# Patrologia Latina, volume 100 — English translation

# Patrologia Latina, vol. 100

## Volume front matter

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library**, complete, uniform, convenient, economical, containing all the holy Fathers, doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed throughout the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with several manuscripts, and corrected with the utmost care; continually elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all the works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of importance;

adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; enlarged by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by others possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is readily apparent to the reader which Fathers commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture, and in which places of their works they did so. An exceedingly accurate edition, easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection itself—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and short works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

## Second series

In which appear the Fathers, doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III, edited by J.-P. Migne, editor of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition is sold in two hundred volumes for one thousand francs; the Greek-Latin edition in thirteen hundred volumes for eight hundred francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

After the first edition, prepared by the most distinguished man, D. # General preface  
### J. Frobenius

[Col. 0009A] **I.** The jurist Henry Canisius, at the beginning of the seventeenth century ordinary professor of the sacred canons at the University of Ingolstadt, celebrated for many literary labors and a most diligent investigator of ancient monuments, had discovered several short works of blessed Alcuin lying hidden in libraries and destined to be brought by him into the public light. He rightly judged that certain other short works of that most distinguished teacher had either completely perished or were still held captive in the libraries, awaiting the assistance of learned men. He wished that they might be released from those undeserved fetters and chains, so that at last they might appear in the light and fly through the mouths of learned men.

“Would that,” he says, “there were someone who would bring all Alcuin’s monuments to light, or at least collect in one volume those which have already been brought to light, and publish them together.” *Thesaurus Monumentorum*, vol. II, Basnage’s edition, pp. 484–485.

**II.** What Canisius had desired, the first of all men to undertake with the greatest care and diligence was the man likewise of great reputation among scholars, D. Andreas Quercetanus of Tours. Moved by love of his native country, as he himself declares at the beginning of the preface to his edition, he collected all the short works of blessed Alcuin, whether already published or gathered from the manuscripts of Paul Petau, Auguste de Thou, the Putean brothers, Sirmond, and others; and he published them anew at Paris in 1617, partly in fuller and more corrected form, and partly as works then discovered for the first time.

**III.** Yet the diligence of this eminent man, however great, did not extend to the foreign libraries of Italy, Spain, England, and Germany. In those libraries, however, various works by this most celebrated writer of his time had once been copied and preserved in great rivalry by his disciples. Other learned men—Martène, Mabillon, Baluze, Pez, and others—who had the good fortune to penetrate those repositories of ancient monuments, discovered more manuscript works of blessed Alcuin. These could be added to the earlier collection, so that a new edition might eventually be made more complete and more perfect. To this end, these men committed their new discoveries to the public, adding them to their collections and mixing them with other short works as they happened to come upon them in the course of their investigations.

A serious inconvenience consequently remained: scholars who wished to learn something about blessed Alcuin suitable for their own studies were forced to search for his letters, commentaries, treatises, and poems scattered through vast and scarcely accessible volumes. This inconvenience could be remedied only by means of a single new collection and edition. It became still greater after copies of Quercetanus’s edition also became exceedingly rare, so that now it is found in only a very few libraries.

[Col. 0010A] **IV.** The plan of preparing a new edition had therefore been initiated in France at the beginning of this century, and hopes had been raised that it would soon be obtained and completed. Until now, however, expectation had been disappointed, and the plan had produced no result. The most distinguished man, D. Antoine Rivet de la Grange, a Benedictine of the Congregation of Saint Maur, in his highly esteemed work *Literary History of France*, vol. IV, p. 343, expressed the wish that at least the labor which he himself had devoted to reviewing all the works of blessed Alcuin, both genuine and spurious, might move some well-educated man to undertake the work so long awaited.

A desire to satisfy in some fashion the wishes and aspirations of D. Rivet and other learned men took hold of me when, by the will of those on whose decision I depended, I was appointed to administer our library of Saint Emmeram, which contained a large number of manuscripts of exceptional antiquity and excellent quality. When I discovered certain codices bearing unmistakable signs of an age of more than nine hundred years and containing various works of blessed Alcuin, I compared them with the edition of D. Quercetanus and easily perceived that, with their help, many gaps in that edition could be filled, countless errors corrected, and the true reading restored in many places. Moreover, several short works appeared which had until then been sought in vain and were partly unknown to scholars; the circumstances concerning all of them will be presented in their proper places.

I therefore began to put my hand to the work—not indeed with the intention of undertaking a new edition of those works myself, but of extending a helping hand if some man equipped with the scholarly apparatus which I recognized myself to lack should at last be willing to devote himself seriously to the task.

**V.** It happened most opportunely that I was informed by the distinguished D. Oliver Legipont, a monk of Saint Martin at Cologne, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a most learned ascetic and, while he lived, my closest companion in literary correspondence, that a man endowed with varied learning, D. Ildephonsus Catelinot, a member of the Benedictine Congregation of Saints Vitonus and Hydulphus at Saint Michael above the Meuse, had long since begun this work and already had all of Alcuin’s works prepared for the press in two volumes. I later learned this more fully and with greater certainty from the literary history of Lorraine by the illustrious Calmet and from the *Literary History of France*, vol. VIII, “Avertissement,” p. x.

I therefore approached this most learned man, D. Catelinot, by letter, promised him my assistance, and willingly placed at his disposal and service whatever resources I had in hand for completing the work he had begun. I also communicated certain things which I believed had not come to his attention.

I hope it will not be unwelcome to scholars if I append here the reply sent by this excellent man, dated 13 February 1754, from which both the study he had devoted to this new work and the reason for the edition’s long delay may be learned:

“For several years,” he says, “I have been undertaking a new edition of Alcuin’s works, and in the space of three years I completed it as far as lay within my power. But, alas, it has remained unpublished and dormant since 1745. I also brought the Benedictine library to completion. For in our regions only works written in the French language struggle beneath the press, while Latin works lie in the cupboards and dust of libraries. Added to this is the serious scarcity of manuscripts, by whose assistance and labor new editions are prepared.

“Such is the poverty in our France and Lorraine that, during the course of my work, we were able to discover only one manuscript, namely the treatise on the Procession of the Holy Spirit, which our Alcuin addressed to the emperor Charlemagne, crowned in the year 800. What sort and size of treatise it is, Antoine Rivet announces in his *Admonition* to vol. VIII of *Gallia Litteraria*, pp. x, xi, and xii [lacuna].

“Pray for a sinner of eighty-three years and ten months, who needs no assistance in walking, seeing, or hearing; but who possesses a sound mind in a sound body, which is God’s gift, and to him I return it with heart and soul.”

Thus far the venerable old man.

**VI.** When I received this excellent man’s letter, I easily realized that the edition of blessed Alcuin’s works would either be delayed for a long time, abandoned altogether upon the death of this old man, who had already been burdened by so many years, or appear only with the deficiency of many monuments relevant to the work that still lay hidden in various libraries.

For an entire year, conscious of the weakness of my powers, I deliberated whether I should myself undertake this difficult labor. At last I decided to attempt the work. At the beginning of 1755 I communicated this plan to D. Catelinot by letter, trusting at that time that, through the new Benedictine literary society conceived and being brought to birth by the mind and pen of the illustrious D. Legipont, whom I have mentioned above, I might obtain greater assistance and resources conducive to carrying out the task more easily.

D. Legipont informed the Reverend D. Calmet of this undertaking by letter and invited the learned members of the Lorraine congregation, of which Calmet then had charge, to permit themselves to be associated with the society. In particular, he persuaded D. Catelinot to surrender to me his collections, prepared for a new edition of the works of blessed Alcuin, so that they might be published in the name of that society in a fuller and more corrected form.

The excellent D. Catelinot agreed to D. Legipont’s request and, almost forgetting his own glory, fulfilled what had been asked with the greatest goodwill and without delay. Thus, in April of the same year, he sent me his entire apparatus, together with certain preliminary materials, various notes, and most learned observations. At the same time, with great humility, he begged me “that, if at any time some or all of the works of so great a man, blessed Alcuin, should be published, his name be spared. For,” he says, “the name of the literary society is far more illustrious and worthy to be placed before so magnificent an edition.”

**VII.** Yet the undertaking of that Benedictine literary society, which D. Legipont had worked to promote with the greatest enthusiasm, could not be brought to its desired conclusion while he lived. When he departed to the heavenly dwelling, it perished completely in its cradle—a fact I report with sorrow—as the literary correspondence by which the conceived offspring ought to have been animated was simultaneously broken off.

The entire burden of the proposed labor of preparing a new edition of blessed Alcuin’s works therefore fell upon my weak shoulders. Yet I did not wish to withdraw them. Reflecting that difficulties must not be fled but overcome, believing that we can do all things through him who strengthens us, and trusting at the same time that this labor would contribute to the glory of God, to some benefit of the Church, and even to the advantage and whatever advancement of literary studies, I stirred myself to undertake the work courageously.

Relying therefore on the hope of divine assistance, I resolved to seek the help of learned men, especially those who, wherever they might be, were entrusted with guarding the treasures of ancient monuments; and to knock at the doors of both nearby and distant libraries in which I knew or suspected that codices relevant to the work lay hidden.

I wrote to the learned custodians of those libraries and to other men of great name and authority, asking them either to open their hidden treasures or to order that they be opened; and I asked that, first, catalogues of the works preserved by them, and then the works themselves which I selected, or variant readings excerpted from them, be communicated to me for my use.

The matter succeeded more happily than I could have hoped, so that my Alcuin emerged far richer than he had been in the collections of D. Quercetanus or D. Catelinot. I shall now briefly explain through whose assistance and by what means I accomplished this.

**VIII.** My first assistance came from the libraries of the most illustrious cathedral chapters of Salzburg and Freising, through the help of the most reverend capitular canons of those churches, especially D. Count de Saurau, at that time the reverend archbishop and prince of Salzburg’s plenipotentiary legate to the imperial diet here at Regensburg; and D. Baron de Wertenstein, privy councillor of the most serene and eminent Bavarian cardinal, bishop of Freising, and so forth—both of whom, to the grief of all good men, had been taken from us only recently.

With the greatest goodwill, both men supplied several codices from those precious repositories of antiquity which I wished to inspect. With their assistance I obtained various unpublished materials, some of which I could use to correct published works, others to supply especially notable deficiencies, and still others to enlarge the work with new short writings, as I have always recorded in their proper places.

**IX.** I found the eminent D. Cardinal Passionei no less benevolent and no less inclined to assist my studies. He had already earned the highest distinction through his work on blessed Alcuin, whose letter to Eanbald—now, according to the order of this new edition, number fifty-six—he had illustrated with notes rich in varied learning.

> According to the recension of this new edition, number fifty-six. Editor, vol. I, p. 63.

This great man, renowned for his learning and, while he lived, an excellent patron of scholars, was appealed to by me. First, he arranged for an index to be sent to me listing all the short works relating to Alcuin preserved in the exceptionally rich Vatican Library, over which he then presided with the greatest credit to his name. Thereafter he instructed the custodians of that library to have copied and sent to me whatever I had selected from the same index.

From there I received:

1. A booklet of blessed Alcuin addressed to the monks of Gothia against the heresy of Felix, previously unavailable, published by us with a preface by the distinguished D. Foggini.
2. A booklet on the Antichrist falsely attributed to Alcuin.
3. A booklet on the Parts of Speech; concerning it, see the preliminary notice to Part V of Alcuin’s works.
4. Sheets containing calculations of the lunar cycle and the preparation for leap years.

Finally, I received certain variant and better readings, which I added in their proper places.

**X.** Enriched by these benefits of the eminent cardinal and encouraged by confidence in such prompt goodwill, I did not hesitate to seek his advice also concerning whether those famous books which are called the *Caroline Books*, *On the Non-Worship of Images*, should be published among the works of blessed Alcuin or omitted, since certain writers wished to attribute them to our Alcuin.

At the same time I asked him to have those books collated with the manuscript of the Vatican Library which Augustinus Steuchus, in *On the False Donation of Constantine against Lorenzo Valla*, book II, p. 111, had written was preserved there in Lombard script. My chief purpose was to determine whether the final chapter of those books, as it appears in the edition of Severinus Binius, is genuine, or whether, as Goldastus contended against Binius, it is spurious and fabricated.

The most learned cardinal did not conceal the opinion he held, but deigned to disclose it to me in a letter written from Rome on 29 January 1759, in these words:

“In the Vatican Library there is no manuscript containing those books which are commonly called the *Caroline Books*, *On the Non-Worship of Images*. As for the refutation of them composed by Hadrian I and addressed to Charlemagne, it exists in two manuscript codices, namely Reg. Vat. 1041 and 1062. Both codices, however, are paper and quite recent.

“Although the form of the letters clearly shows that both were written in France, neither indicates from which older codex, or in what library, it was copied. For the rest, I have no doubt that Codex 1062 is the very one which Severinus Binius says was sent from France to Gregory XIII.

“Since you earnestly ask whether I think it proper to assign these works a place in the appendix to Alcuin’s works, I shall answer frankly: I do not think so. For I see no conjecture of any weight that would suggest that Charlemagne used Alcuin’s assistance in composing the books called the *Caroline Books*.”

Thus far the most wise cardinal. I followed his advice all the more willingly because no argument of any weight occurs in support of the contrary opinion, whereas many serious arguments altogether persuade me that blessed Alcuin was not the author of those books. I have set these arguments out below in the preface to the spurious works.

**XI.** Since this first attempt had succeeded so happily, I decided to explore additional avenues, by which I did not hesitate to expect that I would find still greater resources and learned men equally ready to assist my studies.

To make this happen more readily, in 1760 I had printed by the Montagian press a prospectus of all the short works that ought to appear in the new edition and the order in which they ought to appear. I added a list of certain manuscript codices lying hidden in various libraries. In this way, as though by a general letter, I invited and challenged learned men to contribute their own materials to the work.

Nor was the invitation fruitless. Sooner than expected, certain men celebrated both for their learning and for their published books voluntarily offered their assistance, without having to be individually entreated. Among the first were the illustrious D. Christian Ludwig Scheidius, historiographer of the most serene Guelph family and author of the highly praised work *Origines Guelficae* and many other works; the distinguished D. Christian Adolph Klotz, professor of eloquence and philosophy at the University of Halle, celebrated for various scholarly works and literary controversies; and then the illustrious D. Christian Frederick Temler, secretary to the royal Danish majesty.

I soon received from D. Scheidius a letter full of courtesy, in which he devoted all his assistance to me with the greatest willingness and promised to persuade learned Danes and Englishmen to show similar goodwill by sending them the prospectus I had published.

D. Klotz did still more. In order to make the newly published prospectus known to the entire literary world, he reviewed it with high commendation in the *Acta Eruditorum Lipsiensia* for the year 1760, p. 233. Later, in a letter, he encouraged me to continue vigorously with the work I had begun, offering whatever assistance lay within his power. He also sent me a little-known booklet of rare learning, in which the learning of Alcuin’s disciple Saxo Carolinus is discussed at Wittenberg under the presidency of D. Johann Wilhelm von Berger.

**XII.** As for the extraordinary kindness and singular zeal of the illustrious D. Temler in assisting my labors, I scarcely know with what words of praise to honor it. This distinguished man, previously unknown to me, having learned of my plan from the Leipzig *Acta*, soon sent me certain variant readings from the letters and books on the Trinity, copied from an old edition of the *Homiliary of the Doctors* and formerly noted by the celebrated Baluze. He encouraged me to make whatever use I wished of his services.

Relying on this excellent man’s goodwill, I asked him to put me in contact with any learned men he knew in England, so that they might seek out the writings of blessed Alcuin which I knew, from the catalogues of manuscript books in England and Ireland and from other scholarly reviews, to be preserved in the libraries of that country, and send me what I had requested for the glory of their fellow countryman.

The illustrious man did not fail to respond to my requests, but his efforts there were frustrated. He received from England a reply utterly unworthy of learned men and displeasing to us: they ordered us to wait more than a year until the desired materials could be copied, while at the same time they wished to demand more than one hundred pounds sterling for the writing and labor of a single week.

I would have been willing to accept the first condition; the second, however, which seemed disgraceful to us—and to whom would it not?—I was obliged to reject.

Yet fortune, which had been less favorable in England, did not abandon me completely. Through the kindness of the most distinguished D. de Brequigny, a member of the Royal Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres, I received the letters which I most desired to obtain. While he was searching the libraries of England in 1764 by order of the Most Christian King, he had copied them from a manuscript in the Harleian Library.

This literary treasure must therefore be credited to the goodwill of this excellent man by all scholars, as I have related at greater length in the preliminary notice to the *Appendix*.

**XIII.** The aforementioned D. Temler again attempted, for the purpose of assisting my labors, another route—namely, in Spain. I hoped to obtain from the libraries of that country, especially the Escorial and Toledo, certain monuments which I knew were preserved there and which would contribute to illuminating the history of the Adoptionist error, in which Alcuin played a major part.

In particular, I sought the unpublished letter of the Spanish bishops who followed Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo, addressed to the bishops of Gaul, Aquitaine, and Austria. It was chiefly on account of this letter that the Council of Frankfurt of 794 was convened. Because the letters had supposedly been worn away, D. Henry Flórez had given only its beginning and conclusion in his *España Sagrada*, vol. V, p. 557.

I likewise wished the books written by Etherius and Beatus against the rising Adoptionist error—first published by Peter Stevartius together with other ancient writers at Ingolstadt in 1616—to be collated with a manuscript and corrected from it, since that edition seemed defective and incomplete in certain places. I had decided at some point to include those more accurately corrected books in the appendix to the works of blessed Alcuin, as I indicated in the prospectus of those works that was printed and circulated.

To satisfy this desire, the aforementioned Temler approached a friend living in Spain, equally prompt and zealous in helping literary scholars, namely D. Charles Christopher Pluer, chaplain of the Danish royal embassy at Madrid.

This most distinguished man immediately moved every stone and tried every possible avenue. He tirelessly solicited the learned men whom he believed might contribute something for this purpose, asking them to comply with my wishes.

Yet his efforts encountered many obstacles. The doors of those libraries were so tightly barred that no foreigner had access to them, nor was anyone permitted by any means to release the manuscripts stored there from their fetters and chains for the use of others.

Nevertheless, the aforementioned D. Pluer found a man of great reputation among both Spaniards and foreigners, D. Gregory Mayans, a nobleman of Valencia. Since he had once been prefect of the royal library, there appeared great hope that whatever my wishes required might be obtained through him.

The aforementioned D. Pluer wrote to me concerning D. Mayans in a letter dated 10 June 1765, written from Portugal to the mineral springs in the mountains of Granada, as follows:

“There are by no means lacking in Spain men outstanding in wisdom and learning, whose leader and standard-bearer must undoubtedly be regarded as the celebrated Gregory Mayans. This man devoted himself exclusively to letters together with his most learned brother Antonio.

“When Gregory was serving the king as librarian, he voluntarily resigned the office in order to yield to envy. Yet so far was this change of circumstances from diverting him from the love of letters that it seems rather to have added a spur to him.

“It is certainly true that, apart from Gregory, no one can be found throughout Spain who combines with solid scholarly distinction an equal eagerness to serve.”

I therefore disclosed my desire by letter to this man, who had been so highly praised to me, and requested whatever assistance he might be able to provide. The outcome was fortunate: at last he extracted from his friends the important unpublished letter of the bishops who followed Elipandus, and arranged for it to be promptly delivered to me after it had been copied from a Toledo manuscript. He added a letter of his own, which I presented in print to establish the credibility of the matter.

The excellent man could not, however, obtain the codex containing the aforementioned *Apologeticus* of Etherius and Beatus, with which Stevartius’s insufficiently accurate edition could have been collated, despite all his efforts. For this purpose I had sent him a printed copy of Stevartius’s volume, as he informed me in another letter, which I have likewise presented here.

This was the reason for my change of plan—a plan which D. Catelinot also approved—concerning the inclusion with these works of the same books, as I had initially proposed in the prospectus of those works mentioned above.

What further suggestions the same D. Mayans, deeply devoted to my studies, offered for the elucidation of the writings and acts of the Adoptionists may be understood from his most courteous and learned letters, which I have reproduced in Appendix II.

**XIV.** Having attempted these routes in Lorraine, Italy, England, and Spain, with results that were not altogether fruitless, and wishing to reach the goal I had set myself more successfully, I could not refrain from consulting the more important libraries of France as well. The members of the celebrated Benedictine Congregation of Saint Maur had worked with particular distinction in those libraries.

D. Catelinot, whom I mentioned above, might have turned me away from this plan by writing to me that there was such a scarcity of manuscripts in France and Lorraine that in the course of his work he had been able to discover only one, namely the booklet on the Procession of the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, I also wished to test the matter for myself.

I therefore wrote to the Reverend D. Boudier, then superior general of that congregation, asking him to persuade some of his members to lend me their assistance. The most courteous man did not fail to respond to my requests, and I later experienced his goodwill as extremely useful in other matters as well—something that will be celebrated in our lasting memory.

At his command, the most learned D. Philip Louis Lieble, librarian at the Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, first sent me a catalogue of all the manuscript short works relating to Alcuin preserved in the Royal Library at Paris. Thereafter he sent variant readings excerpted from them with the greatest care, together with certain unpublished materials, namely Alcuin’s letter to George, patriarch of Jerusalem, and the short work on Orthography.

To this man’s industry I likewise owe my knowledge of those letters which, after being confined for so long in the libraries of England, were recently released from their bonds by the illustrious D. de Brequigny, whom I mentioned above and discussed at greater length in the preliminary notice to the supplement to the letters.

> See what follows the Notice in this new edition, where the entire history of the discovery of this treasure is narrated in the very words of that celebrated academician.

[Col. 0016B] **XV.** Another most learned member of the same congregation, D. Jacques-Claude Vincent, librarian of the Abbey of Saint-Remi at Reims, was prompted by my very devoted friend D. Jean-François, a Benedictine monk of the monastery of Saint-Symphorian at Metz and author of a new history of that city, to provide me with considerable assistance.

He collated the manuscript works of Alcuin preserved in the library of Saint-Remi and in that of Saint-Thierry near Reims. The variant readings sent to me were especially useful for restoring the true reading in many places.

I also wished that the ancient life of blessed Alcuin might be collated with the manuscript codex preserved at Reims in the library of the monastery of Saint Mary, which D. Quercetanus had used, although his edition seemed to me faulty in some places.

But I encountered what had formerly happened to D. Mabillon, who, as he himself relates in the preliminary observations to the *Life of Blessed Alcuin*, no. 3, had once seen that codex and later searched for it so that it might be collated with the printed editions, but could not obtain it. Even now no trace of this Life is found either in the aforementioned library or in its catalogue of manuscripts, as I learned from a letter written to me on 10 March 1776 by my very dear friend D. Charles Lancelot. Through the labors and singular industry of this man, our monastery of Saint Emmeram must credit him with a fuller knowledge of the sacred languages and of refined literature.

**XVI.** Finally, the beneficence of the most reverend and at the same time most illustrious in dignity and varied learning prince of the Holy Roman Empire and abbot of Saint Blaise, D. Martin Gerbert, must be recalled with a grateful heart.

To him we owe the fact that certain letters relating to Amalarius, bishop of Trier, and Peter, abbot of Nonantola, have now attained the public light. Through him also the controversy concerning the author of the letter *On the Ceremonies of Baptism*, which Canisius and Quercetanus believed to be Alcuin’s, was brought into the light, and Sirmond’s opinion in favor of Amalarius was confirmed.

[Col. 0016D] Nor should we pass over without praise two men who have deserved extremely well of the republic of letters and are celebrated for the extensive learning which they proved through their distinguished works: D. Oefelius, custodian of the Electoral Library of Munich, and D. Kollarius, custodian of the Imperial Library of Vienna, both most diligent guardians and cultivators of learning.

The first, after searching through the exceedingly rich treasure entrusted to his care, handed over to me whatever he found suitable for my purposes. In addition, he offered many suggestions most useful to my labors.

The second kindly granted me a catalogue of all the manuscript codices relating to Alcuin preserved in the extensive Imperial Library, and thereafter arranged for variant readings to be extracted from them and sent to me, together with an unpublished letter to Aquila, which now bears the number 121.

> [New edition, vol. I, p. 161.]

XVII. Such, for the most part, are the resources which, with the assistance of learned men, I obtained for completing, enlarging, and correcting the Works of blessed Alcuin. As for mentioning the remaining items that came to me from certain other libraries, since they are of lesser importance, there is no reason to detain the reader longer. For I have always mentioned in the Preliminary Notices every little work that proved useful to me. It remains, therefore, to recount briefly what else I have accomplished in this edition, referring the reader, for the sake of brevity, to what I prefaced in the same Notices added to the individual Parts.

XVIII. With the help, naturally, of ancient manuscript codices—indeed, for the greater part contemporary and of the finest quality—as well as of certain separately edited works whose copies I obtained from the various libraries I have acknowledged, I corrected the edition of D. Quercetanus almost everywhere, except in the books written against Felix and Elipandus, for which no ancient codices could be found. I restored many corrupt passages to their integrity; I collected certain records that had remained buried and hidden until our own times, and enriched this edition with them. Among these, above all, the more than seventy letters must be mentioned, which I was obliged to add by way of an Appendix, since the earlier portions had already been almost completed at the press before those letters reached me from the Harleian Library.

[@ [Col. 0017C] See the Preliminary Notice of the new editor.] I marked the remaining anecdotes, and those now brought to light for the first time, in the Catalogue of Works that follows immediately, for the sake of brevity, with an asterisk (*). Furthermore, I separated works of doubtful authenticity, and those altogether spurious and attributed to blessed Alcuin, from the genuine works with which they had been mixed in the earlier edition. Concerning these, learned readers will not find it burdensome to consult the Preliminary Notices prefixed to each work. Finally, I thought it appropriate to append a threefold Appendix to this entire collection, and I have also explained the reasoning behind that decision in the Preliminary Notice.

XIX. When all these matters had almost been completed at the press, an exceedingly ancient manuscript codex happened by good fortune to come into my hands. Written around the middle of the ninth century, it had recently been found [Col. 0017C] in the library of the College of Saint Paul in this city of ours, [Col. 0018A] Regensburg. Its anecdotal contents had to be supplied among the additions and supplements at the end of the Works.

XX. Finally, I directed my care toward making this edition as useful as possible to readers. Accordingly, I endeavored to illuminate certain passages through my own notes and those of others. I cited, from the best editions, the sayings of the holy Fathers and sometimes their complete commentaries, which blessed Alcuin incorporated into his commentaries and treatises. I recorded differing and occasionally better readings, and performed other services that it would be tedious to mention here and that an attentive reader can easily detect in the work itself.

XXI. As concerns the order in which the individual works have been arranged in this collection, it differs from that which they occupy in the edition of D. Quercetanus. I began with the letters which the aforementioned editor placed next to last, chiefly for this reason: they are more eagerly sought by learned men, and a large part of what I have discussed concerning the Life of blessed Alcuin flowed from them as from a most limpid source; [Col. 0018B] and therefore they ought to be regarded as the most faithful testimonies to everything that is narrated and critically examined there. The letters are followed, according to the dignity of their subjects, by exegetical, dogmatic, liturgical, and moral works; historical works, or Lives of the saints; poetic, grammatical, rhetorical, and dialectical works; and finally those astronomical works that survive, concerning the course and leap of the moon and the leap year. The same order is then observed in the doubtful and spurious works.

These, for the most part, are the services which, in this latest edition of the Works of blessed Alcuin, I have been able to perform according to my limited ability amid the many and varied duties imposed upon me—duties that by themselves demand almost the whole person. This responsibility also prevented the work, begun when I was in a state of greater leisure, from being completed sooner or polished more carefully. May kindly and learned readers judge this with fairness and goodwill. [Col. 0018C]

# FROBENIUS’S COMMENTARY ON THE LIFE OF BLESSED F. ALBINUS, OR ALCUIN, COMPOSED ANEW FROM AUTHENTIC RECORDS AND HIS WRITINGS

## PROEM

[Col. 0017C]

Learned men who have devoted their efforts to collecting the works of the Fathers of the Church and of other celebrated writers of antiquity, or to publishing them in new editions, have applied all diligence not only to illuminating their writings, but also to arranging their deeds and actions and assigning them to their proper times. Their purpose was that not only the learning and doctrine of men so illustrious in their age might be transmitted to the people of our own time and to posterity, but also that the virtues with which they once shone might be set before us for imitation.

We have believed it to be our duty to follow the same plan in this new edition of the Works of blessed Alcuin. For although an old and nearly contemporary anonymous writer commended the Life of this blessed man to posterity from the account of his disciple Sigulf, learned men have long complained that his narratives lack solid critical foundation and are sometimes deficient in truth. Therefore the distinguished D. Andreas Quercetanus deemed it necessary to apply several corrections to that account and to compose anew a Life of blessed Alcuin from his own writings and Works published by him; [Col. 0018C] he prefixed it to his edition in place of a preface.

That industry was then sufficient to provide fuller knowledge of our Alcuin from the little works that had at that time been discovered. Nevertheless, since we have found that new light can be brought to the commentary of this most illustrious man from writings recently discovered, which had escaped D. Quercetanus’s notice, and that matters still obscure could be more fully clarified, learned readers, we trust, will judge that our labor in composing anew the Life of this blessed man and resolving certain questions raised here and there will be neither unwelcome nor useless. Yet we did not wish to deprive their reasonable desire to inspect and consult the original Life and the commentary of D. Quercetanus from time to time; rather, we shall present both at the end of this work of ours.

# CHAPTER ONE

## On the various names, homeland, parents, brothers, and other matters concerning blessed Alcuin

I. The name Alcuin is found written in various ways in different writings and codices. In the older and more correct documents, especially in the letters that we find written in an almost contemporary hand, he himself, as may be conjectured, most often expressed his name by writing either Albinus or Alchuinus, or, when he wrote more familiarly to his David, Homer, Damoetas, and other friends, Flaccus Albinus or Albinus Flaccus.

I therefore believe that the remaining forms, such as Alboinus, Alkoinus, Alchwinus, Alquinus, and so forth, as they are found written by later authors, should be attributed to the ignorance of scribes or to the harsh aspiration of those dictating. Some therefore investigate the origin of this name with excessive ingenuity through entirely fictitious derivations and combinations of words, following Heuterus, who in his *Etymologies* interprets *Alcwin* as “one who increases and enlarges everything,” from the word *Gwin*, which among the Germans signifies profit.

In any event, Alcuin or Alchuin appears to have been a native Germanic-Saxon name, which he later wished to express in the better and more Latin form Albinus. He seems to have done this in the letter written to Elipandus, who, alluding to this name in his *Responsoria*, [Col. 0019B] calls him, in a notable taunt, “Albinus, most black with blackness.”

II. The cognomen Flaccus, which he sometimes placed before and sometimes after his name, seemed to the distinguished Quercetanus, in the preface, no. 2, to have been received at baptism. It is more likely, however, that this name was an adopted one, which blessed Alcuin customarily used among his familiars, whom he had as companions in cultivating the liberal arts and sciences, following the custom of his age. Concerning this custom he writes in Letter 184 (now 125) to Gundrada, surnamed Eulalia:

> “Familiarity often causes a change of name, just as the Lord himself changed Simeon into Peter, and named the sons of Zebedee sons of thunder. You can prove this also from ancient or recent days.”

Flaccus, therefore, was a name adopted by Alcuin, or chosen by him; Alcuin or Alchuinus, however, was his original and proper name. For this reason, instead of the title of his Works which the distinguished Quercetanus, misled by the authority of Sixtus of Siena and certain others, first used—as he himself admits in no. 2 of the preface—by writing *Albini Flacci Alchuini*, we have everywhere written *Flacci Albini seu Alcuini*. In the text itself we always write Alcuinus, since we have found that learned men do so more frequently. But it is not worthwhile to dwell on these matters any longer.

III. Great care must be taken that our Albinus or Alcuin not be confused either with Albinus, abbot of Canterbury, praised by the venerable Bede in the preface and in Book V, chapter 21, of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, and to whom there survives a letter of that same Bede in Mabillon’s new edition of the *Analecta*, p. 398; or with Albinus, chamberlain of Pope Leo III, whom Einhard mentions in his *Annals* under the year 799; or finally with Albuinus, a monk of Hersfeld.

There are fewer people who have allowed themselves to be led into this confusion concerning the latter two. Concerning the former Albinus, however, whom the venerable Bede mentions, most writers of the somewhat later period have been mistaken. Clement Reynerus, a man otherwise exceptionally learned, argues at length in *Apostolatus Benedictinorum in Anglia*, treatise I, section I, pp. 34 ff., that Bede’s Albinus—the man whom he calls a disciple and teacher of Charlemagne—is the same person as Alcuin. He says that this is the common tradition of historians, and does not consider the difference between the ages of Bede and Alcuin, which D. Quercetanus had raised as an objection, to be insuperable, because, as he believed, Alcuin reached or even exceeded the age of one hundred, since in Letter 38 (now 43) to Charles he indicates that he was a very old man.

IV. This opinion of Reynerus, however, is solidly refuted by R. P. Michael Alfort in *Annales Ecclesiastici Britannicae*, vol. II, under the year 710, no. 4 and following. He demonstrates that the alleged tradition of historians is neither common nor that of men bearing the seal of antiquity, but rather that of certain writers of the Middle Ages who, attending to only a few details, pronounce their judgments too readily.

Thus, as Harpsfeld writes in century IX, chapter 14, cited by the same Alfort, those who think that Alcuin was a Kentish man and was placed in charge of the monastery of Saint Augustine there were misled by the similarity of the names and by a certain proximity of the times. And indeed, if those writers had examined more carefully the venerable Bede’s account of his Albinus, they would very easily have detected their error.

For in Book V, chapter 21, Bede relates that Albinus had already succeeded Adrian in the administration of the monastery of Saint Augustine at Canterbury in the year 710. In the preface he praises him as a most reverend and learned abbot, and says that he had been instructed—not by Bede himself, but by Theodore, archbishop of blessed memory, and by Abbot Adrian—in that church at Canterbury, where Bede never exercised the office of teaching.

Moreover, the venerable Bede praises that Albinus as “before all others the author and helper of his little work, the *History of the English People*,” and professes that he used his assistance and counsel in composing that History. Anyone even slightly attentive will easily perceive that none of this can apply to our Alcuin. If you wish, consult what Alfort solidly argues against Reynerus in the cited place. Below we shall likewise demonstrate that blessed Alcuin was never a disciple of the venerable Bede.

Anastasius the Librarian, in the *Life of Pope Adrian I*, mentions a certain Albinus whom he calls King Charles’s favorite and says was sent with Bishop George and Abbot Gulfard by the king, who was about to undertake war against the Lombards, to the apostolic see in the year 773. But this Albinus the favorite is different from our Alcuin, who in that year was still residing at York and had not yet migrated to Gaul. Nevertheless, our Alcuin too is called King Charles’s favorite by Sigebert of Gembloux, Trithemius, and others, whose testimonies we shall present below in their proper place. See Mabillon, *Annales*, Book XXIV, no. 45, p. 226.

V. Let us now discuss briefly what we have been able to extract from reliable records concerning the homeland and parents of this Flaccus Albinus or Alcuin. Some Scottish historians thought that he was born in the Scottish regions of Britain. Among them was Buchanan, Book V of the *History*, who argued that he derived his name not from a family but from the Scottish people, who call themselves Albinos in their own language.

Others, as D. Quercetanus noted here, are also to be found who said that he was born in the county of Middlesex, not far from London. Yet nothing can be produced from the records of antiquity in support of one region or the other. We must therefore approve solely the opinion of those writers who affirm, on the basis of Alcuin’s own testimony, that blessed Alcuin was born at York in the kingdom of Northumbria. He himself writes thus in Letter 5 (now 6) to the people of York:

> “You cherished the fragile years of my infancy with maternal affection; you patiently endured the playful period of my childhood with pious patience; and by the disciplines of paternal correction you educated me to the perfected age of manhood.”

Indeed, should one not be considered born in the place where one not only grew into manhood but also spent one’s childhood, even one’s infancy? But perhaps the frequent mention that blessed Alcuin makes in his letters of the Northumbrians, who possessed the Scottish regions as far as the Firth of Edinburgh, gave the aforementioned writers on Scottish affairs grounds, as D. Quercetanus says, for suspecting that he was born in Scotland. Richard Smith’s *Flowers of the Ecclesiastical History of the English*, Book II, chapter 12, section 3, no. 2, also deserves to be read on this question.

VI. It is not established with equal certainty from what rank, or from which parents, blessed Alcuin was descended. He himself was almost entirely silent on the matter, and none of the writers of his acts or Life has disclosed it. The author of his Life asserts at the beginning of chapter 1 that he sprang from a noble lineage of the English people. Again, in no. 7 of the same chapter, he indicates that the pupils of the school at York, among whom Alcuin was numbered, belonged to the class of nobles:

> “There was,” he says, “a school of students formed from the sons of nobles for Bishop Ecgbert, to whose discipline the boy Alcuin had also been entrusted.”

The nobility of blessed Alcuin’s lineage is especially evident from the fact that he was related by kinship to the family of Saint Wiligis, the father of Saint Willibrord. Under that title he himself obtained, by legitimate—hereditary, as I interpret it—succession, a maritime cell constructed by Saint Wiligis in the promontories near the Ocean Sea and the River Humber and subsequently possessed by his descendants. He testifies to this himself in the letter to Beornrad prefixed in this edition to the Life of Saint Willibrord, and in chapter 1 of that Life.

Furthermore, Alcuin sings of the noble lineage of Saints Wiligis and Willibrord in the elegy appended to this Life of the saint, or chapter 33. Of Saint Willibrord he writes:

> This priest was noble, sprung from a great lineage.

Of Saint Wiligis:

> He was a man worthy among the people, Wilgis by name,  
> Living among a noble people beyond the Humber.

For this reason, when Charlemagne summoned him with the prospect of a generous reward, blessed Alcuin replied:

> “Although I am richly endowed with no small inheritance in my paternal region, I gladly reject it and delight to remain here in poverty, so that I may be of service to you.”  
> *Life*, chapter 2, no. 12.

VII. Such, and no more, is what can be said about the lineage of blessed Alcuin. As for the names and condition of his parents, the age in which he lived has granted us no information. He did, however, have brothers and sisters in England, as he indicates clearly enough in Letter 102 (now 130) to Aquila. Expressing to this intimate friend the singular love with which he embraced him, he writes:

> “I would have you believe, dearest Father, that I could not read the little letters from my brothers or sisters overseas with as much pleasure as those from your affection across the Alps; nor does such weariness fatigue my heart after them as follows the beloved sight of your face.”

But whether that same Aquila or Arno—first bishop and then the first archbishop of Salzburg—with whom blessed Alcuin shared all the secrets of his heart through frequent letters, should be counted among his blood brothers, authors do not agree.

Certain distinguished men—Mabillon, Book XXIII of the *Annals*, p. 87; and in the historical *Eulogy* prefixed to the *Life of blessed Alcuin*, chapter 1, no. 3; Rivet, *History of French Literature*, vol. IV, p. 296; Ceillier, *General History of Sacred Authors*, vol. XVIII; Quercetanus in the preface, chapter 1, no. 1; and D. Catelinot in manuscript—declare without hesitation that blessed Alcuin was the blood brother of that same Arno.

Their almost sole basis for asserting this is drawn from Letter 86 (now 91), which bears the heading “Albinus sends greetings to his dearest brother (germanus), Bishop Aquila,” and from Letter 78 (now 83) to the brothers of Juvavum, where he calls Aquila their father and shepherd, but his own brother (germanus):

> “Formerly,” he says, “to the pious Father Aquila, bishop, my brother (germanus) and your shepherd, etc.”

Nevertheless, other equally distinguished writers—Cointius, Pagius, Hansizius, and others—contradict this opinion. They rightly judge that the terms “brother” and “blood brother” should be understood not of blood relationship but of a union of spirits.

For anyone reading Alcuin’s letters to Aquila, says Hansizius in *Germania Sacra*, vol. II, p. 102, no. 12, can readily see that Alcuin deliberately gathered every title capable of expressing the most sincere affection and friendship with which he was drawn to Arno like another Pylades. It was surely unnecessary to press such expressions of affection so often upon a blood brother.

Moreover, as D. Mabillon thought, it is hardly probable that Arno was born in Britain, which was Alcuin’s homeland. Rather, he was probably a Saxon or a Bavarian and grew up in the bosom of the Church of Freising, as the same distinguished man, D. Hansizius, argues with substantial evidence in the same place, no. 1 and following.

I cannot refrain from adding my own judgment to that of these and other learned men, and I believe that it can be strengthened further by the following considerations. In Letters 76 (now 91) and 92 (now 108), Alcuin himself quite openly declares in what sense he calls Aquila his brother—namely, in charity, not by blood.

In the former he wishes the words of greeting, carried by the hands of a passing traveler on a little sheet, to reach more quickly “the son of my charity, who is a father in merits, a brother in charity, and a son in age.” In the latter he also asks Aquila not to forget “a father in old age, a son in merits, and a brother in charity.”

At the beginning of Letter 115 (now 154), he seems likewise to explain that he was united to his Aquila by faithful and familiar custom rather than by natural kinship. He says:

> “Love, long bound together in faithful brotherhood, is often renewed by new letters, so that what is firm in faith may be recognized as sweet in familiarity.”

Similarly, he begins Letter 177 (now 118), addressed to his beloved son Aquila, as follows:

> “I know that you are a father in dignity and merits, but out of the sweetness of charity I have bestowed upon you the name of son, because nothing ought to be dearer to a father than a son.”

In all these passages there is plainly nothing from which one could conclude that blessed Alcuin recognized Aquila as his blood brother. Rather, he always calls him brother with the affection with which he calls him son, namely, from the sweetness of charity.

Indeed, from the words of Letter 102 (now 130), cited shortly before, it is more readily understood that blessed Alcuin did not count Aquila among his brothers. There he declares to Aquila, his sweetest Father, that he takes greater pleasure in his letters than in those which he would receive from his brothers and sisters whom he had left behind in Britain.

If he had regarded Aquila equally as a natural brother, he would certainly have used a different style, one from which it could be understood that he considered Aquila dearer than his other brothers. If, however, anyone should prefer to interpret the words of Letter 102 as referring not to natural brothers and sisters but to those called so through affection, I shall not object. For by this very fact it will become clear in what sense blessed Alcuin was accustomed to call other friends, and especially his Aquila, brothers.

VIII. Having now established what could be extracted from the cited documents concerning the homeland, parents, and brothers of blessed Alcuin, we have neglected no diligence by which the time or year of his birth might be drawn out and determined either from his original Life, from Alcuin’s own writings, or from other ancient records. Yet nowhere did anything certain come to our aid for this purpose.

The more celebrated writers of our own age almost all agree that blessed Alcuin was born before the death of the venerable Bede—that is, before the year 735. Mabillon, Book XXI of the *Annals*, no. 17, p. 94, and Book XXIII, no. 37, p. 187; Rivet, *History of French Literature*, vol. IV, p. 295; Ceillier, *General History of Sacred Authors*, vol. XVIII, p. 248.

They therefore place the year of blessed Alcuin’s birth around 735, the year in which, as will become clear somewhat below, the venerable Bede died. We too follow their calculation, if only because it agrees very well with the remaining events of his life and conflicts with none of them.

# CHAPTER TWO

## The education and teachers of blessed Alcuin

IX. We have shown above, in chapter 1, no. 5, that Alcuin was educated at York just as he was born there. After spending almost all the years of his childhood in the monastery there and absorbing the first elements of learning, when he had already memorized the reading of the psalms, he was entrusted to the discipline of Hechbert or Ecgbert, the archbishop of that see, so that he might be nourished with stronger food of learning and piety, as the author of his Life writes in chapter 1, no. 7.

That most religious prelate had succeeded the younger Wilfrid, who had sought solitude, in the York see—not in 735, as Alfort argues under that year, no. 18, and under the year 738, no. 1, but in 732, as the old writer who continued Bede’s history of the English testifies. Under that year, in which Cuthbert, bishop of Lindisfarne, died, he also recorded Ecgbert’s ordination.

It is moreover clear from Alcuin himself, in his poem on the bishops of York, that Ecgbert held the see of York for thirty-four years:

> He ruled the church for thirty-four years.

It is agreed among the authorities, as Alfort himself admits, that Ecgbert died in the year 766. If you subtract thirty-four years from that date, the year 732 remains as the beginning of his episcopal rule.

This Bishop Ecgbert, whom William of Malmesbury calls an arsenal of all the liberal arts, established in his monastery a school for the sons of nobles. Some were instructed in the rudiments of grammar, others in the study of the liberal disciplines, and others in the knowledge of the divine Scriptures.

Among all these schoolfellows, Alcuin surpassed the others in zeal for learning and piety. He adhered to his teacher with such confidence and fidelity that he did nothing which his teacher’s authority had not approved. Indeed, he was not ashamed to disclose to him even the secrets of his heart, including the impulses of lust by which he was sometimes assailed, mindful of what the most holy legislator of monks, Benedict, prescribed for his followers in chapter 8 of his Rule:

> “They are not to conceal from their abbot the evil thoughts that come into their hearts.”

This is certainly the most immediate remedy for subduing those most dangerous temptations.

X. When Ecgbert died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December in 766, Alcuin “received, by divine favor, Elcbert or Aelbert, a blessed and illustrious man, as teacher in the place of the one he had lost,” as the author of the Life writes in chapter 2, no. 9.

I do not think this should be understood as though Aelbert first assumed the office of teaching in the school at York only after Ecgbert’s death. Rather, Aelbert had been appointed head of the school at York by Ecgbert while he was still alive, as Alcuin himself testifies in the poem on the Bishops of York. After relating that Aelbert, once ordained a priest, always remained inseparably attached to his bishop, he adds:

> By him he was appointed protector of all the clergy,  
> And at the same time was set over York as teacher.

Although Ecgbert, driven by apostolic zeal, never ceased teaching boys and young men, he nevertheless entrusted the principal care of the schools to Aelbert, being greatly occupied with the concerns of his church. To Aelbert, whom he regarded as his own principal teacher, Alcuin attributes almost all his progress in learning in that same poem.

Accordingly, he praises him above all for wisdom, learning, and the office of teaching, showing what disciplines of various kinds he taught before attaining the episcopate, and that he had visited foreign regions:

> Led onward by love of wisdom;  
> If he found anything new in books or studies  
> That he could bring back with him, he sought it out in those lands.

In this literary pilgrimage, I think Aelbert had the young Alcuin as his companion. For I understand the beginning of Letter 222 (now 53) in this sense, where Alcuin says that he once followed the footsteps of his teacher and stopped among the Corbieans [or the Morbacians?], and saw and loved the praiseworthy way of life of that community. See the notes on that same letter.

Alcuin further relates in the cited passage that when Aelbert returned from that journey, he was compelled to assume pastoral care, yet did not lessen his devotion to reading and teaching:

> Nor did he, because of the weight of his cares,  
> Diminish his former zeal for reading the Scriptures;  
> Becoming both a discerning teacher and a pious, holy priest.

Finally, he relates that the same Bishop Aelbert, full of days and merits, before his death entrusted the episcopal dignity to his fellow student Eanbald, and to Alcuin the treasures of books—that is, the care of a library filled with excellent books—and the governance of the school itself. We shall return to this below, in chapter 4.

XI. Since we have begun to speak of the teachers of blessed Alcuin, it will not be superfluous—indeed, it will be necessary—to inquire whether the venerable Bede should also be numbered among them.

Almost all writers of the earlier period take this as indisputable. More recent writers, however, subject everything to stricter criticism and refute it. They demonstrate by weighty arguments that the venerable Bede died around the year 735, when they believe blessed Alcuin had scarcely been born, or at least was still too young for the more rigorous disciplines.

Certainly he was a boy when he was first entrusted to the discipline of Ecgbert, archbishop of York, who had been ordained in 732, as we said shortly before. The venerable Bede died in the first years of that same prelate’s episcopate, as is clear from Alcuin’s own testimony, which we shall cite at the end of this chapter—namely, in the year 735, three years after Ecgbert’s ordination, when Alcuin is thought scarcely to have seen the light of day, or at least, as we first said, was still a boy.

XII. The celebrated writer Francis Chiffletius, however, takes a very different view of the age of the venerable Bede in the dissertation that he prefixed to his new edition of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English People* compiled by the venerable Bede. There the learned man tries to establish by several arguments that the venerable Bede prolonged his life until the year 762 and finally died at the age of ninety, as the author of Alcuin’s Life testifies.

If this is true, then his age would certainly not prevent Alcuin from having been Bede’s disciple; for in that year, 762, he would himself have been nearly thirty years old. Chifflet’s singular opinion therefore cannot be passed over without examination.

XIII. The principal and almost the sole foundation on which this opinion of his seems to rest is built upon a testimony which, as he thought, admits no exception—namely, that of an eyewitness who stood beside the blessed man as he lay dying: Cuthbert, his disciple. There survives a letter by Cuthbert to Cuthwin concerning the death of the venerable Bede, frequently published, including in Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints*, Benedictine century III, part I, p. 537, and in a supposedly more accurate form by Chifflet in the cited work, chapter 2 of the dissertation, p. 11.

Chifflet constructs his argument as follows in chapter 1, p. 4:

> “Cuthbert expressly says that Bede breathed out his blessed soul on Wednesday evening, the seventh day before the Kalends of June, that is, precisely on May 26. For in the year of Christ 762, Easter fell on April 18 and the Ascension on May 27. Therefore, what Cuthbert had stated beforehand—that Bede lived until the day of the Lord’s Ascension—must be understood exclusively, or taken as referring to the ecclesiastical day of the Ascension, which began with first vespers and therefore with the close of Wednesday.”

Thus Chifflet.

But I do not know by what deception or inadvertence the learned man could have asserted that Cuthbert expressly said that Bede breathed out his blessed soul on Wednesday evening, the seventh day before the Kalends of June. For we do not read in Cuthbert’s letter that Wednesday fell on that day of the Kalends of June. Rather, it is stated clearly enough that the feast of the Ascension itself was celebrated on that day, the seventh day before the Kalends of June.

After Cuthbert, near the beginning of his letter, has related that Bede fell ill almost two weeks before the feast of the Resurrection and lived until the day of the Ascension—that is, the seventh day before the Kalends of June, for that is how he connects the words—[Col. 0024D] he relates, after a considerable interval, that Bede spent Wednesday from morning until evening and finally, while singing “Glory be to the Father,” and so forth, breathed out his last spirit from the body.

This account certainly does not convey the sense that D. Chifflet invents, namely, that the venerable Bede breathed out his soul on Wednesday evening, the seventh day before the Kalends of June. It conveys only this, as the text has it: that the venerable Bede lived until the day of the Lord’s Ascension, that is, the seventh day before the Kalends of June.

This means precisely the same as if he had said: “He lived until the day of the Ascension, that is, until the seventh day before the Kalends of June.” Thus, according to Cuthbert’s meaning, the seventh day before the Kalends of June and the day of the Lord’s Ascension were one and the same day.

Cuthbert’s testimony, therefore, in which D. Chifflet placed the principal support of his opinion, rather contradicts it, because according to the rules of computation the day of the Ascension fell not in the year 762 but in the year 735 on May 26—that is, the seventh day before the Kalends of June.

XIV. Since, therefore, the principal argument by which the distinguished Chifflet sought to extend the death of the venerable Bede to the year 762 does not at all support his purpose, but rather confirms, through that testimony of Cuthbert, the account added by the author of the *Chronology of the History of the English People*, as well as the opinion of Simeon of Durham, or Turgot, in Book II, chapter 4, of *The Church of Durham*; of Stubes, a Dominican, in the *Acts of the Bishops of York*; and of the very learned men Pagi, Mabillon, and other more recent critics, by which Bede’s death is placed in the year of Christ 735, the remaining arguments lose all force for proving that he died at the age of ninety.

Those arguments by which D. Chifflet seeks to establish this from the testimony of the writer of Alcuin’s Life, from the addition of the Carthusians of Cologne to the Martyrology, from Bede’s epitaph reported by Wion in *Lignum Vitae*, Book V, chapter 101, and finally from certain letters of Lullus, archbishop of Mainz, lose all persuasive weight for that purpose.

For those additions of the Carthusians of Cologne to Usuard’s Martyrology are too recent to be able to carry authority against so many other more ancient testimonies, since they were first made and published in the year [Col. 0025B] 1521, as Chifflet himself admits.

The epitaph reported by Wion is likewise more recent, and in it this inelegant verse is read:

> In this life he lived three times thirty years.
and Wion remarks that this [epitaph] was also placed upon Bede’s sacred relics after they had been transferred from Girvum, where they had originally lain buried, to Durham around the year 1000—nearly three hundred years after the venerable man’s death. Nothing of this sort, however, is found in the other epitaph published by Mabillon from the Thuaneus manuscript in his edition of the *Life of the Venerable Bede*, p. 539. See also the *Acta Sanctorum* of Antwerp for 27 May, note e.

The occasion for the error concerning Bede’s age of ninety years was doubtless supplied by the author of the *Life of Blessed Alcuin*, whom D. Chifflet likewise employed in support of his opinion, writing in chapter 1, no. 7, that Bede departed to the Lord at the age of ninety. Yet that author clearly indicates that he has no certain knowledge of the matter, saying that he learned it from the account of certain persons. He therefore did not derive this information concerning the age and death of the Venerable Bede from Sigulf, Alcuin’s disciple and companion, from whom he had learned the other events of Blessed Alcuin’s life, but from certain others, whose testimony he leaves doubtful.

The same author there adds, on the basis of others’ report, a similar tale concerning the time Bede spent writing his books:

> “In the nineteenth year of his age,” he says, “he became a levite, but in the thirtieth a priest; from that time onward, until his fifty-ninth year, he strove with no idle labor to insert into books worthy of remembrance, by his own pen, those things which he had learned during the preceding thirty years for the benefit of the Church. For another thirty years, they say, he corrected what he had written.”

A fabrication! Indeed, this testimony of the aforesaid author becomes wholly worthless when he writes in the same place that Bede died in the year 731, on the Lord’s Ascension, 26 May, and that he departed to the Lord at the age of ninety; for in this the author is mistaken in several ways. How, for example, can Bede be said—as I use the words of D. Chifflet himself, in the place cited, p. 6—to have died in the year of Christ 731 at the age of ninety, when in that same year he himself testifies that he was no more than fifty-nine years old? Or how can it be said that Bede died in 731 on the Lord’s Ascension and on 26 May, when according to the rules of the ancient calendar it is absolutely certain that in that year, 731, the Lord’s Ascension occurred not on 26 May but on 10 May?

D. Chifflet indeed thinks that this error should be attributed not to the author but to the copyist, and therefore that 762 ought to be read in place of 731, since he does not doubt that the author himself wrote it so. Yet who cannot see that this conjecture of Chifflet’s, unsupported by any suitable argument, arose from an opinion once adopted and firmly held? The testimony of the author of the *Life of Blessed Alcuin*, therefore, being so manifestly erroneous, is useless and unfit to confirm Chifflet’s opinion.

### XV

Finally, the argument which D. Chifflet constructs from certain letters of Blessed Lull, archbishop of Mainz, included among the Bonifacian letters in volume XIII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* from the edition of Nicholas Serrarius, carries no greater weight. From these letters the learned man attempts to establish that the Venerable Bede did not depart this life until after the martyrdom of Saint Boniface, and therefore lived beyond the year 755 and died at the age of ninety.

This is how he reasons in the place cited, pp. 6–7, from letters 89, 95, 111, and 150:

> “Letter 150, in which Bede is said to have recently shone in the Church, has been wrongly attributed in the printed editions to Saint Boniface of Mainz, since it truly belongs to Lull, his successor. I demonstrate this by two arguments. The first is drawn from the three letters mentioned above. In the first, Lull had asked Cuthbert for all Bede’s little works; since he obtained only a few, mentioned in letters 89 and 95, it remained for him to request the others that he lacked, and this he does in that letter 150. The second argument is that Bede is known to have outlived Boniface. For Boniface, by a glorious martyrdom, prepared his life for heaven in the year of Christ 755. Thereafter Lull, already bishop after Boniface, sent a silken pallium to honor the relics of Bede, recently deceased. The letter to Abbot Cuthbert in the collection is therefore Lull’s—letter 150—in which he mentions Bede as having recently shone in the Church and thus as having by then completed his earthly life.”

After these premises Chifflet concludes:

> “Since it is therefore evident from these considerations that Bede was alive beyond the year of Christ 755, the exact age of ninety years which we have established from his epitaph and other arguments fixes his death in the year 762, which was Lull’s seventh year in office after Boniface.”

### XVI

It is certainly astonishing that Chifflet should have wished, on such slight and almost nonexistent grounds, to remove letter 150 from Saint Boniface and claim it for Blessed Lull. His first argument proves only that Lull could have written as the author of letter 150 wrote; it does not prove that Lull, rather than Boniface, actually wrote in that manner. His second argument is an obvious begging of the question.

For the conclusion that Lull was the author of letter 150 rests upon the claim that he wrote it already bishop, after Saint Boniface had been crowned with martyrdom in 755, and that he sent with it a silken pallium to honor Bede’s recently extinguished relics. On the contrary, that Boniface outlived Bede is established by other certainly genuine letters of his in the frequently mentioned collection, letters 8 and 9.

In the first, the holy man asks Egbert, archbishop of York, to undertake to copy and send him certain treatises from Bede’s works:

> “Whom,” he says, “as we have recently heard, divine grace has permitted to shine in your province.”

In letter 9 he similarly asks Abbot Huetbert:

> “that you may be pleased to send us written copies of some works of the most diligent investigator of the Scriptures, the monk Bede, who, as we have recently heard, shone among you in the house of God.”

Thus, just as Chifflet infers from the words of letter 150—where mention is made of Bede as having recently shone in the Church—that he had by then died, so from the similar mention made by Saint Boniface in letters 8 and 9 it is rightly inferred that Bede died before Saint Boniface’s martyrdom and therefore before the year 755. Since Saint Boniface uses in those letters the same style as the author of letter 150, there is no reason why this letter—whose authorship no one before D. Chifflet had questioned—should be taken away from that holy apostle of the Germans.

I should also point out that letter 150 of the aforesaid collection, which Serrarius copied as unpublished from Baronius, volume IX of the *Annals*, p. 96, does not differ from letter 9 of the same collection, but is one and the same letter. The only difference is that where the former, namely letter 150, reads, “We ask that you send the rest, etc.,” the latter, namely letter 9, reads, “We ask that you send some, etc.” And where the latter reads, “And if it is not burdensome for you to send us one bell,” the former reads, “that you send us one of them”—in Baronius, “one part”—“as a great consolation of our pilgrimage.”

### XVII

What we have argued thus far against D. Chifflet receives further, decisive support from Alcuin himself, who writes in his *Poem on the Bishops of York* that Bede died during the first years of Egbert’s episcopate in that Church. There he sings:

> In the first years of that blessed prelate’s rule,  
> The distinguished priest, Bede by name and merits,  
> Seeking the stars, closed the eyes of his present life.

As we have shown above, Egbert ascended the see of York in the year 732 and died in 766. Bede’s life therefore could not have reached, as Chifflet believed, the year 762, which belonged not to the first but to the final years of Egbert’s episcopate.

### XVIII

Perhaps a longer examination of that singular opinion of D. Chifflet may seem superfluous and foreign to this place. Nevertheless, precisely because of its singularity, we could not pass it over, so that no doubt might remain that Blessed Alcuin could not have been a disciple of the Venerable Bede around the year 735, since Bede had already died in that same year.

## CHAPTER III

### Blessed Alcuin’s Monastic Profession, According to the Observations of D. Mabillon

### XIX

Since in the preceding chapters it was shown that Blessed Alcuin was educated, nurtured, and formed in virtues and learning from infancy in the church of York under the instruction of Egbert and Aelbert, it will not seem inappropriate to inquire here what manner of life he professed there—namely, that of canons or clerics, or that of monks.

Mabillon found that no one in his time had treated this question, although certain writers, especially Benedictines, counted the blessed man among their own, while some more recent authors disagreed. Therefore that most distinguished man, highly experienced in treating matters of this kind, undertook to examine the question more carefully in his *Elogium* prefixed to the *Life of Blessed Alcuin*. He brought forward in good faith the arguments of both sides—not merely those already advanced, but also those that could be advanced. We have thought that readers would prefer to see these arguments presented here in condensed form rather than that we should burden them with all their length, or impose our own arguments in a matter which that celebrated man had nearly exhausted. Nevertheless, we have occasionally inserted a few points which we believed suitable for strengthening D. Mabillon’s position.

### XX

First, Mabillon proves conclusively that Alcuin was not only educated in the church of York but also incardinated and bound to it as a member. No one who has read the letters he himself wrote to the York brethren will deny this. In a letter formerly numbered 7, now 6, he declares himself a son of that church—not merely on account of the benefit of education or subjection, in which sense all Christians may be called sons of Mother Church, but by reason of adoption, through which he deserved to be joined to their congregation as a member and participant in the same sheepfold, household, and family.

He continually lived in that community and, when at times obedience drew him abroad, returned to it. There he was keeper of the library; there he was head of the school. Such an office is rarely entrusted in religious communities to outsiders when suitable members of the household are available. Hence, when Eanbald the Elder, archbishop of York, died while Alcuin himself was in Gaul, Alcuin was summoned to the election of a new prelate. He writes in letters 48 and 49, now 54 and 55, that the severity of a fever and the king’s delay in Saxony prevented him from attending.

### XXI

Since these things were so, there can now be no doubt that Blessed Alcuin professed the institute then flourishing in that church and community. That institute was originally monastic. For the Venerable Bede, in his letter to Egbert the bishop, calls the York congregation a monastery; and there the discipline of regular life was maintained.

In letter 5, now 6, Alcuin exhorts the York brethren to observe it:

> “Let the discipline of regular life,” he says, “order you.”

By these words he understands monastic discipline, for he adds:

> “and let the moderation of ecclesiastical piety make you venerable.”

Here he indicates a distinction between regular discipline and ecclesiastical, or clerical, discipline, and exhorts them to both because those brethren professed both. Similarly, as in other letters he exhorts other monks, he urges them there to humility and obedience, which are virtues proper to monks and the foundation of monastic life.
