Moreover, in his poem on the York bishops he says that the younger Wilfrid, before being ordained bishop, was vicedominus and abbot at York, for in cathedral churches of monks there was, besides the bishop, also an abbot who exercised particular care for regular life.

In the same place he says that Aelbert, Wilfrid’s successor after Egbert, had been entrusted to the monastery—that is, the York monastery—from childhood and, after completing ten years as bishop, returned to the same monastic enclosure so that he might serve God alone.

Finally, it is recorded in the anonymous booklet on the *Life of Saint Liudger*, published by Mabillon in the *Acta Sanctorum*, Benedictine century IV, part I, p. 37, chapter 5, that Saint Liudger was educated at York under Alcuin as his teacher, in a monastery of monks.

Therefore a monastic institute flourished at that time in the York congregation, and specifically a Benedictine one. For Saint Wilfrid I, archbishop of York, is said to have introduced the Rule of Saint Benedict into his diocese and, through its aid, improved the institutions of the churches. This is reported by Eddius Stephanus in Mabillon’s *Life of Saint Wilfrid*, chapter 14; Mabillon himself excellently elucidates the passage in his preliminary observations, nos. 10 and 11, p. 673.

What is more, John the Deacon testifies in the *Life of Saint Gregory the Great*, book IV, chapter 82:

> “At that time scarcely any monk could be found in those regions who did not observe the Rule of Saint Benedict both in his profession and in his habit.”

To these arguments of D. Mabillon another may be added from letter 58, now 73, to the priest Calvinus. From it we learn that Calvinus was a member of the York church and took part in the election of the bishop of that see. He also lived as a monk with the monks in the cell of Saint Stephen. There Alcuin exhorts Calvinus to cultivate, besides his other virtues, discretion,

> “which,” he says, “is said to be the mother of virtues among monks,”

namely, in chapter 64 of the Rule of Saint Benedict.

### XXII

You may object that Sigulf and Fridugis, Alcuin’s disciples who were educated in the school of the York church, wore canonical dress.

D. Mabillon replies: first, it is nevertheless not certain that they were truly incardinated in the York church, as this is certain of Alcuin; second, perhaps that church contained a mixed congregation of canons or clerics and monks; third, perhaps the clerics there, although wearing canonical dress, lived a monastic life, as Adam writes concerning the church of Bremen.

### XXIII

A second argument for Blessed Alcuin’s monastic profession is drawn from the fact that Charlemagne selected him as abbot to correct the morals of the monks of Tours. Secular abbots were never employed or considered suitable for such a task, as may be seen in the privilege granted to the monks of Corbie by Pope Nicholas I and in canon 3 of the Council of Trosly.

### XXIV

A third argument is drawn from the zeal and concern for promoting monastic discipline which Blessed Alcuin displayed. This is attested by his many letters written to monks of various monasteries—Fulda, Corbie, Morbach, Salzburg, Lérins, and others—all of whom, as D. Mabillon demonstrates in various places, professed the Rule of Saint Benedict.

What deacon of those times, what cleric or secular canon, however learned a public teacher; indeed, what bishop, unless he had been taken from among monks, would write with such zeal for the regular discipline of monks? Such ardent zeal and such great concern could surely be found only in a man who, so to speak, had been imbued and nourished from his earliest years with the monastic spirit.

### XXV

From this follows the fourth argument of D. Mabillon: that filial affection toward Saint Benedict, which Alcuin reveals in more than one place, especially in epigrams 196 and 254. There he at once longs so ardently for the increase of his father’s flock and desires so fervently to merit the favor and assistance of that most holy parent that no alumnus of Saint Benedict could be carried toward him with greater fervor.

### XXVI

The fifth argument is drawn from the formulas of confession which Blessed Alcuin composed. In them he calls Saint Benedict his father and expresses his desire to follow in his footsteps. On the use of the Psalms, see below, chapters 4 and 9. In chapter 11 he goes through all the degrees of humility established by Saint Benedict; and in chapter 3 and elsewhere he humbly professes himself a violator of the holy Rule.

But, you will say, Alcuin says these things not in his own person but in the person of the monks whom he governed and for whom he supplied these formulas.

Let it be so. Then the religious whom he governed were Benedictine monks; therefore he too was a Benedictine monk; therefore he speaks these words also in his own person, unless it is conclusively proved that he was not a monk.

### XXVII

The final argument which D. Mabillon draws in support of Blessed Alcuin’s Benedictine monastic profession comes from the confession or profession of faith published by D. Peter Chifflet under the name of that same blessed man and included by us among works of doubtful authenticity. It plainly demonstrates that the author of the aforesaid confession was a monk, as he expressly professes himself to be there. He acknowledges his blessed monks as his fathers in the place cited, part II, no. 9; and, having assumed the monk’s habit, he laments that he bears the false name of monk and has done nothing worthy of that name and habit, and so forth, in part IV, no. 16.

Indeed, although some have called into question whether Blessed Alcuin was the true author of this confession, D. Mabillon nearly establishes the point in his dissertation, which we cited above. Blessed Alcuin was therefore a monk.

### XXVIII

D. Mabillon considered these arguments, which establish Blessed Alcuin’s profession of monastic life, so weighty that they seemed to remove every objection. Nevertheless, that equally learned and modest man does not conceal that certain objections of greater importance may be drawn from the *Life of Blessed Alcuin*.

First, the author of that *Life* compares the conduct of Blessed Alcuin with that of Blessed Benedict, abbot of Aniane, and proposes the former for imitation by canons and the latter for imitation by monks.

Mabillon replies, in no. 20, that at that time there were monks of a milder and less strict way of life, and that the author may therefore have called them canons—such as the monks of Saint-Denis and Tours, some of whom called themselves monks and others canons.

Hence Charlemagne says in a letter to Albinus and the congregation of the monastery of Saint Martin, which we published in volume XCVIII of the *Patrologia*, col. 921:

> “Whether you are called canons or monks.”

And Ardo testifies in his book on the *Life of Saint Benedict of Aniane*:

> “There were certain monasteries following canonical institutions but ignorant of the precepts of the Rule.”

Blessed Benedict of Aniane restored these to regular form at the command of Louis Augustus.

The fathers of the Council of Tours, held in 813, likewise compel monks and abbots of a less disciplined life, in canon 25, to return to their former state, especially abbots,

> “who appeared to conduct themselves among their brethren more canonically than monastically.”

It may also be answered that by the name “canons” the aforesaid author understood monks of cathedral churches, such as existed in England and Germany and also at Rome; the commonly circulated Anastasius calls them “canonical monks” in his account of Pope Gregory IV.

The life of Alcuin, since he was usually compelled to live at the royal court and among courtiers, was more canonical—or milder—than monastic. The author of his *Life* could therefore propose it for imitation by canons, though not by solitary monks, even if Alcuin himself held the monastic Rule by profession and had been prevented or dispensed, against his will, from observing its strictness because of his public duties.

I add that just as monks once lived in certain cathedral churches, so now in certain principal and royal abbeys, and even in public schools, some monks lead a life more canonical than monastic. You would be proposing such men inopportunely for imitation by monks generally.

### XXIX

Objection 2. The praised author of the *Life* calls Alcuin a monk without a monk’s vow in chapter 3. He was therefore a monk by his way of life, not by profession.

The answer is easy. These things are written of Alcuin while he was still a boy, at an age when he was not permitted to profess monastic vows.

### XXX

Objection 3. The objection may be repeated from chapter 8 of the *Life*, where the author reports that Alcuin, already advanced in age, wished to leave the world and asked Charlemagne for permission to lead a monastic life in the monastery of Fulda according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. But he was compelled to remain among the monks of Saint Martin, where his life was no less monastic.

“You will therefore say that Alcuin was not truly a monk, but one only in aspiration, affection, and conduct.”

Mabillon replies that the author of the *Life* must be interpreted through Alcuin himself. When he writes that Alcuin wished to leave the world, the word “world” should be understood as referring to secular occupations, by which the blessed man was continually distracted while longing for the quiet appropriate to prayer and study.

Writing of this desire to King Charles in letter 101, now 129, he says:

> “For nearly five years before this, I considered withdrawing from secular occupations—God is my witness—with no feigned intention.”

A little later he says that he desired

> “to live and rest among the brethren in the church of Saint Martin,”

not at Fulda.

Although Alcuin lived in that same monastery at Tours with brethren who at that time lived in a more canonical manner, his life was nevertheless not inferior to the monastic life which he had learned from childhood. He made every effort to restore them

> “to the dignity of monastic life,”

as he himself declares in letter 195, now 149, to the emperor Charles.

### XXXI

These are the arguments which may be brought forward to prove Blessed Alcuin’s monastic profession. This conclusion may also be confirmed, and not slightly, by what the Venerable Bede relates at the end of chapter 24 of his *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*:

> “When peace and the serenity of the times smiled”—that is, while he was writing this in the year 731—“many among the people of the Northumbrians”—Alcuin’s homeland—“both nobles and commoners, after laying down their arms, took care to enroll themselves and their children in monastic vows after receiving the tonsure, rather than to exercise themselves in military pursuits.”

It should be believed that Blessed Alcuin’s parents, born at that same time, followed this custom and wished to enroll their son in monastic—or, as I interpret it, monkish—vows.

### XXXII

These arguments, most of which we have condensed from D. Mabillon’s observations, together with those which we ourselves have added, will appear, unless we are greatly mistaken, very close to the truth. We have not seen any learned man expressly attack Mabillon’s dissertation, although some think that it has not yet been fully demonstrated.

What stands in the way of their agreement is the authority of the author of the *Life*, almost contemporary with Alcuin, who may seem plainly to have been unaware that Blessed Alcuin was truly a monk by profession. See Le Cointe, year 802, no. 95.

Perhaps, however, that author had before his eyes the condition of the monastery of Tours as it existed in his own time, nearly twenty years after Blessed Alcuin’s death, under his successor Fridugis. Saint Odo, abbot, portrays that condition in the following words, quoted by John the Monk in book III, chapter 1 of his *Life*:

> “Some years ago, while the monastic congregation continued at the church of Saint Martin at Tours, they began to abandon their proper way and customs and to corrupt their life and profession according to their own desires. For, abandoning their native and customary garments, they began to wear colored and flowing cucullae and tunics adorned with the pallium, and so forth. They did these and many similar things against the rights of the Rule.”

Ademar, the monk of Angoulême, explains this matter in his *Chronicle*:

> “At that time, the monks of Saint Martin at Tours, with no one compelling them, laid aside the monastic form before the body of that same saint and assumed the canonical form, and so forth.”

D. Mabillon proves in his *Elogium of Blessed Alcuin*, chapter 8, nos. 41 and 42, that this change occurred under Fridugis, the abbot and successor of Blessed Alcuin.

Attending to this later condition and failing to turn his mind back to the monastery of Tours in its earlier state, the author of the *Life of Blessed Alcuin* may have thought that Alcuin, as father of that congregation, had also professed its canonical way of life.

### XXXIII

Whatever the truth may be, the Benedictine order is rightly proud that so blessed and celebrated a man was first educated within that order and instructed in letters and virtues; that afterward he became a teacher and abbot of Benedictine monks; and that he preserved the spirit of Saint Benedict until death, being joined by vow and desire to this holy order. Nothing could have prevented him from fulfilling that desire except the greater utility of the Church and the public good.

### XXXIV

It should not be passed over here that Blessed Alcuin, in his letters, never calls himself a monk, but either a levite or, what signified the same thing at that time, a deacon. Isidore explains this usage in book VII, chapter 12 of the *Etymologies*. It was then customary for each person to take his appellation from the ecclesiastical office corresponding to the degree with which he was invested, while the title of monk or even abbot was often omitted.

Nowhere does Alcuin even indicate by a word that he was a priest, nor is it written that others raised him to that rank. Nevertheless, some more recent writer, in Mabillon’s volume XXVI of the *Annals*, p. 342, no. 90, maintains that when Charlemagne and his sons received holy communion in the church of Saint Stephen at Tours, Alcuin performed the office of priest, with the deacon Sigulf assisting him, as the author of the *Life of Blessed Alcuin* relates in no. 18.

The most learned Mabillon, however, refutes this opinion of that critic and certain others in the same place. He solidly demonstrates that the words of the author of the *Life*,

> “When Alcuin, after the communion of the body and blood of Christ, mixed it for them with his own hand,”

do not mean that Alcuin gave Charles and his sons communion of the body and blood of Christ. Rather, they mean that after a priest had given Charles and his three sons—Charles, Pippin, and Louis—the communion of the body and blood of the Lord, Alcuin offered them a drink, perhaps in the church’s sacristy, as was formerly customary.

Certainly, as the well-cited Mabillon rightly argues there, no one would say that Alcuin was a priest unless he were entirely unfamiliar with his writings and letters, or unless he had read his *Life* with scarcely any attention. In most of his letters he is called a levite, a humble levite, or even a deacon—never a priest or presbyter.

Einhard, who knew him personally, calls him, after his death—so that no one may suppose that he was ordained a presbyter before his death—only the deacon Albinus. In his *Life* it is said that he came to Francia as a deacon, no. 12; that he celebrated Mass daily in levitical fashion with his priest Sigulf, no. 26; and finally, it is implied that he died a deacon, no. 28. For he is said to have been led into heaven by the ministry of the heavenly levites Stephen and Lawrence and to have stood among them clothed in a most splendid dalmatic.

These points are so evident that anyone ought to be embarrassed to linger longer over a question of such little weight.

## CHAPTER IV

### Blessed Alcuin’s School and Disciples in Britain

### XXXV

We have the Venerable Bede as a most authoritative witness, in various chapters of his *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, that the study of both sacred and secular letters—established there long ago by the Romans but later disrupted by the incursions of the Saxons and Danes—flourished again after Christian religion had been brought to that island and firmly established through the care of Saint Gregory the Great, supreme pontiff. Likewise, after the arrival of Abbot Adrian and Bishop Theodore, men outstanding in every kind of learning, public schools of Greek and Latin education were restored and so frequented that from those schools there later emerged not only bishops but also kings and princes distinguished for learning and wisdom.

Polydorus Vergil, in book IV of his *History of England*, p. 68, counts among these schools the school of Cambridge, founded, as he believes, by Sigebert, king of the East Angles. The Venerable Bede calls him in book II, chapter 15,

> “a man in every respect most learned and most Christian,”

and in book III, chapter 18, writes of him that, after receiving baptism in exile in Gaul, he soon desired to imitate the things which he had seen well ordered in Gaul and established a school in which boys might be instructed in letters,

> “with the assistance of Bishop Felix, whom he had received from Kent, and who provided them with teachers and tutors according to the customs of Kent.”

Bede says nothing about Cambridge; therefore Vergil’s account must be attributed to conjecture. Nor can what the same learned man thinks in the same place—that the fact that England afterward always produced men distinguished in learning should be attributed especially to King Sigebert, and that he was the first to lay the foundation of letters there—be reconciled with the narrative of the Venerable Bede. For according to Bede, that Bishop Felix, who promoted King Sigebert’s project, obtained the first teachers and tutors from the school at Canterbury, which had already been founded.

### XXXVI

It is likewise scarcely credible that John Bale, whose authority some others have also trusted, reports from the annals of the University of Cambridge that Blessed Alcuin taught all the liberal arts there after Bede.

This account, drawn from certain obscure annals, deserves no credence, first because it proceeds from an insufficiently careful writer, such as learned men portray Bale to have been; see Struve, *Bibliotheca Historica et Literaria*, volume II, p. 1220, § 20. Second, it is not likely that the Venerable Bede ever held a teaching office at Cambridge. As we showed above in chapter 2, and shall establish hereafter concerning Blessed Alcuin, he spent his entire life, both learning and teaching, in the church or monastery of York, until he finally departed for Francia.

### XXXVII

Thus only the school of York in England was privileged to have Blessed Alcuin first as a disciple and afterward also as a teacher. At that time it was the most celebrated of all the schools on that island whose memory still survives.

We have already indicated in chapter 2 that it was first established by Egbert, archbishop of that see, and afterward endowed with even greater renown by his successor Aelbert. Under the institution of these most learned prelates, nearly all the sciences and liberal arts were taught there with great diligence and with much benefit to the many students: grammar, rhetoric, dialectic, jurisprudence, poetry, astronomy, arithmetic, music, and ecclesiastical computation. Alcuin himself lists all these in his poem on the bishops of York.

The greatest attention, however, was devoted there to sacred learning and divine Scripture, to a fuller knowledge and understanding of which all the other studies were directed. For this purpose, some diligence was also devoted to learning the sacred languages, Hebrew and Greek, as much as the circumstances of that age allowed.

### XXXVIII

After Blessed Alcuin had passed through all these classes of study in this school with the greatest application and with no less success, he not only earned from his fellow students such an extraordinary reputation for varied learning that, as the author of his *Life* testifies, they honored him as a second master; he was also judged worthy by his teacher, Archbishop Egbert, to be entrusted with the office of teaching in the same school and to be appointed Aelbert’s colleague in that office.

Indeed, before the year 766—that is, before the death of Egbert, which occurred in that year—he had already attained such fame that Blessed Liudger, moved by it, devoted himself in that same year to his instruction and received spiritual teachings from him among the other disciples. This is attested by Alfrid in book I, no. 9, of the *Life of Saint Liudger*; the same testimony is also found in the other *Life*, book I, chapter 5.

The most learned Mabillon agrees on this point. From the same *Life of Saint Liudger*, in book XXIII of the *Annals*, no. 37, he concludes that Blessed Alcuin was placed in charge of the schools of York around the year 758, during the episcopate of Egbert.

### XXXIX.

When blessed Alcuin was directing the schools of York, there was a great influx of students from every quarter, including from foreign regions. Among the foreigners, the first to be named is the man of whom we have already begun to speak: Saint Liudger, the first bishop of Mimigardeford, or Münster, a man renowned for holiness and apostolic zeal.

For when he had once been sent to England by his abbot Gregory, the successor of Saint Boniface in the church of Utrecht, and was staying at York, he came to the attention of blessed Alcuin. He was so delighted by Alcuin’s learning and eloquence that, after returning to Utrecht, he was immediately seized by a desire to return to the same school. Accordingly, he wearied both his abbot and his guardian Thiadgrimus with constant petitions to obtain this permission, and at last persuaded them to consent to his desire.

[Col. 0033C] Liudger, therefore, bound by his vow, returned to York and remained there under the instruction of blessed Alcuin for three and a half years. Then, when an unforeseen circumstance arose, he was compelled against his will to return to his homeland in order to avoid the English hostility toward the Frisians. By then he had been instructed in those disciplines that made him worthy to undertake, with the greatest glory to his name, an episcopal and apostolic office in his homeland.

Alcuin gave him as a traveling companion a certain deacon named Putul, who was making his way to Rome. After receiving priestly ordination there, Putul later returned to York and subsequently came with the same teacher of his to Gaul.

It is credible that at that time many other men or youths from foreign nations came to the schools of England, which were then celebrated for their learning—especially to the school at York, directed by blessed Alcuin. But who they were, we do not know, since the surviving records fail us.

### XL.

Among the countrymen of blessed Alcuin who were his disciples, the following became especially well known. [Col. 0033D] We shall try briefly to clarify some aspects of their lives that may appear obscure.

The first to be mentioned is the younger Eanbald, surnamed Symeon, successor in the see of York to the elder Eanbald, once a fellow student of blessed Alcuin in the same school. The elder Eanbald died on 29 July 796. We have recorded more about the younger Eanbald in our notes to Letters 50, 58, 170, 173, and 174—now 56, 64, 73, 114, and 115—written to him; for the sake of brevity, we refer the reader to those notes.

### XLI.

Another disciple of blessed Alcuin who must be recalled here was Wizo, or Withso, his native name, I believe, as he is called in Letter 118, now 157. In the Colbertine manuscript, as we observed in the notes there, the heading reads: “Letter to Candidus, that is, to Wizo.”

The author of the Life numbers him among blessed Alcuin’s disciples at section 14 and bestows upon him the epithet “magnanimous.” Alcuin himself likewise indicates in Letter 118, now 157, that Wizo had once been his disciple, writing that he had instructed him, together with his companion Nathanael, or [Col. 0034A] Fridugisus, “in the school of learning concerning the divine commandments.”

The same point is suggested in the preface to the Commentaries on Ecclesiastes, dedicated to Onia and Nathanael, where Wizo is designated as a priest. Leland, *On the Writers of Britain*, chapter 100, page 133, rightly identifies this Candidus as a pupil of the church of Lindisfarne.

Together with several other countrymen and fellow students, he accompanied his teacher Alcuin to Francia. After some time, however, around the year 796, he returned to Britain for reasons unknown, as is recorded in Letter 39, now 44, to Damoeta. Since he remained there longer than Alcuin wished, Alcuin discreetly requested his return from Higbald, bishop of Lindisfarne, in a letter to the people of Lindisfarne, a fragment of which we printed in the notes to Letter 8, now 9.

There is no reason to doubt that blessed Alcuin’s desire was fulfilled by Higbald. For this same Candidus, unless we are seriously mistaken, was the man whose loyalty and diligence [Col. 0034B] Alcuin subsequently entrusted with various matters to be handled and concluded with King Charles, with certain bishops, with courtiers, and with friends. This is clear from Letters 92, 105, 109, 110, and 123—now 108, 133, 145, 146, and 162—and from others.

When Candidus was setting out for Rome, to the thresholds of the apostles, apparently out of devotion, Alcuin encouraged and entreated him in a poem to venerate there devoutly the ashes of the holy apostles and of the other saints, to commend himself to their intercession, and to return only with a gift of sacred relics. We shall give the poem below.

This same Candidus may perhaps have been the author of a certain work, hitherto unpublished, *On the Image of God*, which is preserved in Appendix 2. We have stated our conjecture about it in the preliminary notice there.

This Candidus, the disciple of blessed Alcuin, must be distinguished from another Candidus, a monk and priest of Fulda, whose proper name was not Wizo but Bruun. He himself expressed his name at the end of the metrical preface to the Life of Saint Eigil, abbot, in these words:

> Here ends the preface of Candidus [Col. 0034C] to Modestus, who is called by his proper name Bruun and Richeo.

He does the same at the end of chapter 17 of the same Life, writing:

> And what I, once nourished in this court,  
> Bruun, priest and monk and humble teacher,  
> depicted by my own ingenuity, and so forth.

### XLII.

Fridugisus was Candidus’s companion and fellow student at the school of York under the instruction of blessed Alcuin, as the anonymous author of the Life testifies in chapter 8, section 14. Among the learned men of his time he bore the surname Nathanael, as I observed in the note to Letter 118, now 157, from the heading of the Colbertine manuscript.

Alcuin calls him sometimes a deacon, in the preface to *Ecclesiastes*, and sometimes an archdeacon, in Letter 183, now 124. That he was a countryman of blessed Alcuin, his pupil at the school of York, and later his companion in Gaul is suggested not only by the preface and letter just cited, but also by the exceptional confidence and familiarity [Col. 0034D] that Alcuin showed toward him in conducting his affairs. A prudent man would scarcely have extended such confidence to pupils from a foreign land whose abilities he had not yet adequately tested.

Alcuin chose him to carry to Charles the sacred books that he had most carefully corrected, in order to obtain the imperial crown, as appears from Letters 103 and 185, now 131 and 135. While Fridugisus was living at the palace, Alcuin instructed him and Candidus concerning the dispute between the monks of Tours and Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, so that they might defend the cause of those monks, as appears in Letter 118, now 157.

When Fridugisus was staying with the king at Aachen, Alcuin urged him to adorn his female pupils Lucia and Columba, who were present at court, with the beauty and flowers of his wisdom, in Letters 98 and 185, now 126 and 135.

Finally, when weakened by illness, Alcuin judged this beloved disciple of his above all others worthy to succeed him in governing the monastery of Tours, even though Fridugisus did not profess the monastic life but the canonical. The same Fridugisus later also became abbot of Sithiu, Saint Bertin’s [Col. 0035A] monastery.

Under his direction, a more relaxed discipline of the canons later revived in both monasteries, and the spirit of Saint Benedict was completely extinguished. He also possessed great influence at the imperial court. For he subscribed the testament of Charlemagne and became chancellor of Emperor Louis. He died in 834. See Mabillon, *Eulogy of Blessed Alcuin*, section 45; *Annals*, book XXVIII, section 16; book XXIX, section 32; and book XXXI, section 67.

He wrote several works, of which nothing now survives except a letter *On Nothing and Darkness* to the nobles of the palace, published in volume II of Baluze’s *Miscellany*, page 403. In this work Fridugisus investigates, with philosophical subtlety, the nature of nothing, from which God created the world, and of the darkness that was over the face of the abyss. He argues that nothing is something and that darkness is a substance. His arguments, however, are mere sophisms, although otherwise the style he employs is pure, clear, and even fluent.

Mabillon conjectures that Fridugisus wrote the poem *On the Cell of Cormaric*, which we present among the doubtful works. In it he complains that the cell [Col. 0035B], now enjoying its own abbot, namely Jacob, and formerly attached to his monastery at Tours, has been taken away from him.

He also wrote against Agobard, bishop of Lyons, criticizing somewhat sharply certain errors that he attributed to him. This little work of Fridugisus, however, still lies hidden. In his defense, Agobard reproached Fridugisus for the harshness of his style and for certain greater errors against sound theology, in volume I of his works, pages 165 and 191. The discussion of Fridugisus by D. Rivet deserves to be read, volume IV of *Literary History of France*, page 512 and following.

### XLIII.

We have not wished to separate Onia the priest from Candidus and Fridugisus, although little is known about his life or deeds. Nevertheless, he appears to have been a countryman and disciple of blessed Alcuin, as may be inferred from the heading of the Commentaries on Ecclesiastes, where Onia is joined with Candidus and Nathanael and is said, like those two, to have once been brought up as a son in the nest of paternal devotion and instructed under the wings of paternal [Col. 0035C] learning.

From the same heading, where he is distinguished by the title of priest and placed before his companions, it is sufficiently clear that he was also employed in secular affairs at court and was very dear to blessed Alcuin. In Letter 183, now 124, Alcuin commends him equally with Symeon, Martin, and Nathanael to the remembrance of George, patriarch of Jerusalem. In Letter 227, now 230, he expresses to him his sadness at Onia’s absence. In Letter 228, now 231, he admonishes him to love God, to remember the poor, the afflicted, and strangers, and to assist them with alms, protection, and consolation.

### XLIV.

Among the disciples of blessed Alcuin, the author of the Life numbers a certain Osulfus in chapter 8, section 14. There can be no doubt that he too was taught by Alcuin at the school of York. D. Mabillon considers him likewise a countryman of blessed Alcuin, *Annals*, book XXVII, section 29, although in his eulogy appended to the Life [Col. 0035D] of blessed Alcuin, chapter 11, section 66, he says that Osulfus, together with Onia, Candidus, and Nathanael, was an auditor at the monastery of Tours among those who accompanied Alcuin from England.

It is certainly clear enough from the account that the anonymous author of the Life of blessed Alcuin gives of Osulfus’s death at the cited passage, section 15, that Osulfus was not by origin a Gaul or Frank. Blessed Alcuin, speaking prophetically to another disciple of his, Raganard, foretold concerning Osulfus, who was deaf to every admonition regarding a better life:

> “He will die neither in this region”—namely Francia, where Alcuin was then living—“nor in the land where he was born.”

The outcome later proved this true, for he died in Lombardy.

Osulfus, therefore, was undoubtedly the disciple to whom Alcuin wrote Letters [Col. 0036A] 157 and 158, now 206 and 207, as to a prodigal son: at first well formed in the best morals and liberal disciplines, illuminated by the salt of wisdom, and diligent in the sacred Scriptures, but afterward joined to bands of prostitutes, banquets of drunkards, and the vanities of the proud.

“Once,” he says in the former letter, “I begot you, nourished you, fed you, and brought you to full manhood … so that the whole region might sing your praises”—namely Britain, as is read in the Salzburg manuscripts, as I observed there.

In the other letter, he proposes to him, as an example to encourage him toward the correction of his life, a fellow student of his “who now presides over a most noble bishopric.” This was plainly none other than Eanbald, archbishop of York.

Osulfus, therefore, was educated and instructed with him in Britain, at the school of York, under the teaching of blessed Alcuin. Theodulf of Orléans praises this same Osulfus, together with Fridugisus, for his learning in book III, poem 1, addressed to King Charles. Concerning both of them he sings, verse 175:

> Let the worthy deacon Fridugisus stand, joined with Osulfus;  
> Both know the arts, both are well instructed.

Whether this Osulfus is the same man as the one who related many notable things [Col. 0036B] about Charles the Younger in Letter 179, now 120, we do not know.

### XLV.

It is plausible that Osulfus, who was called by that name in his native language, later acquired among schoolmen the designation Cuculus, since Alcuin laments in poem 77 a fall like the one for which he reproves Osulfus. The addition that we published in volume II, poem 6, also belongs to this matter; it was discovered later in a manuscript of Saint Paul’s College at Regensburg.

Certainly, under this familiar and adopted name lies concealed a certain disciple of blessed Alcuin, educated at the school of York and the companion of his teacher in Gaul. Alcuin once sent him to his own Symeon, or Bishop Eanbald, with gifts, as is understood from Letter 171, now 65. He also used his services to convey excellent advice to the same Eanbald when he was afflicted by various adversities, as is read in Letters 174, now 115, and the following letter.

### XLVI.

Cuculus’s companion and fellow student was [Col. 0036C] Calwinus, an English priest. In Letter 58, now 73, addressed to him, Alcuin instructs him with salutary teachings. In another letter, 175, now 116, addressed jointly to Calwinus and Cuculus, he urges them to recommend to Symeon, or Archbishop Eanbald, whatever might console him in his adversities and move him to live a life appropriate to his office and dignity.

From Letter 58, now 73, we learn that Calwinus presided over a cell of Saint Stephen and was a monk and father of monks, as we observed in the notes there. Certainly he was a member of the church of York and took part by his vote in the election of Archbishop Eanbald, as Alcuin suggests in these words:

> “Whom”—Symeon—“you elected to the honor of the pontificate.”

### XLVII.

Among the more distinguished disciples of blessed Alcuin, the anonymous author of the Life names first Sigulf the Elder. From Sigulf’s account the author learned what he committed to the memory of posterity, [Col. 0036D] and his testimony is all the more worthy of belief because, as we read at the end of the prologue to that Life, “he alone, after the departure of Saint Edbert”—I believe this means Bishop Aelbert—“was deemed worthy to know his exceptional secrets.”

According to the same author, chapter 5, section 11, Sigulf was “a man beloved by God, distinguished by nobility of mind and body, a priest and guardian of the church of the city of York.” He was joined to blessed Alcuin by such close friendship that, wishing for this reason to remain constantly with him, he desired to associate himself with Alcuin, who was then conducting schools in Francia.

Before Sigulf accompanied Alcuin to Francia, however, he had already come there as a boy with his uncle Autbert, a holy priest:

> “By whom he had been brought to Rome to learn the ecclesiastical order and sent to the city of Metz for the sake of singing.”

After losing his uncle on the journey through death, Sigulf nevertheless “returned to his own homeland with much benefit.”

Alcuin praises him as an exceptionally devoted student [Col. 0037A] of sacred reading in the letter prefixed to his *Questions and His Answers on the Book of Genesis*. In that work Alcuin sought, as time permitted, to satisfy Sigulf’s desire by explaining certain difficulties in the book. There Alcuin calls him his brother and his companion, inseparable and faithful for a long time.

From this confidence and familiar association, I infer that Sigulf, under the instruction of blessed Alcuin in England, had already advanced beyond his other fellow students toward manhood and was older than they. Hence perhaps he received the name “the Elder.” For this reason Alcuin associated him with himself in the teaching office and entrusted him with the care of the students whenever other affairs repeatedly prevented him from attending to them.

Despite this confidence and esteem, Alcuin sharply reproved him when he had secretly allowed his students Adalbert and Aldric to read the poet Virgil against Alcuin’s command. Although Alcuin, as the author of the Life relates in chapter 10, section 19, had enjoyed reading Virgil [Col. 0037B] in his youth, he later did not want his disciples to do so:

> “The divine Poet is sufficient for you; you do not need to be polluted by the luxuriant eloquence of Virgil.”

To Sigulf, therefore, who had violated this command, he said:

> “Where did we get you from, Virgilian? Why did you begin and choose, against my will and advice, to act without my knowledge so that you might read Virgil?”

Greatly ashamed by this rebuke, Sigulf humbly threw himself at the feet of his teacher, who had penetrated his hidden thoughts, repented, and confessed that he had acted most foolishly.

I suspect that this Sigulf was the sick son to whom Letter 231, now 188, was written. He wished Alcuin to advise him “whether it would be better to await the breath of his final day in canonical dress or in monastic holiness.” The holy man replied that nothing should be changed in the present danger, and that in every condition one’s thoughts and will should always be directed toward the greater advancement of the Church. Nevertheless, if he recovered, he could put on the monastic cowl:

> “For the sake of prayer,” he says, “and for the consolation of fraternal [Col. 0037C] intercession, rest among the monks appears desirable.”

Indeed, when Sigulf was already abbot of Ferrières—for Alcuin, wishing to free himself from all external affairs, entrusted the governance of that monastery to him—he continued to wear the canonical habit until old age. Later, he voluntarily resigned the abbey to his disciple Adalbert and, having taken the monastic habit on the advice—unless I am mistaken—of that same Alcuin, submitted himself to his aforesaid disciple and successor as an outstanding example of modesty. We learn this from Letter 29 of Abbot Lupus.

The school of Ferrières owes its origin to Sigulf; afterward it became much more celebrated under Abbot Lupus. See *Literary History of France*, volume IV, page 242, section 37.

This Sigulf must be distinguished from another man of the same name, whom the author of the Life of Alcuin mentions in chapter 11, section 20. He was a monk and disciple of Saint Benedict of Aniane, as D. Mabillon correctly observes in his notes to the prologue of Alcuin’s Life.

Nevertheless, we cannot agree with the opinion of that very distinguished scholar when he distinguishes there from this man, who dictated the deeds of his teacher, another Sigulf, [Col. 0037D] a priest and very familiar with Alcuin, who is mentioned in the same Life at section 11. He gives no reason for his opinion, nor have we found any reason for it in the Life in question or elsewhere.

### XLVIII.

Among the more celebrated disciples of blessed Alcuin, whom he imbued at York with the sciences and liberal arts, Joseph must finally be counted. In Letter 132, now 174, to Bishop Remigius, Alcuin calls him his disciple and, in the preceding letter, his beloved son.

That Joseph was a Briton is suggested by a fragment of a letter written by Alcuin to him, which we reproduced from Ussher in the notes to Letter 3. In it Alcuin writes about Colcu, a lector in Scotland, in these words:

> “Your teacher Colcu is well.”

Joseph, therefore, had at some time been under the instruction of this Colcu in Britain and afterward joined the scholars [Col. 0038A] at York because of the school’s renown.

Later he went to Francia with this other teacher of his, Alcuin. Certainly he was staying there with Alcuin around the year 790, as is understood from the same Letter 3, which Alcuin wrote from Francia to Colcu, the lector in Scotland. As we stated there in the notes, agreeing with D. Mabillon, Alcuin tells Colcu that he and Joseph were enjoying excellent health in those lands.

The celebrated Mabillon, in his eulogy of blessed Alcuin, chapter 11, section 67, has no doubt that this Joseph was the man who, at the command of this teacher, abridged Saint Jerome’s Commentaries on Isaiah. He likewise testifies that this epitome survives in manuscript under the title *Joseph the Abbot* and records its beginning and end.

The author himself declares that the work was begun at the command of blessed Alcuin and dedicated to his name in this verse:

> Thus it pleases Albinus that we undertake such a labor.

And again, near the end of the poem:

> Thus, obeying your commands, dearest one,  
> I have dedicated to you, Albinus, these things collected in brief.

Finally, he continues in prose:

> “These things I have excerpted in a brief discourse, [Col. 0038B] as I was able … just as you commanded, dearest master Albinus, in devoted obedience. For you instructed me to follow in everything only the absolutely necessary meaning and the path of Hebrew truth … and to avoid uncertain and confused tracks.”

From this one may conclude that the study of Hebrew learning was not absent from the school of blessed Alcuin.

Joseph died before his teacher, since Alcuin commends his soul to the prayers of Bishop Remigius in the Letter 132, now 174, cited above.

### XLIX.

We have wished to recall these more celebrated disciples of blessed Alcuin, leaving aside many others whom he taught in Britain for the sake of brevity, insofar as this may contribute to illuminating the writings and deeds of that most celebrated author and to honoring the reputation of his teaching.

Nothing, however, contributes more to the glory of this immortal man than the fact that the kings, princes, [Col. 0038C] queens, and royal virgins of England, together with its bishops and priests, abbots and monks, and other men distinguished by civil and ecclesiastical rank, made use of his teachings and advice. This is documented by the many letters written to those various persons, filled with salutary admonitions and teachings particularly suited to each condition of life.

### L.

I cannot refrain from warning learned readers at this appropriate point that certain English writers—Harpesfeld, Pits, and Bale, whom the Magdeburg Centuriators copy—were seriously mistaken when they numbered among England’s learned women Gisela and Richtrude, also called by their adopted names Lucia and Columba, to whom blessed Alcuin dedicated his Commentaries on the Gospel of Saint John.

It is surprising that the learned D. Alford added his authority to this opinion in his *Anglo-Saxon Ecclesiastical Annals* under the year 770. For it is clearer than daylight, at least from the words of the letter of those virgins prefixed to those [Col. 0038D] Commentaries and written from Paris to Alcuin while he was at Tours, that they had Alcuin as their teacher not in England but in Gaul. They write there:

> “The bearer of your letters will be able to reach the city of Paris from Tours much more easily …”

But we shall return to these virgins below, when we discuss the school of the palace.

## CHAPTER V

### The Calling of Blessed Alcuin and His Arrival in Francia

### LI.

The fame of so distinguished a teacher could no more be confined within York itself than it could remain within the boundaries of Britain. It spread also into other regions, especially Francia and Gaul, at precisely the opportune time when the governance of both those extensive kingdoms was held by that Charles who, because of his deeds of exceptional wisdom and courage, acquired the name “the Great,” a title that afterward could never be erased.

### LII.

After the death of his father Pippin and his brother [Col. 0039A] Carloman, Charles alone ascended the throne. Looking over the condition of his kingdom, he sorrowfully observed that it was utterly corrupt both in political and ecclesiastical affairs, savage with barbarism, and deprived of every cultivation of morals and letters.

Indeed, it is the common judgment of all writers possessing some knowledge of literary antiquity that barbarism and ignorance, from the fifth century of the Christian era—which must be regarded as the first epoch of the universal collapse of letters—made such excessive advances, and grew so powerful during the first sixty or seventy years of the eighth century, that they appeared to have reached their final completion, admitting no further remedy.

Certainly the monk of Angoulême, in his Life of Charlemagne, writes under the year 787 that before Charles’s time “there had been no study of the liberal arts in Gaul.”

This should not, however, be understood as though no cultivation of letters or liberal arts had ever flourished in Gaul during earlier times, before that fifth century. For we know from Tacitus, Eunomius, and the rescript [Col. 0039B] of the Emperor Gratian preserved in the Theodosian Code—where he commands Antonius, the praetorian prefect of Gaul, to establish literary schools in every metropolitan city and to appoint suitable teachers for them with adequate provision—that before those disastrous times, when Gaul was disturbed by the invasion of the barbarians and by the civil conflicts that later arose, the finest studies had flourished and schools had been established and organized there.

But those seats of learning were later overthrown by the repeated incursions of the barbarians, as we have said, and by the storms of civil discord. Leisure and repose, the friends of the Muses, were taken away, so that under the Frankish kings who preceded Charles no home remained for them. This is what the monk of Angoulême wished to relate at the passage cited.

### LIII.

It is not necessary here to say more [Col. 0039C] about the wretched condition in which Charles found his kingdom, completely disfigured and desolated by prolonged barbarism, since the distinguished author of *The Literary History of France* has discussed it with the greatest learning, volume III, page 417, and volume IV, page 1 and following.

I wished, however, at least to touch upon and mention it briefly, so that it might be more clearly understood what the entire literary world owed to the efforts of Alcuin, that foremost restorer after Charlemagne. We shall recount those efforts in this and the following chapters.

### LIV.

After Charles had restored most of his kingdom to peace and tranquility, whether by arms or by prudence, that great prince rightly judged that no remedy would be more effective for removing barbarism throughout his kingdom than diligent cultivation of morals and intellects.

The obstacle to carrying out this most prudent plan was that he could scarcely find in the regions subject to Frankish rule men endowed with sufficient piety, learning, and experience to undertake with credit and hoped-for success the task of teaching the uneducated and refining the barbarians.

It was therefore necessary to seek such assistance from foreign [Col. 0039D] regions, especially Italy and Britain, where at that time particular attention was being devoted to the cultivation of literary studies and morals. The wisest king’s plan is praised by Alcuin in Letter 101, now 129, addressed to this “David” of his, in these words:

> “I recognized your concern, my lord David: you encouraged everyone to learn wisdom, indeed you urged them on with rewards and honors, and you endeavored to summon from various parts of the world lovers of wisdom to assist your good will. Among them you took care to enlist me also, the least of its humble servants, from the farthest borders of Britain.”

### LV.

The first men to become known to Charles during his several journeys through Italy were Peter of Pisa, a deacon and elderly man, and Paul Warnefrid, likewise a deacon and a monk of Monte Cassino [Col. 0040A]—men highly esteemed for their varied learning and skill in teaching.

Charles invited them to his court, intending them to serve as professors of the sciences in his palace and as assistants in his plan to restore literary studies and organize and establish schools.

Obeying the command of the great prince, after Charles had captured Pavia in 774, they are believed to have gone with him to Gaul to perform that office.

The learned D. Lebeuf discusses both men and various little works of theirs, recently discovered by him, with great distinction in *Dissertation on the Ecclesiastical and Civil History of Paris*, volume I, page 370 and following. There, on page 386, he likewise observes that Charlemagne had already seriously considered restoring literary studies in his extensive kingdom before the arrival of blessed Alcuin.

I would not deny this. Nevertheless, I am certain from what will be said later—and other learned men likewise openly affirm it—that apart from blessed Alcuin no one collaborated with the king’s intention with greater zeal and diligence. Thus it is chiefly to Alcuin’s account that we must credit what the great king [Col. 0040B] afterward established for the benefit and advancement of the best studies, and even for the wise constitution of the happy condition of both commonwealths, ecclesiastical and civil, which ordinarily flows from them.

After this brief preface, let us now begin to discuss the calling and arrival in Francia of the teacher of this court and of the entire Frankish kingdom.

### LVI.

As we have already noted elsewhere, blessed Alcuin first came to the attention of Charles, king of the Franks, “when he was once sent to him by his teacher,” as is read in his Life, chapter 6, section 12.

The event took place before the year 780, when some believe that Alcuin returned from Rome after receiving the pallium for Eanbald the Elder, the new archbishop of York. The author of the Life clearly records this at the same passage.

Certainly, at an earlier time, when Alcuin was still an adolescent—and therefore near the twenty-seventh [Col. 0040C] year of his life, which Alcuin himself establishes as the limit of adolescence in the *Disputation of Boys*—that is, around the year 762, if we correctly reckon his birth as occurring in 735, Alcuin undoubtedly traveled through Francia to Rome.

It was then, namely, when he attended at the royal city of Pavia the disputation between Peter the Pisan and Julius the Jew, as we learn from his Letter 85, now 101. On that journey Alcuin may first have had the opportunity to come to the attention of Charles, who, as we suppose, was not yet governing the kingdom—before the death of his father Pippin.

At another time, or perhaps on the same occasion, blessed Alcuin came to Francia in the company of his teacher Aelbert, and therefore before the year 766, when Aelbert was elevated to the episcopate. He stayed among the monks of Corbie—though I believe Morbach is meant—as he writes at the beginning of Letter 222, now 53.

When these facts are considered together, it is highly probable that Alcuin, not yet beyond adolescence, accompanied the same Aelbert, not yet a bishop, as he traveled through foreign regions and visited the holy places of Rome. Alcuin describes this journey [Col. 0040D] of his teacher in the poem *On the Pontiffs of York*. He adds that when Aelbert was returning to his homeland, kings and rulers received him honorably as a supreme teacher and valued him so highly that they tried by every means to keep him with them:

> So that, flowing with divine dew, he might water their fields.

But Aelbert, desiring to serve the advancement of his own homeland more than that of a foreign region, did not allow himself to be detained. He continued his journey to England and to his own church, whose bishopric he received not long afterward.

### LVII.

When Aelbert departed, Charles—if this may be inferred from the foregoing and from the account of the anonymous author of the Life of blessed Alcuin—turned his attention and hopes toward Alcuin, Aelbert’s companion. From that association Charles could have come to know the young man’s abilities and literary learning, and he wished that, once his teacher had refused the office, Alcuin himself might at some time become the teacher of his court and kingdom. This desire of Charles was eventually fulfilled when the following opportunity arose.

In the year 780, Aelbert, archbishop of York, who had been elected in Ecgbert’s place and died in the tenth year of his episcopate, not long after returning from the journey we have just mentioned, was succeeded by Eanbald the Elder, Alcuin’s fellow student. [Col. 0041A] Eanbald selected this very close friend of his as his legate to obtain the archiepiscopal pallium from the Apostolic See. Perhaps he had no one else whom he considered more suitable for successfully carrying out this business.

Alcuin complied, undertook the journey, and came to Rome for the sake of this legation, as the author of his Life testifies at the cited passage. In my opinion, this was blessed Alcuin’s second journey to that city, where Adrian I was then pope. We mentioned his first journey by the preceding number.

After returning with the pallium, Alcuin, as the author mentioned above relates, met King Charles [Col. 0041B] at the city of Parma. For, according to the annalists of that time—Loisel, Tilius, Einhard, the Saxon Poet, and others—Charles went to Italy with Queen Hildegard around the end of that same year, 780, and celebrated the Christmas festival at Pavia. At the beginning of the year 781 he continued his journey through the city of Parma and, as may be understood from the Life cited above, celebrated Easter at Rome.

It was therefore on this very journey and in that year, before Easter, that blessed Alcuin found King Charles at Parma and was granted admission to speak with the king, who had already known him.

### LVIII

Charles received the man, already highly esteemed by him from their earlier association and thereafter increasingly commended by the growing reputation of his learning, with the greatest goodwill. He did everything, whether by persuasion or promises, to draw him into his kingdom as director of the schools which he was then considering with particular attention.

Alcuin regarded it as almost a sacrilege to resist too stubbornly the solicitations of so great a king, who was burning with the utmost zeal for the welfare of the commonwealth and the Catholic Church [Col. 0041C]. He therefore accepted the office offered to him on the condition that, once his embassy had been completed, he could obtain the consent and permission of the bishop and king whom he served in order to undertake it.

With this condition—which certainly ought to have been regarded as entirely reasonable—blessed Alcuin was accordingly dismissed by the king and continued his journey to his homeland. There, after completing his mission and giving an account of his embassy before Archbishop Eanbald, he at the same time explained to him the will and desire of Charles, king of the Franks, and asked what he wished or ordered to be done. Eanbald consented to these entirely reasonable requests; the king to whose authority he was subject likewise agreed, but both added the condition that Alcuin should not, by remaining too long in a foreign region, deprive his own country of services so advantageous to it, but should return at the appointed time to the kingdom and church to whose service he was bound.

### LIX

[Col. 0041D]

Having obtained this permission, Alcuin made all the necessary preparations for undertaking the journey and for fulfilling this new office worthily at the court of the king of the Franks. He also selected and took with him—as may be inferred from the course of his Life—certain companions and associates, formerly his pupils at the school of York, who could provide him with comfort and assistance in the province entrusted to him. He now went to Francia for the third time and offered King Charles his services and assistance in whatever matters he judged would benefit the king and his kingdom.

### LX

D. Rivet, *Histoire littéraire de la France*, volume IV, p. 296, and D. Ceillier, *Histoire générale des auteurs sacrés*, volume XVIII, p. 249, assign this return of Alcuin to Francia to the year 780, or approximately that year. Yet it is clear from what we presented above in no. 57 from the annals of that period that his return occurred later, and scarcely before the year 782 [Col. 0042A]. According to those witnesses, Alcuin first encountered Charles at Parma before Easter in the year 781; it was there that the king first invited him to remain in his kingdom.

If we consider the length and difficulties of the journey which Alcuin had to undertake both on his way to his homeland and on his return to Francia, together with the various affairs that had first to be settled at home before his departure, it is scarcely credible that all this could have been completed in that same year. We therefore believe that the blessed Alcuin’s arrival on this occasion at the court of Charlemagne should be assigned to the aforementioned year, A.D. 782. In agreement with this opinion of ours is the celebrated compiler of the *Rerum Gallicarum* writers, D. Bouquet, volume V, p. 604, note a at the end.

### LXI

When Alcuin returned from England, Charlemagne received him with the greatest goodwill and, as the often-mentioned author of his Life says, embraced him as a son embraces his father. Not long afterward he entrusted two monasteries [Col. 0042B] to his administration: Bethlehem, also called Ferrières, in the district of the Gâtinais, in the province of Sens; and Saint-Loup at Troyes, in addition to the coastal cell of Saint-Josse among the Morini.

Through these benefactions Charles intended not so much, says D. Rivet in the place cited, p. 296, to enrich this new teacher of his with wealth as to ensure that, through his care and vigilance, regular discipline might be restored in those monasteries and strengthened by suitable studies. In this way, at last, blessed Alcuin’s residence in Francia and at the royal court began to be established. At the same time that great king began to use the counsels of the same teacher not only in restoring literary studies but also in arranging the political and ecclesiastical order of his kingdom.

“From that time onward,” says the aforementioned D. Rivet in the place cited, “King Charles regarded Alcuin as his teacher and thereafter always honored him, undertaking nothing of greater importance without consulting him. His assistance was sought in every more difficult matter whose outcome was uncertain” [Col. 0042C]. The same appears to have been done in the composition of those most wise laws promulgated by Charlemagne and celebrated under the name of *Capitularies*, as may be gathered from the conclusion of the preface of Benedict the Levite to Book V of the *Capitularies*, in Baluzius, volume I, p. 805.

At least, I think no one will deny that those enactments of Charlemagne which were ordered for the restoration of literary studies and for the establishment of schools everywhere in cathedral churches and monasteries proceeded from the counsel and suggestion—or even the pen—of blessed Alcuin. Since they therefore also belong among his distinguished achievements, we cannot pass them over entirely; in the following chapter we shall indicate them briefly, while also recounting the immense benefit that flowed from them to the Church and the whole kingdom of the Franks, together with the perpetual glory of their august author and illustrious teacher.

## CHAPTER VI

### Measures and remedies adopted for restoring literary studies [Col. 0042D]

### LXII

After blessed Alcuin’s arrival at Charlemagne’s palace, and after other learned men from Italy—whom, as we said, the king had already summoned—had gathered there as well, the king, relying upon their advice, undertook the great work which he had long revolved in his mind with profound purpose. Opening war against the long-established barbarism and ignorance, if one may put it so, he began to attack them.

### LXIII

As though sounding the trumpet for this battle, he first summoned and roused the metropolitans, bishops, abbots, and others of his kingdom to whom the matter belonged. He sent letters to all of them, commonly called encyclical or general letters. Baluzius, volume I of the *Capitularies*, p. 201, presents an example addressed to Baugulf, abbot of Fulda, which Sirmond had published from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint Arnulf at Metz.

In these letters Charles states that it had seemed useful to him and his advisers “that in the bishoprics and monasteries, besides the order of regular life and the practice of holy religion, diligent attention should also be devoted to teaching literary studies, according to each person’s capacity” [Col. 0043A].

The king, who was attentive to everything, had noticed that in writings frequently sent to him by certain monasteries “the meanings were indeed correct, but the language uncultivated”; “because,” he says, “what pious devotion faithfully dictated inwardly, the uneducated tongue was unable to express outwardly without reproach, owing to negligence in learning.” He therefore feared “that, just as prudence in writing was deficient, so too there might be in them a much greater deficiency than there ought to be in the wisdom required for understanding the Holy Scriptures.”

Moved by this concern, he exhorts them henceforth not to neglect literary studies, to establish schools everywhere, and “for this work to choose men who possess both the will and the ability to learn, as well as the desire to instruct others” [Col. 0043B].

The most religious king expressed the purpose of this enactment in these words:

> “For we desire you, as befits soldiers of the Church, to be devout inwardly and learned outwardly, chaste in good living and scholarly in good speech; so that whoever, because of the name of the Lord and the nobility of your holy conduct, seeks you out in order to see you may return rejoicing, giving thanks to almighty God, having been instructed by your wisdom, which he has received through reading or singing, just as his sight is edified by the sight of you.”

Truly admirable was the zeal of so great a king for promoting the best studies among ecclesiastical men and for the good that would thereby flow to the whole Church.

From the same zeal, in the Aachen Capitulary of 789, no. 70, in the same Baluzius, volume I of the *Capitularies*, p. 237, he prescribes the studies that should be pursued in schools, and “commands all the orders of the holy Church of God and the dignities of secular power that schools for boys who are learning to read should be established; that in every monastery and bishopric they should learn psalms, musical notation, chants, computation, and grammar [Col. 0043C]; and that they should also possess Catholic books that have been properly corrected . . . . They must not allow their boys to corrupt them either by reading or by writing; and if there is need to write a Gospel, Psalter, or Missal, men of mature age should write it with every care.”

### LXIV

The first concern of King Charles and the teachers of the court, especially Alcuin, was therefore to acquire the books considered necessary for teaching and learning, selecting them and having them properly corrected. This remedy for cultivating minds ought, in the natural order, to precede everything else; for from books poorly arranged and incompetently written it is inevitable that the doctrines themselves should become confused and minds disordered.

In fact, amid the great barbarism of that age, it was difficult to find books free from various lacunae, solecisms, and numerous other errors [Col. 0043D]. The writers of the age preceding Charles, being themselves exceedingly ignorant of grammar and orthography, sprinkled with new errors whatever codices they had received for copying—even when those codices had already been corrupted—so that very often scarcely any meaning could be extracted from them, while just as often they led the reader’s mind in the opposite direction. Learned and diligent investigators of that period know that codices of this kind still survive from that age in ancient libraries.

It is especially regrettable that even the books serving ecclesiastical use, indeed the Holy Scripture itself, were subject to this defect.

### LXV

Charles was therefore particularly concerned that men destined for ecclesiastical ministry should possess well-corrected sacred books. He entrusted the task of correcting them to Paul Warnefrid and Alcuin.

Paul received an order from the king to revise the homilies arranged for the nocturnal office, which were teeming with innumerable convolutions of errors and solecisms. This is stated in the letter prefixed to Charlemagne’s *Homiliary*, found in the Cologne edition of 1539, separately published by the distinguished Baluzius in volume I of the *Capitularies*, p. 203, and by D. Mabillon, *Annals*, Book XXVI, no. 62 [Col. 0044A]. In it the most religious king writes to the devout readers subject to his authority:

> “Because we are concerned that the condition of our churches should always advance toward better things, by vigilant application to letters we strive to restore the workshop almost obliterated by the negligence of our ancestors, and by our example we invite as many as we can to become thoroughly acquainted with the liberal arts . . . . Finally, because we found that the readings compiled for the nocturnal office by the futile labor of certain men—though undertaken with a correct intention, yet with insufficient competence—were less suitable, since they were presented without the names of their authors and were full of innumerable convolutions of errors, we have not allowed solecisms to resound discordantly in the divine readings amid the sacred offices during our days. We have determined to direct our attention toward reforming the course of those readings for the better. We have entrusted this work to Paul the Deacon, our familiar servant, to polish.”

### LXVI

[Col. 0044B]

The author of Alcuin’s Life reports in chapter 12, no. 24, that Alcuin likewise undertook a similar work and labor, in these words: “He collected two volumes of homilies from many works of the Fathers.”

D. Rivet, *Histoire littéraire de la France*, volume IV, p. 337, no. 5, nevertheless calls this assertion into question. He considers it unlikely that the labor of collecting homilies for the use of the churches of Francia would have been necessary after a collection of this kind had been made at the same time by Paul Warnefrid at the king’s command and with his approval. D. Mabillon, however, in the place cited, distinguishes two *Homiliaries*, one by Paul and the other by Alcuin.

### LXVII

It is established with greater certainty that blessed Alcuin, at Charles’s command, corrected a book called the *Comes*, otherwise attributed to Saint Jerome. It contained the epistles and Gospels customarily read on the individual feast days throughout the year. According to D. Mabillon in the place cited, no. 61, a book of this kind is preserved in a manuscript of that period in the library of Chartres. Around its middle are found these words [Col. 0044C]:

> “Let your discernment, reader, know that this codex, which ecclesiastical men call the *Comes*, was taken from that codex which, as is established, was polished and corrected by Albinus, a most learned man, at the command of Charles, the most wise emperor, with the file of accuracy. Although this codex was possessed by many, it was nevertheless read by most in a corrupt and insufficiently punctuated form. Therefore it was the concern of this worshiper of God that it should be corrected to purity by the aforesaid man and divided according to the rules of grammatical art for the sake of pronunciation; so that, in this way, the text of the same codex might open a smooth path to its readers, bring nothing discordant to the ears of its hearers, and not allow the simple to fall into error. For our part, we took care to transcribe this book so accurately and distinctly as it stands corrected and punctuated by that same teacher.”

### LXVIII

[Col. 0044D]

This labor, so immensely beneficial to literary culture, was so dear to King Charles that he himself did not hesitate to undertake it during certain intervals when he was free from the gravest affairs of the kingdom.

According to Lambecius, *Bibliotheca Vindobonensis*, Book VIII, p. 645, there is preserved in that same imperial library a very ancient and exceedingly rare parchment manuscript which, in the judgment of D. Lambecius, formerly belonged to the private library of Charlemagne. It contains an *Exposition attributed erroneously to Origen on the Epistle of the holy apostle Paul to the Romans*. Its writing, sprinkled with several errors, was corrected in Charles’s own hand. The following verses, written beneath it in an equally ancient script, bear witness to this:

> The king Charles, strongest hero who lays low the fierce in war,  
> Second to none in the brightness of his heart,  
> Not allowing the thorns of errors to creep through books,  
> Has corrected them well, exalted in every pursuit.”

“From these verses,” says the aforementioned D. Lambecius, “it most clearly and without any controversy appears that whatever in this codex has been corrected in the text itself, written between the lines, or noted in the margin was written by Charlemagne’s own hand. Consequently this literary monument, out of the veneration owed to so great a monarch, is almost beyond valuation” [Col. 0045A].

The same celebrated librarian then reports that various other codices corrected by the hand of the same king are preserved in that imperial library at Vienna. This can be recognized by comparing their script with the corrections in the earlier codex. See Kollarius, *Analecta Monumentorum Vindobonensium*, volume I, p. 724, note a.

Who could sufficiently marvel at and praise the sublime genius of this greatest of princes, who knew how, with the same hand with which he defeated so many enemies of his vast kingdom, to conquer barbarism as well?

### LXIX

Moreover, the most religious king was especially concerned that the books of Holy Scripture, corrupted in many ways through the carelessness of copyists, should be restored to their purity:

> “Therefore, with God’s help, we have corrected with the utmost exactness all the books of the Old and New Testaments that had been corrupted through the incompetence of scribes,”

as he writes in the letter cited above, prefixed to the *Homiliary*.

Since he considered no one more suitable than Alcuin for completing this work [Col. 0045B], he entrusted its care to him. This is understood from the letter prefixed to Book VI of the *Commentary on John*, addressed to Gisela and Columba, p. 591. There Alcuin writes that the king’s command—by which he had been charged with correcting the Old and New Testaments—prevented him at that time from sending the two women an exposition of the whole Gospel of Saint John:

> “Perhaps I would have sent you an exposition of the whole Gospel, if the command of the Lord King in the correction of the Old and New Testament had not occupied me.”

Alcuin eagerly undertook this most necessary and useful labor and continued it so steadily that, when the work was almost completed, he was able to offer it to the same emperor as a most welcome gift on Christmas Day in the year 800, when Charles was to be crowned with the imperial crown at Rome. In this way he could also testify to his joy at the acquisition of that new majesty. This is understood from letters 103 and 185, now 131 and 135 [Col. 0045C].

### LXX

“According to Baronius, volume IX of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, under the year 778, a codex, the work of Alcuin, exists in the Vallicellian Library, where it is preserved like an immense treasure, since learned men who in our own time have again labored to correct the Vulgate used it as an ancient witness and accorded it the greatest weight.”

At the end of that Vallicellian codex, according to the same Baronius, Alcuin added verses divided into various epigrams. We shall give them, with a certain supplement, in poem 5.

It is plausible that this was the very codex used in the year 1236 by the Dominican Fathers who, at the command of their master general, Father Jordan, and Hugh of Saint-Cher, prior of the Paris convent, labored to correct copies of the sacred Bible. On this matter see Le Long, *Bibliotheca Sacra*, volume I, p. 239.

### LXXI

[Col. 0045D]

Copies of the sacred codex thus corrected were soon disseminated throughout the churches and monasteries and transcribed by industrious and skilled scribes. We have a witness to this in Angelomus, a monk of Luxeuil and almost a contemporary of Alcuin. In his commentary on Genesis, in Pez’s *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, volume I, p. 148, at the end, he writes that he had seen and carefully examined that sacred Bible corrected at Charlemagne’s command. In it he approves, according to his own judgment, the reading of the word *Saraam*, which others wrote with two r’s and one a.

### LXXII

[Col. 0046A]

I have no doubt that blessed Alcuin applied to other books, too—books needed for learning or teaching the liberal arts—the same diligence that he devoted to correcting sacred codices, or that he arranged for it to be applied through his companions or pupils.

It seems highly probable to us that Alcuin also corrected, for the use of students, the book *On the Seven Arts*, published incompletely by Quercetanus among Alcuin’s works, removing the errors with which most copies had been corrupted. Its true author is M. Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator, though it was attributed to Alcuin and, in a single ancient codex of Jacob Sirmond, assigned to him—perhaps because it bore his name owing to the correction he himself had applied to it.

See what we said in the preface to the little works on Grammar, Orthography, and so forth, where we explain why we have omitted that book from this collection.

### LXXIII

While occupied with such labors, Alcuin was likewise concerned that all books intended for the use of churches, monasteries, and schools should be correctly copied according to the rules of orthography and without errors. To ensure that this might succeed more effectively, he judged it necessary above all that the scribes employed for this work be properly instructed in the art of writing correctly, that is, in orthography.

For this purpose he composed a little work on that same art, which we present partly from manuscript codices and partly from the Venerable Bede. There we also explain why we consider this book to be a genuine work of Alcuin.

### LXXIV

In the future, bishops and abbots everywhere imitated the care and concern for purging previously corrupted books [Col. 0046B] and for writing new copies correctly and according to the rules of orthography—care and concern which King Charles had commended by his commands and Alcuin by his example, teaching, and exhortations with the greatest zeal.

Irrefutable testimony to this is provided by the many codices still surviving in ancient libraries: works of Holy Scripture, the holy Fathers, councils, laws, and even secular authors, which are the clearest witnesses to the diligence of that age. We have a large number of them before our eyes in our library of Saint Emmeram, remaining from the beginning of the ninth century. They were written out in a finished script and, as is noted in some of them, subsequently reviewed and purged of errors.

Thereafter, through the industry of this most celebrated teacher of all the sciences, there were also added treatises on the art of speaking, composing, and disputing well. He later gathered their rules in the *Dialogues on Grammar, Rhetoric, and Dialectic* [Col. 0046C].

### LXXV

Once the art of orthography had been restored, the best books serving the schools had been acquired, and the libraries likewise supplied with a great abundance of outstanding authors, nothing further stood in the way of the progress of the sciences to be taught in public and private schools.

The bishops and abbots, therefore, attentive to the very serious commands of the most wise king and roused by the frequent exhortations that Alcuin conveyed to them in almost every letter he wrote, devoted all their efforts to copying and collecting books and establishing schools.

Among the first and most celebrated episcopal schools of that time—at least those whose monuments still survive—were the school of Lyon under Bishop Leidrad and that of Orléans under Bishop Theodulf.

Leidrad is believed to have been summoned by Charlemagne from his homeland in Noricum to assist in reforming discipline and restoring the study of the sciences. In the year 798 he was made bishop of Lyon [Col. 0046D]. In a letter to King Charles, preserved in volume XIV of the Lyon edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 233, he reports concerning the school he had established that in the church of Lyon there were singers so learned in that school that they could also instruct others in singing. There were also some who had progressed so far in letters that they could properly understand the spiritual meaning of the holy Gospel; and others who knew how to interpret the books of the Prophets, Solomon, the Psalms, and even the little book of Job, which is certainly one of the more difficult books.

### LXXVI
