Theodulf, regarded as the principal restorer of studies after Charlemagne and Alcuin, was summoned from Italy by that king around the year 771, as some maintain, because of his outstanding learning; afterward, around the year 794, he was promoted to the bishopric of Orléans.

In letter 193, now 147, Alcuin calls him “a lamp of brilliant light and overflowing wisdom, and a most distinguished man whose age is in its bloom and whose wisdom possesses living vigor.” The various literary monuments published by Theodulf, in Sirmond, volume II of the *Works*, pp. 666 ff. of the Venice edition of 1728, prove that Theodulf deserved this distinguished praise [Col. 0047A].

Thus, a few years after obtaining the bishopric of Orléans—approximately in 794 or 797, according to Sirmond’s calculation—he issued a Capitulary. In chapter 19 he decreed that priests who wished to send their nephews or some relative to school should be permitted to do so.

The schools mentioned there were: one in the church of the Holy Cross, which is the cathedral; another in the monastery of Saint Aignan at Orléans; a third of Saint Benedict in the monastery of Fleury; and a fourth of Saint Lifard in the monastery of Meung. It is also indicated there that schools had been established in other monasteries which had been entrusted to Theodulf to govern.

Pagius, following Cointius under the year 787, no. 85, under the year 735, no. 7, believes that these schools were not public but private. Mabillon, however, in the preface to the fourth Benedictine century, no. 187, maintains that they were public.

Besides these larger schools [Col. 0047B], Theodulf established other, smaller ones in chapter 20. There he urged priests to teach infants and small children throughout villages and hamlets with the greatest charity, demanding or accepting no payment for this except whatever might voluntarily be offered by the parents out of charitable devotion.

Rivet, already cited many times, has admirably illuminated Theodulf’s life and writings in volume IV of his *Histoire littéraire*, pp. 459 ff.

### LXXVII

[Col. 0047C]

Hildegarius, bishop of Meaux, received that Capitulary and, in a well-attended synod, ordered the clergy subject to him to observe its decrees carefully, as D. Mabillon reports having read in the Gembloux codex, *Analecta*, new edition, p. 412, column 2.

Other bishops also admirably imitated the zeal of these men. I consider it beyond doubt that they made and promulgated similar constitutions in their dioceses for restoring literary studies.

For it is clear from various monuments of that period and of the succeeding age that schools were reformed in all the older bishoprics of the kingdom of the Franks, while in those recently founded they were established together with the bishoprics. The same must be said of the monasteries then living under the rule of Saint Benedict.

To discuss individually here all those schools—episcopal and monastic, public and private, large and small—which arose from these constitutions and efforts would be too lengthy and inappropriate. Those who wish to know more about them will find ample satisfaction in the works of the most learned men: D. Lanoius, *On the More Celebrated Schools*, volume IV, part I of his *Works*, pp. 1 ff.; D. Mabillon, preface to the fourth Benedictine century, p. 128, § 8; and D. Rivet, in the work cited, no. 21 ff.

### LXXVIII

[Col. 0047D]

To prevent literary studies, begun and organized with such excellent success, from growing cold again among those entrusted with their care, and to ensure that they might flourish more and more, the highly gifted King Charles employed a means previously unfamiliar and scarcely ever attempted in earlier times.

Sometimes in conversations and sometimes in letters, he proposed various questions to bishops, abbots, clerics, and monks, especially to heads of schools: sometimes concerning more difficult passages of Holy Scripture; sometimes concerning matters of ecclesiastical antiquity and ancient discipline; sometimes concerning the thickets of grammar and dialectic; and sometimes concerning astronomical phenomena and their calculations.

By this ingenious method he compelled them never to cease investigating the truth, treating the sciences, and examining, reading, and rereading books, so that they might become more capable and ready to respond solidly and learnedly, either in writing or speech, to the difficulties posed by the most learned prince after careful investigation.

Indeed, such stimuli, sent forth by so great a prince, could not fail to be extremely useful and effective for cultivating and advancing the sciences and establishing their study firmly [Col. 0048A].

Questions of this kind sent to metropolitans concerning baptism and the ceremonies preceding and accompanying it still survive. Several letters responding to them also survive: those of Amalarius of Trier, volume II, p. 520; of Odilbert of Milan, in D. Mabillon’s new edition of the *Analecta*, p. 75; of Leidrad of Lyon, in the same work, p. 78; of Theodulf of Orléans, in Sirmond, volume II of the *Works*, Venice edition of 1728, p. 679; and of Magnus of Sens, in Martène, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, Book I, p. 158.

He also asked that other questions be clarified, concerning the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, in Mabillon, in the place cited, and concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, as is read in the preface of Theodulf of Orléans to Charlemagne, prefixed to his little work *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, in Sirmond, in the place cited, p. 695.

He had earlier consulted blessed Alcuin about this same difficulty. Alcuin promptly complied with his command in the little work *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, which we present from a manuscript of Laon [Col. 0048B].

Above all, however, Charles was accustomed to trouble this teacher of his with such literary questions—concerning grammar, dialectic, liturgy, the Bible, and astronomy. Alcuin satisfied him in various letters and other writings.

Regarding Charles’s habit of questioning, Alcuin speaks in letter 124, now 163, about letters sent to him by the same king:

> “In these commendable lines of your wisdom I found that, as is your custom, you wished to rouse my sluggishness through your most prudent questions.”

And in letter 125, now 164, responding to other questions from the king, he begins as follows:

> “After reading through the written series of your wondrous wisdom, we found it shining with the splendor of eloquence, most subtle in the profundity of its meanings, and most delightful in the pleasure of its inquiry. From this it can plainly be recognized that God bestowed upon your imperial prudence not merely the power to govern the world, but above all for the protection of the Church and the adornment of wisdom; and that he granted you holy diligence [Col. 0048C] to polish the minds of the young, which had been covered with the rust of a certain inertia, into intellectual sharpness. For, beyond imperial and public concerns, you inquire into evangelical questions for us to unravel in the manner of an academy, and so forth.”

Theodulf, bishop of Orléans [Col. 0048D], praises this same practice of exercising learned men through various questions in a letter to Magnus of Sens, in Sirmond, volume II of the *Works*, p. 679. Speaking of the questions posed by the king concerning ceremonies, he says:

> “These questions, as I am certain you know, were not posed by royal necessity because he needed to learn, but from a desire to teach; nor so that, once they had been resolved, he himself might be instructed about what he did not know, but so that others might be roused from the sleep of sluggish torpor toward the useful resolution of matters. For it has always been familiar to him to exercise bishops in the investigation of the Holy Scriptures and in sound and sober doctrine; the entire clergy in discipline; philosophers in knowledge of divine and human affairs; monks in religion; everyone generally in holiness; leading men in council; judges in justice; and so forth.”

### LXXIX

By these means Francia and the whole kingdom subject to the scepter of Charlemagne emerged from the ancient darkness of ignorance and barbarism. The light of the sciences shone in both ecclesiastical and civil affairs, long afterward illuminating the schools that had already been established and guiding those that were to be founded.

Eventually, however, the kingdom was divided among several princes far inferior to their father in authority, intelligence, prudence, and greatness of spirit. Dissensions arose among them, along with civil wars, incursions by barbarian nations, and neglect of the laws and of good political order. These causes made that once most flourishing empire fall back into the abyss of its former confusion.

D. Rivet discusses this revolution, most destructive to all the Muses, and the wretched condition of literary studies in Gaul in the ninth century, learnedly in volume IV of his *Histoire littéraire de la France*, pp. 217 ff.

Leaving these matters aside [Col. 0049A], lest we merely repeat what has already been done, let us discuss the teaching office which blessed Alcuin held at the royal palace.

## CHAPTER VII

### Blessed Alcuin’s teaching at the Palace School, and his pupils there

### LXXX

[Col. 0049B]

Charlemagne’s love for the Muses continued to grow day by day, as he learned, increasingly through his association with the teachers of his court and through almost daily experience, how much prosperity they would bring to his kingdom.

He was therefore not content that they should be confined within the walls of churches and the cloisters of monasteries, as he had ordered in the preceding constitutions. He also established a home for them in his own royal palace and founded a public school there, so that the royal offspring, the nobles and courtiers, and their sons and daughters might all have readily available the means of cultivating their intelligence and minds.

Charles wished to lead all of them by his own example, so that they might be more diligently encouraged to pursue literary studies. Indeed, he did not consider it unworthy of his majesty to descend from the royal throne and act almost as a pupil on the benches of the learned men whom he had summoned to the court.

The humility and diligence of that king, the most powerful in all Europe, cannot be praised adequately by any eloquence. “The nobility of his mind is marvelous,” says Alcuin in *On the Nature of the Soul*, “since amid the many cares of the palace and occupations of the kingdom he took pains to learn fully the mysteries of the philosophers—something which scarcely anyone else, sluggish with leisure, now strives to know.”

Certainly it must be regarded as something miraculous that, in the palace of so great a king—where every day so many affairs of a vast empire demanded attention; where the trumpets of the most terrible wars so often sounded; and where the most serious matters with the Roman pontiffs, the emperors of the East, the English, and the Spaniards had to be settled through envoys sent in every direction—there could still be found room and leisure for the Muses.

Nevertheless [Col. 0049C], the genius of that greatest prince was equal to joining and reconciling things that seem so utterly opposed to one another.

### LXXXI

All writers who recount his achievements agree that blessed Alcuin taught letters in this palace school; this is also demonstrated by his own Letter 67 (now 82) to the lord King, where, already residing at Tours after leaving the court, he complains that certain teachers had altered the lunar calculation, writing as follows:

> “I am unskilled, I am ignorant, not knowing that an Egyptian school is flourishing in the palace of David’s glory. When I departed, I left Latins there; I do not know who introduced the Egyptians.”

Therefore he taught there, since when he departed he left his pupils there. Indeed, he held the foremost place among the other teachers. Charles bestowed such honor on no one else besides Alcuin: after hearing Peter of Pisa only in the study of grammar, as Einhard relates in *The Life of Charlemagne*, he deemed Alcuin worthy to be his teacher in the remaining disciplines—rhetoric, dialectic, and especially astronomy. [Col. 0049D]

The author of Alcuin’s *Life*, chapter 2, no. 12, likewise testifies to this when he asserts that Charles, after Alcuin had returned from England, “had learned through Alcuin to refresh himself somewhat in the liberal arts, but because of his exceedingly great eagerness he could not be satisfied.” Alcuin himself boasts of the honor bestowed on him by the king in Epigram 260, sent to his brothers at York, in these verses:

> For such gifts please your father,  
> who now makes noble arts resound  
> in royal ears, and leads the fathers  
> across the meadows, following after  
> him who reigns with the splendid crown  
> of lofty wisdom.

And in Epigram 231 he lists certain studies that he practiced with this august pupil of his, singing as follows:

> O David, my sweet love, farewell throughout the ages;  
> how I would always wish to have you present!  
> May I be permitted to play with you in Pierian verse,  
> or climb with you the lofty stars of the highest heaven; [Col. 0050A]  
> or learn with you the beautiful forms of numbers,  
> or enter into the astonishing sayings of the ancient Fathers;  
> or handle the sacred teachings of eternal salvation,  
> by which the path may carry you with me above the stars.

### LXXXII

When, therefore, at the beginning of a letter written to Alcuin, Charles addresses him—as reported in Letter 124 (now 163)—by the title “most beloved teacher in Christ,” we judge that this title was bestowed on him not only as a mark of honor, as Baronius interprets it under the year 778, no. 15, but also on account of his teaching. Indeed, the testimonies cited thus far clearly establish that Alcuin not only discussed mathematics and philosophy with Charlemagne, as Baronius writes in that passage, but also instructed him in at least those sciences.

The same father of ecclesiastical history, in the place cited, considers Charles to have been so thoroughly instructed in sacred matters that he occupied the position of teacher rather than pupil. “For,” he says, “in that discipline it was not Charles who consulted Albinus, but Albinus who consulted Charles, whenever something seemed doubtful, obscure, or difficult to him,” and he believes this to be demonstrated by Alcuin’s letters to Charles concerning Septuagesima, and so forth, Letter 65 (now 80). From Charles’s reply, Letter 12, *Patrologia*, vol. XCVIII, col. 911, Baronius concludes that “Charles greatly surpassed in knowledge of sacred matters the man whom he calls his teacher, Albinus.”

I do not know whether any learned person would not consider this celebrated writer’s estimate of Charles’s sacred learning excessive. Certainly Charles consulted Alcuin more often in sacred matters than Alcuin consulted Charles, as several letters demonstrate: Letter 123 (now 162), concerning the difference between *aeternum* and *sempiternum*, and so forth; Letter 124 (now 163), concerning the two swords; Letter 125 (now 164), concerning the hymn said after supper; and Letter 126 (now 165), concerning the price of human salvation. Baronius did not see these letters, since they had not yet been published at that time.

Charles needed Alcuin’s assistance to refute the errors of Felix and Elipandus, and for this purpose he persuaded him to hasten his return from England. For Charles’s instruction in the faith of the holy and undivided Trinity, Alcuin wrote and dedicated to him a little book on that same doctrine, “because,” he says, “no one ought to know better or more than the emperor.” He adds that he was doing this in order to fulfill the duty of his title, “by which certain people call him a teacher”—namely, the king himself, whom he is instructing.

It must therefore remain firmly established that Alcuin was the teacher or master of Charlemagne in both sacred and secular letters. But since Baronius and others generally recognized only Alcuin’s final journey to Francia, which took place in 792 or at the beginning of the following year, when Charles was already advanced in age, they could not explain whether, or what, Alcuin had taught Charles; so says Pagi under the year 782, no. 8 at the end.

### LXXXIII

The liberal studies to which the king himself devoted attention, as Einhard testifies in *The Life*, no. 19, in Bouquet, vol. V of *Scriptores rerum Gallicarum*, he also ordered to be taught to his children, both sons and daughters. [Col. 0050D] Once the palace school had therefore been very well organized and was frequently attended by King Charles himself, the royal princes Charles, Pippin, and Louis; men and youths of the highest nobility, Angilbert, Adalhard, and Damoeta; and also the royal maidens, both Gisl(a)s, Charles’s sister and daughter; Richtrudis, surnamed Columba, and Guntrada, surnamed Eulalia, together with many others, eagerly following the footsteps of their father and king, committed themselves to the teaching and discipline of blessed Alcuin.

Alcuin thereafter addresses all of them by the names of sons and daughters, certainly for no other reason than that, while they lived at the palace, he exercised a father’s care for them through various instruction in letters and morals. He likewise wrote several letters to them, filled with various teachings and composed with the seriousness of style that teachers ordinarily use when instructing their pupils.

### LXXXIV

To the younger Charles, the king’s son, after he had received the royal crown from Pope Leo III, Alcuin gives exhortations in Letter 178 (now 119) and the following letter: to practice justice and mercy toward the Christian people; to choose good counselors rather than flatterers—men who are pious, prudent, and God-fearing; and to imitate the best examples of every virtue, his father, the excellent emperor.

To Louis, his brother, wishing to satisfy the latter’s desire, he wrote several admonitory letters, as we learn from Letter 179 (now 120) to that same Charles. It is regrettable that all these letters have either perished or remain unknown. That the royal youth Pippin was educated in Alcuin’s school is demonstrated by his *Disputation with Albinus*, which we shall give below, and by Letter 33 (now 38) to him, in which Alcuin offers this beloved son of his excellent guidance for conducting his life.

### LXXXV

Angilbert, later abbot of Centula and numbered among the saints, must also be counted among the pupils of blessed Alcuin in that same school. His illustrious lineage is demonstrated by his singular familiarity with Charlemagne, by his marriage to Berta, Charles’s daughter, and finally by the distinguished public offices he held.

“He was raised from the earliest beginnings of infancy in Charles’s palace,” as we read in a certain letter of Adrian I to Charles concerning the Second Synod of Nicaea, *Patrologia*, vol. XCVIII, col. 1247. He was therefore a pupil of blessed Alcuin in that palace; this is inferred from several letters written to him after he had entered public affairs, containing paternal admonitions and instruction, which we present under nos. 21, 22, 23, and 215 (now 25, 26, 27, and 28). We have noted more about him in various places. His eulogy and life may be found in Mabillon, at the place cited.

### LXXXVI

Angilbert’s fellow pupil in the palace was Antonius, or Adalhard, later abbot of Corbie and likewise enrolled among the saints after his death. His life and eulogy are also found in Mabillon, at the place cited, p. 306 and following.

Alcuin, as a teacher, advises him as a son in Letter 144 (now 189), and in another letter mentioned there, to take care of Homer—or Angilbert—who had been excessively enticed by secular spectacles but later, as Alcuin recalls having learned from Antonius himself in Letter 213 (now 191), turned to better things.

In Letter 112 (now 151), Alcuin advises Antonius to obtain at court permission for his brother Bernarius, whom he likewise calls his son, to return to his monastery when returning home from the monastery on the island of Lérins. On this matter, see what we have noted concerning that same letter. Bernarius himself, therefore, had previously been a pupil of Alcuin in the palace school, together with Adalhard.

### LXXXVII

We believe the same must be said of Flavius Damoeta, as is clear from Letters 39 and 41 (now 44 and 46) written to him, in which Alcuin calls him “son,” which is equivalent to “pupil.”

He was a secular man devoted to military service. In the first letter Alcuin exhorts him, as he is setting out against the enemy—namely, against the Saxons in 796—to fortify his journey by confession, strengthen it by almsgiving, and have himself fortified on every side by the prayers of God’s servants, so that he might return victorious to his homeland with the king and his other fellow soldiers. In the second letter he urges him, amid the occupations of the world, also to watch over the salvation of his soul through good works and, in hearing various cases, to observe justice and mercy. [Col. 0051D]

This Damoeta must therefore be distinguished from Riculfus, archbishop of Mainz, who is given the surname Damoeta in Letter 40 (now 45) in the Petavian codex used by D. Quercetanus, and in Letters 181 and 182 (now 122 and 123), recently discovered in the Harleian Library.

For Riculfus, having been promoted to the see of Mainz already in 786 or the following year, could not have been a military commander ten years later. This same Riculfus, however, unless we are greatly mistaken, had Alcuin as his teacher in the palace school before assuming the government of the aforementioned church. In Letter 182 (now 123), Alcuin calls him “a most eagerly desired son.” There he also professes to rejoice greatly over Riculfus’s prosperity, praiseworthy conduct, and zeal for truth, in accordance with the instructions given to him, using the words of the Apostle John: “I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in faith and truth.”

### LXXXVIII

Since the address “son” has the same meaning as “pupil,” as we already indicated above in no. 84, and since the distinguished D. Mabillon agrees with us in *Annals*, book XXV, no. 38, p. 267, we judge that there can be no doubt that all those whom blessed Alcuin calls his sons or daughters honored him as their teacher, whether in humane letters, sacred learning, or moral discipline.

From this we may safely add to the number of his palace pupils Rigbod, surnamed Macharius, archbishop of Trier, as appears from Letter 129 (now 169). In the notes there, from a contemporary codex of the monastery of Saint Maximin, we showed that he was promoted to that see in 791, not in 776, as Charles Cointius asserts from an old history of Trier in 804, no. 34, vol. I of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, and Mabillon in *Annals*, book XXIV, no. 68. Mabillon consequently says:

> “If Richbod was Alcuin’s pupil before becoming bishop, he must be said to have used him as his teacher in Britain.”

The most reverend D. de Hontheim initially embraced Mabillon’s opinion in vol. I of his *History of Trier*, p. 136, note (b). But after learning more certain facts from the San-Maximinian manuscript, written in the age of Charlemagne, he changed his opinion in the preface to vol. I, p. LXIII, note, where he reports these words of that codex:

> “In the year 791, Lord Charles proceeded with the Franks and Saxons, with the Bavarians and Alemanni, and with his other peoples, into Pannonia beyond Omundesdorf; and he returned with the glory of triumph and wintered at Reganesburg. The bishops Egilramnus, Wiomadus, and Sinpert died.”

By the consensus of all historians, Wiomadus was the immediate predecessor of Richbod in the see of Trier. Richbod could therefore have been Alcuin’s pupil in the palace of Charlemagne before his episcopate, that is, before this year 791. See the same D. de Hontheim, vol. III, p. 1006.

To these pupils we believe that Aquila, or Arno, first bishop and afterward archbishop of Salzburg, may also be added, on the basis of Letters 30, 54, and 55 (now 35, 68, and 69), and others; and Hechstannus, or Altapetra, on the basis of Letter 138 (now 182).

Finally, all those who remained in the palace with the lord emperor during his Roman journey may be included. To them Alcuin, then teaching at the monastery of Tours, wrote Letter 130 (now 121), in which he says:

> “O how happy was the day when, amid our labors, we played at serious literary pursuits; but now everything has changed. The elder remained behind, begetting other sons, and mourns that the former ones have been scattered.”

### LXXXIX

Let us now turn to the noble women whom Alcuin first taught in the palace and afterward nourished through his letters with various forms of instruction.

The first among them is Gisla, or Gisala, and Gisela, surnamed Lucia, Charlemagne’s sister by Bertrada. She was, as Einhard writes in the place cited, no. 18, “dedicated from her girlhood to a religious way of life,” and later became abbess of the monastery of Chelles, “whom Charles greatly honored with filial devotion.”

This is the Gisla whom Alcuin calls his spiritual sister in two letters, Letters 98 and 99 (now 126 and 127), written to her; the second of these was prefixed to his commentaries on the Gospel of Saint John.

She burned with a great desire to advance through Alcuin’s instruction in knowledge of Sacred Scripture. Thus she and Rictrudis, surnamed Columba, write to him:

> “After we had drunk something, venerable teacher, from the honey-sweet knowledge of Sacred Scripture as expounded by your keen understanding, our desire for this most sacred reading, as we confess, burned in us from day to day, and so forth.”

They then say that they are burdened by a twofold sorrow: first, “because they had undertaken the diligent pursuit of this excellent study too late”; second, “because now, although we have great devotion, your distance, they say, stands in the way of our desire.”

Those holy virgins were then living in their monastery at Chelles, not far from Paris, while Alcuin, residing at Tours, was farther away from them than he had been able to instruct them orally, as formerly in the palace. Hence they ask him not to abandon them “the consolation of his writings”:

> “For just as the tongue of one speaking profits the ear of the listener, so the pen of one writing profits the mouth of the reader; and the sense of the one guiding reaches the inner chambers of the heart, just as the words of the one instructing do.”

Finally, following the example of blessed Jerome, who at the requests of noble women composed many little works on the obscurities of the prophets and sent them from the fortress of Bethlehem to the Roman citadels, they ask him to send them an exposition of the Gospel of Saint John adapted to their understanding:

> “Much more easily,” they say, “can the bearer of your papers travel from Tours to the city of Paris than Jerome’s from Bethlehem to Rome.”
>
> [Note: From this it is clearer than the sun that most English writers erred in asserting that these virgins had been taught by Alcuin in England.]

This desire Alcuin fulfilled. First, because of the circumstances and suitability of the approaching Easter solemnity, he sent them that part of his commentary on the Gospel of Saint John which is contained in the two final books, the sixth and seventh. In the following year he sent the preceding five books as well, as is understood from the letter of Lucia and Columba—the names of Gisla and Rictrudis—which was prefixed to the complete commentary.

The three letters that we present from the Harleian Library manuscript under nos. 188, 189, and 190 (now 138, 139, and 140) also seem to belong to these women. The first mentions certain works of Venerable Bede, which Alcuin allowed them to copy. Among them was undoubtedly Bede’s treatise on the Epistles of the Apostles, which Alcuin writes that Gisla possessed in Letter 143 (now 187) to one of his sons or pupils.

In Letter 190 (now 140), after exhorting them to preserve equanimity in prosperity and adversity, Alcuin advises them that if perhaps a more difficult passage in apostolic authority tires them, they should refresh the sharpness of their weary minds by inserting lighter reading—namely, by reading the *Lives of the Fathers* and the miracles of the saints found in Saint Gregory’s *Dialogues*, written, as he says, in most lucid eloquence and confirmed by sentences of Sacred Scripture.

### XC

D. Mabillon rightly warns that another Gisla must be distinguished from Gisla or Gisela, Charlemagne’s sister: namely, his daughter by Hildegard, in the *Acta Sanctorum*, fourth century, part I, p. 449, in the preliminary observation to the history of the translation of Saint Bathildis, no. 3; and in *Annals*, book XXV, no. 81, and book XXVI, no. 61.

Alcuin himself distinguishes the two: in Letter 100 (now 150), he calls the elder one his sister and the younger one his daughter and “most noble maiden.” D. Mabillon also observes this in *Annals*, book XXVI, no. 93, in these words:

> “There was another Gisla, Charles’s daughter, likewise a religious woman, whom Alcuin customarily called not his sister but his daughter.”

It is therefore surprising that the same celebrated writer, a little earlier in the same place, no. 61, asserts that this Gisla was the daughter of Charlemagne, “at whose request Alcuin undertook commentaries on the Gospel of John, elaborated in seven books, of which he dedicated the first five to Gisla and Rictruda, and the other two to Gisla and Columba, his sister.”

In both those letters, however, Alcuin calls Gisla not his daughter but his sister, and calls himself her brother. Gisla, therefore, at whose request Alcuin wrote those commentaries, was not Charlemagne’s daughter but his sister, as we said in the preceding section.

We likewise do not know on what basis another assertion of the same distinguished man rests, in *Annals*, book XXV, no. 81 and elsewhere, where he makes Rictrudis—joined to the elder Gisla in religious profession and devotion to Sacred Scripture—the sister of the younger Gisla. For nowhere do we find Rictrudis mentioned among Gisla’s sisters or among Charlemagne’s daughters.

In the letters that Alcuin sent to both women together with his commentaries on John, he likewise always calls Rictrudis not “sister,” as he calls Gisla, but “daughter.” Nevertheless, it is sufficiently clear from her close association and equal devotion with Gisla the elder, the abbess, that Rictrudis, surnamed Columba, was of very noble birth and a religious woman of the same monastery at Chelles.

### XCI

Among the maidens of the highest nobility living in Charlemagne’s palace, Eulalia desired to be instructed in the teachings of blessed Alcuin. She also asked to be taught by him *On the Soul*, or concerning its nature, properties, and virtues. He fulfilled this request in the little book that we published in volume II.

Eulalia is an assumed name, or surname, of Guntrada, bestowed on her by Alcuin out of familiarity in Letter 184 (now 134), as we noted there and elsewhere. We also observed that this Guntrada is none other than the woman whom Paschasius lists among the sisters of Saint Adalhard, abbot of Corbie, in his *Life*, in Mabillon, fourth Benedictine century, part I, p. 321, no. 33.

Charles valued her above the other maidens. For, as the same Paschasius testifies, she was closer to the king and highly commended to him both for her nobility and for her chastity. Alcuin suggests the same at the end of *On the Soul*, writing that she daily made use of the wisdom of Charles, the most wise emperor, and reverently gazed upon his face. Therefore, in the letter cited, he seeks her intercession with Charles, asking that the king not be angry with him because, having been summoned to Charles, he had been prevented by illness from coming.

In the cited little book *On the Soul*, chapter 14, Alcuin testifies that although he had as yet rarely seen her with his own eyes, he had nevertheless heard others speak of her reputation for study. Paschasius, in the place cited, commends her chastity in these words:

> “The noblest virgin of the noble, who amid the erotic fires of the palace and the beauty of young men, amid the soothing delights and all the blandishments of lust, alone, as we believe, deserved the palm of chastity, and so forth.”

Alcuin also testifies in the cited letter that he had heard the same praise of her chastity and honor. He therefore urges her “to be an example of every virtue to the other maidens in the palace, so that, he says, they may learn from your holy conduct to guard themselves, or to rise again when they fall.”

### XCII

Before we conclude this chapter on the palace school, it is worth briefly touching on a twofold question that has sometimes been debated among scholars:

1. Whether the University of Paris owes its birth to this school and its origin to Alcuin or Charlemagne.
2. Whether the school was fixed in one place, or whether it followed the court as it moved from place to place.

As for the first question, a large number of writers long maintained the affirmative position, and Caesar Egasius Bulaeus defended it with much learning in vol. I of his *History of the University of Paris*, p. 91.

Nevertheless, in our own age the negative position has prevailed. It is supported by very weighty writers: Mabillon, preface to the fourth Benedictine century, part I, § 8; Launoy, *On Celebrated Schools*, vol. IV of his works, part I, chapters 1, 2, and 59; and Claudius Joli, *On Schools*, part I, chapter 22. D. Rivet added his support in vol. IV of his *Literary History of France*, p. 10, no. 16, where he says that the affirmative view cannot be maintained except in the sense that the palace school, which had been at Paris on several occasions, may have inspired the citizens of Paris with a particular love of letters and thereby encouraged them in later times to establish a public school in the city.

The antiquity of the origin of that university, the most celebrated in the whole world, and the discovery of certain traces of it before the end of the ninth century are nevertheless demonstrated by the same D. Rivet in the place cited, p. 250, no. 49. The learned man warns there, however, that this must not be understood as referring to a school distinguished by its own faculties, but to a permanent public school, [Col. 0055A] outside the cathedral churches and monasteries, intended and open for the instruction of the young people of Paris and of anyone arriving from elsewhere.

Regarding the second question, D. Mabillon, in the place cited, no. 179, replies that it seems certain to him that the palace school was established in one place. For, he says, the entire company and equipment of teachers, pupils, and books could not easily be moved from place to place whenever the king changed his residence, which happened frequently. Likewise, the celebrated scholar believes that the very extensive library—from which Louis Augustus later supplied the deacon Amalarius with an abundance of books for extracting a rule for canons, as reported by Ademar, monk of Angoulême—was kept not in a wandering court but in a fixed palace.

Nevertheless, the contrary opinion seems more probable to the distinguished D. Rivet, in the place cited, no. 15. Certainly D. Mabillon himself admits in the place cited that the palace scholars sometimes moved from place to place with the royal retinue and that Alcuin, the director of the palace school, was almost never absent from Charlemagne’s company.

“What greater difficulty,” Rivet asks, “was there in carrying to the court’s various stations the books needed for the school’s exercises than the other things serving the use of the entire court and the whole retinue?”

That school therefore moved together with the court and the courtiers who were to be instructed there: at one time it was at Aachen, at another at Thionville, then at Worms, Regensburg, Würzburg, Frankfurt, Mainz, or Paris. In these and other places, afterward, with Alcuin undoubtedly serving as its midwife, other celebrated schools arose or were reformed. D. Mabillon enumerates many of them in the cited preface, beginning at no. 180 and following, as does Launoy in the work cited on the more celebrated schools. All of them therefore rightly venerate and celebrate Charlemagne and Alcuin as their first founders and restorers.

## CHAPTER VIII

### The return of blessed Alcuin from Francia to England, and from there again to Francia. [Col. 0055C]

### XCIV

After blessed Alcuin had spent nearly eight years at Charlemagne’s palace and had been occupied there organizing the school and teaching various sciences, he remembered the obligation by which, on account of his native land and ecclesiastical orders, he was bound both to his own king and to the bishop—or church—to whom he had pledged himself. He therefore decided to return once more to his homeland and earnestly requested this from King Charles, to whom he had thus far consecrated both his services and his labors.

At first Charles resisted and was distressed that a man whom he valued so highly—a counselor so wise, and a teacher whom he wanted to make so useful and necessary to his entire kingdom, so that through his work it might flourish in morals and the sciences—should be taken away from him.

Recognizing, however, that because Alcuin was subject to another’s authority he himself lacked the power of command, Charles turned to entreaties and promises. According to the anonymous author of the *Life*, chapter 6, no. 12, he addressed him as follows:

> “We have earthly riches in sufficient abundance, excellent teacher, and we gladly honor you as a father with them. We ask that you, long desired and scarcely ever found, may illumine us with your own piety’s reward.”

Moved more by this extraordinary benevolence and favor of so great a king than by the riches offered him, Alcuin promised to comply with Charles’s request as soon as Charles, through his own intervention, had obtained from Alcuin’s king and bishop—whom he was obliged to obey—permission for him to return and remain permanently in Francia.

> “My lord king,” Alcuin replied, in the place cited, “I do not intend to refuse your will once the authority of the canons has been upheld. Although enriched in my paternal region by a considerable inheritance, I gladly reject it and delight in remaining here as a poor man so that I may be useful to you. It is for you alone to obtain this from my king and bishop.”

### XCV

Recognizing the justice of this request, Charles finally consented to Alcuin’s departure, undoubtedly also sending, as Alcuin had asked, letters to the king and bishop to whom he was subject, requesting the permanent release of a man whom he so greatly desired to retain.

It is believed that on this occasion Charles also took the opportunity to return to peace, with Alcuin as mediator, with Offa, king of the Mercians. At that time, namely in the year 790, some disagreement had arisen between them, inflamed by the devil’s instigation, so that navigation for merchants had ceased on both sides.

For Alcuin had heard from certain people that he was to be sent to Offa to settle those disagreements, as he himself writes in a letter to Colcu, a reader in Scotland, written in that same year, as we observed in the notes there.

Indeed, while writing this letter to Colcu, Alcuin was still uncertain whether, and when, the king would release him to return to his homeland, and whether he would receive instructions to negotiate peace with King Offa. For this reason he sent ahead the gifts that, from the generosity of King Charles and from his own resources, were to be distributed among the churches, monasteries, and hermits of Britain, which he mentions in that letter.

Shortly afterward, however, it must be that he set out for his homeland in that same year, because in fact he was there in the year when Ethelred was restored to the kingdom of Northumbria, as we shall immediately explain.

### XCVI

After Alcuin arrived there from Francia, a great revolution took place in the kingdom of Northumbria. The Northumbrians, having recently become hostile to King Osred, demanded Ethelred as king—the man whom twelve years earlier, in 778, they had expelled—and raised him to the throne. Hoveden recounts this in these words:

> “In the year 790, Ethelred was freed from exile and once again enthroned in the seat of the kingdom through the grace of Christ. King Osred, however, having been ensnared by the treachery of his own princes, was deprived of the kingdom, tonsured in the city of York, and afterward, compelled by necessity, sought exile.”

Unless we are greatly mistaken, this is the revolution in the kingdom of Northumbria, Alcuin’s homeland, which kept him in England longer than he wished, even though he had obtained permission from his king and bishop to return to Francia. He himself writes of this upheaval in a letter to certain friends, a fragment of which we presented from the Malmesbury manuscript in the note to Letter 2, in these words:

> “Blessed be God, who alone does wondrous things! Recently Athelred, son of Ethelwold, came forth from prison to the throne, and from misery to majesty. We have been detained by the upheaval of his kingdom, so that we have not come to you.”

He mentions the same upheaval in the cited Letter 2, writing to his own Aquila:

> “The upheaval of our kingdom still keeps me here this year.”

We assigned the year 790 to this letter, but this should not be understood to mean that it could not have been sent in the following year or somewhat later, as I indicated in the same note. For such a revolution ordinarily throws the whole order of the state into confusion, and a longer period of deliberation is needed to restore it to a peaceful condition. To accomplish this, Alcuin’s assistance and a longer stay in his homeland could have been useful or even necessary.

What other necessity could have kept him there longer, unless it was that, at the urgent request of his countrymen, he might assist them with his counsel amid such great confusion in all affairs?

### XCVII

Whether Alcuin, now residing in England, actually negotiated the restoration of peace with Offa, king of the Mercians, at the command of Charlemagne, and whether the reconciliation of the two kings’ dispositions and the restoration of the former freedom of the prohibited navigation should be credited to him, is not entirely clear.

For the successful outcome of that affair is credited in the *Fontanellian Chronicle*, chapter 15, in Bouquet, *Scriptores rerum Gallicarum*, vol. V, p. 315, not to Alcuin but to Gervold, bishop of Évreux and abbot of Fontenelle. The cause of the disagreement is also revealed there.

It is written that Gervold, who for many years had been appointed by Charlemagne as collector of tributes and customs at various ports and cities, especially at Quentovic, had on that account gained the acquaintance and friendship of King Offa; that he had often served as Charles’s ambassador to that king; and that most recently he had gone on account of the king’s daughter, whom Charles the Younger—Charlemagne’s son—was seeking in marriage.

When King Offa refused to agree to this marriage unless Berta, Charlemagne’s daughter, were given in marriage to his own son, Charles, angered, forbade anyone from the island of Britain or from the English people to reach the coast of the Ocean Sea in Francia for the purpose of trade.

“But lest this should happen,” says the author of that *Chronicle*, “it was prevented by the admonition and supplication of the venerable Father Gervold mentioned above.”

Nevertheless, even if this account is reliable, nothing prevents Alcuin from having been employed together with Gervold to promote the same affair.

Certainly it is clear from Letter 42 (now 47) that Alcuin had always been concerned for the friendship of the two kings and for peace between his own people and the Franks, and that, whenever it had been injured, he had worked successfully to restore it. In that letter he assures King Offa “that Lord King Charles had often spoken with him about him in a friendly and faithful manner, and that he was his most faithful friend.” For this reason Charles had sent worthy gifts to Offa and to the episcopal sees of his kingdom.

What those gifts were after the friendship had thus been restored is understood from Charlemagne’s letter to King Offa, which we present in volume II. In it Charles calls Offa “that venerable man and most beloved brother,” and, at his request, grants pilgrims traveling to the thresholds of the apostles free passage through his kingdom. To merchants pursuing profit he grants security, once the established customs duties have been paid, and protection against oppressors.

Some of the gifts were sacred objects intended for the episcopal sees of Offa’s Mercian kingdom; others for the episcopal sees of Ethelred’s Northumbrian kingdom; others, secular objects, for the metropolitan sees; and others for King Offa himself—namely, a belt, a Hunnish sword, and two silk cloaks, as though spoils brought back from a battle against the Huns.

Those gifts intended for Ethelred and the episcopal sees of his kingdom, however, did not then arrive there. For when the letters and the aforementioned gifts had been handed to the messengers, as Alcuin writes in the cited Letter 47, “sad news arrived concerning the faithlessness of the people” of Northumbria “and the murder of King Ethelred,” who had been killed by his own people on 18 April in the year 796.

This impiety so angered Charles “that, withdrawing the generosity of the gifts, he threatened every evil against this faithless and, as he calls it, perverse people, murderers of their lords.” Nevertheless, Alcuin testifies in the same place that he himself calmed this anger.

It is easy to believe, however, that the gifts intended for Offa himself and for the episcopal sees of his kingdom were afterward sent there, since those people were neither accomplices in that faithlessness nor consequently participants in the indignation they had deserved.

Certainly Alcuin himself, as he writes in Letter 43 (now 48) to King Offa, was ready to come to him with Charles’s gifts in that same year—before, I think, he undertook the administration of the monastery of Tours. It nevertheless seemed better to him to remain on pilgrimage:

> “Not knowing,” he says, “what I could accomplish among those among whom no one can be secure or make progress through wholesome counsel.”

### XCVIII

From what has been related somewhat more fully, it is clear that Alcuin did everything possible to make the kings of the Franks and the Mercians friends and to confirm them in friendship and peace. It should therefore be considered highly probable—as we indicated in the preceding section, and as all the most distinguished writers agree—that in the year 790, when he departed from Gaul for his homeland, he received from Charlemagne a commission to negotiate peace with King Offa, and that this undertaking, perhaps carried out together with Gervold, abbot of Fontenelle, had a successful outcome.

### XCIX

After Ethelred had been restored to the kingdom of Northumbria, as we recalled above in section 96, peace was not restored at the same time. Osred, recently thrown from the throne, was plotting a new uprising with certain princes who supported him and was stirring up fresh disturbances in order to recover the kingdom from which he had been expelled. He was nevertheless later captured by King Ethelred and, at the king’s command, killed in the year 792, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, as Hoveden records together with others under that year.

As we said above in section 96, this upheaval in the kingdom delayed Alcuin’s journey to Francia for some time. But when he saw that, through his efforts and counsel, he could accomplish nothing in his homeland, he therefore refused thereafter to return there for the same reason, as he declared to Offa in Letter 43. Now, after first obtaining permission from the king and from his own bishop, and undoubtedly for the same reason, he undertook his journey to Francia, urged also by Charlemagne, as we shall explain. We believe that this occurred either around the end of 792—perhaps after Osred’s murder, carried out in the middle of September of that year—or around the beginning of the following year.

For when the synod against Felix of Urgell was held at Regensburg in 792, Alcuin had not yet returned from Britain to Francia, as he himself writes in Book I Against Elipandus, section 16. In 793, however, he was already living in Francia when the church of Saint Cuthbert at Lindisfarne was destroyed by pagans, as we learn from Letters 9 and following.

Once established in Gaul, he wrote to his dearly beloved brothers of the Church of York, from whom he had been separated with the greatest sorrow, a letter full of affection and gratitude. In it he gratefully recalled the benefits bestowed upon him from infancy and childhood through mature age, and promised to keep them perpetually in his prayers.

Nor was he forgetful of his other friends left behind in his homeland. He wrote letters to the people of Lindisfarne, to Aedilhard, to the king and princes of Northumbria, and to the monks of the Wirenses and Gyrvenses. In these letters he lamented the unhappy events that had befallen them after his departure and instructed them with excellent teachings concerning the means by which they ought to turn aside the divine vengeance from themselves.

Because he had departed for a foreign land, he also turned upon himself the suspicion or accusation of certain people, as though he had simultaneously defected from loyalty to King Offa and to his own people. He removes this suspicion from himself in his letter to the priest Beorninus, saying:

> “Just as I shall faithfully preserve, insofar as I am able, those friends whom God has given me, so also shall I preserve those whom I left in my homeland.”

From what has already been said, it is clear how unjust this accusation against him was. On the contrary, Malmesbury wrote of him very truthfully in Book I of *The Kings of the English*, chapter 6: in the court of Charles he had not forgotten his fellow countrymen, but had labored to preserve them in the emperor’s friendship.

### C

Meanwhile, while Alcuin was remaining in his homeland, we shall relate in our historical Dissertation, section 15 and following, how the disturbances of Felix, bishop of Urgell, who was introducing new doctrines in Francia, and the efforts of Elipandus and the other bishops who supported him against Catholic truth in Spain, arose.

To calm these disturbances and restrain these tumults in the Church and kingdom, the most Christian king Charles undertook everything possible. He was therefore preparing to confer for this purpose with Adrian, the supreme pontiff, with the bishops of the whole kingdom, and with other men commended to him by their ecclesiastical learning and zeal for the faith. He judged that no one’s assistance would be more useful than Alcuin’s for extinguishing that controversy.

Accordingly, he summoned Alcuin from England, undoubtedly by letter, and urged him to hasten his journey to Francia as quickly as possible, so that he might assist the king in overcoming the newly arisen sect that appeared to be opposed to Catholic truth.

Alcuin himself testifies in the preface to his books Against Elipandus and in Book I, section 16, that he came to Francia at the summons of the most Catholic king, although not without the will and providential dispensation of God. See also what we have said on this matter in the cited Dissertation, section 25.

### CI

Alcuin therefore obeyed the divine summons and the king’s will, left his homeland, and returned to Francia for the second time, now to remain there permanently.

This occurred after Felix had been condemned for his error at the Council of Regensburg and had abjured his heresy there and afterward before Adrian I, the supreme pontiff—only to return once more to his vomit.

Alcuin’s first concern after his arrival in Gaul was therefore to recall this same Felix from error to Catholic truth. In earlier times he had commended himself to Felix’s intercessions as a man renowned for his reputation for piety and holiness. Alcuin now wrote to him in letters composed in a charitable style. He later wrote similar letters to Elipandus. When they resisted, he refuted them most solidly in many books, and did so with such success that the Church’s deliverance from those disturbances and restoration to its former tranquility within six or seven years must be attributed above all to Alcuin’s labors.

We have treated all these matters more fully in the historical Dissertation already cited; to repeat them here would be to do the same work twice.

### CII

Just as King Charles, at the beginning, while Alcuin was directing the palace school, entrusted to him the two monasteries of Ferrières and Troyes, so now, when Alcuin had returned from Britain for the second time and was henceforth to remain in Gaul, he placed him in charge of the monastery of Saint Martin at Tours, three years after his return, as we learn from the anonymous author of his Life, chapter 6, section 12.

Let us now discuss his administration of that monastery and the school established there.

## CHAPTER IX

### Blessed Alcuin’s administration of the monastery at Tours and the school established there

### CIII

After returning from England, Alcuin continued for several years to spend most of his time at the king’s court, where he undoubtedly again directed the school previously established there. At the same time, the king employed him in handling various affairs of the kingdom. This latter fact is understood from the beginning of the letter he wrote to the people of York shortly after his return. There he mentions the tribulations of secular distress that had overtaken him and various journeys, perhaps undertaken in the king’s company, through places associated with the holy martyrs or confessors of Christ.

His principal labor, however, was devoted to refuting and, if possible, completely overthrowing the new sect of the Adoptionists. About a year after his return, namely in 794, he attended the Council of Frankfurt, convened against Elipandus, together with certain of his fellow countrymen; by the final canon he was admitted to the fellowship of their suffrages and prayers. On this matter see our earlier Dissertation, section 34.

### CIV

At length, as this man, distinguished both for learning and for piety, experienced with advancing age frequent weaknesses and various illnesses—of which he often complained in his letters to friends—and noticed that the strength of both body and soul was being broken, partly by the hardships of travel and partly by the unremitting labor of literary work, he began to long for solitude and quiet. There, freed from the occupations of the world and from other affairs that distracted the mind in many directions, he could devote himself solely to the service of God and the salvation of his soul.

He expressed this desire to a certain archbishop in Letter 168, now numbered 62, in these words:

> “Let the most loving affection of your fatherhood know that I, your son, having laid aside the occupations of the world, desire to serve God alone.”

He adds the reason:

> “Because every person must prepare himself with vigilant care for the meeting with the Lord his God, and all the more those who are worn down by years and frequent illnesses.”

Yet he was unable for a long time to achieve the goal of this most ardent desire. Thus he wrote to his dearest Homer, who was departing for Rome, I think in 796:

> “When you departed, I often tried to reach the harbor of stability, but the Ruler and dispenser of all things and of souls has not yet granted what he once caused me to desire.”

According to the author of his Life, he wished to spend the remainder of his life peacefully and quietly in the monastery at Fulda. He writes in chapter 8, section 14:

> “When, therefore, he felt himself afflicted beyond his usual measure by old age and illness, he indicated to King Charles that, as he had long considered within himself, he wished to leave the world. He asked permission to lead a monastic life at Saint Boniface’s, according to the rule of Saint Benedict.”

D. Mabillon calls this account into question in his *Eulogy of Blessed Alcuin*, section 61. He believes that Alcuin did not desire the monastery at Fulda as his retreat, but rather the monastery at Tours, which Alcuin himself seems to indicate in Letter 101, now numbered 129, written to his David in 801:

> “By God’s mercy, I desire without any doubt to live and rest among the brothers faithfully serving God in the church of Saint Martin.”

It nevertheless seems to us that these apparently contradictory statements can be reconciled if the account of the author of the Life is referred to the period when Alcuin was still at the royal court and had not yet been placed in charge of the monastery at Tours, whereas Alcuin’s own words refer to the later period, when regular discipline had been restored in that monastery and, after the monasteries had been distributed among his disciples with the king’s permission, he no longer wished to move elsewhere but desired to live and die among the brothers of the church of Saint Martin because of their praiseworthy way of life.

The author of the Life therefore combined in a single narrative two matters belonging to different periods: Alcuin’s desire to withdraw to Fulda and his intention of dividing the monasteries entrusted to him among his disciples. This is by no means unusual among ancient writers who paid insufficient attention to historical criticism.

Furthermore, from Letter 192, now numbered 142, to the brothers of Saint Boniface, or the people of Fulda, recently discovered for the first time, which we have assigned to the year 801, it is clear that Alcuin had once been received by those brothers with great affection and joy, and that from their manner of life he had conceived both happiness and a desire to associate with them more often. Nevertheless, because the king opposed it, he was unable to fulfill that desire.

Whatever the case may be, it can be inferred from Letter 19, now numbered 23, to the brothers of Saint Martin that Alcuin likewise aspired to the monastery at Tours. At the beginning of that letter he declares that he desires to be one of them.

He nevertheless submitted the determination of his wishes to the king’s will.

### CV

Alcuin, now an old man, troubled by frequently recurring illnesses and especially distressed by his weariness with the noise of courtiers and secular affairs, did not cease imploring the king’s clemency that he might be permitted to spend the few remaining days of his life in some quiet place.

At last the king yielded to the most persistent prayers of his beloved teacher. It happened that the abbey of Saint Martin, the most famous in the whole kingdom, became vacant through the death of its abbot, Itherius. This provided the king with a suitable opportunity to satisfy Alcuin’s wishes to some extent.

King Charles therefore placed Alcuin in charge of this monastery, freeing him from the affairs of the court. The anonymous author of the Life briefly describes the matter in chapter 6, section 12:

> “After a considerable period had elapsed, after Albinus had returned to Charles for the second time, he was appointed shepherd of the monastery of Saint Martin at Tours.”

That this occurred finally in 796 is inferred from the following words of a letter written to David, the father of his homeland:

> “Almost five years ago, I considered, God as my witness, withdrawing from secular occupations with a sincere heart; but by the counsel of your pious providence I was transferred to the service of Saint Martin, for the benefit, by God’s gift, of the Catholic faith and ecclesiastical ordinance.”

This letter was written in 801, as we have shown in the notes there. Alcuin, therefore, was placed in charge of the monastery at Tours five years before the writing of this letter—that is, in 796.

### CVI

Although this most pious man, keeping the eternal years in mind, desired to be freed not only from the affairs of the court but also from all secular occupations, even through this withdrawal to the monastery at Tours he did not wholly attain what he desired. He was now entangled in new concerns that cannot be separated from the administration of temporal affairs and the governance of souls.

There were two principal matters that required Alcuin’s attention there and that he was to undertake at the king’s command. First, he was to recall the monks of that monastery, who were living too loosely, to a better way of life. Second, he was to restore the study of letters there, which had almost everywhere fallen into decline.

Let us now see how he accomplished both.

### CVII

Even before Alcuin was placed in charge of that monastery, its regular condition was dear to him. He was always burning with the most fervent zeal to advance monastic discipline in every monastery.

For this reason he wrote Letter 19, now numbered 23, to the brothers of that church. In it he earnestly exhorted them to vigils in praise of God; to pour out heartfelt prayers to God; to humility, so that what they professed inwardly might appear outwardly; to obedience, so that they might not do the evil things that were forbidden but might do the good things that were commanded; and to love of God and neighbor.

> “These,” he says, “are the three commandments that will open the gates of heaven to monks.”

He then instructs and teaches the elders what they owe to the younger men, and finally exhorts the younger men to be subject to their elders and teachers as to fathers.

Before Alcuin assumed the governance of that monastery, however, although those brothers had been bound by the rule of the monks according to an ancient institution, their morals and manner of life were said to be far from praiseworthy. Their life had been so discredited before the king himself that they were apparently believed not even to know whether they wished or ought to profess themselves canons, monks, or neither.

Charles reproaches them for this in Letter 119 among the Alcuinian letters, now numbered 158:

> “You yourselves also know how your life has now frequently been discredited by many—and not without reason. For at one time you said that you were monks, at another canons, and at another neither.”

One of the reasons, therefore, why King Charles entrusted Alcuin with the governance of the monastery at Tours was that those brothers might be moved by the teaching, wisdom, and example of so celebrated a man and recalled to a better way of life. The most pious prince himself reveals this reason for his appointment when he continues in the letter just cited:

> “And, both to give you counsel and to abolish your bad reputation, we chose for you a suitable teacher and ruler and invited him from distant provinces, one who could instruct you in the right way by words and admonitions and, because he was religious, could form you by the good example of his conduct.”

### CVIII

The industry and efforts of this new abbot did not fail the king’s counsel and intention. When he began his administration, he took the beginning of reform from repentance, following the example of Saint John the Baptist and of our Savior himself. He knew well that conversion must begin with repentance for former transgression.

He therefore wrote to these brothers of his a letter on the Confession of Sins, which you will find in Volume II. He directed it especially to the younger plants of the religious community, judging—and rightly—that the corrupt morals and discipline of a religious or any other community could scarcely be corrected by a better or easier means than by thoroughly forming and cultivating the young people attached to such a body through teachings of piety and virtue.

At the same time, however, he asked the elders and teachers to contribute their own efforts to this end.

I have no doubt that this blessed man, who prescribed various other instructions for regular life in frequent letters even to the brothers of other monasteries while absent from them, now offered many more admonitions to his own sons who were present and also committed them to writing.

I believe that the booklet *On the Use of the Psalms* belongs here. Its preface to Charles, which concerns another short work, or *Offices for the Weekdays*, was attached to it by mistake, as we noted in the preliminary notice.

That booklet concerns monks in particular. It teaches which psalms ought to be recited in various circumstances and necessities, with what devotion, with which accompanying prayers, and in what spirit of penitence.

Certainly D. Mabillon, in Book XXVI of the *Annals*, section 47, judged that the following words found in the same booklet referred to the brothers of Saint Martin:

> “At every moment I violate the promises by which I pledged that I would keep the holy rule.”

And also:

> “Grant me, though I am most frail, to follow and imitate the footsteps of your beloved father, Benedict.”

Likewise:

> “I sought the monastery and undertook the monastic life; but wretched as I am, I am often entangled in various ways in frivolities, and so forth.”

There are also many other passages of this kind appropriate to the devotion of monks.

“From these passages,” says D. Mabillon in the cited place, “it is clearer than daylight that monks still remained in the church of Saint Martin and continued there throughout Alcuin’s entire administration.”

It is therefore false that, according to a certain Touraine chronicle, King Charles established canons in the church of Saint Martin by the authority of Pope Adrian and placed Alcuin over them.

The same point is confirmed by a decree of Charles granted to Alcuin near the beginning of his administration, in favor of the abbot and monks of Saint Martin, which we shall give in Volume II.

### CIX

The efforts that he devoted to reforming the discipline of the monastery entrusted to his care were not fruitless. He judged and experienced the conduct of his brothers to be so good and honorable that in Letter 101, now numbered 129, he declared to the king that he desired without any doubt to live and rest among them while they faithfully served God.

In Letter 195, now numbered 149, published for the first time from a manuscript of the Harleian Library, he defended them before the king against unjust informers and offered the following excellent testimony to their conduct, invoking the divine name:

> “I call upon God as witness to my conscience that I have never understood them to be such as I hear them described by certain people who are readier to accuse than to save. As far as it can be seen and known, they perform their duties in the churches of Christ worthily before God; indeed, I testify most truthfully that I have not seen others celebrating more perfectly in any place. Their life can be examined by the perfect man, incorruptible judge, and faithful envoy Wido, who, scrutinizing all their affairs, learned what they had done and how they had lived. Nor was I slow to admonish them concerning the propriety of monastic life.”

No stronger testimony can be brought in support of the excellent discipline and conduct of the brothers at Tours that flourished among them under Alcuin’s administration.

### CX

The second benefit, as we said, that Alcuin rendered there while living in his monastery at Tours was the establishment of a school of learners and teachers and the continuous practice of the liberal arts and other literary studies.

This wise man, instructed by extensive experience, knew very well that no remedy could be applied more suitably or effectively for reforming the morals of a religious community than the cultivation of the mind.

By this method and through this art, the concepts of virtue that have been suppressed partly by ignorance and partly by desire are brought back to life. The lights of truth are kindled after the darkness in which human nature has been immersed through the corruption of sin or voluntary negligence has been driven away.

By this path knowledge of God, supremely good, omnipotent, and all-wise, is acquired; the religion by which he wishes to be worshiped is learned; and it is taught by what means one may reach him as the ultimate end and supreme happiness.

Finally, through this path the best citizens of the commonwealth are formed, and each person learns what he owes to his ruler, his homeland, and his neighbors.

### CXI

Alcuin accomplished with the greatest industry what he had conceived in his mind. In Letter 38, now numbered 43, he explained to King Charles the studies with which he had begun to educate his pupils:

> “I, your Flaccus, according to your exhortation and good will, strive to distribute to some beneath the roofs of Saint Martin the honey of the sacred Scriptures. I endeavor to intoxicate others with the old pure wine of the ancient disciplines. I shall begin to nourish some with the fruits of grammatical subtlety. I desire to illuminate certain others with the order of the stars, as though with a painted roof on the summit of a great house—becoming many things for many people, so that I may educate as many as possible for the advancement of God’s holy Church and for the adornment of your imperial kingdom, lest the grace of the Almighty in me be empty or the generosity of your goodness fruitless.”

Nothing, therefore, was omitted from this school that could contribute to cultivating minds and filling souls with sacred and secular learning.

The newly established school, however, lacked a sufficient supply of books, by whose aid so extensive an institution could be properly maintained, advanced, and stabilized, especially books of the kind to which Alcuin had been accustomed in the school at York.

Therefore, in the same letter, he asked the king to allow him to send back there some of the boys—namely, his pupils, several of whom, as we saw above in chapter 5, section 59, and shall see below in section 104, he had brought with him from his homeland—so that they might “receive whatever is necessary there and carry back to Francia the flowers of Britain.”

> “Thus,” he says, “let there not be merely a enclosed garden at York, but at Tours let there be the streams of paradise with the fruits of the trees, so that the south wind, when it comes, may blow through the gardens of the Loire,” and so forth.

From this it is understood that Alcuin took care to equip the library at Tours according to the model of the one that he had possessed at York “through the industry of his teacher and his own sweat,” and which he himself described in his poem on the bishops of York, verse 1535 and following.

### CXII

We believe that, with the king’s permission, some of Alcuin’s pupils went to York to bring back the books that were wanted, and that the people of York were not reluctant to share them.

Since at that time, because every codex had to be written individually and because scribes were slow and scarce, copies of books were not as numerous as they became after the invention of the art of printing, we therefore think that such exemplars were lent to the people of Tours not for retention but for copying, after which they were to be sent back to York.

For this purpose, and so that the library at Tours might thereafter be made richer, scribes were needed who knew how to write books in a script as neat as circumstances then allowed and according to the rules of grammar and orthography. At that time few such scribes could be found at Tours or elsewhere.

Alcuin complains of this scarcity in Letter 85, now numbered 135, to Charles:

> “The distinctions and subdivisions of points, although they produce the most beautiful ornament in sentences, have nevertheless, because of rusticity, almost fallen out of use among scribes. … I, therefore, although making little progress, struggle daily with Touraine rusticity.”

To remedy this difficulty and defect, Alcuin devoted great effort at the beginning to teaching, as he had earlier done in the palace, the first elements of letters, the rules of grammar and orthography, and the method of writing correctly and accurately.

For this purpose he hung in the scriptorium [Museum], for those copying books, a poem—number 67 in our edition (Volume II)—so that it might continually remind them what they ought to observe when writing. There he advises them, when copying volumes of sacred Scripture or of the holy Fathers, to take care not to insert or mingle their own words anywhere; to seek out correct exemplars of the books they were to copy; and

> “By cola to distinguish the proper senses and by commas,
>
> And to place the points, each in its proper order,
>
> So that the reader in church may not read something false,
>
> Or perhaps suddenly fall silent before the holy brothers.”

The most pious man also took care and watched diligently lest those whose morals he intended to reform through literary studies should be corrupted by books of pagan authors. He therefore forbade his pupils to devote themselves to reading the ancient poets, especially Virgil.

This is gathered from the account of the author of his Life concerning the old man Sigulf, chapter 10, section 19. Alcuin rebuked Sigulf because he had secretly handed Virgil to Adalbert and Aldric for reading, thereby transgressing the command that he himself had given to his pupils. At the same time he reminded them that

> “the divine poets” were sufficient for them and that they had no need to be polluted by the luxurious eloquence of Virgil’s language.

### CXIII

Once a sufficient supply of well-written books had been obtained through this industry, the instruction of the pupils became easier. Among them the teacher himself distributed them according to each one’s capacity and level, and he consequently pursued the teaching of all the disciplines that he had mentioned in the letter cited above in section 111.

The school at Tours soon became so celebrated everywhere that people possessed by a desire for knowledge flocked to it from all directions, just as they had earlier to the school at York.

There were educated there famous men who thereafter spread, throughout and beyond the realm of Francia as far as it extends, the seeds of learning that they had received at Tours under Alcuin’s instruction. Thus the school at Tours became the mother of so many other schools founded in various places.

Let us list in the following chapter the more distinguished and better-known pupils of blessed Alcuin.

## CHAPTER X

### The more distinguished pupils of blessed Alcuin in the school at Tours

### CXIV

Among Alcuin’s students in the school at Tours, D. Mabillon, in his *Eulogy*, section 66, also numbers Onia, Candidus, Nathanael, Witso, Raganard, Waldram, Osulf, Simeon—later bishop of Worms, praised in Letter 73—and Sigulf, according to whose account the Life of blessed Alcuin was written.

We have nevertheless stated above in chapter 4 that Alcuin had all of these men as pupils not in the school at Tours in Gaul but in the school at York in England. It is more reasonable to believe that some of them, if not all, were brought from England by their teacher, at the request and certainly with the permission of King Charles, and served first as his assistants in the palace school and later also in the school at Tours, rather than as pupils.

This is especially clear in the case of Sigulf, whom Alcuin once severely chastised because he had permitted the students entrusted to him by Alcuin’s instruction to read Virgil and other pagan authors contrary to Alcuin’s prohibition. See chapter 10, section 19 of the Life.

He also ordered Nathanael, or Fridugis, to act in his place in instructing the royal maidens Lucia and Columba, who were living in the palace where Nathanael also resided. In Letter 135 Alcuin exhorted him

> “not to hide from them the beauty of his wisdom, but to water within them the flourishing plots of good will.”

Witso, whom D. Mabillon distinguishes there from Candidus, is the same person as Candidus; Witso was an additional name of Candidus, as we observe elsewhere.

Simeon, whom the same distinguished man, in the cited place, makes bishop of Worms, is likewise a surname of Eanbald, archbishop of York, as we have learned from letters recently discovered in the Harleian Library.

### CXV

It is credible that all those teachers who, while Charlemagne was still alive and at the beginning of the reign of Louis the Pious, were placed in charge of schools—whether episcopal or monastic—that were being reformed or newly established should be counted among Alcuin’s pupils. Most of them, moreover, probably completed their studies at Tours.

Since the evidence is lacking, however, we shall list here only those about whom certain testimony exists and who became more distinguished than the others: namely, Rabanus, abbot of Fulda and later archbishop of Mainz; Hatto, his successor in the abbacy of Fulda; Haimo, or Haymo, later bishop of Halberstadt; Samuel, bishop of Worms; Adalbert, successor of Sigulf in the abbacy of Ferrières; Aldric, bishop of Sens after having been abbot of Ferrières; and finally Amalarius, deacon of the Church of Metz.

### CXVI

Browerus reports in his notes on Rabanus’s poem 13, from a very ancient Fulda codex, that Rabanus was sent together with Hatto by their abbot to Tours, to Albinus the teacher, for the purpose of learning the liberal arts.

Rabanus himself declares in the preface prefixed to his commentaries on the Books of Kings that he received the surname Maurus from his teacher Alcuin. He says that, in the passages he explains himself, he marked in the margin the letter M, “expressing the name Maurus, which my teacher, Albinus of blessed memory, bestowed upon me.”

This is why Alcuin always addressed him by that name. Thus, in Letter 111, now numbered 140, addressed to him, he writes:

> “To Maurus, blessed child of Saint Benedict,”

and he begins poem 250 as follows:

> “These verses, holy child of Benedict, Maurus,
>
> Albinus the poet has sung to you in little lines.”

The disciplines that Rabanus learned at that time under Alcuin’s instruction he himself recalls in the poem that he presented to Saint Martin in Alcuin’s person and that is prefixed to the books *On the Praises of the Cross*. We include it among the spurious poems in Volume II, poem 17. In it Alcuin is introduced singing of Rabanus:

> “Indeed, when I was the humble guardian and servant
>
> Of this church”—that is, of Saint Martin—“reading sacred doctrines,
>
> I taught this boy, with the nourishment of the divine word,
>
> The ethical lessons and the studies of wisdom, and so forth.
>
> For his abbot, the ruler of the Fulda flock,
>
> Sent him here to your dwelling, Father,
>
> So that he might read with me the art of scholarly meter,
>
> And joyfully prepare the sacred Scripture in due form.”
