Rabanus nevertheless listened to Alcuin at Tours for only a short time, if D. Mabillon’s conjecture is correct. In Book XXVII of the *Annals*, section 12, Mabillon judges that Rabanus, already a young man and somewhat educated—for he had been ordained a deacon the previous year—was sent to Tours by the abbot Ratgar, to whom Baugulf had ceded the abbacy in 802, two years before the death of blessed Alcuin.

There is nevertheless nothing to prevent his having been sent there at an earlier time by Baugulf, Ratgar’s predecessor, and from having remained there long enough to learn the liberal arts, philosophy, ethics, and sacred Scripture.

Certainly, from poem 13, in which the famous man seemed to attribute Rabanus’s mission to Ratgar, nothing else is learned except that through Ratgar’s generosity he obtained books and that, after compiling them himself and subsequently having them taken away, he modestly requested their return. He sings there:

> “Your goodness has now granted me permission to study books,
>
> But my poverty stifles the powers of my intellect.
>
> Since I feared that my wandering mind might lose whatever
>
> My teachers had taught me by word, I committed it all to pages.
>
> Hence these glosses and little books now survive,
>
> Which I beg you to order returned to the unworthy man.”

### CXVII

Rabanus had as companions in study at the academy of Tours Hatto, Haimo, and Samuel, whom I mentioned above.

Concerning Hatto, who among learned men was surnamed Bonosus, this is established from Browerus’s notes on poem 13, as we said in the preceding section.

The same may be inferred concerning Haimo from the preface to the work *On the Universe*, which Rabanus dedicated to him:

> “I remember, holy father, the good zeal for study that you possessed in boyhood and youth in the exercise of letters and the meditation of sacred writings, when you read with me not only the divine books and the explanations of the holy Fathers concerning them, but also the diligent investigations of the wise men of this world concerning the nature of things, which they composed in their descriptions of the liberal arts and in their investigations of other matters.”

This testimony establishes that Haimo was Rabanus’s fellow student. It could not have been elsewhere than where Rabanus himself, in boyhood and youth, as he says here, was trained in sacred learning and the liberal arts—a training which he himself testifies in the passages cited in the preceding section took place under Alcuin as teacher.

Haimo therefore also learned the same sciences and arts under the same teacher, studying together with Rabanus.

Nevertheless, D. Mabillon, in the *Eulogy of Haimo* in the *Acta Sanctorum*, century IV, part I, page 619, section 7, understands Rabanus’s cited words to Haimo as referring to the school at Fulda, although he subsequently considers true what Trithemius writes: namely, that Haimo was a student of Alcuin together with Rabanus in the monastery at Tours.

Certainly Haimo was Rabanus’s companion in monastic profession at the monastery of Fulda; he later became abbot of Hersfeld and finally, in 841, succeeded Thiatgrimus in the episcopal see of Halberstadt.

Concerning Haimo, who among learned men bore, according to the custom of that age, the surname Praeclarus, and concerning his various writings, one may consult D. Mabillon in the cited place and D. Rivet, *Literary History of France*, volume V, page 111 and following.

### CXVIII

Among these same companions of Rabanus at the school of Saint Albinus in Tours must be numbered Samuel, later made abbot of Lorsch and subsequently, in 838, promoted to the episcopate of Worms while retaining the administration of his monastery, as D. Mabillon relates, *Annals*, book XXXII, no. 3. For Rabanus himself testifies that Albinus was the common teacher of both, in poem 21, in these verses:

> What Albinus once rightly taught as master,  
> Let this breast hold fast; let every work approve it.

This Samuel was Rabanus’s fellow teacher at the school of Fulda, just as he had earlier been his fellow student at the school of Tours, as is clear from the following verses of the same poem:

> Once I rejoiced that you were my companion,  
> Beloved brother, among the readers.

He then adds:

> Now too I rejoice that you retain the rights of a master,  
> That you increase in virtue and occupy your father’s place.

These words suggest that Samuel, already abbot and bishop, retained and exercised the office of teaching, being at once father and master. Mabillon, *Eulogy of Blessed Rabanus*, § 3, no. 10. In letter 143, Alcuin, writing to a certain son or disciple of his, says that he had once composed, under his own name and that of his fellow student Samuel, a letter *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs*. I have no doubt that this is the same Samuel of whom we are speaking; but who his fellow student was is unknown. Alcuin praises his devotion, the beauty of his sacred wisdom, and his zeal for learning it—“which,” he says, “is especially suited to your present years, whether for the blessedness of eternal life or for secular honor.” This son of Alcuin was therefore a layman; and this prevents us from affirming with certainty that he was Rabanus.

### CXIX

The author of the *Life of Blessed Alcuin*, no. 14, unquestionably lists Adalbert among Alcuin’s disciples at the school of Tours. He says that, together with Raganard and Waldram, Adalbert remained constantly attached to Alcuin toward the end of Alcuin’s life, insofar as Sigulf, under whose discipline they were placed, allowed it. Adalbert’s companion was Aldric. Alcuin entrusted both of them to Sigulf for instruction, though under his own direction; and when Sigulf granted them permission to read Virgil in secret, Alcuin rebuked him more sharply, as is reported in the same work, no. 19.

After Sigulf had lived honorably into old age under the canonical habit, he voluntarily surrendered the administration of the abbey of Ferrières, with the consent of the brothers and the approval of Emperor Louis; he assumed monastic religion and thereafter wished to be subject to this disciple of his, as Lupus writes in letter 29.

After Adalbert’s death in the fourth year of his administration, Aldric was elected abbot by unanimous consent of the brothers. Emperor Louis gave his assent and support to this election, as the anonymous author of the *Life of Blessed Aldric* reports in Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, fourth century, p. 570, no. 11. This election took place in 822, as the same D. Mabillon proves from a letter of Louis Augustus, *Annals*, book XXIX, no. 30, p. 473, although in his preliminary observations on the same *Life of Blessed Aldric*, no. 4, he had thought that it occurred around 824.

This Aldric “received the insignia of monastic discipline in the monastery of Ferrières under Alcuin the abbot, his literary teacher,” as we read in his *Life*, no. 4. Louis Augustus appointed him royal tutor because of his reputation for piety and learning. It is exceedingly probable that the anonymous author of the *Life of Alcuin* undertook that work at the urging of Aldric, whom he says was still alive at the time, no. 19; this is also the conjecture of D. Mabillon, preliminary observation in the *Life of Blessed Alcuin*, no. 1.

From this passage it is clear that the *Life* was written after 822, when Aldric was elected abbot of the monastery, but before 829, when he was elevated to the archbishopric of Sens, as D. Mabillon proves in his note to no. 13 of the *Life of Aldric*. For further information concerning his praiseworthy deeds and holiness, see that work.

### CXX

Finally, among Alcuin’s more distinguished disciples must be placed Amalarius, priest and monk of Metz. He himself declares as much in chapter 58 of *On the Order of the Antiphonary*, where he says: “When I seemed to be a boy before Albinus, the most learned teacher of our entire region”—whether at Tours or at the palace is uncertain.

Amalarius nevertheless directed the palace schools after Alcuin, when Claudius the Spaniard had been promoted by Louis Augustus to the see of Turin, as D. Mabillon shows in the preface to the fourth Benedictine century, nos. 181–182. All learned men now agree that this Amalarius, surnamed Symphosius among men of letters, must be distinguished from the archbishop of Trier of the same name. Concerning him and the writings of Amalarius of Metz, one should consult D. Rivet, who wrote learnedly about them after D. Mabillon, *Literary History*, vol. IV, p. 531; D. Ceillier, *History of the Sacred Authors*, vol. XVIII, p. 552 and following, should also be added.

### CXXI

Among Alcuin’s poems, under no. 268, there is an epitaph of the monk Paul, who, as it says there, was instructed in sacred letters at the monastery of Saint Martin. It also reports that Paul lived for seven decades, or seventy years. At such an age it is scarcely credible that he was instructed in letters by Alcuin, who was no older than he was; alternatively, one must say that Alcuin was not the author of that epitaph, which D. Mabillon calls extremely rough.

If anyone nevertheless wishes to regard this Paul as a disciple of Alcuin, this may be admitted in the sense that he lived under Alcuin’s obedience and spiritual direction in the aforesaid monastery, already an old man when Alcuin assumed its administration.

It must certainly be believed that Alcuin had many more disciples in that celebrated school, since it was regarded as the parent of so many other schools that were later founded or restored throughout the Frankish kingdom by Alcuin’s disciples. I have wished to mention here, however, no others than those for whom reliable evidence exists and who attained greater renown among posterity.

### CXXII

Some writers thought that Blessed Alcuin taught letters not only at the palace and in the monastery of Tours, but also elsewhere in France—namely, at Paris, Fulda, the monastery of Saint Gall, and Soissons—and even at Rome.

John Trithemius, *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, book II, chapter 26, writes of Alcuin:

> At Charles’s command, he was the first to establish the Parisian school, transferred from Rome, where he also educated many distinguished disciples from among the monks.

And in volume I of the *Hirsau Chronicle*, p. 11, he says that Albinus, the teacher of Emperor Charlemagne, introduced at the monastery of Fulda the practice of placing highly learned teachers over the monks, so that they would instruct them not only in the divine Scriptures but also in every branch of secular learning, and so forth.

Neither assertion, however, rests on any ancient testimony. Neither in Alcuin’s life nor in his writings is there any trace that, during the time he stayed in France, he directed schools at Paris, Fulda, or anywhere else in that kingdom, except at Tours and in the royal palace.

The palace school was not fixed with the court in one place but was itinerant, as we noted above. From the time Alcuin came from England to Charles until the time he was transferred to the monastery of Saint Martin, however, the court does not appear to have been established even once at Paris, as D. Mabillon says, *Annals*, book XXV, no. 15.

Alcuin did at one time visit the brothers of Fulda, and was received by them most graciously and with great joy, as he writes at the beginning of letter 192, now 142; but there is not even a hint that he was the master of that school. During that visit, however, he could have given them various counsels for advancing literary study and become the author of the practice among the people of Fulda that Trithemius mentions in the cited passage. Something similar may have occurred at the monastery of Saint Gall, at Soissons, and elsewhere.

Finally, nowhere is it stated that Alcuin ever stayed for a longer period at Rome or served as director of its schools. He went there twice: once with his teacher for the sake of literary advancement, and again as an envoy to obtain the pallium for Eanbald, the recently elected archbishop of York. Once these matters were completed, however, he returned again to his homeland, as we have said elsewhere.

## CHAPTER XI

### Other Deeds of Blessed Alcuin at Tours

### CXXIII

After Blessed Alcuin had made the school of the monastery of Tours highly renowned by furnishing it with an excellent method of teaching and learning, had thoroughly cultivated a great many students who came even from foreign regions in literary studies, and had led the minds of the brothers living there from idleness to labor and from laxity of life to stricter observance of the rule and discipline, he considered it his responsibility to secure permanence for a work so happily begun.

Accordingly, he was also concerned with temporal goods, without which a religious community devoted entirely to literary study and the practice of piety cannot be maintained. He therefore took care to obtain from the royal authority charters and privileges by which the goods, possessions, and immunities already granted or to be granted in the future might be so secured that the brothers of that monastery could never be disturbed by anyone in their peaceful use of them.

### CXXIV

Thus, relying upon the clemency of Charlemagne, which he had often experienced, this most diligent steward sought out all the older charters of privileges, immunities, and donations formerly given to the church of Saint Martin for the support of the poor and the allowances of the monks, and confirmed by the hands of previous kings, including Pepin, Charlemagne’s father. He presented them to the king to be reread and humbly asked that the king deign to confirm them by his own authority as well.

The king, always most generous toward such sacred foundations, did not fail to respond to these pious requests of his teacher. He therefore ordered a most extensive royal writ—or, as it is called, a diploma—to be issued. In it, not only are the things previously bestowed upon that monastery by his predecessors and other benefactors confirmed and newly received under royal protection, but it is also forbidden under a severe penalty that either the royal fisc or any other judicial authority should presume to undertake anything against those privileges or against the goods and possessions of the monastery.

We present a copy of this writ in volume II of our edition. Some consider it to have been issued at Laon around the beginning of Alcuin’s attainment of the abbacy; others date it to the year 800, perhaps obtained on the occasion when Charlemagne was at Tours that year for the sake of prayer, as the annalists of that period report.

### CXXV

In the same year—namely, the thirty-second of the Frankish kingdom and the twenty-seventh of the Lombard kingdom—in the month of June, two other writs were issued at Alcuin’s request for the monastery of Cormery. Alcuin had likewise received its administration from Charles after the death of Itherius, its first founder.

For in 791 Itherius founded a cell of Saint Paul in the district of Tours, at Angers, on the river Indre, in a pleasant place called Cormaricus by the ancients. He resolved to build there a church in honor of the Holy Trinity with three altars, and donated many things and possessions for the support of the brothers serving God there and for the comfort of travelers, as is read in Itherius’s charter in D. Mabillon, appendix to volume II of the *Annals*, p. 714, no. 32.

There he asks his successor, who would soon follow, and the abbots succeeding him, to complete and preserve for the praise of Almighty God and the growth of the cell what he had arranged but had not yet been able to bring to completion, and to prefer increasing rather than diminishing anything bestowed upon it.

### CXXVI

Blessed Alcuin judged that this admonition of his most pious predecessor should not be neglected. Accordingly, after obtaining the administration of Saint Martin’s abbey—which Itherius had wished the cell of Cormery to depend upon—he devoted his care to that place, first so that all the goods and possessions bestowed upon the cell might be permanently secured by royal authority; and second, so that the place might be entrusted to monks professing the Rule of Saint Benedict.

King Charles had already dealt with the construction of this monastery, I think, through Itherius himself with Pope Hadrian I, and afterward also with Hadrian’s successor Leo, through Angilbert, as may be gathered from Charles’s letter to Homer, which we published in volume II, Appendix 1.

Concerning the same matter, Alcuin several times wished to be informed by his Aquila in letters 52, now 66, and 55, now 69, written in 797, about what was being done at Rome or at the court.

Alcuin therefore obtained permission from Charlemagne to establish in the same cell of Saint Paul monks who would live according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. From the same king he also obtained, first, that the place should always remain united and subject to the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours and its abbots; and second, that the goods donated to that place, or to be donated in the future, should be preserved for it inviolate.

In another writ, Charles granted at Alcuin’s request the privilege

> that the monks living in that monastery under the Rule of Saint Benedict should have the freedom to send two ships up and down the Loire River for their necessities, and so forth, without being required to pay any toll on that account.

Both writs were issued in the year 800, in the month of June, at Tours—namely, when Charles, as we said above, was staying there for the sake of prayer.

### CXXVII

Alcuin took the first inhabitants of this monastery, who were to profess the Rule of Saint Benedict there, from Gothia: they were disciples of Blessed Benedict, abbot of Aniane. He informed his very dear friend Aquila of this in letter 92, now 108, in these words:

> Recently I established a certain community, almost eight miles from the monastery of Saint Martin, for monastic life and regular religion, initially from brothers from Gothia, where Abbot Benedict established the regular life. But now, God willing, some are coming who are devoting themselves to it with holy devotion.

Ardo, a disciple of Saint Benedict of Aniane, also mentions this foundation in his *Life*, in Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, fourth century, part I, p. 205, no. 36, in these words:

> Alcuin too, of English origin, a levite by rank, renowned for wisdom … having heard and experienced the fame of the man of God’s holiness, joined himself to him with inviolate affection, so that from the letters he often sent to him a single little book was formed by their being gathered together. After giving him gifts, he earnestly asked that monks be given to him. When the venerable Father immediately agreed, he sent horses to carry them; and he placed them in the monastery he had built, called Cormery. There were, as I think, twenty of them, with a master set over them. Through the good example of their conduct, a great multitude of monks was gathered there.

They increased so greatly that in the seventh year of Louis Augustus—Charlemagne’s son—there were already fifty monks there. In that year, 820, the same emperor first granted them the power to elect an abbot from among themselves according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, though with the consent of the abbot and community of Saint Martin.

This was later confirmed by Pope Urban II in 1096 at the Council of Tours, so that the elected abbot of Cormery was to take his staff from the tomb of Saint Martin; after his death, the same staff was to be returned to that place, as a perpetual reminder of his subjection. This is found in the papal letters in volume I of the *Spicilegium*, in Mabillon’s *Eulogy of Blessed Alcuin*, no. 57, p. 176.

### CXXVIII

What we have related concerning the introduction of Benedictine monks into the monastery of Cormery refutes the conjecture of the most celebrated D. Charles le Cointe. In volume VI of the *Ecclesiastical Annals of France*, under the year 791, no. 50, he writes:

> Under the provost at Saint Martin’s the canons lived; but the monks, who had been unwilling to relax, remained under the stricter rule, though both groups used one common abbot and all obeyed one superior, each according to his own institution. From this Itherius the abbot received the occasion to found a cell at Cormery, where he established and endowed monks, as the charter described above teaches.

This is the charter of Itherius, whom we mentioned above in no. 125.

The same learned le Cointe, in the same place, no. 52, after rightly refuting the fable that the brothers of Saint Martin had been expelled by an angel in a single night, adds:

> Moreover, once the monastery of Cormery had been built and endowed, the monks of Saint Martin flocked there; and at Tours only the canons remained in the church of Saint Martin.

Even if we are willing to grant D. Cointius that monks and canons lived together under Itherius as abbot at the monastery of Saint Martin—a claim that nevertheless lacks suitable testimony—we cannot grant that the same abbot built the cell of Cormery for the purpose of transferring there the monks who had previously lived under the stricter rule in the monastery at Tours, and that, once these had been transferred, only canons remained there.

Certainly, even after Itherius’s death, while Alcuin was administering the monastery of Saint Martin, almost all the brothers living there were devoted to the monastic rule, as we have already shown elsewhere from D. Mabillon. This is also clearly evident from Charlemagne’s writ for the same monastery cited above, in which no provosts or canons but only an abbot and monks are mentioned.

Furthermore, the testimony of Ardo and Alcuin’s own letter to Aquila, quoted in the preceding section, demonstrate that the monks of Cormery were taken not from the monastery of Saint Martin but from the school of Saint Benedict of Aniane, and that they were established there not by Itherius but by Alcuin:

> Recently, says Alcuin, I established a certain community … initially from brothers from Gothia, and so forth.

He therefore did not find them previously introduced there by Itherius.

### CXXIX

Among the monks whom Blessed Benedict, abbot of Aniane, sent to Cormery, one named Sigulf is mentioned. He must therefore be distinguished from Sigulf, Alcuin’s disciple brought from England, as we have already noted elsewhere.

The author of the *Life of Alcuin*, chapter 11, no. 20, mentions this Sigulf of Cormery in recounting the fraud of the carriers and adulterators of wine, whom Alcuin had sent for the refreshment of the brothers of Cormery, whom he loved. Using the services of this same Sigulf, Alcuin detected and reproved the fraud.

Afterward Blessed Alcuin repeatedly visited that monastery and inspected the schools established there, as may be gathered from a poem once published among the Alcuinian poems under no. 222, but now relegated to the doubtful works, in volume II of our edition; see our notes there.

In another poem, which we present among Alcuin’s genuine works under no. 106, likewise in volume II, the cell of Cormery is praised above great cities for its literary studies and the moderation and sobriety of its life.

This monastery still exists under the celebrated Benedictine Congregation of Saint Maur, as D. Mabillon testifies in his *Eulogy of Blessed Alcuin*, no. 57. But to comment further on these matters does not belong to the present place.

### CXXX

Shortly before his death, as D. Mabillon believes, *Annals*, book XXVII, no. 30, Blessed Alcuin founded and endowed, for the benefit of the poor and especially travelers, a hospice or hospital—“as they call them”—at a famous place in the district of Troyes, between two bridges and two waters of the Seine, called the Twelve Bridges. The same Mabillon presents the charter of this foundation, drawn up by Alcuin, in the cited *Eulogy*, no. 59. So that nothing relating to the works and piety of so great a man might be lacking, we have decided to reproduce it here.

#### Charter of the Donation of Blessed Alcuin for the Hospice of the Twelve Bridges

In the name of the Lord, who reigns forever.

I, Alcuin, although unworthy, rector and governor of the monastery and possessions of Saint Martin, the most illustrious confessor of Christ, dictated this charter at the command and by decree of Lord Charles, the most serene emperor, so that in the future no disturbance might thereafter be inflicted by my successors or by any person whatsoever upon the matters written below.

Under the inspiration of Christ our God and with the favor of Lord Charles, I resolved to build, for the reception of travelers as an act of almsgiving, a hospice in the very celebrated place called the Twelve Bridges, for the sake of the aforesaid lord emperor, his offspring, all his descendants, and the welfare of the Frankish army. This I have done. From my lord I received a small portion of land between two bridges and the two waters of the river Seine, as is contained below within the boundaries set out in his charter. Upon it I built an oratory of the most blessed Mother of God, Mary, and hospital buildings for the perpetual reception of travelers, as we have said.

My lord also added, by written charter and instrument and by the authority of his holy name, ten *mansi* of land in the Rheims region of Champagne, at a place called Marmorico Villa. Leotard, a nobleman, also gave from his own property, as a perpetual alms, land and possessions in two places, namely, Ferroco and Marniaco. Frambert the priest also gave something at a place called Brituaria.

His nephew, named Marato, likewise gave land under a contract of sale at a place called Mariniaco, for which I gave him four pounds of silver.

Then, by the authority of the lord emperor, we transferred to the same place what lies at the place called Patiaco, and at the villa of Dofio and Muerneto, as is contained in due order in the donation; and at another place called Patiaco on the Igrua, as well as at Curcella and the villa of Cavanno, which Sigbert and his parents assigned to Saint Martin.

Also in the villa of Collorio, in the Flaviacense valley, and at Muilliare, which Adalbert, son of Beringarius, assigned on behalf of his kinsman Ermenfred to the holdings of the same saint, as is contained in the individual legal donations, everything belonging or pertaining to those places.

Other free men living in those regions also gave small portions of land in different places in perpetual right, such as at Mount Gratian, and so forth.

I therefore hand over all these things, lawfully possessed and held, belonging to the aforesaid church of Blessed Mary, by the legal arrangement written below, in perpetual right as an alms of our Lord and of myself, to Jesus Christ and Saint Martin, for the perpetual reception of the poor. Thus, according to the possibility and blessing of the Lord, which I believe he will grant that place and the possessions belonging to it through the intercession of Blessed Mary and Saint Martin, travelers may perpetually receive assistance there, through the alms of my lord King Charles, of his descendants forever, and of the kings of the Franks, for the remedy of my soul, the prosperity of my successors, and the salvation of the holy family of Saint Martin.

I beseech, by the name and majesty of the Holy Trinity, by the blood of our redemption, and also by the terrible judgment at which each person will give an account of his faith and all his works, that this donation of my lord, my own donation, and the reception of travelers there may remain eternally firm and inviolable in perpetual right under the protection and administration of the abbots of Saint Martin. Let it not be transferred as a benefice to anyone, but be assigned under their governance for the service of the faithful and those who fear God.

I especially adjure him, by communion in the holy cross and the Holy Trinity, to provide faithfully and cause to be distributed to the poor whatever God’s blessing may cause to bear fruit in those portions of land. Let him also cause all present and future princes and those exercising authority, after hearing the authority of our most beloved lord emperor and my own, to ensure without disturbance that the decree of our will remains firm, so that he too may deserve to become a participant in this blessing forever, believing with us that anyone who gives his assent to this declaration may, by God’s mercy, cause it to profit him equally as an alms, just as it does me, who, with God’s help, first of all arranged that these things should be done.

Great and most kindly is the goodness of the Lord and our Redeeming God, who will render an everlasting reward to every person of good will and sound faith.

This single charter may suffice in all places and legal proceedings concerning ecclesiastical donations, transfers, leases, and claims, even if it is read in the presence of the faithful and worshipers of God. I adjure them, by the name of the eternal God, by the authority of his redemption, and by the grace of baptism, which they were worthy to receive from their earliest cradle, that whoever hears this document give his assent, according to his ability and the authority granted to him, to our donation.

Otherwise, if he fails to do so, he will have to account before holy Mary and Saint Martin, with me accusing him; and in place of the poor and travelers he will receive the reckoning of his condemnation at the future judgment, when Christ comes in his majesty to judge all human deeds.

May this charter, [lacuna] together with its small possessions, remain free from every hindrance and liability imposed by counts, vicars, judges, and every authority. And so that it may be believed more firmly, my lord deigned to confirm it below with his own hand and, more securely, with the wax of his ring, so that no sacrilegious or reckless person might presume to invalidate anything written in it.

### CXXXI

Mabillon published this charter in *Acts of the Saints*, fourth Benedictine century, p. 177, and added the following note:

> There is no indication of the date on the parchment from which this copy was transcribed. Later, Ingelwinus, abbot of Saint Martin, assigned this hospice to the monastery of Cormery, so that the monks of that monastery might restore it to its former condition, and that the poor there might always be supplied with provisions and other necessities according to the previously established number, namely twenty, and might have there a refuge for their safety against the persecution of the pagans, as is read in the diploma of Charles the Bald issued at Verberie on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the thirteenth indiction and the twenty-fifth year of his reign. At present, in that place called Pontes (Ponte), there is a priory subject to the abbey of Cormery.

The same Mabillon assigns this charter to the year 804 in the *Benedictine Annals*, book XXVII, no. 30, and believes that Alcuin issued it shortly before his death.

### CXXXII

Finally, the blessed man, devoted to the beauty of God’s house and an exceptionally devout worshiper of sacred relics, devoted himself to repairing sacred buildings and constructing oratories, as he himself writes in epigram 116, in these verses:

> This little house, reader, which you see prepared,  
> Is known to have been founded for the sacred relics,  
> … Albinus the poet ordered these buildings to be prepared.

And in epigram 118 he sings:

> Albinus, coming from the poet’s distant land,  
> … Here he ordered the long-ruined vaulted roofs,  
> As you see, reader, to be entirely renewed throughout the hall.  
> Here, establishing places most suitable for sacred relics,  
> So that the saints’ resting place might receive fitting honors—  
> As it is proper on earth to venerate the holy ones,  
> Whom God wished to reign forever in heaven.

D. Mabillon wishes the references here to the long-ruined vaulted roofs to be understood of the vaulted oratories of the basilica at Tours, *Annals*, book XXVII, p. 361.

## CHAPTER XII

### Blessed Alcuin’s Bodily Illness and Resignation of the Administration

### CXXXIII

Although Blessed Alcuin, after the indulgence of his august disciple and most munificent benefactor had permitted him to withdraw from the court to his monastery at Tours, had been freed from the court’s more frequent business and secular cares, he was not yet permitted to enjoy there the quiet for which he had long sighed and which, weighed down by old age, he considered necessary for seriously attending to the greatest of all concerns—namely, his soul—and for reviewing the course of his past life, so as to prepare a way for himself to meet the Lord, the strict Judge.

Indeed, even in this retreat he was occupied, or rather burdened, by many labors that scarcely allowed him to think of the quiet for which he yearned. The restoration of the schools and of literary study; the composition of various treatises on sacred Scripture, Christian doctrine, moral teaching, and so forth; the correction of copies of sacred Scripture; the instruction of disciples who flocked to him; the writing of letters, often on matters of great importance, to kings, bishops, princes, monks, disciples, and friends; the reform of religious discipline among the people of Tours; and his concern for the churches and other monasteries entrusted to his care scarcely left an hour free for him to devote to himself, his own interests, or his rest.

Moreover, King Charles, who took the greatest pleasure in his company, sometimes wearied him by requiring him to resolve various questions and sometimes summoned him to the palace to seek his advice. This eventually became extremely burdensome to the old man, worn down by labors and gradually afflicted by many bodily illnesses. He complains about this several times in his letters and begged the king to allow him to enjoy the quiet he desired at Saint Martin’s.

Thus, in letter 81, now 96, written, unless we are mistaken, in 799, he begs not to be compelled to undertake the long and laborious journey to Rome that the king had planned for the following year in order to settle the disputes of the Romans—a journey the king had already arranged that year after Pope Leo’s arrival and return, and to which Alcuin too had been invited by the king.

> I believe that my frail little body, weakened by illness and daily pains, can in no way complete that journey. I would already have had the desire, if I had the power to undertake it.

He later expressed that same desire and the impediment caused by his illness to Aquila, or Arn, archbishop of Salzburg, in letter 92, now 105. There he expresses his sorrow that the frailty of his little body, weighed down by many small burdens of hardship, prevented him from undertaking the journey and from using the long-desired opportunity to serve Leo, the supreme pontiff, who was afflicted in so many ways.

The letter of King Charles in which he invited Alcuin to undertake the Roman journey with him in the year 800 is missing. Another letter of his is likewise missing, in which he reproached Alcuin, who was excusing himself from the journey, for preferring the smoke-blackened roofs of Tours to the gilded arches of Rome. Alcuin nevertheless mentions both letters in letter 93, now 109.

The king nonetheless yielded to his teacher’s prayers, while ordering that, although Alcuin remained at rest at Saint Martin’s, he should send his own “boys”—that is, as we interpret it, servants and vassals who would convey his gifts—to accompany the same journey. Alcuin replied there with great confidence in the king’s clemency:

> Concerning our boys, whom you command to go to Rome on their father’s feet, I should like to know when, where, and with whom they are to meet your blessedness. … I admit that, at your command and with your assistance, they can undertake the sweat of my labor. But I do not yet grant them my gifts, which I used frequently to receive through your generosity.

### CXXXIV

Alcuin was therefore permitted on this occasion to remain at rest in his monastery. He also began to deliberate about choosing from among his disciples assistants in the administration of his monasteries and about completely laying down the burden of pastoral care, so that he might prepare himself more freely for death, which he constantly held before his mind’s eyes as imminent.

He requested and obtained permission from the king to do this. Concerning the matter he wrote to his very dear friend Aquila in letter 176, now 159, written in the year 800, after Felix of Urgell had been convicted of heresy at the Council of Aachen in the preceding year and afterward handed over to the care and custody of Leidrad, bishop of Lyon, in these words:

> Then, so that you may know how great a mercy God has shown me: from among my own sons I chose assistants for myself in all the possessions I held in various places, with my lord David agreeing in every respect with my requests.

He communicated the same thing in letter 175, now 158, to his beloved disciples Calwin and Cuckoo, writing:

> As I said to Cuckoo, after laying down the burden of pastoral care, we sit in quiet at Saint Martin’s, watching for the moment when the voice comes: “Open to the one who knocks; follow the one who commands; listen to the one who judges.”

In this division of the monasteries, the monastery of Saint Martin fell to Fredegisus, or Fridugisus, the deacon surnamed Nathanael; the monastery of Ferrières fell to the elderly Sigulf. We have said more about them above in chapter 4.

D. Mabillon, in the *Eulogy*, chapter 10, no. 62, remarks that it is surprising that he entrusted both monasteries to two canons. For Fridugisus and Sigulf were canons, although Sigulf later changed his canonical habit, as Lupus writes in letter 29.

Alcuin was succeeded at the cell of Saint Judoc by Warembald, whose privileges Pope Leo III confirmed, as is read in *Gallia Christiana*, volume IV. That cell was later restored and united to the monastery of Ferrières under Abbot Lupus, as D. Mabillon reports from a letter of the same Lupus to Guigmund, *Annals*, book XXXIII, no. 76.

The names of the abbots who presided over the monastery of Saint Lupus of Troyes immediately after Alcuin are now lacking, as le Cointe says, volume VII, under the year 804, no. 66.

### CXXXV

The same most celebrated Cointius, in the place cited, no. 67, writes that modern scholars dispute whether Alcuin continued to discharge the office of abbot until his death, or whether, worn out by old age and bodily illness, he divided among his disciples, before the year 804 in which he died, the monasteries entrusted to him. D. Coint himself favors the opinion of those who say that Alcuin retained the governance of those monasteries until his death. The learned man endeavors to prove this from various letters written by Alcuin to Charles in the years 800, 801, and later. In them Alcuin indeed indicated that he wished to be released from secular affairs, but added no word about assuming the monastic habit or resigning his abbeys; indeed, he desired to live and die among the canons of Saint Martin.

“Therefore,” Coint continues, no. 69, “the burdens of the world, the distribution of which he finally obtained among his disciples after repeated requests, must be distinguished from the administration of the monasteries, which should not be counted among secular occupations unless it is compared with the private and tranquil life of a monk.”

The learned writer adds that the elderly Sigulf, who obtained the abbacy of Ferrières after Alcuin, remained at Tours—far from that monastery, as the author of Alcuin’s Life testifies—with Alcuin until his death. “We therefore,” le Cointe concludes there, “do not think that the monasteries which had been entrusted to Alcuin were divided among his disciples by the emperor Charles before Alcuin’s death.”

### CXXXVI

Nevertheless, despite the difficulties raised by this most celebrated author, we believe that we must adhere to the testimony cited above from Letters 175 (now 158) and 176 (now 159), which D. Coint, since they were published only later, had not seen. From these letters we learn that, four or at least three years before his death, Alcuin had been released not only from secular occupations but also from the burden of pastoral care—which certainly cannot be distinguished from the administration of monasteries—and that he had transferred pastoral care, or the direction of souls, to disciples chosen to assist him.

Nor is there any difficulty in the fact that Sigulf, to whom the abbacy of Ferrières, far distant from Tours, was assigned in that division, was staying at Tours during the final years of Alcuin’s life and even on the very day on which Alcuin departed this life. Just as Alcuin had administered that same abbey while absent for many years, so Sigulf could have done the same, or at least could have come occasionally to his master, to whom he was deeply devoted, and especially have attended him during his final agony—perhaps at Alcuin’s own request.

Nor does the fact favor D. le Cointe’s opinion that Alcuin, in letters written to Charles in the year 800 and later, added no word about assuming the monastic habit or resigning his abbeys, but desired to live and die among the canons of Saint Martin. For from the testimony of the author of his Life we know that long before this he had desired to lead a quiet and tranquil life among the monks of Saint Boniface at Fulda, and that, after his monasteries had been divided among his disciples, he thereafter led a life “in no way inferior to the monastic life, devoted exclusively to fasts, prayers, mortification of the flesh, almsgiving, the celebration of psalms and Masses, and the other virtues by which human nature can be adorned.” *Life*, chapter 8, no. 14.

Nor does Alcuin write anywhere, as D. le Cointe claims, that he desired to live and die among the canons; rather, he desired this among the brothers of Saint Martin, who, as we have often intimated elsewhere, professed the monastic rule under his governance.

Finally, Alcuin’s Letter 38 (now 43) to Charles does not favor D. Coint’s opinion. Although that letter shows that, at the time when it was written, Alcuin governed the school at Tours and was occupied with teaching various disciplines, the learned man’s conjecture is slight when he assigns the letter to the year 801—when Charles had already been crowned emperor—solely because the letter calls his realm imperial:

> “So that I may educate as many as possible for the advancement of Holy Church and for the adornment of your imperial realm.”

It is much more probable that Alcuin wrote this shortly after undertaking the direction of the school at Tours, as we noted regarding that same letter. The “imperial realm” there seems to signify nothing other than a very extensive kingdom with unlimited power of command. In the same sense, Charles’s kingdom is sometimes called an empire by writers before he himself had been crowned emperor, just as Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, says at the beginning of the *Sacrosyllabus* that the Council of Frankfurt of 794 was convened by decree of his empire.

### CXXXVII

Blessed Alcuin, therefore, released by the king’s permission from secular affairs and at the same time from pastoral care, in the manner we have described, applied himself more fervently from the year 801 until his death—and until he had to render an account to the supreme Judge—as the burdens of old age and illness increased.

Nevertheless, Charles Augustus, his disciple, had become so accustomed and devoted to his teaching and counsel that, by every means, he attempted to call the man away from his solitude, even though Alcuin continually pleaded his bodily infirmities, and to draw him to the court, undoubtedly for matters that had arisen. We understand this from certain letters written after the year 800.

In Letter 104 (now 132), written in 801 to Charles, he says:

> “Behold Flaccus, his body worn out, having laid aside the belt of military labor, has chosen with his whole desire, according to the most pious counsel of his lord David, to serve God alone in quiet peace. Why is he again compelled to fight and to sweat beneath the burden of arms, when the weakness of his frail body denies him the ability to lift anything from the ground?”

And in Letter 106 (now 134), written in the same year, unless I am mistaken, or in a later one, although he had wished that, after the passing of those days, he might at least once more be able to see the king’s face, he nevertheless now “humbly as a suppliant, suppliantly as a humble man, devoutly as a devotee, begs” that he may be permitted to carry out his duties at Saint Martin’s, because, he says, “being very weak in body, I am able to accomplish nothing else by way of travel or labor . . . .”

He informs his Aquila of the same summons to the palace and to the lord king, of the bodily weakness that prevented him from performing that service, of the burden of secular business laid aside, and of the terror of divine judgment, which he already felt approaching, in Letters 108 (now 145) and 109 (now 144). In the former he invites Aquila to come to him at the house of Saint Martin, so that they may discuss together the preparation of his soul for death and divine judgment:

> “And when these counsels have been completed between us”—which, he says, “I cannot mention without tears”—“let the final farewell be spoken between Aquila and Albinus.”

And in Letter 191 (now 161), written in 801, he informs this friend, especially dear to him above others, that at Easter he had been brought almost to despair of life by the severity of his fever:

> “But the Lord,” he says, “had mercy on me because of the prayers of his servants. Yet the daily labor of that same chastisement remains—not, however, to the peril of life, but, as I hope, to the cleansing of my sins.”

### CXXXVIII

Finally, as the infirmities of his body increased day by day and he judged that the dissolution of his body was not far distant, he considered it his duty, before his death, to offer due thanks to Charles Augustus, his greatest benefactor on earth, for the abundance of piety and kindness with which Charles had enriched him from the time of his first arrival in Francia. He did so in Letter 106 (now 134):

> “For what,” he says there, “could have been added to the happiness of my journey, or to the judgment of your goodness toward me, who was unworthy of all these lavish gifts? Or what acts of thanksgiving worthy of your mercy can I offer, except to beseech, through the continual diligence of pious prayer, the clemency of the most merciful almighty God?”

He repeats this thanksgiving afterward in the poem appended to the same letter, and there bids his David a final farewell, singing:

> May gentle Christ repay you with manifold gifts  
> For all the goodness of yours that you have bestowed on me.  
> As many grasses as the earth contains, or sands as the shore,  
> So many, through God’s mercy, David, receive as your farewell.

### CXXXIX

Perhaps the verses in Poem 6 of Charles to Alcuin, which we judge to have been falsely attributed to him among the poems in volume II, belong here. In them Charles appears to pray that his beloved teacher may have a blessed departure from this world:

> Beloved teacher, . . . therefore I wished in my songs  
> O venerable one, to console your old age with the Muses . . .  
> And may you flourish in the worship of God through nourishing virtues,  
> Following toward better things the paths of a holy life,  
> Until you come also to the heights of the heavenly kingdom,  
> Rejoicing with the saints, joined to Christ forever.  
> And carry me with you by your prayers, I beg you, teacher,  
> To the pious heights of the merciful King, toward which you go.

### CHAPTER XIII

**The death, tomb, epitaph, and commemoration in the calendars of Blessed Alcuin**

### CXL

Thus the most celebrated Alcuin, once the teacher of the most powerful king and emperor Charles the Great and of the entire Frankish and German nations, whose deeds and merits we have so far recounted and sketched in a modest style, finally completed his days. After growing old amid the many labors he had endured for the Church and the commonwealth, he reached that goal toward which all mortals hasten.

Perceiving this, the most pious man longed with his whole desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ. To reach this goal successfully as well, he omitted nothing by which he might render God propitious to him through works of penance and through the intercession of the saints.

Therefore, so that the death which he represented to himself as near might also continually remain before his eyes, he chose a place where he would rest after death. He used to go there in the evening and sing the evangelical hymn, or canticle, of Saint Mary, the *Magnificat*, with the antiphon “O Key of David,” etc., which the Church uses in the Office during the seven days before the feasts of the Lord’s Nativity. He sighed:

> “Come and lead out the captive from the prison house, the one sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death.”

To this devotion he also added certain verses from the Psalms that suggested a desire for eternal blessedness; they are recorded in his *Life*, chapter 14, no. 24.

### CXLI

He also judged that the season of Lent, which he had always celebrated with the greatest devotion and with contrition of flesh and spirit, was now especially appropriate, so that he might prepare himself not only for the paschal solemnity but also for eternal joys.

He was possessed by the desire that, with divine grace assisting him, he might prolong his life throughout that entire solemnity and finally depart this life on the day when the whole work of our Redemption was completed and confirmed through the coming of the Holy Spirit. This he also obtained.

On the night of the feast of the Lord’s Ascension, as the author of his *Life* testifies in the place cited, no. 28, he fell exhausted upon his bed from a serious illness, so that he even lost the power of speech. “And when paralysis supervened, on the seventh day before the Ides of May, Thursday, toward evening after sunset,” as the Masciacense Annals, cited below, record, he was overcome.

On the day of Pentecost itself, after the morning Office had been completed, when dawn was already shining, at the hour when he had customarily entered to celebrate the levitical Masses with his Sigulf, his soul was released from the flesh—fourteen days before the Kalends of June, in the year 804 from the Incarnation of the Lord—as the author of his *Life* explicitly testifies, chapter 15, no. 29. All later writers agree with him, as do the ancient Annals of Lambeck, Petau, and others in Bouquet, volume V of the *Scriptores Rerum Gallicarum*. There, on page 16, note (k), Alcuin’s death is reported from the Masciacense manuscript as follows:

> “Alcuin died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, on the first day of the week, the day of Pentecost, at daybreak, with the moon six days old, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 804, indiction 12, in the thirty-sixth year of the reign of lord Charles; paralysis having supervened on the seventh day before the Ides of May, Thursday, toward evening after sunset, with the moon twenty-five days old.”

Over the place where the blessed man died, a globe of fire was seen by Joseph, archbishop of Tours, and many others. At the very hour of his death, a gathering of heavenly levites was shown to a certain solitary living in Italy; in their midst Alcuin was seen ascending to heaven, clothed in a most splendid dalmatic, as the author of his *Life* relates in the place cited, chapter 15, no. 30.

### CXLII

The most celebrated writer D. Mabillon, although he acknowledged that the day of death marked by the author of the *Life* should be retained, nevertheless thought in his *Elogium*, chapter 13, no. 71, that the year should be corrected on the basis of certain arguments and conjectures, and that Alcuin’s *Life* should be extended at least to the year 809.

But after considering the matter more carefully, he perceived that the arguments advanced there in favor of his opinion could not prevail over the authority and explicit testimony of the contemporary author of the *Life* and of the ancient Annals—not only the Frankish but also the German ones. Accordingly, he corrected this opinion in the additions and corrections to Part I of the fourth century of the Benedictine history, page 767, where he wished the whole of no. 77 of his *Elogium* to be deleted and the following substituted:

> “What I have hitherto reported concerning the year in which Alcuin died certainly involves difficulty; nevertheless, the authority of his *Life*, derived from a contemporary, must be preferred, especially since it is supported by ancient annals, not only of Frankish but also of German affairs. Among these, the oldest Fulda Annals have the greatest weight with me; Lambeck calls them ‘new’ in volume II of the *Imperial Library*, where they were printed. Those Annals accordingly report Alcuin’s death in the thirty-sixth regnal year of Charles the Great, which corresponds to the Christian year 804, as follows: ‘In the thirty-sixth year, Alcuin died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May’—read ‘June.’ His death must therefore unquestionably be assigned to this year.”

Thus writes the most modest of men. “If the continuators of the Bollandists had wished to take this into account,” says D. Mabillon in Book XXVII of the *Annals*, no. 71, “they would not have wasted their labor refuting this opinion, as they did in volume IV of May, in the preliminary commentary to the *Life of Blessed Alcuin*, no. 5.”

Therefore, lest we too waste our labor by lingering over the refutation of the most celebrated man’s arguments—arguments which he himself has now abandoned and which have found no subsequent adherent—it will not be worth the effort to discuss them.

### CXLIII

Joseph, then archbishop of Tours, who, as we have said, saw a globe of fire shining over the church of Saint Martin at the death of the blessed man, heard that Alcuin had already died and hastened there with his clergy. With the greatest reverence he kissed the eyes of the blessed man and washed them with his own tears.

Although Blessed Alcuin, who despised himself and all outward pomp, had arranged for a tomb to be prepared not inside the church of Saint Martin but outside it, or beside it, wishing by his own example to show what he had urged others to do in Letter 150 (now 199), namely, not to think about adorning a tomb—“This,” he said, “is vanity of vanities; it is better to clothe the soul with these resources than to adorn the filth of the flesh”—nevertheless the aforesaid archbishop, because of the opinion he had formed concerning the blessed man’s eternal happiness, ordered that he “be buried with the greatest honor within the basilica of Saint Martin, so that those whose souls are joined in heaven might have their bodies placed together in one house on earth.” *Life*, chapter 15, no. 32.

This clear testimony of a contemporary author overturns the assertion of William of Malmesbury, monk, Book I of *The Kings of England*, chapter 3, who wrote that Alcuin had been buried in the monastery of Cormaric. The error of Brower, Book I of the *Fuldish Antiquities*, chapter 10, likewise collapses: he asserted that Alcuin lay buried in the celebrated monastery of Hersfeld.

A certain crude epitaph of an Albinus, which had recently stood in the church at Hersfeld and which D. Quercetanus later appended to the *Life of Blessed Alcuin*, gave Brower the occasion for his error. That epitaph, however, certainly does not concern our Alcuin, but rather Albinus or Albuinus, undoubtedly a monk of Hersfeld. Concerning him, the Hersfeld Chronicle records under the year 1034:

> “Alwinus, provost at Hersfeld and most learned in the philosophical arts, who had previously been a most renowned schoolmaster, succeeded that same Bruno at Nienburg.”

Later, D. Mabillon says in his *Elogium*, no. 77, it may have happened that, when the monks of Hersfeld had received from their predecessors the report that an Albuinus was buried in their church, they supposed through confusion of names that this was the great Albinus, or Alcuin, and then composed that crude epitaph for him.

Hermann Kirchnerus therefore unjustly numbers our Alcuin among the teachers of his native Hersfeld in his *Oration*, volume II, page 62, Marburg edition of 1607, perhaps deceived by that same epitaph.

The true and genuine epitaph of Blessed Alcuin, which he himself dictated while alive, was written on a bronze tablet and fixed to the wall near his tomb. The author of his *Life* appended it at the end, where it may also be found published by us.

### CXLIV

The age at which Blessed Alcuin died cannot be determined, since although the year of his death is known, the year of his birth is nowhere recorded. The common opinion is that he was born around the year 735 from the Incarnation, as we noted earlier, chapter 1, no. 8. From this opinion it follows that he reached his seventieth year.

The author of his *Life* describes the whole course of his life, and the works with which he filled it, in a few words that nevertheless contain much in summary, in chapter 13, no. 26:

> “He fled idleness in every way. For he was either reading, or writing, or teaching his disciples, or devoting himself to prayer and the chanting of psalms, indulging his body only in its unavoidable necessities, etc.”

The truth of this account is shown even more clearly by his own writings, which plainly reveal a man continually occupied with various labors, applying every moment of his time to teaching truths, communicating knowledge, giving counsel, instructing people of the highest and lowest condition, and directing ecclesiastical and moral teachings to bishops, priests, monks, counts, and judges.

It is therefore not surprising that after his death the reputation of his sanctity shone everywhere. We have highly authoritative witnesses from his own time.

Rabanus Maurus inserted the name of his teacher into the sacred calendars on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, volume VI of his works, page 187, in these words:

> “The deposition of lord Alcuin.”

And in the letter prefixed to his *Commentaries on the Kings*, volume III of his works, page 45, he calls him “the teacher of blessed memory.”

Hincmar, bishop of Reims, calls him “holy and venerable Alcuin” in his treatise *On the Non-Trinitarian Deity*, volume I of his works, chapter 5, page 473, and chapter 11, page 507. At the end of the letter to Charles the Bald prefixed to his *Book on Predestination*, he calls him “a religious and learned man” and counts him among those Fathers of the Church “whose faith and teaching the Apostolic See of Rome not only accepted with the greatest kindness but also exalted with many praises.”

Ardo Smaragdus says in Book 36 of his *Life of Saint Benedict of Aniane*, cited by Mabillon, that Alcuin was “illustrious in wisdom and venerable for the merit of his holiness.”

The Fulda Annalist, under the year 794, commends him with this eulogy:

> “In these times Alcuin, surnamed Albinus, is held to be illustrious in holiness and learning.”

Bouquet, volume V, page 330.

Finally, he is called a saint in a brief chronicle of Tours. It reads:

> “In the year 804, Saint Alcuin died.”

Cited by Mabillon in his *Elogium*, no. 78.

The eulogies of more recent writers—Mabillon, Henschenius, and others—agree with these testimonies; all proclaim Alcuin Blessed. These testimonies are entirely worthy of belief, given the authority of so many serious writers. But the testimony of God himself is greater: it is found in the miracles which God chose to perform through Blessed Alcuin, in confirmation of his faith and piety, both during his life and after his death. The author of his *Life* recounts these miracles on the testimony of those who were able to bear witness as eyewitnesses.

“Nevertheless, nowhere, so far as I know,” says D. Mabillon in the place cited, “has the Church celebrated Alcuin’s feast day, not even the Church of Tours,” although that Church experienced his holiness and guards the remains of his mortal life.

### CXLV

Perhaps, however, this point in Alcuin’s otherwise irreproachable *Life* ought to be taken ill, as being contrary to the laws of the Church and to monastic humility: namely, the statement that he simultaneously held several abbeys in Francia—the abbey of Tours with the cell of Cormaric, Ferrières with the cell of Saint Josse, and the abbey of Saint Loup at Troyes.

Yet, although this example is of such a kind that no one would easily wish or ought to imitate it, it must nevertheless be said that this plurality of benefices was free from all fault. He neither sought those several abbeys out of ambition nor retained them out of avarice. Rather, they were almost forced upon him against his will by King Charles, who—being himself a most generous king and most devoted to the public good—wished to entrust those abbeys to Alcuin for no other purpose than that he might reform monks who had fallen into a looser way of life and spend all the revenues for the use of the brothers, for their advancement in learning, for the support of guests and pilgrims, and for the expenses of the journeys that frequently had to be made, now to the court, now to England, and elsewhere.

How entirely Alcuin’s mind was detached from the desire for riches and from payment for his labors can be understood from the answer which, according to the author of his *Life*, chapter 2, no. 12, he gave to the king when the king attempted to draw him to himself by means of rich gifts:

> “My lord king, I do not intend to refuse your will . . . I would gladly have been enriched by a considerable inheritance in my native land, but, having rejected it, I take delight in remaining here poor.”

What his view of wealth and poverty was, he makes clear in Psalm 131, verse 15, volume I, page 388:

> “The poor of Christ are those who do not love this world, whether they possess riches or do not possess them. For riches have been given to some for distribution to the needy, not for possession by themselves. They ought to place neither their hope nor their satisfaction in them, but to trust in the name of Christ, in the righteousness and charity of God and neighbor. This is the fullness of the saints, not the riches of the world.”

He also indicates to the priest Eada, in Letter 140, how far he himself was from the desire for riches and how painfully he felt that he had been cast from the quiet state of poverty which he had once professed into the whirlpool of wealth. He asks Eada to restore him by the prayers of his devotion to that same degree of poverty in which Eada himself stood—whom we understand clearly to have been a monk:

> “You hold in your hands what we once intended to hold. But the waves of this world have swept our little boat with stormy winds into the whirlpool of riches . . . . . Poverty is tranquil. If it is guided by the rudder of humility and the sail of charity, then, with the Holy Spirit blowing, it will arrive at the harbor of eternal blessedness.”

### CXLVI

Elipantus, bishop of Toledo, judged that Alcuin deserved censure not only for the abundance of his wealth but also for the number of his servants, since he said that Alcuin possessed twenty thousand of them, volume I, page 869, no. 4, of this edition.

In fact, Elipantus either did not know, or deliberately concealed for the sake of slander, that those servants—if their number was indeed so great—were not household servants assigned to Alcuin’s personal service, but serfs bound to cultivate the lands of the churches and monasteries over which he presided.

Thus, in the letter to Laidrad and his associates prefixed to his books against Elipantus, Alcuin declares that he had never purchased anyone for his own service:

> “Rather,” he says, “I desire in devoted charity to serve all the servants of Christ my God.”

Although, therefore, a plurality of benefices or abbeys is ordinarily condemned by ecclesiastical laws if it is sought out of ambition or retained out of avarice, it is nevertheless free from blame if it is prudently judged—and judged by the very custodians of the Church—that greater benefit can thereby flow to the churches from the dignity and merit of the person being advanced.

Such certainly was the condition of the monasteries in the kingdom of Charlemagne that, at that time, it was more beneficial for many of them to be governed by one abbot so holy and wise than for each to be governed individually by men unequal to the task in piety and learning.

D. Basnage is therefore unjust toward Alcuin when, in his historical observations concerning the Felician heresy and the books of Etherius and Beatus, volume II of Canisius’s *Thesaurus of Monuments*, page 290, he approves Elipantus’s slander against Alcuin in these words:

> “Finally, Elipantus deservedly exposes Alcuin as inflated, on account of the number of his servants—twenty thousand—and the abundance of his riches, which are unbecoming in a monk who has renounced the world.”

Thus Basnage croaks with the crows. D. Madrisius rightly criticizes him as unjust not only toward Alcuin but also toward the other writers who opposed Felix and Elipantus, in his *Works of Saint Paulinus*, pages 226 ff., in a special criticism of Basnage’s historical observations concerning the Felician heresy and the books of Etherius and Beatus.

### CHAPTER XIV

**The learning and teaching of Blessed Alcuin**

### CXLVII

We do not think that, even in our own times, anyone will wish or be able to make doubtful or to dispute the praise of learning belonging to Blessed Alcuin, whose life we have thus far described according to our modest ability and whose works, discovered after the first edition, we now publish. Indeed, no one in the future will fail to judge him superior to all the illustrious men of his age who gained distinction through some reputation for learning.

The many testimonies to be produced later—of those who lived with him, of those who followed close after him, and finally of those who, down to our own times, have mentioned him among illustrious men and ecclesiastical writers—amply demonstrate how high an opinion was always held of his vast learning and unimpaired teaching in faith and morals.

What is more, his own works and studies on subjects of various kinds, by which he enriched the Church and the commonwealth of letters, most clearly prove that there was scarcely any art or science—if medicine alone is excepted—which he did not teach, which he did not treat in his writings, and which he did not strive, with entirely successful effort, to illuminate according to the genius of his own age and of his time. He was a grammarian, rhetorician, poet, philosopher, theologian, and even—although some deny it—a jurist.

Indeed, contrary to what D. Mabillon believed in the preface to Part I of the fourth century of the Benedictine history, no. 176, certain records of his knowledge of laws and jurisprudence survive. We believe that these include both the *Dialogue on Rhetoric*, in which he discusses with his disciple Charles Augustus many subjects relating to Roman law, and certain capitularies of Frankish law, in the compilation of which that same most wise legislator also made use of Alcuin’s assistance, as Benedict the Levite testifies in the preface to Book V of the *Capitularies*, volume I, Baluze edition, page 806.

### CXLVIII

This master possessed an excellent command of the Latin language, although he sometimes appears to depart from the rules of grammatical art. He himself reveals the cause of this deficiency in Letter 85 to his David, where he writes:

> “As for the fact that in letters or punctuation the writing does not proceed as scholastically as the order and rule of grammatical art requires, this is often caused by the speed of the mind, when the reader’s attention hastens to run ahead of the work of the eyes. Nor, fatigued by pain in my head, can I examine what suddenly flies from the mouth of the one dictating.”

Nor should we doubt that Alcuin was fairly well versed in Greek and was not wholly a stranger to Hebrew. His Greek learning is attested by Letter 23 (now 27) to Homer, where he examines certain particles of the Greek language with complete critical precision.

As for his knowledge of Hebrew, however, nothing at all remains from which we can determine how far he advanced in it. The passages sometimes cited by certain writers in Alcuin’s favor—from the *Questions and Answers on Genesis*, the *Commentary on Ecclesiastes*, or the *Interpretations of the Hebrew Names of Christ’s Forefathers*—do not come from Alcuin’s own treasury but are copied almost in their entirety from D. Jerome. This was also observed by the most learned Vallarsius of Verona in the preface to volume IX of the works of Saint Jerome, in the latest edition of 1738.

For this reason, that very learned man also rejects the opinion of a recent admirer of Alcuin, Hody, who asserted that Blessed Alcuin, when correcting copies of Sacred Scripture, had also employed knowledge of the original Hebrew and Greek languages. D. Vallarsius says in the same place that Alcuin did not undertake this task for himself, nor did he have the intention of consulting the original texts. His entire effort consisted in gathering Jerome’s version manuscripts from every quarter and carefully comparing them with one another, so that he might determine which reading ought to be approved on the basis of the authority of those manuscripts that appeared to be of better correction and quality.

Although this is so, it is nevertheless exceedingly probable that Alcuin, always eager for every kind of learning, wished to learn everything for which he had an opportunity to learn in his native England.

Certainly, we have an unimpeachable witness for the long flourishing of the study of the sacred languages there, extending into Alcuin’s own time: the Venerable Bede. In Book IV, chapter 2, of his *History of the English People*, he testifies that in his own time there survived among the disciples of Bishop Theodore and Abbot Hadrian men “who knew the Latin and Greek languages equally as their own, in which they had been born.”

The study of the sacred languages likewise flourished in the school at York, as is evident from the collection of books preserved there, which Alcuin describes in these verses of his poem *On the Pontiffs of the Church of York*:

> There you will find the traces of the ancient Fathers:  
> Whatever the Roman possesses in the Latin world,  
> Whatever illustrious Greece has transmitted to the Latins,  
> Whatever the Hebrew people drank in the heavenly rain,  
> Whatever Africa scattered with its light-bearing radiance.

The Venerable Bede himself therefore knew these languages; his disciples knew them; Blessed Alcuin’s teachers knew them. Why should Alcuin himself, so diligent a disciple of theirs, not also have mastered them? The same conclusion follows from the testimony of his disciple Joseph, whom he instructed, when abridging Blessed Jerome’s *Commentaries on Isaiah*, to follow the path of the Hebrew truth, as we stated above, no. 48.

Most writers of England agree on this matter, especially John Bale, who, relying on the authority of the Annals of the University of Cambridge, says that “Alcuin was skilled in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew.” Nor do the Magdeburg Centuriators deny this, when in Century VIII, column 777, they say that Alcuin acquired knowledge of the Latin, Greek, and Hebrew languages.

### CXLIX. On the Style Which Blessed Alcuin Used in His Many and Various Short Works

It is difficult to render a fair judgment concerning the style that blessed Alcuin used in so many and varied works; for not everyone always forms the same opinion of a particular writer’s style. This difficulty increases when the writings of some ancient author must be recovered from old transcript copies, frequently transcribed with very many errors, while almost all of the author’s autograph manuscripts have perished. For the errors and lacunae found in them alter the style and sometimes make it obscure, difficult, and less fluent.

The style of the same author likewise sometimes changes according to the diversity of the subjects treated. Thus, in Alcuin you will notice one style in his letters, another in his theological, dogmatic, and polemical treatises, and another in his philosophical works. This diversity also proceeds from the fact that he adapts himself to the style of those writers whose lights he has used—now Jerome, now Augustine, now Gregory the Great, now Bede, and now others.

[Col. 0082B]

I therefore think that the judgment concerning his own proper style should be formed chiefly from his letters, from his books against Felix and Elipandus, and from his poems. In the letters—at least those that we possess corrected and complete—I do not know what there is to criticize in his style. Against Felix and Elipandus he uses a modest and serious style, suitable for refuting and correcting opponents. Several poems, to which greater care was evidently devoted—such as that on the Bishops of York, on the vicissitudes of human affairs, on studies at the king’s court, on the Nightingale, on the Cuckoo, and so forth—are not without talent, flavor, and certain poetic sparks.

Nevertheless, we do not claim that the style of these poems, letters, and other writings is to be compared with the style of Cicero, Virgil, and the like, or with that in which Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, and others became famous.

[Col. 0082C]

We are certain of this: Alcuin’s style is better than any that could reasonably be expected from a writer of his age, which was still largely obscure; and it is equally as good as the style of many Latin writers of our own age, in which we grieve that the Latin language is neglected and despised in many schools, to the greatest detriment of literary culture unless a remedy is supplied.

But concerning this matter, as also concerning Alcuin’s literary learning in grammatical, philosophical, mathematical, and other subjects, let learned men themselves judge from the works placed before them. We likewise leave for the attention of scholars and the knowledge of readers a large part of those doctrines concerning faith and morals that blessed Alcuin himself held in mind and commended to his disciples, lest we become excessively prolix in reviewing them individually. Nevertheless, it is useful to recall the principal ones in separate paragraphs, so that it may be understood what care, what religious system, and what purity and integrity of moral discipline existed in those times.

[Col. 0082D]

## § I. On the Canon of Sacred Scripture

### CL. 

He judges the complete canon of the sacred books, which he describes in poem 6, to possess such authority that:

> “Concerning these no one is now permitted to doubt.”

He immediately gives the reason in these verses:

> “For these books truly have a heavenly origin,  
> since the Spirit of God himself dictated them.”

We have thought it necessary to warn the reader here that the final verses, which close the complete poem in the Vienna manuscript, are found appended to the first part of the same poem in a nearly contemporary manuscript, discovered later in the library of the College of Saint Paul at Regensburg. There, after the verse:

> “For Christ’s praise and for salvation throughout the ages,”

[Col. 0083A]

they read:

> “When the sacred books had been utterly burned  
> by hostile devastation, Ezra, fervent for God, restored this work.”

D. Lambecius, from whom we borrowed this poem, reads *Et Rado*—“And Rado”—where the text has *Ezra Deo*, through an easy error in reading ancient script: namely, taking *Ez* for *Et*, and overlooking in the final syllable *do* the stroke placed above it, which indicates that *Deo* is to be read instead of *do*. The distinguished Gentilottus has already noted this omission in Lambecius in the *Analecta Vindobonensia* of D. Kollarius, vol. I, p. 630, although that eminent man was himself deceived, thinking that the stroke indicated the letter *n* and that *Radon* should be read instead of *Rado*.

We, however, have no doubt that in the Vienna manuscript, as also in that of the College of Saint Paul at Regensburg, one should read not *Et Rado*—“And Rado”—but *Ezra Deo*—“Ezra, for God.” Ezra is Esdras, as is clear from this verse of the same poem:

> “Hence the little book of Ezra, Nehemiah, Judith, and Esther.”

Indeed, many have believed that Esdras restored the sacred books once burned or lost during the Babylonian captivity.

[Col. 0083B]

D. Calmet discussed this controversy learnedly in the dissertation prefixed to his commentary on the Books of Esdras.

The common opinion that has prevailed until now—that Rado, abbot of Saint-Vaast, had the sacred Codex restored through the work of blessed Alcuin for his monastery—therefore loses its plausibility. Alcuin makes no mention of this work either in Letter 46 (now 51) to the monks of Saint-Vaast, although in that letter he mentions the titles of the churches and altars dictated by him, as well as the Masses and homily that he composed in honor of Saint Vaast for the use of the monks of Saint-Vaast; nor does he mention it at all in poem 41, in which he lists all the ornaments and gifts presented by Rado to the church and monastery of Saint Vaast.

I shall therefore believe that Alcuin added that poem to the sacred Codex corrected by him at the command of Charlemagne and, in Lambecius’s judgment, still surviving in the Vienna library.

[Col. 0083C]

The note that we previously gave concerning the same poem 6, at the verse *Rado*, must therefore be corrected, since at that time we had not yet seen the manuscript of Saint Paul.

### CLI. 

In the first part of the aforementioned poem, the Book of Tobit is omitted, unless a verse is missing there, perhaps omitted through the copyist’s carelessness; for in the second part, which in both manuscripts is joined to the first without a new title, the same book is also included.

Alcuin believes that the author of the Book of Revelation is John, who wrote the Gospel and reclined upon the Lord’s breast at the Supper. He places the Book of Ecclesiasticus among the Scriptures inspired by God in chapter 14 of *On the Virtues*, addressed to Count Guido; and in chapter 17 of the same work he praises it as Holy Scripture. Nevertheless, in Book I against Elipandus, no. 18, when answering an argument drawn from Ecclesiasticus 36:14, he seems somewhat doubtful whether that book should be counted among the prophetic or sacred books, because Saints Jerome and Isidore number it among the apocrypha. See, however, what we noted concerning that passage in the place cited.

[Col. 0083D]

## § II. On the Trinity and the Incarnation

### CLII. 

Just as blessed Alcuin followed the teaching of the holy Fathers and the primitive Church as his norm concerning the canon of the books of Holy Scripture, so too did he follow it in all the other dogmas of the faith.
