He could not be turned away from it, especially concerning the mysteries of the Trinity and the Incarnation, by any subtleties or arguments of heretics or philosophers. Rather, in his books on the Trinity he gently instilled those dogmas, always received in the Church, into his disciples; and in his books against Felix and Elipandus he defended them vigorously.

He openly professed that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, of one substance, one essence, and one power. He professes the Father to be from himself, the Son begotten from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeding equally from the Father and the Son. In Book I *On the Trinity* he teaches that Christ is at once true God and true man in the unity of person; likewise in Book III, chapter 14, of the same work, and in Book I against Elipandus, no. 21. He teaches that the blessed Virgin is truly the Mother of God, in the same work and in Book VI against Felix, no. 9.

[Col. 0084A]

I do not wish to set out more of these matters at length here, since his teaching concerning these mysteries is abundantly available in the cited books on the Trinity and against the aforementioned authors of Adoptionism.

## § III. On Grace and Free Will

### CLIII. 

Blessed Alcuin teaches and defends in various places both the freedom of the will and the necessity of grace. Thus, in Book II *On the Trinity*, chapter 8, he says:

> “If there is no grace of God, how is the world saved? And if there is no free will, how will the world be judged?”

In the same place he says:

> “Without the assistance of divine grace, free will can neither be converted to God nor make progress in God.”

In Letter 55 (now 69) he prays for prevenient and subsequent grace in these words:

> “Grant the will and the accomplishment; grant that your mercy may go before us to begin, and follow after us to complete.”

Concerning accompanying grace and perseverance, he writes in Letter 76 (now [Col. 0084B] 91):

> “We are born in sins, but by grace we are reborn; and may that grace accompany us as we run in good works and make us persevere to the end.”

Finally, in chapter 9, verse 11, of his *Commentary on Ecclesiastes*, he says that the Pelagian sect is destroyed by the Apostle’s words in Romans 9:16, “It depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy,” because:

> “Without the grace of God, there will be neither a good will in a human being nor the power to perform a course of good works without God.”

## § IV. On Baptism and Confirmation

### CLIV. 

Concerning baptism, in Book II against Felix, no. 16, he teaches that no one could receive adoption as sons of God or remission of sins in the baptism of John. In Book II on John, chapter 5, he teaches that someone baptized by a heretic, schismatic, or any criminal should not be rebaptized if the confession of the Holy Trinity was made.

In his letter on the ceremonies of baptism and in Letter 75 (now 90), he describes the rites of baptism and confirmation according to the practice of the Church and the teaching of the holy Fathers. In the same letter to the people of Lyons, and in Letter 97 (now 113) to Paulinus, he reproves certain Spaniards who, “contrary to the universal custom of the Church,” affirm that under the invocation of the Trinity only one immersion should be performed in baptism.

In the same letter to Paulinus he also accuses others of error who, wishing to perform a threefold immersion, repeat the invocation of the Trinity at each immersion, naming the three persons three times:

> “What need is there to repeat a third time what is sufficient when said once?”

In the cited letter to the people of Lyons he proves the necessity of three immersions by the authority of Pope Saint Leo, Saint Jerome, and Saint Ambrose. Concerning the letter of Saint Gregory the Great to Leander, bishop of Seville, which had been brought against him, he remained uncertain whether it was Gregory’s or had been written under his name by some author of that party:

> “For we did not find it in his book of letters, which was brought to us from Rome.”

[Col. 0084D]

Alcuin must therefore be pardoned for having delivered a harsher judgment against those Spaniards who maintained a single immersion. For he was an extreme opponent of every novelty in the Church and adhered to the practice that prevailed in his time in the Roman Church and in the churches of England, Gaul, and Italy, as well as to the teaching of the holy Fathers whom he cited. Among these may be counted Tertullian, in *Against Praxeas* and *On the Soldier’s Crown*; Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, in *Catechesis* II; Saint Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 27; and others cited by Martène, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, vol. I, p. 129, no. 7; and finally Paulinus of Aquileia, in the treatise that D. Mansi, after we had discovered it long ago in the Salzburg library, inserted into his new edition of the Councils, vol. XIII, p. 921.

This controversy continued for some time after Alcuin and was finally settled at the Council of Worms in 868, where canon 5 decrees that both practices—namely, single and triple immersion—are to be held correct and irreproachable in the holy Church of God.

[Col. 0085A]

### CLV. 

Basnage, volume II of Canisius’s *Thesaurus Monumentorum*, p. 397, note (h), on the letter to the people of Lyons, where Alcuin writes that the three nights and three days during which Jonah was in the belly of the whale and Christ in the heart of the earth can, by synecdoche, signify the three immersions and three elevations in baptism, attacks him in these words:

> “Alcuin was enamored of numbers, and therefore childishly tried to extract mysteries from them to the point of absurdity.”

In my opinion, Basnage did not consider that this sharp criticism simultaneously attacks the earlier Fathers, who certainly were not children—and specifically the most holy and renowned pontiff Leo I, who interpreted the words of Saint Paul in Romans 6:3 in the same way. Relying on Leo’s authority, Alcuin cites his words there from Letter 17 to the bishops of Sicily, which read:

> “The threefold immersion imitates the three-day burial, and the raising from the waters is like the one who rises from the tomb.”

[Col. 0085B]

Let impartial judges of these matters determine what is childish in this interpretation, and whether Basnage’s criticism of the ancient teachers of the Church is not itself more childish.

## § V. On the Confession of Sins

### CLVI. 

Alcuin compares penance with baptism and calls it the second baptism in the Church, by which we are cleansed through humble confession made to priests from the sins committed after the first baptism.

> “Do we not,” he says in Letter 96 (now 112) to the monks of Gothia, “in holy baptism owe to the priests of Christ the confession of our faith, and are we not thus, through the priestly ministry and by the operation of divine grace, cleansed from all sins? Why, then, in the second baptism of penance, through the confession of our humility, should we not likewise, by the same merciful divine grace and priestly assistance, be absolved from all the sins committed after the first baptism?”

And in Letter 79 (now 94) to Aquila, he impresses upon pastors of souls that they should encourage the faithful to purity of confession and contrition in penance:

> “For this is the second baptism in the Church: whoever has fallen into some offense after the first baptism is corrected in this second one.”

Moreover, in the cited letter to the Goths, he reproves and refutes a wicked custom that had taken root in that province: laypeople refused to confess their sins to priests, thinking it sufficient to confess them secretly to God.

He proves the necessity of confession to priests, first, from the fact that Christ gave priests the power to bind and loose:

> “What does priestly power loose if it does not consider the bonds of the one who is bound?”

Second, he proves it from the example of the lepers whom the Lord sent to the priests to be healed; and third, from the example of Lazarus, whom he commanded to be loosed through the disciples:

> “Could he not, by the same word with which he commanded the dead man to come forth from the tomb restored to life, have loosed the dead man’s burial wrappings?”

Fourth, he proves it from the example of David, who accused himself of his sin before the prophet Nathan:

> “He disclosed his wound to a human being and immediately received a remedy from God.”

[Col. 0085B]

He proves the same point from the Sacramentary of the Church, saying:

> “If sins are not to be disclosed to priests, why are prayers of reconciliation written in the Sacramentary? How does a priest reconcile someone whose sin he does not know?”

Finally, he asserts that confession is necessary for those who have made themselves liable to grave sins either by consent, by action, or by an evil habit. He compares such people with the three dead whom Christ raised. Confession is necessary for them as preparation for worthily receiving the body and blood of Jesus Christ:

> “Consider these things, dearest brothers, and if anyone lies in any one of these three kinds of death, let him hasten to the most approved remedies of confession . . . so that he may receive the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ not for the judgment of condemnation but for the salvation of sanctification.”

Blessed Alcuin gives similar instructions concerning the necessity and usefulness of confessing sins to priests to the brothers at Tours, vol. II, p. 154.

[Col. 0086A]

In Letter 39 (now 44), he also urges Flavius Damoetas, as he prepares to set out to fight the enemy, first to expiate his sins by confession. Canisius praises this as an ancient military custom; we have quoted his words in the notes to the cited letter.

## § VI. On the Eucharist

### CLVII. 

Blessed Alcuin’s mind and judgment concerning the mystery of the Eucharist and the dogma of transubstantiation are known from several of his letters, namely Letters 36, 75, and 124 (now 41, 90, and 163). He expresses it especially in Letter 41, where he asks Paulinus in these words:

> “Please do not forget the name of your friend Albinus in your holy prayers, but store it in some treasury of memory and bring it forth at the fitting time when you consecrate the bread and wine into the substance of Christ’s body and blood.”

No testimony more clearly supportive of the dogma of transubstantiation believed at that time could certainly be given.

> “This is our faith, this is the faith of our ancestors”—  
> an observation found in the words of the learned D. Mabillon, *On Gallican Liturgy*, p. 95, Paris edition of 1729—  
> “which I wish our estranged brothers would finally, even if late, acknowledge, and no longer challenge us with that fictitious innovation which they accuse Paschasius Radbertus of introducing in the ninth century. The authority of Alcuin alone, so clear and manifest, ought to settle this controversy . . . Whoever detracts from the credibility of such evident words is a lover not of truth but of contention, error, and schism.”

D. Basnage attempted to corrupt this meaning of Alcuin in volume II of his *Church History*, Book V, pp. 899 and following. We refuted him in our observations on his criticisms directed against D. Mabillon’s discussion of the author of the *Booklet of the Confession of Faith*, volume II, p. 384.

[Col. 0086B]

### CLVIII. 

At that time there was an opinion among certain people in Spain that salt should be placed in, or mixed with, the sacrifice—that is, with the matter of the Eucharistic bread. Blessed Alcuin rejects this in Letter 75 (now 90), asserting:

> “Neither does the universal Church observe that custom, nor does Roman authority preserve it. There are three things to be offered in the sacrifice: bread, water, and wine . . . The bread that is consecrated into Christ’s body must be perfectly pure, without the leaven of any other contamination; the water must be completely pure, without any defilement; and the wine must be thoroughly pure, without any mixture of another liquid except water. From water and flour the bread is made that is consecrated into Christ’s body; water and wine will be consecrated into Christ’s blood.”

[Col. 0086C]

These words demonstrate with the greatest clarity that the use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist was almost universal in Alcuin’s time, and therefore before the schism of Photius—not only in Britain, where he was born, and in Gaul, where he lived for a long time, but also in the Roman Church and throughout the whole Western Church. D. Mabillon demonstrated this learnedly, in his usual manner, in the dissertation *On Unleavened and Leavened Bread*, chapter 9, volume I of the posthumous works, p. 155.

[Col. 0086D]

### CLIX. 

To this passage of Alcuin, which we have just transcribed, D. Basnage adds the following note:

> “It could easily be proved that the Spanish theologians of that time were not advocates of transubstantiation, if we were permitted to draw an argument from the salt mixed with the bread.”

Wonderful! Why should it not be permissible to draw an argument by which the truth of something could easily be proved? If we rightly understand Basnage, it could easily be proved from salt mixed with the bread that the Spanish theologians of that time were not advocates of transubstantiation. Yet he was not permitted to use that argument.

What prevented him? The learned man knew well enough from other, stronger documents and testimonies that the Spanish theologians of that time, as also in earlier periods, were advocates of transubstantiation. It was therefore not permissible to oppose to them a very weak argument derived from the custom of certain people of putting salt into the sacrifice—just as it is not permissible to argue from the use of leavened bread that the Greeks are not advocates of transubstantiation.

The learned man would therefore have been wiser to suppress this note.

## § VII. On the Intercession of the Saints, Purgatory, and Prayer for the Dead

[Col. 0087A]

### CLX. 

Among the dogmas of the Catholic faith are also included blessed Alcuin’s teachings concerning the intercession of the saints, purgatory, and prayer for the dead. It would be lengthy to set out here all the passages in which blessed Alcuin’s belief concerning the invocation and intercession of the saints—whom the Church venerates as blessed and rejoicing in the vision of God in heaven—is made clear.

It will suffice to cite at least two testimonies: one by which he inspires others with confidence in the prayers of the saints, and another showing his own confidence in their intercession. To the brothers at Tours he writes in Letter 19 (now 23):

> “O happy household, rejoicing in such a shepherd . . . For you have the grace of God assisting you, and a great intercessor, namely Saint Martin, praying for you; because, since you stand every day in his service in his house, you have him in heaven as your advocate at every hour.”

For himself he prays in this manner to Saint [Col. 0087B] Willibrord, vol. II, p. 195:

> “O most blessed priest of Christ, do not abandon us laboring on earth, but do not cease to help us from heaven through your prayers. Your life among human beings was always proved for God; may your prayers before God always be earnestly offered for human beings . . . O happy soul, who have left behind the labors of the world and entered heavenly rest with the fruit of your many toils . . . We believe that in the presence of the Lord your God you can obtain everything that you ask, and so forth.”

From these words it is also clear that blessed Alcuin had no doubt that holy men enjoy God’s presence and vision in heaven before the day of the final judgment. Indeed, in Letter 97 he reproves those who held the contrary opinion as wounding the unity of the holy Catholic Church and the truth of the universal faith.

### CLXI. 

Concerning the purifying fire of certain just persons, he writes in Book III *On the Faith of the Trinity*, chapter 21:

> “There are certain just people subject to some minor sins [Col. 0087C] who have built upon the foundation, which is Christ, hay, wood, and straw; these are purified by the heat of that fire, and once cleansed from them they will be made worthy of the glory of eternal happiness.”

Alcuin depicts this fire in his poem on the Bishops of York, verse 905, and verses 987 and following.

He teaches that the intercessions of the living benefit these souls in Letter 134 (now 178) to Eadberht, bishop of Hexham, in these words:

> “The suffrages of the living benefit the dead, either for the forgiveness of sins or for an increase of glory.”

In Letter 151 (now 200) to Eadgifu he writes:

> “If two people are friends, the death of the one who goes before is happier than that of the one who follows; for the former has someone who, out of fraternal love, intercedes for him daily and washes away the errors of his former life with tears. Do not doubt that the care of pious solicitude that you show for his soul is beneficial. It benefits both you and him: you, because you act in faith and love; him, so that either his punishment may be lightened or his blessedness increased.”

## § VIII. On the Church

[Col. 0087D]

### CLXII. 

To avoid being too lengthy in reviewing blessed Alcuin’s teachings concerning the dogmas of the faith, it will suffice to mention one further point: this teacher, whom the Western Church of his age scarcely had anyone greater, and certainly no one more renowned, consistently adhered to the authority of the Catholic and Roman Church. He urged his disciples, and all others whom he knew to attribute too much to their private judgment, personal knowledge, and spirit, to follow that authority.

In Letter 15 (now 18), he recognizes Hadrian I, the Roman pontiff, as the vicar of Saint Peter and heir of that wondrous power of binding and loosing. In Letter 20 (now 24), he calls Leo III a pontiff elected by God, the vicar of the apostles, heir of the Fathers, prince of the Church, and nurturer of the one immaculate dove.

[Col. 0088A]

In Letter 75 (now 90) to the brothers at Lyons, he writes:

> “Let no Catholic dare to contend against the authority of the Church. And lest he be found a schismatic rather than a Catholic, let him follow the most firmly established authority of the holy Roman Church, so that from the place where we receive the beginnings of the Catholic faith, we may always receive the models of our salvation; lest the members be separated from their head; lest the bearer of the keys of the heavenly kingdom cast out those whom he understands to have departed from his teachings.”

For this reason, in Book I against Felix, no. 6, he calls “the Roman Church the head of the other churches.” In Book VII, no. 13, he teaches that “the Roman Church is to be followed by Catholics and those who believe rightly.”

### CLXIII. 

This was the teaching of that most renowned master of all Gaul, France, Germany, and England, and of that illustrious doctor of the eighth-century Church. It was not newly fabricated, but handed down from the time of the apostles and preserved amid the earlier clouds of ignorance and barbarism.

This was the faith of the supreme and most powerful king and emperor, Charlemagne. This was the faith of all the pontiffs of that age, of orthodox princes, archbishops and bishops, and of all faithful Christians. It is therefore astonishing that in more recent times even among learned and educated men there should have been some who wished to assign or fabricate a more recent origin for those dogmas.

[Col. 0088B]

Yet this is the laborious but fruitless diligence of the heterodox, by which they attempt to draw from themselves a spirit of innovation and to cover their own inventions with the disguise of antiquity.

### CLXIV. 

Canisius states in the preface to the reader of Alcuin’s *Dialectic*, volume II of Basnage’s edition of the *Ancient Lessons*, p. 486, that Calvin assumed the name of this orthodox doctor at the beginning, by a mere transposition of letters, through the utmost fraud and imposture.

Spondanus says something similar in volume III of his *Church Annals*, Ticinum edition, p. 61, no. 9, where he writes:

> “He himself—Calvin—at one time called himself Alcuin by transposing the letters, as in the Strasbourg edition of his *Institutes* of the year 1539, imitating the name of that great Alcuin who was the teacher of Charlemagne.”

The *Commentaries of Alcuin—or rather of Calvin—on the Books on the Trinity* are likewise listed in the Index of Expurgated Books, which D. Basnage cites in his observations on the same *Dialectic of Alcuin*, p. 487, and in another Index of Forbidden Books published at Rome in 1704, which we ourselves examined.

[Col. 0088C]

D. Basnage, however, believes that the expurgators, Spondanus, and Canisius were deceived in this matter by a common rumor, and wishes others to believe this until the Strasbourg edition of Calvin’s *Institutes* mentioned by Spondanus appears.

We consider the reasons for his opinion, which D. Basnage presents in the cited place, not contemptible—especially since in the latest edition of the Index, revised by order of Benedict XIV and published in 1758, those commentaries of Alcuin or Calvin are not listed. Instead, they are attributed to Lucas Lossius in these words:

> “Lossius, Lucas: three books of Alcuin, abbot of Tours, on the faith of the holy and indivisible Trinity, illustrated with commentary. Index of Trent.”

Although we have searched extensively for these commentaries, we have not yet been able to obtain them.

### CLXV. 

It would be superfluous to discuss at length here, or to review individually, the teachings concerning Christian morals that blessed Alcuin inculcates everywhere, with the greatest zeal, seriousness, and a certain authority as a teacher, upon people of every rank and condition [Col. 0088D]: kings, princes, judges, military commanders, pontiffs, abbots, monks and nuns, widows and virgins, and entire peoples.

The attentive and devout reader will find them in great abundance not only in his moral works but also in his familiar letters. It would certainly be desirable that in our own times those who are called to the public office of teaching, to the counsels of princes, and to the governance of courts as arbiters of consciences, following Alcuin’s example, would lay aside servile fear and human regard and, modestly but fearlessly, insinuate the truth to the highest and the lowest. In this way they would follow Alcuin’s counsel to Beorninus the priest in Letter 7 (now 8):

> “Whenever, dearest brother, time or place presents itself, always persuade every person to follow God’s will: [Col. 0089A] the king gently, bishops honorably, princes confidently, and everyone truthfully.”

It would also be desirable that princes and other persons of higher rank, following the example of the most powerful king and emperor Charles, would lend benevolent ears to such teachers, counselors, and governors, and protect and support them by their authority against malicious whisperers.

### CLXVI. 

From what we have so far discussed concerning the life of blessed Flaccus Albinus, or Alcuin, from his own writings and works, it can be understood that the praises bestowed upon him by ancient and modern writers are not undeserved. We shall set forth those writers’ testimonies and encomia after his Life, written by an anonymous contemporary and published by the distinguished D. Quercetanus.

The chief thing to praise in so eminent a man is that, although others thought highly of his learning, he himself submitted his writings to the judgment of others with great humility and modesty.

Thus he writes in Letter 67 (now 82), a reply [Col. 0089B] to the lord king:

> “As for your familiar and salutary care, at the end of your letter, to admonish me that if anything requires humble correction it should be corrected: by God’s gift I have never been obstinate in my error, nor confident in my own opinions, nor so constituted that I could not readily assent to a better judgment . . . I beg you to understand this entirely of your wisdom: I write to you not as to one who does not know, but as to one who approves; and I direct [Col. 0090A] the perceptions of my smallness not as to one who is ignorant, but rather as to one who corrects.”

In Letter 85 (now 101) he writes:

> “We give thanks to your revered piety because, according to the command of your instruction, you had the booklet sent to you read aloud to your wise ears, and because you ordered its errors to be marked and sent it back for correction—although it could have been corrected better by you, since another person’s judgment very often has greater value in any work than that of its own author.”

Thus writes, and thus humbly thinks of himself, that great restorer of every branch of learning and first teacher of entire nations, Alcuin. Would that most modern teachers and writers possessed such modesty—those who are so tenacious of their own opinions, even in matters of religion and morals, that they do not permit themselves to be corrected either by ecclesiastical or civil authority.

Would that the princes of the earth also, stirred by the example of the most Christian king and emperor Charles, would use the power and authority they have received from God, oppose by severe laws the audacity of writers of this kind and their alleged freedom to think and write [Col. 0090B], remove booklets harmful both to religion and morals—by which the minds of their subjects must be corrupted—and order those already circulated to be suppressed and burned!

These, then, are the matters concerning the life of blessed Alcuin that we have wished and been able to discuss. The industrious reader will find many other relevant matters in the preliminary notices that we prefixed to almost all of his short works.

# THE LIFE OF BLESSED FLACCUS ALCUIN

First published by D. André Quercetanus from an old manuscript of Saint Mary of Reims.

## PRELIMINARY NOTICE

[Col. 0089C]

The name of the writer of this Life is unknown. Its authority must be assessed from the period in which he lived and from the witness whose report enabled him to learn the deeds of blessed Alcuin.

He undertook this work when Aldric was presiding as abbot over the monastery of Ferrières, as he himself writes below in chapter 10, no. 19. From this it is understood that this Life was written before the year 829, when Aldric, having been abbot, became bishop of Sens.

Moreover, at the beginning and end of the prologue he testifies that he learned the deeds and virtues of blessed Alcuin from his disciple Sigulf, whom he also calls his own instructor. It is therefore highly probable that this anonymous writer was a monk of Ferrières, whose abbot Sigulf had been before Aldric.

André Quercetanus first published this Life from a very old Reims manuscript, written, according to D. Mabillon, in the author’s own period. The Surian edition was made according to the Chesne edition, with chapter divisions added in the margin. We have retained these together with D. Mabillon, although D. Henschen preferred another division for 19 May; he also introduced several corrections into the same work for the reader’s convenience, [Col. 0089D] which we shall indicate everywhere.

## AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

[The supplied source ends here.]

## I

With Christ’s heavenly right hand sprinkling rain and his grace assisting, most reverend Father, equally dear to me, you command me to write for you, in speech perhaps unpolished and from a small source yet filled with truth, what I have been able to learn—reported by the most faithful disciple Sigulf—about the beginning and end of the admirable life of Father Alcuin, for the edification of some. You assert that you have long endured no slight thirst for this account—not because your inward parts, inflamed by heavenly fervor, cannot be refreshed by the lives, pious deeds, and studies of countless saints, whom it is established that they purchased through their own blood or through renunciation of the world and its pleasures, thereby gaining fellowship with the Lamb and with heavenly virtues. Rejoicing with them in one sweet song and an insatiable jubilation, they have made the narrow and constricted way broad and passable by means of garments or palm branches—by which the fruitful mind is adorned—and by having Christ, the humble rider, borne upon the backs of the children of the Hebrews and of the she-ass.

But since, while the world and its concerns grow old and drift away, scarcely anyone can be found who is able to follow in every respect the arduous footsteps of the ancients—those who, the nearer they are proved to have been to the highest Head, the more illustrious they were in the immensity of their deeds, firmly sustaining the Lord’s tabernacle like columns, so that it might never fall or be shaken by the flooding of waters or the assault of winds—you rightly assert that it is therefore most necessary that, if Christ’s grace has granted us someone in our own times whom we should piously imitate, such a lamp should be placed not under a bushel nor beneath the repose of a bed, but upon a lampstand, so that those entering the Church may be illuminated by its clear light.

For the Father of the household himself, who at the first hour and likewise at the eleventh hired laborers for the vineyard and commanded that he give them one wage—if we cannot be hands, or the beard hanging about Christ’s mouth, or teeth white as snow, capable of chewing a crust of bread for little children, or eyes more beautiful than wine by which virgins are nourished, shall we therefore be separated from the desirable body of the Lord? Rather, let us be rooted and founded in the same faith, hope, and charity, according to the Apostle, so that many of us may become one body of the Lord, while the distinction of the stars remains in charity.

## II

Indeed, the apostles were eyes, contemplating as best they could the splendor of the eternal sun through purity of mind, like Peter, chief of the apostles, and the virgin John. The one, avoiding the opinions of many heresies, confessed one person of the living Son of God, consisting of two substances, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 12:16). The other, pouring out his soul within himself and transcending all created things, ascended to him through whom all things were made; and, having drunk from his breasts, he poured forth a mystery unheard of throughout the ages, saying: “In the beginning was the Word,” and so forth.

The blessed martyrs were a brazen breast, preaching clearly, and an iron one, enduring the fires of raging persecutors: Cyprian, Laurence, Dionysius, and Maurice. Holy confessors and teachers arose as a stomach in which the nourishment of doctrines might be stored: Martin, Hilary, Benedict, that outstanding father of monks, Ambrose, Gregory, Jerome, and Augustine.

All these, therefore, rewarded with the Samaritan’s two denarii, devoted within the inn to the wounded man whatever they were able to accomplish by their own labor; now they are gloriously enriched with the wage they awaited.

But now, since iniquity abounds, the apostles—according to the prophecy—and since the charity of many has grown cold, we have become like orphans without a father, sitting upon the knees of our mother, who stands in the middle of the sea and is shaken on every side by the bitterest waves. We need to be fortified by the support of the earlier Fathers and nourished by their life-giving provisions, lest we perish from hunger on the difficult road of our course. Rather, let us leave the ship weighed down with the merchandise of the world and cling truly to the Head, saying: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song of Songs 1:4).

For those who know themselves to be with him know that he—the mountain pleasant to deer seeking the heights—has also deigned to open a refuge for humble hedgehogs, saving both human beings and animals.

## III

Therefore, those whom both excessive age and bodily weakness burden, since they cannot fully follow the ancients, should at least follow the footsteps of those whom clear indications have most certainly proved to have lived together with them in their own time and to have pleased Christ: namely, the monk Benedict, abbot of Aniane,

[Note: “Abbot of Aniane,” that is, Benedict of Aniane.]

and Alcuin, in every respect worthy of canonical imitation.

Obedient to your commands, most holy Father, I shall undertake his life with my pen—not fragrant with the distinction of secular eloquence, but writing of his life with a stammering of sense corresponding to the stammering of my body. I testify before God Jesus that I have not attempted this out of the pride of self-exaltation, but because I desired to benefit the souls of many.

I shall therefore write faithfully what I learned only from his most faithful disciple, namely Sigulf, my instructor and the beloved father whom you too possessed,

[Note: “Father” here means spiritual father.]

who, after the departure of Saint Edbert, alone among all mortals deserved to know his outstanding secrets.

[Note: It may perhaps be necessary to read “Elchbert” here, on the basis of chapter 11 below.]

Therefore, Lord, venerable Father, I beg you to support me in this labor with your pious intercession, since you now command me, who have hitherto kept these things silent, to sound them forth with open mouth.

# CHAPTER I

## Alcuin’s childhood and first studies

### IV

The man of God Albinus sprang from the noble lineage of the English people, but became nobler still when he was reborn through the life-giving waters of Jesus Christ. When he was weaned from his mother’s bodily breasts, he was handed over to the Church to be nourished at her mystical breasts. Even then Jesus, possessing his little body by his gracious favor, did not permit it to be polluted by the foul games and obscene acts of the ancient enemy, since he had predestined it, before Albinus was born, to consecrate his dwelling there.

### V

While he was still a little boy, he often attended church with the others during the daylight hours appointed by the canons, but only rarely at night. When he was still in his tenth year, it happened one night that he lay apart in a house with a simple, tonsured peasant.

That simple peasant had asked the teacher of the distinguished boy, for the comfort of his nighttime solitude, to order some boy from the school to sleep with him in his cell for one night, since he presently had none of his own people with him. By God’s providence, the boy Albinus, who was more a lover of Virgil than of the Psalms, was granted to him.

Now, near cockcrow, as usual the signal for the night watches was sounded by the custodian, and the brothers performed the appointed office. But the simple peasant, turning onto his other side—for he was excessively negligent in such matters—snored as he slept. When the invitatory psalm had already been sung according to custom with its antiphon, the house was suddenly filled with truly dreadful spirits. Surrounding his bed, they said: “You are resting well, brother.”

When he suddenly awoke, they repeated the same words, adding: “Why,” they asked, “while the brothers are keeping watch in church, are you alone snoring here?”

What more need be said? He was usefully beaten so severely that, through this salutary change, he offered all an example of caution and of the chant: “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm 76:11), while his eyes anticipated the night watches.

While he was being beaten, the noble boy, trembling lest the same thing happen to him, said these words in the depths of his heart, as he later testified:

> “O Lord Jesus, if you now rescue me from the bloody hands of these beings, and if thereafter I am not attentive to the watches of your church and the ministries of praise, and if I love the melody of Virgil more than that of the Psalms, then let such a scourge of punishment fall to my lot. I earnestly beg only this: deliver me.”

So that this might be impressed more deeply upon his mind, after the beating of the peasant had ceased at the Lord’s command, the evil spirits, turning their eyes here and there, carefully examined the boy’s whole body and head, wrapped entirely in cloth, while he was completely unaware and breathing. Their leader asked his companions:

> “Who else is resting here in the house?”

“It is Albinus,” they replied, “the boy hidden in the bed.”

When the boy realized that he could not remain concealed, he was flooded with an excessive rain of tears; and, as he had previously been suppressed by fear, he now burst into a great uproar of childish cries. They wished to inflict punishment upon him mercilessly, but were unable to do so, and discussed what they ought to do with him.

Yet, restrained by the Lord’s sentence from satisfying their desire, they foolishly but nevertheless prudently said:

> “Let us not punish him with sharp blows, since he is still inexperienced. Let us correct only his feet, in which the hardness of calluses resides, by cutting them with a knife; and we shall now confirm his promised amendment.”

When his feet had been stripped of their clothing and placed in the hands of the evil ones, Albinus quickly fortified himself with the sign of the cross and, singing Psalm 12 with all his devotion, caused the evil band suddenly to disappear. The half-dead peasant, with the agile boy going ahead of him, fled for refuge to the protection of the saints in the basilica.

### VI

O ambusher of the heel, whose bread is dust, not the grain of the Lord—you who are crushed by the Head! O enemy of the pious! Were you mad, you who once sought, without right, to become a dweller of heaven, seated beside the Most High? If, as you boasted, you were like the Most High on the mountain of God, in the incomprehensible light of radiant splendor, why do you diligently strive under the cover of night to examine your evil acts while kindling darkness against human beings?

Indeed, I shall confess that, as the consequences teach, you rightly judge yourself to have been made the prince of your own darkness by your very presence. For although you appear as an angel of light, you try to take away our inward light with your foul dust.

But if, being an Ethiopian as you are, you attempted to do this to the boy Albinus by instilling excessive fear and thereby dimming the brightness of hope, you have been overcome by a humble human being—you who had overcome the proud human being. Yet if you had known, you would not have crucified the Lord of glory, nor would you have sought to shear the calloused soles of Christ’s worshiper Albinus,

[Note: The words enclosed in brackets in the printed text yield no intelligible sense.]

[“which fruits of deeds you were preparing for yourself unwillingly by wondrous art”; the bracketed text is unintelligible.]

You hid beneath his feet a net of capture, and you yourself, like a bird supported by the wings of a dove, with feet made firm like those of a deer and set on high places, rejoiced to dwell in the wilderness, as David fled from Saul.

You opened a pit and dug it out, and, confused, you fell into it yourself, without the prey you desired. Your own arrows turn their sharp points against you and inflict immeasurable pain.

You fell to the earth, wounding the nations of the saints; you are trampled beneath Albinus’s feet and cast with contempt from the tomb you loved, because the strong one has been defeated by one stronger.

Your heavy scepter, O exactor, and the yoke imposed upon our shoulders have been overcome by a boy who was still too young to call anyone his father or mother. With your spoils, the mother Church adorns herself, forgetful of you and of your people; fruitful in spiritual gifts, she celebrates with the Lord the insignia of heaven in hymns of praise.

We always give thanks to you, Lord, good Jesus, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout the ages. Whatever good we do, begin, or complete belongs to you, according to the one who teaches us your grace and says: “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish” (Philippians 1:13). So too the Psalmist says: “My God, his mercy will come before me” (Psalm 36:11). And again elsewhere: “And your mercy shall follow me all the days of my life” (Psalm 22:6). You yourself also said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

# CHAPTER II

## Alcuin is entrusted to Hechbert’s discipline in the monastery at York

### VII

When matters concerning the beginning of the aforementioned boy had thus begun, he thereafter advanced, in a certain likeness to the Lord, in age and wisdom and in true, living philosophy, obeying his commands more closely.

After he had recited from memory a reading from the Psalms, he was handed over to Hechbert, bishop and most learned disciple of Bede of the English people, as to a teacher like himself, to be fed—as though ignorant of milk—already upon strong food.

[Note: Hechbert was Egbert, said to have been the brother of King Eadberht; he succeeded Saint Wilfrid II in the archbishopric of York in 732.]

Seeing Christ’s lofty grace shining vigorously in the boy, since he was exceptionally perceptive, Hechbert gradually began to reveal his own secrets to him more privately, rejoicing because he had discovered that Alcuin would most certainly become his imitator.

He had a school of boys, sons of noblemen. Some were instructed in the rudiments of grammar; others in the disciplines of the liberal arts; others in the divine Scriptures. After rubbing these in the Father’s hands, they conveyed into their own breast five barley ears and seven wheat ears, together with a pair of fish.

All were instructed with equal care and the greatest propriety in faith, hope, charity, humility, fasting, chastity, obedience, and the most devoted attention to the offices of the Church. They were shaped not so much by words as by the example of the holy father Hechbert, a Christian bishop worthy in every respect. In him the teaching that had shone forth in his own teachers was brilliantly displayed: in Gregory, the holy apostle of the English; in Augustine, his disciple; in Saint Benedict; and likewise in Cuthbert and Theodore, who followed the first Father and apostle in every respect . . .

and in the man exceedingly beloved by the Lord, the presbyter Bede, his own teacher. From the beginning of his life, Bede had been consecrated to the Lord like Samuel. Unacquainted with any defilement of garment, he was entrusted by his parents to monastic rules and strengthened by his example whatever he taught in word.

After he had fought the good fight, completed his course, and kept the faith, and had doubled his Lord’s talent with interest, on the day he wished and requested—namely, the day on which Christ, the King of glory and triumphator over all, ascended into heaven, in the year 731 from the Lord’s incarnation,

[Note: Rather, in the year 735. See Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, century 3, part 1, in the eulogy of the Venerable Bede. See also above, in the Life composed by us, chapter 3, sections 11 and following.]

on the seventh day before the Kalends of June—having completed 127 years since the death of Saint Gregory, he departed to the Lord at the age of ninety,

[Note: This tradition could easily have been corrected by reading Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History*, at whose conclusion Bede testifies that he was putting the final hand to the work at the age of fifty-nine in the year 731, whereas this author wrongly places his death in that year. Mabillon.]

as some assert. In the nineteenth year of his age he became a deacon, and in the thirtieth a priest. From that time until his fifty-ninth year, with diligent labor, he endeavored to insert into books worthy of remembrance whatever he had learned during the preceding thirty years for the benefit of the Church. For another thirty years, they say, he corrected what he had written and also instructed his disciples to no small degree in all the liberal arts.

Before he fell ill, he dictated and composed, with his own melody, this antiphon, highly suitable to the solemn occasion:

[Note: Bede did not compose this antiphon; rather, in a letter his disciple Cuthbert records that, when near death, he frequently used it: “According to our custom and his own,” says Cuthbert. Mabillon.]

> “O King of glory, Lord of hosts, who today ascended triumphantly above all the heavens, do not leave us orphans, but send upon us the Spirit of truth promised by the Father. Alleluia.”

Hechbert, following Bede’s footsteps, devoted his entire treasure to the Lord’s words, searching out the inner chambers of the Scriptures. From sunrise, unless unavoidable hindrance intervened, or some outstanding solemnity or great festival of the saints occurred, he very often remained in bed until about the sixth hour, and sometimes until the ninth, unfolding to each of his disciples the mysteries of Scripture appropriate to him.

Then he would rise and flee to the most private prayer, offering the Lord rich holocausts with incense and rams. Afterward, following the example of blessed Job (Job 1:5), lest his sons should fall into the pit of blessing—or, as the variant reading has it, the pit of cursing—he sanctified them, offering Christ’s body and blood for all.

Finally, as evening approached—especially outside Lent—he took at all times, in summer as in winter, a frugal but suitably prepared meal with his companions. He did not spare the reader’s tongue, so that he might be refreshed by both kinds of bread.

You would then have seen the boys before the Father sharpening themselves with prepared weapons, discussing privately what they would afterward unfold publicly in due order. Is it not possible to say of this also: “As an eagle stirs up its nestlings to fly, and hovers over them, spreading its wings, taking them up and carrying them upon its shoulders” (Deuteronomy 32:11)?

# CHAPTER III

## The religious devotion of the adolescent Alcuin

### VIII

Alcuin, adorned with the flower of adolescence, surpassed all these in humility under instruction.

Hechbert,

[Note: Clearly Hechbert.]

the father of the poor, a great lover and helper of Christ, was accustomed to pour out the most private prayer twice a day, with the watering of a purest spring, kneeling with both knees on the ground and raising his hands toward heaven in the form of a cross for a long time—before taking food, and before celebrating Compline with all his companions.

After Compline had been celebrated, none of his disciples ever dared commit his limbs to bed without first receiving his blessing upon his head.

He loved them all, but loved Albinus especially, because of the distance between their merits, since Albinus was the most faithful follower of his deeds. Among his other virtues, this was granted to him in particular: he never chose to do anything on his own unless the authority of his teacher, approving it, had granted it;

[Note: Perhaps “concederet,” “granted,” rather than “conderet.”]

and he never endured any of the enemy’s inward schemes or snares that he would conceal outwardly from his teacher without any embarrassment.

As a result, he conquered most gloriously by this wondrous method the goad of untamable lust that he had once experienced: he dashed the Babylonian infants against the rock, crushing the head of the serpent that lay in wait for his heel.

He was careful lest Christ’s words be spoken of him: “Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved” (John 3:20). Rather, he desired to belong to those of whom it follows: “But whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be revealed, because they have been done in God.”

O true monk—a monk without a vow,

[Note: The Rule of Saint Benedict prescribes in chapter 8 that monks should not conceal from their abbot the evil thoughts that arise in their hearts. Mabillon.]

whose example a monk bound by duty is very rarely found to follow.

Let us therefore imitate Albinus, the pious youth of the Lord, fleeing the palpable Egyptian darkness. Let us turn night into day and, after darkness, hope for light, escaping from the prison of the prince of darkness.

Let us diligently remember the scales of Behemoth, by which his body is compacted, each pressing against the next: one is joined to another, and not even a gap enters between them; one clings to another, and those holding each other cannot be overcome. His strength is in his loins, and the sinews of his testicles are intertwined. He sleeps beneath the shade, in the secrecy of the reed, and in damp places.

We rejoice, Albinus, in your corrected childhood, while God uses the enemy’s malice for your good. We venerate the purity of your mind in adolescence and your most steadfast strength in the great contest. In that great contest, the flesh, often stirred by the spirit of combat, and the bones—which in many cannot enjoy peaceful rest—remain unharmed in you while the Lord guards you.

You deserved to have the Lord Christ as the guest of your mind. With him protecting you, you could say:

> “In you I shall escape temptation, and in you I shall leap over a wall; you have made my way blameless and my arms like a brazen bow.”

Let us therefore see with what darts this soldier is again sought out and torn from the opposite side, and let us arm ourselves with the invincible weapons of the ancient Fathers, after the manner of the army of Judas Maccabee.

# CHAPTER IV

## He overcomes the envy of his companions and is carried into ecstasy

### IX

13 Kalends of December.

[Note: The year was 766, in the thirty-fourth year of his episcopate. See the poem on the bishops of York, book 2, verses 1284 and 1395.]

After Alcuin had been deprived by the loss of his father Hechbert, by divine gift he received in place of the one he had lost the blessed and illustrious man Ealhbeorht, who was in every respect like his teacher.

When Alcuin surpassed his companions not only in the beauty of wisdom but also in other virtues, appearing second to none, he perceived that in many matters their hearts were disturbed by the spirit of envy at his progress. They could not look upon him with a clear eye or address him with gentle words.

When he consulted his teacher about this, Ealhbeorht urged him to heap burning coals upon their heads by acts of kindness. Having heard his father’s most salutary advice, Alcuin did not cease from his rational intention

[Variant: “orationis,” “prayer,” rather than “rationis,” “intention.”]

until he had obtained evident spiritual healing from the Lord. He repeatedly placed himself beneath their feet, even when they unjustly reproved him, lest they hear any word from his mouth contrary to the teacher’s command.

Thus, when they had suddenly been changed, they rejoiced to have every sort of affection for him from the Master. The little ruler was drawn by the hand of the weaned child from the cave in which he lay, and gentle embraces like those of doves were established there.

The virtues of the saints are certainly great, through which bodies are healed; but those by which souls are cured must be considered no less worthy of wonder and veneration.

Let us venerate Albinus, therefore, marked by this virtue and by wondrous devotion. He refused to know the wormwood of secular learning, so that he might enter into the power of God. Indeed, he despised the world lying in evil, so that, made higher than the world, he might be joined to him who is higher than the heavens.

He had read in the Apostle: “The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the law of God” (Romans 8:7). If the most noble Albinus had wished to follow it, God would have struck down all those who dared such things with punishment that would not long be delayed.

Now, having leaped across the slippery paths of adolescence with worthy praise, he was fixed like the sun in the middle of the vault of heaven, with the great heat of youth.

He had also been taught, with Moses, Egyptian wisdom; he had cut off its hair and nails; he had climbed the mountain on which God could be seen; he had seen the rod turned into a serpent and, when the serpent was touched by the tail, turned back into a rod; and he had learned that the abyss calls to the abyss.

Standing close to his footsteps, he follows the one who proclaims good things upon the mountains, announcing them, so that he might be able to hear the voice of the watchmen when it was raised.

### X

While reading the Gospel of John before his teacher together with his fellow students, Albinus reached the passage that only the pure in heart know how to understand mentally: the passage beginning where John says that he reclined upon the Lord’s breast and extending to the point where he recalls that Jesus went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron.

As Albinus was spiritually intoxicated by this Gospel reading, sitting before his teacher’s little bed, he was suddenly carried away in spirit into ecstasy. The same entire world that once, beneath the rays of the sun, had been shown before the most holy Father Benedict was now displayed before Albinus’s eyes, gathered together within one enclosure or court of mares.

[Note: Henschenius believes the reading may be: “within one enclosure, or court of mares.”]

While Albinus fixed the attention of his eyes upon what he saw, he perceived the whole surrounding enclosure encircled, as it were, by blood.

His fellow students, turning their eyes toward him with great wonder—for he appeared to have no blood at all—tried to awaken him as though he were asleep. At their noise, blessed Ealhbeorht directed his eyes toward Albinus, gazed at him silently for a long time, and said:

> “Read, my sons, and do not awaken this one, so that, indulging in sleep for a little while, he may afterward hear me more effectively as I teach.”

When Albinus had returned to himself and had received the reading, the Father ordered everyone to go outside, keeping Albinus alone with him. The Father then said to him:

> “What did you see? I beg you, do not conceal it from me.”

Albinus wanted above all to keep secret what he had seen, fearing that he might fall into the pit of pride, and answered:

> “What, my lord Father?”

The blessed man replied:

> “Do not, my son, do not hide it from me. I am not asking you about it out of vain curiosity, but for your benefit.”

When Albinus saw that he could not conceal it, he humbly described how he had seen the entire world.

Then the Father said to him:

> “See, my son, see to it that you do not tell anyone except the one whom, after my departure, you will have as your most faithful attendant. Command that man also to keep it secret until your death.”

Obeying this counsel, Albinus revealed the matter concerning himself during his lifetime only to Sigulf.

Whoever therefore desires to know how Albinus could see the whole world within one enclosure should consult book 2, chapter 35, of the *Dialogues* of Saint Gregory.

Meanwhile, let him understand that in the vision of the world heaven and earth were not contracted, but the soul of the seer was enlarged. Caught up in the Lord, he could see without difficulty everything that existed beneath God.

Perhaps someone will also ask more carefully why he saw it under this form, and why it appeared surrounded by blood. Let him know that the entire sheepfold of the holy Church is surrounded by Christ’s blood, so that the redeemed, from the rising of the sun to its setting, having been delivered from the hand of the enemy by Christ’s Passion—which at that moment undoubtedly occupied Albinus’s mind more fervently while he was reading it before his teacher—may say: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good,” and so forth.

The whole world is therefore seen enclosed within one enclosure and surrounded by Christ’s blood when everything that has been symbolically accomplished by the holy Fathers and written from the beginning of the world is unlocked by Christ’s Passion alone. He is the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David.

But if by the rounded enclosure one wishes to understand the life of his carnal companions surrounded by blood because it was shown to him so that, having trampled it underfoot, he might despise it, let this be left to individual judgment.

# CHAPTER V

## Alcuin is ordained a deacon and comes to Francia

### XI

After this, growing from virtue to virtue, he was consecrated a deacon on the day of the Purification of Saint Mary—for on that same day he had previously lost the hair of his head.

Since he already knew that his blessed father Ealhbeorht, whose illness had been foretold, would soon pass to Christ, and since he did everything with his counsel, as was said above, Alcuin carefully asked him what he wished and commanded him to do after they had been separated by death alone.

The Father gave him this answer, which now makes the Lord’s will clear:

> “I want you to go to Rome, and, returning from there, visit Francia. For I know that you will produce much fruit there. Christ will be the guide of your journey, bringing you there and directing you as a stranger, so that you may be a conqueror of the most impious heresy that will attempt to assert that the man Christ is adoptive, and so that you may be a most steadfast defender and most renowned preacher of the faith of the Holy Trinity. You will therefore remain in the land of your pilgrimage, illuminating the souls of many.”

After blessing him with the blessings of the Fathers mentioned above and commending him to Christ Jesus, so that Christ himself might preserve him, the joyful Father Ealhbeorht, bishop, departed to God on the sixth day before the Ides of November.

[Note: The year was 780. See the cited poem, book 2, verse 1583.]

The pious Albinus mourned him with tears as a mother, yet refused to accept consolation.

The deacon, having inherited the holy blessings of the Fathers, took upon himself with hereditary right the great responsibility of multiplying his Lord’s talent splendidly. He taught many in Britain, and afterward not a few in Francia.

At that time there was associated with him a man beloved by God, distinguished by nobility of mind and body, Sigulf the presbyter, guardian of the Church of the city of York. He remained permanently attached to Alcuin. As a boy he had come to these regions with his uncle, the presbyter Autbert, who had taken him to Rome to learn the ecclesiastical order; he had also been sent to the city of Metz for the sake of chant.

There he labored for some time amid great scarcity of bread and with much fruitfulness. After he had sent his holy uncle to the Lord, he returned to his native land.

These two loved each other so greatly that you would have seen in them Rebecca joined to Isaac and Anna joined to Tobias.

When almighty God wished to glorify Francia with spiritual riches, as he had previously glorified it with earthly ones, giving it a king after his own heart—most distinguished in faith, courage, and love of wisdom, and in the ineffable beauty of his body—he stirred Albinus’s mind

[Variant: “moved Albinus’s mind,” rather than “stirred.”]

so that he might fulfill the counsel and command of his father.

# CHAPTER VI

## Alcuin teaches Charlemagne the liberal arts and is placed over three monasteries

### XII

Having therefore been ordered by Eanbald, archbishop and successor of Ealhbeorht, to obtain the pallium for him from the pope, Alcuin came to Rome.

When he was returning after receiving the pallium, he encountered King Charles in the city of Parma. Addressing him with great persuasion and prayers, the king asked him to return to him in Francia after completing his mission. For he knew that Alcuin had formerly been sent to him by his teacher.

Alcuin, desiring to serve the advancement of others as the king had asked, acted with the authority of his own king and archbishop, but only on the condition that he return to them again.

With Christ providing guidance, he reached King Charles. The king embraced him as a father, since he had been introduced by Alcuin to the liberal arts. Charles knew that he had received some refreshment from them, but because of his great eagerness could not be satisfied.

After spending some time with him, Charles gave him two monasteries: Bethlehem, also called Ferrières, and Saint-Loup at Troyes.

[Note: The monastery of Ferrières was situated in the diocese of Sens; Saint-Loup was in the suburb of Troyes. Mabillon. Alcuin appears to speak of these in letters 52 and 53, now numbered 66 and 67.]

But finally Albinus, unwilling to abandon without the authority of his king and bishop the place where he had been educated, where he had also lost the hair of his head and had been consecrated a deacon, asked the great king to grant him permission to return to his homeland.

Charles addressed him in a gracious voice:

> “We possess sufficient earthly riches, most excellent teacher, with which we rejoice to honor you as a father. We beg you to illuminate us, together with the treasure of your piety, through those things you have long desired and have scarcely at last found.”

Albinus replied:

> “My lord king, I do not intend to reject your will once it has been confirmed by the authority of the canons. Even though I am enriched by a considerable hereditary possession in my paternal region, I gladly despise it and rejoice to remain here poor, so that I may be of benefit to you. Your task is only to obtain this for me from my king and bishop.”

At last, overcome by reason, Charles consented to let him go, but did not give peace to his mind until, when Albinus had returned to him for the second time,

[Note: Perhaps “when he was about to return to him for the second time.”]

he had firmly obtained that Albinus would remain with him permanently.

After no small period of time had passed, once Albinus had returned to Charles for the second time, he was appointed shepherd of the monastery of Saint Martin at Tours.

[Note: See letter 101, now numbered 129, and the charter of Charles the Great, volume 2, p. 566; *Patrologia Latina*, volume 97, column 990.]

Governing that monastery, along with others, worthily for God, he strove as far as he could to correct the lives of his subjects. Those whom he had received as untamed, he worked diligently to make rational and honorable in conduct and seekers of wisdom.

# CHAPTER VII

## He refutes the heretic Felix at Aachen

### XIII

Meanwhile, a heresy hostile to God, which was flourishing in parts of Spain and asserted that the Son of God was adoptive according to the flesh, reached Charles’s ears.

When the great and entirely Catholic king learned this by direct experience, he struggled with all his strength to destroy the seed of the devil and uproot the weeds completely from God’s wheat.

Calling his instructor Albinus from Tours and Felix, the wretched author of this heresy, from the regions of Spain, he assembled a great synod of bishops in the imperial palace at Aachen. Sitting among them, he ordered Felix, although he resisted vigorously, to dispute rationally with the most learned Albinus concerning the nature of the Son of God according to the flesh.

What silence there was among the bishops at that time! How clear and unconquerable was the confession and defense of the faith of Charles and of his teacher, supported by royal authority!

Felix fled through many hiding places, but Albinus pierced him with still more darts, so that he nearly completed all the cities of Israel, until the Son of Man should come. For from the second hour until the seventh, scarcely anything else was done.

When his foolishness had finally been exposed to all, and the heresy had been refuted by everyone with apostolic authority, it remained disgracefully hidden from Felix alone, until he read with lamentation the words of the martyr Cyril, sent to him by Albinus:

[Note: Cyril was Cyril of Alexandria, who could be called a martyr because of the many things he endured in disputing and writing for the sake of the faith.]

> “That nature which was corrupted through the devil has been exalted above the angels because of Christ’s triumph and has been placed at the right hand of the Father.”

When Felix read this sentence, he testified aloud and with abundant weeping that at last he had recognized his error and had acted impiously.

But since, turning to another subject, I have touched only briefly upon this matter, whoever thirsts to know it more completely should read Alcuin’s letters to Felix and Elipandus, as well as their letters to him. He will be able to know without hesitation what he desires.

By Christ’s granting, I have thus far written a little about the beginning of Albinus’s life [Col. 0098D], which I judged not to be known to everyone—not as I wished, but faithfully, as best I could. From here I shall try to drag my pen, battered at the lips, toward its conclusion, even if it must creak along in contempt; for I did not think it proper to insert into this little work what everyone knows about him.

## CHAPTER VIII

Alcuin, wishing to withdraw to Fulda, is retained at Tours. His disciples.

**XIV.** When, therefore, he felt himself more than usual afflicted by old age and illness together, he indicated to King Charles that he wished to leave the world, as he had long considered doing. He asked permission to live a monastic life at Saint-Boniface according to the rule of Saint Benedict and, if possible, to divide among his disciples the monasteries entrusted to him. But the formidable yet pious king refused one request with every earnestness of entreaty: the other he gladly heard, begging him to remain at Tours in complete tranquillity and with the highest honor, and not to decline [to devote his care] to him and to the whole holy Church committed to him. As for the burdens of the world that he himself had borne, he most willingly distributed them among the disciples, as Alcuin had requested.

Albinus therefore did what the wisest king had asked, seeking not what would be useful to himself but what would benefit many; and he awaited his final day at Tours. His life was in no way inferior to that of a monk. For the character he had displayed in the Fathers named above continued in him: in fasts, prayers, mortification of the flesh, almsgiving, the abundant celebration of psalms and Masses, and in the other virtues by which it is possible for human nature to be adorned [Col. 0099B]. Except on the days of the Resurrection and of festivals, he prolonged his fast until evening, sparing the food in which he took greater pleasure. Consequently, he often rejoiced to possess in his mouth a sweetness granted from heaven so great that human speech cannot express it.

At that time he could dictate whatever he wished, with no labor at all and with the greatest speed, so that he could say: “I have loved your commandments, Lord, above gold and topaz. How sweet are your utterances to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Psalm 118:127). As a young man he had not loved the secret chanting of the Psalms as much as other reading; now, as an old man, he could never be satisfied with their singing.

Every day he poured out a most secret prayer, as was said above of his master, together with the prolonged extension of his hands in the form of a cross, in the same manner and with many sighs—for he was very rarely able to shed tears. He likewise taught this to his disciples, foremost among whom were the distinguished old Sigulf and the great-hearted Withso; after them came Fredegisus [Col. 0099C] and his companions. In his final period Raganardus and Waldramnus, who are still alive, remained constantly with him. There was also Adelbertus, of blessed memory, at that time Sigulf’s son, as far as he was able; afterward he became a venerable Father; and there were many others, whose names may Christ know.

These men, carefully watching over themselves, diligently took precautions lest they do anything blameworthy in his presence, and often even when he was absent. For they knew that he was bound to God and illumined by His Spirit, although, because old age and illness resisted him, he could no longer see clearly with his bodily eyes. They therefore feared that their actions could not remain hidden from him.

**XV.** Since he was filled with the spirit of prophecy, he foretold to certain persons things that would happen to them, just as he did to Raganardus concerning Osulfus [note: Concerning his fall, Epistles 158 and 159—now 207 and 208—appear to be understood here]. For the same Raganardus, while asleep, saw a dreadful vision which it is better to keep silent about. The next day he reported it to the same Father in fear, afraid that it concerned him.

But the Father [Col. 0099D] replied with great sorrow:

“O Osulfus! Miserable man, how often have I warned you, how often have I corrected you! I labored greatly with your uncle so that he might reform himself and begin to walk in the way of God’s commandments. I foretold to him that, unless he did so before he departed from the world, he would be struck by the plague of leprosy; and so it happened. Therefore I also foretell to you, my son, concerning Osulfus, about whom this vision has occurred, that he will die neither in this region nor in the land where he was born.”

The outcome afterward confirmed this, for he died in Lombardy.

The same Raganardus also attempted, unknown to everyone, to afflict himself by excessive vigils and an immoderate excess of abstinence, so that through this lack of restraint he fell gravely ill with fever. When Albinus came to visit him, he ordered everyone except Sigulfus to leave the house. Then he rebuked him, saying:

“Why did you attempt to act so intemperately without anyone’s advice? For when I observed that you wished to do this, I ordered you also to sleep in the house where I sleep. But as soon as you knew that everyone was asleep, you secretly lit a candle, concealed it in a lantern, went to that place, and kept vigil throughout the night.”

Whatever he had done there secretly, he knew—as God alone knew—and he himself disclosed it to him, adding:

“When you were also going with me on an errand and I ordered you to drink wine, you craftily said, ‘I have drunk sufficiently, lord Father, with my uncle.’ But when you came to your uncle and he too ordered you to do this, you said that you had drunk with me. You wished to deceive us, and you were deceived. Therefore, once you have risen from this fever, beware of such things, and never again attempt to do anything of the kind recklessly.”

**XVI.** Hearing these things from the man who was called the Old One, Raganardus blushed deeply and was greatly frightened, knowing that he had been discovered and that his secrets could not be hidden from Albinus. In amazement he said, “How did this become known publicly?” To this day he himself testifies before God that no human being had known it beforehand, until the man revealed it, but that God alone had known it.

Finally, repenting of what he had foolishly done, throughout the rest of Albinus’s life he undertook nothing of this sort without his counsel and command.

## CHAPTER IX

He foretells the arrival of Benedict, abbot of Aniane.

**XVII.** Very often, when messengers sent by the king or by other friends were still far away, he foretold their arrival, the reason for their coming, what they were bringing, and what they might be seeking to carry away with them. Some of his disciples, hearing such things, blamed his old age as though it were senile, until they had tested them.

The man of God Benedict, who was more closely bound to him by friendship than any other monk, often hastened from the regions of Gothia to receive from him counsel for his own salvation and that of his people. On one occasion he wished to come in such a way that no one at Tours would know of it until he stood at the door of Albinus’s house.

When he was still not nearby, Albinus called one of his men and said:

“Hurry to meet Abbot Benedict at such-and-such a place, and tell him to come quickly to me.”

The messenger of Father Albinus did as he had been ordered. After three days he reached the place that Albinus had indicated, found Benedict, and delivered the message entrusted to him. Astonished that his attempt had been discovered, Benedict quickly came to him at Tours.

As they joyfully kissed one another, Benedict the revered Father began humbly:

“Lord Father, who foretold my arrival to you?”

“No man made it known to me in words,” he replied.

“Who, then, my lord? Did you perhaps hear it through someone’s letter?”

“No,” he said, “truly, through no letter.”

The same man asked him again:

“If you learned it neither from any human speaker nor from anyone’s letter, I beg you, my Father, tell me how you knew it.”

Albinus replied:

“Do not question me about this any further.”

When the venerable Benedict was about to return [Col. 0100D], he asked Albinus to reveal the special prayer with which he prayed for him. Albinus answered:

“This is what I ask of Christ: ‘Lord, grant me understanding of my sins, grant me to make a true confession and perform worthy penance, and grant me forgiveness of my sins.’”

The man of God Benedict said to him:

“Let us add one phrase to this prayer, my Father: ‘And after forgiveness, save me.’”

Albinus, rejoicing, said:

“Let it be so, most reverend son; let it be so.”

Again Benedict asked him to tell him what words he silently uttered with his lips whenever he saw the cross and bowed toward it. Albinus replied:

“We adore your cross, Lord; we recall your glorious Passion. Have mercy on us, you who suffered for us.”

Afterward, having accompanied him for a short distance, Albinus sent him home rejoicing, to his own people.

## CHAPTER X

He foretells the rule of Louis, son of Charlemagne. He forbids his disciples to read Virgil.

**XVIII.** The great king and powerful emperor Charles, wishing to pray and at the same time to enjoy a long-desired mutual conversation with Albinus, undertook to visit the tomb of Saint Martin with his sons Charles, Pippin, and Louis. While holding Albinus’s hand there, he secretly said:

“Master, which of these sons of mine, in your judgment, will God grant me as my successor in this dignity, which He has given me, though I am unworthy?”

Albinus turned his face toward Louis, the youngest of them, but the most distinguished in humility—a quality for which many regarded him as contemptible—and said:

“You will have the humble Louis as an outstanding successor.”

At that time Charles alone heard this. But later, when he saw those same kings walking upright and Louis walking humbly into the church of Saint Stephen for the sake of prayer, he sat in the place where he wished to be buried and said to those standing near him:

“Do you see that Louis is humbler than his brothers? Surely you will see this man become his father’s most exalted successor.”

Moreover, after Communion of the Body and Blood of Christ, when Charles was mixing it for them with his own hand, Louis, distinguished above all in humility, bowed before the holy father and kissed his hand. Then the man of God said to Sigulfus, who was standing beside him:

“Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. Surely after his father, France will rejoice to have this man as emperor.”

This we now both see and celebrate. Those who seemed to be cedars have been cast down, and the fruitful olive tree has been exalted in the house of the Lord.

The Father instructed Charles with great care in the liberal arts and in the divine Scriptures, to such a degree that he became the wisest of all the Frankish kings who had lived since Christ’s coming. He also taught him, for every period of his life, which penitential psalms he should chant with the litany, prayers, and petitions; which he should use for special prayer; which in praise of God; which in every kind of tribulation; and which he should sing so as to exercise himself in divine praises.

Anyone who wishes to know this should read his little book addressed to the same king, *On the Manner of Prayer* [note: We present it under the title *Offices for the Weekdays*, vol. II of this edition. See also the preliminary notice there].

**XIX.** When still a young man, the same man of God had read the books of the ancient philosophers and the falsehoods of Virgil. Now he did not wish either to hear them himself or to have his disciples read them.

“The divine poets are sufficient for you,” he said, “and you do not need to pollute yourselves with the luxurious eloquence of Virgil’s language.”

Sigulfus the Old One secretly attempted to act against this command, and afterward was publicly ashamed of it. Calling in Adalbertus and Aldricus, whom he was then raising as his sons, he ordered them to read Virgil in his presence in the utmost secrecy, forbidding them to let anyone know in any way, lest it come to Father Albinus’s attention.

But Albinus, calling him to himself in his customary manner, said:

“Where have you come from, Virgilian? Why have you begun and wished, against my will and counsel and without my knowledge, to read Virgil?”

Sigulfus threw himself at his feet, confessed that he had acted most foolishly, and humbly repented [Col. 0101D]. After rebuking him, the merciful father kindly accepted his satisfaction and warned him never again to do anything of the kind.

[Note: Aldricus, abbot of Ferrières and afterward bishop of Sens, had Adalbertus, praised here, as his predecessor. It is therefore clear that this Life was written before 829, when Aldricus, having been an abbot, became bishop of Sens. Mabillon.]

The worthy Aldricus, still living, the abbot, testifies that neither he nor Adalbertus had made this known to anyone, but that they had remained completely silent until then, as they had been instructed.

## CHAPTER XI

He knows hidden things. He extinguishes a fire. He heals the sick.

**XX.** The father himself had ordered one hundred measures of wine to be given to the brothers of Cormaric, whom he loved greatly [Col. 0102A]. When the wine was being carried to the monastery, he instructed the administrators, through Sigulfus, the monk of Abbot Benedict [note: “The monk of Abbot Benedict.” Is this therefore someone different from Sigulfus the Old One?], to detain the carriers of the wine until, in their presence, the wine was transferred from the vessels in which they had brought it into other containers. For some of them, secretly taking wine from it, had mixed in enough water so that the vessels would be full when they reached the monastery; the brothers proved with complete certainty that this had indeed been done.

**XXI.** Aigulfus, an English-Saxon priest, also came to Tours to visit the same father. When he had begun to stand before the door of his house, four of the Touronian brothers happened to be together. Looking at him and thinking that Albinus knew nothing of what they were saying, they spoke among themselves:

“This Briton or Scot has come to that other Briton who lies inside. O God, deliver this monastery from these Britons! For just as bees return from every direction to their mother, so all these men come to him.”
