The priest entered Albinus’s house and afterward reported to him, among other things, what he had heard. Albinus asked him:

“Do you know who they are?”

“Truly, I neither knew them nor was able, out of shame, to look at them when they were saying these things.”

But Father Albinus said:

“Certainly I know who they are.”

He therefore called them by their own names and ordered them to come to him, saying:

“These are the men.”

Pitying their foolishness, he spared them and said:

“May Christ, the Son of God, forgive them.”

After giving each of them a cup of wine to drink, he again ordered them gently to go outside. Aigulfus later investigated the matter carefully through others and proved that they were the same men.

**XXII.** I do not think that I should pass over in silence another event known to many. The custodian of Saint Martin’s tomb was responsible for the wax and all the vestments belonging to the basilica. Entering the sacristy where these things were kept, with a lighted candle, he fixed the candle to a post and forgot to take it when he left. He secured the door with its lock and went away.

The burning candle fell upon the wax. The wax, producing great flames, sent out fire with considerable force toward the vestments hanging from poles; the vestments reached up to the roof. When the custodian perceived this, he fled with the key to another monastery [note: “To another monastery.” Mabillon believes that “another monastery” here means another basilica, since, he says, basilicas were not rarely called monasteries, and at least two churches existed in the Martinian monastery. Henschenius, however, believes that the custodian truly fled to another monastery out of fear of the punishment he had deserved].

People rushed together from every side and beat upon the door, but it could not be opened by any effort. The clerics threw outside whatever precious things they had in their houses. The church of Saint Martin was being stripped of its vestments, and no one could hope for anything other than the burning of the entire monastery. The lead roof was being stripped away.

Albinus was present, though he could no longer see with his eyes. He asked what was happening. One of his disciples, the Old One, said to him:

“Go away from here, my lord Father, lest you be struck to death either by the lead thrown down from above or be burned by the fire. Certain destruction awaits.”

When Albinus wished to leave, the Old One said to him again:

“My lord Father, go to the tomb of Lord Martin and intercede for us.”

Albinus did so. When he reached the place, he stretched himself upon the ground in the form of a cross and uttered a groan toward heaven. Then, in a wondrous and incredible manner, as soon as Albinus threw himself upon the ground, the whole fire was extinguished, as though it had been drowned in an immense river.

When the clerics saw this, they rejoiced with great astonishment and hurried to the place where Albinus lay prostrate before Saint Martin’s tomb, praying to God in the form of a cross on their behalf. Raising him from the ground, they blessed God [Col. 0103A], who through Albinus’s prayers had saved the entire structure of Saint Martin’s monastery from being consumed by fire.

“These are your worthy examples, holy Martin: once, when you sought to flee from fires, you could not; turning to God in prayer, you extinguished those threatening fires. Truly lofty is the faith which by its own warmth could extinguish fiery globes.

“It is no wonder if the elements abandon their proper force at Albinus’s prayers and commands, since he himself rests in the heart of the one who loves those who love him and does not permit those walking in fire to be blackened by the flame.

“In these things we adore you, glorify you, and praise you: you who, just as you deigned to promise your servants who keep your commandments, have also shown most clearly through your works in your Albinus that promise. You indeed said, Christ Jesus: ‘If you ask anything of me in my name, I will do it,’ namely, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.”

**XXIII.** This too must be recalled to the Lord’s praise: many sick people who repeatedly came to Albinus received bodily health after receiving his blessing in faith.

It is also reported that at one time, according to some distinguished witnesses, a poor man whose eyesight was severely obscured by darkness came to the door of Albinus’s outer house and asked that water be given him with which he might wash his eyes. For he said that it had been revealed to him that, if he washed his eyes with it, he would recover his sight [editorial note: “if”—the edition reads *quas*].

Without Albinus’s knowledge, therefore, water with which he had washed his face and eyes was collected and secretly given to the poor man who requested it. The poor man washed his eyes with that water in complete faith, drove away the darkness, and recovered clear sight.

“We too are illumined by your sweat, Father, and by your devout teaching the sins of our souls are washed away, while you no longer knowingly tire yourself with the labor of the eyes. You yourself could scarcely see with bodily vision, yet you always strove to illumine the minds of others; those whom you could not instruct in person, you taught in your absence through letters, writing many things useful to the whole Church.”

## CHAPTER XII

The various works he wrote.

**XXIV.** At the request of Emperor Charles he wrote a most useful book on the Holy Trinity (vol. I of this edition), as well as works on rhetoric, dialectic, and music (vol. II). He wrote to Gundrada on the nature of the soul (ibid.). At the request of the women Gisla and Richtrude, he composed a remarkable work on the Gospel of John, partly from his own material and partly from Saint Augustine (vol. I). He also wrote on four of Paul’s Epistles, namely, to the Ephesians, to Titus, to Philemon, and to the Hebrews (ibid.). To Fredegisus, on the Psalms (ibid.). To Count Wido, homilies on the chief vices and virtues (vol. II). To his Sigulfus, very useful questions on Genesis (vol. I). On the Proverbs of Solomon and Ecclesiastes (ibid.), and on the Song of Songs, an exceedingly eloquent work in concise form (ibid.).

Under the names of “Frank” and “Saxon,” he wrote a highly eloquent little book on grammar in the form of questions and answers (vol. II). He collected two volumes of homilies from many works of the Fathers [note: These are certainly distinct from those of Paul Warnefrid; Alcuin’s, however, still lie hidden]. He wrote on orthography (ibid.). In the hundred and eighteenth Psalm he also employed a golden style (vol. I).

There are many other works as well; whoever reads and diligently examines them will find no small edification for himself, as also in the letters addressed to many people. Spending the remainder of his life in these and similar works, he lived a heavenly life on earth.

Placed in the final watch, he awaited the coming of the Son of Man, so that he might enter with him into the wedding feast. Every night he washed his bed with tears, always fortifying himself with the intercession of the saints, whose solemn observances he celebrated every day, lest the ancient enemy pierce him with any of his arrows. The enemy could never enter his house so secretly that he would not suddenly be detected by him and driven away by the sign of the cross.

## CHAPTER XIII

He drives away the devil by prayer. His devout practices.

**XXV.** One night, wishing as usual to pour out prayer secretly with the chanting of psalms, he was overcome by an immense sleepiness. Rising from his bed, he took the cloak from above him. When sleep again weighed upon him, he removed all his clothing except a shirt and undergarments.

Nevertheless, since the sleepiness continued, he took a censer, went to the place where the fire was kept, filled it with coals, placed incense upon them, and perfumed the entire room with a sweet odor. At that hour the devil presented himself to him visibly in bodily form: a huge, very black and deformed, bearded man, heaping blasphemous darts upon him.

“What are you doing, hypocrite Alcuin?” he said. “Why do you strive to appear righteous before men, when you are a great deceiver and impostor? Do you think that you can make Christ accept you through these pretenses of yours?”

But the unconquerable soldier of Christ, standing with David in the tower that is furnished with the entire armor of the brave and a thousand hanging shields, said in a heavenly voice:

“The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? He is the strength of my life; whom shall I dread? Hear, Lord, my murmur; attend to the voice of my cry, my King and my God, for to you I pray, Lord. In the morning you will hear my voice; in the morning I shall prepare myself for you and, rising in the middle of the night, shall contemplate you in order to give you thanks. The proud heap falsehood upon me; but I shall search out your commandments with all my heart. Let my heart be made perfect in your commandments, and let those who unjustly crush me be put to shame, while I shall not be put to shame when day dawns and the shadows bend.”

Finally, the enemy was driven away, and he himself, having completed his prayer, rested. At that hour only one of his disciples, named Waldramnus, who is still living, was awake, secretly observing all these things—a witness, that is, to what had happened [Col. 0104C].

**XXVI.** Following the Apostle’s counsel, the same father used a small amount of wine—not because of a desire for gluttony, but because of the weakness of the flesh. He fled idleness in every way: he was either reading, writing, teaching his disciples, devoting himself to prayer and the chanting of psalms, or attending only to the unavoidable needs of the body.

He was a father to the poor, humbler than the humble, an inviter of the rich to compassion, superior to the proud, a discerner of all things, and an excellent liberator. Every day he celebrated the solemnities of Mass with great care and reverence, assigning particular Masses to each day of the week [note: Alcuin also sent those Masses to other churches and commended their use. See Epistles 46—now 50—and 192—now 142—and the preliminary notice to the *Book of Sacraments*, vol. II].

On Sundays, after dawn had begun to appear, he never at any time surrendered himself to sleep. Quickly preparing himself in levitical fashion, he celebrated with his priest Sigulfus the solemnities of the special Masses until the third hour; then, with great reverence, he entered the public Mass.

His disciples, wherever they were occupied with their duties, especially when they were assisting at the work of God, took care that he should see nothing blameworthy in them.

## CHAPTER XIV

The death of blessed Alcuin.

**XXVII.** Albinus, now desiring to be dissolved from the body and to be with Christ, implored Him that, if possible, he might depart from the world on the day when the Holy Spirit was seen to come upon the Apostles in tongues of fire and fill their hearts.

For his evening office, at the place he had chosen to rest after death—namely, beside the church of Saint Martin—he chanted the evangelical hymn of Saint Mary with this antiphon [Col. 0105A]:

“O key of David [note: This is one of the famous antiphons recited at Vespers during the seven days before the Nativity of the Lord; it belongs to 20 December. Henschenius], and scepter of the house of Israel, who open and no one shuts, who shut and no one opens: come and lead the captive out of the prison house, the one sitting in darkness and the shadow of death.”

After the Lord’s Prayer he recited these verses:

“As the deer longs for springs of water…”  
“How beloved are your tabernacles, Lord of hosts.”  
“Blessed are those who dwell in your house…”  
“To you I lift up my eyes.”  
“One thing I have asked of the Lord.”  
“To you, Lord, I lift up my soul,”

and other passages of this kind.

**XXVIII.** During Lent, therefore, as he had always been accustomed to do, he most devoutly observed the season with every mortification of flesh and purification of spirit. Every night he visited the basilicas within Saint Martin’s monastery, washing himself of his sins with many sighs.

When the solemnity of the Lord’s Resurrection was being celebrated, on the night of His Ascension he fell into bed, exhausted by a grave illness unto death, and could not speak. Finally, three days before he departed, he chanted in his customary jubilant voice the antiphon “O key of David” and recited the verses mentioned above [Col. 0105B].

On Pentecost, after the morning office had been completed, at the same hour when he was accustomed to enter the Masses at the appearance of dawn, the holy soul of Albinus was released from the flesh. Through the ministry of the heavenly deacons, who had with them the blessed protomartyr Stephen and Lawrence the archdeacon, it was led with the army of angels to Christ, whom he loved and sought; and it enjoys His glory in heaven happily throughout all ages, having served Him faithfully in the world.

## CHAPTER XV

A splendor of light appears at his death, and other wonders occur. His burial.

**XXIX.** He died full of days, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 804.

That same night an immeasurable brightness of splendor was seen above the church of Saint Martin, so great that those standing far away thought the whole church was burning with fire [Col. 0105C]. Some saw that splendor throughout the entire night; to others it appeared three times.

When dawn arose, the already immense globe of light seemed to have come over the place where Albinus lay and, as his soul departed, to have pierced heaven. Archbishop Joseph testified that he and his people had seen it throughout the night. Many who are still alive in body also testify to it.

To far more people, however, the brightness appeared not on that night but on the preceding one—namely, the first Sunday after the Lord’s Ascension—in precisely the manner just described.

**XXX.** At the same hour, an army of heavenly deacons also appeared to a solitary living in Italy, resounding in the air with ineffable praises of Christ. In their midst Alcuin, wearing a most splendid dalmatic, stood and entered heaven with them, to minister with perpetual joy to the eternal Pontiff.

On that same day of Pentecost, the solitary told this to a certain brother of Tours, who customarily visited the shrines of the Apostles and had come to him. He asked him:

“Who is that abbot who lived at Tours in the monastery of Saint Martin? What was his name? Or, if you were able, when you left there, how was he in body?”

The brother answered:

“He is called Alcuin, and he is the finest teacher in all Francia. When I set out to come here, I left him in good health.”

The solitary replied with tears:

“Indeed, he enjoys the most blessed health.”

He then told him what he had seen on that day as dawn was brightening. The brother returned to Tours and reported what he had heard.

**XXXI.** Father Sigulfus, washing the father’s body honorably with water together with certain others, placed it upon a bier. He himself at that time had a severe headache, but, sound in spirit through faith, he quickly found healing for his head.

Raising his eyes toward his master’s bed, he saw a comb with which Alcuin used to comb his own head. Taking it in his hands, he said:

“I believe, Lord Jesus, that if I comb my head with this comb of my master, I shall immediately be healed through his merits.”

When he drew the comb through his head for the first time, every part it touched became completely sound. Continuing to comb all around, he lost the entire pain.

Another of his disciples, named Eangist, was gravely afflicted by an immense pain in his teeth. At Father Sigulfus’s urging, he touched his teeth with the same comb, and immediately, because he did so with faith, he received healing through Alcuin’s merits [Col. 0106B].

**XXXII.** When Joseph, bishop of the city of Tours, a good man beloved by God, heard that blessed Alcuin had died, he hurried there with his clergy. He watered Alcuin’s eyes with his own tears and kissed them for a long time.

Using prudent counsel, he ordered that Alcuin not be buried in the place outside that the Father himself had wished for [note: Alcuin did not approve the zeal of certain people in preparing their own tombs. See Epistle 150—now 199], but most honorably inside Saint Martin’s basilica, so that, since their souls were joined in heaven, their bodies might lie together in one house on earth.

This was done. Over his tomb was placed, as he himself had ordered, the inscription that he had dictated while alive, written on a bronze plate and set into the wall.

## THE EPITAPH OF ALCUIN

“Here, I beg you, traveler, as you come, pause for a little while,

and ponder my words in your heart, so that from your likeness and mine

you may recognize your fate:

[Col. 0106C] Let the form be changed: as mine is, so yours shall be. [Another reading: “Behold, the form is changed.”]

What you are now, I once was, a traveler famous throughout the world,

and what I now am, you too will be.

I pursued the pleasures of the world with empty love;

now I am ash and dust, food for worms.

Therefore remember to care for your soul

rather than your flesh, for this remains while that perishes.

Why do you prepare estates for yourself? You see how little space

holds me here in this small chamber; so small will yours also become.

Why do you long to have your body clothed in Tyrian purple,

when a hungry worm will soon eat it in the dust?

As flowers perish when the threatening wind arrives,

so your flesh—and all your glory—perishes.

Repay me in kind, reader, I beg you, for this poem,

and say: ‘Grant pardon, O Christ, to your servant.’

I ask that no devout hand violate the sacred rights of the tomb

until the angelic trumpet sounds from the heavenly citadel:

‘You who lie in the tomb, rise from the dust of the earth;

the great Judge is present, with countless thousands.’

My name was Alcuin, ever loving wisdom.

For my sake, as you read this inscription, pour forth your prayers.”

The following words were appended to this epitaph by someone else:

“Here rests the lord Abbot Alcuin, of blessed memory, who died in peace on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June. When you read this, all of you, pray for him and say: ‘May the Lord grant him eternal rest.’”

[Note: D. Quercetanus reported another epitaph here from Browerus, *Antiquities of Fulda*, book I, chapter 10, which recently existed in the church of Hersfeld. It is not Alcuin’s, however, but rather that of Albuinus, provost of Hersfeld, highly learned in philosophical studies and formerly a famous schoolmaster, as is recorded of him in the *Hildesheim Chronicle* under the year 1034. See Mabillon, *Elogia*, no. 77, and Henschenius’s note on chapter 4 of the *Life*. This epitaph therefore has no place here.]

## PREFACE OF D. ANDREAS QUERCETANUS TO BLESSED ALCUIN, ABBOT

Printed in many places in the preceding commentary.

[Col. 0107A] Since I had long resolved to confer this gift upon my native church and city of Tours—that it should see brought to light not only its ancient history, which I have in hand, but also the writings of the fathers who flourished there—it seemed proper to begin with blessed Flaccus Albinus, or Alcuin, formerly abbot of Saint Martin.

I chose him both because he was, in every field, the most learned and educated man of his age, and because the better part of his works had either remained unknown to this day or certainly survived mutilated and corrupted in many places.

An anonymous author recorded many things about him, relating whatever he had been able to learn from the faithful Sigwulf, his constant companion, for the benefit of posterity. Many things were also recorded by ancient and more recent historians. I have carefully collected and arranged the testimony of all of them, and have likewise arranged for it to be printed together with his Life and epitaph.

But so that what they omitted or received incorrectly may be understood, I shall trace the whole matter back to what are called the pure sources—that is, to Alcuin’s very own writings.

## CHAPTER ONE

Alcuin’s homeland, lineage, and native soil.

[Col. 0107B] Alcuin repeatedly testifies that he originated from Britain, but he leaves uncertain from what stock or from which parents, although it may be established from this one fact that he was born of no humble lineage: he always possessed great influence and authority among the kings, bishops, and other nobles of his island, and he had as a brother the bishop of the church of Juvavum, now called Salzburg, named Aquila [note: See Epistles 36 and 102].

Whether he was born in the Scottish regions of Britain, as Scottish historians maintain [note: Hector Boethius and John Major], or not far from London, in the county of Middlesex, as I find some have thought; or rather, as I believe, in the kingdom of Northumbria, at York, he does not make sufficiently clear.

Certainly Eginhardus, an author of his own time,
@ [Col. 0107D] In the *Life of Charlemagne*, he calls him a man of Saxon origin and himself indicates, in more than one passage and in unambiguous language, that he was educated from childhood at York. Yet the frequent mention in his letters of the Northumbrians, who held the regions of Scotland as far as the Firth of Edinburgh, gave Scottish historians occasion to suppose that he was born in Scotland.

## CHAPTER II

### His name and surname

Thus, born in the province of York, he bore the surname Albinus or Alcuin, taken from his family and not from the Scottish people, who, as George Buchanan asserts, call themselves *Albini* in their own language.

@ [Col. 0107D] Book V of the *History of Scotland*. Flaccus, however, was his proper name from baptism. This is so certainly true that he himself sometimes calls himself Flaccus, sometimes simply Albinus or Alcuin, but more often Flaccus Albinus or Flaccus Alcuin. Therefore those who, reversing the order, call him Albinus Flaccus Alcuin—following Sixtus of Siena

@ [Col. 0107D] In the *Holy Library*—and certain others, are acting contrary to the truth. Although at first we followed their authority and therefore almost always gave him that name as well, those too are mistaken who call him merely Albinus, with Alcuin as a surname.

@ [Col. 0108D] Eginhard and certain others. Albinus and Alcuin, Alboin or Albuin, Alchoin, Alquin, Alchuin, Alchwin, and Alkoin are found indiscriminately in both manuscript and printed books. This undoubtedly arose from the varied pronunciation and spelling of different nations. For those who preferred a softer mode of pronunciation and consistently avoided the collision of the tongue with the rougher part of the palate easily changed the sound *Alchuini* or *Alchoini* into *Albinus* or *Alboinus*, while some pronounced it Alcuin or Alquin, and others Alkoin or Alchwin. The most authoritative witnesses to this are both William, the monk of Malmesbury, and our own author. In their copies the name varies everywhere and without distinction in this way.

Although some assign another cause for this change,

@ [Col. 0108D] Henry Canisius, in his notes on Alcuin’s Letter 1: namely, that Flaccus deliberately changed the barbarous form of his native name into a Roman one, calling himself Albinus instead of Alcuin, just as happened with Winfrid, who was called Boniface, with Willibrord, who was called Clement, and with many others of that age. But, apart from the fact that in these cases it was a proper name, not a surname—which they are said not to have possessed—that was changed, if the differences among the languages are taken into account, it is certain that the syllables *qu*, *cu*, *chu*, *chw*, *ko*, *cho*, *bi*, and *bo* always represented the same sound. This can be detected from the single example of Matthew of Westminster. The man whom he calls Albinus, bishop of Lichfield, under the year 734, he names Alwin in 737. Pontus Heuterus, although not a particularly reliable or careful writer, interprets Alcuin etymologically as *Alwin*, that is, “one who accomplishes and increases everything”; perhaps from the verb *gwin*, which even today means “profit” to the Germans.

## CHAPTER III

### His education, instruction, and teachers

But, passing now from his name to his education and instruction, some believe that this Alcuin first assumed the monastic habit in the monastery of Saint Peter at London,

@ [Col. 0108D] As John Bale states in the first century of his *English Writers*, and that he was almost universally regarded, by both ancient and modern writers, as a disciple of the Venerable Bede.

Whether these things are true must here be examined somewhat more carefully. As regards the first point—where he spent his childhood and youthful years—he himself reveals this in a letter that he wrote to the brothers of the church of York (Letter 6), in these words:

> “You cherished the tender years of my infancy with maternal affection; you patiently endured the unruly period of my childhood with loving patience; by the disciplines of paternal correction you educated me to the maturity of a fully grown man; and by instruction in the sacred disciplines you strengthened me.”

And if we also wish to believe him concerning the second point, he states that Egbert, bishop of York, rather than Bede, was his teacher. For in the letter that he sent to Eanbald, the second successor of Egbert, he speaks as follows:

@ [Col. 0108D] A fragment of it appears in William of Malmesbury and in this work, after Alcuin’s letters.

> “Praise and glory be to God, who preserved my days in good prosperity, so that I might rejoice in the advancement of my dearest son, who would labor in my place in the church where I was nourished and instructed, and preside over the treasures of wisdom in which my beloved teacher, the archbishop Egbert, left me as heir.”

And in Letter 1 to Charles, king of the Franks, where he discusses bringing to Francia books that he had formerly possessed in his homeland of York, he says:

> “But, your servant says, I lack some of the more refined little books of scholastic learning which I had in my homeland through the good and most devoted diligence of my teacher Egbert, and also through my own inadequate exertions.”

Although the name Egbert is found neither in the manuscript nor in the printed copy at this point, William of Malmesbury, when citing the passage,

@ [Col. 0109D] Book I, chapter 3, of *The Deeds of the Kings of England*, adds it; and the subsequent mention of the city of York proves that the passage must necessarily be understood of him.

Moreover, whenever Alcuin refers to Bede, he calls him either simply “Bede the priest” or, with an added expression of honor, “the most distinguished teacher of his age.” For, writing to the monks of Wearmouth,

@ [Col. 0109D] Letter 14. Bede had both learned and taught letters in their monastery, and Alcuin says:

> “Consider the most distinguished teacher of our age, Bede the priest: what eagerness to learn he possessed in his youth, what praise he now enjoys among human beings, and how much greater the glory of his reward with God.”

Why would he have begrudged Bede this praise, and why would he not have called him his own teacher rather than the teacher of his age?

It is true that Bede testifies in the preface to his *History of the English People* that he undertook that work at the urging of an abbot named Albinus, whom he calls a man learned in every respect. But, apart from the fact that he mentions him only as an equal and a friend, not as a disciple, if this Albinus were our Albinus or Alcuin, it would plainly have to be said that he lived far beyond the age of one hundred. For Bede died in the year 731, as Sigebert and others note. Consequently, the Albinus whom Bede mentions must be considered an entirely different person from our Alcuin, and perhaps identified with that Alwin or Albinus who, according to Matthew of Westminster, was bishop in Mercia at Lichfield in 734 and died in 737.

## CHAPTER IV

### His learning and vocation

@ [Col. 0109C] Alcuin, therefore, was educated in the church of York, where he was also ordained as a levite or deacon, and had as his teacher not Bede, as most writers relate, but Archbishop Egbert, whom William of Malmesbury calls “the arsenal and treasury of all the liberal arts”

@ [Col. 0109D] Book I, chapter 3, of *The Deeds of the English*, and who is said to have established a most distinguished library at York. Within a short time he deserved to be counted among those who, after Aldhelm and Bede, were the first to excel among the English in every kind of learning.

For, besides the more humane arts and disciplines, he became most learned also in philosophy, mathematics, and every branch of divine knowledge. He was skilled in the Latin, Greek, and Hebrew languages, as readers of his writings will readily discover throughout. He was also celebrated to some degree for poetry, if the barbarism of his age is taken into account.

Accordingly, when his teacher Egbert was dying, he left him as heir to the treasures of wisdom over which he presided.

@ [Col. 0109D] Alcuin, in the letter to Eanbald already cited.

Alcuin then became head of the school at York and himself later had many disciples distinguished for learning and piety. Among them are Eanbald, who afterward became archbishop of York,

@ [Col. 0109D] William of Malmesbury, Book III of the *Bishops of England*;

Saint Ludger, the first bishop of Münster,

@ [Col. 0109D] *The Life of Saint Ludger* in Surius, chapter 7, and in the book entitled *Stars of the Illustrious Men of Germany*;

and another man named Joseph, who praised that same Ludger in several verses.

@ [Col. 0110D] These verses appear in Surius, *Life of Saint Ludger*, chapter 9.

## CHAPTER V

### Where he taught while living in Britain

Whether this highly learned teacher taught only at York at that time is not entirely certain or clear. For the annals of Cambridge University state—as the author of the *Centuries of Illustrious British Writers* reports—that he publicly taught all the liberal arts there after Bede, and that he eventually lectured at York under Egbert, as the leading philosopher of his age.

Yet Alcuin himself is nowhere found to have indicated this. Unless someone wishes to infer it from these words of his in a letter to Charlemagne (Letter 43):

> “In the morning of my age, when my studies were flourishing, I sowed [the seeds of learning] in Britain.”

But since elsewhere he explicitly shows that he had been the teacher of the brothers of York, this seems chiefly to be understood of York. That he spent the greater part of his youth there in learning and teaching is demonstrated most clearly by these words, written in his old age to the same brothers of the church of York:

> “You,” he says (Letter 6), “are always in my heart and first upon my lips among my prayers. Most devout fathers, whether during the common hours of holy prayer or in the private intercessions of your supplications, I beseech you by the love of God to keep Alcuin, your son, continually in your heart and on your lips. You also who are sons in age but fathers in the holiness of your merits, I implore by the divine mercy never to forget in your holy prayers the teacher of your learning. For the Searcher of my heart is my witness that he always desired, with devotion, your progress in ecclesiastical disciplines and spiritual doctrine. And if you have received anything less, I believe it cannot be attributed to my fault.”

## CHAPTER VI

### Among whom he was held in esteem, and his various embassies

Whatever the truth may be, through this praiseworthy profession of learning he became famous throughout Britain and was held in high esteem not only by the bishops and abbots of the island, but also by the kings and princes themselves. This is demonstrated by the letters he wrote with great familiarity to Aethelard, metropolitan of the Doroan church and primate of Britain (Letter 10); to Offa and Egfrid, kings of the Mercians (Letters 49 and 50); to Aedilred, king of the Northumbrians (Letter 11); to Aedilthid, a servant of God and formerly a queen (Letter 199); to Osbald and Osberth,

@ [Col. 0110C] the dukes of Northumbria (Letter 11); and to many others.

He also undertook two embassies on important matters, one to the Roman pontiff and the other to Francia. William of Malmesbury records one of them in Book I, chapter 3, of *The Deeds of the Kings of England*; Alcuin himself hints at the other in Letter 101, in these words:

> “When I was a young man, I went to Rome, and while I was staying for some days in Pavia, a royal city, a certain Jew named Julius held a disputation with Master Peter.”

By “Master Peter” he means that elderly deacon Peter, surnamed the Pisan, who is said to have been the teacher of Charles, king of the Franks, in grammar.

@ [Col. 0110D] In Eginhard’s *Life of Charlemagne*.

## CHAPTER VII

### He is summoned to Francia by Charlemagne; the reasons for his summons

Not long afterward Charles himself, that most glorious king, who had experienced his learning and wisdom both in Francia, when Alcuin had been sent to him to negotiate a peace treaty, and in the city of Pavia, while Charles was staying there, honorably summoned him from the distant borders of Britain. He wished Alcuin to serve as an assistant to his good purpose of advancing the study of true wisdom and to restore to the light nearly all the liberal disciplines that had then been extinguished throughout Gaul.

Alcuin gives this as the reason for his summons in Letter 23, now numbered 129, to King Charles, where he says:

> “I recognized that you, my lord David, always loved and praised this excellent concern of yours: to exhort everyone to learn true wisdom, indeed to urge them on by rewards and honors, and to summon from different parts of the world lovers of wisdom to assist your good purpose. Among these you took care to summon even me, the least of them, a humble servant of that holy wisdom, from the farthest regions of Britain. Would that I might prove as useful a servant in the house of God as I am ready to obey your will! For I loved with diligence what I understood you wished to find in me, since I recognized that you cherished it in your most sacred heart.”

He seems also to refer to this in poem 209, in these words:

> Albinus, coming from a foreign poet’s world,  
> Charles, illustrious king of this world, receives him—  
> Him whom renowned Britain sent to these lands,  
> Both with the love of sacred wisdom  
> And because of affection.

But in a letter to Laidrad, bishop of Lyons, Nefridius, bishop of Narbonne, Benedict the abbot, and also the most holy bishops, abbots, and brothers in the regions of Gothia, he adds another reason: namely, that he might assist the most devout King Charles in defending the Catholic faith against Felix, bishop of the see of Urgell, and his heretical followers. He declares that this had also been foretold to him, while he was still in Britain, by a certain holy man endowed with the spirit of prophecy:

> “I never attached anyone to my service, but rather desired, with devoted love, to serve all the servants of Christ, my God. For the opportunity to render that service, I came—by a divine dispensation, as I believe, and by God’s command—to Charles, the glorious prince and king of this realm, worthy to be named with every honor. A certain holy man, endowed with the spirit of prophecy, had foretold to me in my homeland that this was God’s will. A venerable man, wholly devoted to God, had also given me this instruction as a teacher: if anywhere I heard new sects arising that were contrary to apostolic teachings, I should immediately devote my entire self to the defense of the Catholic faith.”

And in Book I *Against Elipandus*, speaking of Charles, he says:

> “I did not come to Francia to corrupt him, for he cannot be corrupted, but to assist him in the Catholic faith in which he was nurtured from his earliest age and most excellently instructed by Christian parents and Catholic teachers.”

From all this it is clear that those writers are mistaken who say that Alcuin remained with Charles because he had been captivated either by the pleasantness of the land or by the king’s courtesy, when he had been sent to him by Offa, king of the Mercians, to establish friendship.

@ [Col. 0111D] William of Malmesbury, Book I of *The Deeds of the English*; Polydore Vergil, Book V of the *History of England*; and others.

They are likewise mistaken who assert that he was sent by Achaïus, king of the Scots, at Charles’s request.

@ [Col. 0111D] John Major, Book XI, chapter 13, *On the Deeds of the Scots*; Hector Boethius, Book X; and Buchanan, Book V.

Finally, they are mistaken who report that, “having heard how gladly the most devout of kings, Charles, received learned men, he voluntarily boarded a ship and came to him.”

@ [Col. 0112D] The monk of Saint Gall, Book I of *The Deeds of Charlemagne*; William of Nangis; and others.

## CHAPTER VIII

### The time of his arrival and the condemnation of the Felician heresy

As for the time of his arrival in Francia, no ancient writer seems so far to have recorded it, not even the Anonymous author who composed his life at the dictation of Sigulf. But if the sequence and order of events are carefully considered, it can be discovered that he was not summoned before the year 792 or 793.

Roger of Howden, in the first part of his *Annals*, and after him Matthew of Westminster in the *Florarium*, report that in the year 792 King Charles sent to Britain a synodal book that had been forwarded to him from Constantinople and that contained many improper things contrary to the true faith. Against it, they say, Albinus wrote a letter wonderfully supported by the authority of divine Scripture and brought it, in the name of the bishops and princes of England, to Charles, king of the Franks.

This also agrees, chronologically, with what Alcuin himself says in Book I *Against Elipandus*:

> “Before I had come to Francia at the command of that most wise king Charles, this same sect of your error, while that glorious prince was presiding and Felix—whom you are accustomed to praise greatly—was present as the defender of your party at that time, was debated in the most famous place called Regensburg. By the synodal authority of the priests of Christ who had assembled from different parts of the Christian empire, it was condemned with an eternal anathema; indeed, it was utterly exterminated by the blessed Pope Hadrian, who at that time governed the see of the holy Roman Church with apostolic authority. Then Felix, unhappily fleeing to your regions, attempted, at your request, to revive the smoldering ashes of infidelity.”

For in the year 792, according to the *Annals* of an unknown author, the Felician heresy was first condemned at Regensburg, although its author himself denied it. He was also brought by Engilberth, abbot of the monastery of Centula, into the presence of Hadrian the pope and, after making a confession, condemned it again.

## CHAPTER IX

### He writes an exhortatory letter to Felix, who answers him in an extensive treatise; and he urges the leading teachers of Francia to labor in defense of the Catholic faith

Alcuin therefore arrived in these regions around the year 793. At the beginning of his arrival, he took care to send Felix an exhortatory letter urging him to join the Catholic unity. Felix attempted to answer him not with the brevity of a letter,

@ [Col. 0112D] These are Alcuin’s words in Book I *Against Elipandus*,

but with the length of a treatise, and in it opened most fully all the hiding places of his impiety. He asserted that Christ was both the old man and a titular God, an adopted Son, in need of a second regeneration, and many other things inconsistent with ecclesiastical doctrine.

Concerning this treatise Alcuin himself says elsewhere (Letter 83):

> “Recently a little book was sent to me by Felix the unfortunate. When, out of curiosity, I read through a few pages of it, I found worse heresies—or rather, more blasphemies—than I had previously read in his writings. He asserts that Jesus Christ is neither truly the Son of God nor truly God, but only a titular God.”

Felix had earlier also written a disputation with a Saracen. When Alcuin, at the request of King Charles, diligently sought it, asking whether any of his own people had heard of it, he was told that it could be found with Laidrad, bishop of Lyons (Letter 101). Therefore he promptly sent a messenger to that bishop, in case the work could be found there and dispatched as quickly as possible to the royal presence.

Meanwhile, however, he undertook to answer Felix’s other treatise and begged the pious and wise King Charles to give him assistants in the defense of the Catholic faith: Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia; Richbodus and Theodulf, bishops; and other distinguished teachers and masters.

He himself testifies to this in Letter 84 to Charles, where he says:

> “Regarding the book of the unfortunate man—not a teacher but a subverter—I am very pleased that your most holy will and devotion has taken responsibility for answering it in defense of the Catholic faith. But I beg you, if it pleases your piety, to have one copy of that book sent to the lord pope, another to the patriarch Paulinus, and likewise to the bishops, teachers, and masters Richbodus and Theodulf, so that each may answer on his own behalf. Your Flaccus is working with you to give an account of the Catholic faith. Let him be given enough time to examine quietly and carefully, with his pupils, the opinions of the Fathers: what each one would say concerning the propositions that the aforementioned subverter has set down in his book. Then, at a time appointed by you, let the answers of each be brought before your authority. Whatever propositions or opinions in that book are found to be contrary to the Catholic faith, let all of them be destroyed by Catholic examples. And if the writings of all resound equally and harmoniously in the profession and defense of the Catholic faith, it may be understood that one spirit speaks through the mouths and hearts of all. But if something different is found in the words or writings of any one of them, let it be seen who relies upon the greater authority of the holy Scriptures or the Catholic Fathers; and let the palm of praise be awarded to him who adheres more closely to divine testimonies.”

And in Letter 83 to the same Charles:

> “The answer to this book, or rather to this error, must be considered with great diligence and with many assistants. I alone am not sufficient to answer it. Let your holy piety provide suitable assistants for this work, so difficult and so necessary, so that this impious heresy may be completely extinguished before it spreads more widely throughout the world of the Christian empire, which divine piety has entrusted to you and your sons to rule and govern.”

## CHAPTER X

### He praises the books of Paulinus the patriarch and Etherius the bishop against Felix

Thus, roused as if by a trumpet call, the more learned and more experienced in divine matters directed the darts of their pens against this Felician—or rather Hispanic—heresy. Paulinus, among others, with whom Alcuin had already formed the closest friendship, attacked it in three books. He dedicated them to King Charles the Great and appended at the end a *Rule of Faith* written in verse. At his pressing and venerable commands, he begged that these books be delivered into the hands of the most reverend and most learned Albinus, his spokesman, conspicuous for the highest religious devotion.

@ [Col. 0113D] In a letter to King Charles, a fragment of which survives among the works of Paulinus of Aquileia, in volume 100 of Migne’s *Patrologia*.

Thus he addressed Alcuin, who writes that he received the books and was himself honored by Paulinus with such a distinguished encomium, which he extols with marvelous praises in Letter 113. There he speaks of them as follows:

> “How much more, when I reviewed your little book on the most sacred faith, adorned with the purity of Catholic peace, most delightful in the beauty of its eloquence, and most firmly grounded in the truth of its meanings, did I loosen all the reins of my soul into joy! There I saw four rivers of virtue flowing from one most luminous and health-giving fountain of paradise, irrigating not only the meadows of Ausonian fertility but the fields of the whole of ecclesiastical Latinity. There also I understood that the golden streams of spiritual meanings abounded in the gems of scholarly refinement. You have produced a work that will be of the greatest benefit and is absolutely necessary in the exposition of the Catholic faith—a work that I long desired and repeatedly urged the lord king to undertake: that the symbol of the Catholic faith should be gathered into a single document in the clearest meanings and most lucid language and distributed to all the priests throughout the individual parishes of episcopal jurisdictions, to be read and committed to memory, so that although they spoke different languages, one faith might nevertheless resound everywhere.”

For this reason many also considered these works worthy of being printed together with Alcuin’s writings. We have done so, with the assistance of the manuscript of the most distinguished and learned Putean brothers; I believe no one will fail to approve this as fair and reasonable.

But besides this Paulinus, Etherius—or Hitherius—bishop of Osma, and Beatus the abbot published, at the same time, two books against the same error. They were recently made public at Ingolstadt. Concerning them our Alcuin, addressing Felix, says:

> “As for your claim that a certain Beatus the abbot and his disciple Hitherius the bishop were the first to oppose your sect, we praise them for having attempted to defend the truth.”

@ [Col. 0113D] Book I *Against Felix*.

Whether the bishops Richbodus and Theodulf rendered similar assistance is not yet known.

## CHAPTER XI

### He answers Felix’s treatise in seven books and finally makes him Catholic; he also attacks Elipandus in four other books

Alcuin, as he himself left on record,

@ [Col. 0114D] Book I *Against Elipandus*,

answered Felix’s treatise with seven books composed in his devotion and refuted all the doctrines of his depravity. These books, which until now have been wrongly attributed to Paulinus, were read and approved in the presence of King Charles and the priests of Christ. They possessed such force and authority that

> “the same Felix, in the thirty-second year of the aforementioned glorious prince,”

@ [Col. 0114D] These are Alcuin’s words in the passage cited,

> “came voluntarily, when summoned, to the palace at Aachen. There, in the presence of the lord king and his nobles or priests of God, he was heard rationally and convicted truthfully. Giving glory to God and confessing the true faith, he returned to the peace of Catholic unanimity with his disciples who were then present.”

But this occurred only after his error had again been condemned at Frankfurt. For the *Annals* of an unknown author report that in the year 794:

> “A synod was held at Frankfurt, in which the Felician heresy was condemned for the third time before the bishops of Germany, Gaul, and Italy, in the presence of the great prince Charles and of Theophylact and Stephen, bishops and legates of Hadrian the pope; and the condemnation was confirmed by a binding decree.”

After this Charles entered Saxony with his army and returned to Aachen in the year 796. Felix was brought there by Laidrad, bishop of Lyons, “and presented before him,” to use Felix’s own words,

@ [Col. 0114D] In his confession of faith,

> “and received permission from him to present to the bishops, abbots, and other teachers whom the command of the glorious prince had summoned to him the opinions that he believed he had derived from the books of the saints concerning the adoption of the flesh in the Son of God, or his titular status in his humanity. Thus his assertion might be judged valid by them, not through violence but through an examination of the truth, if they did not reject it on the authority of the holy Fathers.”

And so it was done. For the opinions he brought forward concerning the dispute mentioned above—that is, concerning the adoption of the flesh and the titular status—they excluded on the authority of the holy Fathers, including Cyril the bishop, the blessed Gregory, pope of the city of Rome, the blessed Leo, and other holy teachers previously unknown to him. They also relied upon the authority of the synod recently assembled at Rome for this purpose, at the command of the glorious and most devout Charles, against a letter that Felix had formerly written to the venerable Albinus, abbot of the church of Tours—for this is how he designates our Alcuin, and below we shall say more about his abbeys.

At that synod Pope Leo was present—he had succeeded Hadrian in that same year—and fifty-seven other bishops were seated with him, along with many priests and deacons, in the house of the blessed Apostle Peter. By the authority of all these, then, they excluded the opinions just mentioned—not, as has been said, by any kind of violence, but by the reasoning of truth, as was proper.

Convicted by their authority, by the truth, and by the consent of the whole universal Church, Felix joined himself to their better understanding rather than to the one he had previously followed. With God’s favor he returned to the universal Church with all his heart—not with any pretense or veil of falsehood, as before, but with true belief of heart and confession of mouth.

Thus far the words of Felix, who was no longer to remain unfortunate.

What part Alcuin had in his conversion, he himself briefly explains when addressing Elipandus:

> “I did not make Felix a martyr with Rufinus; rather, by God’s mercy, I made Felix, formerly an accomplice in your error, a Catholic.”

@ [Col. 0114D] Book I *Against Elipandus*.

Not long afterward he also attacked Elipandus, bishop of the see of Toledo, who was attempting to revive the ashes of his disciple, now buried, in four other books of great learning. But whether he overcame him and brought him back to the unity of the Church is not found in Alcuin’s writings.

## CHAPTER XII

### He instructs King Charles in every kind of discipline; and whether David was Charles’s proper name or an assumed one

Since Alcuin’s chief distinction also lay in teaching, after he had been summoned from England, where he had taught, to Gaul, we must now see how he displayed all the treasures of hidden philosophy with an extraordinary eloquence before the disciples who flocked to hear him in great numbers from the farthest parts of the world.

Having become a new citizen of Francia, he thereafter remained closely attached to Charles as a diligent and faithful companion. Above all, he filled his mind with every discipline, so that no one in the whole world was his equal in the sciences.

This can easily be inferred either from Alcuin’s rhetorical and dialectical dialogues with him or from the dedicatory letter of the books on the Holy Trinity. In that letter, when he sent these books to Charles, already crowned emperor—that is, after the year 800—he states that the ruler of the Christian people ought to know everything. While showing the office by which some called him “teacher,”

@ [Col. 0115D] These are Alcuin’s words,

he rebukes certain people who considered it of little use for the king’s most noble mind to wish to learn the principles of dialectical discipline as well.

The same is shown by poem 199, in which he addresses the youth of the city of York:

> Such gifts please your father,  
> Who now causes noble arts to resound in royal ears  
> And leads him, following the Fathers, through their meadows,  
> As he reigns beneath the beautiful crown of lofty wisdom.

@ [Col. 0115C] It is shown even more clearly by the following verses of poem 270:

> O my sweet beloved David, farewell through the ages.  
> How I would always wish to have you present!  
> How I would wish to play with you in abundant verse,  
> To climb with you toward the lofty stars of the highest heaven,  
> To learn with you the beautiful forms of numbers,  
> Or to penetrate the wondrous sayings of the ancient Fathers,  
> Or to discuss the sacred commandments of eternal salvation—  
> What path might carry you with me above the stars.

In this passage, as almost everywhere else, he calls Charles David. I scarcely dare affirm whether this was his proper name or an assumed one. Certainly the following words of Alcuin addressed to him suggest that it was not an assumed name (Letter 96):

> “May abundant blessing upon the illustrious sons of your nobility increase through your benefactions, just as, through the holiness of your namesake, the most beloved King David, the power of the throne, as we read, was preserved for all his grandsons according to the established rules.”

For, as a certain very learned man says, Alcuin would not have called David the namesake of King Charles if his intention had been to give Charles that name merely because of his resemblance to and imitation of David.

This also seems to be confirmed by another testimony of Alcuin himself, where he writes (Letter 17):

> “David, formerly king of the preceding people, chosen by God and beloved by God, and the distinguished psalmist who subdued nations on every side to victorious Israel by the sword and stood forth among the people as an excellent preacher of God’s law—through the extraordinary nobility of whose sons Christ, the flower of the field and of the valleys, blossomed for the salvation of the world—has in these present times granted to his people a king of the same name, virtue, and faith as ruler and teacher. Under his protection the Christian people rests peacefully in the heights above, and he stands as a terror to pagan nations on every side.”

Perhaps, the aforementioned very learned man adds, his name was changed when he was baptized or anointed king. The same thing was done, he says, with Pippin, king of Italy, his son.

That it was his proper name, however, is discouraged by the custom of that and the following age, in which I find that our kings were commonly addressed by writers with the name David. Thus Amalarius, bishop of Trier,

@ [Col. 0115D] At the end of the preface,

and Pope Stephen, in Thegan’s work,

@ [Col. 0115D] *The Book of the Deeds of Louis the Pious*,

call Louis, king and son of Charlemagne, a new and second David. Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, compares Charles the Bald, son of Louis, with David in counsel.

@ [Col. 0115D] Letter 93.

The Italians, in Liutprand of Cremona, the deacon,

@ [Col. 0115D] Book V of the *History*, chapter 14,

bark that King Berengar had come as another David, and in their blind judgment even prefer him to Charles the Great. To mention some more recent examples, Simon Grebanus likewise calls Charles VII David

@ [Col. 0115D] In his epitaph,

and all men recently publicly called Henry the Great “David”

@ [Col. 0115D] In funeral sermons.

## CHAPTER XIII

### He is appointed teacher to Louis and Pippin and instructs many other distinguished men in Gaul

However the matter may stand, Alcuin’s reputation with King Charles was certainly so great that he was not only called his teacher

@ [Col. 0115D] Alcuin, Letter 162, and the monk of Saint Gall, Book I,

and favorite,

@ [Col. 0115D] Anastasius the Librarian, in the *Life of Hadrian I*,

but was also chosen above all others by Charles to educate his sons Louis and Pippin in the precepts of learning.

This is learned partly from Radulfus, dean of Tongeren, Book I *On the Observance of the Canons*, and partly from the disputation that Alcuin himself conducted with Pippin, a noble and royal boy.

And because he was the most experienced and learned teacher of the whole region

@ [Col. 0116C] This is shown by the encomium that Amalarius of Metz gives him

@ [Col. 0115D] Book *On the Order of the Antiphon*, chapter 52,

he was heard with great attendance and admiration from other men as well, and had many disciples distinguished for their learning. Among the foremost of them was Amalarius himself, then a boy.

@ [Col. 0115D] Amalharius himself, at the place cited above; thereafter bishop of Trier; Rhabanus Maurus

@ [Col. 0116D] Flodoardus, book III of the *History of the Church of Rheims*, chapter 21; also still a boy, to whom Letter 150 is extant, but later a great and celebrated man—for he eventually became archbishop of Mainz; Bishop Haymo

@ [Col. 0116D] Trithemius, *On the Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, book II, chapter 26; Usualdus, abbot of Saint Salvator

@ [Col. 0116D] Alcuin, Letter 20; who wrote a *Martyrology of the Saints*

@ [Col. 0115D] Book V of the *History*, chapter 14; Richbod, surnamed Macharius, bishop of Trier before Amalharius

@ [Col. 0116D] Letter 169; Peter, archbishop of Milan

@ [Col. 0116D] Letter 167; Saint Aldricus, abbot of Ferrières

@ [Col. 0116D] *Life of Saint Aldricus*; and many others.

## CHAPTER XIV

### In what places he taught, and whether he was the first founder of the University of Paris

There is not, however, general agreement about the places in which he earned lasting renown among all by educating the young in this way. Trithemius writes more than once that he stayed at the monastery of Fulda and there nurtured many highly distinguished disciples from among the monks

@ [Col. 0116D] At the place cited, and in the *Chronicle of Hirsau* under the year 890; among them he names Haymo, Usuardus or Isuardus, and Rhabanus. The author of the *Ecclesiastical Chronicle of Augsburg*, chapter 10, testifies that he taught at Saint Gall

@ [Col. 0117A] and there became renowned before a noble audience. More recent writers also

@ [Col. 0117D] Polydore Vergil, book V of the *English History*, and Nicolaus Serarius, book IV of the *History of Mainz*, assert that he discharged the office of lecturer in Paris, following the opinion and authority of those who have handed down that the foundation of this most celebrated marketplace of the sciences was laid by him together with several other very learned men. But whether this is true, he himself declares nowhere in his writings. He certainly reports that he maintained public schools in Francia, in Letter 43 to Charlemagne, in these words: “But now, as my blood grows cold, as it were toward evening, I do not cease sowing in Francia.” And in Letter 86 to the same man:

“Nor, he says, ought the wearisome sluggishness of those who attend the lectures to be fairly attributed to the goodwill of the teacher, if, with very many following the renowned zeal of your purpose, perhaps a new Athens might be completed in Francia—indeed, one much more excellent, because this one, ennobled by the teaching of Christ the Lord, surpasses all the wisdom of academic training. The former, instructed only in the disciplines of Plato and formed by the seven arts, became renowned. This one, moreover, enriched by the sevenfold fullness of the Holy Spirit, surpasses the whole dignity of secular wisdom.”

But in which provinces of Francia did he sow seeds of this kind of learning? Or in what city or town of Gaul was this Athens completed? Perhaps in eloquent Paris, Lutetia, to which, as is read in the *Great Belgian Chronicle*, King Charles transferred the school from the city of Rome—something that had earlier been transferred there by the Romans from Greece? There are many reasons that forbid us to believe this.

First, Alcuin nowhere mentions either Paris or Lutetia. Second, although he was in many places of Gaul, whether with King Charles—as at Aachen, according to the author of the *Life of Saint Ludger*, book I, chapter 34—or without King Charles, as in the Belgian region

@ [Col. 0117D] Letter 86; at Tours

@ [Col. 0117D] Letters 43, 109, 101, and 132; at Centula

@ [Col. 0117D] Preface to the *Life of Saint Richarius*; at Saint-Amand

@ [Col. 0117D] Letter 102; and elsewhere

@ [Col. 0117D] Letter 100; he never, however, indicates in explicit words that he taught except either in the king’s palace or at Caesarodunum of Tours.

That there was a school in the palace is demonstrated by these words of his to Charles

@ [Col. 0118D] Letter 173:

“I, ignorant and unaware, did not know that an Egyptian school was operating in the palace of David’s glory. When I departed, I left Latins there; I do not know who introduced Egyptians in their place.”

That he also educated Gallic youth at Tours, he repeats not once but frequently. In Letter 43 to King Charles:

“I shall send back some of our boys, who will carry the flowers of Britain into Francia, so that there may be not merely a closed garden at York, but in the region of Tours the outpourings of paradise with the fruits of its trees; so that, when the South Wind comes to breathe upon the gardens of the Loire, their spices may flow forth.”

Likewise, in Letter 101:

“Thus I, although making little progress, struggle with the rusticity of Tours. Let your authority educate the palace boys.”

And if it is permissible to rely also on supplementary testimonies, where can that new Athens of which I have just spoken be situated more appropriately than in a school of this kind at Tours? For the monk of Saint Gall writes as follows about the matter

@ [Col. 0118D] Book I of *The Deeds of Charlemagne*:

“King Charles gave Albinus the abbey of Saint Martin near the city of Tours, so that whenever he himself was absent, Albinus might rest there and teach those who flocked to him. His teaching bore such abundant fruit that the Gauls, or Franks, of our own day became the equals of the ancient Romans or Athenians.”

## CHAPTER XV

### By what benefits Charles honored him

But since we have mentioned the abbey of Saint Martin, it is worthwhile now to investigate by what benefits King Charles honored this distinguished teacher, or what gifts he bestowed upon him in his kingdom. For it may be learned even from Letter 134 to Charles that many acts of royal kindness were performed for him. There he says:

“May the most holy Trinity repay your goodness, most beloved David of all, with everlasting blessedness for whatever devotion or kindness you have shown toward me, your servant. Just as you mercifully promised when I first came to you, so you have faithfully fulfilled everything; and, to crown the fullest truth, which always dwells in the treasury of your heart, you have added a hundredfold, as is clearer than daylight to the eyes of all and resounds in the ears of many throughout distant lands.”

In particular, he gave him the abbey of Saint Lupus of Troyes, as an anonymous author of his *Life* reports. Alcuin himself also seems to indicate this in Letter 126 to his sister, in these words:

“I was exceedingly pleased by the cross which your kindness sent me. And I believe that you will have an eternal reward from God for that work, as well as the constant intercessions of Saint Lupus and praiseworthy thanksgivings from those who are accustomed to flee to his patronage.”

He also possessed the abbey of Bethlehem, or Ferrières, in the district of Wastina, as is recorded in the *Life of Saint Aldricus*, archbishop of Sens; and likewise the cell of Saint Judoc, entrusted to him for providing hospitality to pilgrims.

Lupus of Ferrières gives testimony concerning this in Letter 11 to King Lothair, when he himself had received the same cell from Louis the Emperor, son of Charlemagne:

“The cell of Saint Judoc,” he says, “which the great Charles had once entrusted to Alcuin for dispensing alms to pilgrims, your father of blessed memory granted to us on the condition stated in his decree: that whatever remained from the alms should accrue to our use.”

Nor do I doubt that this cell was different from that maritime cell which Alcuin writes that he likewise left by lawful succession

@ [Col. 0118D] Preface to the *Life of Saint Willibrord*. For the patron of the former was Saint Andrew, whereas that of the latter was Saint Judoc. The former was distinguished by the body of Saint Wilgisius, the latter by the relics of Saint Judoc. Both, however, were maritime: the former in Northumbria, on promontories surrounded by the Ocean Sea and the River Humber; the latter in a maritime place of Belgium

@ [Col. 0118C] formerly called Wicus, either from the winding curve of the sea, which in Saxon is called *wic*, as Rhenanus teaches; or from a secure station, where people dwell in closely joined buildings, if *wic* denotes this, as Hadrianus Junius argues; or from a castle, if *wic* means “castle,” as the old author Alfricus asserts. It is now commonly called Saint-Josse-sur-Mer.

That the place of Saint Judoc was once called Wicus, or Wici in the plural, and that it was also possessed by our Alcuin, he himself clearly declares in Letter 44, where he complains about his solitude:

“I remain at home almost as if deprived of my children. Damoetas has withdrawn to Saxony, Homer to Italy, Candidus to Britain; Martin, sick, has remained at Wici, at Saint Judoc.”

Likewise, in Letter 96 to King Charles:

“On my return from Wicus, because of necessary matters which we had to arrange there, your most sweet letters came to meet me.”

Finally, he received from the same King Charles the abbey of Saint Martin of Tours to govern, when he was considering withdrawing altogether from secular occupations. He himself bears witness to this in Letter 129 to the same king, when he says:

“For nearly five years before this, I considered, God as my witness, withdrawing from secular occupations with no false intention. But, by the counsel of your pious foresight, I was transferred into the service of Saint Martin, a service profitable to the Catholic faith and ecclesiastical discipline, God granting it.”

Before this transfer, however, I do not know whether the following event occurred at this monastery, which Odo of Cluny

@ [Col. 0118D] in his *Treatise on the Translation of the Body of Saint Martin*; Helinandus

@ [Col. 0118D] in Vincent of Beauvais, book XXIII, chapter 173; the author of the *Great Belgian Chronicle*

@ [Col. 0118D] under the year 770; and many others relate: that all the monks there were killed by angels in a single night because, forgetful of their former religious discipline, they wore silk garments and walked in gilded shoes. Only one was spared—the one who saw the angels striking them and prayed that he might be reserved for doing penance, finally prevailing upon them.

Ademar of Angoulême postpones this to a much later period and asserts that it happened for another reason as well:

@ [Col. 0119A] “Then,” he says

@ [Col. 0119D] “namely, while Charles the Bald was reigning, the monks of Saint Martin of Tours, compelled by no one, cast aside the monastic habit before his body and put on the canonical habit. But soon a plague broke out among them, so that they all died in one night, and thereafter the place was inhabited by canons.”

These words arouse in me the suspicion that what is found in the *Chronicle of Tours* is not yet altogether certain:

“In the year 796, King Charles established canons in the church of blessed Martin of Tours, by the authority of Pope Hadrian, and placed his teacher Saint Alcuin over them as abbot.”

## CHAPTER XVI

### He was Charlemagne’s counselor and was sent by him as an envoy to Rome

Moreover, this man, enriched with so many and such distinguished abbeys, not only presided over them with great renown for holiness and learning, but also did not remain detached from civil affairs and the administration of the state. For Charlemagne always made him his intimate counselor and, as the author of the *Life of Saint Aldricus*, archbishop of Sens, says, “determined all the affairs of the imperial court, and the more important matters, according to his judgment.”

Therefore he is often recorded as having been summoned by him to court

@ [Col. 0119D] Letters 109 and 132; even while he was absent. He was also sent by that prince as an envoy to Rome, together with Bishop George and Abbot Gulfard, to inquire about the rights of Saint Peter against the king of the Lombards, as Anastasius the Librarian reports in his *Life of Pope Hadrian I*.

When some disagreement had arisen between King Offa and the aforementioned

@ [Col. 0119C] Charles, he was still chosen above all others to be sent to those regions on behalf of peace

@ [Col. 0119D] William of Malmesbury, books 3 and 4 of the work cited. Finally, when Charles was planning to go to Rome in the year 800, he wished to take Alcuin with him

@ [Col. 0119D] Letters 96 and 109. But Alcuin excused himself in two letters, preferring the smoke-blackened roofs of Tours to the gilded citadels of Rome

@ [Col. 0119D] Letter 109; and he asked the king to allow him faithfully and earnestly to aid his journey through prayers with God’s servants at Saint Martin

@ [Col. 0119D] Letter 96. Once this request had been granted, Alcuin learned that Charles wished to travel along the Gallic coast before crossing into Italy. He nevertheless thought he should meet him at Centula, at Saint Richarius. There, celebrating the Paschal feast with him

@ [Col. 0119D] *Life of Charlemagne*, and Alcuin’s preface to the *Life of Saint Richarius*, he wrote, or rather corrected, the *Life of that same Saint Richarius the Confessor*, which he also dedicated to the most devout King Charles in a dedicatory letter.

## CHAPTER XVII

### He taught at Tours until the final day of his life, and there wrote many volumes

After returning from there to Tours, he retained until the final day of his life the pattern of life he had established at the beginning. For there he lived piously and holily, and, continuing to educate the young of Gaul, he earned for himself a fame that would never die by the frequent and fruitful publication of volumes.

Above all, he composed there the *Questions*, or, as he himself calls them, the *Interrogations on the Book of Genesis*, and dedicated them to Sigulf, his old and inseparable companion and future successor in the abbey of Ferrières. He also prepared an *Enchiridion*, or pious and concise exposition of certain psalms.

Likewise, he wrote commentaries on Ecclesiastes, which he dedicated to his beloved disciples, the priest Onias, the presbyter Candidus, and the deacon Nathanael. He also composed those splendid seven books of further commentaries which, at the request of the consecrated virgins Gisla and Richtruda, once his disciples in England, he wrote on the Gospel of Saint John.

Moreover, at the command of King Charles, he then corrected all the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments and sent the corrected copies to him from Saint Martin

@ [Col. 0120D] The letter prefixed to book VI of the *Commentaries on Saint John*, and Letter 131. He arranged David’s Psalter for the week, which John Bale cites under the title *Offices for the Weekdays*, and which has therefore now been published by us for the first time from the very ancient codex of the most illustrious Jac. Aug. Thuani.

He collected from the ancient Fathers of the Church homilies, or sermons, to be read throughout the year

@ [Col. 0120D] An anonymous author in his *Life*. He wrote a book *On Virtues and Vices* for Wido, or Witton, count of the British March

@ [Col. 0120B] The anonymous annalist and the *Life of Charlemagne*. He composed a booklet *On the Antichrist*, which some formerly attributed to Rhabanus and others even to Saint Augustine. He abridged with remarkable skill the *Life and Miracles of Saint Martin*.

Finally, he wrote many letters full of learning to Hadrian and Leo, the supreme pontiffs; to the glorious King Charles; to Angelbert, chief officer of the palace of King Pippin; to Megenfrid, treasurer of the royal palace; to Aericus, or Ehericus, duke of Friuli; to Magenhar, count of Sens; to Flavius Homer, chamberlain of King Charles; to Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia; to Laidradus, bishop of Lyon; to Nefridius, bishop of Narbonne; and to many other men of great authority and power.

For the rest of his books, it is not so clearly established where or when they were composed, except for the *Life of Saint Willibrord*, which he wrote in England, and the works on rhetoric and dialectic, which he prepared in the king’s palace

@ [Col. 0120C] We also attribute to him the *Books of the Sacraments* and *On the Divine Offices*, because they were printed earlier under his name, although we are not without grounds for conjecturing that he never wrote the latter. For its author, whoever he may be, declares himself an inhabitant of Braccate Gaul (chapter 34); and, in an ancient manuscript written in the old style, with whose help we restored twelve complete chapters, he attributes the question concerning the birthdays of the saints appended to chapter 18 to the monk Elpricus, who, according to Trithemius, flourished in the year 1040. Moreover, in that work (chapter 32) the institution of the feast of All Saints on the Kalends of November is mentioned, although from Sigebert and others it is readily learned that this feast began to be celebrated in Gaul and Germany only long after Alcuin’s death, namely in the year 835.

Whatever the truth may be, many further writings of his are reported, which have so far remained hidden through either the ravages of time or negligence.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### His death, burial, and sanctity

@ [Col. 0120D] Thus distinguished by the fame of so many and such great adornments of intellect, leading a religious life under the shadow of Charles’s power and beneath the shelter of his piety

@ [Col. 0120D] Letter 133; directing all the consolation of his weakness and old age toward God, among the brothers faithfully serving God in the church of Saint Martin, he at last rested happily, as he had desired

@ [Col. 0120D] Letter 129. In the year of Christ 804, according to the testimony of nearly all the ancients

@ [Col. 0120D] Odorannus, the *Chronicle of Tours and Limoges*, the anonymous author of his *Life*, and others; and, flying away to the rewards of heaven on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, he was buried by his own people in that same church, with the epitaph that he had set up for himself while still alive.

For it is false both that William of Malmesbury asserts

@ [Col. 0121A] Book I, chapter 3 of *The Deeds of the Kings of England*, that he died at Saint Paul’s in the monastery of Cormaric; and that another, more recent writer records

@ [Col. 0122A] Browerus, book I of the *Antiquities of Fulda*, chapter 10; that he was buried in the church of Hersfeld near Fulda.

Finally, after the last day of his life, he also earned the title of blessed, or saint

@ [Col. 0122A] as the anonymous author of his *Life*, Flodoardus, book III of the *History of Rheims*, chapter 21; a canon of Saint Martin in the *Chronicles*; and Rhabanus, archbishop of Mainz, in his *Martyrology*, teach.

These, for the most part, are all that it has been possible to learn about Alcuin from his own works.

## I. Einhard, *Life of Charlemagne*, in Bouquet, *Writers of the History of Gaul*, volume V, p. 99

In the study of grammar he listened to the elderly deacon Peter of Pisa; in the other disciplines he had as teacher Albinus, surnamed Alcuin, likewise a deacon, a man of Saxon origin from Britain, learned in every field. Under him he devoted a great deal of both time and labor to learning rhetoric and dialectic, but especially astronomy.

## II. Saint Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, in a letter to Charlemagne concerning the books he wrote against Bishop Felix, in Madruzius, *Works of Saint Paulinus*, p. 168

“For these particular first offerings of my prayers I hasten to present uniquely, moved by the purest devotion of my heart, in the presence of the orthodox prince and lord of the earth, so that this little gift of ours—though not precious, whatever it may be—may be brought without delay to the hands of the most reverend man, most skilled and distinguished in divine matters, namely Albinus, your foremost spokesman of the highest religious devotion, and, above all, the sweetest honey of your flourishing favor toward me, under the pressure of your venerable commands.

I do not know whether I could ever bestow upon his inviolable charity, through my own strength, these things gathered together in another volume. Not because he needs them, but so that it may be understood more clearly how the sweetness of love and friendship toward him, with which my heart is filled, may continually grow sweetly within me as it is tasted.”

They also embrace with equal reverence the opinions of those who, by divine favor, flourished in the Church in understanding, Catholic doctrine, and holiness of conduct after the canon itself had been composed by blessed Gelasius, and who wrote or taught nothing discordant or different from the faithful—and therefore Catholic—teaching of those orthodox Fathers listed in that same canon. Such were the venerable presbyter Bede; and Paulinus, of venerable memory, patriarch of the Aquileian see; and Alcuin, a religious and learned man [Col. 0126A]. The Roman Apostolic See not only most graciously accepted their faith and teaching, but also praised them highly, as we find in the writings of that holy see which our church received from the same mother of churches, in the time of the Emperor Charles of blessed memory, when a synod was held concerning the known infidelity of Felix and its proceedings were sent to the Roman Church, as to the summit of the churches. Anyone who reads their writings also understands how worthy they are of praise and acceptance. Flodoard, in his *History of the Church of Rheims*, book III, in Sirmond, vol.
