### XXXIX. Huldricus Mutius, *Chronicle of the Germans*, book VIII, in Pistorius, vol. II of the *German Historians*, page 677, Regensburg edition, 1726

[Col. 0129B] He—that is, King Charles—used Peter of Pisa as his teacher in Greek letters. In dialectic, rhetoric, astronomy, and all the mathematical disciplines, he used as his teacher the Briton Alcuin, a deacon. The authors write that this Alcuin was sent by the king of England as an ambassador to Charles concerning important affairs of the kingdoms; and thus the two became dear to one another that Alcuin remained with Charles.

### XL. A German poet cited by Camden, in Alford, vol. II of the *Annals of Anglo-Saxon Ecclesiastical History*, under the year 800, no. 8

What do you not owe to Alcuin, eloquent Lutetia? He happily began there to restore the good arts and alone to drive barbarism far away.

### XLI. Francesco Petrarch, book V of the *Senile Letters*, letter 2

[Col. 0129C] Concerning Charles, who earned among the Gauls the surname “the Great,” his teacher Albinus, in his history of him, after saying that for several years before his death he had been accustomed to suffer frequent fevers, added: “And then indeed,” he says, “he did more according to his own judgment than on the advice of physicians, whom he almost hated.” This is related in precisely the same words by Einhard in the *Life of Charles the Great*, in Bouquet, vol. V of the *Historians of Gaul*, no. 22, page 98.

### XLII. Donato Acciaiuoli, in the *Life of Charles the Great*, in Quercetanus, in this passage

Charles had as his teacher Albinus, later surnamed Alcuin, an exceedingly learned and supreme philosopher. From him he received not only the pursuit of wisdom but also instruction in oratory and the art of reasoning. Through his efforts, they say, Charles first established the Parisian school.

[Col. 0129D] ### XLIII. Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Alcuin, or Albinus, a monk and deacon, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours, English by nationality, formerly a pupil of the presbyter Saint Bede, was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in knowledge of secular letters, second to no one of his time, excellent in verse and prose. Summoned from Britain by the Emperor Charles the Great, he was held in such intimacy by him that he was called the emperor’s cherished teacher. Under his instruction the emperor himself strove to be initiated into all the disciplines of the liberal arts.

He wrote many distinguished volumes, among which are reported:

*On the Holy Trinity and the Faith*, 3 books. “To the glorious Lord Charles, emperor.”

*To the Questions of Fredegisus*, 1 book. “To my most desired son.”

*To Eulalia, on the Reason of the Soul*, 1 book. “To the most beloved in the love of Christ.”

*To Count Guido, on the Virtues*, 1 book. “To my dearest son Guido.”

One book of *Sentences*.

One book *On the Song of Songs*.

Seven books *On the Gospel of John*.

One book *On Genesis*.

One book *On Ecclesiastes*.

Fourteen books *On the Epistles of Paul*.

One book *On the Apocalypse of John*.

One book *On the Adoption of the Sons of God*. “To the venerable one and in Christ ...”

One book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*. “We believe in one God.”

One book *Mirror for Little Ones*. “In divine Scripture.”

One book *On the Proper Meaning of the Names of God*.

One book *Life of Saint Vedast*.

One book of *Letters to Various Persons*.

One book, *Dialogue for His Disciples*.

One book, *Enchiridion on Certain Psalms*.

One book *On the Liberal Arts*.

He is also said to have written many other works, which nevertheless have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the reign of Charles the Great, in the year of the Lord 770.

The same Trithemius, book II of *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, chapter 26, gives almost the same account, but adds the following:

After Bede’s death he came to Gaul with three monk-companions and, having stayed for some time in the monastery of Fulda, raised many illustrious disciples from among the monks. Among them he had as his principal pupils Haymo, later bishop; Isuard the monk; and Rhabanus Maurus, then a boy, who later grew into a great man. Finally, having been made abbot of Saint Martin of Tours through Charles’s provision, he shone forth as a man distinguished in learning and holiness.

After this he adds certain works to the preceding catalogue, namely:

One book of *Questions on Genesis*.

One book *On Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews*.

One book *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*.

*On Grammar*; *On Logic*; *On Orthography*; *On Music*; *On Astronomy*; *On the Poetic Art*; *On the Scattering of Letters*; *On Meters*; *On Arithmetic and Geometry*; *On Rhetoric*.

One book of *Letters*, which are rarely found together.

*Prognosticon concerning the Future Age*.

### XLIV. The Author of the *Chronicle of Chronicles*

[Col. 0130C] Alcuin ... a man exceptionally learned in the Greek and Latin languages, as well as the foremost theologian and philosopher of his time, was held in the highest esteem by Charles the Great for these reasons, since he made him learned in dialectic, rhetoric, and astronomy. ... Since he was regarded as a learned theologian, he published books *On the Trinity*, together with *Questions*; *Mirror for Little Ones*; *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*; *On the Reason of the Soul*; and many other books pertaining to the Christian religion.

### XLV. Polydore Vergil, book V of *English History*, page 106, Basel edition, 1570

Charles the Great, seeing that Albinus, or Alcuin, who had been sent to Gaul by Offa, king of the Mercians, for the purpose of establishing friendship, possessed very extensive learning and therefore deserved to be honored, made him his guest from an ambassador, and his teacher from a guest [Col. 0130D]. I believe he imitated the ancient example of the Athenians, who, after Gorgias had been publicly sent to them by the Leontines as an ambassador and had completed his embassy, detained him at Athens, captivated by his eloquence.

Thus Alcuin, an Englishman who afterward remained in Gaul, began to teach the liberal arts at Paris. Through his influence, not long afterward Charles himself first established a school in that city, and another in Italy at Ticinum, now called Pavia, and so forth.

### XLVI. Albert Krantz, book I of the *Metropolis*, chapter 6

Alcuin was a foremost man with King Charles, on whose advice, especially in sacred matters, he conducted everything. It was he who first commended Ludger to the king.

### XLVII. Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca Sancta*, book III, page 362

Albinus Flaccus, surnamed Alcuin, a monk, deacon, and abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours [Col. 0131A], English by nationality, a pupil of the presbyter Bede, a man celebrated in every branch of learning in his time, and teacher of Charles the Great Augustus, wrote the following volumes on sacred Scripture.

For the presbyter Sigulfus, a brief commentary on Genesis, interpolated from the opinions of the Fathers and arranged by question and answer in simple historical narration. Its beginning is: “To my dearest brother in Christ, Sigulf.”

A brief commentary of moral annotations on the fifteen Songs of Ascents—that is, from Psalm 119 through Psalm 133—which begins: “The steps are ...”

On the seven Penitential Psalms, concise, pointed, and remarkably meaningful annotations according to the moral sense, beginning: “The title of the psalm ...”

One book *On Ecclesiastes*, for Onia and Candidus.

One book *On the Song of Songs*.

Seven books of concise and lucid commentaries on the Gospel of John.

Fourteen books on all the Epistles of Paul.

One book on the Apocalypse [Col. 0131B].

At the command of Charles the Great he also collected and arranged in order the homilies of the outstanding doctors of the Church on the Gospels, which are read publicly in churches throughout the year. They number 209, namely: 48 by Augustine, 6 by Jerome, 10 by Ambrose, 1 by Hilary, 2 by Fulgentius, 4 by Origen, 17 by Maximus, 11 by Chrysostom, 1 by Severianus, 21 by Leo, 39 by Gregory, 48 by Bede, and 1 by Isidore.

Among those inscribed under the names of Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, and occasionally Bede, however, there are not homilies, but centos of explanations taken from the commentaries of these authors, which have been counted in this volume among the old homilies. He flourished under Charles the Great Augustus, in the year of the Lord 770.

### XLVIII. John Leland, *On British Writers*

At that time ... Ecgbert established at York an exceedingly elegant library for the benefit of posterity, being a man plainly born to advance learning. And so that such great treasures might not lack a vigilant guardian, he appointed to this new undertaking his pupil Flaccus Albinus, a man strong in eloquence, learning, and finally judgment.

In the same work, chapter 87, page 119, he calls Albinus the most learned among the learned men of his age.

In the same work, chapter 88, page 121:

Offa, the most powerful prince of the Mercians, together with the other petty kings of England, had very just reasons for sending ambassadors to Charles the Great. When he was considering whom above all he should send, Albinus came to mind, and he appointed him to this necessary and useful embassy. Thus he crossed into Gaul with other men both highly learned and prudent, and set forth before Charles the Great the causes of the English princes with great skill, greater eloquence, and greatest prudence. Charles was so delighted—beyond what anyone could believe—by the man’s eloquence and wisdom, and also by the sweetness of his character, that he retained him in Gaul, perhaps with King Offa’s consent, by offering most honorable conditions.

Charles himself was of excellent talent and not averse to letters. Therefore he asked Albinus how he might cultivate his Franks in the learned arts. Albinus’s sound counsel was not lacking: first, with remarkable diligence, he instructed Charles himself by publishing several little books for this purpose, which still exist; then, through public lectures, he drew the Frankish nobility to Paris; finally, he encouraged the common people themselves, each according to his distinguished talent, to pursue the best studies. Hence, within a short time, a great number of students flocked to Paris. This was the origin of the University of Paris, which it owes to our Albinus.

If anyone now wishes to know what more he accomplished in Gaul, let him read through his book of Letters, and he will be fully informed. Meanwhile, we shall list the books he published, on the testimony of Donatus the Gaul, a by no means untruthful historian.

*On the Trinity*, 3 books. “To the glorious Lord Charles.”

*On Genesis*, 1 book. “How It Is Harmonized.”

*On the Song of Songs*, 1 book.

*On Ecclesiastes*, 1 book.

*On the Gospel of John*, 7 books.

*On the Epistle to the Hebrews*, 1 book.

*Dialogue for His Disciples*, 1 book.

*On the Reason of the Soul*, for Eulalia. “To the most beloved.”

One book of *Sentences*. “Moses through revelation.”

*Life of Saint Vedast of Arras*.

One book of *Poems to Various Persons*. Among them there is one concerning the seven sciences. To these Trithemius also adds the works listed above; see no. 43.

We have also seen:

*On the Adoration of Images*.

*On the Genealogy of Christ*.

*On Astronomy*.

*On Dialectic*.

*On Rhetoric*—unless someone thinks these little books should be counted among the dialogues.

*On Orthography*.

A little book *On Auricular Confession*, which found its way into his book of Letters.

One book of prayers, called *Mass Prayers* [Col. 0132B].

*On the Sanctuary of God.*

@ [Col. 0131D] Perhaps: *On Divine Offices.* This book, however, is falsely attributed to Albinus.

*Life of Saint Martin*.

One book of *Homilies*.

*Albinus’s Dogmas for the Emperor Charles*.

The *Lord’s Prayer*, the *Apostles’ Creed*, and the *Song of Ambrose* in verse.

*On the Eight Parts of Speech*, in dialogue, with Franco and Saxo as interlocutors.

Thus far concerning the books published by him.

The same Leland, in the cited work, chapter 100, concerning Candidus, page 133, writes as follows:

Through the care of this Higebald, bishop, it finally came about that Candidus, migrating to Gaul, betook himself to Flaccus Albinus, as to the most abundant stream of letters flowing in that age. ... I know clearly that Albinus dedicated certain commentaries to Candidus the presbyter and Nathanael, otherwise called Naitanus the deacon. It is therefore credible that Nathanael of Lindisfarne was at some time a familiar associate of Albinus and most closely connected by friendship with Candidus. Of the books written by both men, the knowledge that remains is cold and meager. A curse upon the Danish pirates, the plunderers of the Lindisfarne library.

### XLIX. John Bale, Englishman, *Second Century of British Writers*

Flaccus Albinus, also called Alcuin the deacon, is thought by some writers to have been from York, while others say that he came from near London. He was first the most devoted pupil of Bede, and later of Archbishop Ecgbert. He was regarded as by far the most learned of the theologians of his age, indeed of all the English after Bede and Aldhelm, so that he became the teacher of Charles the Great and the first founder of the University of Paris.

The annals of Cambridge state that after Bede he publicly taught all the liberal arts there, being skilled in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew. They also state that he later lectured at York under Ecgbert, as the leader of the philosophers of his time.

[Col. 0132D] Sent by Offa, the most powerful king of the Mercians, to the aforesaid Charles to confirm a treaty of peace and to conduct other affairs of the kingdoms, Alcuin’s almost incredible learning was recognized. He became a guest from an ambassador and finally a cherished teacher from a guest, just as Gorgias once was among the Athenians.

Thereafter Caesar Charles regarded him above all others as his instructor in rhetoric, dialectic, mathematics, and theology. Under him he also learned extensively the art of calculation and the various courses of the stars.

Concerning him Bebelius writes in a certain preface.

@ [Col. 0131D] This preface was placed before the edition of the *Commentary on Ecclesiastes* published at Basel in 1531.

Adrian Aerntspergius expressed the same judgment concerning Alcuin in a letter to Georg, Baron of Graveneck, abbot and prince of the Holy Roman Empire at Kempten, prefixed to the book *On the Use of the Psalms*, which he had printed at Cologne in 1571 through Maternus Cholinus, in octavo. He writes:

“Albinus,” he says, “is everywhere a pious, concise, mature, serious, and learned author, and especially worthy, before many others, of being placed in people’s hands [Col. 0133A]; for his style is simple and pure.”

He was first abbot at Canterbury, in the monastery of Augustine, and finally at Tours, in the monastery of Saint Martin, by the gift of Caesar Charles, for whom he was then responsible for almsgiving and sacred counsel. He transferred the school from Rome to Paris around the year of salvation 791—it had previously come there from Athens through a very similar effort—and, having first laid the foundations of study through John and Claudius, wonderfully illuminated it with public lectures.

The following little works of this most celebrated man, composed as piously as eloquently, have come down to posterity:

### L. Barthius, *Adversaria*, vol. III, book CXLIX, chapter 5

In Albinus—Alcuin Flaccus—there was no less learning than in any other writer of the great nations; there was even a greater fervor of Christian gentleness, humility, and holiness than in many men of better times. Only purity of expression was lacking, because he despised it, adapting himself to the understanding of his age, which rejects everything that would exceed the eloquence of interpreters of Scripture. Indeed, when reading his letters, one might say that one was reading the zeal and holiness of Jerome’s age, were it not for those rasping scratches of barbarisms. Even with these, however, they are not to be despised.

[Col. 0134B] ### LI. William Cave, *Literary History*, vol. I, page 637

Whatever deeper learning and whatever more polished literature Gaul displays in this and the succeeding centuries must all be credited to Alcuin. The Universities of Paris, Tours, Fulda, Soissons, and many others owe their origin and growth to him. If he did not personally preside over them or lay their foundations, at least his learning shone before them, his example led the way, and the benefits he obtained from Charles increased them.

### LII. D. Andreas Quercetanus, in the dedicatory letter prefixed to his edition of the *Works of Blessed Alcuin* and addressed to the most illustrious D. William Vair, chancellor of France

He calls blessed Alcuin one of the foremost companions of the imperial court, so well instructed through experience and practice in the conduct of affairs and in every art that King Charles always relied upon his most prudent counsels. Gaul honors his blessed memory because, although through his singular reputation for learning and wisdom he possessed great favor and authority with Charles the Great, he used this good fortune not for his own advantage but for the common good of the state.

A little farther on he praises him as a man preeminent in wisdom, counsel, and every science of his age; conspicuous for the splendor of his holiness; shining in uprightness of character; eloquent; and a promoter of every branch of learning.

Baronius, under the year 770, calls Alcuin “a distinguished Doctor.” Under the year 802, he calls him “the torch of this age.” Harpesfeld, in the ninth century, chapter 2: “The ornament of our England and of this entire age.” The Magdeburg Centuriators, in the eighth century, concerning Alcuin, column 780: “Under his teaching he made the Franks equal to the ancient Romans.” And column 782: “He was distinguished not only in knowledge but also in integrity of character.” Twinus, book II of *The Antiquities of Oxford*, section 113, calls Alcuin “a most divine man.”

Many other testimonies and praises by more recent writers, especially Englishmen, concerning the holiness and learning of blessed Alcuin and his distinguished services to sacred and secular society would remain to be cited. But, lest we become too lengthy, we omit them. For what we have presented thus far abundantly proves how highly Alcuin was always and everywhere regarded.

# The First Part of the Works of Blessed Flaccus Albinus, or Alcuin, Teacher of Charles the Great — Letters

## Frobenius’s Notice
[Col. 0135A] {1} The first of those who published several letters of blessed Alcuin gathered together in a single collection was Henricus Canisius, who brought altogether sixty-seven to light from a manuscript codex of the library of Saint Gall, in volume I of his *Antiquae Lectiones*, no. 61. Basnage subsequently had them reprinted in the new edition of Canisius, volume II, part I. D. Andreas Quercetanus published the same letters—generally mutilated in the earlier editions, corrupted through the carelessness of scribes, and gaping in many places—in a more corrected form; he also added several others, transcribed from a very ancient manuscript belonging to the distinguished Paul Petau, and inserted them into part II of the Works of blessed Alcuin, though he omitted the learned notes with which Canisius had illustrated his own letters. Later, the celebrated men Lucas d’Acheri, Jean Mabillon, Edmund Martene, Étienne Baluze, Usserius, Bernard Pez, and others brought still more letters of blessed Alcuin out from the hiding places of various libraries and scattered them into public circulation, inserted in their *Spicilegia*, *Analecta*, and *Thesauri Anecdotorum*. The most celebrated Mabillon was the more fortunate among them: he found no fewer than twenty-six previously unpublished letters in a manuscript codex of our monastery’s library of Saint Emmeram, and presented them in his *Analecta*, from page 398 to 408 of the recent edition. By a happy conjecture he recognized that they belonged to blessed Alcuin; for they appear everywhere mutilated in the aforesaid codex, so that they present rather specimens of general formulas for writing letters than the form of complete letters, the names of those by whom or to whom they had been written, together with other individual circumstances, having naturally been omitted. The title prefixed to those letters in the codex itself also left the reader uncertain about their author. It reads as follows: “Here begin certain letters excerpted from the books of certain noble [according to Mabillon, incorrectly, ‘new’] teachers.” Nevertheless, the celebrated scholar’s conjecture, in assigning them to Alcuin, did not at all deceive him, as will soon become clear, although in explaining them he occasionally departed involuntarily from the truth, as we note in the appropriate places.

[Col. 0135C] We have discovered almost all of these formless Mabillonian letters, such as they stand written in our codex, complete in two ancient manuscript codices of excellent quality and nearly contemporary with one another, from the library of the most illustrious cathedral chapter of Salzburg, which were most generously made available to us. Most of them were addressed by blessed Alcuin to Aquila, or Arno, first bishop and afterward first archbishop of Salzburg. In these letters the individual circumstances omitted from the general formulas into which they had been reduced in the codex of Saint Emmeram are expressed, so that those letters may now plainly be regarded as new ones.

Besides these Mabillonian letters, we present several others from the same Salzburg codices that no one had previously seen or mentioned; we shall give notice of them in their proper places.

Although a sufficiently large number of letters of blessed Alcuin appears in our collection, we know that many others are still missing—letters which he wrote to various persons, including some of the highest rank—and we do not doubt that some may still be lying hidden in the corners of libraries, awaiting an industrious hand, unless, what would be more lamentable, they have perished altogether. Certainly our author wrote so many letters to the blessed abbot Benedict of Aniane, who was bound to him by the closest friendship, that an entire little book could have been made from them, as Ardo Smaragdus testifies in the *Life of Saint Benedict of Aniane*, volume V of Mabillon’s *Acta*, page 205, no. 36. Yet not even one of them seems to have survived.

Blessed Alcuin himself also mentions in his surviving letters many others written to Charlemagne, to Arno, to Paulinus of Aquileia, to the kings and bishops of England, to the leading men of Germany, Gaul, Italy, and elsewhere, which now appear nowhere.

[Col. 0136B] Leland, *On British Writers*, chapter 100, page 123, mentions a letter of Alcuin to Higebald, bishop of Lindisfarne, and quotes from it words by which he refers again, with a certain unspoken purpose, to Candidus, a disciple. Usserius saw a letter to Joseph, different from the one which we present below under no. 131 (now 173). Reynerus, in Alford’s *Anglo-Saxon Annals* under the year 804, no. 20, page 14, lists the one hundred fiftieth letter, to Eadbald, abbot of Gerwich, from which he reports only these words:

> “I believe that it is not unknown to your love, venerable brother, that formerly the holy Fathers, your predecessors, granted me, unworthy though I am, the favor of your familiarity, and ordered the name of my small self to be written in the register of your blessedness, so that I might be one of you, wherever, God willing, I might be.”

An anonymous author of the *Life of Saint Liudger* testifies that Charlemagne ordered this holy man to come to him through letters from Alcuin, whose disciple he had been in Britain. Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, century [Col. 0136C] IV, page 40.

The celebrated Étienne Baluze, volume I of the *Capitularies*, page 1442, relates that, after the edition of the *Capitularies* had been completed, a very ancient collection of Alcuin’s letters was brought to the Colbert Library. From it he transcribed and published, at the cited place, a letter to Candidus and Nathanael. Neither Baluze himself nor any other scholar has reported what other letters are contained there; consequently it is unknown whether they are the same as those published by Quercetanus or others, or different ones. The same must be said of certain letters mentioned in the *Catalogue of the Manuscripts of England and Ireland*, published at Oxford in folio in 1697. There it is stated that manuscript codex no. 5996 of Thomas Gale contains more and better letters of Alcuin than those already published; that manuscript codex no. 931 of Salisbury Church contains Alcuin’s letters and verses to Charlemagne; and that manuscript codex no. 10025 of Sir Symonds d’Ewes contains ninety-one letters of Alcuin, Charlemagne’s teacher, [Col. 0137A] with annotations. In the same *Catalogue*, pages 237 and 262, the collections of John Leland and Richard James from the letters of Albinus or Alcuin are listed. In the old catalogue of the renowned monastery of Saint Peter at Salzburg, seven letters of Alcuin to Arno, bishop of that see, are also recorded; these now escape the eyes of those who search for them.

{3} Everyone will agree that, from these codices—especially those of England—the letters of blessed Alcuin could have been greatly increased and those already published considerably illuminated, had access to them been granted me. But I am now weary of waiting any longer, and perhaps in vain, for the assistance of certain scholars, which has already been solicited in various ways. Therefore, at this point we give all the letters of which we have obtained copies; let those under whose custody the remainder lie hidden no longer begrudge them to the learned public.

The earlier editors whom we mentioned observed no order among the letters except whatever order they happened to find in the manuscript codices or in which the letters came into their hands. We had intended—as we stated in the prospectus of this new edition printed several years ago—to arrange them according to the rank of the persons to whom they had been written. But, advised by the most reverend D. Anselm Desing, abbot of Ensdorf in the Upper Palatinate, a man celebrated for his learning and a most loyal friend, we changed our plan. He said that such an order deserved no attention among scholars; a chronological order would be more agreeable, since it would illuminate and affect the reader more deeply. Following this advice, we have mixed together these letters, published by others either in collected form or piecemeal, or transcribed from manuscript codices, and arranged them according to the sequence of years wherever that could be determined by certain or probable indications. Those in which no indication reveals the time at which they were written have been assigned the final place.

No scholar is unaware of the value that monuments of this kind possess, especially when written by a serious and circumspect man who was thoroughly acquainted with the affairs of his own age. To serve the convenience of readers, we have everywhere added notes to illuminate obscure matters, whenever such notes occurred to us. We have borrowed the remaining notes from Canisius, Mabillon, Basnage, and others, and have corrected their conjectures—occasionally departing from the truth—by means of better letters unavailable to them, while preserving the reverence and modesty owed to such eminent men.

Finally, the learned reader must be informed that the material enclosed in brackets has been added here for the first time from manuscript codices.

## NOTICE OF THE EDITOR OF THE *PATROLOGIA* ON A NEW RECENSION OF THE LETTERS OF BLESSED ALCUIN

Since in this edition of blessed Alcuin we are preparing a new recension of the letters of the holy Father, we wished to give the reader a brief notice. Frobenius, whose excellent edition we follow, had collected only one hundred and sixty-two letters, most of which he had sent to the press, when unexpectedly, though rather late, he received another seventy-one, excerpted from English codices and transmitted by D. de Brequigny. He published these separately under the title *Appendix to the Earlier Letters*. In preparing a new edition, we have inserted the letters printed separately from Frobenius into the earlier collection, restoring to each its chronological order, or the order required by the connection of its subject matter or the identity of the persons involved. We now append the notice that Frobenius prefixed to the letters transmitted to him later.

## NOTICE. (Louis-Georges-Oudard de Brequigny)

[Col. 0137C] “The letters which I present here as wholly unpublished and hitherto almost unknown reached me too late for me to insert them in their proper order among the preceding letters. For they had already emerged from the press to more than the halfway point when the very learned D. Lieble, the present keeper of the celebrated library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, brought me the welcome news that altogether seventy-one unpublished letters of Alcuin had been transcribed from a ninth-century manuscript codex of the Harleian Library in England by the very learned D. de Brequigny, a member of the Royal Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres, who had been sent there in 1767 by order of the Most Christian King to collect literary treasures of this kind. He also reported that this distinguished man was entirely ready to communicate them for a new edition of the Works of blessed Alcuin. Those who are occupied in bringing such treasures out of hidden antiquity will understand how much joy this news brought me.

“I had indeed known for a long time, from the *Catalogue of the Manuscripts of England and Ireland*, published at Oxford in 1697, [Col. 0137D] that among the manuscript codices of Sir Symonds d’Ewes, baronet, under no. 10025, there were preserved ninety-one letters of Alcuin, Charlemagne’s teacher, with annotations, as well as one letter of Charlemagne and seven others of Dungal the abbot. I believe this to be the same codex as that of the Harleian Library, as may be gathered from the account of the distinguished D. de Brequigny which will immediately follow. For this reason I approached the scholars of England through a friend who maintained literary correspondence with them, and asked them to have the aforesaid letters of their fellow countryman transcribed at my expense for the embellishment and enlargement of the Works of blessed Alcuin, and to have them conveyed to me. [Col. 0138C] But my efforts were frustrated by the utterly exorbitant price set for these wares.

“Let me therefore count myself fortunate that these precious remains of antiquity, so long hidden, fell into more generous hands, and hands readier to give; and that through their kindness they reached me while there was still time to join them to the already printed letters in the manner of an appendix.

“Moreover, the way in which the aforementioned most learned D. de Brequigny obtained these letters, and the amount of industry he devoted to transcribing them, he himself explains in a letter sent to me. It will not, I trust, be unwelcome to learned readers if I reproduce it here as a testimony of greater authority.

“Among the most outstanding treasures of the Harleian Library, preserved in the British Museum at London, there is a manuscript codex marked no. 208. It is a parchment volume in the smaller format commonly called quarto, consisting of 119 folios, written in a most elegant script in Gaul, as it appears. That codex contains ninety-one letters of Alcuin, most of them unpublished. I considered it worthwhile to transcribe them, since all the bibliographers whom I have consulted are completely silent about this codex; nor is it mentioned even by the English themselves, either in the more recently published *Biographia Britannica* or in Tanner’s library, the diligent investigator of anecdotal works and manuscripts.

“What especially encouraged me was a note prefixed to the codex, stating that the very learned Usserius had compared these letters with Alcuin’s letters published by Chesnius in 1642 and had marked in his own hand [Col. 0139A] which ones Chesnius had published and which had not yet been committed to print. Hence, I believe, I was not rash in conjecturing that the archbishop of Armagh had then considered sending them to the press.

“And certainly this collection of Alcuin’s letters seemed unworthy neither of public light nor of the labors of so great a man; this will surely be evident to all who examine it. The writers of the *Literary History of France* (volume IV, page 329) believed and deeply regretted that none of the many letters Alcuin had written to Saint Benedict of Aniane had reached us. At least one of them (certainly two) survives among those presented by the Harleian codex.

“The same codex also contains other letters besides those of Alcuin: seven are attributed to the abbot Dungal, brief letters indeed, but all unpublished. Immediately preceding them is a more important letter written by Charlemagne to the emperor Michael. [Col. 0139B] I thought it agreeable to append this, in the place of an appendix, to Alcuin’s letters; I believe that I shall not have done an unwelcome thing by doing so. The letters of Dungal may simply be indicated here and omitted.

“I certainly would not have thought it superfluous to transcribe the entire codex, but, occupied as I was by other matters, I was unable to do so. I undertook only to have transcribed those letters of Alcuin which Usserius had declared unpublished and which I found had not been published subsequently, adding the letter of Charlemagne just mentioned, likewise hitherto unpublished.

“I compared all of these personally with the manuscript codex, and I venture to affirm that they have been copied with the utmost accuracy from the archetype, even with the errors that had crept into the manuscript through the carelessness of the ancient scribe, which were transferred into the copy for the sake of greater fidelity.

“Those letters therefore require correction in not a few places, and indeed illustration in many more; but neither am I equal to undertaking this labor nor is leisure granted me. It will be enough if I have contributed this modest offering of mine to the complete collection of Alcuin’s Works, which a learned man is to publish with every apparatus of scholarship, as a weak and small assistant in a great undertaking.

“I had first arranged for the transcription to be made in London in such a way that each letter would occupy its own quire. But, while the letters were being assembled from these gatherings by a second hand into thicker bundles of leaves, and no separate gathering was assigned to each, the order preserved in the manuscript was reversed through the copyist’s negligence. Yet the original order will be sufficiently clear from the folio numbers of the manuscript codex, which were attached to each letter as it was transcribed.

“I wrote this hastily at Paris, on 10 March 1769, for the use of the most reverend and illustrious D. D. Frobenius, prince-abbot of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg. May I be permitted to offer him my highest greetings and wish him every success.

“DE BREQUIGNY, member of the Royal Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres.”

[Col. 0140B] “Thus wrote the very learned as well as very modest man, to whom all scholars should offer perpetual thanks for discovering this literary treasure, which must certainly be considered of great importance in both civil and ecclesiastical history.

“I corrected the errors of the ancient scribe in the text, while nevertheless recording the manuscript’s reading, so that scholars may judge whether our correction should be approved or rejected.

“The letter of Charlemagne to the emperor Michael, which the distinguished man appended to the Alcuinian letters as an appendix, is the letter which he gave to his envoys, Amalarius, bishop of Trier, and Peter, abbot of Nonantula, when they were sent to confirm peace between the two empires, to be delivered to the aforementioned emperor together with the instrument of peace. We shall place it at the appropriate point among the works attributed to Alcuin, after the short work of that same Amalarius, *On the Ceremonies of Baptism*, hitherto falsely ascribed to Alcuin, together with his *Itinerary*, likewise hitherto missing, and with his letters to Peter, [Col. 0140C] his companion on the journey, and Peter’s replies, likewise unpublished until now.”

## LETTERS. (Alcuin)

{4}

@ [Col. 0139D] This letter is no. 94 among the Quercetan letters and no. 53 among the Canisian letters. According to the most distinguished Madrisius of Udine, in column 525 of volume C of the *Patrologia*, *Works of Saint Paulinus, Patriarch of Aquileia*, it appears to have been written immediately after Duke Aeric’s arrival in Friuli, that is, in the year 787. “For at that time,” he says, “Alcuin was living in Francia, from which Henry (Aeric) had departed shortly before; before entering upon the government of the duchy, he could have visited Alcuin, perhaps to request advice for carrying out his undertaking without offending God.”

## LETTER I. TO DUKE AERIC

@ [Col. 0140D] Aeric is called by others Henry, Eric, and Erich. He was appointed duke of the province of Friuli by Charlemagne in the year 787. For more about him, see Madrisius, at the cited place, in his dissertation on Saint Paulinus’s *Book of Exhortation*. (Year 787.) He praises him for his devotion to sacred reading and his humility; he wishes him victory against the unbelievers; and he proposes Saint Paulinus of Aquileia as a teacher of Christian piety. [Col. 0139C]

“To the venerable man Aeric, duke, Albinus the teacher sends greetings.

“I am sufficiently pleased by your devotion to sacred reading and your practice of devout humility, and by the fact that you did not disdain to visit familiarly the little dwelling of my humble self. Therefore we give thanks for your kindness, and most lovingly [Alcuin: “most diligently”] pray to God for your safety, that he may everywhere make the right hand of your strength victorious against the adversaries of his holy name, and by the power of his great mercy graciously guard it from every adversity of the devil’s deceit and from all the snares of enemies. May he grant that, in observing his commandments, you may fulfill his most holy will as earnestly as human frailty permits, so that he may deign to guide you in prosperity and protect you in adversity. I would perhaps have written more to you, venerable man, about the observance of Christian piety, if my distinguished teacher and pious instructor in the heavenly life, my Paulinus,

@ [Col. 0140D] my Paulinus—whose life has been splendidly illustrated by that same distinguished man, Madrisius, in the works of Saint Paulinus edited by him—had not been present there. Paulinus provided Aeric with what Alcuin here desires for him, through the *Book of Exhortation* which is found in the same collection.”

“From whose heart flows a fountain of living water, leaping up into eternal life” (John 4:14). Take him as your mediator for eternal salvation, so that the foot of your way of life may stumble nowhere; but, running along the straight road, may you, by God’s gracious gift, be worthy to reach the gates of everlasting life. Live and fare happily forever.

{5}

@ [Col. 0140D] This letter is found in the Salzburg manuscript codex and in the Saint-Emmeram codex used by Mabillon. Why the celebrated man passed it over, I do not know. We have supplied within brackets what is found in the Salzburg codex but omitted from ours.

## LETTER II. TO ARNO

(Year 790)

He desires to have him present; he urges him to exercise diligent care for the souls entrusted to his governance; he wishes to greet Laidradus; and he indicates that, because of the recent change of kingdom, he is still being detained in his homeland, England. [Col. 0140D]

“To the beloved Father Aquila, bishop, Albinus sends greetings.

[Col. 0141A] “I recall your love, most holy Father, with a very pleasant remembrance, and I long for a time of affection to come when I may embrace the neck of your charity with the little fingers of my desires. Oh, if only Habakkuk’s translation were suddenly granted to me, how quickly I would rush into the embrace of your fatherhood, and with compressed lips [Alcuin: ‘with lips’] I would kiss not only your eyes, ears, and mouth, but also each individual joint of the fingers of your hands and feet—not once, but many times. But since I am not worthy to come to you in this way, I shall send you more frequently letters of my rusticity, so that they may speak to you in place of my words and say:

> “Ever and forever, most holy bishop, greetings;  
> And may all your friends, I pray, always fare well [Editor: ‘dear friend’].”

“I beg and urge you again and again to consider yourself, to recognize where you are heading, to foresee what you are doing, and to remember before what a terrible Judge you will have to render an account—not only for yourself, but also for each of the souls entrusted to your governance. Therefore labor without slackness; preach in season and out of season [Alcuin: ‘importunately’], that is, to the willing and unwilling; reprove, entreat, rebuke, so that you may deserve to hear from the Lord your God: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord’ (Matthew 25:21). [I beg you to greet Laedredus,

@ [Col. 0141C] Laedredus. I think this is Laidradus, later bishop of Lyon, with whom Alcuin always maintained a close friendship. He was born in Noricum and may at that time have been among Arno’s household, when Alcuin first came to Gaul. a fellow countryman and my friend. Next year I shall inform him with certainty, if he himself is certain what he wants or what he can do.

@ [Col. 0141C] The recent change of our kingdom. In another letter, which we have not yet been able to uncover in full, Alcuin wrote, according to Malmesbury, book I of *The Deeds of the Kings of England*: “Blessed be God, who alone does wondrous things. Recently Athelred, son of Athelwold, came forth from prison to the throne, and from misery to majesty; because of the recent change of his kingdom we have been detained, lest we should come to you.” This change occurred in the year 790, according to Simeon of Durham and other English historians. I believe that Alcuin refers to this same change in the present passage, and that the present letter was written in that year or the next, when Alcuin had not yet returned from England to Gaul. The recent change of our kingdom still detains me this year; may salvation retain you in the eternal kingdom.] Remember our name in your prayers, I beg you. May almighty God remember you in eternal mercy. [I beg you to write to me how you are and what new event has occurred among you in these days. I ask you to commend or write my name through your monasteries and among your friends.] Peace and salvation be with you forever and ever.

{6}

@ [Col. 0141D] This letter, a fragment of which appears in Malmesbury, book I of *The Kings of England*, chapter 4, was transcribed and published in full by James Ussher from two very ancient codices of the Cotton Library, in his *Collection of Ancient Irish Letters*, page 49.

## LETTER III. TO COLCU, A READER IN SCOTLAND

(Year 790)

He recounts various things which he either saw or heard on his journey.

“To the blessed teacher and

@ [Col. 0141D] {7} pious Father Colcu. Ussher calls him a reader in Scotland, perhaps in the monastery of Iona, says Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXVI, no. 10. Alcuin mentions him elsewhere, namely in a letter to Joseph which, according to the same Ussher, still lies unpublished in the aforesaid Cotton codices. There it says: ‘Your teacher Colcu is well, and your friends who are with us are well.’ the pious Father Colcu, Alcuin, humble levite, sends greetings.

“When I heard of the health and prosperity of your fatherhood, I confess that I rejoiced with all my heart. And because I thought you curious about our journey, or about recent events in the world, I have taken care to make them known to your prudence through these letters of my rusticity, whether things heard or things seen.

“First, let your love know that, through God’s mercy, his holy Church in the regions of Europe has peace, prospers, and grows. For

@ [Col. 0142C] The ancient Saxons . . . were converted, when, in the year 785, Widukind and Albio were baptized at the villa of Attigny together with almost all the inhabitants of Saxony, and thus all Saxony was subjected to the Franks, as the annalist of Metz says, as does Charlemagne himself in his letter to Offa, king of the Mercians, volume I of Baluze’s *Capitularies*, page 194 (*Patrologia*, volume XCVIII, column 907). the ancient Saxons and all the peoples of the Frisians were converted to the faith of Christ, King Charles pressing some by rewards and others by threats. But

@ [Col. 0142C] Last year the Slavs . . . the Vionudi, and so forth. This event is reported under the year 789 in the fragment of the *Annals* edited by Chesnius, [Col. 0142D] volume II of the *Frankish Writers*, page 21, in these words: “In the year 789 King Charles was in Slavinia, and the kings of the Slavs came to him—Dragitus and his son, and the other kings Witsan and Drago, with the remaining kings of the Wends . . . and he subjected these nations to his rule. These Wends, or Vionudi, are called by others Wilci, Wilzi, and Wulzi.” Alcuin therefore wrote this letter not in the year 795, as Ussher thought, but in the year 790, when he could say that the Slavs had been subdued the preceding year. last year that same king invaded the Slavs with an army—we call them Vionudi—and subjected them to his rule.

@ [Col. 0142D] The Greeks in the third year, and so forth. Before this letter was written, as I understand it, that is, in the year 788, which is the third year counting inclusively from 790. We should therefore apparently read: “Three years ago.” For the arrival of the Greeks in Italy and the slaughter that occurred that year, see the *Frankish Annals*. But in the third year the Greeks came into Italy with a fleet, and, defeated by the commanders of the aforementioned king, fled to their ships; four thousand of them are said to have been killed and a thousand captured. Likewise,

@ [Col. 0142D] The Avars . . . into Italy . . . and against Bavaria. For this invasion, see the *Annals of Lorsch* and others under the year 788. the Avars, whom we call Huns, burst into Italy and, overcome by the Christians [Malmesbury: “by the commanders of the aforementioned most Christian king”], returned home in disgrace. They also invaded Bavaria, but were themselves defeated and scattered by the Christian army. Likewise, the commanders and tribunes of that same most Christian king took a large part of Spain [Col. 0143A]

[Col. 0143C] Took from the Saracens. This may perhaps be understood of the great expedition undertaken by Charlemagne into Spain in the year 788, in which the annalists of that period report that Pamplona was destroyed and the Spaniards and Basques subdued. took from the Saracens almost three hundred thousand [units of territory] lengthwise along the coast. But alas, what grief! Those same accursed Saracens, who are also called Hagarenes, dominate all Africa and most of greater Asia. I believe that some time ago I wrote to your venerable prudence about their incursion.

“For the rest, most holy Father, let your reverence know that I, your son, and Joseph, your household servant, are, by God’s mercy, well, and that all your friends who are here serve God in prosperity. But I do not know what is going to happen to us.

@ [Col. 0143C] For some disagreement, and so forth. What the cause of this quarrel was, says Mabillon, *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, century IV, part I, page 169, we learn from chapter 15 of the *Chronicle of Fontenelle*, where Charlemagne is said to have ‘requested in marriage’ for his son of the same name the daughter of King Offa; but when Offa would not agree ‘unless Berta, daughter of Charlemagne, were given in marriage to his son,’ Charlemagne, angered by this, ordered ‘that no one from the island and nation of Britain should touch the shore of the Ocean Sea in Gaul for the purpose of trade. But, to prevent this, the prohibition was withdrawn at the warning and entreaty of Abbot Gervold.’ Some disagreement has recently arisen between King Charles and King Offa, inflamed by the devil’s urging, so that navigation for merchants has ceased on both sides. There are some who say that we are to be sent to those regions for the sake of peace [Col. 0143B]

@ [Col. 0143D] To be sent to those regions. Mabillon, at the cited place, page 187, says that this letter was written in England, from which Alcuin was to be sent to Charlemagne. Later, however, the celebrated man took a different view, *Annals*, book XXV, no. 76, and book XXVI, no. 10, where he says that Alcuin, who was then in Gaul, was sent to Britain to arrange peace, and in fact went there around the year [Col. 0144C] 790, although the prohibition of navigation had been lifted through the entreaty of Abbot Gervold. This opinion does indeed appear to agree better with the context of the letter. to those regions. But I beg that, whether we remain or go, we may be fortified by your sacred prayers. I do not know what I have done wrong, since for a long time I have not been deemed worthy to see the sweetest letters of your fatherhood; nevertheless, I believe that I daily feel the indispensable power of the prayers of your holiness.

“I sent your charity some oil, which is now scarcely found in Britain, so that you might distribute it through the necessary places of the bishops for the benefit of the people or for the honor of God [Alcuin: ‘for the benefit of the honor of God’]. I also sent fifty shekels to the brothers from the alms of King Charles—I beg you to pray for him—and fifty shekels from my own alms; and to the southern brethren of Baldhuvinega, thirty shekels from the king’s alms and thirty from my own alms, and twenty shekels from the alms of the head of the household Areidae, and twenty from my own alms; and to each of the anchorites three shekels of pure silver, so that all of them may pray for me and for the lord King Charles, that God may preserve him for the protection of his holy Church and for the praise and glory of his name. May almighty God hear you as you intercede for his holy Church, and cause you to prosper in the blessings of eternal salvation.”

@ [Col. 0144C] Quercetan edition 76, Canisian edition 43, Frobenius 163.

## LETTER IV. TO FELIX, BISHOP

(Before the year 792)

He commends himself to the prayers of Felix, apparently praised by him for his piety. [Col. 0144A]

“To the pious Father

@ [Col. 0144D] Felix, bishop. “This is, unless I am mistaken,” says Canisius, “Felix Hildebald, archbishop of Cologne, and so forth.” But there is no doubt that this is Felix, bishop of Urgell, to whom Alcuin commended himself in this letter before Felix’s error concerning adoption became publicly known. Alcuin himself mentions the letter in another letter to the same man, which I transcribed from a Salzburg manuscript and prefixed to his books against Felix, where he says: “Formerly, hearing the celebrated report of your holiness; . . . I took care to commend myself to your most holy intercessions.” This letter was therefore written before the year 792, when Felix’s error had already become known everywhere. To Felix, bishop, Alcuin, humble levite, sends greetings.

“Through the report of certain brothers you are very well known to us for your piety, although not by sight. Therefore, trusting in the charity which is Christ, I have presumed to commend myself through you to the sacred prayers of yourself and your faithful—not because my merits demand it, but because the good reports about you have moved me. Therefore I humbly beg you to commend me to our Savior with that charity by which he has joined all his own together. For charity despises no one. Through him and because of him who came into this world to save sinners and will come to judgment to crown the just, may I, a sinner, then obtain forgiveness through your prayers, when you, by the mercy of God, receive a crown.

{8} “Stand firm, brothers, and fight manfully for him who fought victoriously for you. For it is not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered to the end, who will be saved (Matthew 10:22). And advance from day to day, like the saints of God who went from strength to strength. I would have written more to you, if it had not seemed superfluous to admonish those whom I ought to ask to intercede for my sins about the virtues. But charity, which despises no one, also endures. What more can I say? Again and again I beg you to receive me in fraternal love into the communion of your prayers, so that God, the rewarder of charity, may receive you into the eternal glory of his kingdom. Farewell, and live happily in the Lord Jesus, dearest brothers.”

## LETTER V. TO CUDRADUS, PRIEST

(Year 793 or thereafter)

He exhorts Cudradus the priest to steadfastness after the devastation of the holy places.

“To the venerable Father

@ [Col. 0144D] Cudradus, priest. Clearly of the church of Saint Cuthbert of Lindisfarne, who successfully escaped the raging hands of the pagans in that devastation which Alcuin repeatedly deplores, especially in letter 8 (now 9), and which occurred in the year 793. To Cudradus the priest, Alcuin the deacon sends greetings.”

[Col. 0145A] I deeply lament the devastation of the holy places [MS: “I groan over” it]; but I rejoice in the constancy of your faith, praising together the clemency of almighty God, who spared you amid the hands of the pagans. Therefore remain with firm faith in the resolve you have undertaken, trusting in the mercy of God, that by his compassion [Supplement: “clemency” or similar] he may preserve you … wherever God wills you to dwell according to fraternal counsel. Yet whether in a place of solitary habitation or in a fraternal company [MS: “fraternal companies,” plural], carefully observe a solitary manner of life, secret prayers, and the discipline of fasting; for it is not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered, and so forth (Matt. X, 22).

And, I beseech you, keep me in your holy prayers in remembrance, as Buitta faithfully promised me in reporting your words. Carefully admonish the brothers who visit you with the consolation of the Holy Spirit, exhorting them to trust in God’s protection and in the intercession of Saint Cuthbert, our Father. Let them place their hope of certain defense not in the clatter of arms or in a heap of falling stones, but in the wall of heavenly piety; and let them transfer the misery of present tribulation to the blessedness of eternal happiness. Let them turn with their whole heart to the Lord, and, if anything in their conduct requires correction, let them correct it without sluggishness, so that their conversion may please God, just as the repentance of the Ninevites pleased him, and he spared the city through the tears of those confessing their sins. God is merciful and compassionate, and abandons no one who hopes in him; for Job’s final state was better than his former one. So, I believe, he will act toward you also, if you turn unanimously to implore his clemency. [Col. 0145C]

@ [Col. 0145D] Edited by Quercetanus, 98; Canisius, 21 (Frobenius, 5).

## LETTER VI. TO THE BROTHERS OF THE CHURCH OF YORK

*(Around the year 793)*

He gratefully declares that he was educated by the people of York from infancy to manhood. He commends himself to the prayers of all of them and exhorts them to guard themselves against vices.

To the most beloved and greatly venerable brothers in the love of Christ,

@ [Col. 0145D] of the Church of York. They evidently professed the institute of Benedictine monks, among whom Alcuin here declares that he was educated and nourished. See Mabillon, in the *Eulogy of Alcuin*, [Col. 0146D] § 3, p. 164. The letter appears to have been written in the year 793, after he had been taken away from their company for a second time and had returned to Gaul; before the disaster of Lindisfarne, I think, since otherwise he would have mentioned it in this or the following letter. To the brothers of the Church of York, the son of your piety, Albinus the deacon, sends greetings.

The whole breast of my devotion is filled with the sweetness of your affection; and if anything can be added to a full measure of love, it is daily heaped up as it grows, so that the sweetness of the mere memory of you drives the troubles of worldly distress, as they arise, far away from the secret chambers of my mind. And this the Lord Christ has deigned to grant me as a singular consolation in the spirit of holiness.

You cherished the fragile years of my infancy [Al.: “the dispositions of my infancy”] with maternal affection; you patiently endured the frivolous season of childhood with pious forbearance; by the disciplines of paternal correction you taught me toward the perfected age of manhood; and you strengthened me through instruction in sacred learning. What more must I say, except that the piety of the eternal King may reward with the perpetual glory of supreme blessedness all the acts of piety that, through you, he has bestowed upon me, his servant? This I ask at every moment of my vigils; this I seek in daily supplication. In this prayer, before the presence of the Most High, I never cease to pour out the innermost tears of my longing at the shrines of the holy martyrs or confessors of Christ, wherever the path of my unsettled journey leads me.

You are always in my heart and first among the words of my prayers. You, most devoted Fathers, whether in the public observances of holy prayer or in the secret intercessions of your supplications, I beseech you by the love of God: keep Alcuin, your son, continually in your heart and on your lips. You also, who are sons in age but Fathers in the holiness of your merits, I adjure by the divine clemency: never forget in your holy prayers the teacher of your learning. For the examiner of my heart is my witness that I always devoutly desired your progress in ecclesiastical disciplines and spiritual doctrine. And if you received anything less than you should have, I believe it cannot be attributed to my fault. Nor, whether absent or present, will benevolence toward your progress ever cease on my part.

O most beloved Fathers and brothers, remember me: I shall be yours, whether in life or in death. And perhaps God will have mercy on me, so that you who nourished my childhood may bury my old age. And even if another place is appointed for my body, nevertheless, whatever rest my soul is to have, I believe that through your holy intercessions, God granting it, rest with you will be given to me; for, as our boy Seneca testifies that he saw, we believe that the souls of our brotherhood are to be gathered in the same place of joy. Although the diversity of merits will cause one to rejoice more blessedly than another, the equality of eternity will make all live happily. And just as one sun shines upon everyone, yet, because of the distance between their eyes, it is not seen equally by all, so eternal blessedness will be granted to all the just in God’s kingdom, although the sublimity of their merits will crown some with greater glory. Prepare yourselves, dearest brothers, with the whole purpose of your intention and action to become worthy of reaching that glory.

Let no carnal desire, no worldly ambition block your path to blessedness. Instead, by the way of truth and holiness, by which the blessed Fathers, our predecessors, reached the heavenly kingdoms, run forward in daily progress, with heavenly grace accompanying you, in a united agreement of piety and a single disposition of will. Drive all sluggishness away from your holy way of life; exchange luxury for chastity; flee drunkenness as though it were the pits of hell; do not seek excessive adornment in clothing. It is better for God’s servants to adorn the soul with ecclesiastical conduct than to dress the body, according to the custom of laymen, in pompous vanity. And it is better to tread the most pure thresholds of the holy mother Church than to frequent the muddy paths of rustic foulness.

Let the discipline of regular life order you, [Col. 0147A] and let the moderation of ecclesiastical piety make you venerable. Ascend to the kingdoms of heaven by the feet of holy humility and the steps of divine charity, through the stages of obedience. Overcome in spirit these things that are perishable and transitory, so that, with divine grace everywhere going before and following you, we may deserve to reach, with every prosperity and joy, the beloved homeland of heavenly glory through the praiseworthy merits of good works.

@ [Col. 0147D] Edited by Quercetanus, 50; Canisius, 24 (Frobenius, 6). We have noted several differing readings from the manuscript codex of Salzburg.

## LETTER VII. TO THE BROTHERS OF YORK

*(Year 793)*

He expresses his joy at a letter received from them, exhorts them to follow the footsteps of their Fathers, and commends himself to their prayers. [Col. 0147B]

To the brothers of the most holy congregation and sweetest affection of the Church of York, Alcuin the deacon, son of that pious mother, sends perpetual honor, peace, and salvation in Christ.

@ [Col. 0147D] From the priest Eanbald. The Canisian codex has “Enbald.” Nevertheless, our reading, drawn from other codices and [Col. 0148D] William of Malmesbury, seems preferable. He is undoubtedly Eanbald, whom Hoveden calls a priest of the Church of York in this year and later its bishop. Letter 50 (now 53) is addressed to him. I received from the priest Eanbald letters from your venerable affection, whose peaceful sequence of greeting in the inscription the same man who carried them greatly enlarged with honey-sweet words of salutation, reporting your perseverance in brotherly love toward us, so that amid the tears of our conversation I thought I could hear your voices in each of his words [Cod. Sal.: “I judged”]. I recognized this most clearly in the letter itself, in which, as I read, it seemed to me that I saw your faces.

May the giver of all good things bring this truly to pass, so that your sorrow may be turned into joy (John XVI, 20) and our joy may be fulfilled in him who also says to his disciples: “No one will take your joy from you” [Cod. Sal.: “may take”] (John XVI, 22)—in him there is unfailing joy, perpetual salvation, blessed prosperity, and glorious blessedness.

{10} In order that he may grant all these things to us through his mercy, let us cling with all our love and all our strength to his commandments. Let us follow the footsteps of the holy Fathers who begot us in Christ, gathered us into this most sacred fold, and nourished us with the milk of paternal piety. Let us believe [Cod. Sal.: “We believe”] that their souls always stand in eternal joys before the presence of the supreme Shepherd and our Redeemer, and that from there they favor our prayers, if they recognize [Cod. Sal.: “they recognize”] that we observe with united devotion the commandments of life that they established for us under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

Let us remember at every hour, dearest brothers, what Fathers and progenitors we had—how distinguished and pious, beloved by God and honored by all the people. Let us not be degenerate sons of their nobility. While we stand among their most sacred relics, let us think of imitating their way of life, so that we may deserve to become companions of their glory. Let not the ambition of the world, carnal delight, the corruption of luxury, or the poisons of drunkenness turn us back from the most upright path of vital life, along which they walked and deserved everlasting glory with God.

Be united in every good counsel, harmonious in every discipline of regular life. First of all, seek with a pure conscience the honor and will of almighty God, who sees the secrets of the heart, so that his grace may cause you to find what is best and nearest to salvation. Let us always have fraternal and peaceful charity, so that, as Christ’s sheep feasting on the pastures of the same life, remaining within the wall of one fold, we may call down God’s mercy upon us in one house of prayer. Let no one, through neglect of his salvation, separate himself from the fellowship of holy prayer at the canonical hours. It is better for the visitation of angels at the appointed hours to find us praying with the brothers than for the fury of the devil to find us torpid in some negligence or luxury. A reward remains eternally for each according to his labor. Whoever labors more will receive a greater reward.

Nor should the labor of our salvation seem difficult. Often harsher medicines are accustomed to provide the desired health. We see through what narrow gate and constricted way (Matt. VII, 14) the holy martyrs entered everlasting life. But we, brothers, can reach the blessedness of that same life by an easier way and a lighter course, since Truth itself says: “There are many dwelling places in my Father’s house” (John XIV, 2). There are many dwelling places because of the diversity of merits; nevertheless, there will be blessed eternity and eternal blessedness for all. For whoever will be there will be blessed and glorious, where the just will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt. XIII, 43).

For just as the persecutors of the holy martyrs were impious men, stirred up by the devil, so our persecutors are, at the devil’s prompting, worldly desire, carnal delight, instability of spirit, and negligence regarding God’s commandments. And just as those holy martyrs, with divine grace assisting them, steadfastly conquered impious tyrants and received the palm of eternal glory, so we also, if with God’s help we overcome our adversaries and bravely resist diabolical suggestions, shall receive the crown of everlasting praise and the palm of eternal blessedness.

Dearest brothers, I beseech you to remember me in your holy prayers, so that my soul may rejoice in you with perpetual prosperity. I, the devoted son of your fatherhood, never forget you; rather, with a love surpassing that for all others, I always love you as though present, daily beseeching God with profound contrition of heart to guard, govern, and protect you with eternal mercy. Farewell in Christ, dearest brothers.

{11}

@ [Col. 0149C] Edited by Quercetanus, 54; Canisius, 32 (Frobenius, 7).

## LETTER VIII. TO THE PRIEST BEORNUINUS

*(Year 793)*

He declares that he has never withdrawn from loyalty to King Offa and the English people; he advises him to urge kings, bishops, and princes to follow God’s will, and commends peace. [Col. 0149A]

@ [Col. 0149C] To the priest Beornuinus. An Englishman, as is clear from the context. He must have been a man of great dignity and authority among kings, bishops, and princes, to whom he could urge and preach God’s will. Alcuin the deacon sends greetings to the priest Beornuinus.

I received your sweet letter of affection, steeped in honey-sweet sentiments and presenting a defense. I trusted its truth more than the false-speaking account of others. For the faith of friendship must stand firm in the heart, not in the changeability of the tongue. Would that I were worthy to preach peace rather than sow discord, and to carry the sign of Christ rather than the weapons of the devil. I would never have written to you if I had not wished to have peace with you and for the peace in Christ that we began to possess to remain firm. Truly—

@ [Col. 0149D] I have never been unfaithful to Offa … Alcuin’s departure from his homeland for Gaul perhaps aroused in certain fellow countrymen the suspicion that he would withdraw even from loyalty to his own people, who had at times been at odds with the Gauls. He removed this suspicion not only by these letters but also by his actions. “For, not forgetful of his fellow countrymen, he labored to keep the emperor in friendship with them,” says Malmesbury, *Book I of the Kings of England*, chapter 3.

I have never been unfaithful to King Offa or to the English people. Just as I shall faithfully preserve, as far as I can, those friends whom God has given me, so also shall I preserve those whom I left in my homeland. My days are few, and I endure even these with the pain of the scourge. Therefore I beseech you, in the Lord, to acquire for me as many intercessors as you can.

This age has been disturbed by many miseries, and there is no refreshment in it except in the mercy of God and the faith of friends. We came naked, and naked we depart (Job II, 21), unless one clothes the soul with good works. Whenever time or place presents itself to you, dearest brother, always urge everyone to follow God’s will: urge the king gently, bishops honorably, princes confidently, and all people truthfully. It is ours to sow; it is God’s to make fruitful.

Let no suspicion of any disagreement between us remain with you. Let us not be among those of whom it was said: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. X, 34). Rather, let us be among those to whom it was said: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV, 27). May the peace of Christ, which surpasses all understanding (Phil. IV, 7), guard our hearts in the charity of Christ [Col. 0150A] and the love of brotherhood. I have written a short little letter, because a little is sufficient for the wise. But may the very many gifts of God glorify you forever, dearest brother.

@ [Col. 0149D] {13} William of Malmesbury published a fragment of this letter in *Book III of the Bishops of England*, reproduced by Quercetanus, *Works of Alcuin*, p. 1672. It now appears complete from the manuscript codex of Salzburg.

## LETTER IX. TO THE PEOPLE OF LINDISFARNE

*(Year 793)*

He laments the devastation of the Church of Lindisfarne, urges prayer, exhorts them to correct their conduct and observe regular discipline, and advises them not to be mentally overwhelmed.

To the most blessed Father, namely Saint Cuthbert [Al.: Cuthbert], bishop, and to the excellent sons in Christ,

@ [Col. 0149D] Hugibald, whom others call Higebald and Hincbald. He governed the Church of Lindisfarne from the year 780 to the year 802, according to Alford. A poem in volume II, part VI, is addressed to the same man. Alcuin wrote another letter to Higebald, in which he wishes the disciple Candidus to return to him; Leland quotes a fragment of it in *On British Writers*, chapter 100, p. 133:

> “If it should please you for him [Candidus] to return to us again, we shall gladly provide whatever we believe may contribute to the advancement of that Church. For whatever I learned from teachers for the benefit of the holy Churches, I especially delight in communicating to the people of our own nation.”

See Letter 39 (now 44), to Damoeta. To Bishop Hugibald [Al.: “Hincbald”] and the whole congregation of the Church of Lindisfarne, Alcuin the deacon sends heavenly blessing in Christ.

[Col. 0150B] The familiarity of your affection [indeed] used greatly to gladden me when I was present; but now, by a reversal of fortune, the calamity of your tribulation, though I am absent, greatly saddens me every day [Malmesbury: “saddened me”]. How—

@ [Col. 0150D] The pagans, and so forth. Concerning this disaster of the people of Lindisfarne, Hoveden should be read under the year 793:

> “In that same year,” he says, “pagans came from the northern region … to the Church of Lindisfarne. They devastated everything in a miserable plundering raid, trampled the holy places with polluted feet, dug up the altars, and seized all the treasures of the holy Church. They killed some of the brothers, carried others away in chains, threw many out naked after tormenting them with insults, and drowned some in the sea.”

Pagius and Alford assign this letter to the following year; but I do not see why it could not have been written in the same year in which that disaster occurred. I have no doubt that, immediately after receiving news of the disaster, Alcuin wished to sympathize with the people of Lindisfarne and exhort them to patience, repentance, and prayer.

The pagans have defiled the sanctuaries of God and shed the blood of the saints around the altar; [they have devastated {12} the house of our hope;] they have trampled the bodies of the saints in the temple [of God] like dung in the street. What should we say except that we must grieve in spirit with you before the altar of Christ and say: “Spare, Lord, spare your people, and do not give your inheritance to the nations, lest the pagans say, ‘Where is the God of the Christians?’” (Joel II, 17). What confidence can the Churches of Britain have if Saint Cuthbert has not defended his own Church with so great a number of saints? [End of Malmesbury’s fragment.]

[Or is this the beginning of a greater sorrow, or did the sins of the inhabitants demand this? For nothing happens by chance [Thus we have emended the text, since the codex read: “For nothing happened by chance”], but it is a judgment of great moment for each person [Latin *magni cuilibet meriti*, sense uncertain]. But now, you who remain, stand bravely, fight courageously, defend the camps of God. Remember Judas Maccabeus, because he purified the temple of God (II Macc. X, 2–3) and rescued the people, as he freed [them] from *extranea* (“foreign things”; manuscript reading uncertain). If anything in your conduct requires correction, correct it quickly. Call back your patrons, who have abandoned you for a time. They did not lack power before God’s clemency, but we do not know why they remained silent.

Do not glory in the vanity of clothing; this is not the glory of priests and servants of God, but their disgrace. Do not erase the words of your prayers through drunkenness. Do not pursue the lusts of the flesh and the avarice of the world; instead, remain firm in God’s service and in the discipline of regular life, so that the most holy Fathers who begot you may not cease to be your protectors. Walking in their footsteps, remain secure in their prayers. Do not be degenerate sons of such great Fathers. They will certainly not cease defending you if they see you following their examples.

Nevertheless, do not be mentally overwhelmed by this misery. “God chastises every son whom he receives” (Hebr. XII, 6); and therefore perhaps he has chastised you more because he has loved you more. Jerusalem, the city beloved by God, perished in the flame of the Chaldeans. Rome, surrounded by the crown of the holy apostles and innumerable martyrs, was torn apart by pagan devastation, but was quickly restored through piety. Almost all Europe was emptied by the swords and fires of the Goths or Huns; but now [MS: “if”], with God preserving it, it shines adorned with Churches like the sky with stars, and in them the offices and practices of Christian religion flourish and increase.

Encourage one another, saying: “Let us return to the Lord our God, for he is abundant in forgiveness” (Isa. LV, 7), and he never abandons those who hope in him.

[Col. 0151C] And you, holy Father, leader of God’s people, shepherd of the holy flock, physician of souls, lamp placed upon a lampstand, be an example in every goodness to all who see you. Be a herald of salvation to all who hear you. Let your companions be honorable in conduct, an example to others for life, not for destruction. Let your banquets be marked not by drunkenness but by sobriety. Let your clothing be worthy of your rank. Do not conform yourself to worldly people in any vanity. Empty adornment of clothing and useless finery are disgrace before human beings and sin before God.

It is better to adorn the soul, which will endure forever, with good conduct than to decorate the body, which will soon rot in dust, with elaborate garments. Let Christ be clothed and fed in the poor, so that by doing this you may reign with Christ. “A man’s wealth is the ransom of his life” (Prov. XIII, 8). If we love gold, let us send it ahead of us into heaven, where it will be kept for us, and we shall possess what we love. Let us love eternal things, not things that perish; true riches, not fleeting ones; everlasting things, not transitory ones. Let us prepare praise for ourselves from God, not from human beings. Let us do what the saints whom we praise did. Let us follow their footsteps on earth, so that we may deserve to be companions of their glory in heaven.

May the protection of divine piety guard us from every adversity, dearest brothers. Farewell in Christ, most beloved, and be strengthened, always making progress.]

@ [Col. 0151D] William of Malmesbury, in the place cited, p. 1673, says that at the end of this letter Alcuin added the following:

> “When our lord King Charles returns home, with the enemies subjected through the mercy of God, we intend, with God’s help, to come to him; and if we can then accomplish anything either concerning the boys who have been led into captivity by the pagans or concerning any of our other necessities [F.: your necessities], we shall carefully bring it to completion.”

@ [Col. 0151D] Edited by Quercetanus, 28; Canisius, 1 (Frobenius, 9); emended from the manuscript codices of Salzburg and Saint Emmeram.

## LETTER X. TO AEDILHARDUS (ATHELARDUS), ARCHBISHOP OF THE CITY OF DOROVERNUM

*(Year 793 or following)*

@ [Col. 0151D] This name, Aedilhardus, varies in different sources; elsewhere it is found written as Edelhardus, Ethilhardus, Adelardus, Athilhardus, and Athelhardus. He was archbishop of Dorovernum, elected in the year 791, as Simeon of Durham reports [Col. 0152D] in Pagius under this year, no. 11. He is mentioned in Ingulf’s *History* and in the letters of King Cenwulf of Mercia to Pope Leo III and of Leo to Cenwulf, which the continuator of Bede transcribed in Book I, chapters 12 and 13. Canisius.—Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, Book XXV, no. 84, p. 291, calls Aedilhard a man of supreme holiness and wisdom, who had once been abbot of Malmesbury, later bishop of Winchester, and finally, after the death of Jaenberht, was elected archbishop of Canterbury. (From Gervase, col. 1642, and William of Malmesbury, Book I *On the Kings of England*, chapter 4.)

He exhorts him to follow the footsteps of his predecessors and to carry out fearlessly the office of shepherd of souls; and he urges him, together with his fellow bishops, to preach the word of God without fear. [Col. 0152B]

To the pious Father and prelate of the holy see, Aedilhard, archbishop, Alcuin the humble levite sends greetings.

Having heard the very sweet words of your salutation and the health of your prosperity, which is greatly necessary to many, I confess that I rejoiced greatly. With all the gladness of my mind I beseech the most merciful piety of the Lord and our God Jesus Christ to preserve your [blessedness] in longstanding prosperity, for the growth of his holy Church, so that through your most devoted teaching the word [Cod.
