Sal.: “words”] of eternal life may grow, spread, and multiply, and so that the number of the Christian people may increase to the praise and glory of our Savior. In this work, holy brother, I beseech you to labor with all your strength. And the nearer the day of recompense approaches, the more earnestly strive to increase the blessedness of your reward.

@ [Col. 0152D] Predecessors. William of Malmesbury says that they were all most holy—Augustine and the others—in Book I of *The Deeds of the Bishops of England*, where their successors may be found. Canisius.

Consider what predecessors you have had [Cod. Sal.: “what predecessors you would have had”]: learned teachers and supreme lights of all Britain [Cod. Sal.: “of this whole province”]. While you pray among their most sacred bodies, you will certainly be aided by their prayers, if neither the fleeting flatteries of the world withdraw you from their footsteps nor vain fears make you afraid of princes.

Always remember that your throat must be God’s trumpet and your tongue the herald of salvation to all. Be a shepherd, not a hireling; a ruler, not a subverter; light, not darkness; a city fortified with firm faith, not a house ruined by rains; a glorious soldier of Christ, not a contemptible apostate; a preacher, not a flatterer. It is better to fear God than a human being; to please God than to flatter a human being. What is a flatterer except a smiling enemy? He destroys both himself and his hearer. These are the ones who sew cushions beneath every elbow (Ezek. XIII, 18), making Christ’s sheep sick rather than healing them.

{14} You have received a pastoral rod and a staff of fraternal consolation: the former for governing, the latter for consoling. Let the grieving find consolation in you, and let the rebellious feel correction through you. The power of a judge is to kill; yours, however, is to give life. Why do you fear a human being because of the sword, when you have received the key of the kingdom from Christ? Remember how much he suffered for you, and do not fear speaking for him. He hung upon the cross, fastened by nails, for love of you; and you, seated on the throne of your dignity, would remain silent through fear of a human being? Not so, brother, not so. But just as he loved you, so love him. Whoever labors more will receive a greater reward.

If you suffer persecution because of the word of God, what could be more blessed? For the Lord himself says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 10). And: “The apostles went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were considered worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus” (Acts V, 41). And: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the coming glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

If you rebuke an offender and he corrects himself at your rebuke, you also have a reward with God, and he will have salvation from God. If he hates your rebuke [Canisius and Cod. Sal.: “if he hates you when you rebuke him”], condemnation is his, and blessedness is yours.

Be a consoler to the unfortunate, a father to the poor, approachable to all, while taking care always to understand what answer you should give to each person. Let your answer always be seasoned with the salt of wisdom—not rash but honorable, not wordy but restrained. Let your conduct be distinguished by humanity, praiseworthy for humility, and lovable for piety, so that you may instruct those who live with you or come to you not only by words but also by example.

Let your hand be generous in almsgiving, ready when giving, and cautious when receiving. Prepare for yourself a treasure in heaven (Acts XX, 35). “A man’s riches are the ransom [Al.: “plunder”] of his soul,” because “it is more blessed to give than to receive” (Luke XII, 33). We have found one precious pearl; let us give everything we have and buy it (Matt. XIII, 46).

Let the reading of Holy Scripture be found frequently in your hands, so that you may be able to fill yourself from it and feed others. Let vigils and continual prayers be yours, all the more because you must intercede for the entire Christian people. Your place is to stand between God and human beings, bringing God’s embassies to the people and interceding with God for the people’s sins. Make yourself worthy, by his gracious gift, to be heard by him. [This] dignity consists in purity of life and confidence in preaching, as Truth itself testifies: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke XII, 35). The holiness of chastity is signified by the loins, and the brightness of preaching by the lamps.

Remember that a priest is the angel of the Lord, God Most High, and that holy law is to be sought from his mouth, according to what we read in the prophet Malachi (II, 7). He is also a watchman placed in the highest position. Hence a bishop is called, as it were, a watchman [Cod. Sal.: “over-watchman”], who must, with prudent counsel, provide for Christ’s whole army—what must be avoided and what must be done.

These men, that is, priests, are the lights of God’s holy Church and teachers of Christ’s flock. In the front line they must raise the banner of the holy cross without sluggishness and stand fearlessly against every assault of the hostile army. These are the men who received the talents and who, when our King, God Christ, returns with the triumph of glory to his Father’s seat, will have to render to that same great Judge on the final day [Cod. Sal.: “on the day of the final judgment”] an account of how much each one gained through the labor of preaching in his office (Matt. XXV).

Therefore, dearest brother, prepare yourself as a suitable minister of the word of God. Admonish your fellow priests also most diligently to labor with all earnestness in the word of life, so that they may appear glorious before the eternal Judge with the manifold profit of their stewardship. Be united in every counsel of piety and steadfast in every judgment of equity. Let no terror of human dignity separate you; let no blandishments of flattery divide you. Rather, join yourselves together like a battle line in God’s camp, in the firmest unity. Thus your concord will finally appear terrifying to everyone who wishes to contradict the truth, as Solomon says: “When a brother is helped by his brother, a city is made firm” (Prov. XVIII, 19).

{15} You are, as Truth says, the light of all Britain [Cod. Sal.: “of that province of ours”], the salt of the earth, a city set upon a mountain, a lamp raised upon a lampstand (Matt. V, 13–15). Again, as the blessed prince of the apostles testifies: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood.” Through the urgency of your preaching, we shall become what follows in that same Epistle: “A holy nation, a people for acquisition,” so that through you the power of him who called us all from darkness into his marvelous light may be proclaimed. “Once not a people of God, but now a people of God” (I Pet. II, 9–10).

Thus our Fathers, by God’s providence, although—

@ [Col. 0153D] The pagans. Read Gildas, *On the Ruin of Britain*, and William of Malmesbury, *Book I of the Kings of England*, chapters 1–4. Canisius.

although pagans, first possessed this homeland through military strength. What a great disgrace, then, that we Christians should lose what those pagans acquired? I say this because of—

@ [Col. 0153D] The scourge. He undoubtedly refers to the devastation of the Danes begun in the year 793; see the letter to the people of Lindisfarne. From this Pagius must be corrected, since he dates this letter [Col. 0154D] two years earlier.

the scourge that recently befell the regions of our island, which—

@ [Col. 0154D] For nearly three hundred and fifty years. Namely, from the year 449, when the Angles and Saxons came to Britain. Pagius, in the place cited.—He says “nearly,” not exactly, for five years are lacking from that number.

has been inhabited by our ancestors for nearly three hundred and fifty [Al.: forty] years. It is read in the book—

@ [Col. 0155D] In the book of Gildas. That is, of Gildas. Gildas wrote after the middle of the sixth century, in the year 564, and died in the year 570, as Usserius argues. Others maintain that he was still alive in the year 581, almost ninety years old, and that he published the letter *On the Ruin of Britain*, together with a correction of the ecclesiastical order. Alcuin praises this letter here; therefore there can be no doubt that it is genuine, since it had already been praised by the Venerable Bede. Basnage.

In the book of Gildas, the wisest of the Britons [Cod. Sal.: “Brectons”], that those same Britons [Cod. Sal.: “Brectons”] lost their homeland because of the plundering and avarice of their princes, the iniquity and injustice of their judges, the negligence and sluggishness of their bishops in preaching, and the luxury and evil conduct of the people.

Let us beware lest these same vices take root in our own times, so that divine blessing may preserve for us in good prosperity the homeland that, in his mercy, he has deigned to grant us. In order that the most abundant piety of almighty God may bring this about, you who, together with the apostles, have received from Christ the key of the heavenly kingdom and the power of binding and loosing: open the gates of heaven to God’s people through continual preaching, and do not remain silent, lest the sins of the people be imputed to you. For God requires from you the souls that you have received to govern. Your reward is multiplied by the salvation of your subjects.

Console the fainthearted (1 Thess. 5:14), strengthen the humble, lead those who are straying back to the way of truth, instruct the ignorant, exhort the knowledgeable, and confirm everyone by the good examples of your life. Chastise the stubborn and those resisting the truth with the shepherd’s rod; support the rest with the staff of consolation. And if you are united in mind, who will be able to resist you? Or who will have peace with God if he does not obey the preaching [perhaps, the preachers] of his salvation, since Truth itself says to the preachers of God’s word: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16). Again, to strengthen them and inspire them with confidence to speak God’s word, the same Truth says: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19; 18:18). Secular power and spiritual power are distinct: the former carries the sword of death in its hand; the latter, the key of life on its tongue. To the latter it is said: “Do not fear them.” Of the former it is said: “They kill the body, but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:26–28). Of spiritual persons also it is said: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matt. 18:20). “If God is for us,” says the Apostle, “who can be against us?” (Rom. 8:31). If Christ is in the midst of his own, who will be able to harm them? Therefore you, priests, ought to have confidence to preach; the rest, humility in hearing and obedience in doing what you command. Let those—that is, the secular leaders—be your defenders, and you their intercessors, so that there may be one flock under one God, Christ the shepherd, and that this homeland may be preserved by him [another reading: “from war”] for us and our descendants in everlasting blessing; so that from this life we may deserve to reach that other life which has no end and is most blessed in perpetual peace.

In order that we may deserve to reach it, you should often say with Moses, the servant of God, with devout heart: “Look down, Lord, from your sanctuary and from your lofty dwelling-place in heaven, and bless your people (Israel) and the land that you have given us” (Deut. 26:15). Again, cry out with tears with Joel, the prophet of God: “Spare, Lord, spare your people, and do not give your inheritance over to the nations as a reproach” (Joel 2:17). As the Apostle James commands: “Pray for one another, so that you may be saved; for the continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful” (James 5:16). The Apostle Peter likewise says: “All of you be united in prayer, showing sympathy toward the brotherhood, humble and merciful” (1 Pet. 3:8). The Vessel of Election also commanded prayers {16} to be made for all, for kings and for all who are placed in high positions (1 Tim. 2:1–2), so that the grace of almighty God may grant the Christian people peaceful times with prosperity, to the praise and glory of his name.

[Col. 0155D] **{17}** The manuscripts of Salzburg and St. Emmeram omit this poem. Quercetanus printed it twice: once attached to this letter and again among Alcuin’s poems.

Eternal city of God, salt [another reading: sun] of the earth, lights of the world,  
The twice six signs of heaven, the months, and three times four years,  
And the hours of the day, and the stones in Christ’s breastplate—  
Your tongue can open or close heaven.  
Teachers of life, great healers of salvation,  
You are living fountains, sacred rivers of paradise;  
You are the Church’s glory, the people’s hope, the gate of light.  
Illustrious offspring, noble temple of Solomon.  
Through you, O Fathers, all Britain in our time  
Flourishes, fruitful in the merits of virtues.  
Together, united in mind, defend Christ’s camp,  
And overcome the wicked weapons with the shield of faith;  
United in heart, strong in heavenly virtue,  
Just in judgment, humble—

[Col. 0156D] With modest piety. Not without cause does he urge modesty upon the clergy of Canterbury. I understand this also of modesty in clothing, the limits of which they plainly exceeded, as is evident from the letter of Saint Boniface to Cuthbert, cited by William of Malmesbury in *Book I of the History of the Kings of England*, chapter 4. He adds: “Indeed, concerning the scantiness of clerical clothing, Alcuin indirectly chastises Athelard, Archbishop Cuthbert’s successor, warning him that when he went to Rome to visit Charlemagne, he should not bring clerics or monks dressed in multicolored and ostentatious garments, because Frankish clerics were not accustomed to clothe themselves except in religious dress.” CANISIUS.

With modest piety, teachers of the people, guides and nourishing shepherds,  
Always and everywhere be faithful to God.  
Multiply the talents entrusted to you by pious labor,  
So that you may receive the greatest rewards in highest heaven,  
Holding heavenly kingdoms with Christ and the saints,  
And may Christ preserve you everywhere mindful of me.  
I am called Alcuin, devoted to your love.  
O shepherds, Fathers, farewell forever!  
And you, holy Father, pious Aethelhard [another reading: “Aedilharde, priest”],  
May you now prosper and flourish, through Christ’s gift, forever.

[Col. 0157D] Edition: Quercetanus 29; Canisius 2; Frobenius 10, collated with the manuscripts of Salzburg and St. Emmeram.

## LETTER XI. TO KING AETHELRED AND THE PRINCES AND PEOPLE OF THE NORTHUMBRIAN NATION  
*(Around the year 793)*

He urges them to be grateful to God; to desire heavenly things rather than earthly; not to seek riches through injustice; to flee vices and sins; to be fathers to widows and orphans; to preserve harmony and peace; and to submit themselves to the preaching of the priests.

[Col. 0157A]

To the most excellent son, King Aethelred of Northumbria—who is also called Aethelred in some places, and in the following letter Edilradus in the Salzburg manuscript. He became king in 774, was later driven from the kingdom by his own people in 778, restored to it twelve years later, that is, in 790, and was finally killed in 796, as Hoveden accurately relates. See Pagi under those years, and Cointius under the year 796, no. 172—Aedilred [another reading: Aethelred], king, and most beloved friends:

To Osbald the patrician—Canisius thinks this is the Osbald of whom Hoveden reports under the year 796 that, after King Aethelred was killed by certain princes of his own nation, he was appointed king; after twenty-seven days, however, abandoned by the entire royal family and the company of the princes, he was driven into exile, and so forth—to Osbald the patrician,

And to Osberht the duke—perhaps the man whom William of Malmesbury calls the patrician of the Mercians, to whom Alcuin wrote another letter, two fragments of which we shall give below from the same Malmesbury—to Osberht the duke and to all friends of brotherly affection, Alcuin, levite, sends greetings of eternal blessedness.

The sweetness of holy love often compels me to remind you of our ancient friendship, of the salvation of your souls, of the truth of faith, and of the concord of peace that you ought to maintain among yourselves; for a friendship that can be abandoned was never true. A faithful friend is long sought, rarely found, and difficult to preserve. Seeking you, I found friends; I shall keep my friends and shall not abandon you, whom I have begun to love. And even if your tongue is silent about me, nevertheless my letters will not be silent about you, but I continually admonish you out of devoted concern, since I always desire your prosperous welfare.

Consider who delivered you from manifold tribulation, how often, by his mercy, you escaped present death, and how often you were rescued from the hand of your enemies. Remember who gave you all the honors you possess, bestowed prosperity upon you, granted you health, and made you greater than all your enemies. Do not be ungrateful for all these blessings, because gratitude for these benefits will merit everlasting life. Nor can the happiness of this age be eternal. Strive most diligently so that, after these earthly honors, you may deserve to possess heavenly ones.

All the delights of this age flee like a fleeting shadow; only what you have done for the love of God remains as a good reward. The road from earth to heaven appears long. The ladder by which one ascends must be exceedingly firm; the fall into hell is easy. Yet this ease has great difficulty, namely, the everlasting fire that burns without extinguishing those who fall into it. The difficulty of ascending to heaven, however, has great joy when one reaches the place to which one ascends—everlasting blessedness indeed.

If perhaps you ask how one ascends to heaven, or how one falls into hell: through evil works, therefore, a person rushes into hell [manuscript: “the lower regions”]; through good works, however, he ascends to the heights. Evil works are these: carnal pleasure, worldly ambition, greed and every evil desire, drunkenness [manuscript: violence], robbery, lies, sexual immorality, fornication, envy, murder, drunken revelries, banquets, enmities, pride, and perjury. As the Apostle says: “Those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:21), unless they are corrected by confession, prolonged penance, and abundant almsgiving. Each one of those things that I have listed can close the kingdom of God and open infernal punishments to a person. Woe to the soul that is compelled always to endure burning flames.

Good works, however, are those by which we can ascend to heaven: love of God, honor and fear of him, vigils [**18**] and prayers to God, love of human beings, mercy toward people, and forgiveness toward those who sin against us; justice in judgments, truth in words, patience in adversity; repaying evil to no one with evil; almsgiving to the poor, kindness toward all people, devotion toward friends, right faith in God, firm hope in his goodness, modesty in clothing, moderation in every use of the world, restraint in food and drink, humility in mind, uprightness in conduct, and fairness throughout one’s life.

These are the steps by which one ascends to heaven; these are the habits that make people worthy of praise; these are the works that merit everlasting joys; this is true wisdom: that a person should provide for himself how he may live happily forever. A person cannot perish altogether like any animal, but after this life he will live forever: well, because of good works; badly, because of evil works; for God will repay each person according to his works (Matt. 16:27).

Do not love unjust riches, because every injustice is punished by God, and God’s blessing is better than all the riches of the world. Whatever is loved in this age is lost; whatever is given for God is possessed. To whom will you be generous if you are stingy toward your own soul? Or who will be faithful to you if you yourself are unfaithful to yourself? Why do you place your hope in another, while you do not wish to benefit yourself? You will die, O human being, and will leave behind everything you possess. Here, in this world, you wish to be a rich stranger and a guest for a short time, yet you do not wish to be rich there, where you will always be? Send your riches on ahead, so that you may possess forever what you love in this age. Build for yourself, through good works, a blessed dwelling.

How wretched will be the person who will burn forever in fire, who will be surrounded by dreadful darkness, who will hear nothing except the voices of the weeping and the horror of gnashing teeth (Matt. 8:12), who will feel nothing except devouring flames, immense cold, and the poisonous teeth of worms! To escape these horrors, O friend, no labor ought to seem hard to you, so that you may deserve to reach that blessedness which is most delightful in eternal peace and most happy in eternal glory. Let no worldly ambition, no carnal pleasure, and no vengeance against enemies impede your course. But run while you have the light (John 12:35); work while it is day, so that you may reach perpetual light and deserve to reign with Christ and his saints in everlasting glory.

I admonish by these little letters not only you, most illustrious men and dearest sons, but also all the princes of your beloved nation and the persons of its various dignities—whether the ranks of ecclesiastical piety or the exalted positions of secular power—with a common regard of charity. As one devoted to your affection like a foster child, I beg you most diligently to obey God’s commandments and to be subject to the preachers of your salvation.

It is their duty—that is, the duty of priests—not to keep silent about God’s words; it is your duty, O princes, to obey humbly and fulfill them diligently. It is the king’s duty to suppress all iniquities by the power of his piety, to be just in judgments, and ready to show mercy. As he shows mercy to his subjects, so God will show mercy to him. He should be sober in conduct, truthful in speech, generous in gifts, prudent in counsel; he should have advisers who are wise, God-fearing, and adorned with honorable conduct. He ought not to covet another’s inheritance, nor be greedy, nor seize things violently, since the Apostle says: “Neither thieves, nor the greedy, nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10). And often through his acts of plunder he loses what is his own, because God hears the groaning of the oppressed.

[Col. 0159C] We also read that the king’s goodness is the prosperity of the whole nation, victory for the army, temperate weather, abundance of the earth, blessing upon his children, and health for the people. It is a great thing to rule an entire nation; indeed, the king is so called from ruling. Whoever rules the people subject to him well receives a good reward from God, namely, the heavenly kingdom. He reigns very happily on earth who will deserve a heavenly kingdom in exchange for an earthly one.

Through prayers and vigils he ought to persist in seeking God with all the greater urgency because he must pray to God not only for himself but also for the prosperity of the entire nation. Likewise, princes and judges of the people, {19} let them preside over the people [of God] in justice and piety. Let them be like fathers to widows, orphans, and the wretched, because the equity of princes is the exaltation of the people. Let them be defenders and guardians of Christ’s churches, so that through the prayers of God’s servants they may live in prolonged prosperity. For the Church is Christ’s bride, and God Christ, the bridegroom of his holy Church, takes vengeance on anyone who attempts to violate her or seize what belongs to her.

[Col. 0159D] You have seen how kings and princes have perished. William of Malmesbury gives an extensive account of the disasters of the kings of Britain and Northumbria in *Book I of the History of the Kings of England*, chapter 3, where he says that most of the Northumbrian kings ended their lives by almost domestic destruction. CANISIUS.

You have seen how your predecessors, kings and princes, perished because of injustices, robberies, and the uncleanness of their lives. Nor did they, fearing God, abstain from such capital sins; nor, what is worse, did they take care to heal the monstrous wounds of their crimes with the medicines of penance. Instead, they rotted in their sins until God’s judgment suddenly fell upon them in terror, and they perished so miserably before the eyes of all as they had shamelessly and without any reverence feared neither to become entangled in the worst crimes.

Alas, how wretchedly they lost the present life! But far more miserably they are tortured in everlasting punishments. Fear their destruction, and guard yourselves against such impieties in which they perished. The same God watches over your [hearts or] works who did not spare their crimes. Many strive to gather wealth through robberies and iniquities, and do not know that because of unjust greed they quickly lose both earthly goods and never acquire heavenly ones.

[Col. 0160B] Men and brothers, beware of such iniquities in yourselves, so that you may deserve to have almighty God favorable to you in the present life and the giver of eternal goods in the future. Maintain peace and kindness among yourselves; mercy and justice toward all people; and preserve bodily chastity, so that the Holy Spirit may dwell in your hearts. May he always suggest wise counsel to you and defend you from every visible and invisible enemy.

Be faithful to your lord, so that through your concord your kingdom may be enlarged, whereas it often used to be diminished through discord. Truth itself says: “Every kingdom divided against itself will not stand” (Matt. 12:25). Just as the greatest empires declined and fell apart through internal dissensions, so, conversely, even the smallest cities or provinces of any state grew and advanced through peaceful concord and at last ruled over kingdoms stronger than themselves.

[Col. 0159D] Fear the scourge. See what we noted about this scourge in Letter 8 to the Lindisfarne community.

Fear the scourge that came upon the church of Saint Cuthbert, a most holy place and one exceedingly rich [manuscript: enduring for a very long time] in the suffrages of many saints, but now miserably devastated by pagans. Whoever does not fear this, correct himself, and weep before God for the prosperity of his homeland has not a heart of flesh but one of stone.

It is the duty of bishops to correct monasteries, arrange the life of God’s servants, preach the word to God’s people, and diligently instruct the people entrusted to them. It is the duty of laymen to obey the preaching, to be just and merciful, so that divine blessing, through its great mercy, may deign to preserve the homeland for us and our descendants in good prosperity—the homeland which, through the right hand of his piety, he deigned to forgive to our parents.

[Col. 0160D] Edition: Quercetanus 39; Frobenius 11, collated from a manuscript with the manuscripts of Salzburg and St. Emmeram. It appears to have been sent together with the preceding letter to the king alone.

## LETTER XII. TO KING AETHELRED  
*(Year uncertain)*

He urges him toward royal virtues.

To his most beloved lord, King Aethelred [Salzburg manuscript: Edilradus], Alcuin, deacon, sends greetings.

[Col. 0161A] Because of the intimacy of our affection, I have taken care to write these personal letters to you alone. And because I shall always love you, I shall never cease admonishing you, so that, subject to God’s will, you may become worthy of God’s protection, and so that the nobility of your royal eminence may be honored by great nobility of character.

A person is not free or noble if he serves sins, since the Lord says: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). It is not fitting for you, seated on the throne of the kingdom, to live by rustic manners. Let anger not rule you, but reason [manuscript: grace]. Let mercy make you lovable, not cruelty hateful. Let truth be heard from your mouth, not falsehood. Be conscious of chastity, not lust; of restraint, not luxury; of sobriety, not drunkenness. Do not be notorious for any sin, but praiseworthy [Col. 0161B] in every good work. Be generous in giving, not greedy in seizing. Let justice adorn all your acts. Be an example [manuscript: model] of uprightness to all who see you. Do not, do not seize what belongs to others, lest you lose what is your own as well. Fear God, who said: “With the judgment you judge, you will be judged” (Matt. 7:2).

Love God Christ and obey his commands, so that by his mercy he may preserve in blessing for you, your sons, and your friends the [kingdom] that he wished you to possess, and may deign to grant you the glory of future blessedness [Salzburg manuscript: will deign]. May almighty God cause you, most beloved son, to flourish in the happiness of your kingdom, the dignity of your character, and enduring prosperity.

[Col. 0161D] This fragment was preserved for us by William of Malmesbury, *Book I of the History of the Kings of England*, chapter 3. Edition: Quercetanus, p. 1667.

## LETTER XIII. FRAGMENT. TO KING AETHELRED  
*(Year 793)*

He speaks of the affliction of the church and city of Lindisfarne.

[Col. 0161C] Behold, the church of Saint Cuthbert, sprinkled with the blood of God’s priests and stripped of all its ornaments, a place more venerable than any other in Britain, is given over to pagan peoples for plunder [another reading: destruction]. And where Christian religion first took its beginning in our [another reading: Northumbrian] nation after the departure of Saint Paulinus from York, there the beginning of misery and calamity has begun.

[Col. 0161D] Saint Paulinus, the first bishop of York; concerning him see the Venerable Bede, Book II, chapter 8, and elsewhere.

What does the rain of blood signify, which during Lent we saw falling threateningly from the north side of the house, in clear weather, from the highest part of the roof, in the city of York—which is the head of the entire kingdom—in the church of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles? Can it not be thought that blood is coming upon the earth from the northern regions?

[Col. 0161D] In the printed editions Quercetanus restored this letter to its complete form with the help of a manuscript. It is number 49 among his editions, number 23 among Canisius’s, and number 13 in Frobenius; here several passages have been corrected from the Salzburg manuscript. **{21}**

## LETTER XIV. TO THE BROTHERS OF THE CHURCHES OF WIRAE AND GYRVUM  
*(Year 793)*

[Col. 0161D] Wirensis and Gyrvensis: the monastery of Saint Peter at Wira, or Wiremouth; and that of Saint Paul at Girvum (Jarrow), in England, at the mouth of the river Wira. A certain Benedict adorned both banks of the river with churches and built monasteries there, differing in nothing through their union in charity and observance of the rule. CANISIUS. See William of Malmesbury, *Book IV of the Bishops of England*, at the end. Clement Reynerus mentions another letter to Eadbald, abbot of Gerwum, in Alford, *Anglo-Saxon Annals*, under the year 804, no. 20, p. 14, quoting these words: “I believe it is not unknown to your affection, venerable brother, that formerly the holy Fathers, your predecessors, granted to me, unworthy though I am, the favor of your fellowship, and ordered the name of my smallness to be written in the register of your blessedness, so that I might be one of you wherever, by God’s will, I might be.”

He urges ordered charity; observance of regular or canonical life and of the rule of Saint Benedict. He terrifies them by the example of the Lindisfarne community; discourages devotion to clothing; and commends confession of sins and penance.

[Col. 0162A]

To the most holy brothers in Christ of the Church of Wira and the Church of Gyrvum, the humble levite Alcuin sends greetings.

Ever since I was able to know it, I have loved your religious devotion, and I have great confidence in the prayers of your unanimity. Even now, although I am far away in body, I am always present among you in spirit, because the breadth of charity is divided by no distance and enclosed by no boundaries. Rather, the more brightly it burns in the chamber of the heart, the more widely it habitually spreads the flame of its sweetest ardor.

Just as a spring watering paradise spreads broadly throughout the world through four channels, so the fountain of charity, the heart teeming with flowers of virtue, flows into four streams of love. Thus Saint Augustine said in Book I of *On Christian Doctrine* (chapters 23 and following):

“Since, then, there are four things to be loved: one that is above us, another that is what we are, a third that is beside us, and a fourth that is beneath us. God is above us. Our neighbor is beside us. Our body is beneath us. No commandments needed to be given concerning the second and fourth [the manuscripts read: ‘are given’]. For however far a person may fall from the truth, love of himself and love of his body remain with him. Therefore Scripture commanded that God and one’s neighbor be loved. No class of things that ought to be loved has been omitted from these two commandments.

“The health of the body is to be loved for the sake of serving God, and the integrity of the soul is to be loved in God. One’s neighbor—that is, every human being—is to be loved for God’s sake, and God is to be loved above all. ‘You shall love,’ he says, ‘the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself’ (Matt. 22:37, 39).

“Let us learn that every human being is our neighbor from the example of the wounded man and the Samaritan. Who does not see that no one is excluded from the duty of mercy, since it is extended even to enemies, the same Lord saying: ‘Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you’ (Luke 6:27)?” [Salzburg manuscript: “since” instead of “when”]

If enemies are to be loved, how much more brothers, who are contained within one fold?

You, most holy brothers, born into spiritual teaching from the same [Salzburg manuscript: “holy”] Fathers, led for a long time through the pastures of life by the same [Salzburg manuscript: “and by good”] shepherds, and instructed in similar institutions of regular [Salzburg manuscript: canonical] life, observe most diligently the unanimity of peace and concord.

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matt. 5:9). Let there be no schisms of hidden rivalry among you, because God Christ is the God of peace and charity, and whoever remains in charity remains in God (1 John 4:16).

Love of neighbor is shown in the service of mercy and in instruction for salvation. Whoever has God’s word in his heart should teach his neighbor; whoever has the resources of the world should help his neighbor; whoever possesses knowledge of any service should assist his neighbor. God himself commands this: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. 7:12).

Observe the order of regular [or canonical] life [Col. 0163B] which the most holy Fathers Benedict and Ceolfrid established for you.

[Col. 0163D] Benedict was the man surnamed Biscop, who, with the assistance of King Ecgfrith of Northumbria, founded the monastery of Wira, or Wiremouth, in 674. Ceolfrid was the first abbot of the monastery of Gyrvum. “For King Ecgfrith of Northumbria,” writes Florence of Worcester under the year 682, “for the redemption of his soul, also gave Abbot Benedict another estate of forty households. There, after sending twenty-two monks and the provost and abbot Ceolfrid, his exceptionally energetic co-worker in all things, he ordered a monastery to be built for the blessed Apostle Paul at the place called Gyrvum.” The Venerable Bede professes that he was educated by these abbots at the end of his *History of the English*, in these words: “Born in the territory of the same monastery, when I was seven years old I was entrusted by my relatives to be educated by the most reverend Abbot Benedict, and afterward by Ceolfrid.” See Alford, *Anglo-Saxon Ecclesiastical Annals*, under the years 674, no. 5, and 682, no. 2.

Guard it most diligently, so that with Benedict and Ceolfrid you may deserve to possess the eternal reward of blessing. This is your praise, this your honor among human beings, and this your reward before God.

Do not conform yourselves to the people of the world in the vanity of clothing, the luxury of drunkenness, the wantonness of jesting, or the insolence of idleness. Rather, with all modesty and piety, let your conduct be pleasing to God and venerable to human beings, as befits the children of the holy mother [Church] and the pupils of monastic life.

You who are the Fathers and shepherds of the holy congregation, teach with the greatest diligence the family entrusted to your governance in fraternal love, and show every example of goodness in yourselves. Admonish the elders as fathers, with honor {22}; correct the younger as sons, with complete affection. In a spirit of gentleness and with honorable speech, instruct them all. Let the rule of Saint Benedict frequently be read in the assembly of the brothers [so that it may be expounded in their own language], so that it can be understood by everyone.

Let each person correct his life according to its instruction, so that what you vowed before the altar to God may be preserved by you inviolate. The Prophet says: “Vow and fulfill your vows to the Lord your God” (Ps. 75:12). For an unfaithful promise displeases God (Ecclus. 5:3).

Consider whom you have as your defender against the pagans who have appeared around the boundaries of the coastal settlement. Do not place your hope in weapons, but in God, who never abandons those who hope in him. Do not trust in [carnal] flight, but in the prayer of your Fathers. In this way you will finally be their sons, if you strive to cling to their footsteps. For holiness does not help those who do evil in a place; rather, the integrity of religion makes those who do good holy and worthy of divine protection.

Who does not fear the terror that occurred in the church of Saint Cuthbert [Salzburg manuscript: Cuthberct]?

[Col. 0164D] The terror that occurred, and so forth. See what we noted in Letter 8 to the Lindisfarne community.

Therefore correct your conduct, lest the just perish because of the sins of the wicked; lest the Lord’s vineyard be given over to the teeth of foxes to gnaw; lest pagans trample the sanctuaries of God. This seems impious; but it is far worse if the devil’s cruelty [because of our crimes devastates the inner chambers of our hearts]. Because of inner enemies, outer enemies have power.

If, therefore, God is the inhabitant of our hearts because of good conduct and purity of life, he will never allow his enemies to ravage what belongs to us. How great a multitude of the Assyrian army perished because of the prayer of one righteous king beloved by God?

Let the chastisement of others be your admonition, and let the tribulation of a few become the salvation of many. You live by the sea, from which the plague first burst upon us. In us has been fulfilled what was once proclaimed through the Prophet: “From the north evil burns forth, and fearful praise will come from the Lord” (Jer. 1:14; Job 37:22). Behold, a fleeing robber has overrun the northern parts of our island. Let us mourn what our brothers have suffered. Let us beware lest something of this kind happen to us. Let us go before the face of the Lord in confession and weep before the Lord who made us (Ps. 94:2, 6), so that he who is Creator and Redeemer may also be Protector and Ruler, and by the good merits of life and the purity of religion may defend his sheepfold by the right hand of his power.

Remember how noble were the Fathers you had, and do not be degenerate sons of such ancestors. Look at the book-treasure [read *thesauros*, “treasures,” in place of *thesaura*], consider the beauty of the churches and the splendor of the buildings. Recall the order of regular life.

How blessed is the person who passes from these most beautiful dwellings to the joys of the heavenly kingdom! Let the boys become accustomed to standing in praise before the heavenly King, not to digging the dens of foxes or pursuing the fleeting courses of hares. How impious it is to abandon the service of Christ and follow the tracks of foxes! Let the boys learn the sacred Scriptures, so that when mature age arrives they may be able to teach others. Whoever does not learn in childhood does not teach in old age.

Recall the most noble teacher of our time, Bede the presbyter: what zeal for learning he had in his youth, and what praise he now has among human beings, he has a much greater glory of reward with God.

[Col. 0164D] From these words Canisius infers that Alcuin was not Bede’s disciple. “For why,” he says, “would he have begrudged Bede this praise and not called him rather the teacher of his own than of his time?”

Therefore, following Bede’s example, awaken the minds of those who are asleep. Attend upon teachers, open books, examine the letters, understand their meanings, so that you may be able to nourish yourselves and provide others with the food of spiritual life.

Avoid hidden feasts and secret [Salzburg manuscript: constant] drunkenness as though they were the pit of hell. Solomon says: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant. But their guests are in the underworld” (Prov. 9:17–18), wishing it to be understood that demons are present at such [wicked] banquets.

As children of God, you ought to display nobility of character, holiness of life, and modesty in clothing. “A person’s laughter, appearance, and manner of walking,” according to Solomon, “declare what he is” (Ecclus. 19:27).

**{23}** What appears to be praise in laypeople—that is, attention to clothing—is recognized as blameworthy in clerics, and especially in monks. Even the prince of the apostles prohibited women from wearing costly clothing and arranging their hair in curls (1 Pet. 3:3). If this were not a sin, Pope Gregory says, the Pastor of the Church would never have prohibited women from the luxuries of clothing.

Let everything among you be done honorably and in due order, so that God may be praised in your good conduct, your honor among human beings may increase, and the reward of your merits may be multiplied with God.

The time of [the present] life is short, the final day uncertain for everyone, and we are quickly snatched away to judgment. Whoever each person then wishes to be, let him now show himself to be that person with all his strength. If, through the weakness of the flesh, he commits any sin, let him wash it away through confession [Salzburg manuscript: “if a sin has been committed, let it be washed away”] and erase it through penance, lest he be condemned in punishment but crowned in glory.

You have holy Fathers who gave you birth as helpers, if you become doers of their instructions. The angelic ranks and the hosts of all the saints also rejoice with you in your good works [they desire to have you as companions in their blessedness]. Indeed, God himself, who wishes all human beings to be saved (1 Tim. 2:4), has prepared for you the glory of the eternal kingdom.

Do not, through sloth of spirit [your spirit] or carnal pleasures, defraud yourselves of eternal goods. Rather, apply yourselves with every effort so that here you may have God as your defender and there as your rewarder, who may cause you to advance in every goodness and establish you blameless [Col. 0165D] before the presence of his glory.

I beg you, let your piety read calmly through what our charity has written devotedly, wishing you present prosperity and future blessedness. I also earnestly ask, through the richness of charity, that you remember my smallness in your holy prayers, and preserve inviolate the fellowship that you granted me [edition: “remember to preserve it”], so that through your intercessions I may deserve to receive forgiveness for my sins, while you may have with God an eternal reward for brotherly love.

May the right hand of almighty God protect you from every visible and invisible enemy [Col. 0166A], and make you flourish everywhere in every good thing, dearest brothers.

## LETTER XV. TO THE BROTHERS OF THE CHURCH OF GYRVUM

He urges them toward virtues worthy of monks and toward following the footsteps of their fathers and teachers.

To the most holy in Christ—
@ [Col. 0165D] To the brothers of the Church of Gyruum. See above, Letter 14, addressed to the same men and also written to the brothers of Wearmouth. The humble deacon Alcuin sends greetings to the brothers of the Church of Gyruum.

Mindful of your piety, by which you have graciously received me into the fellowship of your holy prayer in the embrace of charity, my humble self has decided to recall to your memory, in this little letter, your pledge of fidelity. I wish you, through Christ’s mercy, eternal blessings, and through the intercessions of your affection, that I may be rescued from eternal torments, so that, when the crown of praise is reckoned to you on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0166B], I may receive from that same Judge at least the forgiveness of my sins.

@ [Col. 0165D] I think this passage, corrupt in the manuscript, should be restored [Col. 0166D] so that the meaning emerges as follows:

Nor should the generosity of charity be separated by the distance of lands. Nor is it unusual that the generosity of charity should be separated by distance, since it ought always to be present among God’s servants through him who said: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. 18:20). Whatever has begun among friends in him must remain with inviolable firmness, because “whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

Therefore, let us remain steadfast in the solidity of brotherly charity, attending to nothing else in it except humility and obedience; and let each one help the other with holy assistance. Since charity is of the highest importance for every person, how much more so for Christ’s servants, whose entire worth of life [Col. 0166C] consists in the virtue of charity, humility, and obedience. In these virtues we desire your holiness to advance daily, because those who share nothing, in accordance with their rule of life, with worldly pomp or the vanities of pleasures ought to have their whole life perfected by strict observance of the rule.

Remember, dearest brothers, the most noble fathers and parents of your beginning, who begot you in Christ, and the most noble teachers whom you had in your community of brotherhood. Clinging to their teachings, living by their examples, and following their statutes, you will certainly be joined to their blessedness in the age to come. Blessed is the place that has deserved to have such teachers from God; and blessed are those who strive to keep their precepts in that place [Col. 0166D].

What use is the empty splendor of clothing to God’s servants, who have bound themselves by the vow of monastic life—a splendor that benefits not even worldly people and greatly harms those who serve God? What use is frequent banqueting, which commonly turns the soul away from the religion of the better life? No one who strives to care for his soul can be unaware how many evils drunkenness produces.

Let the elders instruct the young by good examples; and let the Father who presides know that he will have to render an account for the sheep whom he has received to govern. Let each person examine himself, and consider how [Col. 0167A] he may please God and how he may work for the salvation of his soul. But you especially, dearest brothers, ought to remain in God’s service and advance in the study of reason [perhaps: prayer], because of your excellent parents and your few [perhaps: not few] teachers.

What benefit is an abundance of books if there are no readers in them and no one to understand them? What good does the praise of parents accomplish if their followers do not afterward follow their precepts?

You are sons of saints, a noble race and a royal priesthood, nurtured in the Church of Christ. Show your nobility by good conduct, so that many may be instructed by your good examples, and whoever sees you outside may learn from you how he ought to live. For often, from the conduct of a few, those who are outside [Col. 0167B] name the life of those who are within.

The Apostle says: “As long as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I glorify my ministry” (Rom. 11:13). Thus each person ought to adorn his own person or vocation with religious conduct, so that he may have praise among human beings and deserve to receive eternal life with the saints.

May almighty God protect your holiness, which intercedes for us, and cause you to advance in every good work, dearest brothers!

## LETTER XVI. TO THE BROTHERS OF THE CHURCH OF SAINT PETER

He commends himself to their friendship, formerly promised; praises their observance of the rule; and exhorts them to virtues proper to monks.

[Col. 0167C] To the most holy

@ [Col. 0167D] In the Church of Saint Peter. There are many churches, and many monasteries dedicated to the patronage of Saint Peter the Apostle. Among these is reckoned the monastery of Wearmouth, or Wiremuth, in England, which was built by the blessed Benedict Biscop together with another monastery, Girvum, on the opposite bank of the river Wear, consecrated to the holy Apostle Paul [Col. 0168D]. See our notes on Letter 14. The present letter was therefore written to the monks of Wearmouth, among whom the Venerable Bede—whom he praises as the teacher and patron of that place—was nurtured and educated.

To the brothers serving God in the Church of Saint Peter, the humble little servant Alcuin sends greetings of everlasting glory.

Friends are very often separated in bodily appearance, but they ought never to be separated by the sweetness of charity. Where true love exists, there the memory of brotherhood is firm; where the root of a promised friendship is fixed in the treasure of the heart, there it is certain that branches clothed in the flowers of faith have sprung forth, until they have refreshed one another with the fruits of eternal blessedness, possessing true charity between them. This is what I, in my humility, desire firmly to cling to your minds, just as your predecessors once promised me through their pious good will.

Your place of habitation was very desirable to me, although the condition of my wandering life [Col. 0167D] had carried me far from you—not in affection, although in body. For everything I saw among you, whether in the dwellings of your houses or in the conduct of your regular life, pleased me greatly. Would that the obedience, humility, and observance of the regular life of your piety may always please God.

This is your praise before human beings: that you remain steadfast both in your clothing and in all the disciplines of monastic life, just as your fathers, men beloved by God [Col. 0168A] and honored by human beings, established them—those who were the first founders of your community. It is certain that they often visit the places of your habitation; and whenever they find people living honorably and guarding their statutes, they rejoice with them and never cease to intercede for them before the merciful Judge. It is also beyond doubt that visits from angels frequently occur in holy places.

For it is reported that our teacher and your patron, the blessed Bede, said: “I know that angels visit the canonical hours and brotherly communities. What if they do not find me there among the brothers? Will they not say, ‘Where is Bede? Why has he not come with the brothers to the appointed acts of worship?’”

Common prayer is great before God, and great is the fellowship of charity; it is much better to pray, eat, and sleep together with the brothers than to remain alone in a private dwelling at one’s peril. For the devil can more easily overcome one who is alone than one who is surrounded on every side by brotherly assistance, as Scripture says: “A brother helped by a brother is like a fortified city” (Prov. 18:19).

Your praise consists in living honorably and keeping the religious character of your vows. What need have you of the splendor of clothing? From it there will be more blame than praise. For it is vanity and pride, and nothing else—and the destruction of the regular life. It is better to adorn the soul with good conduct, which remains forever, than to adorn the body, which is reduced to dust, with ostentatious colors; or to feed it with luxurious banquets as food for worms [Col. 0168C].

Consider these things, dearest brothers, and follow what may advance you toward eternal blessedness. Obey your fathers, honor the elders, visit the sick, and teach the young well, so that you may have people able to stand at your graves and intercede for your souls.

Consider in your minds what sort of people those now lying in the graves were, and how blessed are the souls of those who brought their days to the end in religion, regular life, bodily chastity, and obedient charity. The kingdom of heaven belongs to them—a kingdom they acquired through labor. May they intercede for you daily, so that, by God’s gift, you may deserve to reach their company.

May almighty God deign to gather the holiness of your unity into eternal [Col. 0168D] blessedness, brothers of the Lord!

{24}

@ [Col. 0168D] {25} This fragment of a letter is found connected by Quercetanus, on page 1623 of Alcuin’s works [Col. 0169D], with part of a letter that we have found complete in volume I of the Councils of Britain, page 159, addressed to Athelard; see below. The present fragment, however, plainly belongs from its context to Charlemagne, Alcuin’s David. Here Alcuin seems to be attacking a new error: some people found it difficult to confess or believe that Christ’s flesh had been changed into spiritual glory after the resurrection. We do not know in what year it was written, unless it is to be referred to the beginning of Alcuin’s controversy against Felix and Elipandus, that is, to the year 793 or the following year.

## LETTER XVII. TO CHARLEMAGNE (Around the year 793)

He praises him for secular power and the preaching of divine law, as ruler of the people and teacher. He attacks the error of the Adoptionists.

When our son Candidus, but your faithful servant [Col. 0169A], came to us, he greatly rejoiced us by announcing your prosperity and sweetly refreshed us with the abundant greetings of your affection. He also enriched the affection of our inmost mind by the praiseworthy presentation of your gift. Moreover, through proofs of your mind, he explained your devotion on our behalf: how you had striven, through pure and holy inquiry, to examine the truth of the catholic faith; and, strengthened by apostolic preaching, he declared that your wisdom always kept to the royal road, in the plain language of truth.

“Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord”; and blessed is the people exalted by such a ruler and fortified by such a preacher. In his right hand he brandishes both the triumphant sword of power, and on his tongue resounds the trumpet of catholic preaching.

Thus David of old, king of the preceding people [Col. 0169B], chosen by God, beloved by God, and an outstanding psalmist, subjected the nations on every side to Israel’s victorious sword and stood forth among the people as an eminent preacher of God’s law. From the distinguished nobility of his sons, for the salvation of the world, Christ—the flower of the field and of the valleys—blossomed from the staff (Song 2:1). In these times, he has granted his people a king, ruler, and teacher of the same name, virtue, and faith as David.

Under his shadow the Christian people rests peacefully in the things above [perhaps: in the higher places], and appears terrible on every side to pagan nations. His devotion does not cease to fortify the catholic faith with evangelical solidity against the sects of perverse doctrine, lest anything new and inconsistent with apostolic teachings arise anywhere through secret infiltrations; but rather, through the light of heavenly grace, may the catholic faith shine everywhere.

Alas, to our grief, certain exiles from this light do not fear, with impious audacity, to deny that Christ, born of the holy Virgin, is true God and the proper Son of God. This error, it seems, has secretly crept so far into the minds even of certain faithful teachers that it appears difficult for them to confess or believe that Jesus Christ, who sits at the right hand of the Father and will come in the glory of the Father’s majesty to judge the living and the dead, is God.

Nor do they acknowledge that the flesh of Christ our God—which hung for us upon the cross—has now been changed into spiritual glory, contrary to the saying of the Apostle concerning the transformation of our body: “It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body” [Col. 0169D] (1 Cor. 15:44). Nor do they consider that same man’s statement—for he was chosen by God as preacher of the world—when, distinguishing the resurrection of the righteous from that of the impious, he said: “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed” (ibid., v. 51).

If transformation into spiritual glory is promised to our works according to the measure of their merits, how much more should the glorious glorification of Christ’s body be believed to have occurred after the resurrection? [Col. 0170A] The Apostle says concerning the glory of our resurrection: “He will reform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:21).

We preach and confess one true God and one Son of God in two natures, namely divine and human: our Lord Jesus Christ reigning with the Father and the Holy Spirit. We do not divide his power or partition it, as though one power were greater and another lesser, because true eternity—or the divinity that is in Christ Jesus our Lord—admits neither division nor partition.

The Apostle says: “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way” (2 Cor. 5:16); that is, he who was mortal on earth in that nature which could die now reigns wholly spiritual in heaven, in the majesty of his divinity. After the resurrection he said to the Apostles: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28:18). The prophets had long before said that this power would be given to the Son of Man.

@ [Col. 0170D] {25} Here I have judged that the letter which is number 97 in Quercetanus and number 14 in Frobenius, addressed “To Someone,” should be broken off. See the preceding note.

@ [Col. 0170D] Editions: Quercetanus 63; Canisius 28; Frobenius 15.

## LETTER XVIII. TO POPE ADRIAN I (Year 794)

He commends himself to the pontiff’s grace, declares him to be the vicar of Saint Peter and heir of his power, and prays that he may grant the requests he is sending through Angilbert.

To the most blessed, most worthy of all honor, and great pontiff

@ [Col. 0170D] To Pope Adrian, who began his pontificate in 772 and died in 795.

To Adrian, Pope, the humblest of all the sons of Holy Church, Albinus sends greetings of eternal blessedness.

The piety of your goodness—venerable and praised throughout the whole world—has brought me, an insignificant servant of Holy Church, a certain confidence in asking your clemency, excellent Father, so that you may deign, through the love of paternal affection, to gather me, unworthy though I am, into the embrace of your most holy intercession.

I know with complete certainty that your Holiness’s devotion continually intercedes for the Christian people of the whole world. Yet I believe that you have acted with particular care for those who commend themselves to your fatherly kindness with earnest humility and flee with greater confidence to the support of such authority.

I know that, through the unity of sacred baptism, I belong to the flock of that Shepherd who did not hesitate to lay down his life for his sheep (John 10:11). Through the piercing glory of his resurrection, he commended these sheep to the blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, to be fed, in return for his threefold confession of magnificent love (John 21). To him also he entrusted the eternal power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth (Matt. 16:19).

As I recognize you, most excellent Father, as the vicar of this most holy See, so I also confess you to be the heir of its wondrous power. Behold, I am one little sheep of your rule [Col. 0171A], but grievously diseased with the stains of sins. Therefore I offer my whole self to your Holiness, most merciful Father, to be healed. By the medicinal power that, after the long succession of the holy Fathers, is known to have been handed down to you by God through Christ, command that I be released from the bonds of sins by the saving word of your piety.

For I see that, in accordance with the rule of evangelical humility, I may say: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but speak the word, and my servant will be healed” (Matt. 8:8). As soon as he hoped, he found; as soon as he believed, he received.

O most blessed tongue of your mouth, in which lies the medicine of eternal salvation, through which heaven is opened to believers! I beg you never to let it be silent. Let it always admonish and heal; let it always open the gates of perpetual blessedness to those who flee to it.

O Lord Jesus, grant him to flourish and live in long-lasting prosperity; and since you have given such a shepherd to your people, deign to preserve him for many years by the right hand of your mercy, so that, coming before the throne of your glory with the multiplied reward of his labor, he may deserve to hear: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:21).

I would now insert in this letter some requests concerning my own needs. But since the chosen envoy of my lord the king, namely my most beloved son

@ [Col. 0171D] The envoy of my lord the king … Angilbert. Angilbert was sent twice by Charlemagne to Adrian. First, in the year 792 after the Synod of Regensburg, when he brought Felix of Urgel to Rome; and again in 794, after the Synod of Frankfurt, when he conveyed to Adrian the capitulary against the synod held at Nicaea concerning the erection of sacred images, as appears from Adrian’s words in his response to Charlemagne. Mabillon, volume II, book XXVI of the Annals, page 313; Pagius under the year 794, no. 12; and others think that this letter was written on the occasion of the second embassy. At the time of the first embassy, in the year 792, Alcuin had not yet returned from Britain to Francia.

Alcuin himself also indicates rather clearly in this letter that, before Angilbert departed for Rome on this occasion, he had already served as an envoy to Adrian, whose goodness, after returning, he used very often to recount to the lord king. [Col. 0172D] “Baronius recites this letter in the appendix to the year 772 and thinks it was sent by Alcuin when Charlemagne, having received news of Adrian’s election as Roman pontiff, sent Angilbert as envoy to Rome. But, as we have just said, Angilbert undertook only two embassies, and Alcuin did not remain in Francia before the year 781 or the following year.” Pagius, cited above; see also his note under the year 773, no. 1.

Angilbert is being sent to the most blessed paternal presence of your supreme authority {26}. I did not think it necessary to put into writing what that faithful and prudent man will be able to explain more effectively in person to Your Excellence’s ears, according to the command of my lord the king.

Among the other missions of his most faithful embassy to you, he has also commended to that aforementioned secretary of the royal will my requests concerning my needs. We have found him to be altogether faithful to all his friends, and especially to you, as is truly fitting, most holy Father. He used very often, in the presence of many witnesses, to recount your goodness to the lord king in words of praise, and he strove to speak of the outstanding acts of piety performed by you in words of pure faith, so that he might show the fidelity of his pious affection and implant love for your fatherly kindness in the minds of many.

@ [Col. 0172D] Editions: Quercetanus 82; Canisius 66; Frobenius 16.

## LETTER XIX. TO THEOPHILUS (Year 794)

He praises his writings as expressing apostolic faith and desires to be instructed by him. [Col. 0172A]

To the best

@ [Col. 0172D] To Theophilus. Perhaps to Theophylact, bishop of Todi, who presided over the Council of Frankfurt in 794 as legate of the Apostolic See, a place where Alcuin could easily have formed a friendship with him. This Theophylact is also called Theophilus by Regino and by the annalist of Metz; this confirms our conjecture.

To Theophilus, disciple of the twice-twofold evangelical truth and of the four-horse team of holy virtues, a four-horse team of faithful friends, full of charity, sends greetings in a ship across the Alpine waters.

We received the letter of Your Dignity, truly, as we recognized, painted with the flowers of charity and filled with the honeyed flavor of spiritual joy. Hence we, disciples of your holiness, refreshed, satisfied, and greatly delighted by the abundance of the dew-bearing nectar that we fully drank from its bosom, recognized that the heavenly treasure of charity is stored sufficiently in your breast and that from it, across the broad spaces of the earth, rivers of saving doctrine flow abundantly [Al.: stream forth], irrigating the dry hearts of those thirsting for the fountain of righteousness—not with the sevenfold flood of the Nile, but with the sevenfold abundance of the Holy Spirit, streams of living water leaping up into eternal life (John 4:14).

Therefore you have earnestly endeavored, through generous piety, to offer us the most lucid cups of apostolic faith. We received them with every hunger of charity and drank them with great thanksgiving. We found in them not even the tiniest impurity of an atom, trembling with varied movements in the sunlight, but a crystalline purity shining brightly, so that the rays of the heavenly sun wonderfully illuminated the lamps of our hearts.

[Col. 0172C] {27} We considered these things more carefully and desired them more ardently; we read them repeatedly, chose them always, and, rejoicing, praised God, who in his customary mercy has granted such a light to our times [Al.: to our labors].

Therefore we pray with greater earnestness that the light of the wisdom given you by God may shine from the heart of your charity through the mouth of your truth, so that every hearer may be built up and the one giver of all good things may be glorified in you and through you.

May your letter of exhortation run to us more often. Let neither Alpine cold, nor the roughness of the roads, nor the overflowing of rivers hinder it in any way. Charity conquers all things, concerning which the sweet-voiced Psalmist sang: “Many waters could not extinguish charity, nor could rivers overwhelm it” (Song 8:7).

Let charity write from the abundance of the heart, so that we may be built up through the diligence of reading. At the conclusion of this little letter, we beg what we desired at its beginning: deign to steer the vessel of our life by the prayers of your holiness.

@ [Col. 0173D] {28} Editions: Quercetanus 79; Canisius 25; Frobenius 17.

## LETTER XX. TO USUALDUS (Year 794)

He exhorts the monks to virtue; says that he assisted their petitions before the king; and commends himself to their prayers.

To the most holy community of the Lord God, Savior of the world, and to the pious Father

@ [Col. 0173D] To Usualdus. Since the manuscript of Saint Gall lacks this name, Canisius wondered whether the congregation of the Holy Savior might be the oratory that King Liutprand, according to Peter Oldrad, archbishop of Milan, in a letter to Charlemagne, built in his palace at Pavia in honor of the Savior of the world. Mabillon, however, in book XXVI of the Annals, no. 8, has no doubt that this Usualdus was abbot of the monastery of the Holy Savior on Mount Amiata near the Etruscan city of Chiusi. Another opinion was once held by a very celebrated man, who in the Acts of the Saints of the Benedictines, 4th century, part I, page 575, believed our Usualdus to have been abbot of the monastery of Saint Nabor near Metz, which in antiquity was called the New Cell of the Holy Savior. This opinion gains strength from the memory of Angilram, who had been archbishop of the church of Metz.

To Usualdus, Albinus, the humble deacon, sends greetings.

We praise the admirable conduct of your blessedness and the life worthy of your name, and we praise the Lord [Col. 0173B] in you, who has deigned to have such confessors of his holy name. For you are not called monks of the Holy Savior by a special title without possessing in merit what you are called by name.

Indeed, so noble a king ought to have noble ministers: outstanding in conduct, harmonious in peace, chaste in body, sober in mind, excellent in every goodness, accustomed to the most glorious triumphs. They must not defend their life by flight, but stand firm in the battle line, fight manfully, and conquer bravely, so that with the glorious palm of victory you may deserve to enter the city of the eternal King.

Considering this, brothers, exhort one another each day, until Christ is named in you. Bring the begun journey of your blessed life to a firm conclusion, so that each one may become worthy to say with the Apostle: “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith. As for the rest, there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just Judge, will give me on that day” (2 Tim. 4:7–8).

As far as I was able, I assisted your request and desire before the lord king, according to what the envoy of your brotherhood suggested to me. I also brought as an assistant

@ [Col. 0174D] Liutgard, the fourth wife, after the death of Queen Fastrada, of the emperor Charlemagne; she died at Tours in the year 800 (Annals of the Franks).

I brought the most pious woman Liutgard. But we beg you to deign to repay our labor on your behalf with your most holy prayers. For formerly, through

@ [Col. 0174D] Angilram, bishop of Metz, who died in 791. Pagius.

I commended myself to your holiness through Angilram [Al.: Engilram], archbishop and first chaplain of the holy chapel. But now, as though prostrate at the knees [Al.: feet] of each one of you, I beg that you deign, by your merciful prayers, to carry me, tossed about on the sea of this life [Col. 0173D], into the harbor of everlasting rest [Col. 0174A], by the gift of divine grace. Thus may I deserve to obtain the salvation of my soul through the help of brotherly intercession, and may you deserve to receive worthily from God the reward of eternal recompense for your service of charity.

May almighty God hear the prayers of your piety, grant that they benefit many, and deign to give you the rewards of everlasting glory, dearest and most desired brothers.

@ [Col. 0174D] Edition: Quercetanus 87 from the manuscript; Frobenius 18.

## LETTER XXI. TO CERTAIN PEOPLE (Around the year 794)

Among the people of York, Alcuin excuses his absence and exhorts them to harmony with their father Eanbald.

To the most holy and beloved in Christ

@ [Col. 0174D] Brothers and sons—namely, the people of York, as is inferred from the words: “Remember what sort of fathers we had, who begot us in the Lord.” He therefore writes to those whose community he professed to share and whose common Father he acknowledged—that is, the people of York.

To the brothers [Col. 0174B] and sons in Christ, greetings.

I rejoice greatly in your advancement in the Lord, desiring that you may flourish in present happiness and future everlasting blessedness. Therefore I do not cease to admonish you frequently concerning the harmony of peace and the counsel of salvation, although with little ability, yet not with little charity.

I have not found the opportunity to come as quickly as your holiness requested, because of certain needs of the Church. Already I am wholly with you in desiring your prosperity, although absent in body, yet not in affection.

Above all I beg that you be harmonious with our most pious

@ [Col. 0174D] Father Eanbald, I think, the elder. Alcuin therefore wrote this letter after he had returned to Francia for the second time, where he was detained by certain needs of the Church—namely, the refutation of the Felician heresy—before the year 796, when that Eanbald died.

Our Father. Keep the fear of the Lord before your eyes, speak together about what you hope is pleasing to him, accomplish it manfully, and hold to it firmly. Let no one be able to tear apart the bonds of your unity [Col. 0174C].

Stand steadfast in the fear of God, since he has mercifully provided for your honor—he who never abandons those who hope in him. If anything in the customs of human life among you needs correction, correct it quickly and with every effort, so that the Holy Spirit of the Lord may deign to remain with you.

And if God, who said, “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. 18:20), is among you, who can be against you? And if his love burns in your hearts, who can harm you?

You have the saints of God as helpers in every good work, if you strive with all your strength to follow the footsteps of the saints. Remember what sort of fathers we had, who begot us in the Lord. Emulate their life, so that with them you may deserve to share eternal blessedness. Remember me in your holy prayers, and may almighty God grant that your unity advance in every good work, beloved brothers.

## LETTER XXII. TO SOMEONE

He urges his son and companion in pilgrimage toward virtue. He recalls and commends the study of wisdom and brings teachings formerly given back to memory.

A father to his son, a peacemaker to a pilgrim, a teacher to a disciple, a companion to a fellow traveler: everlasting salvation.

I have a great desire, dearest son, for your salvation and prosperity. Therefore I have taken pains to send you this letter of exhortation in place of words of paternal affection, begging you, with enduring love of mind and the complete devotion of virtue, to keep God before your eyes and in your memory, so that his most merciful kindness may guard you amid adversity and prosperity, and so that, proceeding along the royal road, you may deserve to reach the gate of the everlasting city.

Let Christ be in your mouth and heart, and constancy in your works. Do not act childishly or pursue youthful desires; but be perfect in all honesty, self-control, and moderation, so that God may be praised in your conduct and the father who begot you may not be blamed.

Be sober in food and drink, caring more for your health than for bodily pleasure or the utterly vain praise of human beings, which accomplishes nothing if your actions displease God. It is better to please God than

@ [Col. 0175D] Actors. Perhaps this should be read as “histriones,” actors, with whom he said above, in Letter 213 [now 191], that his Homer was greatly delighted. Hence the suspicion may arise that this letter was written to that same Homer, or Angilbert [Col. 0176D]. (In Frobenius, Letter 230.)

It is better to please God than actors, and to care for the poor than for mimes. Let your banquets be honorable and your guests religious. Be an elder in conduct, although younger in years. Everything excessive is harmful.

@ [Col. 0176D] Italy is an unhealthy homeland, etc. See what we noted in the notes to Letter 137.

Italy is an unhealthy homeland and produces harmful foods [Col. 0175C]. Therefore, with the greatest care, consider what foods you use, when you use them, in what manner, and with whom; and especially avoid habitual drunkenness, because from the heat of wine the burning of fevers commonly assails the unwary.

My spirit is deeply weary because of your absence. O how sweet life was when we sat quietly among the cases of wise writings, amid an abundance of books and the venerable opinions of the Fathers—things lacking nothing that religious life and the pursuit of knowledge demanded.

Nevertheless, let us use our present lot according to the virtue of the soul, trusting in divine grace, which never abandons us if we place all our hope in it. But I, weary and sad, shall await the desirable sight of your face, not knowing whether I shall deserve to see you coming, or whether you, when you come, will deserve to find me. For God’s judgments are hidden.

Let each person prepare burning lamps for himself, so that at whatever hour he is commanded to meet the Bridegroom, he may deserve to enter the chamber of the eternal King with the light of good works.

If you saw any good custom in us, follow it, so that you may deserve to receive God’s blessing from it. But if you saw any error or ungodly path, shudder at it and flee from it, lest you be entangled with us in our sins.

Do not forget the daily course of the synaxis, with the solemn celebrations of Masses and the vigils of the saints, which, as you saw, are observed daily in our chapel [Col. 0176A]. Use elders and wise men as counselors. Remember Rehoboam, the son of Solomon.

Let every kind of wantonness be far from your conduct. Let your words be truthful, your conduct honorable, your body chaste, your dress religious, your food and drink moderate, and let there be appointed times for what you ought to do. Let your mouth not become accustomed to undisciplined speech.

Let your words be simple, without oaths, full of truth, and seasoned with the salt of wisdom. Let the heart judge before the tongue speaks. There are many jealousies and treacheries among human beings; there are many friends at the table and few in times of need.

Why write more, when you know very well what I often used to recommend to the heart of your charity? From the merits of obedience, paternal blessing will, as I think, come to sons [Col. 0176B].

Consider Reuben; remember Judah—born from one father and mother, yet possessing different blessings because of different merits. Peter and Judas were both chosen for the apostolate, but they did not both follow the Lord with equal devotion. Therefore one was raised to the primacy of the apostolate, while the other was handed over to the prince of demons.

Stephen and Nicolas were chosen equally for the ministry of the altar, but because their faith was unlike, an unlike end followed them.
