The Scriptures are full of lessons concerning obedience; the world is full of examples of what happened to each person through humble obedience. Yet the multitude of these examples is surpassed by the wonderful example of our Redeemer, concerning whom the Teacher of the Gentiles says:

“Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus: who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him a name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:6–11).

@ [Col. 0176D] Edition: Quercetanus 31; Canisius 15; Frobenius 19. {29}

## LETTER XXIII. TO THE BROTHERS OF SAINT MARTIN IN THE CITY OF TOURS (Around the year 795)

He wishes to be with them and exhorts them to virtues appropriate to monks.

Most holy brothers in Christ, and those serving the blessed Martin, confessor of Christ, Alcuin, the humble Levite, sends greetings.

From the time I was able to know of your blessedness, I have always wished to love you, because your holiness pours love for you into my heart, and I desire to be one of you. Thus, if I could not be one of you by merit, I might nevertheless be joined to you by the charity of brotherly love, so that on the great day of the resurrection I might share in the lot of those whom so great a shepherd will present to his king. O happy community, rejoicing in such a shepherd and having such a teacher for the day of the Lord [Editor: “leader”]! Happy is the one who follows his footsteps with his whole will, so that, cleaving to his commands, he may deserve to be associated with his glory.

For this to happen, let no desire of the world and no carnal longing draw you away. You must not neglect your own salvation, nor think lightly of the glory prepared for you in God. For you have God’s grace assisting you, and a great intercessor, namely Saint Martin, who daily prays for you: because you stand every day in his service in his house, you have him in heaven as your advocate at every hour.

Therefore, dearest brothers, strive with the greatest diligence to ensure that the visitation of his most holy Spirit often finds you keeping vigil in divine praises. In the place which he chose for himself as his sweetest resting-place, pour out your prayers as though you were speaking in the presence of God and his saints. Let there not be one thing in your heart and another on your lips, for a human being hears what the mouth says, whereas God sees what the heart thinks; “for God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Psalm 50:19). And “everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). Through humility, obedience, and charity, the monk ascends to heaven.

It is therefore not praiseworthy to imitate the Fathers’ habit in clothing while neglecting the observance of the commandments which they established for those serving God. Whoever wishes outwardly to appear before human eyes as a sheep in his clothing should strive inwardly, in the hidden places of his heart and before God’s sight, to be what he wishes to be thought outwardly before human beings.

The charity which God commanded must therefore be twofold: that is, charity toward God and toward one’s neighbor. The one is above us—namely, God; the other is beside us—namely, the human being. God is to be loved with all one’s heart, with all one’s soul, and with all one’s strength. We are to love our neighbors as ourselves (Matthew 22:37, 39). If anyone asks who one’s neighbor is, he should understand every Christian, just as we read in the Gospel about the Samaritan who helped the wounded man (Luke 10).

Obedience likewise must be twofold: not doing the evil things that are forbidden, and doing the good things that are commanded. These two things—charity and obedience—are to be fulfilled with the utmost humility. These are the three commandments that will open the gates of heaven to monks.

From these roots, then, other virtues grow up, like the abundance of branches, and from them the fruit of eternal life is born. Most holy Fathers and brothers, I beg you, do not consider me presumptuous for writing these things to you. My charity compelled me—

> **Editor’s note:** “My charity compelled me.” These words sufficiently suggest that this letter was written before Alcuin was placed over those monks. Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXVI, no. 47.

—my charity compelled me to break forth in this letter, wishing that God might grant you every good thing [Canisius: “give”], so that in this age you might have honor among human beings and in the age to come eternal life with God’s saints.

But you who are elders, admonish your juniors in a spirit of gentleness, as the Apostle commanded, because their salvation is your reward (1 Corinthians 4), and their instruction is your recompense. For whoever plants a tree expects to receive a reward from its fruit. Regard the young as sons, so that they may regard you as fathers. Instruct them by good examples; admonish them as dearly beloved; correct them as fellow servants. For this is brotherly charity: that all of you should strive to lead one another, as yourselves, to the crown of heavenly blessedness.

Young men, be subject to your elders as to fathers (1 Peter 5:5), just as it is read in the Gospel concerning God Christ, that he was subject to his parents (Luke 2:51). If God, who became human and is Lord of all, does not disdain to be subject to human beings, how much more ought you, boys and young men, to be subject to your teachers, so that through their good instruction you may deserve to advance, flourish, and be exalted in the Church of Christ, and, by God’s gift, attain eternal life with them.

Deign always to intercede for me, so that through your prayers I may deserve to receive forgiveness for my sins and, with you, hear the gracious sentence on the last day of our Lord Jesus Christ: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34).

May God’s eternal grace preserve you, brothers;

May you, mindful of my name and of me, remain well forever.

> **Editor:** Quercet. 72; Canisius. 27; Froben. 20.

## LETTER XXIV. TO POPE LEO III  
*(Around the year 796.)*

He commends himself to the apostolic concern of the supreme pontiff, as vicar of the apostles and prince of the Church, through Angilbert.

> To the most blessed lord, worthy of every honor and mention—

> **Editor’s note:** To Pope Leo. This is Pope Leo III, who assumed the pontificate after the death of Pope Hadrian in the year 795, on the feast of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, as Anastasius reports in the *Life of Hadrian*. He died in the year 816.

To Pope Leo, Albinus, the humble Levite, sends greetings of eternal glory in Christ.

I beg that your most holy piety, dearest Father [Al.: “most glorious Father”], receive with a kindly spirit the little letter of our lowliness, and recognize me as a devoted servant of your affection. As far as I have been able, I have always loved the most blessed princes and shepherds of the holy Roman See, desiring through their most holy intercessions to be numbered among Christ’s sheep, which Christ God, after the glory of his resurrection, entrusted to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to feed.

I confess that it is truly fitting that the entire multitude of that flock, although dwelling in different pastures of the earth, should be subject to its shepherd by one faith of charity; and that, as befits a devoted shepherd, he should take great care of the flock entrusted to him, foreseeing [Al.: “providing”] through diligent admonition of piety and the intercession of holiness that none of them should begin to stray through the precipices of error from the way of truth and the everlasting pastures of life. The health of the flock is the shepherd’s glory, and its increase is his eternal reward.

Behold, most holy Father: you are the pontiff chosen by God, the vicar of the apostles, heir of the Fathers, prince of the Church, nourisher of the one spotless dove. In you may faith shine forth, devotion blaze, and charity abound [Al.: “shine forth, blaze, and abound”]. Gather us, children of God’s holy Church, with the affection of paternal compassion, through your most holy prayers and the sweetest exhortations of the sacred writings, within the strongest sheepfold of the Church’s solidity, lest any one of us, wandering outside, be found abandoned to be devoured by wolfish rapacity.

For the shining ranks of the heavenly army first came to announce the joys of the nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ to shepherds who had devotedly kept watch over their flocks. We do not doubt that, through your most holy vigils in pastoral concern, most proven archimandrite, angelic visitations from the heavenly seats stand beside you; and we believe that, with their help, whatever you ask of divine piety you are able to obtain.

Therefore I, the least servant of the most sacred sheepfold and a little sheep sick with sins, encouraged by the hope of your exceptional goodness, prostrate in spirit before the most holy feet of your fatherhood, humbly beg that you deign to loose the harsh bonds of my sins through the ecclesiastical power of apostolic authority, and that through the prayers of paternal piety you strive to direct the remaining course of my life toward the gates of the everlasting city.

I ask for great things indeed, but charity knows how to give great things. Christ’s clemency does not despise a widow who asks on behalf of her daughter—

> **Editor’s note:** “One who asks on behalf of a widowed daughter.” “I correct this conjecturally,” says Canisius, “although I would rather read: ‘the Canaanite woman asking on behalf of her daughter.’ It is not established whether she was a widow. The manuscript reads: ‘a widow asking on behalf of her son,’ where it seems to join two distinct miracles.”

—but says: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish” (Matthew 15:28). Faith urges me to ask these things; hope confirms that I shall obtain them; charity, I believe, does not presume to refuse them. Christ did not hesitate to die for us when we were enemies; how much more should it be believed that you, holy Father, desire to pray for your friends?

Under you as shepherd, may Christ’s flock increase. You are the comforter of the sorrowful, the helper of the afflicted, the hope of those who cry out to you, the light of life, and the ornament of religion. The place in which you stand makes you honorable to all; nobility of character makes you praiseworthy; and devotion of piety makes you lovable. Since you occupy the seat of the holy Fathers, may you always cling to their examples, so that with them you may deserve to enter the joys of the Lord your God, receiving the manifold reward of your labor.

My dearest son Angilbert—

> **Editor’s note:** Angilbert. This was Angilbert’s third embassy to Rome. Immediately after his election, Pope Leo sent Charlemagne, in order to bind him to himself, the keys of Saint Peter’s confession and the banner of the city of Rome, together with other gifts, through his legates. He asked him to send one of his leading men to Rome to receive the Roman people’s new oaths of faith and submission. Angilbert was sent there, evidently around the beginning of the year 796. Mabillon. See Charlemagne’s letters to Homer, or Angilbert, and to Pope Leo in volume 98 of *Patrologia*.

—Angilbert [Al.: Engilbert] can make known to you our lowliness’s devotion toward the apostolic See, as well as our request. I have recognized him as very faithful to your piety, and therefore entrusted him with the causes of our need, so that through his mouth your pious ears may hear the supplications of my heart.

> **Editor:** Quercet. 92; Froben. 21; Canisius. 46, collated with the manuscripts of Salzburg and Saint Emmeram.

## LETTER XXV. TO HIS DEAREST SON HOMER  
*(ANGILBERT; 796.)*

He commends his remembrance to the patronage of the saints and urges him to bring him ecclesiastical works of beauty.

To his dearest son, the man tossed by the waves, greetings.

When you departed, I tried repeatedly to reach the harbor of stability; but the ruler of affairs and dispenser of souls has not yet granted me the ability to do what he once made me willing to do. Still the wind of temptations lashes the little branches of thoughts growing from the root of my heart, so that the flowers of consolation and the fruits of refreshment cannot be nourished. “All night we labored and caught nothing” (Luke 5), because Jesus has not yet stood upon the shore, commanding the net to be cast on the right side of the boat.

Do not forget the patronage of the saints. Do not neglect to acquire ecclesiastical works of beauty when they come before your eyes. Our rusticity is greedy for such things; your nobility is generous in all things. Remember the poet’s prophecy:

> “If you bring nothing, Homer, you will go outside.”

Who doubts that this was prophesied concerning you and your journey? If the Sibyl foretold Christ and his labors as destined to come, why should Naso not have foretold Homer and his journeys? I have played for a little while with rhetorical elegance for the refreshment of my spirit.

But, returning once more to the sequence of matters with wrinkled brow, I earnestly ask you, as a like-minded friend and guardian of my spirit, to entreat God, together with the suffrages of the holy apostles, for the counsel of salvation for our souls. For, as I recognize, a certain chain of necessity binds us both and does not permit us to enter the camp in the free course of our will. No one can break the shackles except him who shattered the iron bars of hell, who is “the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6): the way for those proceeding through him, the truth for those coming to him, and the life for those remaining in him.

What more do I have to write, since you know everything necessary? Send me letters whenever the opportunity arises for the bearer, so that I may learn of your prosperity and your journey—

> **Editor’s note:** Your journey, namely the Roman journey. While Alcuin returned to Gaul, Angilbert went to Rome three times: in 794, 796, and 800, as stated above. It is uncertain in which of these years the present letter was sent. Mabillon dates it to 796.

—when or whither, by God’s mercy, you will come.

May Christ make everything prosper for you, Homer!

May he preserve you always and everywhere. Farewell!

> **Editor:** Quercet edition. 42; Canisius. 51; Froben. 22.

## LETTER XXVI. TO ANGILBERT, PRIMICERIUS OF KING PEPIN’S PALACE

He commends to Angilbert’s favor a man journeying as a pilgrim to the sacred thresholds of the apostles, and asks that sacred relics be sent to him.

To his faithful and venerable friend Angilbert, primicerius—

> **Editor’s note:** Angilbert. “He was called Homer by an additional name. In the year 783 he flourished at the court of Pepin, king of Italy, and there held the office of primicerius of the palace. Around the year 787 he married Berta, daughter of Charlemagne. Around the year 790, with Berta’s consent, he withdrew to the monastery of Centula. In 792 he brought Felix of Urgell to Rome. In 794 he carried the acts of the Council of Frankfurt to Rome. In 796 he was sent by Charlemagne to Pope Leo III. In 800 he accompanied Charlemagne on his journey to Rome. In 811 he subscribed Charlemagne’s testament. He died on 18 February 814.” Bouquet, *Collection of the Historians of Gaul*, volume 5, page 408, note b. Mabillon places this letter in *Annals*, book XXV, no. 38, under the year 783, but in book XXVI, no. 44, under the year 796. Nothing certain can be established from this. We join it with the other letters to the same man.

Albinus, the humble Levite, sends greetings to Angilbert, primicerius.

Mindful of the friendship agreed between us, I have ventured to send you this letter, begging you kindly to receive its bearer—

> **Editor’s note:** The bearer of this letter. Mabillon thinks it may be possible to infer that he was the presbyter Fortrada, whose name is mentioned in Letter 210.

—and to commend the lord King Pepin to the favor of his journey.

> **Editor’s note:** “King Pepin, son of Charlemagne, king of Italy,” says Canisius. Basnage, as well as Petavius and Bollandus, considers it more probable that this Pepin was king of Gaul, not Italy. The tenor of the letter, however, contradicts this, since it is addressed to Angilbert while he was in Italy, as the person to whom he commends the bearer of the letter, who was seeking the thresholds of the apostles. Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, fourth century, part 1, page 94, §4.

I beg you to ask King Pepin to assist him. The reward of kings in aiding the unfortunate—and especially pilgrims seeking the sacred thresholds of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles—is held to be great in the sight of divine mercy.

Moreover, dearest brother, I earnestly beg you to arrange to send me gifts that are especially sweet and greatly necessary to me: namely, some relics of the saints. “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). May he make you abound in every good thing and establish you in the glory of the saints, whose relics your benevolence may send to me.

May you flourish, son, with crowns of virtues, with the beauty of wisdom, with holy love toward God, and with good faith toward human beings forever.

> **Editor:** Quercet. 27 from a manuscript; Froben. 23.

## LETTER XXVII. TO HOMER  
*(ANGILBERT; YEAR UNCERTAIN)*

He sends a twofold solution to grammatical questions proposed to him by the king.

Flaccus Albinus sends greetings to Flavius Homer.

I wonder why my sweetest David wished to question the sluggish dullness of Flaccus’s laziness about palace questions, and to recall to the camp of battle the man who had earned the name of a veteran soldier, so that he might calm the tumultuous minds of the soldiers; especially since books of secular literature and the wisdom of ecclesiastical solidity, as is right, are found among you, and in them true answers can be found to everything that is asked.

Nevertheless, I have considered, as far as I could, this distinction between two parts of speech. Running through the examples of earlier teachers, I found that they too disagreed with one another on these matters. Therefore I thought it appropriate to send you the authority of this exact measure [possibly: “examination,” *examinis*], so that you may learn their opinions, whether concerning the construction of the parts or the propriety of the rules.

The first question concerned *rubus*: what gender it should have. We find various examples concerning this noun. For in the meter composed in the *Heptateuch*, the following verses are read:

> “In which, by the conspicuous lamp of flames, he sees  
> the curved bramble shining and not consumed by the fires.”

Likewise Ambrose, in the *Paschal Hymn*:

> “And the flame, calling the servant forth,  
> do not destroy the thorny bramble.  
> Though you are a consuming fire,  
> you do not burn what you illuminate.”

A certain grammarian likewise says:

> “Likewise, feminine nouns of this second declension, lacking a plural number, whether names of kingdoms or trees: *tyrus*, *cyprus*, *populus*, *cypressus*, *alnus*, *fraxinus*, *rubus*.”

Donatus likewise said concerning trees:

> “In the neuter, the fruit; in the feminine, we often name the trees themselves.”

Note that he said “often,” not “always.”

Paterius, however, drawing on the words of Pope Saint Gregory, assigned it the masculine gender:

> “For when he addressed Moses through the burning bramble, what else did he show except that he would be leader of that people, who would receive the flame of the law and yet in no way avoid the thorn of sin?”

Isidore likewise says in his *Commentary on Genesis*:

> “But it is read that the Lord appeared in that same bramble.”

Arnobius, in the dispute he had with Serapion, treated *rubus* as masculine, saying:

> “And just as the bramble truly had the flame, so truly the Son of Man suffered; and just as it truly was not set on fire, so truly the Son of God did not suffer.”

Josephus likewise says in his *Histories*:

> “After the sacrifice had been made, Moses ministered to the people beside the bramble which had escaped the flame of fire.”

Virgil too, a falsifier of no contemptible authority, says:

> “May honey flow for him, and may the harsh bramble bear amomum.”

Nevertheless, if it were feminine, the verse could stand through synaloepha.

Priscian, the most truthful teacher of the grammatical art, says this about *rubus*:

> “The particular names of each tree are feminine, except *oleaster*, which both the form of its ending and its declension prevent from being feminine. For *siler*, which is neuter, is not to be placed among the trees, nor is *rubus*.”

Among these authorities, let your prudence see what should be followed. Some of these examples may have been corrupted through the fault of a copyist, with *u* written for *a*, or even *a* for *u*. Nevertheless, it seems more certain that the word is masculine than feminine.

The second question concerned *de*, *dis*, and *des*: whether the form should be *dispexeris* or *despexeris*. The form *des* cannot occur because of the following *s*, which, as Priscian holds, requires *dis*. But the inquiry concerns only *de* and *dis*.

It seems necessary to consider how the matter stands in Greek: which preposition occurs there, whether one signifying *dis* or one signifying *de*. Priscian says that *de* has several meanings and is not used for one Greek preposition alone, but for three, or perhaps more, saying:

> “*De* signifies not only τὸ ἀπό, ‘from,’ but also τὸ ἐπί in the commemorative sense, as in *de partibus orationis*, ‘concerning the parts of speech.’ It is also taken for κατὰ in local composition, as in *deduco*, ‘I lead down’; *descendo*, ‘I descend’; *detraho*, ‘I draw away’; *dejicio*, ‘I throw down’; *despicio*, ‘I look down upon’; *derideo*, ‘I mock.’ It is also intensive, as in *deprehendo*, ‘I seize’; *dedo*, ‘I surrender’; *depravo*, ‘I corrupt’; *deprimo*, ‘I press down’; *deminuo*, ‘I diminish’; *deisco*, ‘I gape open’; *deterreo*, ‘I frighten away’; *deligo*, ‘I bind’; *decurro*, ‘I run down.’ It is also privative, as in *desperatur*, ‘despair is entertained’; *demens*, ‘mad’; *desum*, ‘I am lacking’; *dejerat*, ‘he swears falsely.’”

Note that he said *despicio*, from which *despexeris* will follow. For *spicio* receives many prepositions in composition and none in independent use, because *spicio* is not in use by itself. We find *aspicio*, *respicio*, *suspicio*, *despicio*, *conspicio*, and *prospicio*. Both *despicio* and *dispicio* are found.

For this reason I said above that one must consider which preposition had been placed in the Greek, and from this recognize which should be written in Latin, because such a doubt can be resolved by considering the preceding language. For the Greek verse reads:

> “Hear, O God, my prayer, and do not despise my supplication”:  
> Ἐνώτισαι, ὁ Θεὸς, τὴν προσευχήν μου, καὶ μὴ ὑπερίδης τὴν δέησίν μου  
> (“Give ear, O God, to my prayer, and do not overlook my supplication”) (Psalm 54:2).

Likewise, in Psalm 21, the verse “My God, you are from my mother’s womb” has in Greek:

> Ἀπὸ γαστρὸς [Ἐκ κοιλίας] μητρός μου Θεός μου εἶ σύ  
> (“From the womb [from the belly] of my mother, you are my God”).

Where we say *de*, “from,” *ἀπό* is read.

Likewise, where we have “He will descend like rain upon a fleece” (Psalm 71:6), Greek has:

> καταβήσεται ὡς ὑετὸς ἐπὶ πόκον  
> (“He will descend like rain upon a fleece”), with *ἐπί* above, as in the verse from which this inquiry arose.

For blessed Jerome too, in his *Treatise on the Epistle to Titus*, said without doubt that these prepositions, namely *περί* and *κατά*, pertain to contempt. He likewise makes *contemnit* and *despexit* equivalent. Yet contempt can be good or bad: good when someone despises and scorns torments or reproaches for Christ’s name.

He teaches that these distinctions lie only in the prepositions by these words, where the Greek reads, in the Epistle to Titus, περιφρονείτω, and in the passage addressed to Timothy, καταφρονείτω. He asserts that the Apostle Paul uses different prepositions according to the variety of circumstances. Thus he wrote to Titus:

> “Let no one despise you” (Titus 2:15).

And to Timothy:

> “Let no one despise your youth” (1 Timothy 4:12).

In both passages, because of the Greek prepositions *περί* and *κατά*, he renders the sense with *despicit*. He confirms the same point by the example of the Stoics, who distinguish words with great subtlety.

*De* also has other meanings in Greek, as in:

> “The Lord looked down from heaven” (Psalm 32:13),

which in Greek reads:

> ἐξ οὐρανοῦ ἐπέβλεψε Κύριος [ἐπέλεβψεν, ὁ Κύριος]  
> (“From heaven the Lord looked down [the Lord looked down]).”

Here *ἐξ*, “from,” is used for *de*.

Likewise, where we say:

> “He does not fail from her streets” (Psalm 54:12),

Greek reads:

> Οὐκ ἐξέλιπεν ἐκ τῶν πλατειῶν αὐτῆς;  
> (“It does not depart from her streets.”).

Here too *ἐκ*, “from,” is used for *de*.

According to Priscian, *di* and *dis* have the same meaning as *ab* and *abs*. They are separative, as in *divido*, “I divide”; *diruo*, “I tear apart”; *distraho*, “I draw apart”; *discurro*, “I run in different directions.” Among the Greeks, the preposition διά performs this function.

> **Editor’s note:** See below, volume 2, the book *On Orthography*, under the words *de* and *dis*. In addition to these matters, it should be noted that the Greek text is presented here from the edition of the distinguished Quercetanus, while in the margin we have added the reading of the Septuagint interpreters from Walton’s edition in the *Polyglots*.

For where we say:

> “Let us break their bonds” (Psalm 2:3),

Greek has:

> Διαῤῥήξομεν τοὺς δεσμοὺς αὐτοῦ [αὐτῶν]  
> (“Let us tear apart his [their] bonds”).

Likewise, where we have:

> “Lord, divide them from the few, from the earth” (Psalm 16:14),

Greek reads:

> Κύριε, ἀπὸ ὀλίγων ἀπὸ γῆς [ἀπολύων ἀπὸ γῆς] διαμέρισον αὐτούς  
> (“Lord, divide them from the few, from the earth [releasing them from the earth]”).

Having considered these matters, see, either from knowledge of the preceding language or from the sequence of the constructed sentence, which preposition ought rather to be placed in that verse. These two things are especially accustomed to resolve doubt, lead the reader to a certain meaning, and bring contentious scholastic questions to an end.

For this reason I set out the opinions of the ancient authorities concerning *rubus* and the authority of the Greek language concerning the prepositions, lest anyone attack my opinion with accusations or criticize it as presumptuous if it were supported by no examples from the ancient teachers. For truth is often despised in an insignificant person, although nothing ought to be preferred to it, if only one awaited judgment in such questions and did not defend the presumption of one’s own opinion.

## LETTER XXVIII. TO HIS SON HOMER

> **To his dearest son Homer—**

> **Editor’s note:** Homer. There is no need to note here that Alcuin designates Angilbert by the name Homer; this has been discussed frequently elsewhere. (Froben, Letter 215.)

Albinus, matricularius, sends greetings to Homer.

Through God’s grace we are somewhat better; nevertheless, the chastisement of fevers does not leave us on successive days. Blessed is the one who receives labors in this age and will have rest in the future.

We also give thanks to your prudence for the admonition contained in your sweetest letter. We greatly desire and have kindly received the exhortations of your affection, because perfect charity does not cease to advise others of what it recognizes as best for itself. This is full and perfect love: that each person should wish prosperity not only for himself, but also, mindful of his brothers’ salvation, should not cease to admonish them, whether present in words or absent by letter.

To my son Antonius, your brother, I beg you to send these other letters as cautiously as possible, with the little sheet closed just as it is. If it arrives unsealed in his presence, it will become worthless in his eyes. Nevertheless, I would like you to look at it again when he sends it; but let faithfulness be preserved, so that it is first sent to the one to whom alone it is intended.

> **Editor’s note:** Antonius. To Adalhard, whom he urged in Letter 190 to consult Homer about what should be advised to Adalhard’s brother Bernarius, who had been summoned from Lérins to the palace. This may perhaps be the same letter which he wished to be faithfully transmitted here while sealed.

If you have Jordanes’ *History*, send it to me for information about certain matters.

> **Editor’s note:** Jordanes’ *History*. This is the history of Jordanes concerning the origin and deeds of the Getae or Goths, edited and provided with notes by the Benedictine Dom Giovanni Garet of the Congregation of Saint Maur, and so forth. It is considered more correct in volume 1 of the celebrated Muratori’s *History of Italy*, beginning on page 186.

You, dearest sons, strive to serve God in all charity and holiness, remembering all the good things he has done for you in this age, but especially on account of the hope of future glory and the rest of eternal blessedness. For innumerable are the gifts of his mercy toward us sinners. Therefore let us love him in the manner in which Truth itself says:

> “If anyone loves me, he will keep my words; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

What is more blessed than to have the Father and the Son, together with the Holy Spirit, dwelling within us, and to be defended from every adversity by his visitation, whose vision will make all the saints rejoice in the everlasting age?

May divine grace guard you everywhere, dearest son!

> **Editor:** Quercet. 63; Canisius. 59; Froben. 24.

## LETTER XXIX. TO PAULINUS, THE PATRIARCH  
*(796.)*

He commends himself to his constant remembrance and the bearer of the letter to his protection.

> To the venerable man Paulinus—

> **Editor’s note:** Paulinus. His life, deeds, and writings were excellently illuminated by the highly learned Dom Giovanni Francesco Madrisi of Udine, a priest of the Congregation of the Oratory, in a volume on the works of Saint Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, published at Venice in 1737 in folio.

> **Editor’s note:** We reprint this edition of the works of Saint Paulinus in volume 100 of this *Patrologia*.

Albinus sends greetings to Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia.

Having received the expressions of your wisdom and the gifts of your charity through this bearer of the present little letter, I rejoiced greatly, learning of your prosperity and of your remembrance of me. I humbly beg that you always retain me in your holy prayers with paternal devotion, ever mindful of the kindly devotion which Job had toward his sons. The health of a son is the father’s reward, and a wise son is the praise of his parent.

> **Editor’s note:** Through this bearer of the present little letter. The distinguished Madrisius thinks that this bearer was Ericus, duke. But so great a man would have deserved to be named by Alcuin here and not passed over without praise. I think that this man was of humbler condition, one whose needs Paulinus could assist.

May the present bearer of this letter, at our request, be commended to your help and protection. By the living service of his tongue he will show you either our needs or his own. A fuller account of our greeting—

> **Editor’s note:** Angilbert. Angilbert was going to Rome. The year is uncertain. Following Mabillon, Madrisius, and others, I have assigned the year 796 rather than another.

—our mutual son Angilbert, God willing, will deliver to you when he goes to Rome. But no little sheet is sufficient to express the sweetness of the charity which my soul had drawn with full mouth from your breast. The Spirit of truth is witness, through whom charity has been poured into our hearts (Romans 5:5).

Living happily, live happily, best of Fathers.

And, mindful always and everywhere of your son, farewell.

> **Editor:** Quercet. 95; Canisius. 62; Froben. 25.

## LETTER XXX. TO PAULINUS  
*(796?)*

He expresses his desire to converse with Paulinus, sends him three little notes, and recalls a gift sent by Liutgard.

Albinus sends greetings to the lord Father Paulinus.

From this it may be known how great my eagerness would be to speak with you, if the unjust distance between our lands did not prevent the opportunity for conversation: because of matters that arose, I placed three little notes together in the right hand of a single bearer. One concerned my anxiety, another my little gift, and the third the cause of my daughter Liutgard—

> **Editor’s note:** Liutgard. Perhaps the queen who married Charlemagne in 794 and died at Tours in 800. Concerning her, the distinguished Madrisius says in *Life of Saint Paulinus*, chapter 16, page 46: “She cultivated refined letters and pursued their teachers with royal favor.” This is evident from this and other letters of Alcuin.

—a religious woman devoted to God. For she sent your holiness two bracelets of refined gold, weighing twenty-four denarii less than the new coinage of the king, which would make a full pound, so that you might pray for her with your priests, asking that divine clemency might order her days toward the salvation of her soul and the exaltation of his holy Church. I, confident in your faith, urged her to do this.

But you, holy Father, mindful everywhere of me and of her, fare well in the charity of Christ.

> **Editor:** Quercet. 65; Canisius. 49; Froben. 26.

## LETTER XXXI. TO BISHOP AGINUS  
*(796.)*

He asks that relics of the saints, formerly promised, be sent to him through Angilbert.

Albinus, the teacher, sends greetings to his dearest Bishop Aginus.

> **Editor’s note:** Aginus. “I suspect,” says Canisius, “that this letter was written to the bishop of Agen, and that one should read *Agini episcopo*—‘to the bishop of Agen,’ which was the chief city of the Nitiobriges, concerning whom Ptolemy writes in book 2, chapter 7.” Mabillon and Pagi, however, maintain that he was the bishop of Bergamo, to whom Angilbert turned aside on his journey to Pope Leo III in the year 796. There was also a certain Aeginus, bishop of Verona, whom Cointius numbers among the suffragans of the Church of Aquileia under the year 795, no. 25.

May your charity remember that in our recent conversation you promised to send me some relics of the saints, so that God might be honored in them, our life protected with them, and your reward increased on their account.

Behold, a faithful bearer is here, namely my son Angilbert [Al.: Engilpertus], through whose hand you will be able to send whatever your friend may arrange to send us [possibly: “whatever our friend may arrange to send us”]. I beg you faithfully to complete what you cheerfully promised. For if your goodness does anything in response to this religious request, our humility will receive it with the greatest gratitude and will not cease, according to the opportunity of the time and our recognition of your will, to repay you.

And wherever the patronage of the saints is carried, prayers are offered there every day for you.

May divine blessing accompany you everywhere, most holy Father.

> **Editor:** Quercet. 75; Canisius. 40; Froben. 27.

## LETTER XXXII. TO ITHERIUS  
*(796.)*

He consoles a sick man and, as a friend, urges him to prepare himself for eternity.

Albinus sends greetings to his dearest Father Itherius.

> **Editor’s note:** Itherius. Abbot of the monastery of Tours, whom Alcuin consoles and kindles by this letter in his final struggle. He died in 796, the year in which Alcuin succeeded him in the administration of the same monastery. Mabillon, *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, fourth century, part 1, page 171.

Let us give thanks to God Jesus, who wounds and heals, scourges and consoles. Bodily pain is the salvation of the soul, and temporal weakness, everlasting health. Let us willingly accept and patiently endure the will of our Savior. But now do not delay. Do what you are going to do. Run while you have the light (John 12:35). Hasten to him who calls you. Let the will anticipate what necessity compels. Be a wise scribe, a faithful merchant. Sell earthly things; buy heavenly ones. Why wait for the uncertainty of tomorrow? Let there be no delay in the salvation of the soul. What is conceived in the mind should be accomplished in action. What weakness desired, let health carry through. He who knows all things is witness of my heart that I urge you to this with complete charity and faithful counsel. I know that after you I shall not have such a friend in your place. But I would rather have you as a friend remaining permanently in honor than perishing, and rejoice in you as an intercessor with God rather than as a benefactor in this world. Let us ask God for help, so that he may confirm the counsel of his friends, show his own the way of salvation, and direct into the path of peace those whom he redeemed with his own blood. Behold the price at which we were bought! Let us not love those things that separate us from him who loved us even unto the death of his flesh. We have served the world long enough: let us live for our God through the few days that remain, so that we may be made worthy to see the face of him who said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). Read joyfully, and begin steadfastly; complete it successfully, and may the Lord be with you forever.

> [Col. 0187D] Edited by Quercet. 7; corrected in several places from the manuscript of Salzburg, which bears this title: *Dictated by Albinus the teacher*. It is immediately preceded there by a work of the same subject, *Dictated by Paulinus the patriarch*, which you will find published among the Councils of D. Mansi, volume XIII, p. 921.

## LETTER XXXIII. TO THE LORD KING (Year 796)

He congratulates him on the subjection of the Huns, explains how they should be instructed in the faith, and shows what order is to be followed.

To the most excellent lord and most devoted in every honor of Christ, Charles, king of Germany, Gaul, and Italy, and to the holy preachers of the word, Albinus, the humble little son of holy Mother Church, sends greetings of eternal glory in Christ.

Glory and praise to God the Father and to our Lord Jesus Christ, because, through the grace of the Holy Spirit and through the devotion and ministry of holy faith and good will, he has extended the kingdom and recognition of the true God belonging to your Christianity, and has led very many peoples far and wide from the errors of impiety into the way of truth. What glory will be yours, O most blessed king, on the day of eternal recompense, when all those who through your good solicitude have been converted from the worship of idols to the knowledge of the true God will follow you, standing in blessedness before the tribunal of our Lord Jesus Christ? And from all these the reward of everlasting blessedness is increased.

Behold with what devotion and kindness, for the extension of Christ’s name, you have labored to soften the obduracy of the unhappy Saxon people through the counsel of true salvation. But because divine election does not yet appear to have been present among them, many of them remain to this day, destined to be condemned with the devil in the filth of their most wicked custom. Nevertheless, it has pleased Christ to reward your excellent will, O lover of truth and of the salvation of many, with greater glory and praise. He has subjected to your scepters peoples and nations of the Huns, fearsome for their ancient ferocity and strength, serving under your authority [or: “for their honor”]. And, with grace going before, he has bound their long-exceedingly proud necks to the yoke of the sacred faith and poured the light of truth into minds blind from ancient times.

> [Col. 0188D] “But now.” That is, after “God subjected the peoples of the Huns to Charles’s scepters and poured the light of truth into blind minds”—namely, in the year 796. This letter, therefore, was written in that same year; there is no reason, with Pagi and Cointius, to postpone it until 798. See also below Letter 31 [now 36] to Arno.

But now let your most wise and God-pleasing devotion provide for the new people pious preachers, honorable in conduct, instructed in knowledge of the sacred faith, and imbued with the evangelical commandments. Let them also be attentive to the preaching and examples of the holy apostles, who customarily served milk—that is, gentle commandments—to their hearers at the beginning of the faith, as the Apostle Paul says: “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as little children in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food. For you were not yet able, and even now you are not able” (1 Corinthians 3:1–2).

By this the preacher of the whole world, with Christ speaking through him, signified that a new conversion of peoples to the faith should be nourished with gentler commandments, like an infant age with milk, lest the fragile mind, through more severe commandments, vomit up what it has drunk. Hence the Lord Christ himself, when those questioning him asked why his disciples did not fast, replied: “No one puts new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wineskins burst, the wine is spilled, and the wineskins perish” (Matthew 9:17). For, as blessed Jerome says, one thing is the purity of a virginal soul unpolluted by any contagion of former vice, and another is that which has been subject to filth and to the lust of many.

With these matters thus considered, let your most holy piety wisely determine whether it is better at the beginning of the faith to impose upon unformed peoples the obligation of tithes, so that their full collection may be exacted from every household; or whether one should consider whether the apostles, taught by God Christ himself and sent to preach to the world, exacted tithes or commanded them to be given anywhere.

> [Col. 0189D] See Letter 37 [now 42], to Megenfred.

We know that tithing our possessions is very good. But it is better to lose it than to lose the faith. We, born, nourished, and instructed in the Catholic faith, scarcely consent to tithe our possessions in full. How much less will a tender faith, an infant mind, and a covetous heart consent to such generosity? But once the faith has been strengthened and the custom of Christianity established, then, as to mature men, stronger commandments should be given—commandments that a mind solidified in Christian religion will not reject.

This too must be considered with the greatest care: that the office of preaching and the sacrament of baptism be carried out in due order. Otherwise the sacred washing of baptism in the body will be of no benefit if recognition of the Catholic faith has not preceded it in the rational soul [the Salzburg manuscript reads *intenti*, incorrectly; “attentive”]. The Apostle says: “Let all your things be done honorably and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40). And the Lord himself, commanding his disciples in the Gospel, says: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

Blessed Jerome, in his commentary which he wrote on the Gospel of Saint Matthew, explained the order of this command as follows: “First let them teach all nations; then, once taught, let them immerse them in water. For it cannot happen that the body receives the sacrament of baptism unless the soul has first received the truth of faith. They are baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that, since their divinity is one, the gift may be one, and the name of the Trinity is one God. Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (ibid., verse 20).

A most important order. He commanded [the apostles] first to teach all nations, then to immerse them in the sacrament of faith, and after faith and baptism to command what was to be observed. And lest we think the things commanded were trivial, he added shortly afterward: “All things whatsoever I have commanded you.” Thus those who have believed and have been baptized in the Trinity are to do everything that has been commanded.

Therefore infants who do not yet use reason, being liable to the sins of others, can be saved through the sacrament of baptism by the faith and confession of others, provided that, when the appropriate age arrives, they preserve the integrity of the faith confessed on their behalf [the Salzburg manuscript reads “preserve” rather than “will preserve”]. The Apostle says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10). That confession of the mouth benefits salvation which is firmly held by belief of the heart.

The order, therefore, which, as I think, must diligently be observed in teaching a man mature in age is the one that blessed Augustine set out in the book whose title is *On Instructing Beginners*. First, a person must be instructed concerning the immortality of the soul, future life, the recompense of good and evil, and the eternity of both destinies. Next, he must be instructed concerning the sins and crimes for which he will suffer eternal punishments with the devil, and the good deeds and benefactions for which he will enjoy everlasting glory with Christ.

Then the faith of the holy Trinity must be taught with the greatest care, and the coming into this world of the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, for the salvation of the human race must be explained. The mystery of his passion, the truth of his resurrection, the glory of his ascension into heaven, and his future coming to judge all nations must also be explained; likewise the resurrection of our bodies and, as we have said above, the eternity of punishments for the wicked and rewards for the good. The new mind must be strengthened in these matters.

Strengthened and prepared by this faith, a person is to be baptized. At the appropriate time, evangelical commandments are then to be given repeatedly through diligent preaching, until he grows into a perfect man [“perfect” supplied by the editor], becomes a worthy dwelling for the Holy Spirit, and is a perfect son of God in works of mercy, just as our heavenly Father is perfect—he who lives and reigns in perfect Trinity and blessed unity, God and Lord throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

> [Col. 0189D] Edited by Mabillon, 2; Pez, 2; corrected and supplemented from two Salzburg manuscript codices. I infer that it was written in 796 from the death of Eanbald, bishop of York, which occurred in that year and is mentioned in the following letter, written after this one. Arno was therefore in Rome that year, perhaps discussing with the supreme pontiff the care of the newly converted people of the Avars, entrusted to him by Pippin.

## LETTER XXXIV. TO ARNO (Year 796)

He longs for his return and wishes to be informed about various events. He states that he will go to the Palace in July. He urges him to beware of the error of the Spaniards.

To the venerable winged creature and truly most beloved Eagle, Albinus sends greetings.

I eagerly await the joyful news of how the Eagle, flying high, crosses the Alpine ridges and, wearied by flight, folds his wings in the regions of Rhaetia [the Salzburg manuscript reads “Recia”], or what news he may bring me

> [Col. 0189D] **Concerning the regions of Saint Paul.** Thus the Salzburg manuscript reads; the word *Paul* or *Paulus* is omitted in the Codex Benedictoburanus used by Pez. It should doubtless be read: “concerning the regions of Saint Paul”—namely, the monastery of Cormaric, whose approval from the Apostolic See he also shows himself concerned to obtain in other letters.

concerning the regions of Saint [Paul] and the counsels of the Romans, and whether, if it can be done—which we greatly desire—it may come to pass by God’s grant. Therefore I beseech all winged powers descending from the heavenly seat to make my Eagle come quickly to us, safe and prosperous in every way. We, meanwhile, hasten like a summer swallow to the Palace in July [Mabillon: “desire to hasten to the Palatine regions”]. I do not know what will happen on our journey [whether

> [Col. 0190D] **To the banks of the Meuse.** Perhaps in the monastery of Saint Servatius at Maastricht on the Meuse, which he mentions again in Letter 87 [now 103].

we shall be allowed to catch fish like little divers at the banks of the Meuse; or whether

> [Col. 0190D] **The Loire River.** The *Liger*, the Loire, at the monastery of Tours, to which Alcuin invites Arno in Letter 87 [now 103] in these words: “Would that the Eagle had flown … as far as the fishing of the Loire River.”

we shall return to the Loire and there gather salmon by swimming]. Nevertheless, I hope to remain in these regions until [the month of August], if this pleases our God and the lord king, and there await whatever I am to hear concerning the Eagle’s desired arrival. And while you read through this little letter, quickly send another in return, so that I may know what the Eagle is going to do with his little birds, or what he may do, believe, or what the nobility of the Romans may have that is new

> [Col. 0191C] **Avaria.** Pez incorrectly reads *avaritia*, “greed.” Misled by this, the distinguished P. Hansizius, volume II of *Germania Sacra*, p. 105, interprets the passage as referring to “the Simoniacal heresy, concerning whose overthrow he had written to Engelbert, his legate in the city, so that he might urge it most diligently upon the pontiff.” *Avaria* [is the correct reading].

concerning the arrival

> [Col. 0191D] **Arrival.** “At that time,” says Hansizius in the cited passage, “an ambassador to Charles, in the name of the emperor of the Greeks, Thectistus, sent by Nicetas, governor of Sicily, was arriving”—namely, in the year 797. But I do not see how this embassy relates to the Roman nobility. I would rather interpret the passage as referring to the arrival of the Roman nobility, which had been chosen to convey, together with the keys of Saint Peter, the banner of the city of Rome to Charles in 796.

or what you may have heard concerning the heights of Greece

> [Col. 0191D] **Concerning the heights of Greece.** “The empress Irene,” Hansizius again says, “most recently deposed her son Constantine, having his eyes gouged out on June 15.” But while Alcuin was writing this letter, he could scarcely have known of that upheaval in the Greek empire. The deposition and blinding of the emperor occurred on June 15; but Alcuin evidently wrote this letter around the same time or much earlier, as is shown by the words: “We hasten to the Palace in July”—that is, in the future. I think it more likely that Alcuin wished to be informed about the scandal arising from Constantine’s repudiation of his lawful wife and the persecution stirred up against the holy men who condemned that marriage in 795. See Pagi under that year.

and whether you had brought any relics of the saints with you, by which you could console your Albinus. Things are prosperous for us, God granting it, except that fever and weakness keep me exhausted. Yet “the weaker” will be “the stronger,” according to the Apostle (1 Corinthians 1:25); and bodily weakness often benefits us, so that the strength of faith may grow in the soul.

[Even now all Spain is wandering in Adoptionism.]

Pray for us, that the Holy Spirit the Paraclete may inspire the souls of his servants to defend the truth of the Catholic faith, because the time has come, as we read that it was foretold in the holy books. But you, together with your companions, always follow sound doctrine and diligently preach the Catholic faith, so that you may be worthy to possess an eternal reward with abundant fruit. Live happily and rejoice in the love of Christ with all your companions, dearest Eagle.

> [Col. 0192C] We have transcribed this letter, hitherto unpublished, from the Salzburg manuscript. It was written after the preceding letter: in that one he asks what had happened in Avaria; in this one he receives the answer.

## LETTER XXXV. TO [—] (ARNO) (Year 796)

He tells the same man that he has received his letter. He commends the soul of Archanbald [Eanbald] to his prayers. He sends a letter to the king, written concerning preaching among the pagans.

To the pious Father, faithful brother, and dearest son, greetings.

We have received your letter of charity. You sent me great “eulogies,” when I learned, venerable Father, of your health and prosperity, which pleases me more than a thousand talents of gold and silver. You have also freed me from great anxieties, because you informed me what had happened in Avaria. As for your sons, whom you commended to me, they are already making progress, God granting it, and you will receive them as better men, or commend them to the lord king. Whatever the lord king entrusts to you to do, strive to entrust to me. Since my soul is wearied by your absence, I ask you to intercede carefully for the soul

> [Col. 0192D] **Of Archbishop Archanbald.** I understand this as referring to Eanbald, archbishop of York, who was Alcuin’s fellow student, as the anonymous poet—or rather Alcuin himself, in the poem concerning the bishops of York—testifies. We shall include that poem among his other poems. Eanbald died on the fourth day before the Kalends of August [July 29] in 796, according to Hoveden.

of Archbishop Archanbald, who was both father and brother to me, and a most faithful friend, as well as my fellow student under my teacher. Behold, I alone remain from that school, and I shall not be alone as long as I have you, faithful and friendly men.

As for your request that I write something concerning preaching to the pagans, because of the shortness of time and the bearer’s haste I have not found anything to dictate on that subject. Nevertheless, taking counsel with your fatherhood,

> [Col. 0192D] **I sent you a letter.** Certainly the one given shortly above as number 28 [now 33].

I sent you a letter which a few days ago I directed to the lord king on this same matter. At a suitable time

> [Col. 0192D] **I shall write more fully.** He fulfilled this promise in the following letter, number 31 [now 36].

I shall write more fully on all these matters to your venerable affection.

“Woe to the world because of scandals!” (Matthew 18:7). For what good thing does the insane desire for gold not overturn? Yet God is powerful to recover what has been begun and to complete what has not been accomplished. Let his mercy be entreated to help his servants in the pious labor of preaching, so that praise may be given to his name forever. Keep this little letter with you, reading and pondering it, until you receive a fuller method of catechizing.

Even if for now [the manuscript reads *sic novo*, uncertain] you may not be permitted to speak with me until I come to the lord king (I hope to remain all summer in those regions), we shall be able to meet

> [Col. 0192D] **In Alsace.** That is, in Elisatio—l’Alsace—where it is clear from this that Alcuin had some possessions or perhaps a monastery. You may join *in Alsace* with the preceding words: “if it is permitted for you to remain in Bavaria,” because we have some property in Alsace.

in Alsace, if you are permitted to remain in Bavaria, because we have certain possessions in Alsace. Therefore your messenger has told me all this, but let letters speak more fully, because the memory of country people is fragile. Farewell in peace.

> [Col. 0192D] Edited by Quercet. 104, from a manuscript (Froben, 31). Now corrected in several places from the Salzburg manuscript. This is the fuller instruction concerning the preaching of the faith among the Avars newly converted to the faith, which he had promised in the preceding letter. It was given in the same year, unless I am mistaken, although the distinguished Hansizius assigns it to the following year, namely 797. See also above Letter 28 [now 33], to Charles.

## LETTER XXXVI. TO ARNO (Year 796)

He instructs him concerning the preaching of the faith among the Avars recently converted.

To the sweetest brother and most holy bishop, the Eagle, Albinus sends greetings.

Your parents gave you a prophetic name, although they were ignorant of God’s dispensation, before whom all future things are already accomplished. He who, in supreme piety, ordained you to minister heavenly mysteries to the peoples has, from the height of heavenly grace, given you the keenest sight of spiritual eyes, so that you may draw fish wandering on the sea of this world out of its salt waters for giving life, not death; wash them in the sacred bath of the glass-like font; and make them stand ready for the banquets of the eternal King in the fire of the Holy Spirit. Thus you may become a true hearer of the apostolic calling, as Christ said when, amid the stormy waves, he saw the brotherly partnership of two brothers laboring: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4:19).

He did not restrain them from the duty of their former craft, but commanded that, casting their nets on the right, they should bring better fish to the shore of the most steadfast solidity. Strive with the full intention of your mind to pursue these fish, most effective laborer of the divine work, so that Christ himself may deign through you to preach to the peoples from the keel of your ship [*carinae*, sense uncertain] and may be the merciful helmsman of the little boat from which he commanded you to spread the nets of apostolic preaching into the sea of the deepest gentility. Then, through the mercy of his great piety, you may hear him commanding you and your companions: “Bring here some of the fish that you have just caught” (John 21:10).

Be obedient to his will, according to the name of Simon, who dragged to the Lord’s banquet a net full of 153 great fish (John 21:11). If you wish to know who these fish are in this specified number, they are those who, from the Decalogue of God’s commandments or from the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, have been chosen after the final resurrection for the everlasting banquet with Christ.

Therefore the net of that fishing, unlike the earlier catch, is not said to have been torn, because there no guest is invited except one who has been chosen and ordained for everlasting peace. Accordingly, if you count the individual numbers from one up to seventeen by successive additions, always adding the later numbers to the earlier ones, the total of the calculation rises to 153. And if you divide these seventeen into two—namely, ten and seven—the ten signifies the legal commandments, and the seven signifies the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Again, if you divide seven into two parts, namely three and four: the three signifies faith in the holy Trinity, in which faith all nations are to be saved; and the four signifies the four regions of the whole world into which that faith has been spread. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ commanded his disciples, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:19).

In these very few words he set out the order of the whole sacred preaching. He said “teach” twice and “baptize” once. First of all he commanded that the Catholic faith be taught, and after the faith had been received he ordered baptism in the name of the holy Trinity. Then he commanded that the person imbued with faith and cleansed by holy baptism be instructed in the evangelical commandments.

Hold firmly everywhere to this order of catechizing adults, most holy teacher. But to the more fragile age holy Mother Church has granted that one who is bound by another’s sin, through the paternal transgression, may be freed through another’s profession in the mystery of baptism. And if this were not so, how many infants would perish, from whose number heavenly Jerusalem is built daily? What benefit is baptism without faith, since the Apostle says: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11:6)?

We read that the difference between the impossible and the difficult is this: what is difficult can be done, though barely; what is impossible cannot be done at all by human frailty. Therefore the Lord himself, when the apostles were astonished and asked who among the rich could be saved, replied in the Gospel: “With human beings this is impossible, but with God all things are possible” (Matthew 19:26). For this reason the wretched [Saxon] nation so often lost the sacrament of baptism: it never had the foundation of faith in its heart [the printed edition reads “the sacrament of faith,” but “foundation” is required by the context].

But this also must be understood: faith, as Saint Augustine says, arises from the will, not from necessity. How can a person be compelled to believe what he does not believe? A person can be driven to baptism, but not to faith. So it is with those heretics who affirm the adoption of the flesh in Christ: they cannot in any way be converted to the Catholic faith, because they have no desire to recognize the profession of orthodox faith together with the universal Church.

A person who possesses rational understanding must therefore be taught and drawn by preaching of many kinds, so that he may recognize the truth of the sacred faith. Above all, the mercy of almighty God must be entreated for him, because the tongue of the teacher labors in vain if divine grace does not steep the hearer’s heart. The Truth himself says: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). And so that you may understand that the holy Trinity works the salvation of humanity equally, the Lord himself also says elsewhere: “No one can come to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). Likewise he says concerning the Holy Spirit: “Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). What the priest visibly effects in the body through water in baptism, the Holy Spirit invisibly effects in the soul through faith.

There are three visible and three invisible things in the sacrament of baptism. The visible are the priest, the body, and the water. The invisible are the spirit, the soul, and faith. Those three visible things accomplish nothing outwardly if these three invisible things do not work inwardly. The priest washes the body with water; the Holy Spirit justifies the soul through faith. This is what the Apostle says: “For we are God’s fellow workers” (1 Corinthians 3:9; the source cites “III John 1:8”). A human being cooperates with the Holy Spirit in the salvation of a person. But the person who is to be baptized must also cooperate with both in his own salvation—that is, with the Holy Spirit and the priest—humbly presenting his body for the sacred mystery of washing and voluntarily presenting his soul for reception of the Catholic faith.

All these matters must be carefully considered by the teacher at the beginning of the faith and in the sacrament of baptism, for the salvation of the recipient; and the mystery of so great a sacrament must not be carried out negligently.

This too must be weighed with the greatest care: how the newly planted growth should be cultivated, so that the first flowers of faith may reach the increase of fruits, lest they wither in the frost of any kind of harshness and fail to grow toward the sweetness of the desired fruit. An infant age must be nourished with the sweetness of its mother’s milk, and an unformed soul must be fed with the gentler commandments of divine sweetness. Solid food is for strong men, and higher commandments belong to those whose senses have been trained in the law of God.

Thus the Apostle, writing to certain brothers of more fragile understanding, says: “I gave you milk for food, not solid food [another reading: ‘milk to drink, not food’], because you were unable to receive it; indeed, even now you are unable, because you are carnal. For the carnal person does not perceive the things that are of God; the spiritual person judges all things” (1 Corinthians 3:2)—that is, discerns and judges them.

Hence the Truth himself, in the Gospel, when certain people criticized why the apostles did not fast as the Pharisees and the disciples of John did, replied: “No one puts new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wineskins burst, the wine is spilled, and the wineskins perish” (Matthew 9:17). Who are the old wineskins except those who have hardened in the errors of paganism? If you give them the commandments of the new preaching in a more severe form at the beginning of the faith, they burst and return to their former customs of unbelief.

A mind strengthened for a long time in consecration to the sacred faith is therefore more steadfast for every work than one initiated by a new preaching. Saint Peter acted one way after he had been filled with the new wine of the Holy Spirit, when he answered Nero in the Roman Palace on behalf of the Christian faith, and another way in the house of Caiaphas, when he answered a servant girl concerning his discipleship to Christ. Here he was more timid; there, more steadfast. The former was an example of weakness; the latter, of courage.

After the resurrection, Christ, in his merciful regard, restored him to the primacy of his former dignity through a threefold profession of love and entrusted to him the sheep whom he had redeemed with his own blood to be fed (John 21). Thus the good shepherd might understand that those who offend should not always be corrected with harsh denunciation, but often with the admonition of merciful consolation.

For our Lord Jesus Christ himself, when the Jews tested him concerning the adulterous woman, did not immediately pronounce the severity of the legal sentence. Instead, bending down in an example of humility, he wrote on the ground (John 8), signifying that a teacher should first depict the sins of his own weakness in the dust of his heart and thus judge the sins of others more gently.

If this rule of consideration must be carefully applied in every age and calling, how much more must it be observed with great moderation of piety in those who have recently been converted from the error of ingrained custom to the Christian faith? Likewise, those who had received the sacraments of the Christian faith from infancy but were later deceived by the devil’s fraud and, through long habit, followed carnal lusts—or who were bound by any other chains of sin—should first be consoled with gentler verbal encouragement, lest, terrified by harsher corrections, they recoil from the remedies of repentance.

There are certain illnesses that are better treated with sweeter medicines than bitter ones, and certain others that are better treated with bitter medicines than sweet ones [the bracketed words are supplied by the editor]. Therefore the teacher of God’s people, although he must shine in the house of God with every lamp of virtue, must especially possess the understanding of the keenest discernment, so that he may know what is suitable for each person, sex, age, calling, and even time.

Blessed Gregory, the most illustrious teacher, diligently investigated all these matters in his book *Pastoral Care*, distinguished them according to persons, confirmed them with examples, and strengthened them by the authority of divine Scripture. To the reading of that book I refer you, most holy bishop, asking you to keep it often in your hands like a handbook and retain it in your heart.

And because I know that you, most blessed Father, possess, read, and firmly retain in memory very many books of the holy teachers, and recognize especially your diligence in the divine writings, it seems superfluous for me to occupy the ears of your wisdom with the little letters of my ignorance. Only the cause of charity can justly, as I think, excuse my presumption before the eyes of your authority, lest the affection that burns within the heart appear mute outwardly in words.

For this purpose words seem to have been given to human beings: that they might pour the secrets of the heart into the ears of their brothers. For this purpose letters are written: that where the sound of words cannot reach, the service of written characters may run, so that signs of mutual charity may be displayed in written lines to the eyes of brothers; thus there may be presence of souls in charity where, because of the distance of places, there is absence of bodies.

O happy and blessed life, where what is always loved is seen, and what is seen never becomes wearisome! Where God is eternal love, eternal praise, glory, and blessedness for all. Draw me, your intimate friend, with you toward this life and happiness through continual prayers and exhortations, so that, after the stormy tempests of this life, I may deserve, through Christ’s mercy, to reach with you the harbor of everlasting rest.

May God, Jesus, cause your holiness to flourish in every good thing and to advance toward everlasting happiness, most longed-for brother in Christ.

> [Col. 0195D] Edited by Quercet. 90, from a manuscript (Froben, 31).

## LETTER XXXVII. TO THE LORD KING (Year 796)

He prays for captives in the Hunnic war and for enemies.

My most beloved, sweetest, and most longed-for David! Your Flaccus is sad because of your illness. I desire and entreat God with all my heart that you may quickly recover, so that our joy may be complete in you and your health be whole in soul and body.

My lord, may your piety remember the captives,

> [Col. 0197D] **While your Pippin is with you.** Undoubtedly at Aachen, to which he came after the Hunnic expedition in 796, as the Frankish annals relate. Charles granted Alcuin’s request concerning the redemption of the captives, as is evident from the beginning of the following letter to Pippin.

while your Pippin is with you, in thanksgiving for the wondrous benefit that divine mercy accomplished with you concerning the Huns

> [Col. 0197D] **Concerning the Huns.** Whom Pippin subdued in this year, 796, as the annals of that time testify.

and for the prosperity of the events that lie ahead, so that his most merciful power may quickly subject all adversaries of his holy name to your feet. And, if it can be done and seems fitting to your prudence, may some indulgence and remission also be granted to those who have sinned against you. Nevertheless, because their circumstances are unknown to me, I speak more cautiously about these matters. You yourselves know best what is useful for the kingdom given to you by God and beneficial to the peace of God’s holy Church.

In all things, by doing what you do, do the will of God, so that his most holy grace may protect, govern, and guard you everywhere as you advance, my lord, sweetest and most longed-for.

> [Col. 0197D] Edited by Quercet. 91, from a manuscript (Froben, 33). Given in 796, after Pippin returned from the Hunnic expedition to Aachen, to Charles, his father. See the preceding letter.

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO PIPPIN (Year 796)

He offers excellent instructions for the conduct of life.

To the most noble and most beloved son,

> [Col. 0198D] **Pippin.** Pippin, formerly called Carloman, son of Charlemagne and Hildegard. See more about him in Pagi, from the year 776 through 810, the year of his death.

To Pippin, Albinus sends greetings in the love of Christ.

We give thanks for your benevolence, as well as for the piety of the lord king, who piously consents to the request for the redemption of captives. I know that by such works of mercy you earn blessing and attain the long prosperity of your kingdom. And you, most excellent young man, strive to adorn the nobility of your birth with nobility of character; contend with all your strength to fulfill the will and honor of almighty God, so that his immeasurable mercy may exalt the throne of your kingdom, enlarge its borders, and subject nations to your power. Be generous toward the wretched, compassionate toward strangers, devoted in the service of Christ, treating those servants [F.: “to those”] and churches honorably, so that their diligent prayer may assist you. Be upright in conduct and chaste in body. Rejoice

[Col. 0198D] With a wife, etc. Which wife? None is identified anywhere. with the wife of your youth, and let no strangers share in her, so that the blessing given you by God may extend into the long succession of your grandchildren. Be strong against adversaries, faithful to friends, humble toward Christians, terrifying to pagans, approachable to the wretched, prudent in counsel. Make use of the counsel of the old and the service of the young. Let judgments of equity prevail in your kingdom, [Col. 0197D] and let the praise of God resound everywhere at the proper hours, especially in the presence of your piety. For such devotion in ecclesiastical duties will make you beloved by God and honorable among men. Let thoughts of sobriety be in your heart, words of truth in your [Col. 0198A] mouth, and examples of uprightness in your conduct, so that divine clemency may everywhere exalt and protect you. I ask that this letter go with you as a testimony of my love. Even if it is not worthy to hang from the belt of your veneration, nevertheless may its admonition be worthy to be stored in the heart of your wisdom.

May you live, flourishing in God, joyful and rejoicing in salvation.

May the right hand of Christ protect and guide you. I ask you to commend the name of Albinus everywhere,

O son, to the servants of God throughout your realms.

[Col. 0198D] Edited by Quercetanus, p. 112; Canisius, p. 61 (Frobenius, p. 34). Corrected from the manuscripts of Salzburg and St. Emmeram.

## LETTER XXXIX. TO PAULINUS THE PATRIARCH

He wishes to know what Paulinus intends to do for the conversion of the people after the defeat of the Huns, and repeatedly asks that letters be sent to him.

[Col. 0198B] To the most beloved Father and pious pontiff, Paulinus the patriarch: Albinus, son of your affection, sends perpetual prosperity in Christ.

If I enjoyed the presence of your blessedness every day, I would nevertheless [Edit.: “then”] never be satisfied with the sweetness flowing like honey from your mouth; rather, however much my eager mind drank from the fountain of the life-giving stream, by that much [Cod. Sal.: “nevertheless”] would its thirst increase. But now such great distances divide us from the familiarity of personal conversation that scarcely a bearer of a little letter on his journey can be found. And in the narrow chamber of my breast the pot of charity boils, yet it has no one to whom it may display the brilliance of its splendor or set out its cooked banquets of charity; and, so to speak, an abundance of sweetness has been turned into the hunger of bitterness. The vine flourishes in its shoots, but the cultivator of this unfruitful vineyard does not [Edit., you do not] feed himself. The farmer draws pearls from the gravel [Edit., glory], but gold for the work of the crown is lacking. He who suffers such things with me [Edit.: “of the fathers”] knows what these images signify. Perhaps the reader of this letter remembers himself to be such as he recognizes me in these images; and especially you, holy Father, from whose heart the fountain of true charity flows [Edit., of life, charity flows], and from whose belly rivers of living water flow. And he who promised these things for the consolation (*consolationem*; Cod. Sal. and St. Emmeram: *consolatione*) of our hope dwells in your breast: he is the power and wisdom of God, in whose power and grace wondrously

[Col. 0198D] The people of the Avars have been conquered. In the year 796—as we have already noted several times from the Frankish Annals—the people of the Avars [Ed.: “race/stock of the Avars”] were defeated; their envoys were sent to the lord king, [Col. 0198D] promising peaceful submission and the faith of Christianity. And if this is true, with divine grace going before them, who ought to withdraw from so pious and praiseworthy a labor of the servants of God, so that the devil’s savagery may be destroyed and the service of Christ the Lord [Cod. Sal., of God] may increase?

[Col. 0199A] {46} But since the eyes of very many are fixed upon you, excellent Father, wondering what your revered holiness intends to do—for proximity of place suits you, the distinction of wisdom [is available to you], the excellence of authority belongs to you, and everything that seems necessary for such a work is united in you—therefore the curiosity of my littleness desires [to know] through you [Edit., “for that reason”] the truth of this holy undertaking and seeks the counsel of your prudence; indeed, it urgently asks to know what your good will has resolved to do about it. The work is difficult, but, as Truth itself attests, all things are possible for the one who believes (Mark 9:22). He who made a preacher from a persecutor (1 Tim. 1:13), and raises the poor from the dungheap so that he may sit with princes (Ps. 112:7), [Col. 0199B] can bring forth from the dry ground of my heart, cautiously, streams of a living fountain leaping up into eternal life. How much more can he pour forth from your overflowing breast streams like those of the Gihon, flowing [Cod. Sal., from your exceedingly abundant breast-stream, Gihon waters] across the whole breadth of the Nile’s fields, to make flowers of various kinds fruitful? I ask you to let the son of your charity, united with you in spirit, hear through you what paternal prudence foresees must be done. Thus the most certain counsel of salvation ought to be hoped for from the mouth of him in whose breast the sevenfold [Spirit] of counsel is known [to be] to dwell.

A little earlier I sent two short letters to your fatherhood, one through Saint

[Col. 0199D] Bishop of Istria. All the bishops of the province of Aquileia were formerly called bishops of Istria, as is clear from the Roman council under Agatho, where Ursinus of Ceneta, under the patriarch Agatho, and the other bishops of the Mediterranean sees are called bishops of Istria (Madrisius, Works of St. Paulinus, p. 205). Perhaps this bishop was Aginus of Pergamo, or rather the bishop of Verona, who was with Alcuin in this year, as may be inferred from Letter 26 to the same man (now 31). On Duke Aericus, see Letter 1. the bishop of Istria; [Col. 0199C] the other through the venerable man Duke Aericus.

[Col. 0199D] These words, corrupt in the printed edition, are restored from the manuscript. And may this third letter at least deserve some exhortation from your blessedness, lest, if charity is scorned, it begin to write a fourth [letter] with a wrinkled brow or a complaining pen.
