Do not remain silent any longer, to the increase of my sadness, but by the spirit of consolation given you by God, do not hesitate to send me frequent letters of the consolation of your kindness, so that, assisted by your good exhortations and holy prayers, I may deserve, with divine mercy helping, to share eternal life with you, for the increase of your everlasting reward.

[Col. 0199D] These verses are absent from the Salzburg and St. Emmeram manuscripts.

May wisdom (*sophia*), holy Father, flourish forever and ever in your breast,

with divine gifts.

And may the right hand of almighty Christ preserve me

safe and increase me in heavenly merits,

until the blessed gate of heaven receives you.

Remember me there—[F. supplies: I beg] always in your mouth.

[Col. 0199D] Edited by Quercetanus, p. 62; Canisius, p. 68 (Frobenius, p. 30). In the manuscript of St. Gall the heading is indeed lacking, [Col. 0200D] but from the context it is certain that the letter was sent to Paulinus of Aquileia. CANISIUS.

## LETTER XL. TO A CERTAIN PERSON (PAULINUS)

After Paulinus’s long silence, he expresses his joy at having now received letters. He then launches into praise of Paulinus and, mindful of his approaching death and his own sins, humbly commends himself to Paulinus’s prayers.

[Col. 0200D] While the burning sun of Cancer. From this the learned Madrisius infers that the letter was written after the middle of June. I draw that inference no more from this than from the words below, where he says: “Thus he knows . . . that I do not exaggerate in this letter’s bosom the leaves of words withering in the autumnal cold,” etc.; from these words one may infer that the letter was written in autumn. Without doubt the particle *sicut* (“as”) should be supplied at the beginning; nor is the time of writing expressed here, but rather the heat of the breast is expressed through comparison with burning Cancer. As the fiery sun of burning Cancer rises as a constellation, and the dry earth awaits rain under excessive and prolonged heat, so your will, O excellent Father, thirsty for the cooling of great love, had long desired letters from your blessedness in my breast. Again and again, at every moment of the hours, this burning declaration revolved in my mind: “When will the desired, sweetest letters of mine arrive? When shall I see the tokens of salvation from my beloved? When will a page of Ausonian nobility reveal to me the prosperity of my desired friend, so that I may see whether any memory of our friendship joined in Christ remains in his breast; whether he keeps the name of his Albinus, written by the pen of charity in the secret place of his heart, just as the most sweet name of Father Paulinus, inscribed in eternal letters, lives by perpetual affection in the heart of his son?”

[Col. 0200D] Behold, it has come, etc. Namely, the reply that had been desired, which Alcuin finally extracted from him after sending three letters. See the preceding letter near the end. Behold, the page of paternal affection has come, which I had long desired, sweeter to my palate than all honey and more honorable in my eyes than all refined gold. I received it joyfully with both hands and embraced it with my whole breast, suspended between hopes, wondering what it would tell me about my Paulinus. Once the seals were broken, I opened a path with eager eyes through each line; recognizing in them the desired soundness of the hoped-for salvation of the Father, I immediately kissed each individual letter, and poured out my whole self to God Christ in acts of thanksgiving, saying: “You will give joy and gladness to my hearing, and the bones that have been humbled will rejoice” (Ps. 50:10). And though I had previously been humbled in sorrow, I have now been exalted in joy. And if anything could have been added to a full measure of charity, I would certainly have heaped upon my former [Al., first] fullness of love the abundance of new joy. Therefore whoever, wounded by the honey-sweet arrow of charity, receives in his heart wounds sweeter than every honeycomb, knows that I am not exaggerating in the bosom of this little letter leaves of words withering in autumn’s cold; rather, from the living fountain of truth, to water the true flowers of love, this willing right hand of my heart draws up these words, so that I might pour the drops of my great love into your inward parts.

You have brought forth many examples overflowing with the rare-flowing nectar of the most holy marriage-song of your heart, so that I see the Aristotelian proverb more truly fulfilled in you: Aristotle, who wrote the exceedingly subtle arguments of the *Perihermenias*, is said to have dipped his pen in his mind. But I recognize you as bringing forth, abundantly from the eternal treasury of charity, things new and old, and as having dipped your pen in piety through faith in brotherly love. Your most holy heart is the promised land, flowing with the honey of wisdom and overflowing with the light of the sweetest charity. There the true and glorious Solomon has built, with the jewels of the virtues, a temple for his beautiful dwelling and majesty—not one destined to perish in Chaldean flame, but one destined to remain in eternal peace. In it the Holy of Holies is accessible to the highest and true pontiff, Christ alone, not once a year (Heb. 9:3–7), but always and forever. There is the ark of wisdom and the tablets of the two testaments. The cherubim in the multitude of knowledge cover all these things. Beneath their wings the divine oracles answer the peoples, and rivers of living water leap forth into eternal salvation for those who thirst (John 4:14). Let the thirsty come there from the parched regions of earthly ignorance and drink.

What is not found in so overflowing a treasury of your heart? Its inhabitant is recognized as the one in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Col. 2:3), who has the key of David: he opens and no one shuts; he shuts and no one opens (Rev. 3:7). Whatever he wishes for the advancement of others, he opens with the key of perpetual eloquence, the key of charity; and whatever he wishes in the secret treasury of your breast, he closes with the key of wisdom. This is the most holy ladder of Jacob’s dream (Gen. 28:12), by which devout understanding customarily penetrates the secrets of heaven through the seven steps of spiritual gifts; and again, for the building up of the people subject to him, it descends by the steps of brotherly love, so that he may become an ecclesiastical teacher, sharing divine contemplation with Mary, and again, with Martha, anxious in diligent service for the guests at the Lord’s table (Luke 10:39–40). On these two wings the souls of the saints are borne daily, with great glory of merit, to the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom; by these same wings they cross the stormy gulfs of this world in a secure vessel and reach the harbor of perpetual rest with the merchandise of the virtues.

But I truly fear—and I do not say this without the greatest pain of heart—that I shall not see the face of your blessedness again in this life, because we are traveling a difficult road along the path of separation. Through the valley of tears we hasten toward an uncertain end; and soon fragile flesh will return to where it was taken from (Ps. 103:29). All its beauty, struck and scorched by the burning wind (Job 27:21), will wither, and a person will go to the house of his eternity (Eccl. 12:5). Around him those who mourn will stand in the street [Al., house], and the spirit will return to God who gave it. Where then will be the allurements of bodily pleasures? [Col. 0202A] Where the proud ambition of worldly pomp? Do not all these things vanish like smoke dispersed into the air by the windy eddies of storms? And the more anyone has loved these empty delights in the world, the more he will hate them when presented before the eternal Judge. Blessed is the one who has turned necessity into will and, pierced by love of Christ, has voluntarily lost what he will be compelled by death to lose.

Mindful of my misery, I dictated these words amid tearful complaints—not so that you might correct me, which is unnecessary, on the basis of my words, but so that you might mourn with me over my iniquities; and so that you, my most holy helper, might lift up by your prayers me, who am feeding pigs in a distant region amid every impurity, and restore me, long lost [Al., endangered], to the banquets of paternal affection (Luke 15:13–15). The dust of wicked thoughts has therefore clung to the eye of my heart, so that I am unable either to see or perfectly to love the highest good of blessedness. If I saw it, I would certainly love it. But from you, who received the spirit of consolation from him who wills all people to be saved (1 Tim. 2:4), I earnestly request the support of continual prayer, so that the physician of eternal peace may anoint with the collyrium of his mercy the eye blinded by wicked desires, enabling it to see the true light of perpetual goodness and to love what it sees.

Remember the gentlest mind of the Samaritan, who tended the wounded man, deprived of every means of help, with oil and wine; bound him with a bandage of compassion; lifted him onto his beast; led him to an inn; and gave two denarii for him [Col. 0202C] so that he might be cared for (Luke 10). What is gentler than this compassion? What example is more beneficial? The Creator of all things gave himself up as the price for humanity, to free those whom he created. I confess that I am one of those whom he redeemed. But while greedy for another’s beauty, I went from my father’s tent to see the women of Canaan; the evening wolves found me, seized me, tore me apart, and left me wounded. At last, with divine grace going before me, I came to myself and said: “I will rise and go to my father” (Luke 15:18); and I ask you, most gentle shepherd, to guide me on this journey, as I have said.

The same one who commanded Lazarus to come forth from the tomb could therefore have loosed his bonds. But to demonstrate that he had given holy teachers the power to loose, he said to those standing around: “Unbind him and let him go” (John 11:44). You, excellent shepherd, therefore, at God’s command, loose from me the deadly chains of sins, so that, restored to freedom and life, I may deserve to recline among the guests of God Christ at the banquets of eternal blessedness.

{49}

[Col. 0201D] Edited by Quercetanus, p. 113; Canisius, p. 63 (Frobenius, p. 36); mutilated and incomplete throughout. It may have been written in the year 796, [Col. 0202D] when Paulinus undertook the preaching of the Gospel among the Huns.

## LETTER XLI. TO PAULINUS THE PATRIARCH (Possibly 796)

He asks Paulinus to remember him in the holy Mass. He requests that a fragment of the holy cross and other relics be sent to him, and exhorts Paulinus to undertake the labor of preaching.

To the most holy patriarch Paulinus: the humble levite Alcuin sends greetings.

[Col. 0203A] Bodily absence ought not to divide affection, because a friendship that can be abandoned was never true. From the time I came to know you, sweetest friend, I have always loved you, and my heart made a pact of friendship with your heart. Thus I wrote the name of my Paulinus not on wax, which can be erased. I ask you, do not forget the name of your friend Albinus in your holy prayers; but store it in some treasury of memory and bring it forth at the proper time,

[Col. 0203D] Where you consecrate bread and wine into the substance of the body and blood of Christ. A truly illustrious testimony for the doctrine of transubstantiation as it was believed at that time. “This is our faith, this is the faith of our ancestors,” says the celebrated Mabillon in his book on Gallican Liturgy, p. 95. “Would that our estranged brethren might at last, even if late, acknowledge it, and no longer provoke us with that fictitious innovation which they accuse of having arisen under Paschasius Radbertus in the ninth century. The authority of Alcuin alone, so clear and manifest, ought to settle this controversy . . . . Whoever detracts from faith in such perspicuous words is a lover not of truth, but of contention, error, and schism.” where you consecrate bread and wine into the substance of the body and blood of Christ.

I have long awaited the promises of your affection—that is, the protection of the life-giving cross or of other relics. I beg you, do not defraud me of so great a gift; nor do you, with regard to truth . . . . . I do not want you to plead the length of the journey. Charity will find wings for flying, and rivers will not overwhelm it (Song 8:7). The wings of faith in the palace of the king are sufficient; neither willingness to receive nor faithfulness to return is lacking in them. If our request has any weight with you—and may your request always have weight with God, who has placed you in so exalted a position, where the accomplishment of that same God, our Lord Jesus Christ, . . . . .

See how exalted this name is. Strive to be what you are called by name. Cry out without ceasing; raise your voice like a trumpet (Isa. 58:1). Let your throat be God’s trumpet. Preach in season and out of season (2 Tim. 4:2). Be a cock in preaching, girded in chastity. Be a ram, exceedingly strong in truth, whom no king will be able to resist (Prov. 30:30–31). Be a lamp upon a lampstand in the house of God (Matt. [Col. 0203C] 5:15). Your tongue closes and opens heaven (Rev. 3:7). It first opens it through devotion to preaching. Follow the example of Christ, who traveled through cities, fortified towns, villages, and farms, preaching the Gospel (Matt. 9:35); he did not even shrink from entering the houses of tax collectors or sinners for the opportunity to preach (Luke 5:29). Let hope of reward be the comfort of labor.

What am I doing, foolish as I am, against the philosophical proverb—carrying wood into the forest and watering rivers with trickling drops? I have extended my small measure through rhetorical imagery. I beg you by the love of him who preferred the widow’s two small coins to the gifts of the rich (Mark 12:42–43). Charity bears all things; whoever remains in it remains in God (1 Cor. 13:7), because God is charity (1 John [Col. 0203D] 4:16).

{50}

[Col. 0204D] Edited by Quercetanus, p. 105, from a manuscript (Frobenius, p. 42).

## LETTER XLII. TO MEGENFRIDUS (Possibly 796)

He teaches about the order and manner of preaching; he censures greed and the excessive collection of tithes; he laments that many seek the honors of the priesthood but avoid its rank and ministry. He wishes that Charles be asked to send more good workers into the harvest.

[Col. 0204A] To his most beloved friend in the love of Christ and of the royal palace,

[Col. 0204D] Archarius Megenfridus. He is also called Magenfridus and Maganfredus, commander of the Saxon army in the Hunnic expedition of 791. See the Saxon poet and Einhard’s *Annals* under that year. Here he calls Meginfridus the king’s chamberlain. Thus *archarius* means chamberlain, or, as Alcuin explains in more words a little below, administrator of treasures and keeper of counsels—virtually an intimate counselor. See Du Cange’s *Glossary*, under *Arcarius*. to the chamberlain Megenfridus, Flaccus Albinus sends perpetual soundness.

It is customary for a little letter written by the pen of charity to run among friends, displaying the ardor of its breast to friendly eyes through fraternal writing, so that what lies hidden within the mind may appear outwardly in written form. Therefore, remembering you, dearest friend, I have taken care to send you these letters of admonition for your salvation—and indeed for that of many others. Do not judge me excessive in these letters, but devoted, desiring both the prosperity of the present life and that of the future, so that you may live happily in this temporal life [Col. 0204B] and reign blessedly with Christ in the eternal one.

Every person must consider with the greatest diligence what he ought to flee and what he ought to pursue. The Psalmist presents these two things in a very brief verse, saying: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 33:15). It is not enough merely not to do evil, unless one also does good, if one desires to possess eternal glory. Hence Truth itself, in the Gospel, replied to someone who questioned him: “If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19:17). But each person must weigh at what rank God has placed him and with what talent he has enriched him. For the Lord did not entrust his money for multiplication only to bishops or presbyters; he entrusted talents of good works to every dignity and rank, [Col. 0204C] so that each person might strive faithfully to administer the grace given to him and endeavor to distribute it to his fellow servants. One receives the talent of preaching, another of wisdom, another of wealth, another of some form of administration; perhaps someone receives from God, the dispenser of all these good things, the gift of a particular craft. In all these things faith and devotion must be observed, so that each person may labor faithfully and strive manfully to multiply his lord’s money, in order to deserve to hear the desirable words: “Well done, good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful over little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. 25:21).

Those who receive the money of preaching must carefully consider what suits each place [Col. 0204D] and time, and also in what order the preaching of Christianity ought to be begun and completed. For our Lord Jesus Christ, returning in triumphal glory to his paternal seat, commanded his apostles, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the [Col. 0205A] Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matt. 28:19–20).

[Col. 0205D] Faith must be taught first. Alcuin writes the same thing to Charlemagne in Letter 28 (now 33), and to Arno in Letter 31 (now 36), in the year 796: “Faith must be taught first, and thus the sacraments of baptism must be received. Then the evangelical commandments must be handed down. But if any one of these three is lacking, the hearer will not be able to possess the salvation of his soul. Faith also, as Saint Augustine says, is voluntary, not compulsory. A person may be drawn to faith, but cannot be forced. You may be forced to baptism, but that does not advance faith. Unless it is the age of infancy, which may be saved through the sins of others and the confession of others, a person of mature age must answer for himself what he believes or desires. And if he professes faith deceitfully, he will not possess salvation truly.” Therefore preachers ought to teach the pagan people the faith in peaceful and prudent words. The Lord knows those who are his; and he opens the heart of those whom he wills, so that they may understand what is said by the teacher. But after the reception of faith and baptism, gentler commandments must be offered to weaker minds. For the apostle Paul, writing to the young people of Galatia [Corinth], says: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3:2). Solid food belongs to strong men—that is, the greater commandments belong to those who have long exercised their senses in the law of the Lord. And just as milk suits fragile infancy, so gentler commandments must be handed down to an untrained people at the beginning of faith.

Accordingly, we read in the Acts of the Apostles (chap. 15:2) that Paul and Barnabas went up to Jerusalem to James and the other apostles over this question: how ought they to preach to the Gentiles? They, prescribing the matter by unanimous agreement, decided that no legal burden should be imposed upon their necks, but only that they should abstain from fornication, blood, what has been strangled, and idols (ibid., vv. 28–29). Indeed Paul himself, the preacher to the Gentiles, boasted that he lived by the labor of his hands. For he says in one of his letters: “You know that these hands served both me and those who are with me, so that we might not burden any of you” (Acts 20:34; 2 Thess. 3:8). And again: “It is better for me to die than that anyone should empty my glory. What is my glory? That I may proclaim the Gospel without expense” (1 Cor. 9:15–18). This is what that great preacher of the Gentiles, specially chosen by God, did, so that he might cut away at the root every occasion of greed among preachers, in order that no one, enticed by any desire, but strengthened solely by the charity of Christ, might preach the word of God, just as he himself commanded his disciples in the Gospel: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matt. 10:8).

If the sweet yoke of Christ and his light burden were preached to the hardest people of the Saxons with as much earnestness as the payment of tithes was demanded, or the necessity of the legal edict for the smallest offenses, perhaps they would not shrink from the sacraments of baptism. Let teachers of the faith finally be instructed by apostolic [supply: examples]. Let them be preachers, not plunderers. Let them trust in the mercy of him who says: “Carry neither purse nor bag” (Luke 10:4), and the rest that follows; and of whom the prophet says: “He never abandons those who hope in him” (Dan. 13:60).

I have written these things to your affection, venerable friend, so that they may assist your admonitions to those who desire to hear counsel from you. My beloved David knows all these things well enough; God has given him both wisdom and good will, and he has turned many peoples toward the love and praise of Christ. He possesses every goodness and power sufficient for doing good. There is only one deficiency [F. perhaps supplies: “is lacking”], because of the dangerous times of this age: he has fewer helpers in the work of the Lord than necessary. Nevertheless, I believe that no one in the world has better men than he does. Let him educate, admonish, and teach them according to the wisdom given him by God. And you, most faithful administrator of treasures, keeper of counsels, and devoted helper, perform his will manfully. Be gentle in counsel and energetic in action, peaceful in the household, prudent in embassies, compassionate toward the poor and wretched, just in judgments, generous in almsgiving, so that from your temporal riches you may deserve eternal riches for yourself in heaven.

The affection I bear my beloved David, and concern for the salvation of many, still compel me to advise you about what I know to be useful before God and honorable before the world. For certain priests of Christ who possess parishes and worldly honors do not wish to possess the rank of ministry; it seems to me better that they should have a full blessing and a full reward with God. At present one man labors for an eternal reward, while they labor for a worldly honor.

[Col. 0205D] I think the reading should be: “But they are deprived of the power of binding [Col. 0206D] and loosing”—the most illustrious gift in the Church of Christ, which Christ gave to the apostles, etc. A notable passage against commendatory bishops, parish priests, and others who seek honors but avoid ministry. “But they are deprived,” if I may say so peacefully, “of the power of binding and loosing,” the most illustrious gift in the Church of Christ, which Christ gave to the apostles and, through them, to their successors. It is also dangerous for churches that have no pastors for Christ’s flock to remain without a shepherd for long. Ravenous wolves enter, but there is no one to drive them out. “The mistress of the nations sits alone and widowed, and there is no one to comfort her” (Lam. 1:1–2). Truth itself also says: “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the workers are few; ask the lord of the harvest to send workers into his harvest” (Luke 10:2). And for you, dearest friend, the harvest among the Christian people is indeed plentiful, but in some places there are no harvesters. You, however, ask the lord of the harvest—that is, my beloved David—to send workers into his harvest, so that, when asked, he may say to them, as their own protector and only lover, Christ God, said to his disciples: “Go; behold, I am sending you” (Luke 10:3). He is the lord of the vineyard. Let him send workers into his vineyard and say: “You also go into my vineyard, and whatever is just you will receive for [Col. 0207A] the labor of my vineyard” (Matt. 20:4, 7). He [F., they] is the power and administration of Christ’s vineyard, that is, of the churches of God. To him belong praise and glory, and eternal reward, if they are properly ordered and governed and have as many pastors as can be found,

[Col. 0207D] The passage is corrupt., worthy and pleasing to God. He is the one in this kingdom who can preach to everyone and receive from all the churches reward and blessing in this age, and eternal blessedness and blessed eternity with Christ and his saints.

[Col. 0207D] Edited by Quercetanus, p. 1; Canisius, p. 3 (Frobenius, p. 38). It appears to have been written not long after he was appointed abbot of the monastery of St. Martin at Tours and opened schools there, around the year 796. I infer this because, when he wrote this letter, he had not yet been supplied with the books necessary for teaching.

## LETTER XLIII. TO CHARLEMAGNE (Year 796)

He expresses his joy at the king’s prosperity. To advance his studies, he asks that his books be brought from England. He lists the benefits of literary study and advises that the palace youths devote themselves to it.

[Col. 0207B] To the most pious, most excellent, and most worthy of all honor, David the king: Flaccus Albinus sends eternal salvation in true blessedness in Christ.

The sweetness of your holy affection abundantly refreshes the eagerness of my heart at every hour and even at every moment; and the face of your excellence, which I was accustomed frequently to contemplate with affection, fills all the veins of my memory with great and desirable joy. As though it were the image of many riches in my heart, the name and appearance of your goodness are stored there. Therefore it is a great joy for me to hear the glad news of your sweetest prosperity. To learn this news as well, I have sent, as you know, this little boy, the client [Al., little client] of my littleness, [Col. 0207C] so that, rejoicing in the safety of your exalted position, I might praise the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ with thanksgiving. Not only I, the least little servant of our Savior, ought to rejoice with your prosperity and exaltation, most illustrious of powers; the whole holy Church of God, with unanimous harmony of charity, ought to give thanks to the Lord God almighty, who in these final and most dangerous times of the world has, in his most merciful gift, bestowed upon the Christian people so pious, prudent, and just a ruler and defender. He strives with all his purpose to correct what is crooked, strengthen what is right, exalt what is holy, gladly spread the name of the Lord God Most High across wide regions of the earth, and endeavor to kindle the light of the catholic faith in the farthest parts of the world. This, O sweetest David, is your glory, praise, and reward on the day of the great judgment and in the perpetual fellowship of the saints: that you should strive most diligently to correct the people entrusted by God to your excellence, and endeavor to lead souls long blinded by the darkness of ignorance into the light of true faith. Divine recompense will never be lacking for the best intentions or good efforts; rather, whoever labors more in the will of God will receive greater reward in the kingdom of God. The time of this life runs swiftly, flees, and does not return [Al., does not look back]; {53} but the ineffable mercy of God foresaw that the human race should labor briefly and be crowned eternally. Therefore time ought to be precious to us, lest through negligence we lose what we could obtain eternally through the practice of a good life. Nor will we be able to love anything on earth as much as the blessed rest will be loved in heaven. Whoever then desires to possess it should now strive to earn it through good works. The gate of the heavenly kingdom therefore stands open to all alike, but those are permitted to enter who hasten toward it bearing abundant fruit of goodness.

But I, your Flaccus, in accordance with your exhortation and good will, strive to distribute to some, throughout the buildings of Saint Martin, the honey of the sacred Scriptures; I endeavor to intoxicate others with the old wine of ancient disciplines; I shall begin to nourish others with the fruits of grammatical subtlety; and I desire to illuminate certain others with the order of the stars, as though with the painted roof of some great house. I have become all things to all people (1 Cor. 9:22), in order to instruct as many as possible for the advancement of God’s holy Church and for the adornment of your imperial kingdom, so that the grace of almighty God in me may not be empty (1 Cor. 15:10), nor the generosity of your goodness fruitless. But in part I, your little servant, lack the more refined books of scholastic learning that I possessed in my homeland through the good and most devoted—

> **[Col. 0207D]** William of Malmesbury cites this somewhat differently in Book I, chapter 3, of *The Deeds of the Kings of England*, and in Book III of *The Deeds of the Bishops*: “Give me the more refined books of scholastic learning, such as I had in my homeland through the good and most devoted diligence of my master, Archbishop Egbert. And if it pleases your wisdom, I shall send back some of our boys, who may collect from there whatever is necessary for us and bring back to Francia the flowers of Britain, so that there may not be merely a closed garden at York, but also, at Tours, the outpourings of paradise.” From this we infer two things: first, that Alcuin completed his studies at York; second, and much more clearly, that he established his school not at Paris or in the monastery of Fulda, but in the city of Tours on the Loire, from which so many men distinguished for their learning later emerged. **BASNAGE.**

…through the diligence of my master, or even through whatever labor I myself have contributed. Therefore I say this to your Excellence, lest perhaps your counsel, so desirous of every kind of wisdom, should approve my sending back some of our boys, who may obtain for us whatever is necessary from there and bring back to Francia the flowers of Britain: so that there may be not merely a closed garden at York, but at Tours the outpourings of paradise with the fruits of its trees, so that the South Wind, coming, may blow through the gardens beside the Loire, and their spices may flow forth; and finally may come to pass what follows in the *Song*, from which I have taken this example: “Let my beloved come into his garden and eat the fruit of his trees.” And let him say to his young men: “Eat, my friends; drink and be intoxicated, my dearest ones. I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5:1–2).

Or that exhortatory saying of the prophet Isaiah concerning the pursuit of wisdom:

> “All you who thirst, come to the waters; and you who have no silver, hasten, buy, and eat. Come, buy without silver and without any exchange, wine and milk” (Isa. 55:1).

These are matters that your most noble purpose does not overlook: how throughout all the pages of sacred Scripture we are exhorted to learn wisdom. Nothing is higher for attaining the blessed life, nothing more delightful for discipline, nothing stronger against vices, nothing more praiseworthy in every dignity; and, even according to the sayings of the philosophers, nothing is more necessary for governing a people, nothing better for ordering life according to the finest morals, than the glory of wisdom, the praise of discipline, and the effectiveness of learning. Hence the wisest of men, Solomon, exclaims in praise of it [Alt., explains]:

> “Wisdom is better than all the most precious things, and nothing desirable can be compared with it. She is the one who exalts the humble and honors the exalted. Through her kings reign, and lawgivers decree what is just. Through her princes rule and the powerful determine justice. Blessed are those who keep her ways, and blessed are those who watch daily at her gates” (Prov. 8:11 ff.).

Exhort all the young men in your palace, lord king, to learn this with every effort and to possess it through daily practice, so that they may advance in it during the flowering of their age, be deemed worthy to bring their gray hairs to honor, and through it be able to attain everlasting blessedness. For my part, according to the measure of my little intellect, I shall not be sluggish in sowing seeds of wisdom among your servants in these regions, mindful of that saying:

> “In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening let not your hand cease; for you do not know which will grow, this or that. And if both together, so much the better” (Eccl. 11:6).

> **[Col. 0209C]** “In the morning … I sowed in Britain.” From this some conclude that Alcuin traveled through the principal academies of Britain. The *Cambridge Annals* report that Alcuin taught at that academy after Bede. But nothing prevents his remaining at York and spreading the light of learning throughout all England. This passage proves more clearly that Alcuin was an old man when he established his school at Tours. **BASNAGE.**

In the morning, when my studies were flourishing with the vigor of youth, I sowed in Britain. Now, as my blood grows cold, I do not cease sowing in Francia, as in the evening. For I hope that both may grow at once, by God’s gracious gift. For my broken body, the saying of Saint Jerome is a consolation; he says in his letter to Nepotianus:

> “Almost all the virtues of the body change in old men, and, as wisdom alone increases, the rest diminish.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The old age of those who instructed their youth in honorable arts and meditated day and night on the law of the Lord becomes more learned with age, more seasoned through experience, wiser with the passage of time; and it gathers the sweetest fruits of its former studies.”

In that letter, whoever wishes may read more about the praise of wisdom and the studies of former times, and understand how earnestly the ancients strove to flourish in the beauty of wisdom. I have recognized your devotion—beloved of God and praiseworthy in life—as always advancing and rejoicing in this pursuit, and adorning the nobility of your worldly lineage with a greater nobility of mind. May our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the power and wisdom of God, guard and exalt you, and bring you to the glory of his blessed and eternal vision.

> **[Col. 0209D]** Edited by Quercetanus, p. 93; by Canisius, no. 47; by Froben, no. 39.

## Letter XLIV. To Damoeta, His Son  
*(Year 796)*

He prays for prosperity for him as he goes to war, and grieves at the absence of his friends.

### Flaccus Albinus

> **[Col. 0209D]** To Flavius Damoeta. That this was a distinguished man, energetic both at home and in military affairs, is evident from this and the following letter, where it is clear that he was appointed in Charlemagne’s army, against the Saxons, to administer justice, as these words show: “In hearing diverse cases, let justice always resound upon your lips.” **CANISIUS.**

To Flavius Damoeta, his dearest son, Albinus sends greetings.

I rejoice with your affection and congratulate you on the faith you have shown, because I have always found you faithful everywhere and have recognized you as benevolent toward me, like a son toward his father. Nor have I found you otherwise, since your will has always followed mine. Therefore my heart is weary because your face is absent; nevertheless, I always keep you present in the love of my heart, and I beseech God for your prosperity, that he may deign to preserve you for me in joy, and for yourself in safety, through long years. But I am very anxious—

> **[Col. 0209D]** Concerning his journey to war. The Saxons are meant, as below. Mabillon judges that this occurred in the year 783. I prefer the opinion of Pagi, who, in no. 22, assigns the year 796 to this letter.

—about the journey of your departure to war, because many dangers commonly arise in such undertakings. Yet whoever has justice on his side in going forth and fighting for God may have confidence in the aid of him for whose love he does not fear undertaking so great a labor. But you, remember to strengthen your journey with confession, fortify it with almsgiving, and surround it on every side with the prayers of God’s servants, so that the angel of the Lord may protect and accompany you amid all adversity, and so that you may go in safety and return in peace.

> **[Col. 0209D]** Strengthen your journey with confession. He exhorts the soldier to expiate his sins by sacramental confession before battle, following the praised custom of ancient soldiers, who, among the Normans as well—of whom William of Malmesbury, Book III of *The Deeds of the Kings of England*, relates that they devoted the whole night to confession of sins and in the morning received Communion in the Lord’s body—infantry with bows and arrows, and so forth. **CANISIUS.**

I remain at home almost as though bereft of sons. Damoeta has gone to Saxony, Homer to Italy,

> **[Col. 0210D]** Candidus to Britain. Leland, in *On British Writers*, chapter 100, p. 133, makes this Candidus a foster son of the Church of Lindisfarne and a disciple of Bishop Higebald. There he reports a fragment of Alcuin’s letter to that same Higebald, in which he discreetly recalls Candidus; see above, Letter 8 (now 9), to the Lindisfarne community.

Candidus has gone to Britain; Martin has remained sick at Vico, near Saint-Josse,

> **[Col. 0210D]** At Vico, near Saint-Josse. We have spoken elsewhere of the cell of Saint-Josse granted to Alcuin by Charles. From this passage Baluzius, in his note on Letter 11 of Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, concludes that Vico, or Quentavicus, is the same as the monastery of Saint-Josse, commonly called Saint-Josse-sur-Mer.

and for his recovery I earnestly beg you to implore God’s mercy. Concerning Mopsus, who, as you heard, fell ill at Saint Martin’s, I have heard nothing certain; nor, after your departure, have I seen any messengers from him. But I was almost wholly swallowed up by grief at—

> **[Col. 0210D]** My daughter. Who was this person, for whose health so many prayers, so much almsgiving, and such great anxiety were offered? I venture to say that she was Liutgard, Charlemagne’s wife, whom Alcuin elsewhere calls his daughter. **CANISIUS.**

—my daughter, who for almost three days was given up for dead; but now, by divine mercy, through the prayers of God’s servants and the generosity of almsgiving, we have been greatly comforted concerning her, for she has recovered well. See through what waves your father has been tossed! You, dearest son, strive to intercede for him with the fellow soldiers of your rank, so that the Spirit of consolation may deign to settle these movements of his soul in tranquil peace, and may bring his beloved David and all of you, victorious, back to your homeland with joy. May divine mercy make you a citizen of the eternal homeland, dearest son.

## Letter XLV

[Note: [Col. 0211D] In Canisius and the Salzburg codex the heading “To Riculf, archbishop of Mainz,” etc., is absent. Quercetanus found it in the Petavian codex; Basnage nevertheless says that it does not prove Damoeta to have been a bishop. Rather, the preceding and following letters suggest that he was a layman who administered justice among soldiers in Saxony with great fairness.]

### To Riculf, Archbishop of Mainz, Surnamed Damoeta

He laments the absence of friends and exhorts him to the love of eternal things.

To his most approved friend Damoeta, Albinus sends greetings.

The time during which I have not seen the face or heard the words of your affection seems very long to me. My mind rejoiced as much in your presence as [Note: [Col. 0211D] He is saddened in absence. This and what follows agree with the preceding letter, in which he complains that he has been left almost bereft of sons and alone at home; thus this is the same Damoeta, a layman, not a bishop.] it is saddened in absence. What can the mind do but mourn when it has few friends? Alas, they are almost always absent. Yet I shall do what I can: I shall remember you before the Lord, praying that his mercy always grant you prosperity and fill your breast with his love. These are true riches, which never deceive their possessor and are not lost even in death, but grow more abundant when that which is loved is seen.

This is the difference between temporal and eternal things: a temporal thing is loved more before it is possessed, but becomes cheap when it arrives; the eternal is loved more ardently when possessed than when desired. Therefore let us love eternal things more than temporal ones, so that we may deserve to live blessedly and happily in eternity. Farewell for ever.

[Note: [Col. 0212D] Quercetanus edition 68; Canisius 41 (Froben 41).]

## Letter XLVI. To Damoeta

He gives thanks for a gift, exhorts him to give justice to everyone, and longs for his friend’s return.

[Note: [Col. 0212D] The words “To the most distinguished man,” and what follows, were absent from the Saint Gall codex used by Canisius.] To Flavius Damoeta, most distinguished man, Albinus sends many greetings of lasting peace.

I rejoice greatly in your prosperity, and have been very glad at the gift of your affection, giving as many thanks as I counted teeth in the gift.

[Note: [Col. 0212D] A remarkable animal. Alcuin jokes here about a comb sent by Damoeta, bearing an animal’s head. This relates to poem 219 in Quercetanus, apparently connected with this letter: “A beast had suddenly crept into our house, in which there was the marvel of two heads … one jaw joined them; it bristled with sixty teeth. Its food grew from a living body; it ate neither flesh nor crops nor fruits nor drink, and its mouth did not gape. You know, my Damoeta, what this beast is.”]

A remarkable animal: it has two heads and sixty teeth, not of elephantine size but of ivory beauty. I was not frightened by this beast’s horror but delighted by its appearance. I did not fear that it would bite me with its grating teeth; rather, I smiled to soothe the hair of my head with its gentle flattery. I perceived not fierceness in its teeth but loved the affection of its sender, which I have always found faithful in him. Yet as much as I rejoice in the sweetness of love, so much do I grieve [Note: [Col. 0212D] At the length of absence, namely during the Saxon campaign mentioned above in Letter 39, now 44.] at the length of absence. I would not have wished those whom the sweetest bonds of one affection unite to be separated from one another for so long. What can I do except follow with tears the friend whom my mind desires to have present, until he returns?

O dearest son, amid the occupations of the world do not forget yourself. While the body is fed with feasts, let the soul be refreshed with alms; while limbs weary from travel are restored by rest, let the mind be strengthened in God by prayers. In the hearing of diverse cases, let justice always sound in your mouth; from your inmost heart let consolation [Note: [Col. 0212C] Alcuin: *proveniat*, “come forth.”] go out to the wretched; let the hope of equity not fail those who come to you, nor the aids of mercy those who seek refuge with you. Mercy done to the poor is rewarded with eternal blessedness. Doing this, my son, may you flourish in every beauty of virtue; may divine protection accompany you wherever you go, lead you prosperously everywhere, and quickly bring you back to us in all well-being, that a father’s love may rejoice in his son and God be praised everywhere, who will present his servants joyfully to one another. Be strong, well, and flourishing, sweetest Damoeta.

[Note: [Col. 0213C] Malmesbury, book I of *The Kings of England*, chapter 3, records this and the following fragment of the same letter; Quercetanus, pp. 1667–68.]

## Letter XLVII. To Offa, King of the Mercians (A.D. 796)

[Note: [Col. 0213C] To King Offa. Offa, the very powerful king of the Mercians, ruled from 756 to 796, dying on 26 July, according to Hoveden, p. 406.]

He reports that Charles is angry with the Northumbrian people over the murder of King Ethelred.

Let your venerable affection know that Lord King Charles has often spoken to me of you lovingly and faithfully, and that you have in him a most faithful friend. Therefore he sends worthy gifts to your affection and through the episcopal sees of your kingdom. Likewise, he sent gifts to King Ethelred and to his episcopal sees [Note: [Col. 0213C] He sent gifts. What they were may be learned from Charlemagne’s letter to the same King Offa, to be given in the appendix, Quercetanus p. 1670.]—but, alas, after the gifts had been sent and letters entrusted to messengers, sad news came through envoys returning from Scotland by way of you, concerning the unfaithfulness of the people and [Note: [Col. 0213D] The killing of the king: Ethelred, king of Northumbria, was killed by his own people on 18 April 796. This letter is thus dated after that day.] the murder of the king. Charles withdrew his largesse and was so angered against that people—whom he calls faithless, perverse, and murderers of their lords, worse than pagans—that, had I not interceded for them, he would already have taken from them every good he could and devised every evil against them.

[Note: [Col. 0213D] This is the second fragment of the letter to Offa reported by Malmesbury at the place cited; Quercetanus p. 1667.]

## Letter XLVIII. To Offa, King of the Mercians

Wishing to return to his homeland, England, he is kept back by the perjuries and devastation of his people.

I was ready to come to you with King Charles’s gifts and return to my homeland; but for the peace of my people it seemed better to remain in pilgrimage, not knowing what I could do among people among whom no one can be safe or make progress in wholesome counsel. Behold: [Note: [Col. 0213D] Holy places devastated by pagans, etc., in the preceding years; see Letter 8, now 9, to the Lindisfarne community and those following.] holy places devastated by pagans, altars defiled by perjuries, monasteries violated by adulteries, and [Col. 0213C] the land defiled by the blood of lords and princes.

[Note: [Col. 0213D] Quercetanus edition 38 from manuscript (Froben 44). Its date is uncertain, but it has been suitably joined to the other letters to Offa.]

## Letter XLIX. To Offa, King of the Mercians (date uncertain)

[Note: [Col. 0213D] To King Offa. Offanus and Offa are the same name, as Bede and Bedanus, Columba and Columbanus, Thega and Theganus. The editor displays a very rare silver coin of King Offa, found some years earlier in his abbey garden and kept in his coin cabinet; he considers it undoubtedly the likeness of the same Offa to whom Alcuin wrote these familiar letters, and leaves the reverse inscription and further questions of English medieval coinage to British scholars.]

He sends a pupil to England at the king’s request to teach in the schools, and exhorts him to royal virtues.

To the most excellent lord King Offa, Alcuin, humble levite, sends greetings.

[Col. 0214A] Always wishing faithfully to please your will, I have sent you this dearest son of mine as you asked. I beg you to treat him honorably until, God willing, I come to you; do not allow him to wander idly or serve drunkenness, but provide him pupils and command him to teach diligently. I know that he speaks well, and would that he prospers well; for my pupils’ progress is my reward with God. I am very pleased that you show so much zeal for learning, that the light of wisdom may shine in your kingdom, where it is now being extinguished in many places. You are Britain’s glory, the trumpet of preaching, sword against enemies, shield against foes. Keep God always before your eyes; do justice and love mercy, for whoever forgives is forgiven [Col. 0214B] (Matthew 6:14). Learn to love the commands of Christ God, that his blessing may follow you and your descendants in every goodness and prosperity for ever. May divine grace attend you and your kingdom with a heavenly blessing, most excellent lord.

[Note: [Col. 0214D] Quercetanus edition 48 from a manuscript collated with the Salzburg codex (Froben 45).]

## Letter L. To Ecgfrid, King of the Mercians

He exhorts him to virtue.

To the most noble young man [Note: [Col. 0214D] Ecgfrid, son of Offa king of the Mercians. Alford says that Offa had him crowned king in 787, perhaps in the presence of the Mercian synod, so that he might learn to wield the scepter while his father lived. The letter’s context shows it was written before his parents’ death; its precise year is unknown. He succeeded in 796 and died in that same year, five months after coming to power, according to Malmesbury.] Ecgfrid, humble levite Alcuin sends greetings.

Knowing you to be a youth of good disposition and the highest nobility, I have presumed to send you exhortatory letters. Not because you lack the admonition needed from your wisest and best parents, whose examples of honor are the people’s lessons of salvation [Col. 0214C], but to show you my affection’s faithfulness, wishing you to prosper in God, be adorned with the flowers of virtue, and benefit all the English peoples in prosperity. See from how noble parents you are born and with how great care you are raised. Do not be degenerate in morals when you are noble by birth. Learn their examples diligently: from your father authority, [Note: [Col. 0214D] From your mother, mercy. Alford calls her Zuendrida, related to Charlemagne according to Matthew Paris, and says that she was earlier called Drida. His hostile comment is that her *pietas*, a feminine noun, became *impietas* when she acquired power.] from your mother mercy; from both, devotion to Christian religion, persistence in prayer, generosity in alms, and sobriety in all life. Be the staff of their old age, humbly obedient to their commands, so that their blessing may follow you for ever. For Solomon says that a parent’s blessing exalts children (Sirach 3:11), and likewise: “A wise son is the glory of his father” (Proverbs 10:1). Do not be subject to luxury but to God, for the Holy Spirit dwells in a chaste body and a soul unstained by vices. It does not become you, born upon a royal throne, to be rustic in manners or wanton in speech. Temperance and honorable life will make you lovable and praiseworthy to all peoples. Begin to earn good things by your conduct, keeping God everywhere as your protector. Your prosperity rests on his mercy. If you love him with all your heart and submit yourself with all purpose to his will, he will exalt you in the present kingdom and grant you eternal glory in the future. May divine mercy make you flourish in every goodness, dearest son!

[Note: [Col. 0215D] Edited by Martene and Durand, *Veterum Scriptorum et Monumentorum Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, pp. 49–51, from an 800-year-old Vedastine manuscript. Dated about 796, when Rado received the abbey of Saint Vedast; Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXVI, no. 50.]

## Letter LI. To the Vedastine Monks (about A.D. 796)

He sends several verses and Masses, commends himself to their prayers, and exhorts them to religious virtues.

To his dearest brothers in Christ, Albinus, humble levite, sends greetings.

As the gracious affection of the lord abbot and of you all required [Col. 0215C], [Note: [Col. 0215D] Verses: they are printed in volume II, nos. 41–66.] I composed verses for each church title and individual altar, would that as fittingly as willingly; for your holiness’s command compels swift dictation. Yet let your piety protect what our humility has obediently written.

[Note: [Col. 0215D] Masses means a sacramentary; see below in volume II and its preliminary notice.] I also brought some Masses from our missal for the daily and ecclesiastical offices: first in honor of the supreme Trinity, then for praying for the intercession of saints and asking the assistance of angels, which is very necessary to those laboring in this pilgrimage. Afterward we added a Mass of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, to be sung on some days if anyone wishes, and also a Mass of Saint Vedast, your father and [Note: [Col. 0216D] Our protector. From this passage Alcuin seems to have been especially devoted to Saint Vedast; at Abbot Rado’s request he wrote Vedast’s Life about 796. At about the same time he probably composed titles to be inscribed in the Vedastine church. Martene.] our protector, that his familiar advocacy might bring eternal consolation to his servants. We added prayers also for sins and for those who give alms, so that anyone wishing to make an offering either for his own negligences or for another’s good works [Col. 0216A] might have intercessions suited to his intention.

I think you have all these things better written in your sacramentaries or kept in daily custom. Yet, lest I be disobedient to your love, I wrote what we have in our practice and thought useful to you, begging you to remember my name among these or other intercessions of your holiness. I confess that I have great confidence in your holy prayers for winning the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ. May he keep you, make you advance in every goodness, and deign to hear your prayers both for the salvation of the living and the benefit of the dying.

But you, brothers, remain firmly in unity of love and diligently stand in humble obedience [Col. 0216B]. This is your honor before people; this is your road to God’s kingdom. In these things you should hope for reward from God. Let the elders lead the younger to these most holy paths; correct them in a spirit of gentleness and give them good examples, so that, clinging to your most holy footsteps, they may deserve eternal life with you in Christ. Do not seek the world that you have despised, often singing with the Prophet: “Incline my heart to your testimonies and not to avarice” (Psalm 118:36). For greed is the root of all evils. It is better to have God in the heart than coins in the purse.

Practice the study of sacred reading most diligently among the labors of obedience, so that either work or book may always be seen in your hands [Col. 0216C]. For in holy books God speaks to man, and in prayer man speaks to God. What should be sweeter than hearing God speak? In them the sinner finds consolations and the benefactor joys. As light delights the eyes, so reading delights hearts. Observe the guard of the mouth diligently: always utter words that build up those who hear, for the salvation of others is your reward. Let the Lord’s praise always sound in your mouth, as the Prophet says: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise is always in my mouth” (Psalm 33:2); and again: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me; there is the way by which I will show him God’s salvation” (Psalm 49:23).

[Note: [Col. 0216D] A homiletic exhortation. Alcuin fulfilled this promise in a homily, or exhortation to imitate Saint Vedast’s virtues, to be printed below in its place.] Dearest brothers, I have not yet had time to dictate a homiletic exhortation; but if life remains, with the Holy Spirit inspiring, I shall not forget your request and my promise. May divine mercy make you flourish and advance in every goodness, dearest brothers. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0216D] In Martene’s manuscript there followed verses to be inscribed in Saint Vedast’s church; they are printed in volume II, no. 41.]

[Note: [Col. 0217C] Quercetanus edition 64; Canisius 22; Froben 52.]

## Letter LII. To the Brothers Serving in the Church of Saint Liudgar, Bishop (A.D. 796)

He excuses his failure to visit them and exhorts them to virtues suitable to monks.

To the venerable brothers in Christ [Note: [Col. 0217C] Church of Saint Liudgar. Canisius reads Leodegarius, which he understands of the people of Autun, whose church had Saint Leodegarius as bishop; Mabillon understands the Murbach monks, whose basilica was named for Saint Leodegarius.] serving in the church of Saint Liudgar the bishop, Alcuin, devoted to your progress in Christ, sends greetings.

I received with a most grateful heart the welcome greeting of your blessedness, which faithful brother Odilleoz brought to the ears of my smallness. I greatly desire to be helped by the prayers of your holiness in the stormy voyage of this life, so that under the most merciful guidance of our Savior, through your intercession, I may deserve to reach the harbor of perpetual rest.

[Note: [Col. 0217D] Why he did not come to them. If the letter was written to the Murbach community, as Mabillon thinks, Alcuin excuses himself for not visiting when he came to Alsace in 796, where he had business perhaps not far from Murbach; he may also have come at another time.] That I did not come to you was not, God is witness, from any contempt, but lest the life of my disorderly conduct create scandal to your religious community [Note: [Col. 0217B] Alcuin: *regioni*, “region.”]; I wished to build, not destroy (Sirach 34:28), to gather, not scatter. There is no greater condemnation for Christ’s sheep than a wandering and misleading shepherd. How can a traveler who follows one wandering through bypaths keep the royal road? Does not the spear-shaft follow the point in the blow?

But you, dearest brothers, follow with all strength the examples of the holy Fathers and enter together into the footsteps of their obedience [Note: [Col. 0217B] Edition: *precibus*, “prayers.”]. Love, obedience, and humility open heaven’s gates to monks—not the love [Note: [Col. 0217D] Drinking from a full cup. Mabillon says this alludes to German customs; Canisius says Alcuin refers to the custom of drinking in saints’ names and for their love to obtain a blessing.] that is drunk from a full cup, but that which dwells unfeigned in the brotherly breast, seeking not its own good but another’s (1 Corinthians 13:5), desiring to benefit all and not please itself. Nor is it merely humility outwardly shown by bowing the head, but that which in the heart’s reflection judges itself lower than all before the sight of the highest Judge. What shall I say of obedience [Note: [Col. 0217C] Mabillon: *loquar*, “shall I say.”], when the whole monastic life consists in the simplicity of obedience? A father and pastor will give God account of what he commands [Col. 0218A] and the examples by which he lives before them; likewise sons and flock will give account to the judge of all of the devotion with which they obey paternal commands.

Therefore keep peace and concord among yourselves with all your heart. Nothing without peace pleases God, not even an offering at the altar. Let each outdo the other in honor, according to the Apostle (Romans 12:10). Let elders admonish younger men as sons in a spirit of gentleness (1 Peter 5); and let the younger fulfill the Fathers’ commands, as though divinely spoken, with all humility, preserving in the fear of God the chastity of their own bodies, so that the Holy Spirit may deign to dwell in them. “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3:17). Be zealous in reading holy Scripture, so that you can build up and console one another [Col. 0218B]. Whoever will not learn in youth cannot know in old age. As the worldly miser strives daily to increase his wealth, so let the servant of God strive daily to gather the treasures of wisdom into the sacks of his breast, that he may be a learned scribe in God’s Church, bringing from the treasury of his heart new and old gifts of heavenly knowledge to his fellow servants (Matthew 13:52), and, according to Daniel’s prophecy, teaching many, may shine in perpetual blessedness like a firmament adorned with stars (Daniel 12:3).

I beg you, brothers, do not judge me presumptuous because of this little page of admonition. Read with the eyes of humility what I dictated with the tongue of love, and strengthen my weakness with the aid of your prayers, that by God’s mercy I, a sinner, may deserve to receive pardon for my sins [Col. 0218C] and with you hear that desirable voice: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34).

## Letter LIII
@ [Col. 0217D] **To the Brothers of Corbie.** Thus, indeed, the title of this letter is given in the Harleian manuscript, although the very inscription that follows this letter seems to contradict it: “To the brothers serving God under the protection of the blessed bishop Leodegar.” For both Corbies, the old and the new, had been dedicated under the patronage of other saints: the former to the holy apostle Peter, as we noted in connection with Letter 191; the latter initially to Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, and then to Saint Vitus the Martyr. The inscription of the preceding letter, “To the brothers in the church of Saint Liudger or Leodegar, bishop,” is, in Mabillon’s judgment, to be understood of the monks of Murbach in Alsace. For that monastery was founded about the year 727 by Saint Pirmin, and was dedicated to the honor of Saint Leodegar because Eberhard, the count and founder of the place, was related to this saint through his mother’s family. His grandmother was Bereswinda, sister of Sigrada, Leodegar’s mother. The head of that same holy martyr was also deposited there at the very foundation of the monastery and is still preserved there; consequently, although the monastery was originally built also in honor of Mary, the holy Mother of God, and of Saint Michael the Archangel, in the course of time Saint Leodegar was preferred to the other patrons of the place, as Mabillon proves from the charters of Charlemagne and Emperor Lothar, *Annals*, book XX, p. 77.

**TO THE BROTHERS OF CORBIE.** He praises their good manner of life, which he once experienced among them. He commends himself to their prayers and exhorts them to the pursuit of virtue.

To the most holy brothers in Christ, serving God under the protection of the blessed bishop Leodegar, Alcuin sends greetings.

**Long ago**

@ [Col. 0219C]

**Long ago, following the footsteps of my teacher.** Alcuin had two teachers at York, Egbert and Aelbert, as we explained in the general preface. It is not established that Egbert ever came to Gaul or Alsace, where the monastery of Murbach is situated; but concerning Aelbert, who had been placed in charge of the schools at York by Egbert, his predecessor as bishop, it is related that, eager for broader learning, he traveled through foreign regions for love of knowledge, in case he might find and bring back any books or new instruction. He also went to Rome, where he was honorably received by kings and the highest-ranking men and was almost detained there, etc. Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXIV, p. 211, no. 12. The author of the poem *On the Bishops of York*, whom we believe to be Alcuin himself, likewise testifies, verse 1525, that Alcuin always remained devoted to his father and teacher Aelbert:

> Yet to another he handed over treasures dearer than all else,  
> His books, to his son who always remained devoted to his Father.

I therefore believe that Alcuin at that time accompanied his teacher on the journey, and that on the same occasion he came to the notice of Charlemagne, “who, as the author of the *Life* bears witness, knew him because he had once been sent to him by his teacher.” I think this is also to be understood of the journey undertaken before the year 780, which Alcuin relates about himself in Letter 101: namely, that as a young man he went to Rome, spent several days in the royal city of Pavia, and attended the disputation of the Jew Julius with the teacher Peter.

Following the footsteps of my teacher, I saw and loved the praiseworthy manner of life of your community, and I desired to be among you myself, as one of you. Therefore I beseech your most devout affection, dearest brothers, that you deign to have me as a brother in your holy prayers, as one of you, so that through the intercession of your holiness I may deserve to receive from God Jesus forgiveness for my sins. He is the salvation and blessedness of all who hope in him. You always honor and love him in the holy observance of the regulated life, so that he may find in you a dwelling worthy of himself, as we most certainly believe. What prosperity could be lacking to that community where he is in the midst of them who said: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matt. XXVIII, 20)?

Always maintain true peace in holy charity, obedience without murmuring, and humility without pretence. These are the chief virtues of monastic life and are pleasing to the Holy Spirit as a dwelling place. And instruct your boys and young men with every diligence in chastity, holiness, and ecclesiastical discipline, so that they may be considered worthy to occupy your place after you and, through constant practice, to intercede for you in holy and acceptable prayers before God.

May the Lord God, who has gathered you into the fold of holiness, deign himself to increase your number and grant you to stand at his right hand on the day of judgment, to hear the loving sentence with which he will say to his saints: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom that has been prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV, 34).

@ [Col. 0220D] **Edition of Quercetanus, 88, from a manuscript (Frobenius, 48).** It was sent to the brothers of the church of York, which was then vacant of its pastor, namely in the year 796, when Eanbald the elder died on the fourth day before the Kalends of August and the younger succeeded him (Roger Hoveden, under this year).

## LETTER LIV

**TO THE MOST BELOVED FRIENDS AT YORK.** *(Year 796, in August.)*

He exhorts them to avoid the stain of simony in the election of a bishop.

To the most beloved friends, greetings.

[Col. 0220A] I ask you, by the faith of charity, to act faithfully and wisely in the election of a bishop, if an election must take place.

@ [Col. 0220D] **Before I come.** Thus Alcuin was summoned, as a member of that church, to be present at the new election, but he was prevented from coming by a fever and by the king’s delay in Saxony, as is read in the following letter.

Before I come, I appeal to you again and again by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ: do not under any circumstances allow anyone to acquire a bishopric through the heresy of simony, because, if this happens, it will be the utter ruin of the people. This is the worst heresy, namely simony, which Saint Peter condemned with an eternal anathema (Acts VIII, 14, 20 ff.). Whoever sells a bishopric will receive gold, but will also lose the kingdom of God.

Until now the holy church of York has remained inviolate in its election. See that it is not stained in your days. If it should—God forbid—lose its ecclesiastical authority, I fear that you may lose the eternal kingdom. [Col. 0220B] Judas sold the Bridegroom, that is, Christ. Whoever sells the bride, that is, the Church, is guilty of the same crime, because Christ and the Church are one body, as the Apostle testifies (Eph. V, 23). The seller, however, must be outside the Church; and whoever is outside the Church, where will he be except with the devil in eternal perdition? Do not fear having heard the truth spoken to you. For the books produced by the Holy Spirit testify to what I say. I desire you to be without blemish in the sight of God, to reign happily in this age, and to rejoice forever with Christ. Live and prosper happily in Christ.

{63}

@ [Col. 0220D] **Edition of Quercetanus, 52; Canisius, 30 (Frobenius, 49).** Written to a friend, perhaps a bishop or someone powerful in secular authority, who might protect the new election of a bishop—of York, I think—against every act of violence.

## LETTER LV

**TO A CERTAIN PERSON.** *(Year 796, in August.)*

He asks him to defend the church from every act of violence while a new bishop is being elected, and to keep the eternal days in mind. [Col. 0220C]

To the beloved lord of all, eternal salvation in Christ.

**Having heard from**

@ [Col. 0220D] **From Eanbald.** This Eanbald may perhaps be the same person whom Letter 7 (now 6) calls a presbyter and who shortly afterward was elected bishop of the church of York.

Having heard from Eanbald, your servant, of the health and prosperity you desired, I confess that I rejoiced greatly, because the charity and faith that once began to dwell in our hearts can never depart. And the closer the time of recompense approaches, [Col. 0221A] the more carefully he ought to observe it, so that whoever first passes from this world may feel that he has left a friend behind in this world. But as for me, your son, the severity of fever and

@ [Col. 0221C] **The king’s delay in Saxony.** Concerning this delay of the king, the chronicle of Moissac under the year 796 says: “That same summer King Charles himself remained in Saxony with his two sons, namely Charles [Col. 0221D] and Louis, etc.”

The king’s delay in Saxony kept me from coming to you, as I desired. May divine mercy grant me to see your face in joy before I die. I also desire and beseech you that, if it can be done, I may find you in that dignity of honor in which I saw you when I was departing. Nevertheless, if something else should please your mind, I ask that you absolutely permit no violence to be done to the church of Christ; but let the brothers

@ [Col. 0221D] **By free election.** See the preceding letter.

By free election, in the fear of the Most High God, let them choose the best person, with God’s help. For in the holy canons a terrible anathema is pronounced against all who inflict any violence upon the church of Christ. Know that you have always loved our family and have done them many good deeds. But now we especially need to do good to them, so that wherever our eternal rest shall be, there too they may be perpetual intercessors for us.

@ [Col. 0221D] **The brief exhortation that follows is absent from Canisius; it was supplied by Quercetanus from a manuscript.**

Now is the time for us to foresee the eternal days and, with all moderation and integrity and generosity in almsgiving, to prepare a way for ourselves to heaven. All glory is transitory and will depart like a shadow (Job VIII, 8, 9). Therefore let us hasten to eternal glory through good works. Let us avoid all the vanities of the world, so that we may deserve to reach the heavenly blessedness. Let us live for God through the days of this life that seem to remain for us, so that after this life we may attain his mercy. May divine clemency grant you happy days in this life and deign to bestow upon you eternal glory with his saints, most beloved lord and father.

@ [Col. 0221D] The distinguished Justus Fontaninus first published this letter, together with the notes of Abbot Domenico Passionei, later a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, in the *Appendix to the Vindications of Ancient Charters*, p. 266. Basnage subsequently appended the same letter to the Canisian collection. Everywhere, however, it is mutilated at the beginning and end; here we present it complete and more accurately corrected from the Salzburg manuscript. We have abridged the longer notes of His Eminence Passionei, although they are full of sacred learning.

## LETTER LVI

**TO EANBALD, BISHOP.** *(Year 796, around the month of August.)*

He congratulates him on attaining his dignity, exhorts him to pastoral care and to arranging everything well, and commends himself to his memory and prayers.

To his most beloved son in Christ,

@ [Col. 0221D] **To Eanbald.** Malmesbury calls him the third successor of Egbert, *History of the Kings of England*, book I, chapter 3, p. 24, edition of Henry Savile. Hence an error undoubtedly entered the same Malmesbury, *On the Bishops of England*, book III, p. 269, where, omitting Egbert’s successor Ethelbert, he conflates both Eanbalds into one in these words: “This Egbert’s successor was the elder Eanbald, an energetic disciple of Alcuin.” These words should be corrected as follows: “His successor was Ethelbert, after whom the elder Eanbald was substituted; and after his death came the other Eanbald, an energetic disciple of Alcuin.” Eanbald I died in 796 on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, and Alcuin’s disciple Eanbald II was immediately substituted for him; he received the pallium from Rome in 797. **Alford.**—Alcuin therefore wrote this letter to that disciple of his in 796, to instruct him concerning the episcopal office. **Passionei.**

To Archbishop Eanbald, his devoted father in all things, Albinus sends greetings.

[Laus et gloria Domino Deo omnipotenti, qui dies meos in prosperitate bona conservavit, ut in filii mei charissimi exaltatione gauderem, et aliquem ego ultimus Ecclesiae vernaculus, ejus donante gratia qui est omnium bonorum largitor, erudirem ex filiis meis qui dignus haberetur {64} dispensator esse mysteriorum Christi (I Cor. IV, 1), et laborare vice mea in Ecclesia, ubi ego nutritus et eruditus fueram, et praeesse thesauris sapientiae, in quibus me magister meus dilectus]

[Praise and glory be to the omnipotent Lord God, who has preserved my days in good prosperity, so that I might rejoice in the elevation of my most beloved son; and so that I, the least servant of the Church, might, by the grace of him who is the giver of every good thing, instruct one of my sons who would be considered worthy to be a steward of the mysteries of Christ (I Cor. IV, 1), to labor in my place in the Church where I had been nurtured and instructed, and to preside over the treasures of wisdom in which my beloved teacher]

@ [Col. 0222D] **Helbrechtus.** Malmesbury has “Egbert.” I consider the reading of the Salzburg manuscript preferable, and I think that by this name we are to understand another teacher of Alcuin’s, called Aelbert by the Anonymous Poet and Elcbert in the *Life of Alcuin*. Just as Malmesbury conflated the two Eanbalds, as we said in the note above, so here he confuses Egbert and Helbrecht. See volume II, the poem *On the Bishops and Saints of the Church of York*, verse 1532 ff.

**Helbrechtus, archbishop,**

@ [Col. 0222D] **Left an heir.** See the cited poem *On the Bishops of York*.

Left an heir. But now I must pray with all earnestness for divine mercy, that he who was always a consolation to me through his obedience may survive me in this life—not that I wish for my death, but that his life may be prolonged. For it is not sons who ought to inherit for their fathers, but fathers for their sons.]

Behold, dearest son! Through God you possess everything that a human being could hope for, and even more than our littleness [Al., wickedness] would dare to hope. Now, however, act manfully and bravely. Complete the work of the Lord that you have in your hands, for the reward of our soul and the salvation of many souls. Let your tongue not cease from preaching, your foot from going about among the flock entrusted to you, or your hand from laboring so that alms may be given and the holy Church of God may everywhere be exalted. Be an example of salvation to all. Let there be in you an example of the holiest conduct (I Thess. I, 7); in you, consolation for the afflicted; in you, strength for the doubtful; in you, the rigor of discipline; in you, confidence in truth; in you, the hope of every goodness. Let not the pomp of the world exalt you; let not luxury of food weaken you; let not the vanity of clothing soften you; let not the tongues of flatterers [Col. 0222C] deceive you; let not the hostility of detractors disturb you; let not sorrows break you, nor joys lift you up. Do not be a reed shaken by the wind (Matt. XI, 7), a flower falling beneath the breath of a storm (James I, 11), a crumbling wall (Ps. LXI, 4), or a house set upon sand (Matt. VII, 24, 26); rather, be a temple of the living God, built upon a firm rock, whose inhabitant is the Paraclete Spirit himself. How many days do you think you may have? Imagine in your mind something like fifty years—and behold, these too have an end. Nor should you expect to reach even that point. Let the weakness of your body make you strong in soul, and say with the Apostle: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (II Cor. XII, 10). Let the chastisement of the body be the soul’s progress. Show yourself gentle and humble toward the better, harsh and stern toward the proud, becoming all things to all people so that you may win all (I Cor. IX, 22). Let honey and wormwood be in your hands; let each person eat from them whatever suits him. Let the one who wishes to feed on gentle preaching receive honey; let the one who needs stern rebuke drink from the wormwood—yet in such a way that he may be permitted to hope for the honey of forgiveness if the rosy shame of repentance comes first.

Let all your affairs be conducted honorably and in due order (I Cor. XIV, 40). Let a time be appointed for reading; let [prayer] have its appointed hours; and let the solemn celebrations of Mass take place at their proper time. “The one who observes the day observes it for the Lord” (Rom. [Col. 0223B] XIV, 6). Let joy at banquets be modest; let joy during fasts be chaste; let the face be washed with repentance; let the head be anointed with the oil of mercy, so that everything may be acceptable to the Lord God, who chose you as his priest. For every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters pertaining to God (Heb. V, 1). Aaron stood with the censer of his dignity between the living and the dead, so that the anger of God might not burn further against the people (Num. XVI, 47, 48). The priest of God must be a preacher of [the Word] and of his will to the people, and an intercessor with God for the people, as a mediator between God and human beings. Whoever climbs to a lofty place must beware lest he fall, because the fall from a higher place is known to be more dangerous. “Let him who stands take heed lest he fall” (I Cor. X, [Col. 0223C] 12). Let him who lies strive to rise; and let him who runs beware lest he stumble, lest another receive his prize. We must all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each person may render an account of what he has done in the body (Rom. XIV, 10; II Cor. V, 10). Then there will be no time to buy oil; therefore let us take thought beforehand, lest we then have empty vessels (Matt. XXV). Let the preacher’s loins now be girded and his lamps burning in his hands (Luke XII, 35), so that then he may shine like the sun in his Father’s kingdom, be praised by his Lord for the multiplication of the money entrusted to him, and be honored with eternal glory.

Do not think that you are the lord of the world, but its steward. Let the number of your relatives not make you greedy, as though you ought to gather an inheritance for them. There will be no lack of opportunity for gathering if the tinder of greed, which is the root of all evils, catches fire. No heir is better than Christ; no one is a more faithful guardian of your treasure. For the hand of the poor is Christ’s treasury. Whatever you are pleased to entrust to them from your possessions, send it through the hands of the needy. Let your almsgiving be twofold: one part for saving souls, the other for helping the bodies of the needy.
