Therefore presbyters are to be considered worthy of double honor, according to the Apostle, because they are proved to carry out a twofold ministry (I Tim. V, 17). “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX, 6, 7); whoever sows in blessing will reap blessings, and whoever labors more will receive greater reward.

Let your companions be adorned with honorable morals, not conspicuous for the vanity of their clothing but praiseworthy for the dignity of their conduct. “A wise son is the glory of his father.” Let them not be followers of drunkenness but lovers of sobriety, so that many may be built up by their good examples. Let no empty talk or vulgar jesting be heard from their mouths, but holy psalmody. Let them not ride through the fields reciting verses while chasing foxes, but with you

@ [Col. 0223D] **While riding, let them sing psalms.** See Mabillon’s discussion of the Gallican cursus, p. 443, and the *Life of Saint Epiphanius, Bishop of Ticinum*, which is included with the writings of Ennodius in volume I of Sirmond’s works, col. 1666. Thomassin collected various examples of bishops who rode while singing psalms in the preface to the second edition of the Psalter. **Passionei.**

@ [Col. 0224C] **While riding [the Salzburg manuscript has “by alternating with equal voice”], let them sing psalms with sweet modulation.** Never put on the mantle of sacred blessing without the ministry of the deacons standing by. Have subdeacons also, and the other ecclesiastical grades in due order, so that the Church, sevenfold in the gifts of the Holy Spirit, may shine with the sevenfold distinction of ecclesiastical orders. Let each order have the place and clothing appropriate to its dignity; and if the order of elders and dignitaries is to be observed at banquets, how much more in the Church of Christ? Let the clergy be honorable in dress and steadfast in countenance; and, singing with a measured voice, let them strive to please God rather than human beings (I Thess. II, 4). Excessive raising of the voice is a sign of boastfulness; but let everything be done in humility and honorably, and let them not disdain

@ [Col. 0223D] **To learn the Roman orders.** This letter is evidence of the antiquity of the Roman order; certainly no more substantial or older mention of it has yet been brought forward. Concerning it, see Mabillon, volume II of the *Italian Museum*. **Passionei.**

@ [Col. 0224C] To learn the Roman orders, so that, according to the measure of their strength, they may imitate the head of the Churches of Christ—blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whom our Lord Jesus Christ appointed head of the flock chosen for himself—and may deserve to receive his eternal blessing. Like a most wise bee, prove by learning everything that belongs to honorable conduct, and retain by choosing whatever seems best.

Let your holy diligence foresee

@ [Col. 0224D] **Teachers for the boys.** Alcuin speaks frequently of these matters. Saint Augustine, sent there by Saint Gregory, introduced into England the practice of educating boys, as John the Deacon relates in the *Life of that holy pontiff*, book II, no. 7. **The same.**

@ [Col. 0224C] Let teachers be provided for the boys; let the clergy [Baluz., “clerics”] be divided into separate groups according to the manner of those who read books, those who serve in singing, and those assigned to the study of writing. Have teachers for each of these orders as well, so that those who are idle may not wander about aimlessly through various places, engage in empty games, or be given over to other foolish pursuits. Let your most careful foresight consider all these things, dearest son, so that in the principal seat of our people there may be found a fountain of every goodness and learning, from which the thirsty traveler or lover of ecclesiastical discipline may be able to draw whatever his soul desires. [You have me as your most devoted helper in all these matters, although I live in a foreign land.]

[Col. 0225A] Let your most diligent piety also consider where

@ [Col. 0225D] **Hospices.** On these, see Louis Thomassin, *On Ancient and New Ecclesiastical Discipline*, part I, book II, chapter 89. **Passionei.**

@ [Col. 0225C] Let your most diligent piety also consider where you should order hospices—that is, hospitals—to be established, in which the poor and travelers may receive daily hospitality, [and from our possessions may obtain support].

Behold, I am wearied by a twofold burden, namely old age and illness; and perhaps the dreaded day is approaching when the pitcher will be shattered above the spring and the golden cord will return [to its place] (Eccles. XII, 6). Let the dust return to its earth and the spirit to God who gave it (Eccles. XII, 7); and I tremble with great fear, wondering how he will examine me when I am then to be judged. You, most faithful son, labor for the soul of your father, whether now, while he is in this dust of death, or then, as he hastens toward judgment, so that he may have rest and also forgiveness of his sins, and so that the stains [Col. 0225B] that have clung to him from this muddy dwelling of the little body may be washed away through fraternal intercession.

But even after this writing, I commend all my sons, brothers, and friends to your most careful fidelity, whether they are with me in my pilgrimage or seem to be dwelling with you in their homeland. Regard them as your own and not as strangers. Let them all look to you, rejoice in you, and find consolation in you; let them honor you as a father. Love them as sons, so that there may be one peace and harmony among all in the charity of Christ. May he, in his great compassion and mercy, cause all of you to abound in heavenly blessing, protect, govern, and guide you, and cause you to advance in every goodness, for the increase of my mind and the progress of your salvation, for the exaltation of many, [Col. 0225C] so that very many may be instructed by your {66} good examples and may deserve to come with you to everlasting life.

I ask that this little letter be written out more carefully, that it go with you and remain with you, and that it speak to you often in place of a father’s voice, my son, my dearest son, and my most desired son in Christ. May almighty God, in his great compassion, cause you to prosper for many happy years in this present life, for the exaltation of his holy Church, and may he deign to grant you eternal glory in the life to come.]

@ [Col. 0225D] **Edition of Quercetanus, 77; Canisius, 44 (Frobenius, 51).**

## LETTER LVII

@ [Col. 0225D] **To Bishop Aethelred.** Canisius has this inscription, which Quercetanus omitted. I have no doubt, however, that it should read “To Aethelhard.” For he warns him not to abandon the flock entrusted to him by God to govern merely by fleeing the persecution of his people. This warning concerns Aethilhard, bishop of Canterbury, whose subsequent flight is also censured in Letter 75.

**TO AETHELRED, BISHOP: THAT HE SHOULD NOT ABANDON HIS FLOCK.** *(Year 796.)*

He consoles him in persecution and tribulation and exhorts him to manly perseverance, so that he will not flee from the sheep. [Col. 0226A]

Having received your letter, holy brother, I rejoiced at your well-being but was saddened by the tribulation and persecutions that, as I learned from your letter, you are suffering from your people. Nevertheless, we read that those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake are blessed, as the Lord says, “for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 10). Therefore I urge you, venerable brother, not to cease striving manfully in complete faith and tireless devotion for the sheep entrusted to you by Christ, lest you be judged by that very Lord and shepherd of all to be a hireling who flees rather than a steadfast shepherd (John X).

{67} Look to him who laid down his life for his sheep (John X, 11), who, giving a general command to all, said: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke IX, 23). To whom are you leaving the flock of Christ as you depart? I do not say this as though I were making excuses for failing to do good to the servants of God, but rather to exhort you to bring the good works you have begun to the end of eternal salvation. “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22). Therefore

@ [Col. 0225D] **I wrote to King Offa.** This letter is missing; it might perhaps reveal what that tribulation was which Aethelhard had to suffer from his people. The persecution discussed here is therefore not the one that King Offa of the Mercians inflicted upon the church of Canterbury by transferring the bishoprics subject to that metropolitan see to Lichfield, as Canisius thought at this point. Rather, King Offa is not reproached here as a persecutor but is appealed to by Alcuin as a defender against other persecutors. It is therefore also clear that the present letter cannot be dated later than the year 796, in which King Offa died.

I wrote to King Offa so that he might assist and defend you, according to his ability [Al., power], and protect the holy Church, so that you might be permitted to serve God and multiply your talent in the place where you received it, and await the reward of eternal blessedness, as your Lord says: “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matt. XXV, 21).

## LETTER LVIII

**A CONSOLATORY LETTER TO A MOTHER ON THE DEATH OF HER SON.** *(Year 796.)*

@ [Col. 0226D] **To a most beloved mother in Christ.** As I infer from the words of this letter, she was a certain English matron: “Not knowing, amid the misery of this storm that recently disturbed our people.” He undoubtedly refers to the disturbances that arose in 796, after the killing of King Æthelred of Northumbria and King Ecgfrith of Mercia, through various invaders of the kingdom. Someone might perhaps think that this mother, whom Alcuin consoles over the death of her son, was Quendrida or Quindreda, the mother of the aforementioned Ecgfrith, unless one prefers to understand her as Eadgyth, whom he likewise consoles for a similar reason in Letter 200. But why would Alcuin write two consolatory letters concerning the same matter to the same mother?

To the most beloved mother in Christ, Alcuin the deacon, a faithful son in charity, sends greetings.

Many are friends in prosperity but few in adversity; and the rarer they are, the dearer they become, while minds change along with the world. Some rejoice in another’s happiness but avoid the storm of misfortune [Manuscript: “he avoids”]. For just as light and darkness alternate in their turns, so the prosperity and adversity of this life are changeable. Yet the sorrows that occur must be endured with courage, and the joys that gladden us must be received with moderation. Therefore a modest and devout mother ought not to grieve excessively at the death of her son; rather, she ought to prepare herself through worthy merits to reach that life where no enemy is feared and no friend is abandoned.

A good mother has Christ as her consoler in place of her son, and he never abandons those who hope in him. It is better to rejoice in one who is alive than to grieve over one who is dying [Manuscript: “to rejoice in the living, to grieve over the dying”]. Why do we mourn what we cannot change? A dead person cannot be recalled to the present life; a living person can reach the dead. The body that we cherish with such care will afterward be food for worms. The soul, therefore, will rejoice or grieve according to the quality of its merits; [Col. 0227B] and the dwelling it prepares for itself during these few days will be the one it receives for eternity. Therefore we must labor at every moment for the soul’s rest, so that, since it must live forever, it may also live forever in blessedness and happiness.

I ask you, sweetest mother, to have me, although unworthy [Manuscript: “unworthy” in a different form], as a spiritual son in place of your natural son, loving you with no less faith, although possessing less dignity. Do not grieve over the distance or the lowliness of my appearance, while the charity of the Holy Spirit remains faithfully with you through my consolation; and whatever is best in me—that is, unfeigned faith and unfailing charity—you will always have with you.

Not knowing, amid the misery of this storm [Manuscript: “the misery”], which recently disturbed our people, where your fortune or your will would lead you, I therefore did not know with what counsel to strengthen you, except that you should serve the Lord Jesus with your whole heart and place all the hope of your consolation in his compassion. He says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI, 28, 29).

## LETTER LIX

**TO EDILBURGA.** *(Year 796.)*

He recalls teachings once given to her; grieves over the infidelity of her homeland; and commends the noblewoman Liudgarda to her prayers.

To his most beloved daughter in the Lord,

@ [Col. 0227D] **To Edilburga, undoubtedly abbess of some monastery in England.** For Alcuin asks her to have Liudgarda, a noblewoman—perhaps a queen, the wife of Charlemagne—entered in the ecclesiastical records of her sisters, certainly nuns. I have no information about the family into which this maiden was born, or who her sister was who had been deprived of her husband’s marriage-bed. The infidelity of her homeland, which Alcuin accuses here and about which he often complains elsewhere, is certainly that which the nobles and people perpetrated against their legitimate kings in the year 796; see Letters 46, 47, and others. At that time I find two distinguished women deprived of their husbands’ marriage-beds: one, Elfleda, Queen Offa’s daughter, the widowed wife of King Æthelred of Northumbria, who was killed by his own people that year; the other, Alfrida, or Alfreda, or, as others write, Ætheldryth, a royal maiden, another daughter of Offa, betrothed to Æthelberht, king of the East Angles, but who never reached her husband’s bed, since her fiancé had first been treacherously killed in 793 at the instigation of his mother Quendrida. Perhaps Edilburga, to whom this letter was written, is no different from Alfrida, the sister of Alfleda, who after the killing of her fiancé became a nun and abbess of Crowland. The names of persons vary greatly among those ancient writers, and in obscure matters some allowance must also be made for conjecture. See Alford, *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Anglo-Saxons*, under the years 792, no. 2, and 794, no. 6, and elsewhere.

To Edilburga, greetings.

[Col. 0227D] Since the jealous distance between our lands prevents the sweetness of mutual conversation, we are given the opportunity to show the sweetness of charity through the service of letters, so that [Manuscript: “and”] what the voice cannot accomplish, the writing may express. Therefore we ought to attend to exhortations concerning salvation with no less reverence than to the admonition of personal conversation. In the latter, fear often persuades agreement; in the former, the faith of the reader cooperates in salvation.

Those teachings with which I admonished you, venerable daughter, with awareness of the knowledge of the supreme God, we considered it sufficiently necessary to beg you to retain firmly in your mind [Manuscript: “diximus,” “we said”]. I cannot entrust to writing anything new that I did not then impress upon you in speech [Perhaps: “that I now impress upon you”]. You yourself know how diligently I urged you concerning purity of body and holiness of soul; how I instructed you concerning the duty of humility, vigilance in prayer, generosity in almsgiving, purity of confession, firmness of faith, and the observance everywhere of holy charity, so that by these steps you might ascend to the height of heavenly glory.

Behold, the infidelity of my homeland now so horrifies me that I fear returning [Manuscript: “timeo,” “I fear”], not knowing what good I can accomplish there, except to mourn its impending ruin and to turn again and again to the lamentations of the weeping Jeremiah. In the fourfold order of the alphabet [Manuscript: “albabeti”] he mourned Jerusalem as it was falling, and some part of this ruin has, as I think, stirred hot tears in you on behalf of your beloved sister [Manuscript: “delicte”]. Nevertheless, she who has been deprived of her husband’s marriage-bed must be exhorted to serve Christ in a monastery and to make her temporary sorrow an incentive to everlasting joy.

[Col. 0228C] I ask you faithfully to remember our name, together with all your companions, in your most holy prayers. Also hold in your affection as a sister the noblewoman Liudgarda, who sent you a cloak as a small gift; and order her name to be written, together with the names of your sisters, in the ecclesiastical records. Her friendship is honorable and useful to you. I have sent to your affection a small flask and a paten.

@ [Col. 0228D] “To offer … the offering.” Concerning the daily offerings of princes and other faithful people at Mass, read the celebrated D. Martène, *De Antiquis Ecclesiae Ritibus*, book I, part I, pp. 378 ff., Rouen edition, 1700.

—to offer in them an offering to the Lord God with your hands. And while you look upon it with your eyes, say: “Christ, have mercy on your little servant Alcuin.” I would also like you to make it your daily practice to offer a gift to God at the altar, because apostolic authority established this custom; therefore it must not be omitted but diligently continued.

Live happily for God, dearest daughter, always—

[Col. 0228D] And, mindful of sweet Alcuin, farewell, dear friend.

## LETTER LX. TO KING EARDWULF (Year 796)

He exhorts the king, elevated to the throne, to procure both his own salvation and that of his people. He frightens him by the example of his predecessors.

[Col. 0229A]

To the illustrious man

@ [Col. 0229C] King Eardwulf.

The older writers call him Eardulf, changing the first two letters. According to Hoveden, fol. 406, after King Æthelred of Northumbria was killed by his own people in 796, he succeeded to the throne. “Eardulf,” he says, “son of Earnulf, summoned from exile, was raised to the royal insignia, and at York, in the church of Saint Peter, at the altar of blessed Paul—where that people had first received the grace of baptism—was consecrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of June.” See Pagius on this year, no. 25, and Alfort on the year 794, no. 6.

In this letter Alcuin exhorts Eardwulf, rescued from present dangers and recently raised to the royal throne, to procure both his own salvation and that of his people.

To King Eardwulf, Alcuin the deacon sends greetings.

Mindful of the friendship once agreed between us, and greatly rejoicing also in your revered greeting, I have undertaken, in a few written lines, to admonish your praiseworthy person concerning the prosperity of the kingdom granted to you by God [Ms., “conferred”], and concerning the salvation of your soul, and concerning how the honor entrusted to you may, by God’s gift, remain secure.

You know very well from what dangers divine mercy has delivered you, and how easily, when he willed, he advanced you to the kingdom. Always remember and give thanks for such great gifts of God bestowed upon you, especially by doing, insofar as you are able to understand it, his will with your whole heart; and be obedient to the servants of God who remind you of his commandments.

Know with absolute certainty that no one else can preserve your life except the one who has now delivered you from death; nor can anyone protect and keep you in this position of honor except the one who, in his gratuitous goodness, granted this dignity to you.

Diligently preserve mercy and justice in your mind and in your kingdom, because, as Solomon says—and still more because God grants it—“By mercy and justice the throne of the kingdom is established” (Prov. XVI, 12).

Consider most attentively for what sins your predecessors lost their lives and kingdom; and take the greatest care to avoid doing such things, lest a similar judgment befall you. God condemned some for perjury; he punished others for adultery [Ms., “adulterous women”]; he avenged the greed and frauds of others; the injustices of others did not please him.

God is not a respecter of persons (Acts X, 34), but those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God. First educate yourself in every goodness and sobriety; then educate the people over whom you appear to preside in every modesty of life and dress, in every truth of faith and judgment, in observance of God’s commandments, and in uprightness of conduct.

Thus you will both strengthen your kingdom, save your people, and free them from God’s anger, which for a long time had been threatening them through unmistakable signs.

[Col. 0230A] Such a quantity of noblemen’s and rulers’ blood would never have been shed among them, nor would the pagans have so devastated the holy places, nor would such injustice and arrogance have prevailed among the people, unless God’s manifest vengeance were threatening the inhabitants of the land.

But you, preserved, as I believe, for better times and kept for the correction of your country, with God’s grace assisting you, labor with all your determination for the salvation of your soul according to God’s will, and for the prosperity of the country and people entrusted to you. Thus, through the correction of those subject to your authority, the present kingdom may be happily established for you and your grandsons, and the glory of the future kingdom may be granted to you eternally.

I beg that this little document be kept with you and read frequently, in memory of your salvation and our affection, so that almighty God may deign to preserve you, for the advancement of his holy Church and for our prosperity, flourishing in the kingdom for a long time and progressing in every good work.

Live and fare well, by God’s gift, forever and ever.

## LETTER LXI. TO OSBALD (Year 796)

He exhorts Osbald, whom he suspects of regicide and of disturbances among the people, to change his life and to take thought for his own salvation and that of his people.

To his beloved friend

@ [Col. 0229D] Osbald.

Alcuin calls him a patrician in Letter 11, and here regards him as suspect in the killing of his lord, namely King Æthelred, and in the shedding of much blood among princes and people during those disturbances.

The following account of Roger of Hoveden, p. 406, in the letter cited earlier, is relevant here. He writes:

“In that same year (796), King Æthelred was killed at Corbridge, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May. Osbald the patrician was established as king by certain princes of that people; but after twenty-seven days he was abandoned by the entire royal family and by the princes, driven into exile, and expelled from the kingdom. He withdrew to the island of Lindisfarne with a few companions; and from there he reached the king of the Picts by ship with some of his brothers.”

Alfort incorrectly connected the killing of Æthelred, king of Northumbria, with the year 794, contrary to the authority of the author of Huntingdon, p. 344, whom he himself cites; moreover, he assigned Æthelred only five years. The author of Huntingdon writes: “In the eleventh year of the British king”—that is, of the king of the West Saxons—“the Northumbrians killed their king Æthelred.”

In addition, the lunar eclipse that occurred in the seventh year of King Æthelred, on the twenty-eighth day of March, a Monday, after midnight, as Calvisius observed in his chronological work, belongs to the present year of Christ, 796, to which the same Æthelred lived (Pagius on the year 796, no. 25). See also Letters 11 and 47.

To Osbald, Alcuin the deacon sends greetings.

I am sorry for you because you did not obey me. Two years ago I urged you in my letters to abandon the secular life and serve God according to your vow. Behold, now a worse reputation and a more unfortunate cause have disturbed your life.

Nevertheless, return—return and fulfill what you vowed—and seek the means by which you may attain the service of God, lest you perish with the ungodly, if you are innocent of your lord’s blood; but if you are guilty by consent or counsel, confess your sin, reconcile yourself to God, and flee the company of criminals.

The friendship of God and the saints is better for you than that of those who act wickedly. Do not add sin to sin by laying waste your country and shedding blood. Consider how much blood has been shed through you or through your relatives: the blood of kings, princes, and the people.

Unhappy is the generation through which such evils have befallen the country. I beg you by God: free yourself, lest your soul perish [Col. 0231A] forever.

While you have the light, run, hasten, hurry to the mercy of God, who is ready to receive penitents and console those who turn back to him, lest a day come upon you when you wish to act but cannot.

Do not set shame before yourself as an obstacle to abandoning what you have begun [Ms., “putting down what you have begun]. Greater is the shame of allowing your soul to perish forever than of abandoning wicked men in the present. Rather, if you are able to convert any of them from the wickedness they have obtained [read: perpetrated], do so diligently, so that you may receive the reward both for your own conversion from evil and for that of another.

This is charity, which “covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. IV, 9). By doing this, live happily and fare well in peace.

I beg that this little document be read frequently in your presence, so that you may remember yourself in God and understand how great a concern I, though now far away, have for your salvation.

If you are able to persuade the people among whom you will be an exile concerning their salvation, do not neglect it, so that, by God’s gracious gift, you may arrive more quickly at your own salvation as well.

## LETTER LXII. TO A CERTAIN ARCHBISHOP (Year 796)

He announces that, having laid aside worldly occupations, he is preparing for the Lord’s coming.

To the most holy father, the archbishop, Alcuin, your humble son, sends greetings.

Let your sweetest paternal affection know that I, your son,

@ [Col. 0231D] Having laid aside worldly occupations.

This relates to what Alcuin writes to Charles in Letter 129, written in 801:

“Almost five years ago”—that is, in 796—“I considered, God as my witness, not with a false heart, withdrawing from secular occupations; but, by the counsel of your pious foresight, I was transferred into the service of Saint Martin, profitable, by God’s gift, to the Catholic faith and ecclesiastical order.”

Hence I judge that the present letter was written in 796, when Alcuin, having laid aside worldly occupations, left the court and withdrew to the monastery at Tours. We have said more about this withdrawal in the General Preface.

Having laid aside worldly occupations, I desire to devote myself to God alone. Therefore I beg your Holiness that the blessing and prayer of your exceptional sanctity may reach me, so that divine clemency may deign to preserve the few days of my life that remain in his holy service, for the salvation of my soul.

Since it is necessary for every person to prepare himself with watchful care for the coming of the Lord his God, how much more necessary is it for the elderly, who are worn down by years and frequent illnesses, to adorn their lamps with anxious care, so that, by God’s gift, they may be made worthy to meet the heavenly bridegroom with shining lamps, and not be forced to stand outside while others enter the banquet of the heavenly King.

May the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ grant that I, your son, may enter it with you, most holy Father, in perpetual prosperity. May the Lord God cause the venerable gray hairs of your Holiness to flourish with the gifts of holy virtues [Supply: “to flourish,” or something similar], most desired Father!

## LETTER LXIII. TO KING COENWULF OF THE MERCIANS (Year 796)

Having been raised to the kingdom, he exhorts him to royal virtues.

[Col. 0232A]

To the most excellent man

@ [Col. 0231D] Coenwulf.

He is called Kenulf by others. After the death of Ecgfrith, he assumed the diadem of the Mercian kingdom in 796, before the ninth day of November, according to the calculation of the celebrated Pagius on the year 796, nos. 25, and 821, nos. 22 and 23.

To Coenwulf, king of the Mercians, Albinus, the humble levite, sends greetings.

I take great joy in your goodness, modesty, and noble conduct, as is entirely fitting for royal dignity: the higher someone is in honor above others, the nobler he should be in every perfection of character, in the beauty of justice, and in the holiness of piety.

For, as is read in ancient histories, the clemency of a king ought to surpass the customs of all men. Holy Scripture also says: “Mercy and truth exalt the throne” (Prov. XX, 28). And in the Psalms it is said of almighty God: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV, 10).

The more brightly a person shines in works of truth and mercy, the greater the image of divinity he possesses within himself.

Always keep in mind the one

@ [Col. 0232D] who raised you from poverty.

Indeed, as Alfort says concerning the year 797: “Kenulf succeeded Ecgfrith by no right or title of blood, but solely through the merit of his virtues. He was a grandson of Penda, through his brother Chenalch, who fathered Kentwin; and Kentwin fathered Cuthbert, the parent of Kenulf.”

He raised you from poverty and set you over the princes of his people. Recognize yourself more as a ruler, shepherd, and steward of God’s gifts than as a lord or exactor.

Always keep in mind the conduct of your most excellent

@ [Col. 0232D] predecessor.

This refers to Offa, king of the Mercians, who died this year, as we have often said.

Always keep in mind the conduct of your most noble predecessor: his modesty in daily life and his zeal in correcting the life of the Christian people. Whatever he arranged well in the kingdom given to you by God, let your devotion diligently continue; but if he acted in any matter greedily or cruelly, recognize that you must avoid this completely.

For it was not without cause that his most noble

@ [Col. 0232D] son, Ecgfrith,

lived for so short a time after his father. The reason for this premature death Alcuin assigns in a letter to the patrician Osbert, which is no longer extant:

“He was not taken away in death because of his own sins, but because his father shed much blood to secure his kingdom.”

William of Malmesbury, book I of *The Kings of England*, chapter 4.

Often a father’s merits are avenged in his children [Ms., “the children”].

Have wise counselors—men who fear God, love justice, desire peace with their friends, and display faith and holiness in a devout way of life.

The English people are being wearied by many tribulations on account of their sins. Through the goodness of kings, the preaching of Christ’s priests, and the religious devotion of the people, they must be raised again to the height of their ancient honor, so that the blessed offspring of our fathers may deserve to possess perpetual happiness, stability in the present kingdom, and strength against its enemies; and so that the Church of Christ may grow and prosper, as it was ordered by the holy Fathers.

Always hold Christ’s priests in honor, most illustrious ruler. For the more reverently you honor the servants of Christ and preachers of the word of God, the more Christ, the true and gracious King, exalts and confirms your honor, with his saints interceding.

May the supreme mercy of the eternal King grant that you reign in long-lasting prosperity and deign to bestow upon you the blessedness of the everlasting kingdom, most desired lord.

## LETTER LXIV. TO SIMEON (Year 796)

He commends the memory of the teachings formerly handed down to him and adds new ones.

To the son of revered dignity and sweetest affection

@ [Col. 0233D] Simeon, the high priest.

It is now clear from another letter of Alcuin’s in the Harleian codex, addressed to Eanbald, archbishop of the church of York, surnamed Simon, that the name Simeon is an assumed name of Eanbald the Younger, archbishop of York; that letter will be presented shortly.

To Simeon, the high priest, Albinus sends greetings of present prosperity and perpetual blessedness in Christ.

I have great confidence in your faith and great praise for your goodness; and I have a great desire that you progress from day to day in the charity of Christ, in the conduct of a religious life, and before God in the glory of the saints’ merits. I have often taken care to admonish your holiness about these things in my letters, so that, just as by God’s gracious gift—and with me instructing your tender years—you were happily

@ [Col. 0233D] brought to this degree of most holy dignity,

so, with all the affection of my heart, I may desire God—and pray to him—that you always stretch forward with the Apostle until you reach the exalted crown of everlasting blessedness.

I have filled your ears with prayers while present and your eyes with the written lines of my pages while absent, to such an extent that now I am unable to find anything new that could be added to the devotion of my past diligence, except that you may recall the words [Ms., “beloved things”] of paternal affection with a watchful mind and take care to reread frequently the writings of pious admonition.

If in these writings you find anything inadequately expressed by the style of my affection, it is not through any fault of my will but through the forgetful error of ignorance, which nevertheless may rightly be forgiven. And would that the devotion of your blessedness were as ready to complete the series of written admonition as my rejoicing affection is ready to admonish.

Only this one thing seemed to me firmly necessary to advise you in this document: do not permit the nobility of mind that I knew to be most fully in you, or the integrity of holy faith that you were accustomed to possess toward everyone, to be corrupted or changed by the counsels of friends or by any ambition of worldly desires.

[Col. 0233D] Not every friend can be a counselor, as Scripture says: “Let your friends be many, but your counselor one” (Ecclus. VI, 6).

Do not allow your goodness to be obscured by the wickedness of others. I do not want the love that you have earned through good piety and goodwill from your own people or from strangers to be overwhelmed by another’s negligence or malice; but may you progress in wisdom, love, and honor before God and men, so that you lack nothing in any grace, but everywhere appear devout and pleasing to God and to all the people.

May God Christ increase, exalt, and preserve forever the authority of your blessedness and the affection of your good will, most beloved lord and son in Christ, and most desirous of every good thing.

## LETTER LXV TO SIMEON THE PRIEST

In prosperity and adversity he advises moderation of spirit; he sends gifts and advises that the clergy be taught the Roman Order. He announces that he is somewhat better after illness. He commends devotion to sacred reading and wisdom.

Albinus

@ [Col. 0234D] To Simeon the priest.

I believe this is the same person to whom the preceding letter was written, and for that reason I wished to add this one, although the year and place from which it was sent are entirely uncertain.

To Simeon the priest, greetings.

I rejoice in your tribulation and prosperity, my dearest son, because bodily tribulation is the soul’s salvation, while prosperity in this life is the joy of friends.

Remember that all the saints suffered tribulations in this world, the bitterness of which is not equal to the reward of future blessedness. Whoever carries the greater burden on his back feels the greater sweat in his body. What is the honor of this world except a heavy burden for the traveler? A traveler who is free goes more happily than one weighed down by the size of his baggage.

Nevertheless, God gives to each according to his own dispensation—this to some, that to others. But let each person labor faithfully, so that he may reign happily with Christ.

@ [Col. 0234D] The cuckoo.

Concerning it, see below the letter to Calvinus and Cuculus.

I sent your holiness a spring cuckoo, together with the little gifts of my poverty. Now, however, I have sent you and the brothers and friends a little wine, and one hundred pounds of tin [perhaps, “pewter”] for carrying out necessary works; and

@ [Col. 0234D] four little cups.

*Caucellus* is a small vessel, a diminutive of *caucus*. The *Rule of the Master*, chapter 27, says: “If he wishes to drink water, let him drink not from a jar in one draught, but according to the measure of a cup, a little pitcher, or a small vessel.” See Du Cange, *Glossary*, under *Caucus* and *Caucellus*.

It seems fitting that the little house of the bells should be roofed with tin, for the sake of its ornament and the renown of the place.

I do not know why you asked me about the ordering and arrangement of a little Missal. Do you not have an abundance of sacramentary booklets arranged according to Roman custom? You also have enough Sacramentaries of the older custom. What need is there to compose new ones when the old are sufficient?

I would have wished you to begin introducing the authority of the Roman Order among your clergy, so that examples might be taken from you and the ecclesiastical offices celebrated among you with reverence and praise.

“But assistants are few,” you may say. Yet the greater the labor of good intention, the greater the crown with which the sum of happiness will reward it. He labors happily who builds himself a house in the kingdom of God, preparing great things from small ones and eternal things from fleeting ones, buying heavenly things with earthly things; for the purchase of one pearl he abandons everything in order to possess the one he has found and preferred above all the delights of treasures.

[Col. 0235A] The bird mentioned earlier was able to tell you about my illness. Glory to God! We are somewhat better, but the body’s full strength has not returned. Therefore order people to pray for us more diligently, because the time is approaching when this lodging must be abandoned and the unknown sought.

But may your prayer and the very welcome, indeed exceedingly necessary, gifts of alms come after us. Let faith be shown in the son, so that the Father may rejoice in a wise and faithful son. He does not die who lives in a prudent son.

Renew your devotion to sacred reading in every way, lest our labor in collecting books perish. Do not find it burdensome to give the weight of gold for the acquisition of wisdom, since, according to Solomon, nothing in this world can be compared with it (Wis. VII, 8–9).

And again he says: “What use are riches to a fool, if he cannot buy wisdom?” (Prov. XVII, 16). Wisdom will find a pleasing dwelling in the heart of one who is proved to love her. “A multitude of the wise is the health of the world and the praise of the city in whose citadel she dwells.”

May she, with the Lord Jesus granting it, have a dwelling in your breast, dearest son, forever and ever.

@ [Col. 0235C] Mabillon edition 4, Pez edition 4 (Froben edition 52). Compared with the Salzburg manuscripts. Dated to the year 797, when the Nones of August fell on a Saturday, as the distinguished Hansizius correctly noted, *Germania Sacra*, vol. II, p. 105.

## LETTER LXVI. TO ARNO (Year 797, August)

He rejoices at news of his arrival, wishes to learn many things from him, and instructs him about his own stay.

To his most beloved father, the Transalpine Eagle, Albinus the teacher sends greetings.

I rejoice that I have heard at least some report of your arrival, greatly desiring to see the face of your blessedness [Col. 0235C] and to hear your wished-for speech, and at the same time to learn about the prosperity

@ [Col. 0235D] of the apostolic lord.

“Hence a twofold undertaking had to be carried out by Arno at Rome this year. One matter was public: to settle the disputes that were burning between the pope and the Romans, which the embassy of Angilbert the previous year had not at all calmed. The other was private and concerned his own church. For he wished both to strengthen the diocese recently acquired in Hunnia and to prepare a metropolitan dignity for it.”

—of the apostolic lord, and to learn what has taken place in those regions, how your embassy turned out for you, and whether

@ [Col. 0235D] concerning the cause of Saint Paul,

the monastery of Cormaricus, about which elsewhere—

the matter concerning Saint Paul can be advanced. I beg you to take care to entrust all these matters to me through a swift messenger.

According to the itinerary I have arranged, God willing, we plan to come next Saturday, that is, on the Nones of August, to the monastery of Saint Amandus; to remain there on Sunday; and then to proceed to

@ [Col. 0235D] our estate at Baralla.

The place is unknown to me, and is not mentioned either by the geographical writers whom I have consulted or elsewhere.

We plan to remain at our estate of Baralla [Pez., “Barallam”] for four or five days, not far from Saint Amandus, but approximately fifteen miles away; and then to proceed to

@ [Col. 0235D] Causiacum.

The monastery of Causiacum—Choisy—is situated on the Aisne River near Compiègne. Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXX, no. 15.

We shall reach Causiacum and remain there for a week; and then proceed to

@ [Col. 0235D] Saint Lupus.

A monastery in the suburb of Troyes, entrusted by Charlemagne to Alcuin’s care, about which elsewhere.

Between these places, God willing, you have me for the whole month of August and part of September, if you can in any way arrange for our meeting.

Meanwhile, while we are nearby, write back to me and tell me how many days I should wait for you, because I have nothing in these regions where I can wait, owing to the poverty of our resources. Whatever was there was entirely consumed last year by our friends, who acted kindly and used our goods as their own.

As soon as your letter can reach us, let the messenger hurry so that he may find us nearby. If the king orders you to remain at the palace, Liutgardis and the children will not prevent you from coming to us, since they are going to

@ [Col. 0235D] Liutgardis.

Queen, wife of Charlemagne, who died at Tours in the year 800, on the day before the Nones of June. Loisel, *Annals*.

—Nivielle.

@ [Col. 0236C] Nivielle.

Nivielle, Nivialla, or Nivigella, a monastery built by Itta, or Iduberga, wife of Pippin, mayor of the palace, at the urging of Saint Amandus. Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXXIII, no. 7.

Nivielle, where they are to celebrate

@ [Col. 0236D] the Mass of Saint Mary.

He undoubtedly means the feast of the Assumption of Blessed Virgin Mary, which was also celebrated at that time on 15 August. See Du Cange, *Glossary*, under *Missa*.

Come—come quickly, if it pleases God, Saint Martin, and Saint Amandus, so that we may see one another. I would by no means have wished to go farther before seeing the face of your blessedness.

Send word through our estates; whatever is there will all be prepared for you. I greatly rejoice at the prospect of your conversation, because I do not know when it will take place if not now.

Read happily, and come prosperously, best father, most faithful friend, and dearest in Christ.

@ [Col. 0236D] {69} Mabillon edition 5, Pez edition 5 (Froben edition 53), compared with the Salzburg manuscript. Since his name is absent everywhere, someone might doubt whether this letter was written to Arno or to another friend residing in the king’s retinue. Comparison of this letter with the preceding and following ones seems to favor Arno.

## LETTER LXVII. TO *** (Year 797, August)

He indicates the places where he is staying, wishes to learn news, and sends certain little gifts.

[Col. 0236C]

To his most beloved son, greetings in the sweetness of true charity.

I awaited a letter or messenger from your affection. But thirdly,

@ [Col. 0236D] Gisela, sister of the lord king,

See Letters 98 and 99, now 126 and 127.

Gisela [Pez., “Kysla”], sister of the lord king, sent messengers to me, asking me to come to her because of certain necessities. But now, God willing, I shall go to visit her, and from there to

@ [Col. 0236D] Saint Lupus.

See the preceding letter, in the notes.

—to Saint Lupus, and there I especially hope to remain for the entire month of September. If from there you hear anything about your journey, or

@ [Col. 0236D] about the return of the lord king.

The distinguished Hansizius asserts that this and the other matters mentioned in this letter belong to the year 800. “From this,” he says, “it is clear that Arno had recently come from Italy to the king and returned with him to Rome.”

But Alcuin is not asking to be informed about the king’s departure; he is asking about his return. I interpret these words as referring to Arno’s journey to Rome in the year 797 and to the king’s return from the Saxon expedition. Concerning that expedition, Einhard writes in his *Annals* for the same year:

“The king entered Saxony to crush the obstinacy of that faithless people and to lay it waste; nor did he desist until he had traversed all its borders, for he advanced as far as its furthest limits, where it is washed by the Ocean between the Elbe and the Weser.”

Hence Alcuin’s fear concerning the extremely harsh air of the Ocean, the very bad land, and the envious or untrustworthy people—the Saxons.

—about the return of the lord

[Col. 0237A] [king], or about the progress of his army, do not delay to send me word. Thus, in October, I may go to

@ [Col. 0237D] Ferrarias.

The monastery of Ferrarias, entrusted to Alcuin, is situated on the Clareja—Clairy—which flows into the Loing, in the district of the Wastinenses—Gâtinais—of the diocese of Sens. Its founder formerly called it Bethlehem, as Lupus, the abbot of that place, testifies in Letter 13 (Mabillon, *Life of Saint Aldric*, *Acta Sanctorum*, fourth century, part I, p. 566).

—to visit Saint Peter at Ferrarias. I hope to remain there until the middle of that month. I have therefore written these things to you so that you may know our route and where your messenger may find us.

But also

@ [Col. 0237D] concerning our brother and friend.

Perhaps Candidus, as may be inferred from the following letter, where he complains that Aquila had not wished to send him any news about his Candidus, as he had requested in this letter.

Concerning our brother and friend, whom I once again left with you, send me word. I am very anxious about the lord king and the Christian people because of the extremely harsh climate, that very bad land, and the envious people—if God will be favorable to them and to the defender of his holy Church. May he preserve him for a long time together with his faithful servants.

@ [Col. 0237D] I have sent you

This is the beginning of the letter in Mabillon.

I have sent you one carpet and one thin little cloak, begging you not to despise the smallness of the gift. These are the two small coins that the widow offered in the temple treasury, whom the Lord Jesus praised because she offered with complete charity (Matt. XII, 42).

Live in a manner pleasing to God in every good work, and, praying for us, fare well forever.

@ [Col. 0237D] {70} We have transcribed this letter, hitherto unpublished, from the Salzburg and Saint-Emmeram manuscripts. The passages enclosed in brackets occur only in the Salzburg manuscript. Alcuin received Arno’s letter mentioned here while he was still staying at Saint Lupus, where in the preceding letter he had said that he would remain for the entire month of September. It was therefore sent in the same year, 797. (Froben edition 54.)

## LETTER LVIII. TO ARNO (Year 797, September)

He indicates that he has received Arno’s letter and complains about his silence concerning many matters.

To his most beloved son, the Eagle, Alcuin sends pious and peaceful greetings in Christ.

Having heard of your prosperity through the letter that you sent us

[and which reached us on the Ides of September. But it is strange that you did not wish to send me any word about my Candidus [Ms., “Cando”].

@ [Col. 0238C] I sent a letter … on the seventh day before the Ides of August.

The letter, or preceding epistle, as is clear from a comparison of the two. On that day Alcuin, if he followed the route he had planned in these letters, was at Baralla, around 10 August. He came to Causiacum, where he stayed for a week. From there he went to Saint Lupus, where he remained for the rest of August and the entire month of September; at that place he received Arno’s letter on the Ides of September. From there, or from the monastery of Ferrarias, to which he went in October, he wrote the present letter.

I sent you my letter some time ago through one of your clerics, whose name I do not recall, as I think, on the seventh day before the Ides of August. I do not know whether it reached you. In that letter I was anxious to hear something from which I might learn where you would send it, or on what day, or from what place, or how you had planned to act according to God’s will, and when I might hope that you would come to these regions.

I am therefore hurrying to Saint Martin, where, God willing and with the lord king’s consent, I plan to spend the winter].

Would that my Eagle come flying to pray at Saint Martin’s, so that I might embrace his sweetest wings and hold him whom my soul loves, nor release him until I lead him into my mother’s house (Song III, 4), and he kisses me with the kiss of his mouth (Song I, 1), and we rejoice together in ordered charity.

[“I might have told you something if I had you present: why did you not wish to inform me how the apostolic lord had received you, and what had pleased you in those regions? Or how

@ [Col. 0238D] Father Paulinus,

the patriarch of Aquileia.

From this it is clear that Arno returned from Italy this year.

—my father Paulinus had dealt with you, and where he had gone? You did not wish to satisfy my inquisitive mind. Therefore I now wished to write you a shorter letter, though not with little affection. What I have written, I have written” (John XIX, 22).

I beg you to return this second letter to my Candidus, if he is alive and if he is with you. I do not know why he too remained silent, since you wrote to me, unless perhaps Albinus has departed from his lips, while his affection never departs from my heart.]

May you always, forever, be well, thrive, and flourish, dearest son.

@ [Col. 0238D] Mabillon published this letter in truncated form, as he found it in the manuscript of Saint Emmeram. Here it appears complete from two manuscripts of the Salzburg library. (Froben edition 55.)

## LETTER LXIX

@ [Col. 0238D] {72} The name of the person to whom this letter was addressed is not expressed in the manuscript codices. Nevertheless, it is certain that he was the man who held authority over the monastery of Saint Rupert at Salzburg. And who else could he have been but Aquila, or Arno, who governed that monastery together with the bishopric?

TO ARNO, BISHOP OF SALZBURG (Year 797)

He commends a certain son to him; wishes to be informed about the king’s return, the cause of Saint Paul, and other matters; he longs for the vision of God and exhorts him to desire heavenly things.

[Col. 0238C]

@ [Col. 0238D] This inscription differs in several respects from that of the manuscript of Saint Emmeram, or Mabillon’s manuscript, which reads as follows:

“To the venerable Father, beloved teacher, and desired brother, by God’s will bishop or abbot, I, an unworthy servant of the servants of Christ, send greetings in the joy of complete charity.”

“To the venerable Father, beloved brother, and desired son, greetings in the joy of complete charity.”

[Col. 0239A] [I am very pleased with the harmony between my son and your brother, whom you came to visit when summoned. And you did well by urging me to return to his affection, from which I was never estranged, although I had recognized some doubt about my fidelity in your most gracious letter. As for what he said—that I should have kept him in my household for instruction—I had never heard this from anyone before. Nevertheless,] know that pride does not like to dwell in the chamber of humility, because what the latter builds the former destroys. Behold, insofar as it lies with me, I keep my hands open to embrace him when he comes, not to reject him when he begs. I have resolved to maintain this toward everyone: to cast no one away, but to draw toward me whomever I can. [How much less, then, should your holy and venerable prudence have believed in a quarrel with a man so tested, a person so praiseworthy, and one so long joined to me by such great benefits. What you wrote rather harshly about my son, your brother and nephew, let your affection and piety see to it that our labor does not become fruitless and that the soul for which Christ did not hesitate to die is not lost. Behold, I have sent him back to your affection, so that you may deal with him as seems right to your prudence [Al.: providence]; for he, or the benefices he possesses, is in your power. Act according to what you understand from his merits, which are before your eyes, not according to the words of the envious. For nothing can prosper with me in a spirit of sadness. One of two counsels seems best to me: either commend him to our lord the king through our favor, or keep him with you until, from his conduct, you learn what is useful for him, until our conversation may again take place, God willing. Yet it may be better that he have something for consolation, in accordance with his promise of humility and obedience, lest he be swallowed up by continual grief (2 Cor. 2:7). And if]

[Col. 0239D] Witto. Witto, perhaps Witzo or Candidus, a disciple of Alcuin, mentioned elsewhere more frequently. Witto should come to you; he can learn from him. And if he comes, God willing, look carefully to it lest his residence with you prove fruitless, so that just as his absence saddens me, his presence may gladden you, and my deficiency become your advancement. And if you wish him to spend some time in the monastery

[Col. 0239D] of Saint Hrodbert. Of Saint Rupert, now Saint Peter’s at Salzburg. of Saint Hrodbert, should it be necessary for him to remain there for some time because of assistance from the people and knowledge of the language,

[Col. 0239D] Aedilbertum. Perhaps this is Adalbert, a disciple of Alcuin, [Col. 0240D] later abbot of Ferrières? keep Aedilbert with him, so that, accustomed to our learning and brought up in their customs, he may serve as a mediator for the advancement of both parties. Nevertheless, [Col. 0239D] let it be done as you think best, and inform me as soon as possible what pleases you. And

[Col. 0240D] Concerning our lord the king’s return. From the Saxon expedition; see Letter 53 (now 57). concerning our lord the king’s return,

[Col. 0240D] and your journey. See the same place. and your journey or residence, and concerning our lord the pope,

[Col. 0240D] The matter of Saint Paul. See the same place and elsewhere frequently. and the matter of Saint Paul, and the other matters that are necessary or pleasant for us to hear {71}. Know this with complete certainty: in the regions of Tours scarcely any wine remains, and the abundance of grain will barely last until the middle of the following year. Therefore, God willing, I shall go to visit the brothers and arrange their affairs, returning afterward to stay again in these regions. If it had pleased our lord the king to allow you to winter at Saint-Amand, perhaps, Christ in his mercy, it would have been advantageous for us to live together for some time, so that the prophetic bread might be broken among us, concerning which it is said: “Break your bread for the hungry” (Isa. 58:7). [And] we would have been able to sing continually with one voice and one faith: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke 11:3). [And] to feed upon him who said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever” (John 6:51–52). O how delightful is charity, how sweet his presence, and how blessed the life in which what is always loved will never be lacking! What now burns for the absent one [Al.: in absence] then rejoices in the one present. Although God is present everywhere, he is seen one way in an image through a mirror, and another way in his presence face to face; concerning this the Truth himself says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). Let the heart now be cleansed in this pilgrimage, so that in our homeland we may be permitted to enjoy that most blessed vision. Let us use this perishing world in imperishable charity, so that we may enjoy God in enduring glory. O Lord, [Jesus,] make us love you and hate the one of whom you said: “The world hates me” (John 15:18). Grant that through you we may receive the gift of the Paraclete Spirit, whom the world cannot receive because it neither sees him nor knows him (John 14:17). Do not, according to the promise of your truth, leave us orphans, but send into us the Spirit of truth, who will remain with us forever (ibid., vv. 16–17). O King of glory and Lord of hosts (Ps. 23:10), our warrior and our peace, who said: “Take courage; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33), conquer also in us, your servants. [You know] that without you we can do nothing (John 15:5). Grant your servants to speak your word with confidence, and by their deeds, while they speak, to show what they proclaim with their mouths. Grant both the will and the accomplishment (Phil. 2:13); grant that your mercy may go before us (Ps. 58:11), and that your mercy may follow us (Ps. 22:6)—go before us to begin, follow us to complete [Al.: fulfill]. What more do we have to say except, “Your will be done,” since you desire all people to be saved? (1 Tim. 2:4.) Your will is our salvation, our glory, and our blessedness.

Through a kind of rapture of mind, venerable brother, I have spoken these things—not as orderly as the brevity of a letter demands, but as fervently as the deepest contrition of my heart required. Yet you, sweetest Father and my familiar friend, patiently endure the tears of my heart, and store within yourself what you have heard from me. Who knows, except the one who knows all things, whether tomorrow I shall be permitted to write to you, or the day after tomorrow to speak or hear sweet conversations [Al.: consolations] with you? Today that mercy which has bestowed upon me all the good things I possess has given me the opportunity. Therefore I ought not to be silent, since I do not know what the coming day may bring. But you, united brother, keep eternal days always in mind, and run with patience the course Christ has shown you; for whoever follows him does not walk in darkness but will have the light of life (John 8:12). Let him be your food and drink, your charity and glory. Let worldly ambition, the attentions of flatterers, the appearance of vanity, the fear of the powerful, and the threats of the cruel not overthrow your heart; but build your house upon the firm rock (Matt. 7:24–25), from which no storms can tear you away. Stand fearless, despising the tongues of detractors and taking no account of the mouths of those who praise. With the help of heavenly grace, seize for this way of life as many as you can—through prayers, admonitions, corrections, and examples—so that, with the fruit of manifold labor, you may appear worthy of manifold reward in the presence of the Lord your God. And remember to assist me, who share in your salvation, by your continual prayers for holiness, so that the Savior of all may deign, through the abundant clemency of his mercy, to save me, pierced by many wounds of sin, and to place me, even if last, with you in the portion of eternal blessedness, dearest Father, brother, and son.

[Col. 0241D] Edited by Quercetanus, p. 108, from a manuscript (Frobenius, 56).

## LETTER LXX. TO BISHOP SPERATUS (A.D. 797)

He dissuades him from the vanities of this life, but impresses upon him the duties proper to bishops.

To the most holy brother and dearest son,

[Col. 0241D] To Bishop Speratus. No one reveals of which see he was bishop. Nevertheless, from this letter itself it seems possible to infer that he held a bishopric in England; for he urges him: “Read frequently the booklet of blessed Gregory, our preacher.” See also the following note. To Bishop Speratus, Albinus, a humble Father, sends greetings.

The love of your charity greatly refreshes me every day, and the certainty of your fidelity abundantly gladdens my mind, so that your name for goodness and the face of your sweetness remain deeply fixed in my mind among the earliest friends of my insignificant self. And as much as the memory of charity gladdens me, so much does the tearful distance of absence make me sad. Yet what is necessarily to be endured must be borne patiently. Let the letter as it runs show in writing what the tongue cannot make resound in the ears, so that through the service of the eyes he may recognize what once the ministry of the ears disclosed to the heart’s secret place.

Let your venerable holiness often consider the changing events of the world, and retain in an unforgetful mind what fate remains for us. Let the examples of the entire human race teach us how dangerous the day is, how fearsome the judgment that awaits us at an uncertain time. Let us prepare ourselves to meet the great King (Amos 4:12), so that we may find him merciful, whom no one can escape. What gift we are carrying in our hands must be considered daily, since Scripture says: “You shall not appear empty before the presence of the Lord your God” (Ecclus. 35:6). No display of metals, no brilliance of gems, no vanity of clothing, [Col. 0242A] and no luxury of the world will be acceptable there to that most just Judge. Only generous almsgiving and the multiplication of good merits will be of benefit. Whatever is done here is judged there. Every goodness will be crowned with perpetual reward, and every iniquity condemned to eternal torments.

Let these things cling to our minds; let prudent caution foresee them. We must consider with the greatest care how the soul, lest it mourn on that day in want of good merits, may rejoice in the simple fruit of goodness. May your fraternal concern often rouse my sluggishness through the sequence of the sacred Scriptures. For the words of my exhortation are written with the pen of true affection. Let us do good daily while we have the opportunity (Gal. 6:10), lest darkness overtake us (John 12:35), and lest that fearful day find us unprepared. But you, with pastoral piety and priestly authority, should strive not only to awaken my sluggishness by your letters, but also to proclaim with pious fatherly care to all who hear you that they must keep watch. If the priestly tongue is the key of the heavenly kingdom, it is fitting that his throat be the trumpet of the eternal King, as the prophet says: “Cry out, do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58:1). Who prepares for battle if the herald does not cry out in the camp? Who, girded with weapons, resists the enemy’s entrance if the watchman sleeps on the lofty summit of the tower? Who defends the flock from the wolves’ fury if the shepherd lurks among the forest thorns of lust? Who points out the pastures of the flowering countryside to the flock if the guide wanders with errant steps through pits? Read frequently, I beg you, the booklet of blessed Gregory, our preacher, on pastoral care, so that in it you may recognize the danger of the priestly office and not forget the reward of the servant who works well. Let this book cling frequently to your hands; let its meaning be firmly fixed in your memory, so that you may know how each person should approach priestly honor, with what great consideration one who has approached it must examine himself, by what examples he must live, with what intensity he is commanded to preach, and what is fitting for each person. He has described all this with the greatest discernment.

You know very well with what intensity

[Col. 0241D] That most illustrious king. I think this was Offa, king of the Mercians, who in 787 had his son Ecgfrith crowned king; after his father’s death, however, he held the kingdom for only five months, being taken by death “not on account of his own sins, but because his father had shed much blood for the confirmation of his kingdom,” as Alcuin says elsewhere in a letter to the patrician Osbert, which is lost, and from which Malmesbury quotes these words in Book I, chapter 4, of *The Kings of the English*. See Alford, *Anglo-Saxon Annals*, for the years 787 and 796. that most illustrious king prepared his son [Edit.: for his son], as he thought, to inherit the kingdom; but, as the outcome of events showed, he removed him from it. From this you can understand worldly wisdom, and how true is what the Psalmist sings: “Unless the Lord builds [guards] the house, those who guard it watch in vain” (Ps. 126:1). Man thinks; God judges. Human prudence is uncertain in worldly affairs. Let this alone not deceive anyone considering the future: charity performs what is required in the commandments of God during the times of this life. Let your hand be generous in almsgiving; let your tongue be diligent in preaching; let your life be sober in conduct; let priestly authority be present in correcting the reprobate; let kindly concern be present in refreshing the humble. Let you have clear confidence in asserting the truth, sparing no person so as to withhold a just judgment. Let your daily practice in ecclesiastical offices be venerable, so that everything your dignity ought to observe in the worship of God may be done honorably. For it is better for a priest of Christ to be praised in ecclesiastical service than in the preparation of banquets (Prov. 23:20). What praise is it to pile up your table so high that it can scarcely be carried, while Christ is hungry at the door? He will say on the terrible day: “As long as you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” (Matt. 25:40).

By all means have in your retinue a prudent steward who will provide for the poor with solicitous piety. It is better for the poor to eat from your table than actors or any sort of pleasure-seekers. Avoid those who pursue drunkenness as though it were a pit of hell, as blessed Jerome says. There are two evils. First, to act against the commandment of God, who says: “Beware of all drunkenness and gluttony” (Luke 21:34). Second, to seek praise from what should have led one to repentance. Blessed is the man who does not turn toward vanities and false madnesses (Ps. 39:5). The pomp of clothing is madness, as is the constant luxury of drunkenness, the prophet saying: “Woe to you who are mighty for drinking wine, and strong men for mixing drunkenness” (Isa. 5:22). Whoever delights in these things, as Solomon says, will not be wise (Prov. 20:1). In you, let there be an example of complete sobriety and self-restraint. Let the words of God be read at a priestly banquet. There it is fitting to hear a reader, not a harpist. The house is narrow; it will not be able to contain both. The heavenly King does not wish to have fellowship in name only with pagan and ruined kings, because that eternal King reigns in heaven, while the ruined pagan laments in hell. Let the voices of readers be heard in your houses, not the crowd of laughter in the streets.

Have such companions among the clergy that from their conduct your authority may be praised. “A wise son is the glory of his father, and a foolish son is the disgrace of his mother” (Prov. 10:1). How, as the Apostle says (1 Tim. 3:5), can one care for the Church who does not know how to rule his own household? The little sheep that eats from the shepherd’s table wanders with straying steps. How can one have a cautious manner of life who runs with unrestrained foot through the breadth of the fields? And the teacher’s wisdom is increased by the instruction of his pupils: whoever diligently teaches what he knows often learns, by divine grace, what he does not know. Cursed is the one who hides grain from the peoples (Prov. 11:26), and blessed is the one who sows over every field. “In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not let your hand cease. For you do not know which will prosper, whether this or that,” although both are good (Eccles. 11:6). No one will be everlasting in this world; therefore let each person strive to live well where he will be everlasting. Do not, I beg you, despise the exhortations of charity. I know [Edit.: know] that you understand all these things better and practice them more perfectly. But the affection of great love compels me to advise you toward what is best. It is fitting that humility gratefully receive what charity willingly offers.

May the supreme mercy of God for many blessed years

Preserve those dear to you, and you together with them; may you remember Albinus, and may Christ remember you forever;

May everlasting glory without end now be yours.

## LETTER LXXI. TO BISHOP SPERATUS

He desires his friendship to continue and exhorts him to a life worthy of a bishop.

To his dearest Father,

[Col. 0245D] To Bishop Speratus. Of uncertain see in England; a Letter 56 (now 70) to him also survives. To Bishop Speratus, Alcuin, his faithful friend, sends greetings.

Everlasting charity compels me frequently to send little letters to your affection, although you seem less inclined to repay us in your own letters. Nevertheless, I do not cease wishing you prosperity, and through written pages to make known to your holiness that my mind in no way forgets you, but holds the memory of your name with every firm root.

I remember your sweetness and the brotherhood we shared when we were together in bodily presence, which ought also to be preserved spiritually and not erased by any distance of lands, so that the friendship once agreed upon may be maintained forever. But you, most holy Father, consider carefully the place of your name, where you remain and where your dignity has been established, and fulfill in deed what everyone calls you. Preach confidently to every person, in season and out of season, to the willing and unwilling alike (2 Tim. 4). Let examples of holiness shine in your conduct, and let the preaching of truth gleam in your words, because these two things especially belong to a bishop: that he live by good conduct and not be silent in the words of preaching, as the Truth himself says: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12). Chastity of conduct is shown in the loins, and the light of God’s word in the lamp. Have irreproachable companions, so that outsiders may learn the religious life from them; and let all who come to you be edified, either by you yourself or by them. Do not abandon the study of reading, but keep with you such young men as will always learn and will rejoice more in learning than in becoming drunk; in serving God rather than pursuing the pomps of the world. Prepare yourself to be such as you would wish to stand before Christ’s tribunal. Always remember me in your prayers, so that divine clemency may bring my days to a perfect end, and so that you may have a good reward through me, and I remission of sins through you. May faith and holy love never grow cold in our minds, but increase ever more and more, Christ our God in his mercy willing, who may be favorable to us forever. I wish you health and progress in the charity of Christ, sweetest Father!

[Col. 0245D] Hitherto unpublished; we print it from a Salzburg manuscript (Frobenius, 57).

## LETTER LXXII. TO THE PRIEST SIMEON (ABOUT A.D. 797)

He urges him to carry out the episcopal office diligently in the dangerous times prevailing in Britain. [Col. 0245A]

To his dearest son,

[Col. 0245D] To the priest Simeon. I think he is the same person whom he calls “the chief priest” in the letter to Calvin. Leland, *British Writers*, p. 126, says the following about him: “Flaccus Albinus makes clear mention of Simeon in his letter to Calvin . . . There is also a letter of Albinus to Simeon himself, in which, after praising him, he reminds him of his duty and otherwise urges him, who is hastening forward of his own accord. In Albinus there is no record of the see of his bishopric. My opinion is that he was a bishop in Gaul.” Thus Leland. Nevertheless, from the text of the letter itself it seems to me much more likely that he was a bishop in Britain; for he urges him, [Col. 0246D] since the times in Britain are dangerous because of the deaths of kings, if a storm threatens from there, to steer Christ’s ship manfully, and he indicates that they shared a common teacher, certainly in Britain. To the priest Simeon, Albinus, Father, sends greetings.

If there is reason to rejoice at an ascent, there is reason to fear a fall, because a fall from a higher place is more dangerous. Therefore, in accordance with your name, be an overseer not only of the flock entrusted to you but also of yourself, so that in a few days of labor you may deserve to have a very great reward of blessedness. The times are dangerous in Britain; the death of kings is a sign of misery; discord is the beginning of captivity; and the things you have often heard foretold by our teacher are hastening to become true. Do not be eager for gold and silver, but for the gain of souls. Remember me daily in prayers and almsgiving, and remember yourself in observing God’s commandments. Even if a storm threatens from every side, steer Christ’s ship manfully, so that at last you may reach the harbor of prosperity with your sailors. Let your tongue never be silent from holy preaching, nor your hand grow sluggish in good works; and wherever you go, let the book of Saint Gregory’s *Pastoral Care* go with you. Read and reread it frequently, so that you may recognize yourself and your work in it, and have before your eyes how you ought to live and teach; for it is a mirror of pontifical life and a medicine against each wound of diabolical deceit. Let your spirit not soften under the flattery of princes, nor grow sluggish in correcting those subject to you. Let the flatteries of the world not deceive you; let passing honors not exalt you; let popular favor not overturn you. Be a most firm pillar in the house of God, not a reed shaken by the wind (Matt. 11:7). Be a lamp placed upon a lampstand, not hidden under a bushel (Matt. 5:15). Be for all a way of salvation, not a channel of perdition, so that through you many may be corrected, saved, and reach eternal life with you. Live, fare well, prosper happily in the work of God, and always remember us.

[Col. 0246D] Edited by Quercetanus, p. 101, from a manuscript (Frobenius, 58).

## LETTER LXXIII. TO THE PRIEST CALVINUS (ABOUT A.D. 797)

He exhorts him to despise the riches and honors of the world; he wishes the chief priest Simeon to be admonished frequently; he urges him to beware of flatteries, to devote himself diligently to the care of souls, and to practice Christian virtue. [Col. 0246A]

To his dearest son,

[Col. 0246D] To the priest Calvinus. No one identifies who he was. From the mention of the bishop Simeon, he may be understood to have been an Englishman. See the following column, note a. To the priest Calvinus, Albinus, a devoted Father in charity, sends greetings.

Although friends may be separated in bodily appearance, they can nevertheless always be present through the duty of charity. Those who are joined by the sweetness of affection are not separated by distance of lands. This is what never passes away, if it is faithfully possessed in truth. Alas! those are rarely found whose uncorrupted faith outwardly displays true charity, which has many adversaries, but especially the riches of the world, which assail the hearts of those who seek them under a deceptive appearance, so that scarcely any spark of ancient affection shines amid the shadowy darkness of earthly desires. Expel this poisonous desire of the world far from your mind, dearest son, God showing mercy and grace assisting, so that you may serve Christ God in tranquil peace, in the hope of sweetness, in faith of truth, and in the perfection of charity, possessing the world as though you did not possess it. But if you feel that secular possession is an impediment to the peaceful service by which you ought to serve the Lord God, it is better to cut the cord of that iniquity than to prolong lamentations in vain hope for a long time, not knowing what the coming day may bring. There are people who fall through hope, promising themselves a long life; suddenly they are snatched from this light, and what they planned they do not accomplish. Let the prudence given you by God foresee where your mind is leading you, and do not delay in choosing what is best for you.

You should know with what desire and tranquility you possess the honors of the world. If the religious commitments you previously had [variant: the religious commitment which you had] create no impediment for you, I desire that you always retain them in the service of Christ. I do not think you lack anything in

[Col. 0246D] the cell of Saint Stephen. Whether this cell was the monastery of Saint Stephen of Cauciacum (Choisy), near Compiègne, to which Calvinus may perhaps have withdrawn after coming from England, or whether it should instead be sought in England, I do not know. the cell of Saint Stephen for an honorable manner of life, so that [F. supplies: not] you need not wander abroad through various regions, hear the infidelities of others, grow angry at the sins of strangers, and lose the sweetest tranquility of your mind. Nevertheless, as I said, let your wisdom consider what advantage you have in possessing other people’s property: whether it is enough for you to distribute alms to the wretched; whether you can maintain a school of readers; whether you can clothe the poor; whether you can receive travelers; whether you can live peacefully; whether you can keep peace with those outside. There are many enemies of the Church of Christ who daily strive to seize something either by entreaty or by force; they are friends only in words, but enemies in deeds.

The perversity of these people often greatly disturbs the guardians of the Churches of Christ, as you can understand from the case of my dearest son,

[Col. 0247D] Simeon the chief priest. Mabillon calls him bishop of Worms in his *Eulogy of Alcuin*, §12, no. 66. But I think it more likely that he held a bishopric in England. [Col. 0248D] See the preceding letter to Simeon himself. Simeon the chief priest, who suffers the same troubles from the impious as his predecessors suffered from the enemies of Christ. Their opposition perishes [F.: perished] at its appointed end according to the judgment of the just God {76}, just as certain destruction remains for those who now oppose the preaching of our aforementioned son and the servants of God, since they come after you.
