Yet never cease to assist his good will with prayers and to admonish him with exhortations, so that he may act manfully; for your prosperity consists in his salvation, and in the advancement of his good will a reward for us all will be reckoned with God. For I, though an unworthy Father, nourished, educated, and brought to perfection the man whom you chose for the honor of the pontificate. Admonish him frequently concerning persistence in prayer [F.: preaching] of God’s word and the goodness of patience, which is greatly necessary for one dwelling among wolves and serpents. Let him remember Christ’s saying: “Take courage; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). Let him also consider very frequently in his mind what the Truth himself commanded his disciples when he sent them to the office of preaching: “Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves. Therefore be wise as serpents and simple as doves. Beware of men” (Matt. 10:16–17). Admonish him carefully not to be a lover of the world, not to consent to flatterers, and not, on account of the crowd of relatives, to entangle his mind in desires for lands or riches, but to keep everywhere and in everything the royal road with divine rigor. Christ is a better relative and friend than the numerous kinship or friendship of the whole world.

See what charity does. When I began to admonish you in a familiar style, suddenly the flame of charity carried me over to him. But forgive me for inserting these few remarks about his progress into the little letter intended for you: I wish you also to advance in this happiness of paternal faith before God, so that in all things you may be an assertor of his truth, not a flatterer of falsehood. Someone aptly defined a flatterer by saying: “A flatterer is a smooth-tongued enemy.” And he spoke truly; for there are many flatterers of the rich and few admonishers. One persuader of truth is better than a thousand flatterers of falsehood. Therefore beware of this vice in every way, dearest son, and let your speech always flourish in truth. Although truth has a wrinkled brow, it usually possesses sound counsel. If we shall have to give an account for every idle word (Matt. 12:36), how much more for a harmful or deceitful one? “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11). Speech was given to a human being for the service of truth, not for the iniquity of falsehood. A flatterer is never a true friend, but, as they say, a smooth-tongued enemy. You would be offering a sword smeared with honey to a friend. It is better to heal a wound with a cautery than to nourish it with flattery so that it becomes worse [variant: worse].

Let your sagacity consider the time, place, and person: what should be said, at what time, in what place, and to which person. These things can be read and discerned very well in the book of blessed Gregory called *Pastoral Care*. Let sacred reading never leave your hands at appropriate times. Let reading and prayer have their appointed turns. Let neither night nor day be prolonged in banquets, drunkenness, or unnecessary conversation. Amid cups, let the sound and speech of edification be heard before those who admonish [F.: those who are present], either openly before everyone or before each person sitting nearby. Let the youthful age of your charges be preserved by your words from the flame of vices, so that their age may advance you toward the reward of eternal recompense. Let no soul be worthless to you, since the Lord of all deigned to die for it. Do not say in your heart, “What does it matter to me whether he acts well or badly?” Where is charity if you do not care to correct the one who is in error? Remember the Apostle saying: “Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (2 Cor. 11:29.) He made another’s sin his own grief. What will you have to show your Redeemer and the Judge of all on the great day if you do not have souls to display, redeemed from the devil’s slavery by your labor? As many as you recall from iniquity in this exile through your teachings and lead back to the way of truth, so many rewards you will unquestionably receive on that day. Therefore let charity in doing good to all never cease; let the tongue in speaking of good to all never cease—persuading some through prayers, correcting others with severity, according to the measure of each person’s age or character. Be a lamp in the house of God, and through you let many be illuminated and recalled from the darkness of vices to the way of everlasting light. The grace of the assisting God will not be lacking to you if the will for holy admonition is present. Write the Gospel {77} in your heart, and let the miracles and words of our Lord Jesus Christ remain in your memory; and instead of the Psalms, sing the Gospel frequently, especially according to John, in which loftier mysteries are found. In this work I am laboring from the books of the Fathers

[Col. 0248D] The exposition. He completed it later, around the year 800; see it below in Part II of the Works. to produce an exposition in a brief discourse: a necessary work, and a pleasant one for you if it is completed by God’s gift and can reach you.

But keep peace with everyone [F.: with human beings], war with vices, harmony with the brothers, and pleasant conduct with those who are associated with and live according to the conduct of the saints. Patiently endure your injuries; or rather, forgive, so that you may be forgiven. Be restrained in food, sparing in drink, sober in speech, devoted in vigils, ready for every work of God, kind toward the poor and sick, a comforter of the sorrowful, an assistant to those who labor, compassionate toward the misery of all, and generous in almsgiving according to the resources available to you, remembering the Gospel widow’s two small coins and the prophet who says: “Break your bread for the hungry” (Isa. 58:7). Beware, looking ahead with discernment, that almsgiving may be a consolation both to the giver and to the recipient. Discernment is everywhere of the greatest value, and

[Col. 0249D] Among monks. From this you may infer that Calvinus was a monk in the same cell of Saint Stephen. among monks is said to be the mother of virtues, as Solomon testifies: “Let your eyelids go before your steps” (Prov. 4:25), that is, let discernment go before your actions. The Apostle also agrees with this saying: “Let all your things be done honorably and in order” (1 Cor. 14:40). And a certain comic poet says: “Nothing in excess.” Temperance must be observed in everything; it is the royal road of our whole life, inclining neither to the right nor to the left, but proceeding cautiously and wisely, like a prudent traveler hastening toward the citadel of the heavenly city, going from virtue to virtue until the God of gods is seen in Zion (Ps. 83:8)—that is, in the watchtower of eternal blessedness, which is the reward and recompense of the labor of all the saints. There the pure in heart are blessed, because they will see God (Matt. 5:8). There those who suffer persecution are blessed, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven (ibid., v. 10). There blessed are those who dwell in the house of the Lord, because they will praise him forever and ever (Ps. 83:5).

Keep this little letter with you, dearest son, as a companion, speaking to your heart in place of paternal affection, admonishing you not only concerning your own salvation but also concerning the advancement and prosperity of many, and commending me myself to your heart every day, so that true charity may make us flourish in the commandments of Christ God, to whom be praise and glory forever and ever.

{78}

[Col. 0249D] We have copied this letter, previously unpublished, from a Salzburg manuscript; it was written at the same time as the letter to Athelard, which follows (Frobenius, 59).

## LETTER LXXIV TO THE NATION AND PEOPLE OF THE CANTUARIANS (A.D. 797)

He extols their faith and nobility with praises; exhorts the priests and nobles; laments their calamities; and advises them to try to bring Archbishop Aedilhard back from his flight. [Col. 0249C]

To the most noble nation and praiseworthy people, and to the imperial kingdom of the Cantuarians, Alcuin, a humble Levite, sends greetings.

Very desirous of your honor and your salvation, I have taken care to send these few little letters jointly to you, because of my excessive love for your prosperity. You, however, are the beginning of the salvation of the English, the source of prosperity, the harbor of those who enter, the praise of triumph; you are the origin of wisdom, and from you the power of the empire first proceeded, and the origin of the Catholic faith arose. Among you the brightest lights of Britain rest, through whom the light of truth shone throughout Britain. In you both the splendor of philosophical discipline shone forth and the radiance of holy religion gleamed. Among you there were at once devout teachers of the ecclesiastical faith, the wisest princes of royal dignity, men most courageous in war, and men most just in judgments—conspicuous for nobility of character, prudent in counsel, praiseworthy in piety, honorable in appearance, venerable in countenance, and most distinguished in every dignity. Consider these things carefully, most wise men, in whom the glory of Kent now rests, and strive to imitate the long successions of your most noble ancestors. [Manuscript: *studimini*.] [Col. 0249D]

First of all, let those who serve God in Christ’s Church diligently learn [manuscript: *deserviant*, “may serve”] how they may please God (Colossians 1:10), and how they may firmly preserve and preach the Catholic faith which our teachers first founded among them; for ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of God. “If the blind leads the blind, both fall into the pit” (Matthew 15:14); and, conversely, “a multitude of the wise is the salvation of the people” (Wisdom 6:26). Bring teachers and masters of Holy Scripture to yourselves, lest there be a lack among you of the word of God, or of one who can govern God’s people; lest the fountain of truth dry up among you. Do not adorn yourselves, contrary to ecclesiastical custom, with vanity of clothing; rather, show yourselves noble and adorned in character, and prepared by preaching the word of God, so that the laymen and your warriors may through you become strong, and the people may walk along the way of salvation. [Col. 0250A–B]

Likewise, let the nobles who are among the people govern their dignities with counsel and preside over the people through justice, loving their ancestral statutes in judgments more than money, which subverts the words of the just. With united counsel, let them act manfully for their nation in whatever is good. Set over yourselves rulers distinguished by nobility, devout in the dignity of their character, and honorable in the splendor of justice, so that divine mercy may deign to govern, preserve, and exalt your nation. [Col. 0250C]

Yet the greatest danger threatens this island and the people dwelling in it. Behold, something never before heard of: a pagan people habitually devastates our shores by piratical robbery—the Danes, namely, who began ravaging the shores of Britain in 793 and returned frequently thereafter. And those very peoples, kingdoms, and kings of the English are at variance among themselves; and scarcely anyone now—something I shall not say without tears—is found from the ancient stock of kings, and they are all the more uncertain in their origin because they are lesser in courage. [Codex Harleianus: *incertioris ... minoris*.] [Col. 0249D–0250D]

[Note: “Scarcely anyone now … from the ancient stock of kings” may be compared with William of Malmesbury, *On the Kings of the English*, book I, chapter 1: “After them”—the children of Withred and the kings of Kent, the last of whom was Alric, who died in 794—“the noble stock of kings withered, and the noble blood cooled. Then every most shameless man, whom either a tongue had won wealth or a faction had armed with terror, aspired to tyranny and began to abuse the royal insignia. Among these was Aedilbert, also called Pren, who, when he had ruled the Kentish people for two years, ventured against the Mercians at greater strength than his own; captured by them, he surrendered his hands to chains and his body to captivity.”]

Likewise, throughout Christ’s churches the teachers of truth have perished. Almost all follow worldly vanities and hate the regular disciplines; and their warriors are more devoted to greed than to justice. Learn from Gildas the Breton, a most wise man—read “Gylbum,” but it should be *Gildam*; the manuscript has *Giraldum*. His Life was published by the Antwerp hagiographers on 29 January, and his letter *On the Ruin of Britain* is found in volume VIII of the *Bibliotheca Sanctorum Patrum*, Lyon edition, p. 707—and see from what causes the ancestors of the Britons lost their kingdom and homeland. Consider yourselves also, and you will find almost the same things in yourselves. Fear for yourselves the judgment of Truth himself, who expressed it concerning the Church when he said: “Every kingdom divided against itself will not stand” (Luke 11:17). Behold how great is the division among the peoples and nations of the English; therefore they fail within themselves, because they do not preserve peace and faith among themselves. [Col. 0250D–0251A]

Recall to yourselves, if it seems good to you, your bishop Aedilhard, a venerable and wise man, and strengthen the condition of your kingdom for the better by his counsel, correcting in your conduct whatever displeases God and striving to do those things that can call his mercy back upon you. It is not good that the seat of Saint Augustine, our first preacher, should remain vacant; nor can anyone else in any way be ordained in his place. The ruin of a people is everywhere to disobey its priests and drive away from itself the preachers of salvation. Submit yourselves humbly to your bishop and preacher of your salvation, so that divine grace may accompany you in all your works. Believe me: you cannot otherwise have God favorable to you. Through him, I believe, you can have present peace and hope for eternal salvation. Take counsel for your prosperity and act manfully in whatever you find to be good. Turn yourselves to prayers, supplications, and fasts, so that divine mercy may be reconciled to you, preserve you in your praise and salvation, grant you a secure dwelling in your homeland, and give you a glorious rule in the eternal homeland. May the right hand of almighty God protect and govern you, and deign to exalt you with present happiness and eternal blessedness, desirable and venerable brother-men. [Col. 0251B–C]

[Note: “Recall … Aedilhard.” He had recently temporarily abandoned his see while fleeing the impious invaders of the kingdom. See the following letter.]

[Editorial note: William of Malmesbury cites part of this letter in book I of *The Deeds of the Bishops of England*, under Ethelard. Jean du Chesne published most of it among Alcuin’s letters as no. 97, but truncated at the beginning and joined to another letter, the one addressed to Charlemagne. David Wilkins printed it complete from the manuscript of the distinguished Usher, volume I of *The Councils of Britain and Ireland*, p. 159, assigning it to the second year of Pope Leo III and the fifth year of Athelard’s archiepiscopate at Canterbury, A.D. 797. (Froben edition, p. 60.)]

## Letter LXXV: To Athelard, Archbishop of Canterbury (797)

He urges him to repent of his flight from his see and to restore order to the Church; he is to restrain the clergy from vanity in clothing and from immoderate feasting.

To the man of highest dignity and Father of ecclesiastical goodness, Athelard, archbishop, Alcuin, your faithful son, sends perpetual goodness in Christ.

Our son, returning through you, reported the sweetest words of your affection and at the same time carried in his hands the welcome little gifts of your kindness. Rejoicing in these, I recognized that you still retain in your memory the friendship once agreed upon, just as truth always shines forth as something tested in a perfect man. Therefore I give thanks for your goodness, desiring with all my heart that you may preside over the Christian people in long prosperity and exalt the holy see with fitting honors—the see which for a time you abandoned, according to the counsels of Christ’s priests, because of the impious invaders of the kingdom, as the aforementioned young man reported to me. [Col. 0251D–0252A]

[Note: “Because of the impious invaders of the kingdom.” It is therefore clear that Aethelhard, disregarding Alcuin’s earlier letters, temporarily left his see on the advice of his priests. Among these invaders was perhaps chiefly Aedilbert, surnamed Pren, who succeeded Alric in the kingdom of Kent—or rather, as Alford says, then presumed to royal dignity. He perhaps compelled Aethelhard, who had attached himself to Kenulf, king of the Mercians, to abandon his see after being excessively harassed during Pren’s usurpation. Kenulf later removed Pren from the kingdom in 798, after conquering Kent. See the preceding letter to the people and nation of Canterbury. Alford must be corrected, for he thought this letter was sent in 790 to Lambert, archbishop of Canterbury.]

Concerning this matter, your venerable authority thought it right to ask me through him what I thought. What else can my smallness say except to agree with the counsel of Christ’s holy priests? Yet if they have such authority in their advice that a shepherd ought to flee when the wolf comes, how great is the excellence of the Gospel, which calls him a hireling, not a shepherd, who timidly flees from the wolf’s rage (John 10:12–13). Perhaps they object with the words of Truth: “If they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matthew 10:23). Yet it must be discerned of what time and what persecution this was said. [Col. 0252A–B]

[Note: “What follows here” was joined in the Quercetan edition, p. 1623, to the letter “to a certain person,” namely to Charlemagne, which is letter 14, now 17.]

Again Truth himself says: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep, but the hireling flees” (John 10:11–12). By reading this in the homilies of blessed Pope Gregory, our preacher, you will be able to understand it very well. You yourself are conscious of the reason for which you left your see—whether through fear of death or the cruelty of torments, or because of the horror of idolatry, as the most holy bishop of that same see, Laurence, is said once to have desired. Yet, chastised by apostolic authority, he is said to have reconsidered his plan and withdrawn from what he had begun (*resipuit*; alternative reading: *resipiscit*, “he reconsiders”). Whatever the reason may have been, it seems good, in consideration of my affection, that repentance should be made for it. This could, as it seems, be done honorably if a fast were proclaimed by the common consent of the whole nation: you on account of having abandoned the see, and they on account of having accepted the error, so that God might be reconciled to all of you. Let prayers, almsgiving, and the solemn celebrations of Mass also be performed diligently everywhere, so that God may blot out whatever any of you has done in this matter. [Col. 0252B–C]

By your venerable wisdom, let the study of reading be especially brought back into the house of God, so that there may be young men reading there, a choir of singers, and the practice of books. Through your diligence, let the dignity of that holy Church be renewed, so that they may have from whom to choose a bishop for themselves. Likewise, let your preaching take place everywhere: whether for all the bishops in a common synod, concerning proper ordinations, zeal in preaching, ecclesiastical offices, the sanctity of baptism, and generosity in almsgiving; or concerning care for the poor in each church and parish, especially among the venerable people over whom God has willed you to preside as shepherd. Often a wounded soldier fights more strongly, just as a tired ox drives its hoof more firmly into the ground. Just as the devil rejoiced at your flight, see to it that Christ rejoices in the abundant benefit you bring to souls, and that your reward grows greater, since Truth himself says: “There is greater joy in heaven before the angels of God over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine who have no need of repentance” (Luke 15:7). Considering all these things most diligently, always advance in the love of Christ, loving him with all your heart, all your strength, and all your mind—him who exalted, honored, and preserved you until the day of your salvation. [Col. 0252D–0253A]

But you should diligently strive, as far as you are able, to drive entirely away from yourself and your fellow priests—or rather, from the entire clergy and the ranks of ecclesiastical dignity—the utterly vain fashion of clothing and the immoderate use of banquets. Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, washed away the stain of a threefold denial (John 21:15) through the truth of a threefold confession; wash away your flight, a simple error, through the manifold good of preaching. Above all, let the reading of the Holy Scriptures be renewed through your most holy care, let ecclesiastical dignity be exalted everywhere, and let the holy see, which was first in faith, be first in all wisdom, holiness, and honor, so that there the questioner may find what he seeks, the ignorant may learn what he desires, and the knowledgeable may see what he may praise. [Col. 0253A–B]

And since the unity of the Church, which has been partly severed—not, as it seems, through a reasonable consideration, but through a certain desire for power [Malmesbury: *pietatis*, “piety”]—could, if possible, be peacefully reunited and the division repaired, it seems good to deliberate on this with the counsel of all Christ’s priests and your fellow bishop of the Church of York [Usserius: *coepiscopis*, “fellow bishops”]; yet in such a way that the pious father is not deprived of the pallium during his lifetime, although the ordination of bishops should revert to the holy and first see. [Col. 0253B–D]

[Note: “If it could be done.” William of Malmesbury reads: “And if it could be done that it might be peacefully reunited and the division repaired, it seems good that this should be done with the counsel of all Christ’s priests and your fellow bishop of the Church of York; yet in such a way,” and so forth.]

[Note: “The pious father.” This is evidently Aldulf, or Advulf, bishop of Lichfield, whom Offa, king of the Mercians, had caused to be marked with archiepiscopal honor and the pallium after all the Mercian churches had been withdrawn from the primate of Canterbury. Athelard nevertheless restored the dignity of his own see, with Kenulf, Offa’s successor, promoting the matter by letters written in his own name and that of all the bishops of Britain to Leo III. Alcuin therefore advises here that the bishop of Lichfield be deprived of metropolitan jurisdiction, though not of the pallium, and that the ordination of bishops revert not to him but to the first see, namely Canterbury, to which metropolitan dignity belongs. See the preceding letter.]

Let your most holy wisdom consider all these things, so that a concord of charity may arise among the chief shepherds of Christ’s churches.

If, then, I have dictated anything excessive in these little letters of mine, I beg that your holy patience receive it kindly and not impute it to me as a writer, but attribute it to you as the one who commanded it. I have not acted with presumptuous rashness, but with humble obedience, considering what might benefit many, whether there was fault in the flight or not. Nevertheless, insofar as my devotion could consider the matter, it is better to do what I advise than to omit it. With wholly affectionate charity I admonish you to preach the word of God earnestly. This is your office, this is your reward, these are the fruits of your labor, this is the dignity, praise, and honor of a priest, so that through the manifold fruit of his labor he may appear in the sight of the Lord his God and become worthy to hear the desired voice: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25:21, 23). May almighty God cause your fatherhood to flourish abundantly in every perfect work, for the exaltation of his holy Church, most holy Father! [Col. 0253D–0254A]

[Editorial note: This is letter ten in Canisius, third in Quercetanus, and sixty-first in Froben. Quercetanus published it in a much fuller form from a manuscript. We have adopted several corrections from the Vatican manuscript.]

## Letter LXXVI: To the Lord King (797, in November)

On the calculation of the lunar leap. [Col. 0254B]

To the most desired lord David, king, distinguished by every adornment of wisdom, Flaccus Albinus sends greetings of perpetual peace and glory.

Words of greeting often flow from the fountain of charity; or, if the distance between lands denies the services of the voice, let the letters of affection, formed in ink, return again and again. Therefore, with a simple prayer, I beseech permission for the little letter of my smallness to come frequently before the presence of your authority, bearing whatever we may judge to be either pleasing to your wisdom or necessary to my smallness. And at the proper time may your Flaccus be read in letters, who once was heard in words. [Col. 0254B]

[Editorial note: This is the end of the letter in Canisius. The reason for this present little letter was the lunar leap, which could most certainly be observed in the bright moon of November of this year, the last year of the nineteen-year cycle.]

[Note: The last or final year of the nineteen-year cycle within the period during which Alcuin remained in Francia was 797. In that year the fourteenth moon fell on 17 April, just as in the following year, which was the first of the nineteen-year cycle, it fell on 5 April. This calculation also agrees with that of Venerable Bede; see volume I of his works, p. 365, in volume XC of Migne’s *Patrologia Latina*. Therefore the present letter was certainly written in November of 797.]

Thus this moon of the month of November, which for eighteen years was reckoned as having thirty days, must in the nineteenth year of the aforementioned cycle be reckoned as having twenty-nine days. Consequently, after the twenty-ninth day, which falls eight days before the Kalends of December (24 November), the seventh day before the Kalends is counted as the first day; thus on the Kalends of December the moon is seven days old, though according to the regular epacts it is reckoned as six days old. October, November, and December will therefore all have twenty-nine days. But if anyone neglects to do this with an obstinate mind, relying more on the regular rules than on the calculation of the leap, and wishes the moon of November to have thirty days and the sixth moon to fall on the Kalends of December, he will soon become entangled in a great error concerning the fourteenth moon of the Paschal feast. [Col. 0254D–0255A]

If the moon is reckoned as sixth on the Kalends of December, it will necessarily be eighth on the Kalends of January, ninth in February, and eighth in March; on the Kalends of April it will be ninth, on the fourth day before the Nones of April it will be tenth, on the third day before the Nones eleventh, on the day before the Nones twelfth, and on the Nones thirteenth. Yet according to the calculation of the Paschal feast this must become the fourteenth moon, as is most truthfully sung and most firmly held by all in the Paschal tables. Those who consider the matter carefully can see how great and how pernicious an error may arise concerning the fourteenth moon, the Lord’s Day of Easter, and the age of the moon on that same day, if someone fails to leap over one day in the age of the moon by the calculation of the leap in the month of November. Nor does the lunar age in January, February, March, and April agree with the regular tables, which must be observed over nineteen years in order to determine the age of the moon in each month on the days of the Kalends. [Col. 0255A–B]

There is also another matter in this calculation of the leap which is sometimes more difficult to compute but must necessarily be understood. I know that it will be most familiar to your keen wisdom that in common years, according to the number of epacts, which increase by eleven days each year, the fourteenth Paschal moon anticipates the fourteenth moon of the preceding year by eleven days [alternative readings: *undecima*, “the eleventh,” and Vatican manuscript *duodecim*, “twelve”]. This is easy to discover through the common years. In embolismic years, therefore, the fourteenth Paschal moon is shifted by nineteen days according to the number of the years of the nineteen-year cycle from the fourteenth moon of the preceding year, so that the common shortfall is supplied by the embolismic years and the number of days becomes equal in the nineteen solar years and the nineteen lunar years. [Col. 0255B–C]

Between the fourteenth moon of the last year of the often-mentioned cycle, which falls on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, and the fourteenth moon of the first year of that same cycle, which falls on the Nones of April, there are found not eleven days, as in other common years, but twelve. Thus the day which was removed from the lunar age in the month of November may be found here in April among the epacts, while the calculation of the epacts increases by eleven days each year. [Col. 0255C]

In this year, because of the leap, twelve days are found between the fourteenth moon of the last year and the fourteenth moon of the first year, so that the embolismic month of this year has thirty days according to the calculation of embolisms: the eighteen epacts of the last year, to which, if you add the eleven that ordinarily increase each year, and one day of the leap, the total is thirty. Therefore, in the first year of the often-mentioned cycle no epacts are written, and children sing “from none to eleven.” But if the days of the entire lunar year are counted from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May to the Nones of April, there are found not, as in other years, 354 days, but 353 days. Unless, perhaps, a leap year is approaching, which usually adds one day either to the solar or, as I think, to the lunar year. [Col. 0255D–0256A]

The way in which this calculation of the leap increases each year of the nineteen-year cycle toward the reduction of one day is computed in various ways. But this calculation seems easier: we should know that each year of the nineteen-year cycle adds to the eleven epact days one hour, one point, and one-nineteenth part of a point. From these hours and points, one day is gathered over nineteen years. For twenty-four hours make a complete day; four points make an hour, and sixteen points make four hours. Add to the three points that remain nine nineteenth-parts of a point, and they make four points, that is, one hour. [The text reads *novam*; Froben reads *nonam*.] If you add this to the four hours mentioned above, the result is five hours; and if you add these five hours to the nineteen hours, the result is twenty-four hours, one complete day in nineteen years, full and perfect according to the rule of the sun and moon already called *zodiaci*; Froben reads *zodiacicam* (“zodiacal”). [Col. 0256A–B]

And so that the cause of the lunar leap may be understood more clearly: a somewhat earlier and faster hour of its kindling generates it, just as the eleven days of the epacts usually do in the course of each year. For example, if the kindling of this moon of November took place at the sixth hour of the day, then in the following year the kindling of that same moon will occur one hour, one point, and one-nineteenth of a point before the sixth hour. Thus the whole sixth hour, together with one point of the fifth hour and one-nineteenth of a point of that same hour, will be anticipated. In this way it customarily increases year by year until it amounts to a complete day, which consists of twenty-four hours. [Col. 0256B–C]

I have taken care to recall these matters to your most excellent wisdom [Vatican manuscript: *extollentissimae*, “most exalted”], my sweetest David—not introducing what is unknown, but repeating what is known because of the present moon, in which the calculation of the leap seems especially worthy of consideration. Although we know that others calculate the leap differently and wish to insert it elsewhere, nevertheless, because of the calculation of the Paschal moon, which must remain altogether inviolate and unchangeable according to the ancient institutions of the holy Fathers and the custom of the whole holy Church, it seems that it should be noted especially in the month of November. [Col. 0256C]

Forgetting the old proverb, “You do not carry wood into the forest,” I have sent these little letters to your riches under the name of a small gift, knowing that you remember the praised widow who, when the temple had been cared for [Vatican manuscript: *aurato*, “gilded”], added two small coins, and those who brought goats’ hair for the adornment of the tabernacle (Exodus 25:4 and following). And since you are kind to all, you recall everyone’s favor upon yourselves; while your piety generously does good to all, it draws everyone’s riches to you, as the Apostle says: “Whoever sows with blessing will reap from blessing eternal life” (2 Corinthians 9:6). [Col. 0256D]

[Editorial note: Malmesbury preserved this and the following letter, or the relevant portions of the letters, in book I of *The Deeds of the Bishops of England*, under Ethelard. Quercetanus copied the present letter from him and printed it in Alcuin’s works, p. 1671. It appears to have been written in 798, when Athelard undertook a legation to Pope Leo III on behalf of King Kenulf, the bishops, and the entire Mercian people, especially for the restoration of the dignity of his see. (Alford, *Annals of the Anglo-Saxon Church*, for that year, nos. 2 and following; Froben edition, p. 62.)]

## Letter LXXVII: To Ethelard, Archbishop of Canterbury (798)

He prays for a prosperous journey for him as he goes to Rome and asks him to remember him before the holy apostles. [Col. 0257A]

To the most holy Father and greatly venerable member of Christ, Ethelard, archbishop, Alcuin the deacon sends greetings in the love of Christ.

Hearing of your health and prosperity, and of your conference with Eanbald, archbishop of York, my son, I was greatly pleased, hoping that from the conversation of your holiness the honor of the holy Church would be exalted and the life of those who serve God in it corrected. [Col. 0257D]

[Note: “Conference.” In letter 60, now 75, Alcuin urged him to confer with all the priests and with Eanbald, his fellow bishop of York, in order to repair the division. “From this passage,” says Alford, “and from the letters of King Kenulf to Pope Leo III, it is sufficiently clear that Ethelard first convened a synod of bishops before undertaking the journey to Rome, so that what he proposed to Leo might be spoken not so much with his own voice as with the assent and support of all orders.”]

For this reason I advised, in other letters of mine, that your holiness remain in your homeland, unwilling for the light of Britain to be extinguished. [Col. 0257A–B]

[Note: “In other letters.” See letter 60, now 75.]

But let it happen as God wills, so that it may benefit Christ’s churches. May God make your journey prosperous, and, with his angel accompanying you, may he lead you safely there and bring you safely back (Tobit 5:20–21), sweetest and most beloved Father. Above all I ask that you remember me before the holy apostles, just as we delight in remembering you before Saint Martin. [Col. 0257B]

[Editorial note: From the passage in Malmesbury cited above. This letter was written after Athelard’s return from his Roman journey, which Alford assigns to 798. He adds: “The dignity of the Canterbury Church was indeed restored by this first embassy of Ethelard … but because new signs of difficulties appeared day by day … the Roman see was appealed to again, and Ethelard returned to the City in the following year, 799.” Concerning both embassies, read Westminster, the Saxon Chronicle, and Worcester, cited by Pagi under the year 796, nos. 27 and 28. Froben edition, p. 63.]

## Letter LXXVIII: To Ethelard, Archbishop of Canterbury (798)

He prays for his happy return from the Roman embassy, on account of the restoration of the dignity of the Church of Canterbury.

To the most holy and in every honor most worthy lord Ethelard, archbishop.

After reading the letters concerning your prosperity, the success of your journey and your return to your homeland, and the manner in which you were received with apostolic kindness, I gave thanks with all the affection of my heart and with the greatest joy of mind to the eternal Lord God, who by a great gift of clemency directed the path of your pilgrimage along a prosperous journey, granted you favor in the sight of the apostolic Father, and allowed you to return having accomplished both your embassy and your desire. He has also deigned through you to exalt again to its former summit of dignity the most holy see of our first Teacher, namely Augustine, archbishop of Canterbury and apostle of England, which appeared for a time to have been divided by a fissure of disagreement and by the envious contention of certain persons. [Col. 0257C–0258A]

[Note: “Our first Teacher.” Namely Augustine, archbishop of Canterbury and apostle of England. Alcuin wrote another letter to Athelard when he was about to depart for Rome. Malmesbury summarizes it in book I of *The Kings of the English*, chapter 4, in these words: “Alcuin indirectly chastises Athelard, archbishop and successor of Cuthbert, concerning the scantiness of clerical garments, warning him that when, on going to Rome, he visited Emperor Charlemagne, he should not bring clerics or monks dressed in multicolored and pompous garments, since clerics were accustomed to be clothed only in religious garments.”]

Blessed is the one who strives to preserve the unity of peace through fraternal love; but much more blessed is the one who labors to restore the torn members of charity, disrupted by others, to the structure of a single body. Therefore, now that divine grace is at work, the unity of the members adheres to its proper head, priestly dignity rejoices in its ancient honor, brotherly peace shines among the chief bishops of Britain, and under the two metropolitan cities one will of piety and concord flourishes, as I understood when I read it in the letters of your blessedness. [Col. 0258A]

[Editorial note: Quercetanus, edition 18, from a manuscript; Froben, p. 64.]

## Letter LXXIX: To the Lord King (798 or 799)

He commends his friends who have traveled from England to Rome. [Col. 0258B]

To the most desired lord David, king, Flaccus, registrar, sends eternal salvation in Christ.

The sweetness of your affection and the confidence inspired by your proven piety frequently urge me to send little letters to your authority and, through the service of syllables, to seek to accomplish what bodily frailty prevents my will from accomplishing. But the novelty of the circumstances that have arisen again compels me to produce new letters, so that the little note may convey the feeling of my heart and pour out prayers into the ears of your piety—prayers which, as I truly confess, have never been rejected in the sight of your mercy. Nor do I believe that my prayers for your stability and salvation have been rejected in the sight of God, since divine grace willingly receives tears that flow from the fountain of charity. [Col. 0258B–C]

I have been told that some of the friends of your Flaccus wish to approach your piety: Edelard, namely, metropolitan of the Church of Canterbury and bishop of the first see in Britain; also Ceilmund, formerly a minister of King Offa from the kingdom of the Mercians (text: *Mercionum*; Froben: *Merciorum*); and Torhcmund, the faithful servant of King Ethelred of Northumbria, a man proven in faith and vigorous in arms, who bravely avenged the blood of his lord. [Col. 0258C–0259A]

[Note: “Edelard.” Namely Aethilard, archbishop of Canterbury, who went to Rome to Leo III in 798 and again in 799 to restore the dignity of his see, which had been greatly damaged during the reign of Offa, king of the Mercians. See letter 60, now 75, to Adelhard. On that occasion Aethilard could have approached King Charles with his companions.]

[Note: “Torhcmund.” The manuscript reads “Hedilredi,” that is, of King Ethelred of Northumbria, who was killed by his own men in 796. See letter 42, now 47, to King Offa.]

All these men have been very faithful to me and helpers on my journey, or defenders of my boys who traveled here and there. I beg your excellent clemency to receive them with your customary kindness, for each of them was necessary to me in his own place. I have often learned that devout priests dedicated to Christ’s service, as well as strong and faithful men in secular dignity, are pleasing to your praiseworthy equity. For it is certain that every good person, proven in his own conscience, does not hesitate to love good people, having been taught by the example of almighty God, who is the supreme good. And every rational creature certainly possesses whatever good it has because it has been illumined by his goodness. Truth himself says: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). [Col. 0259A–B]

May the grace of Christ grant you perpetual light,

together with the saints, David, beloved of God. [Col. 0259B]

[Editorial note: Quercetanus printed this letter in two places: once on p. 1141, and again, from a corrected manuscript, in a fuller form with additions in several places, on p. 1465. It was written in 798, as appears from what follows. The very learned Father Ildephonsus Catelinot wished in his manuscript collection to remove it from the body of the letters and place it among Alcuin’s liturgical works. I nevertheless judged that it should be retained here, lest it be necessary to separate and disperse so many other letters dealing with various dogmatic, moral, philosophical, and astronomical questions.]

## Letter LXXX

[Note: Another heading in the earlier edition, p. 1141, reads: “To Charlemagne, emperor of the Gauls.”]

### To the Lord King (798, around Septuagesima)

On the calculation of Septuagesima, Sexagesima, and Quinquagesima. [Col. 0259B]

Blessed be God the Father almighty, who created and honored you; and blessed be our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who redeemed and chose you; and blessed be the Spirit Paraclete, who illumined you and enlarged your heart with every brightness of wisdom and knowledge, most beloved David and sweetest lord! And blessed be the holy Trinity, one almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who has granted me, his little servant, though unworthy, such a lord, friend, and helper of his grace; who through his servant, my teacher of blessed memory, graciously deigned to minister to me. And blessed be your power and kingdom, and those of your sons and your sons’ sons, through the everlasting generations of the age. May the blessing of the saints come upon you and your descendants on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose most holy will [alternative reading: “and may your own most holy will”] always flourish, flower, and grow in your heart, most illustrious ruler and defender of Christ’s Church.

I am filled with joy at hearing of your prosperity and exaltation, and wholly cheered with delight when I received, read, and kissed the letter of your blessedness. Therefore I venture to write something more familiarly to your affection and to present to your venerable gaze the little questions that have been proposed. Knowing that inquiry into scholastic learning and zeal for ecclesiastical discipline are pleasing and agreeable to your illustrious wisdom and sweetest intimacy—and that whatever is seasoned with the salt of urbanity is welcome to your intellectual ears and lovable to your keenest eyes of knowledge—we judged it right to direct to your most holy prudence what the scholarly youth of beginners is accustomed to thrust into dull ears [Al., *flaicinis*, perhaps *Flaccinis* or *Flaccianis*, that is, those of Flaccus], and to seek from there the comfort of an answer whence we know the rivers of wisdom to flow, although I confess that your most holy wisdom may regard these questions as unlearned. And lest my rusticity should presumptuously answer anything [Al., “lest someone presumptuously answer my rusticity”], we thought it safe to consult your praiseworthy genius and radiant keenness of learning. For just as worms fly into summer windows, so little questions settle upon my ears. And, stirred up by the suitability of the present season, they now ask according to ecclesiastical custom why the seventieth, sixtieth, or fiftieth order is said or observed on the Sundays before Lent.

If I answer that this is the custom of the Church and that the practice of this observance has been established by Roman authority, it seems too little to them to have answered by authority and custom alone, unless some reason is added to the authority; for they say that nothing has been established in ecclesiastical customs by the principal teachers without a cause. Their understanding is especially unsettled because the stated number does not correspond to the order of the days. Where they say “seventieth,” there are not seventy days until the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ. Likewise, where the number sixty is marked among the Sundays, it in no way agrees, by my reckoning, with the number of days until Easter. Again, if I say that it has been stated by synecdoche—that is, the whole by a part—this tropical expression, as you know very well, is recognized as extremely common in the Holy Scriptures, as in the three days and three nights during which our Lord Jesus Christ is read to have rested in the tomb (Matt. 12:40), which must be understood in this way, and in many other passages. To mention them all would exceed the size of a book. Yet they add that they ask why seventy, or sixty, or fifty are said in such a period [Al., “why Septuagesima, or Sexagesima, or Quinquagesima is said over so long a period”].

When I was at Rome, I heard certain teachers saying that Eastern peoples customarily fast for nine weeks, Greeks for eight, and Latins for seven; and that from this the Roman Church had taken the custom of calling the Sundays Septuagesima, Sexagesima, and Quinquagesima. Since I did not hear this from such teachers as I would dare to submit myself to their authority, I was wholly unable to affirm it. Therefore something still remains to be sought that agrees with the period and accords with reason, without conflicting with the number.

It seems to me that the day can be called the seventieth on account of the ten weeks extending from that day itself to the close of Easter [Al., “Easter”], when the white garments are removed from those recently baptized. Thus we also read in the Apostle: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses” (Rom. 5:14); and this signifies up to the final times of the Law, which was given through Moses and continued into the times of Christ our God. Moreover, it can be called the sixtieth because there are sixty days up to the middle of Easter, which will be the Wednesday of Easter week. The fiftieth, however, runs up to the holy day of the Lord’s resurrection. The fortieth number also runs, together with its Sunday, toward the mystical Passover of the Hebrews, which our Lord Jesus Christ celebrated with his disciples and which we call the Lord’s Supper.

Nor does the typological interpretation seem to disagree with these explanations. The number seven is known to correspond to the Holy Spirit in many passages of Sacred Scripture. Thus, after seven weeks, the Holy Spirit was sent from heaven in tongues of fire upon the hundred and twenty names of believers (Acts 2:3); and we read of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit in the prophet (Isa. 11:2–3). At that time especially, when the white garments are removed from the baptized, it is fitting that they receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands by the bishop, having received remission of all sins in baptism; and for seven days they customarily attend the holy sacrifices in an angelic [Al., evangelical] garment of chastity and with the lights of heavenly brightness.

The number six corresponds to the perfection of our life, because in six days the almighty Creator completed all his works (Gen. 1:31; 2:1). And this same number six, as your most learned sagacity knows, is perfect by its parts. The number five, multiplied by tens, proceeds to the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, signifying to us the remission of all sins and the justification of life in Christ. The number forty, multiplied four times by tens, is clearly a type of penitence in many passages. Thus our Lord himself fasted for forty days (Matt. 4:2), whose first preaching was: “Do penance; the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3:2). And just as Moses dedicated the Law and Elijah prophecy through forty days of fasting (Exod. 34:28; 1 Kings 19:8), so our Lord himself dedicated the evangelical preaching through a fast of forty days. As your ingenious and excellent prudence in all the disciplines of philosophy knows, the number forty—which, as we have said, corresponds to penitence—when divided through its own divisions and increased by its parts reaches fifty, which is the number of remission; for through penitence we must hasten toward the remission of our sins.

Something remarkable can also be found in this consideration and correspondence of the number six; and, in a certain way, the beginning of this computation agrees with its wondrous conclusion according to the rules of numbers. Thus, between the seventieth and the sixtieth there are six days; likewise between the sixtieth and the fiftieth; and again between the fiftieth and the fortieth the number six is found. Thus there are three sixes, making eighteen [Al., “eighteen days”]. If this number is considered and divided rationally into three equal parts, there will be three sixes; and it is the ratio of one to two, signifying the single death of Christ God in relation to our double death. For we were subject to two deaths—that is, of soul and flesh [Al., body]. But by his single and innocent death he destroyed our double death; and by his single resurrection he showed us and forgave our double death [Al., “ours”]: one death now in the soul, the other in the body on the great day of his coming, so that then there may be one glorious man in body and soul, who previously was one mortal man in soul and body—the soul through sin, the body through corruption.

Likewise, if the end of the calculation is considered, it seems fittingly to agree with this reasoning. Between Holy Thursday, the day of the Lord’s Supper, on which the number forty runs its course, and the Lord’s resurrection—that is, Sunday, on which the number fifty is reached—there are two days. Again, from the Sunday of the Lord’s resurrection [Al., “the day of the Lord’s resurrection”] until Wednesday, when the number sixty is reached, there are two days. Again, from Wednesday until Saturday, where the number seventy is completed, there are two days. When these days are joined—two and two and two—they make six. And if this six is divided into two and four, the same ratio of one and two is found in it. Thus this correspondence pertains to the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ; the earlier one pertains to the Passion, in which we were redeemed, and this one to justification, as the blessed Apostle says: “Christ suffered for our redemption, but he rose for our justification” (Rom. 4:25).

From this speculation you can demonstrate to your familiars how delightful and useful is knowledge of the discipline of arithmetic, which we believe is well known to your diligence and made known through you to others. I could have said more about this, but I did not wish to exceed the limits of the little sheet, especially since I was writing not to one who was ignorant but to one who knows all these things very well. Therefore I have merely sampled these matters in very few words, because I knew that all of them were thoroughly familiar to you. And, as it is said, “With the wise one must use few words” (Eccl. 5:1). Also: “Blessed is he who speaks into an attentive ear” (Prov. 20:12), that is, into one that understands.

Therefore, at the end of the letter, I must say with the queen of Sheba: “Blessed are your men, and blessed are your servants—those who stand before you always and hear your wisdom. Blessed be the Lord your God, in whom you have been pleased, and who has set you upon the throne of Israel, because the Lord loved Israel forever; and he appointed you king, that you might exercise judgment and justice” (1 Kings 10:8–9).

@ [Col. 0263D] Although we have already reprinted this letter among the works of Blessed Charlemagne, we present it here because of its close connection with the preceding and following letters. (In Froben, letter 66.) EDITOR.

## LETTER LXXXI. TO ALBINUS, THE ABBOT

@ [Col. 0263D] Letter. Quercetanus’s edition, p. 1147. Here we present the same letter in a more carefully corrected form from the manuscripts of Salzburg and St. Emmeram. I think both letters concerning Septuagesima were written in the year 798, in which year Alcuin also replied to this letter of Charlemagne through the following letter. The occasion for investigating this matter was provided by his students, “stirred up by the suitability of those times” [Col. 0264D]. Therefore these letters were written at the time of Septuagesima in that year.

Charlemagne replies to the preceding letter concerning the meaning of Septuagesima.

Charlemagne, by the grace of God king of the Franks,

@ [Col. 0264D] Emperor. This word is absent from the manuscripts of Salzburg and St. Emmeram; nor does it appear in Goldast, who published this letter in *Constitutiones imperiales*, vol. III, p. 137. It is likewise omitted in the *Chronicle of Centula*, in Pouget, p. 624, note a. And rightly so, for this letter was given before Charlemagne had been declared emperor, as we said in the preceding note. Emperor of the Lombards and patrician of the Romans, to our most beloved teacher and to Albinus the abbot, whom we name with love, eternal salvation in our Lord Jesus Christ.

A letter sent by your religious prudence reached us. After the praises and blessings due to almighty God, it brought to us and to our descendants a desirable blessing with the greatest benevolence [Al., “and the greatest benevolence”]. After this, its text proceeded with an inquiry into why Septuagesima, Sexagesima, and also Quinquagesima are said or written in order on the Sundays before Quadragesima. Then, taking up the matter and traversing the fields of arithmetic, your diligence endeavored to explain fully to us whatever it had perceived concerning this subject [Al., “determined”]. But while our mind ranged here and there, we considered through careful investigation that not only within the days prescribed by you but also through individual weeks and through the entire cycle of the year [Gold., “the entire cycle”]—by intervals of hours, points, or moments—the mysteries of numbers can be discovered by those who are trained in knowledge of this art. Therefore, since it pleased your affection to consult our royal court on this matter, we do not refuse to disclose to you in a connected discourse whatever our serenity thinks about it [Al., “thought”].

Since inquiry and consideration demand it, we must ask why some abstain for six weeks, others seven, others eight, and still others nine. We endeavor to indicate the reasoning of our understanding to your familiarity through these written lines. Those who observe six weeks and devote themselves to abstinence, subtracting the six Sundays on which fasting is by no means permitted, offer a tenth of the days of their bodies and fast for thirty-six days, as the blessed Gregory, that remarkable teacher, instructs; and although two days seem to remain in this period until the holy Resurrection, it has pleased the teachers of the holy Church of God to call this time Quadragesima.

As devotion increased, Pope Telesphorus—who shone as the ninth in the holy Roman Church after Peter, prince of the apostles—dedicated seven weeks to abstinence. And by what other name could this period more properly be called than Quinquagesima in due order? From this point onward, after the reasoning had been gathered, those who observed eight weeks gradually called it Sexagesima [Gold. adds: “who endeavored to observe them, gradually [called them] Sexagesima”]. Likewise, those who observed nine imposed the name Septuagesima according to the foregoing reasoning, and they judged these names not according to the number of weeks or days but according to the sequence of the names [Al., “numbers”]. It would be as though there were now some who wished, for a just reason, to add a tenth week and, because of the number of weeks, ought to call it Decagesima [Al., Decimagesima], or by some other name; or, because of the number of days, to call it Septuagesima or Octogesima, proceeding along the straight path while preserving the order of the names.

Since, therefore, with divine grace assisting us, we have written to your affection as it seemed to us concerning the names Septuagesima and Sexagesima [Al., Quadragesima], and Quinquagesima, we now take up our pen to write to you, according to the capacity [Gold., “sagacity”] of our understanding, about the observance and worship of these weeks.

Quinquagesima is called and observed by some so that, by fasting, they may offer a tenth of their days to almighty God and imitate our Lord Jesus Christ, who completed a most holy fast of forty days. From Quinquagesima until Easter there are seven weeks, which make fifty days. If you subtract from them the eight Sundays on which fasting may not be observed, forty-two days remain; and these two days—namely, Thursday and Saturday—those who follow this practice dedicate to fasting because they exceed the number forty, while others hold them in veneration [Al., “for refreshment”] on account of the Lord’s Supper and Holy Saturday.

Sexagesima, as we judge, is observed by some so that they may give a tenth of the days of their bodies [Al., “of their bodies”] to almighty God, imitate our Lord Jesus Christ by fasting in portions within the number forty, and be able to leave Sunday or Thursday free from fasting. From Sexagesima until the holy day of the Lord’s Resurrection there are eight weeks. If from each week you subtract Thursday and Friday [literally, “the first and fifth day”], as well as the holy day of Easter itself, only forty days remain for abstinence.

Melchiades, an African by birth, a man wholly apostolic and the thirty-fourth after holy Peter, whom the blessed Sylvester succeeded in the chair [Al., “to the chair”] of apostolic dignity, established that no believer should presume to fast on Sunday or Thursday [literally, “the first or fifth day”] for any reason.

@ [Col. 0265D] “For why . . .” In the manuscript of St. Emmeram it reads as follows: “For why should there be no fasting on Sunday, since the Savior himself handed this down? There is no need to repeat it at length.” “For why should fasting be broken on Sunday, since the Savior himself handed this down? There is no need to repeat it at length.” We have judged that Thursday was released from fasting because of the great mysteries contained in it. On that day the holy chrism is prepared for washing away the primordial sins of the whole world [Al., “for washing away . . . the sin”]; on that day reconciliation is made for penitents; on that day the Redeemer of all, dining with his disciples, broke bread and likewise gave them the cup

@ [Col. 0265D] “As a figure.” The manuscript of St. Emmeram and Goldast read: “In figure.” These words are not to be understood in the Calvinist sense but in the Catholic sense, as they are explained in the work of D. Arnauld, *On the Perpetuity of the Faith*, vol. I, p. 765. as a figure of his body and blood, and gave us a great Sacrament for our benefit (Matt. 26:26–27). On that same day, after many mysteries, God and our Lord Jesus Christ, in the sight of his holy disciples, entered the heavens in a glorious Ascension (Luke 24:51; Acts 1:9). But lest the discourse be prolonged further, we do not fail to know that you have read much concerning this solemnity in the sayings of the venerable orthodox holy Fathers.

Finally, Septuagesima, as we judge, is observed by some so that they may offer a tenth of their days to God [Al., “to the Lord”], and may release themselves from fasting on Sunday, Thursday, and also Saturday [literally, “the first, fifth, and seventh day”]. From Septuagesima until Easter there are nine weeks, making sixty-four days [Gold., “sixty-three”]. If from each week you subtract the three days named above, as well as the most holy Paschal day, thirty-six days remain for abstinence [Al., “of abstinence”]. These people endeavor to break the fast on Saturday, on which God rested from all his works (Gen. 2:2), not merely because of Jewish superstition or because of the legal commandments of the Old Testament, which are a shadow of things to come, but lest they give offense to the Jews [Al., “be scandalized”; Gold., “become sabbatarians”]. The principal reason is that, when that day grows toward evening, the joy of the holy resurrection is solemnly celebrated by the faithful. But since “each person abounds in his own understanding” (Rom. 14:5), whether this is so or something else, we prejudice nothing that is consistent with faith and religion [Al., “we have prejudged nothing”; another Al., “it is prohibited”; another Al., “we have preached it”].

@ [Col. 0265D] “But concerning this.” We have added this clause, which was absent from the printed editions, from the manuscript of Salzburg, Goldast at the cited place, p. 138, and D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. IV, p. 470. “But concerning what your little sheet went on to report—that much could be said about this, but that you did not wish to exceed the limits of the sheet, especially since, just as few words should be used with a wise person, so we in turn have written a few things in few words. As for your use of the queen of Sheba’s words to Solomon concerning the blessedness of the servants who stand before us and hear the words of our wisdom: if you know this to be true, come, stand before us, listen, and together let us delight in the Lord amid the flowering meadows, rejoicing in the varied flowers of the Scriptures.”

@ [Col. 0265D] This letter is numbered 13 in Canisius, 9 in Quercetanus, and 67 in Froben; there it is mutilated, here complete. Several corrections from the manuscript Reg. Vat. no. 226 are now added.

## LETTER LXXXII. TO LORD KING  
*(Year 798.)*

He replies to the preceding letter and sends calculations of the lunar leap.

The desirable [Al. and Vatican manuscript, “desired by me”] and long-awaited face of your good letters suddenly shone forth, and after a very long time the lines of your most holy name refreshed my eyes, eager to see them. Although something reprehensible may have been sung in the following sequence of my little letters, I nevertheless drank in everything with honeyed sweetness when this desirable and much-loved name appeared at the beginning. I confess [Al., “I shall confess”] that it was also most welcome to me to deserve, even in this way, to kiss the syllables of your blessedness: what perpetual and inviolate affection could not earn, at least the sudden pretext of rebuke might extort—knowing that the wounds of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses of one who hates.

Nor is it surprising if the sluggishness of a little donkey should endure a whip upon its back. I, sluggish; I, forgetful of myself, perhaps rightly endured the whip of your boys. The old Entellus, his body exhausted, laid aside his boxing gloves long ago; he yields them to those flourishing in youth. Therefore one of them struck the old man with a tremendous blow, so that darkness passed before the old man’s eyes; and only with difficulty, after his strength had returned, did the blood that had grown cold around his heart warm again.

And, to come to the matter and begin to heal the head I have struck with the fomentations of ignorance: I, unskilled; I, ignorant, not knowing that an Egyptian school was active in the palace of David’s glory

@ [Col. 0266D] This is the end of the letter in Canisius:

@ [Col. 0266D] “When I departed.” Namely, when I departed from the palace school for Tours, I left the Latins there. I do not know who introduced

@ [Col. 0266D] {93} “the Egyptians.” I think I can conjecture who those Egyptian teachers were from a poem of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, to Angilbert. In that poem he attacks with false and bitter taunts a certain Scot living and teaching at court. For the Scots, who originated in Ireland, once followed the Alexandrian Paschal cycle, according to which they celebrated Easter on the fourteenth day of the moon whenever it fell on a Sunday. Perhaps this was Clement the Scot, whom Charlemagne is reported to have left in Gaul to teach, according to the monk of St. Gall at the beginning of book one. MABILLON. *Acts of the Saints*, fourth century, part I, preface, p. CXXXI. “the Egyptians.” Nor was I so unlearned in the calculations of Memphis as I was devoted to Roman custom. Wishing to begin the year, together with the birth of Christ and the increasing light, according to the Latins—not with the Egyptians, whose name is interpreted as “darkness,” beginning from the darkness that follows—for I know that once, with Moses, I must leave the darkness of the Egyptians, and now, in the promised land of light and joy, stand honored in freedom with Jesus our leader, and in no way, according to what my leader, indeed our Lord, said, return again to the darkness of Egypt.

Therefore I wonder why your boys wish to begin the proper year from the month of September and to connect a part of the completed nineteen-year cycle with the following cycle, turning the tail toward the head, rather than, after eliminating all the increases and decreases of the moon and stars, enter wholly freely into the new year and the beginning of the cycle that follows.

Yet I would like to ask these same boys whether it seems more appropriate to take the lunar ages of one year as regulars, and those of the first year as well, or even those of two years—that is, of the last year of the nineteen-year cycle and the first of the following. And whether it is closer to reason to insert the leap at the end of the nineteen-year cycle or in the middle of any year. I would also like to know how they wish to calculate the lunar ages from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, where the fourteenth moon

@ [Col. 0267D] “Of the last year.” Namely, of the recently elapsed year 797, in which the fourteenth moon fell on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, according to the nineteen-year cycles of the Venerable Bede. This letter, therefore, was written in the year 798. “Of the last year,” up to the month of September, in which month the fifth [day] is sung among the Egyptian boys? How can it happen that one moon always has thirty days and another twenty-nine, while the individual [lunar ages] can remain fixed throughout those months? And, as I think, what they will criticize among the Latins they find also among the Egyptians. Perhaps what they do not wish to happen in November must necessarily be found in some other month. Nor do I wish to pull a contentious rope with anyone, nor to entangle myself in the little questions of others. Let each person abound in his own understanding.

As for what you took care to admonish me familiarly [and beneficially] at the end of the letter, that if anything should humbly be corrected, it should be corrected: by God’s gift I have never been stubborn in my error, nor confident in my own judgments. Nor am I such that I could not readily agree with a better opinion, knowing that it is said that one ought to use the ears more often than the tongue. I beg your wisdom to understand this entirely—not that I write to you as to one who does not know, but as to one who approves; nor as to one who is ignorant, but rather as to one who corrects, I direct the thoughts of my littleness.

The evangelical widow did not put two small coins into the treasury (Mark 12:42) because the temple was in need, but because of her devotion. Nor does our humility offer gifts to God as though he lacked anything, but rather to one who possesses all things (2 Cor. 6:10). So also my littleness truly acknowledges that, if I attempt to write anything to you, who are not in need but understand far better, I do so as I ought. “A wise son is the glory of his father” (Prov. 13:1).

As for your saying [Vatican manuscript, “judging”] that it was unworthy to repeat what was already known, I do not know what the rusticity of Flaccus could thrust, as something unknown, upon rich wisdom [Vatican manuscript, “Davidic wisdom”]. But if what is known and formerly heard may not be introduced, what shall we do with letters, even syllables and words, which we necessarily use every day, unless we begin devising rules of a new grammatical art?

It would have been much better for me to eat the purest bread upon the table of your delights than to count grains of wheat with Menalcas in a bakery, from which bread is to be made. If it pleases you, let us enter for a little into the little bakeries of the calculators, or the sooty kitchens of the mathematicians, and we shall bring forth what was once known but is now almost forgotten, according to the prophecy of your Virgil. For:

[lacuna] “I often remember, while singing, laying the long days to rest as a boy. Now so many songs are forgotten by me, and my voice itself has fled from Flaccus. [lacuna]”

Nevertheless, to answer the questions in your little sheet—not supported by riches of wisdom but moved by the letters of your authority, and protected in the lap of your piety—I shall endeavor to set forth a few things about the various reasoning of the lunar leap. First I shall state what I learned in the books of the teachers; second, what I was able to investigate by persuading myself through reasoning [Vatican manuscript, “by reasoning”]; third, what I was able to remember from the mathematical discipline once heard {92}. Thus the manifold lunar leap may be unraveled in manifold ways, as Solomon says: “A threefold cord is not easily broken” (Eccl. 4:12). Likewise, while speaking of wisdom, he added, saying: “Behold, I have written it for you three times” (Prov. 22:20).

These thoughts I have endeavored to direct to your authority, my lord David, most keen investigator of natural things and most devoted investigator of the causes of every kind of reasoning—not distinguished by a spirit of boasting but devoted to the duty of humility, prepared to obey your most holy commands. And if you can find anything worthy of the gaze of those letters and of your keenest eyes, I know that I must give thanks to God, the giver of all gifts [printed edition, “givers”]. If the pen has quickly written anything otherwise than you deserved, I confess that it must be attributed to me; and it must be corrected by the pen of your excellent goodness, while I am protected in the lap of your piety.

@ [Col. 0268D] “These calculations of the lunar leap,” some of them in

@ [Col. 0268D] “Another little sheet.” This little sheet is undoubtedly the one that we present below among the philosophical works from the manuscript of the Royal Swedish Library, Vatican Library no. 226. See also below, letter 84 (now 100). “I distinctly marked these calculations of the lunar leap in another little sheet. As I said, I wrote some from the reading of the thoughts of the Fathers; others I investigated through conjecture based on reasoning; others I gathered from the various calculations of mathematicians [from the Vatican manuscript: “I gathered from suspicions”], so that I would not remain silent before the commands of your venerable dignity and be guilty if I seemed disobedient to so great an authority. Knowing that you can understand and investigate all these matters much more truly and sagaciously, I nevertheless did not refuse the services of Flaccus’s rusticity, so that I might do what you commanded, expecting the reward of obedience and hoping not for the injury of rebuke, because the accustomed goodness of your heart can never be changed but remains inviolate and always progresses toward better things, until, with the Lord God, the Son of God, showing mercy, it reaches the glory of eternity with abundant praise for its merits.”

At the moment when your servants and the sons of our devotion were setting out, the honey-sweet lines of your sweetest authority arrived,

@ [Col. 0269D] “Lines.” Or, the letter of Charlemagne concerning Septuagesima, which we gave above. From it, therefore, we also learn the year in which it was given. “lines,” in which you responded reasonably to the questions of our littleness. And as though dripping sweetness like a honeycomb (Song 4:11), so I read the words of your sweetness, in which I recognized both cheerfulness and truth; and, giving thanks to God, I praised both—the beauty of wisdom and the strength of humility—since you deigned to hear the little sheet of our rusticity, not merely to read it through but also to answer it.

I also found written with affection in those letters of your goodness, as though spoken in my own words, how the queen of the South had come to hear Solomon’s wisdom (1 Kings 10), and how I had exclaimed that those who stood beside Solomon’s wisdom were blessed; and by these words you wished to summon me to that blessedness. I accept this [“grace,” Al., “gratitude”] according to the health of my body, with the grace of God going before me and guiding me safely into the presence of your blessedness.

Yet let your mercy know that this blessedness praised by the queen of the South was not in the land of the Philistines but in Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of peace. Therefore I humbly beg that your Flaccus may be permitted to reach this blessedness in the land of peace and joy, not in the land of dissension and

@ [Col. 0269D] “Saxon.” As I understand it, this was done in the present year, 798, and is described by the Annalist of Lambec and others; see Pagi for this year, no. 4. “war.” What is Flaccus’s weakness worth amid weapons? What is a little hare among boars? What is a little lamb, nourished and raised in peace and unpracticed in battles, among lions? Since you possess the commands of the Lord God, let the timid man remain at home, lest he make others afraid. And Virgil, writing to Augustus:

[lacuna] “You pursue the boars; I guard the nets.”

I beg that these prayers may enter the heart of your piety, so that you may wish and permit me, with palm branches (John 12:13) and singing children, to go out to meet the triumph of your glory; and, while Jerusalem, the desired homeland, and the temple of the wisest Solomon are being built by art [F., “built”], to stand before your beloved presence and say: “Blessed is the Lord God, who has brought [and brought back] beloved David with prosperity [Col. 0269D] and safety to his servants.”

It appears to have been written in the same year as the other letter that immediately follows, in which he defends his calculation concerning the increase of ten and a half hours proposed here. (In Froben, letter 68.)

## LETTER LXXXIII. TO LORD KING  
*(Year 798.)*

Concerning the course of the sun through the signs of the zodiac, and how the leap year arises from it. He praises the study of astrology, arithmetic, and every branch of philosophy. He asks for assistants to refute Felix and encourages the king to defend the truth.

To David, beloved by God and chosen by God, king, Flaccus sends perpetual salvation in Christ in faith and charity.

The sweetest gifts of your piety [printed edition, “your piety”] to me

@ [Col. 0270D] Fredegisus. Is this Fredegisus the same as Fridegisus, Alcuin’s disciple, whom he addressed by the name Nathanael in his letter to Candidus and Nathanael? “Fredegisus, your little servant, brought.” In them I recognized both affection toward me and wisdom in you, as though, in a certain way, the gifts of four days represented the four primordial days of creation.

And because on the first day light was created (Gen. 1:3 and following), on the first day he showed me the material of light. Oil.

On the second day the Creator extended the beauty of the firmament between the waters and the waters; on the second day, in the gifts, I recognized the priestly garments as demonstrating the division between the bodies of the priests and those of the people.

On the third day the earth appeared with its ornaments; on the third day, the most pleasing appearance of gold, which is drawn from the earth’s womb, was sent to me.

On the fourth day the sun, the honor of the world, with the stars of heaven, was introduced [Vatican manuscript, “placed”]; on the fourth day, a certain bright and rounded object in the likeness of the sun,

@ [Col. 0270D] “Honor of the table.” I interpret the jar filled with wine. “honor of the table,” was brought to me. It has twenty-seven semicircles; if these are doubled, they make fifty-four, corresponding to the hours of the lunar course through which it customarily travels through the individual signs. It has a round circle in the middle, corresponding to the sun’s perpetual roundness.

Concerning its course, the aforementioned boy reported to me that you were seeking wisdom about how ...

@ [Col. 0270D] **Ten and a half hours.** In the following letter he asks about this calculation: what is to be changed? Do ten and a half hours usually accumulate in each month? The reasoning for this is subtle, but very easy for your keenness to understand.

Thus, in the first year after the intercalary year, at the beginning of the first hour of the night, the sun enters Aries; after thirty days and ten and a half hours it will leave Aries—that is, at the eleventh hour of the thirty-first night, and at the second point. At the third point of that same eleventh hour it enters Taurus, and remains there for thirty days and ten and a half hours. It will leave Taurus not from the full daylight hour [Perhaps: “the ninth hour of the day”]. And there you have one hour out of four points in the two signs. Thus the two signs make sixty days and twenty-one hours.

At the tenth hour of the day it enters Gemini. It will leave Gemini at the full seventh hour of the night and at two points of the eighth hour. At the third point of the eighth hour of the night it enters Cancer. It will leave Cancer at the full sixth hour of the day. And there you have a second hour and four points of the two signs.
