Thus Gemini and Cancer make sixty days and twenty-one hours. You have [Cod. Vat.: “And you have”] in these four [Col. 0271A] signs forty-two hours and one hundred twenty days.

{94} It enters Leo at the seventh hour of the day. It will leave Leo at the fourth hour of the night and at two points of the fifth hour. At the third point of the fifth hour of the night it enters Virgo. It will leave Virgo at the full third hour of the day. You have one hour out of the four points of Leo and Virgo. These two signs contain sixty days and twenty-one hours. [Col. 0271D] The Vatican manuscript omits the bracketed words: “And these six signs make one hundred eighty-three days.” And there are, as I said, one hundred eighty-two days. And the third: half a day from twelve hours, and three hours beyond the quarter-hours. The sun enters Libra at the fourth hour of the day. It will leave Libra at the first hour of the day and at the second point of the second hour of the night. It enters Scorpio at the third point of the second hour of the night. And it [Col. 0271B] leaves Scorpio at the full twelfth hour of the night. You have one hour out of the four points. Thus these two signs make sixty days and twenty-one hours.

The sun enters Sagittarius at the first hour of the day. It will leave Sagittarius at the full tenth hour of the day and at two points of the tenth hour. It enters Capricorn at the third point of the eleventh hour of the day. It will leave Capricorn at the full ninth hour of the night. These two signs contain sixty days and twenty-one hours. Add these to the signs written above. You have three hundred days and one hundred five hours.

The sun enters Aquarius at the tenth hour of the night. It will leave Aquarius at the eighth hour of the day and at the second point of the eighth hour. It enters Pisces at the third point of the eighth day [Cod. Vat.: “of the eighth hour of the day”]. It will leave Pisces at the full sixth hour [Col. 0271C] of the night. These are the six hours that accrue from the points of the individual signs. These two signs contain sixty days and twenty-one hours. Add these to the days or hours written above, and the twelve signs make 360 days and 126 hours.

Divide 120 hours by twenty-four, and there are five times twenty-four, which is five days. Thus the entire year consists of 365 days and six hours, because previously you had 126 hours. These six hours, multiplied over four years, make twenty-four hours, which is one day—the day that the Latins call the intercalary day. If this day were not added in February of the fourth year, the sun would enter Aries on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, at the first hour of the night; and after 120 years the sun’s delay, when it ought to have entered Aries, would cause it to enter Taurus instead. unless thirty days were added to its course in 120 intercalary years.

[These and similar calculations are so delightful in contemplation to those who understand them, just as the other philosophical arts ordinarily are to the student who learns and understands them.]

@ [Col. 0271D] Thus the true reading is restored from the Vatican manuscript. In Quercetanus it was corruptly written as follows: “These in such calculations become so sweet, and contemplation to the ignorant, as the other arts of philosophy are accustomed to be to the learner” [Col. 0272D] “and to understandings.”

For philosophers were not the creators of these arts, but their discoverers. The Creator of all things created them within nature as he willed. Those who were wiser in the world were discoverers of these arts within the natures of things, as you can easily understand from the sun, the moon, and the stars. For what else do we contemplate and admire in the sun, moon, and stars except the wisdom of the Creator and their natural courses?

It is therefore reported that the patriarch Abraham understood and worshiped God the Creator through the discipline of astrology. From this he was called the Friend of God, and, when tested in faith, was found already strong. For the Hebrews say that he came out of Ur of the Chaldeans (Gen. XII, 1, and XV, 7), that is, from the fire of the Chaldeans. The Chaldeans worshiped fire as God.

@ [Col. 0272D] **My teacher.** Egbertus, or Aelbertus? archbishop of York. See the letter to Eanbald and Malmesbury, Book I of *The Deeds of the Kings*, chapter 3.

My teacher used often to say to me: “The wisest of men were those who discovered these arts within the natures of things. It is a great disgrace if we allow them to perish in our own days.” [Col. 0272B] But now the faintheartedness of many does not care to know the principles of things that the Creator established in nature.

You know very well how sweet arithmetic is in its principles, how necessary it is for understanding the divine Scriptures, and how delightful is the knowledge of the heavenly stars and their courses. Yet there are few who care to know such things; and, what is worse, they criticize those who study them. Their ignorance of natural things could in some way have been blameless, if they had wished to devote themselves to the divine Scriptures and labor in those matters in which the knowledge of eternal life is contemplated; and if they could thereby have defended the Catholic faith truthfully and stood confidently against the adversaries of Christ, through whom the devil’s cunning strives in many ways to attack the Catholic faith.

And these are the times of which blessed Paul foretold: “Now the Spirit expressly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy” [Cod. Vat.: “of the deceitful spirits of demons speaking in hypocrisy,” etc.], “having their conscience branded” (I Tim. IV, 1–2).

If you wish to know how ten and a half hours accrue to the solar course in each year [F.: “in each month”], multiply ten by ten: the result is one hundred, because one hour contains ten minutes. (Ten times ten minutes make one hundred minutes. Give each day 140 [F.: “of 30”] days three minutes, and the result is ninety minutes.) Ten minutes remain. Add to these the five minutes that result from half an hour, and there are fifteen minutes.

[Col. 0272D] Divide these by thirty: thirty times half a minute makes fifteen minutes; thus in thirty days three minutes and half a minute accrue daily. If you wish to know how much accrues daily toward the intercalary day, divide five minutes by thirty: there are six times five. One-sixth of a minute accrues daily, so that half an hour is completed in one month.

Multiply this half-hour by twelve, and the result is six hours. Multiply these by four: four times six makes [Col. 0273A] twenty-four, the number of hours in one day [Supply: “which”]. It accrues over four years, so that an intercalary day can be made. Thus in the fourth year there are 366 days.

This number six has great importance in the circle of the year. For 360 is made up of six times sixty. If sixty is divided by ten, you will find that the number sixty is perfect through ten, just as six is perfect through one. For one, two, and three make six, and it is a perfect number in its parts.

In the same way, sixty possesses a certain perfection when divided by the number ten. For once ten, twice ten, and three times ten make sixty. For the value that six has in the first sequence of numbers, in reaching ten, the number sixty has in the second sequence of numbers, in reaching [Col. 0273B] one hundred.

The five days that remain beyond the 360 days in the individual months are one-sixth of each month. The six hours from which, in the fourth year, the sixth day accrues likewise possess their perfection in the division of the number six, as we said shortly before.

And just as the most equitable Creator accomplished all the works of the primordial world in six days, so that it might be signified, through the perfection of the number six, that he made all things perfect in their natures, so that same great, wondrous, perfect Creator is perfect in his nature. It pleased him [Cod. Vat.: “it pleased”] to complete all things in the perfection of the number six.

Therefore on the sixth day the human being was created, perfect in soul and body; for whose sake all things were created, which are read to have been established in six days. Hence God himself, the Son of God, who is the power and wisdom of God (I Cor. I, 24), came into the world in the sixth age of the world to save the human being whom he had created on the sixth day.

Thus the number six has great importance both in the creation of the primordial creatures and in the succession of the ages, which proceeded through six ages, and because in the sixth age the Son of God came to restore the human race to the original dignity of its creation.

Such calculations, O most beloved [and sweetest] David, ought to be written to you by me, not to just any rustic. I know that your wisdom has been educated in them, and I recognize that they altogether please you, so that your mind may rejoice in the principles of things, just as mine greatly rejoices when I frequently send such matters to you.

Blessed is the Lord God in his gifts, who has granted you the most illustrious knowledge of the divine law [Col. 0273D] and the most delightful understanding of natural things. For his ineffable mercy we must all give thanks with the continual and wholehearted intention of our will, because he has granted us such a lord and ruler. And by constant prayers we must ask his most merciful power that he may deign to preserve you for us in lasting prosperity and health,

@ [Col. 0273D] **Most deeply desired David.** This is the end of the letter in the Vatican manuscript. Hence I might suspect that in what follows a new letter begins, which through the copyist’s carelessness has been appended here to the preceding one.

**Most deeply desired David.**

Recently there came to me

@ [Col. 0273D] **Recently … a little book.** This is evidently Felix’s reply to Alcuin’s letter, written in the pen of charity. Here Alcuin asks that the refutation of the error be entrusted to several people, especially Pope Leo, Paulinus, Richbodo, and Theodulf, as appears in the following letter.

A little book sent by Felix the unhappy recently came to me. When, out of curiosity, I hurried through a few pages of it, I found worse heresies—or rather, greater blasphemies—than I had previously read in his writings. He asserts that Jesus Christ is neither truly the Son of God nor even truly God, but only so-called God.

He does not consider what the distinguished preacher says about the divinity of Christ: “Whose are the fathers, from whom is Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. IX, 5). And I hope that more may be found there that appears to oppose the Catholic faith. If nothing else against the Catholic faith is found, this alone is sufficient for his destruction.

“Woe to the world because of offenses!” (Matt. XVIII, 7). Behold: he who is worshiped by the angels in heaven is denied by men on earth as being truly God.

The response to this book—or rather, to this error—[Col. 0274B] must be considered with great care and with the assistance of many people. I alone am not sufficient for the response. Let your holy piety provide suitable assistants for this work, so arduous and necessary, so that this impious heresy may be utterly extinguished before it spreads more widely through the world of the Christian empire, which divine mercy has entrusted to you and your sons to rule and govern.

Rise, man chosen by God; rise, son of God; rise, soldier of Christ, and defend the bride of the Lord your God. Think of your bride: if someone wished to dishonor her, how patiently would your enemy endure this? Consider also that an insult against your son will reach you; how much more, then, must an insult and reproach against the Son of God, your Savior, your protector, and the giver of all good things, be avenged by you with all your strength? [Col. 0274C] Stand manfully for her whom you received from your God to rule and preserve, so that secular power may advance you toward the riches of spiritual glory.

@ [Col. 0274D] This letter is number 11 in Canisius; number 4 in Quercetanus, who supplied the deficiency in the preceding letter from a manuscript. (In Frobenius, p. 69.)

# LETTER LXXXIV. TO THE LORD KING  
*(In the year 798.)*

He replies to Charlemagne about composing a poem, the appearance of the star Mars, refuting Felix’s little book, questions put to him by the king’s daughter, and correcting calculations according to the Egyptians.

To my sweetest and truly most beloved lord David, magnificent and God-crowned king, Flaccus, veteran soldier, perpetual greeting.

The most joyful little sheet of your letters came to me, refreshing me in fever, reviving me in sleep, and indeed striving to restore me, sluggish with the disease of inactivity, to my former strength. It reminded me to mingle the sweet melody of versification amid the dreadful clash of weapons and the hoarse blasts of trumpets, so that the fierce movements of men’s minds might be soothed by some melody of musical sweetness; even though the most noble steadfastness of your mind remains perpetually in one and the same citadel [Al.: “ark”] of solidity, and flourishes with unshaken strength at the balance-point of justice.

[Col. 0275A] Yet you wished the ferocity of your boys to be softened by the sweetness of some poem; and you foresaw this also with the wisest counsel, because the harshness of an angry mind often fails to achieve the effect [Al.: “affection”] of sound advice, just as continual softness of spirit is accustomed to weaken strength.

But between these kinds of illness prudent moderation stands on a middle path: here it calms swelling fury, there it raises a sluggish spirit; and the royal road settles everything through the counsel of peace. We read in the ancient books of history that this kind of virtue is especially necessary to those engaged in warfare, so that wise moderation may direct and govern everything that ought to be done.

For three things seem to require consideration in an enemy: strength, cunning, and peace. First, whether the adversary can be overcome by public force. [Col. 0275B] If not, the matter must be referred to stratagems and devices of cunning. And if this too achieves nothing, then the hatreds of enmity seem to be removed through the counsel of peace.

Yet if the Flaccine [Al.: “Flaccian”] pipe can soothe savage spirits in any way, I think it should be completed with every care, according to the suitability of the time and the person. Meanwhile I, your Flaccus, am going faithfully and with every diligence to carry out what your sweetest authority wished to entrust to me through your faithful Magamfredus [Al.: “Magenfredus”].

@ [Col. 0275D] **Magamfredus.** Perhaps the same person as the one mentioned in letters 37 and 105 (now 42 and 133).

And let your goodness know with complete certainty that no one has a greater desire—as is right—to fulfill the need for your assistance.

Thus a friend is so called as though he were a guardian of the spirit; that is, one who strives with every concern of loyalty to guard his friend’s spirit intact, so that the sacred right of friendship may nowhere be violated.

Few understand this. Almost everyone seeks to preserve friendship according to the quality of his own spirit, not according to the satisfaction of the other spirit, who is his friend [Al.: “of this person”]. And if this must be carefully observed in a friend [Al.: “spirit”] and an equal, so that the integrity of his spirit may remain inviolate, how much more must it be observed toward a lord, and toward such a person as loves to exalt and govern his subjects with every honor?

The proverbial saying of the ancients therefore shines brightly: “A friend is sought for a long time, found with difficulty, and preserved with difficulty.” And in Holy Scripture: “There is no comparison with a faithful friend” (Eccli. VI, 15).

@ [Col. 0275D] From these words it may be gathered (says Canisius) that this letter was written in the year 799. For at that time the mathematicians of those days rejoiced that the star Mars had appeared again. Nor do I interpret this passage of Alcuin in any other way. The Engolismensian, in his *Life of Charlemagne*, says: “In this year, that is, from the incarnation of the Lord 799, the star Mars could nowhere be seen in the whole sky, from July of the preceding year until July of this year.”

And this is what Alcuin means when he says: “which the sun held for a very long time, but abandoned through fear of the Nemean lion.” For on 23 or 24 July the sun enters the sign of Leo. CANISIUS.

But it must be said, on the basis of the Tilian and Loiselian Annals, which the Engolismensian copied, and of the Chronicle of Ado, that the discovery of the star Mars occurred in July 798, after it had remained hidden from that month of the preceding year, 797, until then. For this reason we believe that the present letter belongs to the year 798.

Now, after we had sought it for so long amid the weapons of Mars, the star of Mars suddenly shone forth. The sun had held it for a very long time, but abandoned it through fear of the Nemean lion, who, it is said, was placed in the heavens [Al.: “clothed”] in memory of Hercules’ strength; and the star was assigned to Cancer for two months [Al.: “for three months”],

@ [Col. 0276D] **And proceeding by another route.** This is the end of the letter in Canisius; the rest was added from a manuscript by Quercetanus.

and proceeding by a different route, it will soon make that retrograde motion. The Dog Star also added itself, with its shining face, greatly beloved by physicians who awaited rewards. But the reason why the sun had kept it hidden for so long is, according to the ancients, the sun’s rays, which, as is said, produce the unequal courses of the planets.

For this reason they are perhaps called “wanderers,” because they are known not always to have a fixed and uniform course. If this is so, as some calculators prefer, let the Egyptian boys say why the sun and moon are counted among them, when both these stars have fixed courses in years, months, days, hours, and moments.

They do not wander in the sense, they say, that they appear to move against the heavens, while they complete the boundaries of their courses at the most certain times; [Col. 0276B] whereas the courses of the five stars are very often borne irregularly through the breadth of the zodiacal circle, either wandering, standing still, or moving backward.

@ [Col. 0276D] **Concerning the little book.** More about it elsewhere.

As for the little book of the unhappy man—not a teacher but a subverter—I am very pleased that your most holy will and devotion is taking care to respond in defense of the Catholic faith. But I ask, if it pleases your piety, that a copy of that little book be sent to the apostolic lord.

Also another [copy should be sent]

@ [Col. 0276D] **To Paulinus the patriarch.** Of Aquileia. **To Richbodo, or Richbodo, bishop of Trier,** as Mabillon seems to think. **To Theodulf, bishop of Orléans.**

To Paulinus the patriarch; likewise to Richbodo and Theodulf, bishops, teachers, and masters, so that each may respond individually on his own behalf.

Your Flaccus is laboring with you to give an account of the Catholic faith. Let him be given sufficient time so that he may quietly and carefully consider, with his boys, the opinions of the Fathers: what each one would say concerning the propositions [Col. 0276C] that the aforesaid subverter set forth in his little book.

At the time appointed by you, let the responses of each be brought before your authority. Whatever in that book—whether propositions or opinions—is found to be contrary to the Catholic faith, let all of it be destroyed by Catholic examples.

And if the writings of all alike and concordantly resound in their profession or defense of the Catholic faith, it may be understood that one Spirit speaks through all their mouths and hearts. But if anything different is found in anyone’s statements or writings, let it be seen who relies upon the greater authority of the holy Scriptures or the Catholic Fathers; and let the palm of praise be awarded to the one who adheres more closely to the divine testimonies.

Concerning the questions that

@ [Col. 0276D] **My daughter.** Which daughter? I have no certainty; perhaps Gisela, Charlemagne’s daughter?

my daughter, your most faithful servant, asked me, I do not recall in orderly fashion, except that, as I think, she asked about the psalms that we sang in the chapel at the evening hour of this present day.

First, then, she asked about the place where the Prophet says, “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. CXV, 11): how can the person who never speaks, such as infants and mutes, be a liar? And again, why did he say in the same psalm, “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me?” (ibid., verse 12)? What is it that the Lord has repaid us? Certainly, good things in return for our evils.

She also asked something about the moon, concerning the verse in which he says, “The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night” (Ps. CXX, 6). From this she added a question about the nature of the moon: if it were of a cold nature, how could it burn?

We do not doubt that all these matters are known to your wisdom. Therefore there is no need for me now to explain interpretations of these questions.

We also had a conversation

@ [Col. 0277D] **Concerning the columns, etc.** I understand this to refer to the basilica at Aachen, about which Einhard, in his *Life of Charlemagne* in Bouquet, p. 99, no. 26, relates the following: “He built a basilica of the greatest beauty and adorned it with gold and silver. Since he could not obtain columns and marbles for its construction elsewhere, he arranged for them to be brought from Rome and Ravenna.”

about the columns that were set in the beautiful and wondrous work of the church, which your wisdom directed. [Col. 0277B] She also asked me something small about Donatus, though I do not know what.

But I received with the greatest gratitude what your most holy benevolence took care to urge us to do: to inquire of the Egyptian boy about changing certain calculations involving ten hours or the quarter-hour [Al.: “quadrantal”] calculation. It is altogether pleasing to my mind that things unknown may be asked of you, or errors corrected through you.

For among familiar persons and in the sacred names of charity, it ought to be observed that in letters passing between them correction should sound more than reproach. In this way all are able to learn, understand, and reach the way of truth.

A horse with four feet often falls; how much more often does a human being, possessing one tongue, fall in speech from time to time? Nor am I ashamed to ask, hear, and agree with the principles of truth. No age, as the comic poet says, ought to be too late for learning wisdom.

Therefore I ask, and in asking I earnestly wish to hear, what must be changed in the calculations of ten and a half hours in each month, and what contrary to the reasoning of nature is found in the calculation that

@ [Col. 0277D] **Our little sheet.** That is, in the preceding letter.

our little sheet sent to your authority. Unless perhaps the notary’s hand had changed words, syllables, or letters—which often happens not only with Latin boys but also with Egyptian boys—as I learned had happened in our earlier little sheet,

@ [Col. 0278D] **In the earlier little sheet, concerning the reduction of the intercalation.** See Letter 67 (now 82) and the notes.

through your most devoted inquiry concerning the reduction of the intercalation. Thus the copyist’s error will in some way be attributed to the one dictating.

But I ask that the most merciful goodness of your wisdom take care rather to correct my error than to place the writings of my insignificance in the hands of those who reproach. For there are people who seek praise for themselves from another’s reproach. This is weak praise and not especially praiseworthy.

It is better to correct a friend than to reproach him, to show oneself wise than to mark another spitefully. I would never have written such things if I did not believe your goodness to be the defender or corrector of our ignorance. [Col. 0278A]

As for what has now happened concerning the star Mars alone, the same often happens in these regions with all five wandering stars: they remain hidden longer than the regular account of the ancients proclaims. And perhaps

@ [Col. 0278D] **Not equally.** Alcuin seems to have suspected an inequality in the terrestrial globe.

not equally, for us who dwell in these northern regions, do the risings and settings of the stars occur as they do for those who live in the eastern or southern parts of the world, where the teachers who published for us the principles and courses of heaven and the stars lived chiefly.

For many things are changed by the diversity of places, as your wisdom knows very well. Now, as we said before, we hasten to fulfill your service faithfully enough, while also praying for the clemency of the Lord our God, that he may soon cause his people to return with honor and praise, after all the enemies of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ have been subjected; may he govern you everywhere, guard you, and make you victorious over all your enemies, whether visible or invisible, so that, with the crown of glory, you may happily reign for many years and, together with his faithful, reach the kingdom of eternal blessedness.

@ [Col. 0278D] **Edition.** Quercetanus, 5, from a manuscript (Frobenius, p. 70). It was written in the year when the star Mars came into view again, namely, 798. See the note to the preceding letter.

# LETTER LXXXV. TO THE LORD KING  
*(In the year 798, in July or August.)*

He replies from memory to the king, who asked various questions about the courses of the stars.

To David the most noble in every kind of virtue and most distinguished by every adornment of wisdom, Flaccus, veteran soldier, sends greetings.

[Col. 0278C] A traveler came flying, holding in his hand a question-filled sheet from your authority, shorter in syllables than the eagerness of my mind would have wished, but more profound in its questions than the modest capacity of my little intellect could reach.

It exhorted an old man of fragile understanding to investigate heavenly matters—one who has not yet learned the principles of earthly things, nor been able to explain the wandering courses of the stars that move through heaven, and who is wholly unable to recognize the natures of the herbs growing on earth.

And it is astonishing how anyone can bring their wandering paths back to a fixed order. {100} They are therefore called wandering stars because they are thought to have uncertain courses.

Or what can our insignificance fail to discover in the moon’s daily labors, when we possess regular accounts, investigated through the numerous arguments of Catholic teachers and ancient philosophers? What could be said more clearly about the agreement of the solar and lunar courses through the signs of the bright zodiac than what the master Bede, investigator of such questions, left for us in his writings?

Or what can be investigated more sharply than what Pliny Secundus, the most devoted investigator of natural things, explained concerning the course of the heavenly stars? But while we are

@ [Col. 0279D] **While traveling.** Through Belgium? As in the following letter.

traveling, the presence of those books in which these matters are discussed is lacking. We dare not rashly respond to the deepest questions of your wisdom. We ask your clemency to order that the first little books of the aforesaid teacher Pliny Secundus be sent to us, in which he strives to explain numerous and obscure arguments concerning the varying course of the stars. Perhaps, with God’s gift, we may be able to extract something from them here or there that might seem worthy to be shown to your most holy presence.

Nevertheless, so that your sheet should not find me so unprepared—or dulled by the sleep of inactivity, as though nothing were stored in the secret chamber of my memory that I could produce in answer to the questioner—I shall say what, by asking rather than explaining, was able to present itself suddenly to my troubled mental vision. I shall reserve a fuller response, if it should be needed, for the books of the aforesaid teachers.

Your first question, then, concerning the agreement of the 360 divisions and the lunar course through the twelve signs, was as follows; I shall set down the same words:

“Just as, in the solar course, after the division of days, hours, and points has been made, an agreement has been found between 365 days and a quarter [Cod. Vat.: ‘after a division has been made of 360 parts and 365 days’], so also in the lunar course make twenty-seven days and eight hours agree with the 360 parts of the zodiac.”

I will not evade saying what I think your keenness perceives here in this inquiry: either something must be added to the lunar course in each sign, so that it may reach the lawful and defined divisions of the entire year marked out in the zodiac, or the number of divisions must be reduced so that the lunar course may agree with the divisions of the zodiac.

The aforesaid master Bede seems to explain this question as well as he could in a certain chapter, whose beginning I think is: “But if someone ignorant of the signs, yet eager to understand the lunar course, etc.”

Through the twelve divisions by which the moon moves away from the sun each day, Pliny Secundus says that the moon, if I remember correctly, completes the zodiac thirteen times in its twelve months. He says “in its months,” not “in the sun’s.” He also added that the moon travels through each sign in two days, six hours, and two-thirds of an hour.

If this is true, the number of 360 divisions seems to correspond very well to the lunar course. I thought it not unworthy to demonstrate this by the division of a single figure rather than by multiplying words, since a few words are sufficient for the wise.

The formula of this figure

@ [Col. 0279D] **The formula of the figure.** Quercetanus omitted this formula, because, I believe, it was missing in the manuscript.

I thought it better to place the formula after the text of this letter than to divide the sequence of our discussion with it. In that figure the difference between the hours may also be recognized, if anyone wishes to examine it more carefully, because solar hours are counted differently from lunar hours [Cod. Vat.: “because the hours of the signs are counted differently, and the solar hours differently”].

In some places the points themselves are also counted in one way and in another, so that in some calculations an hour is found to contain five points, and in others four. Even portents are set out differently by calculators, while mathematicians also customarily divide them differently.

We likewise find that minutes are set out differently in the most subtle arguments of mathematicians, so that they even customarily speak of “minutes of minutes.” But these matters belong elsewhere. Let us now attend to what is immediately before us.

As for the divisions of the signs by hours, and how the nine lunar hours would correspond to five solar days, I remember sending you a separate letter about this.

@ [Col. 0280D] **In another … letter.** This is number 25 in Quercetanus’s edition; we will present it among the philosophical works.

Therefore I have judged it superfluous to say anything about it now. We do not fail to know that the division of hours by twelfths is familiar to you, just as you read in the book *On Times* [Perhaps: of the Venerable Bede].

And because it is laborious to divide the lunar course by twelfths of hours, calculators are content instead to reduce the lunar course to measurements of hours or days, lest an excessive number of twelfths become tiresome to the reader.

Nevertheless, we think that what remains in each sign—that is, two days and six hours, or eight twelfths of one hour—ought specifically to have been stated in the place where he says, “It is laborious to divide the hours in each sign minutely by twelfths.”

For this reason he said that two hours should be subtracted from three signs: the twenty-four twelfths of three signs complete two hours, while a complete hour ought to contain twelve twelfths. We do not fail to know that all these matters were already known to your wisdom.

Therefore we begin to speak about the star Mars, concerning which things are seen. Its investigation used to weary our minds for a long time, so that even when it appeared it did not satisfy our curiosity. It recently appeared to us while the sun was remaining in Leo, approximately, as we think, at the time when the image of that same Mars was discovered among us.

Concerning this star also, your venerable dignity

@ [Col. 0280D] **In another letter.** Namely, the preceding one.

in another letter, immediately after it had been seen by us, we took care to say something according to the capacity [Al.: “ease”] of our investigation.

But now, in response to the exhortation of your letter, we have investigated it somewhat more carefully. For you set down these words of inquiry:

“And concerning Mars, which last year was intercepted from human sight in the sign of Cancer by the sun’s light, what do you think: did this happen through the principle of its natural course, through the sun’s power, or by some portent, so that it completed the course of two years in one? For recently, when the sun was leaving Leo, it appeared to us in Cancer.

“If it accompanied the sun, how swift was its course? If it remained stationary in Cancer for the entire year, while the sun migrated into the other signs, why could it not be seen in Cancer?”

This is a scholarly and very acute argument, to which we shall reply briefly, insofar as God grants us the ability.

But as it was said there that the star of Mars had been intercepted from human sight in Cancer by the sun’s light, I do not think that the star of Mars was intercepted in Cancer by the sun’s light throughout the whole preceding year. Rather, I think that Cancer, at the appropriate time and in accordance with the natural order of its course, was, together with the star of Mars, hidden from human sight by the interposition of the earth. Therefore, in the preceding year I do not remember seeing it in Cancer, while Cancer was pursuing the order of its course by night above [F., beneath, as below] the earth. Nor do I consider it portentous that it did not appear to us for so long a time, but rather a consequence of the natural order of its course. For if it did not appear in the constellation of Cancer in the preceding year, and now appears in Cancer, it is recognized as completing not the course of one year but a period of two years, since now, in the second year, it is situated in another constellation.

As for what was added—“If it remained stationary in Cancer for the whole year, while the sun moved into the other signs, why could it not be seen in Cancer?”—the answer is that Cancer itself, in which it remained stationary, could not be seen. But as soon as Cancer could be seen, that star too was seen along with Cancer, which in the preceding year had naturally withdrawn beneath the earth during the nights.

[Col. 0281B]

@ [Col. 0281D] In another little document. This document has not yet been discovered. In another little document I wrote about the power of the sun, which produces unequal courses in the wandering stars, as the poet says:

“… The sun divides the seasons of the year,  
… It changes night and day,  
… and, with rays reaching toward the stars,  
it restrains them and checks their wandering courses by its stationary position.”

This is what Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars very often appear to undergo. But let your venerable wisdom and most acute knowledge determine whether anything worthy or probable ought to be seen either in this explanation or in that one, or whether something else should be believed concerning such great questions. I did not suppose that you were questioning me on account of ignorance. Whatever your opinion may be, I beg you not to disdain making it known to us with kindly goodwill. I am not an excessive defender of my own opinion, but a devoted pursuer of truth.

The figure appended below has, in its first line, the hours in which the individual signs rise, set, or move from their position. In the second it has ten points in each sign. The third counts the degrees contained in each sign. The fourth gives the days during which the moon remains in each sign. The fifth gives the hours added to the days. The sixth gives eight ounces, which remain from the number of hours and are called a *bisse*. I have gathered all these details into a single formula for ease of understanding the moon’s course—provided, however, that the calculation which your most excellent wisdom sought has been correctly established.

@ [Col. 0281D] Quercetanus’s edition, 10; Canisius’s, 14 (Frobenius, 71). Here collated with the Vatican manuscript.

## LETTER LXXXVI. TO THE LORD KING (Year 798)

The reasons are assigned why the moon may appear smaller or larger than the astronomers’ calculation indicates.

[Col. 0281D]

May the merciful God grant you perpetual salvation throughout the ages,

and the honor of empire, beloved David.

The words of your venerable authority, sweeter than every honeycomb, through the arid—

@ Belgicae. I understand this as referring to the journey undertaken by Alcuin to the monastery of Wicus, or the cell of Saint Josse, which Charles entrusted to his care and which was situated in Belgium; see also Letter 12 among the Chesnian letters, now 96. As I was traveling across the fields of Belgium, they came before me. While reading there about the prosperity of your blessedness and perceiving the beloved welfare of your faithful people, I devoted my whole self to giving thanks to the Lord God Jesus Christ, knowing with complete certainty that happy times had come for the Christian people through the exaltation and welfare of your happiness. For this I rejoice always to pray to the Lord; I continually desire to hear the same report, and, desiring always to hear of your safety as a longed-for gift appointed by God, I welcome it with every joy.

For who would not rejoice in the perfect soundness of his head, unless perhaps he were frenzied or insane? Such a person, I think, ought to be bound with the tightest bonds of Hippocrates [Vatican manuscript, “he judged”]. Even though, according to the Apostle’s teaching, no one hates his own flesh, but rather nourishes and cherishes it (Ephesians 5:29), how much more ought one to rejoice in the health of the head, in which lies the perfection of the whole body and all the glory of the limbs’ structure?

[Col. 0282B]

@ [Col. 0282D] {104} This is the end of the letter in Canisius; the remainder was added by Quercetanus from a manuscript.?

But although you have suddenly transported me from the dusty clods of Campania to the most noble and acute consideration of the heights of heaven, you are again striving to renew within the secret chamber of my heart the knowledge of Pythagorean discipline, from which it has not yet departed, since you have found me never idle in the consideration of such honorable arts, although less learned in them.

Nor should the tiresome sluggishness of readers justly be attributed to the goodwill of a teacher, if, while many follow your illustrious intellectual purpose, perhaps a new Athens might be perfected in Francia—or rather one much more excellent, because this one, ennobled by the teaching of Christ the Lord, surpasses all the wisdom of academic training. That Athens was merely educated in Platonic disciplines and was distinguished after being formed by the seven arts; this one, moreover, enriched by the sevenfold fullness of the Holy Spirit, surpasses all the dignity of secular wisdom. From his gift, if I am able to offer anything worthy in answer to your questions, I shall bring it forth.

The inquiry of your ingenious and most illustrious wisdom was this: Why does the appearance of the lunar body seem smaller to the eyes of those who observe it than the curiosity of those making calculations would find it among the numbers of the nights, or the diligence of those considering it in the degrees of the Zodiac would perceive? And why did the moon in Gemini, in its visible aspect, not reach the same degrees on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April [text, “week”; Vatican manuscript, “seven”], to which the multiplied calculation by points ought to have brought it? [Col. 0282D]

And you propose three causes of this variation, supposing that any one of them might be responsible, using the very words that your letter, worthy of your praiseworthy wisdom, sounded in our ears: whether “the obliquity of the said Zodiac; or the course of the star-wanderer itself through the ether; or some unusual diminution of its legitimate light, never seen in past ages,” might have caused it. As we too looked more keenly upon this diminution in the moon’s calculation, the same movement that had occupied your minds touched our own hearts with a complaint.

But, in addition to the three causes of this diminution proposed by your venerable inquiry, we have found by probable reasoning three other causes, by which this great diminution could, in accordance with the investigations of the ancients, have been defended. For this diminution in the appearance of the lunar body commonly occurs after the calculation of the intercalary leap has been completed—a calculation that is scarcely completed even once in nineteen years. And as the final year of the nineteen-year cycle approaches, in which one day must be skipped according to the calculation of the leap, the moon is very often seen larger than the reckoning of its age indicates. Likewise, after this leap-calculation, during the first years of the nineteen-year cycle, it is often found smaller than the memory of the calculators’ recitation declares.

There is also another reason why the moon sometimes appears smaller than the calculation of those counting it shows: namely, when the moon is kindled shortly before evening, or for only the space of one hour, and immediately after sunset it must be counted as the first moon. It is not surprising if the moon appears smaller in its second, third, or any of its other ages than it would if it were kindled after the first hour of the night and, after twenty-two or three hours, when it reached evening, were counted as the first. This too may be a reason why at times it appears smaller in appearance than it is reckoned in age.

This diminution also frequently presents itself to careful observers in Aries or in the signs near it, if the moon’s kindling occurs there. Thus, in the sign of Aries, it commonly happens in a remarkable way that one sees the last moon of the preceding month in the morning and the new moon of the following month appear in the sky that same evening: having been kindled, as it were, at the sixth hour of the day, it shows the preceding moon already passed in the morning and then displays the coming moon in the evening.

But whether one of the causes introduced by your authority was responsible [Vatican manuscript, “may be responsible”], or one of those proposed by our own diligence, it is nevertheless necessary that the Paschal moon remain in every respect inviolable. For it could not have happened that none of the earlier teachers or holy Fathers had observed this diminution in the moon’s appearance, those who discovered the reckoning of the Paschal moon with sagacity at the Council of Nicaea and arranged it in accordance with Catholic practice, so that by every perpetual right the most holy festival of the Lord’s resurrection might be celebrated harmoniously throughout the whole world [Col. 0283D].

If a more reliable explanation of this diminution can be found in Pliny, whether because of the leap recently completed or because of the bissextile day soon to come—

@ [Col. 0283D] Because of the leap recently completed (in the year 797), or because of the bissextile day soon approaching (in the year 800). This letter therefore appears to have been written in the year 798.

—whether because of the leap recently completed or because of the bissextile day soon to come, I ask that your prudence order an inquiry and endeavor, with your customary benevolent devotion, to make the result known to us. For, while we remain at home, the cloudy rising of waters’ mist, or, as we travel through Belgian dust, the windy scattering of dust, causes our eyes to grow dim. Therefore may your goodness not disdain to help one who is seeking, and to allow one who willingly follows to be led into the way of truth [Vatican manuscript, “to draw him after itself”].

May Christ, illustrious through heavenly gifts,

enlighten you, beloved David, and fill your heart with love of peace.

May the sweet love of life, sweet praise, and sweet glory

be your perpetual salvation, beloved David.

@ [Col. 0283D] {105} Mabillon’s edition, 7; Pez’s, 1, collated with the Salzburg manuscript. It appears to have been written in the year 798, when, as the Salzburg Anonymous on the conversion of Bavaria and Carantania says, “the emperor ordered Arno the archbishop to proceed into the regions of the Slavs, to take charge of that whole region, to cultivate ecclesiastical practice, and to strengthen the peoples by preaching the faith and Christianity,” in Hansiz, *Germania Sacra*, volume II, p. 108. (In Frobenius, Letter 72.)

## LETTER LXXXVII. TO ARNO (Year 798, at the beginning of June)

He exhorts him to perform his apostolic work properly as he sets out for Hunland.

To his dearest like-minded friend, Aquila, chief overseer, in the love of Christ, greetings.

On the Wednesday after holy Pentecost I received a letter from your blessedness, written with charity, strengthened by counsel, and sealed with faith. In it I heard what I had desired and recognized what I had hoped for. The hope of counsel did not deceive me, nor did the cooperation of fellowship delay me.

Your journey, undertaken now in order to establish the truth of the matter, has been arranged in the present circumstances; and the strength of the army that goes with you has been directed toward your safety [Al., “your defense”]. In a certain sense this too has proceeded from the Huns themselves; therefore undertake this journey joyfully in the hope of God’s will. May we, God granting it, see you returning in peace and with sound counsel to these regions, as I suppose.

I ask you, however, as soon as you return, to send us a letter of your affection, so that our curiosity may learn the certainty of events through your report. That kingdom was long stable and strong; but stronger is he who conquered it, in whose hand are all the powers of kings and kingdoms, and who exalts whomever he wishes (Psalm 74:8), visits and enlightens the heart of whomever he wishes, and converts it to his service.

And if his grace looks upon the kingdom of the Huns, who is there who would dare withdraw from the ministry of their salvation? Few days of this life remain to us, and it is greatly to be desired—and God’s mercy must be entreated with the whole heart—that they may be completed in his work [Al., “made firm”]. For each person’s life is judged more by its end than by its beginning. We are born in sins (Psalm 50:7), but we are reborn by grace; may grace accompany us as we run in good works and make us persevere firmly to the end.

But you, holy Father, faithful friend, beloved brother, dearest son, go with good success and with divine grace accompanying you into the work of God, and return to us with joy. Be a preacher of mercy, not an exactor of tithes, because a newborn soul must be nourished with the milk of apostolic compassion until it grows and is strengthened enough to receive solid food. The tithes, as it is said, overturned the faith of the Saxons. Why should a yoke be imposed upon the necks of ignorant people that neither we nor our brothers have been able to bear?

Therefore we trust that the souls of believers will be saved in the faith of Christ. Go now, dearest brother, in the blessing of God and the consolation of the Holy Spirit. Your Albinus is with you in his heart; would that you might soon have him as a companion in the work of God. We, the members of the household, do not cease praying for you, that divine grace may go before you and follow you everywhere, so that you may return to us with abundant fruit of pious labor.

You have good and religious companions with you, in whose speech and conduct the name of the Lord Jesus may be glorified. We shall always remain anxious about your return until we see the one whom we love and embrace with our hands the one whom our heart desires.

@ [Col. 0285D] A third part of your labors. “Certainly worthy of remembrance is the gift that King [Charles] made to Arno: in each place that he would cultivate through apostolic labors, he granted him a third part.” Hansiz.

He also granted you a third part of your labors in each place—whether bishopric or monastery—to be handed over as your alms, if your life should accompany you on the journey [Salzburg manuscript, “if he should accompany you”], and he ordered this to be confirmed by written schedules [Salzburg manuscript, “he orders”].

Behold, as the paper fails, not charity, we lay down the pen, adding only these words of greeting: May you live happily for God; may you go forward and flourish in the work of God; and may the right hand of the supreme King protect and defend you everywhere as you go and return, venerable, beloved, and sweetest—

@ [Col. 0285D] {106} Mabillon’s edition, 13, where it is mutilated. Here it is presented complete from the Salzburg manuscript. It is a reply to Arno’s letter when he had gone, or was about to go, to Hunland in the year 798, grieving that he was compelled to be absent from his own sheep. Alcuin replies: “Nor do your former sheep hinder you,” etc. (In Frobenius, Letter 73.)

## LETTER LXXXVIII. TO ARNO (Year 798, in October)

He exhorts him to perform his apostolic office diligently and not to allow himself to be hindered either by bodily weakness or by concern for his own sheep.

To his dearest Father in Christ, Aquila, Albinus, weak [Col. 0285C] in the longing of complete charity, greetings.

The letters of your faith and steadfast charity found me [in the house of Saint Martin] [on the day before the Nones of October], but, by God’s gift, in better health. May he grant that you too may be better and better through the highest grace of God, and may he cause the work of God that you have in hand to grow through the great breadth of the people. May your spirit not grow lukewarm, and may the frequent weakness of your body not terrify you. For power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9).

Blessed is the place and hour in which the supreme ruler of the earth has established you. But run by running, so that God may bring your course to completion, that you may preserve the faith, and that a crown of glory may remain for you thereafter (2 Timothy 4:7–8). As for us, the bonds of sins—partly the chains of the world, partly the bonds of illnesses—deny us the ability to run, and what is ready in the will grows weak in the flesh (Mark 14:38). But let the will of the Lord be done; and may he who began in the spirit complete his work.

Let all nations know [that they are] like a drop from a bucket—

@ [Col. 0286D] These words, omitted by Mabillon, are to be supplied from Isaiah 40:15: “Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket, and are accounted as a speck on the scales; behold, the islands are like fine dust.”

Who am I, except the tiniest dust? Yet he who raised me from dust can make of a creature whatever he wills, because he does everything that he wills in heaven. He who transferred the weary hands of a fisherman from the hook to the key of the kingdom of heaven, and from a persecutor of the saints made him a preacher to the peoples—considering this, do not despair either of your brother’s salvation or of your own effectiveness.

The days of labor are few, but those of reward are many. Labor—[Al., “I labor”]—labor for me and for yourself, so that your labor may benefit me; may my will, if it can do anything, assist you. Draw me after you by the prayers of your holiness; we shall run together until the King brings us into the wine cellar, arranging in us the sweetness of his charity (Song of Songs 2:4).

And since the voice of your affection cannot reach us, let a letter, which they call a report, come more frequently. “A brother who is helped by a brother is like a fortified city.” How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things (Romans 10:15).

[“Lift up your voice like a trumpet, and remember,” he said [so the manuscript; perhaps it should read, “remember to follow him who said”]: “I have other sheep that are not from this fold; they hear my voice, and I must bring them too, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd” (John 10:16). Nor do your former sheep hinder you from bringing others and making one fold.

Let your wisdom recognize what our devotion signifies. We shall educate the boy whom we have in our household as a son, and, God willing, make him a perfect man. We shall be his assistants according to the circumstances of the matter and the requirements of the time; and, if God wills that we see one another face to face, then, concerning him—as concerning many others—we shall adopt a plan for salvation. As your Albinus was, so shall he also be forever.]

For he who began the good work of charity in us, may he complete it and, I believe, bring it to the great reward of faith. But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved (Matthew 10:22). May the Lord guard your going in and your going out, from this time forth and forevermore (Psalm 120:8).

Live happily and flourish in the work and word of God. Farewell, brother, forever. Always remember to pray for us, and may God always remember to help you.

@ [Col. 0286D] Quercetanus’s edition, 86, from a manuscript; Frobenius, 74.

## LETTER LXXXIX. TO LIOBRADUS (Year 798)

He desires the friendship of Liobradus [Leidradus], the elected bishop of Lyon.

To the bishop, brother, friend,

to Liobradus, the elected one.

@ [Col. 0286D] Mabillon thinks that “Liobradus” should be read “Liodradus”; this is Leidradus, elected bishop of Lyon in 798 and first ordained in the following year. See *Literary History of France*, volume IV, pp. 433 ff.

To Liobradus, the elected one, Albinus sends greetings.

I give thanks to God, who has deigned to grant me such a friend, in whose faith truth, in whose goodness kindness, and in whose counsel salvation have always been found. And the rarer it is nowadays to find such people, the more highly they ought to be valued.

As the gleam of gems shines amid sandy gravel, so a proven friend is most gratefully discerned, embraced, and held amid the clamorous crowd of the multitude. According to the proverb of antiquity, such a friend is long sought, scarcely found, and difficult to preserve. It is easy to recognize the interpretation of this proverb in your own case. And, remarkably, while everyone wishes to find such a friend, scarcely anyone desires to be one. This is because, although they hear the Lord’s command with open ears, they nevertheless value it little in their deaf hearts: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same for them” (Matthew 7:12).

Among the other marks of virtue that belong to this command, this too is included: whoever wishes to find a faithful friend must himself be a faithful friend to every human being, whether in the salvation of the soul or in secular assistance, insofar as the matter and person of each individual require.

As for what you wished to ask me about certainty regarding my intention or location, I have nothing certain to report to you yet, except that, if God has mercy and life accompanies us, you will still see my face, although I do not know where or when, because of the occupations of both you and me.

Strive to send me letters often, according to the opportunity offered by those who carry them, so that I may have occasion to write back to your affection and also to communicate whatever may occur to me. Only earnestly entreat the Lord Jesus to direct, according to his great mercy, the life of his servant toward the fulfillment of his most holy will and toward the advancement of the Christian religion, according to the measure of our strength.

[Col. 0287C]

May eternal peace govern you, beloved bishop of Christ;

always and forever, beloved bishop, farewell.

@ [Col. 0287D] {111} Quercetanus’s editions, 69 and 70; Canisius’s, 8, collated with the Salzburg manuscript. (In Frobenius, Letter 75.)

## LETTER XC

@ [Col. 0287D] To the brothers of Lyon. The monks of the Island of Barbara, or Athanacum, concerning whom see Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXVI, no. 71. Canisius says that this letter lacks any title in the manuscript, but from the name of Leidradus, bishop of Lyon, it is evident that it was written to these same brothers.

## TO THE BROTHERS OF LYON (Year 798)

He warns them to beware of the various errors of the Spaniards. He answers a question concerning the observance of the Sabbath before the Sunday of the Resurrection.

@ [Col. 0287D] Leidradus the elected bishop had not yet been ordained; that ordination first took place in the year after his election, in 799. See the preceding letter.

Having heard of the praiseworthy concern of your religious conversation in Christ through Leidradus the elected bishop, I confess that I was filled with great joy, because Christ, the fountain of all goodness, still has confessors of his holy name in these days, when the charity of many grows cold (Matthew 24:12). They cast off the burdens of secular occupations and long to place Christ’s easy yoke upon their own necks {107}; they retain in their breasts, with sweetness, true charity that casts out fear (1 John 4:18), and show it truthfully in their works.

But now the course of the journey that has been begun must be completed with the greatest cheerfulness of mind, because “whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22). For if sluggish laziness secretly creeps in, concealing the good work, the wickedness of an evil work soon grows openly. The origin of wickedness is the loss of goodness. And when a person follows the inclination of his own will, he soon loses the effect of divine service.

This was the first fall of the angel: rejoicing in his own power, he turned away from the highest good. He who had been more glorious than the others in his creation became more wretched than all in his destruction. From the point where pride raises itself, there it is most greatly cast down. Therefore humility of obedience is especially necessary for those who serve God. [Through the steps of humility one reaches the summit of exaltation.]

Christ is read to have been subject to his parents (Luke 2:51), so that by the example of his humility he might form us for good obedience. What is the life of monks except charity, humility, and obedience? These are the paths that lead a person traveling along them to the citadel of the eternal city, provided that the Catholic faith, which works through love, accompanies the one running along these paths.

But, dearest brothers, beware with your whole attention of the new sects of Spanish error. Follow the footsteps of the holy Fathers in the faith, and join yourselves to the universal Church in most holy unanimity [Al., “unity”]. It is written: “Do not move the boundaries of your fathers” (Proverbs 22:28).

@ [Col. 0287D] Concerning the Symbol of the Catholic faith. Canisius interprets these and the following words as referring to the addition of the word “and the Son”—*Filioque*—which was being debated at that time. It seems more probable to me, however, that Alcuin is here simply exhorting the people of Lyon to reject the sects of Spanish error, lest they add new names—“adoptive,” “nominal”—to the Symbol, or introduce unheard-of traditions into practice, such as using salt in the sacrifice, omitting the triple immersion, and so forth.

Do not insert new [names] into the Symbol of the Catholic faith, and do not embrace in ecclesiastical offices traditions unheard of in ancient times. Proceed along the public road of apostolic teaching, and do not turn aside to the right or left from the royal way along the byways of any novelty.

As for the adoption that certain people attempt to thrust upon Christ God in an insulting manner—

@ [Col. 0288D] From synodal authority. Namely, from the acts of the Council of Frankfurt of 794, or perhaps of Aachen in 799. What seems to stand against this, however, is that Leidradus is here called “elected,” whereas in this year he had already been confirmed.

—you have an answer from synodal authority. The unity of person in Christ’s two natures confirms that he is, by nature, the Son of God the Father. For one person cannot in any way be both proper and adoptive. Therefore Christ is the proper [Salzburg manuscript, “natural”] Son of God the Father, and we are adopted through him; he is not adopted together with us. Just as he alone is without sin, so he alone is without adoption, while the Father testifies at his baptism: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). And the Apostle says: “He did not spare his own Son” (Romans 8:32). What more should we say about these matters, concerning which you have been sufficiently instructed, except that whoever believes him to be adopted by God the Father is not believed to be adopted by God the Father through him?

[Col. 0289A]

We have also heard that some people in those regions assert that salt ought to be put into the sacrifice of the body of Christ.

@ [Col. 0289D] We rejected Basnagius’s criticism of this passage in the preface.

This custom is observed neither by the universal Church nor by the authority of Rome. According to the Apostle John, there are three that bear witness: the Spirit, the water, and the blood (1 John 5:8). There are three things that ought to be offered in the sacrifice of this testimony: bread, water, and wine.

For just as the spirit gives life to the body (John 6:64), so bread strengthens the human heart. Just as Christ freed us by his blood, so he also gladdens us with wine. Likewise concerning water: “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst” (John 4:13).

Thus [Salzburg manuscript, “namely”] the bread that is consecrated into the body of Christ, without the leaven of any other contamination, must be most pure; the water must be pure from every defilement; and the wine, without any mixture of another liquid [except water], must be most thoroughly purified. Therefore water is appropriate to both. From water and flour the bread is made that is consecrated into the body of Christ; water and wine are consecrated into the blood of Christ.

For if water and salt, as the authors of this sect say, have one nature, soak one piece of fresh meat in water and sprinkle another with salt. You will quickly see whether water and salt have the same effective power. Did Christ’s flesh decay in the tomb, so that his body now needs salt in the sacrifice?

Therefore, when salt is commanded to be present in sacrifices under the Old Law, this was a sign intended to signify a future reality, not an observance to be maintained in the present age—just as all the sacrifices of the Jewish Law “happened to them as a figure,” according to the Apostle (1 Corinthians 10:11). These things, however, were written for us. “For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6).

The figure of this most sacred offering had already gone before in Melchizedek, who used to offer wine and bread to the most high God (Genesis 14:18).

The sanctification of this mystery also foreshadows the effect of our salvation. In the water the people of believers are understood. In the grains of wheat from which flour is produced so that bread may be made, the gathering of the whole Church is signified; by the fire of the Holy Spirit it is cooked into one body, so that its members may be joined to their head. Likewise, in the water mixed with wine, as we said, the figure of the nations is signified. In the wine the blood of the Lord’s passion is shown. And so, when water is mixed with wheat or wine in the sacraments, the faithful people are incorporated into and joined to Christ [the bracketed words are supplied by the editor].

But the brevity of a letter prevents me from arguing at length about such figurations. The Carthaginian canons also state, in chapter 24, concerning the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood: “Nothing more is offered than the Lord himself handed down; that is, bread and wine mixed with water” (Third Council of Carthage).

A third question has also been brought to us from Spain—which was once a nurse of tyrants but is now a nurse of schismatics—against the universal custom of the holy Church of God, concerning baptism. Some assert that, under invocation of the Trinity, a single immersion ought to be performed.

[Col. 0290A]

The Apostle seems to be opposed to this practice in the passage where he says: “For you have been buried with Christ through baptism” (Romans 6:4). For we know that Christ, although this must be understood synecdochically, was in the tomb for three days and three nights, as he himself said to the Jews: “Just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights” (Matthew 12:40).

@ [Col. 0289D] “Three nights” may signify three immersions, and “[three days]” three elevations. Just as Christ rose on the third day, so may we, raised on the third day from the font of the life-giving bath, walk with him in newness of life (Romans 6:4). We also read in the letter of Saint Pope Leo, which he wrote concerning baptism to all the bishops of Sicily, where, after an appropriate sequence of argument, he added the following:

“Although, therefore, both those things that pertain to Christ’s humility and those that pertain to his glory converge upon one and the same person, and everything in him that belongs to divine power and human weakness tends toward the effect of our restoration, nevertheless, specifically in the death of the crucified one and in the resurrection of the dead one, the power of baptism creates a new creature from the old. Thus, in those who are reborn, both the death and the life of Christ may work. For blessed Paul the Apostle says: ‘Do you not know, brothers, that all who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death? We have been buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be together in the likeness of his resurrection,’ and the rest, which the teacher of the nations discussed more fully in order to commend the sacrament of baptism (Romans 6:3–5).

“And it is evident from this teaching that, for the regeneration of the sons of men and their adoption as sons of God, that day and that time were chosen in which, through the likeness and form of the mystery, the things performed in the members might correspond to those accomplished in the head himself. Thus, according to the rule of baptism, death has perished [Salzburg manuscript, “has intervened”] through the slaying of sin, and the threefold immersion imitates the three-day burial, while the raising from the waters [is] like one rising from the tomb” (Letter 16, chapter 3, volume LIV of *Patrologia*, column 697).

Blessed Jerome also says in the second book of his *Treatise on the Epistle of Saint Paul to the Ephesians*, in his exposition of the statement, “One God, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all, who is above all, over all things, and in all of us” (Ephesians 4:5–6), concerning the triple immersion:

“If, as the Arians suppose, God the Father alone is God, then by the same reasoning the Lord Jesus Christ alone will be Lord, and neither will the Father be Lord nor the Son God. But far be it from us to say that there is no deity in lordship or lordship in deity. There is one Lord and one God, because the lordship of the Father and the Son is one deity. Therefore one faith is also said [to exist], because we believe similarly in the Father and in the Son and—

@ [Col. 0290D] And in the Holy Spirit. Supply from the published editions of Saint Jerome: “we believe.”

—and in the Holy Spirit. And one baptism: for we are baptized in the same way into the Father, into the Son, and into the Holy Spirit; and we are immersed three times, so that the Trinity may appear as one sacrament. We are not baptized into the names of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, but into one name, which is understood to be God.

“And I wonder by what reasoning Arius, Macedonius, [and Eunomius], in discordant impiety yet agreeing together, suspect a diversity of natures in one word, one work, and one sacrament, and, while holding a filthy fountain from the creature in the Son and in the Holy Spirit, have drawn off different streams of heresies.

“‘One baptism’: this is also directed against Valentinus, who contends that there are two baptisms, and against all heretics, so that they may know that they do not possess baptism, but that in the one Church of Christ there is one life-giving font. One baptism can also be spoken of in this way: although we are baptized three times because of the mystery of the Trinity, nevertheless it is reckoned as one baptism.

“One baptism also exists in water, in the Spirit, and in fire; and concerning this the Lord says: ‘I have a baptism with which I must be baptized’ (Luke 12:50). And elsewhere: ‘You shall be baptized with my baptism’” (Mark 10:39).

There are also verses of blessed Ambrose—

@ [Col. 0291D] Of Bishop Ambrose. Whether he was the Ambrose of Milan or the Ambrose of Alexandria is uncertain. These verses are not found among the works of Ambrose of Milan. According to blessed Jerome, the Alexandrian wrote a volume containing many verses. Canisius.

—of Bishop Ambrose, most distinguished for his treatment of the excellence of the number three, which it pleased us to insert in this letter in confirmation of the triple immersion.

Everything threefold flourishes beneath the majesty of the Thunderer. Three—the Father, the Word, and likewise the Holy Spirit—are one. The threefold saving form of the cross is one, the redeeming one. The third day received the Lord returning from death. [Col. 0291C] Three days held Jonah beneath the whale’s entrails. Three boys saw [or perhaps, sang of] God in the blazing furnace. Thrice, proclaiming the holiness of Sabaoth, the blessing sings praise. **Anyone to whom the full grace of washing is given must be immersed three times in water.** Every action is established and confirmed by three witnesses. In the third month the seasons return to their appointed members. There are three ages: youth’s flower, maturity’s strength, and infirm old age. There are three measures—

@ [Col. 0292D] Can., “middle,” as in Sidonius, Book II, Letter 1: “Whatever is to be hoped for, it pleases me that it should come about through you, under your leadership.” —in legal cases: judge, defender, and plaintiff. There are three stages in the ages of the world: origin, passage, and end. Three things that touch hope: rest, light, and the glory of life.

@ [Col. 0292D] “But these principal teachers.” With these words Letter 70 of the Quercetan edition begins. It is a continuation of the preceding letter and should be joined to it, as in the Salzburg manuscript. “But these principal teachers and most holy Fathers have left us testimonies in their written statements.” For our part, according to the smallness of our understanding, it seems to us [Col. 0291D] that, just as the inner man must be reformed in faith in the Holy Trinity according to the image of his Creator, so the outward man must be cleansed by a threefold immersion, so that what the Spirit invisibly effects in the soul, the priest may visibly imitate in the water. For original sin was committed in three ways: through delight, consent, and deed. Thus every sin is accomplished either by thought, word, or action. Therefore a threefold washing appears suited to the threefold kind of sins: either because of original sin, which brings destruction upon infants, or because of those sins which, in people of more mature age, are added by will, word, or deed.

But so that you may understand the meanings of this most sacred mystery, in accordance with the understanding of the holy Fathers and the statutes of the Church, I shall set forth for your charity the same sacraments according to the Catholic interpretation. For we believe that no one may doubt that everything performed in them has been established with great holiness and venerable significance. First, the pagan becomes a catechumen, approaching baptism so that he may renounce the evil spirit and all his destructive pomp. He is also exsufflated, so that, once the devil has been driven away, an entrance may be prepared for Christ our God. He is exorcised—that is, the evil spirit is adjured—to depart and withdraw, giving place to God [the true God]. The catechumen receives salt, so that his rotten and transitory sins may be cleansed by the salt of wisdom, through the divine gift. Then the true faith of the Apostolic Creed is handed over to him, so that the empty house, abandoned by its former inhabitant, may be adorned by faith and prepared as a dwelling for God. Then the scrutinies are performed, so that it may be examined repeatedly how firmly, after renouncing Satan, the sacred words of the faith that has been given have been rooted in his heart. [His nostrils are also touched, so that, for as long as he draws breath through his nostrils, he may persevere in the faith he has received.] His breast is likewise anointed with oil [in the same way], so that the entrance may be closed to the devil by the sign of the holy cross. His shoulders are also signed, [so that he may be fortified on every side. Likewise, by the anointing of the breast and shoulders] the firmness of faith [Col. 0292C] and perseverance in good works are signified. And thus, in the name of the Holy Trinity, he is baptized by a threefold immersion. And rightly so: the human being, who was created in the image of the Holy Trinity, is recalled to that same image through invocation of the Holy Trinity. And the one who fell into death through the third degree of sin—that is, through action—may, having been raised from the font for the third time, rise again through grace to life. Then he is clothed in white garments, because of the joy of regeneration, the purity of life, and the beauty of angelic splendor. Then his head is anointed with sacred chrism and covered with a mystical veil, so that he may understand that he bears the dignity of royal and priestly rank, having been brought forth from anathema, according to the Apostle: “You are a royal race, offering yourselves to the living God as a holy sacrifice pleasing to God” (1 Peter II, 9, and Romans XII, 1). Thus he is strengthened by the Lord’s body and blood, so that he may be a member of the one who suffered and rose again for him. Finally, through the laying on of hands by the chief priest, he receives the Spirit of sevenfold grace, so that he may be strengthened by the Holy Spirit to preach to others—he who in baptism was endowed with the grace of eternal life.

You see how faithfully, reasonably, and prudently all these things have been handed down for us to observe. Let no Catholic dare contend against the authority of the Church; let no sober person contend against rational custom; let no believer contend against the understanding of piety. And so that he may not be found a schismatic rather than a Catholic, let him follow the most approved authority of the Holy Roman Church: so that from the place where we receive the beginnings of the Catholic faith, from there we may always have models for our salvation; so that the members may not be separated from their head; so that the bearer of the keys of the heavenly kingdom may not reject those whom he understands to have strayed from his teachings.

@ [Col. 0293D] “But the letter, etc.” Thus Alcuin possessed an incomplete manuscript of the letters of Saint Gregory. For the letter about which Alcuin here raises a doubt is known to be genuine, addressed to Leander of Seville, from Isidore of Seville, the Fourth Council of Toledo, and John the Deacon. But we shall say more about this elsewhere. “But the letter which they say was written by Saint Gregory concerning single immersion, we did not find in his Letter Book, which was brought to us from Rome. We did, however, examine all the others in that Book which he had written to the churches, bishops, and kings of the western regions. Therefore we are uncertain whether it is his, or whether it was written under his name by some author of this school.”

As for the observance about which you asked, concerning the holy Sabbath that precedes the day of the Lord’s resurrection, it seems to us most fitting that it should be kept joyfully with every form of veneration. And whatever on other days during the Lenten meals is done either for the sake of health or under the compulsion of any necessity, it seems worthy to us that it should not be rejected on that day—not for the satisfaction of the appetite, but for the veneration of holiness. God therefore does not ask so much what we eat as he considers how readily we abstain from what is forbidden, or with what moderation we use what is permitted. In all these matters, consideration of the times and the appropriateness of brotherly love must be observed. Therefore we read that the Lord said to the Jews in the Gospel, when he proposed the parable of the children concerning John’s abstinence and his own accommodation to human beings: “Wisdom has been justified by her children” (Matthew XI, 19). That is, the children of wisdom understand that in all things and everywhere reasonable moderation and peaceful harmony are praiseworthy. Your holiness, dearly beloved brothers, recognizes all these things better in practice than we are able to express them in words.

You, however, carry out the journey of eternal salvation, with great devotion of mind and body, so that you may deserve to attain the everlasting crown of heavenly glory. And I beg you to keep me familiarly in your holy prayers. “The continual prayer of a righteous person has great power,” according to the Apostle James (James V, 16)—how much more that of many brothers? God, the witness of hidden things, knows how greatly I desire that you should advance in every goodness; and may he grant that you pass from the grievous misery of this mortality to the joys of eternity.

@ [Col. 0293D] “Of this letter.” This concluding clause is absent from the Salzburg manuscript.
