Hilary of Arles discusses the statutes of the monks of Lérins [Col. 0294D] in the Life of Saint Honoratus. “I ask you to arrange for a copy of this letter to be sent to the brothers who serve God on the island of Lérins, [Col. 0294A] because they were accustomed to question my smallness about matters of this kind.”

@ [Col. 0294D] Mabillon edition: largely mutilated. We give the complete text from the Salzburg manuscript. (In Froben, Letter 76.)

## LETTER XCI. TO ARNO (A.D. 799)

He desires to see him; laments the dangerous times; reports that he has been summoned to the palace and that Felix is to be brought by Laidrad to the king, etc.

To [the Eagle], dearest among all the birds of Alpine height: Albinus sends greetings.

O, if Habakkuk’s translation to you were granted to me, with what tenacious embraces I would clasp your neck, O sweetest son! Nor would the length of the [summer] day, though it wearied me, make me press your breast against mine or join mouth to mouth any less, until I had kissed each limb of your body with the sweetest greetings. But because my sins prevent this from being possible in my sluggish body, I shall accomplish what I can with greater urgency, dipping the pen of affection into a tearful stream, so that the sweetest words of greeting may be written on this little sheet and may come by the hand of a traveling messenger to the son of my affection, who is a father in merits,

@ [Col. 0294D] “A brother in affection.” Alcuin explains himself similarly in Letter 92 [now 118] to the same man. See what we said about this in the preface, where we inquire whether Arno was Alcuin’s blood brother. —a brother in affection, a son in age; so that he may read me mourning, although he does not see me rejoicing. O harsh separation in the heavy burden of the body! O sweet union in the inward parts of love! O true brotherhood, which is never divided, which burns no less in absence than it shines in presence! May our memory with you always flourish in this regard, I beg, so that our frailty may be supported by your prayers, and the name of the one who loves you may not depart from your heart; but may there be unity in Christ, without whom no love is perfect.

{112} We have many concerns about the Catholic faith, because there are very many opponents. Therefore we need to be strengthened by the intercessions of many, so that, with God’s grace, we may be of benefit to many. The times are dangerous, and tribulation continually comes upon tribulation. The people are in want, the rulers in labor, the Church in anxiety, the priests in complaints. Everything is disturbed; yet I believe that he will have mercy whose mercy is beautiful in a time of tribulation. We have greatly rejoiced that you have always been intent upon his praise and honor. For [Candidus] refreshes our spirit concerning your religious life, whether in your household [Col. 0294D] or on the road. Therefore it is not my task to admonish one who is already doing these things, nor to complete what is already full, but to rejoice with those who rejoice and to praise God for your progress. “While you can, perform the works of God” (John VI, 28); and “while you have the light, walk” (John XII, 35), until you reach “the prize of the heavenly blessedness” (Philippians III, 14). [Would that, when summer arrives more quickly, we might deserve to see you. For in mid-May, God willing, I expect to be at the palace, [Col. 0295A] according to what the lord king has commanded us. And

@ [Col. 0295D] “Felix has sworn to come.” He was to be brought by Laidrad to the council at Aachen, as can be gathered from the following letter; hence this was written in the year 799. Felix, the advocate of novelty, has sworn to come to the lord king to give an account of his faith. Therefore pray more earnestly for us.] But I, a native son of the holy Church of God, must stand with you; and what the unanimity of Christ’s priests believes and preaches, I labor for, speak of with my companions, and will open my mouth on behalf of the sons of the holy Church of God, if he fills it who says: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm LXXX, 11). I desire to teach the way of the Lord, strengthen those who waver, exhort those who stand, and raise up those who lie fallen, through him and in him “who raises up the oppressed and releases the captives” (Psalm CXLV, 7–8). The Lord Jesus Christ, for whom and through whom I speak, that we may testify that he is true God and true Son of God before all who wish or do not wish to hear, [Col. 0295B]

[Our little books, which

@ [Col. 0295D] “Hildegarius.” Without doubt some disciple of Alcuin at the monastery of Saint Rupert. See the following letter. —Hildegarius carried from Saint Martin, namely Saint Ambrose’s work On the Catholic Faith addressed to the Emperor Gratian, and the Treatises on the Prophets Joel and Amos. If these little books remained in the monastery, bring them with you by all means if you come; otherwise send them back to us. But if he carried them away with him, have him sent so that he may return them, so that he may have the blessing of Saint Martin, since they are from that man’s repository, and we do not wish anything belonging to him to be lost through us. You did well by that aforementioned boy when you allowed him to serve the world, because he did not wish to persist in the study of ecclesiastical life; and do not be angry with me on his account. I knew that he did not want what I knew you wanted; but I did not wish him to be separated from you through me, since he belonged to you by blood [Col. 0295C]—I fear, not by spirit. Nevertheless, one must not despair concerning him: God is able to raise up sons of Abraham from these stones (Matthew III, 9). Do a kindness, I beg,

@ [Col. 0295D] “Mago.” By this name he indicates Adalbert, concerning whom elsewhere. See the following letter. —to my black Mago; for he will be useful in the house of God. He was always with us and possessed good will and humility, whether in the service of God or in the study of reading. Whatever he may have received, make him share with many, so that the word of God may grow in the Church which, by God’s dispensation, you serve. Greet, I beg, all our brothers in peace and charity, and our Father

@ [Col. 0295D] “Alimum.” He was bishop of Säben, who signed the Synod of Dingolfing in the year 772. —Alimum the bishop, and your other fellow priests. Always exhort them to the duty of preaching. Remember that

@ [Col. 0295D] “The archiepiscopal pallium,” with which Arno was honored in the preceding year, as is now also clear from this letter, [Col. 0296D] which was sent in 799 shortly after the beginning of the year, namely before March. See the following letter. —when you received the pallium from the apostolic see, you received a greater burden and became indebted to every person and rank, preach the word of God with confidence.] Do not, do not be silent, but cry out and do not cease. “Raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isaiah LVIII, 1), show everyone the way of eternal salvation, and say: “Run! This is the royal road; this is the public highway that leads to the palace of Christ God, in which there is peace, praise, and glory.” When you arrive there, remember me.

[On the Kalends of November

@ [Col. 0296D] “The Solemnity of All Saints.” Quercetanus states in the preface to Blessed Alcuin, no. 17, that this solemnity began to be celebrated on that day—that is, on the Kalends of November—in Gaul and Germany long after Alcuin’s death, namely in the year 835. This assertion is refuted by the present passage. —the solemnity of All Saints. Behold, venerable Father Arno, you have the solemnity of All Saints designated, as we said, which you should continually retain in your mind and never cease to honor at its annual season, observing and attentively considering that if Elijah, one of those saints, was able in the Old Testament, by his prayer, whenever he wished, to close heaven against transgressors and open it to the converted (1 Kings XVII, and James V, 17), how much more can All the Saints in the New Testament? For there the keys of the heavenly kingdom have been specially and openly entrusted to them, and they can close heaven against unbelievers and open it to believers if they are honored by the faithful with inward love and celebrated with a glorification worthy of them. So that this may rightly be done by us, may the true light, which enlightens every human being (John I, 9), Christ Jesus, enlighten our hearts; and may the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding (Philippians IV, 7), through the intercession of all his Saints, guard them until the day of eternity. Let us precede this most holy solemnity for three days by fasting, praying, singing Masses, and giving alms for one another with sincere devotion.]

@ [Col. 0296D] We give this letter, hitherto unpublished, from the manuscripts of Salzburg and Saint Emmeram; the passages enclosed in brackets occur only in the Salzburg manuscript. (In Froben, Letter 77.)

## LETTER XCII. TO ARNO (A.D. 799, IN MARCH)

He reports that he has received the letter with gifts and indicates that he will be with the king in mid-May, when Felix too is to be brought. [Col. 0296C]

To his dearest son, the Eagle: Albinus sends greetings.

Having received, with great joy and gladness, the priestly gifts of your affection, together with your sweetest letter, in which your love—which I have often tested and have always loved—was fragrant to me, sweeter than every honeycomb, I stored the memory of your face and name within the secret chambers of my heart, like a desirable treasure [edition: “is stored”]; and what appears black in the hair is loved as white in the heart. But I beg with all my might that, if it can be done, this coming year I may see the sweetest eyes [of my Eagle], so that I may embrace and kiss you not only with my mouth but also with my whole heart. [Long ago I wrote a longer letter to your affection [Col. 0296D] and sent it to brother Chlotar, so that it might reach you through your men. Therefore I now speak only a few words in this present little sheet. For your letter, together with the gifts, came to me on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, and I immediately wrote this one, greatly desiring to see you. Now, God willing, I am planning to be with the king in mid-May, because

@ [Col. 0297D] “Laidradus . . . Felix.” From this we learn the year in which the letter was written, namely 799, when Laidradus brought Felix to Aachen; we have discussed him elsewhere. —our son Laidradus is to bring that Felix with whom we are engaged in a dispute of words. And would that our dearest Father Paulinus might come! If an opportunity arises for you, I greatly desire that we may have you present], because I have much to discuss with you which, because of the untrustworthiness of those who carry letters, I do not wish to disclose in writing. But be more cautious amid hostile arms. It is your task to preach, not to fight; to make peace, not discord; to recall people to life, not send them to death, as your holiness knows very well.

{114} [Hildegarius carried two books of Saint Martin with him, as

@ [Col. 0297D] “In another letter.” Namely, the immediately preceding one. —I indicated to you in another letter. I ask you to have them brought here: Saint Ambrose’s On the Faith, and the Treatises on the Prophets Joel and Amos. And

@ [Col. 0297D] “My Mago.” Adalbert. See note c to the preceding letter. —greet my Mago and treat him well, for he is a good brother; and all the sons of the holy Church

@ [Col. 0297D] “Ratbertum.” Undoubtedly Rutbertus, or Rupertus; from the context it seems that the text should read: “Treat well all the sons of the holy Church at Saint Rupert’s,” that is, of the Salzburg monastery. —treat Ratbertus well, and greet them all in the name of Albinus, together with your other fellow priests, and pray for us.] And may the Lord God direct our hearts (2 Thessalonians III, 5) and our minds toward the salvation of many, so that the word of God may advance and shine in the ears of many, and the Catholic faith may be stored in their hearts. May God’s Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, preserve you and your faithful, and cause you to flourish always and forever in the duty of charity and the truth of faith, dearest son.

@ [Col. 0297D] Quercetanus edition 78, Canisius 20, Froben 78. Compared with the manuscripts of Salzburg and Saint Emmeram. Mabillon, in Book XXVI of the Annals, no. 58, assigns it to the year 796. Hansiz, volume II of *Germania Sacra*, page 103, believes it was written in 794, when Elipandus, after Felix had been recalled to heresy following the Synod of Regensburg in 792, endeavored to spread the poison beyond Spain into Gaul and Germany; {116} against this he urges the brothers of Juvavum to arm themselves with devotion to the sacred writings. It nevertheless seems to me that the present letter is the one mentioned in the following letter to Arno, which was written in 799, and therefore that it belongs to the same year, in which the case of Felix was no less than on other occasions being debated.

## LETTER XCIII. TO THE BROTHERS OF THE CHURCH OF JUVAVUM (A.D. 799)

He praises their regular way of life and exhorts them to perform the duties of monks well. [Col. 0297C]

To the most holy brothers in Christ of the Church of Juvavum, the humble Levite Albinus sends greetings in the charity of Christ.

Hearing of your praiseworthy way of life in Christ and of your unanimity, my spirit rejoiced with great joy and longed with an even greater desire to see your community in person and to commend myself with humble devotion to your sacred prayers. But because this has so far been prevented by the varying course of events and the great distance of the lands [which does not permit me bodily to go where my mind, with supreme desire, always longs to be present], I have taken care to send these little letters of my smallness in fulfillment of this duty, so that you may recognize in these lines the desire of my heart, which long ago I also sought to entrust to the pious Father, Bishop Aquila,

@ [Col. 0298D] “Aquila, my own brother.” Canisius added a note to this passage; and we have discussed in the preface whether it should be inferred from this that Aquila, or Arno, archbishop of Salzburg, was Alcuin’s blood brother. —your shepherd, my own brother, striving [Col. 0298A] to be spiritually one of you and one with you, desiring that your holiness might lift me from earthly desires and place me with you in heavenly longing.

O how blessed is the life of monks! Pleasing to God, beloved by angels, honored by human beings. Whoever lives faithfully here among human beings undoubtedly reigns happily among the angels. The primitive Church, through the apostles, initiated this life in Judea; of them it is read that all things were held in common and that no one claimed anything as his own (Acts IV, 32). I think this should be observed not only in secular possessions but also in spiritual desires, so that all may desire one thing and may practice the good of obedience more than the inclination of their own will. If Christ did not come to do his own will, as he himself testifies in the Gospel, but the Father’s (John V, 30 and VI, 38), how much less should a monk do his own will rather than Christ’s? Let him be not sluggish in the work of God but diligent; let him consider not only what is commanded but also how what is commanded may be accomplished, lest the evil of murmuring grow in anyone. If some of the people of God perished in the wilderness because of the sin of murmuring, how much more should a monk of the monastery be punished with spiritual retribution if he does not fear allowing his mind to grow insolent through the evil of murmuring?

{115} Therefore let him receive with thanksgiving what the shepherd’s care has provided as sufficient for him. Let there be holy peace and concord among all; chastity of life in the young; seriousness of character [Col. 0298C] in the old; fervor in work among the young. Let no one withdraw from the canonical hours or the regular psalmody. It is better to praise Christ with the assemblies of angels than to enjoy sluggish sleep in torpor, or, while awake, to pursue empty desires. And let not only the words of sacred reading resound in the mouth, but let inward compunction of heart follow the words of the reader or singer. Under no circumstances should the reading of Sacred Scripture depart from your hands at the appointed hours, because, as you have heard, various heresies are now striving to stain the purity of the Catholic faith.

Therefore arm yourselves with knowledge of the truth and with the judgments of evangelical authority, so that you may be able to resist those who contradict the truth. How does an unarmed person fight? [Col. 0298D] Or how can one teach who has refused to learn? Riches are spiritual; wisdom is in the heart, as Solomon says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the prudent” (Proverbs XXI, 20).

[Col. 0299A] Learn diligently the truth of the holy faith, store what you have learned in the treasure of your hearts, hold fast to God with the firmest hope, and love, honor, and praise him with the most fervent charity. For this is the better portion that Mary chose, sitting beside the Lord’s feet; it will not be taken away from a human being forever (Luke X, 39, 42). But Christ is loved more ardently after this life in proportion as his goodness is understood more perceptively.

Yet there is no need for my smallness to admonish you about each individual matter, since you have the well-known books of sacred instruction and your pious Father and shepherd present among you, who will be able to admonish you by the living voice better than my written letter. Nevertheless, to show you the charity I owe you, I have sought to address you in a few lines, so that you might recognize the confidence of my affection toward you.

@ [Col. 0299D] “To the aforementioned Father,” namely Aquila. “From this,” Hansiz says, “it is clear that Arno also held the superintendence of the monks.” —Therefore obey the aforementioned Father with all humility (Hebrews XIII, 17). He must give an account to God of his care for you, and you likewise must give an account of your obedience to him. He has been placed in great danger on your behalf; strive to intercede for him with great charity, so that he may have a reward for you before God and you may have rest with him in the kingdom of God. The education of sons is the praise of teachers, and the progress of the flock is the reward of shepherds.

With divine grace assisting, guard yourselves, brothers, in all chastity, humility, concord, and charity, “bearing one another’s burdens” (Galatians VI, 2, 5). Let no evil, immodest, impatient, or useless speech proceed from your mouth (Ephesians IV, 29); but speak what is holy, devout, and just, and worthy of your holiness, for the exhortation of those who hear. Let God always be honored in your mouth (Romans XV, 6), and pursue with your whole purpose the things that belong to true peace; then the God of peace will be with you, and the peace that surpasses all understanding will guard your hearts in all goodness and piety (Philippians IV, 7, 9). “Blessed are the peacemakers [for they shall be called sons of God]” (Matthew V, 9). It is the highest nobility to be a son of almighty God. But this great nobility must be earned by the dignity of one’s conduct. For you are not your own, but Christ’s, who bought you at a great price—that is, with his blood. “Carry God in your body” (1 Corinthians VI, 20), so that God may deign to dwell in your hearts, and so that from this brief and laborious life you may deserve to arrive at eternal rest [Col. 0299D] and blessedness, with the holiness of blessed Hrotbert and the other Fathers interceding for you. May divine mercy cause you to flourish in every good, dearest brothers.

@ [Col. 0299D] Mabillon edition 11, Froben 79. This appears more complete from the Salzburg manuscript.

## LETTER XCIV TO ARNO (A.D. 799, IN MARCH)

He sends Easter poems and wishes the parish priests, or pastors, of his diocese to be admonished concerning uprightness of life and the proper performance of their duties. [Col. 0300A]

To the Eagle flying through the Alps, running across the plains, and walking through the cities, the humble earth-dweller sends greetings.

[“I have sent Easter poems to your peace, as the Magi dictated them to me. You should judge whether they are suitable for writing or useful for reading.

@ [Col. 0299D] “I also sent a letter to the brothers.” These brothers are the monks of Saint Peter, or Saint Rupert, to whom we have just given the preceding letter. —I also sent a letter to the brothers, asking that it be read in your presence, so that you may commend me to their prayers, as well as to those of your

@ [Col. 0299D] “Parishioners.” He means the pastors or parish priests of his diocese. See Du Cange, *Glossary*, V, “Parochianus.” —parishioners who are accustomed to come for the dedication of the holy chrism. I would also have written to them for the sake of your charity, if it were not too presumptuous. Nevertheless,] admonish them concerning chastity of life, uprightness of conduct, vigilance in prayer, and perseverance in supplication; and let each one have the people entrusted to him well instructed in the will of God and his church properly directed. [And let them take especially diligent care of widows, orphans, and the poor (Ecclesiasticus IV, 1–2 and following; VII, 36). Let them also have scholars, and make them learn the psalms and ecclesiastical song diligently, so that in every church the daily course of praise to God may be performed.] Let each one honor his ministry in the Lord, so that there may be no reproach in Christ’s priest but praise in the preacher of truth (2 Corinthians VI, 3). [And let them exercise holy baptism with the greatest diligence, because nowhere is error more dangerous, nor, if it is properly observed, more fruitful.] Let each exhort people to purity of confession and compunction in penance, because this is the second baptism in the Church: whoever, after the first baptism, has fallen into some offense is corrected in this second one. May God be your helper everywhere, so that you may advance in every good work and be considered worthy of a manifold reward in the sight of the Lord your God. Until the Kalends of May I shall expect your arrival in these regions.

@ [Col. 0300D] “The king is going to Saxony.” In the year 799 King Charles celebrated Easter at Aachen on the day before the Kalends of April; afterward he entered Saxony and took up position at Paderborn with his army, as the Frankish Annals testify. The timing of that journey therefore agrees with the time when the letter was written. —We hope that the king will go to Saxony. As for my own situation, God willing, when you come we expect to learn something more certain. Only assist our frailty with your prayers, so that Christ may direct us according to his merciful will, so that we may do what is pleasing to him (Ecclesiasticus II, 19). May Christ God deign to preserve your blessedness in good health for the advancement of his holy Church, desired Father!

{117}

@ [Col. 0300D] Quercetanus edition 11, Canisius 4, Froben 80. In Quercetanus it also appears under the title: “Laments over the misery of this age.”

## LETTER XCV TO THE LORD KING (A.D. 799)

He gives thanks for gifts received and complains about the disturbance of the Church and kingdom. He urges the king to devote the greatest care to the Church, with somewhat less severity toward the Saxons. [Col. 0301A]

We give thanks to your most merciful goodness, sweetest David, because you deign to remember our smallness and to make known to us what your faithful servant has sounded into our ears. Nor do we offer continual thanks to your piety only for this, but for all the good things that, from the day when my smallness became known to you, he has brought about with me. You began excellently, but you have brought things to an even better completion. Therefore, in continual prayers, I beseech the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that he who has granted you every good thing in earthly happiness may deign eternally to grant you far better realms of eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0301B] I would advise your venerable dignity about very many matters in person, if either you had the opportunity to listen or I had the eloquence to speak, because the pen of my affection often prompts the secrets of my heart to discuss your excellence’s prosperity, the stability of the kingdom given to you by God, and the advancement of the holy Church of Christ, which has been disturbed by the manifold wickedness of evil people and stained by the criminal enterprises of the worst men—not only by persons of low rank but also by those of the greatest and highest standing. This is very much to be feared. For until now there have been three highest persons in the world: [namely,] the apostolic eminence, which ordinarily governs, in the office of a vicar, the see of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. What, however, was done to the man who

@ [Col. 0301C] He is speaking of the cruelty perpetrated by the Romans against Leo III, Roman pontiff. —had been ruler [Col. 0301C] of that aforementioned see, your venerable goodness has taken care to make known to me. Another is imperial dignity, and [Col. 0302A]

@ [Col. 0301C] “The Second Rome.” Constantinople, which is also commonly called Rome by historians—Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chapter 8, and elsewhere—and even in the constitutions of the emperors. It received the name New Rome from its founder Constantine. Sidonius also says in the *Panegyric*:

“Hail, summit of scepters, queen of the East,

Rome of your world.”

—of the secular power of the Second Rome. How impiously

@ [Col. 0301C] “The governor of the empire.” “That is, the emperor Constantine, seized in the year 797 by his mother Irene and her counselors, and blinded and killed, according to the author Theophanes.” Canisius. —the governor of that empire was deposed is widely reported by rumor, not by outsiders but by his own people and fellow citizens. The third is royal dignity, in which the dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ has appointed you ruler of the Christian people: superior to the other aforementioned dignities in power, brighter in wisdom, and more exalted in the dignity of your kingdom.

Behold, in you alone the entire salvation of Christ’s churches rests, leaning upon you. You are the avenger of crimes, the ruler of those who stray, the consoler of the sorrowful, the exaltation of the good. Did not the extreme examples of impiety arise in the Roman see, where the religion of the greatest [Canisius: greatest possible] piety once shone? They, blinded in their own hearts,

@ [Col. 0301C] “They blinded their own head.” “These words are spoken severely and truly against the Roman people, who rose up against Pope Leo III, struck him, and mutilated his eyes in the year 799, according to Anastasius the Librarian.” Canisius. —blinded their own head. Nor does there seem to be fear of God there, nor wisdom, nor charity. What good can be there where none of these three is found? If they had fear of God, they would not have dared; if wisdom, they would never have wished to do it; if charity, they would certainly not have done it. The times are dangerous, foretold long ago by Truth itself, because “the charity of many will grow cold” (Matthew XXIV, 12).

@ [Col. 0301D] “In no way is care for the head to be omitted.” I judge it worthwhile to transcribe here the interpretation that Pagius inserted into the text of this letter under the year 799, no. 3. He gives it as follows:

> “In no way is care for the head [that is, the Roman pontiff] to be omitted … Let peace be made with the wicked people [namely, the Romans], if this can be done. What is possessed must be held on to, lest, on account of acquiring what is lesser, what is greater [namely, the Lombard kingdom] be lost. Let the proper fold be preserved [and therefore the Romans were not [Charlemagne’s] own subjects], lest the ravening wolf lay it waste [that is, lest some tyrant arise to whom the Romans might flee if they were too severely oppressed]. Thus let one toil over what belongs to others [namely, in arranging the Roman commonwealth], so that no harm may be suffered in what belongs to oneself [that is, in matters pertaining to the Lombard kingdom].”

From this interpretation the celebrated writer concludes:

> “From these words we understand that the Constantinopolitan emperors did not at this time possess the city of Rome; nor did Charles possess its dominion; nor was he the colleague of the supreme pontiff in the administration of the city. Otherwise Alcuin would not say that there were three supreme powers in the world, and that the loss of the Italian kingdom would be greater than the acquisition of Rome and of a foreign city. Thus, by this letter of Alcuin alone, the opinion of Marca and Cointius is overturned: they maintain that from the year 796 the dominion of the city and of the Exarchate of Ravenna belonged jointly to the pontiff and Charles, and that both governed them with equal right. For if this had been so, Alcuin would not have called the Romans foreigners, nor would he have warned Charles to beware lest, on account of acquiring what was lesser, he lose the entire kingdom. At this very time the duke of Benevento was in arms against the Franks, and the recent change of affairs in the city of Constantinople gave reason to fear that, if disturbances arose in Italy, the Greeks—hostile to the Franks—would encourage them. Hence Alcuin advised Charles to beware of those reefs.”

Thus far Pagius. I fear that the celebrated man has departed too far from Alcuin’s meaning in this interpretation. Here, then, is another interpretation, which I submit for judgment to learned men:

> “In no way is care for the head [the Roman pontiff] to be omitted. Let peace be made with the wicked people [the Saxons, whom he reproaches by the same name in the following letter; with whom also, in this year 799, he negotiated peace through his son Charles, and from whom he carried away a multitude of people, with women and children, and settled them throughout various lands in his territories [*Chronicon Moissiacense* and the *Annals of Lambecius*]. With the Roman people, however, Charles at that time [Col. 0303C] was waging no war; nor was it the whole people, but only certain leading men who plotted the death of Leo]. Let the threats be relaxed somewhat, lest the [Saxons], hardened, flee … What is possessed must be held on to [in the lands of Saxony], lest, on account of acquiring what is lesser [namely, the enlargement of an earthly kingdom], what is greater [the salvation of the Church and of its head] be lost. Let the proper fold be preserved [the Church, which is properly called the fold of every believer; and Alcuin would not have wished by that name to designate the Lombard kingdom, as Pagius supposes], lest the ravening wolf lay it waste [namely, after the shepherd has been struck down]. Thus let one toil over what belongs to others [among a people not yet acquired], so that no harm may be suffered in what belongs to oneself [namely, in matters concerning the welfare of the Church, which ought to be the possession of every believer, and especially of its supreme advocate, as it were].”

Let the learned decide which of these interpretations ought to be preferred, or which should be considered more consistent with Alcuin’s meaning.

“In no way is care for the head to be omitted. It is less serious for the feet to hurt [Muratorius: ‘to remove’] than the head. Let peace be made with the wicked people, if this can be done. Let the threats be relaxed somewhat, lest, becoming hardened, they flee; but let them be kept in hope until they are recalled to peace by wholesome counsel. What is possessed must be held on to, lest, on account of acquiring what is lesser, what is greater be lost. Let the proper fold be preserved, lest the ravening wolf lay it waste. [Col. 0302C] Thus let one toil over what belongs to others, so that no harm may be suffered in what belongs to oneself.”

[Col. 0303A]

@ [Col. 0303D] “Long ago … I spoke about the exaction of tithes.” In letters 28, 31, 37, and 72 [now 33, 36, 42, and 87]. “Long ago I spoke to your most holy piety about the exaction of tithes, because perhaps it is better that the public necessity be relaxed, or at least suspended for some time, until faith takes root in their hearts—provided, however, that that homeland is judged worthy of God’s election. Those who departed were excellent Christians, as is known in many cases. But those who remained in the homeland [Canisius: ‘of the homeland’] remained in the dregs of wickedness. For Babylon, because of the sins of the people, was appointed as a dwelling-place of demons (Rev. XVIII, 2), as we read in the prophets. None of this can be hidden from your wisdom. For we know that you are exceedingly learned in the sacred Scriptures and in secular histories. From all these things God has granted you complete knowledge, so that through you God’s holy Church may be governed, exalted, and [Col. 0303B] preserved among the Christian people. Who can say how great a reward will be presented to your excellent devotion by God? For neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him (I Cor. II, 9).”

May gentle Christ mercifully from heavenly Olympus

Rule, exalt, protect, adorn, and love you. My mind greatly rejoices

That your own faithful goodness most graciously receives the aged king. I pray that he may look upon these little letters of ours

With a merciful eye—letters written by love of your piety. May the holy stars of heaven,

Or the green grasses of earth,

All things cry out together: “David, prosper everywhere!” Earth, heaven, sea, human beings, birds and beasts

[Col. 0303C] Cry with one voice: “Farewell, father!”

@ [Col. 0304C] Published by Quercetinus, 12, from the manuscript [Frobenius, 81]. It was written before Pope Leo came to Charlemagne in the year 799.

## LETTER XCVI TO THE LORD KING  
*(Year 799)*

He gives thanks for the king’s remembrance of him in letters and for the many benefits he has received. He praises and urges the king to render justice to the apostolic see. He excuses himself from undertaking the journey to Rome. He expresses the wish for peace with the Saxons.

To the lord David, most beloved king in the Lord of Lords, Flaccus, faithful herald of everlasting blessedness in Christ, sends greetings.

As I was returning from

@ [Col. 0304D] Wicus. The seaside cell of Saint Judoc among the Morini, today Saint-Josse-sur-Mer. Charlemagne entrusted this monastery to Alcuin’s governance when Alcuin returned from England to Francia in the year 792 or the following year. At Wicus, where we had necessary matters to arrange, the most sweet letters of your Excellence met me as I was visiting your most religious

@ [Col. 0304D] sister. Namely, Gisla, perhaps at the convent of Chelles, of which she was abbess. Mabillon: “your sister.” These letters were welcome in your prosperity and praiseworthy in the divine mercy, which never abandons those who hope in it, just as

@ [Col. 0304D] We recently heard about the apostolic lord, Pope Leo, whom divine mercy did not abandon but miraculously rescued from the hands of robbers, restoring to him the use of his eyes and tongue, as the writers of that time testify; Alcuin himself also intimates this here in the words, ‘what the divine goodness mercifully accomplished,’ etc. “we heard through your most gracious letters what had recently been done concerning the apostolic lord; he too rejoices to come into the presence of your most blessed presence,”

@ [Col. 0304D] To arrive. Pope Leo came to Charlemagne while the latter was staying at Paderborn [then called Paderbrunna] in the present year, 799, and there was received with truly royal magnificence, as Anastasius testifies. “to arrive,” as your letter of kindness made known to us. We give many thanks to your goodness for having deigned, in your customary piety, to remember our name. We give your distinguished piety continual thanks not only for this present remembrance, but also for all your goodness, which you have always shown toward our exile in word and deed: faithful in promises, true in fulfilling what you promise. Therefore your faith, your unfeigned charity, and your continual intercession constantly embrace your blessedness in the secret treasury of my heart.

O sweetest glory of the Christian people! O defender of the churches of Christ! Consolation of the present life! All must exalt your blessedness with every prayer and assist it with intercessions, so that through your prosperity the Christian empire may be protected, the Catholic faith defended, and the rule of justice made known to all.

Behold what has been done concerning the apostolic see in the chief city, in the most excellent dignity—matters that are preserved solely by your judgment—so that, tempered by prudent deliberation and by the wisdom God has given you, what must be corrected may be corrected, and what must be preserved may be preserved; and so that what divine mercy has mercifully accomplished [Col. 0304C] may be raised to the praise of that name which saved its servant and delivered him from the persecution of execrable infidelity. May your supremely wise prudence of mind, understanding everything that is appropriate to each person, act and accomplish in doing good or in punishing what pleases God, so that the good will shown toward you by all may be praised and loved. Let your piety recognize this with complete certainty: no gifts of gold or silver from any human beings bring the soul of your Flaccus as much joy as your letters of blessedness restore him with complete gladness. Therefore, with a suppliant prayer I beg you to command more often that this be done—the thing you recognize that I always love.

[Col. 0305A] {120} “As for that long and arduous journey

@ [Col. 0305D] of going to Rome.” “For this service,” says Pagius under the year 799, no. 4, “King Charles had already sent several bishops and abbots [namely, in the present year].” See the letter to Arno below. “of going to Rome, I do not think that the feeble little body of my frailty, broken by daily pains, can undertake. I would already have had the desire, if I had the power to carry it out. Therefore I beseech the most merciful benevolence of your fatherhood to permit me faithfully and earnestly to assist your journey by my prayers, while serving God at Saint Martin’s. Would that divine grace might one day grant you freedom from the wicked Saxon people, so that you could travel, govern kingdoms, administer justice, renew churches, correct the people, decide what is just for each person and dignity, defend the oppressed, establish laws, console pilgrims, and everywhere show to all the way of age [perhaps: of truth] and of heavenly life. May your piety’s arrival be a consolation to everyone, and may abundant blessing for the illustrious sons of your nobility increase through your benefactions, just as, according to what is read, through the holiness of your namesake, David, the king most beloved by God, royal power was preserved for all his grandsons. For in these and similar exercises of religion, the exaltation of your sons, the prosperity of the kingdom, the health of the people, the abundance of crops, and the delight of every good thing increase; and for you, sweetest David, the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom grows and is augmented through Christ God, for everlasting days.

May Christ, everywhere merciful,

David, beloved of the people, grant you counsel of peace together with salvation. May the Almighty’s right hand always defend,

[Col. 0305C] Making you and your people victorious together. May his name be praised eternally throughout the whole world

Because of the help of piety shown through you. Behold, O hope of all life, pattern of salvation,

How everything rejoicingly returns to you.”

@ [Col. 0305D] “He who comes sorrowful.” “He seems,” says Canisius, “to allude to Charlemagne’s second Roman expedition. He went to Rome four times: in 774, to vindicate Hadrian and the Roman Church against the injuries of Desiderius the Lombard; then in 781, to fulfill a vow; third, against the duke of Benevento in 786; fourth, to restore Leo in the year 800, when he was proclaimed emperor.” To me, however, these words seem to refer to the sorrowful arrival and joyful return to the city of Pope Leo; the further context of the poem, compared with the text of this letter, also suggests this quite clearly. These verses are appended by Canisius to letter 7 [Frobenius, 93], which is now letter 109.

He who came sorrowful, let him now return joyful to the city,

Through the Father’s gracious gifts and sacred counsel. Finding what he seeks, attaining whatever he hoped for,

Let him also bring back hymnic praises to him who in our age

Granted the world such a ruler

Under the governance of sacred justice.

{121}

@ [Col. 0305D] Frobenius, 82. Mabillon published this letter, though not in its entirety, from the manuscript of Saint Emmeram; Pez published its beginning from the Benedictine manuscript. Here it appears more fully from the Salzburg manuscript, with those passages enclosed in brackets supplied accordingly.

## LETTER XCVII TO [—]  
*(Year 799)*

He longs for the recipient’s presence and laments the atrocious deed at Rome; he urges him to the work of preaching and the practice of virtues. He congratulates him on receiving the pallium, while urging him to fulfill his ministry well. [Col. 0306A]

To my most beloved son in charity and venerable father in holiness, a devoted friend in the faith sends greetings.

I would have had many things of great necessity to discuss with you, if time and place and the presence of your face were available—whether concerning the general condition of the Church’s holiness or concerning the particular vicissitudes of affairs relating to us. But this will happen when he who disposes all things in heaven and on earth wills it; may he at some time grant us to exchange words of charity and to reveal the heart’s ardor through peaceful speech.

But you, dearest of all and most closely joined to my heart among all Christ’s priests! I beg you to make intercessions for us, so that divine mercy may cause you to advance in every good thing and may deign to guide us toward the progress of our salvation. The occupations of this age are many, its varieties are diverse, and its events are miserable; and the Church of Christ is attacked in many ways, not only by pagans but also by false brothers (II Cor. XI, 26; Gal. II, 4). And where the fountain of equity and justice ought to flow out to all through the channels of holiness, there, above all, the marshy depth of iniquity exhales its foulness—as perhaps you will hear from the most holy see, what crimes and

@ [Col. 0306D] “Of excessive atrocity.” This was perpetrated against Pope Leo in the year 799, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, during the Greater Litania, as may be gathered from the following words: “While such things are being done to the head.” “of excessive atrocity is reported to have recently taken place. We must fear not only this crime of most impious depravity but also the portent of a greater evil. While such things are being done to the head, it is dreadful to consider what may happen to the body. Justice is suffering, iniquity is abounding, charity is growing cold (Matt. XXIV, 12; II Tim. II, 17), and unbelief is spreading like poison and, like a cancer, does not cease to stain the members of Christ. Therefore, while you have the opportunity, labor in the word of preaching, in the power of charity, in the example of holiness, in the duty of piety, in the distribution of alms, and in steadfastness of mercy and piety, so that you may deserve to pass from the misery of this darkness to the light of everlasting blessedness; and do not cease to draw me with you, as a son, brother, and companion united with you in your salvation, through constant prayers and admonitions, so that together we may be made worthy to say, by the gift of the dispenser of eternal goodness: ‘The king has brought us into his wine-cellars; we will exult and rejoice in you’ (Song I, 3).”

[

@ [Col. 0306D] “I rejoiced greatly,” etc. The passages enclosed in brackets in the manuscript of Salzburg are inserted between the preceding and following material. It is easy to judge that a new letter begins here. The preceding words bear the appearance of an epistolary conclusion, whereas these are of the kind with which a letter properly begins—namely, words of congratulation, addressed, I think, to Arno of Salzburg on his new dignity and the honor of the archiepiscopal pallium. Hence I think it happened through the error of scribes that, in the manuscript of Saint Emmeram used by Mabillon, the exhortation beginning with the words “The movements of an agitated spirit,” which belongs to this new letter, was attached to another; and that in the Salzburg manuscript this new letter was joined to the preceding one without a new heading—something that experts in ancient book production know to be by no means unusual. Nevertheless, because of the authority of the Salzburg manuscript, I did not wish here to separate one letter from the other, although in my judgment they are distinct and were written in different years. Let learned men judge whether one should follow my conjecture. If it is thought that some weight should be given to it, then this new letter must be assigned to the year 798, to which the ancient records unanimously agree that the pallium was granted to Arno. But if the manuscript’s authority is preferred, and both parts are judged to constitute only one letter, it must nevertheless be certain, against the distinguished Hansiz, that Arno publicly assumed the archiepiscopal dignity both before the year 800 and before April of the year 799, when that atrocious act was perpetrated against Pope Leo, and that Alcuin sent a congratulatory letter before that year 800—that is, before the middle of the year 799. See Hansiz, vol. II of *Germania Sacra*, p. 110.

“I rejoiced greatly when I heard that your blessedness bore the holiness of the shoulder-cloth [the pallium] and stood firmly in the highest stability of ecclesiastical honor. Would that this benefit many and especially profit you, so that the name of God and our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified in you; and remember that you are more a minister than a lord, because of him who said: ‘I am among you as one who serves’ (Luke XXII, 27). If that God and Lord of all, redeemer and savior of the human race, did not disdain to come and serve, not to be served (Mark X, 45), how much more ought we to consider the measure of our poverty, to minister the offices of salvation to all who belong to us, and to serve with the devotion of charity, since by steps of humility one reaches the height of the heavenly kingdom.

“Therefore the Prophet, moved by divine love, says: ‘Let not the foot of pride come to me’ (Ps. XXXV, 12)—that is, let no trace of pride remain in his heart. How much more, then, should we, raised from the dung of poverty to the seat of glory (Ps. CXII, 7), elevate our dignity through the ministry of humility. This is what makes the ignoble noble and raises an earthly creature to the heavenly tribunal.

“Whenever you are clothed in the pallium of holiness, think constantly and see the sign of the holy cross fixed upon it, whether in front or behind. Remember that you must follow him who carried his cross, on which he prepared the trophy of our redemption. When you see it, kiss and venerate it, as befits the holiness of this sign; and remember that you must follow him who said: ‘Whoever wishes to come after me, let him take up his cross and follow me’ (Matt. [Col. 0307C] XVI, 24). Therefore Christ carried it first, and after him Simon was found, who carried Christ’s cross, placed upon him, following in his footsteps. This is recognized as having been done as a sign of our conduct; for Simon means ‘obedient.’ Everyone who wishes through obedience to come to the triumph of glory [the editor supplies: ‘or something similar’] thinks of carrying Christ’s cross. For this, by steps of humility and strides of patience—or by being ready to die for the truth, by enduring the scandals of fraternal perversity, or by grieving in compassion over the troubles of one’s brothers—[the text is incomplete].”

May the agitated movements of your spirit be composed in tranquil peace, so that nothing may be done in anger, but everything with counsel—“buying up the time, until the anger passes” (Eccl. XXXII, 24)—and so that whatever prudent wisdom of counsel suggests ought to be done may then be said or done. May the feeling of your heart hear the cries of the poor, and may your generous hand refresh their misery. It is a great thing to have God as your debtor,” because the reward of Christ’s poor repays benefits, and what the wretched person cannot repay, the Lord of all will deign to recompense. Let your continual thought be in the sacred Scriptures, and let the joy of the banquet be praise of the Redeemer. While the body is nourished with food, let the mind be warmed by divine reading, lest the soul, hungry while the body is intoxicated, mourn. Let what is eternal be nourished more than what will perish. Let the mind examine heavenly things and continually foresee its future dwelling, so that through the labor of a short time it may deserve everlasting rest.

I would have written more to you if I did not know that a little is sufficient for the wise. One word in the heart of a thoughtful person accomplishes more good than many thousands in the heart of a scorner. Do not cease sowing the seed of salvation in the hearts of many, so that from the salvation of many you may deserve to receive abundant recompense before God’s mercy. Live happily, flourishing and advancing in the charity of Christ and in the commandments given by God for the eternal blessedness of the human race. Remember me, dearest father, brother, and son, and may you prosper forever in Christ.”

@ [Col. 0308D] Edited by Mabillon, 10 [Frobenius, 83], collated with the Salzburg manuscript.

## LETTER XCVIII TO ARNO  
*(Year 799)*

He urges him to guard himself against the dangers of the world and makes known his love for him.

Albinus sends greetings to the evangelical Eagle.

The temptations of this age are exceedingly numerous, and many are the dangers for those who love the world. Behold how suddenly they have departed [Col. 0308C]

@ [Col. 0308D] “Very brave men.” Namely, Henry or Eric, duke of Friuli, overcome by an ambush of the citizens near Tarsatica, a city of Liburnia; and Gerold, prefect of Bavaria, killed in battle against the Avars on the Kalends of September in the year 799. See the Frankish Annals under this year. “very brave men, who guarded and even extended the boundaries of the Christian empire. We mourn not only this loss but also fear the sign of a greater danger. Therefore, dearest father, guard yourself with every vigilance, and labor in the house of God, so that your labor may advance you toward eternal salvation. Nothing stable can be established in this world except the charity of Christ and his service. For, as the Apostle says, ‘the form of this world is passing away’ (I Cor. VII, 31). Only that remains which we do for the love of God and in obedience to his commandments.

“Rescue yourself, as far as you can, from the dangers of this life. Let your throat be a trumpet over the house of God. Be the standard-bearer of spiritual warfare and a leader in Christ’s battle line, so that the kingdom in the land of the living may be enlarged for you and you may place no hope in this land of the dying. Rather, where eternal life is, let your attention, hope, and desire be directed there at every hour. Say to Christ God: ‘My soul desired you in the night, and my spirit watched for you in my inmost being’ (Isa. XXVI, 9). [Col. 0309A] Those who guard Christ’s camp must remain awake and not sleep, because the glory of the everlasting kingdom is promised to those who watch and do not grow numb through sloth.

“I would have written to you more often if report had told me where your little letter might have found you. Nevertheless, the memory of your name is written in my heart with the stylus of charity—not with a perishable pen, but with enduring sweetness, repeatedly echoing from the innermost affection of my heart: ‘When will that day come when I may embrace my Eagle and clasp the neck of my venerable Father in sweet embraces?’ Do you see what true charity is like? It cannot be divided by any distance of lands or erased by any forgetfulness; rather, it grows more and more.

“Happy is the soul that loves God, freed from the bonds of this age, so that it may advance in the solidity of truth and arrive at the vision of divine blessedness, where there is tranquil joy and everlasting life without any disturbance. To this happiness, holy father, strive to lead me with you through prayers, so that in Christ we may enjoy the sweetness of everlasting charity. Greet in my name all the sons of God’s holy Church who serve God with you, and write my name in their hearts through the devout affection of prayer; may Christ God command that their names be written in the heavenly book, he who said to the companions of his labor: ‘Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven’ (Luke X, 20). Farewell, all of you, happily in Christ’s blessing, most beloved brothers.”

## LETTER XCIX TO [—]

@ [Col. 0309D] Frobenius, 172. This letter is wholly enigmatic at its beginning, and it is impossible to guess who is meant by the names of the cock, the sparrow, the blackbird, and so forth. The Eagle is undoubtedly Arno, archbishop of Salzburg, to whom this letter may perhaps have been sent; the Lion is Pope Leo of Rome, who, after barely being rescued from the atrocious hands of the Romans in the year 799, went to King Charles in Saxony. Arno also came there and rendered his services to Pope Leo; afterward, at the king’s command, he escorted him to Rome. But no other writer has noted what Alcuin seems to imply here when he says that Arno, in that same year 799, was still staying at Rome when the atrocious crime against Leo was committed and accompanied him to Saxony: “Concerning the Eagle, who recently, abandoning the heights of the Roman citadel …” For in the year 797 he was sent to Rome as an envoy by King Charles; but the distinguished Hansiz proves at length, in volume II of *Germania Sacra*, under Arno, nos. 20 and 22, that he returned from there in the following year, and this also seems capable of being gathered from the preceding letters. Perhaps in the year 799, when hatred against Leo was burning more fiercely, he was sent there again to settle the disagreements. But who can draw light from these shadows of riddles? (Year 799.) The letter is enigmatic at the beginning. He seeks the recipient’s charity. [Col. 0309C]

“The first letter of the first and the fifteenth of the sixth, a number sacred in its degrees and perfect in the works of God, sends greetings.

“Why has that brother come empty-handed? On his tongue he carried ‘Ave’ to the ears; in his hands, cuckoos; he brought nothing.” But you who sit at the crossroads, why did you entrust nothing certain to him who dwells in Maresa? Ravens flying over the roof-tops cry out, while the dove raised on the floors of the Church remains silent. I would believe it if it had said anything about the Eagle, who recently abandoned the heights of the Roman citadel to drink from the springs of the Saxon countryside and to see the Lion ruling all creatures and [Col. 0309D] wild beasts; or what our blackbird, flying among those [birds], might have entrusted to the monastic cock, who is accustomed to rouse the brothers for the morning vigils; so that through him the solitary [Col. 0310A] sparrow on the roof might know what agreement existed between the Lion and the Eagle; whether the Eagle’s youth had been renewed to its former cheerfulness according to the prophecy of the Psalmist (Ps. CII, 5); whether new roofs were rising in the marshy pools of treachery; and whether the Lion, following the ibexes [manuscript: ‘hibices’], was considering crossing the Alpine hills.

“The sparrow has open ears; but, as I see it, in the proverbial tale the wolf took the cock’s voice, lest, if he sang, the apostolic denial should be renewed in the City of ancient power, and the last error should be worse than the first.

“What wrong has charity committed, which saw ‘valen’ written [sic], when I hear that partridges running through the fields have come to the cock’s dwelling?” Perfect charity casts out fear (I John IV, 18); with the pupils of its shining eyes it sees everything clearly, and with the bright gaze of piety it will always find the sure rule of wholesome counsel. As it appears, the cock has been turned into a cuckoo, which is accustomed to be silent when the sun rises under the summer constellation of Cancer, while the nest-bearing sparrow rings alike under every star on the sooty roofs; now it flies in the month of the Septentriones to revisit the beloved, so that it may feed the chicks whose beaks gape eagerly with grains of piety—wishing that one day, over the banks of the fish-filled

@ [Col. 0310D] “river.” This undoubtedly refers to the Loire, the river flowing past Tours. In letter 29 [now 34] he says of it: “I do not know what will happen concerning our journey … whether I shall return to the river of the Loire and there gather salmon while they swim.” And in letter 87 [now 103] he wishes that “the Eagle [Arno] might fly as far as the fisheries of the Loire.” “fish-filled river,” I may hear the cock’s voice sounding powerfully [perhaps: ‘with force’; *valide*], and that he who is accustomed to rouse himself on his own wings for the morning melodies may come to encourage the sparrow in the midst of the chicks.

“O how sweet is the voice of charity! How lovely are the exhortations of genuine affection that customarily resound in the ears of the heart! Do not close your hands, full of seeds, because he who hides grain will be accursed, while he who multiplies it will receive a blessing (Prov. XI, 26). What will the judgment be on one who denies to a petitioner what he ought to have pressed upon one unwilling to receive? How does one who is not sown grow? What reward should be expected by one who produces no fruit? Or how does fruit grow if seeds are not scattered? Blessed are those who sow beside all waters, setting down the foot of the ox of ecclesiastical order and of the ass of the plebeian court; and if you did not do so in the morning of early life, do it now, in the evening of your final gray hairs. It is better to be a steward of everlasting bread than a distributor in rustic commerce, because ‘whatever a person sows, that he will also reap’ (Gal. VI, 8).

“Behold where charity has brought me! Forgetting myself, I carry goatskins to Christ’s sanctuary. For your heart is recognized as Christ’s treasury [manuscript: ‘treasure’], from which rivers of living water customarily flow [Col. 0311A] (John VII, 38). If I have exceeded the proper measure, may he forgive me; [perhaps read: because charity] has no measure and bears all things.” Draw me after you by your prayers, so that we may run together toward the prize of the heavenly calling. Strength fails unless fraternal consolation lifts up the weary and raises the fallen. What is there that charity cannot do, when it is in him who can do all things? Do not neglect your brother’s salvation. Christ gave himself for sinners; why do you withhold words of exhortation from one to whom he did not deny his blood? Surely you ought not to regard anyone as a stranger, since all are citizens in Christ.

“Charity does not regard persons; it has no pierced sacks, nor does it heap thick mud upon itself. Rather, it is modest, kind, merciful, and gentle. May he preserve you in it who gathered you into his fold, transferring you from the waves of the savage sea, so that you might be a ram whom no power of iniquity could resist. Help the one who prays, so that he may conquer in him who conquered the vanities of this age in you; he who said to his disciples in a consoling voice: ‘I have said these things to you so that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have distress, but take courage, because I have conquered the world’ (John XVI, 33). May Christ, the Son of God, make you victorious and hear you in every prayer, dearest brother.”

@ [Col. 0311D] Edited by Quercetinus, 14; Canisius, 5 [Frobenius, 84], collated with the Vatican Royal manuscript.

## LETTER C TO THE LORD KING  
*(Year 800)*

He replies to Charles’s repeated letters. He praises his zeal for religion, piety, and royal power, and mentions certain computational charts.

[Col. 0311C] To David, king blessed and resplendent with every adornment of wisdom, Flaccus Albinus sends greetings in Christ.

Although recently I sent two writings to your clemency, one of which fulfilled the duty of greeting, while the other met the requirements of a reply, nevertheless, upon receiving your blessedness’s letter, it seemed appropriate to reply to both [Alcuin: “to both letters”; perhaps “in some fashion”]. I received it with reverence, filled with the light of knowledge and the pursuit of truth, and with great eagerness in giving thanks I blessed God, who abundantly fills the breast of your piety with the power of faith and the experience of reason. Thus it is clearly shown that in you the prerogative of priestly teaching, the piety of your will, and royal power shine forth above all: for the Catholic faith, which everywhere ought to be one and different in no respect, through your most holy concern,

@ [Col. 0311D] “With the errors of schisms brought to rest.” I understand this to refer to the Felician heresy, quieted by the Council of Aachen toward the end of the year 799. “with the errors of schisms brought to rest, is recognized as being preached and flourishing. And as far as you surpass others in royal power, so far you surpass all in the splendor of wisdom and the fervor of holy religion. Happy is the people that rejoices in such a ruler: {124} in whose prosperity the salvation of all consists; in whose cheerfulness everyone’s spirit will rejoice, as it is said: ‘In the cheerfulness of the king there is life’ (Prov. XVI, 15). [Col. 0312A] His throne disperses iniquity; his countenance preserves reverence even unto equity. For what the apostolic Fathers once accomplished in their writings for the confirmation of the Catholic faith in various parts of the world, your most holy concern does not cease to fulfill.

“We proclaim this as a remarkable and distinctive gift of God’s piety in you: that with as much devotion as you strive to cleanse and protect the churches of Christ inwardly from the doctrines of the faithless, with just as much zeal you strive outwardly to defend or extend them against the devastation of pagans. With these two swords divine power has armed [your] venerable excellence on the right and on the left; in them you stand as a praiseworthy victor and glorious triumphator. Hence you wished to summon the devotion of my littleness to the kind of inward battle. I gladly submitted to the sweat of that struggle, [Col. 0312B] so that—”

[Col. 0311D] **In the little book.** Namely, in the books against Felix, which he submitted to the king’s examination and approval after that Council of Aachen had ended. See the letter prefixed to those books [Col. 0312D] and our Dissertation on the Heresy of the Adoptionists. In the little book which I recently sent to Your Piety, this may be recognized, although I have not yet learned that the same text of the little book has been confirmed by the seal of Your Authority. And I think this happened either through the bearer’s delay or through lack of time. In no way does Your customary goodness refuse, in several little letters, to do what it is known to have done more often in rarer ones.

As for the sheets of calculations concerning the lunar cycle and the preparation of the bissextile year, which you entrusted to our devotion for examination, we found them most diligently worked out with respect to their measurements, most acutely devised, and most nobly presented. And what my devotion once began concerning the bissextile year with a few little calculations, your most sagacious investigation has completed abundantly. Nevertheless, it should be considered [Col. 0312C] why, in certain months, the calculation of the solar cycle did not reach the same days in the second, third, or fourth year. Likewise, it seems that an easier and more straightforward reckoning of the lunar cycle may be found. Although this excellent and most acute calculation is understood to proceed distinctly and carefully down to a single scruple or *silicus* [Alternative: *siliculus*]. I have sent to Your Excellence the thread of certain calculations—

[Col. 0312D] **On the course of the sun and moon through the zodiac.** What Alcuin wrote about the sun’s course through the zodiac is perhaps what is found above in Letter 83. But it is clear from comparison with both that the sheet containing the calculations of the moon’s course through the individual signs belongs to Letter 85. You will find the same sheet among the *Philosophical Opuscula*, vol. II.

—on the course of the sun and moon through the zodiac. If it should please your most acute intelligence to add a woof to it, perhaps some kind of garment may be woven for the palace boys against the cold of ignorance, just as you declare that you did very well in the arrangement of the earlier fabric. It is my task to dig atoms of gold from the bosom of the earth, or from dusty clods. It is yours, with reverence, to wear upon your head a royal diadem, [Col. 0312D] resplendent with the gems of wisdom, so that Your Praiseworthy Power may flourish in every kind of virtue and, through the manifold praise of its merits, may deserve to reach the glory of the heavenly kingdom, with Christ ruling and granting it.

Hardly, hardly does a wicked fever permit me to live upon the earth,

yet you wish me to climb the heavenly path. [Col. 0313A] Through fields, hills, grasses, and green meadows,

while dear health urged me to seek it, suddenly your piety

commanded me, with feeble feet, to climb the stars of the highest heaven.

And to distinguish the signs of the lofty zodiac by their divisions,

and determine what order, position, and number they have.

Would not the fields of Hippocrates be worth more at a touch

when traversed with Flaccus and his boys,

than to describe with a ray the signs of the plowed heaven,

or to count the days of the moon and sun?

Yet, as the illustrious poet sang in a brief line,

“Love conquers all”; may love conquer us also.

At your command I have briefly described the regions and stars of heaven,

for great love possesses my heart.

Now let Your Piety see whether there is anything here worthy of approval,

[Col. 0313B] or whether anything on the page should be erased with pumice. {125} If your judgment never deceives the image,

I shall fear no one and flee no one, David, glory of the world!

If these things should perhaps prove worthy of your favor,

I think the old man himself will soon begin greater things,

if the eternal God adds years to his life.

It is His goodness that whatever work [Alternative: “assistance”] we have comes from him.

As the little sheet passes over hills and flowing fields,

may this couplet always sing upon his lips:

“May the blessing of the eternal King increase and exalt your life,

O David, beloved of God.”

[Col. 0313C] **Edited by Quercetanus, p. 15, Canisius, p. 6 (Frobenius, p. 85), now collated with the Vatican manuscript.** [Col. 0313D]

## LETTER CI

**TO THE LORD KING [Vatican manuscript: EMPEROR]. (Year 800.)** He gives thanks for the little book against Felix, which was read and sent back; he excuses some of its errors. Concerning Felix’s dispute with a Saracen, and that of a certain Jew with Master Peter. He sends certain specimens of diction. [Col. 0313C]

To the most pious and excellent lord David the king, Flaccus, wounded by the pen of charity, sends greetings.

We give thanks to Your Revered Piety because—

[Col. 0313D] **The little book . . . sent to you.** He means the seven books against Felix, which in the preceding letter he complained had not yet been secured by the seal of royal authority. **BASENAGE.**

—you had the little book sent to you, in accordance with the command of Your Orders, read aloud to the ears of your wisdom; and what you ordered to be marked as its errors, you sent back for correction. Although it could have been better amended by you, since another person’s judgment in any work very often has greater force than that of its author, nevertheless you did somewhat less than the full duty of charity would have required: you did not likewise mark the ideas expressed without learning or written in a non-Catholic manner. For, as the sequence of Your Most Sagacious Sheet made known to us, I formed some suspicion that not everything read there was to be approved, since you ordered defenders of that work to be sent to Your Excellence, even though no one can be a more suitable defender or corrector of the words of my littleness than you yourselves. For the authority of the one who commands ought to defend the diligence of the one who obeys.

As for the fact that the writing does not proceed as scholastically in its letters or divisions as the order and rule of grammatical art demands, this is often caused by the mind’s speed, [Col. 0314B] when the reader’s attention hastens ahead of the eyes’ task. Nor can I, fatigued by headache, examine what flies suddenly from the mouth of the one dictating. And whoever does not wish to have another’s negligence imputed to him should not impute it to another.

I therefore neither saw Felix’s disputation with the Saracen, nor was it found among us. Indeed, I had not even heard that man’s name before. Yet, when I inquired more carefully whether anyone among our people had heard of him [Alternative: “had heard of his reputation”], I was told that he was at—

[Col. 0313D] **Laidradus.** We have spoken of him several times elsewhere. It might have been found with Laidradus, bishop of Lyon.

Therefore, in haste, I sent our messenger to the aforesaid bishop, in case he might be able to find it there, so that it might be sent to Your Presence as quickly as possible. (Here the letter ends in the edition of Canisius.)

[Col. 0314C] {126} While—

[Col. 0313D] **I, a young man.** For this reason I cannot agree with the celebrated Mabillon, who in *Benedictine Annals*, book XXV, no. 22, and in the *Acts of the Saints*, fourth century, in the *Historical Eulogy of Alcuin*, chapter 1, no. 26, judges that this disputation took place during the Roman journey which Alcuin undertook in 781 to obtain the pallium for Eanbald, bishop of York. For it is scarcely credible that Alcuin would have called himself a young man when he was already at least forty years old. I suspect that Alcuin had gone to Rome long before, perhaps when he first came to the notice of King Charles. For, according to the anonymous author of Alcuin’s Life, before Charles received him at Pavia as he returned from Rome with the pallium, he “knew him, because long ago he had been sent to him by his master.” On that occasion, while still a young man, he could also have gone to Rome and stayed at Pavia.

—I, a young man, went to Rome and stayed for several days at Pavia, the royal city. A certain Jew, named Julius, had a disputation with Master Peter.

[Col. 0314D] **With Master Peter.** Namely, Peter of Pisa, whom Charlemagne, already an old man, heard teaching grammar, as Einhard testifies in the *Life of Charlemagne*, in Bouquet, *Collection of the Historians of Gaul*, vol. V, p. 99, no. 25.

And I heard that this same controversy had been written down in that city. This was the same Peter who became renowned while teaching grammar in your palace. Perhaps—

[Col. 0314D] **Your Homer.** This is Angilbert, about whom elsewhere. Your Homer must have heard something about it from the aforesaid teacher.

I sent to Your Excellence certain—

[Col. 0314D] **Specimens of diction.** I understand this to refer to the *Orthographical Opusculum*, which we present from the Salzburg manuscript in the second volume of the Works.

—specimens of diction, confirmed by examples or verses—

[Col. 0314D] **Of the venerable Father.** Undoubtedly of the Venerable Bede. See the preliminary notice to the same *Orthographical Opusculum*.

—confirmed by examples or verses of the venerable Father, and certain figures of arithmetical subtlety—

[Col. 0314D] **Figures of arithmetical subtlety.** Perhaps this refers to *On Arithmetical Subtleties for Sharpening the Young*, a little book which we shall also publish in the second volume, transcribed from the Reichenau manuscript.

—certain figures of arithmetical subtlety, for the sake of amusement, in the little sheet which you sent us blank, so that it might return clothed, though it had presented itself naked to our eyes. I considered it worthy of being honored by our letters, since it had come to us ennobled by your seal. And if the aforesaid specimens should have fewer examples [Vatican manuscript: “should possess fewer examples”]—

[Col. 0315D] {127} **Beseleel.** This is an adopted name, taken from Bezalel, highly skilled in architecture, whom Moses placed in charge of constructing the tabernacle of the covenant (Exod. XXXI, 36, 37, etc.). Here, however, Einhard, Charlemagne’s notary and the author of his Life, seems to be indicated; he was in charge of building affairs in the royal palace and therefore was also given the name Bezalel by Walafrid Strabo in a poem which he wrote about that same Einhard or Eginhard:

“No less reverence must be shown to the great Father Bezalel, the craftsman, who, prudent, first understands every work of the artisans.”

Your Bezalel—and indeed our familiar helper—will be able to add something from his fatherly verses; likewise, he can consider the principles of figures in the little book on arithmetic.

[Col. 0315D] **Distinctions of points.** Some call Alcuin the originator of points, commas, and other marks for distinguishing sentences in writing. From this passage it is clear that he attempted to revive those marks after they had long been neglected, and that for this reason he had to wage daily war against the rusticity of Tours. The distinctions or subdivisions of points, although they make a most beautiful ornament in sentences, have nevertheless almost disappeared from scribes because of their rusticity. But just as the glory of all wisdom and the ornament of salutary [Vatican manuscript: “secular”] learning are beginning to be renewed through the industry of Your Nobility, so it seems entirely fitting that the use of these marks should also be restored in the hands of writers. Thus I, although making little progress, fight daily against the rusticity of Tours. [Col. 0315B] May Your Authority educate the palace boys so that they may express most elegantly whatever your mind has dictated in the clearest eloquence, so that the sheet of the royal name, running everywhere, may display the nobility of royal wisdom.

May wisdom flourish with you in eternal gifts,

so that praise, honor, and power may remain yours.

My sheet, tell the beloved David as many holy greetings as you have letters, with my sweet love.

[Col. 0316D] **Edited by Quercetanus, p. 66, collated with two Salzburg manuscript codices (Frobenius, Letter 102).**

## LETTER CII. TO ARNO (Year 800)

He teaches that the world must be despised and that one must strive toward eternal things. He says that he has come to the dwelling of Saint Amandus to visit Arno, but regrets that he did not find him there. [Col. 0315C]

To my dearest brother, Aquila the bishop, Albinus sends greetings.

If a welcome messenger had come to me, I would have written to your affection more often, so that I might fill with letters what I could not with words, and so that, while the tongue was silent, the written letters might display the sweetness of charity. God granted this to the absent as a consolation: that they might speak through sheets of paper and convey necessary things into one another’s hearts, while the mind, enclosed in the heavy prison of the body, cannot unfold the swiftness of its nature; yet fraternal love sends written signs to one another. What do you think should be said about the glory of the saints, where no sluggishness of bodily burden obstructs the pious will, so that it may fulfill whatever pleases it? What is the world except misery, a fleeting shadow, and a deceptive pleasure? Let us hasten with the full concentration of our minds toward that rest which no sorrow disturbs. Let us ascend by the steps of charity to that city in which God alone reigns as king forever, in which complete blessedness flourishes and prevails without any misery. So that we may deserve to reach it, let us exhort one another with the same King’s assistance, and let the swifter course of charity draw along the slower one through diligent admonition. Correct my negligence with fraternal care, or raise me, lying prostrate, by the prayers of your holiness, so that, under the guidance of a brotherly right hand, the one who has until now rolled in the mire of the world may not grow weary on the way of truth.

[Col. 0316D] **“Coming, I was coming.”** Hansizius thinks that Arno, returning from Pannonia in 799, began planning to visit the monastery of Elnon-Saint-Amand and had previously informed Alcuin of this by letter; the distinguished scholar believes this may be gathered from the following letter. Alcuin, he says, meanwhile went to that monastery, and because he had not yet found Arno there, addressed him again in this letter. I, however, think that both letters belong to the year 800, and that this one was sent before Arno had departed from Salzburg, while the following one was sent when he had already arrived at the monastery of Elnon. See the notes to the following letter.

I was coming to the sweetest dwelling of our protector, Saint Amandus, seeking my beloved, so that I might refresh my soul with his sweetest conversation. But because the desired bird had not yet flown from the Juvavian nest [Salzburg manuscript: “Juuovian”], I sent him this inviting little sheet, so that he might recognize our prosperity or show us his presence [edition: “indicate it to us”]. A faithful friend is long sought, scarcely found, and difficult to preserve; his sweetness surpasses all the pleasures of the world. What are riches without friends? The miser seeks gold; and what is in gold except a vain appearance? Is not one loaf better for the hungry than a mountain of gold? Gold can benefit the giver, not the possessor. Therefore let us give away riches in the present, so that we may possess them in the future. For the poor man’s hand is Christ’s treasury. No keeper of riches is better than Christ. May divine grace assist you, dearest brother, in progressing forever.

{128}
