[Col. 0316D] **Edited by Mabillon, no. 3; Pez, no. 3 (Frobenius, no. 87). It now appears in a more accurate form from the Salzburg manuscript codices.**

## LETTER CIII. TO ARNO (Year 800)

From a letter received from Arno he learns of his return; but he learns nothing about the Christianization of the new people, nothing about Arno’s stay, and nothing about the hope of a mutual conversation, although he greatly desires it.

To the most holy bishop and sweetest son, Aquila, Albinus sends greetings.

I received the sweetest letter of Your Affection, and I read it joyfully because it acknowledged your prosperity and return, expecting what it would announce to me—

[Col. 0316D] **Concerning the Christianization of the new people.** I take this to refer to the people of the Huns, who in the previous year, 799, defected from the faith which they had promised the king, as the annalists testify. It was Arno’s responsibility to ensure that they did not at the same time abandon the faith promised to God; this matter also concerned Alcuin.

—concerning the Christianization of the new people and the progress of what had been accomplished there. But I found nothing about these matters. Nevertheless, God willing, when I see you—or compelled by necessity—you have [Pez: “will have”] to say what the little sheet kept silent about [Pez: “contains”]. I also asked how long Your Blessedness would have to remain in these regions. But I did not find this either. Therefore, being more uncertain about our meeting, what should I entrust to writing? Yet, if you are permitted to remain at the monastery until Easter, perhaps during Lent we shall visit you, sitting in the bed of your delights. I, however, am still uncertain about my journey because of the report flying from the mouths of many—

[Col. 0317D] **The king visiting the shrine of Saint Martin for the sake of prayer.** The king also came there in 800 after Easter. From this I infer that the present letter belongs to that year.

—the king visiting the shrine of Saint Martin for the sake of prayer, and necessity obliges me to await him [F.: “to expect him?”] and prepare lodging for my most beloved lord. And would that Aquila had flown among the other company of holy birds [as far as] the fishing grounds of the Loire!

The lord king also ordered me to come to the monastery of Gisela, his most holy sister—

[Col. 0317D] **Gale.** In French, Chelles, four miles from Paris on the Marne. See the letter to Gisela, Charlemagne’s sister.

—to Gale [Salzburg manuscript: “Cale”] to meet Angilbert; but I still do not know when [Pez: “how”] this is to happen. If this has been arranged before the king’s arrival, then you will come to meet us at—

[Col. 0317D] **To the cell of Saint Stephen at Coisacum.** In French, Choisy. See Letter 52 (now 65), to Arno.

—the cell of Saint Stephen at Coisacum, and [Pez: “or”] at—

[Col. 0317D] {129} **Noviantum Curtulum.** In the Benedictoburan manuscript the word *Noviantum* is absent; Hansizius, wishing to supply it by conjecture, substituted *Baralla*. But the Salzburg manuscript overturns that conjecture. *Noviantum*, or, as it is named in a charter of Charlemagne given in 770 for the monastery of Tours, *Novientus*, is a village near Paris on the Marne. See Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, col. 33; Martinière, *Grand Dictionnaire géographique*.

—Noviantum Curtulum, our place. But write back to me as quickly as possible [Salzburg manuscript: “as much as you can”] about the length of your stay with Saint Amandus, and what—

[Col. 0318D] **To Leidradus.** In the previous year he had brought Felix from the regions of Spain to Aachen, and was soon to depart there again; but at present he was staying at Tours with that recently converted Felix in order to restore his health. See Letter 92 (now 108).

—and what you wish to entrust to Leidradus [Salzburg manuscript: “Laidradus”]. He scarcely lives if he will not see our faces together. [Col. 0317C] For he has been very ill throughout the whole year, and with his soul dissolved [Salzburg manuscript: “with his soul’s counsel”] he desires to deliberate with us. Many good things have taken place in those regions, glory to God! But he is uncertain whether it is better to labor in the ministry of preaching or to lead a quiet life. But, God permitting, we shall hear these matters more certainly from him himself. I have also instructed, by letter and often by word of mouth, the brothers—

[Col. 0318D] **The brothers of Saint Servatius.** This monastery is situated at Maastricht on the Meuse; formerly it belonged to monks, but now to canons. Mabillon.

—of Saint Servatius to serve Your Authority, just as they serve me.

I would write more to you about the urgency of holy preaching and about the uprightness of conduct among the pagans, because the dignity of the preachers’ way of life usually instructs them, just as does the truth of their words [Alternative: “in preaching”]. [Col. 0318A] But because I hope, by God’s mercy, to see you soon, I thought it better to discuss these matters in conversation than to make them known in writing. Nor does your mind possess a greater ardor for our conversation than mine. Therefore let us ask God’s clemency to grant, in his mercy and in our prosperity, that we may soon see one another face to face. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ cause you to progress in every goodness, dearest son [Mabillon manuscript: “most reverend father”!]. [Amen.]

[Col. 0318D] {130} **Edited by Mabillon, no. 17 (Frobenius, Letter 88). What was omitted in Mabillon’s edition is supplied here from the Salzburg and Saint Emmeram manuscript codices. It is uncertain to what year this letter should be assigned, for Alcuin often entertained the hope and desire of enjoying Arno’s presence. I have appended it to the preceding letter, with which it also agrees. Nevertheless, it may be inferred from the following letter that Arno satisfied his desire before departing from Gaul.**

## LETTER CIV. TO ARNO (Year uncertain)

He is grieved because Arno’s presence, long awaited in vain, did not come; but he mitigates his grief with sighs for the heavenly homeland. He gladly receives the gifts sent to him. [Col. 0318B]

To the Father of my sweetest affection [to Aquila the bishop], the Swan from overseas, borne on the wings of holy charity, sends perpetual greeting.

I looked, I hoped, I desired—and behold! The one I looked for did not come; the one I hoped for I did not see; the one I desired I did not receive. My expectation has been frustrated; my hope has been emptied. And if only presence had replaced hope! Then there would now be complete joy. But, alas, in place of expected gladness, unexpected sadness has stolen in. My misfortune obstructed your way of coming and took from me the happiness of rejoicing. What will a mind wounded by love do now? Is there any consolation capable of refreshing even slightly so great a wound? [Col. 0318C] Or do you utterly reject hope from yourself as a false comforter? Or, amid the darkness of your misery, do you take it up again like a spark of some burning flame? Behold, the flame of charity sets the whole breast aflame; if hope joins it as a companion, it burns happily, provided that what it desires truly comes to pass. Hope is good in absence, but love in presence is better. For our hope, like an anchor, draws us toward the solidity of the heavenly homeland (Hebr. VI, 18–19); but perfect happiness will come when the vision of love is complete, and God will be seen in his glory, who is now loved in our hearts (I Cor. XIII, 12). But let the pilgrimage of this exile be endured patiently until the presence of the desired and most blessed homeland arrives. We need patience (Hebr. X, 36), whether in awaiting hoped-for blessedness or in the absence of dearest friends. Let us always possess today in charity, but in hope the desire for tomorrow, so that what is loved today may come.

Behold, my mind is tossed by various thoughts, hoping that you, as an adviser, will come like a harbor of firm stability. But, as I see, it is carried farther from the desired quiet by the waves, tossed upon the open sea, and ignorant of which harbor it will reach. Nevertheless, through the constant prayers of Your Holiness, may you deign, by God’s granting of grace, to lead your doubting friend amid the disputes of his thoughts toward firm counsel of salvation. Everywhere there is ready the merciful hearer of holy prayers, who [Col. 0319B] is accustomed both to hear the prayers of brotherly love and to assist those who hope in him through the spirit of consolation (Ps. XVII, 31). Let us raise our hope toward his sweetest clemency, while remaining without doubt concerning his assistance, for he enlightens every person who comes into this world (John I, 9). Let us implore him incessantly with the whole intention of our heart and the whole affection of our mind, so that he may enlighten the eyes within us, lest we ever fall asleep in the death of ignorance (Ps. XII, 4).

[I received the gifts of Your Affection with as joyful a spirit as I recognized that you sent them with complete charity. But as happily as my mind rejoices in the gifts, so sadly it groans over the absence of Your Blessedness. But what of these things? Let charity live in Christ! Let him who is absent in body be present in spirit, [Col. 0319C] until, God granting it, blessed presence arrives, which can never come to an end. May the Lord God, in his mercy, guard you everywhere as you progress in his will, dearest brother!]

[Col. 0319D] **Edited by Mabillon, no. 23; supplemented from the Salzburg manuscript (Frobenius, Letter 89).**

## LETTER CV. TO ARNO THE ARCHBISHOP (Year 800)

He rejoices in Arno’s visit but grieves at the brevity of his presence; he raises his desire toward ever-enduring joy. He urges him to give pious exhortations to the brothers and to all the sheep.

To Aquila the archbishop, deservedly desired and loved, the humble Levite Alcuin sends greetings.

Much sweetness came to me—

[Col. 0319D] **From the visit.** The distinguished Hansizius thinks that this visit of Arno to Alcuin took place in the year 800, when Arno had returned from Rome to the king and had made a journey to the monastery of Elnon ( *Germania Sacra*, vol. II, under Arno, no. 33). We follow his conjecture here.

—from the visit of Your Revered Affection. Although you were laboring, I was nevertheless refreshed by the consolation of your piety, so that, according to the response of blessed Benedict—

[Col. 0319D] **From the Life of Saint Benedict, in Saint Gregory the Great, Book II of the *Dialogues*.**

—I seemed to have Easter in the arrival of your affection. [Col. 0320A] But I mourned the brief duration of your long-desired presence; and as joyful as I was at the sight of your face, so deeply was I tormented by your departure. But what of these things? Such is the joy of this world, admonishing us to strive toward the future joy [Mabillon: “future rejoicing”], which will never have an end; once its sweetness has been tasted, it never ceases to be present, and toward it we must hasten with the whole eagerness of our mind. What is that joy like which will have no disturbance and will never fear an end? It must now be possessed in hope; after the end of this life it must be possessed forever. How blessed is that love among brothers which lives without end and increases without weariness.

Holy Father, exhort our common sons—

[Col. 0320B] **Adhelricus . . . Adalbertus . . . Guntarius.** Adhelricus is perhaps Aldricus, later abbot of Ferrières, who, even after Arno’s death, was sent by Emperor Louis in 822 to establish regular discipline in the monastery of Elnon (Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXIX, no. 30). Adalbertus was likewise abbot of Ferrières; the author of Alcuin’s Life testifies that he was a disciple of Alcuin and Sigulfus (Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints*, Benedictine fourth century, part I, p. 167). Here he is expressly called “Magus,” so that there can no longer be doubt that the same name in Letters 76 and 77 (now 91 and 92) refers to this Adalbert. I have not determined who Guntarius, Arno’s attendant, was.

—Adhelricus the Levite, Adalbertus Magus, and Guntarius, attendant of Your Piety—to prepare themselves worthy of this charity. Persuade them to obey paternal commands, to be truly brothers in the Lord and sons of the eternal Father, coheirs with Christ God (Rom. VIII, 17). These things are not to be urged by your pastoral concern only upon them, but are to be impressed upon all the sheep of the flock entrusted to you: that they remain in holy charity and chastity. The world lies in wickedness (I John V, 19), and many turn away from the way of truth and the precepts of faith, serving the world more than God, without considering that the eye of the divine majesty watches over them everywhere, and that he will repay each according to his works (Matt. XVI, 27). Therefore, most illustrious preacher of the word of God, insist in season and out of season (II Tim. IV, 2), because many resist sound doctrine, loving themselves and not seeking eternal things. From among them, with divine assistance, rescue as many as you can from the flames of everlasting destruction and gather them into the folds of Christ’s sheep, so that through their salvation your glory may be increased on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

May divine paternity guide Your Fatherhood and cause you to progress in the house of God until the perfect day, dearest Father.

{131}

[Col. 0320D] {132} **Edited by Quercetanus, no. 21, from a manuscript (Frobenius, no. 90).**

## LETTER CVI. TO THE LORD KING (Year 800)

**An epitaph.**

[Col. 0320D] **For Liodgarda.** Or Liutgard, the wife of Charlemagne, who, at Tours, where she had come with the emperor for the sake of prayer, was seized by illness and died on the day before the Nones of June in the year 800 (from the Loiselian Annals and others).

For Liodgarda, a noble woman.

To the most pious and peaceful lord king and most excellent [Col. 0320D] triumphant victor, glory and salvation of eternal blessedness.

Lord Jesus, our hope, our salvation, our consolation, who with your most merciful voice commanded all who groan under the burden of any labor, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI, 28). What is more delightful than this promise? What is more blessed than this hope? Let every grieving soul and every contrite heart come to him, pouring out tears in the sight of his mercy; let it not hide its wounds from the physician who says: “I kill and I make alive; I strike, and I heal” (Deut. XXXII, 39). He scourges in wondrous ways so as to educate his children, for whose salvation he did not spare his only Son. Who is against us if God is for us (Rom. VIII, 32, 31)? Who can sadden us if God makes us glad? I do not want God to say to you: “O soul, why do you groan? Why do you lament my judgments? I gave; I have taken away” (Job I, 21). What do you have apart from me (I Cor. IV, 7)? Why does what pleases me displease you? Everything you have is my gift, not your own possession. Prepare yourself so that you may be a participant in my blessedness. For your sake I descended and suffered what you have read in my writings, so that I might prepare a dwelling for you in my Father’s house. Do not delay, my sister, my bride; arise, hasten, and come to the banquets of my glory (Song II, 10). Great, blessed, incomparable are the things I have prepared for you. And although they are great, do not be anxious or doubt their price. Your kingdom is worth as much as you are. Give yourself, and you will have it. The eternal King desires your beauty. Let there be no wrinkle or stain in you (Eph. V, 27). If any dust from your earthly dwelling has clung to you, wash it away with tears, so that the one who desires you may find you beautiful, lovely, and worthy of desire. Do not grieve over another’s happiness, for it has ended its thorny labors and flown to him who made it. Such is the condition of our frailty after the sentence of the first condemnation: we are born in order to die; we die in order to live. Surely the entrance into life is happier than death? It is said that someone replied, when he was being consoled over the death of his son: “I knew that I had begotten a mortal.” Why do you grieve over what we cannot avoid? Often grief will be healed by time, though reason cannot heal it. Let us send gifts of charity after our dear ones. Let us offer the gift of our salvation for them. Let us show mercy to the miserable, so that God may show mercy to them. What we do for them in faith benefits us also.

[Col. 0321D] Lord God, gentle and merciful Jesus, have mercy on the one whom you have taken from us. Hear us through the medicine of our wounds [perhaps: “your wounds”], which hung upon the wood and sits at your right hand interceding for us (Rom. VIII, 34). I know your mercy, for you desire all people to be saved (I Tim. II, 4). Forgive her debts (Matt. VI, 12), whatever she contracted after the water of salvation. Forgive, Lord; forgive, we beseech you. Do not enter into judgment with her. Let mercy triumph over judgment (James II, 13). For your utterances are true, in which you promised mercy to the merciful (Matt. V, 7)—and you gave them the means to become such. You have mercy on whom you have mercy; have mercy, Lord, on your creature, so that your creature may praise you and sing your mercies forever. And may the soul that will survive beyond this life always say: “I will praise my God in my life; I will sing to my God as long as I am” (Ps. CXLV, 1).

May she always live happily forever, I pray;

may my dear daughter, I ask, be dear to God.

[Col. 0321D] **Edited by Quercetanus, no. 22, from a manuscript (Frobenius, no. 91).**

## LETTER CVII. TO THE LORD KING

**A consolation for the death of Liutgard.**

To the desirable and truly most blessed David the king, Flaccus Albinus sends greetings.

I know that Your Glorious Power does not rule Jerusalem, destined to perish in the fires of the Chaldeans, but governs and directs the city of perpetual peace, built by the precious blood of Christ [Col. 0322B], whose living stones are gathered by the cement of charity, and whose heavenly building rises in height with walls formed from the various gems of the virtues. Of this the Psalmist says: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the dwellings of Jacob” (Ps. LXXXVI, 2). And elsewhere: “Mount Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great king” (Ps. XLVII, 3). Therefore I, a very small portion of this city, established under the shelter of Your Piety, strive, in dutiful service, to send little letters frequently for the joy of your mind: an official gift of our devotion, not necessary to your abundance; wishing, through the kindness of your consolation, to heal the grief of your wounded spirit, because I have often experienced that the familiar gentleness of Your Highness sympathizes with the sufferings of the humble. For the Lord himself, the source of all consolation and salvation, wept with those who wept for the friend whom he came to raise (John XI, 33, 35), sharing the grief of others according to human feeling rather than mourning the death of his friend—especially since he knew beforehand that he would restore him to life that same hour. The children of Israel mourned Moses, but under the Law, not under the Gospel (Deut. XXXIV, 8). Therefore Jesus, because of the sacramental significance of his name, is not read to have followed the people’s tears, but rather appears as one who would live again after death. At the beginning of Judges, in accordance with the historical order, the mourning of the wise is represented as lasting one day, but that of the wicked throughout all the days of his life. In the wise person, what is mourned is a separation from human intimacy, not destruction. In the wicked, everlasting destruction must be accompanied by perpetual mourning. Yet the father lives on in the son, the teacher in the disciple, and the friend in the friend, if the dignity of conduct and the nobility of wisdom remain in those who come after them.

What if, in the misery of my human condition, my son should die before his father in the flower of youth? “The just man is taken away, lest wickedness should alter his heart” (Wis. 4:11). “The judgments of the Lord are a great deep” (Ps. 35:7). Nothing will happen in the world without cause, nor will a single sparrow fall into the fowler’s snare without our Father who is in heaven; not a hair from the head perishes (Matt. 10:29; Acts 27:34). For we ought not to grieve when one of our dear ones departs from pilgrimage to the homeland, from the dying to the living, from exile to the kingdom. Let the words of truth be our consolation: “He who believes in me, even if he has died, will live. And everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” (John 11:25–26). Therefore let us know that our dear ones, dying in works of charity, live for God and die to the world. By works of mercy they say daily with the Apostle to Christ: “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). Happier is the one who leaves his friends surviving him than the one who will survive his friends. The death of a good man is a migration to a better life; it is not to be mourned but congratulated (John 5:24).

Let us rejoice in the mercies of our Redeemer. Before Christ’s coming, Abraham was in the underworld; after Christ’s Passion, the thief was in paradise. By Christ’s death, death itself died; the fiery sword guarding paradise was extinguished by Christ’s blood. And blessed Peter, an earthly man, opens the gates that the heavenly Cherub had closed; and from a fisherman’s net he suddenly transferred his hand to the keys of the kingdom of heaven. In the Cherubim there is a multitude of knowledge, but in Christ a multitude of mercy. Formerly God was known only in Judaea, but now among all nations there is one voice: Christ, who made us from slaves into friends and transformed us from fugitives into sons. He assumed the nature of our mortality into the glory of his divinity. In this let the human race rejoice, knowing that the nature of our weakness has been raised above the angelic choirs and sits in the heavens at the majesty of the Father’s glory. What condition of human mortality [the passage is corrupt: *Quae conditio mortalitatis timens humanae*] ought to disturb you after such great glory of your nature? Your equality [with the heavenly beings] is utterly certain; only clothe yourself in the wings of charity’s covering, so that you may fly to where Christ ascended. Do not be distressed by the death of your dear ones, but rejoice with their joy.

Christ gave himself over to death for you. Why do your tears oppose Christ, who snatches your dear ones from death to life, from labor to rest? The day of a good man’s departure is happier than the day of his birth. The former is the beginning of rest, the latter of labor; the former the entrance into joy, the latter into sorrow. We are born in order to die; we die in order to live better. This life is a road for those traveling to their homeland. If it is rough, if it is narrow, it must be walked courageously. If it is level, if it is prosperous, it must be traversed cautiously, because it has many ambushers. The providence of God knows, therefore, for whom a long journey along this road is beneficial and for whom it is best to bring the labors of this pilgrimage quickly to an end. Let God’s judgments please us. “The Lord is just, and his judgments are right” (Ps. 118:137). That mind pleases God most which finds all God’s pleasing things pleasing. Let us praise, love, and pray that his will may always be done in us—his will, to which good things always please—and that we can possess and accomplish nothing good except through him. If what we have is good and lovable, he has granted it to us. Let us give thanks to him; with the whole attention of our mind let us offer him a sacrifice of praise, in which he promised us eternal salvation through his Prophet, saying: “The sacrifice of praise has honored me; there is the way by which I will show the salvation of God” (Ps. 49:23). This is angelic joy, the gladness of the saints, our consolation. For heavenly Jerusalem, which is built from living stones, does nothing else in its homeland, as the Psalmist speaks and sighs in our voice: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house” (Ps. 83:5). And as though someone had asked what that blessedness was—to dwell in the house of the Lord—he answered: “For ever and ever they will praise you.” This praise will be without weariness and without failure; without end it becomes sweet in the hearts and mouths of those who sing. Whenever we perform it on earth, we imitate the angelic life. This sweetness drives all the world’s sadnesses from the soul and mitigates all grief. And the more abundantly someone enjoys God’s gifts, the more he should acknowledge himself a debtor to the mediator of all the good things he possesses.

If, then, it seems right for a person to give thanks for any benefit or service, how much more ought thanksgiving to be offered to God? He gave everything that appears good in this world, and he will give all the good things that can be desired or possessed in the world to come, where God himself will be all in all, who now distributes to each according to the measure of his goodness (Eph. 4:7). Then there will be every goodness, every blessedness, and complete sufficiency in all. May God, Jesus, bring you after the labors of this life to the happiness of that supreme blessedness and unfailing glory, most longed-for lord and most worthy of every honor.

May Christ grant you true riches, beloved David,

Together with the saints in the citadel of heaven.

{134}

[Col. 0323D] Edited by Mabillon, p. 19, where it is more than half mutilated and otherwise incomplete. (Froben, p. 92.) Here we give it complete from the Salzburg manuscript, from which the material enclosed in brackets was copied. It is now clear from this that it was written neither to Richbod, bishop of Trier, as the author of the *Gallia Litteraria*, after Mabillon, asserted in vol. IV, p. 329, nor to Paulinus of Aquileia, as the distinguished Madrisius wished on p. 251, but to Aquila or Arno.

## LETTER CVIII. TO ARNO. (A.D. 800)

He urges him to defend Pope Leo against his adversaries. He complains that the Huns have revolted from subjection and that pagan ships are ravaging the shores of Aquitaine. He relates that he has founded a new monastic community. He sends greetings to Bishops Alimo, Remedius, and Paulinus. He reports certain matters concerning Elipandus and Felix.

[Col. 0324D] To the most blessed lord and, deservedly, bishop [Aquila], worthy to be embraced by the wings of perpetual charity, the humble deacon [Alcuin] sends greetings.

Rejoicing at the sweetest reading of your letters and at the most delightful message of your prosperity—as though some refreshment had come to me amid the heat of fevers, and, scorched by the flames of the dog days, I had been revived by the dew of your greeting—I rose wholly strengthened in hope when I heard what I had always desired and read in your letters what I had always longed for: the safety of apostolic authority and the steadfastness of holy religion in him whom—

[Col. 0325C] A confessor of Christ. Clearly, Pope Leo III, as the context of the letter itself demonstrates. He is called a confessor because he suffered persecution and torments for Christ, although afterward he died a peaceful death. “Confession,” says Saint Cyprian in the book *On the Simplicity of Prelates*, “is the beginning of glory, not the crown’s reward; it does not complete praise but initiates dignity.” I think it right for all the churches of Christ to name and venerate him as a confessor of Christ. I would desire his presence above that of all other men of this life, if the health of my little body allowed me to carry this out. [I had long desired this with the greatest longing of my soul, to such an extent that, I confess, I appealed to your faith: if such progress of mine could have been made under his authority for the Churches of Christ as my devotion desired, I would have resolved to stand before his presence above all the pleasures and honors of the world; if I had been granted leave to calm the ardor of his spirit, and to exhort, under the authority of his holy name, through the various regions, peoples, parishes, cities, and provinces of the world; to explain the principles of the Catholic faith to many persons; and, according to the custom of the holy Fathers, to impose religious admonition through circulating little letters. But, as I see, because my sins prevent this, it has not yet been possible, on account of the weakness of my little body, weighed down by many small burdens of trouble. Moreover, he himself has not commanded me anything about this, although, according to the dignity of the world, it ought especially to have been done at his command; through others, however, he firmly commanded me this, as though he wished it to be done.]

[Col. 0325D] He himself, however, said nothing about it. From this passage I gather that Alcuin had not yet received the king’s letter, in which, while writing to him, he reproached him “for preferring the smoke-blackened roofs of Tours to the gilded arches of Rome.” He himself, however, said nothing about it.

I also understand that there are many rivals of that aforementioned apostolic lord who seek to depose him by crafty insinuation,

[Col. 0325D] These statements agree with what Anastasius the Librarian reports in his *Life of Leo III*, in these words: “While the most serene king himself had held him [Leo] in great honor for some time, these aforementioned wicked men plotted . . . to bring false charges against the most holy pontiff, and afterward to send them to the aforementioned king—charges which they could in no way prove; for through their treacheries and iniquities they uttered such things, desiring to humble the holy Church, which ought not even to have been spoken.” seeking to charge him with adultery or perjury, and then [perhaps: so] arranging that he should purge himself of these crimes by the solemnity of a most serious oath; thus secretly persuading him to resign the pontificate without an oath and to lead a quiet life in some monastery. This must absolutely not be done, nor should he himself consent to bind himself by any oath or surrender his see. I would answer on his behalf if I had stood at his side: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at him” (John 8:7).

I remember reading once, if I recall correctly,

[Col. 0325D] In the canons of blessed Silvester. I think, in the Roman Synod under Pope Silvester, although modern critics attribute his decree to the spurious works introduced by Isidore Mercator. in the canons of blessed Silvester, that a pontiff must be accused and brought to judgment by no fewer than seventy-two witnesses, [Col. 0326A] and that their way of life must be such that they could stand against such authority. Moreover, in other canons I read

[Col. 0326C] “The Apostolic See . . . is not to be judged.” Undoubtedly from the Synod of Sinuessa, convened in the case of Pope Marcellinus in the year 303. Alcuin’s counsel, following the archbishops and bishops—including Arno—declared: [Col. 0326D] “We do not dare to judge the Apostolic See, which is the head of all the Churches of God. For by it and by its vicar we are all judged; but it is judged by no one, just as was the ancient custom, etc.” Anastasius, cited above. On these and similar canons, consult Peter de Marca, *Concordia Sacerdotii*, book I, chapter 11, and others. that the Apostolic See has judicial authority but is not itself to be judged. I have considered consigning all this, and much more, to him in my letters because of his Catholic charity. Who can be a pastor in the Church of Christ and remain free from danger if he who is the head of Christ’s Churches is cast down by evildoers? He will stand or fall for his own Lord. But he will stand, for “the Lord is able to make him stand” (Rom. 14:4).

But you, dearest son, son of my prayers, [son of the Church of Christ, nurtured in his sheepfold among his holy sheep, to whom the Shepherd of all shepherds said three times, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:15–17)], labor for the safety of your head, for the preservation of the supreme shepherd, [Col. 0326B] for the authority of the holy see, and for the integrity of the Catholic faith, lest the Shepherd of shepherds be exposed to the wolves’ bites. I, for my part, accompany the devotion of your excellent piety with tears, pursue it with prayers, and support it with the aid of my letters. Be cautious about whom you entrust with your counsels; prudent in your replies; truthful in your judgments; careful to discern what is appropriate for each person; and {135} do not forget the father in age, the son in merits,

[Col. 0326D] the brother in charity. See Letter 76 (now 91). the brother in charity. Let it come—indeed, let the day come, when he who has ordered all days is pleased to permit the desired embraces of father and son to unite, and for them to exhort one another in mutual conversations [the same: consolations].

[Third cause: you

[Col. 0326D] You were. Perhaps we should read “you had been”; “of my journey,” to which he had said above that he had been called or invited. you were the cause of my journey. The first was the Churches of Christ; the second was the lord king, because in [Col. 0326C] tears

[Col. 0326D] I left him in tears. Clearly the king, whom he had come to Tours this year, 800, to venerate Saint Martin, and who was departing. I left him in tears, wishing to inscribe the perpetual memory of his joy upon my soul; the third was to see the sweetest face of your charity. But until now I have been prevented from bringing about what I greatly desired. It will therefore happen through your holy prayers, when he is pleased who is without whom nothing good can be done.]

[Col. 0326D] The earlier letter. This letter of Arno to Alcuin, containing those false charges brought against Pope Leo III, was handed over to the fire by Alcuin himself, lest a scandal might arise from it among the uninformed, as the context itself relates. The earlier letter that reached us under your name, containing certain complaints about the character of the apostolic lord and about your danger before him on account of the Romans, was brought to me, as I believe, by your cleric named Baldricus. He brought me a cape sewn in the Roman fashion, a linen garment, and a woolen one. But because I did not want the letter to fall into someone else’s hands, only Candidus read it through with me, and so it was committed to the fire, lest some scandal might arise through the negligence of those who kept my little letters [perhaps: of the person who kept them].

[Col. 0327D] The destruction of the Huns. They had revolted in the preceding year, as the annals report. The destruction of the Huns, as you said, is nevertheless our negligence: we have been laboring among the accursed race of the Saxons, despised by God up to this point, and have neglected those whom, as it seemed, we could have held in greater favor with God and glory among men. I do not dare to impose upon you alone so much labor on my account through the prayers and tears that I often shed because of your absence. Nevertheless, it is not an empty journey to come for the protection of Saint Martin and to commend your life to his holy prayers.

[Col. 0327D] Pagan ships. I think these were the Normans, who, as Einhard testifies in his *Life of Charlemagne*, “were devastating the Gallic and German shores with continual ravaging. Therefore Charles, by placing stations and patrols at all the ports and mouths of rivers where ships seemed able to enter, prevented the enemy from coming out by such fortification. He also prepared a fleet for the Norman war, etc.” The annals refer this to March of the year 800. The pagan ships, as you have heard, did much harm through the islands of the Ocean in the parts of Aquitaine. Some of them nevertheless perished, and about one hundred and five of those raiders were killed on the shore. This incursion is a great chastisement, unknown in earlier times to the Christian people, because perhaps the servants of God do not keep the vows that they are accustomed to make. Therefore, dearest son and deservedly revered brother, exhort your brothers to live according to the rule and to preserve their original devotion firmly, as Scripture says: “Vow and pay your vows to the Lord your God” (Ps. 75:12). Again: “It is better not to vow than not to fulfill one’s vows” (Eccl. 5:4).]

[Col. 0327D] For you are close to the borders of the pagans. The letter was therefore given to Arno while he was staying at Elnon, not at Salzburg; for no danger from the Normans ravaging the Gallic and German shores could threaten him there. See Hansiz, vol. II of *Germania Sacra*, p. 113, no. 33. For [Col. 0327C] you are close to the borders of the pagans. May our Lord God be your salvation, protection, and mercy, he who says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). There is great upheaval in the world, and unbelief in the minds of many, and negligence in the name of monks. They want to be called [something] and not to do it, as Scripture says: “The sluggard desires, and does not desire” (Prov. 13:4). That is, he wants to be blessed but does not want to labor in order to become blessed. [

[Col. 0327D] I have recently founded a certain community. Clearly at Cormaric; for this year, on the Nones of June, Alcuin obtained letters from Charles, who was staying at Tours, allowing him to establish monks there. See those letters in vol. II of the Appendix. I have recently founded a certain community, about eight miles from the monastery of Saint Martin, for monastic life and regular religion, initially from brothers from Gothia, where Benedict established a regular way of life. But now, God willing, some are coming and devoting themselves to the holy life.] One must not limp in God’s service but walk along the royal road, so that, with divine grace assisting, one may eventually reach the desired shore. [Whatever I hear about your canonical way of life, I confess that it pleases me greatly. Let this also be added to the reward of your diligence: that the brothers under your authority may live according to the holiness of the regular life. I have heard nothing else, nor should I say less than what I recognize to be advancing through fraternal charity.] To the people also, as I have often begged, preach the word of God insistently (2 Tim. 4:2), lest any soul be dependent upon your judgment or be demanded from you. Show them the way of salvation, strengthening some in private conversation and others by public preaching. Give exhortations to each according to the manner appropriate to his condition or person: [Col. 0328B] to the authorities and judges, justice and mercy; to the younger, obedience; to the elders, humility and faith; to all, fairness, love of God and neighbor, bodily chastity, kindness, and piety in almsgiving, so that, with the manifold fruit of your labor, you may deserve to reach the seat of eternal blessedness through the mercy of him who says: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). I also beg you, according to my hope and your faith, to remember me with your holy brothers in continual intercession, so that, when the course of our contest is nearly complete, I may deserve to receive forgiveness of my sins and some share of blessedness among the citizens of the heavenly dwelling. [Col. 0328C] [I would write more according to the desire of our heart, if this messenger, having been sent by your command, did not have to return quickly; nevertheless, from these very few letters you will be able to recognize the ardor of our charity toward you.] May divine grace accompany you everywhere, lord father and dearest friend.

[Col. 0328D] In the manuscript of Saint Emmeram the text continues thus: “And if an opportunity arises for you to see our friend, greet him a thousand thousand times. The little book, etc., as inside . . .”

[I beg your humility, in my official capacity, to greet the dearest father,

[Col. 0328D] Bishop Aelim. He is undoubtedly Alimus, bishop of Säben or Brixen. See Letter 91. Bishop Aelim, together with the other brothers and fellow priests of your holiness. Likewise greet Remedius, our most dear and faithful friend, the decurion [from the curia].] And if an opportunity arises for you [

[Col. 0328D] Patriarch Paulinus of Aquileia. It is now clear that Alcuin is speaking here of Paulinus’s books against Felix of Urgel. Mabillon, conjecturally, since the manuscript he used did not contain the name Paulinus, attributed the little book mentioned here to Richbod, bishop of Trier. But that otherwise extremely careful man did not see this complete letter; from the mutilated letter the error was easy. The author of the *History of the Literature of France*, vol. IV, p. 329, must likewise be corrected. Patriarch Paulinus] to see him, greet him a thousand thousand times. I was reading the little book of the Catholic faith that he sent to the lord king, and it pleased me greatly in its eloquence, in the flowers of its diction, in its exposition of the faith, and in the authority of its testimonies, so that I thought nothing needed to be added to these matters concerning the questions recently debated between us and the party of Felix. The Church and the Christian people are fortunate as long as they have [the lord king, or] such a defender of the Catholic faith. [But something still remains to be done. For a certain Elipandus of the city of Toledo, a bishop in name but not in dignity, persists in the condemned heresy despite synodal authority and apostolic censure. Yet let your affection know that our son

[Col. 0329D] Laidradus. The distinguished Madrisius maintains in his work on Saint Paulinus, p. 222, nos. 62 and 65, that Laidradus did not return to Spain after the year 799, when Felix had already been converted. But he is mistaken, as is clear from this passage, and we shall demonstrate further in our dissertation on the Felician heresy. Laidradus, your brother bishop, has, by God’s gift, achieved and daily continues to achieve great progress in those regions. As religious and truthful men from those regions told me, as many as twenty thousand—bishops, priests, monks, the people, men and women—have been converted, lamenting their former error and rejoicing, giving thanks to God daily in their recognition of the truth and steadfastness in the Catholic faith. Concerning Felix himself you have already heard through our letters, or rather through the report of others, what happened, and how he was recently at Saint Martin with the aforementioned

[Col. 0329D] Our son, namely Laidradus. son of ours; and he loves me greatly, and all the hatred he had held against me has been changed into the sweetness of charity.] That you asked me, through the sequence of my letters, to address your holiness frequently: God, who witnesses my heart, knows how greatly I desire this, so that it may happen as often as the time and the messenger permit. I wish you to have me present in my letters, so that nothing may be lacking to us in the communion of charity except the presence of our eyes. But [Col. 0329C] much greater and better than this is the perpetual presence of holy charity in Christ Jesus our Lord.

[Col. 0329D] Quercetan edition, p. 13; Canisius, p. 7. Now corrected in places from the Vatican Royal Manuscript 69. (In Froben, p. 93.)

## LETTER CIX. TO THE LORD KING. (A.D. 800, IN AUGUST)

He replies to Charles’s letter announcing victory over the enemies and the miraculous recovery of Pope Leo. He declines to undertake the journey to Rome.

To the most beloved lord and most worthy of every honor, King David, Flaccus, a veteran soldier, sends perpetual salvation in Christ.

We received the letters reporting your prosperity and our consolation with great love and fitting favor, praising the clemency of almighty God, who has caused you and your faithful followers to flourish in prosperous success, [Col. 0329D] and has subjected the enemies of his name to your power—

[Col. 0329D] He has subjected them beneath his feet. In the preceding year, 799, Charles completed the Hunnic war through his son Pippin and the provincial prefects. According to Einhard in his *Life of Charlemagne*, he subdued the Britons on this side of the Channel and successfully conducted affairs against the Saracens, as related by the annals commonly attributed to Einhard, Charlemagne’s own notary. He has subjected them beneath his feet. May God do this, and add this also (1 Kings 3:17), so that by the triumph of your terror he may everywhere subject hostile nations [Col. 0330A] and, by the sweetest yoke of his love, subject fierce hearts to the Christian faith, so that God alone and our Lord Jesus Christ may be believed in, worshiped, and loved. Let your most illustrious [power and most holy] will labor with every effort for this: that Christ’s name may be glorified and his divine power become known throughout many kingdoms of the earth through the triumphs of your courage, so that not only the greatness of your power may show you to be a king, but also your zeal in sowing the word of God may make you a preacher in praise of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore divine grace has wonderfully enriched you with these two gifts: the rule of earthly felicity and the breadth of spiritual wisdom, so that you may advance in both until you reach the happiness of eternal blessedness. Spare [your] Christian people [Col. 0330B] and defend the Churches of Christ, so that the blessing of the heavenly King may make you strong against the pagans. One of the ancient poets is read to have said, when, if I remember correctly, he was singing of the praise of the emperors of the Roman realm, what they ought to be:

> To spare the subjected and to subdue the proud.

Blessed Augustine explained this verse with much praise in his book *The City of God*, although we ought to attend more to the evangelical precepts than to Virgil’s verses. For Truth itself says: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7). And elsewhere: “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36).

[Col. 0330C] As for what your proven will, in Christ, of kindness toward the apostolic shepherd has taken care to communicate to us—

[Col. 0330D] Miraculous recovery. Some doubt whether Pope Leo was entirely deprived of his eyes and tongue by the assassins. But the writers of that period plainly agree that he recovered the use of his eyes and tongue, together with good health, not without a miracle. See Anastasius the Librarian, *Life of Leo*; the *Lorsch Annals*; the Saxon Poet; Theodulf of Orléans, book III, poem 6, to Charlemagne; and others. it is fitting that all the Christian people rejoice in this clemency of divine protection and praise the name of our holy [Cod. Vat.: the holy] God, who never abandons those who hope in him, who restrained impious hands from the wicked outcome of their will—those who, with blinded minds, wished to extinguish his light and, by their own impious counsel, deprive themselves of their own head. Whatever should be done concerning them, your most prudent wisdom must consider; it knows best what is appropriate for each person and what ought to be repaid to each by deed, and how that pious shepherd, freed by divine protection from the hands of his enemies, may safely serve God Christ in his own see.

[Col. 0330D] As for the fact that your letters of kindness charge Flaccus with the fault of silence, whom [perhaps: him] the fervor—

[Col. 0330D] The month of August. Charles “arriving at Mainz at the beginning of August, announced a journey into Italy,” says the Loiselian annalist under the year 800; therefore he received that letter from Alcuin in the same month of that year. Pagi, under this year, no. 8. of August makes sluggish, not ineffectual in will, concerning our boys whom you command to go to Rome on their father’s feet, I should like to know when, where, and with whom they ought to meet your blessedness. Concerning them we find written in the letter of your excellence: “Those who, while you are at rest, can undertake your duties in your place.” I admit that, when you command and assist me, they can undertake the labor of my sweat. But I do not yet grant them my offices, which I was accustomed frequently to receive through your generosity. For Moses also, whom you set before us as an example, after the battle had been fought and the Amalekites defeated, himself distributed the recovered spoil to the people (Exod. 17:13). And David, after Syria had been subjected through Joab, the commander of the army, dedicated the gold and the most precious gems for the adornment of the temple (2 Sam. 8:11). He also placed the crown of the king of the Ammonites upon his own head, although Joab had borne the labors of the campaign (2 Sam. 12:30).

But concerning what you wished to reproach me for as well—that I prefer the smoke-blackened roofs of Tours to the gilded arches of Rome—I know that your prudence has read that Solomonic saying: “It is better,” he says, “to sit in a corner of the roof than in a common house with a quarrelsome woman” (Prov. 21:9). And, if I may say so peacefully, iron harms the eyes more than smoke. Tours, content with its smoky roofs, remains in peace by God’s gift, through the providence of your kindness. Rome, however, which was founded amid fraternal discord, does not cease to retain the poison of dissension implanted in it; and it compels your revered dignity to hasten from the sweet dwelling places of Germany [Col. 0331C] in order to restrain the destructive power of this pest. We, for our part, accompany your absence with tears and your journey with continual prayers, humbly beseeching divine clemency that it may lead you and your followers safely in every prosperity and bring you back rejoicing. {139} Yet I by no means agree that the letters of your piety should forget me; let them come more often in the spirit of consolation, so that they may be kissed, read again and again, and preserved with perpetual sweetness in the treasure of the heart.

May Christ grant happy times of this kingdom

And of the eternal one, beloved David,

[Col. 0331D] Basnagius says at this point that the remaining verses are absent from the Quercetan edition, in which only the first two are given. The learned man did not notice that Quercetan published the remaining verses at the end of Letter 12, now 96; they seem to belong there more than here, since that letter concerns Leo’s return to the city, which occurred in the preceding year. to you.

[Col. 0331D] Baluzius published this letter in book I of the *Miscellanies*, p. 377, from which we have transcribed it. (In Froben, p. 94.)

## LETTER CX. TO THE ABBOTS AND MONKS OF GOTHIA. (A.D. 800)

He addresses the error of the Adoptionists, which he says he has already refuted in a short book sent through blessed Benedict and will now refute in a larger work. [Col. 0332A]

Albinus, humble servant of Christ and servant of Saint Martin, sends eternal salvation in Christ to all the abbots, brothers, and sons who are

[Col. 0331D] in the regions of Gothia. Gothia is also called Septimania by another name. Felix of Urgel “administered a poisonous draught of the Adoptionist heresy to many throughout Septimania,” as Jonas of Orléans writes in book I *On the Cult of Images against Claudius of Turin*. This circumstance troubled Alcuin, lest the monasteries recently partly founded and partly reformed by blessed Benedict of Aniane should be infected by that poison. in the regions of Gothia, most dear in Christ, sends greetings of eternal blessedness.

Having received the sweetest letters of your blessedness, together with the exceedingly pleasing and greatly necessary gifts of your holy prayers, I rejoiced with every joy and gladness of mind, placing great confidence in your most sacred intercessions to Jesus, the Son of God, who for the salvation of the world deigned to become man: so that he who was eternally born as God from the Father should be born temporally from a virgin, and the same one should be man who was also God, and the same one God who was also man; and there should be no separation of person or sonship, lest there be two Sons, one proper and the other adoptive, or two Gods, one true God and the other titular [“called”] God—something wholly impious to believe and proclaim. For the Son of God, in the propriety of his person and the dignity of his sonship, united man to himself, so that there might be one Christ, one God, and one Son of God, wholly in what is his and wholly in what is ours, perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity. This can be proved by many evangelical and apostolic testimonies, and also by the traditions of the holy Fathers, as has been partly done in the little book [Col. 0332C] that we sent through blessed

[Col. 0331D] In the little book . . . that we sent through blessed Benedict. [Col. 0332D] We shall give this little book, which has remained hidden until now, from Vatican Palatine Manuscript 290 below, before the seven books against Felix. See our dissertation on the Adoptionist heresy. Benedict was abbot of the monastery of Aniane, which is the head of the other monasteries of Septimania or Gothia, now called Languedoc by the French; Alcuin had a friendly relationship with him. Benedict, for your consolation and confirmation in the Catholic faith. But in the hands

[Col. 0332D] The larger work. Namely, the seven books against Felix of Urgel. we now have a larger work because of the other matters that we read in the little book

[Col. 0332D] Of the venerable Felix. This is an address used for a friend, not an adversary. The present letter was therefore written after Felix had been convicted by Alcuin at the Council of Aachen in 799 and had been reconciled with him. See what we said in the aforementioned dissertation. of the venerable Felix; and, God willing, we are sending it to you after it has been read and approved by our bishops and

[Col. 0332D] And the lord king. See the letter to Charlemagne prefixed to the seven books against Felix. the lord king. Meanwhile, may your holiness assist us with your holy prayers, so that the Lord God may open to us the recognition of truth, the confidence to preach, and steadfastness in the Catholic faith. “The prayer of a righteous man has great power” (James 5:16), and how much more the prayer of many.

{140} This novelty of expressions in connection with adoption, and the designation of Christ, must be utterly detested by all the faithful, and this division in Christ [Col. 0333A] our Lord must be carefully avoided. We know that there are two perfect natures in Christ and one person: that he is both mortal and immortal. Just as a human being is mortal in the flesh and immortal in the soul, yet is one human being, one person, and one son wholly proper to his father, and cannot be divided so as to be partly a “designated” man and partly a true man: so also Christ, although mortal in the flesh and immortal in his divinity, is nevertheless one Jesus Christ and one Son of God. As I said, a human being is one son, although mortal in the flesh and immortal in the soul. In no way, therefore, can one Son, with one Father, be both proper and adoptive. And if Christ the Son of God is one in one person, he is altogether either wholly proper or wholly adoptive. But it is better that, because of the excellence of the nature [Col. 0333B] [Leg., “the excellent nature” or “of the nature”] of the Son of God, who is proper and eternal, the assumed humanity should be made the Son’s possession, than that, because of the humanity, the eternal Son of God should be humbled into adoption. A proper son and an adoptive son absolutely cannot be one son in relation to one father, though they can be so in relation to two fathers.

Considering these matters carefully, hold them firmly in your minds, and steadfastly preach that there is one Son and one God, and that he is the same proper, true, and perfect Son; for all truth is in Christ, with no fiction, and the whole fullness of divinity (Col. II, 9), with no diminution or defect;

@ [Col. 0333D] Nor did he . . . need baptism. Alcuin refutes this error in Book II Against the Same Man. nor, as it is read in the little book of the aforementioned Felix, did he need baptism; rather, immediately, without sin and every stain of sin, he was conceived by the Holy Spirit as true God and true [Col. 0333C] man. And if the blessed Virgin could beget for herself a proper Son, who had been the Son of God from eternity, how could God the Father not have his own proper human Son, who was born in time from the Virgin? There is altogether one person in both natures, Christ and the proper Son of God, in relation to both parents. You will read all these matters more fully, with the help of that same God about whom we are speaking, in the same little book that we now have in hand. Only remain firm in the faith and do not hesitate at all [Supple, “remain”]; for, as the Apostle says, without faith it is impossible to please God (Hebr. XI, 6).

Maintain fraternal charity among yourselves with the utmost diligence, and unity in complete Catholic peace, in right faith, and in unfeigned humility. Preserve your obedience [Col. 0333D], according to the purpose of the regular life, with every effort, and remain steadfast in your places, where you have given yourselves to God; do not abandon your monasteries and wander through the vanities of the world. For the time of this life is short (I Cor. VII, 29), and the sufferings of this world are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to come (Rom. VIII, 18). The yoke of Christ ought not to seem hard or burdensome to your blessedness, but light and easy, as he himself says: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. XI, 30). “Not the one who begins, but the one who perseveres, will be saved” (Matt. X, 22; and XXIV, 13). Call to mind Judas [Col. 0334A], who became a betrayer from among the apostles. Consider Saul, who was changed from a persecutor into a preacher. Remember the monk Malchus, whose history blessed Jerome has recently published in a letter: how, apparently out of concern for piety, he left the monastery, abandoning his father, and into what tribulations he later came; and how he mourned the monk whom he lost in the desert, though he had been lost to the monastery. Rarely does the devil fight against God’s servants with an open face; rather, under the appearance of piety, he suggests that leaving the monastery is more useful than remaining in it. A sheep that leaves the fold and withdraws from the shepherd is exposed to the bites of wolves. It is better not to make a vow than not to fulfill one’s vows. Scripture says: “Vow and pay to the Lord your God” (Ps. LXXV, 12). God is faithful in the promises of blessedness that he makes [Col. 0334B] to those who love him (James I, 12). And truly you say [Sense corrupt]: “He will repay the promises of truth.” Remember the Apostle saying: “Brothers, stand firm and immovable” (I Cor. XV, 58). And again: “Let the one who stands take heed lest he fall” (I Cor. X, 12). John stood when he saw Christ. Therefore, dearest brothers, watch and stand firm in the faith, act manfully (I Cor. XVI, 13), and let your hearts be strengthened in every good work. The Psalmist says: “Wait for the Lord, act manfully, let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord” (Ps. XXVI, 14).

{141} What does “wait for the Lord” mean except: wait with a steadfast mind until the day of recompense comes to you? Perform every work manfully, and let your heart be strengthened in persevering in what you have begun; and “wait for the Lord”—whatever tribulation or labor he permits within you, [Col. 0334C] endure it manfully. “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord will deliver them from them” (Ps. XXXIII, 20). Let no labor seem hard to one who loves God, for he is the faithful rewarder and an able helper; he never abandons those who hope in him. Let a person answer the devil’s suggestions: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me” (Ps. CXVII, 6), that is, carnal pleasure. Again: “Depart from me, you evildoers, and I will search out the commandments of my God” (Ps. CXVIII, 115). And again: “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. May the Lord guard the going-out and coming-in of his servants, from this time forth and forever” (Ps. CXX, 2, 8). Read these things happily, dearest brothers, and faithfully fulfill them. May the Lord God help you and cause you to advance in every good thing; may he hear [Col. 0334D] your prayers for all people and for me, your faithful helper; and may the Lord God guard you in eternal peace and perfect charity, brothers, men and dearest sons.

@ [Col. 0334D] Edited by Quercet. 99 from a manuscript (in Froben. 95).

## LETTER CXI. TO THE BROTHERS IN GOTHIA. (Year uncertain.)

He exhorts them to repentance, to observance of the regular life, and to courage in the tribulation that has arisen.

To the most holy brothers in the charity of Christ, and to those faithfully serving God in various parts of Gothia, Alcuin, humble levite, sends greetings.

[Col. 0335A] We read that the Lord commanded his disciples to have the crowds recline in groups of fifty, fifty by fifty; he wished all of them to be refreshed by the solidity of one bread (Luke IX, 14). The number fifty, in which the Law was given, signifies the remission of sins: this is the Paraclete Spirit himself, sent by the Father and the Son, who descended upon the one hundred and twenty; all the faithful receive remission in the grace of that Holy Spirit, first in the sacrament of baptism, and second in the tears of repentance, by which the sinful soul, cleansed, will deserve to attain the vision of God the Savior. Truth itself says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8). “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI, 2). “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting the salvation [Col. 0335B] of our souls” (II Cor. VII, 1). Knowing and understanding these things perfectly, dearest brothers, let nothing sordid remain in your conscience, whether contracted from the frailty of the flesh or instilled by the agitation of the spirit, so that the Holy Spirit may find in your hearts a dwelling worthy of himself. Let the malignant enemy find no share of his malice in your good way of life, nor discover in your hearts the entrance he seeks. Rather, strengthen your souls with every safeguard: with the protection of charity, the guardianship of obedience, the wall of humility, the observance of chastity, and the bond of holy peace. Fight manfully against the ancient enemy and, with united hands, overthrow him who goes about roaring, seeking whom he may devour (I Pet. V, 8). Carry on your foreheads the banner [Col. 0335C] of the cross, and in your hearts the defenses of charity and the foundation of the Catholic faith. Raise yourselves to God with firm hope, and his crafty cunning will have no power against your unanimity. Be more ready to obey your elders with humble minds than to judge, through the fault of murmuring, whatever work is imposed upon you.

You have vowed to serve God and to be governed by your fathers’ counsels. Do not exalt yourselves above your superiors, nor judge their actions or counsels; be content simply with their judgment, whatever you do, and with the precepts of the regular life, in which humility in obeying with charity is especially commanded. Let all your hours be found useful to your souls, whether in manual labor, in the study of reading, or in the grace of prayer. Let the laborer pray in his heart, so that he may be considered worthy of a double reward. Likewise, during the nourishment of the body, let the soul be nourished by thanksgiving to God; or, if the body is afflicted by labor, let the mind be strengthened by compunction. When a monk is thus armed with this double support, the ancient enemy will be able to harm him in nothing (Rev. XII, 9), though he seeks through mental wandering to diminish the reward of the one who labors.

[Col. 0336A] I, for my part, troubled by the storms of the world, have toiled in vain with much labor in many places; but now, as though shipwrecked, by God’s mercy I have been cast into the harbor of rest. As I lie there weary and wounded, I beg your unanimity to assist me by the constant exercise of your holy prayers, so that one day I may deserve to reach the flourishing fields of virtue and, in good security, serve him alone in whom alone is the hope of complete salvation; without him, neither can the fallen rise again nor the one standing well stand with a firm step.

I have sent small gifts to your affection, but, God as my witness, not with small charity—so far as its little spark can glow in the breast of a sinner. Even if God had not yet granted me to stand with you in the holiness of life, nevertheless his most merciful grace has truly [Col. 0336B] poured your charity into my heart, and I desire and humbly pray that through your most holy prayers he may deem the offering of my will acceptable to God and receive his gift into my soul. He is accustomed to give grace for grace; from his fullness we have received whatever good we appear to possess. May his charity always be in the heart, praise in the mouth, and in good works the sign of perfect love.

I desired to write many things to your blessedness, but, [Col. 0335D] distressed by news of tribulation. We do not know what this tribulation was. Eginhard, in his Annals under the year 793, reports that the Saracens entered Septimannia, fought with the Franks, and returned victorious; from this, danger may have threatened the monks of Gothia, or Septimannia, and tribulation may have arisen. Accordingly, it might seem plausible to anyone that this letter was written in that year. Yet in that year Alcuin was not cast into the harbor of rest but summoned to new labors. For this reason it seemed more prudent not to assign the present letter to any certain year; nevertheless, I judged it advisable to join it to the preceding letters, since they were written to the same people. distressed by the news of tribulation, I dictated these few words. Whatever the tribulation may be, I beg you to act manfully and remain steadfast in spirit, knowing that God never abandons those who hope in him (Ps. XVII, 31). And if, under the pressure of any tribulation, it should be necessary to change your place, let the observance of the regular life never be changed; [Col. 0336C] nor let bodily tribulation weary the constancy of your spirit. Night and day take their turns. The storm of the sea is calmed by the tranquility of clear weather. Nor can perpetual prosperity be found in this present world, because we are in exile and are born for labor (Job V, 7). Just as blows train children to learn the beauty of wisdom or to become accustomed to good conduct, so we too are admonished by labors and sorrows to hasten toward the rest of perpetual blessedness. It is darkened by no pain or labor and brought to an end by no limit; rather, it remains stable forever in perpetual joy and happiness. To attain it, let no labor frighten away your holy purpose, {143} and let no allurements of this world draw you back; but, dearest brothers, be strong in spirit and steadfast in every good work [Col. 0336D], knowing that your labor is not in vain before God (I Cor. XV, 58), and that the one who labors more will receive greater reward. May the Lord God, who has gathered you into the charity of one fold, deign to help you with eternal blessing within the walls of the Catholic faith and in the riches of holy charity through good works, and to guard you forever—fathers, brothers, and most dearly desired sons, most sweet to my heart’s affection.

@ [Col. 0337D] Edited by Quercet. 71, Canis. 26 (Froben. 96); corrected from the manuscript of Salzburg, which has this title: “Against those who do not wish to give confession to priests.”

## LETTER CXII. TO THE BROTHERS IN THE PROVINCE OF THE GOTHS. (Year uncertain.)

He refutes the error of those who do not wish to confess their sins to priests, and establishes the necessity of confession. [Col. 0337A]

To the most beloved men, brothers and fathers, in the province

@ [Col. 0337D] of the Goths. Canisius, considering this word corrupt in the manuscript, wishes it to be read “Scots.” But there is no reason to correct the manuscript, since it is certain that Alcuin also wrote other letters to the monks of Gothia, or Septimannia. of the Goths, Albinus, humble servant of the Church of Christ, the deacon, sends greetings.

The abundant praise of your intelligence and religion has often sounded in our ears, whether on account of the most sacred life of the monks or the religious conduct of the laity: the former are said to desire to devote themselves to God alone, free from all the noise of worldly disturbance, while the latter are said to lead a most chaste life, with rational reflection, amid worldly occupations. [Col. 0337B] [What could be more delightful than this exchange of fraternal charity?] The former do not cease to help their fellow members by daily prayers; the latter eagerly support their intercessors with the consolations of the present life. Thus each pours back upon the other the grace of blessing given to each by God. Therefore, taught also by the examples of your piety, we ask that the course of our voyage be directed by the prayers of your holiness toward the harbor of perpetual rest.

We too have taken care, in the mutual duty of charity, to send your holiness a few little letters of pious admonition, on account of certain customs that are said to have taken root in your regions. It is said, however, that none of the laity wishes to give his

@ [Col. 0337D] confession. This is an outstanding testimony by Alcuin in favor of auricular confession against even the heretics of modern times who assert that it is sufficient to confess sins to God alone. Alcuin speaks of this matter frequently elsewhere, as in Letters 13, 39 (now 14, 44), and so forth. See Mabillon, Preface to Part I of the Third Century of Benedictines, p. 9. confession to priests, whom we believe to have received from God Christ, together with the holy apostles, the power of binding and loosing (Matt. XVI, 19; XVIII, 18). What does priestly power loose if it does not examine the bonds of the bound? The physician’s work will cease if the sick do not reveal their wounds. If bodily wounds await the hands of a fleshly physician, how much more do wounds of the soul demand the consolations of a spiritual physician? You must confess to God, O man, whom you cannot hide from, whether you wish it or not; yet you neglect to make satisfaction to the Church of Christ, in which you sinned. Why did Christ himself command the leper whom he cleansed to show himself to the priests (Matt. VIII, 4)? Why did he command others to loose Lazarus, who had been raised after four days (John XI, 44)? Could he not have loosed the dead man’s bandages by the same word by which he commanded him to come out of the tomb, restored to life [Col. 0337D]? Why did he ask the blind men who cried out to him what they wanted (Matt. XX, 32)? Could he, who was able to restore the desired light to their eyes, have been ignorant of the desire of their hearts? Perhaps, if you could hide from God as you can from a human being, you would be unwilling to confess to God more than [Col. 0338A] to a human being. This seems to be a kind of pride: to despise a priest as judge.

{144} If you say: “It is good to confess to the Lord” (Ps. XCI, 2), it is good also for you to have a witness to this confession. Although

@ [Col. 0338D] Confession does not always signify repentance. On this subject St. Augustine speaks elegantly in Sermon 8, On the Words of the Lord. CANISIUS. confession does not always signify repentance, but very often praise, as Truth itself said in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Father of heaven and earth” (Matt. XI, 25), that is, “I praise you, Father of heaven and earth.” And in the Creed it is said: “I confess one baptism,” and the rest, which refer to the same verb. In this passage the verb “I confess” designates a confession of faith, not of sins. Are you ashamed to show a human being, for your salvation, what you are not ashamed to perpetrate with a human being for your destruction? You wish to have your maidservant conscious of your wickedness, yet you do not wish to have Christ’s priest as an assistant in your reconciliation? You fell through an enemy, and you do not wish to rise again through a friend? You have greatly offended your Lord, and you do not wish to have another reconciler except yourself? Do you trust that you will be saved through your own prayers? You reject the apostolic command that says: “Pray for one another, that you may be saved”; and again:

@ [Col. 0338D] If any one of you is a sinner. He elegantly applies, in an accommodated sense, St. James’s words: “Is anyone among you sick,” etc., to the soul of the sinner. CANIS. If any one is a sinner, let the priest pray for him, so that he may be saved. What do you say to these words, which are read in the same epistle: “Confess your sins to one another” (James V, 14, 15, 16), so that your offenses may be blotted out? What does “to one another” mean except person to person, the guilty person to the judge, the sick person to the physician? Wisdom itself also said through Solomon: “The one who hides his crimes will not be directed aright” (Prov. XXVIII, 13), that is, the one who strives to conceal his sins will not be directed aright [Col. 0338C] in the way of salvation.

Can our crimes be hidden from God, who sees, knows, and considers everything? We can hide what we do from a human being, but not from God. Did David not say in the presence of the prophet Nathan, who reproved him for his sin: “I have sinned against the Lord” (II Kings XII, 13)? Behold, so great a man wished to have a prophet as the witness of his confession. And because he was not ashamed to confess what he had done wickedly, he immediately heard: “The Lord has taken away your sin.” He disclosed his wound to a human being and immediately received a remedy from God. Indeed, in Leviticus, very often, at the Lord’s command, the sinner is sent to the priest with a victim; offering it to God, he is to pray for him, and the sinner will be forgiven (Lev. V, 12). What are our victims for the sins we have committed except confession of our sins? We must offer it purely to God through the priest, so that through the priest’s prayers the offering of our confession may become acceptable to God, and we may receive remission from him who does not despise the sacrifice of a troubled spirit and a contrite and humbled heart (Ps. L, 19).

Christ came into this world to be judged by enemies for our crimes, so that he might redeem us from the service of the devil; and we disdain to be judged by God’s holy priests so that we may be freed from the bonds of our sins? He, without any sin, did not refuse to stand before the judgment of human beings, even wicked ones; and we, with many sins, disdain to undergo the judgments of human beings, even holy ones? In holy baptism, must we not give to Christ’s priests the confession of our faith and the renunciation of Satan, and thus, through the priestly ministry, with divine grace at work, be washed from all sins? Why also, in the second baptism of repentance, through the confession of our humility, should we not likewise, with the same divine mercy, be absolved by priestly assistance from all the sins committed after the first baptism?

If sins are not to be disclosed to priests, why are prayers of reconciliation written in the

@ In the Sacramentary. Does he mean the Sacramentary of St. Gregory the Great, in which prayers of reconciliation are found? CANIS. Are prayers of reconciliation written in the Sacramentary? How does a priest reconcile someone whose sin he does not know? If wars are to be conducted by counsel, according to Solomon (Prov. XX, 18), with what boldness do we confidently fight against the devil without the counsel of ecclesiastical commanders? Again, from the same speaker we read: “A brother who is helped by a brother is like a fortified city” (Prov. XVIII, 19). Who will the priest of Christ, the commander of God’s army and ruler of his camp, help, if no one deigns to seek from him the aid of salvation, and if no one shows him the hidden wounds of the devil’s deceit for treatment by his healing right hand?

[Col. 0339C] {145} Therefore remedies have been placed in the churches in vain, and by synodal authority committed to writing against all the wounds of our sins, inflicted upon us spiritually or bodily either by the cunning of the ancient enemy or by neglect of God’s commandments, if they are not revealed to those appointed in the Church of Christ to heal the festering sores of our crimes. For, the Apostle says, “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X, 10). Not only confession of the Catholic faith, but also pure confession of sins [with contrition of heart] profits us toward eternal salvation, as Scripture says: “Declare your former wrongs, so that you may be justified” (Isa. XLIII, 26). And again: “The righteous person is the first to accuse himself” [Col. 0339D] (Prov. XVIII, 17). If the righteous person, how much more the sinner?

If perhaps you say with the Psalmist: “I said, I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord” (Ps. XXXI, 5), I too will say with the same Psalmist: “Because I was silent, my bones grew old” (ibid., v. 3). And again with another prophet: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel I, 17). What does it mean for beasts to rot in their dung except that criminals lie in the corruption of their sins? Whoever sins lies down; whoever confesses rises [Cod. Sal., “will rise”]. Whoever does penance returns to his father, as the prodigal son is read to have said in the Gospel: “I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven [Col. 0340A] and before you” (Luke XV, 18). But it is sufficient to make confession once to a priest in the presence of divine mercy. We judge, however, that it must always be made to the Lord with tears and contrition of heart. For everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his works may not be reproved; but whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be revealed, because they have been done in God (John III, 20–21).

You, therefore, brothers, are sons of light and not of darkness, a people acquired and not a people of perdition, a holy nation (I Pet. II, 9), acquired by Christ’s blood. Walk as sons of light in all goodness [Col. 0340B] (Eph. V, 8–9), piety, and chastity, putting off the old man with his sins and putting on the new, who has been created according to God (Col.
