III, 9–10). Let your way of life be heavenly, not earthly. Love justice and hate iniquity. Let the one who is healthy defend himself with the shield of faith, lest the secret arrow of the ancient enemy be able to wound him (Eph. VI, 16). But if anyone is wounded because of the frailty of the flesh or negligence in vigilance, let him hasten to the medicine of confession, lest through the enticement of evil habit the sin scarcely be capable of being uprooted [Cod. Sal., “of uprooting”]. For the Gospel history relates that the Lord Jesus Christ raised three dead persons: the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue in the house (Mark V, 38 ff.), the son of the widow outside the city gate (Luke VII, 12 ff.), and Lazarus, four days dead, whom he called from the tomb to life (John XI). What are these three dead persons except three kinds of sinners [Col. 0340C], whom divine grace now habitually raises each day through confession? He raises the daughter in the house when he calls back from the perpetration of sin the one consenting to sin in his heart. He raises the widow’s son outside the city gate when he causes one sinning outwardly in deed to flee to the remedies of repentance. But the one stinking in the evil habit of sin he raises when he draws tears of repentance from his heart and commands, by ecclesiastical authority, that he be loosed, so that he may be worthy of the Lord’s communion and become a participant in the sacred altar.

Think on these things, dearest brothers, and if anyone lies in any one of these three kinds of death, let him hasten to the thoroughly tested medicines of confession and wash himself with the saving medicine of repentance, so that he may [Col. 0340D] communicate in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ not to the judgment of condemnation but to the salvation of sanctification. And always remember with thanksgiving how divine mercy transferred you from the land of darkness and cold, from the region of ignorance and iniquity, into places of light and joy, into tabernacles of abundance and justice; and how, with fatherly kindness, it chose you for itself as sons, so that through you its name might be proclaimed among the nations. Follow the footsteps of the holy Fathers, and do not introduce new sects into the religion of the Catholic faith. Beware of the poisonous leaven of wandering corruption; but in sincerity and truth eat the spotless loaves of the sacred faith, and drink the wine [Col. 0341A] that divine Wisdom mixed for her chosen ones; and sing to your God, in concord of peace and unanimity of perpetual charity, a hymn of praise; with the heavenly host, praise God with a harmonious voice and say: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II, 14). May divine grace go before you, mercy follow you everywhere, and may it cause you to flourish in every good work, most beloved brothers and most holy fathers.

@ [Col. 0341D] Edited by Quercet. 81, Canis. 60, Froben. 9.

## LETTER CXIII. TO PAULINUS THE PATRIARCH. (Year 800.)

He praises his little book on the exposition of the faith and urges him to combat certain errors arising in the Church.

[Col. 0341B] To the most beloved lord in the Lord of lords, and pious Father Paulinus, patriarch, greetings.

I seem to have some refreshment for my spirit, so that the flame of charity hidden in my heart may perhaps be able to draw forth some spark, lest what burns within grow entirely numb, now that a suitable opportunity has occurred for me to write something to your charity. What else? When I am permitted to behold letters from your blessedness, sweeter than every honeycomb, do I not seem to myself to dwell entirely among the varied flowers of paradise and, with the eager right hand of my desire, gather spiritual fruits from them?

How much more so when I saw your most sacred little book of the faith,

@ [Col. 0341D] Your little book of the faith. I think he means none other than the work he immediately below calls “the exposition of the Catholic faith.” See the following note. reviewed, adorned with the purity of Catholic peace, most delightful in the beauty of its eloquence, and most firm in the truth of its meaning [Col. 0341C]: I released all the reins of my heart into joy. In it I saw four rivers flowing from one most lucid and health-giving fountain of paradise (Gen. II, 10), irrigating not only the meadows of Ausonian fertility but also the fields of the whole ecclesiastical Latin tradition. I understood there also that the golden streams of spiritual meanings abounded in the gems of scholarly elegance. You have produced a work destined to benefit very many and absolutely necessary

@ [Col. 0341D] In the exposition of the Catholic faith. The learned man evidently means the work “The Rule of Faith, promulgated with the point of a metrical style,” which appears among Paulinus’s works in the Madrid edition, p. 169; see the same man’s Life of Saint Paulinus, chapter 14, no. 4. But Alcuin would hardly have considered that poem important enough to be given to each priest in each parish under episcopal jurisdiction to read and commit to memory. I think this exposition of the faith, and the explanation of the entire Creed, was another work of Saint Paulinus, which has not yet seen the light. in the exposition of the Catholic faith, a work I long desired and often urged the lord king to have: that the symbol of the Catholic faith might be gathered into a single sheet in the clearest meanings and most lucid language, and distributed to all the priests in each parish under episcopal jurisdiction, to be read and committed to memory, so that, although they spoke different languages, one faith might nevertheless resound everywhere.

Behold! What my humility desired, your sublimity has fulfilled. With the author of our salvation you have a perpetual reward for this good will, and among human beings the praise of this perfect work. May your ever-fervent charity always fortify the camp of the eternal King on every side with unconquerable shields of faith, lest the cunning of the ancient enemy be able to find any entrance for his wickedness. Although he has a thousand arts of harming, it is much more necessary for us {147} to have a thousand arts of defending those who believe in him who said: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John XVI, 33). His mercy foresaw for us the temporary time of struggle, so that the reward might be eternal. He first trampled upon the head of the lion and the dragon; and he gave us the power to tread upon serpents and scorpions (Luke X, 19), and to overcome all heretical perversions, which are the gates of hell. But you, apostolic man, armed with this power, fight manfully and conquer bravely [Col. 0342B], so that you may reign happily with Christ. Alas, what grief! Many are accustomed to tear with heretical claws the seamless tunic of Christ woven from above, and to do in the peace of the Church what the soldiers did not dare to do during Christ’s passion. Therefore, venerable Father, most learned athlete, and most beloved teacher, let us always remain fellow soldiers in Christ’s camp and, in one battle line, fight under the banner of the holy cross with united counsel and strength, so that through us he who cannot be conquered may conquer his adversaries.

@ [Col. 0342D] {148} Now again. He seems to be criticizing Elipandus’s obstinacy after Felix’s conversion. The letter therefore belongs to the year 800. See Letter 105. Now again the ancient serpent, crushed not by a club of Hercules but by an evangelical club, is trying to raise his head from the thorn bushes of the Spanish countryside and from the caves of poisonous unbelief, and to mix new toxins of cursing into the former cups of wickedness. But also the coldest [Col. 0342C]

@ [Col. 0342D] north wind. The controversy over performing a single immersion in baptism was being debated not among the northern peoples but among the Spaniards, already in the time of Leander and Gregory I. The expression is therefore figurative, indicating another Spanish error. BASNAG. the northern wind, driving the solid wall of the Church from another side, is striving to alter the rule of the Catholic custom of holy baptism, and, under the invocation of the Holy Trinity,

@ [Col. 0342D] A single immersion. See Letter 90 to the brothers of Lyons. asserting that a single immersion ought to be performed and neglecting to imitate our Savior’s three-day burial in baptism, although the Apostle said: “For you were buried with Christ in baptism” (Rom. VI, 4; Col. II, 12). Others, however, wish to perform three immersions and to invoke the Holy Trinity at each immersion; thus they strive to name all three persons three times, whereas Truth itself commanded: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19). What need is there to repeat a third time what, once said, is sufficient?

[Col. 0342D] There is also, among certain people, a hidden doubt as to whether the souls of the holy apostles and martyrs and of other perfect people are received into the heavenly kingdom before the day of judgment.

@ [Col. 0342D] We touched on this error briefly in the Preface. With these and similar darts, drawn, as I believe, from the quivers of unbelief [Col. 0343A], some people seek to wound the unity of the holy and Catholic Church and the truth of the universal faith; they also infect the clearest cups of ecclesiastical faith with the filthiest dregs of errors and attempt once more to turn into waters of folly the nuptial wine that Christ, from water, beneficially changed for the Virgin Mother (John II, 3–9), that is, for the holy Church, to drink. But it is yours, O chosen shepherd of the flock and guardian of the gates of the city of God, who hold the key of knowledge in your powerful right hand and conceal five clearest stones in your left, to crush entirely, with one blow of truth, the Philistines who blaspheme the army of the living God in the one most proud Goliath (I Kings XVII). It is ours, with hands raised heavenward with Moses, to assist you by prayers of humility (Exod. XVII, 11), and, with David, to watch [Col. 0343B] from the most strongly fortified tower of the city until a watchman, crying out from the high summit, announces your victory to us (II Kings XVIII, 24 ff.). Everyone’s eyes look to you, desiring to hear something heavenly from your overflowing eloquence; and, through you, they eagerly await the swift melting of the coldest hailstones beneath the fervent sun of wisdom—stones that do not fear striking the pinnacles of the wisest Solomon. But you are a burning and shining lamp (John V, 35); we rejoice to exult in your light, so that, with you shining and leading us toward the light that enlightens every person coming into this world (John I, 9), and with the grace of that same eternal light assisting us, we may deserve to arrive there.

@ [Col. 0343D] Froben. Letter 173.

## LETTER CXIV. TO AEDILHARD, ARCHBISHOP. (Year 800.)

[Col. 0343D] I gave the fragment of this letter above as Letter 62 (now 77), from the Malmesbury manuscript; it has now fortunately been found complete in the manuscript codex of the Harleian Library. See what we noted there; although the year must be corrected, and this letter seems to belong to the year 800, on account of what we note in Letters 116 and 117.

He praises him for his meeting with Eanbald concerning the honor of the churches and the reform of the clergy. He urges him to return quickly to his flock after completing his embassy; he sends his saddle and his horse.

[Col. 0343C]

To the most holy Father and greatly revered among the members of Christ, Aedilhard, archbishop, Alcuin the deacon sends greetings in the love of Christ.

Hearing of your health and prosperity, and of your meeting with my son Eanbald [read: Eanbald], bishop of York, pleased me greatly. I hope that from the conversation of your holiness the honor of the churches of Christ may be exalted, and that the life of those serving God in them may be corrected—since for a great part it has long been corrupted and has almost been brought to the level of the vanity of laymen—so that only the tonsure seems to distinguish it [Col. 0343D], while in other respects it is in many ways similar, whether in the vanity and arrogance of clothing, the excess of banquets, or the other matters that your holy discernment knows very well. Therefore, in other brief letters of mine, I urged your holiness to remain in your homeland, unwilling that the light of Britain should be extinguished or the trumpet of truth fall silent; but let what pleases God and benefits the churches of Christ be done [Col. 0344A]. If you go with the intention that I read in the letter of your blessedness, I confess that it would please me greatly—provided, however, that you find someone who will fulfill your good desire.

Return, return, holy Father, when your mission of piety has been completed, to the lost sheep, lest the flock, without a shepherd, wander and fall among the briars of vices; it could scarcely be corrected even with its shepherd present. As there are two eyes in the body, so I believe and desire that you two shine across the whole breadth of Britain: do not remove the right eye from your homeland. Remember your most holy predecessors, our fathers and shepherds, with what diligence they labored in the word of God and for the salvation of the Christian people, so that, following in their footsteps, you may deserve to share their fellowship in heavenly glory.

[Col. 0344B] But if you reach the lord king, advise your companions, and especially the clerics, to conduct themselves honorably in all holy observance—in clothing and in ecclesiastical order—so that wherever you go you may always leave an example of every kind of goodness. Forbid them to use garments of gold or silk

[Col. 0344D] Malmesbury remembers this admonition addressed to Aedilhard in Book I, chapter 4, of *The Kings of England*, whose words we have quoted above in the notes to Letter 63 (now 78). in the presence of the lord king; let them go about in humble dress, according to the custom of the servants of God. In every place may you go in peace and with honorable conduct; may knowledge of you arise according to the custom and practice of this people.

I have sent you, as you instructed me, the saddle on which I am accustomed to ride, prepared in the manner in which the shepherds of the churches in this region commonly have them; and also a horse to carry the saddle while you ride upon it [Col. 0344C], if it pleases your piety.

[Col. 0344D] I sent my servant. He met Aedilhard at Saint Judoc and received him there kindly, as he writes in the Letter to Eanbald that follows. I sent my servant so that our people might receive you honorably, as far as I have the means, and so that the command of your holiness might be carried out. Through him you can again inform me by letter of your journey, and whether, on your return, your goodness intends to come to Saint Martin, our protector and your intercessor. May God grant you a prosperous journey; and, with his angel accompanying you, may the Holy Spirit guide and lead you safely and bring you back. May he grant that for many happy years you advance in holy preaching for the salvation of many and the increase of your reward in eternal glory, sweetest and most dearly desired Father!

At the end of this little letter I beseech your charity to remember my name in your holy [Col. 0344D] prayers, as I have often asked and your kindness has promised. But now I especially entreat you to remember me before the holy apostles and martyrs of Christ, just as we gladly have your remembrance before your Saint Martin.

[Col. 0345C] Froben, Letter 174.

## LETTER 115. TO EANBALD, ARCHBISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF YORK, CALLED SIMON. (Year 800.)

[Col. 0345C] *Called Simon.* This title is found in the Harleian manuscript itself. From it we learn that the Simeon the priest to whom Letter 57 (now 72) was written, and whom Alcuin calls, in Letter 58 (now 73), addressed to Calvin, “most beloved son and chief priest,” is the same person as Eanbald, archbishop of York, to whom Alcuin, following his usual practice, gives the assumed name Simeon. See my notes on the letters cited, where, before seeing the present letter, I inferred from the context—against the distinguished scholars Mabillon and Leland—that this Simeon was to be sought neither in Gaul nor in Worms, but in England.

He consoles the afflicted man and urges him to patience; he dissuades him from fleeing his church.

[Col. 0345A]

To Simeon, the priest, son of my vows, Albinus sends greetings.

On his way to Rome, your fellow bishop and religious man Aedilhard encountered my envoy at Saint Judoc.

[Col. 0345D] *At Saint Judoc.* I think one should read *Jodocus* or *Judocus*: a seaside cell otherwise called Wicus, or a small monastery entrusted by Charlemagne to Alcuin in 793, when Alcuin was returning from England to France; today Saint-Josse-sur-Mer. See Letters 39 (now 44) and 81 (now 96), in the notes.

As he was kindly received by me [perhaps: “by my agency”] at his own request, he had with him two other bishops and our friends Ceommund and Toretmund. For their companionship I sent my letters to my lord King David

[Col. 0345D] See Letter 74 (now 89), from which it is understood that Ceommund, or Ceilmund, was a minister of Offa, king of the Mercians; and that Toretmund, or Torhemund, was the faithful servant of Ethelred, king of the Northumbrians. From the present passage it further appears that Aedilhard had two bishops as companions on his journey to Rome. The Saxon chronicler and the Worcester chronicler mention only one of them under the year 799: he calls him Cinebriht, bishop of the West Saxons, while here he calls him Kinebert, bishop of the city of Winchester. No one reveals the name of the other. Pagius, under the year 796, no. 28.

Among the other things that the aforementioned venerable Father himself took care to report to me in his letters, he informed us of your affliction. Because of this I hastened to send these consolatory words to your charity, entreating you to act manfully in the sight of God and to be strong-hearted. It is neither always night nor always day, but each takes its turn; so it is with the adversity and prosperity of this age. Today a storm threatens, but tomorrow calm smiles upon us. Let the anchor of hope be fixed in Christ. Let him who rejoices in prosperity fear adversity; and let him who is wearied by adversity hope that prosperity will soon arrive. Gold of perfect beauty cannot exist unless it has been tested in a furnace of heat. I think that part of your affliction arises from yourself, since you

[Col. 0346C] *Who perhaps receive the king’s enemies.* Roger of Hoveden, in Alford under the year 801, no. 2, reports that “in those times Eardulf, king of the Northumbrians”—within whose territory the church of York was situated [Alford, at the cited place]—“led an army against Kenulf, king of the Mercians, because he had received his enemies. Kenulf himself, gathering an army, brought with him abundant assistance from other provinces. After a long campaign between them, at last, on the advice of the bishops and nobles of the English on both sides, they made peace through the favor of the king of the English.” Perhaps Eanbald, during the period when the kingdom of Northumbria declined after the murder of Ethelred in 796, and when its kings, according to Malmesbury, Book I, chapter 26, were subject to the will of the king of the West Saxons, attached himself to the party of Kenulf, king of the Mercians; perhaps he likewise received Eardulf’s enemies and protected their lands, thereby drawing upon himself Eardulf’s hatred and persecution. At any rate, this is Alcuin’s own suspicion.

Perhaps you receive the king’s enemies, or protect the possessions of his enemies. But if you suffer justly [manuscript: “you will suffer”], why are you troubled? [Col. 0345C] If unjustly, why do you not remember the tribulations of the saints? “You have heard of Job,” says the apostle James, “and you have seen the end intended by the Lord” (James 5:11). Whoever shares in the tribulation of the saints will also share in their glory. Do not contemplate flight, but hope for the crown.

Stand firm in the battle line, like the standard-bearer of Christ’s army. If the one carrying the standard flees, what does the army do? If the trumpet is silent in the camp, who prepares for battle? If the commander is fearful, how will the soldier be saved? “You have not yet,” says the Apostle, “resisted unto blood; and you have forgotten your consolation; God chastises every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:4–6). A son ought not to grieve over the correction of paternal affection. “The wicked,” says Scripture, “raged against the just, but the Lord will break their teeth” (Psalm 57:7), and he reduces their attacks to nothing. Read carefully how the aged Mattathias, when death itself was close at hand, exhorted his sons to act manfully and fight bravely against the enemies of God; and how the saints were crowned through tribulations, and how little—indeed, how nonexistent—is the glory of the sinner. Among other things he says: “Do not fear the words of a sinful man, for his glory is dung and worm. Today he is exalted, and tomorrow he is not found; for he has returned to his earth, and his thought has perished [manuscript: ‘will perish’]” (1 Maccabees 2:62–63).

[Col. 0346B]

There is no need to seek examples from the ancient ages when you have enough before your eyes in the present. You yourself have seen how the kings and princes who opposed your predecessors and the Church of Christ perished. Does God sleep over their crimes because they think they can rage with impunity and do not believe that God’s eye watches over their madness? They have become fools in their wisdom because they do not fear God the judge. But let your patience and good will pray for them, lest God perhaps grant them repentance and they become, from enemies, friends of God [perhaps read: “so that they may be saved”]. But if their destruction has been predetermined [manuscript: “their treachery has been fully completed”], your holiness will by no means be without the reward of eternal happiness [Col. 0346C]. Their pride vanishes like smoke, while your patience shines like light toward the perfect day.

I beseech you: may the reading of these letters strengthen your heart to act manfully and stand steadfast in the battle line of Christ’s army. Who ought to tremble with Christ as leader, when he goes before the ranks of his own battle? He first carried his cross to his passion, ready to suffer for the salvation of the world, proclaiming to all: “Whoever wishes to come after [Col. 0347A] me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24). “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). Strengthened by these testimonies, run after Christ with fearless step, so that you may deserve to possess his mercy forever.

I know that my day has drawn near, and I rejoice to have you survive me. But you must act concerning my soul as a faithful son acts concerning his father; and as I instructed Cuculus to tell your blessedness, I have done. By God’s mercy I desire to live in quietness, for he says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29). May the greatest grace of God accompany you on all your ways, defend you, guide you, [Col. 0347B] and govern you, my son, my most beloved son!

[Col. 0347D] Froben, Letter 175.

## LETTER 116. TO CALVIN AND CUCULUS. (Year 800.)

[Col. 0347D] Alcuin wrote another letter to Calvin alone, Letter 58 (now 73), in which he also mentions the affliction of Simeon, the chief priest, or Eanbald.

He suggests what should be suggested to Simeon (Eanbald), the bishop placed in affliction. He indicates that he has laid down the burden of pastoral care.

Albinus sends greetings to Calvin and Cuculus, his most beloved sons.

I have heard of the tribulations of our most beloved son Simeon. You, however, exhort him to act faithfully and not to be faint-hearted in temptations. His predecessors used to suffer such things; and not they alone, but all the saints. John the Baptist is recorded to have been killed for his testimony to the truth. Let him take care that there be no other cause of temptation in his case except the preaching of truth. I fear that [Col. 0347C] because of the possession of lands, or even

[Col. 0347D] *The receiving of the king’s enemies.* Perhaps Eardulf’s. See note *e* to the preceding letter.

the receiving of the king’s enemies he may be suffering something. Let what belongs to him be sufficient for him; let him not desire what belongs to another, since such things often bring danger upon those who possess them. While he thinks he is benefiting a few, he harms many, for whom it is necessary to intercede daily [manuscript: *cotidie*, as always], or he may harm the flock he ought to govern.

And why does he have such a large number of soldiers in his retinue? He seems to have them out of a motive of mercy; but they harm the monastic communities that receive him and his men. As I hear, he has many more than his predecessors had. Likewise, those men have more followers—that is, more low-born soldiers—than it is fitting for them to have under their authority.

[Col. 0347D] *Our teacher.* Egbert or Aelbert? Both were Alcuin’s teachers; both were archbishops of York. See Letters 38, 50, and 68 (now 43, 56, and 83).

Our teacher did not allow any of his attendants to have more than one man, apart from the stewards of his household—that is, only two in all [Col. 0347D]. It is foolish mercy to benefit a few, perhaps guilty people, while harming many, including good men. Let him not accuse me for suggesting such things [Col. 0348A], but let him correct himself for doing them. As I said, we, Cuculus,

[Col. 0347D] *Having laid down the burden of pastoral care.* Alcuin, having assumed the direction of the monastery of Tours in 796, went there after leaving the affairs of the court. He also wished to be released from the burden of pastoral care, or from the administration of the monasteries previously entrusted to him; this he finally obtained from King Charles, who, as the anonymous author of Alcuin’s *Life*, chapter 8, testifies: “The burdens of the world that Alcuin had, he most willingly distributed among his disciples, as he had requested.” I think this happened in the year 800. For in the following letter to Arno, certainly written in that year, he writes: “Then, so that you may know how great a mercy God Almighty has shown me—for all the possessions that I had in various places, I chose helpers for myself from among my own sons, with my lord David approving all my requests.” I therefore think that this letter and the two preceding ones should be assigned to the year 800.

Having laid down the burden of pastoral care, we sit quietly at Saint Martin’s, awaiting the time when the voice will come: open to the one who knocks, follow the one who commands, heed the one who judges. May your holy solicitude help me, so that, with God’s gift, I may escape that day. And admonish all our friends to remember me in their most holy prayers, especially our son Simeon the priest, in whom above all I place my trust. May God be favorable to him in this life, so that he may deserve to receive future blessedness with the saints of God. Live happily forever, most beloved sons [manuscript: “most beloved son”]. Greet Credulus and our other friends on behalf of my name.

[Col. 0348D] Froben, Letter 176.

## LETTER 117. TO AQUILA, THE BISHOP. (Year 800.)

He replies to letters received from him and gives thanks for his gifts; he mentions a certain impious and cruel murder; and he narrates what was done in the case of Felix of Urgel in the presence of the king and the Fathers.

[Col. 0348B]

To Aquila, bishop and man of divine charity, Alcuin, a servant of the holy Church of God, sends greetings.

Charity alone joins those who are absent and makes those present rejoice. It is joyful everywhere and rejoices with all good things everywhere; it is fortified on the right and on the left by hope and faith. It begins in time but endures forever. Without it there is no virtue, without it there is no good, without it no one is granted the vision of God; for if God is not loved here, he will not be seen there, where the highest blessedness of his lovers is to see God. Truth itself says: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21).

Therefore, most beloved Father, let us love him whose vision is eternal blessedness. But if you perhaps ask how God is to be loved, he who spoke before will answer you: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (ibid., verse 23). And if you continue to ask what his word is, learn from him who is the Word of God, when he says: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John 15:12). “How,” says the Evangelist, “do you love God, whom you do not see, when you do not love your brother, whom you do see?” (1 John 4:20). Let this be firmly rooted in our minds; let it be held in eternal memory. You, chief priest of Christ, keep it continually in your heart and strive to preach it to all. In this matter also continually admonish me, your faithful lover, for the salvation of my soul, and assist me with your prayers, so that I may advance in it until, under God’s guidance, the course of my life reaches its perfect end. Nor is it necessary for my insignificance to multiply syllables of admonition for you, since I know that, by the inspiration of divine grace, your most sublime holiness both knows everything very well and accomplishes it even better. Yet, lest you rightly accuse me of silence, the most sweet charity of your name compels me to write something to you as opportunity permits.

[Col. 0349C] *While I was traveling from the palace.* The following notes will make it clear that this letter was written in the year 800. In that year King Charles was at Aachen around the end of June, when Alcuin says that he returned from the palace. After the death of Queen Liutgard—which occurred that year on the day before the Nones of June—he returned “through Orléans and Paris,” as the Loiselle annalist relates; the annals of Metz and Saint-Bertin, together with Einhard, agree with him (*Bouquet, Historians of France*, vol. V). From this I infer that Alcuin accompanied Charles when he returned from Tours to Aachen.

While I was traveling from the palace on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, four leagues [*leuca*, “league”] from Saint-Amand,

[Col. 0349C] *In the little dwelling of Saint Martin.* I think he means the village of Baralla, about which he writes to Arno in Letter 66: “I have arranged to remain four or five days at our village of Baralla, not far from Saint-Amand, but about fifteen miles away.”

in the little dwelling of Saint Martin your faithful servant Dominic found me, with both hands filled by the gift of charity: the right with the honey-sweet letters of your affection, the left made most pleasing by a twofold kind of gift. [Col. 0349B] No delay of tardiness held me back from having this little letter, which you now hold in your hand, written that very day, after summoning a notary, so that I might satisfy your venerable will. Thus you would know with certainty how great is my haste to fulfill the commands of your desire. Then, so that you may know how great a mercy God Almighty has shown me—for all the possessions I had in various places,

[Col. 0349C] *I chose helpers for myself from among my own sons.* Our renowned Mabillon once believed in his *Eulogy of Blessed Alcuin*, section 11, number 62, that Alcuin divided the administration of his monasteries among his disciples in 804: the monastery of Saint Martin to Fridugisus and Ferrières to Sigulfus, and that he did not die until 815. But the distinguished man later withdrew this opinion in Book 27 of his *Annals*, page 367, and at the end of volume V of the *Acts*. The present letter leaves no doubt that in this year 800 Alcuin chose from among his disciples helpers in the administration of his monasteries and possessions. See note *e* to the preceding letter.

I chose helpers for myself from among my own sons, with my lord David approving all my requests.

But you, by prudent counsel, consider the will of Almighty God and the honor of the holy Church of God, so that the better man may be chosen as head of the churches of the order, and so that an impious crime may not be left unpunished. It is less dangerous to offend human beings than God. If every murder is punished by the laws, what judgment should be made

[Col. 0349D] *Concerning that murder.* Alcuin is here speaking of the murder, or violent death, of a certain person holding a higher ecclesiastical dignity; and that it was perpetrated impiously and cruelly in a notable place and at a notable time is sufficiently shown by the context itself. It cannot at all be understood of the cruelty inflicted by the Romans upon Pope Leo in the preceding year. He was not killed, but blinded and mutilated in the tongue, and left half alive. Nor in Rome in this year was the selection of a new pontiff being discussed by the envoys of King Charles—a course Alcuin opposed in Letter 118 (to Arno)—but rather the restoration of Leo to his own see. No other bishop is mentioned by the historians as having been cruelly killed in that year or the preceding one. Could Alcuin’s words instead refer to the death of John, patriarch of Grado, whom John, duke of Venice, caused through his son Mauricius to be thrown from a very high tower? But the unanimous opinion of historians is that this death occurred in 802 or the following year. On this, see Dissertation 6 of M. de Madrisi’s *Works of Saint Paulinus of Aquileia*.

of that murder which was committed so impiously and cruelly against such a person, in such a place, and at such a time? I fear that it may one day be avenged by pagans if Christians do not impose a punishment proportionate to such impiety. Yet I am not recommending anyone’s death, since God says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel 33:11). Rather, let punishment be imposed by wise counsel through other kinds of penalties, or by condemnation to perpetual exile, so that all may recognize that the rulers of the Christian people possess the zeal of the Lord; that the dignity of the priesthood may remain inviolate; that the voice of the corrector may be free; and that the defiance of the one who speaks back [perhaps: “the slanderer”] may be suppressed. It is thought

[Col. 0350C] *And that your case with the Saxons may be brought to an end more quickly.* No one says that Arno had any case with the Saxons. I think that in the words “it is thought, and your case,” there is a corruption, and that perhaps one should read “it is thought safe,” or something similar. Certainly, the persistent resistance of the Saxons still caused King Charles much trouble in this year and prevented the remaining affairs of the kingdom and the Church from being handled more successfully. Hence in Letter 95 he also advised the king “to make peace with the wicked people—the Saxons.” And in Letter 96 he says: “Would that divine grace might at some time grant you freedom from the wicked people of the Saxons, so that you could travel, govern kingdoms, and administer justice.” Again, in Letter 108: “The destruction of the Huns is our negligence toward those laboring among the accursed race of the Saxons . . . and our neglect of those whom we could have had with greater reward before God and glory before human beings,” and so forth.

it is thought, and that your case with the Saxons may be brought to an end more quickly, if truth can nevertheless be found amid lies. Moreover, the devil seeks causes of every kind so that justice and the protection of the holy Church may be hindered. Ah, may that day come when I may be permitted to see the sweetest face of your piety and hear your most gracious speech.

When

[Col. 0350D] *When we had a dispute with Felix.* Namely, at the Council of Aachen toward the end of the year 799. In that year, the thirty-second of the glorious King Charles, Alcuin engaged Felix in a rational disputation in his presence, “and truly defeated him and made him Catholic,” as he himself writes in Book I *Against Elipandus*. It must therefore be held with certainty that the present letter was given in this present year 800, after the sixth day before the Kalends of July.

We had a great dispute with the heretic Felix in the presence of the lord king and the holy Fathers, but he remained hardened for a long time and acknowledged no authority except the judgment of his own sect, thinking himself wiser than everyone else in the very matter in which he was more foolish than all. But when divine mercy finally visited his heart, he confessed that he had been led astray by a false opinion and declared that he firmly held the Catholic faith. [Col. 0351A] Since we did not know the secrets of his heart, we left the matter to the judge of hidden things, entrusting him to

[Col. 0351C] *To Bishop Leidrad.* Bishop of Lyon, who was sent to Spain this year with Nefridius and Benedict to eradicate completely the impiety of the heresy spread there by Felix and Elipandus. Alcuin confirms this here, and we have explained it elsewhere.

to Bishop Leidrad, our most beloved son, so that he might keep Felix with him and test whether what he claimed to believe was true. And

[Col. 0351D] *If he had wished to condemn his former error by his letters, etc.* Felix had therefore not yet issued at the Council of Aachen the confession that he later sent to the clergy and people of Urgel; he published it only afterward.

if he wished by his letters to condemn his former error, which he had previously preached obstinately. The lord king had earlier considered sending him

[Col. 0351D] *To Archbishop Riculfus of Mainz.* Two letters to him survive in the Harleian codex, which we present below.

to Archbishop Riculfus, to be preserved and corrected; and that his priest, who was worse than his teacher, should be sent to you and your prudence was also said. But while they declared that they had been converted [manuscript: “converted,” singular] to the Catholic faith, they were then given to our aforesaid brother to be tested as to what the truth was. And he [Leidradus], with

[Col. 0351D] *With the abbots Benedict and Nefridius.* Alcuin sent books against Elipandus to them and to Leidradus; see the letter prefixed to those books. It is remarkable that Nefridius, who was bishop of Narbonne, is here placed after Abbot Benedict and called an abbot. He was nevertheless also abbot of the monastery of Urbion, commonly called that of the Blessed Virgin of Crassus. See Mabillon, Book 27 of the *Annals*, no. 49, page 376.

the abbots Benedict and Nefridius, was sent into those western regions [Col. 0351B] to extinguish and remove the infidelities of this most depraved assertion. With ecclesiastical writings our insignificance assisted them as far as it could,

[Col. 0352C] *With ecclesiastical writings.* These are enumerated by Alcuin in another letter to the same men: a letter to Elipandus; [Col. 0352D] his reply to that same letter; four books against the same man; Elipandus’s letter to Felix after Felix’s conversion; and Felix’s confession of faith published after his conversion.

especially with the little book that we recently published against that Felix’s little book,

[Col. 0352D] *Which he sent to us the previous year.* It follows from this that the year in which Alcuin received Felix’s little book, which Felix composed in opposition to his brotherly exhortation, was 799. Therefore Letters 83, 84, and 90—which, before seeing the present letter, we assigned to 798—must be connected with that year.

which he sent to us the previous year.

My Candidus has praised your way of life and your devoted zeal for every kind of goodness, together with your holy concern for ecclesiastical authority, so highly that I am almost ashamed of my own laziness.

I considered it rash to write any brief words of admonition to your venerable authority unless I recalled blessed Jerome’s saying that gold found in a dung heap should be praised and inserted into the Lord’s treasury. For the blessed apostle Paul transferred the gold of wisdom, found in the dung of the poets, into the riches of ecclesiastical understanding; and all the holy teachers instructed by his example did the same. A rose born among thorns is recognized as possessing grace of incomparable fragrance and color. In the same way, let your piety read my letters as a rose among thorns, so that, if you find any good fragrance in them, thanks may be given to the giver of all good things, who is able to create a rose from dust and raise the poor from dung, so that he may possess a throne of glory and sit with the princes of his people.

I sent to your charity three little gifts: a tent, to protect your venerable head from the rains; a little mantle, to warm your sacred breast; and a cup, in which bread may be enclosed [perhaps: “dipped”] at table, so that these objects, in their several places, may continually impress upon your holiness the memory of my name.

[Col. 0352D] Froben, Letter 177.

## LETTER 118. TO AQUILA. (Year uncertain.)

He expresses his affection to Arno, whom he calls his son, and wishes him every good thing.

To his most beloved son Aquila, Albinus sends greetings.

I know that you are a father in dignity and merit, but out of the sweetness of charity I have given you the name [supply: “of son”], because nothing ought to be dearer to a father than a son—especially when the son surpasses his father in every goodness and dignity. Whether entering or leaving, waking or [Col. 0352B] sleeping, the sweetness of paternal affection always follows you. Would that you might have it in mouth and heart, in the service of the holy altar, in tears

[Col. 0352D] *Before the feet of the holy apostles.* Arno was therefore in Rome when this letter was written. Since he visited there several times—namely, in 797 on behalf of his own church, in 799 in the retinue of Pope Leo, and since he may also have stayed there for some time in the year 800—it remains uncertain to which of these years the letter belongs. I have nevertheless judged it should be joined to the preceding letter to the same Arno.

before the feet of the holy apostles. Indeed, wherever you go, may it go with you, and may its eternal memory remain with you, because the affection of that charity always follows you as you go and return.

Know with absolute certainty that an anxious mother awaiting the arrival of her traveling son does not long for him as ardently as the burning desire of my heart awaits the sight of your face. I have written little, although you know much more and understand better what pleases God according to human judgment and conjecture. May God give you counsel in your heart, confidence in your mouth, and perfection in your works, so that in every respect you may please him who raised you from dung and set you among the princes of his people. Without him we can do nothing good; in him the one who resolves to do or say everything for his name in faith and charity can do all things. May his charity shine with perpetual flames in your heart and extinguish every flame of earthly desire, so that God alone may always be in the mouth, heart, and charitable works of your life. In him, I pray, may you live happily in enduring prosperity, my most beloved son!

[Col. 0353C] Froben, Letter 178.

## LETTER 119. TO CHARLES, THE YOUNG KING.

He congratulates Charles, son of Charlemagne, because he has received the royal title with a crown from the apostolic lord; and he offers excellent counsels for ruling well, after the example of his father.

[Col. 0353A]

To the illustrious man worthy of every honor

[Col. 0353C] Charles, the young king. He was the eldest son of Charlemagne by Queen Hildegard, born in 772, and later distinguished by his successful deeds and victories. He died before his father in 811.

To Charles, the young and renowned king, Albinus sends greetings.

I have heard

[Col. 0353C]

that the apostolic lord placed upon you the royal title with a crown. There is a profound silence among writers concerning this royal coronation of Charles by the apostolic lord. Everyone among the annalists of that age agrees that Pippin and Louis, the younger sons of Charlemagne, were anointed kings by Pope Hadrian I in 781; but all are silent about Charles, the eldest. We now possess Alcuin’s clear and indisputable testimony to this event, which I think should be referred to this year 800 and to the day on which his father Charles was likewise adorned with the imperial crown by Pope Leo III. For here Alcuin calls him the ruler and emperor of the Christian people. My conjecture also seems to be strengthened by the testimony of Anastasius the Librarian in his *Life of Pope Leo III*, where he says: “Immediately the most holy bishop and pontiff anointed Charles with holy oil, and his most excellent son as king, on the very day of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ.” I know that the distinguished Dom Martin Bouquet, volume V of the *History of France*, page 466, in the notes, along with others, interprets this of Pippin, son of Charles, who, having come into the city with an army under the leadership of Winigis, duke of Spoleto, was there anointed king [Col. 0354C]—namely, of Italy. But, as we said above, Pippin had already been anointed king of Italy by Pope Hadrian long before. Anastasius, therefore, must be understood to mean Charles, son of Charles, the eldest, who was now crowned by Pope Leo as the future successor in the kingdom. I also think that Frodoard sang of the same event, in Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, part II, third century, page 504, in these verses:

[Col. 0354D]

> From the apostolic seat the king receives the august crown;  
> The honor of the Roman Fathers is proclaimed increased;  
> The scepters of the Frankish empire shine with splendor;  
> And he born to kingship rises to the kingdom by sacred anointing.

Who is more born for kingship than the firstborn? Therefore Sirmondus wished, without justification, to correct the heading of poem 25 in book IV of the poems of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, addressed to King Charles—namely, the son of the great Charles. For, as Alcuin asserts here, he was a king not merely in the honor of the name but also in power: “the apostolic lord imposed upon you the royal name, with the consent of my lord, the most excellent David, together with the crown of royal dignity.” Hence I rejoice, indeed I rejoice, in the honor both of name and of power, wishing your dignity and nobility to benefit many peoples, nations, and churches of Christ for salvation, to be renowned throughout the world in the glory of triumph, and likewise to be terrifying to the adversaries of the Christian religion; may you flourish and prosper in lasting prosperity, always pursue better things with God’s blessing, ascend to higher things, and grow until the perfect day of eternal blessedness.

Therefore, my most beloved son, practice and cause to be practiced justice and mercy among the Christian people, because these are the things which, as Solomon testifies (Proverbs 16:12), exalt the throne of a kingdom and make royal power praiseworthy and pleasing to God. Have good, pious, prudent counselors who fear God, men in whom truth reigns, not greed, because bribes blind the hearts of the wise and overturn the words of the just (Exodus 23:8). Let no one’s wickedness obscure the name of your dignity; and what you yourself do not wish to do, do not permit others, because of their greed, to carry out wickedly, since the fault of subjects is often charged to their masters. Nor should the impious will of certain people, under the name of your blessedness, fill their purses with the mammon of iniquity.

You need not seek examples far away, for in the household in which you were raised you have the finest examples of every goodness. And believe with complete certainty that, by God’s gift, you will obtain the blessing of that most excellent and in every virtue most noble father of yours, the ruler and emperor of the Christian people, if you strive to imitate his nobility, piety, and entire moderation of conduct; and that you will fully merit the Lord’s mercy, which is better than all the glory of the world. Wherever you travel, may the footsteps of piety always follow you, so that you may have praise among human beings and an everlasting reward before God.

May the world’s great hope always flourish forever.

May Christ be your love, light, way, life, and salvation.

[Col. 0354D] Froben, Letter 179.

## LETTER 120. TO THE SAME.

[Col. 0354D] We join this letter to the preceding one, addressed to the same Charles, although from its wording it cannot be established with any great certainty whether it was written in the same year or in some other year. Nevertheless, from the words “Nor permit judges subject to your authority,” and so forth, it seems possible to infer that Charles already possessed royal power at that time.

He again exhorts Charles to royal virtues and to imitate his father’s example. He prays for prosperity for him.

[Col. 0354B] To Charles, a lord deservedly distinguished and most worthy of royal honor, his son, Albinus sends triumphal salvation in Christ.

I rejoice, my most beloved son, in your devotion to good will, which I have heard about from your servant Osulf—both concerning the frequency of your almsgiving and concerning your humility in the Mandatum (the foot-washing). Know with complete certainty that all these things greatly please God and win for you a perpetual blessing from his mercy. You, my son—my most beloved son—practice and cause to be practiced, as far as you are able, the honor of almighty God always, in every goodness and piety, following the examples of your most excellent father in all honesty and sobriety, so that the divine mercy of Christ our God may grant you to possess his blessing by hereditary right.

[Col. 0354C] Be a compassionate hearer of the poor, discerning their cases with the greatest justice; and do not permit judges subject to your authority to judge for fees or rewards, because bribes, as Scripture says, blind the hearts of the wise and overturn the words of the just (Exodus 23:8). Keep as your honored servants those who are servants of Christ in truth, because some come in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves; yet the Truth says: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:15–16). Have wise counselors who fear God, not flatterers, because a flatterer, as it is said, is a smooth-tongued enemy and often deceives those who consent to him. Be prudent in thought and cautious in speech, always placing your hope in God, who never abandons those who hope in him.

Would that I might more often send a little letter of admonition to Your Nobility, as your most noble—

[Col. 0355D] Chlodwig, your brother. From this passage it becomes clear that Alcuin also wrote several letters to Louis, the third son of Charles the Great by Hildegard, later emperor, although none of them has yet been discovered. Chlodwig, your brother, repeatedly asked me to send him admonitory letters, which I have already done and, God willing, shall continue to do; he is also accustomed to read them with great humility. This is my greatest joy: when I hear of the good conduct you display, as is fitting. For it is a gift of God and a prosperity of the kingdom when the rulers of the Christian people live with the most refined morals and conduct themselves among human beings in a manner pleasing to God. It is entirely certain that heavenly blessing reaches the nation and kingdom from this; may God deem your nobility worthy to possess it eternally. Flourish, prosper, and grow, advancing in every good thing and prosperity for the exaltation of his holy Church, my sweetest son!

[Col. 0355D] Froben, Letter 180.

## LETTER 121. TO THE SONS RESIDING IN THE PALACE WITH THE LORD EMPEROR  
*(Year 800.)*

[Col. 0355D] Residing in the palace with the lord emperor. Below he asks them to remember him at the threshold of the holy Apostles, and says that his little letter would fly beyond the Alpine hills. He therefore wrote this letter while the emperor was in Rome and Alcuin was at Tours, in the year 800 or the following year.

He displays his affection for his sons and entrusts his memory to them at the threshold of the Apostles.

[Col. 0355C] To his dearest sons in Christ, their father sends perpetual salvation.

I would have had very much to write to you if a dove or raven were present, one that could have carried my little letters to you on a faithful flight. Nevertheless, I have sent these few lines into the air, so that the wind might carry them into your hands—unless perhaps the west wind should change into the east wind. Let the north wind or the south wind rise and carry my little letter, so that it may bid you farewell and announce to you our prosperity, as well as my great desire to see you soon in that state of health which a father wishes for his sons. I, troubled and fearful, watch to see when this may happen, and what I shall hear about you.

Oh, how happy was the day when, amid our labors, we played together at serious literary pursuits. But now everything has changed. The old man remains, begetting other sons, lamenting those who came before and are scattered; but what does the accursed hunger for gold not accomplish! Nevertheless, let there be spiritual presence where there is bodily separation. With abundant tears remember your father at the threshold of the holy Apostles, praying for prosperity for my sinful soul, that it may be freed from the bonds of the crimes it has committed from the first day to the last of this life.

What happened, my sons? Why did the little letter not fly beyond the Alpine hills, through the hands of the returning Saxons, to the holy shrine of the city of Troyes?

[Col. 0355D] This, I think, should be understood as referring to the church of Saint Lupus, or the monastery in the suburb of Troyes, which Charles the Great entrusted to Alcuin’s care; he also mentions it in Letters 66, 67, and elsewhere. “The holy shrine of the city of Troyes”; and from there, might it fly through the hands of our people to the venerable church of the city of Tours?

[Col. 0356D] Froben, Letter 181.

## LETTER 122. TO RICULF, ARCHBISHOP, ALSO CALLED DAMOETAS  
*(Year uncertain.)*

[Col. 0356D] Also called Damoetas. The Harleian manuscript itself has this heading. Before this letter came before my eyes, I believed, with D. Basnage, that the heading of Letter 40 in Quercetanus—“To Riculf, archbishop of the city of Mainz, also called Damoetas”—was erroneous; and I thought that the name Damoetas belonged not to some bishop but to a secular man who presided both over warfare and the administration of justice. I believed this could be inferred from two other letters, namely 44 and 46, especially since the heading was absent both in Canisius and in the old Salzburg manuscript that was available to me. But now, from this and the following letter, it is perfectly clear that Alcuin also called Riculf, archbishop of Mainz, Damoetas.

He exhorts him to labor and to apostolic virtues. [Col. 0356B]

To the great fisherman Damoetas, Albinus sends greetings.

May he who, walking beside the Sea of Galilee, commanded the brothers who were fishing together, saying, “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4:19), deign to lead you, laboring upon the sea of this life, into the harbor of perpetual rest, together with the abundant fruit of your labor. Cast your net on the right side of the boat (Mark 1:17), so that it may be filled from the depths of this world with great fish, whose names may be written in heaven (John 21:6). Do not be terrified by the stormy tempest which the Lord, walking upon it, trod beneath dry feet, and upon which he looked with compassion at Peter as he was sinking [perhaps the reading should be: “freed him by his compassion, just as he looked upon him when he was denying him,” and so forth], so that the stain of the threefold denial might be cleansed by the glory of a threefold confession (Matthew 14:25, 30). Remember Solomon’s command: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do it earnestly, for there is neither work nor reasoning in the underworld” (Ecclesiastes 9:10), that is, in the grave, toward which the flesh hastens.

Let your hand be apostolic in almsgiving, and your tongue devoted to the ministry of preaching. Remember the Lord saying, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it.” Let your banquets be held with complete sobriety, as the Lord commands: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke 21:34). Let your right hand often be burdened with the pages of the Gospels, so that your soul may be nourished with spiritual food. Let the examples of the saints be before your eyes, those who courageously conquered the world and now reign happily with Christ. Do not fall short of your predecessors, so that, since you occupy their chair, you may be made worthy to equal their merits in heaven.

Do not find it burdensome to read this little letter of charity, nor think it superfluous, because it presents things already known. If small gifts of refined gold please those who are known to you, let the consolations of spiritual wisdom please you as well. In the former there is a fleeting delight of the eyes; in the latter, an unfailing treasure of the soul. For the Truth says: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matthew 7:12).

My mind awaits the writings of Your Blessedness with great longing; therefore I strive to send my letters to your authority more often, wishing that you might not only make progress through my letters but also frequently encourage me through yours.

[Col. 0357D] Froben, Letter 182.

## LETTER 123. TO DAMOETAS, THE HIGH PRIEST  
*(Year 800.)*

He exhorts Damoetas, who was in Rome, to strive to repair the division in the Church; he rebukes disagreement among the peacemakers. He wishes not that something new be established, but that ancient things be repaired. [Col. 0357B]

To the venerable Father and magnificent member of Christ,

[Col. 0357D] To Damoetas, the high priest. That is, to Riculf of Mainz, to whom the preceding letter was written; see its note. To Damoetas, the high priest, the humble master Albinus sends greetings.

According to the opportunity afforded by the bearer, the charity known to our minds urges my tongue to dictate something of a fatherly greeting to Your Belovedness, so that you may know that the flame of our ancient love shines undiminished in my breast. I shall never cease to love the one whom I have always found faithful, because charity which can be abandoned, according to the old proverb, was never true.

Having therefore heard of your prosperity, your praiseworthy conduct, and your perseverance in the truth—

[Col. 0357D] And how you stood with the apostolic lord. From these words and from the rest of the tenor of this letter, I consider it beyond doubt that Damoetas, or Riculf, accompanied Leo III, together with Hildebold of Cologne, Arno of Salzburg, and other bishops and royal envoys, when the pope returned to Rome in the autumn of 799 from the court of Charles the Great, and that in this year and the next he took part in the judgment against the impious adversaries of that most holy pontiff, although no other writer of that period has reported this about Riculf. Yet Alcuin’s testimony is sufficient, being superior to all exception. And when I heard how you stood with the apostolic lord, in accordance with the letter of my request, the innermost chambers of my heart immediately sprang forth into joy, once the reins of sadness had been loosened and their doors opened; in a full voice I began to sing with the Apostle: “I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in faith and truth” (3 John 4). And I marveled that certain wise men had read, with the deaf ear of their hearts, the apostolic preface: “There is no authority except from God; and whoever resists authority resists the ordinance of God” (Romans 13:1–2). For all things that come from God are ordered.

Therefore I would have had sufficient material for disputing this matter. But knowing that your prudence understands all these things perfectly, and that you pass with the swiftest perception through the series of my letters, I offer only this admonition: let the deeds most upright correspond to the name of your highest dignity, and let conduct marked by complete equity adorn the most holy priestly mantle of honor, so that what appears upon the shoulder to the eyes of many may be proclaimed and loved by the mouths of all in your conduct.

Formerly we recognized you laboring all night with blessed Peter amid the waves. But now, at God’s command, you must cast the net on the right side of the boat with the blessed prince of the Apostles (John 21:11), so that you may catch, without a tear in the net—that is, in the perfection of the Catholic faith—153 great fish, whose meaning I remember once explaining to Your Holiness.

[Col. 0358D] Whether Alcuin did this in words or in writing is not clear from the passage. In the preceding letter he touched upon this passage from John’s Gospel, but left the mystery of that number of great fish unexplained—unless someone should wish to suppose that the letter has been mutilated. Alcuin nevertheless explained the same mystery in his commentary on the Gospel of Saint John, at chapter 21:11. I remember explaining it. But, alas, what grief, that so great a tear has suddenly been made in the apostolic net, where that greatest fisher of souls rests in his most sacred body! Scarcely could the assembled crowd of holy teachers from different parts of the world repair the tear of impious dissension with the threads of pious charity. Moreover, as I have heard—and I shall not say this without pain—the teachers themselves are wickedly in disagreement with one another.

Some wish to put a patch of raw cloth into an old garment and make the tear worse (Matthew 9:16; Mark 2:21); others, with better counsel, wish to reform old things and restore them to their ancient order. We have heard that your most holy concern labors together with the latter, and I greatly rejoiced that, according to God, you are sowers of pious peace and ecclesiastical harmony. In this I always desire your goodwill to labor, remembering the Lord’s sweetest gift to his own: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you; not as the world gives do I give to you” (John 14:27).

The saints, peaceful in every good thing, ought to be at peace with one another in one way; sinners are very often known to have peace among themselves in another way, as is read in the holy Gospel concerning Herod and Pilate (Luke 23:12). But that peace which is accustomed to exist among the saints was foretold by the prophet at the Lord’s command, when he said: “Love peace and truth, says the almighty Lord” (Zechariah 8:19). And the distinguished Preacher says: “May the peace of Christ, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts in charity and holiness” (Philippians 4:7). May your religious piety and venerable authority always pursue this peace with all who serve God. The angelic host sang of this peace when the Lord was born, saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). In this peace, and in every good thing, I desire Your Blessedness to advance, with divine grace assisting, venerable lord and most dearly desired son!

[Col. 0359C] Froben, Letter 183.

## LETTER 124. TO GEORGE, PATRIARCH OF THE CITY OF JERUSALEM

[Col. 0359C] He extracted this previously unpublished and hitherto unknown letter from the Royal Paris manuscript no. 2826 and kindly communicated it to me—a most learned man and my dearest friend, D. Lieble, the Benedictine and librarian of Saint-Germain, mentioned above.

[Col. 0359D] To George the patriarch, and so forth. At the suggestion of the aforementioned D. Lieble, I learned of this letter from the excellent preliminary treatise on the bishops and patriarchs of the holy Church of Jerusalem, prefixed to volume III of the May Acta Sanctorum, p. 40, no. 174, by D. Daniel Papebrochius, S.J. There he testifies that George’s name is certainly expressed in the Life of Saint Stephen the Sabaite, published in volume III of the July Acta Sanctorum, on July 13. For there, chapter 5, no. 49, one reads:

> “The most holy patriarch, the lord Elias, returned with joy and honor to his own see, and for quite many years enjoyed the dignity of the patriarchate; and when he departed holily from this life to God, he left his own syncellus, George, as his successor in the Theadelphian see.”

Papebrochius then notes that this George is called Gregory in the Bruges manuscript, a neighboring and easily interchangeable name; but in the manuscript of Roubais he is called Sergius. The learned man believes that this George was ordained around the year 799 and was that patriarch of Jerusalem on whose behalf “a certain monk coming from Jerusalem brought King Charles, in the year 799, a blessing and relics from the holy place of the Lord’s Resurrection,” as the annalists Einhard, the Bishop of Metz, and others relate. They further testify that in the year 800, after the king had celebrated Christmas at Aachen, he released the aforesaid monk and sent him away with Zacharias, the priest of his palace, with much money to distribute among those holy places, among the poor, and among people afflicted by many hardships. See also R. P. Michel Le Quien, O.P., Christian Orient, vol. III, p. 317. On this timely occasion, therefore, I have no doubt that Alcuin sent this letter to George the patriarch by the priest Zacharias.

He congratulates George on his dignity in the holiest place and exhorts him to patience amid the persecution of unbelievers. He commends himself and his companions to George’s prayers. [Col. 0359A]

Blessed be God and our Lord Jesus Christ, who visited his people, chose the city of Jerusalem, made it most holy by the blood of our redemption, and most glorious through the resurrection of that same God and our Lord. Blessed also is his mercy, by which he chose you, most holy patriarch George, in the holiest places of his dwelling and of our redemption, as an intercessor for his holy Church, which throughout the whole breadth of the world [perhaps: “manifests,” rather than “offends”] praises, venerates, and adores the name of the Lord, the eternal God. May you be in that place a preacher of the most blessed peace in which he himself walked with feet holier than those of the whole world, he who said: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27); may you be the ruler of his people and a preacher of the truth to all visitors to the holy places. Blessed are you, to whom it has been granted to pour out tears at the feet of him who, with a merciful countenance, said to the sinful woman who washed his holy feet with tears: “Because she loved much, many sins are forgiven her” (Luke 7:47).

Exhort your companions in tribulation, through pious prayers, fatherly affection, and holy longing, to remain steadfast in the faith of Christ God and patiently to endure the various persecutions of unbelievers, remembering him who, for their salvation, hung upon the cross and said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). “The sufferings of this present time,” says the distinguished Preacher, “are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to come, which will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18). No soldier will be crowned except one who fights lawfully. The labor of the tribulation of this life is brief, but the reward that will be given to those who conquer is eternal. Let no one of the faithful forget the most delightful promise of our Lord Jesus Christ, who said: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

[Col. 0360A] I also beg, through his mercy, that you remember me in your holy prayers—he who said: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew 18:20). This promise is perfectly fulfilled in those who are joined not only bodily but also by perfect charity.

I, Albinus, have a name among acquaintances [the manuscript reads *notes*; perhaps read *nostros*, “our people,” or *nostrates*, “our countrymen”], and among the sons of the holy Church of God. Know also that your name is remembered with us during the offices of the sacred altar. Take courage, brothers, as men, in Christ Jesus and in his strength, and act confidently in the Catholic faith. Be patient toward all, knowing that your labor is not in vain in the Lord (1 Thessalonians 5:14; 1 Corinthians 15:58); rather, the one who labors more will receive the greater reward. Ascend in mind and holy desire to him who said: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24).

We desire that, with the grace of Christ cooperating, what the Prophet once said may be fulfilled in you: “From Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2:3). From there let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matthew 5:16).

May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to hear Your Holiness, who intercedes for the holy Church of God, and make you advance in every good thing for the salvation of many [“salvation” or something similar is missing]. Venerable lord patriarch and most desired Father, I beg you also to deign to intercede for our sons: for Bishop Symeon, for the priests Onia and Martin, and for the archdeacon Nathanael—

[Col. 0360D] Concerning Symeon, Onia, and Nathanael, Alcuin’s disciples, we have made further observations elsewhere; who Martin was is unknown.

—and for the others who are with us and who do not cease to intercede for your blessedness. I wish you farewell forever in the name of the Lord God Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0360D] Froben, Letter 184.

## LETTER 125. TO GUNDRADA, A VIRGIN ALSO CALLED EULALIA  
*(Year 800.)*

[Col. 0360D] Also called Eulalia. It is now clear from this heading in the Harleian manuscript that Eulalia, to whom Alcuin addressed the little book On the Nature of the Soul, which we shall present below among the moral treatises, was really named Gundrada. She was certainly a sister of Saint Adalhard, abbot of Corbie, concerning whom Paschasius Ratbertus writes in the Life of Saint Adalhard, Acta Sanctorum of the Order of Saint Benedict, fourth century, part I, p. 321, no. 33:

> “A virgin, the noblest of the noble, who amid the alluring pleasures of the palace and the beauty of young men, amid the soothing delights and every enticement of lust, alone, as we believe, deserved to carry away the palm of chastity and was able, as they say, to pass through the impurities of the flesh along an uninjured path.”

Alcuin here testifies that this praise of chastity and propriety had also reached his own ears.

He instructs Gundrada how to live virtuously at court. He wishes to be commended to the king through her and to have his inability to reach the king excused.

To Eulalia, his venerable daughter in Christ, Albinus sends greetings.

[Col. 0361A] Familiarity often brings about a change of name, just as the Lord himself changed Simon into Peter and named the sons of Zebedee “Sons of Thunder” (Mark 3:16–17); this you can also prove in ancient times or in these more recent days.

You, most illustrious virgin and bride most worthy of God, guard yourself in every chastity of body and soul, because, according to the Apostle, God’s virgin ought to be chaste in body and soul (1 Corinthians 7:34). Be an example of every goodness to the other virgins in the palace, so that from your holy conduct they may learn to guard themselves or to rise again when they fall. Let them go before the face of the Judge through conversion. Let them be noble in conduct, as they are noble by birth. Let them not serve carnal desire but the teaching of Christ. Let them live honorably before human beings and worthily before God.

Let them repent of the past and guard themselves against the future, because Scripture says: “God grants penitents a share in righteousness” (Ecclesiasticus 17:20). Everything we do in secret is known to the Lord; and if the tongue has not uttered it [perhaps the reading is *dixerit*, “has spoken”], conscience will not be able to conceal it. Everything closed is open to God. Let a person believe that all sin is pardonable if, in confession, he goes before the face of God (Psalm 94:2); yet many things done in secret are spoken of publicly, because “a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5:14). The lowliness of a poor person hides enormous crimes; dignity, though often present, scarcely conceals what it does. What is done within the walls runs through everyone’s mouth. Understand what I say, and forgive the one who says it.

May the goodness of chastity and propriety that I have heard about you never depart from you. Do not let security deceive you; let your praise not diminish but increase, and may your present happiness advance toward eternal happiness. Remember that you are a guest for a brief time. Be consolation to the miserable and counsel to the fearful; a noble vessel of the holy Scriptures and a dwelling place of heavenly wisdom. Adorn your soul with evangelical commandments: modest in speech, prudent in counsel, patient under insult, humble in your words, watchful in prayer, generous in almsgiving, and praiseworthy in every goodness.

For me also, I beg you, speak as an intercessor for your prosperity to my lord David, so that he may not be angry with his servant—

[Col. 0361D] Because I was unable to come. He had been summoned by the king to accompany him when he was setting out for Rome in the year 800; he excused himself from the hardships of that journey because of bodily illness and his love of quiet in the monastery of Saint Martin, in Letter 93, now 109, to the king. See also Letter 92, now 108, to Arno.

—because I was unable to come as he wished, being continually hindered by illness. My only work is to persist in prayers and prepare eternal dwellings for myself, according to the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, who does not abandon those who hope in him. Farewell in eternal blessedness, my dearest daughter!

[Col. 0361D] Quercetanus edition 56; Canisius 55; Frobenius, Letter 98.

## LETTER 126. TO HIS DEAREST SISTER  
*(Year 801.)*

He praises her piety and exhorts her to labor for eternity; he gives thanks for the cross she sent.

[Col. 0362B] To his dearest sister in Christ.

[Col. 0361D] Sister. Namely, his spiritual sister Gisla, who was the natural sister of Charles the Great and at whose request Alcuin also undertook his commentaries on the Gospel of John. There was another Gisla, Charles’s daughter, whom Alcuin usually called not his sister but his daughter. Mabillon, Annals, book 26, no. 93.

I truly confess that I greatly desired to come to you because of certain matters which I wished to discuss with you. But I was prevented by the severity of fevers, which still wear me down intermittently. Therefore I shall take care to hurry to meet the king sooner, before the winter cold. I am greatly pleased by your labor in the church of the holy Mother of God—

[Col. 0362D] Church of the Mother of God. “Gisla, abbess of the Parthenon of Chelles, at this time, in the year 800, arranged for a new basilica to be built there in honor of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God, and transferred the nuns there from the basilica of the Holy Cross. Some years later the body of Saint Balthild was transferred from the crypt of the Holy Cross into that same church of Saint Mary, which Lady Gisla had built from its foundations,” as is read in the History of the Translation of Saint Balthild in Mabillon, Acta Sanctorum, fourth Benedictine century, part I, p. 452, no. 8. See also Mabillon, Annals, book 26, no. 93. Nevertheless, I believe the present letter was dated not in the same year, 800, but in the following year, because in the year 800 Alcuin could not have met King Charles before winter, since after August of that year the king was already on the road toward Rome.

—and in the advancement of the church of the holy Mother of God, and in the study of books. Therefore, in these labors, we rejoice to assist your diligence as far as we can. And the boy—

[Col. 0362D] Fredegisus, Alcuin’s disciple and later his successor in the governance of the monastery of Tours.

—Fredegisus will bring you assistance at a suitable time. Your progress in God is a great joy to my heart. Therefore strive most diligently to complete what you have begun, with God’s mercy assisting. Everyone will receive a reward according to his labor; and the one who labors more will receive the greater reward. Now is the time for working; the time for recompense will come. Let us prepare ourselves now to be the kind of people we wish to be then. A little is enough for the wise. I know that the keenness of your mind has understood all these things better than I have expressed them in writing and will fulfill in deeds what I can scarcely explain in words.

Would that the time might soon come when I could share with you the anxieties of my heart, so that my spirit might be consoled by the consolation of your piety [Alcuin’s reading: “perfection”]. I am greatly pleased with the cross which your kindness sent me. And I believe that you will have an eternal reward from God for the work involved in it, as well as the continual intercessions of Saint Lupus—

[Col. 0363D] Saint Lupus. “From this,” says Mabillon in the cited passage, Annals, “we understand that this cross was sent to Alcuin for the basilica of Saint Lupus at Troyes, over which Charles had placed him.”

—and the praiseworthy thanksgivings of those who are accustomed to seek refuge in his protection.

Now, gracious sister, farewell; O sister, dearest to us!

Now and always, sweet friend, farewell.

[Col. 0363D] Quercetanus edition 60; Canisius 56; Frobenius, Letter 99.

## LETTER 127. TO HIS MOST BELOVED SISTER

He gives thanks for a cloak and other gifts; he remembers Angilbert, his sister Ava, and Columba.

To his most beloved sister in Christ.

[Col. 0363D] Sister. Likewise, according to Mabillon, Gisla, the sister of Charles the Great.

We have had, by God’s gift, favorable solemnities during these most holy days; the lord king was joyful, and the entire palace was filled with gladness. And I, your brother, also felt great joy at your prosperity and greeting, and at the most welcome gift of the singing of psalms and celebration of Masses, which you sent me with great affection. But also—

[Col. 0363D] A cloak.
