Similar to the one which King Witlaf of Mercia, when giving one, says in the donation preserved in the history of Ingulf: “I also offer to the secretary of the aforesaid monastery, for the service of the most holy altar, a scarlet cloak which I wore at my coronation, to be made into a cloak or chasuble.” Canisius.

—the cloak you sent me, perfectly suited to me, pleases my heart greatly. When Angilbert comes, perhaps we shall have something more definite to report to you. Strengthen your mind in the service of God and in the salvation of your soul. Build for yourselves courageously an eternal house in heaven, so that you may have ready the blessedness with Christ and his saints which many desire in words but do not accomplish in deeds. But you, labor by days, hours, and moments, so that you may abundantly possess what you may love happily.

I believe that you will faithfully act upon the prayers of—

[Col. 0363D] Ava. She seems to have been that servant of God who diligently arranged for the books of the New and Old Testament to be copied; on this account Alcuin praises her in poem formerly numbered 204, now 5.

—our sister Ava [Alcuin: Eva]. But at my request add something more, because she was faithful to me. And where is faithfulness made more evident than after the death of a friend? Say—

[Col. 0364D] Columba. To her, together with Gisla, Alcuin dedicated the last two books of his Commentary on John.

—Columba, that she may commit to memory what she has received, until the one who is to add more comes. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matthew 5:6). May he who came to enlighten the world and drive the darkness of ignorance from the hearts of believers fulfill your desire and illuminate your heart with charity. May life and salvation, by Christ’s gift, accompany you forever.

[Col. 0364D] Mabillon 8, amended in places from the Salzburg manuscript. Frobenius, Letter 100.

## LETTER 128. TO GISLA, DAUGHTER OF CHARLES THE GREAT

He grieves that illness prevents him from seeing the king’s face and enjoying Gisla’s conversation; he exhorts her to virtue.

To his dearest daughter in Christ.

[Col. 0364D] Daughter. Gisla, the third daughter of Charles the Great by Hildegard, as Einhard writes in the Life of Charles. Mabillon.—Certainly Alcuin would not have called Gisla, Charles’s sister, a girl when she was already of more advanced age.

To his faithful daughter in charity, the Father sends perpetual prosperity [and so forth].

[Col. 0364A] The inconveniences of bodily weakness distress my paternal heart above all because, as soon as I wished, I could not present myself to the affection of my lord [David and to yours]. Yet I trust in the mercy of him who is accustomed to raise up the crushed and heal the sick, that he may still fulfill my wish of seeing the face of my lord [most beloved] and enjoying the conversation of your intimacy.

But you, dearest daughter, remember to adorn your dignity with honorable works of mercy and holiness of life, so that your conversion may be praised more for its virtue than for the splendor of gleaming gold. If anyone considers the divine commandments more carefully, he will find in them [both] praise in the present life among human beings and the glory of eternal reward with God. Strive, most noble girl, to learn and fulfill these things with the greatest diligence and deepest devotion, so that you may become worthy [Col. 0364B] of being loved by God and praised by human beings. Then Flaccus has reason to rejoice with every joy, [and, like the old man Entellus, to dance], and to leap for joy with all his strength.

> With distinguished character, virtues, and life as your crown,  
> May you flourish and prosper, dear daughter, for your sake.

@ [Col. 0364D] Quercet’s edition, p. 23, from a manuscript. There it is entitled: “On the praise of wisdom and on the desire for a tranquil life.” Its principal purpose, however, is to express his joy and offer congratulations on Charles’s return from Italy after he had attained the insignia of the Roman Empire. That return occurred in the year 801, after Easter, on 25 April. After the feast of Saint John he returned to Gaul. *Annals of Tilianus.* (Froben, Letter 101.)

## LETTER 129. TO THE LORD KING

*(Year 801, around the end of May.)*

He expresses his joy at Charles’s return from Italy and sends Candidus to meet him with gifts.

To the most desired lord and most worthy of every honor, David, father of his country, Albinus, registrar, sends greetings of present and future blessedness.

Blessed be the Lord God, and blessed be his perpetual mercy toward his servants: for whose prosperity and safety he has led you safely and brought you back in peace, O sweetest David; he has preserved, honored, and exalted you, and in every place of your arrival he has caused the light of justice and piety to shine before the face of your blessedness, so that all the darkness of iniquity and the cloud of perversity might be scattered by the most serene splendor of your wisdom.

Blessed is the nation for which divine mercy has provided so pious and prudent a ruler. Happy is the people governed by a wise and pious prince, as we read in that Platonic saying: kingdoms would be happy if philosophers—that is, lovers of wisdom—ruled, or if kings devoted themselves to philosophy; for nothing in this world can be compared with wisdom. It is she who raises up the humble, makes the powerful glorious, and exists as something praiseworthy in every person; in her are the honor and beauty of the present life [Col. 0365A] as well as the glory of eternal blessedness, because only true wisdom will make our days blessed and everlasting.

I have always recognized that you, my lord David, loved and proclaimed this wisdom with your excellent zeal; that you urged everyone to learn it, indeed even encouraged them with rewards and honors; and that you endeavored to summon lovers of it from different parts of the world to assist your good will. Among these you took care to summon me also, the least little servant of that holy wisdom, from the farthest ends of Britain; and would that I were as useful a little servant in the house of God as I am ready to obey your will! For I diligently cherished in your most sacred heart what I understood you wished to find in me.

Therefore each day, with eager attention of heart and my ears hanging upon the words of those who arrived, I anxiously asked what they were reporting to me about my sweetest lord David: when he would return home, when he would come back to his country. At last, although late, the longed-for voice of those who shared my desire sounded in my ears: “He will come now, now!”

@ [Col. 0365D] “He has already crossed the Alps.” “Charles himself, after celebrating the feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist at Ivrea (a city of Piedmont), crossed the Alps and returned to Gaul.” *Annals of Loiselianus*, under the year 801. He has already crossed the Alps, the one whose arrival you so fervently desired in your heart, O Albinus.

Then, repeating my cry again and again in a tearful voice, I exclaimed: “O Lord Jesus, why do you not give me the wings of an eagle? Why do you not grant me the translation of the prophet Habakkuk in one day, or even one hour, so that I may embrace and kiss the feet of that dearest man of mine and, beyond everything that can be loved in this world, see his most radiant eyes, so sweet to me, and hear his most delightful words? Or why, hostile fever, do you overwhelm me at an inopportune time and not permit me to employ my accustomed bodily vigor, so that what cannot happen quickly may at least happen late?”

Nevertheless, rejoicing at this most welcome news of your arrival, I immediately

@ [Col. 0365D] sent Candidus. This is that Witso, Alcuin’s disciple, whom Pezius incorrectly confuses with another Candidus, a monk of Fulda, concerning whom see *History of the Literature of France*, vol. V, p. 10. — CATELINOT.

I endeavored to send our Candidus to meet your most holy affection, carrying in his hand a little gift as a token of his lord’s favor, certain of [perhaps: a welcome token from] your client, and carrying in his mouth the necessary wishes of his master. I ask that your kindness graciously listen to him.

It is time for weakness to acknowledge its own frailty and to devote itself entirely to the stability of the soul, so that although the outward person is worn down by years or the affliction of illnesses, the inward person may nevertheless be renewed from day to day by the desire for eternal salvation. My mind awaits your piety’s counsel concerning how this ought to be done. For if the rash presumption of combatants often falls into danger, how much more does one who is thinking of entering a spiritual contest sweat through uncertain victories in turn, if he is not guided by prudent counsel?

To prevent this, Holy Scripture has forbidden it, saying: “Do everything with counsel; afterward you will not repent” (Ecclesiasticus 32:24). Knowing this very well, and trusting less in my own judgment, I have resolved to submit myself to the counsel of your prudence. For, as I truly confess, whatever your pious foresight has arranged for me to do through the grace of the merciful God, I have found to have turned out entirely well for me. For nearly

@ [Col. 0366D] five years ago. That is, in the year 796. From this passage, therefore, the time when Alcuin began governing the monastery of Saint Martin can be established.

Nearly five years ago, I considered withdrawing from secular occupations, God is my witness, with no pretended intention. But, on the advice of your pious foresight, I was transferred into the service of Saint Martin, profitable, by God’s gift, to the Catholic faith and ecclesiastical discipline. Nevertheless, the affection of my former intention has not departed from my heart, as I already told your piety when the past year had ended.

Let your goodness consider all these things and arrange them by a pious promise, because, as I have said, the entire intention of my mind looks most truly to the counsel of your goodness. It trusts no other person [perhaps: it does not entrust itself to anyone else], because all the consolation of my weakness and old age rests upon you.

I desire, without any doubt, to live or rest among the brothers faithfully serving God in the church of Saint Martin, by God’s mercy; and I perpetually desire that your affection may share with me in eternal life in the presence of that most blessed breast [perhaps: protector] of yours. I earnestly beseech God that the present life of your Excellence may be assisted, protected, and sustained by the intercession of that holy protector of yours; and that after this life you may deserve to enjoy eternal blessedness with him, my most beloved and most desired lord David.

{152}

@ [Col. 0366D] Mabillon’s edition, p. 16, where the heading is: “To the venerable Father, teacher of evangelical reading.” But here it is published complete and corrected from a manuscript of Salzburg. (Froben, Letter 102.)

## LETTER 130. TO ARNO

*(Year 801.)*

He replies to a letter and removes an unfavorable suspicion from himself. He says that he advised the king whom he should choose as envoys to administer justice. He asks that prayers be offered for him and that he be commended to Pope Leo, Patriarch Paulinus, and Peter of Milan. Finally, he urges him to work toward restoring peace among ecclesiastical persons. [Col. 0366C]

To the venerable Father, eagle of the Gospel, Albinus sends greetings.

The lines of your affection came to me sweeter than honey and more precious than refined gold, sealed with the sweetest little gifts. In them I recognized the perpetual vigor of holy charity in the secret chamber of your heart, which neither Alpine cold nor Italian heat could overthrow; but amid all the changes and shadowy storms of this age it continually rises anew, like the morning star.

Concerning this the Truth himself says: “I give you a new commandment” (John 13:34). New, because it is evangelical; old, because it is legal—in it hangs the whole Law and the Prophets (Matthew 22:40); in it the fullness of all grace consists. New, because it casts out fear (1 John 4:18): what was burdensome through fear will be light through love, as the fountain of charity testifies: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30).

The whole sequence of your little letter shone with the honey of this teaching. Believe me, sweetest Father, that I could not read the little letters of brothers or sisters from across the sea with such sweetness as I read your affection’s

@ [Col. 0367D] brothers and sisters. Alcuin here seems quite clearly to exclude Arno from the number of his brothers. See our preface.

@ [Col. 0367D] Transalpine. Arno was therefore at that time across the Alps in Italy, indeed in Rome, as is also made known by other words of this letter.

transalpine letters; nor does such weariness fatigue my heart after them as follows after the beloved sight of your face. But whatever divine wisdom commands must be endured patiently, for it orders all things gently (Wisdom 8:1) and pours into the hearts of its servants, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, the sweetest gifts of charity. Charity rejoices in being strong amid adversity and humble amid prosperity; in both it is powerful in him who can do all things, secure concerning itself and solicitous concerning its own.

I considered it superfluous to write much about this to your Reverence, because I recognize by many proofs that you are wholly within it. In it you must courageously conquer adversaries and fight bravely against the enemies of the Church [Col. 0367B] of Christ, so that a crown of praise may come to you and yours on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

I was reading certain apologetic words inserted into your letter, thinking that I was angry over some brother, which I certainly was not:

[or that you had heard from another what I wrote, which was in no way true. But to show you the truth of the matter, the occasion of this thought arose from the fact that you took away from me another person who could have made progress. Without any harm to charity, I disclosed my suspicion, not at all thinking that you might suspect benevolence toward me because of my letters, as though another person were not progressing because of my negligence;]

while I truly thought that he would be mine if he had wished to be yours, mindful of that saying of the wise Seneca: “The world has destroyed ‘mine’ and ‘yours.’”

[Never consider anything among your people so intimate that it is not also mine; and know that nothing among mine is alien to you.]

For what God has joined, let no human being separate (Matthew 19:6); nor should what is joined in minds be divided by distance. Where there is one charity, there is no separate will.

[But as for what your good foresight judged ought to be commended to my sweetest David for the salvation of many,

@ [Col. 0367D] On the selection of envoys. Charles seems to have followed this counsel of Arno and Alcuin in the year 802. “For the most pious emperor,” as the *Chronicle of Moissac* says, “did not wish to send his poorer vassals to administer justice, on account of gifts; but he chose archbishops and the remaining bishops and abbots, together with dukes and counts, who would no longer need to accept gifts from the innocent, and so forth.”

concerning the selection of envoys who are ordered to travel about [to administer] justice, know with certainty that I have often done this myself and have also urged his counselors to do it. But, alas, people are rarely found whose mind, firmly established [F.: strengthened] in the fear of God, rejects every form of greed and wishes to follow the royal road amid the miseries of rich and poor, as Solomon testifies: “Gifts blind the hearts of the wise and overthrow the words of the just” (Ecclesiasticus 20:31; Exodus 23:8).

Yet if those are just whose words wicked greed can overthrow, or if those can rightly be called wise whose hearts are blinded by gifts, then, as the Apostle says, greed is the root of all evils (1 Timothy 6:10). Whoever follows it can in no way walk along the way of justice.

As for me, recognizing my wounds only very slowly, I go about near the threshold of blessed Saint Martin, our Father and your protector, repeating your name daily among the most beloved persons; and I am weakened not only by the many scars of my former life, but also by adding at every moment new pains, worse than the earlier ones, to my ulcers.]

Therefore I earnestly implore the familiar charity of your affection to strive to seek for me, although I am unworthy, through the continual prayers of your holiness before the most merciful Savior, the medicine of perpetual health; and to take care to commend me to every servant faithful to God and Christ whom you find, and to those joined to your Reverence by the bond of sacred affection;

[and especially to my most beloved lord Pope Leo, to Paulinus the patriarch, and to Peter, archbishop of Milan, as well as to other men of religious life, whose names are written in heaven (Philippians 4:3)], so that, I beg you, you may inscribe the name of my smallness in their hearts, in order that through the prayers of many saints the many bonds of my sins may be loosed.

But you, most holy Father, carrying in your mouth the branch of the peaceful olive into the ark of the Lord (Genesis 8:11), make the dissensions of others into your rewards by calling them back to the concord of holy peace, so that the people may obey their ruler, the flock its shepherd, and the sons their own Father, while the Father rules his sons in peace and gentleness, so that in all things there may be one concord of charity and no root of bitterness may further put forth branches of poisonous dissension

@ [Col. 0368D] among the most holy persons of ecclesiastical rank. These were certainly the dissensions in Rome on account of Leo III; although the judgment against the parricides had ended, the parties had not yet been fully reconciled. This matter was entrusted especially to Arno, as is perfectly clear from this letter. In my judgment, therefore, this letter belongs to the year 801.

among the most holy persons of ecclesiastical rank. Let the trumpet of truth be in your mouth, so that peace and truth may always be heard from your lips; and may what the Psalmist sang be fulfilled not only in you but also through you for the benefit of many, where he says: “Mercy and truth have met each other; peace and justice have embraced one another” (Psalm 84:11).

This is your work in the present light; this is your reward in eternal glory. For a certain poet said concerning the work of a poem about the Gospel:

> This work, this indeed, perhaps, will rescue me from the fire,  
> when the fire-breathing Judge descends from his citadel.

I shall say:

> This work, this indeed, may not only rescue you from the fire,  
> but also make you ascend to the citadel of heaven.

Read happily, acknowledge humbly, and faithfully accomplish what charity has written and Christ has commanded to be done.

@ [Col. 0368D] Quercet’s edition, p. 20, from a manuscript. (Froben, Letter 103.)

## LETTER 131. TO THE LORD KING

*(Year 801.)*

He sends through his servant sacred books that he has collected into a single volume and corrected. [Col. 0368D]

To the most desired and deservedly beloved King David, [Col. 0369A] Albinus sends greetings of present prosperity and eternal blessedness in Christ.

After long deliberation about what my devotion might find worthy to offer to the splendor of your imperial power and the enlargement of your most abundant treasury, lest my little talent should grow sluggish in useless idleness while others offered various gifts of wealth, and lest my smallness’s messenger should come empty-handed before your blessedness, at last, inspired by the Holy Spirit, I found what would be fitting to offer in my name and what might be pleasing to your wisdom.

Thus it is plainly evident in the most sacred solicitude of your piety what the Holy Spirit is working through you for the salvation of the whole Church, and how greatly all the prayers of the faithful should desire that your empire extend through all your glory, so that it may be pleasing within to all who are faithful to God and fearsome without to all [perhaps: to all] the Lord’s adversaries.

But when I sought and considered what could be found more worthy of your peaceful honor than

@ [Col. 0369D] gifts of divine books. He is speaking of a codex of the Holy Scripture in the Vulgate edition, which, at the urging of Charlemagne, he purged of the many errors of the scribes who copied it. We have spoken elsewhere about this codex. See Mabillon, Book XXVI of the *Annals*, no. 61. I think this gift was offered by Alcuin to Charles, recently crowned with the imperial crown: “To the splendor of imperial power,” while others were also offering various gifts of wealth on the same occasion. The letter therefore belongs to the beginning of the year 801.

the gifts of divine books, which, dictated by the Holy Spirit and produced through the ministry of Christ God for the salvation of the whole human race, were written with the pen of heavenly grace; these books, joined together into the sanctity of one most splendid volume and carefully corrected, I have taken care to send to your most illustrious Authority through this most illustrious son of yours and faithful servant, so that he might stand in the joyful service of your dignity with full hands.

He, weakened by a long illness, hurried to approach your piety as soon as he had recovered somewhat, by God’s mercy. But I also send you the little gifts of my tears in prayers at Saint Martin’s, with a faithful promise, for the prosperity of your most desired Authority. Let him serve the most pious Lord as is fitting; I shall pray for my most beloved lord as the visitation of the Holy Spirit deigns to illumine my heart. If my devotion could have found anything better, I would certainly offer it with willing heart for the increase of your honor.

@ [Col. 0370D] Quercet’s edition, p. 17, from a manuscript. (Froben, 104.)

## LETTER 132. TO THE LORD KING

*(Year 801.)*

Called to court, he excuses himself on account of old age; and he declares that the most wise king has no need of his counsel. [Col. 0369D]

To the deservedly praiseworthy King David, worthy to be embraced with every service of charity and greatly desired by us, Albinus, the most humble little servant of the holy Church of God, sends perpetual salvation in eternal glory.

Because the flame of perpetual charity continually burns [Col. 0370A] in my heart, it seems right that, at suitable intervals, it should sparkle outward through the service of letters, lest what is nourished by the continual kindling of new benefits grow cheap through silence.

Behold, Flaccus, with his body worn out and having laid aside the belt of military labor, has chosen, according to the pious counsel of his lord David, to serve God alone in tranquil peace with his whole desire. Why, then, is he again forced to fight and sweat beneath the burden of arms, when the frailty of his weak body denies him the ability even to lift himself from the ground? Unless perhaps, at a later time, he whose mercy raises up the fallen and releases the bound (Psalm 145:8) deigns to grant him strength.

Perhaps some dialectician will say: “He is strong in counsel, though age-old weakness denies him strength.” But an entirely true response may also be offered to him: If anything worthy has flourished in Flaccus’s heart, the pious David possesses all of it in the most sacred treasury of his heart. Indeed, wherever David is, there also is Flaccus. Let the richest of both in wisdom answer on behalf of both.

And, to put simply what I must simply beg: May the holy mind of my lord, I ask, not become angry at my delay, because I cannot come now. There will be another opportunity, if God wills, at a suitable time. Nor do I think that my devotion can be of greater service to your Excellence anywhere than through continual prayers at Saint Martin’s, so that divine mercy, which has raised you through each office

@ [Col. 0370D] to the highest honor of secular power. From these words I infer that Charles had by then already attained the imperial dignity, which rises above all other secular dignities. The letter was therefore written in the year 801 or a later year.

to the highest honor of secular power, may grant you the use of that honor in lasting prosperity and, from the dignity of this exalted position, may cause you to ascend to the summit of the eternal kingdom [Col. 0370C], where mercy and justice, by God’s mercy, will lead your blessedness.

That man may rightly and happily be called happy who deserves to pass from this present happiness to eternal happiness. And the promise of that most beautiful verse will be fulfilled in him: “The saints shall go from virtue to virtue, until the God of gods is seen in Zion” (Psalm 83:8).

> May the nurturing power of Christ God grant you kingdoms,  
> Golden ones with the saints, David, in the citadel of heaven.  
> I pray that David’s gentle hand may tear the page,  
> Which almighty God may make victorious.

@ [Col. 0370D] Quercet’s edition, p. 24, from a manuscript. (Froben, 105.)

## LETTER 133. TO THE LORD KING

*(Year 801.)*

He announces the death of Maganfred. He intercedes for the brothers and the church of Saint Peter in the city of Benevento and asks that the Beneventans be treated mercifully. [Col. 0370D]

Glory and praise to almighty God for your safety and prosperity, my sweetest David, and for every honor and wisdom in which he has caused you, by special grace, to surpass all others [Col. 0371A]. May perpetual thanksgiving resound and the continual intercession of holy prayers be directed to God, so that you may live, remain strong, and reign in long-lasting prosperity for the correction and exaltation of his holy Church, so that under the protection of your revered power she may serve God in secure peace.

Previously I poured out the prayers of my supplication through your servant Candidus; I ask that your piety receive them with a merciful spirit. Whatever my mind suggested to me, I put entirely into his ears, so that he might preserve it in his heart and disclose it to your piety with truthful mouth.

But new developments in events urge me once again, with the pen of charity, to write the lines of my devotion. I have heard, indeed, what I cannot say without pain and tears,

@ [Col. 0371D] Maganfred. I think this is the same man to whom Letter 42 was written. Maganfred, your faithful man and our dearest friend, died in the land of Benevento. Therefore I have been asked by the brothers

@ [Col. 0371D] The brothers of Saint Peter. This seems to be understood, according to Mabillon, as the Beneventan monastery of Saint Peter *ad Corpus*, which is now a parish church. See Book XXVII of the *Annals*, no. 6.

of Saint Peter to send a letter to your goodness concerning the small estates formerly belonging to that church, so that, if it seemed right to your foresight, your reward might consist of some of them; and likewise concerning the courtyard within the walls of the city, from which a respectable dwelling might be built for the brothers of Saint Peter. In all these matters may your goodness consider what pleases God, what brings honor to your name, and what is pleasing to your goodness.

But a much greater and more necessary matter for the Christian people now arises, for which I must pour out prayers with my body prostrate before the feet of your piety. First, do not be angry with my most faithful charity, by which I truly recognize myself as especially indebted to your kindness. Secondly, and in the innermost affection of my heart, I ask that the most holy consideration of your wisdom provide for what pleases God and what benefits the Christian people

@ [Col. 0371D] Concerning a hostile expedition, etc. I think this is to be understood of the hostile expedition that Pippin undertook against the Beneventans at Charles’s command, when Charles was traveling to Rome in the year 800 and again when he was returning in the year 801. See the Annals of Tilianus, Loiselianus, and others.

in the hostile expedition into Beneventan territory, lest greater harm come upon it from your faithful men. You know very well how divine providence fought on your behalf. The father and brother of this

@ [Col. 0371D] Most wicked man. He undoubtedly means Grimoald, duke of Benevento, who succeeded his father Arigisus, with Charlemagne’s consent, in 788, but later became rebellious and fought with Pippin for a long time. See Erchempert, *History of the Lombards*, Benevento, in Muratori, *Italian Historical Sources*, vol. II, part I, p. 238. Grimoald’s father Arigisus and his brother Romoald, as Alcuin here suggests, were both removed within a short period—indeed, they died in the same year and almost the same month. Pope Adrian agrees in Letter 88 of the *Codex Carolinus*, where he writes to Charles: “When they came [Athalgisus with an army], by God’s will, through the aid of the apostles, they found the plans of the wicked scattered, because they found the duke Arichis, or his son Waldon [Cointius thinks Romoald should be read], dead.”

most wicked man were taken away within a short time. So also, we believe, so he will act if his holy will disposes that this man too should perish, provided that this occurs without any harm to your faithful. Such matters can often reach their conclusion better through counsel than through open assault, over time.

The more a person humbles himself beneath the hand of almighty God, the more quickly he vindicates the injuries of his servants. He says: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay” (Romans 12:19; Hebrews 10:30; Acts 13:22). That is: “Reserve vengeance for me, and I will fight for you.”

For David himself, concerning whom the Lord gave so lofty a testimony—“I have found David, son of Jesse, a man after my own heart” (2 Samuel 19:23)—forbade the killing of Shimei, who cursed him, hoping that God would grant him a blessing in return for his patient humility.

Let this too be arranged by the investigation of your keenest wisdom, considering, according to the vitality of reason and the salvation of your faithful, how their spirits can endure prolonged labor without the presence of your blessedness. I call God as witness to my heart that I have written these things in complete faith and with a perfect desire for your prosperity in every respect. I beg your blessedness to read these same things patiently and not to harbor any anger against my presumption for bringing such matters before your wisdom.

Although my charity may be able to appear foolish, it can never be found unfaithful, either in the smallest or the greatest matter. The confidence of your well-tested humility has dared to write these things.

Perhaps someone may say: “Why does that man meddle in the affairs of others?” He does not recognize that nothing concerning your prosperity ought to be foreign to me, since I testify that I love it more than the health of my body or the length of my life. You are the prosperity of the kingdom, the safety of the people, the glory of the Church, and the protection of all Christ’s faithful. Therefore divine grace has granted us, beneath the shadow of your power and the shelter of your piety, to lead a religious life and serve Christ God in secure peace. [Col. 0372C] Thus, with concerned mind and pious intention, we rightly and necessarily care for and intercede for your prosperity and safety, most desired and most worthy of every honor, King David.

{157}

@ [Col. 0372D] Quercet’s edition, p. 19, from a manuscript. Froben, 106. It was written at the time when he already felt his strength gradually failing and his illnesses growing worse, as he also complains in the preceding letters; it was therefore sent in the same year, 801, or in a later one.

## LETTER 134. TO THE LORD KING

*(Year 801.)*

He gives thanks for benefits received and asks that, because of his bodily weakness, he may be permitted to rest at Saint Martin’s.

To the most pious King David, Albinus sends greetings of perpetual blessedness.

May the supreme God, the Trinity, restore to your goodness, O David, most beloved of all, eternal blessedness for whatever kindness or benevolence you have shown toward me, your servant. Just as, when I first came to you, you mercifully promised, so you faithfully fulfilled everything, and, to complete the fullness of truth that always dwells in the treasury of your heart, you added a hundredfold. This is clearer than light to everyone’s eyes, and the report of many echoes through distant lands.

For what could have been added to the good fortune of my pilgrimage, or to the judgment of your goodness, beyond all these lavish gifts bestowed upon one less worthy than I? Or what thanks worthy of your mercy could I render, except by the continual diligence of pious prayer to implore the clemency of the most merciful almighty God, so that in eternal recompense, in heavenly blessedness, he may repay many times over all the benefits of your most generous goodness to my smallness?

So that I may be permitted to carry out my daily devotion at Saint Martin’s, I humbly beg, suppliant as a suppliant and humble as a humble man, devout as a devout man, because my body has become so weak that I can accomplish no journey or labor. All the dignity and strength of my body, as I truly confess, have departed and gone away, and each day they continue to flee; nor, as I fear, will they return in this world.

I hoped and desired, during the days that have passed, still to see the face of your blessedness, even once. But as the weakness of my frail body grows heavier, I have come to know that this is entirely impossible. Therefore I implore the mercy of your unconquered goodness: may the holy mind and benevolent will that are in you not become angry at my weakness, but in pious compassion grant me, weary as I am, permission to rest, to persist in prayers for you, and to go before the face of the eternal Judge in confession and tears.

Thus, if somehow, by the mercy of God Jesus, I may escape the fearful accusations of the ancient enemy and deserve to have one of the saints as a helper, standing with me and interceding for my frailty, so that I may not be handed over into the hands of my enemies (Ecclesiasticus 4:22).

O how fearful that day is for every person, and how necessary it is for each one to prepare to meet the Lord his God! The very Light that enlightens every person exhorts us and cries out: “Walk while you have the light, lest the darkness overtake you” (John 12:35). And elsewhere he shows how we ought to walk in that light, saying: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

> May the grace of Christ be with you forever, David,  
> So that you may flourish, remain strong, and prevail as a mighty ruler in the world.  
> After this, may you, blessed, possess the heavenly kingdoms,  
> Always together with the saints in the citadel of heaven.  
> May gentle Christ repay you with manifold gifts,  
> For behold how much goodness your kindness has bestowed upon me.  
> As many as are the grasses upon the earth or the sands upon the shore,  
> So much well-being, David, may you have by God’s mercy.  
> May illustrious David live happily through eternal years,  
> Living everywhere in Christ through sacred merits.

@ [Col. 0373D] Froben, Letter 185.

## LETTER 135

@ [Col. 0373D] To Nathanael. He was in fact called by the name Fridugisus or Fredegisus, as I noted at Letter 118 (now no. 157). From this letter we learn that this Nathanael was that envoy of Alcuin, the illustrious son and faithful servant of King Charles, through whom Alcuin offered Charles “for the splendor of imperial power the gifts of divine books, carefully corrected by him and joined together into the sanctity of one most illustrious volume,” as he says in Letter 103 (now 131). See below, col. 375, note a.

## TO NATHANAEL

*(Year 801.)*

He arouses him to piety; he entrusts to him the care of instructing the virgins Lucia and Columba. He entrusts to him a letter to be presented to King Charles together with a gift of Holy Scripture. [Col. 0374B]

Albinus sends greetings to Nathanael.

May he acknowledge you in blessing who was recognized by you when the blessed Philip preached, who called you from beneath the fig tree of the ancient offense to the man from Nazareth; may he grant that you be an Israelite without deceit, so that you may become worthy not only to say in words but also to fulfill in deed: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel” (John 1:45–49).

Follow him until you see him standing with blessed Peter and the sons of Zebedee on the shore and crying out: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find something” (John 21:6), so that after this fishing, when you are invited to the meal, he may say to you among the other companions of the holy fishing: “Come and eat” (ibid., verse 12).

What is sweeter than this meal? What is more blessed than this presence? There eternal joy is enclosed by no end; to it only the great fish will be chosen, those who were caught by apostolic preaching without the net being torn. Their number increases from one to seventeen, on account of the Decalogue and the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. I remember having written long ago to my lord David about the marvelous division and meaning of this number, with a heart warm with charity,

@ [Col. 0373D] In the hot bath . . . This was constructed by Charlemagne at Aachen, as the anonymous poet—or Alcuin himself in the poem on Charlemagne and Pope Leo’s arrival to him—attests, verse 106. See it in volume II of this edition among the doubtful works. There:

[Col. 0374D] Here others labor to find hot baths; the naturally boiling baths open their massive chambers of their own accord; they fashion beautiful seats with marble steps. A spring of excessively bubbling water does not cease boiling with intense heat; it leads streams off into every part of the city.

And Einhard writes of him in *The Life of Charlemagne*: “He also delighted in naturally warm vapors of water, frequently exercising his body by swimming . . . . For this reason he also built a palace at Aachen.” In Bouquet, *Scriptores rerum Gallicarum*, vol. V, p. 98, no. 22. In the bath of naturally hot water [manuscript: *atque*, “and”], where I do not fail to know that you, my pupil, are present.

[Col. 0374D] Greet

[Col. 0374D] Lucia and Columba. There exists in the Harley manuscript a letter to these same women, written when he sent them his already completed commentary on the Gospel of Saint John; for this reason we have prefixed it to that commentary, where you may consult it. “Beg Lucia, our sister, and Columba, our daughter, [Col. 0375A] to remember my old age in their holy prayers and their own salvation in good works; and do not conceal from them the beauty of your wisdom, but water within them the flourishing garden-beds of good will. What is more beautiful than the flowers of wisdom, which never wither? What is richer than the wealth of knowledge, which is never exhausted? Encourage them in these things. Let them live day and night in meditation on the law of God, so that they may find him whom Moses wrote of in the Law and the prophets. Let them hold him fast and not release him until they are led into the storerooms of royal glory, so that, ordered by love, they may be supported by the flowers of eternal blessedness, while the Bridegroom sends from his chamber the left hand of present prosperity beneath their heads, and the right hand of eternal blessedness embraces them.”

[Col. 0375D] But the letter of my littleness. This is Letter 103 (now 131), to the lord king, which he arranged to have delivered and presented to him, together with the most holy gift of sacred Scripture, through Nathanael, who, having recovered from a long illness, hastened eagerly to Rome to crown the emperor, on the very day of the Lord’s Nativity, when Charles himself received the imperial crown from Pope Leo III. “But the letter of my littleness, together with the most holy [Col. 0375B] gift of sacred Scripture, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, and with words of peaceful greeting, return to my lord David, to whom we offer as many thanks and praises for all the good things he did for me and my sons as that book contains syllables; and we wish that as many blessings be given him by God as letters are written in it.

Live happily for God, my son, through your flourishing years,

so that your own Jesus may preserve you everywhere. Without him the world’s wandering glory benefits no one;

Born mindful of the Father, always beloved, farewell.”

[Col. 0375D] Froben, Letter 186.

## LETTER CXXXVI. TO THE SAME

He encourages an honorable and religious way of life and advises him to avoid crowned doves flying through the palace chambers.

[Col. 0375C]

To my sweetest son Nathanael, Albinus the Father sends greetings.

I beg you, my dearest son, to make your life and conduct honorable and religious, and, insofar as possible, without any reproach before God and before human beings, so that it may be understood how great an education you received. Your holiness and venerable religion are praise to me among human beings and a reward before God. Let no crowned doves come to your windows, those that fly through the palace chambers; let no untamed horses burst into the doors of your chamber; and let not the faces of dancing bears be yours to look upon—[the manuscript perhaps reads, “the time”]—but rather the faces of clerics singing psalms. Let your words be modest in truth, your voice measured, and your silences deliberate; and carefully examine the person to whom you speak. Do not involve yourself in the quarrels of others; do not neglect the psalmody of the sacred hours; do not neglect the supreme power of the Mass in the body of Christ; and let charity not be absent.

Let holy reading be performed before you, so that words of preaching may be supplied for those at table. Let your willing and refusing be established in the citadel of your mind, lest you be forced to repent of any deed. Be a father to the poor, so that they may eat of your bread, because Christ is refreshed in the poor. How happy is the table at which Christ is the guest! Be irreproachable in the dignity of your conduct, magnificent in holiness, praiseworthy in the accounting of what is given and received, pleasant in words, joyful in appearance, cheerful toward the wretched, generous toward the poor, becoming all things to all people [Col. 0376B] [the manuscript reads *odorante*, “with a scent,” which makes no sense], so that, through the grace of Christ, you may deserve to receive a reward from all.

[Col. 0375D] Froben, Letter 187.

## LETTER CXXXVII. TO COUNT CHRODGARIUS. (A.D. 801)

He indicates that he is undertaking the education of a little boy and his brother. He urges faithful service and the provision of advice to the king. As Chrodgarius is about to depart to ravage Beneventan territory, he advises him to beware of Italy’s harmful air.

To the praiseworthy man

[Col. 0375D] Count Chrodgarius. The ancient writers are silent about him. That he was in the retinue of Pippin, king of Italy, and was sent by Charles his father, after Charles had been crowned and proclaimed emperor at Rome, while preparing to return from there to Francia in the year 801, with an army to devastate Beneventan territory, is made known by this letter. See the following note. Albinus the deacon sends greetings to Count Chrodgarius.

The service of letters is not to be despised when distance between lands has taken away the use of the tongue for joining friendship. Therefore I have taken care to send you, venerable friend, these lines of my devotion, begging [Col. 0376C] you to strive to commend my prayers among your spiritual friends, wherever you may go, with faithful charity.

You have sent us a good little boy to educate, together with his highly praiseworthy brother, whose conduct suits us exceedingly well in every form of religion and holiness; and the little boy is in need of this. I wish you to send him back to us as soon as possible.

Nor, I beg you, should the admonition of my letters be burdensome to you [so the manuscript reads], since I desire you to advance in God’s will and to work for the salvation of your soul through almsgiving to the poor, justice toward all, mercy toward the wretched, and good counsels that may advance the salvation and prosperity of the lord emperor and the Frankish kingdom.

I have heard that you are going

[Col. 0375D] To devastate the Beneventan homeland. Charles [Col. 0376D] the Great “in the year 800, setting out from Mainz for Rome, ordered an army to go raiding into the lands of the Beneventans with his son Pippin,” as the Tilian, Loiselian, and Metz annals report, in Bouquet, vol. V, *Scriptores rerum Gallicarum*. But the title of emperor, which he here assigns to Charles while advising Chrodgarius to support the emperor and the prosperity of the Franks by his good counsels, prevents me from thinking that Alcuin should here be understood as referring to that expedition. Those same annalists report, however, that in the year 801, after everything had been properly arranged at Rome, the emperor, “having again sent an expedition against the Beneventans, departed from Rome with his son Pippin after Easter, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, and came to Spoleto, etc.” I think Alcuin is speaking of this expedition. See also Letter 105 (now 133) concerning the same matter.

[Col. 0376D] At the end of the volume, in Froben’s edition, between the Errata and Addenda, the following is printed at this point: “Chrodgarius may perhaps be Rotharius (Rotherius, or Rotgerius), a most distinguished duke, accomplished in the Pythagorean language and an excellent standard-bearer, descended from the Frankish race and nobly raised in the court of King Pippin from the illustrious line of Agamemnon, etc.” This is read in the *Life of Saint Austremonius*, in Bouquet, vol. V, *Scriptores Francici*, pp. 432 and 470. Concerning him also, as founder of the Carolfensian monastery, Theodulf of Orléans sings in poem VIII, ibid., p. 421:

“Finally, the mighty count Rotharius, illustrious hero,

founded this work together with his wife Euphrasia.”

To devastate the Beneventan [Col. 0377A] homeland. You know very well what danger threatens you there,

[Col. 0377D] Because of the pestilential air of that land. The Frankish army experienced this in the year 793, as is read in the Annals of Moissac under that year: “In that very winter King Charles sent his two sons Pippin and Louis with a great army into Beneventan territory. And a very severe famine arose there . . . . [Col. 0378D] upon the army that had arrived, so that some were unable to abstain from eating meat even during Lent.”

Because of the pestilential air of that land. Therefore leave nothing concerning your affairs without consideration, especially so that no injustice or negligence in any fault may cry out against you from behind. Use your wisdom for your eternal salvation, because only that is true knowledge which grants human beings everlasting blessedness. I wish you to live happily in this present age and in the age to come, venerable friend!

[Col. 0378D] Froben, Letter 188.

## LETTER CXXXVIII. TO A SISTER AND DAUGHTER. (A.D. 801)

He informs them how highly he values their friendship. He tells them of the good news received from Rome. He sends certain works of the venerable Bede to be copied. He informs them about his own health.

[Col. 0377B]

To the dearest in Christ

[Col. 0378D] Sister and daughter. Perhaps to his sister Gisla and daughter Rictruda, to whom he dedicated his commentary on the Gospel of Saint John, and whom in another letter in the Harley manuscript, which we shall present at the beginning of that commentary, he calls Lucia and Columba. I think that two other letters in the Harley manuscript were written to these same women, in an uncertain year; for this reason I have judged that they should be joined to this one. “To the most grateful sister and daughter, the Father sends greetings of everlasting heavenly blessedness.

“As far as the course of events between us has been able to demonstrate, from the beginning of our acquaintance we have always found your goodness faithful to our interests. Therefore we rightly owe perpetual thanks and praises to almighty God, who, although we are unworthy, has granted us friendship with women of such distinguished rank and such proven faith, and has allowed us to find—something rarely capable of being found among blood relatives—such friendship among strangers; although, so far as the fellowship of Christian faith is concerned, no one should be called a stranger, while so far as the exile of this world is concerned, we are all strangers, [Col. 0377C] as the Psalmist says: ‘Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged’ (Psalm 119:5). The dwelling of this life is an exile, since it compels us to hasten toward the homeland of which it is said: ‘Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they shall praise you’ (Psalm 83:5). Blessed is the one who will pass from labor to rest, where he will live eternally without any disturbance of mind or body.

“We received the expressions of your piety with tranquil hearts, devoutly entreating God’s mercy that you may live happily in this age with enduring prosperity and, after the labors of this life, attain eternal blessedness.

“Our Candidus has returned from Rome, bringing from there entirely favorable reports concerning my lord David and all his faithful subjects; our little sons

[Col. 0378D] Remained with Pippin. That is, in Italy, left there by Charles when he returned from Rome to Francia in 801 for the military expedition against the Beneventans. See the notes to the preceding letter. He said that they had remained with Pippin; he reported that the Apostolic had overcome his adversaries and was in great favor with the lord emperor.

“We have sent the works you requested, begging you to have them copied and returned as quickly as possible, because they are very necessary to us for the benefit of readers. Our master Bede [manuscript: *Boeda*] composed them in simple language with subtle meaning. We have therefore taken care to send you his little works because we understood that you especially desired his words.

“As for my health, know that the fever has partly departed and partly remained. It remains for chastisement; but divine mercy and the intercessions of his saints have spared me more than my merits deserve. Yet the greatest fear of God’s judgment still remains, from which no one can escape. May the goodness of the eternal Father chastise us only with loving compassion and not hand us over to the power of our enemies. To him I shall often say: ‘Deliver my soul from the sword, and my only one from the hand of the dog’ (Psalm 21:21). Again: ‘O Lord, free my soul, for the Lord is merciful and compassionate’ (Psalm 114:4), so that what is said may come to pass: ‘Bless the Lord, O my soul’ (Psalm 102:1). And again: ‘Praise the Lord, O my soul’ (Psalm 145:2). ‘Blessed be the name of the Lord from this time forth and forever’ (Psalm 71:17). May divine grace deign to crown you with perpetual blessing, most beloved ladies in the Lord!”

[Col. 0378D] Froben, Letter 189.

## LETTER CXXXIX. TO A SISTER AND DAUGHTER. (Year uncertain)

He commends charity and the reading of sacred Scripture together with prayer.

[Col. 0378C]

To the beloved persons in Christ, sister and daughter, the Father sends greetings of everlasting heavenly blessedness.

Why has your charity been silent for so long? Have the words of greeting failed, or have no circumstances arisen whose knowledge a letter might convey to our ears? Should distance between lands separate the sweetness of charity, whose flame, according to the words of the Song, could be submerged neither by the depth of rivers nor by the vastness of the sea (Song 8:7), and in which alone, if anyone stumbles, he has become guilty of all (James 2:10)? This is what must shine upon the good and the evil, so that an earthly person may be perfected in it, just as the Father who is in heaven is perfect (Matthew 5:48).

Therefore the child of charity is a child of God, because God is charity (1 John 4:16). May its light sufficiently illumine your hearts and its sweetness abundantly refresh your breasts. This is the sum of all good things; this is the better part, which will never be taken away, but burns more and more in the breast of the one who possesses it. Concerning it two disciples said, after recognizing the Lord in the breaking of bread: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32). Seek it in the holy Scriptures, searching them with the utmost attention, so that you may recognize the Lord speaking to you in them.

What is sweeter than to enjoy conversation with almighty God? [Col. 0379B] For whoever reads the Lord’s most sacred words, handed down to us through his saints, will hear God speaking; and whoever prays speaks to God. May these most sacred exchanges turn day and night into rejoicing; and may worldly occupation not overthrow spiritual delight. For the pleasures and false loves of this age are vanity of vanities; all the delights of this life pass away like a shadow and are easily scattered like foam upon water. Therefore, dearest and noblest virgins, exercise your souls in all holiness and religion and in devotion to reading, so that the Holy Spirit may deign frequently to visit the hearts of your devotion from heaven. He is recognized as dwelling in breasts full of charity and in those who labor with attentive minds in holy wisdom.

[Col. 0379C] Meanwhile I have taken care to give you a foretaste of these things with the pen of holy affection. But if you are concerned to know the effect of your father’s will, know that my illnesses are increasing daily and that my body is being weakened by various pains. The Lord is knocking at the doors, if he finds his servant watchful; and, aided by your intercessions, I strive to keep holy vigils, lest he who commanded his apostles, saying, ‘Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation; the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh [the manuscript reads *heart*] is weak’ (Matthew 26:41), should find me asleep amid the occupations of the world. May Jesus God cause your holiness to flourish in every good work and advance toward everlasting happiness, dearest sister in Christ!

[Col. 0379D] Froben, Letter 190.

## LETTER CXL. TO A SISTER AND DAUGHTER

He advises them to preserve equanimity in prosperity and adversity by the example of the saints, whose lives he wants them to read from the *Dialogues* of Saint Gregory the pope.

[Col. 0379D]

To the persons most beloved in Christ, sister and daughter, paternal affection sends greetings.

We give thanks to divine mercy for your prosperity and health and for all the good things that his ineffable mercy has granted you. We also praise the piety of his constant will, by which he has bestowed upon us, though unworthy, such faithful consolation and such sweet charity in your affection. Therefore it is necessary for all who live piously in Christ to praise his surpassing grace, by which he has had mercy on the human race, and always to attribute whatever good we do to his kindness, without which, as the Truth itself bears witness, we can accomplish nothing. In this goodness may your unity always remain joyful. It must not be broken by the adversities of the world or by the faithlessness of those who love the world, nor should you be sad, even though many adversities befall us. Such is the variety of this present life that prosperity is always mingled with adversity, just as day is changed into night; just as bodily health is afflicted when illnesses come upon it; just as the flower of youth withers when old age arrives; and just as the calm of summer is worn away by winter storms.

Yet none of these things should weary a religious mind. Rather, with stable constancy and upright hope, it should remain firm and immovable before God. Hence, by the testimony of the Truth itself, John the Baptist is praised because he was not a reed shaken by the wind (Luke 7:24): that is, he did not allow [manuscript: *valuit*, “was able”] his mind to turn from the straight path of stability either through the adversities of the world, envious reproach, deceitful flattery, or smiling prosperity. Instead, with equal firmness of mind, he endured adversity and moderated joy. By his example, may the exercise of your minds be strengthened in God, dearest women. Temptations often bring benefit, so that tested patience may increase toward the reward of eternal recompense.

As gold is tested by fire, so the Christian mind is examined through tribulations. Scripture says: “My son, when you approach the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation” (Sirach 2:1), not for security. Strengthen [Col. 0380C] yourselves by the examples of the saints, reading in turn the sweetest examples of their lives and the necessary encouragements of holy words. Let their life be a mirror for you. For the insertion of lighter reading often refreshes the sharpness of a weary mind. Therefore the more difficult meaning of apostolic authority will undoubtedly weary you frequently; but now take into your hands either the *Lives of the Fathers* or the miracles of the saints, many of which are found set forth in the *Dialogues* of blessed Gregory, our teacher, in most lucid eloquence and always confirmed by sentences from sacred Scripture. You will begin to make it your custom to discuss these things among yourselves and to bring them forth at other meals, judging them to be very pleasing to you. Just as a variety of foods removes a diner’s disgust, so a variety of reading refreshes the reader’s mind. Let your charity, with thoughtful foresight, consider all these things and see what suits each time and each person, so that many may advance toward the salvation of their souls through your excellent admonitions.

I have written these things as a fatherly admonition, so that your affection may often have my presence in this letter, just as your charity will remain firmly fixed in our mind. See how plainly one may understand, in mutual charity, what the Lord himself said in the Gospel: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matthew 18:20). Let us not think that this was said only of bodily presence, but rather of the presence of holy charity, which has been poured out through the Holy Spirit into our hearts (Romans 5:5). Since we possess the treasure of true love in our breasts, let each person help the other according to the measure of Christ’s gift, whether in the consolation of worldly necessity or in the sharing of spiritual teaching. Wherever these things take place, it is most certain that Christ is in the midst, diffusing from one religious heart into another the sweetness of charity, so that there may be one harmony among all who love God and one devotion among those who help one another.

As you continually consider these things with sweetness, and remember us, may you, through Christ’s mercy, grow day by day in charity, be strengthened in faith, and remain unfailing in hope of divine goodness. With eternal prosperity, farewell, dearest and most delightful names of holy affection!

[Col. 0381D] Froben, Letter 191.

## LETTER CXLI. TO AQUILA OR ARNO. (A.D. 801, after Easter)

He recalls with joy the prosperity and exaltation of the king. He wishes to be informed about the case of the lord Apostolic, the Beneventan dispute, and the proceedings of the assembly of bishops. He reports on the state of his health.

To the venerable Father and, among the members of Christ, most excellent chief overseer Aquila, Albinus, a brother devoted in charity, sends greetings of unfailing glory [the text has *indeficiens*; perhaps *indeficientis*, “unfailing,” agreeing with *gloriae*].

I rejoice exceedingly in the faith and charity of your blessedness; in the prosperity, health, and exaltation of the pious [Col. 0381C] prince, the great triumphant and

[Col. 0381D] glorious emperor. This makes clear that the present letter was written after Charles received the imperial dignity at Christmas in the year 800, and indeed after Alcuin had somewhat recovered from the illness by which he says he was afflicted around Easter—that is, in the year 801. Glorious emperor, and in the safety of his most noble offspring and of all his faithful people. Yet two matters were absent from your letter: concerning our lord Apostolic Father, how the long dispute between shepherd and people had ended; and concerning the Beneventan dispute. For I am very anxious about my sons, whose life, health, and good works you yourself know very well to be extremely important to me. And I wonder why, through the wisdom and counsel

[Col. 0381D] Of the assembly of many. “For in the year 800,” Charles “held at Rome a very great assembly of bishops, or abbots together with priests and deacons and counts, or with the rest of the Christian people,” specifically to examine and judge the case of Pope Leo III and to arrange other matters both public and ecclesiastical. This assembly continued into the following year, as the Frankish annals of Loisel and others report in Bouquet, vol. V, repeatedly cited. Of the assembly of so many people, for the integrity of that kingdom, the cause of the impious dispute was not brought to an end in some manner. At the same time, I am anxious to hear what was arranged in so great and distinguished an assembly concerning the condition of the holy Church and the firmness of the Catholic faith. Nor should the association of those who came over such a long period have occurred without some great benefit to the Christian people [Col. 0381D]. But may your holiness, most worthy shepherd, lead the flock of Christ entrusted to your care through the pastures of eternal life with every solicitude, so that together with the flock subject to you, you may rejoice in manifold recompense [Col. 0382A] in the kingdom of eternal blessedness.

As for my own prosperity, let your fatherhood rejoice, because the Lord God, who kills and gives life, wounds and heals (1 Samuel 2:6), chastised me around Easter with a severe scourging of fevers and brought me almost to despair of life. But he had mercy on me because of the prayers of his servants. The daily labor of the same chastisement nevertheless remains, though not to the danger of life, but, as I hope, for the cleansing of my sins. Your mind I strive daily to commend to the mercy of almighty God, wishing you to advance in every good work before God. Though my body is almost lifeless, the living power of charity lives in my breast, loving you, my brother Aquila, [Col. 0382B] as a father, because I have always found you faithful. And I acknowledge that few possess this quality: to remain of the same mind toward their friends in prosperity and adversity alike. No one may rightly doubt that this treasure is in your heart, because the charity of God, and also of one’s neighbor, has been poured into your heart through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us, so that we may love one another as Christ also loved us (Romans 5:5).

I greatly desire to see the face of your affection and to be warmed by the comfort of your consolation. It is time to provide for eternal days, which alone can almost rightly be called wisdom. Provision for worldly affairs will benefit us for a short time; provision for perpetual prosperity, however, will be closed by no end. No one should doubt that it greatly advances through fraternal conversation, as the Truth itself says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matthew 18:20). What good counsel will be lacking when so great a mediator is known to be present? May divine grace preserve your blessedness unharmed for a very long time, so that you may benefit many through counsel and example, lord, father, son, brother, and friend!

[Col. 0382D] Froben, Letter 192.

## LETTER CXLII. TO THE BROTHERS OF FULDA. (Around A.D. 801)

He urges religious virtues. He sends a storax-colored pallium for the body of Saint Boniface and a missal booklet.

To the most holy, and to us worthy of all charity,

[Col. 0382D] Brothers of Saint Boniface. The Fulda brothers, since Saint Boniface founded that monastery and was buried there after his glorious martyrdom. To the brothers of Saint Boniface, our Father and protector, the humble Levite Alcuin sends greetings of eternal blessedness in Christ.

Mindful of your sweetest affection, by which you once received me most kindly and with every joy

[Col. 0382D] Received me at that time. It is certain from this that Alcuin was once at Fulda; it remains uncertain, however, whether he opened a school there and personally taught letters, as Trithemius and others thought. Nevertheless, I believe that Alcuin was not idle there and that, because of his ardor for advancing the sciences, he at least offered the people of Fulda excellent counsels for cultivating good letters. This was certainly the duty of a man who exercised a teaching authority not only at Tours but throughout Francia, as Altfrid says in book I of *The Life of Saint Liudger*, no. 9. You received me; and as much as I rejoiced then in your presence, so much is my spirit now tormented by your absence, seeking to see those whom it loves and to have present those whom it cherishes. But since this is not granted to bodily eyes, let perpetual affection be made present spiritually; for charity that can be abandoned was never true.

Therefore let us strive toward that which will never have an end, in which there is blessed eternity and eternal blessedness. To deserve to reach it, let no labor terrify you and let no flatteries of this world draw you back. Rather, let love for him always burn in your hearts—the one who appeared as a third companion on the road to two disciples, who, when he had been taken from their bodily eyes, said: “Was not our heart burning while he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32). Let us seek him in the writings of the holy Fathers, whom those disciples, not yet instructed in the Scriptures, understood. Now everything has been opened; now he himself has opened the meaning, of whom it was said: “Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures” (ibid. 45). Now evangelical truth shines throughout the whole world; now the enigmas of the prophets gleam more brightly than the sun in the churches of Christ. Pursue this light of truth with your whole soul; understand Christ in it, love Christ in it, follow Christ, so that, clinging to his most sacred footsteps, you may deserve to possess eternal life in his most holy presence, mindful of the apostolic command: “Brothers, be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not vain in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 15:58).

Be steadfast in your place and in the devotion of your calling. Do not abandon your most holy Father; stand around his tomb, so that he may offer your prayers to almighty God. Do not covet worldly vanities, but love heavenly blessedness; and do not, as the Doctor of the Gentiles says, conform yourselves to this age, but be transformed in the renewal of your mind (Romans 13:2). For it is shameful for a monk to abandon spiritual warfare and entangle himself in worldly affairs.

Let there be no murmuring among you, no hatred, no envy, no detraction. Do not judge one another; rather, let all your actions be performed in humility and harmony, obeying your superiors not merely outwardly but from the heart, as though before God (Ephesians 6:5–6). Let your obedience, charity, and humility be known to all, so that many may be instructed by your good example and advance in the salvation of their souls. But if the venerable Father

[Col. 0383D] Bonulfus, or, as others write, Baugulfus, who at this time presided over the monastery of Fulda, was the successor of Sturm or Sturmius, who died in 779. In the year 802 he “relinquished the authority he had held and received Ratgar as his successor,” as the Fulda annalist reports. The reason why Baugulfus resigned the abbacy may perhaps have been an illness that rendered him unable to endure the rigors of regular life. Alcuin did not want him judged for this by his brothers. Hence it seems to me that, when this letter was written, either Baugulfus himself or his monks were considering the abdication of the abbacy; and for this reason I think that the letter should be dated shortly before the year 802. A letter of Charlemagne exists addressed specifically to Baugulfus and his entire congregation, although it was also sent at the same time to all bishops and monasteries in the year 787. There the king Charles exhorts all to cultivate and restore the study of letters both in cathedral churches and monasteries. Mabillon thought it probable that “Alcuin himself, who was then in Charles’s retinue, had advised him to send this letter to all bishops and abbots, and that Alcuin himself perhaps dictated it.” It was first published by the learned Sirmond from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint Arnulf at Metz; it is also reproduced in full in Bouquet, vol. V, *Scriptores rerum Gallicarum*, p. 621. Charles Cointius indeed denied that it was addressed to Abbot Baugulfus, on an entirely trivial argument; Mabillon refutes him in book XXV of the *Annals*, no. 64, p. 279. Bonulfus, my most beloved friend, is unable, because of his illness, to fulfill the rigors of regular life, do not judge him, but obey him from the heart and love him as a father, because he will have to render an account for your souls. He labors for you by wandering and running about so that you may be able to live in peace, keep your regular life, and have what your bodies require. You, however, act as beloved sons: fear God, love God, and care for your most holy Father in your prayers, so that he may live happily with you in lasting prosperity and that you, with him and he with you, may deserve to possess eternal life [Col. 0384B].

Instruct, admonish, and teach your young men in every holy discipline and Catholic doctrine, so that they may be considered worthy to stand in your place and to direct prayers . . . to you wherever you remain. Admonish them sincerely concerning bodily chastity, confession of their sins, devotion to reading, and manual labor without murmuring, and concerning all the matters that seem necessary at such an age. Let them become subject to their elders and teachers, with good humility and most devout religion. And you elders who are present, provide good examples for them, so that they may be instructed not only by words but by the religious character of your life. Let them not be luxurious, not slaves to drunkenness, not contemptuous, not followers of empty [Col. 0384C] games; but let them learn to be good officials in the house of God, so that through the intercession of their Father, Saint Boniface, they may deserve to receive blessing and grace from God Christ. And I beg you to keep me in perpetual memory in your holy prayers. For the time is approaching that no one can escape; let each person prepare himself, so that, clothed in good morals, he may not appear naked before the presence of the Lord his God.

I have sent one

[Col. 0384D] Storax-colored pallium. “So called from the color of storax, which is a drop resembling a quince,” says Papias. See Du Cange, *Glossary*, under *Stauracium*. I have sent a storax-colored pallium for the body of Saint Boniface, our Father, in whose holy intercession I have great confidence for my sins, so that I, a sinner, may deserve to receive forgiveness on the day when your holiness receives the crown of eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0385A] I sent
@ [Col. 0385D] “I sent a Missal booklet, etc.” He sent a similar one to the monks of Saint-Vaast. See Letter 51. The author of the *Micrologus on Ecclesiastical Observances*, chapter 60, volume XVIII of the *Bibliotheca Sanctorum Patrum*, p. 489, Lyon edition, says: “At the request of Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, Alcuin composed Mass prayers, so that the priests of that time, newly converted to the faith, not yet instructed in ecclesiastical offices, and not yet supplied with an abundance of books, might at least have something with which they could perform their office on any given day.” But the aforesaid author is greatly mistaken in this, as is manifest from this letter. For Alcuin did not send these Mass prayers to priests newly converted, but to monk-priests long practiced in the divine offices [Col. 0386D]; nor did he send them at the request of Saint Boniface, with whom Alcuin scarcely had any association, but out of charity toward the brothers serving Saint Boniface, and in his honor.

I have taken care to send you, most holy priests, a Missal booklet, so that you may have it for each day on which anyone might wish to direct prayers to God: whether on the occasion of the honor of the Holy Trinity; or concerning the love of wisdom; or concerning tears of penitence; or concerning perfect charity; or when anyone wishes to ask for the assistance of the angels; or of any of the saints; or whether someone wishes to offer prayers for his sins; or for any living friend; or even for many friends; or for brothers departing from this world; or when someone wishes especially to implore the intercession of blessed Mary, the perpetual virgin and Mother of God; or when anyone wishes to sing of your most holy Father Boniface and call upon his most devout presence through prayers. We have taken care to send all these things to you out of consideration for charity, asking your humility kindly to receive what we send you with the fullest charity. Let each person make whatever use of them he wishes, and let no one reproach me for performing the office of charity. For let each person abound in his own understanding, and always do what is pleasing to God and to all the saints, so that they may be found worthy to enjoy with them the perpetual vision of our Lord Jesus Christ.

May the Lord God hear your holy blessedness, mindful of me, in every holy petition, and may he deign to grant you present happiness and future blessedness, dearest brothers. I ask that you inform us by letter, if this letter has reached you, and [Col. 0385C] what your wisdom thinks of it. I have done what was mine to do, fulfilling the duty of charity in the love and honor of our Lord Jesus Christ.

{158}

@ [Col. 0386D] Frobenius 107; Mabillon edition 14, where it is headed: “To an excellent bishop and evangelical teacher,” with the proper name omitted. Mabillon conjectured that it was addressed to Liudger, bishop of Mimigernaford. But this conjecture is overturned by the Salzburg manuscript, from which the text here emerges in a more corrected form. I join this letter with others in which, because of his worsening illness, there is frequent remembrance of death.

## LETTER 143. TO ARNO. (Year 801)

He invites him to come to Saint Martin; he aspires to heavenly things and asks that prayers be offered for him.

To Aquila, an excellent bishop, Albinus sends greetings.

May a little letter written with the pen of charity reach your reverence, most desired brother, whispering in your ears that you should come, if possible, to the threshold of blessed [Martin], our Father and your protector, so that your companion [Albinus] may be able to exchange with you, in familiar conversation, the final words of greeting [Col. 0385D]; for the hour of parting among brothers and separation among friends is hastening. “When a man goes to the house of his eternity, and those who go about in the street mourn around him” (Eccles. [Col. 0386A] XII, 5), then true friendship will be proved, while false flattery will cease. Many promise companionship, but few keep it. Nor is this surprising, because “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX, 16).

But what of these things? Let a man join himself to God, and he will have all that is necessary. “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. VI, 33). The pains and tribulations of this life daily admonish us to join ourselves to God, flee earthly things, and love heavenly things. But alas, what grief! Miserable as we are, we wish to remain long in these miseries, and seek less earnestly the perpetual rest; we gape after our desires, clinging less closely to God’s commandments. He chastises us with fatherly compassion so that in spirit we may flee these temporal things and hasten toward the eternal, where true blessedness is found.

So that I may deserve to reach it, [Col. 0386B] may your holiness, by God’s mercy, assist me through the support of your prayers. I know my danger; I acknowledge my sins. Therefore, as a suppliant, I ask the intercessions of Christ’s servants, that they may have mercy on me. My hope and consolation is God Christ, the Redeemer of all, to whom praise and thanksgiving are due for all the good things that, by his freely given mercy, he has granted me in this world.

Live happily for God, for to live for the world is death;

Indeed, for man to live for God is true life.

@ [Col. 0386D] Mabillon edition 15; Frobenius 108. Here it appears more complete from the Salzburg manuscript.

## LETTER 144. TO ARNO. (Year 801)

He desires to see Arno at Saint Martin and to confer with him about the affairs of his life before he is compelled to depart from this life.

To Aquila, a deservedly beloved lord, pious and peaceful bishop, Albinus sends greetings.

Perpetual charity will always find an occasion for greeting a friend, so that the faithful spirit may rejoice in reading letters, since it has not been granted to rejoice in the presence of the eyes. But the faithful sight of the spirit in charity is better than every gaze of the pupils. Therefore God must be contemplated spiritually, not with bodily eyes, which we share with the little worms. His vision is the whole blessedness promised to the saints in everlasting glory; from it the wicked are removed, lest they see the glory of God.

Let us exhort one another to this vision of perpetual blessedness, because “a brother helped by a brother is a fortified city” (Prov. XVIII, 19). [Yet if these things that I have said about the vision of the spirit should appear very true, [Col. 0386D]] I see that there is a certain loss in being absent from your face, [not on account of the black hairs on your head, but on account of your sweetest eyes and the beloved speech of charity that we have been accustomed faithfully to share among [Col. 0387A] ourselves. For I indeed—

@ [Col. 0387D] “Called to the palace because of illnesses, etc.” See Letter 134 to Charles, described shortly before this. The letter was written while Arno was returning from Rome in the year 801. See also the following letter.
