I have been called to the palace, but because of the weakness of my little body I cannot come, while looking forward to you, with life as my companion, in the house of God and of Saint Martin.] If somehow this beloved desire of mine may come to pass, by God’s mercy, so that we may contemplate one another before the golden cord is broken and the wheel is crushed above the fountain (Eccles. XII, 6), and the outer man goes to the house of his eternity while friends mourn around him, and the spirit returns for judgment to him who gave it (Eccles. XII, 7).

At the terror of this judgment I tremble utterly. Therefore, laying aside the burden of worldly business, I shall choose to serve God alone, even with a sluggish heart and an impeded step, lest that day find me altogether unprepared. But, by God’s mercy, with life as my companion, [Col. 0387B] I shall undertake to heal, according to the counsels of your holiness, the wounds that the misery of this world has unhappily inflicted upon me. When these counsels have been exchanged between us—something I cannot say without tears—let the final farewell be spoken [between Aquila and Albinus].

And I, strengthened forever by your most holy counsels and prayers, shall watch and watch [in the appointed place] for when my Lord returns from the wedding and knocks at the door (Luke XII, 36), to see whether he finds the keeper of the house watching. When the moment of that fearful hour has passed, may I leave your blessedness surviving me, for the necessary intercessions on behalf of my sins. For faith is tested at the end, and is found almost nowhere among men. Everyone greatly needs it, but few seem to possess it.

[Do not be unwilling to read these little letters often [Col. 0387C], which I dictated with tears arising, so that you may keep in mind what my chief desire is toward you; and so that my soul may recognize that what is scarcely found in very many people is certain to be found in you, in the place destined for it.]

May divine mercy, most desired Father, grant you for a long time to advance in the service of holy Church and in the progress of many souls, so that with the manifold fruit of your labor you may deservedly reach eternal blessedness. Again and again I say, and I say with tears: remember me. May almighty God guard you and grant you to flourish in every goodness, sweetest and most beloved of all bishops.

@ [Col. 0387D] Mabillon edition 20 (Frobenius 109). Here it appears more complete from the Salzburg manuscript.

## LETTER 145. TO ARNO, ARCHBISHOP. (Year 801)

He replies to a letter sent to him. He again desires to enjoy Arno’s presence, while prevented from coming to the palace himself. [Col. 0387D]

To the lord deservedly most beloved among the members of Christ [Aquila, archbishop], Albinus, matricularius of Saint Martin, sends everlasting greetings.

[Col. 0388A] While I was on an embassy, a letter from your blessedness reached me, conveying words of the sweetest greeting. After reading it with joyful spirit, I recognized familiar things and considered the things I had desired; I read happily in everything that the most holy devotion of your spirit toward us was watchful. [To these I took care to dictate a brief reply to a notary because of the bearer’s haste, especially since I had previously sent, through Candidus, our son and your faithful servant—

@ [Col. 0387D] “Two little letters.” Perhaps the two preceding letters immediately before this one?

two little letters, one to

@ [Col. 0387D] “To Gandolfovilla.” The Reverend author of the *Prodromus of the Chronicle of Göttweig*, part II, p. 819, identifies Gundulphi villa, or Gundum-villa, from Miraeus, with the district of Toul and interprets it as Gondreville on the Moselle near Toul; although the celebrated Valesius, in his *Notes on Gaul*, p. 239, declares that it refers to Gondecourt in the district of Vabrus near Conflans.

Gandolfovilla and the other to the palace at Aachen. I think that, by God’s mercy, he found you returning there,

@ [Col. 0388D] “Returning, I think, from Rome by way of Gundolfovilla to the palace at Aachen.”

and he was able to disclose to you everything about us by word of mouth: how God’s mercy had looked favorably upon our illness and old age, and had peacefully freed us from the tumult of this world, so that in a quiet way of life I might await the final day, [Col. 0388B] which is far from no one, but is especially to be feared by the one who recognizes that it is near and already standing at the doors.]

But may your holiness watch over Christ’s flock, lest anyone [Mabillon: *anything*], being subject to your admonitions [Frobenius: *abjectis*, “cast down”], and looking to you, fall short of the grace of Christ through wolfish bites; for the destruction of any soul is the shepherd’s loss. {160}

@ [Col. 0388D] “I was summoned to my lord David.” See the preceding letter.

I was summoned to my lord David, but delayed by illness I did not come—or perhaps I was detained by my own will.] Blessed is the man who is chained by God’s chastisement and freed from the troubled storms of this world. I never rejoiced so much when surrounded by worldly riches as I have rejoiced in the quiet consideration of my life.

By God’s mercy, I desire that through your affection there may be accomplished what cannot be accomplished through my own sluggishness: namely, that I may be permitted to enjoy for some hour the embraces and conversations of your charity. There is no bishop whose presence I would rather enjoy, according to God’s mercy, than yours. May he bring this about who said: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. XVIII, 20).

It is dangerous for a fragile spirit to remain amid the tempest of this world. Martha served Christ, but because she was occupied with many things, she is nevertheless said to have heard the Lord say: “But Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her forever” (Luke X, 40, 42).

[If it pleases God that you come to the threshold of Saint Martin, I greatly desire, wish for, and beg it. Otherwise, let your letters come speaking into the ears of your Albinus, so that through their bearer I may be able to sew together and send you a longer little letter [Col. 0388D].]

I was surprised by a certain word in one of your little letters of affection, where I read that, after suitable and desirable thoughts for my spirit, you said that because of your occupations you had been unable to send me a little gift—as though our charity consisted in gold or silver—[Col. 0389A] although it is so great that, as I truly confess, it exists in my spirit, and, as I believe, in yours also, so that compared with that charity every kind of wealth is worthless.

That is the true charity of which you have just written: it does not undergo the dangers of the floods of which it is said, “Many waters shall not overwhelm charity” (Song VIII, 7). May this charity flourish in our hearts, not the empty appearance of gold or silver. These do not benefit those who possess them; rather, they hinder them, unless they have learned to use them for the salvation of their souls by gifts to the poor and have carried this out in deed.

May almighty God protect and guard your holiness, for the perpetual salvation and blessed prosperity of the advancement of many, most beloved and desired lord Father, and most worthy in God of honor.

@ [Col. 0389D] We publish this letter, hitherto unpublished (now 110), from two manuscript codices, one Salzburgian and the other from Saint Emmeram. The material enclosed in brackets is found only in the Salzburg manuscript.

## LETTER 146. TO ARNO, ARCHBISHOP OF SALZBURG. (Year 802)

He declares his affection for Arno. He partly refuses and partly promises to answer his questions. He praises love of the king’s justice and censures the greed of officials. Along with gifts he sends a work on Solomon’s Ecclesiastes to be copied. [Col. 0389B]

To the most reverend Father Aquila, archbishop, the humble matricularius Albinus sends greetings.

On the ninth day before the Kalends of June, at the third hour, a messenger from your blessedness arrived among us, and at the ninth hour of the same day he announced that he necessarily had to return. Therefore, placed within so narrow a space of time, I could dictate nothing else except to give thanks for [Col. 0389C] the sweetest generosity of your charity, and for the proof of the holy faith that we have always truly recognized to dwell in your breast. But the faithlessness of those receiving my letters for delivery to you greatly harms my devotion. For I remember that last year,

@ [Col. 0389D] “When you were returning from Italy.” Namely, in the year 801. The reason why Alcuin cannot here be understood as referring to some earlier return of Arno from Italy [Col. 0390D] is that this letter was addressed to Arno while he was occupied with a public mission to administer justice, and therefore with the office of a royal envoy, which was only undertaken in the year 802, as we shall say below in the note to Letter 112 (now 151).

when you were returning from Italy, I sent you two little letters; similarly, just now, in anticipation of your arrival, I sent two to the palace. But I do not know which of them reached your presence. [For just as the exchange of your conversation was sweet to me, so it is sufficiently delightful for me often to address your authority through literary greetings. And know with certainty that I rejoice greatly when I receive letters from your affection, because there is no bishop in this kingdom whose faith I would more readily trust, whose welfare I would more desire in the Lord, or whose holy consolation, whether in speech or in letters, I would more wish to enjoy. But the misery of this world separates those who are dear, divides harmoniously joined spirits, and thus teaches us more ardently to hasten toward that life where no beloved person will ever be absent and no enemy will ever be present. Whoever recognizes the blessedness of that life easily despises the delights of this world, which are not delights but deceptions, not sweetnesses but bitterness, not true riches but false flatteries. [Col. 0390A] But alas, what grief! Many are lovers of this deception, and few are worshipers of true riches (II Tim. III, 4), while Truth itself says, “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX, 16). Let us strive to be among the few, so that we may deserve to be counted among the chosen.]

What could my sluggishness write about canonical life and regular discipline, or your occupation accomplish? What could my incompetence add to the holy canons or to regular discernment? Or should I admonish you about something in which you were instructed from infancy? Or what can my indolence know about secular judgment, among which affairs I never wished to be involved? Nevertheless, if my diligence can learn anything about it, once I know for certain what you are asking about, I shall not be slow to explain what I think. [Col. 0390B]

@ [Col. 0390D] “Concerning the nature of the Catholic faith.” See the notes to Letter 152.

Concerning the nature of the Catholic faith, at a suitable time, with the divine Spirit inspiring me, I do not refuse to consider something according to the writings of the Catholic Fathers and to transcribe it for the increase of your holiness. I see this as very necessary for many who seek worldly things more than spiritual ones, not knowing that, according to the Apostle’s saying, it is impossible to please God without faith (Hebr. XI, 6).

[As for prayers for you, my mind can in no way forget them. Rather, with a certain sweet remembrance, I keep the name of your blessedness fixed in my heart before God, especially before the tomb of Christ’s confessor and your intercessor, blessed Martin, and I have had it written among the sacrifices of Christ’s holy priests.]

As for the condition of my illness and my disposition, my Candidus was able to tell you everything. Therefore it is superfluous to write anything about it except this: all the dignity of my body has departed, and worldly pleasure has fled far away.

I am very certain of the good will of our lord the emperor: he desires that everything in the kingdom given to him by God be arranged according to the standard of righteousness. But he has not as many helpers of justice as he has subverters, nor as many preachers as predators; for there are more who desire their own things than God’s (Phil. II, 21).

Your holiness should accept no gifts from anyone in legal cases, for you know very well that it is said in the Law: “Gifts blind the hearts of the wise and subvert the words of the just” (Exod. XXIII, 8). This evil is exceedingly prevalent among Christians, because those who are commanded to despise their own possessions seize what belongs to others with injustice. May your good foresight above all forbid this to everyone concerned with the mission of your venerable truth. [Col. 0390D]

We received the very sweet gifts of your affection with every eagerness of mind, although at present my mind desires no little presents because of the repose of my spirit. Nevertheless, gifts from you are always sweet to me, especially garments, which have always been quite suitable for my body.

We have sent your charity two head coverings as a blessing, on account of the two commandments of charity [Col. 0391A], and one fine white little cloak, on account of the harmony of perpetual peace, which ought always to be one and the same between us.

I have also sent, for copying, if you wish, and for returning to us again—for I have nothing else except this one thing—a little work on Solomon’s Ecclesiastes. You will be able to learn the reason and purpose of this work from its own prologue. But I beg that, if you consider it worthy, it be copied quickly and immediately sent back to us, lest the devotion of our labor perish for our boys, since, as I have said, I have nothing else except this alone.

[May almighty God deign to guard you in perpetual prosperity and grant you to flourish in every wealth of holy virtues, lord Father and most desired brother.]

@ [Col. 0391C] Frobenius, Letter 193.

## LETTER 147. TO THEODULF, ARCHBISHOP. (Around the year 802)

He praises his virtues; rejoices over the pallium obtained from the Apostolic See; urges him to preach persistently. He prays for a favorable journey. [Col. 0391B]

To the pious Father and prudent teacher, whom we embrace with every affection,

@ [Col. 0391C] “Theodulf, archbishop of Orléans.” Here the title “archbishop” should be noted. It belonged to him not by reason of his see, which had never been metropolitan, but by personal honor, on account of his having received the pallium from the Apostolic See, as I shall explain below. Alcuin wrote this letter, as is clear from its context, from the monastery of Tours after the year 796, when he withdrew there; and at a time when the strength of his body had already been broken and was gradually failing because of continuous fever. He laments this also in other letters written in the year 800 and later. We shall observe in the following notes that the present letter was written in 802.

To Theodulf, archbishop of Orléans, the humble Levite Alcuin sends greetings.

Words of sweetness habitually flow from an overflowing fountain of charity, because it is a kind of refreshment for a heart burning with love to express in speech what it holds most deeply in mind. Therefore, wishing, through the impulse of private affection, to renew the bond of friendship established through consideration of piety, I wished by this little letter to recall my fidelity to your holiness [Col. 0391C], lest the treasure of memory become worthless through the long rust of forgetfulness.

This was especially because our son Candidus, your faithful servant, often tells us many distinguished signs of goodness in your blessedness, and how freely he had borne testimony to the truth in—

@ [Col. 0391D] “In a public assembly.” I think this should be understood not of a diocesan synod, but of an assembly of the whole kingdom or empire held in the presence of the king or emperor. In my judgment, this could not have been another assembly with which the journey of Theodulf of Orléans, mentioned below, could be connected except the assembly at Aachen in the year 802, in which Emperor Charlemagne “selected archbishops, bishops, abbots, and counts, whom he sent throughout his entire kingdom,” as the Chronicle of Moissac relates. See below, col. 393, note a.

in a public assembly; and how honorable your blessedness’s conduct was among persons both greater and lesser [Col. 0392A]; how devoutly and religiously you diligently observed ecclesiastical offices; and how you hated impious disputes. For all these things most certainly show that you please God, that the grace of the Holy Spirit flows abundantly into your breast, and that the flame which Truth itself testifies that it sends upon the earth, so that it may burn (Luke XII, 49), blazes in your heart, since no floods can extinguish it.

I shall rejoice and rejoice greatly at the increase of your honor and—

@ [Col. 0391D]

“Concerning the seal of priestly dignity, etc.” Until now the opinion of the very learned men Baronius, Pagius, Sirmond, Mabillon, and others had been that Theodulf received the pallium from Pope Stephen IV when, in the year 816, he crowned Emperor Louis at Reims, and that only then was he called an archbishop. But this opinion is completely overturned by this letter, since it is certain that Alcuin did not live until that year.

The poem of Theodulf himself to Modoinus provided the most distinguished men with an occasion for error. They assign it to the year 817, and it concludes with these verses:

> It stands as the work of the Roman bishop alone,  
> from whose holy hand I received the pallia.

They therefore interpreted this passage as referring to Pope Stephen IV, to whom Theodulf had been sent by Louis the Pious, although Theodulf does not name the pontiff there. In fact, in that poem Theodulf complains that he had been condemned to exile through a fault neither proved nor ever confessed by him, and he adds that no one could have exercised judgment over him even if he had confessed, unless it had been the Roman pontiff, or the Roman See, from which he had received the pallium:

> Suppose I had confessed, he says; whose judgment would have had  
> the power to impose upon me the fitting reins of judgment?  
> It stands as the work of the Roman bishop alone, etc., as above.

It must therefore be maintained that, while Alcuin was still alive, Theodulf received not from Stephen IV but from Leo III—and more probably, as we shall say immediately, in the year 802, while he was carrying out a mission in the province of Narbonne as a royal envoy—both the honor of the pallium and the title of archbishop.

Concerning the seal of priestly dignity, which Apostolic authority has added to you, know this with certainty: the splendor of this honor demands persistent preaching. The priestly pallium is a diadem. Just as the brilliance of gems adorns a royal diadem, so confidence in preaching ought to adorn the honor of the pallium [Col. 0392B]. For it possesses its honor in this: that its bearer proves to be a preacher of truth.

Remember that, by priestly dignity, the tongue is the heavenly key of the kingdom and the clearest trumpet of Christ’s armies. Therefore do not be silent, do not keep quiet, do not fear to speak, having Christ everywhere as the companion and helper of your work and journey. For it is not right that so bright a light, so abundant a lamp of wisdom, should be hidden under a bushel, but that, for the honor of its giver, it should shine with the light of truth upon all who enter the house of God. “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Matt. IX, 37). But the fewer they are, the more persistent those who are present must be.

“Raise your voice,” says the Prophet, “like a trumpet” (Isa. LVIII, 1). And another says: “Let there be a trumpet in your throat, like an eagle, over the house of God” [Col. 0392C] [The manuscript should be read thus: “In the throat let there be a trumpet like an eagle,” etc.] (Hos. VIII, 1). Many occupy the earth, but when Christ seeks fruit they will not bring any. You, venerable man, should honor your ministry; preach in season and out of season, and, like a wise banker, multiply the Lord’s money, so that you may become worthy of the payment of the denarius.

[Col. 0393A]

> This work, this work perhaps removes you from the fire;  
> this work, this work inserts you into the heavenly court.

This is the poet’s wording. But Apostolic authority is proved everywhere to admonish us to this; Truth itself also commands it, saying: “Go, teach all nations” (Matt. XXVIII, 19). Likewise the Psalmist declares blessed the one who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night (Ps. I, 2).

Perhaps your wisdom thinks my incompetence babbles excessively; but I desire that the grace of divine mercy bestow upon you greater gifts of spiritual blessedness. Therefore I dictated this little letter with confidence, because I knew that your holiness was rich in the gifts of pious charity and willingly endured words that are known to flow from the fountain of love of truth.

But this above all I beg with a suppliant heart: keep me, a servant of your holiness, commended in your holy prayers, all the more because the day of recompense is approaching. For curved old age compels me, with silent step, to hasten toward the presence of my judge; but continuous fever, like a raging robber, besets the road of my journey, stripping me of the garments of the salvation I desire, so that I can scarcely perform any service in the house of God.

Therefore greater necessity compelled me to hasten to the assistance of Christ’s servants, so that they might strive to help me through holy intercessions, lest my soul be handed over to the enemies of my Lord Jesus Christ. But you, illustrious man, whose age is flourishing, whose wisdom is vigorous, and whose holy dignity is exalted, with the flowers of sacred preaching—

@ [Col. 0393C]

“Your journey’s roads.” I interpret this passage as referring to the journey undertaken by Theodulf after the assembly held at Aachen in October 802, as the Chronicle of Moissac relates. At that assembly, Emperor Charles “selected from his nobles the wisest and most learned men, both archbishops and the other bishops . . . and sent them throughout his entire kingdom.” See the capitulary of that same year in Baluze, volume I of the *Capitularies*, p. 345.

The cited Chronicle of Moissac agrees with this, recording the following: “The most pious Emperor Charles, remembering on his day the poor who were throughout his entire empire and could not fully obtain justice, did not wish to send poorer vassals from within his palace to administer justice; rather, he selected in his kingdom archbishops and the other bishops and abbots, together with dukes and counts, who no longer needed to accept gifts from the innocent, and sent them throughout the entire kingdom, so that they might administer justice to churches, widows, orphans, the poor, and the whole people.”

I have no doubt that in this public assembly Theodulf was assigned that mission and prefecture in the province of Narbonne which he himself describes in Book I of his poems, or in the *Paraenesis to Judges* in Sirmond, beginning at verse [Col. 0394C] 99. He relates how, although tempted by various gifts from litigants, he carried out the office of judge everywhere without corruption, precisely in accordance with the intention expressed by the emperor at that assembly.

[Col. 0394D] I know that the celebrated Mabillon, in Book XXVI of the *Benedictine Annals*, nos. 71 and 72, assigns this mission to the year 798, immediately after Laidradus, his companion on the mission, had been ordained bishop of Lyon. But, with all respect to so eminent a man, I would say that this is confirmed by no ancient witness; nor is it sufficiently certain in what year Laidradus, although perhaps elected in that year, was ordained to his see. Theodulf also calls him the future bishop of Lyon in the cited poem, verse 119.

Notwithstanding these considerations, it seems to me most probable from the foregoing that the public assembly, Theodulf’s journey, and the honor of the pallium—which Theodulf perhaps obtained from the Apostolic See for the greater dignity of his very important office—events that Alcuin mentions in this letter as having occurred at the same time, should all be associated with the year 802, and that this letter likewise belongs to that year.

Remember to fill the roads of your journey with the flowers of preaching, leaving traces of your arrival everywhere. And, I beg you with suppliant prayer, may your Albinus go with you in mouth and heart wherever you go—he who carries you at Saint Martin in the chest of his heart and follows your journey with prayers—wishing that God’s good angel may go with you, so that you may travel prosperously and return to us happily and joyfully.

Use your lot happily, so that you may enjoy your reward eternally. This life is a road; blessed is the one who is not detained on the road by the variety of meadows, so that he fails to hasten toward the beauty of his homeland. Happy is the one who divides the burden of riches into consolations for the poor [Col. 0394A], knowing that the hands of the poor are Christ’s treasury, and that on the great day he will testify that he received whatever was expended for his least ones in this light.

@ [Col. 0394D] Frobenius, Letter 194.

## LETTER 148. TO THE SAME

A wholly allegorical letter in which Theodulf is compared with the Father of the vineyards.

To the great pontiff and Father of the vineyards, Theodulf, Albinus sends greetings.

We read in *Chronicles* that Zabdias was placed over the wine cellars in the time of David, the king greatly beloved by God (I Chron. XXVII, 27). Now, by God’s mercy, a second David rules over a better people, and under him a nobler Zabdi presides over the wine cellars of the vineyards. The king introduced him into the wine cellar with rightly ordered charity, so that the scholars might support him with flowers and surround him with apples, as one languishing with love for him who gladdens the human heart.

Now, if there is no one to strengthen, perhaps there is no lack of one to gladden in the cellars of Orléans, since hope rests in a flourishing vineyard, not in a withering fig tree. Therefore Jotham, David’s counselor, a learned man (ibid., 32), sends to Zabdi, saying: “Let us rise in the morning and see how well the Sorek vineyard is flowering; as a chant is sung over it, let the springs of the cellar be led forth outside.”

But now, with the keys of charity’s storerooms opened, let this little verse be celebrated by the steward of the vineyard throughout the towers of Orléans:

“Eat, my friends; drink and become drunk” (Song V, 1, 2). “I sleep in sweetness, and my heart is awake in charity. Come, receive without any exchange wine and milk” (Isa. LV, 1). “My throat is like the best wine, worthy for my beloved to drink and for his lips to savor” (Song VII, 9). “I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine” (Song VI, 2).

It must not be said: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” (I Kings IX, 7). “I cannot rise and give it to you” (Luke XI, 7). If perhaps three loaves are not at hand, which were lacking in the storehouses of the Gibeonites, by Christ’s blessing seven jars are full of the finest wine (John II), wine that had been kept until now. Who does not know that it is to be mixed by the master of the feast of the city of Tours at the command of the virgin’s son [Col. 0395A]? And this must be preserved, lest new wine be put into old wineskins. No one who drinks old wine immediately wants new, for he says, “The old is better” (Luke V, 37, 39).

Blessed is the one who speaks into a listening ear. Farewell in peace, dearest brother!

@ [Col. 0395C] Frobenius, Letter 195.

## LETTER 149

@ [Col. 0395C]

This is the title of the Harleian codex itself. The present letter should be joined to two others concerning the case of an Orléans cleric who was thrown into prison by his bishop, escaped from it, and fled to the basilica of Saint Martin as to an asylum. These letters are presented below, col. 408 and following.

Alcuin had perceived from Letter 119 (now 158) that the emperor Charles’s disposition toward the brothers at Tours—accused by Theodulf of dishonoring his men, indeed the bishop himself and his imperial command—had been sharply aroused, and that Alcuin himself had in some way been brought under suspicion of neglecting his duty. Therefore, in this letter he first tries, with the greatest submissiveness, to soothe the emperor’s mind and move him to clemency; then he defends his brothers against the unjust accusation of their adversaries, showing that they were diligent and assiduous in celebrating the divine offices, guilty of no injury toward the bishop of Orléans, of no disobedience toward the royal commands, and of no conspiracy to defend the accused. In addition, he discloses the true causes of the riot and of the bishop’s agitation against the men who wished to drag the accused back to his former bonds; finally, he solemnly asserts that at the beginning he knew nothing of the whole affair, but afterward omitted nothing belonging to his duty in order to quell the riot. In confirmation of all this he appeals to the testimony of the royal envoys Wido and Teotbert.

This letter is therefore to be regarded as highly important, because through it that celebrated controversy between the bishop of Orléans and the people of Tours is brought into fuller light, and the innocence of the latter is vindicated by Alcuin’s most weighty testimony.

## TO CHARLES, MOST EXCELLENT EMPEROR  
*(802 or 803)*

He pleads for the brothers of Saint Martin, and defends them and himself against calumny in the matter of the asylum granted to the cleric of Orléans; he discloses the true cause of the riot.

To the most excellent lord and most worthy of every honor, Charles, king, emperor, and Augustus, most victorious, greatest, best, and most serene: Albinus, matricularius, [Col. 0395B] sends eternal salvation in the Lord God Christ, both for the present prosperity and the future blessedness.

On the first page of this letter I see that I must offer thanks with my whole heart to the Lord our God for your safety and welfare, matters greatly necessary not only to me but to all Christians. Then, prostrate in body before the mercy of your pious goodness, with a contrite heart and tearful voice, I must plead for the brothers of Saint Martin, into whose service your goodness has delegated me, although I am less worthy of it.

I call God as witness to my conscience: I have never understood them to be such as I hear them described by certain people who are more ready to accuse than to save. So far as it can be seen and known, [Col. 0395C] they worthily perform their offices in the churches of Christ. I testify most truly that I have seen no others celebrating in any place more perfectly, nor interceding more diligently, in their daily custom, for your safety and for the stability of the Christian empire.

Their conduct and life can be attested by a perfect man, an incorruptible judge, and a faithful envoy, Wido.

[Col. 0396D] **Wido.** A count who governed the March of Brittany on this side of the sea. I believe him to have been the same man to whom Alcuin dedicated his book *On Virtues and Vices*, which will be presented below among the Moral Works, where one may see the preliminary notice. Wido can be heard, since by investigating everything concerning them he learned what they had done and how they had lived.

Nor was I slow to admonish them concerning the propriety of monastic life, as those very witnesses themselves attest, if anyone thinks their testimony worthy of belief. Nor do I know their faults toward their accusers, or why their accusers pursue them with such hatred. And it is remarkable that they should wish to intrude into another’s harvest, contrary to the commandment of the law, when the distinguished Teacher likewise forbids this, saying: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? To his own master he stands or falls. And he shall stand, for God is able to make him stand” (Romans 14:4).

[Col. 0396D] For the city of Tours has a shepherd, and so forth. He is speaking of Joseph, bishop of Tours, who, on the night when Alcuin died, “saw an immeasurable brilliance of splendor over the church of Saint Martin and the blessed soul of that man entering heaven, and, shedding pious tears, kissed the body of the deceased,” as the author of Alcuin’s *Life*, no. 30 and following, relates. “For the city of Tours has a shepherd distinguished in conduct and devoted in preaching, who knows how to provide the measure of wheat to Christ’s household most effectively. Let each shepherd watch over his flock, lest any of God’s grace be lacking in it, so that when the Shepherd of all comes, he may find them worthy to be rewarded with an everlasting recompense.”

With regard to the gathering and riot that arose in the church of blessed Martin, or outside in the atrium, I testify before him who considers the hearts of individuals that it happened neither at my urging, nor with my knowledge, nor even with my approval. I confess that I was never under greater distress on account of the sins of others than I was at that time. Nor, as far as I could understand or hear, was anything done there by the advice of the brothers; indeed, I could not discern even their wish that it should happen. It is beyond doubt that no one who fears God or cares for his salvation ought either to do such a thing—or even to think of doing it.

Was not Teotbert, a venerable man and envoy of your authority, among us for nineteen days for this investigation, with our accusers also appearing before him in turn? Whomever he wished, he flogged; whomever he wished, he put in chains; whomever he wished, he made swear; whomever he pleased, [Col. 0396C] he summoned into your presence. I would have served my Lord Jesus Christ in vain for so long if his mercy and providence had abandoned me so completely that I should fall into so impious a crime in the days of my old age. But I confess most truthfully and without any doubt that I would not wish to have as much gold as all France possesses if such a dangerous riot in the Church of Christ had been organized through my counsel or preparation.

I am poor and a stranger in this world. I fear God and have whatever small concern I can for the everlasting salvation of my soul, although in this life my conduct [Col. 0397A] may have shown this less perfectly. Now, especially, in the days of my old age and illness, I must be particularly on my guard. I know the burden of so monstrous a crime, and I am not unaware that the judgment of my life has drawn near. Out of fear of that judgment, I freed myself from the tumult of this world by the counsel of your beatitude, so that I might serve God alone in quiet and intercede daily for you in tears, in return for all the good things you have done for me, with God’s favor.

Nevertheless, I do not blush to disclose to your excellence the account of this tumult according to the truth, insofar as I have been able to understand it, sparing no one, so that I may bear testimony to the truth. It seems to me that no one sinned more in this impious affair than the guardian of that criminal, through whose negligence such great [Col. 0397B] evils afterward arose. To speak with the peace of those who will read or hear this letter, I judge it more just that the man through whose negligence that accused person escaped from his chains should suffer those same chains than that the fugitive accused should be taken from the church, where he had fled to the protection of Christ our God and his saints, and returned to the same bonds. I do not say this merely from my own judgment, but strengthened by the word of the Lord, who commanded a prophet to say to the king of Israel, who had released the king of Syria from his hands: “Thus says the Lord: Because you have released a man worthy of death, your life shall be in place of his life” (1 Kings 20:42).

Secondly, I understand that the instigators of this tumult were those who came armed, in greater numbers than necessary, from the city of Orléans to the city of Tours. This was especially so because a report spread through the ears of the people [Col. 0397C] that they had come in order to drag away by force the man who had fled to the protection of the Church of Christ and of blessed Martin. It is also common to everyone everywhere to resent the dishonoring of their saints. Perhaps that wretched man even urged the peasants who came to his lodging, while drinking, to defend the church of Saint Martin, lest he be violently dragged away from it.

The third incitement to this tumult occurred when our holy Father and bishop, most inopportunely, entered the church in the presence of the people with the men who were thought to have come to carry off the accused. Perhaps he did this with a simple heart, thinking that no harm could result from it. When the uneducated crowd saw this—for it always acts without deliberation in matters that are unsuitable—they shouted together [Col. 0397D] and ran for clubs. Some energetic men came from outside when they heard the bells ringing; their movement was carried out by the hands of the uneducated, as was ascertained by the envoys of your authority, indeed by our very accusers themselves.

In their presence the holy Gospel was brought, with the wood of the holy cross placed upon it. They made whichever of the brothers they ordered swear an oath. But when the brothers heard the bells, they rushed from the refectory to learn why they had been rung. On coming, they quelled the tumult as far as they could, as I have heard, except for those who, as I judge, were found to be boys and were brought into your presence. They were at fault in that gathering. From them it can be heard what they did; they themselves also swore that no one had urged them to do this, but that they acted only from the impulse of their own foolishness.

Nor was any vassal of Saint Martin there, except one named Amalgarius, who was with me at that very hour. I immediately sent him with other brothers to quell the tumult and rescue the men of the venerable bishop from the hands of the people, lest anything evil be done to them. After the tumult had been quieted, they were led into the monastery, where they could be safe. They, however, burned with such hatred against me that they turned into an evil act the good deed I had ordered them to perform, saying that I had sent them *eulogiae* as an insult—something entirely false. For they did not know that I had been instructed in the Lord’s commandment, which says: “Do good to those who hate you” (Matthew 5:44).

[Col. 0398B] Let your holy piety, most merciful lord, consider these things and learn the truth; and, for the love of almighty God and in honor of Saint Martin, your intercessor, show mercy to his servants. He has always been honored in the kingdom and by the kings of the Franks. In confession of our sins we are accustomed to say to God: “If you should mark iniquities, Lord, Lord, who shall stand?” (Psalm 129:3). Let us say the same to you, since we know that you are the noblest member of that same Head: if you should mark iniquities, lord emperor, who shall stand?

Especially since the distinctive virtue, goodness, and praise of emperors has always been clemency toward their subjects, to such an extent that Titus, that most noble emperor, said: “No one should depart from an emperor in sorrow.” Gladden the hearts of your servants by the supreme gift of your mercy. Let mercy triumph over judgment, since by your praiseworthy piety you have been able to pardon the greatest sins of treachery committed against your authority [possibly: “of those who sinned”]. Forgive our misfortune according to the most pious nobility of your most holy mind, which I have always recognized as flourishing wondrously in the wisdom of your heart. And just as we read that David, the Father of Christ, was praised for the greatness of his mercy and the equity of his judgments, so, with Christ’s gift, we have always known your beatitude to be praiseworthy and worthy of proclamation in these titles of merit.

May almighty God the Father, through his only Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, in the Spirit Paraclete, [Col. 0398D] illuminate, fill, and gladden the heart of your beatitude with every blessing and wisdom; and may he deign to grant your most noble offspring perpetual prosperity, for the salvation of the Christian people, most longed-for, best, and most august father of your country!

May King David Magnus flourish and thrive in wisdom, virtue, and triumphs—a great glory in speech.

[Col. 0397D] **Editions:** Quercetanus 55; Canisius 48; Frobenius 111.

## LETTER 150. TO MAURUS  
*(802)*

He asks Maurus (Hrabanus) for the little book he had promised him.

To blessed Maurus, boy of Saint Benedict: Albinus sends greetings.

[Col. 0398D] **To the boy Maurus.** In Quercetanus’s edition this letter is incorrectly addressed “To Benedict.” He is Hrabanus, Alcuin’s disciple, to whom, according to the custom of that period, Alcuin gave the surname Maurus, as Hrabanus himself testifies in the preface to his *Commentary on the Books of Kings*. Mabillon, *Annales*, book 26, no. 39. It appears to have been sent to Hrabanus after he had returned from the schools at Tours to Fulda, around the year 802. Mabillon, *Annales*, book 27, no. 13.

The little book *On the Praises of the Holy Cross*, which he promised to Alcuin and completed in the thirtieth year of his age, and which, in the year 806, he dedicated to Saint Martin in the name of the already deceased Alcuin, with a prefatory poem entitled “Intercession for Maurus.” Rivet, *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. V; Mabillon, *ibid.*, no. 29.

The little book that you promised, when I asked you to write it: I ask that your promise make it firm and that my joy be fulfilled. When many draw from it, the fountain of a living spring is not dried up; so neither is your wisdom diminished, even though our need draws from it. Do not despise me who ask, nor refuse to fulfill what you promised; but let your truth become my satisfaction. Love the one who loves you, and give to the one who asks,

[Col. 0399D] **“That you may do everything.”** The passage is corrupt. Quercetanus’s manuscript reads: “May you be able to please the one who possesses everything that these things command.” [Col. 0400D] Live happily, and so forth.

because the law commands one to please a parent. May you live happily with your children, and in

[Col. 0400D] **“Among the people.”** In the Saint Gall manuscript, apud Canisius, *poculo* is read. Perhaps *in osculo* should be read. among the people of charity, greet the brothers, praying for me.

{163}

[Col. 0400D] **Edition:** Mabillon 21. We have restored its beginning from the Salzburg manuscript. (Frobenius, Letter 112.)

## LETTER 151. TO ARNO, ARCHBISHOP  
*(802)*

He complains that no reply has been sent to several letters. He grieves that his friend is entangled in secular affairs, and that shepherds of souls are troubled by worldly cares. He commends himself, sick in body and mind, to Arno’s prayers, and sighs for heaven.

To the venerable Father and archbishop Aquila, embraced, honored, and desired under the wings of true charity: the humble matricularius Albinus sends greetings in Christ.

[Col. 0400D] **“At the anniversary time.”** Within the period of one year, as I interpret it.

[At the anniversary time I sent several little letters to your holy affection, written according to the feeling of charity; but I do not know whether they reached the face of your venerable dignity, since I have not yet deserved replies in your customary familiarity—whether this was the negligence of the bearers, or whether the occupation of your holiness prevented you from writing.]

I know that the full affection of your piety remains firmly in your breast, not only toward me but toward all your friends. It will be proved in adversity and praised in prosperity: in whose wings is health, in whose steps is the ladder which the patriarch Jacob dreamed of (Genesis 18:12 and following), an ascent to him who says: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).

Behold the sign of Christ’s discipleship! Behold the gate of the heavenly kingdom! Behold the foundation and summit of our life! Yet it is scarcely believed to be firm where it does not appear by some indication—whether in the consolation of the poor, in exhortation to the brothers who are near, or in writing to those distant in body but near in spirit.

I grieve for you, brother! I grieve from the innermost sorrow of my heart

[Col. 0400D] **“Because of secular affairs.”** After Arno returned from Rome in 801, having settled matters there, he was enrolled among the royal envoys, or public judges. He was their chief in Bavaria, as may be read in several public documents from 802 and the following years in *Historia Frisingensis*, vol. I. Arno bore this office reluctantly, since he considered it greatly derogatory to an apostolic office. See below, Letter 114 (now 153).

because of secular affairs, which impede, by a certain gathering of clouds, the rays of charity that could have illuminated many from the flame of your breast, if they were not obscured by the darkness of earthly occupations. Yet let it keep watch in your heart and, at suitable times, send forth its radiance, so that it may shine for all who are in the house of God (Matthew 5:15)—for those who are not blind so as to see or deaf so as to hear (Isaiah 42:18).

What is the duty of your name, if not to keep your mouth open to all in bearing witness to the truth, through him who says: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80:11)? Do not neglect the grace that has been given to you (1 Timothy 4:14), but attend to it so that it may progress more and more.

“Many are the tribulations of the righteous” (Psalm 33:20), because among the many who are called, few are chosen. And the rarer they are found, the more urgently it is necessary for them to preach the word of God. Almost everyone seeks what is his own (Philippians 2:21), and few seek what appears to belong to Christ. Secular cares disturb shepherds who ought to be free for God. They are forced to wander through the lands and for the world to serve as soldiers of Christ, and, under whatever necessity compels them, they hide the sword of God’s word behind the bars of their mouths. Alas, what grief! Very few possess it, although very many promise that they have it; but on the day of battle they show themselves to be mercenaries, not soldiers.

Having considered these things more carefully, most beloved Father, consider yourself, look around, and attend to who you are, where you are going (Genesis 32:17), and what you will say in judgment, in the presence of him who appointed you as watcher over his people.

Know that I myself have been almost externally freed from secular affairs, but inwardly I have been badly wearied by many occupations and utterly empty disturbances of thought, which prevent me from crying out with a pure heart: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” (Mark 10:47). By your most holy prayers, dearest brother, I humbly and earnestly beg that these things may be driven away, at least to some extent.

Help the one who labors; raise up the one who lies fallen; extend the hand of compassion to a brother almost submerged in the stormy sea of thought. Do not think that I am making these prayers in vain. With God as my witness, I shall say that I greatly need the annoyance of this temptation to be relieved by the prayers of your holiness.

I can restrain my body to some degree, but I cannot constrain the wandering steps of my heart, although I ought to desire heavenly things alone. I have the eyes of my heart almost blinded by the darkness of earthly dust, unless he to whom I must often cry with the prophet illuminates it by the free gift of his compassion: “For you illuminate my lamp, O Lord; my God, illuminate my darkness” (Psalm 17:29). Again: “Illuminate my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Psalm 12:4).

[Col. 0401A] {164}

In part I see where my rest is, where the satisfaction of my thirst lies. Where? In him alone to whom the prophet cried: “My soul has thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm 41:3).

And, turning to himself elsewhere, as though he had found the answer to this petition, he says: “This is my rest for ever and ever; here I shall dwell, for I have chosen it” (Psalm 131:14). In another verse he exhorts himself toward it, saying: “Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you” (Psalm 114:7).

For this benefaction [Mabillon: “For this blessed gift”] he stirs himself elsewhere to praise God: “Praise the Lord, my soul” (Psalm 145:2). And, as though his soul had answered, he adds: “I shall praise my God during my life; I shall sing psalms to my God as long as I am” (ibid.). Since I shall always be, I shall always praise my God, saying: “Let the heavens and the earth praise him, the sea and everything that is in them” (Psalm 68:35).

I have placed these verses together in this way because nothing seems sweeter to me to sing in the compunction of prayer than these verses thus arranged. I ask that, prompted by the reminder of my devotion, you make it your custom to sing them often, with great joy of heart, in remembrance of eternal blessedness and whenever you recall my name, however slightly, in this prayer and in every prayer that brings salvation.

May divine grace deign to hear you, most longed-for lord Father, and sweetest to the love of our heart!

[Col. 0401D] We publish this letter, hitherto unedited, from the Salzburg and Saint-Emmeram manuscripts. The passages enclosed in brackets are found only in the Salzburg manuscript. (In Frobenius, Letter 116.)

## LETTER 152. TO ARNO  
*(802)*

He commends to Arno the care of canons, monks, and the third rank, intermediate between them. He complains of simoniacal depravity, which has also entered the apostolic see. He mentions a letter on confession and a little book on the Catholic faith.

[Col. 0401C]

To the venerable bishop Aquila: Albinus sends greetings.

Some time ago I wrote at length; therefore I have decided now to write only briefly, urging this one thing: that your holy authority speak in God and for God, and trust in God, so that it may be carefully examined what is suitable for each person: what is suitable for canons, what for monks, and what for the third rank, which varies between these two [Saint-Emmeram manuscript: “what”], standing between the canons of the higher rank and the monks of the lower. Such people are not to be despised, because people of this kind are found especially in the house of God.

Above all, give attention to the complete overthrow of the simoniacal heresy, which wickedly rules over many, taking its root from secular judges and extending its branches as far as ecclesiastical persons. Thus those who ought to have uprooted the thorns of avarice are themselves pierced by the thorns of bitterness; these, growing more and more, have almost crept into the apostolic see, from which the palm of piety ought to have grown, flourishing with the fruit of the date-palm. From this the rancor of envy has boiled over.

Forgive me for saying this—or rather, forgive me for fearing that anyone should dare to think something against his own head. Would that the person who says this might be found mistaken, so that the one who ought to make others innocent through the words of holy preaching might himself be innocent!

[My magician]

[Col. 0401D] **“My magician.”** He calls Adalbert by this name. See Letter 89 (now 501).

My magician asked me in a letter expressing his affection—whether at your authoritative command or prompted by his own will—to compose a letter on confession or penance. But I sent him the one which I had long ago dictated and written for the sons of Saint Martin, whose number is great; I judge that this alone can also suffice for your young men. Would that you might come, if possible; but if not, send the Magician at a suitable time, for the reading of a little book which I have recently written

[Col. 0401D] **“A letter on Confession.”** This will be given below among the moral works.

[Col. 0401D] **“A little book … on the Catholic Faith.”** He seems to mean the books entitled *On the Faith of the Holy Trinity*, and so forth, which were presented to Emperor Charles in the year 802 with a dedicatory letter prefixed. See above, Letter 110 (now 149), note c, on the Catholic Faith.

on the Catholic faith, and sent to the lord emperor through this boy. Let this little book by no means escape your hands, but let it by every means be copied, so that you may have it; for it is exceedingly necessary for those wishing to know the Catholic faith, in which the sum of our salvation consists.

May blessed God bless you and yours with an eternal blessing, most beloved lord Father!

[Col. 0402D] **Edition:** Mabillon 24. It appears to have been sent shortly before the following letter, whose note b may be seen in column 405. It has now been restored to its integrity from the Salzburg manuscript. (Frobenius, Letter 113.)

## LETTER 153. TO ARNO, ARCHBISHOP  
*(803)*

He announces that he has received a letter of affection through Bishop Adalwin, who came to Saint Martin. He wishes Odulf to be admonished concerning the administration of justice, the chaplains concerning praiseworthy conduct, the brothers of the monastery of Saint Rhodbert concerning sincere charity, and so forth.

[Col. 0402C]

To the most holy Father raised to the honor of the archiepiscopate of Aquila: the humble [deacon Albinus] sends greetings of eternal peace and prosperity.

When the most sweet brother, [Col. 0402D]

[Col. 0402D] **“Bishop Adalwin.”** Of Regensburg, who presided over this see from 792 until 817, as the old documents of the library of Saint Emmeram testify, where one reads: “792: Sinpert died; Adalwin succeeded. 817: Adalwin died; Baturicus had succeeded.” See the following letter.

Bishop Adalwin came to Saint Martin for the sake of prayer, bringing us the very sweet words of your greeting and announcing the strength of the prosperity we desired. We were, as I confess, greatly rejoiced at his arrival; and, as your affection had instructed, we received him privately and addressed him with the language of the sweetest familiarity.

For, as I recognized in him, he is a very faithful man and devoted to holy religion [Mabillon: “devotion”]. Having examined the words of your greeting that he brought, we found them written with the pen of charity. By the honeyed sweetness of that same charity we have always been refreshed by you and in you; and, by God’s mercy, it can carry us to heaven on the two wings of love.

This is the better portion that blessed Mary chose, sitting at the feet of the Savior and intent on hearing from him the word of salvation (Luke 10:39, 42). Therefore let us remain continually in perfect charity, one part of which stretches toward God in faith and upright conduct, while the other embraces our neighbors in patience and kindness.

May your intention, dearest brother, proceed peacefully along this fourfold way until the God of gods is seen in Zion (Psalm 83:8), in the fullness of blessedness. Remain in these commandments and strive to instruct others, so that they may learn the Catholic faith and demonstrate it by sober conduct in their works, and strive to be patient and beneficent toward the souls who share this labor.

We had nothing new to entrust to your sincerity concerning the palace.

[Col. 0403D] **“Odulf.”** Since this name was absent from the Saint-Emmeram manuscript, Mabillon thought that the reference was to Gerold, prefect of Bavaria; Hansiz thought it referred to Goteram, first count of the frontier district. But we now possess the certain name from the Salzburg manuscript. Odulf appears with Arno among the royal envoys in documents 118 and 128 of *Historia Frisingensis*, vol. I, part II. See also the capitulary of 805, no. 2, in Baluze, vol. I of the *Capitularia*, p. 325, no. 7, and elsewhere in volume 97 of the *Patrologia*. He died in 819, as the *Brief Annals of Regensburg*, edited by Mabillon from the Saint-Emmeram manuscript, testify, *Analecta*, p. 368.

But may your holy devotion preach [Col. 0403D] to our former friend Odulf the word of life frequently, so that he may be just in judgments and merciful toward the poor, because we read: “Mercy and truth preserve the ruler” (Proverbs 20:28), and exalt those who walk in them. Let him always remember whom he would wish to have as his defender in dangers, and let him love him; and, insofar as he is able, let him fulfill his commands in action. Nor should he thoughtlessly expose himself to dangers, as

[Col. 0403D] **“Certain of his predecessors.”** The distinguished Hansiz wishes this to be understood of Gerold and Eric, who were killed in the Hungarian war in 799. Alcuin, however, could have cited a more recent example: Cadaloc and Goteram, who, according to the same *Annals of Regensburg*, were killed with many others in 802 at the castle of Guntionis.

some of his predecessors did, and therefore perished by a shameful death. Let Christ be in his heart, and his commands in his mouth and in his works, so that he may live happily in this world and obtain blessed glory in the next.

Greet your disciples and chaplains in my name, I ask, admonishing them to live honorably before men, so that your dignity may be praised on account of their conduct. Also exhort the brothers of Saint Rhodbert, confessor of Christ, frequently to serve God faithfully in sincere charity, devout religion, and obedience to holy humility, looking toward the reward of everlasting blessedness.

They wage the warfare of the Church in the camp of Christ [Salzburg manuscript: “Let them wage”], so that in the heavenly dwellings they may rejoice with him in everlasting happiness. I wish you to admonish them to remember me—not only them, but all the servants and handmaids of God in your region. May the Lord God increase their number and command their names to be written in the heavenly library.

May divine grace accompany you all and bring you to the glory of everlasting blessedness, most beloved lords!

[I would have written letters of exhortation to each of the persons mentioned above, if the haste of this venerable bearer had not prevented me. [Col. 0403D] But may your goodness, I ask, become a living letter pleasing to God, so that in my name you may admonish each of them [Col. 0404A] concerning the salvation of their souls, and commend them to my prayers, whom Christ deigns to preserve everywhere.]

[Col. 0404D] **Edition:** Mabillon 25. It now appears in an expanded form from the Salzburg manuscript. It seems to have been written after Letters 146 and 148. In those letters he complains that no reply was made to the letters he had written at the anniversary time; here, however, he admits that he received words sweeter than any honey. Once this is established, the present letter must be placed after the year 802, in which Letter 146 was written, since that letter was sent on the ninth day before the Kalends of June, whereas this one was sent on the day of the Lord’s Supper. This is why I have assigned the year 803 to it. (Frobenius, Letter 114.)

## LETTER 154. TO ARNO, ARCHBISHOP  
*(803, on the day of the Lord’s Supper)*

He consoles him, afflicted by secular occupations. He sends a letter through Bishop Adalwin. He promises grateful remembrance for the chasuble.

To the most desirably honored and honorably desired archbishop [Aquila]: the humble [deacon Albinus] sends greetings.

Having received the gifts of your affection, more precious than all gold, and words sweeter than all honey, in which I read of the anguish of your mind

[Col. 0404D] **“Because of secular service.”** This was something Arno, recently enrolled among the public judges, was frequently obliged to undertake.

in secular service contrary to the dignity of your holiness, so that you are not permitted to devote yourself to better offices or to labor for the gain of the flock of souls, I beg your beatitude to consider whether any of the saints ever passed through this world without temptation.

As blessed Jerome says in one of his letters, Solomon alone was always in delights, and therefore perhaps he sinned. The blessed apostle exhorts us to patience: “You have heard of the patience of Job and have seen the end of the Lord” (James 5:11). The Lord himself says in the Gospel: “In your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

Let us turn to Christ with our whole attention and constant prayers, for he is the one refuge from every tribulation. As the Psalmist commands: “Cast your care upon the Lord [Salzburg manuscript: ‘God’], and he will nourish you” (Psalm 54:23). Let us say to God with the prophet: “Be to me a God who protects me and a fortified place, so that you may save me” (Psalm 70:3).

God is he in whose hand is the heart of a king, and he will turn it wherever he wishes. He never abandons those who hope in him. He declares, with a true promise and the strongest consolation: “Everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matthew 7:8), together with the other things that he discusses deeply enough in that same passage concerning hope for the fulfillment of a petition, and confirms by examples.

From the beginning of the world, and also from the birth of the Church, those who served God have always been wearied by tribulations. If you read in the divine books about the course of the world, you will find what I say to be true: either God’s servants suffered open persecution externally, or, in the peace of the Church, they were afflicted inwardly by hidden troubles.

[Col. 0404D] Against all these things, patience alone is effective in the name of God. The Lord himself, conqueror of this world, says to his disciples—or rather to their successors: [Col. 0405A] “In the world you will have distress; but take courage, I have conquered the world” (John 16:33).

We must remember what Truth itself answered its tempters: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matthew 22:21). If we live according to the apostolic example and lead a poor life on earth, as they did, we rightly renounce the service of the world. But now the princes of this world appear to have a just reason for oppressing the Church of Christ with their service.

When blessed Paul the apostle instructed Titus, his beloved son, concerning the individual offices of ecclesiastical dignity, he said among other things: “Warn them”—whom else but Christians?—“to be subject to princes and authorities, to obey their commands, to be ready for every good work” (Titus 3:1). Blessed Peter likewise wrote in agreement, since he was inspired by the same Spirit: “Obey your fleshly masters, not only the good and gentle, but also the difficult” (1 Peter 2:18).

If we must obey even the difficult, how much more ought we, with willing readiness, to obey a most wise prince and one most devoted to holy religion. Nor do I say this because I do not rather wish you, together with your disciples, to lead a quiet and excellent life for God in holy religion, with the most blessed woman who, sitting at the Lord’s feet and hearing heavenly words, chose the portion that will never be taken away (Luke 10:39, 42).

But I fear that, if the matter is stirred up, your beatitude may neither be able to attain what you desire nor retain imperial favor. Therefore, as I said above, the only apparently salutary course is to commend the outcome of our desire entirely to God through prayers in the narrow circumstances of our situation [manuscript: “of our situation”], so that by his holy clemency and goodness he may provide for us how we may peacefully attain our will.

Yet if we must seek our own will, let us remember that he—that is, the Lord Jesus—said of himself: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38). For the will of God is wholly good; and we must ask with every intention of mind and every execution of good works that it may always be done in us.

These things we dictated in haste for the moment, because of the pressure of the festal day. In fact, your Blessedness’s messenger had come to us on the most holy day of the Lord’s Supper, demanding letters from us so that he might not return empty-handed. By God’s mercy, you may hope for a fuller reply, whether concerning the consolation of your labor or even the anguish of your mind, and also concerning the inquiries that

[Note at Col. 0405D: “Emb.” Thus it is read in the manuscript codices. I have no doubt that some proper name lies hidden under this abbreviated word “Emb.” Formerly Emb had it through the agency of the disciples of your charity, most dear to us.]

[I beg you to salute, in my name, your sister, the handmaid of God. Urge her in my words to lead a religious life on earth, so that she may be found worthy to possess blessedness in heaven. Venerable Father

[Note at Col. 0405D: Adalwin. Concerning him, see the preceding letter, which perhaps was that little letter of reply that he says he placed in his hand [Col. 0406D]. From this we infer that that letter too belongs to the year 803. “Bishop Adalwin came to us with great and manifold honor, bearing the syllables [i.e. the message] of your affection; we placed in his hand a little letter of our reply.” You accused me, as I admit justly, of writing to you too slowly or of being negligent in writing [F., “in writing”]; and this was because of the lack of couriers, who are scarcely ever found trustworthy. Thus the great distance between our lands prevents anyone from crossing from these regions to you except rarely. Nevertheless, let your affection know that, after the lord emperor, I would wish my little mind to exert itself for no one more than for you, because I am indebted to no one more, on account of the always most fully proved faith and affection of your Blessedness. One thing was read in the letter that your Reverence has just sent, which I would not have wished to be written, or ever to have happened: namely, that you no longer had hope of seeing my face. This weighed heavily upon my mind, because I asked the one present to dismiss me with the hope of returning to Saint Martin. Let the Lord’s will be done. Or, if it cannot come to pass here in this temporal light, may it come to pass, by God’s mercy, in the eternal one. I shall wear the little chasuble that you sent in memory of your affection at the solemn celebrations of Mass.] Glory and praise to God! Everything is prosperous with us, and with our sons whom you know; they unanimously salute your Blessedness and wish you much health for a long time in the Lord. Know with absolute certainty that we cherish the sweetest remembrance of your name in our prayers at Saint Martin; and whenever the Spirit of the Lord visits the heart with compunction, he always brings the remembrance of your name back to mind. May God, who is rich in mercy (Ephesians 2:4), in everlasting kindness have mercy upon you, Father, brother, dearest son, forever.

[Note at Col. 0406D: Edited by Mabillon, no. 26. It now appears in a more correct form from the Salzburg manuscript. (In Froben, Letter 115.)]

## LETTER CLV. TO ARNO, ARCHBISHOP (Year 803)

He commends himself, as a weak old man, to the sacred memory. He sends two table-vessels and offers repeated thanks for the Mass-chasuble.

To his most beloved son Aquila, archbishop, Albinus sends greetings in the Lord.

Affection once joined by faithful kinship is often renewed by new letters, so that what is firm in faith—which is sweet in familiarity—may be recognized. Therefore I join one little letter to another, so that what is written on the page may be read as having been inscribed on the tablets of the heart [Mabillon, “tablet”], not with perishable ink, but with the everlasting Spirit, who arouses unutterable groanings in my heart for your well-being. Your affection, as I know most certainly, does not forget our name, because frequent illness compels us to remind our friends of the support of holy prayers, so that divine kindness may be propitious toward my sins and my life may be renewed for the better, like the youth of the eagle (Psalm 102:5). May neither my Judge nor my Witness judge me according to my merits, but according to his great mercy spare his confessing little servant, who is a sinner [Col. 0407A]; and may he not abandon him in the days of his old age (Psalm 70:9), but cherish him with the consolation of the Holy Spirit and have mercy upon him. Let your most holy mind and keenest wisdom remember these same words concerning itself: while you have the opportunity (Galatians 6:10), labor at the work of God, so that on the great day of our Lord you may receive the reward of your labor with God’s saints, everlasting. May divine grace guard you, your sons, and your household with everlasting protection, go before you, and increase you in gifts and merits forever. [I have sent two little vessels to your affection, holy Father. I beg you humbly to accept them and to keep them for some time before your eyes on your table, just as I

[Note at Col. 0407C: The chasuble. He also mentions it in the preceding letter; hence we have assigned this one to the same year. “I shall have the chasuble that you sent at the solemn celebrations of Mass.”]

[Note at Col. 0407D: Hitherto unpublished; it now appears from the Salzburg manuscript. (In Froben, Letter 117.)]

## LETTER CLVI. TO ARNO

He sends various short works through Fredegisus and commends this son of his to him. [Col. 0407B]

To the venerable evangelist Aquila, Albinus sends greetings.

I have sent to your affection, through my son Fredegisus, a small handwritten book containing many things on various subjects, namely: brief expositions of the seven Penitential Psalms, also of Psalm 118, and likewise of the fifteen Psalms of Ascents. There is also in that little book a small Psalter said to be that of blessed

[Note at Col. 0407D: Psalter. This is found below among the Offices for the weekdays under the title “Collection of Bede’s Psalter.” “The Psalter of Bede the presbyter, which he collected in sweet verses in praise of God and in prayers for each psalm according to the Hebrew truth.”]

Bede. There is also

[Note at Col. 0407D: A hymn on the work of the six days, etc. I do not know which hymn this is, or whether it belongs to Venerable Bede or to Alcuin.]

a very beautiful hymn on the work of the six days and on the six Ages of the world. There is also in it

[Note at Col. 0407D: A letter on Confession. This is the letter that he recently sent to his Magus. See the preceding letter among the notes.]

a letter on Confession, which we composed for infants and children. There is also in it

[Note at Col. 0407D: An old hymn, etc. See it after the Commentary on the Psalms of Ascents.]

an old hymn on the fifteen Psalms of Ascents. It also contains other prayers, and likewise a most noble hymn composed in elegiac meter about a certain queen

[Note at Col. 0407D: A hymn on Queen Æthelthryth. It is extant among the poems attributed to Alcuin and in volume 3 of the works of Venerable Bede, p. 139. It begins:

“Gracious God, Trinity, who governs all the ages,

“Grant now success to what has been begun, gracious God, Trinity.”]

named Æthelthryth. I have placed this little book in the hands of my son Fredegisus. Ask him for it, lest perhaps, because of his other occupations, he forget to return it to you; and do not allow him to do so unless you have it, whether at home

[Codex: “in the house”]

or on a journey, in memory of me, so that you may hear it as though I were speaking to you in your heart. I would have sent more in it, had his haste not overtaken me; and I had no time to arrange it as I had planned. Fare well in prosperity, and, reading it happily, remember me always in your prayers and fare well without end. I beg your most merciful kindness, dearest Aquila, to receive my son Fredegisus graciously and familiarly, and to help him according to your ability; and may you regard him as a brother in Christ. May Christ preserve you forever.

[Note at Col. 0407D: This letter, whose beginning Mabillon had previously published in *Acta Sanctorum*, fourth century of the Benedictines, part 1, p. 187, the learned Baluze later presented in a fuller form from a manuscript of the Colbert Library, where the oldest collection of Alcuin’s letters is preserved, volume 1 of the *Capitularies*, p. 1442. We have now supplied the deficiency at its end from a manuscript of the Vatican Royal Library, and have added variant readings from another manuscript of Salzburg of excellent quality. (In Froben, Letter 118.)]

## LETTER CLVII

[Note at Col. 0408D: To Candidus and Nathanael. That is, to Wizo and Fredegisus, as the old list placed at the front of the Colbert manuscript teaches; there it reads: “Letter to Candidus, that is Wizo, and Nathanael, that is Fredegisus.” Baluze.—Both were Alcuin’s disciples and were then staying at the prince’s court.]

## TO CANDIDUS AND NATHANAEL

[Mabillon dates it to 802; Baluze to 803.]

He advises them to conduct themselves wisely at court. He instructs them concerning the dispute with Theodulf, bishop of Orléans.

To his dearest sons in Christ, Candidus and Nathanael, Albinus sends greetings. [Col. 0408B]

My concern and my affection for you, sons, keep watch over you at every hour, desiring that by your character and religious life you may please God and my lord David, and that you may be examples of good works to the others who live in the palace. “A wise son is the grace of his father” [Mabillon and the Vatican manuscript: “to the young men; for grace indeed …”]. True wisdom is that which leads to eternal life. Nor has it laid down for us ignoble precepts, but very noble ones, worthy of every honor; through them we can attain [Mabillon: “reach”] eternal life and obtain honorable esteem among human beings. Concerning these precepts I have often admonished you in the school of your instruction [Mabillon: “of our instruction”]. But recently, brought forth from the nest of your father’s education, you flew out into the public air. Let what you heard from us be evident in you. May the father live in his sons, he who now anxiously awaits the day of his death. I desire you to survive him, you whom he had as fellow soldiers in the labor of God’s service [Mabillon: “he desires to have you surviving him”]. I would have many things to write that you ought to observe as necessary; but I know that I have often admonished your affection concerning an honorable life and often followed up and renewed my admonitions in letters. Therefore let us say what now appears necessary both to us and to you.

The venerable Father

[Note at Col. 0408D: Theodulf. Concerning him and his works, see Jacques Sirmond, volume 2 of his works, pp. 665ff., and *Literary History of France*, volume 4, pp. 459ff. Cointius asserted from the charters of Louis the Pious that he was adorned with the pallium by Pope Stephen IV while the pope was staying at Reims in the year 816, and was thereafter called archbishop of Orléans; Pagi likewise says this in the same year, no. 10. But this opinion is completely overturned by the letter to Theodulf, Letter 147 of this edition, note b.]

Theodulf, bishop, is engaged in a dispute with certain brethren, faithful intercessors for your prosperity, concerning a certain fugitive defendant.

[Mabillon: “with the brethren [Col. 0409A] of Saint Martin.”]

The defendant

[Note at Col. 0409C: Salzburg manuscript: “Theodulf the archbishop has a certain dispute with the brethren of Saint Martin, your faithful men, concerning a fugitive defendant, more, as we think, at the request of his own people than from any disturbance or anger of his holy mind. The defendant …”]

after many kinds of punishment had suddenly escaped from his bonds [through the negligence of the guards] and taken refuge in the basilica of Saint Martin, the foremost confessor of Christ, confessing his sins, seeking reconciliation [Salzburg manuscript: “pardon”], and appealing to Caesar, asking for a way to his most holy presence. We returned him to the ministers of the aforementioned bishop, because of the ambushes

[Note at Col. 0409D: Salzburg manuscript: “When he had been returned to the messengers of the aforementioned bishop, so that he might be safely led, under their pledge, to the presence of the lord archbishop for canonical penance, they did not dare to lead him because of the ambushes …”]

prepared for him on the road, as it is said. As they departed, they left him standing before the doors of the church. But after these events, as it was discovered [Mabillon: “as it is conjectured”], very many men of the same venerable bishop came in a hostile manner [Salzburg manuscript: “after some time, the men of the pontiff came in a hostile manner …”]. Eight leading men

[Note at Col. 0409D: “The principal men entered the church on Sunday with our most holy bishop, apparently to seize the defendant lying before the tomb of the holy confessor of Christ, and to profane the sanctity …”]

entered

[Note at Col. 0409D: With our bishop—namely, the bishop of Tours, as Mabillon records in Book 27 of the Benedictine Annals, p. 361, no. 16.]

the church on Sunday with our bishop—not those eight who, according to the prophet, are said to feed the land of Nimrod with swords and spears (Micah 5:6), but to seize the defendant and profane the holiness

[Note at Col. 0409D: “Fearing lest between the altar and the tomb of the most holy confessor there should be a shedding of blood. A certain man of that fugitive’s party was seized in the midst of the crowd to be led outside, and he cried for help. At this, the people, partly seeing and partly hearing what had happened, suddenly raised a great cry, and there was a gathering of the people, especially the poor, from every part of the city. It was reported in the city that the enemy from Orléans had come to profane Saint Martin’s intercessions, because they knew that many men from the aforementioned city lived scattered through the villages. Fear and tumult increased everywhere. Our brethren snatched the aforementioned bishop’s men from their hands, lest they suffer some harm, and drove the people out of the church. But his men say many things that did not happen there, with audacity, and exaggerate what did happen with superfluous words. Let your holiness consider whether it is just that a fugitive defendant who has taken refuge in Christ’s church should be seized by force, and whether it is right …”]

of the house of God and diminish the honor of Saint Martin, the holy confessor of Christ. For they rushed inside the altar railings and expelled the brethren before the face of the altar [Mabillon, perhaps: “our brethren”].
