If they say otherwise, they are utterly false, because none of them bowed his head to God’s altar at that time. It was reported throughout the city that the enemy from Orléans had come to profane Saint Martin’s intercessions, because they knew that the men living in the little villages would come from there. Suddenly a crowd of beggars gathered in the city from every direction, prepared to defend their defender. [Col. 0409C] Fear and tumult increased everywhere. Our brethren snatched the aforementioned bishop’s men from their hands, lest they suffer harm, and drove the people outside the church. But I know that the pontiff named above will make many accusations against our brethren, exaggerate what happened, and add many things that did not happen, just as we read in his letter

[Note: “Up to this point is Mabillon’s fragment.”]

Therefore, dearest sons, I strictly command you to come prostrate before the feet of my lord David, the most just and serene emperor, asking that, when the bishop comes, you be given an opportunity to defend yourselves and dispute with him: whether it is just that a defendant should be seized by force from the church and subjected to the same punishments from which he fled; and whether it is right

[Note at Col. 0409D: Salzburg manuscript: “Let your holiness consider whether it is just that a fugitive defendant should be seized by force from Christ’s church, and whether it is right,” etc.]

that one who appeals to Caesar should not be brought before Caesar; and whether it is lawful that a penitent who confesses his crimes should be stripped of all his possessions down to his shoe-strap; or whether the Lord’s word is rightly observed: “Mercy triumphs over judgment” (James 2:13). In such an act, on the contrary, judgment triumphs over mercy. And where is that mercy so often praised by our Lord Jesus Christ, which is numbered among the evangelical beatitudes: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7)? Likewise the Lord’s command: “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36). Let us also consider the prudent warning where he says: “Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned” (ibid., verse 37); and many other passages read in the authority of the Gospel concerning mercy, and the Lord’s own word where he says: “I have not come

[Note at Col. 0410D: Salzburg manuscript: “It is certain that this same defendant committed many sins and very impious crimes. He has as witnesses priests who are still alive, to whom he made his confession: a Christian from the monastery of Saint Benedict and Adalbert from the monastery of Saint Martin, before he was discovered, bound, or tortured. What is it that the Lord Jesus himself says: ‘I have not come …’”]

to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matthew 9:13). Therefore he did not reject the sinful woman who touched his holy feet; she did not, by her touch, bring reproach upon Christ, but drew forth the insignia of his virtue. For her uncleanness did not defile the world, but the purity of the world purified the unclean woman.

Let us remember that we are servants of the one who, led to the cross, prayed for those crucifying him (Luke 23:34). And how does the venerable Father say that a guilty sinner ought not to be received in the church? If sinners do not enter the church, perhaps no priest will be found to sing Mass in it, nor anyone to answer the cantor, unless it be some newly baptized person, since the apostle John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

Yet in the venerable bishop’s letters we find this same defendant called a devil, not a human being. Do you not consider what the Apostle says: “Do not judge before the time” (1 Corinthians 4:5)? Do we prescribe to the power of God that he should have mercy on whom he wills, when he says: “The last shall be first, and the first last” (Matthew 19:30)? We have an interpretation of this wisdom in Judas and in the thief [supplement supplied]. The one from the apostolate hung from a noose; the other entered paradise from the cross (Luke 23:43).

Blessed Gregory says that there are two things in this same saying that we must carefully weigh. What are they? “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 27:5). The first is that no one should presume greatly upon himself, because even if he has already been called to the faith, he does not know whether he is worthy of the everlasting kingdom. The second is that no one should dare despair of his neighbor, whom he perhaps sees lying in vices, because he does not know the riches of divine mercy.

Is any sinner such that he cannot be cleansed by Christ’s blood, or so deeply submerged in the abyss of crimes that Christ’s mercy cannot heal him? What else does one who says this imply but that Christ died in vain? He died in vain if he cannot give life to some, although he grants us pardon every day. Is it just to deny to others the pardon that we earnestly desire to be given to ourselves? [Edition: “never”] We flee to the church so that our prayers may be heard in it, yet we disdain to hear the prayers of others in it? We trust that our sins are forgiven through the prayers of the saints in the church, yet with hard hearts we bind the sins of one who confesses in that same church?

But the Apostle commands that those who offend be corrected in a spirit of gentleness (Galatians 6:1). And the apostle James says: “If you have bitter zeal and there are contentions in your hearts, do not boast” (James 3:14), [Col. 0411C] and so forth—the things that are read in what follows with terrible condemnation concerning those who possess bitter zeal [F., “in what follows”]. Zeal is good, if it is tempered by a spirit of gentleness. Care must be taken that the ruler show himself to his subjects as a mother through kindness and as a father through discipline [perhaps the text should read: “that the ruler show himself to his subjects as a mother by kindness and as a father,” etc.]. It must also be ensured that neither rigid strictness nor excessive leniency prevail. For discipline or mercy is greatly ruined if either is maintained without the other. Therefore the ark is said to have contained both the rod and the manna (Hebrews 9:4), so that in the ruler’s breast there might be the rod of strictness and the manna of sweetness, as the Psalmist says: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Psalm 22:4). Let there be zeal, but raging moderately [Vatican manuscript: “strict”]. Let there be kindness, but let it not spare beyond what is useful.

But let us see what the holy canons decree concerning fugitives who flee to a church.

[Note at Col. 0411D: Salzburg manuscript: “the unclean: I say this because there are some who say that such sinners ought not to enter Christ’s church. Perhaps few enter. ‘On whatever day,’ says the prophet, ‘the sinner turns, he shall live and shall not die.’ But let us see what the holy canons decree concerning fugitives who flee to a church,” etc. The Salzburg manuscript omits the intervening material.]

In the canon of Orléans (First Council of Orléans), chapter 1, we read: “Concerning murderers, adulterers, and thieves, if they flee to a church, we decree that the following must be observed, as the ecclesiastical canons have determined and Roman law established: they may not be dragged away from the church courts or the bishop’s house, nor handed over to anyone else, unless, after oaths have been given upon the Gospels, they are made secure from death, mutilation, and every kind of punishment.”

O bishop of Orléans, you dare to act against the Council of Orléans, in which, as we read, seventy-two bishops were present! Can it seem just and honorable for the bishop of that city to violate the authority of his own city?

Likewise, the Fourth Council of Orléans, chapter 21: “If anyone, compelled by necessity, takes refuge within the precincts of a church, and someone, disregarding and despising the priest or ruler of the church, should presume to drag him by force or deceit from the sacred places or courts, or perhaps entice him away, that person shall be barred from the church’s thresholds as an enemy of the church until, according to the bishop’s judgment, fitting amendment follows through imposed penance; nevertheless, the person who was seized from the church must first be restored to the church” [perhaps: “after he has been restored”].

Likewise Saint Sylvester, in title 21 of the Fifth Council of Orléans: “Concerning slaves who flee to the precincts of a church for any offense, we decree that what is written in the ancient constitutions be observed. Once an oath has been given by the master concerning the pardon granted, whoever he may be, let the slave go forth secure in the pardon. But if the master, forgetful of his pledge, is proved to have violated what he swore, so that the one who had received pardon is afterward [Salzburg manuscript: “subsequently”] subjected to any punishment for that offense, let that master, who was forgetful of the pledge given, be suspended from the communion of all.”

Likewise the Council of Agde [First Council of Orléans, chapter 1]: “It was agreed that murderers should not quickly be driven from the doors of the church and should be free from every kind of punishment, provided, however, that they make satisfaction to those against whom they are guilty.”

Likewise the Council of Agde: “Every believer who takes refuge in the bosom of the church—that is, of the mother—should not easily be repelled, but in that church should be healed through satisfaction, to the extent that the judges of truth determine.”

We also read concerning the emperor Constantine that, after he had been baptized, on the fourth day [Salzburg manuscript: “on the fifth day”] he established a law of this kind: wherever a church had been built, it should possess this power by virtue of its consecration, that any defendant who fled into it should be defended at the peril of whatever judge was then present.

And, after examining the very careful books of the Romans, we likewise find written concerning fugitives who seek the protection of any church, and concerning those who appeal to Caesar or demand to be led before the prince.

The emperors Theodosius and Valentinian Augustus, in a constitution given to Antiochus, prefect of the praetorium, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April at Constantinople, in the consulship of Antiochus and Bassus [Vatican manuscript: “at Constantinople”], interpretation of Book 4 of the Theodosian Code, “Concerning Those Who Flee to a Church”:  “The church and places dedicated to God must protect defendants who, compelled by fear, have fled there, so that no one may presume to use force or hands in any holy place for the plundering of property [Vatican and Salzburg manuscripts: ‘for violence against and killing the defendants …’]. But whatever space belongs to the porticoes, courts, houses, or areas adjoining the church, we command to be guarded as though it were the interior of the temple, so that the necessity of fear may not compel defendants to remain around the altars and pollute places worthy of veneration.”

The emperors Honorius and Theodosius Augustus, in another constitution given to Ciclianus, the governor, after other provisions, on the ninth day before the Kalends of February [Vatican manuscript: “given”; Salzburg manuscript: “on the Nones of September”] at Ravenna, in the consulship of Honorius for the seventh time and Theodosius for the second time, interpretation of Book 3 of the Theodosian Code, “Concerning the Custody of Defendants”: “On every Sunday, judges shall bring defendants out of prison under reliable guard, so that Christians or priests may provide them with food, and on those days they shall be taken under guard to the bath, out of reverence for religion. If any of the guards neglects to fulfill this, he shall be compelled to undergo the penalty established by the law itself.”

Under the Julian Law concerning public violence, anyone endowed with authority who kills—or orders to be killed, tortured, beaten, or condemned on the public road—a Roman citizen appealing to the emperor [Book 2 and Book 15 of the Theodosian Code, “Concerning Appeals”], is condemned; the penalty is capital punishment for persons of lower rank [edition: “for lower persons”], while persons of higher rank are punished by deportation to an island.

The Julian Law decrees that, on account of violence [Salzburg manuscript: “through public violence”], any judge who tortures a free man or Roman citizen who has appealed to be led into the presence of the prince, kills him, orders him killed, binds him in public chains, beats him with whips, or presumes to condemn him, shall be condemned. For this offense, persons of lower rank are punished capitally [edition: “are placed”], while persons of higher rank are banished to an island.

In Orosius, Book 7, we read about King Alaric, who besieged, entered, and devastated Rome, and about the intention with which that pagan king ordered the holy places to be spared. Let us quote the very words used by that historian, who, after giving an appropriate account of the events, added: “Alaric arrives, besieges trembling Rome, and breaks into the troubled city; yet he first gave orders that, if anyone had fled into holy places, especially the basilicas of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, these should be allowed to remain inviolable and secure above all.”

Anyone wishing to know with what honor he ordered the sacred vessels found in the churches to be carried back may read what that same historian wrote [Vatican and Salzburg manuscripts: “there”].

If anyone considers the testimonies of the canons and laws that we have presented to be lesser authorities [Salzburg manuscript: “considers the authority of the canons or Roman law to be lesser”], let him read the Lord’s own commands concerning cities of refuge, and understand that it was divinely established that defendants and sinners, by the Lord God’s command, should have places of protection where they might be sheltered from the ambushes of their pursuers.

[Note at Col. 0413D: The Salzburg manuscript continues here as follows: “So much so that concerning fugitive slaves he is read in Deuteronomy to have commanded that they should not be returned to their masters because of fear of torture. The same words that are read there are: ‘You shall not hand over to his master a slave who has fled to you, but he shall dwell with you in the place that he chooses, in one of your cities where he finds rest; and you shall not distress him’ (Deuteronomy 23:15–16). These are the Lord’s words, not another’s, and they must be understood with all reverence and observed according to the opportunity of the time. We also read in the histories of the ancients that in almost every city there was an asylum for the refuge of criminals; and if pagans accorded this honor for the sake of refuge, how much more ought Christian churches to retain their honor for the comfort of fugitives?” This is the end of the letter in the Salzburg manuscript.]

It is also read that Rome itself and other cities throughout the world established asylums for the protection of defendants, so that, through the place or temple that was considered holy among them, the severity of the laws might be moderated [Vatican manuscript: “the precaution”].

Is it lawful among Christians for the Church of Christ to be held in less honor than the temple of Jupiter among pagans; or the house of blessed Mary, Mother of God, to be regarded with less veneration than the asylum of the impious Juno; or for Saint Martin himself, a true worshiper of God, to be less honored in a Christian empire than the deceiver Asclepius was honored under pagan rule?

If all these things are read to my lord David, the most Christian emperor and wholly devoted to every honor of God, or are spoken in peaceful words, I know that his most holy spirit, full of piety and most careful in keeping God’s commandments—he who cannot be turned from the way of truth by any gifts—will decide and judge everything as it may please the Lord God Jesus Christ and his saints,

[Note at Col. 0414D: The sense is incomplete.]

and it will be an everlasting reward for him in eternal blessedness and an everlasting blessing for his sons.

Behold the judgment of the holy canons; behold the decrees of the legal writings: they most firmly command that the honor of Christ’s churches be preserved in their protection of fugitives. We never believe that the most Christian and serene emperor, our lord Charles Augustus, would command otherwise, except in accordance with the judgment of the holy canons and the enactments of the legal writings [the words in brackets are restored from the Vatican manuscript and were lacking in the codex used by Baluze], and as his predecessors established. Neither the honor of God’s holy Church nor the reverence and fear due to his great name ought to be diminished in his most excellent kingdom and most powerful empire, or in any dignity and honor, but should always be increased, to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who honored him above all other kings and emperors with the splendor of wisdom and exalted him by the power of his kingdom.

[Note at Col. 0414D: It is useful, because of the historical connection, to append to this letter the reply of the emperor Charlemagne.]

[Note at Col. 0414D]

Baluze says in his notes on the *Capitularies*, volume 2, p. 1062: “This letter of Charles is of great importance, written by a great prince highly skilled both in the rights of the priesthood and in those of the empire. Here you see a cleric judged by his bishop according to the canons and confined in custody because of his offenses; having broken, so to speak, the bonds of the prison, he fled to the church of Saint Martin and abused the sanctity of the place in order to escape the punishment that had been imposed upon him by an excellent judgment. You then see the monks, in order to trade upon the religious authority of their asylum, conceal him in their hiding places and dare to undertake his defense against the bishop, even publicly heaping many insults upon him. This affair seemed so mad and foolish to the wisest of princes that he not only chastised their folly with harsher words, but also ordered that the cleric be returned to his bishop and that the monks come before him, so that they might wash away the crime that had been committed by making fitting satisfaction …”

“Moreover, what happened here to Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, under the rule of Charlemagne later happened almost in the same way to Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, as Flodoard teaches in Book 3 of his *History of Reims*, chapter 21. In listing Hincmar’s letters, he says: ‘To Ebo, bishop and fosterling of the Church of Reims, concerning a certain brother who had fled from this church and was staying with him, so that he might strive to send him back as quickly as possible with careful attention.’”

Baluze first published this letter from an old manuscript of the Colbert Library in volume 1 of the *Capitularies*, p. 413, and thought it was written in the year 803; Mabillon, however, assigned it to the preceding year. (In Froben, Letter 119.)

## LETTER CLVIII. TO ALBINUS, THE MASTER, AND TO THE COMMUNITY OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MARTIN

He reproves the community of Saint Martin for defending a certain guilty cleric who had fled to them, contrary to the judgment of his bishop and contrary to the king’s command, etc. [Col. 0414D]

[Col. 0415A] In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Charles, and so forth, to Albinus, the venerable master, and to the entire community of the monastery of Saint Martin.

The day before the letter sent by you arrived at our presence, letters sent by Bishop Theodulf were brought to us. They contained complaints about the dishonoring of his men, and not so much of them as of the bishop of this city, and about contempt for the command of our imperial authority. We had ordered that command—concerning the return of a certain cleric who had escaped from the bishop’s custody and was hiding in the basilica of Saint Martin—to be written under the authority of our name. You also sent us copies of it [F.: “we sent you …”], in which we do not think that we decreed anything unjust, as it seemed to you.

But when we had both letters reread to us—yours, that is, and Theodulf’s—your letter appeared to us much harsher and composed with anger than Theodulf’s, and in no respect sprinkled with the seasoning of charity toward him. Rather, it seemed to defend the defendant, accuse the bishop, and, under the cover of a concealed name, maintain that he either could or ought to be admitted to an accusation; although both divine and human law have entirely decreed that

[Note at Col. 0416D: “No criminal.” This is read in the *Capitula of Angilram*, chapter 43, and from there in Book 5 of the *Capitularies*, chapter 187. See also Book 7, chapter 85. Baluze.]

no criminal is to be granted the license to accuse another, although he has been defended and protected by you for this purpose under the pretext of the command of our name, since he had already been accused, and
> [Col. 0416D] **In the presence of the people.** This passage is greatly illuminated by chapter 370 of Book V of the *Capitularies*: “He was judged in the presence of the people of his city” [Col. 0415C]. He ought to have had standing to accuse by invoking the imperial name, following the example of the blessed Apostle Paul, who, accused by his own people before the rulers of Judaea but not yet judged, appealed to Caesar and was sent by those same rulers to Caesar to be judged (Acts 25:10–11). This, however, does not at all fit the present case. For the Apostle Paul, accused by the Jews but not judged, appealed to Caesar and was permitted to go before him. But this infamous cleric, both accused and judged, sent into custody and having escaped from custody, entered unlawfully the basilica which he ought not to have entered except after repentance, and, as you say, still does not cease to live perversely. Like the Apostle Paul, he appealed to Caesar, but he will by no means, like Paul, go before Caesar. We command that he be returned to the one before whom he was accused, by whom he was judged and sent into custody, and from whose custody he escaped; and that man is to bring him before our tribunal, whether he speaks truth or falsehood, because it is not fitting that, on account of such a man, any alteration should be made in our first command. But we are also greatly astonished that it seemed to you alone that our authoritative sanction and decree ought to be opposed, although it is plainly evident both from ancient custom and from the constitution of the laws [kings] that right decrees ought to be valid [F., ratified], and that no one is permitted to despise their edicts or statutes.

And in this we could not sufficiently wonder: that you preferred to obey the pleas of that wicked man rather than the commands of our authority, when it is now perfectly clear that, with that same man, the love of discord arising from a breach of charity has forbidden [his] departure from this place [the Latin construction is corrupt] [Col. 0416B] [L., as it were]. You yourselves know—for you are called the community of this monastery and servants of God [and would that you truly were!]—how your life has already been repeatedly defamed by many, and not without cause. At one time you said that you were monks, at another that you were canons, and at another neither.

And while seeking your welfare and the eradication of your evil reputation,

> [Col. 0416D] **A master.** Alcuin, certainly? We chose for you and invited from distant provinces a suitable master and rector, who could instruct you in upright living by words and admonitions and, because he was religious, could shape you by the example of a good way of life. But, alas, everything has been turned in another direction; and

> [Col. 0416D] **The devil found you as his ministers.** Ivo, bishop of Chartres, *Letter* 266, speaking of the monks of the greater monastery of Tours: “The monks, moved by demonic envy.” BALUZ., in the same place. The devil found you as his ministers for sowing discord where it was least becoming—namely, among the wise and teachers of the Church, who ought to have corrected and chastised sinners—and you compel them to burst forth into the sin of envy and anger. But they, by God’s mercy, will by no means give assent to your evil suggestions. You, however, who have proved yourselves despisers of our command, whether you are called canons or monks, know that you must appear before us at our pleasure, according to what our present messenger shall announce to you. And although the letter sent to us concerning the sedition committed here excuses you, come and wash away the stain of the crime with an appropriate satisfaction.

{176}

> [Col. 0416D] We have here transcribed a letter hitherto unpublished from two manuscript codices, Salzburg and St. Emmeram. The material enclosed in brackets is found only in the former. [In Froben, *Letter* 120.]

## LETTER CLIX. TO ARNO

He commends to him a student of grammar, whom he calls a calf.

To the most beloved Aquila, Albinus the matricularius wishes perpetual blessedness in Christ.

[Col. 0417A] I have sent to you the animal—the calf, my *Enchiridion*—so that you may help him and rescue him from the hands of his enemies; and help him as much as you can [“because the venerable bishop is greatly incensed against us,” that is,

> [Col. 0417D] Theodulf. See the preceding letter to Candidus and Nathanael. Whether this calf is the accused man on whose behalf the people of Tours disputed with the bishop of Orléans, as we saw in the preceding letters, cannot be determined from this brief document. Theodulf].

I have also placed in this boy’s mouth—although a calf is, contrary to nature, a rational animal—what he himself has to bellow in the ears of your holiness. [For I have had him [I had him] to be educated with me in my house, and, God granting it, he will be able to make progress in the study of reading or in the discipline of the grammatical art in the house of Saint Martin.]

O Aquila! Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we shall glory in the name of the Lord our God (Psalm 19:8). May you be well and flourish forever and ever.

> [Col. 0417D] This letter is the last one in the Emmeram manuscript codex and was omitted by Mabillon. The style reveals Alcuin’s pen; but whether it was written to Aquila or Arno, or to another friend, is uncertain. [In Froben, *Letter* 121.]

## LETTER CLX. TO ***

He commends himself to the affection of a friend. [Col. 0417B]

To the most beloved Father, an outstanding pontiff. Desiring to bear the light yoke, in whose unity he wishes you salvation.

Letters sweeter to us than every honey were delivered by our brother. While I was preparing to answer their contents, my son arrived; his most welcome visit briefly detained me from a longer response. Yet no worldly ambition will be able to detain my heart from the sweetness of charity. Rather, may it grow more and more from day to day, and each day add an overflowing amount to the full measure of my charity. May almighty God, who has joined us in the charity of the present life, deign to join us in perpetual charity forever.

> [Col. 0417D] This letter, hitherto unpublished, was extracted from an eleventh-century manuscript codex of the library of the Imperial Court at Vienna, catalogued in the theological class under no. 131, and communicated to me by the distinguished Dr. Matthias Reiberer, librarian and historian of the Society of Jesus in Vienna. From his industry the republic of letters eagerly awaits a continuation of *Germania Sacra*, already greatly adorned by the most celebrated Dr. Hansiz. [In Froben, *Letter* 122.]

## LETTER CLXI. TO ARNO

He explains how *substance*, *essence*, *subsistence*, and *nature* are said of God.

Albinus sends greetings to Aquila.

I am astonished that you ask me, within the narrow limits of a single moment, to portray the form of eternal life on a brief tablet. What is the Catholic faith, if it works through love, other than eternal life? To say something about it, lest I appear disobedient to your commands,

> [Col. 0418D] **I dictated in a brief discourse.** I understand these words as distinct from the short work referred to in this letter, in which the form of eternal life is not portrayed but a question quite different from it is answered. Alcuin himself seems to indicate this when he continues: “But concerning what it pleased your holiness to ask me—what difference there is between substance,” and so forth. There Alcuin evidently intended to indicate that Arno had proposed two questions to him: he had satisfied one in a brief discourse, but was answering the other in the present letter. Therefore I do not think it necessary to accept what the distinguished Dr. Reiberer proposed—either that *vero* (“but”) in the words just cited should be replaced by *ergo* (“therefore”), or that the text should be read, with certain words transposed and others supplied, as follows: “I am astonished that you ask me, within the narrow limits of a single moment, to portray the form of eternal life on a brief tablet and to unlock the most sacred recesses of the divinity. To say something about it, lest I appear disobedient to your commands, I dictated in a brief discourse. What is the Catholic faith,” and so forth.

But concerning what it pleased your holiness to ask me—what difference there is between substance, essence, and subsistence, or whether, if it is lawful to say so, the holy Trinity is a nature—one must know that *essence* is properly said of God, who always is what he is, who said to Moses, “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14). For God alone truly is, because he is unchangeable. Whatever is changeable, in a certain sense truly is not, because it can become what it is not, or cease to be what it is.

*Substance*, however, is a common name for all things that exist. Heaven, the sun, the moon, the earth, trees, herbs, animals, all living things, and human beings are called substances; for whatever is not a substance is nothing at all. Substance, therefore, is to be something. God, then, is substance—indeed, supreme substance and first substance, and the cause of all substances, because he is the creator of all things.

Hence, against the poison of Arian faithlessness, we customarily say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one substance, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one substance. For substance is so called because it subsists. Therefore the Greeks customarily say of God: *μία οὐσία, τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις*—“one substance, three subsistences” [manuscript: *Ypostatis*; Latin manuscript: *subsistentias*]. This did not please blessed Jerome, who judged that it was better to say in Latin: “one substance, three persons.” Riches are also called “substance” in ordinary usage, as it is read concerning the prodigal son in the Gospel: “He squandered his substance” (Luke 15:13), that is, his riches.

We freely call God’s *nature* nature, because every nature is nature, and especially that nature which alone is true nature, because it always is what it is, since that nature which always is cannot in any way be changed into another nature. It is frequently found in the books of the Catholic Fathers that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one nature.

But what you say you have read in the works of Saint Augustine—that God begot the Son neither by necessity nor by will, but by nature—we rightly consider to have been said: the Father begot the Son by nature because the Father and the Son are of the same nature, not by necessity or by will. For we read that a certain heretic impiously asked a Christian whether God had begotten the Son willingly or unwillingly. If he said “unwillingly,” necessity would fall upon God; but if he said “willingly,” the heretic would immediately reply that the Son belonged to will, not to nature.

The Christian, however, most vigilantly asked him in return whether God the Father was God willingly or unwillingly. If he answered “unwillingly,” the misery of necessity would follow—a thing it is great madness to believe concerning God. But if he said “willingly,” the reply would be made to him: “Then he too is God by his will, not by nature.” What, then, remained except for him to fall silent and to see himself bound by his own question with an unbreakable bond?

Therefore God is God by nature, the Son is Son by nature, and the Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit by nature; and there is one nature of these three, just as there is one essence, one omnipotence, and one divinity.

For the rest, there are many tribulations of the faithful according to their various circumstances, and each person is subject to temptations in this world, because the place in which we live is exile, not our homeland. These troubles of temptation urge us to seek our homeland and the quiet life, which can by no means be found here except in hope by one who lives for eternal rest. The end.

{178}

> [Col. 0419D] Quercetanus first published this letter among Alcuin’s dogmatic works, on page 765, and later added different and better readings on page 1512. The writers of *Gallia litteraria* judge that it is more correctly placed among Alcuin’s other letters than among his dogmatic works. We have followed their advice. It exists, with corrections, in the royal Vatican codex 69. [In Froben, *Letter* 123.]

## LETTER CLXII. TO THE LORD KING  
*(Year uncertain.)*

He explains the difference between *eternal* and *everlasting*, *perpetual* and *immortal*, *age*, *aeon*, and *time*.

To Lord David, excellent ruler and greatest victor, Flaccus Albinus wishes health.

On the proper meaning of certain names, as I was returning from you [Al., from us],

> [Col. 0420D] **Candidus.** Alcuin frequently made use of his services, as is evident from several letters in which he sometimes calls him Wizo. See *Gallia litteraria*, vol. V, p. 10 ff. Our Candidus proposed questions to us; I decided to remain silent for the time being so that he might investigate them more carefully at leisure. But he, an excessively demanding pursuer of your will and an importunate questioner, did not allow me to delay. Therefore I briefly noted the explanations of these names in a sudden and uncultivated [edition: secretly composed] discourse, awaiting your judgment concerning what has been said, as also concerning all my words and writings. For obedient devotion is praiseworthy when it is approved by the authority of the one who commands.

This, then, is the question presented to us by the same man: what difference is there between *eternal* and *everlasting*, *perpetual* and *immortal*, *age*, *aeon*, and *time*?

First, one must know that *eternal* and *everlasting* seem to signify the same thing. *Eternal* is a simple word, whereas *everlasting* is composed from the adverb *always* and the noun *eternal*. Therefore everything eternal may also be called everlasting; and, conversely, everything everlasting may also be called eternal.

*Perpetual* seems to be derived from *perpes* and to signify that which is interrupted by no interval but always remains in the same condition in which it is.

The difference between *eternal* and *immortal* seems to be that everything eternal is immortal, but not everything immortal is rightly called eternal.

Between *aeon* and *age* one may distinguish in this way: an aeon can be understood as something eternal, whereas an age is something temporal. But let us now examine the difference among these names.

That nature is called *immortal* which cannot die, though it is not necessarily unchangeable—that is, incapable of change. Thus the human soul was created immortal, but it is certainly not unchangeable, because it can be changed from worse to better, from better to worse, from worse to worse, or from better to better, as it is said: “The saints will go from strength to strength” (Psalm 84:7).

God alone is truly immortal and unchangeable, because he alone is truly and properly eternal and always is. Concerning him the Apostle says: “Who alone possesses immortality” (1 Timothy 6:16). He used “immortal” in place of “unchangeable,” because what is changeable in a certain sense dies with respect to what it was, when it begins to be something else that it was not.

Yet *eternal* is often used improperly of what is subject to time or change and is not always of the same kind; therefore it is not properly called eternal. For what changes does not remain. And, as we said above, this is the distinction between immortal and eternal: everything eternal is immortal, but not everything immortal is sufficiently precisely called eternal. For even if something always lives, nevertheless, if it undergoes change, it is not properly called eternal, because it is not always of the same kind, although it may rightly be called immortal because it always lives.

Sometimes, however, what is immortal is also called eternal. Properly speaking, *eternal* has neither anything past nor anything future; whatever is, is always. This is true of God alone. Therefore God alone is eternal according to the proper meaning of eternity.

What we have said about eternal may likewise be understood of everlasting. But what does the Apostle mean when he says, “Before eternal times” (Romans 16:25; 2 Timothy 1:9)? If there are times, how can they be eternal, since times exist only in created things? Perhaps he wished “before all times” to be understood. He preferred to say “eternal” rather than “all,” perhaps because time did not begin from time; for “eternal times” signify the aeon.

The difference between aeon and time is that the former is stable, whereas time is changeable.

An *age* is said to exist after the kinds of things were created and divided into different changes of times; and it appears that the age and times began together. But in many passages *age* is also read in Holy Scripture in the sense of everlasting, as in the words: “For his mercy is forever” (Psalm 106:1; 118:1 ff.). “Forever” means perpetually, because his mercy is eternal and unfailing.

An age is also the order of the world as it runs its course, tending toward the future and leaving the past behind. It is therefore thought that ages are so called because times are continually dissolved within them [F., revolve within them].

There is, however, a distinction when one says *from the age*, *in the age*, and *into the age of the age*. Adam was “from the age,” that is, at the beginning of the age. The other fathers—Noah and Abraham—were in the age but were not from the age, just as the entire succession of the human race was, is, or will be in the age.

“Into the age of the age” refers to the future age, which will exist after this age; it is also called “into ages of ages” (Tobit 9:11). In some passages, however, “into the age of the age” signifies absolutely the eternity of the Lord, since he is shown to have been merciful before the age, in the age, and after that age. Hence it is said of him: “But the mercy of the Lord is from age to age upon those who fear him” (Psalm 103:17).

Likewise, “into the age of the age” (Psalm 9:6; 10:16, and elsewhere) is often used because of the two Testaments, since the New Testament is the age of the former age, just as the future age will be the age of this present one.

An age is also found used for the end of any period or time. For in the Law of the Lord it is said: “Let him be your servant forever” (Exodus 21:6), that is, until the jubilee year.

One must know, however, that *eternal* is customarily understood in Holy Scripture in three ways.

First, it is used properly and truly of what is without any change, as God alone is.

The second usage is when something is called eternal that is not itself eternal in its own nature, but what it signifies is eternal. Thus it is said to Abraham: “I will give you and your seed this land as an eternal possession” (Genesis 17:8). Neither the land itself nor its inhabitants could have been eternal; rather, the land of the living, which is signified by that land, is eternal, as are its inhabitants, concerning whom it is said: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matthew 5:4).

The third usage is when something is called eternal because no end is assigned to it, or because it is arranged in such a way that thereafter it is not to be done, insofar as this concerns the care or power of the one who does or commands it. It is in this manner that a certain poet says:

> He will serve forever who does not know how to use what is small.

For he cannot serve forever whose own life cannot be eternal.

There is, however, a remarkable difference between the essence of almighty God and the revolving times of human life. We read that there are three times—past, present, and future—but in such a way that scarcely anything is present to us, while everything is past or future. [For when I say a word, the preceding syllable, while I say it, was future; and when I say the later syllable, the earlier has passed.] [Al.: “For when I have said a word, its preceding syllable …”]

But for God there is nothing past or future; everything is present, for he said to his servant Moses: “I am who I am.” And: “You shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exodus 3:14).

But if you begin to inquire more subtly, even the two syllables in the expression “eternal God” are not eternal; rather, that which these syllables signify is in every respect eternal. For the words by which we speak are nothing other than signs of the things that we conceive in our minds and by which we wish to bring others to knowledge. These words are never rightly uttered unless they signify truth. Truth is natural to every human being to such an extent that no one ever wishes to hear falsehood in place of truth in such a way that he himself believes what is false—unless he is excessively fickle [Vatican codex: empty] and turned away from all truth.

But since the sequence of this little document is hastening toward its end, it seems appropriate to say something definite about the meaning of *end* itself. There is a passage where *end* signifies what is without end, as in the Gospel: “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John 13:1), that is, he loved them forever.

There is also a passage where it signifies perfection: “For Christ is the end of the law” (Romans 10:4), that is, the perfection of the law.

There is likewise a passage where it signifies Christ himself, as in certain psalm titles: “For the end, David” (Psalms 51, 52, and elsewhere), that is, “for Christ.”

Sometimes *end* also signifies the end of any thing or period, as in Daniel: “At the end of those days” (Daniel 4:31).

Nor should the multitude of words or the length of this little document be held against me, because the length of time—or rather, that which has no time—requires many words to demonstrate what can scarcely be demonstrated. But a pen dipped in the fountain of charity finds it sweet to speak with one to whom all good things are sweet. May God deign to grant him eternal sweetness.

> May the merciful God grant you perpetual salvation throughout the ages,  
> and the glory of empire, O beloved David.

> [Col. 0421D] [Froben, *Letter* 124.] Quercetanus, edition 6; Canisius, edition 12. Here, however, a more carefully corrected text appears from a manuscript of the Salzburg library, where the following title is prefixed: “Explanation of the swords that are mentioned in the Passion.” In the printed editions: “Concerning what is said in the Gospel: ‘Lord, here are two swords.’”

## LETTER CLXIII. TO CHARLES

He explains the passage of Saint Luke, chapter 22:36 and following, concerning the two swords. He complains about certain bishops who wish to prevent priests and deacons from exercising the ministry of preaching, and about the profanation of altars.

To the most desirably venerable and venerably desirable Lord David the king, Flaccus [Albinus] sends greetings in faith and charity.

Having learned from the letters of your most noble piety of your health, greatly beloved by us, and of the prosperity necessary for the entire Christian empire [F.: “I learned”], I poured out the whole affection of my heart in thanksgiving to Christ, the most merciful King. Through diligent prayer, I entreated his mercy, together with all the collaborators in our devotion, that he might deign to preserve, govern, and extend your peaceful and beloved power, for the exaltation of his holy Church and

> [Col. 0422D] **The most sacred empire.** I believe that the Roman Empire is meant here. Hence we judge that this letter was not written before the year of Christ 800.

the long-lasting prosperity of the government of the most sacred empire. Among the praiseworthy pages of your wisdom I also found that you wished, as is your custom, to stir up my sluggishness skillfully through very prudent questions. Rather, through inquiries [“to teach more than to learn what was unknown”], I recognized this, because to ask wisely is to teach, as we find written in a page of your authority. There, after an appropriate statement, we observed the following words written in truthful speech:

> [Col. 0423D] **Here ends the letter according to Canisius:** “Let your diligence therefore know,

> [Col. 0423D] **Most beloved teacher in Christ.** From these words, and from the confession of Charles himself, the testimony of Einhard is confirmed: he relates that Charles had Alcuin as his teacher in the other disciplines, except grammar. To this also refer the verses of Alcuin’s epigram 260 [formerly 199] to the brothers of York, where he sings:

> Such gifts indeed please your Father,  
> who now makes illustrious arts resound  
> in royal ears, and leads the one who follows  
> through the meadows of the Fathers, and so forth.

“Most beloved teacher in Christ, concerning a question proposed to us by a certain man who was not a cleric but a layman, a question concerning the Gospel to which our response was then deferred until the present—not because we would have been unable to answer in accordance with what he asked,” and the rest.

I truly and greatly rejoice when laymen sometimes blossom forth in evangelical inquiry, since I once heard a prudent man say that it belongs to clerics to learn the Gospel [edition: distinguish it], not to laymen. What of this? Everything has its time (Ecclesiastes 3:1), and often a later hour brings what an earlier one could not. Nevertheless, this layman, whoever he was, is wise in heart, even if a soldier in his hands—such men your most wise authority ought to have in great number [edition: ought to have].

But let us turn our pen to the answer to the question, to satisfy the mind of the inquirer, if indeed our smallness is able to satisfy so distinguished an intellect.

The knot of the proposed question, as I found it tied in the letters of your excellence, was of this kind. Let us therefore set down the very words that I read in them:

> “There is a passage in the Gospel according to Luke (22:36, 38, 50) where the Lord Christ, as he was about to go to his Passion, commanded the disciples to sell their tunic and purse and to buy a sword. When they answered that there were two swords there, he said, ‘It is enough.’ We think that Peter used one of them in cutting off Malchus’s ear. At that time the Lord also said to him: ‘Put your sword back into its sheath. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword’ (Matthew 26:52). How is it consistent that the one who then commanded them to sell their tunic and buy a sword immediately said that those who took the sword would perish by the sword? If the sword is the word of God (Ephesians 6:17), and when the Lord commanded them to buy a sword he signified the word of God, how does it fit that everyone who receives the word of God should perish by the word of God?”

The solution is easy if one considers the circumstances surrounding this passage in each of the evangelists and understands the different meanings of *sword*. For *sword* does not signify the same thing everywhere. Thus *lion* has one meaning where it is said, “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Revelation 5:5), and another where it is said, “He prowls around like a lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8). The first lion is Christ; the second is the devil. Although the word *lion* is written with the same letters, it does not have the same meaning in the two passages.

The word *abyss* likewise has many allegorical meanings in Holy Scripture, as diligent readers can easily discover: the abyss signifies the immensity of waters; the abyss, the depth of the Scriptures; [the abyss, the ineffable judgments of God (Psalm 36:6; Romans 11:33)]; the abyss, wisdom; the abyss, human hearts. Many such things are found in Holy Scripture, which have various interpretations according to the qualities of their contexts. The Lord’s speech is full of eyes and may be pierced from every side; it is the deep depth of God’s mysteries. Who can investigate all their secrets?

The sword, therefore, also seems to have many meanings. It signifies the poisonous curses of the Jews against Christ when it says: “They sharpened their tongues like a sword” (Psalm 64:3). It also signifies death when it says: “You who delivered David your servant from the evil sword” (Psalm 144:10). It signifies the tribulation of Christ’s Passion when it says: “And a sword will pierce your own soul also” (Luke 2:35), that is, the tribulation of his Passion will torment your soul.

It also signifies division when it says: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matthew 10:34), that is, to separate the good from the evil.

The vengeance of the sword is also understood by the name *sword*, where it is written: “For he does not bear the sword in vain; for he is God’s avenger against those who do evil” (Romans 13:4).

The judgment of God is likewise designated by the name *sword*: “My sword has drunk its fill in heaven” (Isaiah 34:5). Again: “I will sharpen my sword like lightning, and my hand shall execute judgment” (Deuteronomy 32:41). And according to the Apostle, the word of God is understood as a sword.

But perhaps that layman, who was accustomed to fight with a single sword, thought that it had only one interpretation, not considering that the very sword he holds in his hand is double-edged: with it he tries to take the life of his enemy and rejoices to defend his own. Therefore, according to one meaning, the Lord said in Matthew: “All who take the sword will perish by the sword” (Matthew 26:52). But according to another meaning, in Luke: “But now, let the one who has a purse take it, and likewise a bag; and let the one who has none sell his tunic and buy a sword” (Luke 22:36).

The latter sword seems to have pleased him, while the former displeased him. Therefore he commanded that the former be returned to its sheath and the latter be bought. For this reason we must consider more carefully what each signifies, and the interpretations of the holy Fathers must be brought forward, lest our smallness seem presumptuously to say something.

That sword, according to Matthew, is understood to designate vengeance for our injuries; whoever carries it out will perish in his own crimes, as Truth herself says: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your offenses” (Mark 11:26). Therefore he commands that this sword also be returned to the sheath of the heart, so that there each person, in accordance with the Gospel parable of the two debtors (Luke 7:41 ff.), may forgive his brother from his heart. This is the forgiveness of our offenses: that we forgive those who sin against us, as Truth herself testifies: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:37).

But let us see what that sword can signify according to Luke’s Gospel, from which the whole sequence of the inquiry arose. It is clearly the word of God, which we must buy by selling all the impediments of secular life, and with which we must fight manfully against all the snares of the ancient serpent. Our Savior, returning in triumph and glory to his paternal throne, gave this sword to his disciples, saying: “Go, teach all nations” (Matthew 28:19).

The Lord therefore did not answer concerning the blow of this sword, as the extraordinary inquirer into this question supposed, “Return the sword to its sheath,” but concerning the sword that is read of in Matthew. Concerning the other, he said: “Allow it up to this point” [Salzburg codex: “even now”] (Luke 22:51), so that each might have its own proper meaning.

For in a single event the salvation of some and the destruction of others often arise. Just as in the whole Passion of Christ there is the destruction of the Jews but our salvation, so also the act of apostolic boldness can be understood in two ways, according to the subtlety of allegory, from the Lord’s own words.

Let that man, whoever he is, ask why in one evangelist the Lord commanded a staff to be carried, while in another he commanded that it not be carried; then he will understand that swords have different meanings.

But, according to the venerable command of your wisdom, we must consider “what the purchase [edition: removal] of this sword signifies; what the purse signifies; what the bag signifies; what the tunic signifies; and finally, why it is said that two swords are enough.”

We have spoken in its proper place of the sword’s being returned to its sheath and of the danger facing the one who takes it.

The purchase of this sword is renunciation of the world, concerning which the Lord himself said: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33). This means: a follower of avarice cannot be a preacher of truth, because he destroys by his deeds what he preaches with his mouth.

Thus the hidden substance of riches may be signified by the purse, and public wealth by the bag. Carnal pleasure is represented by the tunic. All these things must be sold utterly—that is, cast away—so that the follower of the sword of God’s word may become a worthy soldier of Christ.

But when the disciples said, “Behold, here are two swords,” and the Lord replied, “It is enough,” the two swords are body and soul. In these each person must fight according to the grace given him by God and in accordance with the will of the Lord God. It will be enough for the will of God if his commandments are fulfilled in body and soul.

But this proposed question also summons another, because “deep calls to deep” (Psalm 41:8). And while I thought I had untied the knot [Editor: “method”] of a powerful argument, behold, I encountered another from the side of a hidden constriction [Editor: “into another hidden construction from the side”], which I shall resolve not for the lay author of the earlier inquiry, but for your venerable dignity.

If this sword, as we said, is the word of God [Col. 0426A], why did it cut off the ear of the adversary, when the word of God ordinarily reaches through hearing to the hidden chambers of the heart, so that there it may bear the fruit of faith—one hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold (Matthew 13:8)? What does this cutting-off signify, I ask, except that the ear of unbelief [Editor: “infoeditatis”] should be cut away, so that the new ear might be healed by the touch of divine grace, and the stripping away of the old man pass over into the glory of renewed formation?

Hence this servant was called Malchus. *Malchus* is translated into Latin as “king” or “one who will reign.” How can he be both king and servant, except because in the old man we were servants of sin, whereas in the new man, healed by the grace of the Lord God [Editor: “holy”], we shall be kings and shall reign with Christ? What does it mean that the Lord himself healed his persecutor, except that every preacher in the Church of Christ should not cease to heal even his enemies by the word of compassion [Col. 0426B]? Thus the Lord himself, at the time of his Passion, did not abandon works of healing even toward his own persecutors.

And so perhaps Malchus was permitted to be wounded so that Peter’s steadfastness might be shown, the Lord’s compassion might shine forth, and an example of every good work might be given to us, so that we might offer the remedies of eternal salvation [Editor: “a gift”] even to our enemies.

Why were two swords found only [Editor: “afterward”] in the Lord’s Passion, and why did apostolic confidence fight with one, while we do not read that the other was drawn from its sheath? We said that the two swords signify body and soul: both must work through one faith, so that the faith hidden in the soul may be displayed outwardly through the body in action. “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” [Col. 0426C] (Matthew 12:34). Therefore the disciples are also said, when they received the gifts of the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire, to have spoken “the mighty works of God” (Acts 2:11). For where charity burns inwardly in the soul through the gift of the Holy Spirit, it immediately shines outwardly in the word of preaching.

The two swords may also, not inappropriately, be understood as faith and works: faith lies hidden in the heart, while the work proceeds openly in deed. To one who considers the matter carefully, this interpretation is also found to correspond to the former, because faith belongs to the soul, while works belong to the body. Let each person therefore direct his attention to the inner chamber of his heart and see how greatly he loves God; then let him bring that same love of God forth into action.

Above all, let the preachers of the Church of Christ show the love of our Redeemer to the people through the diligent words of their preaching. Let them be burning lamps (Luke 12:35) in the house of the Lord; let them be fortified cities planted upon the mountains of virtue, most strongly defended against every ambush of the hostile army. Let them be watchful shepherds, leading Christ’s flock through the pastures of eternal life, so that, with abundant fruit of souls, they may deserve to enter into the joys of their Lord God.

May these men [Editor: “hostia,” erroneously] be always admonished by your most excellent dignity and your most holy will in the love of Christ—indeed, driven by the sweetest exhortations toward the duties of preaching—so that on the great day of our Lord Jesus Christ you too may deserve to hear the gracious sentence: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your Lord” [Col. 0427A] (Matthew 25:21).

Nor should you think that this is to be heard there only by priests or clerics; believe rather that it must also be spoken to good laymen who labor faithfully in the work of God, and especially to those placed in the higher dignities of the world. Their good conduct, holiness of life, and admonitory words of eternal salvation may become a preaching to their subjects. For each person will have to render an account on the day of judgment for the money of his master that he received. And whoever labors more will receive the greater reward.

Therefore, most beloved and honored defender and ruler of the Churches [of Christ], may the venerable devotion of your most holy wisdom exhort some by admonishing them, correct others by chastising them, and instruct others in the disciplines of life, so that, becoming all things to all people (1 Corinthians 9:22), you may deserve to receive an everlasting reward from them all [Col. 0427B]. Thus, with a great and praiseworthy multitude of peoples, may you appear glorious in the presence of the Lord your God.

I also hear of a certain custom in the Churches of Christ that is not sufficiently praiseworthy, one which your most prudent authority could easily correct, if the report is true and not rather a false excuse by which presbyters place upon their bishops what they themselves do not wish to do. For they say that bishops have forbidden presbyters and deacons to preach in the churches, although in the Apocalypse it is read [Editor: “let the bishops and bride say”]: “The Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him who hears say, Come. Let him who thirsts come; let him who wishes receive the water of life” (Revelation 22:17).

The Apostle likewise says: “If something is revealed to another who is sitting, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one” (1 Corinthians 14:30–31), that is, teach. Again, to Timothy: “Let the presbyters who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word and teaching of God” (1 Timothy 5:17).

Let them say in which canons presbyters are forbidden to preach. Rather, let them read and understand how, from the beginning of the nascent Church, there have been throughout the breadth of the world many and remarkable preachers from the various orders of the clergy, including men sent by apostolic authority into different regions; and let them cease to keep as a private possession what could contribute to the greater gain of many souls.

For our Lord Jesus Christ himself assigned to his apostles men of the second rank for the duties of preaching, as is most clearly read in Luke: “After this the Lord also appointed seventy-two others and sent them two by two before his face” (Luke 10:1) [Col. 0427D]. A little later: “He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me; and he who despises me despises him who sent me” (ibid., 16). And there are the other things that are read there concerning the administration of the word of God.

Why are homilies read everywhere in the churches by men from every clerical order? What is a homily except a sermon? It is astonishing that one may read but may not interpret, so that all may understand. What else does this amount to except that the hearers become fruitless, and that Virgil’s line is fulfilled:

> He gives sounds without sense . . . .

[Col. 0428A]

—and not the evangelical command: “What you have heard in the ear, preach upon the housetops” (Matthew 10:27)?

For blessed Jerome says in his letter (52) to the presbyter Nepotian, where he instructs him concerning the office of preaching:

> “It is a very bad custom in certain Churches for presbyters to remain silent and not speak in the presence of bishops, as though they either begrudged them or did not deem themselves worthy to be heard. And if something is revealed to another,” says the Apostle Paul, “who is sitting, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn [Editor: “and all may speak”] and all may be comforted” (1 Corinthians 14:30–31). And: “The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets; for God is not a God of dissension but of peace” (ibid., verses 32–33). “A wise son is the glory of his father” (Proverbs 10:1). Let the bishop rejoice in his judgment when he has chosen such priests [for Christ]. [Editor: “While you teach in the church”; variant: “While they teach in the church”] Let not the shouting of the people but their groaning be aroused. Let the tears of the hearers be your praises.”

This great and admirable teacher set these words against so evil a custom. Much more could be said about it, but a few things suffice for the wise. Nor is it fitting for our rusticity to burden the ears of your praiseworthy wisdom with many words. We ask only, with humble devotion, that you order such matters to be corrected by paternal oversight, if the report is true. Thus may the lofty governance of royal power everywhere benefit all toward salvation, and may the rewards of perpetual honor be increased for you with Christ the Lord our God and his saints.

We have also seen in some places neglected altars of God without a roof, defiled by the droppings of birds or by the urine of dogs [Col. 0428C]. Your venerable will in God can easily correct this through the bishops, so that the table of the Lord may remain in its place with due honor, or be carried into the larger church according to the holy prudence of God’s priests. Let the altar of Christ, or the consecration of his body and blood, be treated honorably; and let the preeminent sacrament of our salvation be consecrated, revered, and guarded with every form of veneration.

[Col. 0427D] This letter is number 106 in Quercetanus’s edition, published by him from a manuscript. It was written after the year 800 to Charles, already emperor. (In Froben, Letter 125.)

## LETTER CLXIV. TO EMPEROR CHARLES

Response to questions about the hymn said after the supper in Matthew and Mark.

To Charles, king and emperor Augustus, best, greatest, and perpetual, by the gift of Christ God, King of kings [printed *Regi*, “to the King”; read *Rege*, “by the King”]; [Col. 0428D] the humble matricularius Albinus sends everlasting salvation in the glory of heaven.

We found your letters, composed with the serious perfection of your remarkable wisdom, shining with the brilliance of eloquence, most subtle in the depth of their meanings, and most delightful through the grace of their inquiry. From this it can plainly be recognized that God has bestowed the imperial power of your prudence not only for the government of the world, but especially for the protection of the Church and the adornment of wisdom, so that through your most holy diligence the minds of young men, covered with the rust of a certain sluggishness, might be polished to intellectual sharpness.

For, beyond imperial and public concerns, you inquire into evangelical questions for us to unravel in an academic manner [Col. 0429A]. Although we know that these same questions are very familiar to your prudence—as your dignity’s letter itself says—you wished, nevertheless, by certain goads of questioning, to rouse the sleepy sluggishness of old age, lest senile inactivity remain silent. Hence I understand that even now you intend more to teach through your graftings [read: “through your inquiries”] than that anything from my response could be added to your overflowing wisdom.

For to ask wisely is to teach. Thus to inquire prudently is a way of discovering, just as Pythagoras is said, through carefully ordered questions, to have taught a certain boy more about geometry than he would have learned from asking what Pythagoras wanted of him. Likewise, we read that the Lord acted in the Gospel through certain parables.

[Col. 0429B] {185} But to respond to what has been asked, insofar as the grace of the one whose discourse gave rise to this inquiry inspires my mind—although my smallness can scarcely offer anything worthy of your brightness, since I do not possess such confidence in my appearance or thoughts as is read of the architect Xenocrates, who, crowned with poplar leaves and clothed in a lion’s skin, walked amid the crowds of the people toward the tribunal of Alexander the Great. When he was asked who he was and where he came from, he replied: “I am Xenocrates, a Macedonian architect, and I bring you thoughts and forms worthy of your brightness.”

Yet I perceive that I possess, concerning the Platonic matters of your excellence, a disposition such as is recorded of the philosopher Aristippus. When he had lost everything in a shipwreck and scarcely escaped alive to shore, he is said to have told his companions: “Go to Athens and tell my disciples to gather those riches which cannot perish in a shipwreck”—meaning wisdom.

Nor would I bring forward these memorials of ancient history were it not that the lines of your authority provoked me to mention the names of philosophers.

With this preface, let us come to the question in your letter. After a suitable preface to the letter, we find it written—as we shall use your own words:

> “From the reading and authority of sacred history itself we have concluded that after the mystical supper either the disciples, or rather the Lord himself, said a hymn. For this reason we were struck with no small astonishment: why has a hymn of such great sweetness, whether said by the Lord himself or, if by the disciples, nevertheless in the Lord’s presence, been omitted by all the evangelists?”

This is the whole substance of the question: why has the hymn of such great sweetness been silently omitted by all the evangelists, when it is absolutely certain from the words of sacred history that a hymn was said after the mystical supper by the disciples, or rather by the Lord himself?

The interpretation of the whole [perhaps: “name”] must therefore first be given. *Hymnus* is a Greek word, and in Latin it may be interpreted as “the praise of a song.” Or, as blessed Isidore says:

> “A hymn is a song of those praising; translated from Greek into Latin, it means ‘praise,’ because it is a song of joy and praise.”

Properly speaking, hymns are compositions containing praise of God. Hence the Book of Psalms is also called by many teachers the Book of Hymns.

When the Evangelists said, “And after a hymn had been said, they went out” (Matthew 26:30; Mark 14:26), many simply transmit it in this way: “After praise had been offered to God, they went out.” Some therefore think that they sang the verse of Psalm 21: “All the fat ones of the earth have eaten and worshiped” (Psalm 21:30). They suspect this from the commentary of blessed Jerome, who says: “And after a hymn had been said—that is, what we read in the psalm: ‘All the fat ones of the earth have eaten and worshiped.’”

There are also those who wish to apply this praise to the preceding verse, where it says: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and those who seek him shall praise the Lord” (ibid., verse 27).

It is possible, however, that the Jews had a custom of singing a hymn of praise after supper, just as travelers passing along a road or laborers working in the fields were accustomed to bless with this verse: “The blessing of the Lord be upon you; we have blessed you in the name of the Lord” (Psalm 128:8).

But leaving aside these and similar opinions of certain people, although they do not seem to be contemptible, let us disclose the clear interpretation of the truth.

It is the custom of the Evangelists for one to say more fully what the others have entirely omitted. Blessed John the Evangelist is especially proven to have done this. An attentive reader will be able to find sufficient examples of this in their writings, but the brevity of a letter prevents us from touching upon them except insofar as they seem necessary for answering this question.

Thus, concerning this mystical supper of the Old and New Testaments, all four Evangelists spoke, reporting either what was done or what was said at it—partly in similar, partly in dissimilar ways—yet all these things are necessarily believed to be true.

What those other three said about the consecration of the bread and the cup, John omitted, dwelling especially upon the display of Christ’s humility, by which he deigned to wash the feet of his disciples. He also devoted a very long and most sacred discourse to those eleven chosen men, speaking to them in secret and spiritual language after the son of perdition had gone out.

When this discourse had ended, the blessed Evangelist added: “Jesus spoke these things, and lifting up his eyes to heaven, he said” (John 17:1). By this he designated not only the words that John himself reports the Lord to have spoken, but also those which the other Evangelists wrote that he spoke at that holy banquet.

When the blessed Evangelist continues by saying that Jesus, with his eyes lifted to heaven, said, “Father, glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you” (John 17:1) . . . through to the place where, after this hymn of praise and the most holy prayer had been completed, he said: “So that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them” (ibid., verse 26)—the pious Savior poured out this prayer for himself and his disciples, indeed for all the faithful who would come until the consummation of the age.

This is the most holy and beautiful hymn, entirely necessary for all believers, which our Lord Jesus Christ, our advocate (1 John 2:1), after completing the banquet of our salvation and of his compassion, sang before his disciples with great sweetness and wondrous graciousness.

This is the hymn that the holy solicitude of your wisdom inquires about. Keep it in perpetual memory, my sweetest David, for the praise of our Lord and Savior and in the hope of eternal blessedness. For the Son could have spoken these same words of hymnlike praise and prayer to the Father silently; but the prayer of the Son is the instruction of the disciples, indeed of all who are accustomed to pray in the praise of the Lord.

No prayer is sweeter than that which is poured forth in praise of divine goodness. Hence the Lord himself says through the Prophet: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me, and there is the way by which I shall show him the salvation of God” (Psalm 49:23).

[Col. 0431D] Baluzius published this letter from the Colbert manuscript in Book I of the *Miscellanea*, page 365; we have added several variant readings from manuscript codex b of the Vatican Royal Library. (In Froben, Letter 126.)

## LETTER CLXV. TO CHARLES THE GREAT

Response to the question of the price of human salvation, and to whom it would be given. [Col. 0431B]

In the name of God Christ, Savior of the world. Albinus sends to David, beloved of Christ the Lord, perpetual peace and prosperity in the Lord.

Wisdom is, as the philosophers defined it, knowledge of divine and human matters. This wisdom your most excellent imperial and deeply religious humility habitually seeks diligently from men, so that it may pour all their perceptions into the treasure of your own heart, and thus be able, from this most abundant treasury of riches, to bring forth new and old things according to the evangelical scribe (Matthew 13:52).

Therefore you have undertaken to direct to the understanding of our smallness [Vatican manuscript: “little understanding”] the question of a certain wise Greek who inquired to whom the price of human salvation should be given—not, as I know very well, because you were ignorant, but to test what the understanding of our smallness had perceived concerning it or learned from teachers.

That wise man is said by certain sons of Catholic learning at the palace to have inquired to whom this price should be given. As it appeared to those who heard his wisdom, he wished to establish that death was the recipient of this price, thinking that there could be no redemption unless there were someone who received the price from the purchaser and, having accepted the price, handed over something belonging to himself to the purchaser. He also tried to confirm this by the authority of the Apostle, because it is said: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses” (Romans 5:14).

To address the depth of this question, I shall proceed to answer its obscurity with the judgments of the Fathers, lest I say anything rash [Col. 0431D].

[Col. 0432D] The sense is difficult; if I wished to answer it fully [the printed text reads “if to answer”; perhaps read “if I wished”], a large book would be required. Nevertheless, I shall so temper my pen that I do not exceed the limits of a longer letter.

First, it seems necessary to ask concerning which death the blessed Apostle gave his testimony: whether concerning the devil, who is often designated by the name of death; or concerning sin, which is the death of the soul; or even concerning the death of the flesh, which is the punishment of sin (Romans 5:12 and 6:23). Then, concerning the price of our salvation, we shall say whatever the one who offered that price for us suggests to our mind.

[Col. 0432A] {187} Discussing sin, the Apostle adds this testimony: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses.” If he had intended this to be understood solely of the death of the flesh, he would certainly have said: “Death reigned from Adam until that day” concerning which he says elsewhere: “The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:26)—the death whose reign in our flesh we still lament.

Hence the Apostle himself also says: “For in this we groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Corinthians 5:4).

Accordingly, we think that by these words the Apostle signifies another kind of death, which is said to have reigned from Adam to Moses—that is, until the final times of the Law and the beginning of grace, which destroyed this reign of death.

The death of which it is said, “Death reigned from Adam,” is without doubt the death of which the Prophet says: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18:4). This reign of death was destroyed when grace arrived, after the blood of Christ erased the bond written by our sins (Colossians 2:14), fastening it to the cross and killing in himself the hostility that existed between God and man (Ephesians 2:16).

But this kind of death had no reign in the soul of Christ our Redeemer, because he never sinned; therefore he did not die. If Christ did not commit sin, which is the death of the soul, and if his flesh, once the sting of death had been condemned, rose from the tomb in the glory of triumph—death no longer ruling over him, as it is said (Romans 6:9)—where is the price that death boasts was handed over to it?

Why did death not retain it, if it received it by right of purchase? Nor does it immediately follow that the price must be given to the one from whom something is said to have been redeemed. For the Prophet prayed that God would redeem him from distress (Psalm 118:143), yet it cannot be said that he gave God something as a price for the distress by which the Prophet was troubled.

Likewise, in another psalm it is said: “Let those redeemed by the Lord say so, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy and gathered from the lands” (Psalm 106:2). The almighty God did not give a price to the nations, kings, or enemies so often [Vatican manuscript: “wholly”] as he redeemed his people from them. Again, in another psalm: “He redeemed us from the hand of our enemies” (Psalm 135:24).

If you attend to the historical account, he gave no price to the Egyptians when he deigned to free the Hebrews from their hands by the blood of the mystical lamb (Exodus 12:13). Here we ought to consider to whom this lamb was sacrificed for the redemption of God’s people: to the most merciful Lord God, or to the most impious king Pharaoh? And whom did its blood, smeared on the doorposts, protect from the destroying angel (ibid., verse 23)?

Does a prison possess power in itself to punish? Or does someone give a prison a price to redeem prisoners from it? Or does the sword that avenges crimes kill through gifts not to harm [variant: “gifts do not kill”; possibly: “gifts avail against the one who is not guilty”], rather than to the judge who has the power to bind or release, to kill and to make alive?

If, therefore, that wise man wishes, on account of the name “redemption,” which Holy Scripture often uses in place of our liberation, to maintain that a sale and purchase with death are necessary for our salvation, where would the prior purchase be, so that a second repurchase from that prior purchase—as he interprets it—may rightly be spoken of?
