When we say “renewal” or “reformation,” we say this because there was a first creation and formation, when human beings were created and formed. Redemption cannot in any way be understood as though there had previously been some purchase. Nor does the word “redemption” pertain so much to purchase as to liberation, as we showed above.

This can also be proved by the words of the Lord himself, where he says: “The Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his soul as a redemption for many” (Matthew 20:28). Who would dare to say that that holy, immaculate soul, separated from all sin, was given to death?

Let us rather see to whom this soul was given for our redemption. Blessed Luke the Evangelist reports that Jesus cried out on the cross: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit”; and, saying this, he expired (Luke 23:46).

“Spirit” and “soul” are different names, but by these testimonies the Lord’s one reality is recognized. He therefore handed over his spirit, not compelled by any necessity, but by his own will, when he wished. Whether we call it soul or spirit, he commended it to the Father and handed it over for our redemption, just as he had said earlier: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18).

Christ laid down his soul for us, and he laid it down when he wished; when he laid it down, he commended it to the Father; and again, when he wished, he took it up. To lay down the soul, therefore, is to die. The flesh laid down the soul, and the flesh again took it up through the power of the Word of God dwelling in it.

What he says here—“I have power to lay down my soul”—is what is said there: “He bowed his head and handed over his spirit” (John 19:30). This spirit is the soul, which Christ laid down when he wished. The power was in him, not in death, as to when he would lay down his soul and when he would take it up again.

What power did death have over our Redeemer, when he accomplished everything by his own will, undertaking to perform for our salvation what he had resolved to perform by a will shared with the Father [variant: “the fatherland”]?

Therefore, Eve, whose name is interpreted as “life,” was formed from the side of the sleeping Adam (Genesis 2:21); so from the side of Christ sleeping on the cross the price of the Church was brought forth. Hence he himself says through the Prophet: “I slept and took sleep, and I rose again, because the Lord received me” (Psalm 3:6).

Unless someone should dare to say that the blood of Christ, which was poured onto the earth by the soldier’s lance (John 19:34), had remained with death [variant: “for death”] as though it were a price, let him hear what blessed Augustine thinks in Book IV of his beautiful work *On the Holy Trinity* (chapter 3). After a suitable discussion of Christ’s death, he says:

> “And one of the disciples, even touching his scars, cried out, saying: ‘My Lord and my God!’ (John 20:28). And when the complete integrity of that flesh appeared, it was shown in it what he had said when exhorting his own: ‘Not a hair of your head will perish’ (Luke 21:18). But if the hairs of the saints will not perish, how much more will the blood of Christ not perish?”

Likewise, blessed Fulgentius, in Book III *To King Thrasamund*, chapter 34, gives this testimony concerning the whole humanity of Christ’s body ascending into heaven in his book *On the Christian Faith*:

> “After he had laid down his soul and had taken it up again according to his whole humanity, he ascended into heaven and sat at the right hand of God” [variant: “sits”].

He redeemed us by enduring various injuries and sufferings. He suffered bonds, was struck with blows, and was scourged. He redeemed us through the blood of his Passion. Finally, he redeemed us by displaying the miracles of his resurrection, as the Apostle says, comprehending everything: “You were bought with a great price” (1 Corinthians 6:20).

But who would have received that price of such power? Let us hear what the eminent interpreter of the Psalms, Cassiodorus, said concerning the verse, “The Lord sent redemption to his people” (Psalm 110:9):

> “It is appropriately said, ‘He sent redemption,’ because captives appeared to need this. But it was such a price that a tyrant would not take it; rather, the one who was being released would receive it. The captive gained his redemption, and the one who was held guilty was thereby enriched, while the tyrant who held him was condemned.”

But we must inquire more carefully and examine with justified attention whether it is more correctly said that death received the price from our Savior, or that death itself was the price of our redemption.

Let us hear what blessed Augustine says about this [variant: “indicates”] in Book IV *On the Holy Trinity* (chapter 12, at the end), where he discusses at length the penal and entirely just misery of our condition and the undeserved death of our Lord Jesus Christ:

> “Through sin we came to death, and he came through righteousness. And therefore, since our death is the punishment of sin, his death became an offering for sins.”

Likewise, in another chapter of the same book, he says this concerning Christ’s death (chapter 13, section 17):

> “For he was not stripped of the flesh by anyone’s right of power [printed “carnally”; read “of the flesh”], but he stripped it from himself. For he who could not die if he did not wish to, undoubtedly died because he wished to. And therefore he openly triumphed over principalities and powers, making a display of them in himself. For by his death he offered for us one most true sacrifice.”

He continues many other remarkable things concerning the same matter.

A little later in the same chapter, under the title “Concerning the perfect and true sacrifice that the Savior himself became for us,” he most lucidly shows who the priest was and what the sacrifice was, for whom and by whom it was offered. He says (Augustine, cited work, chapter 14):

> “What priest, then, is so just and holy as the only Son of God, who had no need to cleanse his own sins through sacrifice—neither original sins nor those added from human life? And what could be taken so suitably from human beings to be offered for them as human flesh? And what is so suitable for immolation as mortal flesh?”

A little later:

> “What could be offered and received with such favor as the flesh that became the body of our sacrifice and of our priest? For since four things are considered in every sacrifice—who is offered to, by whom it is offered, what is offered, and for whom it is offered—the same one true mediator, reconciling us to God through the sacrifice of peace, would be one with him to whom he offered [Vatican manuscript: “only one”]; would make one in himself those for whom he offered; and would himself be both the one who offered and what he offered.”

Is it not clear, once blessed Augustine’s words are properly understood, to whom he offered this sacrifice? Unless someone should dare to say that the sacrifice offered to God the Father was one thing, and the price by which we were redeemed another.

In all the injuries, insults, and sufferings that the only Son of God endured for us, what was accomplished except an offering for our sins, except the price of our redemption? It seems superfluous to ask who received this offering or price, when blessed Paul, taken up into the third heaven, did not hesitate to give this testimony concerning the one who is both priest and victim, price and offering: he “offered himself for us as a sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma” (Ephesians 5:2).

That life came to death is also attested by the same Augustine in his exposition of Psalm 58 (Sermon 2, section 4):

> “What did they do to Christ? They did not kill life, but death. For when death had been extinguished, life rose again.”

Our Savior himself, insofar as he is medicine and salvation, was given to us, as it is said by the Prophet: “A Son has been given to us, and his government has been placed upon his shoulder” (Isaiah 9:6). Isaac, of course, carried the cross upon his shoulders for his own sacrifice.

The same person, priest and sacrifice, was offered by himself to God the Father for our salvation as a fragrant aroma. Concerning him the Prophet says that the Lord swore: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:4).

Blessed Cyprian, an outstanding teacher and glorious martyr, wished to understand this testimony in the following way (Letter 63):

> “For who,” he says, “is more the priest of the Most High God than our Lord Jesus Christ, who offered a sacrifice to God the Father, and offered that same thing which Melchizedek had offered—that is, bread and wine, namely his body and blood?”

He offered it for us so that he might redeem us by that sacrifice. He both offered this sacrifice for us and gave it to us as an everlasting memorial, as it is read in the Gospel:

> “And having taken bread,” says the Evangelist, “he gave thanks and broke it, and gave it to them, saying: ‘This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup after he had supped, saying: ‘This is the cup of the New Testament in my blood, which will be poured out for you’” (Luke 22:19–20).

He is therefore both victor and victim—and victor because victim. He is likewise both priest and sacrifice—and priest because sacrifice. In that nature in which he is priest because he is sacrifice, made higher than the heavens, he is always living to intercede for his own (Hebrews 7:25–26).

The same one is powerful with God the Father and the Holy Spirit; the text then has an incomplete phrase, “life to those believing in him.” The same one—the only-begotten Son of God, with the following words “God and living” grammatically corrupt—is our Lord Jesus Christ, whose praise and glory endure through everlasting ages.

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Paraclete, and in the great name,

May prosperity, glory, life, and salvation be yours.

O my sweet love, David, farewell throughout the ages.

May Christ everywhere be for you praise, light, and strength.

Perhaps an Athenian sophist from the Academic school put forward such a question; with him, as a Platonist, we may for a little while cross swords in argument. Moreover, we read that blessed Paul disputed with the Stoics, in order to lead them from error into the way of truth through the disciplines they themselves professed. For the people of God, being destined to be redeemed from the harshest slavery and enriched with Egyptian wealth, followed a leader directed by God, and from that wealth offered abundant gifts to God for the construction of the tabernacle. [Col. 0436B]

Why should we not, instructed by such illustrious examples, propose syllogisms to that dialectical questioner, so that, wounded by the weapons of his own forces, he may willingly return to the camp of the Catholic army? Tell me, I beg you, tell me, most prudent teacher: is death a substance? Let us see whether it ought rightly to be said that death received so great a reward [Cod. Vat.: “received a price”].

Therefore, if death is a substance, it is God’s creature, since no substance exists unless it is either God himself or created by him. But if death was created by God, no one may doubt that it was created among the works of the six days, because the Creator himself, as sacred history relates, completed his works on the sixth day and rested on the seventh from all his works (Gen. 2:2). [Col. 0436C] If, then, death is not found to have been created among those six days, it is certainly not a creature. And if it is not a creature, then it is not a substance either.

Nor, plainly, did whatever appears to be signified by the name “death” exist before humanity had sinned. What punishment for original sin was established among the original creatures? It is therefore proved that death cannot rightly be called a creature.

But if the aforementioned master does not consider it necessary to believe, on the basis of this dialectical reasoning, that death was not created, let him believe it on the testimony of God or of Holy Scripture, which says, as we read: “God did not make death” (Wis. 1:13). Therefore, if the Lord did not make it, then, as we have said, it is certainly not a creature.

Death appears to be nothing other than absence. For where life departs from youth [F.: “from the living”], there will be that which is called death, just as darkness is nothing other than the absence of light. [Col. 0436D]

But if death is not a creature—as has truly been proved by the testimony of the divine writings and by the rational necessity of argument—how could it have received a price more excellent than all creatures? Whatever is read as having been done through the devil’s envy or Jewish unbelief in the passion of our Lord and Savior was wholly an ordering of divine mercy, using their wickedness to effect his own goodness and advance our salvation.

But whatever the devil thought he had accomplished through their murderous hands [F.: “through their jurisdiction”], all of it was the voluntary permission or disposition of the one who suffered—not the dominion of a mortal necessity. [Col. 0437A] And it is astonishing that one should be thought to have given a price to death who owed death nothing; nor is death, as has been said, a substance capable by right of demanding such a price.

@ [Col. 0437D] The distinguished Baluzius published this capitulary at the cited place, p. 375, under the name of Alcuin. Since it too was addressed to Charlemagne, I have thought it appropriate to append it to the preceding letter, copied from the same manuscript, because it can scarcely find a suitable place among Alcuin’s other works. In my judgment, this capitulary is a response to certain points proposed by the emperor for consultation; those points may perhaps have been more precise, whereas the response is general. (Frobenius, letter 127.)

## LETTER 166

### OR A CAPITULARY OF ADMONITION TO THE SAME CHARLES

The chapters that it is fitting to recall at such a time.

**I.** A testament is confirmed by the death of the testator, as the Apostle declares (Heb. 9:17). Therefore, after the testator’s death, it acquired complete validity. The unanimous consent of all had also confirmed it before his death. What previously could in no way be rejected cannot therefore later be overturned.

**II.** Whoever is found to be ungrateful toward the testator, and moreover insulting, bears witness against himself that he is unworthy of the testament. For example: Canaan’s dishonoring of his father made him a servant; Esau lost his birthright through lack of self-control; Reuben, because of his insult against his father, was placed behind his younger brothers. Finally also: “Whoever curses his father” (Exod. 21:17; Lev. 20:9), and so forth. [Col. 0437B]

**III.** It is natural for children to inherit their fathers’ blessings. Those who prepare disobedience or obstinacy toward their parents, however, fight against the laws of nature. The legitimate heir, therefore, will be the one who has maintained the prescribed order toward his parents.

**IV.** It is one thing to be admitted mercifully without due entitlement; it is another to be credited appropriately as a matter of obligation. What has been granted wholly without entitlement cannot be claimed as a due reward. For differences in merit demand differences in rewards. [Col. 0437C]

**V.** One who is well-born and has lawfully obtained the inheritance, who is found to be neither a despiser of the ancient or the new law, nor wounded by hostility toward his father, nor injurious toward the people, ought, by the Lord’s mercy, to possess great confidence in receiving the inheritance.

**VI.** When the head is broken, it is evident that all the parts subject to it languish, since the soundness of the whole body proceeds from the head’s stability. Subordinate members cannot boast of a health that is plainly absent from the head.

**VII.** Here, if truth is sought, it is not unknown; if reason, it is not ambiguous; if authority, it is not uncertain. For authority rises above, reason is clear, and truth cannot be hidden.

[Col. 0437D] **VIII.** All these matters seem to be included in a threefold division: namely, those who offer counsel, those who cause harm, and those who are always so uncertain between the two that they immediately join whichever side they see prevailing. Those who offer useful counsel must therefore be assisted; those who resist must be confronted courageously; the uncertain must either be drawn over by reason or prudently ignored. Everyone must be shown that authority cannot be corrupted, reason cannot be defeated, and truth cannot be wholly overcome. [Col. 0438A]

**IX.** The people must be guided according to divine decrees, not followed; and honorable persons are more suitable for giving testimony. Nor should those be heard who customarily say, “The voice of the people is the voice of God,” since the tumultuousness of the mob is always close to madness.

**X.** There is a common proverb: “Something is overcome by hardness; from softness nothing remains.” Yet wisdom must also supply constancy, and constancy perfect wisdom, so that constancy may be wise and wisdom constant. [Col. 0438B]

**XI.** The preaching of peace must be practiced in such a way that an assertion of falsehood is not introduced under the name of piety. For just as breaking peace is most evil, so denying truth is blasphemous. Truthful unity and peaceful truth are, in the end, very much in harmony with one another.

**XII.** These and similar matters, I think, must be impressed upon the simple, since ignorance of the truth compels very many to go astray. Once the truth has been made manifest, opponents will be confounded, friends will be strengthened, and all alike will lack an excuse.

I beg you to examine these matters graciously and carefully. The immensity of your fidelity makes my smallness impatient on your behalf and also makes me dare beyond my strength. Indeed, no one loses faith except one who never possessed it. May he in whose hand are kings and the rights of kingdoms multiply, protect, and overshadow your crowns. [Col. 0438C]

@ [Col. 0437D] Edition: Quercetanus 59, Canisius 34. (Frobenius 128.)

## LETTER 167. TO PETER, ARCHBISHOP

He commends himself to his paternal affection and holy prayers.

To his most beloved father in Christ,

@ [Col. 0438D] Peter, archbishop of Milan, to whom he wrote the following letter. He governed the Church of Milan from the year 783 until 804, when he departed to the heavenly realms. See Cointius and Ughelli. — There survives a most elegant letter of this Peter, also called Oldradus, to Charlemagne concerning the translation of St. Augustine to Pavia, carried out in 725. Canisius. — Nothing is found in this letter by which Angilbert, traveling to Rome, is commended to this archbishop, although Mabillon asserted this in book 26 of the *Annales Benedictini*, p. 318.

To Peter the archbishop, Albinus sends greetings of eternal blessedness.

Mindful of your most sweet humility and affection, I groan over the absence of one whose flame of charity burns in the heart of your son. How great is the unhappiness of this age, which separates friends so dear, which separates a son from his father! O, if only I had the wings of an eagle, so that I might fly across the heights of the Alps swifter than the east wind! How quickly I would stand before your fatherly feet, to cool the burning of my breast by seeing my father. [Col. 0438D]

But since this cannot happen, let us clothe ourselves with the wings of a twofold charity: let us always be present in Christ, though absent in this world. What is charity except unity of souls? The Truth himself said this when he prayed to the Father for his own: “Father, preserve them in your name, whom you have given me, that they may be one, as we also are one” (John 17:11). [Col. 0439A]

I, your son, beseech you by the mercy of him who said these things, to keep the name of your son Alcuin stored in the most holy treasury of your paternal remembrance, and to pronounce it, even once, among the most worthy offerings of your prayers to God.

How great a reward remains for you, excellent Father, with the Lord Christ, the remunerator of piety, if you strive through prayers of paternal mercy to lift me, weighed down by the burdens of sins, from the loads of iniquity! I confess that I am an unworthy son of such authority; nevertheless, strengthened by the example of the younger son who departed from his father into a distant land, I dare to say: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; therefore I am no longer worthy to be called your son” (Luke 15:21). [Col. 0439B]

And I believe that, mindful of paternal piety, you ran out to meet the returning man with joyful embraces. I also believe that you remember the wisdom of blessed Job concerning his beloved sons [Al.: “devotion”], since he daily endeavored to offer sacrifices to God for their prosperity (Job 1:5), greatly desiring to nourish for God those whom he had begotten for the world. Therefore, in all temptations he was found tested like gold in a furnace (Wis. 3:6).

For a father’s praise consists in the salvation of his sons, and a shepherd’s reward increases in the multiplication of his flock. Indeed, the chief Shepherd himself, after the glory of the resurrection, entrusted to blessed Peter the sheep which he had redeemed with his loving blood, so that he might feed them, because of the firmness of his threefold confession of love for him (John 21). [Col. 0439C]

It is your duty, holy Father, to assist the absent with prayers, to instruct those present with words, and to strengthen them by examples, so that paternal piety and pastoral devotion may benefit all toward salvation. Fathers customarily store up treasures for their children (2 Cor. 13:14); but you, leave treasures of blessedness to your grandchildren, so that through the long succession of ecclesiastical instruction the glory of the heavenly kingdom may continually increase for you.

I desire, if it can be done, that you refresh me with a letter of your fatherhood, so that the eyes of my longing may read what I would have wished to hear with my ears, if that had been possible [Al.: “if I had been able”]. For the human race has been granted the ability to entrust the secrets of the heart to writing and to make known through silent letters what the speaking tongue cannot express.

The blessed apostle Paul also frequently used to instruct his absent children with pious admonitions [Al.: “with the piety of admonition”], so that the daily reading of letters might impress the eternal memory of a father’s teachings upon the minds of his children. [Col. 0439D] May divine mercy deign to preserve the authority of your holiness, for the exaltation and joy of his holy Church, in lasting prosperity, most beloved Father! [Col. 0440A]

@ [Col. 0439D] Frobenius, letter 196.

## LETTER 168. TO PETER, ARCHBISHOP  
*(Date uncertain.)*

He expresses his gratitude for paternal kindness and commends Liudgarda, who is sending him gifts.

To the most holy father Peter, archbishop, Albinus, the humble son of your charity, sends greetings.

It is sweet for me to write frequently to your reverence, excellent Father, if the reliability and convenience of messengers permitted it. Yet even if paper does not travel, charity does not sleep; it keeps a gentle vigil and wholesomely remembers your paternal kindness, by which you have received me, though less worthy, into the dignity of a son, cherished me with familiarity, and strengthened me with admonition. May the pious remunerator of all good things repay all these deeds with eternal reward. [Col. 0440B]

@ [Col. 0439D] Liudgarda, the wife of King Charles, whom he also frequently mentions in other letters. Liudgarda was a religious woman, faithful to God and to the king. She sent a silver dish and one

@ [Col. 0439D] storax. I think this means a storax cloak, such as Alcuin himself sent to the brothers at Fulda for covering the body of St. Boniface; see the note to letter 142.

She sent a silver dish and a storax as alms on her own behalf to your holiness, so that they might be distributed according to the will of God. Since I, your son, am the mediator in this embassy, I beg you to deign to receive her into the affection due to a daughter. For she has a good will to benefit the servants of the Lord and his holy Church. Therefore pray more earnestly for her salvation and prosperity, so that divine grace may preserve her in lasting health. [Col. 0440C]

@ [Col. 0439D] Edition: Quercetanus 34, Canisius 18; collated with manuscript codices. (Frobenius, letter 129.)

## LETTER 169. TO RIGBOD, PONTIFF OF THE CITY OF TREVES, SURNAMED MACHARIUS

He complains about his friend’s absence and the interruption of their exchange of letters. He rebukes him for his excessive love of Maro.

To his pious father and dearest friend,

@ [Col. 0439D] Macharius. This was the surname of Richbod, bishop of Trier, as may be gathered from the title of this letter, which Canisius wrongly believed belonged to another lost letter. It reads there: “To Richbod, pontiff of the city of Trier,” and so forth. The same man is then called Macharius in the inscription. [Col. 0440D]

The title misled Canisius because the manuscript he used was corrupt. It read as follows: “To Richbod, pontiff of the city of Trier and the assembly,” whereas, instead of that expression, one should read: “surnamed Macharius,” as in Quercetanus.

Richbod, formerly a monk and abbot of Mediolacum (or of Lorsch?), was promoted to the bishopric of Trier in 791, according to a contemporary manuscript of the monastery of St. Maximin cited by Hontheim, *History of Trier*, vol. 1, p. 63. He therefore had Alcuin as his teacher when Alcuin first came to Francia. He is also the man to whom Alcuin wished to entrust Felix of Urgel’s booklet for refutation. Richbod died in 804, according to the annalists of his time, the Lorsch Annalist and others. See Mabillon, book 25 of the *Annales*, no. 44, and elsewhere.

To Macharius, monk and pontiff, Flaccus [Cod. Sal.: “Filius”] Albinus sends greetings in the charity of Christ.

May the world not separate what God has joined [Can.: “separates”]. Behold, may he who came to cast fire (Matt. 19:6) into the hearts of his own make what he has kindled burn. May no floods of unbelief overwhelm the fire that is commanded to burn day and night on God’s altar. Nor let anyone dare to bring a foreign fire into the spiritual tabernacle, lest he be killed by the one who commanded his own fire always to burn (Luke 12:49). [Col. 0440D]

What is God’s fire except charity (Song 8:7)? And what is foreign fire except love of the world? Therefore two of Aaron’s sons were preserved because of the two commandments of charity, while two perished because of their love of the world and of its lover (Lev. 10:1–2). [Col. 0441A]

Mary chose the better part for herself, and it will not be taken away from her (Luke 10:42). Let us love what will not be taken away, and flee what can be taken away. It is impious not to love one who loves us, and not to repay one who repays us.

What does God repay us? He repays our evils with his good things. Let us repay his good things with our own good things. What are our good things except that we love him and keep his commandments? And what are his commandments except that we love one another? “On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets” (Matt. 22:40).

Why have I repeated these matters at such length in my opening, except so that you may know the ardor of my heart? It would almost be better for me to have you present as a poor man than absent as a rich one. What are riches to me if I do not have the one I love, if I do not behold the one I desire? Your power is misery to me. [Col. 0441B]

Where is our sweetest conversation? Where is the desirable study of the sacred writings? Where is the joyful face that I used to behold? Where is the communion of charity that brotherly love exercised from both sides? Where at least is the memory of our name?

Behold, a whole year has passed, during which neither the consolation of a letter has come to my eyes nor the duty of a greeting sounded in my ears. What did the father do wrong, that the son should forget him? What did the teacher do, that the disciple should neglect him? Perhaps the world’s exaltation has disdained the teacher’s name in him? Or has my exile become worthless in your eyes? Or has your love of Maro taken away the memory of me? [Col. 0441C]

O, if only my name were Virgil! Then I would always play before your eyes, and you would examine all my words with complete attention, and, according to his proverb, I would be with you:

> Then supremely happy, than whom no one was happier.

What shall I do? Shall I lament my unhappiness because I am not the one you love? Or shall I praise your wisdom because you love one who does not exist? Flaccus [Canisius: “Filius”] has departed, Virgil has arrived, and Maro nests in the teacher’s place [Can.: “occupies the teacher’s place”].

I dictated this in grief, either because you had forgotten me or because you were absent, rubbing the paper with a somewhat harsher pumice stone, so that perhaps, even in anger, you might write something in reply—for “the weary ox fixes its hoof more firmly” [Can.: “the injured ox”]. [Col. 0441D]

Begin either to defend yourself or to attack me, so that I may understand the study in which you have spent the leisure of this year. Reveal to us the treasure with which you have filled your heart, so that we may rejoice with you in your good fortune. [Col. 0442A]

Would that the four Gospels, not the twelve books of the *Aeneid*, fill your breast, so that that four-horse team may carry you to the palace of the heavenly kingdom, where there is unfailing honor and an everlasting reign, where, I believe, you will remember to intercede for me, since I rejoiced to exhort you to go there.

@ [Col. 0441D] Edition: Quercetanus 40, Canisius 19; collated with the Salzburg manuscript. See the preceding letter. (Frobenius, letter 130.)

## LETTER 170. TO RIGBOD, THE BISHOP ALSO CALLED MACHARIUS

He grieves over his friend’s absence.

To his beloved father Macharius, Albinus, the humble deacon, sends greetings.

@ [Col. 0441D] Cod. Sal.: “To his beloved father, greetings,” with the remainder omitted.

The sweetness of charity cannot be fulfilled by the duties of letters, yet they strive to display some kind of light of it. Just as a present person is pointed out with a finger, so the charity of an absent person is shown through letters. [Col. 0442B]

I confess that the affection of my mind for you is weary of your absence. It would be some refreshment of love if I could either hear the affection of your heart through another’s mouth [Cod. Sal.: “more deeply”], or, when I read your letters, recognize the one whom I desire more ardently. May the world not separate those whom Christ’s charity has joined.

May the longed-for day of seeing arrive through him who created all days for seeing. I would have had many useful things to discuss with you if I had been able to enjoy the intimacy of your conversation [Cod. Sal.: “conference”]. The time will come, when he who orders all times wills it, that I may see you with every sweetness of charity [“that I may be able to see you”]. Farewell, son, brother, and friend.

@ [Col. 0441D] Frobenius, letter 197.

## LETTER 171

@ [Col. 0441D] The Harleian manuscript itself bears this heading, and it is entirely similar to that of letter 167; see there what we noted concerning Richbod.

**TO RIGBOD, ARCHBISHOP, SURNAMED MACHARIUS.** *(Date uncertain.)* He complains about the interruption of their exchange of letters. For the moment, he requests certain writings of St. Leo and the Venerable Bede. He invites him to St. Martin.

To Macharius,

@ [Col. 0441D] Patriarch. Alcuin also gives this title of honor to Arno, archbishop of Salzburg, in the poem appended to the letter in which he dedicated his commentary on the Penitential Psalms to him, in the final verse:

> Under your guidance, father, shepherd, patriarch, priest.

[Col. 0442D] Private writers sometimes give the same title to archbishops of the principal sees, especially those who exercised a certain primacy over other bishops or even over other archbishops. In ancient times the bishops of Trier especially enjoyed this prerogative throughout Gaul and both Germanies. Thus St. Hildulf, in the notice of the privilege granted to the monastery of St. Deodatus (in Surius, under June 19), is called “a man of holy compassion, archbishop, indeed patriarch.” See the *Prodromus of the History of Trier*: *On the Discipline and Doctrine of the Church of Trier under the Romans*, §6, p. 132, and §7, pp. 135–136; and on the same subject under the Franks, §5, p. 313.

Patriarch Albinus sends greetings.

What good do hidden wisdom, an unseen treasure (Sir. 20:32), or silent charity accomplish? Does fire flame in a flint unless it is struck? Why, dearest brother, does your charity fall silent in silence? Why will you not move your tongue to dictate and your hand to write? Why do you bury your talent in the earth? Why does no letter of admonition hasten forth? Let him read what he desires; let him consider what he does.

@ [Col. 0442D] “Mus l cnse bacha.” This is perhaps a Germanic expression designating some smaller river, German *Bach*. — Thus it stands in the manuscript, in which the word *mus* is marked with a cross above it. I fear that the letters of “mus l cnse bacha” have been submerged; nevertheless, if your pipe remains silent for me, I beg that it resound for others, so that sleepers may be awakened, the languishing may be healed, the ears of the deaf may hear, and the lame may strive to run along the path of discipline, so that there may be a reward [Manuscript: “a marvel”] for the one who shows the way of truth. [Col. 0443A] It is written: “Let the one who hears speak the truth.”

I was summoned, but illness hindered my journey. Speak what pleases God and belongs to sound doctrine. I beg you to lend us for the moment the homily of St. Leo and the treatise of blessed Bede on Tobit. But, as I see, you have extended your hand to receive and drawn it back to give. As for the journey that remains along our way, I beg you to assist me with your holy prayers, so that I may deserve to reach the gate of the everlasting city.

[Col. 0443B] If you come by coming, the right hand of God the Father will receive you, and, if the intercession of St. Martin helps you [perhaps: “will help you”]. May divine grace accompany and advance you, most beloved brother, flourishing in every good thing and progressing in the holy study of wisdom!

@ [Col. 0443D] Frobenius, letter 198.

## LETTER 172. TO THE SAME  
*(Date uncertain.)*

He grieves over the absence and expresses joy at the news that Macharius has recovered his health.

To the most holy father Macharius, whom we name with the highest honor, Albinus, the humble deacon, sends greetings.

From the time your charity became known to me, that same charity burned more effectively in my heart with a familiar flame, so that my mind said to me: “I have been wounded by love.” But now, in a certain way, what once tasted sweet in my breast has become bitter. For the long absence of your sweetest face torments the hidden places of my soul, and the sweetest conversation of your wisdom burdens my memory. Not hearing the most desired eloquence of your mouth, nor the most pleasant brotherhood of your heart, which used to breathe words of saving conversation into my ears, I remember that brief saying: “What is sweeter than to have a friend with whom you can speak about everything, as with yourself?” [Col. 0443C]

But let complaints depart where the effectiveness of correction is not thought possible. Let what the frailty of human necessity compels us to endure be borne patiently. Let there be a sweet presence of minds where there is the sad absence of faces. Let the letter of charity, winged with feathers, fly more often, fulfilling the office of the tongue, revealing the secret of brotherly love, and displaying to a son the sweetness of paternal affection, lest prolonged silence be stained by the rust of forgetfulness. [Col. 0443D]

Always eager to hear of your prosperity, and frequently asking those who arrived what news they brought me about my Macharius, I was suddenly struck down by the grievous report of your illness. With all my heart grieving, I watched [expected] for the desired message of your recovery to come to me—for him who lifts up the fallen to heal the brokenhearted, and for my sadness to be turned into joy, which, I pray, may never be taken from my heart, in which I always wish you lasting prosperity and health. [Col. 0444A]

When I heard from those who reported it that your health had been restored, I confess that I was filled with great joy, because I was permitted to hear what I had long desired and had asked God for with greater devotion.

But now, dearest son, brother, father, and friend, let us give continual thanks to God for all the good things he has bestowed on us, restoring you to health and filling me with joy. In doing so, we shall do his will, in whom alone are salvation, life, and unfailing happiness. [Col. 0444B] Let us love, proclaim, and worship him, because this is eternal life.

Therefore, to live in worldly desire is death, not life. The only true life is to live for God, as he himself says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6)—the way by which one travels, the truth to which one comes, the life in which one stands. Live happily forever, son, brother, father, and friend!

@ [Col. 0443D] Edition: Quercetanus 67, Canisius 39. (Frobenius 131.)

## LETTER 173. TO JOSEPH

He sympathizes with his bodily illness and encourages him to patience. He commends himself to his prayers and urges the renewal of the house of God, and so forth.

To his beloved son,

@ [Col. 0443D] Joseph. He was Alcuin’s disciple at the school of York, and there is no doubt that he is the Joseph who, at Alcuin’s urging, abridged St. Jerome’s commentaries on the prophet Isaiah. This *Epitome* of Joseph survives in the manuscript of St. Germain, no. 585. (Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, fourth century, part 1, p. 188 and following.) [Col. 0444D] Alcuin also mentions this Joseph in letter 3, to Colcu, and commends him after his death to Remigius, bishop of Chur, in the following letter. Another letter of Alcuin to the same Joseph, once preserved in the oldest manuscripts of the Cotton Library, is missing. According to Usserius, Alcuin writes in it: “Your teacher Colcu is well, and so are your friends who are with us.”

To Joseph, Albinus sends greetings.

I grieve over your bodily pain, but I rejoice in the happiness of your soul. For “God scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). “He kills and gives life; he wounds and heals” (Job 5:18). May the hope of reward be your consolation in labor. These pains soon end; the rewards of patience never end. “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to come, which will be revealed in the saints” (Rom. 8:18).

Therefore, with thanksgiving, sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise (Ps. 49:14). This is not a punitive tribulation but a propitiation that brings pardon. Gold is refined by fire in the furnace (Prov. 27:21), so that it may emerge purer; so the soul undergoes bodily tribulation, that it may proceed into life more cleansed. [Col. 0444C]

The Lord’s discipline ought not to be a punishment to anyone; rather, let him receive cheerfully what the merciful physician applies for healing. Amid the scourges of piety, let prayers of humility be directed to God, so that he who chastises mercifully may forgive kindly, and eternal salvation may come to the one who suffers. [Col. 0444D]

Do not cease, mindful also of us, to pour out diligent prayers for us, so that divine mercy may provide us with a life of continual prosperity. The fabric of this matter is still being woven with the uncertain thread of peace beneath its covering; and when the garment has been completed, it will soon be sent to your fraternity to be put on. [Col. 0445A]

It pleases me greatly that you have begun to renew the house of God. Endeavor to complete this one also, and have the other, about which I spoke when present, consecrated, so that for the twofold labor of honoring God you may deserve to receive a multiplied reward. Live, flourish, and prosper happily, dearest son!

{195}

@ [Col. 0445D] Edition: Quercetanus 74, from a manuscript. (Frobenius, letter 132.)

## LETTER 174. TO REMIGIUS, BISHOP

He commends to him a merchant traveling to Italy, and the soul of that Joseph to his prayers.

To his sweetest father,

@ [Col. 0445D] Remigius, bishop. Remigius, or Remedius, bishop of Strasbourg, lived in Alcuin’s time and died in 803; see Mabillon, *Annales*, book 27, no. 24. At the same time there was another Remigius, or Remedius, bishop of Chur, whose ecclesiastical canons, collected from the spurious letters of the Roman pontiffs disseminated by Pseudo-Isidore, were published by Goldastus, *Rerum Alamannicarum*, vol. 1, part 1, p. 121. I understand Alcuin to mean this second man. For it was the bishop of Chur, not the bishop of Strasbourg, who could assist merchants traveling to Italy in the mountain passes.

To Remigius, bishop, Albinus, the humble son, sends greetings.

I commend this merchant of ours, carrying the merchandise of Italy, to the protection of your fatherhood by these letters, so that he may travel safely along the roads of your homeland and return safely; and so that in the mountain passes he may not be detained by our customs officials, but may have, through the breadth of charity, a broad path for going and returning. [Col. 0445B]

I beg you to order prayers for the soul

@ [Col. 0445D] of Joseph, certainly the one to whom the preceding letter is addressed—Joseph, my disciple. May you flourish and progress from virtue to virtue (Ps. 83:8), until you joyfully see your God in Zion. And remember me, most holy Father, I beg you.

@ [Col. 0446D] Edition: Quercetanus 56, from a manuscript. (Frobenius, letter 133.)

## LETTER 175. TO REMEDIUS, BISHOP

He gives thanks for the gifts of his charity and urges him to good works.

To the venerable father,

@ [Col. 0446D] Remedius, bishop. I do not doubt that he is the same as Remigius, bishop of Chur, mentioned above. For these names vary among writers for the same person.

To Remedius, bishop, Alcuin, the humble deacon, sends greetings.

Having received the gifts of your charity, we rejoiced greatly at your prosperity, or because you remember us, hoping that through your most holy prayers I am made a participant in divine mercy. [Col. 0445C] Charity among friends is better than gold, and faith among the absent is more precious than gems, where God alone observes and rewards.

Diligently carry out what belongs to you, and multiply the talents of the Lord’s money that you have received, so that you may be made worthy to come with joy before the presence of the supreme King and to hear that desirable voice: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:21).

Now is the time for laboring; then, for resting. Now is the time for earning merit; then, for being rewarded. Make yourself such that what you desire may come to you. Love the one who loves you, so that you may deserve to reach his most blessed seat and say: “As we have heard, so have we seen, in the city of our God” (Ps. 47:9), in which there is complete [Col. 0445D]

@ [Col. 0446D] Remedius, bishop of Chur. See letters 174 and 175 to the same man. I would have you note that this Remedius Decurio, whom Alcuin wished to be greeted through Arno in letter 118, is this same bishop, and that in place of the word *Decurio*, which the Salzburg manuscript has, one should read *de Curia*, that is, “of Chur,” meaning the bishop of Chur.

[Col. 0446A] happiness and no disturbance, supreme rest and everlasting blessedness. May almighty God cause your holiness to flourish in every good thing, venerable Father!

@ [Col. 0446D] Frobenius, letter 200.

## LETTER 176. TO REMEDIUS, BISHOP OF CHUR  
*(Date uncertain.)*

He commends himself to his prayers on account of their old friendship.

To the most desired father Remedius, bishop of the city of Chur, Alcuin, the humble deacon, sends greetings.

Mindful of your affection and of the friendship once joined between us, I have taken care to send these little letters to your reverence, excellent brother, in remembrance of the former pact that we made between us. I beseech you by the kingdoms of the supreme Thunderer to deign, in accordance with the truth of your promise, to keep the memory of my name in your sacred prayers; [Col. 0446B] also command the servants of God who are in the monasteries throughout the extent of your diocese to intercede for me.

For I, wounded by many darts of this world, await with trembling spirit the day on which I shall be summoned to judgment, not knowing what I shall have to answer my judge, Jesus Christ, who granted me so many good things in this world, while I, as though ungrateful for all of them, did many things I ought not to have done.

But you, most holy Father, according to the charity you possess toward the members of Christ and the tested faith you have in our Savior, deign to assist me with continual prayers, so that I may find the Lord my God merciful. Prepare yourself also, according to the wisdom God has given you, in every goodness for his coming, so that, with the manifold fruit of your labor, you may be considered worthy to stand joyful and glorious before the tribunal of Christ, and, from the very brief labor of this life, may deserve, by God’s gift, to enter eternal blessedness with all the saints. [Col. 0446C]

May the Lord Jesus, who said, “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved; he will enter and go out” (John 10:9), guard your entrance and your departure, from now and forever (Ps. 120:8), most holy Father.

@ [Col. 0446D] Frobenius, letter 201.

## LETTER 177. TO THE SAME

He expresses his confidence in his prayers and urges him to carry out his episcopal office well, in hope of an eternal reward.

@ [Col. 0446D] To the most blessed father Remedius, bishop, Alcuin, the humble deacon, sends greetings.

Having graciously received the letters of your venerable affection, [Col. 0447A] which filled me with very great joy—both at the prosperity of your dignity and at the remembrance of your name—I place great confidence, by God’s grace, in the intercessions of your holiness. And the more I recognize myself as a sinner, the more I know that I need your holy prayers. I do not doubt that through the continual supplications of your charity I may obtain some measure of forgiveness; indeed, I rejoice that you yourselves possess a great reward for the integrity of your holy faith. For we have the very true promise of Truth itself, which says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matt. 18:20). Our gathering is in the spirit of charity, not in bodily presence; and nothing is hidden from him to whom all things are present—not the purity of our charity, without which nothing pleases God, nor any offering at the altar. Let us therefore pursue this with the deepest affection of our hearts, so that we may deserve to reach him who is true charity, unfailing blessedness, and blessed eternity, so that our labor may not be fruitless but may attain the glory of perfect recompense.

Do not, in your solicitude for this exchange, ever forget to encourage my sluggishness through the affection of your letters, so that we may deserve to attain that most blessed vision of our Lord Jesus Christ, where there is eternal light and the most joyful repose of perpetual peace. Do not cease to draw all who come to you, or who in any way belong to you, toward the peace of this blessedness by the example of an excellent life; nor be slow to water with your sweetest admonitions hearts that have grown dry, so that the summit of the dignity named above may possess in you a sublimity of merits before the sight [Col. 0447C] of God.

Let your words be seasoned with the salt of wisdom, so that it may be said of you most truly: “Behold the great priest, who in his days pleased God”; may he be deemed worthy to meet his Lord with the talents of the Lord’s money multiplied, and to hear the desired voice: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord God” (Matt. 25:21). For the final day hastens, and weary old age enters our chamber with silent foot. He who knocks stands at the door, if we receive his coming with joyful hearts. Few are the days of our labor, but a reward without number of days follows the one who labors well, by the ordinance of him who orders the eternal day according to the merits of each person. In his house there are many dwelling places; but all of them are filled with the riches of happiness and the glory of blessedness [Col. 0447D], where the saints, after the sweat of this life [Col. 0448A], enjoy eternal peace. From the heavenly dwellings they await our struggle, desiring that their number may be increased through us. Therefore, as you hasten there, most blessed Father, strive—taking me with you through your prayers, according to your most faithful promises—that the crown of your glory may profit me, Christ granting it, for perpetual salvation through God’s mercy. May divine grace cause you and those who faithfully serve with you in the Church of Christ to prosper in all things, most beloved and holy Father.

{196}

@ [Col. 0447D] Edited by Quercetanus, 32; Canisius, 16, compared with the manuscript codices of Salzburg and Saint Emmeram. William of Malmesbury, *On the Bishops of England*, book III, records a fragment of this letter beginning with the words “O most noble offspring” and extending to “may you deserve to attain.” (In Froben’s edition, Letter 134.)

## LETTER CLXXVIII. TO BISHOP AEDILBERT

He commends himself to the prayers of all collectively and individually; he urges them to follow the footsteps of their fathers, to read Holy Scripture, and to instruct the young.

To the distinguished shepherd of dignity,

@ [Col. 0447D] {197} The name Aedilbert is absent from the manuscript codices and from Canisius; nevertheless, it is supplied by Malmesbury in the work cited. In the Salzburg codex the name Alcuin is also absent; in its place are the letters “LCHN,” with the vowels AUI omitted, whose addition produces ALCHUIN. Aedilbert was bishop of Hagulstad in Northumbria: he succeeded Tilhere in that see in 789 and died in 797. See Hoveden and Malmesbury.

To Bishop Aedilbert [Col. 0448B] and to the entire congregation serving God in the church of Saint Andrew, Alcuin, your client in charity [Canisius: “in holiness”], sends greetings in Christ.

Desiring a special friendship, I have taken care to send the little letters of my smallness to your holiness, both to renew the bond of our ancient familiarity and to commend myself to your most sacred prayers. And if, according to the Apostle, “the prayer of a righteous person has great power” (James 5:16), how much more must the prayers of the entire most holy congregation in Christ be effective—prayers which, in the canonical hours each day, may rightly be believed to penetrate heaven in peaceful unity [the Salzburg codex and Canisius: “unanimity”]. Nor should one doubt that the individual prayer of each person in secret reaches the ears of almighty God [Salzburg codex: “should reach”]. Therefore, with all the humility of petition, I commend myself to each one, both to the common prayers of all and to the particular prayers of individuals, insofar as my prayer has any influence with your piety, so that through the prayers of your holiness, released from the chains of my sins, I may deserve to enter with you, dearly beloved brothers, through the gates of life.

O most noble offspring of the holy Fathers, successors of their honor and venerable life,

@ [Col. 0447D] Inhabitants of your most beautiful places. Regarding the construction of the church of Hagulstad, which seemed to wish to rival Roman magnificence, see William of Malmesbury, in the work cited. Hagulstad was a place situated fifty miles from York and served the royal treasury; when the blessed Wilfrid exchanged it with the most blessed Queen Etheldreda for other possessions, it came into his possession. There, with walls raised to a menacing height and various winding passages carried around in spirals, he embellished the buildings wonderfully, partly according to his own judgment and partly through the skill of the masons whom hope of generosity had drawn from Rome. It was then widely reported among the people, and was also recorded in writing, that nowhere around the Alps was there such a building. Now those who come from Rome make the same claim, so that those who see the Hagulstad construction swear that they imagine Roman ambition: so greatly have the injuries of so many ages and wars failed to remove the antiquity from the buildings. Canisius.

inhabitants of your most beautiful places, follow the footsteps of the Fathers, so that from these most beautiful dwellings you may deserve, by God’s gift, to attain the fellowship of eternal blessedness with those who begot you, in the beauty of the heavenly kingdom.

Learn to know and fulfill God’s commands, since he says: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19:17). For this reason the reading of the holy books is necessary, so that in them each person may understand [another reading: “find”] what he ought to follow and what he ought to avoid. Let the light of knowledge remain among you, and through you shine upon other churches, so that your praise may resound on everyone’s lips and an eternal reward may remain for you in heaven. Each person will receive the reward of his own labor. Teach boys and young men diligently the knowledge of books for life [another reading: “on the way”] of God, so that they may become worthy successors to your honor and also intercessors for us. The suffrages of the living benefit the dead, either for the forgiveness of sins or for an increase of greater glory.

He who does not sow will not reap, and he who does not learn does not teach. A place of this kind, without teachers, will either not be saved or will scarcely be saved. It is a great almsgiving to feed a poor person with bodily food; but greater still is it to satisfy the hungry mind with spiritual teaching [Salzburg codex: “soul”]. Just as a provident shepherd takes care to provide the best pastures for his flock, so a good teacher must diligently procure everlasting pastures of life for those subject to him. For the multiplication of the flock is the glory of the shepherd, and the multitude of the wise is the health of the world (Wis. 6:26).

I know, most holy Fathers, that you know these things perfectly and willingly fulfill them. But the charity of the one dictating has snatched words from my mouth, believing that you would read with pious humility what I have dictated in sober devotion to the love of God. Again and again I beg you to deem me worthy to have my name remembered among your familiars [Col. 0449C]. May God himself, Christ, hear your goodness interceding for the whole Church of God, and grant that you may attain the glory of eternal blessedness, dearest brothers.

@ Edited by Mabillon, 22; its deficiency at the end has been supplied from the Salzburg manuscript codex. (In Froben’s edition, Letter 135.)

## LETTER CLXXIX. TO A CERTAIN BISHOP

He longs for eternal things. He urges the diligent fulfillment of pastoral office. He wishes augury, the singing of birds, and sneezing to be abolished.

The shortness of the page cannot explain the sweetness of your affection. But I trust that the faith of your piety holds what the letter of my unskillfulness is not sufficient to express. For although the memory of charity consoles the sadness of absence, and although the eye seeks at every moment the one it wishes to have present, the mind nevertheless never ceases to love him in his absence [Col. 0449D]. Alas, how harsh is the condition of this mortality, which so often separates friends through varying events and does not permit a lover always to see the one he loves! O how happy is eternal blessedness, where what is loved is always seen, and what is not loved is never beheld! We must hasten toward it, so that we may deserve to enter it. Let no labor frighten us away; let no pleasure delay us. Rather, let us strive toward it with all our strength, the more eagerly the more blessedly the one who enters will possess it.

With you, dearest brother, I beg you to draw me along by continual prayers. You, however, are the ram against whom, according to Solomon, no one can prevail (Prov. 30:31); I am a sickly little sheep among the flock of the Gospel pasture [Col. 0450A]. Your tongue is the key of the kingdom of heaven; therefore let it never be silent about good things and never cease from admonition. Let it chastise the proud and obstinate with stern reproofs; let it refresh the humble and quiet with devout exhortations; strive, like a devoted merchant, to increase the talent you have received. The Lord who gave it is not slow to return and demand an account of his money. See and consider more attentively how many souls you have received to govern at the peril of your own soul. Make a profit for yourself from them, not a loss. Return to the example of your Lord God: how he traveled preaching through cities, fortified towns, villages, and even individual houses (Matt. 9:35); indeed, he did not shun the banquets of tax collectors and sinners, so that from the fellowship of familiarity he might obtain an occasion for preaching [Col. 0450B]. Thus, strengthened by his examples, wherever you come to a banquet, do not cease there to perform the duties of preaching, so that in exchange for the bodily things provided to you and your companions, they may receive spiritual things for themselves and their fellow laborers (Rom. 15:27; 1 Cor. 9:11).

Remember how strictly the devout preacher Paul bound himself, saying: “Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!” (1 Cor. 9:16). And again, how terrible were the threats with which the Lord himself charged the prophet Ezekiel when he imposed upon him the duties of preaching: “Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel.” And shortly afterward: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, and he dies in his sins, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. 3:17–18). And again, through the prophet Isaiah, preachers who remain silent are called [Col. 0450C] “mute dogs unable to bark” (Isa. 56:10). Who are the mute dogs except silent shepherds, unable to bark through preaching against the devil’s attacks?

Therefore, dearest brother, I beg you most earnestly to make all who belong to your diocese hear the words of life {198}, either through yourself or through your priestly assistants, so that the salvation of those subject to you may be your glory before God. But if anyone, God forbid, afterward . . . let his blood be upon his own head; and may you be found free from responsibility for his destruction, since you preached to him, even though he did not obey you.

For the ancient enemy rarely fights Christians with open face; rather, under the pretext of piety he conceals the poisons of a deadly suggestion. [Augury, the singing of birds, sneezing, and many similar practices must also be altogether forbidden, since they have no power except among those who believe that they have some power, so that according to their faith it may happen to them. For the evil spirit is permitted, for the deception of those who observe such things, to cause these practices to produce effects, so that auguries may often foretell something true. Thus, even in the Old Law, those who observe auguries are commanded to be punished by death (Deut. 18:10, 12), so that we may know with what punishment souls living under grace must be chastised if they make a habit of this evil.] It is fitting, therefore, that you, as a pious shepherd and prudent physician, guard the flock entrusted to you against these and similar plagues, so that you may deserve to bring it undefiled before the sight of the eternal Judge and become worthy to hear the desired voice: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:21).

@ [Col. 0451D] {199} This letter now appears for the first time from the Salzburg manuscript codex. It lacks an address there; nevertheless, the very character of its style does not allow us to doubt that it is Alcuin’s. To which bishop it was sent, however, is not known from any certain indication. (In Froben’s edition, Letter 136.)

## LETTER CLXXX. TO A CERTAIN BISHOP

He grieves over his friend’s illness; he urges patience, virtue, and care for the students.

When I received the letters of your blessedness, their very appearance greatly rejoiced me, and their meaning filled all my inward parts with joy—except that your illness disturbed my veins. But, according to the Apostle, bodily weakness is strength of spirit. Let the son rejoice, so that he may be disciplined by the father. Gold is tested in the furnace so that it may shine more purely from the flames (Prov. 27:21); and a person is refined in bodily suffering so that his soul may leap out purer from the prison-house of its confinement [Col. 0451B]. Let paternal chastisement please you, because a father’s scourges advance salvation. The days of labor are few, and the reward is everlasting [perhaps: “perpetual”]. Therefore let the tongue labor diligently in preaching, the hand in almsgiving, and the foot in traversing the flock of Christ. Let the mind keep watch in prayers, be strengthened in psalmody, and rejoice in the praise of God. Whatever a person will always be doing in heaven, let him do frequently here on earth. “The sacrifice of praise has honored me,” God says through the Prophet; “there is the way by which I shall show him the salvation of God” (Ps. 49:23).

Let there be humility in heart and body; patience in conduct and speech; a servant of the Lord fervent in mind; peace on the lips and charity in the heart. Let gentle words always be mingled with harsher ones, because soft words penetrate a hard heart more easily than bitter words [Col. 0451C]. Let there be discernment concerning what is appropriate to each time, person, age, and task. Let there be frequent reading, sober fasts, moderate banquets, honor for guests, provision for the poor, care of the household, and diligence among the people.

What am I doing, and what is it that I am writing, except that charity does not know how to be silent, and that it is a kind of refreshment to express in words what inflames the mind? I know that you patiently endure my rusticity and do not reject my little letters of familiarity. Therefore I am not ashamed to write again what I have said before and to repeat what I previously sent. Even if I do not remember what I wrote earlier, I am nevertheless not forgetful of eternal charity.

Now I would like you to hurry to your homeland and arrange the lessons of the boys: who should learn grammar, who should read letters and short books, and who should be deemed worthy to absorb Holy Scripture with a sober mind. But you, holy Father, should devote yourself especially to the Gospel readings and serve the learning of the canonical books of Holy Scripture, because meditation on the divine law befits you, so that it may be said of you: “He will meditate on the law of the Lord day and night” (Ps. 1:2). Thus may your fruit flourish forever [Col. 0452A], and may everything you do prosper for your salvation. And remember me. Farewell, most holy Father.

@ [Col. 0451D] Edited by Quercetanus, 53; Canisius, 31. (In Froben’s edition, Letter 137.)

## LETTER CLXXXI

@ [Col. 0451D] Certainly to a certain bishop and disciple of Alcuin, as the context indicates, but otherwise unknown. TO A CERTAIN BISHOP. He urges piety and the remaining virtues; he commends care for divine praise in the churches entrusted to him.

“The Lord is my portion,” said my soul (Lam. 3:24). “My portion,” said the father to his son, “may you have a portion with the saints forever.”

After reading the letters of your blessedness, I rejoiced at the well-being of your prosperity, whose present supporter I was insofar as I could be, and still am now, though absent and desirous of it. Would that, as you promised in your letter, you might remember the ancient fatherly bond and sweetness between us in the Lord, who may always advance us according to his will and [Col. 0452B] cause us to progress in his commandments. Let us remember that he raised us from the dungheap and placed us among the princes of his people (Ps. 112:7–8)—not through our merits, but through his freely given mercy. Let us always give thanks to him throughout our life, so that he who exalted us may also preserve us.

Adorn most diligently in the praise of God all the churches that, by God’s gift, you have received to govern. Let there be in them the melody of the Psalms at the canonical hours, perseverance in prayer, the solemn celebrations of Masses, and intercessions for you and your friends. Let your conduct, my son, be marked by honesty and temperance; let the cultivation of clothing be moderate; let banquets be characterized not by luxury and drunkenness but by sobriety and suitability to times and persons. Everywhere keep the fear of God before your eyes. Let humility exalt you, truth make you honorable, and mercy make you beloved. Let your hand be generous to the poor and kind to friends. Be a faithful steward of the household of God. Be a pattern of salvation to all who dwell with you (1 Thess. 1:7). And because God has made you noble in honor, be noble also in character. Let the light of your goodness shine before everyone. May the heavenly Father be glorified in you, preserve you in this present life, and grant you eternal glory with the saints in the life to come.

My portion, my portion, may you prosper; may Christ always be your portion.

Be mindful, my portion, I beg you, of your nurturing father.

@ [Col. 0452D] Edited by Quercetanus, 45; Canisius, 36, compared with the manuscript codices of Salzburg and Saint Emmeram. (In Froben’s edition, Letter 138.)

## LETTER CLXXXII. TO THE PRIEST HECHSTAN

He urges virtue and wishes to be commended to the prayers of his friends. [Col. 0452D]

To my dearest son,

@ [Col. 0452D] “High rock.” “I find,” says Canisius, “in the division between Louis and Charles the name ‘Alta Petra’ as a place-name after Saint Ursus at Solothurn and Grandval.” Here, however, it is a proper name, not of a place but of a person rendered in Latin; in German it sounds Hechstanus or Hechstainum, perhaps Hochenstein. Altapetra Albinus sends greetings.

May your reward, in accordance with your name, be high and firm. But work diligently so that this may come to pass by God’s gift. Run while you have the light; ascend daily through each step of the virtues, so that it may be said of you: “The saints will go from virtue to virtue,” and so that what follows may also come to pass: “The God of gods will be seen by you in Zion” (Ps. 83:8). Persist in vigils and prayers, in chastity and humility, in love of God and neighbor, and in observing the other commandments. Adorn yourself with all these things, which nevertheless must all look toward the strengthening of charity, on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. 22:40). Although you may not yet be senior in years, you have begun to be senior in the order of the sacred ministry [Canisius: “in the sacred ministry”]. For *presbyter* means “elder” in the Latin language, signifying that one ought to be old in conduct, perfect in steadfastness, and intent upon preaching the word of God, so that one may fulfill by one’s deeds what one teaches with one’s mouth.

{200} But you, dearest son, prepare diligently for yourself, through good merits, an everlasting dwelling in heaven. Now is the time for laboring and winning God’s favor; then will be the time of judgment and, for good works, of living unto God, because each person will then be judged according to his works (Matt. 16:27). Let the pomp of the world not be sweeter to you than eternal salvation, nor bodily pleasure [Canisius: “affection”] sweeter than the love of God. Whoever loves God here will also rejoice with God there [Salzburg codex: “will rejoice to be with God”]. How delightful is eternal blessedness, and how miserable is everlasting destruction! Prepare yourself in the present for whatever you wish to become in the future life. As a guest for a short time, earn for yourself an everlasting dwelling. Think today that tomorrow you may be dying. Every day must be regarded as though it were the last. Therefore a person must always be ready, so that on whatever day the Judge knocks at the door, it may be opened to him with joy (Luke 12:36).

He will be carried

@ [Col. 0453D] To judgment. Canisius reads: “to the *imalicium*.” “Scriverius read *mallum* in the manuscript notes; and indeed *mallus* is an assembly in which the greater cases were formerly judged. ‘Lest public *malla*—for both *mallum* and *mallus* are used—or judicial sessions be held at the exits or atria of churches, the Synod of Soissons under Charlemagne forbids this; it was held at approximately the time when Alcuin flourished,’ says Basnage. But the manuscript codices remove the doubt, for they read ‘to judgment,’ which reading is also demanded by the context itself.”

the soul to judgment, when it is led from the body.

What then will drunkenness avail? What then will bodily luxury, the pomp of clothing, a ring on the finger, or gold in the purse avail? The rich man dies just as the poor man does, and the condition of both is the same, unless perhaps one proves better than the other. The good person goes into everlasting life; the wicked is handed over to eternal torments. Be a son of life and not of death. Be an heir of heaven with Christ, not food for the fires with the devil. Strive each day to become better, so that you may always deserve to be with God.

Greet in my name

@ [Col. 0454D] Sacen and Begnod. These names occur only in the edition of Quercetanus; they are absent from our manuscript codices, and it is unknown whom they designate.

Sacen and Begnod, servants of God, our friends, sons of eternal life. Ask them to remember us in their prayers, together with their household, which they diligently instruct in the service of God [another reading: “may instruct”], so that they may receive a reward from them and not punishment, praise and not disgrace. For the progress of those subject to them is the salvation of their superiors, and the good shepherd will be crowned through the multiplication of his flock. And you, my son, remember me and yourself in your prayers, so that divine mercy may deign to preserve us by its perpetual gift in eternal salvation. Farewell, farewell, my son, forever.

@ [Col. 0454D] Edited by Quercetanus, 46; Canisius, 37, compared with the manuscript codices. (In Froben’s edition, Letter 139.)

## LETTER CLXXXIII. TO THE PRIEST MONNA AND HIS BROTHER

He urges contempt for the world and humility.

To my dearest friends in Christ, brother and son,

@ [Col. 0454D] Anthropus and Stratocles. These names, like the address to Monna supplied by Quercetanus, are absent from Canisius and from the manuscript codices available to us. Perhaps he calls Monna “Anthropus” by a Greek appellation; for *Monn* or *Mann* means “man” in the German language. Anthropus and Stratocles, the humble levite Alcuin, send greetings.

Charity commonly addresses by letters those whom it cannot see with its eyes, because the letters on a page strive to express the greatness of love, so that what cannot be seen in the mind may be read by the eyes in syllables. Therefore, mindful of your brotherhood, dearest friends, I have sent this letter jointly to you, so that you may know how great is my concern for you—concern which neither the distance of lands [Col. 0454B] nor the passage of time has been able to erase, preventing me from admonishing those whom I love most {201}. I desire both to believe in the prosperity of your salvation before God and to know it in this world. For both to happen, one thing must be pursued: namely, pleasing God. Whatever is loved in the world passes away, and only whatever is done in God remains. Therefore let temporal things not delay those who are journeying toward eternal things, since the disciple whom Jesus loved says: “Do not love the things that are in the world” (1 John 2:15). Can a hungry person fill himself with the shadow of bread? The happiness of the world is shadowy; true happiness is awaited only in the future.

Do not be held by the chains of the world or bound by the snares of the devil. Do not rebuild the chains that you cut off through confession and repentance, so that you may be able to raise free hands [Col. 0454C] to God and pray with a pure heart to him whom you ought to love with your whole heart. Let vigils and prayers be constant for you. “Blessed is that servant whom, when the Lord comes, he finds watching” (Luke 12:37). You must watch in good works, not sleep amid bodily pleasures. Flee drunkenness as a pit of destruction, because according to the Prophet, “wine and drunkenness take away the heart” (Hos. 4:11). Do not pursue the pomp of clothing. “Blessed is the man who does not regard vanities and false insanities” (Ps. 39:5). It is better to adorn the soul that remains than the body that decays into dust with clothing, as a certain philosopher says: “It is ridiculous to seek praise in vanity,” intending the superfluous concern for clothing to be understood as vanity [Canisius: “to be understood”]. And if very many do this, it is written: “You shall not follow the crowd to do evil” (Ecclus. 18:32). For it is better to be saved with a few than to perish with the many.

Know whose examples you follow most diligently, and cling most closely to that person’s merits. Christ made the way to heaven for us through humility; why do we follow the pride of the wicked? Through pride the angel fell from heaven; why does a human being, earth and ashes, become proud? What place should be assigned to a proud human being, if infernal punishments were prepared for a proud angel? There is no need to admonish you as though you were [foolish or] ignorant, since you have the Gospel of Christ before your eyes. Read and understand what must be avoided and what must be observed. Whatever is written there must be done, since Truth itself says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. 24:35). And again: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my words” (John 14:23). The sign of love for God is to observe his commandments; and the reward of love is the vision [Canisius: “visitation”] of divinity, as he whom we are commanded to love himself promises, saying: “He who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21). Pray for me and fare well, brother-men, dearest in Christ.

@ [Col. 0455D] Edited by Quercetanus, 37; Canisius, 42. (In Froben’s edition, Letter 140.)

## LETTER CLXXXIV. TO THE PRIEST EADA

He gives thanks for gifts; he grieves that he has been snatched from the condition of poverty into the abyss of riches; he commends himself to prayers.

To his beloved friend,

@ [Col. 0455D] Eada the priest. Mabillon considers it likely that this man was a monk, *Annals*, book XXVII, no. 31. “This letter,” he says, “makes clear how far Alcuin was from a desire for riches,” on account of which someone might perhaps have considered him worthy of reproach. Eada the priest, Albinus sends greetings.

I received the gifts of your affection with great joy and devotion, desiring, by the gift of Christ God, that you may possess prosperity both in the present and in the future, and recognizing in you the generosity of your former munificence [Col. 0455C]. Therefore you have renewed in us the friendship of our ancient faith. Would that divine mercy might cause to persevere in you until the end of your life what it deigned to work in you from your earliest age. For “the form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. 7:31). Therefore it is necessary that the final days find us clothed in sobriety with regard to the twofold commandment of love. For “whoever offends in one thing,” that is, in one commandment of charity, “has become guilty of all” (James 2:10).

{202} I beg you to have us as companions of your blessedness, just as we desire to have you as a companion of our prosperity. By the prayers of your devotion, lead us into that same degree of poverty in which, with God bringing it about, you wholesomely remain. You hold in your hands what we once intended to hold. But the waves of the world have carried our little boat by stormy winds into the abyss of riches [Col. 0455D]. Yet I beg you to strive to recall me, through prayers of piety, to the harbor of quiet. I desire it, but I do not do it. Peaceful is the poverty that you once loved happily. “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). But if this poverty is guided by the rudder of humility and, with the Holy Spirit blowing into its sail, by the sail of charity, it will reach the harbor of eternal blessedness, where—remembering my name—you may deserve to intercede for me [Canisius: “to plead for my unhappiness”]. [Col. 0456A]

Give yourself to this, I humbly beg, so that you may have a double reward: one for yourself and another for your brother. Would that I may deserve to see you there with joy, if this cannot happen here! May divine grace accompany you and cause you to flourish in every good thing, so that with the manifold fruit of good works you may deserve to enter everlasting life.

@ [Col. 0456D] Edited by Quercetanus, 36; Canisius, 38, compared with the manuscript codices. (In Froben’s edition, Letter 141.)

## LETTER CLXXXV. TO A CERTAIN DISCIPLE

He rejoices at the disciple’s prosperity and study of letters; he urges repentance and struggle against the enemies of the soul. He reproves bodily adornment.

I received the letters of your affection with a grateful hand and read them with a joyful spirit, understanding in them the prosperity of your life and your devotion to literary study, through which the eloquence of the writer shone forth. It is clear to me that this is my greatest joy: to see my sons [supplied] flourishing in purity of conduct and diligence in progress. This is the adornment I desired in them [another reading: “in my own”]. These are the delights with which I wished them to be clothed. This is the cleanliness I longed for in them. These are the banquets in which I loved to see them rejoice. Through these things, too, the soul that hungers and thirsts for righteousness is refreshed. This is the wine that Wisdom mixes for those invited to her table, when she has built her house supported by seven columns (Prov. 9:5, 1).

In this divine house, dearest brother [Salzburg codex: “son”], I beg you always to dwell.
