I beseech you to feed upon its banquets; I desire that you be drunk with the pure wine of this cup [another reading: “of this”], not to pursue the vain pomps of the world or the harmful pleasures of the body, which will not profit those who walk in them, but have plunged their followers into the abyss of eternal destruction [Col. 0456C].

But you, love of my soul, if you have contracted any filth from these things, wash it away with tears, cleanse it through repentance, and erase it with the hand of a better life; mindful of yourself and mindful of me, making my soul rejoice and sparing your own, because your salvation is my consolation. Do not defraud your father of his reward in you. Do not erase the name of son from yourself. If you will not do it for your own sake, do it at least for mine. If you care neither for me nor for yourself, fear, love, and honor God. He is the true Father, the Redeemer, the giver of all good things; he raises up the soul that sleeps amid pleasures.

You must fight every day against three enemies: against the devil, against the world, and against the flesh. How will you be able to sleep securely? While you sleep, those who seek to kill you remain awake. How can you not fear the flames of eternal destruction [Col. 0456D]? You are a guest here for a short time: why do you seek a homeland in your exile and forget the one in which you were enrolled as a citizen through baptism? Consider who hung upon the cross for you [patiently enduring the insults of the envious], whose side, pierced by a spear, poured forth the blood of your redemption. Do not regard the price of your salvation as insignificant. He who made you was handed over for you; indeed, the Creator of all things spent himself as the price of your redemption. Why do you make yourself ignoble, having been bought at so noble a price? Do not make a servant of the devil out of a son of God.

[Col. 0457A] What—

@ [Col. 0457D] “In pompous garments.” It is evident from the words “You are a minister of the sacred altar,” and so forth, that the man whom Alcuin here reproves for the affected splendor of his clothing was a cleric. Let us hear Sidonius reproving the elegance of dress in a churchman: “By conspicuous dress and appearance,” he says in Letter 13 of Book IV, “he does not merely become youthful again but in some way becomes a child again. Indeed, with his garment tightly fitted, his boot stretched taut, his hair cut like a wheel, and his beard clipped close to the skin by scissors and sunk into the hiding places of his wrinkles, having undertaken the profession of religion, let him rather grow strong in the powers of resurgent innocence” [Col. 0458D]. It should be noted here that the ancient Franks used close-fitting garments. Concerning them Sidonius writes in Poem 2:

> The close-fitting garments customary among them constrain the tall limbs of men.

As also concerning the Goths, Sidonius, Book IV, Letter 20. Canisius noted several further observations here about the clothing of the Romans and the ancient Franks from the same Sidonius.

Do you clothe your flesh in splendid garments and not seek the adornments of the soul? Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, who does not turn to vanities and false madnesses (Psalm XXXIX, 5). It is better to hang the necklace of wisdom around one’s neck than to be wrapped in the silk of vanity (Ecclesiasticus VI). It is better to gird one’s loins with chastity than to be bound with numerous belts of pomp, and to carry in one’s hands the lamps of good works, burning brightly, than to make one’s fingers gleam with rings of display (Luke XII, 35). It is better for one’s feet to be made ready for the Gospel of peace than to be tied by a long knot of bandages (Ephesians VI, 15).

Alas, that which perishes is adorned with such diligence, while that which endures is neglected with such heedlessness! The former is adorned, nourished, and clothed with every care; the latter is regarded as a worthless household object, unworthy of any adornment! The earthly is cultivated, while the heavenly is not cared for! The image of God is despised, while the appearance of earth is honored! Let it not be so, my son; let it not be so in you.

You are a minister of the sacred altar, a companion of the highest honor, a vessel of wisdom, the flower of youth: attend to your dignity and be what you are called. Consider that your body will return to dust and your soul will be hurried to judgment. Show yourself now as you wish then to be. Now is the time for laboring; then, for being rewarded. Now is the time for earning merit; then, for receiving its recompense. Whoever labors more will receive the greater reward. Run while you have the light (John XII, 35). Whoever exists today will not exist tomorrow, as Scripture says: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, for you do not know what the coming day may bring” (Ecclesiasticus V, 8). All the glory of the world will fall like the flower of hay. “The grass withers, and its flower fades” (I Peter I, 24). Remember your Creator before the time of affliction comes.

Let us fight bravely and conquer swiftly [Ms.: manfully; another: stubbornly], so that we may be crowned happily. We have as our helper the one whom we also have as our rewarder. He first conquered the enemy so that we might be able to conquer. He triumphed on the cross so that we might reign in heaven. He descended to us on earth so that we might ascend to him in heaven. He became the Son of Man so that we might deserve to be sons of God. To him be praise and glory throughout all ages. Amen.

[Col. 0458D] Edited by Quercetanus, 47; Canisius, 29, collated with manuscript codices (in Frobenius, Letter 142).

# LETTER CLXXXVI. TO A FAITHFUL FRIEND

He indicates the ardor of his charity and urges him to be an example to all in his life. He commends the reading of the holy Gospel and of Saint Gregory’s *Pastoral Book*.

[Col. 0457D] To the sweetest brother and friend in the charity of Christ, greetings.

“An old friend is not like a new one” (Ecclesiasticus IX, 14). A friend who follows fortune and observes the times, who changes according to the character of the place, was never a true friend. O, if I had a voice of iron, and if all my hairs were turned into tongues, so that even in this way the words of my affection might reach the ears of your heart; or if the spirit of prophecy were in your breast, so that you could perceive the secrets of my heart! You would surely believe how my breast is filled with the sweetest savor of your love.

But now I shall do what I can. I send you these little letters, tokens of great affection, so that through them you may understand what can scarcely be understood. Just as a flame can be seen but cannot be touched, so affection can be discerned in writing but can scarcely be felt in the soul of the writer. For just as sparks are scattered from a fire, so love flies through the service of letters. Yet in the hearts of many it is extinguished; therefore it shines more gratefully wherever even some little flame of it burns.

Because I have found true charity in you, most holy brother, no distance between our lands prevents me, as the opportunity of the bearer allows [to visit you], since I desire to enjoy you perpetually in Christ. May his love fill our hearts, so that through love of him our brotherhood may remain inviolable. As a priest of the most high God, as a heavenly trumpet, as a herald of salvation, strive to impress his charity upon the hearts of all. Whatever his holiness rejects, forbid with the greatest urgency; whatever his goodness loves, proclaim with the greatest ardor. Let no power of earthly frailty frighten you; let no worldly ambition restrain priestly severity. “Do not fear those who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew X, 28).

Be a lamp of life to all, a guide along the roads of God, an example of uprightness. Be consolation to the wretched, medicine to the wounded, consolation to the afflicted; be a shepherd, not a hireling; the house of God, not a den of robbers; a flourishing palm, an ever-green olive tree (John X, 12; Matthew XXI, 13; Psalm XCI, 13; Genesis VIII, 11). Do not sell God’s doves. Give freely what you have received freely (Matthew X, 8). Show yourself blameless in all things, so that your life may be the people’s instruction and so that many may be built up by your good conduct (I Timothy III, 2).

Read diligently, I beg you, the Gospel of Christ, as well as the other books of canonical authority. But also examine very frequently the *Pastoral Book* of blessed Pope Gregory. Feed your soul on these feasts, so that you may have the means to refresh others as well.

I beg you also to remember me during the solemn celebration of Mass and your sacred prayers, so that divine clemency may deign to grant me forgiveness of sins and you a crown of merits.

[Col. 0458D] Quercetanus, 102, from a manuscript (in Frobenius, Letter 143).

# LETTER CLXXXVII. TO A CERTAIN SON

He praises the disciple’s devotion and pursuit of wisdom. He urges him to follow not his own ways but exhortations and the examples of the saints. He commends the reading of sacred Scripture, the practice of the virtues, care for young men, and so forth.

[Col. 0459A] Albinus sends greetings to his dearest and beloved son.

The sequence of your letters gladdened my eyes, for in them I saw the evidence of good devotion, the beauty of holy wisdom, and love of learning it—something especially fitting for your years, whether on account of the blessedness of eternal life or of worldly honor. For nothing is more praiseworthy in a person than the beauty of wisdom and the affection of charity.

But what you asked—that I should inscribe my ways for you—seems strange, since you were with me day and night and nothing was hidden from you concerning what was done among us. Nor does it seem fitting that you should wish to follow my footsteps so closely, except perhaps the words of admonition that you heard so often. Rather, let the examples of the saints instruct you, which are read in the holy Scriptures and are recognized as the support of our life.

But you, dearest son, exercise yourself in charity, and remember to adorn your life with ecclesiastical duties. Frequent vigils and prayers, and labor day and night in the study of reading, seeking Christ in the writings of the prophets, where he was foretold, and in the authority of the Gospel, where he was revealed. When you find him, do not lose him (Song of Songs III, 4), but bring him into the house of your heart and have him as the ruler of your life. Love him as your Redeemer and governor, and as the giver of all good things. Keep his commandments (I John V, 3; Matthew XIX, 17), for in them there is eternal life.

Examine yourself with great discernment, considering what you are commanded to do and what to avoid. Whatever you have received from a teacher, or understand through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, pass on and teach with the greatest diligence, so that the gift of understanding may always increase in you, for “to everyone who has, more will be given” (Matthew XIII, 12)—that is, the knowledge of understanding is increased in one who possesses the zeal to teach.

Be like a father to the poor and wretched, humble in serving and generous in giving, so that their blessing may come upon you. Warn the young men who are with you about purity of body, confession of their sins, constant study, sober conduct, avoidance of drunkenness, flight from lust, and rejection of the vanity of this world. Let them learn in youth what they may teach in old age. Let them show honor to their elders, but love ecclesiastical duties.

Therefore see to it that they behold good examples in you, together with the exhortation of the words of the saints. For this kind of religion and devotion to almighty God, may grace pursue you, exalt you, and honor you among men, and grant you everlasting life.

Concerning the books you asked for, namely, blessed Bede’s commentary on the Epistles of the Apostles—

[Col. 0459D] My sister Gisla. I understand this to mean Gisla, the sister of Charlemagne, not Gisla, his daughter. See the notes on Letter 126, to Gisla.

My sister Gisla has it. When she sends it back to me, I shall send it to you. Concerning—

[Col. 0459D] It is therefore clear that Alcuin wrote a work *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs*, but the letter he mentions here has perished.

I once composed, at your request, a letter under your name concerning the Blessing of the Patriarchs—

[Col. 0459D] Samuel. Perhaps this was the Samuel who later became bishop of Worms, a fellow student of Rabanus Maurus, to whom this letter might have been given under Alcuin. Concerning him Rabanus writes in Poem 21:

“For once I rejoiced that you were my companion, etc. What Albinus, the proper teacher, once taught, may this breast retain, etc., and of your fellow student Samuel.”

I do not know whether you asked about this work or about some other author. You asked what the word *epistola* means. For in Greek, *epi* means “upon” and *stola* means “garment.” Hence the Emperor Hadrian—

[Col. 0460D] Epictetus. Alcuin is referring to Hadrian’s question: “What will become of us if you loosen the girdle?” Epictetus replied: “It is a letter.” See the *Altercation of the Emperor Hadrian Augustus and Epictetus* in Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, vol. XIII, p. 560, and p. 563 among the notes.

The philosopher Epictetus was asked, among other questions, what a “girdled thing” was. Seeing him holding a letter in his hand, he replied: “What you are holding in your hand.” He wished to understand it as though the seal of a letter were a kind of outer fastening by which the sheet was clothed from the outside. Keep this interpretation until you find a better or more accurate one.

[Col. 0460D] Frobenius, Letter 231.

# LETTER CLXXXVIII. TO AN ILL SON

He consoles him and urges him to confess his sins.

To his dearest son, the object of his unique affection, greetings in the blessing of Christ.

I hastened to meet the presence of your sweetness, and behold, in place of the joy of seeing you, a letter of sadness has arrived, announcing in tearful words your illness and declaring that you are almost sighing at the threshold of this life. Yet as much as I grieve over your suffering, so much am I gladdened by divine compassion, which has refined you through such a long illness, so that you may appear purer in his sight. “Blessed is the man whom the Lord reproves; for he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews XII, 6).

Let this hope console you, dearest son. If anything worldly has come under your power, send it beforehand to the Lord as a pledge of peace [Ms.: promise]. Carefully cleanse, according to your conscience, every smallest impurity of words and thoughts, indeed also of deeds, before a faithful and prudent confessor, so that nothing may remain by which the Evil One could accuse you before the supreme Judge.

Trust with the strongest hope in the Lord Jesus, who at a single confession promised paradise to the thief. And if his clemency—which is accustomed to kill and to give life—should wish to restore you to your former state of health, let your character then be such as your will is now, and your conduct then such as your thought is now, so that both the suffering of illness and the restoration of health may advance your everlasting salvation.

You have me, insofar as I can be, as a faithful helper either on that terrible journey or as a counselor for the comfort of the present life.

As for what your affection asked concerning the difference between the two places—that is, whether it would be better to await the breath of the final day in a canonical see or in monastic holiness—God is everywhere, and he considers the quality of merits more than that of places. If you have labored more under the shoulder-cloak than under the cowl in God’s service, what reason is there, at the point of death, to cast aside the insignia of your labor [read: insignia] and seek another judgment?

Unless perhaps, under the cowl, should God in his mercy restore you from this illness, you intend to serve as a soldier. Nevertheless, as long as you live, direct the intention of your mind toward the greater advancement of God’s holy Church. Therefore, for the sake of prayers and the comfort of fraternal intercession, it seems desirable that your body rest among monks.

If I have said anything wrongly, do not think that I speak from ill will but from ignorance. You have, I know, pious and prudent counselors with you, whose counsel it seems proper for you to use for the salvation of your soul. As for my smallness, it never withdraws from your affection; and even if it cannot understand as it ought, it nevertheless does not cease to desire as it should.

I ask you, whatever may happen concerning your life, to let me know quickly, so that I may either accompany you as you depart with tearful intercessions—

[Col. 0461D] Something seems to be missing here. May you always have eternal or temporal days of happiness in Christ, by God’s mercy.

[Col. 0461D] Quercetanus, 107, from a manuscript (in Frobenius, Letter 144).

# LETTER CLXXXIX. TO ANTONIUS

He complains of being forgotten, rejects theatrical spectacles, and says that he wrote to Homer about them, and so forth.

[Col. 0461D] To Antonius. He calls Adalhard, abbot of Corbie, by this assumed name, as Pascasius testifies in the *Life of Adalhard*, no. 21, in these words: “For this reason Adalhard was called Antonius by some, as the letters of Master Albinus report.” Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, fourth Benedictine century, part I, p. 316.

To Antonius, Albinus sends greetings.

[Col. 0461C] What a level road it would have been across—

[Col. 0461D] Across the Belgian countryside. I think this should be read instead of “war-like countryside.” For old Corbie was there, as was Adalhard’s patrimony. Mabillon, cited work, *Acta Sanctorum*, p. 307, n. 3.

What a level road it would have been across the Belgian countryside, for running or flying on the wings of charity! I fear that the wings have perhaps been broken, which could otherwise have been inserted into them like the others. Therefore the paternal nest is not visited, nor does the dove even bring little letters on foot, as once, as you read, in Greece. What will Orpheus do about this as he goes?

“Orpheus . . . Orion among dolphins. The estate of the wine-bearer is turned; the judgment is ours.”

{206} I am jesting; I am seriously [perhaps: in earnest] trying often to awaken the sleeper. But neither has there been dancing when the singer sang, nor lamentation when the mourner mourned.

“Let everything become even the middle of the sea; live on, forests,”

said the lover to the woman who despised him. The same poet, in the same work:

“You will find another if this Alexis grows weary of you.”

I thought I would come to you, whisper the sweet things into one little ear, and sing the harsh things into the other; but the Roman count prevented me at an unwelcome time. If he rises up in battle against me, I shall hope in this: “Though an army encamp against me” (Psalm XXVI, 3), because “strength is made perfect in weakness” (II Corinthians XII, 9).

I fear that—

[Col. 0461D] Homerus. Angilbert, with whom Adalhard lived at the court of Pippin, king of Italy. Mabillon dates this letter to the year 791 and observes what the minds of pious men then thought about theatrical spectacles—spectacles which Alcuin could neither tolerate nor conceal even in a courtier such as Angilbert then was. *Annales Benedictini*, Book XXVI, no. 13.

I fear that Homer may grow angry with the letter forbidding spectacles and the devilish fictions that all the holy Scriptures prohibit, to such an extent that I used to read that Saint Augustine said: “I do not know, man, how great a crowd of unclean spirits follows one who introduces actors, mimes, and dancers into his house.” But far be it from a Christian household that the devil should have power there.

I once wrote to you about these matters, wishing health to your dearest son with all the affection of my heart, and wishing through you to accomplish what I recognized could not be accomplished through me. But let your spirit, dearest son, rejoice in the service of God and in the salvation of your brother, so that your reward of merits may increase through the progress of others.

For this reason I often desired letters of exhortation from your affection. But I do not know what cause either removed me from your mind or compelled you to cease exhorting. Blessed is the one who speaks into the ear of a listener. Would that all might hear you with such desire as I, your wholehearted friend, do! Or write even after being rebuked, so that you may vindicate yourself, since when asked you were unwilling to console me.

Farewell in the peace of everlasting blessedness, dearest son.

[Col. 0462D] Frobenius, Letter 212.

# LETTER CXC. TO ANTONIUS

He announces that the brothers of the island of Lérins have arrived and that Adalhard’s brother was summoned to the palace, and so forth.

[Col. 0462C] To his pious, prudent, and religious son—

[Col. 0462D] To Antonius, who is called Adalhard, abbot of Corbie. His father was Bernard, son of Charles Martel, brother of King Pippin, uncle of Charlemagne. He had two brothers, Wala and Bernarius, and two sisters, Gundrada and Theodrada. All of them were always held in the highest regard by Charlemagne. After his death, all except Theodrada were driven into exile by Emperor Louis in 814. Mabillon believes that the reason was none other than that men distinguished by power and intelligence were suspect to Louis—indeed a pious Augustus, but suspicious and fearful. Consult the *Life of Saint Adalhard* in the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Order of Saint Benedict, fourth century, part I, pp. 306 and following.

To Antonius, Albinus the *matricularius* sends greetings.

A certain preacher ought, according to the Apostle, to be persistent; so also a certain affection, though unwelcome, presses itself upon an audience that is scarcely grateful. Nor does it know how to remain silent when rejected; it cannot be overwhelmed by floods or extinguished by storms, lest, once kindled, it be suddenly put out. [This] was the reason for this little letter, which my pen took care to append.

Accordingly, the venerable and religious brothers from the monastery—

[Col. 0462D] From the monastery of the island of Hilirina. Instead of *Hilirinae*, one should read *Lirinae*, or “of the island of Lérins,” as will be clear from the letter to the brothers of Lérins presented shortly afterward.

Accordingly, the venerable and religious brothers from the monastery of the island of Lérins came to us a few days ago, telling us everything prosperous concerning those regions. But they also added that my son—

[Col. 0463C] Your brother. Saint Adalhard had a brother named Bernarius, as we said above. Pascasius Radbertus writes of him in the *Life of Saint Adalhard*, no. 34: “He had the form of Christ’s discipleship with us,” namely at Corbie. Further below, no. 35, he testifies that Bernarius was sent into exile by Emperor Louis Augustus together with his brothers and his sister Gundrada, and was sent back to Lérins: “Our Bernarius,” he says, “is sent back to Lérins,” where he had previously assumed the monastic state.

It is therefore certain from the present letter that Adalhard’s brother—Bernarius, evidently—was a monk on the island of Lérins. Through the efforts perhaps of his brothers, sisters, and relatives, who were held in the highest regard by Charles, he was summoned to the palace. When Alcuin heard this, he advised that he be sent back to his monastery, lest he become involved in the former dangers from which he had escaped there while wearing the monastic habit. This advice was ineffective. For, as can be gathered from the passage cited from Radbertus, Bernarius appears to have remained in the monastery of Corbie with his brothers until the death of Charlemagne.

Afterward, when envy had been aroused against this family, he was sent back to his own monastery of Lérins. The author of the *Life of Louis Augustus* writes: “He restored Adalhard, formerly abbot of the monastery of Corbie, to his previous office; likewise he summoned his brother Bernarius from the monastery of Saint Benedict, reconciled him to his brother, and restored him to the same place.” Perhaps “to the same place” should be read here. Instead of “from the monastery of Saint Benedict,” one should read “from the monastery of Saint Honoratus,” or “of Lérins,” from which Bernarius was recalled after his reconciliation; thereafter he was permitted to live in the monastery of Corbie with his brothers, who were likewise restored to the same place.

At the end of Vincent Barrali’s *Bibliotheca Lerinensis*, Bernarius, Adalhard’s brother, is included among the saints of Lérins, although the author does not state whether he is venerated. Bollandus omits him in the catalogue of saints omitted under January 2.

Your brother, when he had been ordered to go to the palace with the abbot, had begun his journey in the second week after Easter. I wanted you to know this so that you might provide your brother with good counsel concerning what should be done. As far as the judgment of my smallness can see, it would seem very necessary for him to return to his brothers and live the life in which he was saved from the danger of death, in which he nearly perished. Why should he return again to the place where he was almost lost?

It should not seem burdensome to you, together with—

[Col. 0464C] With our Homer. Angilbert, with whom Adalhard spent some time at the court of Pippin, king of Italy. According to the writer of Radbertus’s *Life*, he had been attached to King Pippin so that he might properly instruct the young king and the kingdom itself in the conduct of public affairs and the practice of religion. Alcuin calls Angilbert the chief officer, or first counselor, of King Pippin’s palace in Letter 26. See the following letter.

It should not seem burdensome to you to consult our Homer about the eternal salvation of your brother, and to send word to your friends who are at the palace, so that they may instruct him with good counsel and seek permission for him to return. Warn him in your letters not to be doubtful in spirit or unsteady in his steps, but unanimously to ask the imperial piety for the opportunity to return.

I would have you believe that this little letter was dictated by charity, so that you might have a reward and your brother eternal salvation. Live happily in the charity of Christ and in every holy devotion, dearest son.

[Col. 0464C] Frobenius, Letter 213.

# LETTER CXCI

[Col. 0464C] To Antonius the monk. This is the title of the letter in the Harleian manuscript, although Adalhard was already abbot [Col. 0464D] of the monastery of Corbie, or Saint Peter’s. See column 465, note a.

# TO ANTONIUS THE MONK

He expresses his joy at Antonius’s intended visit. He attacks the vanity of Homer’s actors, complains about the interruption of their correspondence, which he says is not contrary to the regular life, and expresses a desire that he be remembered after his death.

To his dearest son Antonius, Albinus sends greetings.

[Col. 0463C] I rejoiced when I read the little letter that your affection sent me, but even more in the comfort of your brotherhood, because from the day I came to know your family I loved them with the inmost affection of my heart, though not equally as I loved you, since they did not belong to me equally. Of almost all my friends, I loved you as the one most specially mine.

Thank you that at last you have blossomed again, opening your mouth and addressing the Father, whether out of charity or even hospitality.

[Col. 0464D] I entrusted to Hubo. Read *Huboni*, but rather, as I think, *Widoni*, namely that royal envoy whose testimony Alcuin invokes on behalf of the innocence of the Tours monks in Letter 166. He knew all the secrets of their life and conduct, as defender and advocate of the affairs of Saint Martin by royal authority.

I entrusted to Hubo, who presides over the affairs of Saint Martin, the task of satisfying your spirit, arranging to meet you on the appointed day.

What you wrote about the improved conduct of my Homer pleased my eyes greatly. Although he had always possessed honorable character, no one in this world is such that he does not have to forget what lies behind and stretch forward to what lies ahead, until he reaches the crown of perfection.

One matter concerned—

[Col. 0464D] Concerning actors. Alcuin has already mentioned that Homer, or Angilbert, was very devoted to theatrical games and spectacles in Letter 144 to our Antonius. There he says that he had written about these matters long ago, wishing health to his dearest son; I think that this is the letter he means here. The letter he wrote to Angilbert himself, which he mentions both here and there, is still missing. In it he admonished him to avoid such spectacles and devilish fictions, which all the holy Scriptures prohibit, and so forth.

One matter concerned actors, whose vanities I knew threatened no small danger to his soul. This displeased me, and therefore I wrote something about it, in order to show him fully the solicitude of my love. It seemed strange to me that so wise a mind had not understood that he was doing things unworthy of his dignity and not deserving of praise.

I advise your affection that wherever you go, the word of God should shine from your mouth, according to the opportunity of time and place, so that the good reputation of your conduct may be adorned by the urgency of preaching.

When I read at the beginning of the first page of your little letter the apologetic excuses you had arranged, written with a paradigmatic pen, I received them gratefully, although I thought them rather unnecessary. The knower of our hearts knows with what affection I desired the consolation of your letters, and with what fear you had suspended your pen upon the wall of the regular house.

Either I was perhaps so unworthy of a comforter, or I placed my hope in a human being more than was pleasing to God. Nevertheless, I would not want your goodness to have acted thus toward others, but rather to have become all things to all, so that you might deserve to have a reward from God for all.

Christ, as we read in histories, wrote a letter to Abgar, a pagan king. Or was blessed Paul not among those of whom Scripture says, “They were of one heart and soul, and they held everything in common” (Acts IV, 32), and did he do well by writing to his friends? Or, if he did so, did he do wrongly by writing so many letters to his friends? Or how did you dare to read my little letters while not sending yours to me? If it is contrary to the rule to write to others, it is certainly contrary to the rule to read what others write.

With the great desire of my heart I wish that you had in no way sinned more against the custody of the regular life than by wishing to issue letters of exhortation. For you have wounded my heart. But if there is still time for healing, heal the wound of charity with your pen, lest it fester into something worse.

You do not need kinds of medicines purchased at great price, nor must the heart of a lion be extracted at peril. Rather, open the heart of your charity and water with the dew of heavenly blessing the dry fields of my heart, so that they may always begin to bear the [missing: fruit, or something similar] of their former peace and concord.

Did not the family of Saint Peter, at your urging and entreaty, receive you into the bosom of its brotherhood as one of its own?

[Col. 0465D] The family of Saint Peter. That is, the old monastery of Corbie in Gaul, in the diocese of Amiens, dedicated to Saint Peter. Adalhard was first a monk there and afterward its abbot.

If you were afraid to benefit a friend, why did you not exhort a brother and companion of your own brotherhood? Does the constraint of the rule forbid you to exhort your brother? Either what you promised was false, or what you did for your brother was not good.

But let complaints cease; let the consolations of charity arise among brothers, without which nothing can please God. If it is in the heart, let it be recognized in action; if it burns within, let it shine outwardly. For this reason the Holy Spirit was sent in the form of fire and tongues: so that the charity burning within the heart might bring forth the word outwardly, as the poet sang:

“Love presses upon the mind; ardor seethes in speech.”

I, having laid aside the military belt of labor and desiring quietly to serve God, await with excessive trembling the hour when it will be said to me: “Open to the one who knocks; hasten to the tribunal of your Judge, so that you may hear what you have done in your life” [Ms.: what you did].

If this hour should come upon the Father while you, my son, are still alive, then, as a faithful intercessor together with all your companions, stand by me, so that, by the mercy of God Jesus, I may escape the grim faces of my accusers. To him be praise and glory for all his good gifts, which in wondrous mercy he has bestowed not only on me but on the whole human race.

But you, dearest son, prospering greatly and living happily, farewell forever.

[Col. 0465D] Frobenius, Letter 214.

# LETTER CXCII. TO ANTONIUS THE MONK

He greatly desires Antonius’s prayers, so that he may always be able to love and praise God.

[Col. 0466A] To Antonius, Albinus, *mansionarius* and *matricularius*, sends greetings.

I call you a “keeper of the dwelling” because there are many dwellings in the house of the eternal Father (John XIV, 2). I desire you to be not only their inhabitant but also, by apostolic authority, their judge, discerning who is worthy to dwell in which one.

With the whole intention of my heart I beg that you may have your Albinus in your mouth and heart while you offer your soul in the sight of the Holy Spirit, asking that the Spirit, the Paraclete, rescue me from the spiritual temptations of my soul, so that my soul may be worthy to love and praise the supreme good, that is, the true God. For this is the angelic life. They always do this, and continually perform what we must perform more often: whoever loves and praises God more on earth possesses him more fully in heaven.

This life is wretched and entirely full of troubles. We have no salvation except in the Lord God Christ. May your devotion always love, praise, and proclaim him. In your holy prayers always assist your fellow servants, and especially me, a sinner, whom, though unworthy, you have addressed by the name of Father. Greet our brothers, your fellow soldiers, in the name of our office, and especially those whom you know we have loved more familiarly.

May divine grace deign to preserve you all forever in brotherly charity and in the unity of holy peace, dearest brothers!

[Col. 0465D] Frobenius, Letter 232.

# LETTER CXCIII

An enigmatic letter.

[Col. 0466C]

[Col. 0466D] To Antonius, Paulus. These names and the subject of the letter itself are wholly enigmatic, and it would hardly be worthwhile to spend time unraveling them.

To Antonius, Paulus.

The letters that came to me on the sixth day before the Ides of Quintilis at—

[Col. 0466D] Uuicos. Or *Wicus*, the maritime cell of Saint Josse, entrusted to Alcuin’s care by Charlemagne when Alcuin came to Gaul. See the notes to Letter 39 (now 44) and elsewhere.

The letters that came to me on the sixth day before the Ides of Quintilis at Uuicos were full of joy concerning what was mine and what was yours, and concerning the unending [so the manuscript reads; perhaps: the end of the name], which has remained in me until now and, I believe, will remain, although I had suffered most painfully the presence of absence and the absence of presence.

As for a fraternal visit, I often wished for one according to the opportunity of the journey. But the second person of the pronoun knows very well why it did not happen; indeed, I still do not understand how this could have occurred.

Know that letters alone are not enough for what is mine and yours—for these are the things that destroy the world—if “I” and “you” are not present. Up to this point, three letters have been in sadness, with two causing this; but let seven endure everything until six and eight rejoice together, and let seven stand in its proper place. For from the perfection of the number six one ascends, through the grace of seven, to the blessedness of eight.

Let there be a unity of the first and the last through the middle, because all things in creation reach unity through these three terms. And if one is taken from the middle and two from the last, there will be three equal terms, wondrous in the perfection of all creatures, which were created by the three Persons in the unity of power.

Let whoever reads these things understand and praise most subtly the giver of wisdom, and live happily in him.

Greet the brothers: the young and the mature, those who read and understand, those who love and do good, those who worship Christ and possess charity. May all of them fare well, flourish, and blossom eternally in every perfection of life and praise of God.

[Col. 0467D] Quercetanus, 80; Canisius, 45; Frobenius, 145.

# LETTER CXCIV. TO THE COMMUNITY OF SAINT MARY AND FATHER MOROALD

He desires to enjoy their fellowship and friendship.

To the community of the most blessed and most holy Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, and to the pious Father Moroald—

[Col. 0467D] Moroald. Without doubt, the abbot of the monastery of blessed Mary at Farfa. See Mabillon, *Annals*, Book XXVI, no. 8.

Moroald, the least servant of the holy Church, Alcuin sends greetings in the charity of Christ.

Having often heard the reputation of your holiness, I therefore desired to join myself to your intimacy. But now a suitable opportunity has arisen for me, through the present brother, to commend myself to you with earnest prayers.

Therefore, through the Son of the holy Virgin, I humbly beseech your unanimity to deign to receive me, though unworthy, into your hearts and hands—not as an unknown person, but as a brother. For although I have not seen you with the eyes of the flesh, I seem to see you with the eyes of the heart, and I love you greatly. With an attentive spirit I embrace the uprightness of your life, desiring that your blessedness may everywhere advance in the Lord and reach the joy of everlasting peace.

Praying for us, farewell always in Christ, dearest brothers.

[Col. 0467D] Quercetanus, 33, from a manuscript (Frobenius, 146). Which one is the mother and which the daughter? No indication reveals this.

# LETTER CXCV. TO A MOTHER AND DAUGHTER

He urges them to good works and commends himself to their prayers.

Albinus sends greetings in Christ to the mother and daughter.

I received your salutation with a joyful heart, humbly beseeching Christ God mercifully to regard your devotion, to make it advance more and more in his will, and to bring your way of life to your crown of glory. Let the daughter obey her mother in every good thing; let the mother be devoted to the salvation of her daughter. Let both always be diligent in God’s service, doing in chastity what is pleasing to God. Educate the daughter entrusted to you [it seems that *family* should be read] in every fear of God, as though you were to render an account for each person’s soul. Therefore teach your sons and daughters with all diligence, so that you may be found worthy to possess not merely bodily consolation but also spiritual joy. Let Christ not be despised in the ragged poor man, but let him be brought into the house, warmed and refreshed; for the refreshment of the needy is the salvation of the rich. Perform the canonical hours with all devotion in divine praise, so that the concert of your psalmody may be heard by the angels and received by Christ. Let your modesty, according to the Apostle, be known to all people (Phil. IV, 5), so that your present life may be an example leading many to salvation, and your future life may be received from God, the rewarder of all good things, in recompense for your praiseworthy conduct of piety. At the end of this little document, I beseech your goodness to deign to keep the memory of my name among your prayers; and pray for my everlasting salvation with that charity with which, through this letter, I have endeavored to admonish you concerning your own. Reading these lines, remain always in Christ, dearest ladies.

[Col. 0468D] Edited by Quercetanus, p. 100, from a manuscript (Froben, Letter 147).

## LETTER 196. TO EUGENIA, HIS DAUGHTER

He exhorts her to steadfastness in the tribulations which, though innocent, she suffers from wicked kings together with God’s servants. [Col. 0468B]

**Albinus**

[Col. 0468D] **Concerning Eugenia.** It is unknown which virgin she was. I infer from the words of this letter that she was English: “Kings have become tyrants with you.” I think these words should be understood of the kings of England, whose tyranny Alcuin also condemns in other letters.

To Eugenia, his dearest virgin daughter in Christ, Alcuin sends greetings.

After receiving the letters of your affection, together with the sweetest gifts and expressions of thanks, I rejoiced greatly in your faith and charity. I have heard of the tribulations which not only your innocence suffers, but also nearly the whole company of God’s servants, because kings have become tyrants with you, not rulers; and they are called kings not, as formerly, from ruling (*a regendo*), but from plundering (*a rapiendo*).

But be strong in spirit. “Many are the tribulations of the righteous,” cries the Psalmist, so that you may attain what follows: “But the Lord will deliver them from all these things” (Ps. XXXIII, 20). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Brother will hand brother over to death,” and so forth (Matt. X, 21). “But by your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke XXI, 19).

Gold does not shine unless it is tested by fire. Job would lie hidden unless he were tested by tribulations; concerning him the Apostle James, exhorting us to patience, says: “You have heard of Job, and you have seen the end appointed by the Lord” (James V, 11). “Tribulation produces patience,” says the Apostle, “and patience produces testing, while testing produces hope” (Rom. V, 3–4). What hope, if not that of everlasting blessedness?

If you have found a precious pearl, sell everything and buy it; hold it fast and do not let it go (Matt. XIII, 46). “This world lies in the power of evil” (1 John V, 19). There are people who love themselves and do not obey Christ’s Gospel. Each person walks in the way of his own will, not following him who says: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John VIII, 12). Again: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. XVI, 24). The cross is taken up when tribulation is conquered through patience.

“No soldier will be crowned unless he competes lawfully” (2 Tim. II, 5). For a virgin, to compete lawfully means to be holy in body and spirit (1 Cor. VII, 34), and to be a bride worthy of Christ, singing daily: “My beloved is mine and I am his, who feeds among the lilies” (Song II, 16)—that is, among the whiteness of virginity.

Remember the wise and foolish virgins. If the ancient enemy finds no place of temptation within you—that is, in your body—he will certainly seek outwardly how he may weaken your spiritual strength. You must resist him with a courageous spirit. For, says the outstanding Teacher, “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the glory that is to come, which will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18), when “God of gods will be seen in Zion with unveiled face” (Ps. LXXXIII, 8). And wherever the virgin goes, the Lamb follows her (Rev. XIV, 4).

O supremely happy woman, for whom no one is happier,

who, with the blessed Mother of God leading her, will be found worthy to enter all the hidden chambers of the heavenly kingdom.

It does not greatly harm you that you were unable to complete the journey you began, since God has provided something better for you. Spend on the relief of the poor what you had prepared as provisions for so long a journey. Give what you possess, so that you may deserve to receive what you desire. Hold in your heart the fullest charity toward him whom you ask to be your defender in tribulation. The devil cannot easily lay waste to a dwelling in which Christ resides; from his side a thousand shall fall, and ten thousand at his right hand (Ps. XC, 7).

I wish that you may have him as your comforter in all your tribulation, whom you will have as the rewarder of all your penitence. Look to him who says: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John XVI, 33). May his eternal power make you conquer in every tribulation and grant you to receive the palm of everlasting blessedness—he who says: “I will give him the hidden manna” (Rev. II, 17), which no one knows except the one who receives it.

Farewell, dearest daughter, flourishing in every virtue and wisdom.

[Col. 0469D] Edited by Quercetanus, p. 44; Canisius, p. 57, collated with the Salzburg manuscript (Froben, Letter 148).

## LETTER 197. TO HIS SPIRITUAL DAUGHTER (EUGENIA)

He commends chastity together with generosity in almsgiving.

To his dearest daughter in Christ, Eugenia, Albinus sends greetings.

I am pleased often to address your kinship in brief letters, though with no small service of affection, and to introduce into your thoughts the salutary counsels of my admonition, or of your [Salzburg manuscript: “holy”] promise, so that you may strive to preserve intact in body the most noble glory of virginity, remembering the glorious reward of chastity. Behold: throughout the great palaces of the eternal King in heaven, they follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Rev. XIV, 4). What is more blessed than this glory, or more glorious than this blessedness? There the victor over nature will be joined to the Creator of all creatures.

Nor should daily labor deter you, since the hope of so great a reward will console you. The labor of a few days will be repaid with eternal rewards. Let virginity also be fruitful in generosity of almsgiving, and let it not greedily gather fleeting treasures of wealth with an avaricious hand, but let it distribute them with a generous spirit among the members of her Bridegroom. With the two wings of charity and chastity, let her fly upward to the lofty realms of heaven.

Nor let the virgin, freed from the bonds of fleshly desire, be bound by the snares of avarice; but, victorious over herself, let her not succumb to the slothful desire of the world [Salzburg manuscript: “sluggish desire”]. Rather, through works of mercy, like green branches, let her pave a road for herself to the citadel of the heavenly Jerusalem, where, welcomed with angelic praises, she will be led in everlasting joy into the chamber of the great Emperor.

For this to happen, the seeker after this pearl must remain vigilant and not sleep in the slumber of inactivity. Rather, she must often knock through prayers by night and by day at the gates of the eternal city. When she comes, she will find them open—gates which everyone, once led away from this bodily prison, will ardently desire to enter. She must foresee this with the greatest diligence, so that she may then find the gates open, and the angelic choirs receiving the soul with outstretched hands and leading it into the chamber of the King, there to enjoy eternal joys.

Then she will sing forever the song of praise in the presence of her Bridegroom, saying: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all his works; in every place of his dominion, bless the Lord, O my soul” (Ps. CII, 1, 22).

May you live, prosper, and flourish, most noble virgin, in Christ.

[Col. 0469D] {210} Edited by Quercetanus, p. 89, from a manuscript (Froben, Letter 149).

## LETTER 198. TO HUNDRUDE, A WOMAN

He exhorts her to devotion and an exemplary life in the king’s palace. He asks her to greet the queen and Egfrid.

[Col. 0470C] To a woman devoted to God

[Col. 0470D] **Concerning Hundrude.** Mabillon calls her an English matron, Book XXVI of the *Annals*, no. 14. She lived in the palace of King Offa veiled like a nun, as may be inferred from what follows.

Alcuin the deacon sends greetings to Hundrude.

I gratefully received your greeting and your little gifts of kindness. In them I recognized that you possessed an abundant memory of the friendship once established between us [perhaps, “that you held”]. I also believe that your prudence has not forgotten how my devotion, when you were already present, earnestly admonished you concerning the charity of Christ and the integrity of life.

Therefore I do not think it necessary to repeat these matters in many words, but only to request in a few little lines that at every hour and moment you keep the eternal things in mind and prepare yourself for the meeting with the Lord your God (Amos IV, 12), so that without fear you may be able to see the Judge of your life, whom you have loved with all your strength in your heart.

Let your thought be in God’s presence, your life in sobriety, your speech in the modesty of truth, and your works in the integrity of chastity, so that younger people may be instructed by your example, older people may rejoice with you, and all may be edified; so that, in the king’s palace, the devotion of a disciplined life may be seen in your conduct. Thus may the mercy of the supreme King guard you in every prosperity and deem you worthy of eternal reward because you persevere in good works to the end of your life.

I beg you to greet the lady queen on behalf of my insignificance. I would have written her letters of exhortation, if, because of the king’s occupations [perhaps, “royal occupations”], it had been possible for her to read my lines. Nevertheless, let her know with complete certainty that I too, to the extent of my ability, am faithful to her.

Yet what was done concerning the monastery of Inmercum was not what I had hoped from their goodness.

[Col. 0471D] **The monastery of Inmercum.** No one identifies this monastery; it must certainly be sought in England. Let them deal with me as they please. For my faith will not be violated among them, since I believe that they are as much better as they are better in merits and dignity. May the Almighty guard, protect, and rule them everywhere with eternal protection, together with all his faithful.

[Col. 0471D] **Egfrid.** The son of Offa, king of the Mercians, to whom Alcuin wrote Letter 50.

Greet my son Egfrid carefully. I wish that he may flourish in God’s will and in prosperity for many happy years.

Farewell always, sweetest sister.

[Col. 0471D] Edited by Quercetanus, p. 30, from a manuscript (Froben, Letter 150).

## LETTER 199. TO AEDILTHYDA, SERVANT OF GOD, ONCE A QUEEN

He instructs her with the best principles of life.

[Col. 0471B] To his most beloved sister in Christ

[Col. 0471D] **To Aedilthyda, a mother.** Mabillon is uncertain whether this is Alfrida, or Ethedrita, the daughter of Offa, king of the Mercians, whom Ethelred, heir to the kingdom of the East Angles, wished to take as his wife and therefore approached Offa’s palace, but was treacherously beheaded there (Book XXVI of the *Annals*, no. 29; *Acta Sanctorum*, fourth century, part I, p. 565). Alford thinks that she was Etheldrita, whom the Westminster writer calls Etheldreda, wife of Ethelwald, king of Northumbria, concerning whom Hoveden says: “In the year 762 King Ethelwald took Queen Etheldrita on the Kalends of November at Cataract.” *Anglo-Saxon Annals* under that year, no. 1 and following. It is certainly clear from the text that she presided over a great household of men and women; that she was a queen is not equally clear, except from Quercetanus’s heading.

To Aedilthyda, a mother, the humble levite Alcuin sends greetings.

As I gratefully receive the gifts of your kindness and gladly hear the words of your affectionate greeting, I confess that I have rejoiced with great sweetness, recognizing that faithful charity has remained in your heart—a charity which neither the distance of lands can interrupt nor the surge of the sea, tossed by stormy waves, overwhelm so completely that its beneficent generosity could not fly all the way to me. As it is written: “Many waters could not extinguish love, nor could rivers overwhelm it” (Song VIII, 7).

Therefore, the charity that can be abandoned was never true. Nothing brings human beings so close to God as charity. “Whoever remains in charity remains in God,” as Scripture says, “because God is charity” (1 John IV, 16). Concerning this the Savior himself says: “On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. XXII, 40)—that is, on the charity of God and of one’s neighbor.

Through charity toward one’s neighbor one reaches love of God. For the evangelist John says: “If you do not love the brother whom you see, how can you love God, whom you do not see?” (1 John IV, 20). But brotherly charity must be shown both in spiritual admonition and in worldly consolation. For just as the body is nourished by food, so the soul is fed by sacred instruction.

Therefore whoever is able ought to do both: extend with a generous hand to the poor person what he needs, and refresh the hungry soul with salutary admonition—especially those who preside over others and appear to have responsibility for many. Watch over each soul in this work with diligence, as though you were to render an account for them on the day of judgment.

Whoever negligently guards the talent he has received will suffer a punishment worthy of his negligence; but whoever diligently multiplies the Lord’s money will receive a great reward from his Lord God. Those who preside must know that the more they labor for the salvation of their subjects, the greater glory they will receive, since on the day of judgment the Lord God will say to them: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV, 21, 23). What voice is sweeter than this? What hearing is more blessed?

May you deserve to hear this voice, dearest sister. Instruct those subject to you with all earnestness; admonish them with words and educate them by example, because their salvation is your reward. Do not remain silent out of fear of human beings, but speak out of love of God. “Reprove, rebuke, exhort” (2 Tim. IV, 2). Publicly chastise those who sin openly, so that the others may have fear (1 Tim. V, 20). Admonish some in a spirit of gentleness; correct others with the pastoral rod, carefully considering what is suitable for each one.

Some malignant illnesses are cured by sweet potions, others by bitter ones. Honor old women and old men as mothers and fathers; love young people as brothers and sisters; instruct those younger in age as sons and daughters; and care for everyone in Christ, so that you may receive everyone’s reward from Christ (1 Tim. V, 1–2).

The faithful steward should strive to increase his lord’s money—that is, the souls entrusted to him—through diligence, not diminish it through laziness. The good servant will be crowned by his lord, but the wicked will be condemned, as may be understood from what is said in the Gospel by those who read it. Work with the greatest diligence in God’s service, so that you may receive a great recompense in the kingdom of God.

Let your almsgiving go before you and prepare your way. “Gifts enlarge a person’s path and make room for him before a prince” (Prov. XVIII, 16). We are guests and pilgrims on this earth (Heb. XI, 13). Our homeland is in heaven. It is not good to love transitory things and neglect eternal ones. Each person will receive from his God according to his works, for he will repay each one according to his deeds (Matt. XVI, 27).

Let vigils and prayers be frequent for you, and psalmody in your mouth, not empty talk on your tongue. Let the love of God be in your heart, and not worldly ambition in your mind. Whatever is loved in the world passes away; whatever is loved in Christ remains. Willingly or unwillingly, we shall be eternal. Let us strive with all our purpose to live faithfully where we shall always remain.

Frequently honor the feasts of the saints with divine praise and the poor with almsgiving, so that through their intercession you may deserve to share in their blessedness. Let your words be praiseworthy for their truth; let your conduct be lovable for its sobriety and modesty; let your hands be honorable for their generosity. Let the conduct of your whole life be an example of every goodness to others, so that the dignity of your person may be praised by all, loved by many, and through you the name of God may be glorified, as Truth itself says: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16).

We have a great Father, namely, almighty God. How noble in conduct, how modest in speech, how chaste in heart, how merciful to all the son of God ought to be, since he himself commands: “Be merciful, as your heavenly Father is merciful” (Luke VI, 36). Let us imitate his goodness as far as we can, so that we may deserve to have eternal blessedness with him. For he said not only to the apostles but also to us: “I have given you an example, so that just as I have done for you, you also may do” (John XIII, 15). Again: “Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John VIII, 12).

Why does a human being take pride in the riches of the world? Christ became poor for us (2 Cor. VIII, 9), so that through the poverty he accepted for us on earth we might be rich in heaven. For the flesh which we adorn with such care in luxury quickly rots in the earth. Moreover, we think of adorning the tomb; this is vanity of vanities. It is better to clothe the soul with these riches than to adorn the filth of the flesh.

Christ was buried in a cave, not in a temple. I say this because some living people customarily construct their own tomb. What does it matter to me where food for worms rots? We must strive only that the soul may have rest, that it may live happily—since it cannot die.

For the time will come when “this corruptible body will put on incorruption” (1 Cor. XV, 53), and the soul will recover what it left on earth. Then the human being, in soul and body together, will reign with Christ—he who served Christ with his whole soul and body [perhaps, “who now serves Christ wholly in soul and body.”]

{212}

[Col. 0473D] {213} This is here published for the first time from the Salzburg manuscript (Froben, Letter 151).

## LETTER 200. TO EDILTHRUDA

He consoles a mother over the death of her son.

To his most beloved mother in Christ

[Col. 0473D] **To Edilthruda, a mother.** I do not know whether this is the same woman as Aedilthyda, whom Ingulfus also calls Etheldrita and to whom the preceding letter was addressed.

To Edilthruda, the humble levite Alcuin sends greetings.

Because, on account of the distance of our dwelling, I cannot personally admonish your sweetest affection, I do not cease to fulfill through the service of letters what is denied to the ministry of speech. With all the affection of my heart, I desire that you, dearest mother, may everywhere advance in every good thing, so that you may become worthy to be counted among those of whom our Lord Jesus Christ said in the Gospel: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my mother and brother” (Matt. XII, 50).

How is she a mother, unless she is daily brought to birth through holy charity in the depths of a perfect heart? Behold what kind of son a devout mother can have: that very God, King, and Redeemer, also a consoler in every tribulation. “Many are the tribulations of the righteous” (Ps. XXXIII, 20), but Christ’s consolations are greater.

In what event of wretchedness should a worldly person grieve, when he possesses in his heart the source of all consolation, namely Christ as an inhabitant? Rather, one ought to rejoice in tribulations because of the hope of eternal blessedness, as the Apostle says: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts XIV, 21). Again: “God scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII, 6). Again, it is read concerning the apostles: “The apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been considered worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus” (Acts V, 41).

Let your affection know that your spiritual son, the Lord Jesus, is not mortal. He lives—he lives, and he lives and reigns at the right hand of God the Father. Therefore do not grieve over the death of your bodily son; indeed, do not grieve over that of your own body either [the text breaks off: *abso*]. Rather, labor at every hour and moment so that the soul may live happily with Christ, and console yourself in hope of his goodness, because God’s mercies are many.

He has left you alive after your bodily son so that, through your intercessions and almsgiving, God may have mercy on him. Perhaps he died in his sins, but by divine mercy it can come about that he lives. For the thief was hanged with Christ in his crime, yet he was saved by Christ’s mercy.

Do not mourn for one whom you cannot recall. And if he belongs to God, do not grieve that he has been lost; rather, rejoice that he was sent before you to rest. If two people are friends, the death of the one who goes before is happier than that of the one who follows, for the departed has one who daily intercedes for him with brotherly love and washes away the errors of his former life with tears.

Nor should you doubt that the care of pious solicitude which you bear for his soul is beneficial. It benefits you and him: you—[the manuscript is corrupt: *tibi itaque, quae in fide facere dilectione*]—and him, in that either his punishment may be lightened or his blessedness increased.

Great and immeasurable is the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, who wishes all people to be saved (1 Tim. II, 4) and no one to perish. As I said, do not grieve in your tribulations; but if greater ones come upon you, rejoice in them, since the Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the glory that is to come, which will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

As gold is tested in fire, so a person is proved in the furnace of tribulation. While you have control of your possessions, make alms from them, because you do not know what the coming day may bring (Prov. XXVII, 1). No steward can be more faithful to you than you yourself, and God will more willingly accept gifts that go before us than those that follow us.

“For in many things we all offend,” as the Apostle James says (James III, 2). The evangelist John likewise said: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John I, 8). And according to Solomon: “A man’s redemption is his own wealth” (Prov. XIII, 8). From the one who has more, more will be demanded.

We ought to be stewards, not owners, of worldly things; for we are exiles and pilgrims in this life, as were all our fathers (1 Chron. XXIX, 15; Ps. XXXVIII, 13). May their death place our own death before our eyes at every hour, and may their good conduct in Christ be instruction for our life, so that, following their footsteps in faith, charity, and every good work, we may deserve to have everlasting life in heavenly blessedness.

[Col. 0475D] Edited by Quercetanus, p. 35; Canisius, p. 54; collated with the Salzburg manuscript (Froben, Letter 152).

## LETTER 201. TO MAGENHARIUS, COUNT OF THE CITY OF SENS

He exhorts him to virtue and to care for his office.

To his beloved in Christ

[Col. 0475D] **Concerning Magenharius.** The unknown writer of the *Life of Louis the Pious* (*Rerum Gallicarum Scriptores*, vol. VI, p. 90, no. 7) calls him Meginary. He was a wise and energetic man, knowledgeable about the usefulness and dignity of royal government, whom Charlemagne sent to Louis so that Louis might make use of his counsel. Einhard names Meginher as a count among those present when Charlemagne made his testament. BASNAGE.

To Magenharius, count, the humble levite Albinus sends greetings.

I have heard, venerable man, that you desired conversation with my insignificance; and, to speak truthfully, I greatly desired your presence, so that I might console myself through sweet conversation with your wisdom. But since circumstances did not allow this to happen, it seemed fitting to me to fulfill through letters what I could not accomplish in words, to show you my affection, and to offer you useful counsel in writing, so that your advancement might be my fruit.

Since you have been placed in a lofty position on earth, may you, through works of justice and mercy, deserve heavenly honor. Consider how transitory are all the things we possess in this world, and that every human being must earn eternal glory for himself through temporal good works [Salzburg manuscript: “for every human being must earn eternal glory through temporal benefits.”]

Therefore, so that by God’s gift you may attain everlasting blessedness, let no worldly pleasure and no fleshly desire impede you. Be just in judgments, devout in works of mercy, a father to widows and orphans, defending them from every act of violence [Canisius: “defend them”].

Be also like a brother to the churches of Christ, so that through the prayers of God’s servants, amid the dangers of enemies, rivers, roads, and illnesses, the divine right hand may always protect, guide, and preserve you everywhere. Ensure that the poor eat your bread every day, because the consolation of the wretched will be your eternal reward.

Be prudent in counsel, wise in thought, modest in speech, always having God present, so that, speaking his will [Alcuin: “truth”], you may become worthy of his protection. Preserve your body in chastity and your soul in sobriety. Be faithful to the lords whom God has given you, kind to your friends, equitable toward all people, and generous to the afflicted. Forgive your debtors and those who sin against you, so that God may forgive you if you have done anything against his will.

Carefully instruct your subjects also to be just in judgments, merciful to the afflicted, fearful of God, and honoring Christ’s Church, so that their goodness may be reckoned to you as a reward [Salzburg manuscript: “reckoned as a reward”]. The sins of subjects are often imputed to their rulers [Canisius: “are often implicated with them”] if those in authority do not diligently admonish them how they ought to act; just as the goodness of subjects benefits as a reward those lords who earnestly teach them to fear God and obey his commands.

I beg you not to consider me presumptuous for writing these things to you. The charity of Christ, love for your salvation, and confidence in your goodness urged me to write them. I desire that you may possess prosperity in the present and deserve blessedness in the future [Salzburg manuscript: “that you may possess prosperity in the present and deserve future blessedness”].

May divine grace make you flourish in every goodness, dearest man.

{214}

[Col. 0475D] Edited by Quercetanus, p. 115; Canisius, p. 65 (Froben, Letter 153).

## LETTER 202. TO AMIGUS

He expresses his affection to a friend.

To his beloved friend, greetings.

I was pleased to address your gray hairs in this small letter of greeting, though not with a small service of affection, so that you may know that, although I am far away, I nevertheless remember you and have not forgotten the friendship which, when we were together, we maintained with the sweetest affection and consolation. May the charity between us always remain firm in Christ, never destroyed by any wind of false speech, but always standing immovable with solid strength amid all the adversities of this world.

Remember me in your prayers, and fare always well, dearest brother.

[Col. 0475D] Lucas Acherius published this letter from the manuscript of Saint-Germain in volume III of the new edition of the *Spicilegium*, p. 321. After him, Bernard Pez published it in volume II, part I of the *Anecdota*, from the manuscript of Saint Emmeram; we have collated it with the Salzburg manuscripts and two manuscripts of Saint Emmeram.

“Acherius says: ‘I found this letter, and two others—one on the ten words of the Law, and one on the three kinds of visions addressed to Fridugisus—marked with Alcuin’s name among various short works by the same author, in a very ancient written manuscript which the diligent and learned Parisian bibliographer Louis Billaine gave me as a gift. Someone may say: Were you really right to attribute these letters to Alcuin? Certainly; for when I noticed that they breathed the style and genius of so great a man, why should I not attribute them to him? There was no reason not to.’” (Froben, Letter 154.)

## LETTER 203. TO GALLICELLULA

On the comparison of the numbers of the Old and New Testaments.

To my beloved son

[Col. 0476D] **Concerning Gallicellula.** The manuscript copies have *Gallicellulo*. It is an assumed name for one of Alcuin’s students.

Albinus sends greetings to Gallicellula.

Because you asked me to relate, or rather compare, the significance of the numbers found in the Old Law with the authority of the New Testament—and because, while traveling, we have no opportunity to write more—we shall nevertheless begin with ten and continue until we reach one, so that the pen of the writer may run along with the feet of the traveler.

There are ten commandments of the Law, given to the people of God on two tablets through Moses and Aaron (Exod. XX). Christ gave ten minas to the preachers of both peoples (Luke XIX, 13).

Egypt was struck by ten plagues so that the people of God might be liberated (Exod. XII, 3). The Church of Christ was crowned through ten persecutions.

On the tenth day of the first month the Passover lamb was to be selected, and it was to be sacrificed on the fourteenth day of that same month. At the tenth hour [certainly the ninth], the Passover Lamb—that is, Christ—gave up the Spirit on the cross for the salvation of the world (Matt. XXVII, 46, 50; Mark XV, 34, 37).

In the tenth generation the flood came and destroyed the ungodly (Gen. VII). After ten kings, the Antichrist is born at the end of time, and with him all the ungodly perish (Rev. XVII, 12).

The archangel who fell from heaven was covered with nine stones. Nine orders of angels remained in heaven.

Eight souls were saved in the ark (1 Pet. III, 20). Through the eight beatitudes faithful souls are saved in the Church (Matt. V, 3 and following).

On the eighth day every male child in the people of God was to be circumcised [supplied: “every”] (Lev. XII, 3). On the eighth day Christ was circumcised (Luke II, 21), through whose circumcision the eight principal vices are destroyed.

On the seventh day God rested from all his works (Gen. II, 2). In the seventh age the saints rest from the labors of this world.

Wisdom cut out seven pillars to build her house (Prov. IX, 1). Through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit Christ strengthened his house, that is, the Church.

In six days God made heaven and earth and everything in them. All the periods of this world proceed through six ages.

On the sixth day the human being was created from unstained earth. In the sixth age the Son of God became human from an unstained Virgin.

In five books Moses gave the Israelite people commandments for living. Returning to heaven, Christ entrusted five talents to his faithful servant (Matt. XXV, 15).

{215} Four rivers flow from one spring of paradise to water the earth (Gen. II, 10). Four Gospels proceed from one fountain, which is Christ, to water dry hearts so that they may bloom with flowers of virtue.

There are four elements, by which the adornment of the world is chiefly constituted. There are four virtues by which the lesser world—that is, the human being—ought to be adorned.

Adam was tempted in three ways and overcome: by gluttony, vainglory, and avarice. In these same three ways Christ was tempted and conquered Adam’s conqueror (Matt. IV).

The whole world is divided into three parts: Europe, Africa, and Asia [manuscript copies: “and India”]. In these three parts God is worshiped [manuscript copies: “is to be worshiped”] in three ways: by faith, hope, and charity.

God gave Abraham three commands, saying: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Gen. XII, 1). Three things are promised to us: resurrection, life, and glory.

There were two tablets of the covenant, on which the Decalogue was written by the finger of God (Exod. XXXI, 18). There are two commandments of charity, written by the finger of God—that is, by the Holy Spirit—in the hearts of the faithful.

There were two cherubim in the temple. “Cherubim” is interpreted as “a multitude of knowledge” (Num. VII, 89; 1 Kings VI, 23 and following). Therefore there are two parts of knowledge: one is to abandon the devil, the other is to love God.

There was one ark in which the faithful were saved while the world perished. There is one holy Church of God, through which the faithful are saved while sinners perish.

There was one crossing of the Israelite people through the Red Sea, so that they might receive the promised land (Exod. XIV). There is one baptism, through which one must pass to eternal life (Eph. IV, 5).

[Col. 0477D] We published this letter and the preceding one after Lucas d’Acherius, *Spicilegium*, volume III, new edition, p. 322, from two manuscript copies of the monastery of Saint Emmeram and one Salzburg manuscript.

## LETTER 204. TO FRIDUGISUS

On the three kinds of visions.

[Froben, Letter 155.]

Three kinds of visions exist: one corporeal, another spiritual, and a third intellectual. A corporeal vision is what is seen with bodily eyes [Cod. Sal., “we are accustomed to see”]. A spiritual vision is what, when bodily sight has been removed, we perceive in the spirit alone through a certain imagination, as when by chance we perceive something unknown to the eyes: immediately an image of that thing is formed in the spirit, but that spiritual imagination does not appear beforehand, before the bodily perception has been brought to it. An intellectual vision is what we consider solely through the mind’s alertness, as when we read what is written: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. XIX, 19). The letters are read through bodily sight, the neighbor is recalled through spiritual imagination, and love is apprehended solely by the understanding of the mind.

The first kind of vision is known to everyone. The second is likewise familiar to all. The third is unknown to most, because they cannot distinguish what is spiritual from what is intellectual. The Apostle excellently distinguished these two in a single, very brief sentence: “I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray also with the mind; I will sing psalms with the spirit, and I will sing psalms also with the mind” (I Cor. XIV, 15). He called the hidden meanings contained in the holy Scriptures “spirit,” and he called their manifest understandings “mind.” {216} For he wanted us either to pray or to sing psalms with an understanding of what we say. Hence elsewhere he says: “If I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is without fruit” (ibid. 14). Here by “tongue” he designated the obscure and mystical meanings that are usually perceived only spiritually; if we do not understand them, our mind remains unfruitful.

These two kinds of vision are also wonderfully distinguished in Pharaoh and Joseph (Gen. XLI). To Pharaoh, future things were shown in the spirit; to Joseph, their disclosure was made in the mind. The spirit of the former was formed so that he might see; the mind of the latter was illuminated so that he might understand. Daniel’s excellence was likewise tested and proved: he understood the dream of future events that the king saw in the spirit, and he revealed its interpretation to the king (Dan. II and IV). Therefore the one who understood with his mind was more truly a prophet than the king who perceived with his spirit. But these three kinds of vision are also shown in that writing which appeared depicted on the wall before King Belshazzar (Dan. V). Through bodily vision the king saw letters written on the wall, but neither was his spirit formed so that, although he saw them, he could read them, nor was his mind illuminated so as to understand them. Then the prophet arrived, who both read through the spirit the obscurity of the writing and understood through the alertness of his mind its most obscure meanings. These things, dearest son,

> [Col. 0479D] Fridugilse. Thus the manuscript codices have it; but I have no doubt that it should be read Fridugise or Fredegise, for whose sake he gave these responses to questions concerning the Trinity, and so forth.

> Fridugilse, I dictated these words in the cited discourse so that you would not be ignorant of this threefold distinction, which is familiar to everyone but understood by few.

> [Col. 0479D] In the San-Emmeram manuscript, the following words are added at the end of this letter: “Here ends the Book of Albinus the Master, which Bishop Baturicus ordered to be written as a worthy work.” Baturicus was the bishop of Regensburg who succeeded Adalwin in the year 817.

> [Col. 0480D] We copied this letter from the Salzburg codex. We recognize Alcuin as its author from its style and from the position it occupies in that codex, midway among his certain and undisputed letters. We have not been able to discover any trace of the identity of the disciple who brought complaints against Alcuin to the palace and with whom he wishes to be reconciled.

# LETTER CCV. TO A CERTAIN DISCIPLE

> At Froben, letter 156.

He removes the cause of the disagreement from himself and asks to return to friendship.

To his dearest son in the love of Christ, greetings.

I beg you to deign to read these little letters of paternal devotion with your customary affection and piety. Why, dearest son, did you wish to carry the insult of our disagreement into the ears of the palace? There it is being said: “What are we to hope for from the friendship of those who could not preserve faith or concord even among themselves?” This can be more a disgrace than a commendation, more a despair of our faith than a confirmation of your case. And with what face will you be able to reproach one whom you used so often to praise?

I know that your anger seems just to you, for this is the nature of human fury: whatever it does or says appears just to itself. “Be angry and do not sin” (Ps. IV, 5), that is, do not remain in anger. He permitted what belongs to nature; he removed what belongs to guilt. Therefore the Apostle also says: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. IV, 26). Often a defender is better than an accuser, because the former defends for the sake of peace, while the latter accuses for the sake of discord.

Nor do I distrust my case, although it is being debated in the king’s presence. The searcher of hearts is my witness (Ps.
