VII, 10) to how faithfully I have always loved you and how much good I wished for your brother, whom I see you have loved more carnally than you loved your father spiritually, although he had acted proudly toward me [the passage is corrupt]. My lord the king is my witness whether God was the cause of his piety’s first naming the other party, or whether I was the one to entreat him. I would not be ashamed to have both accusations judged in his most holy presence, if we were not disgraced by the mark of disagreement. But the fact that I proceeded without your knowledge was caused by necessity, not by choice.

{217} Why, my son, have you forgotten how, with tears and bowed head, I pleaded with you for peace and concord, for the love of Christ, to whom you are indebted to every person, even without being asked? And if I had killed your brother, you ought certainly to have forgiven me because of Christ’s command; how much more when I harmed him in nothing but rather benefited him altogether. Yet because of this good deed toward him, you have become an enemy to your friend. In the regeneration of the Holy Spirit, your brother is no more your brother than he is mine. And if he had remained in the first generation from which discord arose between dearly beloved persons, and in which you love him more than me, he would be brother neither to you nor to me.

Return, return—not, perhaps, for love of me, but for love of him who, when we were enemies, reconciled us to God through his blood (Col. I, 20). Let him now be our mediator for peace, as he was previously our mediator for life. If you despise these prayers of my humility with a hardened mind and desire to harm me—though you cannot deny that it is lawful to benefit me, unless you wish to erase the paternal and teacherly name from the secret place of your heart or from the speech of your lips; and no one who has ever acknowledged the benefits of charity between us is unaware that this would be impious—nevertheless, with him protecting me for whose love I make these humble pleas, I believe you will not be able to harm me.

Absalom drove his father from the kingdom, but deprived himself of life (II Kings XV and XVIII). Let us fear that what that disagreement suffered carnally we may suffer spiritually, if we do not return to the charity of Christ. “Charity is patient” in enduring, “kind” in giving; “it does not act improperly,” that is, it does not demand more than is due from its brother in a matter; “it hopes all things, believes all things” (I Cor. XIII, 4 ff.). We ought to hope for what is better and believe what is best.

Would that this little letter restore me to my former place with you; and if it cannot accomplish this, at least may it find me excused before my judge, since I have done what I could, even if I could not obtain what I wished. I can—I believe I can—through him who inspired my little heart to ask what I considered pious. May he also inspire your heart to grant what I requested.

> [Col. 0480D] The condition of peace, however, is that a child should not be the father of disagreement, but that the Child should be the “Father of the age to come” (Isa. IX, 6), of whom it is said: “Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my chosen one, in whom my soul is well pleased” (Matt. XII, 18), so that we may be counted worthy to be named among and to be children of those of whom he previously said through the prophet: “Behold, I and the children whom God has given me” (Isa. VIII, 18).

> [Col. 0481D] In Mabillon, letter 9, compared with two Salzburg and San-Emmeram codices. (At Froben, letter 157.)

# LETTER CCVI. TO A DISCIPLE

He reproves him for the perversity of his life and exhorts him to correction.

> [Col. 0481D] To his dearest son. Perhaps Osulf, whom Alcuin frequently rebuked for the corruption of his morals and admonished to correct himself, as is related in the Life of Alcuin. It is certain from the Salzburg codex that he was a Briton; in that codex the region mentioned at the beginning of this letter is called Britain. I think the following two letters and the poem *On the Cuckoo* also belong to the same man.

To his dearest son.

Dearest son, brother, and friend, whose name I desire the heavenly library to preserve forever: long ago I begot you, nourished you, fed you, and, by God’s gift, brought you to the stature of a perfect man—carefully instructed in the liberal arts, illumined by the sun of wisdom, and most excellently adorned with good morals—so that nearly the whole region sings your praise [the Salzburg manuscript codices read: “Britain”], and the fame of your name is wider than knowledge of your face.

Devoted to this distinction of yours, I call Christ to witness that I was your helper; and according to the measure of my strength, though perhaps not competent, nevertheless willingly, as I was able, and even now in your absence, I earnestly pursue you with prayers, having once advanced you in sacred disciplines when you were present. But by the mercy of him who redeemed, illumined, and exalted us and made us participants in his knowledge, I beg you more earnestly not to become angry with my affection, which does not allow me to remain silent, if I speak somewhat harshly to you.

The affection of fatherhood compels me to say what I have learned from a winged rumor, because you are doing certain things that suit neither your dignity nor my affection. I do not wish the fame of your glory to be darkened by black stains, lest someone else steal from you the place owed to you, so that “the last shall be first and the first last” (Matt. XIX, 30).

What is this that I hear about you—not from some single person whispering in a corner, but from many people publicly recounting it with laughter? You are still devoted to childish impurities and to things that you ought never to have done and ought never to have wished to abandon [or: “that you do not wish to abandon”]. Where is your most noble learning? Where is your celebrated diligence in the holy Scriptures? Where is your excellence of character? Where is your strength of spirit? Where is your fear of Gehenna? Where is your hope of glory? How are you not horrified to perpetrate what you ought to have forbidden in others?

Turn, I beg you, within your heart [Cod. Sal., “into yourself”], and say with the prophet: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep day and night” (John IX, 1)—not for Jerusalem, which will be burned by Babylonian fire, but for the soul that will burn in the flames of Sodom. At every moment the grim exactor hastens forward, whom no one can escape. What will you then answer your most just Judge if you do not now correct your foul deeds?

I beg you, dearest son, by the terror of that judgment which we are all compelled to undergo, that from this day, on which you read through this little page—dictated with intimate sorrow, written with pure charity, and sealed with holy faith—you may begin with steadfast courage to break apart and cast far from you the chain of this diabolical suggestion and impious consent, so that you may be able to lift pure and free hands to the Lord your God (I Tim. II, 8).

He is ready to come out to meet you as you return from a distant region, if you do not delay rising and saying: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; therefore I am no longer worthy to be called your son” (Luke XV, 21). He will deign not only to meet you but also to embrace and kiss you, clothe you in the finest robe, adorn you with a ring, provide you with sandals, and, moreover, lead you into the house of his delights. There, joined with the angelic choirs, you will sing in blessed eternity and eternal blessedness: “Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5).

> [Col. 0482D] Quercet. 103; compared with the Salzburg and San-Emmeram manuscript codices. (At Froben, letter 158.)

# LETTER CCVII. TO THE PRODIGAL SON

He reproves the disciple’s perverse habits and urges him to amend his life by the example of a certain man who is now a bishop and was formerly his fellow student.

> [Col. 0482D] To the prodigal son. Mabillon also seems to think that Osulf is designated by this name. See the preceding letter.

To the prodigal son, from his grieving father, greetings.

Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes (Jer. IX, 1), so that I may weep—not for an imaginary city of the Chaldeans destined to perish in flame, but for a soul, the glorious image of Christ, destined to remain for an infinite eternity?

Alas! alas! unhappy soul! Noble through the price of Christ’s blood, but ignoble through the contagion of sin: why have you abandoned the fountain of life and dug for yourself broken cisterns (Jer. II, 13)—cisterns in which there is no water of salvation, but only a wallow for swine [Edit., “cattle”]? Why have you abandoned the father who instructed you from childhood, imbued you with the liberal disciplines, trained you in good morals, fortified you with the precepts of eternal life, and joined yourself to bands of prostitutes, banquets of drunkards, and the vanities of the proud?

Are you not that young man once praiseworthy on everyone’s lips, lovable in everyone’s eyes, and desired by everyone’s ears? Alas! alas! Now you are blameworthy on everyone’s lips, accursed in everyone’s eyes, and detested by everyone’s ears. Who has so overturned you except drunkenness and lust? Who persuaded you, handsome boy, son of the Church, venerable light, to feed swine and eat their pods?

Rise, son, rise and return to your father, and say often, not just once: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you, and therefore I am not worthy to be called your son” (Luke XV, 21). There is still a little light in you; run while you have the light, lest the darkness of eternal destruction seize you now (John XII, 35). Believe in the perpetual light of mercy, so that you may become a son of light.

The Father is merciful; he will immediately come out to meet you as you return and will rush into your embrace. He will order the first robe to be brought to you and will adorn your right hand with the ring of his image. Do not wander any longer through the brambles of vices like a lost sheep, but return to him who left the ninety-nine sheep in the heights of heaven to find the one that had gone astray on earth, bring it back, and place it with the others for the joy of the angels in the heavenly homeland (Matt. XVIII, 12; Luke XV, 4, 7).

Think, yes, think, how great is the joy of the angels over one sinner who repents, and how pious and merciful is he who says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.” Again, through the prophet he says: “On whatever day the sinner turns, he shall surely live and shall not die” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11, 12).

Do not, son, do not despise the one who calls, nor neglect the mercy of the one who shows compassion [Cod. Sal. and San-Emmeram, “of the one who shows compassion”]. Remember the eternal flames of torments, the poisonous teeth of worms, the immeasurable cold, the lamentations of those who weep, the merciless faces of the torturers [Cod. Sal. and San-Emmeram, “the torches of the torturers”], and the endless stretches of misery.

Consider also the most blessed companies of angels, the glorious ranks of the saints, and the ineffable, blessed vision of almighty God, which the saints will enjoy forever. You can still avoid the former and choose the latter. Your lust and wickedness may lead you to that end of the impious; but to this glory and praiseworthy blessedness of the saints your conversion and repentance may, by God’s mercy, bring you.

Enough for you is the past time spent in lusts and pleasures. Come to your senses at last from this destruction of yours, and do not obey diabolical suggestion any longer. Rather, confess your sins and repent in the hope of forgiveness. “Who knows whether he will turn and forgive?” (Joel II, 14). For his mercies are many, and his compassion is infinite toward those who take care to mourn their sins rather than add to them—to cast off the burden of iniquity rather than increase the criminal load.

Remember the thief hanging on the cross, the Ninevites sitting in ashes, and the impious King Manasseh returning from captivity in Babylonia. Just as divine mercy showed compassion to them after their repentance, so most certainly will it show compassion to you, if you wish to return to him with complete intention of heart, conversion of life, and tears of repentance.

Look at your fellow student, who has always clung to God with complete devotion of heart and now presides over a most noble bishopric,

> [Col. 0483D] If this prodigal son is to be sought in England, as may be conjectured from the preceding letter, then these words may suitably be understood of Eanbald, bishop of York, who was also a disciple of Alcuin.

beloved, praised, and desired by all. But you, wretched man, wandering through the thickets of vices, are honorable to no one and blameworthy to all.

Remember how much more distinguished you once were in gifts, better in learning, keener in understanding, and superior in every ecclesiastical discipline. But now you are like an abandoned hut in a vineyard, a dwelling for foxes and wild beasts that are accustomed to ravage Christ’s vineyard.

Your former companion and partner in learning, however, is a temple of the living God and a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, beloved by God and by human beings. Each day he prepares eternal dwelling places for himself in heaven, while you pursue earthly filth and repeatedly rush back toward the mournful path of destruction, destined to plunge down the precipices of vices.

Rise, I beg you, my dearest son, rise and go to your brother [your], of whom I spoke earlier, because one Church begot you both, one discipline instructed you both, and one father instructs you both. Let there now also be one concord between you, one counsel for your salvation, and one dwelling place of ecclesiastical piety.

I know that he greatly rejoices in your progress. Do not despise your father’s prayers; do not neglect my tears as your teacher. Bring me consolation through your salvation, lest the devil boast against me in your destruction.

I nourished you as my dearest son, fed you, and instructed you. Do not be a source of confusion to me, a disgrace to yourself, and a reproach to your contemporaries. Act manfully and take courage in the Lord, and conquer all your adversaries through him who says: “Take courage; I have overcome the world” (John XVI, 33), so that my joy may be complete in you and no one may take your joy from you.

“A wise son is the glory of his father.” You will bring ineffable joy not only to me, who begot you, but also, in accordance with the evangelical parable that I presented shortly before in this same letter, you will bring joy to all the angelic orders. Do not deprive them of their joy or yourself of your blessedness. If you now cause them to rejoice in your repentance, God will grant that you rejoice with them in glory forever.

Let this little letter remain with you and be read often, until what the one who dictated it desires has been accomplished [Cod. Sal., “until it accomplishes what he desires”]. I believe that God will indeed accomplish what paternal charity seeks in a son. But do not delay turning to God, for we do not know what the coming day may bring forth (Prov. XXVII, 1). God certainly accepts repentance today, but he has not promised a long duration of the present life. He has left us uncertain of the final day so that he may always find us ready, with the lamps of good merits, to go out to meet him.

> [Col. 0484D] Quercet. 114, Canis. 64 (Froben. 159).

# LETTER CCVIII. TO THE SAME MAN

He laments the disciple’s perverse habits and attempts to recall him to better things through fear of Gehenna.

> [Col. 0484D] To his dearest son, Osulf. Mabillon.

To his dearest son.

Whom I begot late and dismissed early. He was snatched from my breasts before he was properly weaned. Flesh more hostile than a stepmother seized him from his tender paternal embrace through the whirlpools of lust. Alas, what grief! What shall I do except mourn for one who is perishing, if perhaps he can be restored to life by the warm fomentation of tears?

Woe to the flesh that does not fear the sulfurous fires of the five cities or the flames of the punishments of infernal torments. Bind yourself, I beg you, with the chains of this fear, and test whether you can endure even a single spark of its heat; consider what it would be like if your entire body were tortured by an eternal conflagration.

Look back at last, and do not consent to the one who prepares such fires for you. Rather, discipline yourself and yield to your father’s entreaties. Recognize that you are always present to God’s eyes and before the sight of the holy angels. Be ashamed to do in their presence what you dread to perpetrate in the presence of any human being.

I know that you believe judgment is destined for all, and you believe yourself to be among those who have done the things that the devil daily suggests to you. Behold: yesterday you did the will of your flesh; today you are going into the fire of eternal flame.

> [Col. 0485D] Froben, letter 211.

# LETTER CCIX. TO A FRIEND

He exhorts one who has turned to better things to persevere.

To his dearest friend, perpetual salvation in all present prosperity and eternal blessedness.

I have great joy over the good intention of yours that I heard from our brother Benedict exists in you. I desire, and beseech God, that it may be completed as soon as possible with complete harmony. For it is written: “Do not delay turning to the Lord God, for you do not know what the coming day may bring forth” (Ecclus. V, 8).

Rescue yourself from the prison of these tribulations, which in this world usually torment the minds of the faithful, as it is written: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous”; so may you deserve to experience what follows: “But the Lord will deliver them from all these” (Ps. XXXIII, 20). And take the greatest care that no injustice, while you hold the Lord’s plow, draw you back. No soldier burdened with another’s baggage advances well into battle, except with victorious weapons alone, either for his own defense or for injuring his adversary.

I have told our most faithful brother Benedict everything that seemed necessary for you. [The text concerning “places, assistance, and steadfastness of spirit” is corrupt.] But you should know that wherever there is an association of many people, both good and evil are found. A wise mind should make use of the instruction provided by both: it should avoid the wickedness of the evil and follow the justice of the good.

The rational mind given to the human being ought to discern what should be avoided and what should be followed. One should neither distrust nor trust a place excessively, for if a place could have helped, an angel would never have fallen from heaven, nor would a human being placed in paradise have sinned. Rather, as Truth itself says, the kingdom of God must be sought within us (Luke XVII, 21).

And the Psalmist says: “Fear the Lord, all you his saints, for those who fear him lack nothing” (Ps. XXXIII, 10). Fear of the Lord forbids sin, when a person recognizes and fears God’s presence everywhere, because the one who knows the person’s thoughts, words, and deeds will also be that person’s judge. Nothing of ours escapes him, nor will he leave anything unjudged, because, as it is said, he will repay each person according to his works.

> [Col. 0485D] While we have time, let us do good, because after death there is no time for working, but only time for receiving the reward.

Thinking on these things, dearest son, take care of yourself, remembering from how many dangers God has delivered you. Love him and turn to his mercy, so that your sins may be erased and you may deserve to receive with God’s saints a place of refreshment, light, and peace. Remember me among those who serve God and intercede for you, and may you prosper in perpetual well-being, dearest friend.

> [Col. 0485D] Quercet. 43, Canis. 67; compared with the manuscript codices. (At Froben, letter 160.)

# LETTER CCX. A LETTER OF RECOMMENDATION TO FRIENDS

A letter of recommendation for a certain priest, Fordradus, to friends.

> [Col. 0485D] “Of brotherly affection”

> [Col. 0485D] To friends of brotherly affection, etc. This and the following two letters are letters of recommendation for traveling friends who are making their way to the holy places.

To friends of various ranks and names, Albinus, your fellow servant in Christ, sends greetings.

Although the distance between lands makes the dwellings of Christians different, nevertheless the fellowship of holy charity, under Christ the one shepherd, makes them one flock. In reliance on this fellowship, through the supplicatory letters of our smallness, I most diligently commend to your piety this priest,

> [Col. 0485D] Fordradus. This name is omitted in the other manuscript codices. “Fordredus the abbot, who came to the thresholds of the blessed apostles and to Rome on account of his monastery, is mentioned in letters of Paul I to Ecgbert, archbishop of York, and Eadbert, king of Northumbria, apparently issued in the year 757. But in that year Alcuin would scarcely have been of such age or authority that he could have dictated letters of this kind.” (Alford, *Annals of Anglo-Saxon History*, under that year, no. 2.) But those letters may have been issued later, or Fordredus may have gone to Rome on another occasion as well. See also the notes to letter 22 (now 27).

I commend Fordradus most earnestly, so that, supported by the assistance of your affection, he may more easily complete the road of his holy pilgrimage, and so that the reward of your goodness before the eyes of almighty God {221}–267 may be increased.

> [Col. 0486D] The intermediate numbers are omitted because of the rearrangement of the letters.

> [Col. 0486D] EDIT. PATR. May he who is the way, the life, and the truth (John XIV, 6) deign to show you the way of your salvation, grant you the truth [Edit., “rest”] of eternal glory, and bestow blessed life. [May divine grace assist you, dearest brother, in your progress, forever.]

> [Col. 0486D] Quercet. 51, Canis. 52 (Froben. 161).

# LETTER CCXI. TO ALL FRIENDS

A letter of recommendation for the traveling priest Noroberet to friends.

> [Col. 0486C] To all friends in the love of Christ, the humble Levite Alcuin sends greetings.

Wherever this priest named Noroberet [Al., Norbet] comes into your presence, I beg you to deign to receive him kindly in whatever business or need he may have. You will certainly have God as the rewarder of your goodness, who will say on the day of judgment: “I was a stranger, and you took me in” (Matt. XXV, 35).

And if my littleness can repay you with thanks in any matter whatsoever, I will diligently and faithfully endeavor to do so. May divine mercy receive in its heavenly dwelling the one who receives this man, or others traveling for Christ’s name, into his lodging. Farewell, brothers in Christ.

> [Col. 0486D] (Froben, letter 162.) This letter of recommendation, previously unpublished, comes from the Salzburg manuscript codex. It also exists in the manuscript codex of the royal library in Paris; D. Lieble, librarian of Saint-Germain, sent me a copy from there. He will be praised more fully later.

# LETTER CCXII. A LETTER OF RECOMMENDATION TO FRIENDS

A recommendation to friends on behalf of pilgrims traveling to the thresholds of the apostles.

> [Col. 0486D] To all venerable men, to those possessing various powers and ranks, and to the sons of holy charity, the humble Levite Alcuin sends greetings of eternal blessedness.

We know, therefore, the piety of your goodness: for the love of Christ and the reward of future glory, you kindly receive pilgrims and strangers, especially those who, for ecclesiastical necessity or for the salvation of their souls, are accustomed to visit the sacred thresholds of the holy apostles. Whoever receives these people into his house will have Christ receive him into his glory, because in such people Christ himself will have been received, as Truth itself says in the Gospel: “I was a stranger, and you received me” (Matt. XXV, 35).

Nevertheless, on behalf of the bearers of this letter, I, Alcuin, your faithful friend—O excellent fathers and most holy brothers, most beloved sons!—earnestly beg your charity to receive them kindly in whatever business or need they may have. You have God as your rewarder and me as your debtor, according to the opportunity of time, to satisfy your wishes in Christ.

> [Col. 0487D] Froben, letter 199.

# LETTER CCXIII. TO RAGANBERT, BISHOP

(Year uncertain.)

> [Col. 0487D] In this letter Alcuin complains about a new and unusual exaction that the bishop’s ministers were imposing upon the priests and churches of Saint Martin. Such exactions, which are made under the name of provisions or synodaticum, were formerly permitted by the canons and decrees of councils only in a case of necessity, as may be seen in Thomassin, *Old and New Discipline*, Part III, book II, chapter 32 and following. I do not know of which see Raganbert or Ragerbert—the manuscript has both forms—was bishop. I find no bishop of this name presiding over the see of Tours in Alcuin’s time. I think, rather, that those priests were parish priests in churches situated outside the diocese of Tours but belonging to the monastery of Saint Martin; nevertheless, they were subject to the bishop’s visitation and had to appear at synods.

He complains of new exactions by which the bishop’s ministers were harassing priests serving in the churches of Saint Martin.

To the venerable lord Ragerbert, bishop, whom we honor in the love of Christ, Alcuin the Levite sends greetings.

Remembering the friendship agreed upon between us, I am encouraged to write to you about something that seems necessary to us on both sides. I was told that your young men had imposed some new custom upon the churches and priests of Saint Martin. Indeed, they even said it came from you; nevertheless, I did not believe this of your holiness, thinking that you observe the canons very well, and especially the evangelical saying of our Lord Jesus Christ, where he says: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matt. X, 8).

For they say that your messengers had commanded our priests to provide one and a half modii of bread, one modius of wine, four modii of grain for horses, six cheeses, one hundred eggs, fish, garden produce, and sufficient legumes from each priest; and that if they did not provide these things, they would have an interdict by your authority forbidding them to sing Masses in our churches, nor would they be permitted to allow other priests to sing in the churches of Saint Martin.

It seems strange to me by what authority you wished to excommunicate Christ’s churches. If the priests have sinned, what has the church sinned? Why do your young men not remember how terribly the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, struck down the sellers of grace in the first inventor of this heresy, saying: “May your money be with you unto perdition” (Acts VIII, 20)?

I beg you, most merciful Father, by that charity through which God has joined us, and by that faith in which we made our agreement, not to send anything new against the churches of Saint Martin or against his possessions. Saint Martin is powerful with God to defend his possessions, if it is necessary for him to cry out to God.

If it pleases you, and if it can be done, allow the churches of Christ that are under the immunity of Saint Martin, and in your parish, to remain as they are until we speak together. Whatever authority it is just for you to exercise over them, I do not reject; rather, if they are not obedient to you, I will constrain them together with you. For they ought to come to your synod and give an account of their spiritual offices, while you ought freely to give them the things that belong to God, as I said above, since the Lord Jesus has commanded that spiritual gifts be given freely by everyone.

The intercession of Saint Martin and Saint Aredius will grant you greater prosperity than the council of those who encourage this exaction and the payment of tribute. And even if you wished to impose this upon others, I never thought that you would wish to impose such a necessity upon our people, because of the friendship agreed between us, or rather because of the honor of Saint Martin, whom God has honored with such authority that through his intercessions he can grant aid to all his saints.

May divine mercy protect and exalt your blessedness in safety and happiness, and may it cause you to preach rightly, most holy lord.

> [Col. 0488D] Froben, letter 202.

# LETTER CCXIV. TO NIFRIDIUS, BISHOP

(Year uncertain.)

He asks to be remembered in prayers and commends Benedict as he departs from him.

To his beloved father,

> [Col. 0488D] Nifridius, bishop. This is Nefridius, bishop of Narbonne, who is elsewhere also called Nimfridius and Nibribridius. In the case of the heresy of Felix and Elipandus, he was sent to Urgell with his associates Laidradus, bishop of Lyon, and Benedict, abbot of Aniane. On that occasion Alcuin dedicated to them the books he had written against that heresy, with a letter prefixed to them; this will be discussed in its proper place. See note c, col. 489.

To Nifridius, bishop, Alcuin sends greetings.

I beg your charity to remember me in your sacred prayers together with our brothers. These are dangerous times, and only the one who serves God in perfect charity, right faith, and good hope lives happily; these are the highest truths of those who serve God. Let your holiness exercise itself in these things, so that, with God’s help, you may deserve to pass from the labor of this life to the blessedness of everlasting rest.

> [Col. 0489A] But Brother
@ [Col. 0489D] Brother Benedict.

Benedict, abbot of Aniane, celebrated for his holiness, who under Charlemagne and Louis the Pious reformed the discipline of monasteries, especially those of Aquitaine, and for this reason often visited the court and Alcuin himself, to whom he was closely attached by many ties. Consult his Life in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, century IV, part I, p. 191 and following, and in Bollandus under 11 February.

May Benedict be able to make everything concerning me known to you. I dismissed him in tears. Receive him with joy; and both of you labor as good shepherds in Christ’s flock, doubting nothing concerning the eternal reward that will be given to those who faithfully feed Christ’s flock. Greet all the bishops and fathers of our brothers, in the duty imposed by our name, with charity and good wishes, asking them to remember us in continual intercession, so that they may receive an everlasting reward for my salvation.

{268} May God guard all of them with perpetual protection and grant that they advance in every good work, so that, as the number of their talents increases, they may be made worthy of a manifold recompense before God. May they all live and flourish happily in Christ the Lord our God.

@ [Col. 0489D] Froben, *Epistles*, 203.

## EPISTLE CCXV. TO THE MOST BELOVED FATHERS

*(Year uncertain.)*

He urges them to charity and to the labors of monastic life. [Col. 0489B]

To the most beloved fathers in Christ, perpetual salvation.

Those whom faithful charity always follows should also often be accompanied by a succession of letters, because it is a certain refreshment for one who loves to express in words or writing the fervor of a burning heart. Words have been given for the demonstration of truth, so that what the heart truly conceives the tongue may faithfully utter, and one brother may pour his heart into another’s heart, producing unity of spirit, in which there is communion of charity. For a soul without charity is dead, lacking the image of divine Goodness, in whose likeness we were created and by whose goodness our Savior renewed us. He said: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). I do not think it necessary to write much to your holiness concerning the sweetness of this, which you learned long ago and have shown yourselves to possess. It remains only that you retain it firmly to the end, since “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22).

Greet also,

@ [Col. 0489D] Most holy Father Infridius. It should certainly be read *Nifridius*, with the letters *i* and *n* transposed in the first syllable, as frequently happens in ancient writings. “Shortly before the year 778 he was the first founder, and likewise the first abbot, of the celebrated monastery of Saint Mary of Orbione, or Urbione, so called from the nearby river; it was at one time called Saint Mary of Novalia, from the pleasant valley in which it is situated, and finally it was named Saint Mary of Crassa. He later became archbishop of Narbonne, as we learn from the ancient necrology of the place.” (Mabillon, [Col. 0490D] *Annals*, book XXIV, no. 86, p. 244.) I therefore think that this letter was written to the monks of that monastery.

Most holy Father Infridius, greet our brothers serving holy Mary. They truly chose an excellent mistress, and the excellent bridegroom of that mistress and Queen of Heaven; and it is fitting that the excellent King be served excellently. Let the one who chooses good things [perhaps: *eligit*, “chooses,” or *elegit*, “has chosen”] guard good things, not abandon good things, but retain good things forever. It is little to have begun good things unless the one who chooses good things perseveres in them to the end. What is it to abandon fruitful labor and devote oneself to fruitless labor? The labor of monastic life is therefore fruitful, whereas the labor of the world is fruitless. No one lives in the world without labor; and supremely happy is the one who passes from labor into rest, while unhappy is the one who passes from labor into torment. He labors in order to fare badly, and does not understand what he is doing. Understanding is necessary in life, so that a person may know toward what end the reward of his labor is directed. A small labor in a good person will be rewarded with everlasting rest. May almighty God grant you, dearest fathers, to advance for many years in enduring prosperity for the salvation of many.

@ [Col. 0490D] Froben, *Epistles*, 204. {269}

## EPISTLE CCXVI. TO BISHOP CUNIBERCTUS

He commends the memory of an old friendship. He urges him to the work of preaching, which must not be hindered by any worldly power or vanity.

To the father of venerable dignity,

@ [Col. 0490D] Cuniberctus, bishop. He was in Britain, as I infer from the words “to the inhabitants of our most famous island of Britain,” and so forth. He is undoubtedly Kinebert, bishop of the city of Venta, companion of Æthelhard on the journey to Rome. See the note to Epistle 115. Anastasius Bibliothecarius also mentions a certain Cuniberctus among the most faithful envoys sent to Rome in 799 to judge the case of that supreme pontiff, Leo III. Whether this was the same man as ours is uncertain.

To Cuniberctus, bishop, Alcuin, humble Levite, sends greetings.

Long ago,

@ [Col. 0490D] {270} At an assembly of the holy fathers in synod. It is equally unknown what this assembly was and where it was held, whether in England or in Gaul. In 785 a certain Chumberchus, bishop, subscribed the decrees of the Council of Calchuth. Wilkins, *Concilia Magnae Britanniae*, vol. I, p. 151.

Long ago, at an assembly of the holy fathers in synod, your goodness made with us covenants of charity. Because this bearer now provides the opportunity, our humility has endeavored to renew them in this little letter, lest perhaps your long absence should have caused you to forget our name. Charity does not tolerate forgetfulness, and truth is not tarnished by any length of time, especially in such a person and so distinguished a man of holiness, whose spacious, honey-flowing heart habitually gathers a multitude of spiritual friends. Among them, I beg, may the name of my small self find some place; and your most noble fidelity, as we have said, once did not shrink from promising this. Moreover, my father, I humbly implore you to order the most holy brothers under your governance to maintain the same spiritual concern for us.

I confess to you, most holy bishop, that I have eagerly loved the venerable communities of brothers whom, according to what report has told us, we heard to be serving God with worthy conduct in those regions, although it was not granted to us to approach them in bodily presence. May your piety, for the love of Christ, speak on our behalf to Christ for them; and God will by no means fail to reward your devotion, excellent man. For it befits priestly dignity to show an affectionate concern to all who plead with it, to assist the absent with holy prayers, and to strengthen those present by the urgency of evangelical preaching.

You know very well how great the need of the Christian people is, that the preacher of God’s word should not be silent, and how great the need is among the inhabitants of our most famous island of Britain, where once a multitude of teachers continually proclaimed the words of eternal life. But now, because of sins, the laborers in the Lord’s harvest are few. The fewer they are found to be, the more necessary it is that those who remain should make every effort, through the continual practice of holy preaching, to recall people from the error of life and the excess of many vanities to the practice of modesty, sobriety, and chastity.

Let the mouth of your holiness not be silent concerning the words of evangelical truth, the succession of apostolic teaching, and the most noble conduct of the holy fathers, so that many may be instructed through your most holy devotion and, by the gift of Christ God, an abundant reward may remain for you forever. Let neither royal power nor the arrogance of any worldly eminence prevent your voice from speaking the truth. Let neither the flattery of those who follow you, nor the pomp of worldly luxury, nor the deceptive appearance of gold, nor any pleasure of earthly delight withdraw your holy heart from the confidence required for diligent labor. Rather, let the light of truth shine in all things through you, and let the way of eternal salvation be shown.

The days of labor in this life are few, and the one who labors more will receive the greater reward; but the recompense of heavenly blessedness endures through eternal ages. May almighty God grant that your holy and venerable fatherhood live and advance happily for many years, for the exaltation of his holy Church, dearest father.

@ [Col. 0491D] Froben, *Epistles*, 206.

## EPISTLE CCXVII. TO BISHOPS ALCHARD AND TIFRED

He urges them to fulfill the duty of preaching.

To the most holy and venerable fathers,

@ [Col. 0491D] Alchard and Tifred, bishops. I believe that these bishops are to be sought in England. Indeed, I think I have found them there. Among the bishops who subscribed the Council of Clovesho in 803 and the decree of Archbishop Æthelhard, there is named Alcheard, also called Ealehard, bishop of the church of Elmham; and Tidfrith, bishop of the city of Dunwich. See Wilkins, cited above, pp. 167–168; on p. 152 they are also listed by King Offa among the bishops of the East Angles whom he wished to be subject to the church of Lichfield, which he was raising to archiepiscopal status.

To Alchard and Tifred, bishops, Alcuin the Levite sends greetings.

I beseech your most merciful goodness not to regard the letters of my small self as presumptuous. I have therefore dared to write them in the confidence of your charity, because Christian humility ought to despise no one but kindly receive everyone into the pious embrace of love. I desire that this charity shine abundantly in you through the Holy Spirit, so that rivers of living water—that is, of sacred doctrine—may be seen to flow sufficiently from your hearts, as Truth himself says in the Gospel (John 7:38).

{271} It is your office to preach God’s word to everyone and to shine for everyone in the house of God, so that all may recognize the light of truth through you and be led to the pastures of everlasting blessedness. Your mouth ought to be the trumpet of Christ God, because the tongues of your authority are the keys of heaven, having power to open and close: to open to penitents and to close against those who resist the truth.

Therefore make yourselves worthy of such great excellence through good conduct, knowing that the assiduity of preaching is the priests’ glory. Priestly honor is not a worldly game; rather, the priest of Christ must exercise himself with great diligence in God’s commandments, so that by examples and words alike he may instruct the Christian people.

The venerable brother

@ [Col. 0492D] Lullus, abbot, praised your good conduct to me. In the decree of Æthelhard mentioned above, among the abbots belonging to the diocese of Dunwich, Lulla the abbot subscribed after Tidfrith the bishop.

Therefore I have taken care to commend myself humbly to your holiness, asking you to order that some remembrance of our name be made throughout your churches. I have presumed to ask this not on account of my merits, but out of the charity of Christ. Act accordingly, as I trust in your good piety. May God the Lord increase you in the grace of merits and cause you to advance in all holiness and in the preaching of God’s word, dearest and most desired fathers.

@ [Col. 0492D] Froben, *Epistles*, 207.

## EPISTLE CCXVIII. TO ARDBERT

He urges him to works of justice and mercy; praises his goodness; and commends to him the case of Lullus the abbot. [Col. 0492C]

Alcuin, servant of Saint Martin,

@ [Col. 0492D] To Ardbert, illustrious man. In England, as I infer from the name of Lullus the abbot, who is mentioned in the preceding letter. In two charters of King Ecgfrith of Mercia from the year 796, for the monastery of Saint Alban, printed by Alford in *Annals*, vol. II, under that year, no. 5, p. 678, a certain Heardbert, duke, subscribes. Whether he is the same as this illustrious Ardbert requires further examination, which I leave to other learned men.

To Ardbert, illustrious man, greetings and everlasting blessedness.

On hearing of your praiseworthy conduct, befitting your station, I confess that I rejoiced greatly. You, excellent man, should always do what pleases God and persuade others to do the same, so that God’s blessing may accompany you everywhere and you may advance in the counsels of your salvation, benefiting many and doing justice to the people, mercy to the poor, and honor to Christ’s churches. Thus the intercession of God’s servants may commend you daily to the mercy of the Lord Jesus, because “the prayer of a righteous person has great power” (James 5:16), and how much more the prayer of many.

[Col. 0492D] Care for the poor, who usually stand before the door of your banquet, because Christ is received in the poor. On the day of judgment he will say to those who diligently give alms to the poor: “As often as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40). [Col. 0493A] This is followed by that most blessed sentence which the Lord will speak to those who in this world have dealt kindly [perhaps: “toward”] with the poor, strangers, afflicted, and sick: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34).

I beg you to order that a remembrance of our name be made throughout the churches under your authority. I always rejoice to hear better things about you, knowing that the prosperity of many consists in your good and merciful conduct in the service of Christ.

I would certainly have written more to your dignity if there were such familiarity between us that it would not seem presumptuous for me to intrude suddenly upon your excellence. But because I have written out of the charity of Christ, I beg you to deign to read this humbly; for the bearer of this little note who is present,

@ [Col. 0493D] Lullus, the venerable abbot—see the notes to the preceding letter—used to praise your goodness to me. Trusting in this, we have also written these letters, asking you to receive him kindly in his affairs, with the same piety [manuscript: “piety’s”] that he used to report to us concerning you.

I desire that you live happily in enduring prosperity in this world for many years and, after the end of this life, by God’s gift, may deserve to reach the kingdom of everlasting blessedness, most noble man and most beloved by us.

@ [Col. 0493D] Froben, *Epistles*, 208.

## EPISTLE CCXIX. TO BISHOP LEUTFRED

He consoles him in tribulation.

To the most holy father and most beloved son,

@ [Col. 0493D] Leutfred, bishop. Undoubtedly Leidrad, bishop of Lyons; for this name is represented in various ways by less careful ancient writers. He is called Laedredus in Epistle 2, Liobradus and Liodradus in Epistle 89, and elsewhere Laidradus.

To Leutfred, bishop, Alcuin sends greetings.

[Col. 0493C] I truly confess that your tribulation torments my mind, when I hear that you have been placed in danger and are unable to fulfill the ministry of your office, while a spiritual warrior is compelled to become a carnal warrior. Nevertheless, place your hope in God and console yourself in God’s mercy, hoping in his perpetual goodness, which never abandons those who hope in him. Tribulation presses upon tribulation, because sin increases upon sin. But what should be done in the tribulation that you are suffering,

@ [Col. 0493D] I said to Brother Benedict—abbot of Aniane, mentioned in the following letters; from him Leidrad received twenty monks for the monastery of the Isle of Barbe, which he founded, as Ardo, or Smaragdus, testifies in the Life of that holy abbot, no. 36, in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, century IV, part I, p. 205—that he would be able to show your charity everything that has happened to me.

Pray for God’s mercy upon us, that he may direct our ways according to what pleases his good will and advances our everlasting salvation. Do not in any way consent to involve yourself in the weapons of combatants. Flee to Christ; lie prostrate before him and cry out: “My mercy and my refuge; my protector and my deliverer; in him my heart has hoped.” Fare well in every prosperity.

@ [Col. 0493D] Froben, *Epistles*, 209.

## EPISTLE CCXX

@ [Col. 0493D] To Benedict. Abbot of Aniane, most celebrated for his reputation for holiness and doctrine and for restoring Benedictine monastic discipline, with whom Alcuin maintained a close and familiar friendship. “For when he had heard and experienced the reputation for the holiness of this man of God, he joined himself to him in inviolable charity, so that from his letters, often sent to him and gathered together, a single little book was composed,” as Ardo, or Smaragdus, testifies in the work cited above. It is regrettable that the greatest part of the letters mentioned here has perished, and that only these two, found in the Harleian manuscript, survive.

## TO BENEDICT

He commends to his charity a certain brother whom he calls his son; he commends himself, tossed about in the waves of the world, to Benedict’s prayers. He returns thanks for medicinal herbs, and so forth.

To Father Benedict, may perpetual salvation be granted in blessed Christ.

I am greatly pleased by the faithfulness of your devotion and charity toward your brother and our son, because a friend is proved in adversity, which is what every person most needs when passing from this life, so that through fraternal intercession he may behold the face of his Judge as merciful. Console him, as far as you are able, by words and deeds, until you see what God will do with him.

{273} The waves of the world agitate me with various movements. But you, together with your brothers, as you promised, do not cease to assist me with your prayers, lest the abyss of any desire or sin engulf me. I shall explain to you face to face, God willing, the causes and circumstances of this event of mine, and I shall do what you asked at the appropriate times. I always remember to send the little letters of my small self to your charity, and I beg to receive yours in return. I ask you to take pains to inform me confidently about your progress and prosperity.

[Col. 0494C] I received the medicinal herbs you sent with a grateful heart. Just as you have taken care to provide me with bodily health, so I always desire provision for your spiritual health, wishing that you may advance vigorously in the work you have begun, and

@ [Col. 0494D] The flock that you have gathered—in the monastery of Aniane, which Saint Benedict built at his own expense. “For after leaving the monastery of Saint-Seine, where he cut off the hair of his head and assumed the habit of a true monk, and after living for several years with his disciples in a cell built near Aniane, he constructed a large coenobium called Aniane and ordered a basilica to be dedicated to the Savior and to blessed Mary.” Mabillon, *Preliminary Observations on the Life of Saint Benedict of Aniane*, no. 4—

govern faithfully the flock that you have gathered. Do not in any way grow weary, whether through sloth in thought or through the negligence of some. Let the one who labors more receive the greater reward. I greatly desire to see you this present year, if it can be done, because the familiarity of your humility has greatly pleased my heart. Equality of spirit usually produces the sweetness of affection; and although the merits of their works may be unequal, the desire for salvation can nevertheless be equal. For the sick person desires his health just as the physician does, although the one lies ill while the other is strong in a healthy body. May the merciful God cause your fatherhood, interceding for us, to advance in every good thing.

@ [Col. 0495D] Froben, *Epistles*, 210.

## EPISTLE CCXXI. TO THE SAME

He sends letters to the king and others for Benedict to deliver; he wishes to receive letters from Benedict more often.

May blessed God grant eternal blessing to Father Benedict.

@ [Col. 0495D] {274} I have written some little letters. Of these he mentions only one to the king and another to the brothers. Three letters to the abbots and monks of Gothia survive, namely 132, 133, and 134. Moreover, through blessed Benedict he sent them a little book against the heresy of Felix, for their consolation and confirmation in the Catholic faith, as is read in Epistle 132. Whether he is speaking of one of these letters or of some other letter still hidden from us cannot be determined from this passage. Perhaps on this occasion he also sent the letter to Leutfred presented immediately above, and the one to the friend now presented; for this reason it seemed appropriate to join them here to the letters to Benedict.

I have written several little letters, as you will be able to understand from reading them, if this seems worthwhile to you. Return one to each person, but give the king his with many words of greeting. It seemed better to me that you should speak to his piety concerning us, our wishes, and our son, rather than that I should write something from that place, because letters pass through the hands of many, whereas words remain faithfully in the heart.

I have written the letter to our brothers collectively. If you find anything worthwhile in it, I would have it written out more fully [perhaps: “write it out more fully”]; and if you think anything should be added, do so according to your judgment, because it was dictated in haste to recall the sweetness of our friendship and the diligence of their prayers for us. As you know, we have a great desire, and also a great need, and we have good hope in their most sacred prayers. Where you are, there am I also, and may God be with us forever.

As the opportunity of the bearer permits, let letters come more often. Let not the rusticity for which you are accustomed to excuse yourself make charity silent, lest its flame shine less brightly, but let it shine in little writings, since it burns perpetually in the heart. Go on your way, by God’s mercy, with every prosperity. May my eye see you before I die, not once but often; and, by God’s gift, may you always fare well forever.

{278}

@ [Col. 0495D] In Froben, *Epistle*, 216.

## EPISTLE CCXXII

@ [Col. 0496D] To the Hilliriensian brothers. This is indeed how the title is read in the manuscript, but the following address makes it clear that it should read “To the Lérins brothers.” On the island of Lérins is that monastery, or that community, which Saint Honoratus, bishop of Arles, founded there at the beginning of the fifth century and made illustrious by the holiness of its life. The monks of Lérins came several times to Saint Martin out of devotion, as is evident from Epistle 190 and from the following one. Alcuin also corresponded with them frequently; and he wished a copy of Epistle 90, concerning the various errors of the Spaniards, to be sent by the men of Lyons.

## TO THE BROTHERS OF LÉRINS

He recalls the reputation for their good conduct; commends himself to their prayers; and urges mutual charity and peace.

To the religious congregation of the most holy Father Honoratus, Alcuin the deacon sends greetings.

I greatly rejoice in the excellent reputation of your conduct, in your observance of the rule, and in the pious unity of peace, which we have heard testified to by our own brothers and by others. But hearing all good things about you more certainly through the report of these brothers, and as we desire, we therefore take greater care to commend my small self to your holy prayers, asking you to deign to remember our name, just as your father of blessed memory,

@ [Col. 0496D] Your venerable father—I do not know whether this was Teotgarius, to whom the following letter is addressed, or one of his predecessors—we believe once forgave me. We now strive to renew this through these letters and through the urging of these brothers, because, as I confess, we have great confidence, in the sweetness of our hearts, in the intercession of those who serve God. What I lack in merits, we hope by divine grace to possess through their prayers.

What is there that the devout unity of a holy congregation cannot obtain from him who says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew 18:20)? What is sweeter than always to have Christ present, than to be called sons of God, since Truth himself says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9)? Therefore it is entirely necessary for everyone, but especially for those living a regular life in the sacred order, to observe with every effort the good of concord and the unity of peace. For those who do not preserve the truth of holy peace will surely lose the dignity of sons. “See,” said the distinguished teacher, “if you bite one another, lest you consume one another” (Galatians 5:15).

A person who does not wish to embrace peace cannot rightly be called a son of God. Peace binds together the concord of brothers and the charity of neighbors. “My peace,” said the Lord, “I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27)—that is, “I left you in peace; in peace I will find you.” As he departed, he wished to give what he desired to find in all of them when he returned.

[Col. 0496C] I therefore speak to you more diligently concerning the goodness of this devout peace, dearest brothers, because the devil’s deceit is especially accustomed to shoot the arrow of murmuring among brothers, knowing that perfect charity is not present where the unity of charity is wounded by the weapon of murmuring. “Charity,” as Scripture says, “covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8), and without it sins are not forgiven. The blessed Apostle praised it so greatly that he declares that neither martyrdom, nor contempt of the world, nor the fires of flames is beneficial without its goodness. “For by this,” the Lord Jesus said, “everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).

Every obedience and every submission in humility in monasteries must be strengthened by the protection of charity. This must be done without the false outward display of pretense in the body; rather, we must love one another from the heart and show by our deeds what we have stored in the treasury of the heart. The person who strives to live among human beings in peaceful charity and holy love lives an angelic life on earth. What he begins to possess here in part, he will rejoice to possess fully in heavenly blessedness. This is the better part, which will not be taken away from the one who in this world intends with every effort to embrace Christ’s footsteps in the work of charity. May divine mercy deign to hear your holiness interceding for the Christian people, dearest brothers.

{280}

@ [Col. 0497D] In Froben, *Epistle*, 217.

## EPISTLE CCXXIII

@ [Col. 0497D] To Teotgarius, abbot. It is not sufficiently clear from this letter over which monastery Teotgarius was abbot. Since mention is made here of brothers who came to the monastery at Tours out of devotion and to commend themselves to the intercessions of Saint Martin, it is easy to infer that they were the monks of Lérins whom, in Epistle 212 (now 190), he said had come there a few days earlier; and that Teotgarius was abbot of Lérins. There is also mention of a certain abbot Teotgarius in the Life of Saint Eigil, abbot of Fulda, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, century IV, part I, p. 255, who took part in the dedication of the church at Fulda and the translation of the body of Saint Boniface in 819. But nothing else is said of him there apart from his name. See also book XXVIII of the *Benedictine Annals*, p. 454, no. 13.

## TO TEOTGARIUS THE ABBOT AND THE BROTHERS OVER WHOM HE SEEMS TO PRESIDE

He sends back with a letter brothers who had made a pilgrimage to Saint Martin; he asks pardon for their disobedience and negligence. He wishes those who have gone astray to be recalled, not rejected. [Col. 0497B]

To the most holy Father Teotgarius and to the whole family chosen by God and also blessed, Alcuin, servant of Saint Martin, together with the brothers serving God in his monastery, sends greetings of everlasting blessedness.

I sent words of greeting to your piety through your brother Sizimarius, and now, because of the opportunity provided by these brothers who have come to us, it seemed right and necessary to repeat the same words a second time. I therefore also took pains to send you this letter, because after the aforementioned brother’s departure I began to be afflicted by a severe fever.

For this reason I earnestly beg you to deign to help me in the most holy prayers of your unity, because I know that your religious holiness, devoted to God, has great power in prayer before the heavenly King [lacuna], Truth himself saying: “Whatever you ask, believing, you will receive” (Matthew 21:22). He said “believing,” because “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11:6). Therefore may Catholic integrity remain in your hearts, so that whatever you ask in the name of Jesus you may deserve to receive, whether for the stability of your life and perseverance in good works to the end, or for your friends who have faith in your goodness and charity. For “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8), and “the one who remains in charity remains in God, because God is charity” (1 John 4:16).

[Col. 0497D] In the holiness of this charity I have taken care to send these brothers of yours, and also ours, to your piety. They wished to visit the relics of Saint Martin for the sake of prayer; but they also told me, in strictest confidence, something about their disobedience or negligence, asking us, together with the piety of Saint Martin, to be intercessors for them so that they might be received again in their proper place.

I firmly instructed them to say nothing to anyone about the cause of their negligence, since I did not wish anything to go forth from your most holy congregation except what is best. For there are many who criticize our life rather than follow it, eager to conceal their own criminal sins by criticizing monastics. But whatever we do contrary to what the monastic rule prescribes should remain among us alone, be reconciled, and be brought back into concord, so that the enemies may not rejoice over us.

There is no person who does not sin. It is good to recall a wandering sheep to Christ’s fold, following the example of the one who descended from heaven to seek the lost sheep on earth.

The patience of superiors ought to be the salvation of those subject to them. It is better to forgive those who offend than to expel sinners, because if only the just and healthy remain, perhaps the shepherd alone will remain without a flock. But what if the shepherd himself sins? Who remains in the place consecrated to God?

We must remember the apostle John, who says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). But if we acknowledge that we are sinners and confess our iniquities, saying with the tax collector, “God, be merciful to me a sinner” (Luke 18:13), we have an advocate—that is, the Lord Jesus, our propitiator—with the Father. He gave himself for our sins (Titus 2:14), so that he might redeem us in his blood and acquire for God a people acceptable to him.

[Col. 0498C] Considering these things, dearest brothers, gather the wandering little sheep again with joy, remembering the mercy of the one who left the ninety-nine sheep in the mountains to find the one that had gone astray, placed it on his shoulders, and carried it back to his house of glory, so that the angels might rejoice over the sheep that had been found (Matthew 18:12; Luke 15:4).

Keeping all these things in mind, forgive, so that God may forgive you; for this is the way and the summit of the heavenly kingdom: either not to sin or to forgive those who sin. “Consider yourself,” the Apostle says, “lest you also be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:1–2).

May divine grace deign always to preserve you in the charity of obedience and humility, lord fathers, brothers, and sons.

{281}–283

@ [Col. 0498D] In Froben, *Epistle*, 220.

## EPISTLE CCXXIV. TO FRIDUIN

He congratulates him on having taken charge of the monasteries of Saints Benedict and Ceolfrid and urges him to preside over his flock by a good example. He commends himself to his prayers. [Col. 0498D]

To the most holy father,

@ [Col. 0498D] Friduin. Alcuin congratulates this old friend of his on having assumed the paternal care of Christ’s sheepfold, namely, the monasteries of Girwy and Wearmouth, belonging to Saints Benedict and Ceolfrid. Alcuin also wrote another letter to Eadbald, abbot of Girwy, a fragment of which we supplied from Rainer in the notes to Epistle 13 (now 14). I therefore believe that Friduin was Eadbald’s successor.

To Friduin, formerly known to me and always my friend, Alcuin sends greetings.

[Col. 0499A] On hearing that the paternal care of Christ’s sheepfold had been entrusted to you, I confess that I rejoiced greatly, both at the elevation to so great a dignity and at the opportunity for good work, because you now have the means by which you can make yourself equal to the holy fathers in name and merits.

Therefore, most holy father, take greater care to establish the regular life in this excellent place. We do not urge you to devise anything new, but to renew everything ancient in every way, because the founder and the renewer of the same work may receive the same reward before God. Do not seek a name for yourself through empty flatteries, but seek praise for God through holy admonitions. Live according to the examples of the holy fathers Benedict and Ceolfrid, so that, following their merits, you may be found worthy of their reward.

Do not in any way permit the vanities of clothing, excessive drunkenness, or lustful pleasures to rule either in you or among your brothers; rather, let everything among you be done with regular moderation in food, drink, clothing, and chastity. And just as you are first in dignity, so be first in the practice of every virtue. What will become of the flock if the shepherd goes astray? The flock’s health and growth are the shepherd’s glory and reward. Let bodily things not deceive you, but let spiritual things exalt you. Be a lamp in the house of God and, in every place, a model of salvation. Let the angels, visiting the church’s services and the works of fraternal unanimity, find you above all standing first, working first, and interceding first for the Christian people in every way. Let no special quantity of gold or silver deceive you; rather, let a general and holy way of life make you pleasing to God.

[Col. 0499C] Let the Church and its adornments be your treasure, not a private chest. Let your conscience not condemn you for possessing what you ought not to possess, lest it be said to you: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4:23). Or how will you teach others what you yourself do not do? An error in life closes the teacher’s mouth. It is better to have God in the chest of your heart than gold in the chest of your bedchamber. It is a disgrace to your life for your fingers to shine with gold and your neck to be adorned with silken garments (Latin *siricis*; F. *sericis*); let your breast be adorned with

[Col. 0499D] an orarium. That is, a stole. “It is called an orarium because it is granted to orators, that is, preachers. It admonishes the one who is clothed with it to remember that, under the yoke of Christ, which is light and easy, he has been established.” (Author of the book *On the Divine Offices*, among the spurious minor works attributed to Alcuin, chapter 39.) Let your breast be adorned with an orarium of holiness, not with the empty finery of clothing. It is better for the soul to be beautified with virtues than for the body to be adorned with colored garments.

Consider how few days remain to you, and with what enduring prosperity the first founders of the monastery [Col. 0500A] in which you now serve God lived in holy conduct; and how quickly those were taken from this life who in some measure were violating the statutes of the first parents. Remember how blessed are those who rejoice with God in heaven: they did not earn this by the luxury of life, the vanity of clothing, or the pomp of the world, but by zeal for the Lord, the observance of regular life, greater care for the soul than for the body, and loving concern for the progress of their brothers. Do what [F., “so that”] the honor of the present hour may profit you toward the glory of the time to come. I beg you always to remember me with the brothers, either in a particular prayer of your holiness or in the common fellowship of fraternal intercession, so that God may direct the course of my life toward salvation—not merely my own salvation, but, by the gift of Christ God, the salvation [Col. 0500B] of many. And may divine clemency, with all the brothers,

[Col. 0499D] with the most blessed apostles interceding. Namely, Peter and Paul, to whose honors the monasteries of Girovensis and Wirmuthensis, which Friduinus undertook to govern, were dedicated, as I noted in letters 13 and 219 (now 14 and 16). May the most blessed apostles intercede, and may divine clemency always cause you to advance in every good work and to await the final day in all holiness, so that you may be made worthy to stand before Christ’s tribunal and hear the blessed voice: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34).

[Col. 0499D] In Froben, letter 221.

## LETTER 225. TO THE BROTHERS WHO APPEAR TO SERVE GOD IN VARIOUS PLACES ON THE ISLAND OF IRELAND

[Col. 0499D] This letter is certainly an illustrious testimony to how greatly regular observance, the pursuit of wisdom, the purity of Catholic doctrine, and the zeal of apostolic preaching flourished in the monasteries of Ireland. Probus writes in the Life of Saint Patrick that Saint Patrick spread the faith and monastic life on that island around the year 430. Mabillon proves, from the testimony of the Venerable Bede, that afterward the Irish monks professed the same rule as the English monks, namely that of Saint Benedict. (*Preface to the Third Age of Benedict*, no. 16, and to the Fifth Age, nos. 82ff.)

He rejoices at the report of their excellent way of life that has reached him; he praises the good works that their predecessors once performed in Britain, Gaul, and Italy. He exhorts them to regular life and teaches what the life of rulers, monks, nuns, and all Christians ought to be. [Col. 0500C]

To the most noble sons of the holy Church who, throughout the breadth of the island of Ireland, appear to serve Christ God through a religious way of life and the pursuit of wisdom, the humble levite Alcuin sends greetings of perpetual prosperity in the Lord.

Having heard through the venerable brother,

[Col. 0500D] Dungal the bishop. I do not know who this Dungal was, or of what see he was bishop, unless he was that Dungal, the recluse or monk of Saint-Denis, who among other works wrote a book against Claudius of Turin in defense of the veneration of sacred images. He used to call himself *Peregrinus*, and at the beginning of that same book he testifies that he had come to this land—Gaul—long before. Mabillon conjectures in the work cited that he was Irish or Scottish, and his very name makes this plausible. (Mabillon, *Annals*, book 30, no. 3; *Literary History of France*, vol. 4, p. 493.) Having heard through Dungal the bishop that a religious and God-pleasing fellowship in regular life flourishes among you, I confess that I have rejoiced greatly, because the Lord Jesus is shown, at this ruinous end of the falling age, to possess so many praisers of his most holy name, preachers of the truth, and followers of holy wisdom as I hear the illustrious island of Ireland possesses to this day. Therefore, most excellent fathers, most religious brothers, and most noble sons, I entreat your devout unanimity with all the affection of my heart: strive to renew through constant admonitions, exhortations, and rebukes the ancient custom of holy religion and the pursuit of holy wisdom, so that the light of truth and knowledge may, according to its customary manner, shine most abundantly through you and from you across the congregations of Christ’s Churches and throughout the many regions of the world.

In ancient times, therefore, very learned teachers customarily came from Ireland to Britain, Gaul, and Italy and brought great progress to many of Christ’s Churches. And the more dangerous these times are now known to be, with very many being turned away from the way [Col. 0501B] of truth, according to the apostolic prophecy, the more earnestly the truth of the Catholic faith must be learned and taught everywhere among you, so that preachers of the orthodox faith may have the means to resist those who contradict the truth and openly defeat the adversaries of apostolic teaching. Pseudo-teachers suddenly break forth, seduced by apostate cunning, introducing new and unheard-of sects. While they think that they acquire praise for themselves through new doctrines, they are found blameworthy and hateful to everyone, as we have seen happen in the regions of Spain.

Therefore, most holy fathers, exhort your young men to learn with the greatest diligence the traditions of Catholic teachers and to strive with their whole mind to grasp the principles of the Catholic faith, because “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11:6). Yet the knowledge of secular letters must not be despised. Rather, grammar and the other disciplines of philosophical subtlety should be handed on, as a foundation, to tender childhood, so that by certain steps of wisdom they may be able to ascend to the highest summit of evangelical perfection, and so that, as their years increase, the riches of wisdom may also increase. Do not allow the ardent flame of youth to fall headlong into the precipices of vice, because the Holy Spirit, as it is written, does not dwell in a body subject to sins (Wisdom 1:4–5). Without his grace, human understanding can accomplish nothing of lasting worth. But if a young man appears to possess some gift, it will be taken away from him if he does not take care to preserve himself in chastity. The serene, holy, and most pure Spirit [Col. 0501D] enters a pure and chaste soul. Let the elders admonish their juniors not only with words but also instruct them by good examples. The teacher’s authority is diminished if his teaching is destroyed by his conduct; the teacher’s wisdom should shine in the uprightness of his morals, so that what is heard from his mouth may be seen in his deeds.

If, God forbid, secular rulers are found among you acting against the authority of the Christian religion, let the priests, through diligent preaching, admonish them to abandon evil customs, to adorn their authority with good morals, and to live in chastity, having one wife according to the command of evangelical authority. Let them distinguish the people’s cases by the most just judgment and show mercy to the poor and afflicted. Let them not be quick to [Col. 0502A] shed human blood, because, as the sacred Psalm sings, “men of blood shall not live out half their days” (Psalm 54:24). If they wish to possess the happiness of the present kingdom and authority, let them know that they cannot have it except by God’s granting it; nor can they possess the glory of future blessedness except by the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ giving it. Therefore, let them cling with their whole mind to the evangelical commandments, so that they may be strengthened by divine blessing in the present kingdom and be found worthy to receive with God’s saints the everlasting kingdom.

But whoever has promised to serve God in the conduct of monastic life should know that he is bound to fulfill what he promised, as Scripture says: “Vow and pay your vows to the Lord your God” (Ecclesiastes 5:3). And again: “It is better not to vow than not to fulfill one’s vow.” Let their conduct be chaste and honorable, without any reproach, pleasing to God and honorable among men—not in feasting [286] and drunkenness, not in bedrooms and indecencies (Romans 13:13), but let them clothe themselves with the examples of our Lord Jesus Christ, shining among secular people like stars gleaming in the sky, so that many, illumined by their light, may be encouraged to flee the pleasures of this world and strive to join themselves to their number.

Let women’s monasteries serve God in virginal chastity, with chaste bodies, modesty, and humility. If they have chosen [manuscript: “would choose”] the heavenly King as their bridegroom, let them strive to preserve the chastity owed to their heavenly spouse, so that with the most blessed Mother of God, the ever-virgin holy Mary, they may deserve to follow the Lamb through the heavenly dwellings wherever he goes.

Let everyone alike [*communiter*] strive to preserve the precepts of holy love in complete perfection, in which Christ God established the sign of discipleship, saying: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). Let each person have humility in learning, devotion in teaching, and diligence in works of mercy toward the poor and afflicted. Let no one—elder or younger, secular or monastic, man or woman—be ashamed to confess sins and correct through penance whatever he or she has done against [Col. 0502D] God’s will. It is better to have one human witness of one’s sins for the salvation of one’s soul than to await the accusation of diabolical fraud before the Judge of all ages, before the choirs of angels, and before the multitude of the whole human race. While a person lives in this world, confession and penance are fruitful; at the future judgment, there will indeed be penance for sinners, but it will not be fruitful, because each person will be judged according to his works. Let criminals and those burdened with sins fear the eternal flames of punishment. Let the righteous—and penitents as well—rejoice in the glory of perpetual blessedness with Christ, who says: “The wicked will go into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46). And elsewhere: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew [Col. 0503A] 13:43). May Christ God graciously preserve your blessedness, which prays for us, in perpetual prosperity, most beloved fathers, sons, and friends.

{288}

[Col. 0503C] Froben, letter 217.

## LETTER 226

[Col. 0503C] To the brothers of Saint John the Baptist. That is, to the brothers of the Monastery of Mount Olive, whose founder and first rector was Olomundus or Olemundus. It was once called the Monastery of Saint John the Baptist of Castro-Malasti, in the diocese of Carcassonne, situated in Vallesecura on the bank of the River Duran—the Durance. It is now known only under the name Mount Olive (Montoliou), and it still survives, after various vicissitudes, under the celebrated Benedictine Congregation of Saint Maur. (Mabillon, *Annals*, book 25, p. 251, no. 6.) TO THE BROTHERS SERVING GOD IN THE CHURCH OF BLESSED JOHN THE BAPTIST. He receives the abbot and brothers of the Monastery of Mount Olive into his friendship and exhorts them to fight for the Catholic faith and persevere in regular observance.

To the religious brothers serving God and Saint John, the forerunner of Christ, the humble servant of that same Christ and his forerunner, Alcuin, sends greetings.

For the first congregation that, by God’s providence, I received to govern was consecrated to blessed John the Baptist.

[Col. 0503D]

[This congregation, which Alcuin first undertook to govern, might be thought to have been a coastal cell situated in the province of Northumbria, indeed on headlands near the Ocean Sea and the River Humber, where Saint Wilgisius, father of Saint Willibrord, was buried. Alcuin himself testifies that he received this cell to govern through legitimate succession in the prose Life of that same Saint Willibrord, chapter 1. Yet this opinion seems to be opposed by the fact that Alcuin testifies that that monastery had been consecrated under the patronage [Col. 0504C] of the most blessed Virgin Mary, in the elegy on that same Saint Wilgisius, near the end, in these verses:

“The brothers took care to bury the body in a church

Which stands built near the shores of the sea,

And, consecrated to the most illustrious Mother of God,

Shines forth in your name, Virgin Mary.”

But perhaps that same cell also honored Saint John the Baptist as its patron; for it is very common for the same place to have several holy patrons. Therefore, I think it right to acknowledge you as brothers and fellow-soldiers [Col. 0503B], having one Lord God and one patron, whose intercession may graciously increase our number on both sides. Your father,
