[Col. 0504D] Olomundus. Concerning him, see note b above; he is said to have died in the year 827, on the third day before the Ides of December, according to Mabillon, *Annals*, book 30, no. 21. We have received your father Olomundus in Christ, and our brother in love, with familiar affection, as a kinsman of one household, a worshiper of one Lord, and a fellow servant of one protector. In him I receive all of you as most beloved brothers, asking that you graciously receive me and mine through his hands into your holy prayers. You know very well how great is the communion of true love, which makes those absent in body present in spirit. Bodily absence does no harm where there is spiritual presence.

But you, sons, brothers, and fathers, I beseech you in the clemency of Christ: be united in the Catholic faith, thinking the same thing and willing the same thing. Stand firm in the place of your contest, fearing none of the weapons of the ancient enemy; fight against him with united hands. A soldier fights better in battle with many than if he is found alone outside in the field. By the field I mean the breadth of the world. What have you to do with worldly custom? You have chosen Christ; you have bound yourselves to fight for Christ, persevering in the contest of regular life. Let none of God’s commandments seem harsh to you. Console yourselves with the hope of perpetual reward, knowing that no one is crowned unless he competes lawfully [Col. 0504A] (2 Timothy 2:5). He does not compete lawfully who abandons the place of his contest and lays down the standards of his service. This life is a time of trial. Be strong in trials, steadfast in tribulations, doubting nothing about your reward. The days of labor are few, but the days of recompense are everlasting. Do not be disturbed by your small number, for our leader himself says: “Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32).

Serve God in the profession of regular life, without murmuring or weariness. God the rewarder will never be lacking if your devotion in his service is not lacking. If your devout father wishes to alter or renew something in your congregation—“of your congregation” in the manuscript—do not murmur about it. For just as the very wise bee gathers one sweetness from many flowers, so a prudent father should gather from the conduct of many a single honey of excellent religion. No one field contains every kind of flower; likewise, in no single person can every excellence of character be found. One person abounds in love, another shines with humility, another gleams through almsgiving, another is distinguished by wisdom, and another rejoices in knowledge of the Holy Scriptures. Therefore, a wise person should choose particular things from particular people, so that the splendor of a single crown may be formed in the soul that possesses God, who apportions to each according to the measure of his will or the capacity of the recipient. “Test everything; hold fast what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21)—that is, consider many things and choose whatever is best.

[Col. 0504C] I wish, and I beseech God, that your number may increase and that you may always flourish in holy virtues, so that many may be instructed by your good examples [289] and you may be deemed worthy of a great reward in the sight of the Most High Judge, with blessed John interceding and Christ God showing mercy and granting it. May heavenly grace raise you up and cause you to advance in every good work, most beloved brothers.

[Col. 0504D] Froben, letter 224.

## LETTER 227

[Col. 0504D] There is no indication of the monastery or congregation whose brothers received this letter. Yet all monks should regard as belonging and addressed to themselves the excellent teachings, abundantly scattered by Alcuin here and elsewhere, concerning mutual love, humility, obedience, diligent care for divine praise, regular discipline, and so forth. TO CERTAIN MONKS. He seeks their friendship and prayers. He exhorts them to love, humility, obedience, care for regular discipline, and divine praise.

[Col. 0505A] To the venerable father and the most holy brothers in the congregation of the most blessed confessor of Christ, the humble levite Albinus sends greetings.

I rejoiced to hear of the prosperity of your blessedness, of your religious life, worthy of God and praiseworthy among men. Therefore I commend the name of my littleness more earnestly to your holy prayers, so that you may regard me as one of yourselves. I, a sinner, greatly in need of the intercession of the saints, knowing how powerful are the prayers of the righteous according to the testimony of the Apostle James, place no confidence in my own merits but commend myself entirely to divine grace through the intercession of Christ’s servants. Although, because my sins hinder me, I am not worthy to be counted among them, nevertheless, by God’s mercy, I know how to love them in God and render them due honor [The manuscript is corrupt here]. Therefore I earnestly beg you to receive me with the love with which I humbly ask you. For love is kind; the whole life of God’s servants consists in it. Your unanimity possesses it most excellently, as I hear, and whoever is worthy to possess it will have eternal life through it. Follow it with your whole heart, most beloved brothers, because the whole life of monks consists in love, humility, and obedience. Since your piety has chosen God as its lord and king, love God with all your strength and strive to obey his commandments. Let each person be the other’s teacher in good works, and let each person be the other’s disciple in humble obedience, as the Apostle says: “If something is revealed to one who is sitting, let the first be silent” (1 Corinthians 14:30). [Col. 0505C] “The Spirit blows where it wills” (John 3:8). It is God’s gift if anyone understands rightly or loves justly; God’s gift must be despised in neither age nor person.

Let the elders among you instruct the younger, so that they may be deemed worthy [Forte, “worthy”] to stand in their proper place. Teach them with all gentleness, instructing them in the fear of God, so that they may learn from their earliest years to serve God and be formed by the regular precepts. Let the younger render due honor to the elders. For you are like one body, each a member of the other, so that God may be honored in all things (Romans 12:5), all may be built up, and all may deserve to attain the glory of everlasting blessedness (1 Peter 4:11).

I have written these few little letters to you from the fountain of love, not as to people who are ignorant of these things, but as to those who know them better and practice them more diligently in God. I have also written so that you may know my will regarding your salvation—and indeed that of all God’s servants—and so that you may know the familiarity of my soul with you. May your goodness, in fraternal humility, read and receive with your customary devotion what I have taken care to write to you. May God, the Father of all consolation, graciously console you everywhere [Col. 0506A] and grant you to reach the eternal kingdom, whose praise should always be in the mouth and heart of your love. For this is the life of the saints: praise of Christ’s goodness and love in his presence. This never exceeds [Forte, “falls away”], never passes, and never grows weary. Whoever is more frequently occupied with these things in this mortal life bears a greater likeness to the holy angels. The angels of God always praise God in vigils; and whoever strives to keep vigil for the praises of God leads an angelic life on earth, performing on earth, according to the times appointed for human frailty, what all the saints will do in heaven. Let neither sleep, nor worldly desire, nor vain thought impede the course of your religious life and your divine praises, so that angelic visitations may find each one of you standing in his place and praising God. Therefore, those who strive to praise God in this mortality will go with the Psalmist into everlasting happiness and sing: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm 83:5).

May the Lord God cause your holy unanimity, most beloved brothers, to advance in every good thing and grant you to reach the happiness of eternal blessedness, most beloved brothers.

[Col. 0505D] Froben, letter 225.

## LETTER 228. TO ABBOT ARNOLD

He praises their way of life and exhorts them to religious virtues, especially poverty in banquets, money, clothing, and so forth.

[Col. 0506C] To the venerable father,

[Col. 0505D] Arnold, abbot. I have not discovered which monastery he belonged to. He cannot be the same as Arnulfus, abbot of the monastery of Glonn and of Saint Florentius on the Loire in the diocese of Angers, who was employed as a companion and assistant to Saint Benedict of Aniane in the reform of monasteries, as Louis Augustus testifies in the diploma he prepared concerning the restored monastic order in the monastery of Saint-Denis. See Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, Fourth Age, p. 218. For this Arnulfus could not have assumed governance of that monastery before the year 800, in which year Albaldus, abbot of that place, whom Arnulfus succeeded, was still alive. Mabillon, cited above. To Abbot Arnold and the holy congregation, the humble levite Albinus sends greetings.

Your religious conduct in the Lord pleased me greatly, as did your humility in love, the adornment of the Church, the arrangement of the buildings that I saw in passing, and the very sweet welcome with which you received me in great friendship. I recognized that he who said the following had a dwelling prepared in your hearts: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). Therefore, with humble entreaty, I exhort your brotherhood to remain faithfully in perfect love, so that the harmony of peace may flourish among you, the beauty of obedience may shine in your conduct, [Col. 0506D] the dignity of humility may be seen in all your actions, and bodily chastity may bloom like lilies in the sight of God. Be united in every perfect work, obedient to your spiritual father without any contradiction, because he will have to render an account for you on the great day of the Lord, and you likewise will receive a very great reward on that day for your obedience.

“The kingdom of God is not food and drink” (Romans 14:17), but love in a pure conscience. These, then, are the sacrifices [Col. 0507A] that monks ought to offer to the Lord God at every hour; by these offerings the divine majesty will be appeased; through these paths the gates of the heavenly kingdom are opened. Think on this continually; always remember it; live amid these delights [291]. These are the wedding garments in which you may be made worthy to possess the banquets of the heavenly King. Let none of you pursue avarice or seek to gather passing riches. Let no one possess even a single coin without his father’s permission. Let the joy of common life suffice for each person, whether in clothing or in the religious moderation of food and drink. Only let the spiritual father take care that no one has just cause for murmuring. Let no shortage of any kind destroy the order of regular life; rather, let each person be content, according to the means of the place and time, with the allowance administered to him, and the more humbly he bears want, should it suddenly arise, the greater reward let him receive from God. Whoever desires to fight for the kingdom of God ought not to quarrel over a single cup of wine. The most noble Creator and Father of all wishes to have noble sons. It is a great nobility to be a son of God, but this dignity, so lofty and excellent, must be guarded by great nobility of character and conduct.

What I have written under the compulsion of love, may your humility graciously read with patience. If you find anything worthy of remembrance in these letters of mine, store it in the treasury [Col. 0507C] of your heart for the sake of your salvation and in remembrance of our name, so that divine piety may lead you into the joy of heavenly blessedness and, through your holy prayers, grant me, a sinner, forgiveness of my sins. May the piety of the heavenly King cause your holiness to advance in every good conduct, most beloved brothers.

[Col. 0507D] Froben, letter 226.

## LETTER 229. TO THE PRIEST EANULF

He commends himself to his prayers and exhorts him to fraternal conduct, regular life, care of souls, and so forth.

To the most beloved brother

[Col. 0507D] Eanulf the priest. Nothing else is known about him. From this letter, however, we learn that he was a monk, perhaps in England, and a priest among the monks, entrusted with the public duty of teaching and sowing the word of God. To Eanulf the priest, Albinus sends greetings.

Because love remembers every good thing, I beg you to remember me in your holy prayers and strive to preserve yourself in all chastity [Col. 0507D] in the sight of the Lord God Most High. Maintain humble conduct among the brothers and great concern for regular life, because whoever bears the greater judgment receives the greater honor [Read: “because he bears the greater judgment, who …”]. What is worldly dignity to you, which falls like the flower of hay? I do not want you to wander from place to place, but to remain steadfast in the service of God, in which you were chosen for the service of Christ. Live among the brothers like Lucifer among the stars, so that many may be encouraged by your good examples. Just as I have cared for the salvation of your soul, [Col. 0508A] so care for the salvation of many. Do not despair of the log snatched from the fire, but let it be extinguished in the fountain of penance, so that he who burned in the flame of lust may shine in the flame of love and purity in the sight of God. You know the frailties of youth; you know the river of iniquity, how many are swept through precipices into the abysses of various lusts. Therefore, work with an attentive mind, with God’s help, to recall as many as possible from the error of iniquity through your sweetest admonitions. You will have the greatest reward with God if you do not neglect the salvation of your brothers.

Many are teachers in name, but few are devoted to the office of love. Do not cease to sow the word of God; God knows where he wishes it to fall. His goodness will never be lacking to you in reward. “Whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way [Col. 0508B] covers a multitude of his sins” (James 5:20). May you live among the brothers in gentleness of patience [292], humility of obedience, and sweetness of love, so that the mercy of our Redeemer may cause you to flourish in a variety of virtues and graciously preserve you from every adversity.

I beg you to greet all our brothers whom you know to be joined to me by some bond of love, and always remind, concerning my prayers, all whom you have as friends, whether God-fearing people or companions in holy conduct. Live in all love, and fare well forever.

[Col. 0508D] Froben, letter 227.

## LETTER 230. TO THE PRIEST ONIA

He says that love is sweet in the present and bitter in absence. He exhorts him to virtues. [Col. 0508C]

Albinus

[Col. 0508D] To Onia the priest. This is undoubtedly the same Onias to whom Alcuin dedicated, together with Nathanael and Candidus, his Commentary on Ecclesiastes; we have also recorded certain things about him elsewhere. To Onia the priest, greetings.

It is remarkable that what was sweet has been turned into bitterness. For love is sweet in the presence of the beloved, but in a certain way extreme [Forte, “bitter”] in absence, when one does not see the person one loves and is distressed by that person’s absence. In the blessed and in the kingdom of God, however, it will always be sweet, because the beloved is present to the one who loves him; the vision of him is complete blessedness. To deserve to reach that blessedness, all the harsh things of this life should be regarded as sweet through the gift of patience, and all the sweet things of this world should be reckoned as nothing.

Remembering this, my dearest son, live happily under the fear of God, in the love of Christ, in all sobriety, chastity, [Col. 0508D] and love, advancing day by day in every good work, so that you may be made worthy to attain that love which will never change and will never have an end. Live happily in the love of Christ and in every holy religion, my dearest son.

[Col. 0508D] In Froben, letter 228.

## LETTER 231. TO THE SAME

He commends love toward God and toward the poor, afflicted, and pilgrims.

Albinus sends greetings to Onia the priest.

[Col. 0509A] I confess that the prosperity and joy of your soul greatly please me. Love, as the Apostle says, never falls away (1 Corinthians 13:8); it is always new and ancient—new through presence, ancient through memory. May you always faithfully follow it with every person, as far as lies within you and insofar as it may appear honorable and useful for God’s honor. It is not love that is maintained in drunkenness or glued together in partnership with sins, but an impious will, not a good sweetness. Always love God, who loves the one who loves him and cherishes the one who cherishes him. Have as a friend the one who is a friend to everyone according to his own nature. Remember the poor in almsgiving, the afflicted in defense, and pilgrims in consolation, so that God may repay you on the great day, when he will divide the whole human race into two portions: [Col. 0509B] for some, because of hardness of heart, unfailing flames of torment; for others, because of works of mercy and acts of love, the kingdom of perpetual blessedness. By doing this, live happily, my dearest son.

{293}

@ In Froben, letter 229.

## LETTER 232. TO GISLA

He makes his love for her known, exhorts her to every kind of virtue, and commends the reading of Holy Scripture.

To the most beloved virgin in Christ,

[Col. 0509C] Gisla. Whether she was the sister or daughter of Charlemagne, or some other virgin of great nobility, is uncertain. To Gisla, Alcuin, the humble levite, sends greetings.

I rejoiced greatly at your conversation, most illustrious servant of God, and was comforted by the devotion of your friendship, so that from the day on which I entered into a pact of love with you, I was nourished almost every moment by the sweetness of your affection, considering myself happy while, according to your promise, I enjoyed the protection of your most holy prayer. But now, more than ever, I need to be fortified by the constant protection of your prayers, while I am compelled to attempt the uncertain course of a sea tossed by waves [Manuscript: “to test”], so that divine clemency may graciously lead me to the harbor of salvation and grant me to stand again, rejoicing, in your presence. But I humbly beg you, most devoted virgin of God, not to let the pointed words of my foolishness offend the ears of your prudence. Let holy humility teach you to read through what true affection urges me to write; do not consider my style presumptuous, recognizing it as dutiful; and she receives as an admonisher the one whom she loves in God [F., “may she receive”].

[Col. 0509D] First of all I admonish you concerning the love of God: preserve the nobility of his image, and always remember whose bride you have begun to be. Your bridegroom is exceedingly renowned and glorious; he seeks no other adornment in you except the spiritual kind—not twisted bindings of hair, but upright bonds of good conduct; not the outward, empty brilliance of garments, but the noble inward radiance of holiness and chastity. Beware lest he find anything in you that offends his eyes. And if perhaps—as the condition of human frailty commonly brings about—the malicious spirit should imprint some stain of negligence upon you, remember to wash it away quickly with tears of repentance, [Col. 0510A] lest you remain long without your bridegroom’s embrace, for he is readier to receive you than to lose you—only do not delay returning to him from day to day. For he especially hates these two evils in human beings: negligence in returning, and despair of the one who saves. Let these two things be far removed from our thoughts, and then he will be near to our souls. Therefore he bears the name “Savior,” because he always saves and desires to save, as it is written: “Who desires all human beings to be saved” (1 Tim. 2:4).

Do not glory in earthly nobility, but give thanks to him who, when he willed you to be human, granted you parents so exalted and illustrious. Follow their nobility not with pride but with humility; and rejoice especially in this, that he did not wish you to be the bride of another, but of himself. What greater glory or higher honor could there be for you than to be the bride of that King who is above all kings? And inasmuch as he is higher in power and excellence, so much more diligent must you be in holiness. Holiness consists in works of righteousness, and righteousness is fulfilled in two ways: namely, that we do not do what God has forbidden, and that we do what he has commanded, according to the Prophet: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 33:15).

I consider it superfluous to write to your wisdom about these matters, because in both you have been more abundantly instructed from your earliest age by the best and noblest teachers, and your excellent natural intelligence teaches you everywhere. Moreover, the entire sequence of the holy books chiefly declares this to your ears and repeats it again and again: what every human being must avoid or pursue. Exercise yourself in reading them, for through them God himself, our Lord, speaks to you and shows you the effect of his gracious will. Recognize and consider with what honor his embassy to us must be esteemed. If an embassy and a letter from a king came to you, would you not immediately set aside other concerns, receive and read his letter eagerly and with complete devotion, and hasten to fulfill it? Behold, from heaven the King of kings, indeed your Bridegroom, has deigned to send you, O virgin, his letters through prophets, apostles, and teachers [Ms., “apostolic teachers”]—not entrusting you with some service necessary to himself, but making known what he knew to be necessary for your salvation and glory. Let diligent reading of these letters refresh you, because in them God is recognized; in them the glory of eternal life is announced; in them it is shown what we must believe, hope for, love, and flee.

I have written these things not to instruct one who is ignorant, but to fulfill the duty of charity. Above all, I ask that you preserve yourself undefiled for the day of our Lord Jesus Christ; and that with your whole attention you draw others along with you by admonitions or examples, and run after him accompanied by many, until he brings you into his Father’s house and into the chamber of his mother (Song 3:4), so that you may eat and drink at his table in his kingdom (Luke 22:30), where there is food without disgust, drink without thirst, life without [Col. 0511A] death, joy without sadness, and glory without end. Hasten there, O virgin, so that, always joined to the holy Virgin Mother, you may follow the Lamb through all the inner sanctuaries of the heavenly kingdom. May Christ God deign to preserve and hear your holiness, flourishing in every good work and interceding for me, lady virgin.

{294}–297. FRAGMENT I.

@ [Col. 0511B] D. Quercetanus was unaware of this letter. TO THE BROTHERS OF SAINT NINIAN AT CANDIDA CASA. (In Usserius, *On the Origins of the British Churches*, p. 669.)

To the brothers of venerable affection serving God in the place called

@ [Col. 0511B] Candida Casa. Concerning the location of this place and the etymology of its name, Venerable Bede says the following in *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, book III, chapter 4: “That place, belonging to the province of the Bernicians, is commonly called Candida Casa, because there he built a church of stone, in a manner unusual among the Britons.” And Polydore Vergil, *History of England*, book I, p. 6, no. 10: “Toward the northern coast, near Ireland, lies Nithsdale . . . To the south it adjoins Galloway, better for pasture than for grain; there is Candida Casa, and a very ancient church dedicated to the blessed Ninian and adorned with an episcopal see.” Alcuin the deacon sends greetings to Candida Casa.

I beseech the unanimity of your piety to remember my name and to deign to intercede for my smallness in the church of the most holy Father [Col. 0511B]

@ [Col. 0511C] Bishop Ninian. Venerable Bede likewise calls him Ninia; William of Malmesbury, Nina; others, Ninus or Ninianus. He was the apostle of the Picts, whose land is now thought to be held by the Scots. A critical-historical account of his life is found in the *Acts of the Saints*, September, vol. V, Antwerp edition, pp. 318 ff. Of Bishop Ninian, who shone with many virtues, as has recently been reported to me through

@ [Col. 0512B] Poems. Would that those poems had reached us—as the Antwerp commentator rightly wishes! Since their author lived closer to the age of Saint Ninian, we would possess more reliable documents for illuminating his deeds. For what now survives supplies only uncertain knowledge of the acts of the holy bishop. The poems, written in metrical art, were sent to us through our faithful disciples, the scholars of the church of York. In them I recognized both the learning of their author and the holiness of the one who performed the miracles, from what I read there.

FRAGMENT II. TO THE PEOPLE OF YORK. (In William of Malmesbury, book I of *The Deeds of the Kings of England*, chapter 3.)

“I did not come to Francia out of greed for gold—the one who knows my heart is my witness—nor did I remain there for that reason, but because of ecclesiastical necessity.”

FRAGMENT III. TO OSBERT, PATRICIAN OF THE MERCIANS. (In the same author, at the place cited.)

“Our kingdom of the Northumbrians almost perished because of internal dissensions and false oaths.”

FRAGMENT IV. TO THE SAME OSBERT, PATRICIAN. (In the same author, at the place cited, chapter 4.) [Col. 0512B]

“I do not think that the most noble young man Ecgfrith died because of his sins, but because his father shed much blood for the consolidation of the kingdom.”

@ [Col. 0512B] See above, letter 63, among the notes. The remaining fragments of Alcuin’s letters, which the distinguished Quercetanus added from Malmesbury at the end of his collection, ought to be omitted here, because some letters whose fragments they were have already been given above in full; the rest we have inserted among the notes to other letters.

ALPHABETICAL LIST OF THE PERSONS TO WHOM BLESSED FLACCUS ALCUIN ADDRESSED HIS LETTERS

[Col. 0511C]

To Adalhard, abbot of Corbie. See Antony. To Adrian I, pope. Letter 18. To Æthelbert, bishop of Hexham. Letter 178. To Æthelhard, archbishop of Canterbury. Letters 10, 57, 75, 77, 78, 114. To Æthelred, king of Northumbria. Letters 11, 12, 13. [Col. 0511D] To Æthelthryth, queen. Letter 199. To Eardwulf, king of Northumbria. Letter 60. To Aérico, duke of Friuli. Letter 1. To Æthelred. See Æthelhard. To Agino, bishop of an uncertain see. Letter 31. To Alchard, bishop, perhaps of the church of Elmham in England. Letter 217. {302} To Altapetra, priest. Letter 182. To friends. THE SECOND PART OF THE WORKS OF BLESSED FLACCUS ALBINUS, OR ALCUIN, TEACHER OF CHARLEMAGNE: EXEGETICAL OPUSCULA, OR COMMENTARIES ON SACRED SCRIPTURE

{304} FIRST OPUSCULUM

[Col. 0515C] In Vatican manuscript codex 289 the title of this opusculum is *Albinus’s Little Questions on Genesis*.

QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS ON GENESIS

PRELIMINARY NOTICE

[Col. 0515A]

We have said a few things about Siguulf, or Sigulf, whose questions Alcuin answers here, in the general preface, where the other disciples of Alcuin are also discussed. From the letter to Sigulf prefixed to this commentary, the reader will understand the reason, purpose, and method of raising, treating, and resolving these questions from the book of Genesis; from that letter it is likewise clear that Alcuin is the true author of this opusculum. Nevertheless, some time was spent in doubt concerning the final question, which concerns the blessings of the patriarchs, as to whether it should or could be attributed to Alcuin. Since that question is developed at much greater length than the others and is examined according to both the historical and the spiritual sense, and since in certain manuscript codices it is separated from the rest of the work and written under its own title, it came to appear under another name—now that of Saint Augustine, now that of Eucherius,

@ [Col. 0516C] Eucherius, *On Genesis*, book III, pp. 183–188, Lyons. Now it appeared under the name of others as well. [Col. 0515B] The most recent Benedictine editors of the works of Saint Augustine, of the Maurist Congregation, however, rejected the same commentary to the appendix of volume III of the works as a work falsely attributed to this holy Father and restored it to its true author, Alcuin. See above, letter 143 (now 187), and its notes. Alcuin himself borrowed almost the whole of the earlier part of that commentary, which is more literal and historical, from Saint Jerome’s *Questions on Genesis*, and the final part from the books of Saint Gregory the Great’s *Moralia*, as we have noted in their proper places. From the Augustinian edition we have added at the end whatever is lacking elsewhere.

The first person known to us to have published these *Questions and Answers on Genesis* was Menardus Moltherus, in 1525, in octavo at Haguenau; they appeared there again in 1529, in the same format, under the following title: *Questions on Genesis by Albinus, once tutor of that Charlemagne*. Moltherus prefixed to his edition a dedicatory letter to the distinguished man Lord Laurentius [Col. 0515C] Truchsess of Bomersfelden, dean of the holy Church of Mainz. Because that edition is rare, it will be worthwhile to transcribe here what concerns both the commentary and its author.

“It seemed to me not inappropriate,” says the learned editor, “to send you, whose intelligence is capable and always ready, Albinus’s *Questions on Genesis*, so that you might understand how far from that ancient simplicity of learning our age has fallen in the case of certain men who carry and twist the simple sense of sacred Scripture here and there, up and down, as though by the stormy force of the south wind. Nor is there any need for me to commend the author: antiquity and his position commend him, for he was the teacher of that Charlemagne in the liberal disciplines . . . When distinguished men for their piety and courtesy, Johannes Enolfus, dean, and Pancratius Thiel, scholasticus of the royal church of Saint Cyriacus near Worms in the land of the Vangiones, had lent me this copy—for it belongs to the library of that church—I did not wish, like a greedy moneylender, to lock away the ancient coin . . . I could point out from certain writers entire passages taken from here; but I would not wish this to be understood as though I meant to criticize their diligence or strip a crow of the feathers with which it has been adorned, but so that we may acknowledge as utterly true what that man said: that nothing has now been said which was not said before. Accordingly, nothing is written with such precision that those ancient men, men certainly of keen judgment, did not polish and refine it with the most exact discernment and the final files of criticism.” Thus Moltherus.

From this praised Moltherian edition the work was included in the catalogue of certain ancient theologians entitled ΜΙΚΡΟΠΡΕΣΒΥΤΙΚΟΝ [*Mikropresbytikón*, “Little Presbytery”], published at Basel in 1550, where it appears on pp. 445 ff. Five years later it was inserted in the same city into the *Orthodoxographia of the Ancient Holy Fathers*. Later Magarinus de la Bigne arranged for it to be included in volume IX of the Paris edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* of 1579; finally, the distinguished Andreas Quercetanus, using the manuscripts of the most distinguished Thuanus and the Putean brothers, produced a more accurate and expanded text.

In this edition we have had before us two manuscripts of excellent quality, from the ninth century, preserved in our library of Saint Emmeram. With their assistance, variant readings have been noted, many errors of earlier editions have been removed, and not a few lacunae have been filled. We have enclosed variant readings and supplied material in brackets in the text.

{305}

PREFACE OF ALCUIN

[Col. 0516C]

Alcuin sends greetings to his most beloved brother in Christ, the priest Singuulf.

Because, dearest brother, you have been my inseparable and faithful companion for so long [Al., “so greatly”], and because I know you to be exceedingly devoted to sacred reading, I have gathered together and dedicated to your name a few questions from the book of Genesis which, as I remember, you asked me from time to time, so that you might have something with which to refresh your memory. Memory often loses what it ought to preserve unless it keeps it stored in the treasury of letters—especially in our case, since we are distracted by the occupations of the world and wearied by the various hardships of travel. And because (*quod*; Ms., *quia*) the weight of books cannot be carried with us, we must sometimes cultivate brevity, so that the precious pearl of wisdom may have little weight and the traveler weary from the road may have something with which to refresh himself, without burdening the hand of its bearer with the weight.

There are many exceedingly difficult questions in that same book which I have not wished, or perhaps have not been permitted, to touch upon at present—or because you did not ask me about them. Those questions are chiefly historical and content with a simple answer; the others require greater inquiry and a longer treatment [Col. 0517B] [Manuscript codex: “and require a longer treatment”]. Be content with these alone, dearest brother. And if I have said anything incorrectly in them, strive to correct us, brother [Ms., “with fraternal writing”]; but if anything is correct, give thanks not to me but to the giver, who by his gifts makes you advance and makes me sufficient for you—without whom we can do nothing, but in whom all things are possible for the believer. May he cause us to multiply, to the praise and glory of his name, the bounty of his money entrusted to us by him.

Question 1. How is it consistent that Genesis says, “God rested on the seventh day from all his works” (Gen. 2:2), while the Gospel says, “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17)?

Answer. He rested from the creation of new things

@ [Col. 0517D] The words “and creation” are omitted in the manuscript codices. —and from the creation of creatures, not from the governance of those already created. Therefore God is to be regarded then as Creator in the creation of the world during six days, but now as Governor in all the creatures [Ms., “natures”] of the world.

Question 2. How many rational creatures [Ms., “reasonable creatures”] did God create?

Answer. Two: angels and human beings—the heavens as a dwelling for angels, and the earth as a dwelling for human beings.

Question 3. Why is the sin of the angel concealed in silence in Genesis, while that of the human being is disclosed?

Answer. Because God did not predestine the angelic wound to be healed, but he predestined the human wound to be healed.

Question 4. Why was the sin of the highest angel incurable, while that of the human being was curable?

Answer. [Because] the angel was the originator of his own crime, whereas the human being was deceived by another’s fraud [Col. 0517D] [“was” supplied]. Moreover, the higher the angel was in glory, the greater was his fall; but the more fragile the human being was by nature, the easier was forgiveness.

Question 5. Why was the human being created as the author of his own power?

Answer. So that he himself might be the author of his own life [supplied “or”] or death. But if he had been subject to necessity [Ms., “necessity”], he would possess neither the glory of a good work nor punishment for an evil one; he would be like one of the animals.

Question 6. Why, then, were the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil created in paradise?

Answer. So that through the one the human being might be immortal, and through the other mortal. He used the tree of life as a kind of medicine, so that he might be incorruptible [Col. 0518A]; but the tree of the knowledge of good and evil as though it were poison, so that he might die.

Question 7. Why did Adam, lord of the world, receive a law?

Answer. So that he would not be exalted by his dominion to such an extent, but would know through observing the commandment that he was subject to his Creator [Ms., “Maker”].

Question 8. What does it mean that God breathed into Adam’s face the breath of life (Gen. 2:7)?

Answer. God’s breathing into [supplied “into”] the human face is the imparting [Ms., “creation”] of a rational soul.

{306} Question 9. Why was the human being created on the sixth day, although, because of reason, he was nobler than the other creatures, which were made before him [Edit., “himself”] [“during the six days”]?

Answer. So that the Creator might first prepare the world like a house [Col. 0518B] and afterward introduce its inhabitant, that is, the lord of the house.

Question 10. Why did the Creator, on account of Adam’s [offense (Edit., “curse”)], curse the earth and not the waters (Gen. 3:17)?

Answer. Because the human being ate from the fruit of the earth [Ms., “ate fruit from the earth”] against the prohibition, but did not drink from the waters; and that [Ms., “because”] God predestined the sin which the human being contracted from the fruit of the earth to be washed away in the waters.

Question 11. Why do terrestrial animals bear more of the curse than aquatic animals?

Answer. Because they live more from the cursed earth than aquatic animals do; and therefore after the resurrection Christ wished to eat fish, not any terrestrial animal (Luke 24:43).

Question 12. Why did the Creator himself wish to atone for the human being’s sin [Col. 0518C] by himself and not through an angel?

Answer. Because the merit of one angel was not sufficient for the redemption of the entire human race; nor would the devil have incurred as great a crime (*sceleris*; Ms., *scelus*) by killing an angel as he incurred by killing the Creator.

Question 13. Why is the devil so hostile to the salvation of human beings?

Answer. Because of hatred toward the Creator, envy toward the human being, and despair of his own salvation.

Question 14. Why did God not give the human race [supplied] at the beginning the law that he afterward delivered through Moses?

Answer. Because among the first human beings the law of good nature was observed for a long time. But when the natural law had faded away through the habit of sinning, the written law was given through Moses, so that the good things that were known might have authority, and those that had begun to be concealed might be revealed; [Col. 0518D] and so that the terror of discipline might correct transgressors and restore faith in God.

Question 15. Why was Abel’s sacrifice accepted and Cain’s rejected (Gen. 4:4)?

Answer. [Because] Abel offered God the best and natural things, whereas Cain offered inferior things devised, as it is thought, by human invention.

Question 16. Why is Abel called “just” in the Gospel in a singular way (Matt. 23:35)?

Answer. [Because] three great proclamations of righteousness are said to have existed in him: virginity, priesthood [supplied “and”], and martyrdom [Al., “of virgins, priests, and martyrs”]. In these he first represented the figure of Christ, who was virgin, priest, and martyr.

[Col. 0519A] Question 17. Why was Enoch preserved from death for so long (Gen. 5:23)?

Answer. So that it might be shown what all human beings could have been if they had not sinned.

Question 18. Why is that same Enoch going to die (Rev. 11:3)?

Answer. So that he might pay the debt owed by human nature, and so that no one could do what Christ wished [Ms., “did not wish”—namely, not to die].

Question 19. In how many ways is divine activity understood?

Answer. In four ways. First, in the dispensation of the Word [of God], all things are eternal. Second, in unformed matter, he who lives forever created all things simultaneously (Eccl. 18:1). Third, through the works of the six days he distinguished the various creatures. Fourth, from primordial seeds there arise not unknown natures but those already known, repeatedly renewed so that they do not perish.

[Col. 0519B] Question 20. Which creatures were made from nothing?

Answer. Heaven, earth, angels, light, air, water [supplied “and”], and the human soul.

Question 21. Of how many elements does the world consist?

Answer. Of four: fire, air, water, and earth.

Question 22. What is the nature of each of the elements?

Answer. Fire is of a hot and dry nature; air, of a hot and moist nature; water, of a moist and cold nature; earth, of a cold and dry nature [Ed., “watery”].

Question 23. Of what nature is heaven said to be?

Answer. Fiery, round, and revolving.

Question 24. If it is revolving [supplied “is”], why does it not fall?

Answer. It would fall because of its excessive speed, as the wise men of the world have said, if the encounter with the planets did not moderate it [Edit., “if this course did not moderate it”].

[Col. 0519C] Question 25. Why did God complete the creation of the world by the number six [Ms., “the creatures”]?

Answer. Because that number is read as perfect according to the principles of arithmetic; and so that God might show that he had created all things perfect and very good.

{307} Question 26. What does “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” mean?

Answer. God perfected [Ms., “made”] heaven and earth in the Son.

Question 27. Why is it said that God had planted paradise from the beginning (Gen. 2:8)?

Answer. Jerome holds [supplied “that”] paradise had been planted before the creation of heaven and earth [Edit., “to have been planted”].

Question 28. What is signified by the names “heaven” and “earth” when it is said, “In the beginning God made heaven [Col. 0519D] and earth” (Gen. 1:1)?

Answer. That unformed matter which God made from nothing was first called heaven and earth—not because it already was this, but because it could already become this. For it is read that this starry heaven was made on the second day, and that on the third day the earth appeared and began to be clothed with flowers. Alternatively, by the names heaven and earth spiritual and earthly creatures may be understood.

Question 29. What does “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” mean (Gen. 1:2)?

Answer. Not by wandering about [Edit., “through wandering”], but by power and the command of the one who governs, in order to form and enliven the unformed matter that is signified in this passage by the name “waters” [Ms., “may be signified”].

Question 30. What does “But the earth was invisible and unformed” mean (Gen. 1:2, from the Septuagint)?

Answer. Invisible because of obscurity; unformed because of shapelessness.

Question 31. What does “God said, ‘Let there be light’” mean (verse 3)?

Answer. The writer used “said” in place of “made,” in order to show the speed or ease of God’s work.

Question 32. What does “God called the light day” mean (verse 5)?

Answer. That is, he caused it to be called so.

Question 33. Why is light read to have been created on the first day?

Answer. It accords with God’s works that on the first day temporal light should first be made from eternal light [Ms., “of light”], so that there might be a means by which the other things he created could appear.

Question 34. What does “There was evening and morning, one day” mean (verse 5)?

Answer. That is, the end of a completed work [Col. 0520B] and the beginning of a work begun.

Question 35. What does “God saw that it was good” mean?

Answer. It means that the thing he made pleased him in the goodness in which it pleased him to make it, so that it might remain.

Question 36. Why is it said only of the human being, “Let us make the human being” (Gen. 1:26), whereas of the other creatures it is written, “God said”?

Answer. Namely, so that it might appear that the rational creature being created was made with deliberation [Ms., “because”], and so that its nobility might be shown.

Question 37. Why did he say “Let us make” in the plural?

Answer. So that the one operation of the three Persons might be shown.

Question 38. In what does the human being bear the image of his Creator?

Answer. In the inner human being.

[Col. 0520C] Question 39. Why both “image” and “likeness”?

Answer. The image is in eternity; the likeness is in conduct.

Question 40. Why did he say again, “God created the human being in his image” (verse 27), when earlier he had said, “in our image”?

Answer. So that both the plurality of Persons and the unity of substance might be intimated.

Question 41. Why is it not said only of the human being, once created, “God saw that it was good,” as it was said of the other creatures?

Answer. Because after the human being was created, everything was called very good, as though each thing had previously been good individually. On account of the human being, however, everything was very good, because everything was created for the human being’s adornment [Ms., “because everything is created”]; but the human being was made for the glory and praise of his Creator.

[Col. 0520D] Question 42. What does it mean when it is read [Ms., “he said”], “God rested on the seventh day from all his works” (Gen. 2:2)?

Answer. For [supplied] if you divide the number seven into one and six, there are two first perfect numbers. Unity is perfect in itself by nature and power; the number six is the first number perfect in work and act, and it is fulfilled by its parts, for one, two, and three make six. Therefore [Ms., “but”], in [supplied] the rest of the seventh day it is signified that before the creation of the world God is perfect in himself by nature and power and has rest eternally in himself. Creatures, however, having received actuality from him in creation, possess through him a certain perfection in their natures [Col. 0521A] and [omitted in Ms.] rest in the work of obedience; and rational creatures especially are blessed in [omitted in Ms.] that good by which they rest in their Creator.

Question 43. Why is it said of the Sabbath day, “God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it” (verse 3), while this is not read concerning the other days?

Answer. So that he might show that after the labors of the six ages of this world, the rest of the saints would rest in the eternal Sabbath and blessed repose [Ms., “the saints would rest”], as he will say: “Come, you blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25:34). For this reason that day is also read to be without evening, since the final rest of the saints is everlasting.

Question 44. Why did he say, “These are the generations of heaven and earth” (Gen. 2:4)?

Answer. It is directed against those who affirm that the world had no beginning and has always existed.

Question 45. Why did he say [supplied: “On”], “the day when he made heaven and earth” (verse 4), and not “on the days”?

Answer. He used “day” for the whole period of primordial creation, just as the Apostle says, “Behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2). He wished “day” to be understood as the whole period during which the saints labor in this life for eternal salvation.

Question 46. What does “Every shrub of the field” mean (Gen. 2:5), before it arose on the earth?

Answer. It indicates the speed of God’s work. That is, before any fruits arose or sprouted from the earth by growing, suddenly all the fields and hills were covered with grasses and trees.

Question 47. What does “For the Lord God had not rained upon the earth” mean (verse 5)?

Answer. So that it might be understood how different the earth’s first sprouting was from that of the present time, which is completed only with difficulty and late, after delays, through irrigation by rains. The former, however, appeared immediately at the command of the one who ordered it.

Question 48. What does he again mean when he said, “A fountain rose from the earth, watering the whole face [Ms., “the whole surface”] of the earth” (Gen. 2:6)?

Answer. Either he is speaking only of paradise, which is believed to have been watered by a single fountain; or, if it is to be understood of the whole earth, he intended the abundance of all waters to be understood.

Question 49. “Therefore the Lord God formed the human being from the mud of the earth” (Gen. 2:7). Why, then? Is it not read that the human being had already been created on the sixth day?

Answer. He had already spoken briefly [Ms., “in brief”; another, omits the word] beforehand of the creation of the human being by anticipation [Col. 0521D]; now he has undertaken to explain it more fully by recapitulation.

Question 50. What does it mean when he said, “Therefore the Lord [supplied] God formed the human being from the mud of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life”?

Answer. Clearly, the human being was made from the substance of body and soul. The body was formed from mud [of the earth], while the soul was created from nothing by God’s breathing into it.

### Question 51

What does it mean when it says: “And God placed the man in the paradise of delight, to work it and guard it” (Gen. 2:15)? [Was work necessary for the man in paradise?] Or from whom was he to guard it [Edit., “that”; elsewhere, “that it be guarded”]?

**Answer.** There was no affliction of labor in paradise for the man, but rather the exhilaration of the will, since the things God had created would, with the assistance of human work, yield more joyfully and abundantly [Ms., “more truly”]. “And guard it”: that he might guard that same paradise for himself, lest, if he lost anything, he should thereby deserve to be expelled.

### Question 52

Why is it called “the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (Gen. 2:9)?

**Answer.** Not because the tree itself was rational by nature, or possessed knowledge of good and evil, but because through it the man could experience and know what the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience were.

### Question 53

What does he signify by saying: “You shall surely die” (v. 17)?

**Answer.** He designates the man’s twofold death, that is, of soul and body. The death of the soul occurs when, because of some sin, God abandons the soul. The death of the body occurs when, because of some necessity, the soul abandons the body. Christ destroyed this twofold death by his single death [the word “death” is supplied]. For he died temporarily in the flesh alone, but never in the soul, because he never sinned.

### Question 54

Why is it said: “He brought them to Adam, to see what he would call them” (Gen. 2:19)?

**Answer.** He did not bring them by movement through a place, but by the hidden sign of his power he willed that they should come.

### Question 55

Why did God wish the man to give names to all the living creatures?

**Answer.** So that the man might understand, through the discernment of reason, how much better he was than all living creatures, and might love his Creator all the more because he understood himself to be better than the other living beings.

### Question 56

Why is it said: “But for Adam no helper like him was found” (Gen. 2:20)?

**Answer.** Because among all the living creatures of the earth no rational being was found except him alone.

### Question 57

Why is the woman read to have been built from the side of the sleeping man, and not formed from the earth like the man (v. 22)?

**Answer.** Certainly, for the sake of the mystery: signifying that Christ slept on the cross for the sake of the Church, from whose side the fountain of our salvation flowed.

### Question 58

How does what was said—“Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife” (Gen. 2:24)—apply to Christ?

**Answer.** He left his Father because he did not appear to human beings in the form in which he is equal to the Father. He left his mother when he abandoned the synagogue of the Jews, from which he was born according to the flesh, in order to cling to the Church, which he gathered from the nations.

### Question 59

Why were Adam and Eve not ashamed while they were naked (Gen. 2:25)?

**Answer.** Because they felt no law in their members resisting the law of their mind. They thought that nothing needed to be covered, because they felt nothing that needed restraint. As punishment for sin, it happened to the man that his own flesh became rebellious against him in its movements, because he himself had been rebellious against his Creator in his actions.

### Question 60

Why is the serpent called more cunning than all the living creatures of the earth (Gen. 3:1)?

**Answer.** Not because of its own nature, but because of the inflation of the devilish spirit. For the devil used the serpent as an instrument for carrying out the malice of his cunning.

### Question 61

Why did God permit the man to be tempted, when he knew beforehand that he would consent?

**Answer.** Because it would not have been greatly praiseworthy if the man had not sinned because he was unable to do evil. Even today, without interruption, human beings throughout the human race are tempted by the devil’s ambushes [Edit., “he is tempted”], so that the virtue of the one tempted may be tested, and the triumph of the one who does not consent may appear more glorious.

### Question 62

Was the serpent able to understand the sound of the words spoken by the one who was speaking through it?

**Answer.** It is not believable that it could understand what the devil was doing through it. Rather, just as a demoniac or a deranged person speaks words he does not know, so the serpent uttered words it did not understand.

### Question 63

Why does the woman answer the serpent when questioned (Gen. 3:2) [Ms., “answered”]?

**Answer.** So that her transgression might be inexcusable, since she could in no way say that she had forgotten the commandment which she disclosed to the serpent.

### Question 64

Why was the man made with free will?

**Answer.** Because the Creator did not wish to create as a slave to anyone the man whom he made in his own image, so that through voluntary goodness he might appear praiseworthy, or through evil desire condemnable.

### Question 65

What is true freedom?

**Answer.** The greatest freedom is to serve righteousness and to be free from sin.

### Question 66

How could the woman believe the serpent’s words, that she had been divinely forbidden a good thing?

**Answer.** Because perhaps there already existed in her mind a certain love of her own power and a kind of proud presumption about herself, which through that temptation had to be conquered and humbled.

### Question 67

Why did the woman look at the tree after the serpent’s persuasion (Gen. 3:6)?

**Answer.** So that she might investigate whether there was anything deadly in it. When she found nothing of that kind in it, she tasted from it with greater confidence.

### Question 68

[But] why did the man consent to the woman?

**Answer.** Because perhaps he saw that she had not died from that food. It could also have happened that they thought the Creator had said, “If you eat from it, you shall die” (Gen. 2:17), for the sake of some symbolic meaning.

### Question 69

For what purpose were their eyes opened (Gen. 3:7)?

**Answer.** For what purpose, if not to desire one another? This happened to them as punishment immediately after the sin.

### Question 70

Why did they run in confusion to fig leaves [Ms., “the leaves of the fig tree”] (Gen. 3:7)?

**Answer.** Because they had lost the glory of simple chastity, they fled to the twofold itch of lust. [For this reason the Lord Jesus said to Nathanael: “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (John 1:48), that is, “When you were under the fig tree of original sin, I saw you through mercy, and therefore I descended to set you free.”]

### Question 71

What does it mean that Adam and his wife hid themselves after midday (Gen. 3:8)?

**Answer.** That after the blessed light of paradise’s happiness they hid themselves in the dark misery of this age [Edit., “in the darkness of misery”].

### Question 72

Why did God, as though ignorant, ask where Adam was (Gen. 3:9)?

**Answer.** He did not ask because he was ignorant, but by rebuking he admonished Adam to consider where he was and from where he had fallen.

### Question 73

From what did he think he could hide himself from the Lord’s presence?

**Answer.** This folly befell him as punishment for sin: he thought that he could conceal himself from the One from whom nothing can be concealed [Ms., “whom he wished to hide from him”].

### Question 74

Why did Adam shift the blame for the sin onto the woman (Gen. 3:12)?

**Answer.** To increase his sin, he answered proudly rather than humbly, as though directing a complaint against God: why had God given him such a companion, from whom the occasion of sin had come? Likewise, the woman refers the cause of her guilt back to the Creator, asking why he had created the serpent by which she was to be deceived [“in paradise”].

### Question 75

Why was the serpent not asked why it had done this?

**Answer.** Because perhaps it had not done this by its own nature or will, but the devil had acted through it and by means of it. Therefore it is said to it: “You shall go upon your breast and eat earth” (Gen. 3:14), since the cunning of its wickedness is indicated by the breast. It also devours earth when it feeds and takes pleasure in the luxury and lust of sinners [Al., “is enlarged by them”]. For just as the devil spoke through the serpent, so also the curse is pronounced upon him in the serpent.

### Question 76

What is the seed of the woman, or the seed of the serpent (v. 7)?

**Answer.** The seed of the woman is the whole human race; the seed of the serpent is the beginning of original sin. These two seeds, by divine command, ought to maintain continual hostility toward one another, so that we do not do what the devil wishes, since he never wishes anything that will benefit us.

### Question 77

What are the head of the serpent and the heel of the woman (Gen. 3:15)?

**Answer.** The head of the serpent is the thought of an unlawful suggestion, which we must crush and strike with all our intention against the rock, which is Christ. The heel of the woman is the final time of our life, when the devil strives to attack us more fiercely. If we resist him courageously, we shall receive the victory of perseverance together with our salvation.

### Question 78

When it is said, “And you shall be under the man’s power” (Gen. 3:16; Gal. 5:6; 1 John 4:18), is it being asked whether the woman was also under the man’s power before the sin?

**Answer.** Certainly she was, but under that servitude which works through love and casts out fear. Afterwards, however, she was under the conditional fear of servitude, which operates through discipline.

### Question 79

Why did the earth bring forth thorns and thistles (Gen. 3:18)?

**Answer.** Because through the man’s sin the earth was cursed, so that it would produce thorns and poisonous plants for the punishment or exercise of mortals, so that the man would always have his original crime before his eyes and, thus admonished, would at some time turn away from sins.

### Question 80

Why did God make leather tunics for the man (v. 21)?

**Answer.** To indicate that they had become mortal.

### Question 81

How did the Lord God say of the man after the sin: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us” (v. 22)?

**Answer.** He spoke in the plural, “one of us,” because of the holy Trinity, just as at his creation: “Let us make man in our image” (Gen. 1:26). Here he uses the voice of one deterring others, to instill fear so that they would not sin; or the sense of one reproaching, because Adam not only had failed to become what he had wished to become, but had not even preserved what he had become.

### Question 82

What is the meaning of the Cherubim and the flaming, turning sword that he placed to guard the way to the tree of life (Gen. 3:24)?

**Answer.** It means a certain fiery guard through angelic ministry. Yet the fact that it is called “turning” appropriately signifies that it is to be removed at some point from the gates of paradise.

### Question 83

How did Cain know that the Lord had not looked upon his offerings, but had looked upon Abel’s offerings (Gen. 4:5)?

**Answer.** As is believed, fire sent from heaven received Abel’s sacrifice, as we very often read happened when holy men offered sacrifices. Cain, however, had to consume his own sacrifice with fire.

### Question 84

What does the Lord’s saying to Cain mean: “If you do well, will you not receive? But if you do badly, your sin will immediately be present at the door” (v. 7)?

**Answer.** It means: if you offer your sacrifice with a pure mind, you will be accepted, with God looking favorably upon you and your sacrifice. But if you act badly, whether you enter or go out, your sin will always accompany you, and the Lord will cease to guard your entrance and your departure.

### Question 85

How should “Your desire shall be under you, and you shall rule over it” [Ms., “over him”] be understood (v. 7)?

**Answer.** Because you possess free will, sin does not have dominion over you, but you have dominion over it. It lies within your power either to restrain it or to desire it.

### Question 86

Why did the Lord ask Cain, “Where is Abel your brother?” (v. 9)?

**Answer.** Not as one who was ignorant, but as a judge questioning the guilty man whom he would punish. Cain, to increase his sin, answered him deceitfully and proudly.

### Question 87

How does Abel’s blood cry out to the Lord (v. 10)?

**Answer.** The guilt of that homicide appeared in the sight of the [just] Judge.

### Question 88

Why is Cain cursed in his sin, [whereas in Adam’s sin the earth is cursed] [Edit., “when previously the earth was cursed in Adam’s deed”]?

**Answer.** Because Cain knew the condemnation of the first transgression and was not afraid to add the crime of fratricide to original sin [Edit., “the homicide of his brother”]. Therefore he was judged worthy of a greater curse.

### Question 89

What was the sign of Cain that God placed upon him so that he would not be killed (v. 15)?

**Answer.** It was evidently the sign that he would always live trembling and groaning, wandering and exiled, and would not dare to have a peaceful dwelling anywhere on the earth. Perhaps for this reason he founded a city in which he could be safe (v. 17).

### Question 90

Why did he condemn himself to death by saying, “Everyone who finds me will kill me” (v. 14)?

**Answer.** He said this in despair, or so that by the brevity of death he might escape his present torments.

### Question 91

How will the one who kills Cain be punished sevenfold (v. 24)?

**Answer.** The number seven is very often accustomed to signify fullness of any matter in the holy Scriptures. It is as though he had said that the one who, warned by the bitterness of so great a condemnation, would not restrain his hands from shedding blood was to be punished with the gravest vengeance [“would not restrain” in the Edit.; the Ms. reads “wished to restrain”].

### Question 92

What does it mean that Lamech is read to have said, when Cain killed: “Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, but Lamech seventy-sevenfold” (v. 24)?

**Answer.** Because the sin of homicide is read to have been avenged by the Flood in the seventh generation. But the crime of adultery, which Lamech was the first of all to commit with two wives, could be expiated only by the blood of Christ, who came into the world in the seventy-seventh generation.

### Question 93

From where did the devil’s first evil will arise?

**Answer.** When the cause of the misery of the evil angels is sought, it rightly presents itself: they did not wish to preserve their strength for him who is the supreme good, but turned away from him and toward themselves, taking pleasure in their own power. This is the first defect and the first deprivation of a rational creature. And what else is this vice called but pride?

### Question 94

What is evil?

**Answer.** Evil in itself is nothing except the privation of good, just as darkness is nothing except the absence of light.

### Question 95

Why did the second origin of the world arise through Noah’s three sons (Gen. 6)?

**Answer.** So that the three parts of the world might be filled by the three generations. Shem possessed Asia through his sons, Ham Libya, and Japheth Europe.

### Question 96

Of whom did he say: “When human beings had begun to multiply upon the earth and had begotten daughters. And again: The sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful” (Gen. 6:1–2)?

**Answer.** Scripture wished to call the daughters of men the offspring of Ham, and the sons of God the descendants of Seth [Ms., “Shem”]. The latter were irreligious under their father’s curse; the former were devout under their ancestral blessing. But after the sons of Seth [Ms., “Shem”], overcome by desire, joined themselves in marriage to the daughters of Ham, from such a union men were begotten who were immense in body, proud in strength, and uncultivated in character, whom Scripture calls giants.

### Question 97

What does he mean by saying: “My spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh” (Gen. 6:3)?

**Answer.** In this passage “spirit” signifies anger, and “flesh” the fragility of human nature. It is as though he had said: “Because the human condition is fragile, I will not preserve them for eternal torments, but here I will repay them what they deserve” [Ms., “here” rather than “from here”].

### Question 98

What does that predetermined number signify: “And the days of his life shall be one hundred and twenty years” [Ms., “years”]?

**Answer.** That number was given to the human race for doing penance; but vengeance overtook those who despised it, for the Flood came after one hundred years.

### Question 99

What does God mean when he says: “It repents me that I made man,” and again, “He was touched inwardly by grief of heart” (v. 6)? Can repentance or grief of heart occur in God?

**Answer.** God does not repent of what he has done, nor does God grieve as a human being does, for his judgment concerning all things is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain. Rather, holy Scripture uses familiar words intelligible to us, adapting itself to our smallness, so that from things we know we may come to know things unknown.

### Question 100

“Noah was a righteous and perfect man” (v. 9). If no one is without sin, how can anyone be perfect?

**Answer.** Here some people are called perfect, not in the way in which the saints will be perfected in that immortality in which they will be equal to the angels of God, but in the way in which people can be perfect in this pilgrimage.

### Question 101

What does God’s saying to Noah mean: “The end of all flesh has come” (v. 13)?

**Answer.** “All flesh” signifies all mortals [Edit., “all mortal men”] except those who were to be saved in the ark. They were therefore preserved as a kind of seedbed of the second origin.

### Question 102

“I will destroy them with the earth.” How “with the earth,” when the earth afterward remained?

**Answer.** For teachers report that the earth’s strength and fertility were far inferior after the Flood than before it. For this reason, it is thought, permission was given to human beings to eat flesh; and before the Flood human beings had lived solely on the fruits of the earth.

### Question 103

What are the smoothed timbers from which the ark is commanded to be made (v. 14)?

**Answer.** Strong and indestructible timbers. Another translation says “squared,” so that the ark would not be broken apart either by the force of winds or by the inundation of waters.

### Question 104

“And you shall coat it with pitch.” What is the nature of pitch?

**Answer.** Pitch is an exceedingly hot and powerful glue. Its property is such that when timbers have been smeared with pitch, they can be destroyed neither by worms eating them, nor by the heat of the sun, nor by blasts of wind, nor by the inundation of waters.

### Question 105

What kind of appearance or shape, then, should we understand the ark to have had (v. 15)?

**Answer.** It seems to have had four corners rising from the bottom, gradually drawn inward toward the top, until it was gathered into a space one cubit wide [Ms., “it seems to have been gathered from the bottom upward through four rising corners…”]. Thus it is reported that at its foundations it was three hundred cubits in length, fifty in width, and thirty in height, but that it narrowed toward the peak, so that the uppermost space was one cubit in length and width.

Indeed, no shape could have been more suitable and appropriate for the ark than one in which the top, like a narrow roof, spread out the downpour of the rains, while the squared stability of its bottom rested in the waters, so that it could be neither tilted nor sunk by the force of winds, the violence of waves, or the restlessness of the animals inside it.

### Question 106

How should we understand it as having two chambers and three chambers (v. 16)?

**Answer.** It had two chambers in the lower part and three in the upper part, so that we understand there to have been five divisions of habitation in it. Its lower spaces were assigned to dung and filth, so that the animals, and especially the human beings, would not be troubled by the stench of manure. The upper chamber adjoining this one was assigned to preserving food for the animals.

Thus, they report that the lower sections, which are called “two-chambered,” were divided for these purposes. The upper sections, called “three-chambered,” were assigned first as dwelling places for wild beasts, the fiercer animals, and serpents. Above these were suitable places for gentler animals, and stalls. Above all, in the highest place, a dwelling was assigned to human beings, so that, just as they surpassed all animals in honor and wisdom, they might also surpass them all in position.

Thus five lodgings are understood to have existed in it: first, the dung chamber; second, the storeroom; third, for wild animals; fourth, for tame animals; fifth, for human beings.

### Question 107

How should we understand the door that was built in the side of the ark?

**Answer.** They also report that the door made in the side was positioned so that it had beneath it the lower sections that he called “two-chambered,” while the sections he called “three-chambered” were above the level of the door. From there all the animals entered and were separated into their respective places, with an appropriate arrangement according to what we have said above [Ms., “scattered”].

### Question 108

What mystery does the ark’s measurement contain?

**Answer.** It contains the perfect mystery of Christ’s body. For six times fifty is contained in three hundred, and ten times thirty likewise. So too, if you measure the human body when a person is lying down, its length is six times its width and ten times its height. The length of a person lying down is measured from the crown of the head to the feet, the width from side to side, and the height from the back to the belly.

This figure is known to apply appropriately to Christ because of the long-suffering of the faith that endures all things, the breadth of charity, and the height of eternal hope.

### Question 109

For what purpose was a window commanded to be made at the top of the ark?

**Answer.** So that he would have a place from which he could send out birds to investigate whether the earth was dry [Al., “from which birds could be sent out”].

### Question 110

What is meant by “two and two, seven and seven” (Gen. 7:2)? Are we to understand that four unclean animals and fourteen clean animals were to be brought in?

**Answer.** “Two and two” is not said on account of the number four, but on account of male and female. For there were only two of the unclean animals, and only seven of the clean.

### Question 111

Why did he take the unclean animals in an even number, but the clean in an odd number?

**Answer.** So that Noah would have animals from the clean ones with which to sacrifice offerings to God.

### Question 112

Why were the clean animals more beautiful [Ms., “more numerous”] than the unclean?

**Answer.** Because of their future use for the human race: it was fitting that the clean animals, which would benefit human beings, should be more beautiful [Ms., “more numerous”] than those that would harm them.

### Question 113

It is often asked whether the ark is described as having such capacity that it could carry so many and such animals, together with suitable little compartments and their food.

**Answer.** Origen solved this question by means of the geometrical cubit, asserting that one geometrical cubit was equal to six of our cubits.

### Question 114

What does it mean that all the animals are said to have entered the ark [to Noah] (v. 9)?

**Answer.** They did not enter because Noah gathered them, but because God commanded them. Just as it was said in the first creation, “He brought them to Adam, to see what he would call them” (Gen. 2:19), so, compelled by the divine will, the animals came of their own accord to the ark in the predetermined number.

### Question 115

What should be understood concerning fish or birds [Ms., “flying creatures”] that can live in or above the waters—whether they were in the ark or not—and concerning the very small creeping creatures, such as gnats, flies, and other such creatures?

**Answer.** Saint Augustine solves this question in this way in Book XV, chapter 27, section 4, of *The City of God*:

> “It is often asked about the smallest creatures, not only such as mice and lizards, but also such as locusts, beetles, flies, and even fleas, whether there were not more of them in that ark than the number determined when God gave the command. First, those whom this question troubles must be warned that the statement, ‘which creep upon the earth’ (Gen. 6:20), should be understood in such a way that it was not necessary to preserve in the ark those creatures that can live in the waters—not only those that are submerged, like fish, but also those that float upon the surface, like many birds.

> “Furthermore, when it is said, ‘male and female shall they be,’ it is plainly understood to be for restoring the sex [the text has *sexum*; Augustine, *loc. cit.*, reads: “to be said for restoring the kind, and thereby”]. Who does not see how greatly this can be said to pertain to the kind? And thereby it was not necessary for those creatures to be there which can be born without sexual union from various things or from the corruptions of things. Or, if they were there, as they are accustomed to be in houses, they could have been there without any fixed number.

> “Or, if the most sacred mystery then being enacted, and the figure of so great a matter, could not be fulfilled by the reality of the event in any other way than by having in the ark, in that definite number, all creatures that could not live in the waters because their nature forbade it, this was not the concern of that man or of those men, but of God. For Noah did not catch them and bring them inside; he merely allowed them to enter as they came. This is the force of what was said: ‘They shall enter to you’—that is, not through human action, but by divine will” [Ms., “divine”].

### Question 116

After the door had been closed and no human being remained outside the ark, how could the door have been enclosed and coated with pitch on the outside?

**Answer.** Without doubt this was the work of divine power, so that the waters would not enter through the opening, which a human hand had not sealed [Perhaps, “which” rather than “what”].

### Question 117

How could lions or eagles, which are accustomed to live on meat, have been fed in the ark?

**Answer.** Perhaps other animals, besides the predetermined number, were sent into the ark as food for the others; or perhaps some food other than meat was indicated by the wise man or by God [Ms., “with God indicating it”], which would also suit such animals as food. The latter is more believable.

### Question 118

Of what living creatures was it said: “In which was the breath of life” (v. 15)?

**Answer.** Not only of human beings, but also of all the others that live on the vital breath.

### Question 119

If the water rose fifteen cubits above Olympus, whose height, as is reported, rises beyond this turbulent air where neither clouds are seen nor winds felt?

**Answer.** If the earth could invade the space of that tranquil ether, why could the water not do so as it rose? There are, however, some who think that before the Flood neither the inequality of the earth nor the height of the mountains was as great as it is now.

### Question 120

What should be understood concerning the peace and harmony among the animals, and why animals of different kinds did not attack one another?

**Answer.** Just as they were brought into the ark by God’s will, so they were preserved in the ark by God’s will. Whether they were divided into compartments according to their kinds or remained together, they were nevertheless governed by God’s power.

### Question 121

What should be understood concerning the animals’ drinking, about which Scripture says nothing?

**Answer.** Some think that one day’s supply of food or drink in the ark served the animals for many days, or perhaps for the entire year. But let us abandon uncertain conjectures and grant to divine power the freedom to do with its creatures whatever it wished.

### Question 122

It is asked where the raven rested, if the dove did not find a place on which to rest.

**Answer.** The raven could have settled on the corpse of some animal, which the dove naturally avoids.

### Question 123

Why did the land animals perish with the man rather than the aquatic animals?

**Answer.** Because of the curse of the earth, from which the land animals fed.

### Question 124

What should be thought concerning animals whose nature cannot live always in dry places or always in wet places, such as otters and seals, and many kinds of birds that seek their food in the waters but sleep [Ms., “feed”] and rest on dry land?

**Answer.** Divine power could have adapted either aspect of their nature until the Flood had passed, so that they could live either entirely in wet places or entirely in dry places. Unless perhaps places had been prepared for them outside the ark, in some part of it, from which they could live in the waters and rest on dry land.

### Question 125

Of what spirit did he say: “God brought a spirit, and the waters were diminished” (Gen. 8:1)?

**Answer.** It can rightly be understood as the spirit of which it was said: “The Spirit of the Lord [Ms., “of God”] was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1:2).
