Then it was borne over them so that, when the waters were gathered into their own place, the earth might appear. Now it is said to have been brought, so that, when the waters of the Flood had been removed from the midst, it might reveal the face of the earth.

The word “spirit” can also be understood as “wind,” according to the Psalmist’s statement: “And the spirit of the storm stood still” (Ps. 106:25), by whose repeated blasts the water might be forced to withdraw.

### Question 126

Where did the waters return, when it is said: “The waters returned from the earth, going and receding” [Ms., “returning”] (Gen. 8:3)?

**Answer.** Literally, it appears that all the streams and courses of rivers return through hidden channels of the earth to the womb of the abyss, according to Solomon’s statement: “To the place from which the rivers flow, they return, so that they may flow again” (Eccl. 1:7).

### Question 127

Why did the rain cleanse for forty days, and again, after forty days, Noah is said to have opened the window [of the ark] (v. 6)?

**Answer.** The number forty signifies the tribulation of repentance. That Noah opened the window [of the ark] after forty days signifies that heaven is opened by fasting. For this reason Moses and Elijah, and the Savior himself, consecrated fasts lasting forty days, as though this number were necessary in three periods: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace.

### Question 128

Why did the dove bring back an olive branch (v. 11)?

**Answer.** The dove, representing the Holy Spirit, after the most loathsome bird had been driven away, flies back to Noah after the Flood as to Christ after baptism. Carrying branches of refreshment and light [Ms., singular “branch,” omitting “carrying”], it announces peace to the world.

### Question 129

If God had made all things good, and even very good (Gen. 1), what does it mean that he called some animals clean and others unclean? Can something unclean be good?

**Answer.** Even what is called unclean is good in its own nature; but in comparison with another, better nature, it is regarded as though it were unclean.

### Question 130

Why is the ox better than the lion?

**Answer.** Because its nature is better suited to assist human need, for whose sake all the animals were created.

### Question 131

Why was the man placed in terror to the other living creatures (Gen. 9:2)?

**Answer.** For the comfort that followed the vengeance already completed, so that the few human beings would not be oppressed by the many beasts; and so that they would know that they ought to rule over irrational beings, not rational ones. Hence our first fathers are read to have been shepherds of cattle, not kings of human beings.

### Question 132

Why was the eating of flesh granted to human beings after the Flood and not before (v. 3)?

**Answer.** Because of the infertility of the earth, as is thought, and the frailty of the human being.

### Question 133

Why was the rainbow given as a sign of security (v. 13)?

**Answer.** Because the Creator foresaw the fearful minds of human beings, lest they should be destroyed again by a Flood whenever they repeatedly saw the inundations of rain.

### Question 134

Why was the same sign of security placed in the sky?

**Answer.** So that it could be seen by everyone, and so that, in every tribulation, we might lift the eyes of our heart toward him who dwells in the heavens.

### Question 135

Why is that sign of different colors given to human beings?

**Answer.** For the sake of security and fear. Thus in the rainbow the color of water and of fire is displayed together: in part it is blue and in part red. Therefore it is a witness to both judgments—one already carried out and the other still to be carried out: namely, that the world will be consumed by the fire of judgment, for it will not be destroyed by the water of the Flood.

### Question 136

Were there rains before the Flood?

**Answer.** It appears that there were not, since the rainbow arises only from the rays of the sun and a moist cloud. It could, however, be that the earth was made fertile by the irrigation of dew and springs [as in Egypt].

### Question 137

Why is the righteous man Noah read to have become drunk after the Flood (Gen. 9:21) [Ms., “Why is it not read that before the Flood Noah, the righteous man, became drunk?”]?

**Answer.** Perhaps, as blessed Jerome says, he did not know that it was possible to become drunk on wine. For it is not read that human beings used wine before the Flood. Therefore it is said specifically of Noah: “And Noah planted a vineyard.”

### Question 138

Why did the uncovering of the thighs follow drunkenness?

**Answer.** Because lust very often follows satiety.

### Question 139

Why was Ham cursed in his descendants (v. 25)?

**Answer.** Because punishment awaits those who sin and do not repent. Often, indeed, the wickednesses of the reprobate thrive here unpunished, but are punished in the future. For it was prophesied that the sons of Israel, who would come from the seed of Shem, would receive the land of Canaan after expelling and defeating the Canaanites (Gen. 5).

### Question 140

Which man is intended to be understood as a brother when it is said: “I will require the blood of man from the hand of his brother” (Gen. 6)?

**Answer.** He wished every human being to be understood as a brother, according to the kinship derived from one ancestor [Ms., “he wishes”].

### Question 141

How was the world divided among the sons and grandsons of Noah?

**Answer.** As is thought, Shem received Asia, Ham Africa, and Japheth Europe.

### Question 142

How many nations did each of them beget?

**Answer.** From Japheth were born fifteen sons, from Ham thirty [Ms., thirty-six], and from Shem twenty-seven: seventy-two in all. From these arose seventy-two nations, among whom the Lord sent seventy-two disciples.

### Question 143

Why was it said: “May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem” (Gen. 9:27)?

**Answer.** From Shem the Hebrews arise, and from Japheth the people of the nations. Since the multitude of believers is broad, it received its name of breadth from Japheth, whose name means “breadth” [Edit., “height”]. What is added—“May he dwell in the tents of Shem”—is prophesied concerning us, who, after Israel has been cast out, occupy ourselves with instruction in the knowledge of the Scriptures.

### Question 144

What does the statement in Genesis mean: “From that land Assur went out [Ms., ‘went forth’] and built Nineveh and Robooth, a city [Vulgate: ‘and the streets of the city’]” (Gen. 10:11)?

**Answer.** It does not signify two cities. For *Robooth* means “a street.” The sense is therefore: “He built Nineveh and the streets of the city.”

Inter. 145. How is Nimrod called a giant, a mighty hunter against the Lord (Gen. X, 8–9)?

**Answer.** That is, a suppressor and destroyer of earthly men. Therefore, together with his peoples, he raised up a tower against the Lord, in which impious pride was signified. [Col. 0533A] [Because the dominion of a ruler is expressed in language, pride was there given dominion,] so that the man who refused to understand in order to obey God’s command might not understand the one giving orders. Thus that conspiracy was dissolved, when each person withdrew from the one whom he did not understand and joined himself only to someone with whom he could speak. Therefore the nations were divided by languages and scattered throughout the lands.

Inter. 146. To whom does God say, “Let us go down and confuse their languages” (Gen. XI, 7)?

**Answer.** God’s “going down” means observing human actions or drawing near to their perceptions. But when he said in the plural, “Let us go down,” and again, in the singular, “God confused the speech of the whole earth,” he wished to display the holy Trinity in the distinction of persons and the unity of operation [Col. 0533B] in the divine majesty. Just as at the beginning of the creation of humanity it was said, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness.” And again: “God made man according to his likeness” (Gen. I, 26–27), so that the Trinity might be believed to exist in persons, and unity in power.

Inter. 147. Is it believable that human beings were so foolish as to think they could raise the height of any building into heaven (Gen. XI, 4)?

**Answer.** Pride is ordinarily followed by folly, and humility by wisdom. Therefore the tower is here placed as a symbol of pride. Pride consequently produced diversities of languages [the humility of Christ gathered together the diversities of languages], and those whom the tower had separated, the Church brought together.

Inter. 148. Who was the first of all to seek to rule over human beings [Col. 0533C] and enlarge his kingdom?

**Answer.** The giant Nimrod, who, as is read in sacred history, became the founder of the tower’s construction and of the establishment of Babylon.

{317} Inter. 149. Are the tower and the city one work, or two?

**Answer.** Many consider [it to be] the citadel of the city of Babylon—that famous tower [the reading is restored from the manuscripts]. And therefore that city is called Babylon, that is, “confusion,” because there the speech of the whole earth was confused and human language divided into various tongues. The history of the nations commends the marvelous construction of this city, that is, Babylon. Its height was arranged to be immense, whether this refers to a single tower [of it], which they were especially attempting to raise among the others into heaven, or to all the towers, which are signified by a singular number in such a way that one says *miles* while understanding “thousands of soldiers” [Querc., when we understand many soldiers].

Inter. 150. In which family did the language remain that had originally been given to Adam [Edit., by God]?

**Answer.** As is thought, it remained in the family of Heber, from whom the Hebrews were named, in that part of humanity which remained God’s portion, and in which Christ was also to be born. For it was fitting that salvation should first be proclaimed to the world in that language through which death had first entered the world. The title written on the Savior’s cross also shows that this was the first of all languages.

Inter. 151. If God rested from all his works on the seventh day, how did such a great diversity of languages suddenly appear?

**Answer.** The Creator is not thought to have made something new in this division of languages, but to have divided modes and forms of speech among different kinds of languages. Hence, in the languages of different nations, we find the same syllables and letters of the same power, although joined differently; often, too, the same names or words signify one thing in one language and another thing in another. Thus we say in the Psalm, “with an iron rod” (*in virga ferrea*) (Ps. II, 9), while in Greek it is written, ἐν ῥάβδῳ σιδηρᾷ (“with an iron rod”). Therefore in Latin *sidera* does not signify “iron,” as in Greek, but “stars.”

Inter. 152. What is meant by what is read concerning Abraham’s brother Haran: “Haran died before his father Terah in Ur of the Chaldeans” (Gen. XI, 28)?

**Answer.** *Ur* means “fire,” and the Chaldeans worship fire as a god. But, as the Hebrews relate, Terah was thrown into the fire by the Chaldeans together with his sons because he did not wish to worship fire; in that fire Haran was consumed. This is what is now meant by the statement, “He died before the presence of Terah his father,” as Jerome reports in the *Book of Hebrew Questions* (Patr., vol. XXIII, col. 957), saying:

> “The Hebrew tradition is therefore true: Terah went out with his sons from the fire of the Chaldeans, and Abraham, surrounded by the Babylonian conflagration because he did not wish to worship it, was delivered by God’s help. From that time his days of life and the period of his age are reckoned, from the moment when he confessed God while rejecting the idols of the Chaldeans.”

And thus the extremely obscure question concerning Abraham is resolved. For it is read that Terah, when he was seventy [Ms., seventy-five] years old, fathered Abraham, and that after he fathered Abraham he lived another one hundred thirty-five years, and that all [the days] of Terah [Col. 0534C] were two hundred five years. We likewise read in Genesis: “Abraham was seventy-five years old when he departed from Harran” (Gen. XII, 4), namely after his father Terah had died. Therefore, from the year of Abraham’s birth to the year in which he departed from Harran there are one hundred thirty-five years. But the years that passed before he was delivered from the fire of the Chaldeans by God’s protection are not counted for him. This is Jerome’s explanation.

Inter. 153. How is what is said understood: “The father of Milcah is the same as the father of Iscah” (Gen. XI, 29)? Or who was Iscah?

**Answer.** Terah fathered Abraham, Nahor, and Haran. Haran fathered Lot, Milcah, and Sarai, surnamed Iscah, and they took wives: Abraham took Sarai, while Nahor took Milcah. At that time marriage between paternal uncles and their brothers’ daughters had not yet been prohibited by law.

Inter. 154. What is to be understood in the three departures in which the Lord commands Abraham to leave his country, his kindred, and his father’s house (Gen. XII, 1)?

**Answer.** Nothing other than that we must leave the earthly man, the kinship of our vices, and the house of the father—that is, the world, which is called the devil’s house—as in the Psalm: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. XLIV, 11).

{318} Inter. 155. How many promises did the Lord make to Abraham?

**Answer.** Two. The first was that he would possess the land of Canaan in his offspring. This is signified when it was said: “Go into the land that I shall show you, and I will make you into a great nation” (Gen. XII, 2). The second was far more excellent: that he would be the father not only of the single Israelite nation, but also of all the nations that follow the footsteps of his faith. This is promised in these words: “And all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in you [namely, those who imitate Abraham’s faith shall be blessed in Abraham’s offspring]” (Gen. XII, 3).

Inter. 156. Since Sarai had been taken away by Pharaoh, how can it follow that she was not violated (v. 15)?

**Answer.** According to the Book of Esther, among the ancients any woman who pleased the king was anointed for six months with myrtle oil, and for six months was treated with various perfumes and women’s preparations; only then did she enter the king’s presence (Esth. II, 12). Thus it could have happened that, after Sarai had pleased the king, while her entrance to the king was being prepared throughout the year, Pharaoh gave Abraham many gifts, and afterward Pharaoh was struck by the Lord while she still remained untouched by intercourse with him.

Inter. 157. Was it fitting for Abraham, such a holy man, to conceal that Sarai was his wife, rather than place his hope in God so that he would not be killed by the king (Gen. XII, 13)?

**Answer.** It is shown by this act of his that a person ought not to tempt the Lord his God when he has something to do by rational deliberation. He did what he could for his life; what he could not do, he entrusted to the one in whom he hoped, and to him he also entrusted his wife’s chastity. For neither his faith [and hope] failed. Pharaoh, terrified by God and afflicted with many misfortunes because of him [Ms., her], learned that she was his wife and returned her unharmed and with honor to her husband.

Inter. 158. “And your offspring shall be like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore” (Gen. XII, 17). Who are signified by the stars, and who by the sand?

**Answer.** By the stars [of heaven] are understood the fewer, the stronger, and the brighter; by the sand of the seashore, the great multitude of the weak and carnal.

Inter. 159. What are the Razim and the Zozim [Ms., Raphim; al., Rafim, Zuzim] (Gen. XIV, 5)?

**Answer.** *Razim* is interpreted as “giants,” and *Zozim* as “terrible ones”; they signify mighty men in Arabia.

[Col. 0535D] Inter. 160. [Then] God said to Abraham: “Lift up your eyes and see from the place where you now are, toward the north and the south, the east and the sea [Vulgate, west], for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring” (Gen. XIII, 14). If only the land that he could see while standing in one place toward the four regions of the world was promised to him, does the promised land not seem narrow?

**Answer.** It was not only that part of the land that he could see which was promised to him. For it was not said, “I will give you as much land as you see,” but, “I will give you the land that you see,” while the land beyond it was also given on every side. Therefore he added: “Rise, and walk through the land in its breadth and its length” (v. 17), so that by walking through it he might reach those places which, while standing in one place, he could not have seen with his eyes. That land signified the land which his carnal offspring was to receive; [for his spiritual offspring would possess the breadth of the whole world.]

Inter. 161. What is meant by the words “toward the east and the sea” [Al., “the south”]?

**Answer.** When holy Scripture speaks of the regions of the promised land, it commonly uses “sea” for “west,” because the region of Palestine has the sea on its western side.

Inter. 162. Who are the “equipped men” of whom it is said: “He counted his equipped servants born in his house” (Gen. XIV, 14)?

**Answer.** By “equipped” he meant [young men] ready for battle, and those who had not taken wives. Concerning them he says below: “Except those things which the young men ate” (v. 24).

Inter. 163. “And he pursued them as far as Dan” (v. [Col. 0536B] 14). What place is Dan?

**Answer.** Dan is a Phoenician town now called Paneas, where one of the sources of the Jordan rises; it is called Dan, while the other is called Jor. When these two sources, which are not far distant from one another, join into a single stream, it is called the Jordan. Just as one river comes from two sources, so one name is produced from the two names.

{319} Inter. 164. Who is this Melchizedek, king of Salem, whom the Apostle says was “without father and without mother” (Gen. XIV, 18; Hebr. VII, 3)?

**Answer.** The Apostle said that he was without father and without mother because holy Scripture does not recount his genealogy. The Hebrews say that this Melchizedek, under a changed name, was Shem, the son of Noah. By calculating the years of his life, they show that he lived until the time of Isaac. They also say that all the firstborn were priests and sacrificed offerings to God until the time of Aaron and the ceremonies of the Law, and that these were the birthright which Esau sold to his brother Jacob. This same Melchizedek would rightly have received tithes from the triumphs of his great-grandson [Ms., grandson]. Moreover, they maintain that Salem was the very place later called Jerusalem. This place, they report, was first called Jebus, afterward Salem, and then Jerusalem.

This Melchizedek, however, figuratively signifies Christ according to the Apostle, because Christ is without a mother in heaven and without a father on earth, offering to God for us on earth the bread of his body and the wine of his blood. To him it is said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Hebr. V, 6; Ps. CIX, 4).

Inter. 165. Who was Damascus Eliezer, concerning whom Abraham said, “He will be my heir” (Gen. XV, 2–3)?

**Answer.** He was the son of Abraham’s steward, who afterward, as they say, founded Damascus, gave the city his name, and obtained the kingdom there.

Inter. 166. Was it consistent with Abraham’s faith for him, as though doubtful, to seek a sign from the Lord, saying: “Lord God, how can I know that I shall possess it?” (Gen. XV, 8)?

**Answer.** He was not asking, as though doubtful, whether God’s promise would come to pass, but inquiring how it would happen.

Inter. 167. What, then, was to be understood in that mystical sign concerning the descendants of Abraham’s race? And why were animals three years old to be taken? Why did he divide the animals but not the birds (v. 9)?

**Answer.** The animals three years old signify the three periods in which the people grew to the summit of honor. From the time of the patriarch Abraham, through the promises, the people were joined to God until the time of Moses. From the time of Moses the lawgiver, they were glorified by receiving the law from God, by the display of miracles, by triumphs, and by entering the promised land. From the time of David they were exalted by royal honor and by the building of the temple and the city of Jerusalem.

The ram signifies royal and priestly dignity; the heifer, the people serving under the letter of the Law; and the goat likewise signifies that same people as sinful. The birds prefigured spiritual people and God’s elect. The divisions of the animals therefore show that schisms always exist among the carnal; but in the fact that he did not divide the birds, the peace and unity of spiritual people are understood. The terror that fell upon Abraham toward evening signifies the terror on the day of judgment, which will separate the spiritual from the carnal, setting some at the right hand and others at the left (Matt. XXV). The birds that fly over the carcasses are demons [Ms., demonic powers], which seek to settle upon the carnal; a devoted teacher ought to drive them away by diligent admonition.

Inter. 168. What is meant by what was said to Abraham: “Know assuredly that your offspring will be a stranger in a land not its own, and they will subject them to slavery and afflict them for four hundred years” (v. 13)? From where are these four hundred years of slavery calculated?

**Answer.** [Col. 0537C] It should not be understood as though God’s people were in that harsh slavery for four hundred years, but because it is written: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Gen. XXI, 12). From the year of Isaac’s birth until the year of the exodus from Egypt there are four hundred five years. Therefore, when you subtract twenty-five years—from the promise to Isaac’s birth—from the four hundred thirty years, it is not surprising that Scripture chose to call the complete total of four hundred five years four hundred, since it commonly designates periods in such a way that what slightly exceeds or falls short of the complete sum of a number is not counted.

Thus the statement, “They will reduce them to slavery and harm them,” is not to be referred to the four hundred years, as though they had held them in slavery for that entire period. Rather, the four hundred years refer to the statement, “Your offspring will be a stranger in a land not its own,” because that offspring was a stranger whether in the land of Canaan or in Egypt, before they received the land as an inheritance according to God’s promise. This happened after they had been freed from Egypt. Here, therefore, a hyperbaton is to be understood, and the order of the words is: “You shall know with certainty that your offspring will be a stranger in a land not its own for four hundred years.”

The intervening statement is to be understood as follows: “And they will reduce them to slavery, and they will harm them,” so that this interpolation does not belong to the four hundred years. For in the final part [of those years] of this total—that is [Ms., “this is the difference”], after Joseph’s death—it happened that God’s people endured harsh slavery in Egypt.

Inter. 169. Why is it said in Genesis concerning Abraham’s descendants, “They will return here in the fourth generation” (Gen. XV, 16), while in Exodus it is read, “In the fifth generation the children of Israel went up from the land of Egypt” (Exod. XIII, 18, according to the Septuagint)?

**Answer.** The children of Israel went out of the land of Egypt in the fourth generation. Count the generation of Levi: Levi fathered Gath; Gath fathered Amram [Ed., Abram]; Amram fathered Aaron [Edit., Aran]; Aaron [fathered] Eleazar; Eleazar [fathered] Phinehas. Gath entered Egypt with his father Levi; [again, Eleazar returned from Egypt with his father Aaron]. From Gath to Eleazar four generations are counted.

But when Exodus says that the children of Israel went out of the land of Egypt in the fifth generation, the line of the tribe of Judah is being counted [Ed., “is to be counted”]. Judah fathered Perez; Perez [fathered] Hezron; Hezron fathered Aram; Aram fathered Amminadab; Amminadab fathered Nahshon; Nahshon fathered Salmon. Perez entered Egypt with his father [Judah]; Nahshon is described as the leader of Judah in the wilderness, while his son Salmon entered the promised land. Count from Perez to Nahshon, and you will find five generations.

Inter. 170. “To your offspring I will give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates” (Gen. XV, 18). Of which river of Egypt did he speak?

**Answer.** Not of the great river of Egypt, that is, the Nile, but of the small river that separates Egypt and Palestine [where the city of Rhinocorura is located].

Inter. 171. How is Abraham defended from the charge of adultery, since while his legitimate wife was living he was joined to his servant-woman (Gen. XVI)?

**Answer.** The Gospel law of one wife had not yet been promulgated. He also had a promise from God that his offspring would be multiplied, but he did not yet know from which wife; afterward he was told that he would have a son by Sarai. His intention in producing offspring was therefore pious, because his intention in intercourse was not lustful. Sarai too, since she could not have offspring by herself, wished to have one by her servant-woman. Both consented to the act, because [both knew Sarai] to be barren [Edit., “because she knew herself to be barren”].

Inter. 172. How were “the hand of everyone against Ishmael, and his hand against everyone” (Gen. XVI, 7, 12)?

**Answer.** The angel of the Lord found Hagar beside a spring of water in the wilderness, at the spring on the road to Shur, which leads through the desert to Egypt; [she was hastening to go there]. And he called his name Ishmael, because the Lord heard her humility (*Ishmael* is interpreted as “the hearing of the Lord” [Ms., “of God”]): “He will be a wild man; his hand will be against everyone, and everyone’s hand will be against him, and he will dwell opposite all his brothers.” This signifies that his offspring would dwell in the wilderness—that is, the wandering Saracens, with uncertain settlements, who attack and fight all the nations adjoining the desert on its side [and are attacked by everyone].

[Col. 0539A] Inter. 173. What letter was added to the names Abraham and Sarai, and what was the reason for the change in their names?

**Answer.** The Lord said to Abraham: “Behold, my covenant is with you, and you will be the father of a multitude of nations, and your name will no longer be called Abram; rather, your name will be Abraham, because I have appointed you the father of [many] nations” (Gen. XVII, 4 and 15).

The Hebrews say that God added to Abraham’s and Sarai’s names a letter from his own name, which among them is the tetragrammaton: ה [Ms., *e*]. At first he was called *Abram*, which is interpreted as “exalted father,” and afterward he was called *Abraham*, “father of many.” The word “nations” is not contained in the name but is understood.

Nor is it surprising that, although among the Greeks and certain others a letter appears to have been added, we say that the Hebrew letter ה was added. It is characteristic of that language to write it with ה but read it as *a*, just as, conversely, they often pronounce the letter *a* as *e*.

And God said to Abraham: “You shall not call your wife Sarai [Ms., Sarrai], but Sarra shall be her name” (Gen. XVII, 15). Those are mistaken [Ms., “And they are those”] who think that *Sarra* was first written with one *r* and afterward another *r* was added, because *r* among the Greeks represents the number one hundred. She was therefore first called *Sarri* [Ms., *Sarrai*], written with יר [Ms., with *sin, resh, yod*], the *yod*—that is, the vowel element *iota*—having been removed; an *e*, read as *a*, was added, and she was called *Sarra*.

The reason for the changed name is this: previously she was called “my princess,” the mistress of one household only; afterward she was called simply “princess.”

[Col. 0539C] Inter. 174. Why did Abraham receive circumcision (v. 24)?

**Answer.** Circumcision was entrusted [Ms., “given”] to Abraham so that he might be under the Law, just as Adam was under the command not to eat from the tree, so that it might be demonstrated whether he would fulfill it or not. Believing that he would have a son through whose generation blessing would come to all nations, and in whose grandchildren a unique example of chastity and sobriety would remain, he received the sign of faith on that part of the body from which the son of faith [Edit., “of God”], not of flesh, was to be born. Thus, with no bodily part mutilated to make him more deformed, he became more glorious through the sign of faith in God.

Therefore, to lose something for God is gain, not loss. In receiving the sign of his faith, Abraham was not disfigured but improved. If Adam had kept God’s covenant, Abraham would not have received this covenant. But because Adam first acknowledged the guilt of disobedience in this member, it was fitting that Abraham should receive the sign of obedience in this member a second time [Al., “as the second”], so that it might be shown that the obedient would eventually father children for life, whereas formerly transgressors had fathered children for death.

Inter. 175. Did he say, with a doubtful mind, “Will a son be born to one who is a hundred years old, and will Sarra, ninety years old, give birth?” (v. 17)

**Answer.** These words do not show the disbelief of one who doubts, but the joy of one who marvels. Therefore Isaac was called Abraham’s son because Abraham laughed with joy. [For] this laughter should be understood positively, as in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall laugh” (Matt. V).

Inter. 176. Why did the Lord rebuke Sarra when she laughed, while Abraham also laughed and was not rebuked (Gen. XVIII, 13)?

**Answer.** Abraham’s laughter arose from wonder and joy, but Sarra’s from doubt and disbelief; this could be distinguished by the one who knows human hearts. Therefore this same Sarra, laughing, is corrected; once corrected, she is immediately made fertile, and contrary to the hope she had entertained according to human reasoning, she received from the divine promise what she had doubted she would have.

Inter. 177. How many persons in the Old Testament were named by their proper names before they were born?

**Answer.** Four: Ishmael, Isaac, Solomon, and Josiah, [Col. 0540B] for specific reasons.

Inter. 178. Since the three men who appeared to Abraham were three, how does he address the Lord in the singular, saying, “Lord, if I have found favor before you” (v. 3)?

**Answer.** Perceiving the Lord in the angels, he chose to speak to the Lord rather than to the angels. At times God speaks through angels by means of appearances and bodily forms temporarily assumed from the air before corporeal eyes, just as Abraham was now able not only to see three men, but also to receive them into an earthly dwelling and provide food for their use.

For unless angels, when they announce certain things to us on earth, temporarily assumed bodies from the air, they would certainly not appear to our external sight. Nor would they eat food with Abraham unless, for our sake, they bore something solid from the heavenly element. It is not surprising that those same beings who were received are called at one moment angels and at another the Lord [Edit., “lords”], because the word “angels” expresses those who ministered outwardly, while the title “Lord” shows the one who inwardly presided over them. In this way the command of the one presiding and the service of those ministering are made clear.

{322} Inter. 179. What is the outcry of Sodom, and what is meant by the Lord’s saying, “I will go down and see whether they have completed by their deeds the outcry that has come to me” (Gen. XVIII, 20–21)?

**Answer.** Sin accompanied by a voice is guilt in action; sin accompanied by an outcry is guilt with freedom and boasting. But when he said, “I will go down and see,” and similar things, why does the almighty Lord, who knows all things, appear to doubt before testing, unless to set before us an example of seriousness, so that we do not presume to believe human evils before proving them?

And behold, just as he descended through angels to learn of their evils, he immediately struck the criminals. Yet he is patient, he is gentle—he of whom it is written, “But you, Lord, judge with tranquility” (Wis. XII, 18)—he of whom it is again written, “The Lord is patient.” When he found them involved in such a great crime, it was as though he set aside his patience and did not wish to await the day of the final judgment for vengeance, but anticipated the day of judgment with the fire of judgment.

Behold: when he heard the evil, he believed it, as it were, with difficulty; yet he struck without delay when he discovered its truth by knowing it. He thereby gave us an example: greater crimes should be believed only slowly when they are reported, but punished more quickly when they are truly recognized.

Inter. 180. Why did Abraham say, “I am dust and ashes” (Gen. XVIII, 27), although he had received such great promises from God?

**Answer.** He tempered the sublimity of the promises by submitting himself in humility. It is rightly [Ms., “plainly”] understood what place he had assigned himself, since even while speaking with God he considered himself dust and ashes. If, then, he so despises himself who had risen to the honor of divine conversation [Ms., contemplation], we must carefully consider with what punishment those will be struck who make no progress toward the heights and yet exalt themselves over trifles.

Inter. 181. It is commonly asked whether God’s statement about Sodom—that he would not destroy the place if a hundred or ten righteous people were found there (vv. 26, 32)—was a special judgment concerning that city, or whether it should be understood generally of all places: that God spares any place in which even ten righteous people are found.

**Answer.** It is not necessary that we be compelled to apply this to every place. Nevertheless, it could be said concerning Sodom because God knew that there were not even ten righteous people there. He therefore answered Abraham in this way to signify that not even so many could be found there, thereby intensifying the enormity of their wickedness.

Inter. 182. If Abraham understood God or angels in those three men, and Lot likewise in the two, why did they think that the visitors ate human food?

**Answer.** Perhaps they first supposed them to be human beings in whom they understood God to be speaking. Later, when certain signs of the divine majesty existed and appeared, they recognized them as angels, when they saw them ascend into heaven. But here we must observe how great a good hospitality is. Angels entered a hospitable house; fire entered houses closed to guests.

Inter. 183. If God’s judgment is just, why were infants in Sodom burned together with their parents?

**Answer.** So that the excessively impious crime of the Sodomites might be perceived: their sin reached even to the death of their children, so that no trace of their origin might remain. Was it not provided for them that, by not living long, they would not follow the examples of their fathers, and that in the future they would suffer more lightly, or not at all, having been killed because of another’s guilt? [Col. 0541D] Parents are guilty both for themselves and for their children. Therefore the death of the children is the parents’ crime, and for this reason the children will be their parents’ accusers.

It is some kind of benefit not to be guilty, even though one is not glorious; for it benefits a person not to be poor if he cannot be a king.

Inter. 184. Why, when Lot had been ordered to flee to the mountain, did he prefer Segor so that he might be saved there, and afterward migrate from Segor to the mountain (Gen. XIX, 20)?

**Answer.** The Hebrews relate that Segor, frequently ruined by earthquakes, was first called Bale and afterward Salissa. Lot was afraid and said: “If this city, while the other cities still stood, was often destroyed, how much less will it now be able to escape in the general ruin?” It is certain that this occasion of unbelief also gave rise to the beginning of intercourse with his daughters. For he had seen the other cities destroyed, while this one [stood and he himself had been rescued by God’s help (in the edition, mistakenly, “and this was the one that was rescued by God’s help”)]; therefore he ought not to have doubted what he had heard was granted to him.

Inter. 185. Why, then, are the angels said to have entered Lot’s house as though compelled to be guests?

**Answer.** So that Lot’s charity might be tested, proved, and rewarded, and so that the greatness of hospitality might be shown. The angels entered the hospitable house to rescue their host; fire entered houses closed to guests in order to destroy the sinners within them. Therefore guests are not to be avoided but invited willingly.

Inter. 186. Why was vengeance from heaven inflicted upon the impious inhabitants of those cities (Gen. XIX, 24)?

**Answer.** Because the outcry of sinners is said to have risen to heaven, they therefore had to be punished from heaven.

Inter. 187. Why were they punished with sulfurous fire?

**Answer.** So that the most foul burning of lust might be punished by the most foul burning of flames.

Inter. 188. Why was Lot’s wife turned into a statue of salt (v. 26)?

**Answer.** For the seasoning of the faithful, because the punishment of the wicked is the instruction of the righteous.

Inter. 189. With what intention did Lot’s daughters seek intercourse with their father (vv. 31, 33)? Or can they be cleared of incest, since they did this knowingly, while he acted as though unknowingly?

**Answer.** It appears that Lot’s daughters had learned something about the consummation of the world, which was impending through fire, but, being young women, they did not fully understand what they had learned. [They did not know] that, when the Sodomites had been destroyed by fire, much time still remained for the world; they suspected that something had happened like what they had heard about the time of Noah, and that they alone had been preserved with their father to restore the human race.

They therefore conceived a desire to recover the human race and supposed that the beginning of restoring the world had to be initiated by them. Although they thought it a serious crime to steal intercourse with their father, it seemed to them an even graver impiety, if, by preserving their chastity, they destroyed the hope of human posterity, as they believed.

For this reason they devised their plan: with, as I think, the lesser guilt but the greater hope and justification, they softened and relaxed their father’s grief or severity with wine. Entering on successive nights, each one conceived from him while he was unaware. They did not repeat the act or seek it again. Where is the guilt of lust, when the crime of incest was not repeated in deed? How can something be judged a vice that was not repeated in action?

Inter. 190. If Lot is to be blamed as incestuous [Al., “as uncertain”] in this act, is he or is he not?

**Answer.** Lot is indeed to be blamed in this act to the extent that ignorance caused by drunkenness deserves blame. For the eternal law also condemns drunkenness, which commands that food and drink be taken only for the health of the body. From this we must consider more carefully how great an evil drunkenness is, and those for whom this evil is habitual must fear greatly.

In crime, drunkenness deceives the one whom Sodom did not deceive. The flame of women burns the man whom the sulfurous flame did not burn. Lot was therefore deceived by a contrivance, not by intention; for this reason he stood somewhere between sinners and righteous people, since he was descended from Abraham’s kin [Ms., stock] yet lived in Sodom. Moreover, the fact that he escaped from Sodom, as Scripture indicates, is attributable more to Abraham’s honor than to Lot’s merit.

Inter. 191. Why was the sin of the world avenged by water in the days of Noah, while the Sodomites were punished by fire?

**Answer.** Because the natural sin of lust with women was condemned by the comparatively gentler element, whereas the unnatural sin of lust with men was avenged by the burning of a harsher element. There the earth, washed by water, grows green again; here, burned by flames, it dries up in eternal barrenness.

Inter. 192. Why did Abraham say a second time that Sarra, his wife, was his sister (Gen. XX, 2)?

**Answer.** Because, from Pharaoh’s earlier correction, he was certain of God’s protection—that Sarra could not be violated—but uncertain of his own life, whether he would escape their hands. The beauty of Sarra is indeed astonishing: even at such an advanced age she could be loved so greatly that her husband feared for his life because of her beauty.

[Col. 0543C] {324} Inter. 193. Why did God say to Abimelech, “I spared you so that you would not sin against me” (Gen. XX, 6)?

**Answer.** So that it might be understood that one sins against God when one commits acts that people think should be treated lightly, as though they were sins merely of the flesh.

Inter. 194. Why did Abimelech not die immediately when God said to him, “Behold, you will die” (ibid., v. 3)?

**Answer.** God foretold what would undoubtedly have happened if, by this warning, he had not been guarded from sin through abstaining from it.

Inter. 195. Why did Abraham hold a great feast on the day Isaac was weaned, rather than on the day of his birth or circumcision (Gen. XXI, 8)?

**Answer.** Because of its spiritual significance: joy should then be felt over a spiritual man when he is nourished by solid food of truth [Col. 0543D] and not by the milk of carnal understanding.

### Question 196

For what play did Sarah accuse Ishmael, the son of Hagar (Genesis 21:9–10)?—Answer: The Hebrews explain this in two ways: either that he had committed idolatry, according to what is written elsewhere, “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exodus 32:6); or that, as though he were older, he was jokingly and playfully claiming the rights of the firstborn against Isaac. Sarah, hearing this, could not tolerate it. This is also confirmed by her own statement to him: “Cast out this slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.”

### Question 197

After how many years is a child customarily weaned?—Answer: Among the Hebrews there is disagreement: some assert that the fifth year [Ms., fourth year] is the time, while others say that the period of weaning is completed in the twelfth year.

### Question 198

If Ishmael was thirteen [Al., fourteen] years old when Isaac was born, and the years of weaning are added to his age, how can it be consistent that a youth of such an age sat on his mother’s shoulders, when it is said: “Abraham took bread and a skin of water and gave them to Hagar, placing them upon her shoulder, together with the child, and sent her away” (Genesis 21:14)?—Answer: Every son, according to the idiom of the Hebrew language, is called an infant and a little child in comparison with his parents. The meaning, therefore, is: Abraham placed the bread and the skin upon Hagar’s shoulder; having done this, he gave the child to his mother—that is, he handed him over to her care, entrusted him to her—and so sent her out of the house. This is made clear in what follows, where it is said: “Arise, take the child, and hold his hand” (ibid., v. 18), not so that she should lift him from the ground as though he were lying there, but so that she should hold him by the hand as a companion. And when a child is held by a parent’s hand, concerned affection is displayed.

### Question 199

What is meant by saying that the mother wept and that God heard the child’s voice (ibid., vv. 16–17)?—Answer: The mother was lamenting not her own death but that of her son, and God spared the child for whom his mother’s weeping had been [Ms., was].

### Question 200

How had Abraham planted a field beside the Well of the Oath (ibid., v. 29ff.), if, in that land, as Stephen says in Acts 7:5, he “had received no inheritance, not even enough ground to set his foot upon”?—Answer: The inheritance is to be understood as that which God was going to give by his free gift, not this property that was purchased for a price. The area around the well is understood to have belonged to that purchase agreement, in which seven ewe-lambs had been given, when Abimelech and Abraham also swore an oath to one another.

### Question 201

What does “God tested Abraham” mean (Genesis 22:1)? The apostle James says, “God tempts no one” (James 1:13). How are both statements to be understood?—Answer: In Scripture, temptation is customarily understood in two ways. One is that which occurs through God for the purpose of testing, so that a person may be justified and crowned; concerning this it is said: “The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love him” (Deuteronomy 13:3)—that is, to make you know. The other is that of which James says, “God tempts no one” (James 1:13), by which we become entangled in sin. Of this the Apostle says: “Lest perhaps the tempter has tempted you” (1 Thessalonians 3:5). Abraham, therefore, was tested by God so that he might be proved, justified, and crowned, and so that his obedience, tested by such an ordeal, might become known to later generations.

### Question 202

Of which mountain did God say to Abraham, “Upon one of the mountains that I shall show you” (Genesis 22:2)?—Answer: The Hebrews say that this was the mountain upon which the Temple was later established, [on the threshing-floor of Ornan the Jebusite].

### Question 203

Why, in Abraham’s testing, did God say, “Take your dearest son, whom you love, Isaac” (Genesis 21:12)?—Answer: So that, through the reminder of his affection [Col. 0545A] and the recollection of his name, the burden of the test might be increased, and paternal affection might be tortured by the memory of the promise—for earlier God had said to him: “In Isaac shall your seed be called.” It was as though, if he were killed, the entire hope of the promise [Ms., promises] would be frustrated.

### Question 204

And why was he not permitted to kill his son immediately, but ordered to take him with him for a three-day journey in order to offer him?—Answer: So that, through the length of time, the intensity of the testing might also increase. For the journey extended over three days, and throughout the entire three days the father’s inward parts were tormented by anxieties that continually grew: during all that long interval the father was to look upon his son, take food with him, and have the child hanging upon his father’s embraces for so many nights, clinging to his breast and sleeping in his lap, so that at every moment the pain of killing his son might accumulate within his paternal affection.

### Question 205

If Abraham was thinking, with unwavering and steadfast mind, of slaughtering the boy as a burnt offering to the Lord, why did he say to his servants, “You remain here; I and the boy will go over there, and when we have worshiped, we shall return to you” (Genesis 22:5)?—Answer: [He was thinking of slaughtering the boy both with a doubting mind and with an undoubting mind believing that God would raise him.] Both aspects, therefore, are praiseworthy: his constancy in offering and his faith in the resurrection. He knew with absolute certainty that God could not deceive; and even if the boy were killed, God’s promise would nevertheless remain secure. Hence the apostle Paul had also learned through the Holy Spirit what Abraham had held in his heart, when he praises [Ms., praised] his faith, saying: “By faith Abraham did not hesitate when he offered his only son, in whom he had received the promise [Ms., promises], [thinking] that God is able to raise him even from the dead” (Romans 4:20).

### Question 206

It is often asked where this ram came from, which was sacrificed in place of Isaac (Genesis 22:13): whether it was suddenly created there from the earth, or brought from elsewhere by an angel.—Answer: This ram should be believed to have been real, not merely apparent [Ms., imagined]. Hence teachers judge it more likely that an angel brought it from elsewhere than that the Lord created it there from the earth after the work of the six days.

### Question 207

Why did Abraham call the name of that place “The Lord saw” (ibid., v. 14), when there is nowhere that the Lord does not see?—Answer: He said “saw” for “appeared”; that is, he caused himself to be seen, as in the statement there: “And now I know that you fear God”—that is, “I have caused you to be known” [Ms., “that he may be known”; al., “that you may be known”]. This is a manner of speaking in which the agent signifies what is effected, as when we call cold sluggish because it makes people sluggish. But when he said, “Therefore even to this day it is said, ‘The Lord will see on the mountain,’” a proverb arose among the Hebrews: whenever people are in distress and wish to be uplifted by the Lord’s help, they say, “On the mountain the Lord will see”—that is, just as he had mercy on Abraham, so he will have mercy on us. For this reason they still customarily sound a horn as a memorial of the ram that was given.

### Question 208

“The angel of the Lord called Abraham a second time from heaven, saying: ‘Because you have done this thing and have not spared your only son for my sake’” (ibid., v. 16). Did Abraham not spare his son for the sake of God, but for the sake of the angel?—Answer: Either the Lord Christ is signified by the name “angel,” and he is certainly God; the prophet explicitly calls him “the angel of the great counsel.” Or, God was in the angel, and the angel spoke in the person of God, as also often occurs in the prophets. This seems still clearer in what follows, where we read: “The angel of the Lord called Abraham again from heaven, saying: ‘By myself I have sworn,’ says the Lord” (ibid.).

### Question 209

What does it mean that the same promises, and not different ones, were made to Abraham a second time (ibid., v. 17)?—Answer: It signifies that Abraham would have two kinds of offspring, one carnal and the other spiritual. Therefore the Lord said to him: “So shall your seed be, like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea”: by the stars of heaven, the spiritual are meant; by the sand of the sea, the carnal [Edit., “are understood”].

### Question 210

Why does Scripture mention the sons of Nahor, Abraham’s brother (ibid., v. 20)?—Answer: Because something notable is afterward recorded as having been accomplished by them or by their descendants. Thus Uz [Ms., Chuz] was one of them, and Job descended from his line. For this is written at the beginning of Job’s book: “There was a man in the land of Uz [Ms., Chuz] whose name was Job.” Some, therefore, wrongly thought [Ms., think] that Job was born from the line of Esau, in whose line was Balaam [Ms., “from the people of Esau. The second born of Milcah was Buzi, from whose line was Balaam,” etc.], that diviner who, as the Hebrews relate, is called Elihu in the Book of Job: at first a holy man and prophet of God, later blinded through disobedience and desire for gifts, when he began to curse Israel, and called by the name of a diviner. [It is also said in the same book: “And Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite became angry.” From this Buzi, namely, descended Ham, or his father, Damascus. For that place is called Aram, which is written here in place of Syria, and is read under that very name in Isaiah. Chesed was also the fourth, from whom the Chasdim—that is, the Chaldeans—were later named. Bethuel, from whom came Rebecca and Laban, the father of Leah and Rachel.]

### Question 211

Why was one city, Hebron, called by three names, namely Hebron, Arbe, and Mamre (Genesis 23:2)?—Answer: It was called Hebron after the giants, by whom it was once founded; and Arbe derives its name from the number four, because four patriarchs were buried there: Adam, the great father of the human race; Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The same city was called Mamre after one of Abraham’s friends.

### Question 212

[It is asked] what is signified by Abraham’s saying to his servant, “Place your hand upon my thigh, and swear by the Lord, the God of heaven” (Genesis 24:2–3)?—Answer: The Hebrews relate that he swore by its sanctification, that is, by circumcision. But it is better understood that he swore by the seed of Abraham, that is, by Christ, because the Lord God of heaven was later to come in that flesh which was propagated from that thigh.

### Question 213

How is Abraham’s servant not blameworthy for seeking a sign by an augury (v. 14)?—Answer: It is one thing to ask for some extraordinary event whose meaning is conveyed by the miracle itself [Ms., “which is a sign for the miracle itself”]; it is another thing to observe human errors with superstitious vanity in omens, auguries, and divinations. Some practices are agreements of demonic familiarity, and they are performed with no small sin whenever they are performed. The former kind of request, therefore, is an affirmation of faith, or a joining of faith, to God; the latter is a joining of unbelief to the devil.

### Question 214

What does Rebecca’s departing blessing mean: “You are our sister; may you increase to thousands upon thousands, and may your seed possess the gates of their enemies” (v. 60)? Were those who said this prophets, since they declared what was later to happen [Ms., “what had happened in the future”]?—Answer: They were not prophets, nor did they wish this through such great presumption; but what God had promised to Abraham could not have been hidden from them.

### Question 215

What was the exercise by which Isaac is said to have exercised himself in the field toward evening (v. 63)?—Answer: That exercise signifies prayer, according to the passage where Christ prayed on the mountain; thus Isaac also bore the type of the Lord (v. 62).

### Question 216

What is that land of the South where Isaac lived when his father’s servant returned with Rebecca?—Answer: [The land of the South] signifies that land [Ms., Gerar] from which he had once been brought by his father for sacrifice (v. 65).

### Question 217

What is the *theristrum* with which Rebecca covered herself?—Answer: It is a kind of cloak, like the Arab garments now worn, with which the women of that province cover themselves [Ms., “the *theristrum* is called a cloak, also a kind of Arab garment still worn today”].

### Question 218

Why, after the promise made to him and after the birth of Isaac, in whom God had promised him the multiplication of offspring and the blessing of the nations, did Abraham wish to take another wife (Genesis 25:1)?—Answer: It was not because of lack of self-control, since he was already advanced in age; rather, just as Hagar and Ishmael signify the carnal people of the Old Testament, so Keturah and her sons signify heretics who think that they belong to the New Testament. Yet both women are called concubines, for it is said: “But to the sons of his concubines he gave gifts” (v. 6). Sarah alone is always called his wife.

### Question 219

Who is this Keturah, or from whom did she derive her lineage [Ms., “deriving her lineage”]?—Answer: [Keturah is interpreted as “joined” or “bound”; for this reason] the Hebrews suspect that she was the same Hagar who, after Sarah’s death, passed from being a concubine into being a wife [Al., “became a wife”]. In this way Abraham’s advanced age, now set aside, seems to be excused, so that an old man would not be accused of indulging in lustful new marriages after the death of his aged wife. [It is also related] that the sons of Abraham born to him by Keturah [occupied the land called Arabia as far as the shores of the Red Sea]. It is also said that one of Abraham’s descendants, called Asser [Ms., “was called Assur”], led an army against the Lubians [Ms., Laban], settled there after defeating the enemy, and that his descendants called Africa after the name of Atavi. Other sons of Abraham by Keturah are also thought to have occupied the regions of Judea [Ms., “the region of India”].

### Question 220

How is it fitting for so holy a man as Abraham that it is said, “And, failing, he died” (Genesis 25:8)?—Answer: The Hebrew does not have “failing”; it was added by the translators of the Septuagint.

### Question 221

What does it mean that he is said to have been “full of days”?—Answer: It means that he died full of the works of light and of the day.

### Question 222

What does Scripture mean when it says of the sons of Ishmael, “They dwelt from Havilah to Shur, which is opposite Egypt” (v. 18)?—Answer: Havilah is the region around which the Pishon flows, issuing from Paradise; it was named after a certain Havilah, a grandson of Noah, and is a wilderness opposite Egypt. Shur, too, is a wilderness between Kadesh and Bered, extending the desert as far as the Red Sea and the borders of Egypt.

### Question 223

What does it mean that Ishmael generated twelve princes, or leaders (v. 16) [who gave their names to regions or tribes (omitted in the manuscript)]?—Answer: It signifies that each of Ishmael’s sons gave his name to regions or tribes. His firstborn was Nebaioth [Ms., Nabaoth; al., Nabeoth], after whom the entire region from the Euphrates to the Red Sea has to this day been called Nabataea; it is part of Arabia. Their families, towns, villages, fortified settlements, and tribes are also known by these names. From one of them comes the name Kedar in the desert; another region is called Eduma; Teman [Ms., Theman] lies to the south, and Kedemah to the east.

### Question 224

What does it mean that it is said of the same Ishmael, “He died before all his brothers” (v. 17)? Or who are designated by the name “brothers” [Ms., “reckoned as brothers”]?—Answer: It means that he died in the presence of all his children [Ms., sons], with all his children surviving and none having been carried off by death before him. “Brothers” is used for “sons,” as Jacob demonstrates when he says to Laban: “Let it be placed before my [brothers and] your brothers, and let them judge between us” (Genesis 31:37). For we do not read that Jacob had any other brothers there apart from his children.

### Question 225

It is asked where Rebecca went to inquire of the Lord when her children were struggling in her womb (Genesis 25:22).—Answer: Perhaps she went to the place where Abraham had established an altar in order to pray; or perhaps there were at that time certain men of God through whom God could be consulted.

### Question 226

Is what the Lord answered Rebecca—“Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your womb; one people shall overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger” (v. 23)—to be understood historically or allegorically?—Answer: In both ways. Spiritually, what was said is usually understood as follows: in Esau the elder people of God is represented, that is, Israel according to the flesh; through Jacob, Jacob himself is represented in the Christian people, propagated according to spiritual descent [Ms., “which he propagated”]. But historically also this answer is found to have been fulfilled, when the people of Israel—that is, Jacob, the younger son—overcame the Idumeans, whom Esau propagated, and made them tributary through David. This continued for a long time, namely until the king under whom the Idumeans rebelled and cast the Israelite yoke from their neck.

### Question 227

What was the birthright that Esau sold to his brother Jacob (v. 31)?—Answer: The Hebrews relate that all firstborn customarily performed the priestly office before Aaron was chosen as priest; they possessed priestly garments, and clothed in them offered sacrifices to God. These, they say, were the garments of Esau, with which Rebecca clothed her son Jacob and whose fragrance delighted his father, establishing the beginning of the blessing (Genesis 27:15).

### Question 228

If the will of a righteous man is good, why did Isaac bless not Esau, whom he wished to bless, but Jacob, whom he did not wish to bless?—Answer: The will of a righteous person is good insofar as conscience is concerned; but insofar as foreknowledge [Ms., “presence”] is concerned, it is not free from contrary circumstances. For God alone judges the future. Accordingly, Isaac, as a righteous man concerned with the present condition [Ms., “humanity”], thought the elder son more worthy of the blessing. But God, who knows hidden things, showed that the younger deserved the blessing, [so that in the blessing he might show that the benefit belonged not to man but to God (Edit., “so that he might show the blessing to belong not to man but to God”)]. Therefore it was said in Numbers to Moses and Aaron the priest: “Put my name upon the children of Israel; I, the Lord, will bless them” (Numbers 6:27). It belongs to the priest to bless; it belongs to God to grant the effect of the blessing. Thus Isaac understood through the spirit of prophecy that the blessing had been predestined by God for the younger son, saying: “I have blessed him, and he shall be blessed” (Genesis 27:33).

### Question 229

What does Jacob’s statement mean: “How fearful is this place! This is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Genesis 28:17)?—Answer: These words pertain to prophecy: what was to occur in the promised land was that the true God would be feared and worshiped, a tabernacle would be made for him, and he who is the blessed God above all would walk there on his feet. We should understand “the gate of heaven” as an entrance by which believers gain access to take possession of the kingdom of heaven.

### Question 230

Why did Jacob pour oil upon the stone that he raised as a monument (v. 18)?—Answer: He did not do this out of idolatry [Ms., “he did not make it like an act of idolatry”]. Neither then nor afterward did he worship the stone or sacrifice to it. Rather, it was established as a very clear prophetic sign [Ms., “in a very clear prophecy”] pertaining to anointing. Hence Christ’s name derives from *chrism*.

### Question 231

[It must be asked] how it was said, “Jacob served for Rachel seven years, and they seemed to him like a few days” (Genesis 29:20), when even a short period is usually long to those who are in love.—Answer: It was said because of the labor of servitude, which love made easy and light.

### Question 232

After Jacob’s seven years of service, when he had been deceived by his father-in-law’s trickery and was joined to Leah, was he to receive Rachel only after another seven years of service?—Answer: No [therefore], as some wrongly think, he did not take Rachel as his wife after another seven years, but after seven days of the first marriage. For it follows: “And he went in to Rachel, and he loved Rachel more than Leah, and served her another seven years” (v. 30).

### Question 233

Are the two maidservants, Bilhah and Zilpah, to be called wives or concubines (Genesis 30:4, 9)?—Answer: Perhaps every concubine is called a wife, but not every wife a concubine, according to the manner of speaking in Scripture [Ms., “of the Scriptures.”] Thus Sarah and Rebecca, [Leah] and Rachel cannot be called concubines; Hagar and Keturah, however, and Bilhah and Zilpah are both wives and concubines.

### Question 234

How did various offspring of the flocks come forth from the sight of the various rods (v. 38)?—Answer: Jacob observed the times when the animals were mounted and, after the heat of the day, went eagerly to drink. He placed variegated rods in the channels and, when the rams and he-goats were admitted, caused the ewes and she-goats to be mounted in their very eagerness to drink, so that, from their twofold desire—while they drank eagerly and were mounted by the males—they conceived offspring such as the shadows of the rams and he-goats mounting above them appeared in the reflection of the water. For the color of the images was also varied by the rods placed in the channels.

Nor is it surprising that this should be the nature of conception in women, so that, whatever they have seen or conceived in their minds during the final heat of pleasure in which they conceive, they should produce such offspring, since the same thing is also said to occur among herds of mares in Spain. Quintilian, too, in the case in which a certain married woman was accused because she had borne an Ethiopian [Ms., “because she had borne . . .”], argues in her defense that conception has the nature described above. Many similar things are also said to occur in the offspring of animals. [But] it is also reported to have happened to a woman, as is found written in the books of the very ancient and highly skilled physician Hippocrates. She was about to be punished on suspicion of adultery because she had borne a most beautiful child unlike the family of either parent, unless the aforementioned physician had solved the question by advising them to investigate whether perhaps there was some such picture in the bedroom. When one was found, the woman was freed from suspicion.

### Question 235

Why did Jacob want the early-born animals to be his and the late-born to belong to Laban? Or [Ms., “and”] why did he not, by this method, make everything his own?—Answer: Jacob, prudent and clever, preserved justice and equity in his new method. If all the sheep and goats had produced spotted offspring, there would have been some suspicion [of deceit], and Laban, openly hostile to the arrangement, would have resisted it. Therefore he regulated everything so that he himself would receive the fruit of his labor and Laban would not be entirely despoiled.

Whenever the sheep and goats were mounted early, since the offspring are produced in spring, he placed the rods before them so that varied offspring would be born. Whatever sheep and goats sought the males late, he did not place the rods before their eyes, so that single-colored animals would be born. Whatever was born first belonged to him, because it was [spotted and] varied; whatever came later belonged to Laban, for animals of a single color—whether black or white—were born.

### Question 236

Why should Jacob not be accused of fraud in this matter?—Answer: This event compels us to inquire into its prophetic and figurative meaning, since Jacob certainly acted as a prophet. For we must not believe that he did such a thing except through spiritual revelation.

### Question 237

How does Jacob say ten times to his father-in-law that he had changed his wages (Genesis 31:41)?—Answer: The meaning is that Laban continually changed the agreement after each birth. If he saw spotted animals being born [after a birth], he would say: “I do not want spotted ones to be born to me in the future.” Again, when he saw single-colored animals being born [and Jacob, having heard this, did not place the rods in the channels], he would say: “Future offspring will produce single-colored animals for me.” And what more need be said? Up to ten times, Laban’s agreement concerning his animals was changed, and whatever Laban had determined should be born was turned into the opposite color.

So that no one may find ten birthing periods in six years incredible, read Virgil, where it is said:

> Twice-pregnant ewes . . . .

The nature of the Italian sheep and of those of Mesopotamia is said to be the same.

### Question 238

Why did Jacob set up a stone as a monument (v. 45)?—Answer: It must be carefully observed that they established such monuments as testimony to any matter, not in order to worship them as gods, but so that they might signify something through them.

### Question 239

What does it mean that Jacob swore by the fear of his father Isaac (v. 53)?—Answer: He is understood to have sworn by God, whom his father Isaac feared. He commended this fear earlier also when he said: “The God of my father Abraham and the Fear of my father Isaac” (v. 42).

### Question 240

What are the camps of God that Jacob saw on his journey (Genesis 32:1–2)?—Answer: There is no doubt that they were a multitude of angels. In Scripture, that multitude is customarily called the army of heaven.

### Question 241

How did Jacob have faith, seeing that he feared his brother Esau so greatly (v. 7)?—Answer: In the words of Jacob himself that follow, both human weakness and the faith of devotion are evident: God was to deliver him and to fulfill what he had promised. Nevertheless, we are instructed by this example that, although we believe in God, we must still do what human beings ought to do as a safeguard for salvation, lest, by neglecting such measures, we appear to be tempting God.

### Question 242

How, then, did Jacob ask to be blessed by the one whom he had overcome in wrestling (v. 26)?—Answer: This is a great prophecy concerning Christ. For Jacob is understood here in two ways, namely, as carnal and spiritual. Jacob prevailed over Christ—or rather, in those Israelites by whom Christ was crucified, he appeared to prevail—and he is blessed by him in those who believed in Christ, among whom was the one who said: “And I am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin” (Romans 11:1).

Thus one and the same Jacob is both lame and blessed: lame in the breadth of his thigh, as though in the multitude of his descendants, concerning whom it was said, “They have stumbled from their paths” (Psalm 17:26); but blessed in those of whom it was said, “The remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Romans 11:5).

### Question 243

What was the reason for changing Jacob’s name so that he was called Israel (Genesis 32:28)?—Answer: Various interpretations of this name are proposed, but blessed Jerome gave the following interpretation: [Col. 0552C] “The meaning, then, is this: ‘Your name shall no longer be called Supplanter,’ that is, Jacob; ‘but you shall be called Prince with God,’ that is, Israel. For just as I am a prince, so you, who were able to wrestle with me, shall be called a prince. But if you were able to contend with God or with an angel—for many interpret this in different ways—how much more with human beings, that is, with Esau, whom you ought not to fear.”

### Question 244

What did Jacob mean when he said [to his brother], “I have seen your face as though I had seen the face of God” (Genesis 33:10)? Did words of fear and a troubled mind erupt into such flattery?—Answer: These words are fraternal and were spoken with a kindly disposition, since, after the kindly reception, the fear itself had passed. Perhaps, too, by “God” we should here understand some angel or one of the saints, according to the Apostle who said: “Although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, just as there are many gods and many lords” (1 Corinthians 8:5).

### Question 245

How did Jacob promise his brother that he would follow his tracks when he was heading by another route (Genesis 33:14)?—Answer: Perhaps he followed him for a while. Or he may at first have promised sincerely, but afterward [thinking [Edit., “he thought”]] chosen another course.

### Question 246

How could Jacob’s two sons themselves inflict such slaughter and plunder in a foreign land (Genesis 34:25)?—Answer: The multitude with Jacob was not small, since he had become extremely wealthy; but his sons are named in connection with this deed because they were its leaders and instigators.

### Question 247

What did Jacob mean when he said to his household, “Cast away the foreign gods that are among you” (Genesis 35:2)? And again: “They gave him all the foreign gods that they had, and the earrings that were in their ears” (v. 4). If these were ornaments, did they not pertain to idolatry?—Answer: It is to be understood that these earrings were amulets of the foreign gods. Scripture testifies that Rebecca received earrings from Abraham’s servant; this would not have happened if it were forbidden to possess earrings as ornaments. Therefore those earrings that were given together with the idols, as has been said, were amulets of the idols.

### Question 248

Why is it said a second time to Jacob (v. 10), “You shall not be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name,” and he called him Israel?—Answer: Earlier the angel by no means imposed the name upon him; rather, it was foretold that the name would be imposed upon him by God. What, therefore, is promised there as future is here said to have been fulfilled. Clearly, this name is rightly understood to belong to that promise in which God would be seen in a manner in which he had not previously been seen by his fathers.

### Question 249

What is Ephrath, where Jacob is said to have buried his wife Rachel (vv. 19–20)?—Answer: Ephrath and Bethlehem are names of one place, with similar interpretations: one is translated “fruitful house,” and the other “house of bread,” on account of the bread that is said to have descended from heaven.

### Question 250

Where is the Tower of the Flock, beside which Jacob is said to have dwelt (v. 21)?—Answer: Near Bethlehem, where a flock of angels sang at the Lord’s birth; or where Jacob, while pasturing his flocks, gave the place its name; or, what is more likely, where the mystery of future events was then being revealed through prophecy [Ms., “because the prophecy of future events was already then being revealed through a mystery”].

### Question 251

What does it mean when it is said of Isaac, “And, consumed by age, he died and was gathered to his people” (Genesis 35:29)? How was he consumed, or to what people was he gathered?—Answer: “Consumed by age” means perfected by age. Those who end this life pleasing to God are gathered to the people of the angels or of the holy souls. They are said to be gathered when no anxiety of temptations or danger of sins remains. Reflecting on this, Scripture says: “Before death, praise no one” (Sirach 11:30).

### Question 252

How does Scripture say that, after the death of his father Isaac, Esau departed from the land of Canaan and lived on Mount Seir (Genesis 36:8), when, as Jacob came from Mesopotamia, he is read to have sent messengers to his brother in the land of Seir, the region of Edom (Genesis 32:3), as though he were living there at that time [Ms., “and that he was living there at that time”]?—Answer: It is easy to suppose that, after his brother had departed for Mesopotamia, Esau did not wish to live with his parents, either because of the resentment with which he grieved that he had been deprived of the blessing, or because of his wives, whom he saw to be hateful to his parents. He therefore began to live on Mount Seir. Then, after his brother Jacob’s return and their reconciliation, he too returned to his parents. When they had buried their father together, since that land, as Scripture says, could not contain them because they had become very wealthy, he departed again for Seir and there propagated the nation of the Idumeans.

### Question 253

There were twelve sons of Jacob (Genesis 35:22); and, when all are counted, including Benjamin, Scripture adds: “These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Mesopotamia of Syria” (v. 26).

@ [Col. 0553D] This passage has been corrected from the manuscript, since it is clear that Benjamin was born in Canaan. How, then, are twelve said to have been born in Mesopotamia?—Answer: There is no easier solution to this question than to understand it by synecdoche. For where the greater or more important part is present, it is customary for that which does not belong to the name itself also to be included under that name.

### Question 254

How was Joseph’s dream fulfilled, in which he said that he had seen the sun and moon and eleven stars worshiping him (Genesis 37:9), when it is clear that, while he was ruling in Egypt, his mother Rachel had died long before? Indeed, we do not even read that his father worshiped him.—Answer: In Christ it is easier [Edit., “easy”] to understand the fulfillment of the dream. For to him was given the name that is above every name, so that at his name [Ms., “the name of Jesus”] every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Philippians 2:10).

### Question 255

It is asked why Scripture calls the Ishmaelites, by whom Joseph was sold by his brothers, also Midianites (Genesis 37:28), since Ishmael was the son of Abraham by Hagar, whereas the Midianites descended from Keturah.—Answer: Scripture had said of Abraham (Genesis 25:6) that he gave gifts to the sons of his concubines, namely Hagar and Keturah, and sent them away from his son Isaac into the land [Ms., “to the land”] of the East. Thus they are to be understood as having formed one nation.

### Question 256

How is Jacob’s statement to be understood: “I will gladly descend to my son in the underworld” (Genesis 37:35)?—Answer: These are the words of a troubled and grieving man, exaggerating his misfortunes by this expression as well. Or, by “the underworld” he signified the grave, as though he were saying: “I remain in mourning until the earth receives me [buried], as it has received him.”

### Question 257

How could the story concerning Judah, his three sons, and his wife Tamar (Genesis 38) have been completed within so few years? [Since, then, in the year
[Col. 0554D] **An uncertain reading:** perhaps XVII. It may be supposed that he was sold in the fourteenth year of his age; he had spent thirteen years in Egypt, unknown to Pharaoh. To these thirteen years were added seven years of abundance, making twenty years; two more are added, [Col. 0555A] because Jacob entered Egypt with his sons in the second year of the famine, and twenty-two years are found during which Joseph was absent from his father and brothers. How could these things have happened within this intervening period?] — **Answer.** Holy Scripture often presents many things by recapitulation. It is therefore understood that these events began several years before Joseph was sold. Moreover, as soon as Judah came of age, he fell in love [Ms., “began to fall in love”] with her whom he took as his wife; and this occurred before Joseph was sold into Egypt.

**Question 258.** Why did he say of Tamar, “After she had put off the garments of her widowhood” (verse 14)? — **Answer.** So that it might be understood [Ms., “so that you might understand”] that, from the time of the patriarchs, widows had their own distinctive garments, certainly not garments such as married women wore.

[Col. 0555B] {332} **Question 259.** Why did Judah say, “She is more righteous than I” (Gen.
