XXXVIII, 26)? — **Answer.** Tamar sat at a crossroads or at *capeto*; there a traveler ought to look more carefully to see which road he should take—not in order to satisfy a wandering lust for shameful pleasure, but so that she might receive children from her father-in-law, for a more righteous purpose than that of her father-in-law: he acted for lust, she for the sake of children. Therefore, in comparison with her, he had done the lesser evil.

**Question 260.** If Perez received his name, meaning “division,” because he had divided the second membrane [Ms., “the membranes”], from what did Zara [sic] receive his name (verses 29–30)? — **Answer.** Zara is interpreted as “Rising” or “East.” Thus he is so called either because he appeared first, or because many righteous men were born from him, as we read in Chronicles (I Chron. II, 4).

[Col. 0555C] **Question 261.** Why did the Gentile men who were in prison with Joseph see omens of things to come (Gen. XL, 5)? — **Answer.** Not on account of their own merits, but so that Joseph might be glorified and the one who was hidden might be revealed.

**Question 262.** What [are] the “three branches” (verse 10)? — **Answer.** Three [branches are three] boughs.

**Question 263.** Why did Pharaoh and Herod celebrate the days of their birth with festive honors (verse 20)? — **Answer.** Because they thought that the hour of their birth had appointed them to kingship [Ms., “had appointed them to the kingdom”]. They performed a similar act of worship, so that, since their impiety was equal, their solemnity might also be one.

**Question 264.** What does Pharaoh’s statement mean: “I thought that I was standing upon the river” (Gen. XLI, 1)? — **Answer.** It means the same as what is read elsewhere: “Behold, I am standing beside the spring of water” (Gen. XXIV, 13). In this manner of speech the psalm also says: “He founded the earth upon the water” [Ms., “upon the waters”]. [People are not forced to suppose that the earth floats upon the waters like a ship.] According to this expression, it is rightly understood that the earth is higher than the water. For it is raised above the waters where earthly animals dwell.

**Question 265.** How is the abundance [of grain] compared with the multitude [of sand] (Gen. XLI, 49)? — **Answer.** Because, just as sand is innumerable, so the quantity of grain cannot be contained within the usual mode of counting [Ms., “could not be contained”].

[Col. 0556A] **Question 266.** How should we understand, concerning the holy man Joseph, that he had made his brothers drunk (Gen. XLIII, 34)? — **Answer.** In the Hebrew language [Ms., “in the idiom of the Hebrew language”], “drunkenness” is used for fullness or satiety, as in the psalm: “You visited the earth and made it drunk.” And again: “They shall be made drunk from the abundance of your house.”

**Question 267.** What is meant by Joseph’s repeatedly mocking his brothers and keeping them in such suspense before he wished to reveal himself? — **Answer.** He afflicted them, not to avenge himself upon them [“upon them” is absent in some copies], but to cleanse them from the crime of the former offense they had committed against him; or rather, so that their joy might be increased by the delay, when they saw such glory in the man whom they had believed to be dead at their hands.

[Col. 0556B] **Question 268.** How can it be said, “His sons and daughters went down with Jacob into Egypt” (Gen. XLVI, 7), when Jacob had no more daughters than Dinah alone? — **Answer.** Either we should understand granddaughters by the word “daughters,” or the plural number has been used for the singular, as in the passage: “He sent among them the dog-fly.”

**Question 269.** When Scripture says, “All the persons who came out from Jacob’s loins” (verse 26), what should be answered to those who try to confirm by this testimony that souls, together with bodies, are propagated from parents? — **Answer.** No one should doubt that “souls” is said for “people,” in an expression in which the part signifies the whole [Edit., “in an expression in which the whole is signified by the part”].

**Question 270.** “These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore in Mesopotamia of Syria, together with Dinah: thirty-three persons of her sons and daughters” (verse 15). Were all these thirty-three persons born from Leah in Mesopotamia of Syria, although Jacob stayed there with his father-in-law for no more than twenty years, and seven years passed before he took Leah as his wife? — **Answer.** Therefore Holy Scripture said that all these were born in Mesopotamia because their fathers were born there.

**Question 271.** If the persons who entered Egypt with Jacob numbered sixty-six, and Joseph with his two sons was found there (verses 26–27), how are seventy persons subsequently said to constitute the house of Jacob? — **Answer.** When Jacob himself, as the root, is counted with them, they are known to number seventy.

[Col. 0556D] **Question 272.** While here [in Genesis] we read that there were seventy persons in the house of Jacob, how is it said in the Acts of the Apostles (VII, 14) that Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy-five persons? — **Answer.** Luke could not write something contrary to that Scripture which had already been disseminated among the nations. At that time, in any case, the authority of the Seventy Translators was held in greater esteem than that of Luke, who was unknown and insignificant and was not considered among the nations to be of great credibility [Al., “was not regarded as such”]. This should, however, be observed generally: whenever the holy apostles or apostolic men speak to the peoples, they usually make use of testimonies that had already been disseminated among the nations, although many maintain that Luke the evangelist, as a proselyte, did not know the Hebrew writings.

[Col. 0557A] **Question 273.** When Jacob’s sons were asked what work they did, they answered, “We are shepherds of sheep, as were our fathers also” (Gen. XLVII, 3). Why do we read that the first patriarchs were shepherds of sheep and not [kings] of nations? — **Answer.** Because without any doubt servitude is just, and domination is just, when animals serve human beings and human beings rule animals. For this was said to the man when he was created: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness, and let him have dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, and all things that are upon the earth” (Gen. I). Here it is indicated that reason ought to rule irrational life.

Human beings, however, were made servants of human beings either by iniquity or by adversity. By iniquity, as it is said: “Cursed is Canaan; he shall be a servant to his brothers” (Gen. IX, 25). By adversity, as happened to Joseph himself, so that, after being sold by his brothers, he became the servant of a foreigner. Thus the first servants—those to whom this name was introduced into the Latin language—were produced by wars. For when one human being has been overcome by another, he may justly be killed by the law of war; but because he was spared, he was called *servus*, a servant. Hence also the term *mancipia*, “slaves,” because they are captured by hand.

**Question 274.** What land is Gersen [Al., Gesen] or Ramesse? — **Answer.** The Jews think that it is the region now called Thebaid, and that Ramesse was formerly called Arsenatis.

**Question 275.** How could pasture for cattle be found in the land of Egypt, since that land is not irrigated by rains, while Joseph’s brothers say that they left the land of Canaan because they had found no grass for their flocks (Gen. XLVII, 4)? — **Answer.** Those who know the places report that pasture could be abundant in many of the marshes of Egypt, even when there was a famine of grain, which ordinarily comes from the flooding of the Nile. Indeed, those marshes are said to produce richer pasture when the Nile’s waters rise less.

**Question 276.** What does it mean that so great a man and such a patriarch was so concerned about the disposition of his body, insisting that he not be buried in the land of Egypt but in the land of Canaan beside his fathers (verse 30)? — **Answer.** You should seek the mysteries of these figures, and you will find a source of greater wonder and joy. There is no doubt that the corpses of the dead signify sins in the Law. Hence the statement is derived: “Whoever is baptized by a dead person and again touches him, what does his washing profit him? So also whoever fasts for his sins and then goes out and does the same things again,” and so forth (Eccl. XXXIV, 30–31). The burial of the dead therefore signifies the remission of sins. This is the meaning of the statement: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI, 1). Where, then, were these symbolic corpses of the patriarchs to be buried except in that land where the one was crucified by whose blood the remission of sins was accomplished?

**Question 277.** What does it mean that Jacob, turning toward the head of his bed, prayed to the Lord (Gen. XLVII, 31)? — **Answer.** After his son had sworn to him, assuring him concerning the request he had made, he worshiped God toward the head of his bed [Ms., “he began to worship the Lord”]. For the holy man, obedient and devoted to God, weighed down by old age, had his bed positioned in such a way that, while lying down, he was ready to pray without any difficulty [the added *habitus* is of uncertain force].

{334} **Question 278.** What does Jacob mean when he says, “Your two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are” (Gen. XLVIII, 5)? — **Answer.** He means: just as Reuben and Simeon will be two tribes and will be called by their own names, so Ephraim and Manasseh will be two tribes. They too will produce two peoples and will inherit the land of promise, like my sons. But the other sons whom you beget after my death will be yours; they will be called by their fathers’ names in their inheritance. They will not receive land separately, nor have their own allotments, as the other tribes do; within the tribe of Ephraim [Ms., Ephraim] and Manasseh they will be mingled as appendages of the people.

**Question 279.** Why did Jacob wish to tell his son Joseph, as though he did not know it, where and when he had buried Joseph’s mother (verse 7)? — **Answer.** Perhaps he wished prophetically to recall that Joseph’s mother had been buried there where Christ was destined to be born.

**Question 280.** What is the one portion that Jacob gave to his son Joseph [in addition to his brothers], which he says he took from the hand of the Amorites with his sword and bow (verse 22)? — **Answer.** He signified the city called Shechem in Hebrew and, according to Greek and Latin declension, called Sichima; it is corruptly called Sichar by many, and is now called Neapolis, the city of the Samaritans. *Shechem* in the Hebrew language is translated “shoulder” [Al., “number”], which is why the Seventy [especially] translated it as they did. When he says that he possessed it by his bow and sword, he calls the bow and sword justice, by which he deserved, as a foreigner and sojourner, to be delivered from danger after Shechem and Hamor had been killed. For, as we read above, he feared that the neighboring towns and fortresses might rise against him because of the destruction of the allied city, but the Lord did not allow them to harm him.

[Or it should certainly be understood in this way: “I shall give you Sichima, which [I acquired] by my strength,” that is, with the money which I obtained through much labor and sweat. By saying “above your brothers,” he shows that he gave it to Joseph’s tribe without casting lots; and his mausoleum can still be seen there today.]

# ON THE BLESSINGS OF THE PATRIARCHS

**Question 231.** How are the blessings with which the patriarch Jacob blessed his sons to be understood—historically or allegorically—when he said, “Gather yourselves together, sons of Jacob [and listen, Israel, to your father], so that I may announce to you what will happen in the last days” (Gen. XLIX, 1)? These words seem to convey allegory more than history. — **Answer.** Both are intended: history and allegory. History concerns the division of the land of promise, whose [divisions] were to be allotted to their grandsons. Allegory concerns Christ and the Church and what would happen in the last times. But first the foundations of the historical account must be laid, so that the summit of the allegory may more suitably be placed upon the earlier structure.

“Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength, the beginning of my grief, foremost in gifts [greater in authority]; you have poured yourself out like water; do not increase, because you went up onto your father’s bed and defiled his couch” (verses 3–4).

[Col. 0559D] **From Jerome, *Questions on Genesis*.** The sense here is this: You are my firstborn, greater in strength [the printed “*libris*” is probably an OCR corruption of *viribus*], and according to the order of your birth you ought to possess the inheritance that was due by right to firstborn sons—namely, to receive the priesthood and the kingdom [for this is demonstrated in the bearing of the burden and in mighty strength]. But because you sinned and, like water that cannot be held in a vessel, poured yourself out in the impulse of pleasure [Ms., “of the will”], I therefore command you not to sin further, but to remain among your brothers mourning [Al., “paying for”] the punishment of your sin, because you lost the rank of the firstborn.

[Col. 0559D] **The following is not Jerome’s.** “The beginning of grief” is every firstborn, because the parents’ affections are first moved on his behalf.

“Simeon and Levi are brothers, weapons of iniquity for warfare. Let my soul not enter their council, and let my glory not be in their assembly; because in their fury they killed [a man] and in their will they undermined a wall. Cursed be their fury, because it was stubborn, and their indignation, because it was harsh. I shall divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (verses 5–7).

This signifies that it was not his counsel that they killed Shechem and Hamor, the men allied with them, and that, contrary to what was right, they shed innocent blood in a time of peace and friendship. Filled with cruelty as though by a kind of fury, they overthrew the walls of the foreign city [Ms., “so that they would overthrow them”] (Gen. XXXIV). Hence he says, “Cursed be their fury, because it was stubborn,” and so forth. “And I shall scatter them in Israel.” Levi did not receive a separate inheritance but had a few cities for dwelling throughout all the tribal allotments [Edit., “cities to be inhabited”]. Concerning Simeon, it is written in the book of Joshua (XIX, 1–2) that he too did not receive his own allotment, but obtained something from the tribe of Judah.

“Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hands shall be upon the necks of your enemies; the sons of your father shall worship you. Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to the prey, my son” (Gen. XLIX, 8–9). Or, as it is written in Hebrew: “You have gone up from captivity, my son.” You have lain down and rested like a lion; and like a lioness, who will rouse him?

Because Judah is interpreted as “confession” or “praise,” it is rightly written: “Your brothers shall confess to you, Judah,” or “shall praise you.” Although this contains a great mystery concerning Christ, according to the literal sense it signifies that kings are generated from the stock of David and that all the tribes would worship him. For it does not say “the sons of your mother,” but “the sons of your father.”

The following words, “You have gone up to the prey, my son,” show that he would lead captive peoples away; and according to the more sacred interpretation, that Christ ascended on high and led captivity captive (Eph. IV, 8). Or, as I think more fittingly, captivity signifies the Passion, and ascent signifies the Resurrection.

“He binds his foal to the vine and his donkey to the vine” (Gen. XLIX, 11). This signifies that he joined the donkey’s foal on which Jesus sat—that is, the people of the Gentiles—to the vineyard of the apostles who are from the Jews; and that he bound the donkey on which he sat to the vine, or, as it is found in Hebrew, [to *Soreth*], that is, to the choice vine: the Church gathered from the nations.

When he says, “My son,” this is an apostrophe (*ἀποστροφή*) to Judah [Al., “he turns the address from Judah toward Christ”], indicating that Christ would accomplish all these things.

[Col. 0560D] **The following is not Jerome’s.** When he says, “The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations,” he signifies that rulers from the tribe of Judah would not fail until the time when Christ was born, he who, sent by the Father, is the expectation of the nations.

[“Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea and at the station of ships, reaching as far as Sidon.”]

“Isachar is a strong ass, lying between the boundaries. He saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent; he placed his shoulder under the burden and became a servant to tribute” (verse 13).

[Col. 0560D] **Jerome, *Questions on Genesis*.** Since above he had said concerning Zebulun that he would possess the shores of the Great Sea and would reach Sidon and the other Phoenician cities, he now returns to the inland province. By his blessing he made Isachar, who would possess the most beautiful region beside Naphtali [in Galilee], its inhabitant. He calls him a bony or strong ass, and says that he placed his shoulder under the burden, because he would work very hard in cultivating the land and carrying to the sea the loads produced in his territory, also transporting tribute to the kings.

The Hebrews say that, metaphorically, this signifies that, meditating on the Holy Scriptures day and night, he devoted his effort to labor; and therefore all serve him, as though carrying gifts to a teacher.

“Dan shall judge his people, like another tribe in Israel. Let Dan become a serpent on the road, a horned serpent on the path, biting the horse’s hooves so that its rider falls backward” (Gen. XLIX, 16–18). “I shall await your salvation, Lord.”

Samson, a judge in Israel, was from the tribe of Dan. Thus, seeing in the spirit that Samson the Nazirite would grow his hair and triumph over his slain enemies, he now says that, like a serpent and basilisk lying in wait on the roads, he would allow no one to cross the land of Israel; and even if some reckless man, trusting in his own strength as though in the speed of a horse, wished to ravage it like a brigand, he would not be able to escape him.

He speaks throughout by the metaphor of the serpent and the horse [Edit., “what he says relates to the form of the serpent and horse”]. Seeing, therefore, your Nazirite so strong, who died on account of a prostitute and, by dying, killed our enemies, I thought, O God, that he was your Christ, your Son. [Col. 0561A] But because he died and did not rise again, and Israel was once more led away captive, another Savior of the world and of my people must be awaited, so that he may come for whom this has been reserved; he himself will be the expectation of the nations [Ed., “but he who died and rose again is therefore my Savior,” and so forth].

{336} “Gad, girded, shall fight before him, and he himself shall be girded behind” (verse 19). This signifies that, returning after fourteen years before Reuben, half the tribe of Manasseh, and the sons whom he had left beyond the Jordan in possession [Ms., “his sons beyond the Jordan”], he found a great battle against the neighboring nations and fought bravely after defeating the enemy. Read the book of Joshua son of Nun (XIII, 7) and Chronicles (I Chron. V, 1, 11).

[Col. 0561B] “Naphtali is a released hind, giving beautiful words; or, Naphtali is a watered field” (Gen. XLIX, 21). The Hebrew word *Aiala Selvha* [Edit., *Silvam*] signifies both. It means either that warm waters arise in this tribe, or that it was watered by the streams of the Jordan above Lake Gennesaret. The Hebrews, however, wish “a watered field” to be understood here because of Tiberias, which seemed to possess knowledge of the Law; and they interpret it as the beautiful utterances of the prophets [Ms., “a watered field and the beautiful utterances of the prophets”].

The released hind indicates seasonal crops and the fertility and speed of the land. But it is better if we refer everything to the teaching of the Savior, because the Savior taught there especially, as is also written in the Gospel (Matt. IV, 15).

[Col. 0561C] “Joseph is a son who increases, my son who increases and is beautiful in appearance. Daughters ran upon the wall, but they embittered him, quarreled with him, and harbored envy, having arrows. His bow remained firm, and the bonds of his arms and hands were loosened by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob. From there the shepherd went forth, the stone of Israel” (Gen. XLIX, 22–24).

O son of Joseph, you are so beautiful that a crowd of Egyptian girls looked out upon you from the walls, towers, and windows [Ms., “looked out”]. Your brothers envied you [and provoked you to anger], bearing arrows of spite and wounded by darts of jealousy [Ita Ms.; Al., “and they envied him”]. But you placed your bow and weapons of battle in God, who is a mighty defender; and your bonds, with which your brothers had bound you, were loosed and broken by him. Thus from your seed the strong tribe of Ephraim will arise, steadfast and invincible, harder even than stone, and ruling the ten tribes of Israel.

“Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he eats the prey, and in the evening he divides the spoils” (verse 27). It is evident to all how clearly this is a prophecy of the apostle Paul. In his youth he persecuted the Church (Acts VIII, 3); in his old age he became a preacher of the Gospel (Gal. I, 13).

The Hebrews, however, explained it in this way [Ms., “discussed it thus”]: The altar on which sacrifices were offered and at whose base the blood of the victims was poured was in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin [Al., “had been”]. “This,” they say, “therefore signifies that the priests offer sacrifices in the morning and in the evening divide what has been collected for them from the people according to the Law,” placing the bloodthirsty and voracious wolf in relation to the interpretation of the altar, and the division of the spoils in relation to the priests, who, serving the altar, live from the altar.

[Thus far is from Jerome.]

Thus far [Ms., “however”] concerns the historical sense.

Spiritually, however, Reuben represents the earlier people of the Jews, to whom the Lord says through the prophet, “Israel is my firstborn” (Gen. XLIX, 3). For, in accordance with what was due to the firstborn, it belonged to that people to receive the priesthood and the kingdom.

It is added, “You are my strength.” Certainly this means that the foundation of faith came to that people from the very power of God [Ms., “because the foundation of faith came from that people itself; from it came the power of God”], who is Christ.

But how is he himself “the beginning of grief,” except because he continually inflicts injuries upon God the Father, turning his back [and not his face] toward him? He is “foremost in gifts,” because the oracles of God, the legislation, and the covenant [or promise] were first entrusted to him. He is “greater in authority,” certainly because of the greatness of his strength, since he reigned more abundantly than the others in this world [Edit., “he denied God,” incorrectly].

He was poured out like water by sinning against Christ, like water that cannot be held in a vessel; he was poured out in the impulse of his will [Al., “of pleasure”]. Therefore he added, “Do not increase.” [Because he sinned and denied Christ,] after he was scattered throughout the whole world, he was greatly diminished.

But why did he deserve such things? He adds: “Because you went up onto your father’s bed and defiled his couch.” This happened when he seized the Lord’s body, in which the fullness of divinity rested, hung it upon the cross, and defiled it with iron.

[Col. 0562C] “Simeon and Levi are brothers, weapons of iniquity for warfare” (verse 5). By Simeon and Levi the scribes, Pharisees, and priests of the Jewish people are understood. The scribes of the Jews were associated with Simeon, while from the tribe of Levi came the chief priests, who conspired to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him. Of this conspiracy he says, “Let my soul not enter their council.” For he shuddered at all the crimes that the Jews were to commit in the last times.

“For in their fury they killed a man”—that is, Christ, of whom it is said, “Behold, a man whose name is Rising” (Zech. VI, 12). And elsewhere: “A woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. XXXI, 22). “They undermined a wall”: they pierced with a lance that spiritual and exceedingly strong wall which guards Israel.

“Cursed be their fury, because it was stubborn”—namely, when, inflamed with fury, they delivered Christ to Pontius Pilate, saying, “Crucify him, crucify him” (John XIX, 6). “And their indignation, because it was harsh”—when they demanded the robber Barabbas and asked that the Prince of Life be crucified (Matt. XXVII, 21).

“I shall divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel,” because some of them believed, while others remained in unbelief. Those who separate themselves from them and come to faith are said to be divided; those whose homeland and temple were overthrown, and whose unbelieving nation was scattered throughout the world, are scattered.

[Col. 0563A] “Judah, your brothers shall praise you” (Gen. XLIX, 8). By this Judah the true confessor, Christ, is represented, who was born according to the flesh from his tribe. His brothers praise him: namely, the apostles and all his coheirs, who through adoption have become sons of God the Father and brothers of Christ by grace, while he himself is their Lord by nature.

“Your hands shall be upon the necks of your enemies.” By those same hands and by the same trophy of the cross he both protected his own people and conquered hostile and adverse powers [Ms., “bent them”]. Accordingly, the Father also promises him, saying: “Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet.”

“The sons of your father shall worship you,” because many of the sons of Jacob, worshiping him through the election of grace, have been saved.

“Judah is a lion’s cub” (verse 9), because by being born he became little, as it is written: “A little one has been born for us.”

“You have gone up to the prey, my son”: that is, ascending the cross, you redeemed captive peoples [and, dying, rescued those whom that adversary had invaded. Finally, returning from the underworld, you ascended on high and led captivity captive].

“You have lain down and rested like a lion.” Most clearly Christ lay down in his Passion, when, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit, or when in the tomb he rested securely, as though in a kind of sleep of the body.

But why “like a lion” and “like a lion’s cub”? In his sleep he was a lion, because he fulfilled this not by necessity but by power, as he himself says: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down.”

What he added, “And like a lion’s cub,” means that he died from the same source from which he was born. Christ therefore rested like a lion, because he not only did not fear the bitterness of death, but even in death itself conquered death’s dominion.

When he says, “Who will rouse him?” what else does this mean than what he himself says [Ms., “because no one except himself,” in accordance with what he himself said]: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”?

“The ruler shall not fail from Judah,” and so forth (verse 10). This most clearly refers to Judah. For a long time an unbroken succession of kings from his seed remained among the Jews, until Christ was born; this has already been stated above.

“He binds his foal to the vine” (verse 11). His foal is the people from the Gentiles, upon whom the burden of the Law had never yet been imposed. The apostles who are from the Jews bound this people to the vine, of which it is said: “The vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth” [Al., “he joined it to the vine, namely, to the apostles who are from the Jews. For the vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth is the house of Israel”].

And [they bind it] to the vine which says, “I am the true vine.” To this vine, therefore, he binds his donkey, that is, the synagogue, pregnant [Ms., “slow-moving,” that is], and weighed down by the heavy burden of the Law.

“He washed his robe in wine,” or his flesh in the blood of the Passion; or the holy Church in that wine which is poured out for many for the remission of sins.

“And his cloak in the blood of the grape.” The cloak is the nations, which he joined to his body, as it is written: “As I live, says the Lord, unless I clothe all these as a garment.”

“His eyes are more beautiful than wine” (verse 12). The eyes of Christ are the apostles and evangelists, who provide the Church with the light of knowledge, whose teachings [Al., “writings”] surpass the austerity of the wine of the ancient Law, because they are far milder.

“And his teeth are whiter than milk.” The teeth are the holy teachers, who cut people away from errors and, as though by chewing them, transfer them into the body of Christ. The teachers of the Church have become whiter than the milk of the old Law.

“Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea and at the station of ships” [Ms., “shall dwell”] (verse 13). Zebulun is interpreted as “dwelling-place of beauty” [Al., “of strength”], and it signifies the Church, which dwells on the shore of the sea and at the station of ships, so that it may be a refuge for believers and show the harbor of faith to those in danger.

Against all the storms of the world, it awaits shipwreck with unshaken firmness, solidly resisting the storms of the Jews and heretics, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine. Although it is battered by the waves, it is not broken.

It extends as far as Sidon, that is, as far as the nations. It is also read in the Gospel that some apostles were taken from those places and that the Lord often taught there, as it is written: “The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the people sitting in darkness, saw a great light” (Matt. IV, 16; Isa. IX, 1–2).

Sidon is interpreted as “hunter” or “huntress.” And who are the hunters except the apostles, who, as we said above, were taken from those places? Of them it is said: “I shall send many hunters, and they shall hunt you on every mountain” [Al., “in every place”] (Jer. XVI, 16).

“Isachar is a strong ass” (Gen. XLIX, 14–15). Isachar, which is interpreted as “reward,” refers to the people of the nations, whom the Lord purchased at the price of his blood.

This Isachar is described as a strong ass because formerly the Gentile people, like a brutish and lustful animal [had lived], subsisting without any reason; but now, submitting its neck to the rule of the strong Redeemer, it has come under the yoke of evangelical discipline [Al., “but later willingly bore the yoke …”].

“Lying between the boundaries, he saw that rest was good and the land excellent.” To lie between the boundaries is to rest while awaiting the end of the world, seeking none of the things that occur in between but desiring the final things.

The strong ass sees rest and an excellent land when the simple Gentile people therefore raises itself to the strength of good works [because] it strives toward the reward of eternal life.

Hence he also adds that it “places its shoulder under the burden,” because, desiring to reach the promised rest, it willingly bears all the burdens of the commandments. Thus it became “a servant to tribute,” that is, offering gifts of faith and the offerings of good works to Christ its king.

“Dan shall judge his people, like the other tribes of Israel. Let Dan become a serpent on the road, a horned serpent on the path,” and so forth (verse 16).

Some say that these words prophesy that the Antichrist will come from the tribe of Dan, because in this passage Dan is described as both a serpent and one who bites. Hence Dan was the first of the tribes of Israel to pitch its camp in the north, signifying the one who says that he will sit on the sides of the north, and of whom the prophet figuratively says: “From Dan the snorting of his horses was heard” (Jer. VIII, 16). He is called not only a serpent but also a horned serpent, or *cerastes*. For *keras* in Greek is said to mean “horn” [Al., “Κέρατα … are called horns”].

Thus that serpent is said to be horned, and the Antichrist is appropriately represented by it: he will be armed against the life of the faithful not only with the bite of poisonous preaching but also with the horns of power [Edit., “and also with horns against the powers”].

Who does not know that a path is narrower than a road? He therefore becomes a serpent on the road because he entices those to walk in the broadness of the present life whom he flatters as though sparing them. But he bites when, with the poison of his error, he consumes those to whom he grants liberty.

Again, he becomes a horned serpent on the path because he attacks those whom he finds faithful and sees constraining themselves within the narrow paths of the heavenly commandment—not only with the wickedness of crafty persuasion, but also kills them with the terror of power [Al., “presses them”]. In the anguish of persecution, after the pretended favors of sweetness, he exercises the horns of his power.

[In this passage] the horse signifies this world, which, through its pride, foams along in the course of passing time. And because the Antichrist will seize the end of the world [Ms., “strives to seize it”], that horned serpent is said to bite the horse’s hooves. For biting the horse’s hooves means reaching the end of the age by striking it.

“So that its rider falls backward.” The rider of this horse is whoever is lifted up by the iniquities of this world; hence he is said to fall backward.

This brief commentary is thus concluded in the Benedictine edition of the works of Saint Augustine, Saint-Maur, volume III, Appendix, page 28:

“So that its rider falls backward. The unbelieving Jewish people, caught in the snares of their own error, await the Antichrist instead of Christ. Jacob rightly, in the same passage, suddenly turned into the voice of the elect, saying: ‘I shall await your salvation, Lord’ (verse 18). That is: I faithfully believe not in the Antichrist, as the unbelievers do, but in the true Christ, who is to come for our redemption. Amen.”

{339}

# SAYINGS OF THE BLESSED ALBINUS, LEVITE

On the passage from Genesis: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26).

## PRELIMINARY NOTICE

[Col. 0565B]

This little commentary, found in Ms. J. Sirmond under the preceding title, was appended by the distinguished Quercetanus to the *Questions on Genesis*. It had already been published among the works of Saint Ambrose under the title *A Little Book on the Dignity of the Human Condition* [Col. 0565C], and among those of Saint Augustine with this inscription: *On the Creation of the First Man*. It is now found in the appendices to the works of Ambrose and Augustine. We found it in the manuscripts of Salzburg, Freising, and Saint Emmeram, without an author’s title, indeed, but included among other short works of Alcuin. In the same Salzburg manuscript, marked no. 67, there is also a little work in which the works of the six days and other matters are treated in accordance with a discussion between boys, with questions and answers. There the nature of man is discussed, and that passage of Genesis 1:26, “Let us make man,” etc., is examined in dialogue; the answers, however, are given in the same words that are read continuously in the little commentary now before you. It is certainly uncertain whether these words were first—an easy thing to believe—arranged as a dialogue and later detached from it in the form of a single dissertation, or whether they were first delivered in a continuous exposition and afterward incorporated into a more extensive dialogue. Nevertheless, I am convinced that blessed Alcuin is the true author not only of this little commentary but also of that entire dialogue, or discussion between the boys. We shall, however, place it among the doubtful minor works, where you may see the preliminary notice.

So great [Edit., “the whole”] is recognized to be the dignity of the human condition: man was created not merely by the word of command, as were the other works of the six days, but by the counsel of the holy Trinity and the work of the divine Majesty [Al., “is”]. Thus, from the honor of his first condition, he might understand how much he owed his Creator, since the Creator immediately granted him so great a privilege of dignity in his creation, so that he might love his Creator with all the greater ardor in proportion as he understood that he had been formed by Him in so marvelous a way. And this is so not only because he was so excellently created by the counsel of the holy Trinity, but also because the Creator of all things made him according to His own image and likeness [Col. 0566B], something He granted to none of the other creatures.

This image must be considered more carefully from the nobility of the inner man. First, just as God, being one, is always wholly present everywhere, giving life to all things, moving and governing them—as the Apostle confirms: “In him we live, and move, and have our being” (Acts 17:28)—so also the soul is wholly active everywhere in its body, giving it life, moving it, and governing it. For it is not greater in the larger members of its body and smaller in the smaller members, but is wholly present in the smallest and wholly present in the largest. This is the image of the unity of almighty God that the soul possesses in itself.

It also bears a certain image of the holy Trinity. First, in this respect: just as God is, lives, and has wisdom, so the soul, in its own manner, is, lives, and has wisdom. There is also another Trinity in it, since it was created according to the image of its Creator, the perfect and supreme Trinity, which is in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit [Al., “which is from the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit”] [Col. 0566D]. And although it is of one nature, it nevertheless possesses within itself three dignities, namely, understanding, will, and memory.

The same thing, though expressed in other words, is signified in the Gospel when it is said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Matthew 22:37)—that is, with all your understanding, with all your will, and with all your memory. Now [Ms., “For”], just as the Son is generated from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, so from understanding the will is generated, and from both of these memory proceeds, as anyone of sound judgment can easily understand. For the soul cannot be perfect without these three, nor can any one of these three, so far as its blessedness is concerned, be complete without the other two [Col. 0567A].

And just as God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit are not three gods but one God possessing three persons, so too there are soul-understanding, soul-will, and soul-memory—not three souls in one body, but one soul possessing three dignities. In these three our inner man wonderfully bears the image of God in his nature. From these, as from the soul’s more excellent dignities, we are commanded to love the Creator, so that He may be loved in proportion as He is understood [Al., “He is understood ... He is loved”], and may always be held in memory in proportion as He is loved.

Understanding of Him alone is not sufficient unless the will is directed toward His love; indeed, these two are not sufficient unless memory is added, by which God remains continually in the mind of the one who understands and loves Him. Thus, just as there can be no moment in which man does not use or enjoy God’s goodness and mercy [Col. 0567B], so there ought to be no moment in which he does not have Him present in his memory. Let this suffice concerning the image.

Now understand something concerning the likeness, which is to be discerned in conduct [Al., “in lesser things”]. Just as God the Creator, who created man according to His likeness, is love, is good and just, patient and gentle, pure, merciful, and adorned with the other marks of holy virtues that are read of Him, so man was created to possess love, to be good and just, patient and gentle, pure and merciful. The more each person possesses these virtues within himself, the nearer he is to God and the greater likeness of his Creator he bears.

But if—God forbid—someone, through the byways of vices and the divergences of crimes, should degenerate and stray from this most noble likeness of his Creator, then what is written will happen to him: “And man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them” (Psalm 48:13). What greater honor could man have than to be created according to the likeness of his Maker and adorned with the same garments of virtue with which his Creator is adorned, of whom it is written: “The Lord has reigned; he is clothed with beauty” (Psalm 92:1)—that is, adorned with the splendor of every virtue and the beauty of complete goodness?

Or what greater disgrace, or more unhappy misery, could befall man than, after losing the glory of this likeness of his Creator [Col. 0568B], to sink into the shapeless and irrational likeness of brute beasts? Therefore let each person consider more carefully the excellence of his first creation, recognize within himself the venerable image of the holy Trinity, and strive to possess, through nobility of conduct, exercise of virtue, and dignity of merit, the honor of the divine likeness for which he was created. Thus, when what he is becomes manifest, he may appear like the One who wondrously formed him according to His likeness in the first Adam, and more wondrously restored him in the second [Edit., incorrectly, “in the age”].

# ON THE TEN WORDS OF THE LAW, OR A BRIEF EXPOSITION OF THE DECALOGUE

## PRELIMINARY NOTICE

This very brief exposition of the Decalogue was published by D. Lucas d’Acheri from the manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés together with two other letters of blessed Alcuin: *On the Comparison of the Old and New Testaments* and *On the Three Kinds of Vision* (see Letters 203 and 204), in volume III of the *Spicilegium*, p. 321. We have therefore transcribed it here, both because it lacks the form of a letter and because its subject is connected with the *Questions on Genesis*.

The Lord therefore gave Moses the law of our innocence and of the knowledge of Himself, and established it in ten words, writing it with His finger on tablets of stone. These commandments are distributed in such a way that three concern love of the divine Trinity, while seven concern brotherly love, by which human society is not harmed.

The first commandment of the Decalogue pertains to God the Father, when it says: “The Lord your God is one God” (Exodus 20; Deuteronomy 5). This means that, hearing this, you should worship the one God the Father and not pour out your fornication among many gods.

The second commandment pertains to the Son, when it says: “You shall not take the name of your Lord in vain”—that is, do not suppose that a creature is the Son of God, since every creature is subject to vanity; but believe that He is equal to the Father, God of gods, the Word who was with God, through whom all things were made.

The third commandment, concerning the Sabbath, pertains to the Holy Spirit, whose gift promises us everlasting rest. Since the Holy Spirit is so called, God also sanctified the seventh day [Col. 0568C]; for on the other days the sanctification of works is not mentioned, except on the Sabbath, where it is said: “God rested.” Therefore this commandment pertains to the Holy Spirit, both because of the name of sanctification and because of the eternal rest belonging to the gift of the Holy Spirit.

For it is said there: “Remember that you sanctify the Sabbath day. Six days you shall labor, and shall do all your work. But the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God; you shall do no work on it” (Exodus 20:10). The work of the six days contains the activity of six thousand years; in the rest of the seventh is shown the time of that blessed kingdom which the Jews, celebrating it carnally, await. And lest we falsely deceive ourselves and apply this to faith in a lie, God cries out through the prophet: “Your new moons and your Sabbaths my soul has hated” (Isaiah 1:13). How, then, were or will those Sabbaths be sanctified which God hated? Therefore the Sabbath is sanctified where eternal rest is promised to us after the good works of this life. Accordingly, whatever we do, if we do it for the sake of the rest of the future age, we truly observe the Sabbath.

After these three commandments comes the number seven of the commandments pertaining to love of one’s neighbor. It begins with honoring parents, when it says: “Honor your father and your mother” (Exodus 20:12); this is the fourth commandment. For from his parents man opens his eyes, and this life takes its beginning from their love. Hence this commandment is first, as the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Honor your father and your mother,” which is the first commandment (Matthew 15:4; Ephesians 6:2). But how is it first, unless in the manner already stated, namely, that within the number seven, because it pertains to love of one’s neighbor, it is first on the other tablet? For this is why two tablets of the law were given.

In this commandment, therefore, children are ordered to honor their parents and not to be insulting or insolent toward them, but to show them the reverence owed through the duty of piety and humanity. For if someone withholds honor from his parents, whom will he be able to spare, if he hates his own?

The fifth: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20:14), that is, no one should unite with women outside the marriage covenant in order to satisfy lust. For he specifically commits adultery who approaches another woman besides his own.

[Col. 0569B] It should have said “the fifth,” as above it said “the sixth.”

The sixth: “You shall not kill.” For not only does the person who commits homicide by deed commit murder, but also the one who encounters a hungry or naked person who may die unless he helps him by supplying clothing and food; such a person will therefore be held guilty of homicide.

The seventh: “You shall not steal” [Col. 0570A] (verse 15), which is the vice of rapacity.

The eighth: “You shall not bear false witness” (verse 16), which is the crime of lying and falsity.

The ninth: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (verse 17). In this commandment he forbids the intention of adulterous thought. For one thing is to do something of this kind with a woman other than one’s wife, and another is not to desire another man’s wife; therefore there are two commandments: “You shall not commit adultery,” and “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.”

The tenth: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property.” In this commandment he condemns worldly ambition and restrains the desire for possessions.

Thus the first of these prohibits superstition, the second error, the third love of the world, the fourth impiety, the fifth restrains fornication, the sixth cruelty, the seventh rapacity, the eighth destroys falsehood, the ninth adulterous thought, and the tenth greed [Col. 0570B]. And it should be noted that, just as the Egyptians were struck by ten plagues, so ten commandments are written on the tablets, by which the people of God are governed and demons are slain.

# SECOND LITTLE WORK: THE *ENCHIRIDION*, OR A PIOUS AND BRIEF EXPOSITION OF THE PENITENTIAL PSALMS, PSALM 118, AND THE GRADUAL PSALMS

## PRELIMINARY NOTICE

This threefold little work was occasioned by Alcuin’s frequent discussions of the divine Scriptures with Arno, archbishop of Salzburg, his beloved “Aquila.” When they were conversing about the seven penitential psalms, Psalm 118, and the fifteen Gradual Psalms, whose use in the Church’s office had always been celebrated, Arno asked Alcuin to compose brief expositions of them, as a kind of *Enchiridion*, that is, a handbook, as is learned from the dedicatory letter that follows immediately. Alcuin agreed and afterward sent these expositions to Arno through Fredegisus, together with certain other little books listed in Letter 117, now 153, to the same Arno.

This *Enchiridion*, then, appeared for the first time in print, so far as we have been able to discover, at Paris in 1547, in octavo, from the press of Nicolaus le Riche, or Divitis. Eight years later, that is [Col. 0569D], in 1555, it was given a place among the *Orthodoxographi Theologi*, or sacred doctors of sounder faith, published at Basel, pp. 1085–1122. Again, in the aforesaid city of Paris, a commentary on the penitential psalms, if William Crowe’s *Catalogue of the Scriptures*, p. 41, is to be trusted, appeared separately and without the other two commentaries in 1568, in octavo. Antonius Possevinus, however, in the *Sacred Apparatus*, vol. I, p. 35, adds to that edition also the commentary on Psalm 118 and the exposition of “The Sixty Queens,” etc., as the author of the *History of the Literature of France*, vol. IV, p. 304, reports. The distinguished Quercetanus transcribed the complete little work from the edition of Nicolaus Divitis.

In all these editions the preface, or letter, in which Alcuin dedicated the present work to Arno is missing. It was first published by the celebrated D. Lucas d’Acheri in 1669, *Spicilegium*, vol. IX, pp. 111, 116 of the old edition, or vol. III, p. 323 of the new edition. We found it in two manuscript codices, one belonging to the library of the most illustrious chapter of the metropolitan church of Salzburg, the other to the library of Saint Emmeram. In them this threefold commentary is also contained; we compared it with the editions and corrected it in many places.

In the Saint Emmeram manuscript, verses, or Latin rhythms composed from the beginnings of each of the aforementioned psalms, are appended to the exposition of the Gradual Psalms. They are also found in a manuscript of the library of the famous monastery of Reichenau, which the distinguished D. P. Bernard Liebherr, then prefect of the notable library, communicated to me shortly before the sad departure of its former inhabitants. Alcuin mentions these rhythms under the name of a hymn in the letter cited above, Letter 117, now 153, written to the same Archbishop Arno, in these words: “There is in it”—that is, in the handbook sent to Arno—“an old hymn on the fifteen Gradual Psalms.” By calling it old, he also implies that he himself was not the author of that hymn, but that it was composed by someone else.

[Col. 0569D] In d’Acheri’s *Spicilegium*, at the place cited, the following note is read:

“This very lucid preface had indeed been transcribed from the manuscript of Saint Claudius by Petrus Franciscus Chifflet, S.J. [Col. 0570D], but less accurately, as Baluzius discovered from a copy of Jacobus Sirmond taken from the same manuscript. With its help we corrected quite a few passages, which it would certainly be most useless to record. In that manuscript the following was written: ‘A book of Manno, of blessed memory, offered at the tomb of Saint Eugendus.’”

This book, then, belonged to the monastery of Saint Eugendus, commonly called Eugendi, in the Jura region, now called Saint-Claude, and was offered by Manno, provost of that monastery, says Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. II, book XXXII, p. 629.

## PREFACE

To the most holy Father and supreme pontiff, Bishop Arno, the humble Levite Alcuin [Al., “Archoinus,” incorrectly], greetings.

When I recognized, venerable Father, that your most holy will shone with zeal for the Catholic faith and abounded in God’s gifts of holy charity, and when you wished, as though consulting a father, to ask me, the least little servant of divine Scripture, about many customs of ecclesiastical dignity—lest perhaps something established by which Fathers concerning any matter should remain unknown to your prudence—a conversation suddenly arose between us concerning the psalms of penitence: which they were, how they were to be understood, and how they were to be used. It was soon discovered, from the discernment of the venerable Fathers, that there were seven of them.

You also inquired why Psalm 118 enjoyed such celebrated praise [Col. 0571B], or why it was accustomed to be sung at the canonical hours with such continual observance; and why the psalms were called Gradual, of which no one, while reading the book—

[Col. 0571D] In Acheri’s text, in place of *lectitanti*, one finds *librum delictante*, “while delighting in the book.” This monstrosity so frightened the latest editor of the *Spicilegium*—as he says—that he printed dots in its place to indicate that there was some corruption here [Col. 0572D]. That same editor believes that *delectante* should be read instead of *delictante*, in the same sense in which the verb *delectare* is used in the account of the Translation of the Bodies of Saints Ragnobertus and Zeno, chapter 5, volume II of the *Spicilegium*. In both the Salzburg and Saint Emmeram manuscripts, however, *lectitantem* is found, leaving no doubt that *lectitanti* should be read.

—I think there is no doubt concerning the psalms. You asked that brief expositions of them be prepared for your most discerning holiness, as a kind of *Enchiridion*, that is, a handbook. I gladly assented to your gracious request [Al., “by this request”], and, taking up the treatises of the holy Fathers who had carefully investigated the individual verses in the Book of Psalms, I set out to note what they said about these matters and to gather the sweetest flowers, so as to satisfy the desire of your will.

But first of all I thought it right to draw out the reasons for the numbers: namely, why the penitential psalms were also consecrated by the number seven [Col. 0571C]; why Psalm 118 was divided into twenty-two sections, each of which contained eight verses; and what reason there was for there being fifteen psalms designated by the title “Song of Ascents.”

It is very well known that the number seven has great perfection in its meaning throughout sacred Scripture, especially because Isaiah, the greatest of the prophets, declared [Ms., “foretold”] prophetically that the gifts of the Holy Spirit exist in Christ. There the same prophet, who was privy to the Lord’s secrets, says: “A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and he shall be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord” [Col. 0571D] (Isaiah 11:2).

The Lord Himself also wished to instruct us through seven petitions (Matthew 6:9). In the Apocalypse of John (1:4, 13, 16) He testifies that he saw seven lampstands and seven stars and wrote to seven churches. Many other things are found scattered through the divine books that display the perfection of the number seven [Col. 0572A]. Hence also Solomon’s saying: “Wisdom built herself a house; she hewed out seven pillars” (Proverbs 9:1). These matters require a longer discussion—if, indeed, anyone in our time is capable of explaining all the mysteries of this number.

The number seven was also consecrated at the beginning of creation by the Creator’s rest, and it is clear that the order of the ages proceeds according to the same number. Moreover, when it is divided into the two members of its greater portion, namely, three and four, it possesses the wondrous mystery of the universe. For in the number three the holy Trinity, creator of all that exists, is signified; and in the number four the totality of creatures is represented, whether because of the four regions of the world, or because of the origin of the four elements, or even because of the distribution of time [Col. 0572B], which is known to proceed in four ways. Therefore, because of the perfect forgiveness of sins that we receive in baptism, and also through the tears of confession and repentance, the penitential psalms are consecrated by the number seven.

Likewise, the final psalms of the Psalter, in praise of the Lord God eternal, are dedicated by the same rule of perfection, through the number seven.

Psalm 118, moreover, which is thought to have no equal for the testing [Ms., “purification”] of the soul through adherence to sacred prayers to God, is composed according to the alphabet of the Hebrew language. It appears to consist, according to the number of the letters of that language, of twenty-two sections, each of which contains eight verses, always beginning with the same letter in alphabetical order—perhaps because of the eight evangelical beatitudes, in which the perfection of the legal commandments is understood to reside; or because of the eighth day of circumcision, which in the new man signifies the stripping away of carnal pleasures. The verses of this psalm, taken together, amount to twice eighty-eight, as though an ascent were opened up through the ten legal commandments to the eight beatitudes of evangelical perfection.

Here would now be a suitable place for me to discuss the marvelous correspondence of numbers with the mysteries of our salvation, if my discourse were not directed elsewhere.

Likewise, in the fifteen Gradual Psalms, a most beautiful order of ascent is represented, reaching up to the upper room, in which the Holy Spirit came upon the names of the one hundred and twenty men in tongues of fire with a mighty flame [Ms., “breath”] [Col. 0572D].

[Col. 0572D] Baluzius restored the following wording conjecturally; in the Saint-Claude manuscript, as also in the first edition, it read *sicut putari*.

Therefore, if you begin to count the individual numbers from one through fifteen and gather their entire sum into one total, you will find one hundred and twenty—that is, three times five produces three times forty. This is the number in which Moses, by fasting, merited to receive the law [Col. 0573A], Elijah, exalted by the prophetic spirit, was raised up, and our Lord Jesus Christ Himself, after forty days of fasting, gloriously defeated the evil tempter.

When all these matters have been considered—how great is the excellence of numbers in the divine Scriptures, and how necessary it is for those who read them to know their significance—it is plainly evident. Through them the order of the ages proceeds, and the pattern of our life is established. Hence it is read in sacred Scripture that the Lord the Creator made all things in number, weight, and measure (Wisdom 11:21).

Therefore it seems proper to exhort your holy authority to encourage gifted young men to exercise themselves in such studies, so that, by the fervor of youthful talent [Ms., “with the fervent talent of youth”], they may learn and later, when their years have matured, have something to teach their disciples [Col. 0573B], so that, through the diligent preaching of your holiness, very many may be instructed in the law of the Lord.

It is the priest’s duty, from the lofty height of his station, to preach [Ms., “foresee”] what is appropriate to each person and with what pastures he should nourish the flock entrusted to him, lest some little sheep, wandering from the flock, should through the shepherd’s negligence be exposed to the bites of wolves.

Every teacher, indeed, will have to render an account to his master of the money entrusted to him, and no shepherd should imagine that little danger threatens him when he has received many thousands of souls to account for as his own. Let the good teacher labor diligently in the house of God, so that he may deserve to be gloriously crowned in the kingdom of God. The time of labor will therefore pass quickly, but the blessed reward will never end.

If we seek to live happily [Col. 0573C], let us direct our minds there where true happiness exists, to which no one can attain except supported by charity, which lifts us from earthly things to heavenly ones. Let us meditate on nothing more frequently during the pilgrimage of this life than how we may please our Redeemer and Judge, knowing that we shall not always be here, but shall always exist in another life.

How wretched is the person who, from the labor of this mortality, passes into a greater labor of mortality [Ms., “immortality”]; and how blessed is the person who passes from this labor into rest, whose end will never come. Therefore let us not love transient riches, but those that always remain.

The Lord Jesus did not promise us honors that pass away, but everlasting honors; not earthly glory [Col. 0573D], but heavenly glory; not a long life here, where we are born in sin, live in labor, and die in sorrow, but He promised us eternal life in blessedness [Al., “in perfection.”] He promised riches that do not perish but always remain.

The riches of this age, however, appear to be common to the good and the wicked. The good use them well, for the increase of their eternal salvation; the wicked use them badly, for their own destruction. But the Lord God promised those fervent in charity what nothing could surpass in blessedness: the perpetual vision of His blessedness, toward which we must hasten with purified heart, as Truth Himself says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

[Col. 0574A] Those are pure in heart, namely, whom no stain of any wickedness disturbs, who accustom themselves to praise God with chaste mind through heavenly hymns. They live an angelic life on earth, rejoicing in the praises of God and delighting in psalmody with pure heart.

No mortal will ever be able fully to explain the power of the psalms. In them the confessions of sinners are found; in them penitential tears are stirred; in them contrition of heart is renewed. For the entire Book of Psalms breathes of heavenly mysteries, abounds in spiritual precepts, and is filled with divine praises. Whoever has learned to sing the psalms with attentive mind and to examine them will find in them the whole dispensation of our salvation foretold, and the marvelous delights of heavenly joys.

Therefore, most holy Father, exhort the holy brothers [Col. 0574B] to examine their meanings diligently [Ms., “to learn them diligently”], so that they may know and understand in their hearts what they utter with mouth and tongue, instructed by the apostolic example. For it is written that the Apostle said of himself: “I shall sing with the spirit; I shall sing also with the mind; I shall pray with the spirit; I shall pray also with the mind” (1 Corinthians 14:15).

Let the mind of the one who sings meditate with understanding on the words [Edit., “those who understand”], for the thoughts of each person are open to the Lord, who does not despise the contrite and humbled heart of those who cry out to Him in prayer. Indeed [Ms., “as”], one of the wise has said [“the prayers of the humbled ascend to heaven”].

We have been saved through the humility and mercy of Christ, who says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29). Whoever shows mercy will receive mercy from God, as the Lord Himself says: “Be merciful, just as your heavenly Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36).

The image of God, to which we are being restored in our minds, consists especially in works of mercy. For these, an eternal kingdom is promised to the holy and just, when the sheep will be separated from the goats and will hear the desirable voice of the supreme King and Judge seated upon the throne of His paternal majesty: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34).

Read this, holy Father [Col. 0573D]—be happy [felix] [see the note below]—and remember Albinus, your teacher, for many years, while you stand humbly at the sacred altars of the Lord, so that the merciful Almighty, in His customary mercy, may release the bonds of crimes, whose fitting punishment for abominable offenses [the text is materially corrupt or incomplete], so that he may be able, rejoicing with you, to praise the Thunderer, after the labors of this life, through the Lord’s mercy.

May an all-powerful angel, sent from the heavenly citadel, accompany you as you go through lands, woods, and hills. Through castles and villages, through the mighty rivers of the earth, may he always everywhere, I pray, lead you forth and bring you back, rejoicing, together with the prosperity of holy salvation, you, gracious Father! Through the gift of Christ God, forever.

May you prosper and flourish always, dearest bishop! And with all your sheep, running through the pastures of life, may you gather the holy flowers of virtue [Col. 0575A], while you, Father, shepherd, patriarch, and priest, lead them.

[Col. 0575D] Cointius took from this poem an argument to prove that Arno and Alcuin were not blood brothers, although in one letter Alcuin wrote: “To my sweetest brother and dearest kinsman, Aquila,” etc. He maintains, however, that such letter inscriptions are titles of friendship, not of blood relationship. We discussed this matter in the preface prefixed to these works. Sixtus of Siena calls Alcuin’s annotations on the penitential psalms concise, pointed, and wonderfully significant according to the moral sense.

[Col. 0573D] In the manuscript used by Acherius, the word *felix*, enclosed here in brackets, had been omitted, and at the end, to complete the verse, the word *sacerdos* had been added conjecturally [Col. 0574D]. We restored the word *felix* from the Salzburg manuscript.

# PSALM VI

## VERSE 1

The title of the psalm is: “For the end; of David; in hymns, for the eighth.” Here “for the end” means that David sang hymns and songs with Christ, the End, in view; “for the eighth” means for the hope of the future resurrection.

Here David exhorts the sinful soul by his own example not to despair immediately, even if it has sinned grievously, but, after washing the bed of its conscience with tears of repentance, to return to God the physician, who heals the wounds of its sins.

[Col. 0575D] The manuscripts present this brief introduction as follows: “For the end; in hymns, for the eighth; a psalm of David.” “For the end” signifies eternity. A hymn is praise of the divinity composed according to the rule of some meter. “For the eighth,” however, signifies the Lord’s advent, when, after the week of the age has ended, He comes to judge the world. Hence this psalm also begins with the greatest trembling. In this psalm the human race asks to be corrected and judged by God, but not in anger and fury.

## VERSE 2

“Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger.”

Anger is prolonged indignation, whereas fury is a sudden kindling of the mind. But anger signifies the eternal punishment of the wicked, while fury signifies purgatorial fire; and the penitent man asks God to free him from both.

## VERSE 3

“Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak; heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled.”

The confession of sin is a powerful prayer for mercy. He will find God’s mercy who confesses himself miserable. “For I am weak; heal me,” he says, Lord—as though he were saying: “I am weak through sin; heal me through mercy.” “For my bones are troubled”: by “bones,” I mean all the virtues that, because of their firmness, are called bones.

## VERSE 4

“And my soul is greatly troubled; but you, Lord—how long?”

In the first man, my soul transgressed, lost all the virtues, and was therefore troubled through repentance, so that it might be cleansed. “And you, Lord—how long?” Supply: “How long will you not rescue, correct, and reform my soul, which is greatly troubled?”

## VERSE 5

“Turn, Lord, and rescue my soul; save me for the sake of your mercy.”

For unless He first turns our soul, no one will rescue it from danger [Ms., “unless He first turned our soul, no one would rescue it”]. Or: “Turn, Lord, and direct us through your mercy, and look upon us”—the text has [Ms., “deign to look upon us”]—“since on account of our sins you have turned your face away from us. Rescue my soul,” that is, from the punishment threatening it, “and save me,” not through my merits but through your mercy.

## VERSE 6

“For there is no one in death who remembers you.”

For the dead will not praise you, Lord, but we who live [Ms., “who are living”], because He is not the God of the dead but of the living.

“And in hell who will confess to you?”

[Not as an impossibility, but as something rare, he used this expression.] “For forgiveness” must be supplied; for properly speaking, confession is found in this world, where forgiveness is also found.

## VERSE 7

“I have labored in my groaning.”

Here he explains the measure of his repentance.

“Every night I will wash my bed.”

By “bed,” let us understand bodily pleasure.

“With my tears I will water my couch.”

To water signifies something more abundant than to wash. The “couch” signifies the heap of sins.

## VERSE 8

“My eye is troubled because of anger.”

Because of the Lord’s anger he confesses that the eye [of his heart] is troubled. “O God, through whom the punishments that I fear have been prepared for me, my mind is troubled, and the whole governing power of my heart trembles.”

“I have grown old among all my enemies.”

“I have grown old”—that is, I have remained in the iniquity of the old man Adam—“among all my enemies,” whether among demonic spirits or among our sins.

## VERSE 9

“Depart from me, all you who work iniquity.”

After he himself has obtained mercy, he teaches or exhorts the others to depart from him [Edit., “to conduct themselves as he does, whom he does not wish”]; for he does not wish to have the company of the wicked. [At the same time, it should also be noted—as we said above—that he commands not those who have worked iniquity, but those who are working it, to depart from him.]

## VERSE 10

“Depart, therefore,” he says, “from me, evildoers, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.”

The Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has received my prayer. He repeats one and the same thing in many ways, as joyful and rejoicing people are accustomed to do.

### Verse 11

“Let all my enemies turn back and be utterly ashamed; let them turn back and be very swiftly ashamed.” He does not pray against his enemies but for his enemies, that they may turn away from their sins and be ashamed—not lightly, but intensely; not tomorrow, but quickly and in the present time. Amen.

## Psalm XXXI

The title of the psalm is, “Of David: understanding,” because David understood, and by his example commands us also to understand that no sin is so serious that God will not freely forgive it, if we are prepared to confess it and abstain from wicked ways.

> [Col. 0576D] Manuscript copies: “A psalm of David; to this belongs understanding.” “A psalm of David” contains the voice of the prophet, showing that a person can be saved not by his own merits but by the grace of God, if he confesses. This, then, is what “understanding” means: that the Godhead has granted us understanding of our sins, so that we may earnestly pray for their cleansing.

### Verse 1

“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered.” Their iniquities are forgiven, that is, the iniquities of those whose sins are washed away by the Lord God through confession; and their sins are covered through charity, according to the saying: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8). Or their sins are covered so that here they may be veiled by repentance and not revealed in judgment. Some call those things “iniquities” that are committed before baptism, and “sins” those committed afterward.

### Verse 2

“Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin, and in whose mouth [Ms., in whose spirit] there is no deceit.” What is covered will not be seen; what is not reckoned will not be punished. “And in whose mouth there is no deceit”: that is, in the mouth of the one who confesses himself to be a sinner, like the tax collector who said, “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13). For the person who displeases himself is pleasing to God; there is no deceit in his mouth, but, believing God in truth, he confessed with his mouth what he held in his heart.

### Verse 3

“For when I was silent, my bones grew old, while I cried out all day long.” I did not put forth (*protuli*; Ed., *praetuli*, “put before”) a confession for salvation; therefore all my strength withered in the weakness of the flesh. “While I cried out”—that is, many cry out if they possess anything good, and display it through vanity. The wicked are silent and cry out: they are silent about what it is lawful to speak of, and speak of what they ought to keep silent. They are silent when they conceal their sins; they cry out when they proclaim their merits. They are silent in confessing their sins and cry out in presumption upon their merits. What, then, does “while I cried out all day long” mean except “while I persisted in crying out”?

> [Col. 0577D] Manuscript copies: “They are silent about confession and cry out in presumption. What, then, is ‘crying out all day long’? Persevering in the defense of their sins.”

### Verse 4

“For day and night your hand was heavy upon me; I was turned in my misery while the thorn was fastened into me.” For the sinner, the hand that scourges and punishes with weight is grievous. “Day and night” signifies continuous time. He would not have been humbled beneficially in any other way unless the hand of the Godhead had pressed him down. “I was turned in my misery”: that is, I understood my sin after you made me miserable beneath the weight of your power. “In misery”—that is, in wretchedness. What is the thorn that is fastened into me except the prick of a sinful conscience?

### Verse 5

“I made my sin known to you, and I did not cover my injustices [Ms., my injustice].” To make known and not to cover are the same thing: to confess. For if a human being does not acknowledge sin, God does not forgive [Ms., if a human being acknowledges, God forgives]. Some have thought that “offense” means a light sin, but “injustice” means some enormous and savage crime.

“I said: I will declare my injustices against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the impiety of my sin.” “I will declare,” he said—that is, “I will confess publicly,” so that he may draw others to imitation. The impiety had been in his heart, because [Ms., since] he had determined to remain silent.

He says, “I will declare against myself,” that is, “I will accuse myself.” “And you forgave the impiety of my sin”: when you mercifully forgave what I had previously done.

### Verse 6

“For this [impiety] every holy person will pray to you at an opportune time.” The opportune time for praying about sins is this life, in which the holy pray for this reason: no one is free from sins. Nevertheless, “in the flood of many waters they shall not approach him.” The many waves of the floods will roll the wicked along in judgment, but they will not harm the holy; nor will torments approach the one who does not cease to pray here for his sins.

### Verse 7

“You are my refuge from the tribulation that surrounded me; my exultation, deliver me from those surrounding me.” In this flood I have no refuge except you. “My exultation,” he says, “redeem me.” But you are already exulting—what do you wish to be redeemed from? “My exultation, redeem me.” Do you rejoice and groan? “Yes,” he says, “I rejoice and groan. I rejoice in hope, but I still groan in reality.” Therefore he adds, “Redeem me from those surrounding me,” whether bodily vices or unclean spirits, who hasten with headlong speed to destroy us.

### Verse 8

“I will give you understanding and instruct you in this way in which you will walk; I will establish my eyes upon you.” This is the voice of the Lord, the voice of one giving understanding. For this is the understanding truly indicated by the psalm’s title, which the Lord’s power has mercifully poured into penitents [Ms., pours into them]. He added, “And I will instruct you,” that is, “I will teach the one who does not know the way of salvation.”

> [Col. 0578D] Manuscript copies: “As though I were teaching one who does not know; as though I were girding one who is unarmed with the sword of saving life.”

For the way is the one he had entered: to serve God, after the wickedness of his former conduct had been condemned. It follows: “I will establish my eyes upon you,” that is, “I will direct the light of my understanding toward you.”

### Verse 9

“Do not become like a horse or a mule, in which there is no understanding.” Those who wish to govern themselves not by God’s will but by their own impulse fall, unbridled, into sensuality. The Prophet restrains them with terrifying words, saying: “Bind their jaws with bit and bridle, who do not approach you.” God restrains the pride of the wicked with the bridle and bit of his discipline: those who boast of their merits and remain silent about their sins. “Who do not approach you,” he says—those who withdraw from you through pride [Ms., but withdraw through pride].

### Verse 10

“Many are the scourges of sinners [because they did not wish to repent], but mercy will surround those who hope in the Lord.”

> [Col. 0578D] Thus the printed texts are corrected by the manuscript copies: “That mercy [surrounds them], so that they may merit eternal life. Those who have right hope and faith in God are surrounded by God’s mercy,” so that no place is left by which the hostility of the devil might enter them.

### Verse 11

“Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous, and glory, all you upright of heart.” The Prophet urges the Church to rejoice in the hope of eternal life and regeneration. Yet here also it rejoices in tribulation. “Glory, all you upright of heart,” as Paul says: “Whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31). Those are called upright of heart who are pleased with all God’s judgments, accuse themselves of their sins, and always praise God both in adversity and in prosperity.

## Psalm XXXVII

### Verse 1

The title of the psalm: “A psalm of David, for the end, for the remembrance of the Sabbath.”

“Sabbath” is interpreted as “rest,” because the saints—that is, the holy Church—rest [in that rest of Paradise which it lost in Adam]. The psalm admonishes us that if illness or bodily weakness befalls anyone, he should not cease to seek heavenly medicine, in which he may rest.

In this psalm Christ pleads the cause of his body—not because he himself had sin, but because he was made sin for us, in order to free us from sin.
