At times he speaks in the person of the head alone, who is the Savior himself, born of the Virgin Mary; at times in the person of his body, which is the holy Church spread throughout the whole world. Therefore what the body speaks, the head also speaks. Thus, “the two will be one flesh” [that is,] Christ and the Church.

### Verse 2

“Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury.”

[The entire psalm is spoken in the person of a penitent, but it may be referred to Christ, as may Psalm 68.]

“Lord, not in your anger.” As we have already said, anger is a disturbance of the mind; fury, however, is irrational vengeance accompanied by the bitterness of gall. Therefore this person, who knows himself to be a sinner, asks to be rebuked not in anger but through mercy, and not in fury but through patience. Some, however, understand eternal anger as hell and fury as purgatorial fire; the holy man asks to be delivered from both.

### Verse 3

“For your arrows have been fixed in me, and you have strengthened your hand upon me.” Your arrows are the words of your teaching, which have pierced my heart like a javelin, so that I might repent. “And you have strengthened your hand upon me”: so that, like a good teacher, you might make me corrected after afflicting me with the blows of discipline.

### Verse 4

“There is no health in my flesh because of your anger; there is no peace in my bones because of my sins.” I saw the face of your anger, not anger itself: that is, through the holy Scriptures I understood how much you threatened sinners, and I wasted away, asking that this anger itself not descend upon me. “There is no peace in my bones because of my sins.” I allowed no rest either to my bones or to my limbs until I cleansed them [through repentance].

### Verse 5

“For my iniquities have risen above my head.” For they have grown strong against me, as follows: they have been laid heavily upon me like a burden. My sin is not light to me; rather, I acknowledge that it has imposed the heavy weight of judgment and grown above the crown of my head. As a great burden, so are my sins upon me.

### Verse 6

“My wounds have become foul and putrid because of my foolishness.” My wounds of sin stink and rot, and I eagerly await a physician. And why, you ask [Ms., he says], did they rot because of my foolishness? Because I was unwilling to repent.

### Verse 7

“I have become wretched and greatly troubled, utterly so, until the end”—until I was cleansed by confessing. For sins are not forgiven without confession and sorrow. All day long I went about grieving, judging myself unworthy even to dare raise my eyes toward heaven; but beating my breast I said: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” “All day long” signifies [Ms., shows] the continuation of the sorrow.

### Verse 8

“For my loins are filled with mockeries, and there is no health in my flesh.” He professes himself to be filled and weakened by those mockeries with which the devil entices the human race to sin.

### Verse 9

“I am afflicted and humbled exceedingly, everywhere; I roared because of the groaning of my heart.” We can be bent in body without being humbled in spirit. Therefore here the two are joined together. Since manifold calamity leaves nothing free, he added something still greater by saying “everywhere,” that is, “on every side,” so that he might show that abundant calamity had surrounded him from all directions. “I roared because of the groaning of my heart”: to display the strength of great patience, he asserts that he broke into groaning, not into words.

### Verse 10

“Lord, all my desire is before you.” His desire was such that he deserved to be before God. For whoever asks forgiveness for sins places his desire before God. What is already before him is accustomed to be heard. “And my groaning is not hidden from you”: that is, God knows whatever a person possesses. Whatever I have done wrong, whatever I have done badly, I have disclosed everything to you with groaning, knowing that hidden things are not hidden from you.

### Verse 11

“My heart is troubled, and my strength has left me; and the light of my eyes itself is not with me.” Because of the anger I mentioned above, which I dread incurring. “The light of my eyes is not with me,” because, having set aside the light of truth, I had fallen into the darkness of sins. From the beginning of the psalm Christ had pleaded the cause of his body; now he begins to plead his own particular passion.

### Verse 12

“My friends and my neighbors approached and stood against me.” The Jews are called “friends” because of Abraham. “Neighbors,” because Christ took flesh from their lineage [Ms., assumed flesh from their lineage]. They approached him in order to seize him.

When he says, “My friends and my acquaintances stood against me,” this may also be understood of the disciples, who, terrified by fear during the Passion, withdrew far away, even to the point that Peter denied him; or they stood by accusing him. “And those who were near me stood far away”: namely, the apostles and the other disciples, of whom the Evangelist says: “When they had seized him, all his acquaintances stood far away” (Luke 23:49).

### Verse 13

“And they used force who sought my life.” Those who used force were not acquaintances but Jews: either against Peter, when they said, “Are you not also a Galilean?”; or against John [Ms., James], who, when he was being dragged away, fled from them naked, leaving behind the linen cloth; or even against Christ himself.

[“And they used force who sought my life”: that is, the Jews, as though the strength belonged to them and they had not received that power from God.]

“And those who sought evil against me spoke vanities and meditated deceit all day long.” They meditated many deceits when they asked whether tribute should be paid to Caesar (Matthew 22:17), or whether a woman caught in adultery should be stoned (John 8:4). But they openly introduced deceits when they brought false witnesses (Matthew 26:60). They spoke vanities when they said: “He casts out demons by Beelzebul” (Luke 11:15).

### Verse 14

“But I, like one who is deaf, did not hear, and like a mute who does not open his mouth.” “I continually endured their reproaches and remained continually silent,” he says. Pilate also reveals this when he says: “You do not answer me? Do you not know that I have power to release you?” (John 19:10).

“But I, like a mute who does not open his mouth.” Certainly, even before Pilate our God did not speak. Isaiah speaks of the same person, saying: “Like a lamb led to the slaughter, he did not open his mouth.”

### Verse 15

“And I became like a man who does not hear and who has no rebukes in his mouth.” For when they smeared me with spittle, beat me with a reed, and mocked me while kneeling, I was moved by none of these things and became one who had no reproaches in his mouth. Thus I remained silent when accused, as though I had nothing to answer on my behalf. In all these things Christ gave an example, so that a human being might patiently bear the scourges of correction [Ms., ought to bear them].

### Verse 16

“For in you, Lord, I have hoped; you will hear me, Lord my God.” So that you may raise me up. Or: “[You will hear me],” that is, “See their pride and my humility.”

### Verse 17

“For I said: May my enemies never rejoice over me; and when my feet are shaken, they have spoken great things against me.” The holy apostles may be called Christ’s feet. Firm during the Passion, they ought to have supported him like feet support the body, but they were shaken from faith into unbelief.

Or he speaks of Christ: “My feet may be shaken from their stability, and my enemies may insult me if, humbled by this death on the cross, I do not rise again.” Against me they spoke great things, saying: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.”

### Verse 18

“For I am ready for scourges, and my sorrow is always in my sight.” “I prepare myself,” he says, “to endure the cross, the spear, gall, and vinegar, so that through this death I may redeem [with my blood] the perishing people.” For Christ came for this purpose: to endure the Passion. My sorrow is always before me until I also attain victory in judgment [Ms., until I cast forth victory in judgment].

### Verse 19

“For I will declare my iniquity and consider my sin.” Just as he submitted to the curse in order to free us from the curse of the Law, so also he professes himself a sinner, in order that he might bear our sins and by pious reflection and merciful counsel rescue us from them. “And I will consider my sin.” Christ’s sin is the offenses of the human race, for which he is now also said to be subject to the Father.

### Verse 20

“But my enemies live, and they have been strengthened against me, and those who hate me unjustly have multiplied.”

[Because they were not immediately punished by divine vengeance. “And you have strengthened your hand upon me”: they were strengthened in the letter of the Law, in which they did not understand what had been announced spiritually. “And those who hate me unjustly have multiplied.”]

Certainly they act unjustly and without reason when, from this letter, they believed that their offspring would be multiplied like the stars of heaven.

### Verse 21

“Those who repay evil for good slandered me, because I pursued goodness.” For me, who offered the sweetness of eternal life, they gave vinegar and gall to drink, and they slandered me, saying: “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matthew 27:34; Mark 15:31).

They slandered me because I pursued righteousness, so that, fulfilling the Father’s will, I might accept death for the life of the people.

### Verses 22–23

“Do not abandon me, Lord my God; do not depart from me. Attend to my help, Lord, God of my salvation.” It is manifest, Lord Jesus, that the Father, raising you from the dead on the third day, seated you at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality and power, giving you the name that is above every name. Therefore, since the battles of the flesh are grievous, you, Lord, attend to our help and be our salvation in time of tribulation.

## Psalm L

The title of the psalm [is this, which we are attempting to explain]: “For the end, a psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, when he had gone in to Bathsheba.” The gravity of David’s sin is well known from the history of Kings [Ms., from the history of the magnificent king]; equally well known is the most humble supplication for sin contained in this psalm.

This psalm is fiftieth in the order of the psalms because the number fifty was consecrated in the jubilee year until the true sending of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles; without his grace no one can receive forgiveness [Ms., “and consecrated in the advent of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles through forgiveness, because no one without the grace of the Holy Spirit can receive forgiveness …”].

We have examples in Holy Scripture of the sins of holy people, of their repentance, and of the forgiveness of sins granted to them by God. Therefore let no one doubt God’s mercy, even if he is entangled in the greatest crimes; let no one be ashamed to confess sin, since the prophet David, king of many nations, glorified by promises concerning Christ, did not, when he sinned, blush to confess his sin publicly and to flee through repentance to the Lord’s mercy.

Peter washed away his threefold denial with the bitterest tears. The tax collector departed from the temple justified through repentance. The sinful woman washed the holy feet of the Lord with tears [in repentance], and deserved to hear that, because she loved greatly, many sins were forgiven her (Luke 7:38). Strengthened by such examples, let no one despair of God’s mercy; let no one, however great his crimes may be, be ashamed to confess them; let no one be slow to wash away his iniquity with tears. Since we are all sinners, let each one of us say with the Prophet:

### Verse 3

“Have mercy on me, God, according to your great mercy.” Have mercy because I am wretched; have mercy because your mercy is great. Let none of us, like Adam, flee to harmful excuses, but let him openly bring forth what he acknowledges he has done wickedly. Let him flee for refuge to the most merciful Judge; let him anticipate his face in confession, lest he experience him as angry in the future judgment if he now despises him as merciful.

The time of mercy is now for every person who repents. In the future judgment, however, there will be a time of justice, when each will be repaid according to his works. Who could express how great is God’s mercy toward human beings, by which he clothed the Creator of the world in mortal flesh, so that, always living in his own nature, he might be able to die for our sins in our nature?

“According to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity.” O Lord, although my iniquity is great, the multitude of your mercies is greater. In that mercy I beg you to blot out my iniquities, which I dread as having been written against me, so that, with you showing mercy, I may deserve to be written in your book of life; for no one is written there unless all his iniquities are blotted out here.

### Verse 4

“Wash me more thoroughly from my injustice and cleanse me from my offense.” By the gift of your mercy, wash me, Lord, from the stains of my injustice. Do not merely wash me, but also cleanse me [Ms., purify me], so that nothing filthy may remain in my life. I was able to defile myself, but I cannot cleanse myself unless you, Lord Jesus, make me clean by the sprinkling of your holy blood.

### Verse 5

“For I know my iniquity, and my offense is always against me.” It is our task to know [Ms., acknowledge] our sins and humbly confess them. It is God’s task not to reckon them against us but mercifully to forgive them. Many can know their sins, but only those are shown to acknowledge them properly who condemn them through their own execration. For perfect repentance is to avoid future sins and mourn past ones.

David adds: “And my offense is always against me.” We place our offense against ourselves, or always keep it before ourselves, when we continually hold it in memory in order to pray for it until it is overcome by us and consigned to eternal death, lest it again be able to conquer us as it once did. For as often as we lament sins committed, so often we look back upon them.

### Verse 6

“Against you alone I have sinned and done evil before you.” He confesses that he sinned against God alone, because a powerful king fears no other avenger of his sin. And, to show the greater enormity of his iniquity, he added: “I have done evil before you.” Since I knew that you were present everywhere, why did I not fear to sin in the presence of so great a Judge? In this he accuses his own madness, because he did not dread sinning in the presence of so great a Judge.

It follows: “So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.” The Lord’s words are rightly said to be justified, since without doubt his declarations are always fulfilled; and in his sight no living person will be justified. Therefore everyone must say: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant” (Psalm 142:2).

Our Lord, our warrior, was judged and conquered the most savage enemy of the human race; condemned, he acquitted the world. Therefore, foreseeing in the prophetic spirit [Edit., in the prophecy of the spirit] that sins could be redeemed only in the blood of Christ, he praises his justice, by which he condemned the devil, and his mercy, by which he redeemed the world.

Accordingly, he confesses not only his present sin but also that of his parents, in whom he himself was conceived and born, saying:

### Verse 7

“Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in offenses” [Ms., “gave birth to me in sins”]. Who can make me, conceived from unclean seed, clean, except you alone, God, who are without sin? What wonder is it if I have done so, I who confess myself a sinner in those things—when I know that I was conceived in iniquities through original sin? I contracted sins before I possessed the beginnings of life.

O Lord Jesus, with what praises can we exalt your mercy? What worthy thanks can we render to you, who freed us by your blood from the debt of this written bond, erasing on the cross the acknowledgments of our sins that our first parents wrote against us?

### Verse 8

“For behold, you have loved truth; you have revealed to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.” Just as in the preceding verse he proved through the common offense that no one is exempt [Ms., excepted] from sins, so again, in confessing sins, he spoke the truth, which the Lord requires above all else and more than all sacrifices. For God does not delight in our punishments but seeks confession of error.

“Therefore you have revealed to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom”—namely, those things that God revealed to him in the manifestation of his Son: first, that I might acknowledge that he has a Son; then, that I might know that he would come from my seed in the assumption of flesh, proclaim him, and announce the glory of the resurrection.

> [Col. 0583D] In manuscript copies the earlier passage reads as follows: “First, that he might acknowledge that he has a Son; then, that he might know from what seed he would come in the assumption of flesh, so that he might also foretell the figure of the Passion and announce the glory of the resurrection; and then, he says, that he ought not to have sinned, since he had deserved to recognize such things.”

It follows:

### Verse 9

“You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.” Just as earthly hyssop is suitable for treating the lungs, so that it may dispel swelling, so anyone sprinkled with heavenly hyssop—that is, humility of heart—is cleansed from every evil of pride. Therefore you will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow; and although my sins are like scarlet, they will be made white as snow.

> [Col. 0584D] In manuscript copies: “So that, because my sins are like scarlet, they may be made white as snow.”

Nothing white can be found above snow among bodily things. But he said “whiter than snow” because a spiritual soul, once cleansed, shines far above bodily things. The humility of Christ removes [Ms., saves from] our sins, aptly compared with the humblest herb, hyssop; for just as hyssop removes swelling from bodies, so humility removes the swelling of pride from our souls.

### Verse 10

“You will give joy and gladness to my hearing, and the humbled bones will exult.” Joy was given to his hearing when Nathan said to him, “Your sin has been forgiven” (2 Kings 12:13). Joy refers to absolution; gladness to the possession of everlasting rewards.

“And the humbled bones will exult,” he says: the virtues that had previously been humbled by sin. Or: the hope of eternity [Ms., “the eternity of my hope”], which had been humbled when I sinned, exults when you forgive.

### Verse 11

“Turn your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities.” Do not regard my sins in such a way that they return to your memory. “Turn your face away,” as though he were saying: “Do not see them; do not remember them.” “And blot out all my iniquities”: past, present, and future.

### Verse 12

“Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inward parts.” The Prophet asks that a clean heart be created in him—that is, restored [so that he may see God]. Each person ought to do the same.

[“Create a clean heart in me, O God”: for this reason he asked, so that he might become clean from sin.]

“And renew a right spirit within my inward parts,” by which I may confess you rightly; or renew the right spirit for seeing and discerning, just as it was previously right within me, because it became old through sin. He asks to be renewed by grace and adds, “within my inward parts,” from which he knew the detestable crime of adultery had emerged. For he was asking for a remedy in both parts, since he had sinned in both.

### Verse 13

“Do not cast me away from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me.” Do not cast me away, lest I become an exile from you like Cain. The one who is rejected by a father is cast away from his face. For he knew that healing of mind and the light of wisdom came from that face, and he believed that he would be handed over to the enemy if he were judged to be expelled from the Lord’s countenance.

Then he asks that the spirit of prophecy not be taken from him, a spirit the king possessed as more precious than all other things.

### Verse 14

“Restore to me the joy of your salvation”—namely, the exultation of your Christ, which I possessed in him before I sinned. Christ is the salvation of God the Father, as though he were saying: “Just as I previously foresaw through the Holy Spirit that he would come in the flesh, so now I will act.”

“And strengthen me with a principal spirit,” so that vices themselves may not rule in me [Ms., “so that he himself, not vices, may rule in me”]. “Strengthen me,” he said, lest I sin again, lest I depart from you through the mutability of my soul.

Here the Holy Trinity is to be understood: in the principal spirit, the Father; in the Spirit, the Holy Spirit; in the right spirit, the Son.

### Verse 15

“I will teach the wicked your ways, and the impious will turn back to you.” “I will teach them,” I say, so that, turning away from wicked ways and practicing repentance, they may obtain mercy, just as I have obtained mercy from you. That is, I will set myself forward so that others may imitate my example.

### Verse 16

“Deliver me from bloodguilt, God, God of my salvation, and my tongue will exalt your righteousness.” The Prophet asks to be delivered from bloodguilt—that is, carnal offenses—so that he may cease sinning in this weakness. “Blood” is used for the human body because among its other fluids it appears to be the principal one.

When he says, “God of my salvation,” he signifies the Lord Savior, through whom salvation is given to those who piously believe. He also added, “My tongue will exalt your righteousness”: that is, if you deliver me from bloodguilt, which is understood as sins, my tongue will rightly speak your praise, or my tongue will proclaim your commandments.

### Verse 17

“Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth will announce your praise.” The Prophet’s lips, which had been closed by the condition of sin, are declared to be opened through the benefit of absolution. The mouth is also called the secret place of the heart, from which divine praise proceeds. Therefore, rightly, after the absolution of sin, he declares that his lips must be opened and says that his mouth can announce the proclamations and praise of the one by whom he has been restored.

### Verse 18

“For if you had desired sacrifice, I would certainly have given it; you will not delight in burnt offerings.” Here the Prophet signifies the sacred rites involving the sacrifice of animals, rites that were to be rejected at the Lord’s coming. It is therefore clear that the Prophet had been turned toward God with his whole mind, so that he did not believe himself to be cleansed by the sacrifices performed at that time, but rather by the offering of which he says next [Ms., below]:

### Verse 19

“A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart you will not despise, O God.” As though he were saying: “O human being, if you have sinned, do not seek outside yourself an animal to slaughter; within you, you have something to kill.” After saying which sacrifices God rejects, he now says which ones he seeks.

This is the sacrifice we give to God: the spirit of pride, slaughtered by the humility of confession, from which not blood flows but streams of tears pour forth.

[It follows: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise.”]

He calls “contrite” the heart violently afflicted by the labors of repentance. “Humbled” means humbled before God, so that what had previously been proud through exaltation might become devoted through pious confession.

[“He does not despise”]: for it is clear that God does not despise such offerings, just as he is known to have rejected the earlier sacrifices.

### Verse 20

“Deal kindly, Lord, in your good will toward Zion, so that the walls of Jerusalem may be built.” Zion is interpreted as “watchtower” and signifies the Church, which the holy Prophet asks to be built throughout the whole world. Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace.” Therefore let the walls of Jerusalem be built—that is, let memorials of our immortality be constructed in faith [and hope] and charity.

### Verse 21

“Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings and burnt offerings; then they will place calves upon your altar.” This is said to the Father: “Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness,” that is, the most glorious Passion of the Son, who offered himself as a sacrifice for all, so that the world might receive the salvation it did not deserve by its own works.

When he says “offerings and burnt offerings,” this also concerns the faithful Christians who were to believe after the Lord’s coming. It signifies that the hearts of living human beings, not the limbs of dead animals, are to be sacrificed.

“Then they will place calves upon your altar”: namely, the priests, when the Catholic Church has been built through the Lord’s Passion. For he used “calves” for innocent adults, whose age is in its beginning and whose neck is shown to be free from the yoke of sin.

Or he promises those preachers of the Gospel whose image Luke the evangelist assumed in the figure of a calf; unless perhaps we should understand as calves rather those who offered their souls as a sacrifice of sweetness upon the sacred altars.

We too, your servants, Lord Jesus, humbly beseech you to grant, according to the counsel of your compassion, immeasurable mercy for our great crimes, and, having humbled us through contrition of heart, to prepare us as a worthy and acceptable burnt offering by slaughtering our vices and putting our offenses to death. Amen.

## Psalm CI

### Verse 1

The title of this psalm: “The prayer of the poor man when he is afflicted and pours out his prayer before the Lord.” In this psalm it is the voice of a poor man who is afflicted and groaning, offering his miseries to the most merciful Judge with great humility. As prescribed in the title of the psalm, this poor man begins with a prayer directed to God [with a powerful cry], saying:

### Verse 2

**Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you** [Ms.: *perveniat*, “may reach you”]. This is the voice of one who repents and implores God’s clemency for his sins, asking first of all to be heard. It is a matter of great hope in prayer to believe that one can be heard by God. Therefore let everyone humble himself completely, and, with a humbled and contrite heart, cry out to the Lord, because, as another psalm says, God does not despise a contrite heart.

Prayer is the soul’s gentle supplication, accompanied by compunction of heart; a cry is a confession uttered by the voice with earnestness of heart. First he used the word “prayer”; now he adds “cry,” so that you may recognize that the fervor of his supplication has increased, and understand that his prayer has burst forth into the loudest cry. Let the most devout Christian understand that this manner of holy prayer must be observed: he should pursue in thought the very thing that he has poured forth in words [Col. 0587D; Edit.: “that he should pursue it in thought when he pours forth his words”]. Let him keep in mind the one to whom he is praying; let him exclude all superfluous thoughts, which are suggested by the enemy, so that an effective prayer may reach God through the purity of the heart, as the Apostle says: “I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray also with the mind; I will sing praise with the spirit, and I will sing praise also with the mind” (1 Cor. 14:15). The prayer of the one who sings is acceptable to God only when a pure mind performs inwardly what the mouth expresses.

### Verse 3

**Do not turn your face away from me on whatever day I am in trouble.** The face of the Lord signifies the mercy of God, and this poor man, groaning and repentant, begs that it not be turned away from him. “On whatever day I am in trouble”: whatever temptation [Ms.: “tribulation”] may seize him, he asks for divine help in every distress [Col. 0588A]. Therefore he continues: **Incline your ear to me**, that is, grant me a gracious hearing. “On whatever day I call upon you,” that is, on the day of my tribulation. The day of tribulation and temptation is this present life, in which this penitent hastens to beg that he be heard, lest death overtake him and he be found unworthy of being heard. For in this life there is a time of mercy, but in the future there is judgment, when God will repay each person according to his works.

### Verse 4

**For my days have vanished like smoke.** As smoke is scattered into the air when the wind comes, so all the pride of this life vanishes when death overtakes it [Ms.: “when it comes”]. Whoever is exalted today will not exist tomorrow. Recognizing this, the penitent mourns that the days of his misery are like smoke [Col. 0588B].

### Verse 5

**I have been struck like grass, and my heart has withered.** This penitent has come to a mournful account of human frailty—which quickly falls like grass once it has been dried by some circumstance—in order that he might hasten to receive the remedy of divine mercy by not concealing his misery from the compassionate physician. Whoever advances in the Lord’s commandments will be compared with green and flowering grass, but the sinner will be compared with withering grass [Col. 0588C].

**For I have forgotten to eat my bread** [Ms.: “to consume”]. Bread for us is the observance of the Lord’s commandments, which the sinner forgets to eat when he has bound himself by his own iniquities or sins. Here the nature of sinners is expressed: when sin is desired, contemplation of the Lord is not maintained [Ms.: “because, when sin is desired…”].

### Verse 6

**At the sound of my groaning my bones have clung to my flesh.** It is fitting that the one who loses righteousness should groan, whether in order to gain profit or because he has subjected himself to any sin. “My bones have clung to my flesh,” he says—that is, my strength has been given over to carnal desires, which wage war against my soul [Col. 0588D]. In the soul there ought to be the strength to rule and restrain the unlawful movements of the flesh.

### Verses 7–8

**I have become like a pelican in the wilderness, like a night-raven in a dwelling-place. I have kept watch and have become like a solitary sparrow on the roof.**

He names three kinds of birds and three places where they dwell, through which different kinds of penitents are represented. The pelican is an Egyptian bird, always afflicted by natural leanness and taking delight in solitude, just as penitents ought to do through frequent fasts. Through this kind of bird hermits are beautifully signified: abandoning human companionship, they torment themselves with much affliction, moved by fear of the Lord [Col. 0588D].

The night-raven (*nycticorax*) may be called in Latin “the raven of the night,” loving darkness rather than light; it is known to seek its food at night. Thus the penitent ought during the night to seek the nourishment of the soul with vigilant care, even though he may appear to dwell in an ordinary household among many people.

**I have kept watch and have become like a solitary sparrow on the roof.** The sparrow is a very alert bird, accustomed to live on roofs and pleased by human proximity. He is rightly compared with the person who, fleeing the deceits of the devil’s cunning, hastens to fortify himself within the sacred boundaries of the Church through vigils, prayers, and the tears of repentance [Col. 0589A].

### Verse 9

**All day long my enemies reproached me, and those who praised me swore against me.** They praised me with their mouths but prepared ambushes in their hearts. They praised in order to deceive; they commended in order to overthrow. This comes from the devil, who, if he cannot overthrow Christ’s servant through public sins, attempts to frighten him away from the path of truth through the reproaches and criticisms of those around him.

There are very many who are ashamed to do good, lest they appear unlike the multitude of those doing evil [Ms.: “doing badly”]. This sin too the penitent confesses [Ms.: “professes”] that he has committed.

### Verse 10

**For I ate ashes like bread, and I mixed my drink with weeping.** This grieving man describes the banquets of the penitent and of one who despises this world, because through such a banquet they hope to reach the Lord’s table.

Therefore, sinner, do not despair of the forgiveness of sins. “On whatever day the sinner turns, he shall live and shall not die.” But do not delay turning to the Lord. Forgiveness is certain for you when you turn away from your sins, but tomorrow is uncertain for you. Turn today, lest you die tomorrow. If you lived badly yesterday, live well today, remembering the one of whom the Truth says: “Fool, this night your soul will be required of you” (Luke 12:20). Correct yourself, so that in the body of Christ you may be able to possess this saying: **For I ate ashes like bread**, and so forth.

### Verse 11

**Because of the face of your anger and indignation, for, though you lifted me up, you struck me down** [Col. 0589C]. Here he explains with groaning why he exhausts himself in such great affliction through repentance: namely, because we are born with the anger and indignation of God, which becomes more severe when sins are added. Therefore he says: **For, though you lifted me up, you struck me down.**

Humanity was lifted up by the honor of the image of God and ennobled by free will; but because it used this badly, it was struck down and cast into this valley of tears.

### Verse 12

**My days have declined like a shadow, and I have withered like grass.** Because humanity turned away from God, the days of its happiness declined. What had been light in the Lord became a shadow in sin, and the flower of its life withered like grass. It would never become green again unless it were watered by the blood of Christ.

### Verse 13

**But you, Lord, remain forever, and your memorial from generation to generation** [Col. 0589D]. He who had cast himself down in repentance for his sins even to the ashes raised himself up by praising God for his benefits, saying: “While I wither, you remain forever.” Therefore he most rightly began with the coming of the Lord of his salvation and of divine praise, through whom he knew that the world would be saved.

Here “memorial” means the saving promise concerning the Lord’s future incarnation [Ms.: “who is to come”], which no forgetfulness will erase.

### Verse 14

**You, Lord, will arise and have mercy on Zion, for it is the time to have mercy on her, for the time has come.** It is as though he said: “Why do you delay the salvation of Zion?” Zion is the mountain where the Lord’s temple is, signifying the Church that longs for the Lord’s coming [Col. 0590A; the supplied text has an editorially interrupted passage]. He added: **For the time to have mercy on her has come**—that is, the time of which the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Gal. 4:4).

It must be understood that this penitent is not pleading only his own cause; he also desires the salvation of the whole human race, which could not occur unless the Son of God came.

### Verse 15

**For your servants have loved her stones, and they will have compassion on her dust.** We must observe how precisely the words are fitted to the realities. He calls the stones pleasing: they are the apostles and martyrs, and especially the preachers of truth in Zion, that is, in the Church. The earth, however, signifies sinners, upon whom God has had mercy through the blood of our Savior [Ms.: “of our Salvation”].

The stones are said to be objects of the Lord’s mercy because they are solid in the Lord’s building and secure through their firmness [Col. 0590B]. The earth, however, will be made clean through mercy, so that it may be worthy to be placed in the Lord’s building.

### Verse 16

**And the nations will fear your name, Lord, and all the kings of the earth your glory.** Those whom he named “dust” in the preceding verse he here calls “nations,” since they devote themselves to earthly actions. Kings are all who rule themselves well and know how to preside over others through good example or the words of preaching. They fear the great name of Christ God when his servants—whom he earlier called stones—proclaim his glory.

### Verse 17

**For the Lord has built Zion, and he will be seen in his glory** [Col. 0590C]. Therefore all the nations will fear the Lord, and the spiritual kings will dread his glory, because Zion has been built by the Lord: namely, the mother Church, constructed from living stones, in which salvation [Ms.: “praise”] remains without end.

He who now appeared in humility will be seen in his glory when his city has been established and built [Ms.: “when the structure of his city has been completed”], when he comes in the majesty of the Father and of the holy angels to distinguish between the lambs and the goats.

### Verse 18

**He has regarded the prayer of the poor and has not despised their supplication.** When our Savior came into the world, the prayers of this poor man were heard—prayers that had often been recited previously in the sight of divine mercy. This poor man is one and many: one in charity, many in the breadth of the whole world, possessing one faith, one baptism, and one God.

### Verse 19

**Let these things be written for a later generation, and the people that will be created will praise the Lord** [Col. 0590D]. These prophetic sayings were written, and now they are read in a later generation. That was the first generation in which this Scripture was published; now the people of the succeeding generation read it, because they will be created by the Lord from the multitude of the nations, praising the Lord in the truth of light and not in the figures of shadows.

### Verse 20

**For he looked down from his holy height; the Lord looked from heaven upon the earth.** From heaven the Lord looked upon the earth of our misery through his only Son (verse 21), in order to hear—as the following verse shows—the groaning of those in chains, that is, of the human race, which was bound by the devil’s chains in its first parent and condemned to the everlasting death of destruction [Col. 0591A]. Looking down from heaven, the Lord came to release the captives and give life to the slain.

### Verse 22

**That the name of the Lord may be proclaimed in Zion, and his praise in Jerusalem.** For, as the prophet says, “From Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3). There the name of the Lord was first preached through the apostles. Thus it is read in the Acts of the Apostles that there was a multitude of believers there. It is also clear that the Lord commanded in the Gospel that the apostles preach repentance and the forgiveness of all sins to all nations, beginning first from Jerusalem (Luke 24:47, 53). Concerning them the Evangelist says shortly afterward: “And they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God.”

### Verse 23

**When peoples gather together as one, and kingdoms, to serve the Lord** [Col. 0591B]. For this reason the groans of the poor were heard: namely, so that the people gathering as one might resound with the praises of the Lord. In the words “peoples as one,” the power of catholic unity is signified, because we are all one in Christ, just as the Lord himself, supplicating the Father for his own, prayed that they might be one in us.

**And kingdoms, to serve the Lord.** This service of the Lord is true human freedom. Through the service of God the Church has been exalted to such great glory that even kingdoms serve her—kingdoms that had previously persecuted her.

### Verse 24

**He answered him on the way of his strength.** Who? To whom did he answer? The Christian people answered their God; the Church answered Christ, her head. What did it answer? That it should do what he who redeemed it commands [Col. 0591C]. Where did it answer? On the way of his strength.

What is the way of his strength except Christ, who says, “I am the way and the truth and the life,” without whom we can answer nothing through good works to the Lord’s commands?

**Make known to me the shortness of my days.** This is the voice of the Church, through the apostles, entreating the Lord concerning the end of the world [Ms.: “questioning the Lord”]. They said: “Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the consummation of the age?” (Matt. 24:3). He answered: “First this Gospel will be preached throughout the whole world,” and the other signs of the consummation of the age that are read there.

The penitent calls that time a “shortness of days” because he counts the whole period from the beginning of the world to its end, in comparison with eternity, as a single and very brief moment [Ms.: “is counted”]. This penitent desires to reach quickly the happiness of eternal blessedness, just as the Gospel commands that the servant always be ready.

### Verse 25

**Do not take me back in the middle of my days; your years are from age to age.** Desiring eternity, this poor man does not wish to be taken back to the middle of his life, that is, to the years of youth, in which people especially tend to sin through the fervor of the flesh. He does not desire to return to those days, so that he may deserve to reach the Lord’s eternal years, which are not subject to change. There the succession of times will not exist, but a certain stable and ever-identical life will remain, immune to change.

“The age in which these things are is [the age] of this world, or the generation of this generation,” which is signified in the Gospel where the Lord says: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty” (Matt. 19:28).

### Verse 26

**In the beginning you, Lord, founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands** [Col. 0592A]. This is what is read at the beginning of the sacred Scriptures: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” This the Lord’s praiser says so that we may understand that we have the same one as Redeemer whom we have as Creator. He who created heaven and earth in the beginning plainly exists without a beginning.

“The heavens are the works of your hands,” that is, all things were made by the power and wisdom of God [Ms.: “that is, your powers, because all things were made through the Word of God, that is, through the power of God and the wisdom of God”].

### Verse 27

**They will perish**—that is, heaven and earth, as it is read in the Gospel, “they will pass away”—**but my words will not pass away. But you remain, and they will all grow old like a garment** [Col. 0592B]. He declares that the Lord alone is immutable, while everything will grow old like garments. Here he seems to show the frailty of human flesh. That grows old which is consumed in the manner of a garment through death.

**Like a covering you will change them, and they will be changed.** Perhaps heaven is understood to be the covering of the earth, which is to be changed for the better, as another Scripture indicates: “And there will be a new heaven and a new earth” (Isa. 65:17).

### Verse 28

**But you are the same, and your years will not fail** [Col. 0592C]. He indicates that everything is changeable except the Creator alone, who is always the same as he is, and whose years of eternity will never fail. This does not mean that years are to be understood in God as though one comes and another passes; rather, his eternity, which is always the same, is designated by the name “years.”

### Verse 29

**The children of your servants will dwell there**—that is, the children of the holy fathers, namely, of the prophets, apostles, and teachers of the Church, will dwell in the years of eternity [Col. 0592D]. We must not suppose that the fathers are absent where their children will be. If the children are there, how much more the fathers? If the good disciple is there, how much more the teacher, who is better than the disciple?

**And their seed will be directed from age to age.** Whose seed, except that of the holy teachers [Edit.: “their teachers”], who will be directed into eternal blessedness? Those who kept the right path here will possess there the rewards of blessedness [Ms.: “uprightness”].

Therefore let no sinner delay doing penance, so that he may deserve to attain the glory of this reward. Let him continually remember the first word of the Lord’s preaching, in which it was said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matt. 3:2). Amen.

# Psalm 129

This psalm is the eleventh among the Songs of Ascents. That number signifies a certain diminution of perfection; but it is sixth in the order of penitence, and the number six is known to be perfect in its parts. In this number the Creator himself made all things, to show that everything he created is perfect [Col. 0593A].

This penitent, however, strives through the tears of repentance to reach the perfection of forgiveness, saying:

### Verse 1

**From the depths I cried to you, Lord.** “From the depths,” that is, from the enormity of sins, from which there is no other salvation for him except to cry out to the Lord and hope in his mercy. Therefore he asks that his cry be heard, the cry that he uttered from the depth of sins, saying:

### Verse 2

**Lord, hear my voice.** Those are closest to the Most High who have burst forth from the depths of holy humility, confessing themselves to be sinners and saying that they have cried from the depth of iniquity:

**Let your ears be attentive to the prayer of your servant.**

Who is crying? A sinner, of course. From where does he cry? Even from the depths. What depths? The depths of sins. With what hope does he cry? The one who came to release sins gave even the sinner lying in the depths the hope of crying out and hoping for forgiveness. But what does this sinful man cry? Let us hear.

### Verse 3

**If you observe iniquities** [Ms.: “iniquity”], **Lord, Lord, who will endure?** Behold, the depth from which he cries has appeared [Ms.: “has been opened”]. He cries beneath the waves, as though submerged in the depth of his iniquities, accusing himself in thoughts, words, and deeds, recognizing that the whole of human life is subject to temptations. The text continues by showing the hope in which he cries:

### Verses 4–5

**For with you there is forgiveness.** What is this forgiveness except the blood of Christ, the innocent blood poured out for the forgiveness of our sins? Therefore, Lord, forgiveness is with you, and it encourages me to cry out to you. For if you had wished to be only judge and not forgiver, you would observe our iniquities, and no one could endure.

**And because of your law I have endured you, Lord.** I have awaited you, Lord, who were promised to me in the law. That law made me guilty and compelled me to cry out to you, who are the Lawgiver and the Redeemer, the Son of Man made under the law.

**My soul has waited for your word.** What word? The Word who was in the beginning with God. I have awaited this Word, so that it might become flesh and liberate my soul. In him we have received forgiveness of sins and the promise of the kingdom of heaven. In this Word the prophets hoped; the apostles expounded and saw him; and in this Word believers are blessed, although they did not see him in the flesh. In this Word [Ms.: “word”] all the souls of the saints hope.

### Verse 6

**From the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord** [Col. 0593D]. The morning watch is the revealed resurrection of the Lord our Savior, when, although the Jews were guarding the tomb, he rose through the reality of his restored body [Edit.: “because the Jews were guarding the tomb…”]. Until night—that is, until the end of this age—we must live in this hope, so that now we may rise in soul and on the last day rise in body.

Whoever now rises from the death of the soul through the Word, the Son [Ms.: “the son”] of God, will then rise happily in the flesh through the Word, the Son of Man [Col. 0594A]. In this promise let Israel hope in the Lord. For we have been saved in hope. What we now possess through the sweetness of hope, we shall then possess in the reality of the thing itself. Do not doubt this happiness of the promise, Israel—that is, you who see God.

### Verse 7

**For with the Lord there is mercy, and abundant redemption with him.** Although the sinner is weighed down by the mass of sins, the mercy of God is present in Christ, who came without sin in order to release sins. With him there is abundant redemption, because where sin abounded, grace abounded still more.

### Verse 8

**It is he who redeemed Israel from all his iniquities** [Ms.: “their iniquities”]. Therefore, sinner, do not cease. Cry out from the depths; drive all despair away from yourself. Say—say it again: “If you observe iniquity, Lord, Lord, who will endure?”

Observe him; await him because of his law, the law he gave you in the prayer in which you plead for your sins, saying: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” Hope that you will rise again and in every way become free from sin, because he rose who was the first to be without sin.

Do not say, “I am unworthy of his mercy because of my sins.” Consider that with him there is abundant redemption: he handed himself over in order to redeem you. Liberated through repentance, do not bind yourself again through sin. Serve the Lord as a son, not as a slave, because everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. A slave does not remain in the house, but the son remains with his Father in eternal blessedness. Amen.

# Psalm 142

**The title of the psalm: “A psalm for David himself, when his son was persecuting him.”** In the Books of Kings we read this history: how Absalom expelled his father David from the kingdom. But there is another David who is truly strong of hand, strong in battle, who struck down the most arrogant enemy: our Lord Jesus Christ.

Therefore this David must be recognized as the one whom his son Judas persecuted by handing him over to death. He had sons, concerning whom he said: “The sons of the bridegroom cannot mourn while the bridegroom is with them; but the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will mourn” [Col. 0594D] (Matt. 9:15).

The minds of sinners must mourn if the bridegroom is taken away from them because of their sins. First of all, they must ask to be heard; then, that they not be brought into judgment; and finally, that they be delivered from their enemies, to whose power they have handed themselves over because of their sins.

### Verse 1

**Lord, hear my prayer; listen with your ears to my supplication.** “Hear” means the same as “listen with your ears.” Repetition greatly expresses the petitioner’s earnestness. The humility of tears is the absolution [Ms.: “washing”] of sins.

**In your truth hear me; in your righteousness.** This commends grace, lest any one of us think that it is through his own righteousness that he is freed. It is God’s righteousness that he possesses, because God has given it. “In your righteousness,” we say [Ms.: “let us say”], “hear me” [Col. 0595A]. For when I look only at myself, I find nothing in myself except sin. My entire liberation is your righteousness. Therefore the text continues:

### Verse 2

**And do not enter into judgment with your servant.** Therefore, Lord, do not enter into judgment with me, however righteous I may seem to myself. You bring forth from your treasures [Ms.: “from your treasure”] the rule of equity. You judge me according to my righteousness, and I am found to be crooked.

Why? **Because no living person will be justified in your sight.** This signifies the whole human race, subject to original sin. Therefore no one can be justified unless liberated by your grace. If no one born from a corrupted root will be justified, how much more am I, oppressed by the weight of my own sins?

### Verse 3

**For the enemy has persecuted my soul** [Col. 0595B]. Judas persecuted Christ’s soul; the devil persecuted my soul by persuading me to sin. He humbled my life to the earth when he sprinkled my soul with earthly defilements and soiled it with the dust of vices.

**He placed me in dark places like the dead of the age.** [Alternative form: “The enemy placed me in the darkness of sins, like the dead of the age.”] Those are “the dead of the age” who die in their sins, receiving the recompense [Ms.: “reward”] of their iniquity. Therefore:

### Verse 4

**And my spirit was distressed within me; my heart was troubled within me.** My spirit was distressed within me through repentance, and my whole heart was troubled because of the enormity of my crimes, fearing that the just Judge might condemn me with the dead of the age [Col. 0595C].

### Verse 5

**I remembered the days of old.** The days of old are those in which I lived in sins according to the old man; their memory torments me.

**I meditated on all your works; I meditated on the works of your hands.** I saw and examined all your works, because nothing good can exist in us unless it is brought about by your grace, you who made us. Considering these things more attentively, what did I do? Namely:

### Verse 6

**I stretched out my hands to you; my soul is like land without water before you** [Col. 0595D]. I stretched out my hands in prayers, and in the consolation of the holy cross, on which the hands of my Savior were stretched out, I will pray.

Then he gives a comparison in which the penitent says that his soul desires God as thirsty land awaits the rains, so that it may bring forth desirable fruits.

**Without water before you.** O God, may my soul be watered for you, and, watered by you, may it bear fruit for you.

### Verse 7

**Hear me quickly, Lord, because my spirit has failed.** The animal spirit [or “life-breath”] quickly fails, and the flesh returns to its own earth, and it no longer recognizes its place. A person is born once and reborn once; he dies once and will be resurrected once. Therefore, Lord, have mercy while there is a time for mercy, an acceptable time, and a day of salvation.

I know that the day will come very quickly on which I will be judged according to my works. Have mercy now, Lord Jesus, so that you may have mercy then in judgment.

**Do not turn your face away from me** [Col. 0596A], for if you turn the face of your mercy away from me, I will become like those who descend into the pit. The pit signifies the lower place of hell, where the impious are tormented by everlasting distress. No one will be delivered from it unless the grace of God comes beforehand, before the time of judgment.

The pit may also be understood as the depth of sins. If a sinner reaches it, he will despise salvation by despairing of his soul. The penitent begs to be delivered from it, as from the infernal place, and continues:

### Verse 8

**Cause me to hear your mercy in the morning, Lord, because I have hoped in you.** Behold, I am in the night, but I will hope in you until the night of iniquity passes and the dawn of your mercies comes to me like the light of sunrise.

**Make known to me the way in which I should walk.** That is, make known to me the way of your commandments, so that I may walk in it, enlightened by him who enlightens every person coming into this world [Col. 0596B].

**Because I have hoped in you, Lord.** This is the firm consolation of one who confesses: hope in the goodness of the Lord who saves.

### Verse 9

**Deliver me from my enemies, Lord; I have fled to you for refuge.** Who are the enemies except demons, the ambitions of the world, and carnal desires? Having abandoned these, I have fled to you for refuge—not away from you, as Adam fled into the shadows after the midday of happiness. I have no one to whom I can flee for refuge except you, Lord my God.

### Verse 10

**Teach me to do your will.** Your will is my salvation, since you desire all people to be saved and none to perish.

**Because you are my God.** You are all my good, my entire salvation. I seek the Lord for redemption; I seek a patron for freedom [Ms.: “liberation”]. You are my God; you created me. I cannot be recreated by anyone other than you, by whom I was created.

You created me through the Word, God, abiding with you [Ms.: *manentem*, accusative form of “abiding”]. You recreate me through the Word made flesh for us.

**Your good Spirit will lead me into a right land.** For my evil spirit led me into a crooked land; may your good Spirit lead me into a right land. Your Spirit is always good, but mine is always evil unless it is made good through yours.

### Verse 11

**For your name’s sake, Lord, you will give me life in your righteousness** [Col. 0596D]. Here the most merciful grace of God is commended: through his mercy we have been given life in the name of the Savior, not through our merits [Col. 0596D].

**You will lead my soul out of tribulation.** Holy souls will be led out of tribulation as from prisons when they are freed from the temptations of the enemy and reach rest, where there will no longer be any tribulation from the tempting enemy. Thus the end of the present life is the end of the labor of the saints.

### Verse 12

**For God will scatter their enemies and destroy all who trouble the souls of his servants.** Here the righteous are troubled; there all who suffer persecution for the name of Christ will glory and be consoled in the rest of blessedness, according to the saying of Truth itself: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:10), forever and ever. Amen.

# The Exposition of Master Albinus Flaccus Alcuin on Psalm 118

## Preface

The hundred-eighteenth psalm contains a great mystery within itself. But because it contains the law, commandments, justifications, testimonies, and judgments, and because these differ from one another, it is necessary to distinguish them.

The law, therefore, is what was given through Moses. In Christ it must be understood spiritually, because although the Apostle calls it holy, he nevertheless describes it as a shadow of future things.

The commandments are those in which the observance of the Lord’s precepts is prescribed, according to: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery,” and the rest.

Justifications are those by which God commands, through love of God and of one’s neighbor, that the weeds of hatred be uprooted from the human heart.

Testimonies are those in whose presence the order of holy observances is entrusted to us, as when Moses calls heaven and earth as witnesses, and Paul says to Timothy: “I testify to you,” he says, “in the presence of the living God and in the presence of his elect angels,” and the rest (1 Tim. 5:21).

Judgments are those by which either the righteous will be honored with splendid rewards or transgressors will be condemned to eternal punishments [Ms.: “he will honor the righteous… he will condemn…”].

The ways are the apostles and prophets, through whom one comes to the true life [Ms.: “way”], which is Christ. This entire psalm is written according to the order of the letters: eight verses begin with one letter, then another eight are completed by the following letter, and the same pattern is woven through to the end.

From its beginning this great psalm, beloved, exhorts us to blessedness, which no one fails to desire [Edit.: “which no one fails to expect]. Who has ever been, or can be, or will be found, who does not wish to be blessed?

Why, then, is exhortation necessary for something that the human mind desires spontaneously? Certainly, the one who exhorts acts so that the will of the person with whom he is speaking may be awakened toward the thing for which the exhortation is addressed.

Why, then, are we urged to desire what we cannot fail to desire? Because everyone indeed longs for blessedness, but they do not know how to reach it. Therefore this psalm teaches us, saying:

## Aleph, that is, Doctrine

### Verse 1

**Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.** None can be blessed except the undefiled; and none are undefiled except those who walk in the way. The way, however, is nothing other than the law of the Lord.

Therefore, if he seeks blessedness, let a person be undefiled in the way and walk in the law of the Lord, which is the way of the blessed. Let him not be idle; let him be without blemish—that is, without mortal crime. Yet he distinguishes between blemish and blemish. Since we cannot be without minor faults, at least we must not fall into greater ones [Ms.: “we ought not to fall”].

**Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord:** in the way, in Christ [Edit.: “in the way of Christ”], as he himself says: “I am the way and the truth.” Those who walk in the law of the Lord walk in his commandments.

### Verse 2

**Blessed are those who search out his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart.** They understand that when they have sinned, they have transgressed in the presence of witnesses. He says, however, that they seek him with their whole heart, and not lightly or sluggishly.

### Verse 3

**For those who commit iniquity have not walked in his ways.** The ways are the apostles and prophets, through whom one comes to that life [Ms.: “way”] of which he said: “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14:6), as we have already said. The impious do not walk in this way, because they follow Satan’s way.

### Verse 4

**You commanded that your commandments be kept exceedingly.** He teaches us to keep his commandments not with a lukewarm heart or a careless mind, but firmly and attentively [Col. 0598B]. He used “exceedingly” to mean “very greatly.” God therefore gave this command with great force, and it is greatly necessary to keep God’s commandments.

### Verse 5

**Would that my ways were directed toward keeping your justifications.** Unless our ways are directed by the Lord himself, we will be too weak to keep his justifications because of the frailty of the flesh.

“You gave a command,” he says, “and commanded me to keep it. But would that you would provide help, so that, because you command me, I may be able to do what I have learned must be done because you have taught me.”

### VERSE 6

Then I shall not be put to shame when I have examined all your commandments. “When,” he says, “my ways have been directed by your grace, then, by examining your commandments, I shall not be put to shame, while I regard all your commandments.” For one must not omit some and observe others, but keep all of them equally, lest we be put to shame at the future judgment.

### VERSE 7

I will praise you, Lord, with an upright heart, because I have learned the judgments of your righteousness. I will praise you if my path and my heart have been made straight: I will proclaim you, Lord; I will praise you, and I will confess that this is your work.

### VERSE 8

I will keep your ordinances; do not utterly forsake me. That is: I shall do what you command, if you assist me continually. It is as though he said plainly: Do not allow me to stray from a good work, lest, while I lose the order of right living, I lose the uprightness of speech. He asks not to be wholly abandoned, but rather that divine help may never and nowhere depart from him.

### VERSE 9

By what does a young man correct his way? By keeping your words. The question is: by what does a young man correct his way? The answer is that this correction consists in keeping God’s words. He calls every person “young” who, after putting off the old man of sin, becomes new in Christ [Ms.: “who becomes new from the old man of sin”].

### VERSE 10

With my whole heart I have sought you; do not cast me away from your commandments. “You have caused me,” he says, “to seek you with my whole heart; make me remain in your commandments. Help me so that they may be possible for me, and do not drive me away from them”—that is, do not withdraw your help from me.

### VERSE 11

I have hidden your sayings in my heart, so that I may not sin against you. He immediately sought divine help, lest God’s sayings be hidden in his heart without fruit, if works of righteousness did not follow. For after he had said this, he added:

### VERSE 12

Blessed are you, Lord; teach me your ordinances. Why, indeed, does he say, “Teach me your ordinances,” except because he wishes to learn them by doing them, not merely by speaking or retaining them in memory?

### VERSE 13

With my lips I have declared all the judgments of your mouth. “I have kept silent about none of your judgments,” he says, “but have proclaimed them all completely with my lips”—namely, those things that you told me by your mouth, that is, through the proclamation of your sayings.

### VERSE 14

I have rejoiced in the way of your testimonies, as in all riches. Christ is the way of God’s testimonies, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. Therefore the one who travels along this way rejoices in it as in all riches. Many testimonies of divine love have been fulfilled for us, and there is no doubt that those still expected will also be fulfilled [Ms.: “he does not doubt the things that are expected to be fulfilled”].

### VERSE 15

I will exercise myself in your commandments [Ms., adds: “myself”], and I will consider your ways. Exercise is the constancy of action. Unless this man had been practiced in God’s commandments, he could not have considered his ways—that is, the apostolic and prophetic teachings.

### VERSE 16

I will meditate on your ordinances; I will not forget your words. I meditate on these things and exercise myself in them, so that, not consigning them to oblivion, I may be able to fulfill them completely and perfectly.

## Voice of Gimel

### VERSE 17

Deal generously with your servant; give me life, and I will keep your words. There are four kinds of recompense. Either evil is repaid with evil, as God will repay the wicked with eternal fire; or good with good, as he will repay the righteous with an eternal kingdom; or good for evil, as Christ justifies the ungodly by grace; or evil for good, as the Jews persecuted Christ through wickedness.

Of these four recompenses, the first two belong to justice: evil is repaid with evil and good with good. The third belongs to mercy: good is repaid for evil. But God does not know the fourth [Ms.: “But the fourth does not pertain to Christ”], for he repays no one evil for good.

The third, which I placed in third place, is necessary above all. For unless God repaid good for evil, there would be no one to whom he could repay good for good. Knowing, therefore, that God’s words cannot be kept through obedience unless they are perceived through understanding, he adds this also to his prayer and says:

### VERSE 18

Uncover my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law. “Give me,” he says, “understanding by which I may behold the wonders of your law and see the power of your commandments.”

### VERSE 19

I am a sojourner on the earth; do not hide your commandments from me. Everyone is a stranger wherever he is absent from his homeland. Therefore this man, who has been enrolled as a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem, confesses that he is a sojourner on earth, because he is certain of the promised inheritance. But because human life upon earth is a time of testing, he asks that God’s commandments not be hidden from him during the time of his tribulation and sojourn.

### VERSE 20

My soul has longed to desire your ordinances at all times. Whether I eat, drink, or do anything else, may I always desire, meditate upon, and grasp them. For you justify me; your grace makes me righteous. It is good for me always to desire this and to take delight in this protection of yours. Otherwise I shall not be righteous if your grace is lacking to me or pride has inflated me.

### VERSE 21

You have rebuked the proud; cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments. This rebuke is to be understood as the one that the first parents of the human race deserved through their transgression, turning aside from God’s command through pride, by which they desired not what God commanded to be loved, but what the devil persuaded them to desire out of envy.

Every proud person, therefore, is subject to this rebuke, whether by inherited merit or by the choice of the will. For the proud turn aside from God’s commandments. It is one thing not to fulfill his commandments through weakness or ignorance; it is another to turn aside from them through pride. Then all the ungodly will receive the full curse when they hear: “Depart, you cursed, into the eternal fire.”

### VERSE 22

Take away from me reproach and contempt, for I have sought your testimonies. The saints earnestly and vigilantly sought the divine testimonies, not idly or sleepily, so that they suffered such things; as the Lord commanded: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake,” and so forth (Matthew 5:10). But this prayer is poured out for the persecutors, not by invoking punishment upon them, but so that, when they have been converted to the Lord, reproach may be removed from the martyrs, when those persecutors too have honored the same religion.

### VERSE 23

For rulers also sat and spoke against me, but your servant exercised himself in your ordinances. What the prophet speaks here concerning himself he sees as destined to occur in the apostles and the other martyrs, who suffered many things before kings and governors, as the Lord himself also foretold. Although they were afflicted with various punishments, even to the cutting off of their heads, they nevertheless always exercised themselves in God’s ordinances.

### VERSE 24

For your testimonies are also my meditation, and your ordinances are my counsel. Thus Christ’s servant exercised himself, so that he contended against his persecutors through [the delight of the testimonies]. The counsel of the persecuting rulers was to destroy the martyrs when they had been found; the counsel of the suffering martyrs was to find their enemies destroyed. The former repaid evil for good; the latter, good for evil. What wonder, then, if the former ceased by killing, while the latter conquered by dying [Edit.: “gave life”]?

## DALETH

### VERSE 25

My soul has clung to the ground; give me life according to your word. I understand the soul to be joined to mortal flesh. Therefore, lest sin grow strong, I ask you to give me life, knowing that the desire of the flesh produces death.

### VERSE 26

I declared my ways, and you answered me; teach me your ordinances. He calls human actions “ways.” Without doubt he gives the name “ways” to the action itself. I confessed the ways of my sin, and you forgave me; now grant the instruction by which you may teach me your ordinances [Ms.: “by which I may be instructed in your ordinances”].

### VERSE 27

Make me understand the way of your ordinances, and I will exercise myself in your wonders. Rightly did the holy company seek to understand the way of the ordinances, since it had exposed its own ways—that is, its sins. For unless we condemn those ways, we cannot reach this one. Make me understand—that is, grant me understanding pertaining to blessed life—and I will exercise myself in your wonders, certainly through insight and prudence, so that he may draw the Old Testament toward a spiritual understanding. He calls the ordinances themselves “wonders,” just as above he called them ordinances.

### VERSE 28

My soul has grown drowsy from weariness; strengthen me in your words. In the station of this mortal dwelling, through weariness caused by bodily weakness, strengthen me in your words, so that, once the sleep of sin has been removed, I may vigilantly persist in them.

### VERSE 29

Remove from me the way of iniquity, and have mercy on me through your law. Having been raised to that contemplation of truth, he asks for what was necessary in this world: that the way of iniquity—that is, of the devil [Ms.: “the devil”]—might be removed from his assaults. “And have mercy on me through your law”: for this law has been established by you so that you may always have mercy.

### VERSE 30

I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments. I have chosen the way of truth in which I might run; I have not forgotten your judgments, so that I might run. I have chosen as the way of truth Christ, the Son of God, whom, foreseeing that he would come into the world, I hear saying: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” I have not forgotten your judgments—the judgment that he proclaimed in the Gospels when he said: “This is the judgment: that everyone who believes in the Son of Man may have eternal life.”

### VERSE 31

I have clung to your testimonies, Lord; do not put me to shame. And because, by clinging to these, I have deserved pardon for my former crimes, I ask that you not allow me to be put to shame before you on account of sin.

### VERSE 32

I have run in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart. The enlargement of the heart is love of truth. It is produced by God’s gift, so that one serves him not through fear of punishment but through love of righteousness, when the love of God is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. Therefore he ran in the way of God’s commandments because the Lord enlarged his heart.

### VERSE 33

Set before me, Lord, the law—the way of your ordinances—and I will seek it always. Here again the blessed people advance; in it they ask that the law acquired for themselves be established.

@ Manuscript codices: “At the fifth letter the blessed people brought forth [this prayer], in which they ask that the law be established for themselves.”

Earlier he said: “And have mercy on me through your law,” that is, through the Old Testament. Now, however, he desires a new law to be established for him, namely, with the Lord Christ coming in the flesh, so that the faith of Christians might be strengthened. He said that he would seek it continually; for that is sought which is requested unceasingly with great prayers.

### VERSE 34

Give me understanding, and I will search out your law and keep it with my whole heart. The Church asks to understand the distinction between good and evil, between life and death, and between the letter and the meaning. “Let me understand, proclaim, fulfill in action, and keep it with my whole heart”—that is, with complete love. How beautifully ordered are his words! First he asks that the law be established for him, that is, the New Testament; then that he might deserve to know the intention of that law, so that he might keep it with the full integrity of his heart.

### VERSE 35

Lead me along the path of your commandments, for I have desired it. A path is narrower than a way: it is the narrow and constricted way, that is, the higher commandments that lead to life. We should understand these commandments as those of the New Testament, along which he earnestly prayed to be led. “For I have desired it”—that is, I have desired the divine grace of the New Testament, through which he knew that he would reach the kingdoms of heaven.

### VERSE 36

Incline my heart toward your testimonies and not toward greed, says the Church—that is, toward humility, in accordance with: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29). Through his testimonies God deals with us so that we may worship him freely; greed, the root of all evils, hinders this. Therefore let us not incline our heart toward greed. Let us worship the Lord for the Lord’s sake alone, so that he himself may be the reward of his worship.

### VERSE 37

Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity; give me life in your way. “Turn my eyes away”—that is, my senses—“lest they see vanity,” that is, defection. It is as though he said: In this vanity, which is defection, let me not keep my eyes—that is, my senses—fixed. Rather, he says, give me life in your way: that is, give me life in yourself (*temetipso*; Edit.: *temetipsum*) or in your commandments; give life to my soul.

### VERSE 38

Establish your word for your servant in your fear. The Lord’s word becomes stable in our heart when what that word commands is done; it is torn away when the contrary action is performed. Therefore God’s servant asks that persevering obedience be confirmed in him, so that it may not be moved from its position by any impulse toward evil action [Ms.: “which may not be moved from its position”]. This occurs through the Spirit and through that pure fear which guards against offending love—not through fear by which impiety fears being condemned [Ms.: “lest it be condemned”].

### VERSE 39

Cut away my reproach, which I have suspected, for your judgments are pleasing. In this statement the greatest [Edit.: “example”] of human failing is set forth. Many fall into reproach by suspecting things otherwise than truth has it; he asks that this fault be cut away from him. Suspicion is very often proved uncertain, and it does not befit a Christian man. This suspicion, therefore, leads to reproach, which arises from sin. Rightly did he say that the Lord’s decree was pleasing to him, through which he knew that he had found both rest and an everlasting crown.

### VERSE 40

Behold, I have desired your commandments; give me life in your righteousness. “You have made me,” he says, “desirous of your commandments; make me effective as well. Help me to do what you command; yourself grant what you order.” It is one gift of your mercy, Lord, that, while keeping the holy sayings, we may be given life in your righteousness—that is, that we may confess you equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit [Ms.: “when we confess you equal …”].

### VERSE 41

Let your mercy come upon me, Lord, your salvation according to your word. At the sixth letter the holy way of life arrives; in it the person asks that the saving Lord be granted to him. He is the mercy of sinners and the life of the faithful, through whom salvation came to the nations. “According to your word” means according to your promise, which you promised through the prophets.

### VERSE 42

And I shall answer those who reproach me with a word, because I have hoped in your words. This statement plainly indicates to us that we must answer those who oppose us manfully, lest the presumption of the wicked appear superior. They reproach the Word when they say that the Son is less than the Father. “Because I have hoped”: I shall answer with firmness those who call my hope in you vain, because their hope is empty.

### VERSE 43

And do not take the word of truth utterly from my mouth, for I have hoped exceedingly in your judgments. He asks that no punishment and no terror extort from his mouth the confession of truth.
