When he says “utterly,” he indicates that the word of truth had at some time been taken from certain people, as happened to Peter, who denied the Lord three times before the cock crowed. Yet he wiped away that sin with tears and cleansed it with the shedding of his blood. “For I have hoped exceedingly in your judgments”: the judgments of the Lord were that the crowds of martyrs were driven by various torments toward the kingdoms of heaven [Ms.: “were oppressed by various tortures”].

### VERSE 44

And I will keep your law forever and for ever and ever. This verse and the others up to the end of the letter contain not a petition but a narrative. Above he asked to receive; here he gives thanks for what he has received. “Forever” indicates the whole period of the present life; “for ever and ever” signifies the future age. The law that he desires to keep perpetually is to be understood as love, because it is the fullness of the law; when the other commandments cease, it alone remains forever.

### VERSE 45

And I walked in spaciousness, because I sought your commandments. I have been enlarged through keeping your law, because I sought your commandments. I searched them diligently for this purpose: that I might believe and understand.

### VERSE 46

And I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not put to shame. He spoke of the Lord’s testimonies because he had asked and received the strength to answer those who reproached him with a word. Strengthened by this firmness, he says that before the kings of the world he was not put to shame, but proclaimed the truth in fearless speech [Edit.: “he spoke”].

### VERSE 47

And I will meditate on your commandments, which I have loved. Here he shows the ardor of frequent meditation. No one can meditate on the commandments unless he has gone through them by constant reading. “Which I have loved,” he says; for no one can neglect what he loves. He adds “exceedingly,” beyond which no greater love can be found.

### VERSE 48

And I will lift up my hands toward your commandments, which I have loved, and I will exercise myself in your ordinances. In the preceding verse he said, “I will meditate on your commandments,” which concerns the contemplative faculty; now he says, “I will lift up my hands,” which pertains to the active faculty. For lifting up the hands signifies occupying oneself with good works. One who is held by evil actions does not lift up his hands. “And I will exercise myself in your ordinances”: there he meditated, where the mind’s attention was engaged [Edit.: “Where I meditated, for there the mind’s attention is engaged”]; here he exercised himself, where he sought to advance through the frequent practice of good works.

@ The Salzburg manuscript omits the words enclosed in brackets. They do not indicate that the words had slipped from memory; rather, it reminds us: and]

### VERSE 49

Remember your word to your servant, in which you have given me hope. When it is said to God, “Remember,” the desire of the one praying is revealed: he asks that the promise be hastened. [God is not being reminded as though it had slipped from his memory.] “Remember,” therefore, he says, “your word to your servant”—that is, fulfill your promise—in which you gave me hope, that is, through which you made me hope.

### VERSE 50

This has comforted me in my humiliation, because your word has given me life. Hope of the future life gave consolation amid the troubles of the world. “In my humiliation,” because holy humility is shown by enduring everything patiently. “Because your word has given me life”: he gives the reason why his humiliation was consoled—because the hope of consolation gives life to the afflicted [Ms.: “He says that hope consoled him amid the troubles of the world …”].

### VERSE 51

The proud acted wickedly exceedingly, but I did not turn aside from your law. “The proud acted wickedly.” He wishes the proud to be understood as persecutors of the humble—that is, ungodly persecutors of the godly—and therefore he added: “But I did not turn aside from your law,” because their persecution compelled him to do this.

### VERSE 52

I remembered your judgments from of old, Lord, and I was comforted. “I remembered” from the time when the human race took its beginning. I remembered your judgments; and because I experienced that all your ways are mercy and truth, I received consolation. I was comforted by the help of your grace. Through the Holy Spirit I understood that you were to come in the flesh.

### VERSE 53

Despondency seized me because of sinners who forsake your law [Ms.: “Despondency of spirit …”]. The voice of the Church displays an attitude of compassion, grieving over the transgressions of the wicked. It is necessary that the fault of another distress a holy man, while a devout mind desires everyone to be saved.

### VERSE 54

Your ordinances were songs to me in the place of my sojourning. By saying “songs,” he signifies psalmody performed with great delight. Singing lifts up labors and removes weariness from the mind. “In the place of my sojourning” signifies this world, where everyone who is devoted to the Lord Christ lives as a stranger. After Adam was expelled from paradise, we conduct our sojourn in this land.

### VERSE 55

I remembered your name by night, Lord, and I kept your law. Human weakness must remember the Lord’s name always, but especially and more earnestly during the night, when one is either oppressed by the recollection of riches or tormented by the fire of desire. Above all, one must pray that, if one has begun to keep God’s law, one may not be torn away from it in anything.

### VERSE 56

This has happened to me because I sought your ordinances. This law became for me consolation and [not] a stumbling block, so that I might be able to search out your ordinances more diligently.

### VERSE 57

You are my portion, Lord; I said that I would keep your law. “Portion” derives from “part.” For we belong to the part whose wishes we obey. Hence God is rightly called the portion of the devout, because the devout and holy belong to his kingdom. “I said that I would keep your law”: I said—that is, I resolved and determined. Blessed is the one who has no other portion except the Lord, who does not love honors, riches, or desires, but God alone.

### VERSE 58

I have entreated your face with my whole heart; have mercy on me according to your word. The prophet rightly entreats God’s face [“with my whole heart”], knowing that he has a pure heart. For “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” “Have mercy on me according to your word,” through which you promised that you would not overwhelm the sinner in death, but would mercifully console him.

### VERSE 59

For I considered my ways and turned my feet toward your testimonies [Ms.: “turned away”]. He sets forth the order of human conduct. First we must accuse ourselves, and thus move toward the Lord’s commandments. He considered his ways [Edit.: “my ways”], that is, his human actions, but they displeased him completely; [therefore] he turned his feet to walk toward the Lord’s testimonies. Whoever walks in them has firm footsteps.

### VERSE 60

I am ready and have not been troubled, to keep your commandments. I am ready to preach; I am not troubled at having to endure tribulation for Christ, so that I may keep your commandments. The unjust shafts of those who reproached me did not disturb me.

### VERSE 61

The cords of sinners have surrounded me, but I have not forgotten your law. By saying “cords,” he shows that there are as many snares as there are sins we commit. “Cords of sinners” does not derive from what the sins are, but from what sinners are. The cords of sinners, therefore, are the impediments of enemies, whether spiritual or carnal. [Edit.: “which”] If they entangle the body, let them not entangle the soul. Because of these impediments he did not forget God’s law [Ms.: “In this the man did not forget God’s law …”], because the word of God is not bound.

### VERSE 62

At midnight I rose to praise you because of the judgments of your righteous ordinances. Midnight is profound tribulation, because he was not afflicted [Edit.: “driven away”] in such a way that he could not rise. He rose in order to confess to God that, by his just judgment, power had been given to sinners to persecute the saints. God’s grace helps the saints to undergo such exercises, by which they become more illustrious.

### VERSE 63

I am a companion of all who fear you and keep your commandments. Now the Church is a companion to those who fear God with holy fear and fulfill his commandments; it is their companion in hope, faith, and love.

### VERSE 64

The earth is full of your mercy, Lord; teach me your ordinances. He showed mercy when he came to redeem us; therefore the earth is full of mercy, and therefore the holy Church exists. “Teach me your ordinances”: that is, your commandments, so that I may understand, proclaim, and fulfill them in action.

### VERSE 65

You have dealt well with your servant, Lord, according to your word. The prophet’s voice speaks in the person of the Church. “You have dealt well” when you came in the flesh and redeemed us. “With your servant”: with the Christian people. “According to your word”: the Word of the Father is the Son. “According to your word,” so that you would not punish us when we sinned [Ms.: “me when I sinned”] in anger, but would console us with mercy.

### VERSE 66

Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge, because I have believed in your commandments. God teaches goodness by inspiring the sweetness of love; he teaches discipline when he gives patience amid tribulations; he teaches knowledge when he himself is recognized as the bestower (*tributor*; Ms.: *adtributor*) of saving commandments, because I have believed that I have eternal life in your commandments.

### VERSE 67

Before I was humbled, I sinned; therefore I kept your word. [“Because of the first sin,” he says, “I was humbled, and, lest I be humbled again, I kept your word.”] Thus, through your grace, experiencing punishment proved beneficial, so that I might acquire obedience.

### VERSE 68

You are good, Lord, and in your goodness teach me your ordinances. For no one is good except God alone. He truly wishes to perform God’s ordinances when he does not wish to learn them without God’s gracious sweetness.

### VERSE 69

The iniquity of the proud has multiplied against me, but I shall search out your commandments with my whole heart. He says that the iniquity of his persecutors has multiplied against him, and therefore he asks not to be stained by them. “But I shall search out your commandments with my whole heart,” so that, to the extent that they strive to lead him astray [Edit.: “to restore him”], he may appear to cling all the more firmly to the Lord’s commandments.

### VERSE 70

Their heart has become thick like milk, but I have meditated on your law. “Thickened” may be used in a good or a bad sense; here it is used in a bad sense, namely, for the pride of the wicked, of which he spoke above. Their heart has been compressed, like milk, into a denser substance. Yet they could not separate this man from the Lord’s law, because through devout wisdom [Ms.: “patience”] he overcame them.

### VERSE 71

It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I may learn your ordinances. It is good for me that you turned punishment into discipline and humiliation into instruction, because I desire to know your ordinances in such a way that I may do them. There is no true knowledge directed toward the good [Ms.: “of the good”] unless it is known for the purpose of being practiced [“so that it may be done”].

### VERSE 72

The law of your mouth is good for me, more than thousands of gold and silver. The law of God’s mouth is Christ, who came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it. Foreseeing him, the prophet desires him above all treasures, because he commanded not only that friends be loved but also that enemies be forgiven [Ms.: “because he commanded …”].

## JOD, THAT IS, BEGINNING

### VERSE 73

Your hands made me and fashioned me; give me understanding, so that I may learn your commandments. It is a great thing for a person to understand that he was made and fashioned by God’s hand and formed in his image. If he recognizes this, he ought to ask for knowledge so that he may understand and keep God’s commandments. The hands of the Lord are to be understood as his power and wisdom. “Made” pertains to the soul; “fashioned” pertains to the body. And because the soul is more precious than the body, he placed “made” first.

### VERSE 74

Those who fear you will see me and rejoice, because I have hoped exceedingly in your words. This is the voice of the Church: those who fear the Lord will see its understanding and will rejoice. For when the Church sees others observing God’s commandments, it has great joy. Later they will rejoice with one another in this way, both here and in the future. “Because I hope in your word”—that is, I have hope in Christ.

### VERSE 75

I know, Lord, that your judgments are righteous, and in your truth you have humbled me. By saying that he has known the Lord’s judgments, he signifies that God corrects a person who sins through a swelling of spirit by humbling him, and receives the one who implores him through divine mercy. Who could doubt that the judgment is one of supreme righteousness, when the one who sinned through pride is cleansed by devoted humility?

### VERSE 76

Let your mercy now come, so that it may console me, according to your word to your servant. Let your mercy therefore come according to your promise, so that mortal life may receive comfort through present gifts and patiently await the future blessings of eternity.

### VERSE 77

Let your mercies come to me, and I shall live, because your law is my meditation. It has been sufficiently expressed that through mercy we attain eternal life. That meditation makes blessed those who seek the kingdoms of heaven through holy works.

### VERSE 78

Let the proud be put to shame, because they have acted wickedly against me unjustly; but I shall exercise myself in your commandments. “Let them be put to shame.” Although the proud rage and act wickedly against the saints, the love of the devout does not grow cold, and their exercise in God’s commandments does not cease.

### VERSE 79

Let those who fear you and those who know your testimonies turn toward me. That is, let those who come to know them through my teaching be converted to you. “And those who know your testimonies”: those whom divine reading has instructed, but whom the work of salvation has not yet trained.

### VERSE 80

Let my heart be blameless. Here “heart” stands for the soul, as though he said: Let my soul be without mortal sin. In your ordinances, so that I may not be put to shame—that is, so that I may not suffer eternal shame.

### VERSE 81

My soul has failed for your salvation [Ms.: “in your salvation”], and I have hoped exceedingly in your word. This failing does not mean that he failed in faith; rather, it shows that he was wearied by such immense longing that he reached the most blessed exhaustion. “In your salvation,” which in Hebrew is called *Jesus*; and “in your Word,” that is, in the Only-Begotten, who is the power of God.

### VERSE 82

My eyes have failed for your word, saying, “When will you console me?” Here again he speaks of eyes, but certainly of inner eyes. That failing is praiseworthy and blessed, arising not from weakness of spirit but from the strength of desire for God’s promise. For he says, “for your word”: he declares that he endured this exhaustion until the Lord’s expected incarnation appeared to the eyes of his heart. “When will you console me?” That is, when will what you promised come?

### VERSE 83

For I have become like a wineskin in frost; I have not forgotten your ordinances. Above he had asked to be consoled; now he gives the reason why help should be given. The wineskin signifies the mortal body; the frost signifies the benefit of conversion [Edit.: “conduct”]. Just as a wineskin contracts in icy cold, so the incentives of our fleshly vices are reduced through the affliction of repentance, so that they do not forget the Lord’s ordinances.

### VERSE 84

How many are the days of your servant? When will you execute judgment on those who persecute me? Knowing that the company of the saints is subject to demonic trials until the end of the world, he asks when this world will end, so that the prepared vengeance may be completed against the persecutors—that is, against the devil together with his servants. He desired the judgment to come quickly, in which there will already be rest for the blessed and joy that will endure without end.

### VERSE 85

The wicked have told me stories, but not such as your law, Lord. “They have told me”: he says that the wicked have recounted tales of empty opinions, composed with the pleasing artistry of eloquence. But he found nothing useful in them, as he did in the Lord’s law, in which it is truth, not words, that delights him.

### VERSE 86

All your commandments are truth; the wicked have persecuted me; help me. Against the tales of heretics he says that all the Lord’s commandments are truth. “The wicked have persecuted me”—namely, by teaching perverse things and persuading me of falsehoods. Therefore help me, so that I may contend for your truth even unto death.

### VERSE 87

They almost destroyed me on earth, but I did not forsake your commandments. Bodily vices would have greatly humbled me to the earth, unless I had kept the divine commandments.

### VERSE 88

According to your mercy, Lord, give me life: into eternal life, because I no longer live for myself, but Christ lives in me. So that I may keep the testimonies of your mouth. Either those things that you commanded in the law, or those that you proclaimed in the Gospels.

### VERSE 89

Forever, Lord, your word remains in heaven. He says that the Lord’s word remains in heaven—that is, in the saints, whom he makes live after death and rejoice after tribulation—or in the heavenly powers, which always devote themselves to his service.

### VERSE 90

Your truth is for ever and ever; you established the earth, and it remains. “Age” signifies the Law and the Prophets; “age of age” signifies the Gospels and the apostles, in which there is truth, which is Christ the Lord. As for “the earth,” that is, human nature, he signifies the whole by a part and says that God established it in the saints, so that they might remain in their faith. For unless he himself had established it, they would neither believe nor remain: “You established the earth, and it remains.”

### VERSE 91

By your ordinance the day continues, for all things serve you. Whenever “day” is placed in the singular number, that everlasting day which is to come, without night, is signified. Then all things subject to him serve him. His adversaries too serve him, though unwillingly, while, condemned, they deservedly endure everlasting punishments at his command.

### VERSE 92

If your law had not been my meditation, I might perhaps have perished in my humiliation. The blessed people of the martyrs, afflicted amid such great humiliations of torment, assert that they could perish unless meditation on the law came to their aid with consolation. The law says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution.” This law is faith, which works through love. By remaining in meditation on it, through the help of your grace, one is made worthy not to perish eternally in the humiliation of tribulations.

[Col. 0609D] **VERSE 93.**—“For ever I shall not forget your ordinances, because by them you have given me life.” By “ordinances” he means the observances of the Law under the shadow, which, by signs of the truth, bestowed the benefit of the perfection that was to come. We therefore ought not to forget these ordinances, which granted us the beginnings of faith and life.

**VERSE 94.**—“I am yours; save me, for I have sought your ordinances.” I am your servant, and you are my God; from you I ask to be saved, because I have no vanity [Ms.: “because my belly is not a god”], nor am I devoted to empty glory, but to your ordinances.

{370} **VERSE 95.**—“Sinners awaited me in order to destroy me; I understood your testimonies.” For a long time the hostile powers have attacked me in conflict, but I, understanding your testimonies, received consolation from them.

**VERSE 96.**—“I have seen the end of every perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad.” By “perfection” he means the consummating perfection of all virtues, whose end is Christ, whom he foresaw as coming through faith, and whose commandment’s breadth he marvels at. In this he plainly signifies charity, which in its breadth embraces all the commandments within itself. For when all the commandments come to an end, charity alone will remain forever.

**VERSE 97.**—“How I have loved your Law, O Lord! It is my meditation all day long.” How have I loved your Law? “Thus,” he says, “I have loved the law of faith, which works through love, so that it is my meditation all day long,” that is, throughout the whole of time.

**VERSE 98.**—“You have made me wiser than my enemies by your commandment, for it is mine forever.” The prophet’s enemies are the Jews, who do not understand spiritually. The Prophet declares himself wiser than they because, in these commandments—which he keeps forever—he foresees the Lord who is to come.

**VERSE 99.**—“I have understood more than all those who teach me, because your testimonies are my meditation.” Those whom he called enemies in the preceding verse he here calls teachers, designating, of course, the Pharisaic teachers, who, clinging to the letter, neglected spiritual understanding. The evangelical company therefore understands better than such teachers, because, rejecting their perversions, it received the Lord’s sincere teaching through meditation on his testimonies, understood according to the truth [Ms.: “of understanding”].

**VERSE 100.**—“I have understood more than the elders, because I sought your commandments.” Certainly the new people understood better: they received Christ by seeking his commandments, unlike the Jewish people, which killed him by putting him to death [Ms.: “which believed him worthy of death”].

**VERSE 101.**—“I restrained my feet from every evil way, so that I might keep your words.” “From every evil way”: this saying concerns the members, not the head. For the Savior himself was not assailed by any desires, so that it would have been necessary for him to guard his feet. We can keep the words of God only if we do not follow our evil desires.

**VERSE 102.**—“I have not turned aside from your judgments, because you established the Law for me.” You established the Law of the Gospel for me. For the Mosaic Law was a pedagogue; this Law granted the effect of the whole fullness [Edit.: “The Law of the Gospel granted the freedom of the whole…”]. Rightly, therefore, the holy people rejoiced in this Law, which it had received through faith.

**VERSE 103.**—“How sweet are your utterances to my throat, O Lord, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth.” The throat of the heart signifies its secrets, where the Lord’s utterances are spiritually understood and loved. Honey is open teaching; the honeycomb is secret teaching.

**VERSE 104.**—“From your commandments I gained understanding [because a person reaches the wisdom of hidden things through obedience to the commandments]. Therefore,” he says, “I hated every way of iniquity.” It is necessary to hate iniquity out of love for justice.

**VERSE 105.**—“Your word is a lamp for my feet, O Lord, and a light for my paths.” If the light of God’s word shines within us during the nights of this age, our feet will not fall into the snares of ropes and the pits’ precipices that the hand of devilish cunning has prepared amid our stumbling-blocks. “And a light for my paths”: so that, with this light going before us, while we walk the paths of this life, we may be led to that which is the true way.

**VERSE 106.**—“I have sworn and resolved to keep the judgments of your justice.” By “swore” he names the oath by which he made his resolve, because the mind ought to be so firmly fixed on keeping the judgments of God’s justice that what it has resolved should count entirely as an oath.

**VERSE 107.**—“I have been humbled exceedingly, O Lord; give me life according to your word.” He learned the humility that Christ taught, who is meek and humble of heart. Therefore he now begs that, just as Christ, after the humility of his servant’s form, was exalted into the glory of God the Father, so he too may be transferred from this bodily humility into eternal life.

**VERSE 108.**—“Make acceptable the free offerings of my mouth, O Lord, and teach me your judgments.” This is the voice of the Church, as though it said: May my vows, which I offer to you, be pleasing [to you]—that is, acceptable and delightful. “And teach me your judgments,” that is, your commandments, so that I may understand and fulfill them.

{371} **VERSE 109.**—“My soul is always in my hands” [Ms.: “in your hands”], “and I have not forgotten your Law.” For the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God; in whose hand we too are [Ms.: “they are”], together with our words. “And your Law,” he says, “I have not forgotten.” It is as though his memory were aided by being in God’s hands, so that he would not forget God’s Law.

**VERSE 110.**—“Sinners have laid snares for me.” What snares? Those set beside the way; and if you depart from the way, you fall into snares [Ms.: “because a snare is set beside the way and …”]. What are these snares except the devil’s nets [Ms.: “tangles”], or the demon’s suggestions? Vices and sins may also be understood.

“And I have not gone astray from your commandments.” This is the voice of the Church. I have not strayed from your commandments, but remain constant in their practice.

**VERSE 111.**—“I have acquired your testimonies as an inheritance forever, for they are the rejoicing of my heart.” Your testimonies and your precepts—that is, my inheritance forever, both here and in the future. Since your testimonies are the rejoicing of my heart, they are my joy, because the Church delights and rejoices in God’s commandments.

**VERSE 112.**—“I have inclined my heart.” I was not proud, but humble; and therefore I inclined my heart in order to understand you, because the proud do not incline their hearts toward humility. For what purpose did I incline my heart? The Church says: “To perform your ordinances,” that is, your commandments. “Forever,” for the sake of the reward of eternal life, so that I may deserve to receive it.

**VERSE 113.**—“I have hated the unjust and loved your Law.” After saying, “I have hated the unjust,” he added the reason: “and I have loved your Law,” to show that he did not hate the nature of unjust people because they are human beings, but their iniquity, because they are enemies of the Law that he loves.

**VERSE 114.**—“You are my helper and my protector, and I have hoped greatly in your word.” A helper in the present, a protector in the future. “And I will hope in your Word,” that is, in Christ, because the Word of the Father is the Son.

**VERSE 115.**—“Depart from me, evil ones, and I will search out the commandments of my God.” Here the evil ones are demons, vices and sins, or hostile powers. While they prepare their snares and their worst suggestions for you, you cannot search out the commandments of your God in order to understand them rightly. But if you wish to do penance, you must separate yourself from their company.

**VERSE 116.**—“Receive me according to your utterance, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my hope.” This is the voice of the Church, desiring that the Bridegroom come and receive her as his bride, as he promised in the utterance of the prophets. “And I shall live in justice,” because I am now dead in sins. “And do not put me to shame”: let him whom I await, and whom you promised, come to me.

**VERSE 117.**—“Help me.” He asks for assistance; “and I shall be saved in soul,” if you come and help me; “and I shall meditate forever, without end, on your ordinances.”

**VERSE 118.**—“You have despised all who depart from your ordinances, for their thought is unjust.” It has been explained why frequent meditation on the Lord’s ordinances is undertaken: those who depart from his ordinance are despised by the Lord. An ordinance is the sinner’s pure confession before the Lord. Those who disdain to be saved [Ms.: “healed”] by such a remedy have an unjust thought.

**VERSE 119.**—“I have regarded all the sinners of the earth as transgressors; therefore I have loved all your testimonies.” The Prophet says this in the person of the Church, because before Christ’s coming they were transgressors, being held under obligation on account of the transgression of the first man, Adam. Not all sinners are transgressors, but all transgressors are sinners. Therefore I have loved all your testimonies, so that I might not appear as a transgressor among them.

**VERSE 120.**—“Pierce my flesh with your fear, for I have feared your judgments.” I fear the future judgment. Therefore, nailing all the desires of the flesh to your cross, I am ready to live with you, to die with you, and to be buried with you, so that I may deserve to live with you in the future.

**VERSE 121.**—“I have practiced judgment and justice; do not hand me over to those who persecute me” [Ms.: “those who slander me”]. A person practices judgment whenever he judges himself and condemns his own perversities before the Lord’s tribunal with a just curse. We practice justice when we judge ourselves by justice, when we are the judges [Ms.: “avengers”] of our offenses. He asks not to be handed over to the sinners who condemned sins. Those who persecute are the devil {372} and his ministers, who pursue us with tireless malice. Hence also we pray every day, admonished as we are to say: “Do not lead us into temptation.”

**VERSE 122.**—“Receive [Ms.: ‘choose’] your servant for good; let not the proud slander me.” Receive me—that is, do not let them drive me into evil; receive me for good [Ms.: “in goodness”]. They slander in pride [Ms.: “let them slander”]; defend me in humility, so that the slanders of the proud may not harm me.

**VERSE 123.**—“My eyes have failed in hope of your salvation and in the word of your justice.” My eyes have failed in hope of the word of God’s justice, that is, in hope of the promise of Christ. He said that the eyes of his heart had failed, not because the intention of his desiring soul had been overcome and collapsed, but because it had passed over, with the whole ardor of the mind, into expectation of God’s grace. The justice of God that he mentioned is Christ, who makes people just.

**VERSE 124.**—“Deal with your servant according to your mercy, so that he may fulfill my vows. And teach me your ordinances,” so that I may perceive their humility, as I have often desired.

**VERSE 125.**—“I am your servant; give me understanding, so that I may know your testimonies.” Let me learn them from you, and not from heretics or Jews, because no time is free for me from the exercise [Edit.: “expectation”] of your service.

**VERSE 126.**—“It is time to act, O Lord; they have destroyed your Law.” The Jews, certainly, who did not understand it spiritually. But the time will come when the Lord will cause its hidden things to be disclosed through evangelical preaching.

**VERSE 127.**—“Therefore I have loved your commandments more than gold and topaz.” Just as gold surpasses the value of all metals, so topaz, containing within itself the beauty of all gems, surpasses all their honors. Therefore the Prophet loves God’s commandments above all these things, because in them he understands that the coming of the Lord, who is to redeem the world, has been foretold.

**VERSE 128.**—“Therefore I was directed toward all your commandments; I hated every way of iniquity.” He who loved the Lord’s Law above gold and gems necessarily appeared most upright with regard to all his commandments, and hated the crooked way, because he deserved to love what is perfectly straight. The way of iniquity is the way that leads us to vices; the straight way is the way of virtues, which grants us pardon and salvation.

**VERSE 129.**—“Your testimonies are wonderful; therefore my soul has searched them out.” See that one thing is done in them and another is signified. Therefore, since what is in them is wondrous to me, I search them out more diligently, so that, with you as interpreter, I may understand everything.

**VERSE 130.**—“The explanation of your words enlightens me and gives understanding to the simple.” The holy people say that they have been enlightened by the explanation of the Lord’s words, namely, the words of the Lord’s prophets, which had long been hidden. For example: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive,” etc. (Isaiah 7:14); and: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God,” etc. (Luke 3:6). Now, through the Lord’s coming, with those words enacted and fulfilled, enlightened, they see all things: the Word made flesh, the Virgin having given birth, and the mute having spoken. All these things grant pure understanding to the simple, that is, to the humble.

**VERSE 131.**—“I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit, because I desired your commandments.” I opened my mouth in confession, acknowledging that without you I can do nothing; and I drew into myself the spirit of grace, through which I trust that I can fulfill what I desired, namely, your commandments [Edit.: “through which I consider that I can fulfill…”].

**VERSE 132.**—“Look upon me and have mercy on me, according to the judgment of those who love your name.” That is, according to the judgment you exercised upon those who love your name. For in order that we might love you [Ms.: “that they might love … you”], you first loved us [Ms.: “them”]. It is indeed the Lord’s judgment that he make his name known openly and grant mercy.

**VERSE 133.**—“Direct my steps according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me.” What are “steps,” except [a prayer] that God may cause his commandments, which he [imposes] by commanding, to be fulfilled by assisting? “Steps” signifies the movements of the soul. The holy company asks that these be directed according to the Lord’s word, which shows the right path and commands us to enter it. “And let iniquity not rule over me” [Edit.: “so that … in them”]. He knew that iniquity could not be wholly excluded from this life, and therefore he prays that its dominion [Ms.: “lordship”] may be brought under him.

**VERSE 134.**—“Redeem me from the slanders of men, so that I may keep your commandments.” Act upon me [Edit.: “touch me”] by pouring in your Spirit, so that the slanders of men may not conquer me through terror and lead me away from your commandments to perform their evil deeds [Ms.: “deeds already done”]. For if you do this for me, I shall keep your commandments amid the very slanders.

**VERSE 135.**—“Make your face shine upon your servant,” he says—that is, reveal your presence by helping and assisting. “And teach me your ordinances”: teach me, namely, so that I may do them.

**VERSE 136.**—“My eyes poured forth streams of water, because they did not keep your Law.” This holy man continually practices true repentance and does not cease to wash away ancient offenses with flowing tears, so that you may understand that, unless you do true penance, what you have done is not easily forgiven you. True repentance consists in continually washing away offenses through weeping and not repeating what has been washed away.

**VERSES 137–138.**—“You are just, O Lord, and your judgment is right. You commanded justice: your testimonies, and your truth, exceedingly.” Great is God’s justice in both respects, and right is the judgment by which punishment is decreed for the sinner and justification is not denied to the penitent. “Exceedingly” applies to both, whether to justice or to truth.

**VERSE 139.**—“My zeal has consumed me, because my enemies have forgotten your words.” This zeal is the zeal of love, not of labor. For in holy emulation he wants his enemies to be corrected, grieving and wasting away because they have forgotten God’s words.

**VERSE 140.**—“Your utterance is exceedingly refined by fire, and your servant has loved it.” For just as it consumes sin, so it enlightens the sinner if he turns back. This fire is Christ’s word, concerning which he says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12:49). He says that he loved this fire because it gives life, honor, and a remedy to the human race.

**VERSE 141.**—“I am young and despised; I have not forgotten your ordinances.” Here the meaning of the two peoples is aptly understood: the younger people is despised by the older, yet, through the gift of God’s grace, it has not forgotten his commandments.

**VERSE 142.**—“Your justice is justice forever, and your Law is truth.” The Lord’s justice remains forever, and whoever keeps his truth will rejoice in eternal happiness. The Christian people understood this and therefore was filled with the truth, which is Christ the Lord, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.”

[Col. 0615B] **VERSE 143.**—“Tribulation and distress have found me; your commandments are my meditation.” The savagery of the enemies brings tribulation upon this younger people, but it does not lose charity. Its meditation is God’s commandments, from which it will return love to those who hate it.

**VERSE 144.**—“The equity of your testimonies is forever; give me understanding, and I shall live.” Beautifully, after [Ms.: “against”] tribulations and distresses, which are temporary, the equity of God’s commandments is declared to be eternal, so that each person, in such hope, might despise what he perceives to be temporary. “Give me understanding,” namely, so that I may understand the dangers of this world to be passing and temporary. “Give me life,” through hope of the future reward.

[Col. 0615C] **VERSE 145.**—“I cried with my whole heart; hear me, O Lord; I shall seek your ordinances.” We have often recalled that this cry is not the voice of the body but of the spiritual mind, by which the righteous are heard by God; it especially reveals their devout affection [Ms.: “or he opens their prayers”]. By “ordinances” he means that he is not seeking the riches of the age, nor merely seeking to know the ordinances, but to fulfill them.

**VERSE 146.**—“I cried to you; save me, so that I may keep your commandments.” Now he shows that the preceding cry was poured out to God: namely, that he might strengthen the soul by the reason of faith and grant health to the body, truly so that he might be able to keep the Lord’s commandments.

**VERSE 147.**—“I anticipated the dawn and cried out; I hoped greatly in your words.” The time before dawn is the night-time, which is not yet mature—that is, suitable for doing anything by keeping watch—and it is commonly called an inconvenient hour. He forestalls old vices by youthful chastity, who through the maturity of a vigorous spirit never removes his hope from God’s words.

**VERSE 148.**—“My eyes anticipated you at dawn, so that I might meditate on your utterances.” The light did not find him sunk in sleep, but vigorously watchful and meditating on the divine utterances with the attention of spiritual eyes.

{374} **VERSE 149.**—“Hear my voice, O Lord, according to your mercy, and give me life according to your judgment.” He declares that no person should place confidence in anything except God’s compassion alone, which makes the miserable blessed, the captives free, and the dead alive. “According to your judgment,” by which you spare those who entreat you. For no one can be given life unless he possesses no life of his own.

**VERSE 150.**—“Those who persecute me have drawn near to iniquity” [Ms.: “in iniquity”], “but they have gone far from your Law.” The persecutors draw near when they go so far as to torture or kill the flesh. But the nearer these persecutors are, the farther they are from the law of justice.

**VERSE 151.**—“You are near, O Lord, and all your ways are truth.” Against that nearness of persecution he declares the Lord’s proximity to be his remedy. From it he knew that the help of salvation would come—not through a location on a journey, but through the truth of God’s commandments entering the hearts of the saints.

**VERSE 152.**—“From the beginning I learned from your testimonies that you founded them forever.” What are these testimonies except those by which God testified that he would give his children a king and an everlasting kingdom? Therefore those testimonies are founded forever, because what he promised is eternal; for the foundation of the promise is Christ, in whom the testimonies of this hope are true. He says that he learned them from the beginning because he speaks in the words of the Church, which arose from the beginning of the human race and was absent from no generation.

**VERSE 153.**—“See my humility and rescue me, because I have not forgotten your Law.” “See,” he says here, pertains to the martyrs [Ms.: “what is seen here pertains to the martyrs”], whose bodies are afflicted like the lowliness of beasts. He continues: “And rescue me”—from what, except the pressing necessity of punishments and the danger of death? By “Law” here he means the sentence that says: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). He says that he has not forgotten this until the end of his life.

**VERSE 154.**—“Judge my judgment and redeem me; give me life because of your utterance.” I have judged that I know nothing except Jesus Christ, who was promised to come for the redemption of the world. According to this judgment, therefore, may I be given life by you through your utterances. Redeem me, whom you could not redeem unless I believed. “Give me life because of your utterance”—that utterance in which he promises: “Whoever believes in me will never die.”

[Col. 0616D] **VERSE 155.**—“Salvation is far from sinners, because they have not sought your ordinances.” I think this should be understood especially of the Jews, who made salvation—that is, the Lord Savior—far from themselves by not believing in him. They did not believe the testimonies in which the coming of the Lord Savior had been prefigured. Therefore they were made far from salvation because they rejected the author of salvation.

**VERSE 156.**—“Your mercies are many, O Lord; give me life according to your judgment.” [The Lord’s acts of mercy are those by which he has deigned to help the afflicted and wounded in various ways.] “Give me life according to your judgment.” This is indeed the judgment we ought to ask for when, in satisfaction through humility, we prostrate ourselves and confess our sins. For then it is the Lord’s judgment to have mercy on such people in their confession.

**VERSE 157.**—“Many are those who persecute and afflict me; I have not turned aside from your testimonies.” This is the voice of the Church in its martyrs, who amid torments and multiplied punishments did not yield to their persecutors. Hence also a great multitude of martyrs found the palm, because amid various torments they testified that they had in no way turned aside from the Lord’s testimonies.

**VERSE 158.**—“I saw those who did not keep the covenant, and I wasted away, because they did not keep your testimonies” [Ms.: “utterances”]. Who are those who did not keep the covenant except those who, unable to endure the tribulations inflicted by many persecutors, turned aside from God’s testimonies? “When I saw this,” he says, “I wasted away,” grieving that they had fallen from such great glory.

[Col. 0617B] **VERSE 159.**—“See that I have loved your commandments, O Lord; give me life in your mercy.” That is the fruitful endurance which receives the persecutors’ savagery through love of the commandments.

**VERSE 160.**—“The beginning of your words is truth, and all the judgments of your justice are forever.” “Your words proceed from your truth,” he says, “and therefore they are true” [Ms.: “truthful”] “and deceive no one. By them life is pronounced” [Ms.: “is foretold”] “for the just, and punishment for the wicked.”

**VERSE 161.**—Princes persecuted me without cause, and my heart feared your words. Earthly kings persecuted Christ’s Church without cause, having no reason for persecution, since Christians harmed them in nothing. When they [Edit.: “and they themselves”] could not force Christians to deny the truth, they uttered threatening words and inflicted savage punishments. But the martyrs themselves remembered the Lord’s word: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matthew 10:28).

**VERSE 162.**—“I shall rejoice over your utterances, like one who finds abundant spoils.” Although the martyrs died in a humble condition, they found abundant spoils when they received the divine rewards. They also rejoiced when the persecutors themselves were converted to the Lord, so that those who took innocent lives might the more become spoils [Edit.: “had helped”]. Therefore he says that he rejoices in the Lord’s utterances, that is, in the sacred admonitions, like a victor receiving plunder.

[Col. 0617D] **VERSE 163.**—“I hated iniquity and abhorred it, but I loved your Law.” We must consider carefully that [“he demonstrated love of good things by hatred of evil things, since” (Edit.: “love is of good or evil things; he therefore showed how”)] our mind, if it received iniquity, could in no way unite itself wholly to the Lord’s Law. He does not say that he hated an unjust person, but that he hated iniquity and—rightly—abhorred it, because it is alien to the Law; and that he loved the Lord’s Law with perfect willingness. Who are those who love the Lord [Ms.: “God”], except those who hate iniquities?

**VERSE 164.**—“Seven times a day I have praised you for the judgments of your justice.” If we wish to understand this number literally, it signifies the seven occasions [Edit.: “voices”] by which the devout piety of monks consoles itself: Matins, Terce, Sext, None, Lucernarium, Compline, and Nocturns [Ms.: “Matins, Compline, Nocturns”]. But if you attend to it spiritually, you will recognize that it more wisely signifies continuity, as in the saying: “I will bless the Lord at all times.” He praises God seven times a day because his mind, enduring in complete radiance, hastens toward that seventh day—that is, the Sabbath of sabbaths—which is eternal rest.

**VERSE 165.**—“There is great peace for those who love your Law, O Lord, and there is no scandal for them.” Great peace signifies purity of mind and abundance of faith, which we rightly set against vices. For the person who is scandalized by a brother loves God with false love [Ms.: “by a brother”].

**VERSE 166.**—“I awaited your salvation, O Lord, and I loved your commandments.” We await Jesus, the Lord and salvation of all [Ms.: “I awaited the Savior”], and I have done the things commanded in the Law and the Prophets. The hope of the reward generates love of the commandment.

**VERSE 167.**—“My soul kept your testimonies and loved them exceedingly.” “Kept” pertains to the martyr’s endurance; “loved” pertains to charity, which is stronger than every torment. This love must itself be greatly increased, because there the charity of the whole friendship is unfolded [Ms.: “must be practiced, because it is unfolded through all the efforts of the soul”].

**VERSE 168.**—“I kept your commandments and your testimonies, because all my ways are before you, O Lord.” A person keeps precepts and testimonies when he walks in God’s ways and does nothing in action or thought that would be considered unworthy in the divine contemplation.

**VERSE 169.**—“Let my prayer draw near before you, O Lord; according to your utterance give me understanding.” I ask, Lord, that my prayer be brought near to you, so that, receiving understanding from you, I may ask for nothing except what is proper.

**VERSE 170.**—“Let my prayer enter before you, O Lord; according to your utterance rescue me.” Our holy petition ascends by degrees. Earlier he said, “Let it draw near” [Ms.: “Let my entreaty draw near”]; now he says, “Let it enter.” First it was to draw near, then to be able to enter the Lord’s presence. Above he said, “According to your utterance, give me understanding”; here he says, “According to your utterance, rescue me,” so that there he may see the heavenly things he desires, and here may be cleansed from the stain of eternal desire.

**VERSE 171.**—“My lips shall pour forth a hymn when you teach me your ordinances.” If you open my lips through a pure conscience, then they will utter a hymn worthy of praise—namely, the hymn that I will learn after being instructed in your ordinances.

**VERSE 172.**—“My tongue shall proclaim your utterance, because all your commandments are equity.” There is nothing else in your utterances, O Lord, but peace, equity, and life. I shall believe this in my heart, speak it with my lips, and proclaim it with my tongue [Ms.: “may I proclaim it”].

[Col. 0619A] **VERSE 173.**—“Let your hand come to be, so that it may save me, because I have chosen your commandments.” When he says, “Let your hand come to be,” he designates the Lord Savior, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, through whom all things were made and are governed. Here we must understand “hand” as the right hand. He asks the Savior to come, knowing that through him he would be saved. By saying, “I have chosen your commandments,” he testifies that he has placed every danger after his love of the Lord.

**VERSE 174.**—“I desired your salvation, O Lord, and your Law is my meditation.” I had desired to see the very one whom, even in those times, I believed would come from a virgin’s womb. To demonstrate that this knowledge had come to him from the divine Scriptures, he continues: “And your Law is my meditation.” For in the Prophets he had desired Christ the Lord, whose birth was to come and of whom the Law and the Prophets spoke.

**VERSE 175.**—“My soul shall live, and it shall praise you, and your judgments shall help me.” He speaks to the one whom he desires to behold, promising that his soul will live forever, since he had rightly understood that it had believed. “It shall praise you,” with a new song, namely, through pure faith. By “judgments” he means those words that the Lord promises he will speak to his servants, as in: “Come, blessed ones.”

**VERSE 176.**—“I have gone astray like a sheep that has been lost; seek your servant, O Lord, because I have not forgotten your commandments.” The one sheep is the congregation of the saints and faithful, and their one shepherd is the Lord Christ. Consider how lowly a comparison is used for human beings when they abandon Christ’s grace: they are compared to a wandering sheep exposed to the dangers of wolves [Ms.: “open to dangers”]. And it is rightly said, “that was lost,” so that you may know that it was found by the Lord’s mercy.

To him be glory with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## THE EXPOSITION OF MASTER ALBINUS FLACCUS ALCUIN ON THE GRADUAL PSALMS, WHICH ARE ALSO CALLED THE SONGS OF ASCENTS

Steps belong to those who ascend or descend. But these fifteen steps belong to those who ascend. If you calculate this number—that is, fifteen—from the first to the last, the total is one hundred and twenty. Upon this number the Holy Spirit came in the upper room, that is, in the place of ascent, to show us that by these fifteen steps we must ascend to the height of the highest perfection. Therefore God descended from heaven to us on earth, so that we might ascend from earth to heaven. Therefore he descended into the valley of our tears, so that we might ascend into the blessedness of his joy.

But let us hear where this man, who sang these psalms for our salvation, began his ascent, or how he wished us to ascend. Indeed, the first step of our ascent is humility, so that we may understand that we are sinners and must hasten toward God’s grace. Therefore he says:

## PSALM CXIX

**VERSE 1.**—“When I was in tribulation, I cried to the Lord, and he heard me.” This life is tribulation. Those who cry humbly to God from it are heard, like the Publican who said: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13). But let us see what this penitent man cries out.

**VERSE 2.**—“O Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue.” Lying lips are those that try to urge us toward iniquity by their suggestions; a deceitful tongue is one that wishes to turn us away from the way of justice. The former urge us to sin; the latter holds us back from doing good. But let us consider what answer the Lord gives us to these prayers.

**VERSE 3.**—“What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue?” Behold what will be given to you in answer to the deceitful tongue, which customarily says—not to advise you, but to overturn you—“You cannot renounce the world; you cannot enter so difficult a way and so narrow a gate.”

**VERSE 4.**—“The sharp arrows of the mighty one, with desolating coals.” That is what is said in the Gospel: “For human beings this is impossible, but for God all things are possible” (Matthew 19:26). The arrows of the mighty one are the words of God, which pierce our hearts so that we may despise the world and love God. From these arrows love is aroused, not destruction produced. “With desolating coals,” that is, devastating coals.

But if shooting with words is insufficient, let examples demonstrate the matter. Those who had been black and cold through sins, once again kindled by the love of God, devastated and destroyed the works of the devil in their hearts, so that they might prepare a dwelling for God within themselves. After many sins they loved God greatly; therefore much will be forgiven them [Ms.: “many things are forgiven them.”] He continues:

**VERSES 5–6.**—“Woe is me, because my sojourning has been prolonged! I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has been a great sojourner.” Behold what this man accomplishes, and toward what he seeks to ascend, after being freed from the deceitful tongue, pierced by the word of God, and strengthened by the examples of many.

“Woe is me,” he says, “because my sojourning has been prolonged!” This is the voice of one grieving and lamenting his misery, because his sojourning in the pilgrimage of this mortal life has been prolonged for a long time. A sojourner is one who cultivates foreign soil. Thus he laments his condition and longs to return to his homeland; therefore he adds: “I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar.” Kedar is interpreted as “darkness.” It signifies sinners, among whom the righteous live as pilgrims in this age, while the threshing floor—that is, the Church—has not yet been purified and separated by the final winnowing of judgment. Therefore, desiring to ascend, he says: “My soul has been a great sojourner.” The body is a pilgrim in places, and the soul in its affections. Thus, wounded by the arrow of charity, he yearns with his whole desire for the heavenly homeland. He continues:

[Col. 0621A] **VERSE 7.**—With those who hate peace I was peaceful; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause. Who are those who hate peace, if not those who tear apart the unity of the Church, wishing to appear teachers of truth although they are teachers of error? “When I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause.” Those who strive to attack the teachers of the Church’s faith do so without cause, since these teachers seek to correct them and join them to the unity of the holy Church.

## PSALM 120

The first step of our ascent is the distress of our humility; the second is faith. And it must be understood that these steps of our ascent are nothing other than the progress of our salvation. Therefore, in these songs we are taught to ascend—but to ascend in the heart, in a good disposition, in faith, hope, and love, and in the desire for perpetuity and eternal life. Thus in the following psalm he said:

**VERSE 1.**—I lifted up my eyes to the mountains: from where will help come to me? These mountains are the saints, placed on high and illumined with brightness—but by him who is the true light, which illumines every human being coming into this world. Consequently, through faith this ascending man understood that from this mountain [Edit.: to this mountain], which is raised above the summit of the mountains, he must ask for, hope for, and receive help. Therefore he said:

**VERSE 2.**—My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. And he continued, speaking to that mountain from which he hoped for his one and only help:

**VERSE 3.**—Do not let my foot be moved, and let him who guards you not slumber. Make my foot stand firm in the ascent of my salvation, on the step of humility or right faith. Love moves the foot toward progress [pride moves it toward falling]. Rightly, then, this man, hearing that he should ascend and not fall, and that as a resident alien in the valley [Ms.: from the valley] of weeping he should progress rather than fail through the swelling of pride, says to the Lord: “Do not let my foot be moved” [Ms.: toward moving my foot]. And God says to him: “Let him who guards you not slumber.” Believe in him who never slumbers [Ms.: will never sleep] [and he will guard you]. Who is he who never slumbers, if not the one of whom the Apostle says: “Death will no longer rule over him” (Romans 6:9)? Therefore he added:

**VERSE 4.**—Behold, he will neither slumber nor sleep, who guards Israel. Be Israel—that is, a man who sees God—in faith and love, and his grace will never sleep in its guardianship of you. And as if this man were asking himself [Ms.: had asked], “Who is he who does not slumber?” the answer was given:

**VERSE 5.**—The Lord guards you. And how will he guard you? The Lord is your protection over your right hand. The hand signifies power; the right hand signifies eternal happiness. “The Lord is your protection over your right hand”—that is, if you believe in him, he will protect you so that you may have power to stand on the right side of the eternal Judge and hear the desired sentence: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom,” and so forth. As though he were still asking, the answer is given: In what will the Lord guard him?

**VERSE 6.**—By day the sun will not burn you, nor the moon by night. [The Lord] will guard you—that is, he will preserve you in right faith, whether in eternal things or temporal things; whether in faith in the holy Trinity, which is signified here by the name of the sun, or in faith in the holy Church, which is represented here by the name of the moon—so that your faith may neither wander nor be scandalized. For movement [F.: burning] signifies scandal. [Likewise, there are two commandments of love: love of God and love of neighbor.] Whoever, therefore, goes astray in the very substance of truth is burned by the sun; he is burned by day because he errs in that very wisdom. Whoever is not scandalized in the Church and in the flesh of Christ, who is the head of the Church, is not burned by the moon. “By day the sun will not burn you, nor the moon by night.” Why? Because:

**VERSE 7.**—The Lord guards you from every evil; may the Lord guard your soul. He guards you from scandals in the sun and from scandals in the moon. He guards you from every evil—that is, he guards your soul from every unbelief, so that it may not yield to unbelievers or be broken by tribulations.

**VERSE 8.**—May the Lord guard your entrance and your departure, from this time forth and forever. When we are tempted, we enter; when we conquer [the temptation], we depart [Edit.: we depart from the temptation]. Therefore may he guard us as we enter into faith, guard us as we depart toward rewards—and this forever, where the saints will reign [Col. 0622C] with Christ.

## PSALM 121

This man has now reached the third step of ascent: the desire for the heavenly Jerusalem, toward which he rejoiced to ascend in hope, although he was still laboring here among earthly things. Therefore he said:

**VERSE 1.**—I rejoiced in those things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord. I rejoiced in the prophets; I rejoiced in the apostles; indeed, in all the saints who say to me: “We shall go into the house of the Lord.” They say: “Run, hasten into the house of the Lord”—that is, hurry toward the heavenly Jerusalem.

**VERSE 2.**—Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem. “Standing,” that is, remaining; “our feet,” that is, the rewards of good works; “in your courts, Jerusalem,” that is, in the heavenly dwellings. He says “courts” in the plural, since the Truth itself says: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14:2). As though this lover were asking what this Jerusalem might be, he was told:

**VERSE 3.**—Jerusalem, which is built from living stones; which is built as a city, not of an earthly king but of a heavenly one, not a temporal but an eternal Jerusalem, whose participation is in the same thing. That which is always the same is “the same thing.” What is always the same, if not God, who said: “I am who I am”; who descended so that we might ascend; who shared in our mortality—for “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us”—so that we might share in his eternity [Ms.: his own eternity]? For “from his fullness we have all received.” Who, then, are those who will ascend into this city, to this participation? He explained next, saying:

**VERSE 4.**—For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, the testimony of Israel, to confess the name of the Lord. Not the tribes of the earth, of which it is said: “All the tribes of the earth will mourn over him,” but the tribes of the Lord, whom the twelve apostles will judge, separating them from those who are the tribes of the devil. For their testimony is in Israel—that is, in those who see God. Why do they ascend? “To confess your name, Lord,” as it is said: “Confession and beauty are in his presence” (Psalm 95:6).

**VERSE 5.**—For there thrones have been set for judgment, thrones over the house of David. What are these thrones, if not the holy apostles and preachers of the world, in whom God himself sits to judge the world? For God himself said: “Heaven is my throne” (Acts 7:49). And in the Psalm: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 19:1). Who are these heavens, if not the holy apostles, whose sound has gone out into the whole world? Hence it is said: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom”—that is, wisdom sits in the soul of the righteous. This wisdom is God, who said: “I will dwell in them, and they will be my peoples, and I will be their God” (2 Corinthians 5:16). “Thrones over the house of David”—that is, over David’s household [Ms.: Christ’s]: the house of David is the Church.

**VERSE 6.**—Ask for the things that make for the peace of Jerusalem, and abundance for those who love you. “Ask” is understood in two ways: either “inquire” or “pray”; that is, inquire or pray how you may have peace in Jerusalem. Or the speech is addressed to those thrones, so that at the judgment they may ask who belong to Jerusalem—those of whom it is said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9). Again the speech is addressed to that Jerusalem: “And abundance for those who love you”—that is, those who love the heavenly Jerusalem possess an abundance of every good: here abundance in hope, there abundance in reality. Therefore he continues:

**VERSE 7.**—Let peace be in your strength, and abundance in your towers. That is, in your love; for your strength, O Jerusalem, consists in love of God and neighbor [Ms.: your strength is the love of God and neighbor]. Through this peace and this strength there will be abundance in your towers—that is, in your exalted ones, who shortly before were called thrones. Many stand on the right, but few sit in judgment. He said that they sit in your towers, O Jerusalem, because he is a lover of this peace and this city:

**VERSE 8.**—For the sake of my brothers and my neighbors I spoke peace concerning you. Not for my own sake, not for earthly honors, not for the riches of the world, but for the sake of my brothers and my neighbors—that is, your sons [I speak this peace, I proclaim this peace to them, so that] they may receive this peace and remain in it.

**VERSE 9.**—For the sake of the house of the Lord our God I sought good things for you. That is, so that the number of your sons may increase, so that all may run to you, and each may say to the other: “Let us go into the house of the Lord”; likewise: “Come, let us ascend to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways, because from Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2:3).

## PSALM 122

Let us see what this ascending man, standing in the house of God and reaching the fourth [Edit.: how great] step of confidence, said:

**VERSE 1.**—To you I lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven. Let us lift our eyes from earthly things to heavenly things, from ourselves to the Lord [Ms.: God]. Let us displease ourselves so that we may please God, who dwells in heaven—that is, in the unity of the saints. Just as we must lift our eyes spiritually, so we must understand heaven spiritually. Wherever God dwells, there [our eyes] must be lifted in love [Edit.: there our hearts must be lifted]. [So that this might be understood more firmly, this lover strengthened himself with an example.]

**VERSE 2.**—Behold, as the eyes of servants are on the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a maidservant are on the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are on the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us. When, therefore, you hear “Christ,” lift your eyes to the Lord your God; when you hear “Lord,” lift your eyes to the wisdom and power of God. Lift your eyes to your mistress, because you are a male servant and a maidservant: a male servant because you are the people; a maidservant because you are the Church. Yet that maidservant has become a bride. One person speaks, and all speak in one, because all are one in Christ: one people, one Church, one flock belonging to one shepherd. “Until he has mercy on us”—that is, until he frees us from the tribulations of this life and the troubles of this way, and establishes us in the eternal homeland—us whom here he never ceases to instruct through various temptations. And let us hear what this man cries out:

**VERSE 3.**—Have mercy on us [Ms.: us], Lord, have mercy on us, because we have been filled exceedingly with contempt. Have mercy on us, so that we may hold right faith; have mercy on us, so that we may accomplish works corresponding to faith. “Because we have been filled exceedingly with contempt”—that is, with the temptations of this world.

**VERSE 4.**—And our soul has been filled exceedingly with the reproach of those who abound and the contempt of the proud. And who are those who reproach [us]? He explains next: “reproach toward those who abound” [those who rejoice in the prosperity of this world]; “and contempt toward the proud,” who in their riches [are proud and] despise the poor of Christ, of whom it is said: “Blessed are the poor, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

## PSALM 123

On the fifth step of the Songs of Ascents—that is, in steadfastness of patience—this lover, standing firm, sings these words:

**VERSES 1–2.**—If the Lord had not been among us, let Israel now say, if the Lord had not been among us. This is the voice of the saints, whether martyrs or those suffering tribulations in this world. It is as though they were saying: If the Lord were not our helper, we could never have endured these tribulations, sufferings, and persecutions. But because he is in us, we can easily pass through everything that appears harsh in this world. Let Israel say this—that is, let the man who sees God consider this, because God completes these works in him [Ms.: this work]. When people rose up against us, they might perhaps have swallowed us alive. They rose up to devour us, as though to swallow us alive. Who could endure such savage and relentless persecutions unless the Lord had helped those who hope in him, whom he never abandons? Thus, in the first Psalm of Ascents, he testified that he had been freed from a deceitful tongue and seductive flattery; now, in this psalm, he recounts that he has been redeemed from open persecution through the mercy of God and the Lord, so that he might overcome both spiritual and bodily persecutions, whether in hidden temptation or open persecution. The fact that in the preceding psalms he speaks as though with one voice, but here speaks in the plural, signifies the unity of the body of Christ; it also signifies that there are many members belonging to that head, which is Christ.

**VERSES 3–4.**—When their fury was enraged against us, perhaps the water would have swallowed us up. This is the martyr’s voice, displaying the persecutor’s savage spirit: “perhaps, like water, it would have swallowed us” [Ms.: the waters would have swallowed us]. Water signifies the ungodly people who seek to devour the saints [Ms.: the waters here signify the peoples of the ungodly who seek].

**VERSE 5.**—Our soul passed through the torrent; perhaps our soul would have passed through unbearable water. He signifies the violence of persecution by the name “torrent.” “Unbearable water”—that is, we endured the incredible rage of the wicked; and unless the Lord were among us, our weakness could in no way have escaped these most savage persecutions. This victorious band, turning to praise its deliverer, says:

**VERSE 6.**—Blessed is the Lord, who did not give us as prey to their teeth. Blessed is God, who conquered the world; through him we conquer, and through him we have been freed from the harshest teeth of our persecutors [Edit.: from persecution and the harshest teeth]. And this is because God was among us.

**VERSE 7.**—Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of hunters. This sparrow is Christ. Just as he was freed from all iniquity and from the persecution of the ungodly, and returned gloriously victorious to his Father’s seat, so through him we have been freed and have not been handed over to the snares of the devil’s deceit or into the hands of hunters. We lost our life, but we preserved our faith; and it is better that, having lost it, we have been found, as the Truth itself says: “Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it.” And who is the author [Ms.: doer] of this exhortation, patience, and strength in us, if not he who made heaven and earth? He who made us is himself the one who redeemed us; and he who redeemed us is himself the one who rewards us. To him we always say: “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (verse 8).

## PSALM 124

Now he begins to speak about the stability of the eternal Jerusalem and about the confidence and stability [Ms.: firmness] of those who hasten toward it with their whole desire, saying:

**VERSE 1.**—Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; he will not be moved forever, who dwells in Jerusalem. Faith directed toward God makes life stable; no one who builds his house upon his firm rock can be moved by any temptations. What is Mount Zion if not Christ, who is at the summit of the mountains, who will be raised above the hills, and to whom all nations will flow (Isaiah 2:2)? Zion is the Church, in which there is the mirror of life and the vision of eternity, whose head is Christ. Behold, this ascending man of spiritual steps asks what kind of Jerusalem this is, in which the choir of the saints dwells, and he is answered:

**VERSE 2.**—Mountains surround it, and the Lord surrounds his people, from this time forth and forever. These mountains are angels [they are apostles], prophets, and holy preachers who fortify this Jerusalem. And lest the fact that it has such mountains around it seem a small thing to you, he immediately added: “And the Lord surrounds his people.” Behold what walls, what fortifications, what defenders we have! Let us remain within the enclosures of Jerusalem and not fear the devil’s ambushes or his arrows, since we have such defenders—and this not for a time, but forever. Therefore he says: “From this time forth and forever.” He continues:

**VERSE 3.**—For the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous, so that the righteous may not stretch out their hands toward iniquity. The lot of the righteous is to stand at God’s right hand on the day of judgment. Over their lot—that is, over their assembly—the rod of the ungodly will not come: that terrifying sentence, “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire.” “So that the righteous may not stretch out their hands toward iniquity.” Why this limitation, that the righteous should not stretch out their hands toward iniquity? So that the righteous may endure the wicked as rulers for a time and understand that this will not be everlasting, but may prepare themselves to possess an eternal inheritance. For then every power of iniquity will be destroyed, so that God may be all in all. Let those who are upright in heart consider this: the unjust do not rule forever; their power will be taken away from them, and the Lord alone will reign over his saints.

**VERSE 4.**—And may he do good to the good and to those who are upright in heart. Here, so that they may remain steadfast in faith and good works, and in the future receive eternal glory.

**VERSE 5.**—But those who turn aside into bonds the Lord will lead away with those who practice iniquity. Peace upon Israel. Those who practice iniquity—that is, those whose deeds they imitated, because they loved their present joy and did not believe in future punishments [Ms.: because they loved]. What, then, will those who are upright in heart and do not turn aside possess? Let us now come to the inheritance itself. What is that inheritance? “Peace upon Israel.” What peace? That which surpasses all understanding.

## PSALM 125

This Psalm of Ascents sings the praise of our redemption: how we have been freed from the captivity of the devil’s power and from the bonds of our sins. This lover of our freedom sings [indeed]:

**VERSE 1.**—When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted—that is, rejoicing. Zion is eternal in the angels but captive in human beings. Why captive? Because they have been sold under sin. Why were they sold, if not because they consented to sin? We were made free, but we sold ourselves to sin [because of the consent to sin in our first parent (Edit.: because we became partners in the sin of our first parent)]. But in the second Adam we were freed, and therefore comforted. For not all the citizens of that city are captives; only those who wander from it are captives. Yet consolation belongs to the wretched and the grieving. For now this consolation is in hope; then it will be in reality, when we see face to face. Until now we believe in faith and love in hope.

**VERSE 2.**—Then our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation. In this consolation of our redemption, the mouth of our heart was filled with joy, and the tongue of our heart with exultation: the mouth and tongue of the heart by which, while our bodily mouth is closed, we cry out to God when we pray. “Then they will say among the nations: The Lord has done great things for them.” That is, he has shown mercy to all the nations. For God is not known only in Judea, but from the ends of the earth we have heard the praises of the righteous saying [Ms.: the righteous person saying]: “Hear us, O God our savior, hope of all the ends of the earth and of the distant sea” (Psalm 65:5). Let us all say [Ms.: let them say]:

**VERSE 3.**—The Lord has done great things for us; we have become rejoicing. He has shown us mercy; therefore we have become rejoicing.

**VERSE 4.**—The Lord will turn our captivity, like a torrent in the south. Torrents are called winter rivers, for they run filled with sudden waters and great force. The south wind, however, is warm and melts ice. It signifies the Holy Spirit, who loosens and dries the hardness of our sins, which has been bound by the frost [Latin: zelo; perhaps gelu] of unbelief, and turns our captivity into joy.

**VERSE 5.**—Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.” Likewise: “Blessed are the merciful, for they will obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:5, 7). Those who mourn their sins sow in tears; those who perform works of mercy sow in the valley, as the Apostle says: “Whoever sows in blessing will reap from blessing” (2 Corinthians 9:6). For as much as each person sows, so much will he receive. For the very life into which we have entered is wretched, tearful, and full of labors. Therefore a human being knows how to weep from birth but does not know how to laugh, because he was born for labor, not for joy.

**VERSE 6.**—Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds. This Song of Ascents exhorts us to works of mercy, so that we may go and seek someone to whom we may do good and with whose misery we may sympathize, as the Apostle says: “Weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). Let us cast our seeds upon passing waters, because after a long time we will find them. Therefore he continues: “But coming, they will come with exultation, carrying their sheaves.” Where will they come, if not into the presence of the supreme Judge? What do they carry? Works of mercy. “For I was hungry,” says the Lord, “and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink.” What, then, will they hear? “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world,” and so forth (Matthew 25:34–35). This will be said to those who now wish diligently to sow works of mercy among the poor.

## PSALM 126

These songs, as we have often said, belong to those who are ascending. How are they ascending? By loving God. Whoever loves God ascends; whoever loves the world falls. But the title of this psalm adds: “A Song of Ascents of Solomon.” Let us see why the name of Solomon is added only in this [place]. Solomon is interpreted as “peaceful.” Who is this peaceful one if not the true Solomon, our Lord Jesus Christ, who made peace between heavenly and earthly things in his blood and made the two one, joining the two walls to himself in the cornerstone? For the Church joined two peoples—the people of circumcision and the people of uncircumcision—into one fold, so that there might be one shepherd and one flock. Of this Solomon it is said at the beginning of the psalm:

**VERSE 1.**—Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain [Ms.: labored]. Unless the Lord builds the Church without stain or wrinkle, every preacher labors in vain. Who are those who labor in vain, if not the heretics, who labor to gather a Church but do so without the Lord? Therefore their work is vain. Since the faithful people has been built, our Lord Jesus Christ is its guardian: he builds, preserves, protects, and rewards; he alone is in all things both builder and guardian.
