Therefore he said in the following verse: “Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain.” This is the city so often sung of in these Psalms of Ascents: the spiritual Jerusalem, certainly.

**VERSE 2.**—It is vain for you to rise before the light. For it is vain for a person to labor inwardly without divine grace. [Let grace precede, but let obedience follow; then he does not labor in vain.] Rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow. If you wish to be exalted, be humble here, where he was humble who became poor for us, so that there you may be exalted where he sits at the right hand of God the Father. Rising signifies exaltation; sitting signifies humility. In other passages sitting is understood as the honor of judging, as there: “You will sit on twelve thrones” (Matthew 19:28). Likewise, sitting signifies humility, as there: “Jesus, wearied from the journey, was sitting by the well” (John 4:6). For in another psalm it is also said: “Lord, you have known my sitting down and my rising” (Psalm 139:2)—that is, my humility and my exaltation. Therefore, so that it might be understood to what kind of sitting this referred, he immediately added: “You who eat the bread of sorrow.” Those who groan in this pilgrimage eat the bread of sorrow. Let us therefore breathe after the heavenly homeland with desire: here there is humiliation, there exaltation; here pilgrimage, there the homeland. Let us humble ourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt us at the time of visitation. As though this lover were asking when that resurrection—that is, exaltation—would be, he is answered:

**VERSE 3.**—When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord: sons, the reward, the fruit of the womb. Sleep here signifies death. [Just as] Christ was not exalted except after death, so our exaltation will not be [Edit.: is] except after death; for his resurrection occurred only after he had died, nor will our resurrection occur unless we first die. As though you were asking again [and saying], “To which beloved?” he says: [This is] the inheritance of the Lord, sons, the reward, the fruit of the womb. What is this inheritance? That one, certainly, of which it is said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm 2:8). Who are the sons, the reward [Ms.: “of reward”]?  All the saints, certainly, whom Christ acquired with his blood. “The fruit of the womb”—that is, [the fruit of the Church. “Inheritance,” “sons,” and “fruit” signify one thing, namely,] the assembly of all the saints [Edit.: the congregation], “sons, the reward, the fruit of the womb.” Then he adds:

**VERSE 4.**—As arrows in the hand of the mighty, so are the sons of those who have been shaken out. The arrows are the apostles, whose sound has gone out into all the earth, sent from the hand of the mighty one—that is, Christ. “So are the sons of those who have been shaken out” [those very apostles are the sons of those who have been shaken out]—that is, the sons of the prophets, who by God’s gift [Ms.: from a suitable one] shook out and brought into the light the hidden things and mysteries of Christ’s incarnation and the holy sacraments of the Church, the mysteries of the heavenly treasure hidden from the ages [Col. 0629D]. The apostles are their sons [Ms.: were their sons], because what the prophets announced in an enigma, the apostles preached in Christ as history.

**VERSE 5.**—Blessed is the man who has fulfilled his desire from them; he will not be confounded when he speaks with his enemies in the gate. “From them”—that is, from the preaching of the apostles, from which he fulfills his whole desire and loves heavenly rather than earthly things, eternal rather than temporal things. He will not be confounded when he speaks with his enemies in the gate. The gate is Christ. Whoever preaches Christ, speaks in Christ, and remains in Christ will not be confounded forever. Rather, he preaches in season and out of season—that is, to those willing and unwilling to hear the word of God, to friends as well as enemies. He stands [in the gate (Edit.: out of season)] so that all may hear and all may be built up.

## PSALM 127

This ascending man of the Songs of Ascents comes to the song of the blessed and says from where this blessedness comes [and says to himself]:

**VERSE 1.**—Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways. This is the true [Ms.: truly] blessedness: it consists in the fear of the Lord and in the observance of his commandments. This is the fear of which another psalm says: “The holy fear of the Lord endures forever and ever” (Psalm 19:10). One fear arises from punishment, another from love. Blessed is the one who fears the Lord because of love and observes his commandments in love. As he himself says: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John 14:15).

**VERSE 2.**—You will eat the labors of your fruits [Ms.: the fruits of the labors of your hands]; you are blessed, and it will be well with you. No one eats labors, but what is born from labor—that is, fruit. The holy martyrs labored in this world so that they might receive the fruit of eternal life, so that what was said might be fulfilled in them: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations, and I appoint a kingdom for you, just as my Father appointed a kingdom for me, so that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22:28–30). “You are blessed, and it will be well with you.” Here you are blessed in hope; there it will be well with you in reality, when you see face to face the one whom here you love in your heart.

[Col. 0630C] **VERSE 3.**—Your wife is like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house. The wife of Christ is the Church [the Church, which] is also the bride, abounding in the fruit of good works. “On the sides of your house.” Those are the sides in the house of God that cling more firmly to Christ. “Your sons are like olive shoots around your table.” In Christ there is not one wife and another son, but all are one in Christ. The one whom he previously called “wife” he now also calls “son” [Ms.: “sons”], because the wife and the sons are the Church of Christ. “Like olive shoots.” [The olive] signifies peace. Therefore the sons pass into the peace of Christ in newness of spirit, not in the oldness of the letter [Ms.: may pass]. “Around your table.” The table of Christ is sacred Scripture, from which we are fed, from which we understand what we should love [Col. 0630D] and what we should desire, and toward whom we should lift our eyes.

**VERSE 4.**—Behold, thus will every person be blessed who fears the Lord. He returns to the beginning of the psalm, where he said: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord.” Now he explains what this blessedness is, which is owed to the one who fears God, and how the one who fears God is to be blessed. For he says:

**VERSE 5.**—May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life. He said, “May the Lord bless you from Zion”—that is, from the contemplation of eternal life. That is the true blessing which makes us desire eternal life. Therefore he added: “That you may see the good things that are in Jerusalem all the days of your life”—that is, eternal good things, not temporal ones; things that endure, not things that pass away, which are in the heavenly Jerusalem. “All the days of your life”: you will always rejoice; you will always see good things—that is, Christ, the author of all goodness.

**VERSE 6.**—And may you see the sons of your sons: peace upon Israel. Your sons are the good works that you do; the sons of your sons are the fruits of good works, which are to be seen and received in the future life, where there will be peace upon all who see God. This peace is Christ, which surpasses all understanding. May that peace guard our hearts forever.

## PSALM 128

**VERSE 1.**—This tenth Psalm of Ascents begins thus: “Often they have attacked me from my youth,” let Israel now say. This is the voice of the Church enduring false [Col. 0631B] brothers and looking back to earlier examples [Edit.: looking back at the example], and through those examples exhorting us to endure invincibly, after the example of the Fathers. For the Church was attacked long ago, not recently but always, from the beginning of its existence. Abel was the Church of Christ, but he was attacked by his brother. Likewise, Jacob was the Church of Christ, but he was attacked by his brother Esau. Moses too was very often attacked in the Church of Christ by the people over whom he presided. Christ was killed by the synagogue, but was not overcome [Edit.: separated]. Behold, through examples he taught us to endure false brothers courageously. Let all who love God with a full heart and desire to see God say this, and let them say again:

**VERSE 2.**—Often they have attacked me from my youth, yet they have not prevailed against me. Whether in the Old Testament or in the New, they have never been able to prevail against me so that I would consent to them.

**VERSE 3.**—Sinners built upon my back; they prolonged their iniquities. They built upon my back for me to endure; they laid tribulations upon me, but I bore them until they might be corrected and thus cease persecuting me, or until at the end they might be shaken from my back [Col. 0631D]. I endure to the end, but they will persecute to the end. “They prolonged their iniquities,” because there is no time in this world when the Church of Christ does not suffer persecution from false brothers.

**VERSES 4–5.**—But the righteous Lord will cut down the necks of sinners; let all who hate Zion be confounded and turned backward. That is, he will crush their pride. By “neck” he signifies their pride. Let all who hate Zion be confounded and afraid. Let them be confounded in judgment and afraid in the depths. Those who hate Zion [Zion is the Church]—that is, those who hate the Church and do not wish to obey the word of God. For they are in the Church, but are false brothers, and they hate those who do good within it. See what follows concerning those who hate the Church:

**VERSE 6.**—Let them become like the grass of the roofs, which withers before it is pulled up. [For all the glory of those who are proud perishes in this world.] Just as the grass of the roofs has no root and quickly withers, so they quickly perish: “which withers before it is pulled up”—that is, before they are punished in judgment, they wither, having no moisture of good works.

### VERSE 7

“With which the reaper shall not fill his hand, nor he who gathers sheaves his bosom.” The reapers are the angels; they do not fill their bosoms with their produce, because it is weeds and not wheat. Rather, the weeds are bound into bundles and burned with everlasting fire.

### VERSE 8

“And they who passed by did not say: ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you; we have blessed you in the name of the Lord.’” The prophets, patriarchs, and apostles are those who pass along the road of this age. Their blessing benefits the children of the Church, not the false brothers who attack the Church. For they do not bestow blessing upon those who are to perish, but upon those who are to remain. And what blessing do they give? “They bless,” he says, “in the name of the Lord,” because every blessing and every sanctification is strengthened and confirmed through the name of the Lord.

## PSALM 129

### VERSE 1

There follows the Psalm of Ascents whose beginning is: “From the depths I cried to you, Lord; Lord, hear my voice.” Accordingly, this psalm [manuscript: “from this psalm”] represents a stage of reflection and a station of a certain lament, so that we may understand in what depth we are and from where it is necessary for us to cry out. For this mortal life [Edit.: “depths”] is a depth for us. Whoever understands that he is in the depths should cry out, groan, and sigh until he is rescued from the depths and comes to him who sits above all the abysses, above the Cherubim, and above all that he created—not only temporal things but also spiritual things. Yet he came from there even into the depth of this life, in order to free us from this depth of misery and to urge us to cry out to him who is the true Savior, saying: “Lord, Lord, hear my voice.”

### VERSE 2

“Let your ears be attentive to the prayer of your servant.” The repetition of the cry signifies an inward entreaty. He continues:

### VERSE 3

“If you observe iniquities, Lord, Lord, who will endure?” He reveals from what depth he was crying out: from the abyss of his sins, which had flooded over his head, understanding that this whole life is full of temptations. Therefore he said: “Who will endure?” If you judge us only according to justice and do not grant mercy, there is no one who can endure, because all are children of wrath. Rather, our hope rests upon your mercies and not upon our merits.

### VERSE 4

“For with you there is forgiveness, and because of your law I have waited for you, Lord.” This forgiveness is the blood of Christ, which freed us from the slavery of fear that existed under the old law. “I have waited for you, Lord,” that is, “I have hoped in you, Lord,” just as he says in another psalm: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he regarded me” (Psalm 39:2): I waited through hope, and he regarded me through mercy.

### VERSE 5

“My soul has waited for your word, Lord; my soul has hoped in the Lord.” For what word did it wait? It hoped in the Word who became flesh; through that Word you forgave me all my sins. Yet my soul still hopes in the Lord. What does it hope for? To receive the forgiveness of sins. But I do not yet possess eternal life; and because you have done what you promised, I hope that you will do what still remains, so that after the resurrection of all I may receive eternal life.

### VERSE 6

“From the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord.” The morning watch is Christ—“Christ has risen” (Edit.: “it is Christ who has risen”)—in whom we shall all rise. Therefore, from the watch of his resurrection until night, that is, until the end of the world, let all the saints hope in the Lord. And this hope is entirely certain because:

### VERSE 7

“With the Lord there is mercy, and with him is abundant redemption.” Through him, therefore, we have been redeemed; through him we shall rise.

### VERSE 8

“He himself will redeem Israel from all its iniquities.” “Where sin abounded, grace abounded” [editorial supplement]. For they have been saved by the grace of God through faith, from all their iniquities. He designates all the faithful by the name “Israel,” because all have been redeemed from all their iniquities through the abundant redemption of the Lord Jesus Christ.

We should know that in some passages of these psalms the words sound as though they concern many people, as where he says: “Have mercy on us [manuscript: ‘on us’], Lord, have mercy on us, because we have been filled exceedingly with contempt” (Psalm 122:3). In other passages they sound as though they concern one person, as where he says: “From the depths I cried to you, Lord.” This is because we are many in our members but one in Christ: all speak in one, and one speaks in all. For this ascender says:

## PSALM 130

### VERSE 1

“Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up.” In these words he offers God the sacrifice of humility, as it is read in another psalm: “A contrite spirit”—that is, a humbled one—“is a sacrifice to God” (Psalm 50:19). Thus the prayer of the humbling tax collector was heard more than that of the proud Pharisee.

“Nor have my eyes been lifted up.” He said that the eyes of his heart were not exalted but humbled, because humility is the guardian of all good things.

“Nor have I walked in great matters, nor in things too wonderful for me.” I have not sought to be great among human beings or remarkable by performing signs and miracles, because signs were given for unbelievers, not for believers, so that those who did not believe through preaching might believe through signs. Hence he adds:

### VERSE 2

“If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul: as a weaned child is upon his mother, so is recompense in my soul.”

These two verses seem to sound like a curse and to refer to heretics, who do not wish to be humbled in the peace of the Church but to exalt themselves in the schism of their own doctrine. They did not wish to be nourished by the milk of the mother Church so as to reach solid food, which is Christ. Therefore they have been weaned and rejected by their mother, because they refused to be nourished by the milk of piety. They are teachers of error, although they are not disciples of truth. Therefore recompense will be made to them in their souls [Edit.: “in their hands”]: because through the unbelief of schism they withdrew from the faith in soul, so in soul they will receive whatever they have deserved.

### VERSE 3

“Let Israel hope in the Lord, who is the hope of all who see God.” From this time onward and forever—that is, until eternity, in which we shall see the one in whom we now hope.

## PSALM 131

This is the forerunner of our ascent and leads to the stage of gentleness, in which the most holy David set before us an example, speaking as though in his own person:

### VERSES 1–5

“Remember, Lord, David and all his gentleness.” David is interpreted as “strong of hand.” According to the historical account, he spared the enemy who sought his life, signifying our warrior Christ, who struck down the exceedingly proud Goliath with the stone of his own strength. When we were enemies, he became gentle toward us, so that, instructed by his example, we might be gentle and meek.

“As he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob.” God’s swearing means that he displays the pledge of his promise [manuscript: “that he displays his promises”].

“He vowed a vow to the God of Jacob.” What is Christ’s vow except that he would redeem the human race? Hence he says in the Gospel: “I have completed the work that you gave me” (John 17:4).

“He vowed a vow to the God of Jacob.” In what follows he shows what he had vowed to God: namely, that he would find a dwelling for the God of Jacob—that is, the holy Church—of which it is said in another psalm: “How lovely are your dwellings, Lord” (Psalm 83:2).

But if we act well, we too shall be God’s dwelling and the temple of the living God, as the Apostle said: “You are the temple of God.” Let no sleep, no pleasure of the flesh, and no ambition of the world deter us, so that we fail to find a dwelling for God within ourselves.

### VERSE 6

“Behold, we heard of it in Ephrata; we found it in the fields of the forest.” Ephrata is interpreted as “mirror.” Images are seen in a mirror; this signifies the prophets, who spoke through an image concerning the future house of God. “We found it in the fields of the forest”; there we heard about the house of God—that is, in the breadth [Edit.: “height”] of the nations, which are covered with the brambles and thorns of sins. Yet there is now the house of God there, the Church of Christ, of which the prophets foretold.

### VERSE 7

“We shall enter into his dwelling.” Whose? The dwelling of the God of Jacob. How shall we enter? Through faith.

“We shall adore in the place where his feet have stood.” Whose feet? Those of Christ our Lord, where his footprints are seen, and where the wonders he performed and the firmness of our redemption are proclaimed. For without the charity of this house salvation would not be found [Edit.: “only salvation would not be found”]. He is to be adored where the true faith is said to be [manuscript: “where the true faith is to be adored”].

### VERSE 8

“Arise, Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification.” This is said to Christ, that he should rise from the dead and enter into his rest—that is, after the labor of his Passion, into the rest of heavenly glory.

“You and the ark of your sanctification.” The ark of Christ is the Church of Christ. The resurrection took place first in the head; it will follow in the members, so that what the Truth itself said may come to pass: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me.”

### VERSE 9

“Let your priests be clothed with justice, and let your saints rejoice.” It belongs to the priest to preach justice and to demonstrate it by example; it belongs to the people to rejoice in justice and in the preaching of the priests [Edit.: “the joy … and the preaching”].

Likewise: let the priests be clothed with faith and hope, and let the saints rejoice; for just as Christ rose in glory, so the saints will rise with Christ in glory.

### VERSE 10

“For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your Christ.” This is the voice of the Church pleading with God the Father: “May he not turn away the face of his Christ because of the victory he won over his enemies”—that is, so that he might turn his face away from the Jews [manuscript/editorial wording].

[Edit.: “Pleading on behalf of the Church: ‘Do not turn away the face of your Christ because of the victory David won over his enemies; turn your anger away from the Jews.’ And after the fullness of the nations, all Israel will be saved, which is now saved in the apostles and the others.”]

### VERSE 11

“The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not disappoint him.” The Lord’s oath signifies the confirmation of his judgment. He does not swear in vain, nor will what he promises be without fruit [manuscript: “nor will it be fruitless”]. In swearing truth, he fulfills truth, because truth cannot be deceived.

“From the fruit of your womb I will place upon your throne” [manuscript: “upon my throne”], that is, he will be born from a virginal womb, and I will place him upon my throne.

“A shoot will come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will rise from his root” (Isaiah 11:1). The shoot will come forth from the root of the patriarch; the flower—that is, Christ—will rise from the Virgin’s womb.

Another translation has: “The Lord will swear, and he will not repent.” This does not mean that God repents of anyone; rather, saying that God “repents” signifies that he changes something. “The Lord will swear, and he will not repent,” that is, he wishes to preserve as unchangeable what he does, what he established with David his servant [manuscript: “what is made”].

### VERSE 12

“If your sons keep my covenant and these testimonies of mine, which I shall teach them, their sons also will sit forever upon my throne.”

Certainly, your sons and the sons of your sons [Edit.: *tui et filii*, “your sons and the sons”], if they keep my commandments, will sit upon the throne of your blessedness. For all the faithful are sons in Christ of David and of Abraham, concerning whom the Truth itself says: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matthew 3:9).

### VERSE 13

“For the Lord has chosen Zion; he has chosen it beforehand as his dwelling.” Zion is the universal Church, blessed in the angels and a pilgrim in the inhabitants of the earth; and it too will eventually share in angelic blessedness. This is the dwelling of God forever. Those whom God chose in Christ he chose beforehand—that is, predestined before the foundation of the world—according to the Apostle, who says: “Those whom he called, these he also predestined” (Romans 8:30).

### VERSE 14

“This is my rest forever and ever; here I shall dwell, because I have chosen it.” These are God’s words: “This is my rest; here I rest.” How greatly God loves us, brothers, that because we rest he says that he rests. He himself is never troubled, nor does he rest in that manner; but he says that he rests there because we have rest in him. “Here I shall dwell, because I have chosen it.”

### VERSE 15

“Blessing her widow, I will bless her; I will fill her poor with bread.” Every soul that understands itself to be deserted by every help except that of God alone is a widow according to the world, because the world abandons it. Yet she is not thereby a widow who has Christ as her husband. Therefore the holy Church is a widow in all her members: abandoned and despised by the world, but chosen and betrothed by Christ.

“And I will fill her poor with bread.” Christ’s poor are those who do not love this world, whether they possess riches or do not possess them. For riches are given to some to distribute to the needy, not to possess for themselves. They ought neither to place their hope in riches nor to find their satisfaction in them, but to trust in the name of Christ, in justice, and in the love of God and neighbor. This is the fullness of the saints, not the riches of the world.

### VERSE 16

“I will clothe her priests with salvation, and her saints will rejoice with rejoicing.” Who are the priests? Those who have offered themselves to God as a living sacrifice, pleasing to God [manuscript: “who offer themselves”].

“And I will clothe them with salvation,” that is, with Christ Jesus, who is the salvation of all believers, as the Apostle says: “All of you who were baptized have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Galatians 3:27).

“And her saints will rejoice with rejoicing.” In what will they rejoice? In being clothed with Christ. Therefore he adds:

### VERSE 17

“There I will bring forth the horn of David; I have prepared a lamp for my Christ.” This is to be understood of Christ, not merely of a kingdom [manuscript: “so that hope may be placed in Christ, not in the world”]. The horn signifies kingship and exaltation; David signifies Christ the king.

“I have prepared a lamp for my Christ.” The Truth itself says in the Gospel concerning John: “He was a burning and shining lamp.” He was prepared by God the Father to go before the face of his Christ, as it was said: “Behold, I send my angel, who will prepare your way before you.”

### VERSE 18

“I will clothe his enemies with confusion, but upon him my sanctification will blossom.” “Upon him,” that is, upon Christ, my sanctification will blossom. In his baptism there is the remission of sins, sanctification, and the gift of the Holy Spirit, as John himself bears witness, saying: “This is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit; and I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John 1).

## PSALM 132

He has now reached the psalm of the fourteenth stage [Edit.: “the fourteenth stage”], in which this lover of ascent praises the unity of the saints. He rejoices that he has reached the unity of brotherly charity; therefore he says:

### VERSE 1

“Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one.” What is more beautiful or more pleasant—or rather, what is better—than unity and charity among the members of Christ, whom he has chosen to call brothers? What this unity resembles he explains in the following comparison:

### VERSE 2

“As ointment upon the head, which flows down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron.” Who is this Aaron? Certainly Christ, who alone entered into the Holy of Holies with blood—not another’s but his own—to intercede for us with God the Father.

“As ointment upon the head.” This ointment is the Holy Spirit, who flows down from Christ the head, for Christ is our head.

“It flows down upon the beard,” that is, upon strong and unconquerable warriors who fight for Christ’s name: first the apostles, then the sanctifying [manuscript: “sanctified”] martyrs, and thereafter it reaches all the faithful. Therefore he adds: “Which flows down to the edge of the garment.”

The garment of this priest is the holy Church, consecrated by his blood until the end of the world and woven into a garment for him. Therefore he said “to the edge of the garment,” and then added another comparison with the same meaning:

### VERSE 3

“As the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion.” Hermon is interpreted as “an exalted name,” which is Christ exalted upon the cross and afterward lifted up into heaven. His grace—that is, his dew—descends upon Mount Zion, that is, upon what is holy and perfect in the Church of Christ. Whatever the beard or the edge of the garment signifies, Mount Zion also seems to signify.

He continues: “For there the Lord commanded blessing and life forever.” Where did he command it? Among the brothers who dwell together as one. There he commanded blessing; there those who dwell in harmony bless the Lord; there also they receive eternal life [manuscript: “there also is eternal life”].

Thus far we have ascended by singing the stages to the house of God. Let us see what must be done in it. What, then, except to bless the Lord in heart and mouth with charity, saying with the Prophet:

## PSALM 133

### VERSE 1

“Behold, now bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord.” “Behold, now,” that is, at this time, in which the Lord has gathered us through his only-begotten Son into the house of his love. Let us bless the Lord, not with a transitory but with a lasting praise, exhorting one another to stand and persevere in the praise of God.

“You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.” That is, you who remain in the catholic faith, in the unity of charity, which is signified here by the name “court.” A court is a broad place, open to the sun. Thus our mind, illuminated by the breadth of charity, ought to be open to all in doing good.

He adds:

### VERSE 2

“In the nights lift up your hands in the holy place, and bless the Lord.” The nights signify the tribulations of this age. In them we are admonished to raise our hands to good works and to bless the Lord, not only with words but also with good deeds.

It is easy to bless God in prosperity, but it is especially necessary to praise him in adversity, with Job, who, after everything he possessed had been taken away, said: “Blessed be the name of the Lord from this time forth and forever” (Job 1:21).

He continues:

### VERSE 3

“May the Lord bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth.” Zion is called a watchtower [Edit.: “mirror”]. In it the saints are to be blessed, those who reach the fifteenth stage and received the Holy Spirit in the upper room under the number twelve times ten.

Therefore, if you add together all the numbers from one through fifteen, they make one hundred twenty. This number, consecrated by the coming of the Holy Spirit, signifies that the New Testament is prefigured by the Old and that the Old is fulfilled in the New.

At the first stage, afflicted, we cried out to the Lord; at the fifteenth, liberated from afflictions, we are commanded to bless the Lord—no other than the one who made heaven and earth: “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but he gave the earth to the children of men” (Psalm 113:16), who are commanded to ascend from earthly things to heavenly things.

# AN OLD HYMN ON THE FIFTEEN PSALMS OF ASCENTS

## PRELIMINARY NOTICE

We stated above, in the preliminary note to the threefold Commentary on the Psalms reviewed thus far, that Alcuin was not the author of this hymn. Nevertheless, we judged it appropriate to place it here because it was at least written or dictated by Alcuin and sent to his beloved Aquila, as is evident from Letter 153. This hymn also occupies this same place in a very ancient manuscript codex of our library of Saint Emmeram. We have placed the variant readings in parentheses, taken from the Reichenau manuscript, or Augia the Rich.

I cried out to the Lord when I was troubled,  
and the Lord heard his servant at once.

I lifted my eyes immediately  
to the ancient mountains:  
whence help will come from the Lord Most High?

I rejoiced in all that the Lord said to me:  
“We shall go to the house of God” [manuscript: “of the Lord”],  
in which we shall always remain.

To you I lifted my eyes, O God [manuscript: “O Ruler”] among us,  
you who are at heaven’s summit  
with the host of angels.

“Had the Lord Most High not been among us,”  
let Israel say,  
“we would have been weaker than all.”

Those who trust in the Lord, the greatest ruler,  
are like Mount Zion,  
which is never moved by anyone.

When the Lord immediately turned back Zion’s captivity,  
we were greatly consoled in everything.

Unless God [manuscript: “the Lord”] builds  
and preserves us,  
the labor of all who build houses is vain.

Blessed are the children of men [manuscript: “of all”]  
who fear their Lord,  
and who walk along the narrow way  
with steadfast faith.

Often they attacked me,  
but my adversaries could not prevail;  
they immediately ceased,  
for the Lord strengthened me.

From the depths I cried out humbly and faithfully  
to you, God [manuscript: “Lord”] of victory,  
eternal Father of glory.

My heart was not lifted up in pride,  
nor was I inwardly exalted in my thoughts.

Remember me, Lord God [manuscript: “O Ruler”]  
from heaven’s summit,  
you whom thousands upon thousands of ministers attend.

Behold how good, sublime,  
and how pleasant it truly is  
for brothers to live as one  
and to dwell in the highest life.

Behold, now all servants,  
standing in the house of the Lord,  
bless the Lord of all days.

I beseech the Father of power  
and the Prince of knowledge  
that through these three times five stages  
I may be able to climb to heaven,

and through the ethereal regions  
be carried to places of refreshment,  
so that I may deserve to possess  
excellent rewards.

# THIRD OPUSCULUM: A COMPENDIUM ON THE SONG OF SONGS

## PRELIMINARY NOTICE

[Column 0639A]

The author of the Life of Alcuin himself expressly testifies that blessed Alcuin wrote a brief commentary on the Song of Songs: “In the Proverbs,” he says, “of Solomon, and in Ecclesiastes, and in the Song of Songs, he wrote with rich brevity.” Several manuscript codices confirm the same, since diligent librarians attest that a similar commentary is contained under Alcuin’s name.

Thus, in the catalogue of the manuscripts of the Harleian collection, volume I, manuscript 212, in membranaceo quarto, is recorded as containing, under number 2, Alcuin’s Commentary on the Song of Songs. On folio 100 verso it begins with these words: “Here begins the book of the Song of Songs, that is, ‘the better things of those who are better,’ just as ‘Holy of Holies.’”

Likewise, in the catalogue of the manuscripts of England and Ireland, published at Oxford in 1679, among the manuscript codices of the Jacobaean Library, number 8676 is listed as “Albini’s Commentary on the Song of Songs.”

In the Library of Saint Lawrence at Liège, of the Order of Saint Benedict, there is: “Alcuin or Albinus on Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs.”

The distinguished and celebrated Montfaucon likewise carefully records several codices containing this same commentary in volumes I and II of the *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum*. In volume I, page 628, he writes: “In the Library of the King of England: Alcuin’s work on the Song of Songs.” Volume II, page 1202: “In the Library of Gemmeticum: Alcuin’s Exposition on the Song of Songs.” Page 1222: “In the Library of Saint Albinus of Angers: Alcuin’s Exposition on the Song of Songs.” Page 1239: “In the Monastery Library of Saint Ouen at Rouen: Alcuin on the Song of Songs.” Page 1253: “In the Monastery Library of the Blessed Virgin of Bec: A Brief Exposition on the Song of Songs in the name of the Church and the Synagogue. It is Alcuin’s, as is noted there.” Page 1284: “In the Dijon-Saint-Bénigne Library: Albini’s Exposition of the Song of Songs.” Page 1342: “In the Library of the Savinian Abbey of the Cistercian Order: Alcuin on the Song of Songs.” Page 1361: “In the Monastery Library of Saint Michael in Peril of the Sea: Alcuin’s Exposition on Genesis and on the Song of Songs.”

Finally, in the Oxford-Cambridge *Ecloga*, or catalogue of the manuscripts of England, a *Compendium on the Song of Songs* is attributed to Alcuin. Perhaps this is the same work as the *Compendium* published by the distinguished Patrick Junius, which we present here.

The authority of celebrated writers adds weight to the testimony of these manuscripts: Helinandus, in Vincent of Beauvais, *Historical Mirror*, book XXIII, chapter 173; Trithemius, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and book II of *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, chapter 26; John Bale, *British Writers*, century II; Conrad Lycosthenes, in the *Epitome of Conrad Gesner’s Bibliotheca*; and Possevinus, in the *Sacred Apparatus*, volume I.

It is remarkable that the learned writers of the *Literary History of France*, although they had these testimonies before them, nevertheless denied (volume IV, pages 305, 335, and 336) that any complete commentary on the Song of Songs had flowed from Alcuin’s pen, and maintained that all his labor consisted in the explanation of a single verse of chapter VI, contained in the letter to his disciple Daphnin, which is to be presented at the end of this opusculum.

The testimonies cited do not at all permit this interpretation, since they speak not of the exposition of only one passage or verse of the Song of Songs, but of a commentary on the Song of Songs—that is, on the entire book. These same men, otherwise highly learned, are even more mistaken when they confidently assert, in the cited place on page 336, that the *Compendium on the Song of Songs* published in London in 1638 with the commentaries of Gilbert Foliot by Patrick Junius is nothing other than that same letter to Daphnin. This rash judgment is refuted simply by looking at the edition itself, of which those otherwise excellent men had no copy.

It must therefore be certain, at least on historical grounds, that our Alcuin expounded not merely some passage but the entire book of the Song of Songs in a brief style—or, as the author of his Life says, “with rich brevity.”

It remains to inquire whether this *Compendium*, which we present from the London edition prepared by Patrick Junius, is that very work which Alcuin composed in expounding the book.

In favor of Alcuin stands the authority of the distinguished Patrick Junius, royal librarian and diligent investigator of ancient monuments, who first brought this *Compendium* into public view under Alcuin’s name, without hesitation, from the royal library.

The title of the exceedingly rare little book, received as a gift from the illustrious and learned D. Christian Frederick Temler of Copenhagen, secretary for ecclesiastical affairs to the most powerful king of the Danes, reads: “The Exposition of Gilbert Foliot, Bishop of London, on the Song of Songs, together with Alcuin’s Compendium; now first brought to light from the royal library through the work and study of Patrick Junius, royal librarian.”

On page 275 it begins: “Alcuin’s Compendium on the Song of Songs. London, from the printing house of the royal majesty, 1638.” It is reasonable to presume that Junius would not have done this unless he had been supported by the testimony of some manuscript codex free from every suspicion of novelty or corruption.

This authority is strengthened by manuscript 69 of the Vatican Royal Library, in octavo, written in the tenth century. The eminent Cardinal Passioneo, then prefect of that library and later celebrated with the highest honors in the republic of letters even after his death, made it available to me. In this codex the same *Compendium*, with a few alterations that we note, is included among Alcuin’s letters, although it does not bear his name as a heading.

Finally, the style in which this commentary was written is by no means unlike Alcuin’s style, although in his commentaries—where, for the most part, the opinions of earlier Fathers are culled, as was customary in that age—he does not preserve a consistent character, as he does in letters written from his own genius.

These foundations will seem sufficiently firm to anyone for attributing this *Compendium of the Exposition of the Song of Songs* to Alcuin as its true author, without danger of error. I admit that some doubt concerning the true author of this commentary was introduced into my mind when, while reading through the *Stromata on the Song of Songs* of Angelomus, abbot of Luxeuil, in volume XV of the Lyon edition of the *Bibliotheca Sanctorum Patrum*, pages 415 and following, I found our Exposition contained there for the most part, both in its ideas and even in its wording.

Yet when I observed that Angelomus borrowed nearly everything he commented upon, whether in the Books of Kings or in the Song of Songs, from the sayings of other teachers and expositors, and learned it by lending an ear to a most eloquent master—perhaps Alcuin himself—as he confesses in his apologetic preface to the Books of Kings; and when I further considered that Angelomus also took the beginning of his commentary on the Song of Songs, beginning with the words “Scripture most clearly teaches that Solomon was called by three names,” from the beginning of Alcuin’s commentary on Ecclesiastes, I easily dismissed the doubt I had previously formed.

I now have no doubt that the portions of Angelomus’s commentary agreeing with this *Compendium* were likewise borrowed from the same source. Nothing prevents me from considering Alcuin the true author of this *Compendium on the Song of Songs*, relying especially on the testimony of the writers cited above and on the evidence of several manuscript codices, above all the Vatican manuscript that I use here and the English manuscript used by the celebrated D. Patrick Junius.

# A POEM PREFACED TO THE FOLLOWING COMMENTARY IN THE VATICAN CODEX

Solomon sang this book with wondrous sweetness,  
which contains the noble songs of the Bridegroom and Bride,  
singing here and there the praises of the Church and Christ;  
it recalls the faithful companions, men and women, of the bridal chamber.

These songs, young man, I ask you to remember  
to entrust to your mind.  
These songs are far better than those of false Maro.  
They sing true precepts of everlasting life for you;  
to your ears he will sound badly frivolous and “salty” [perhaps “false”].

# CHAPTER ONE

### VERSE 1

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” The Synagogue desires God to become incarnate and, devoted in love, goes out to meet him as he comes. This is the first voice heard in the Song of Love. When the holy prophets repeatedly showed her the way of life and revealed the coming of the one who, proceeding like a Bridegroom from his bridal chamber, would enrich the world with a new blessing, she began, after the voices of the heralds had passed away, to desire the presence of the king and Savior himself, saying:

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” That is: Let him no longer continually assign angels or prophets to instruct me. Let him come himself at last, the one who has been promised for so long. Let him illuminate me with the light of his presence; let him comfort me, as though offering a kiss and addressing me with his own mouth. That is, let him not disdain to instruct me when I ask about the way of salvation.

This is read as fulfilled in the Gospel: “When Jesus was seated on the mountain, his disciples approached him. And opening his mouth, he taught them, saying: ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven’” (Matthew 5:1).

He therefore says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” That is: Let him touch me with the sweetness of his presence, which I have so often heard promised by the prophets.

[The Vatican Codex, after the text “Let him kiss me,” and so forth, has only this final exposition: “That is: Let him touch me … which I have heard …”]

“For your breasts are better than wine.” The sweetness of evangelical teaching is better than the austerity of the Law.

[The Vatican Codex omits what follows, from the word “wine” to the end.]

Wine signifies the fervor of legal knowledge; milk signifies the beginnings of evangelical faith. Hence Paul says: “I gave you milk to drink” (1 Corinthians 3:2), that is, food.

“The breasts of the Bridegroom are better than wine,” because the rudiments of faith regenerate whomever they do through water and the Spirit and, when the entrance to heavenly life has been opened, lead them forth—something the prolonged observance of the Law was unable to do. The Apostle bears witness to this when he says: “The law brought nothing to perfection” (Hebrews 7:19). By the breasts are understood the teachers who give us milk of knowledge.

### VERSE 2

“Fragrant with the finest ointments.”

[The Vatican Codex: “With the gifts of the Holy Spirit.” It omits the rest up to “Oil poured out.”]

Therefore the Holy Spirit is compared with ointments, because just as ointment heals a wound, so the Holy Spirit drives away vices and cherishes and heals souls.

The ointments with which prophets and priests were anointed under the Law were good, but better are those with which the apostles and their successors have been invisibly anointed. Concerning these Paul says: “It is God who anointed us, and God who sealed us” (2 Corinthians 1:21). And John says: “Let the anointing that you received from him remain in you” (1 John 2:27).

“Your name is oil poured out.”

[The Vatican Codex: “From chrism comes ‘Christ,’ that is, ‘anointed’ from ‘anointing’; this name, together with the grace of the Holy Spirit, is poured out upon all the faithful in baptism.” The rest is omitted up to “Therefore the young women …”]

This is an explanation of the reason: it is not surprising that his members give off the fragrance of ointments, since he himself received his name from ointment.

From *chrisma* comes “Christ,” that is, “anointed” from “anointing”; this name, together with the grace of the Holy Spirit, is poured out upon all the faithful in baptism. Hence Peter says: “How God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts 10:38). And in the Psalms: “God anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 45:7).

He says “oil”: not oil that has merely dripped, but oil that has been poured out. For God does not give him the Spirit by measure, because he himself is full of the Holy Spirit.

“Therefore the young women have loved you.” That is, the souls of the elect, renewed by the grace of baptism.

### VERSE 3

“Draw me after you …”

@ [Col. 0643D] Vatican Manuscript: “That I may follow you as you ascend into heaven”; with other passages omitted up to “Let us run together.” Formerly the Synagogue asked God to come and offer her the kiss of peace; now the Church, knowing that he has already come and has already returned to the heavens, desires to follow him. Since she cannot accomplish this by herself, she implores the guidance of him to whom she longs to come.

**Draw me after you.** That is: because without you we can do nothing, we pray that, as we run toward you, you may sustain us with the right hand of your protection. For we cannot run, or complete our course, unless we run with you as our guide and helper. Hence Paul: “I labored more than all of them, yet not I, but the grace of Christ” (I Cor. 15:10).

**Let us run together in the fragrance of your ointments.** That is: by doing good in cooperation with you, through the increase of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, let us hasten toward fellowship with the heavenly Jerusalem, so that we may follow you as you ascend into heaven.

**The king brought me into his chambers.** That is, into the eternal joys [Col. 0643C] of the heavenly homeland.

@ [Col. 0643D] The Vatican Manuscript omits what follows this note up to “We shall exult.” The chambers of the eternal king are the joys of the heavenly homeland, into which the Church has now been brought through faith and will be brought more fully through reality.

**We shall exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts as better than wine.** In you, not in ourselves, remembering in every respect the grace of faith as superior to the teaching of the Law.

@ [Col. 0643D] Vatican Manuscript: “Turn your attention toward us, remembering in every respect the grace of faith as superior to the teaching of the Law.” The rest is lacking up to “The upright love you,” which means: We by no means exalt ourselves over what we have received, but in everything that we live rightly we shall exult in your mercy, remembering with what compassion you refresh us and how you have deigned to mitigate the austerity of the Law by the grace of evangelical faith.

**The upright love you.** No one loves you except the upright; and no one is upright except one who loves you.

**VERSE 4.—I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.** I am black amid the pressures of persecutions, but beautiful in the splendor of virtues.

@ [Col. 0644D] The Vatican Manuscript omits what follows this note up to “Like the tents.” That is: I appear black in the eyes of my persecutors, but before God I shine adorned with the splendor of virtues.

**Like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon.** Kedar was the son of Ishmael; his name is interpreted as “darkness.” The holy Church says that she is black like Kedar because she has been so darkened by the afflictions of unbelievers that she seemed to have become the enemy of the whole world. Solomon was peaceful both in name and in life; he made his tents from the skins of dead animals. So the Lord creates the Church from those who mortify within themselves the desires of the flesh. Therefore the Church is like Solomon’s curtains.

@ [Col. 0644D] The Vatican Manuscript adds after the text: “Dark in the temptation of demons, beautiful in mortifying carnal desires,” with the rest omitted.

**VERSE 5.—Do not look at me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me.** That is: Do not marvel if I am despised by human beings, because the heat of excessive persecution—or the love of Christ—has discolored me.

@ [Col. 0644D] The Vatican Manuscript adds after the text: “Do not marvel if outwardly I am despised by human beings because of the heat of temptations.” My mother’s sons fought against me; they made me keeper of the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep. The bitterness of persecution by the sons of the Synagogue caused me not to keep the vineyard of Jerusalem, but to become keeper of many vineyards—that is, Churches—throughout the world.

@ [Col. 0644D] The Vatican Manuscript omits what follows this note. The mother of the primitive Church is the Synagogue, to whom it is said through the prophet: “Zion, you shall be called a city, and the mother of cities” (Zech. 8:3).

**VERSE 6.—Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.** Tell me about my shepherd, whom I love with my whole soul, and in what pastures he feeds and where he finds rest, lest, troubled by the heat of temptations, I begin to seek him among the assemblies of his companions—that is, of heretics.

**VERSE 7.—If you do not know yourself, most beautiful among women, go out and follow the footprints of the flocks.** If, under the power [F.: condition] of this temptation, you do not know that you have been betrothed to me, depart from my fellowship and follow the various actions of those who wander. **And pasture my kids beside the tents of the shepherds.** That is: nourish lost hearers who, having followed the teachings of foolish teachers, will stand on the left.

**VERSE 8.—I have compared you, my friend, to my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots.** Just as I freed the former people from fear of Egypt, so I shall free you, my bride, from the hands of persecutors if you trust in me.

**VERSE 9.—Your cheeks are beautiful like a turtledove [Vatican Manuscript: tower].** I have adorned you with so great a virtue of salutary modesty that you do not corrupt the chastity of the faith promised to me through the seduction of wicked teachers. **Your neck is like necklaces.** The holy preachers are signified by the neck: what they teach in word, they display in their works. The perfection of their works is expressed by the necklaces.

@ [Col. 0644D] Vatican Manuscript: “The holy teachers are signified by the neck. Works are expressed by the necklaces, because what they …”

**VERSE 10.—We shall make golden chains for you, ornamented with silver.** Holy Scripture is shown in the chains: inwardly it shines with the gold of spiritual meanings and gleams with the silver of heavenly eloquence.

**VERSE 11.—While the king was at his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance.** While Christ the King rests in the blessedness of heavenly secrecy [Vatican Manuscript: “While the King … rests”], the virtue of the saints supplies us in the Church with a grace of great sweetness.

**VERSE 12.—My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me; he will dwell between my breasts.** The death of my beloved, which he underwent for my salvation, will always remain in my memory.

**VERSE 13.—My beloved is a cluster of henna (*cyprus*) to me, in the vineyards of Engaddi.** He [Edition: *quid*, “what”] who was a bundle of myrrh in the bitterness of his Passion is himself a cluster of henna (*cyprus*) in the sweetness of his resurrection. Myrrh saddens; wine gladdens. **In the vineyards of Engaddi:** because of the divine gifts that, after his resurrection, he bestowed in baptism upon those who share in him. Engaddi, “fountain of the kid,” signifies baptism.

**VERSE 14.—Behold, you are beautiful, my friend; behold, you are beautiful.** You are beautiful in the clean works by which you live soberly in this age. You are beautiful in simplicity of heart, because you devote yourself to good deeds solely with eternity in view. **Your eyes are like doves.** The eyes of your heart are pure and simple, free from every duplicity of deceit; or your senses are endowed with spiritual understanding.

@ [Col. 0645D] Vatican Manuscript: “Behold, you are beautiful, my friend; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are like doves. Beautiful in simplicity of heart and purity of works, because your spiritual senses are endowed with understanding.”

**VERSE 15.—Behold, you are beautiful, beloved to me [Vatican Manuscript: “my beloved”], and comely.**

@ [Col. 0645D] Vatican Manuscript adds after the text: “You alone are beautiful by nature; I am beautiful from you.” The rest is omitted up to [Col. 0646D] “Our couch.” Hearing that the Lord has attributed to her a twofold beauty—namely, of work and intention, together with the simplicity of a pure heart—the holy Church responds in devoted speech: Whatever beauty, grace, simplicity, or hope I have, I received because you gave it; but you are truly and incomparably beautiful and comely, through the eternity of your divine nature and the marvelous dignity of the humanity you assumed.

**Our couch is flourishing.** The bride rests with the bridegroom on the couch when the time of peace is flourishing.

@ [Col. 0646D] The Vatican Manuscript omits the words “The bride rests …” and what follows. The peace of the holy Church both flourishes with holy virtues and multiplies through spiritual offspring.

**VERSE 16.—The beams of our houses are cedars; our ceilings are cypresses.** The beams and ceilings are the teachers of the holy Church, signifying protection [Vatican Manuscript: defensive strength] and beauty; cedar and cypress signify their outstanding virtues and the fragrance of a good life.

@ [Col. 0646D] What follows this note is omitted in the Vatican Manuscript. The Church is sustained by their word and example, so that she is not shaken by heretical depravity. The fragrance of cedar drives away serpents, which suits those who habitually uproot the venomous doctrines of heretics by the power of heavenly speech. The cypress, which does not shed the beauty of its foliage under any force of the winds, expresses the constancy of those who adorn the holy Church with loftier ornaments of virtue, like ceilings.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0646A]

**VERSE 1.—I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.** I am the world’s adornment and the lily of the valleys. [Vatican Manuscript: “I am the world’s adornment and the glory of the humble.”]

**VERSE 2.—As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among the daughters.** You seek rest and the praises of the couch. Remember that you will be made whiter by the thorns of tribulations, and that the fruit of preaching [F.: persecution] is greater than that of repose.

**VERSE 3.—As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons.** Just as an apple tree surpasses forest trees in appearance, fragrance, and taste, so Christ surpasses all the saints [Vatican Manuscript: “all the holy ones”], who are called children of God by grace [Vatican Manuscript: “but”]; he alone is so by nature. **Under his shadow, whom I desired, I sat.** [Col. 0646B] Protected by the same one whose constant presence I sought, I rest and remain secure. **And his fruit is sweet to my throat.** For he refreshes me with the heavenly sweetness of his grace [Vatican Manuscript: “refreshed me”].

**VERSE 4.—The king brought me into the wine cellar.** The wine cellar should be understood as the Church, in whose unity alone the Holy Spirit is ordinarily given and received; his grace is signified here by the name of wine. **He ordered charity within me.**

@ [Col. 0646D] The Vatican Manuscript joins this text with the preceding one. In that cellar charity has been ordered, so that each person loves God with all his heart, more than himself, and his neighbor as himself.

**VERSE 5.—Strengthen me with flowers; surround me with apples, because I am sick with love.** Console me with the examples both of those beginning and of those finishing. Show me the way of salvation while, amid the weariness of this pilgrimage, I still languish with love of the heavenly vision.

**VERSE 6.—His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.** Christ’s temporal gifts are signified by his left hand, and the blessedness of eternal life by his right: here he strengthens the mind through hope, and there glorifies it through reward.

**VERSE 7.—I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the stags of the fields, do not rouse or awaken the beloved until she wishes it.** I charge the peaceful souls of the faithful by their respective virtues [Vatican Manuscript: *quasque* for *suas quamque*], which are signified by clean and ruminating animals, not to obstruct the devoted efforts of the brethren through any untimely interference, but to let each person rejoice in the progress of others as though it were his own.

@ [Col. 0646D] The Vatican Manuscript omits what follows this note. The works of virtue are signified by gazelles and stags, which, in proportion to their purity, are accustomed to scorn—or rather destroy—the violent snares of the ancient enemy. The gazelle climbs mountains, has keen sight, and chooses better pastures.

**VERSE 8.—The voice of my beloved.** The words “This is” are understood: “This is the voice I heard adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken me while I rested in his embrace.” **Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills.** My beloved made such leaps: from heaven into the womb, from the womb into the manger, from the manger to the cross, from the cross into the tomb, and from the tomb he returned to heaven. He is the one raised above all mountains and hills—that is, above the heights of the saints.

**VERSE 9.—My beloved is like a gazelle and a fawn of the stags.** In the assumption of flesh and in humility [Vatican Manuscript: humanity], Christ is compared to a gazelle; in the variety of virtues and the innocence of a fawn of the stags—that is, of the patriarchs. **Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattice.** Clothed in the wall of our mortality, he remained hidden; yet he looked toward us through lattice and windows when he performed miracles, so that through the miracles it might become evident who had remained hidden through his sufferings [Vatican Manuscript: “so that”].

**VERSE 10.—And my beloved speaks to me.** He urges me to preach, saying: **Arise, hurry, my friend [my dove], my beautiful one, and come.** Arise from the bed of repose, on which you seek to care only for yourself. Hurry and come to fulfill the care of salvation also for your neighbors through the diligence of preaching.

**VERSE 11.—For winter has already passed; the rain has gone away and departed.** The cold of unbelief and the rain of iniquity have now departed—those things that covered the whole world until the time of the Lord’s incarnation.

**VERSE 12.—Flowers have appeared on the earth.** That is: the beginnings of faith and justice have blossomed in the world as the Church grew. **The time of pruning has come.** That is: with the useless shoots of vain religion cut away, human hearts are prepared for the future fruit of faith [C. V.: “may be prepared”]. [Col. 0647C] **The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land:** namely, the voice of Christ our Savior saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3:2).

**VERSE 13.—The fig tree has put forth its early figs.** The commandments of the Old Law have fallen. **The flowering vines have given their fragrance:** that is, the evangelical people, or flowering vines, have spread the fragrance of holy conduct far and wide. **Arise, my friend, my beautiful one**—

@ [Col. 0647D] Vatican Manuscript: “Arise, my bride, my friend, and come”—

**and come.** O my bride and friend, to whom I have offered such great blessings, arise and come, and gird yourself for the contest from which you will receive eternal rest.

**VERSE 14.—My dove:** through the infusion of the Holy Spirit. **In the clefts of the rock, in the recesses of the wall.** That is, in the wounds that the Bridegroom received for the salvation of his bride; and in the recess of the wall—that is, in the protection of heavenly virtues.

@ [Col. 0647D] The Vatican Manuscript omits what follows this note up to “Show me.” The dove builds its nest while sitting in the clefts of the rock when the Church places the hope of her salvation in the Lord’s Passion; when, in the sacrament of his death, she trusts that she is protected from the snares of the ancient enemy, as from the attack of a hawk; and when she strives in that same sacrament to create offspring of spiritual children—that is, virtues.

Hence Jeremiah, speaking in the person of Moab and inviting heretics to unity, says: “Leave the cities and dwell in the rock, inhabitants of Moab; be like a dove nesting at the mouth of a cavern” (Jer. 48:28). A wall serves to fortify a vineyard, and here it is explained as made of stones. Hence Isaiah: “A vineyard was made for my beloved on a hill, in a fertile place, and he surrounded it with a wall” (Isa. 5:1–2). This wall signifies protection, because the Lord surrounds the Church so that she cannot be devastated by the assault of unclean spirits.

**Show me your face.** You who wish to hide like a dove in the secret recess of quiet—

@ [Col. 0648D] Vatican Manuscript: “Show me your face. I beg you …,” with the earlier material omitted—

I beg you, come forth into public activity, and show your face through your works. **Let your voice sound in my ears.** Namely, the voice of praise and preaching. For your voice is sweet, and your face is beautiful. The voice of the one is sweet to the Lord who finds it sweet to proclaim the Lord’s words to his neighbors or to resound with praises to the Lord himself; and the faith of the one is beautiful who, adorned with works, does not fear to suffer adversity [Col. 0648B] [Vatican Manuscript: “does not fear it”].

**VERSE 15.—Catch the little foxes for us, which destroy the vineyards.** That is: conquer heretics and schismatics, little in faith [Vatican Manuscript: wicked], crafty in speech, who habitually tear the inexperienced minds of the faithful with the tooth of perverse doctrine. **For our vineyard has blossomed.** That is: the peoples of the elect are sprouting abundantly.

**VERSE 16.—My beloved is mine.** That is: he alone is my beloved and he alone is my helper. **And I am his.** I alone am beloved, because no one rightly loves Christ except the one Church, and no other is loved by him. **He pastures among the lilies.** That is, amid purity of faith and the whiteness of virtues.

**VERSE 17.—Until the day breathes and the shadows incline.** Until the eternal light of the age to come rises and the shadows—that is, the errors of the present life—pass away. **Return, be like a gazelle or a fawn of the stags, my beloved, upon the mountains of Bethel.** I beg you, my beloved, to return more often through the sweetness of your visitation, because with the flesh that you took from the lineage of the patriarchs you ascended above every height of the heavenly mountains, so that by contemplating the eternal homeland you might lighten the labor of my pilgrimage [Vatican Manuscript: “reveal”].

## CHAPTER III

**VERSE 1.—Upon my bed by nights [Vatican Manuscript: “by night”] I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought and did not find him [Vatican Manuscript: “I sought him and did not find him”].** “For a long time,” she says, “I sought the Lord with great zeal, but because [text: *quae*, Vatican Manuscript: *quia*] I was still subject to the allurements of my flesh and blinded by the darkness of deep ignorance, I did not find the light of truth—that is, the Lord.”

**VERSE 2.—I will rise and go around the city; through the streets and squares I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him and did not find him.** I resolved in my mind to rise from the bed of carnal pleasures, to travel through lands and seas, and to approach the schools of the philosophers [Vatican Manuscript: “ministries”]; but even so I did not find him.

**VERSE 3.—The watchmen who guard the city found me [Vatican Manuscript: “The sentries”]. Have you seen him whom my soul loves?** The watchmen are those who guard the Church: the apostles and teachers, who found the Gentile people anxiously engaged in the search for truth [Vatican Manuscript: *sollicitantem*, “actively seeking”].

**VERSE 4.—A little while after I had passed them, I found him whom my soul loves.** When I entrusted myself to their teaching, I immediately found the light of truth that I had long sought [Vatican Manuscript: “that I sought”]. **I held him, and I will not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me.** I held [Vatican Manuscript: “I hold … until …”] him with firm faith, and I will hold him until, at the end of the age, through the ministry of preaching, I bring him into the house and chamber of the Synagogue, which gave birth to me in the Lord; and there will be one flock and one shepherd.

[Col. 0649B] **VERSE 5.—I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the stags of the fields, do not rouse or awaken the beloved until she wishes it.** In the preceding passage we did not find the bride reaching repose through sleep; rather, we found her springing from her bed and hastening with great labor to find her beloved—and the beloved adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem not to disturb her. But perhaps that soul, lulled by a blessed sleep, which knows how to rest in divine love, closes the eye of the heart toward external things and opens it toward internal things. The daughters of Jerusalem are therefore rightly adjured not to awaken the beloved—that is, not to hinder a mind devoted to God from the purpose of heavenly desire by an untimely interruption.

@ [Col. 0649D] After the verse the Vatican Manuscript adds: “Therefore the Bridegroom repeats this verse, so that you might not think that he has less concern for the Church gathered from the Gentiles than for the Church gathered from the Jews, but that there might be one most beloved bride from both.” The earlier and later material is omitted here.

This passage is repeated in the Song of Love so that the Lord may show that he cares no less for the Church from the Gentiles than for the Church gathered from the Jews. For the fact that he adjures the daughters not to awaken the beloved may be understood as his command to those who came to faith from the Jews not to disturb those who came to faith from the error of the Gentiles, nor to oppose their repose.

{398} **VERSE 6.—Who is this who comes up through the wilderness?** The Synagogue marvels at how the people of the Gentiles, cleansed by no ministry of circumcision and instructed by no admonition of the prophets, could suddenly rise from the lowest pleasures through the wilderness of paganism and idolatry to the lofty heights of virtue and the embrace of the Bridegroom.

@ [Col. 0650D] The Vatican Manuscript omits what follows up to “Like a column.” Her faith is all the more wondrous because, having been received from above, she preserves it invincibly, as John testifies when he says: “I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is; and you hold fast to my name and did not deny my faith” (Rev. 2:13).

The wilderness may also signify a way of life separated from the allurements of the world and devoted solely to searching out God’s law and observing the heavenly commandments.

**Like a column of smoke from aromatic spices.** Enkindled by the fire of love, she strives toward heavenly things with every effort of virtue.

@ [Col. 0650D] The Vatican Manuscript omits what follows up to “Myrrh.” Smoke ordinarily rises in part while at the same time part of it is carried upward and disappears. So also, in some of her members, the Church is born anew through the grace of the Holy Spirit; in others, as in those born earlier, she is gathered toward heavenly things. She is compared not to smoke but to a column of smoke, so that the unity of the Church’s faith may be signified.

**Of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer.** Of the mortification of carnal pleasures, the purity of prayers, and the fragrance of every virtue.

**VERSE 7.—Behold, Solomon’s couch; sixty strong men surround it, chosen from the strongest of Israel.** Solomon’s couch is the peaceful way of life of the saints. The sixty strong men are the holy preachers and very strong warriors who, being pure in heart, are worthy to see God.

**VERSE 8.—All holding swords and highly trained for war.** For they hold the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, and complete in their works what [Vatican Manuscript: *quidquid*, “whatever”] they teach with their mouths. **Each man’s sword is upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night.** The terrors of the night are the snares of hidden temptation. The sword is vigilant guardianship, suppressing the desires of the flesh so that the impurity of life does not stain the word of preaching.

**VERSE 9.—King Solomon made himself a litter from the wood of Lebanon.** Solomon’s litter is the holy Church, which raises believers to the banquets of eternal blessedness and is built from the strong in spirit, as from incorruptible wood.

**VERSE 10.—He made its columns of silver.** The silver columns are teachers shining with the light of eloquence. **Its backrest is gold.** The golden backrest is the hope of perpetual rest promised to the faithful [Vatican Manuscript: “perpetual … promised”]. **Its ascent is purple.** What else is the purple ascent but the blood of the martyrs and the Passion of our Redeemer? For no one ascends to the banquet of life except through the mystery of Christ’s Passion. **Its middle he paved with love, because of the daughters of Jerusalem.** Everyone who has love of God and neighbor will arrive joyfully at this rest and these banquets. Christ supplied all these ornaments of the Church because of the excessive love with which he loved us and handed himself over for us.

**VERSE 11.—Go out and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon.** Go out in mind and deed from the turbulent way of life of the world, so that you may be able to see the King of peace. **In the diadem with which his mother crowned him.** See the Lord Christ in the humanity that he received from his virgin mother and placed at the right hand of the Father’s majesty. **On the day of his dispensation [Vatican Manuscript: betrothal].** In the time of his incarnation, when he came forth from the virgin womb to unite the Church to himself as his bride. **And on the day of the joy of his heart.** That is, the redemption of the human race, which was a day of joy for Christ.

## CHAPTER IV

**VERSE 1.—How beautiful you are, my friend, how beautiful you are!** He calls the Church beautiful, and repeats “beautiful,” because he saw her praiseworthy both in action and in preaching.

@ [Col. 0651D] What follows this note is omitted in the Vatican Manuscript up to “Your eyes.” In action, that is, because she ascends like a column of smoke from aromatic spices; and in preaching, because she strives to bring even those nearby into fellowship with her, saying: “Go out and see.”

**Your eyes are like doves.** Your senses are excellent in contemplation of spiritual things and modest [Al.: “venerable”].

@ [Col. 0652D] The Vatican Manuscript omits what follows up to “apart from what lies within,” namely: “By these gifts of mine, which you recently expounded, you have deserved to see and understand my diadem, which you recently proclaimed. Apart from what lies within.” Great indeed is the glory of outward work, but far more incomparable is the reward of eternal recompense, which cannot be seen while we are pilgrims on earth [Vatican Manuscript: “which cannot yet be seen”].

**Your hair is like flocks of goats.** The faithful people may be understood by the hair, for through their great number they provide the Church with its greatest adornment. **That have come up from Mount Gilead.** Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony,” which aptly suits the united multitude of the saints.

**VERSE 2.—Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep.** By the hair are signified those who are more fragile; by the teeth, those who are more perfect and suited to govern the Church. **Which have come up from the washing.** That is, from the font of holy baptism. They have been shorn and washed: stripped by renouncing [Vatican Manuscript: *renuntiantes*, “renouncing”] the world and cleansed by the washing of life. **All bearing twin offspring.** That is, fruitful in a twofold love. **And none among them is barren.** There is no one who does not produce offspring of good works.

**VERSE 3.—Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon [Vatican Manuscript: *cocunea*, “scarlet”], and your speech is sweet.** The scarlet ribbon signifies the doctrine of truth. The bride’s lips are compared to scarlet because the Church never ceases to proclaim the price of the Lord’s blood by which she was redeemed; or because holy preaching flames with the ardor of love.

**Like a fragment of a pomegranate, so are your cheeks, apart from what lies within.** Modesty is expressed in the cheeks, and the Passion of Christ in the pomegranate. The bride therefore has the redness of a pomegranate in her cheeks when she confesses the mystery of the Lord’s Passion in words and proves it by deeds.

**VERSE 4.—Your neck is like the tower of David.** The tower of David is the Church; the neck is the preachers, by whose faith and constancy she stands firm in the same city and is invincible on every side. **It was built with bulwarks.** The bulwarks of that city are the defenses of the holy Scriptures, or the examples of the Fathers who came before.

**A thousand shields hang upon it.** For as many commandments as there are in the divine books, so many defenses there are for our breast, by which we are protected against every snare. **All the armor of the strong.** This is every equipment of action or heavenly doctrine, through which we not only escape but also overcome.

**VERSE 5.—Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle [Vatican Manuscript: *capreae* for *caprae*], which feed among the lilies.**

**VERSE 6.—Until the day breathes and the shadows incline.** The two breasts are the two peoples who come from circumcision and from the Gentiles. Through humility they understand themselves to be small and sinners; but, running in love, they pass through every obstacle of the world. They feed [Vatican Manuscript: “they pasture”] among the lilies—that is, among the purest examples of the holy Fathers—until, when the eternal day breathes, we pass beyond the shadows of present mortality [Vatican Manuscript: “present shadows”].

**I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.** Myrrh expresses mortification of the flesh; frankincense, devotion in prayer. It is as though the Bridegroom said: “I will visit them, and in gracious and merciful illumination I will glorify those whom I see to be exalted in the virtue of Passion or prayer.”

**VERSE 7.—You are wholly beautiful, my friend; there is no blemish in you.** In all who fear God, both small and great.

@ [Col. 0652D] This gloss is absent from the Vatican Manuscript.

**VERSE 8.—Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come.** Lebanon is interpreted as “whiteness”: that is, a soul made white by good works. The Bridegroom urges her three times to come: first, while living [Vatican Manuscript: *viventes*, “living”] in the flesh, through good works; second, after being freed from the flesh, to receive blessed life; third, after receiving the body, to enjoy perfected joys after the resurrection.

**You will be crowned from the summit of Aman [Vatican Manuscript: Amana], from the peak of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.** The evil spirits are called lions because of their pride and leopards because of their cruelty. By the name of mountains are signified the proud hearts of unbelievers, where unclean spirits have their dwelling. When holy preachers convert such people to the way of salvation, they are crowned from the summit and peak of the mountains—that is, from the princes of the wicked—for the crown of glory grows from the labor of the contest.

**VERSE 9.—You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart.** The wounding of the heart signifies the greatness of Christ’s love for the Church. **With one of your eyes and with one lock of your neck.** In the holy unity of the teachers, signified by the eyes, and in the devout unity of the people subject to them, signified by the locks of hair.

**VERSE 10.—How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride.** Again, by the name of breasts the holy teachers are expressed, because they console the weak and sustain the little ones, which is done with milk. **Your breasts are more beautiful than wine.** The sweetness of grace is more beautiful than the austerity of the Law. **And the fragrance of your ointments surpasses every spice.** The most delightful fame of faith, spread [Vatican Manuscript: *diffusae* for *diffusa*] throughout the whole world, is broader than that of the Old Law and of the Fathers [“in it”], which was confined to Judea alone.

**VERSE 11.—Your lips, bride, are a dripping honeycomb.** A honeycomb is honey in wax; honey in wax is the spiritual meaning of divine utterances in the letter. It drips with honey because nearly every sentence has multiple meanings. The bride’s lips are the teachers, who disclose that sacred writings contain manifold meanings.

**Honey and milk are under your tongue.** Milk signifies the instruction of little ones; honey, the stronger teaching of the perfect. Under the tongue means in the meditation of the heart.
