**And the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense.** The Church’s garments are her works, which are compared with the fragrance of frankincense because everything holy that the Church does for the Lord repays, through those works, the service of prayers.

**VERSE 12.—A locked garden is my sister, my bride; a locked garden, a sealed spring.** The locked garden is the Church, which produces many kinds of shoots of spiritual works. It is a spring because it overflows with saving doctrine; locked because it remains fortified by the Lord’s protection; sealed by the word of faith.

**VERSE 13.—Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of orchards.** Through the irrigation of holy baptism the Church sends forth from herself a paradise of pomegranates—that is, of holy martyrs—with the fruits of orchards, namely, the fruit of holy virtues.

**VERSE 14.—Henna (*cyprus*) with nard, nard and saffron.** Henna (*cyprus*) is an aromatic tree signifying the blessing of heavenly grace. Nard expresses a type of the Lord’s Passion; saffron, the fervor of love. Henna (*cyprus*) is joined to nard when divine grace strengthens us to suffer for Christ. Nard is likewise joined to saffron when, through love of Christ, we willingly accept death.

**Cassia and cinnamon.** Cassia [Vatican Manuscript: *casia*] is also an aromatic tree, but a small one, and therefore signifies the humble in spirit. Likewise cinnamon signifies those who despise themselves. It too is a short tree, but fragrant and sweet; humility, however, has great praise and sweetness before God.

**With all the trees of Lebanon.** Just as cassia and cinnamon indicate the humble thoughts of the saints, so the trees of Lebanon demonstrate their lofty actions. Myrrh and aloe are aromatic trees that express continence of the flesh. **With all the finest ointments.** That is, with the more excellent gifts of virtue. These trees are beautifully joined with the ointments, because when we restrain the flesh from wantonness, it follows that we receive greater gifts of the spirit.

**VERSE 15.—A garden spring, a well of living waters that flow with force.** The Church is both: a garden spring because she produces spiritual fruits, and a well of living waters because of the hidden mysteries disclosed to the saints through the revelation of the Holy Spirit [“alone”]. They are living waters because of the divine utterances that proceed from the invisible treasures of divine grace.

**From Lebanon.** He speaks of the Church herself, which is both white through purity of faith and lofty through the glory of virtues.

**VERSE 16.—Rise, north wind, and come, south wind, blow through my garden.** The north wind signifies the adversities of the world; the south wind, its blandishments, because the Church is tested by a twofold assault. **Rise** is the voice of one permitting, not commanding.

**And let its spices flow.** That is: let the constancy of virtues spread wonderful fragrances. **Let my beloved come into his garden.** Let the Lord come into his Church, preserve her everywhere immaculate, and make her fruitful with the fruit of faith [Vatican Manuscript: *fecundam* for *fecundet*]. **And let him eat the fruit of his trees.** Let him willingly look upon and gratefully receive the works of his saints.

{401}

## CHAPTER V
## Chapter V

### Verse 1

“Come into my garden, my sister, my bride.” “Come,” he says, “very often into my Church; and I come in order to correct, assist, and strengthen you.” “I have gathered my myrrh with my spices.” By myrrh, suffering or mortification is expressed; by spices, all the virtues. He gathers myrrh with spices when he brings the martyrs, together with the other elect, to the maturity of their rewards.

“I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk.” In the honeycomb and wine, preachers are understood; in the honey and milk, hearers. The inward Judge approves and rewards both. “Eat, friends; drink and be intoxicated, beloved ones.” Friends are those who do what I command; beloved ones are those who embrace me with complete love. I entreat you: fill your inmost hearts with the deeds of the saints as with choice banquets.

### Verse 2

“I sleep.” By the gift of God’s grace, I worship him in the peace of the present life [Al.: of the Church]. “And my heart is awake.” The more peacefully I am free from external assaults, the more deeply I see inwardly [Cod. Vat.: the more deeply I see within] how good God is.

“The voice of my beloved, knocking.” He knocks at the door of the heart when the Lord stirs us to advance in virtue. “Open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove, my undefiled one.” That is: open your heart to me. My sister, because you are my co-heir; my friend, because you are acquainted with my secrets [Cod. Vat.: with my secret things]; my dove, because you have been illumined by the gift of my Spirit; my undefiled one, because you alone are worthy of my gaze.

“For my head is full of dew, and my locks with drops of the nights.” God is the head of Christ; the locks are the gathered companies of the faithful. In the dew and drops of the nights, the cooling of the love that they ought to have toward God and neighbor is shown in many people. Therefore the Lord necessarily rouses each of the faithful to the work [Al.: office] of preaching. To her, summoned to the labor of teaching, the Church replies:

### Verse 3

“I have removed my tunic; how shall I put it on again?” As though she openly said: “For your sake I abandoned worldly affairs; how shall I take them up again?” “I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” “Already, through the tears of hidden remorse, I have washed away earthly thoughts; how shall I again be defiled by the filth of the world [Al.: by unclean things]?” For the ministry of preaching can scarcely exist without worldly occupation [Al.: preoccupation].

### Verse 4

“My beloved put his hand through the opening.” The beloved put his hand through the opening when the Lord invisibly kindles us, through a hidden inward compunction, to the work of virtue, and recalls to us how and how greatly he suffered for us when he descended from the bosom of the Father.

“And my inmost being trembled at his touch.” Recalling these things, the bride’s inmost conscience is wholly afraid; she accuses the sluggishness of her repose and hastens to the labor of preaching.

### Verse 5

“I arose to open to my beloved.” That is, to preach the word of the Lord. “My hands dripped with myrrh; my fingers were full of [the finest] myrrh.” In the hands, works are signified; in the fingers, discernment. In myrrh are signified self-restraint and sufferings, which are then most excellent when either self-restraint is practised or sufferings are endured solely for the love of God and neighbor.

### Verse 6

“I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved.” He opens the bolt to the bridegroom who, when divine inspiration comes, opens—that is, makes worthy of divine visitation and indwelling—the temple of his breast. [The enclosed words are omitted in Cod. Vat.]

“But he had turned aside and passed on.” Since no one in this life is granted the complete vision of God that will be granted in the future, the beloved is said to pass on; that is, he shows himself as one who will be seen and enjoyed more fully in the future.

“My soul melted when he spoke.” “The more sweetly,” she says, “I received the voice and nearness of my beloved, the more sublimely did whatever was cold within me grow warm through love [Col. 0655B] [and melt (Cod. Vat.: and whatever was rigid melted)].”

“I sought him and did not find him; I called him, and he did not answer me.” The gift of compunction and inward sweetness is not in the power of the one who wills, but in the mercy of the giver. Therefore they do not always possess it equally, because God does not reveal himself in the same way to those laboring in exile as to those reigning in their homeland.

### Verse 7

“The watchmen who go about the city found me; they struck me and wounded me; the watchmen of the walls took away my cloak from me.” The watchmen of the city, that is, of the Church, are the holy teachers. Through constant preaching they go around the hearts of individuals, wound them with darts of heavenly love, inflame them so that they burn more intensely, and remove from them the covering of their former way of life.

### Verse 8

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem: if you find my beloved [Cod. Vat. omits ‘my beloved’], tell him that I am faint with love.” The bride rightly languishes when, struck by the sword of God’s word, she removes her earthly garment. She adjures the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, souls worthy of God—to report the greatness of her love to God and to ask heavenly assistance for themselves, so that they may see his glory.

### Verse 9

“What is your beloved more than another beloved, O most beautiful among women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have thus adjured us?” “I beg you: since you have adjured me in this way, make me also burn through the word of preaching with the love by which you say that you are languishing; and show me what your beloved is like in that respect in which he may be loved, not feared, since perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

### Verse 10

“My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands.” White, because he is without sin; ruddy with the blood of his passion; chosen out of thousands, because he alone is the mediator between God and human beings.

### Verse 11

“His head is the finest gold.” God is the head of Christ, who alone is good and best. “His locks are like the raised branches of palms, black as a raven.” The locks are the throngs of saints who cling to God in faithful service. Raised palms signify eminence before God; blackness, contempt before human beings. Or, they are raised because of victory and black because of afflictions.

### Verse 12

“His eyes are like doves beside streams of water.” The holy teachers are meant, through whom the Church sees what is right. They are rightly compared to doves because of innocence [Cod. Vat. omits “innocence”] and simplicity, and to streams of water because of the divine charisms.

“Washed with milk, and sitting beside the fullest streams.” He says that they are washed with milk, that is, cleansed by the sweetest grace. And they sit beside the fullest streams, that is, beside the abundance of all spiritual gifts. The streams may signify the instruction of the Old Law, and the fullest waters the perfection of evangelical teaching, since preachers bring forth from their treasures things old and new (Matthew 13:52).

### Verse 13

“His cheeks are like plots of spices.” In the cheeks of our Savior, both his modesty [Cod. Vat.: modest piety] and his severity are expressed. In the plots of spices, his virtues, sweetness, and fame of glory are signified. “Planted by spice-merchants.”

“His lips are lilies dripping first-rate myrrh.” The prophets and apostles are meant: the former recounting the mysteries of his future incarnation, the latter narrating what he accomplished. His lips are the words of his teaching; lilies, because they promise the love of the heavenly kingdom; dripping first-rate myrrh, because they preach that one must reach it through contempt for present pleasures.

### Verse 14

“His hands are turned work of gold.” His hands are his works, because he fulfilled by deeds what he taught in words. They are turned work because they hold within themselves the whole rule of justice, as it is said: “It is fitting for me to fulfill all justice” (Matthew 3:15). They are also golden hands because everything he did as a human being he perfected through the glory of his divinity.

“Full of hyacinths.” They arouse us to hope for heavenly things and to love them, because hyacinth is a gem of the color of the sky [Cod. Vat.: in hyacinths].

“His belly is ivory, variegated with sapphires.” The belly of the beloved therefore signifies the fragility of his humanity; ivory, the beauty of chastity; sapphire, the sublimity of heavenly virtues. It is variegated with sapphires because partly the fragility of his humanity is understood through hunger, temptation, weariness, and death, and partly the height of his divinity through miracles, resurrection, and the glory of his ascension.

### Verse 15

“His legs are marble columns.” By the legs, the courses [Al.: gifts] of Christ’s incarnation are indicated. They are compared to marble columns because of their firmness and uprightness. “Founded upon golden bases.” Whatever was done by him or concerning him was arranged before the ages by the counsel of divine foreknowledge [Cod. Vat.: providence; Al.: promise].

“His appearance is like Lebanon; he is chosen like the cedars.” As Lebanon surpasses other mountains in height and in the beauty of its trees, so the Lord Christ surpasses all the saints in the height of their merits and the beauty of their virtues. “Chosen like the cedar.” Just as the cedar surpasses in dignity the other trees that grow in Lebanon, so Christ surpasses in his glory all who are born in the Church to life.

### Verse 16

“His throat is most sweet.” In the throat, the inner sweetness of his words is recalled; whoever tastes it does not hunger. “And he is altogether desirable.” What more do you seek? He is altogether desirable, because he is wholly God and wholly human, and into him the angels long to look. God in the majesty of the Father; human in the virginity of his mother; in the former, the Creator; in the latter, the Savior.

“Such is my beloved, and such is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.” The more devotedly someone loves God, the more familiarly he has God as a friend; and you must understand him in this way if you wish to have him as a friend.

## Chapter VI

### Verse 1

“Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women?” For the sake of poetic beauty, the persons speaking are varied; nevertheless, they signify Christ’s Church, which is expressed under the name of the bride.

“O most beautiful among women.” The individual Churches of the saints are beautiful, but the whole of the holy Church throughout the world is most beautiful.

“Where has your beloved turned aside, and we shall seek him?” He who once lived on earth in bodily form—tell us where he has turned aside, so that we may follow him [Al.: seek him] with you.

### Verse 2

“My beloved went down to his garden, to the plot of spices.” As though she had said: “He went up there from where he came down.” He went into the garden, that is, into his Church, so that he might water it like a plot of spices with the fountain of his grace, and make it sprout with the flowers of virtue.

“To pasture in the gardens and gather lilies.” He pastures in the gardens when he delights in the pious labors of the saints; he gathers the lily when he leads those who attain the perfect [Cod. Vat.: of the perfect] whiteness of merits to the heavenly kingdoms.

### Verse 3

“I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine, he who pastures among the lilies.” I prepare in myself a dwelling-place for my beloved; and he has one in himself for me, for he always pastures among the holy desires of pure minds.

Up to this point it is the voice of the holy Church, praising and seeking the bridegroom. What the one who has been sought replies is now added.

### Verse 4

“You are beautiful, my [friend], sweet and lovely as Jerusalem.” The holy Church is called sweet and lovely like Jerusalem because the desire for her life already resembles the vision of inward peace.

“Terrible as an army drawn up in battle array.” That is, united and joined together in love [Al.: joined], so that no place may be opened to the enemy through the evil of discord; for we are terrible to the enemy only in the unity of peace.

### Verse 5

“Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly away.” That is, the eyes of your mind. Do not seek to know me perfectly on the road of your pilgrimage, which cannot happen; for the more intently you seek to recognize me, the more certainly you will understand that I am incomprehensible. And do not seek on the way the reward that is reserved for you in your homeland.

“Your hair is like a flock of goats that have appeared from Gilead.”

### Verse 6

“Your teeth are like flocks of sheep that have come up from the washing, all with twin lambs, and none among them is barren.” These verses were explained above, but repetition is an indication of firmness. In the hair, peoples are understood; in the teeth, teachers; in the twin offspring, the two commandments of love.

### Verse 7

“Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from your eyes.” The cheeks of the holy Church are the spiritual Fathers, who are wondrous in virtues, worthy of reverence in conduct, and unashamed to glory in the cross of Christ. The things seen in her are very great, but the things unseen and reserved for the future are far greater.

### Verse 8

“There are sixty queens, and eighty concubines, and maidens without number.” Queens are those who, through preaching the truth and faith and through the sacred baptismal font, generate offspring for the eternal King [spiritual offspring], out of love for the bridegroom and with the heavenly reward in view. Concubines are those who teach Christ by preaching or baptizing solely for carnal advantage [Cod. Vat.: who teach for merely carnal advantage]. Therefore the former are designated by the perfection of the number six, multiplied through the Decalogue [Al.: the number ten]; the latter by the imperfection of the number eight, since they do not sincerely observe the Decalogue. Maidens are souls newly reborn through Christ’s grace, whose total number, because of their multitude [Cod. Vat.: because of the multitude], surpasses the number of the heavenly citizens.

### Verse 9

“You are one, my dove, my perfect one” [Cod. Vat.: “You are one”]. Namely, the holy and universal Church throughout the whole world.

“She is one for my mother, the chosen one for her who bore her” [Cod. Vat.: “of my mother … of her who bore her”]. That is, for the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all, from whom the grace of the Holy Spirit descends to us, through which we are reborn to God.

“The daughters of Zion saw her and proclaimed her most blessed; queens and concubines praised her.” Those whom he previously called maidens he now calls daughters. Queens and concubines are the same as before, and all praise the Catholic Church.

### Verse 10

“Who is this who advances like the rising dawn?” The Church advances like the dawn because, with the sun of the true light already risen in her, she is shown to the world after the darkness of prolonged ignorance.

“Beautiful as the moon.” Illumined by the sun of justice, she lights up the night of the world.

“Chosen as the sun.” She bears the image of her Creator in all justice, holiness, and piety [Cod. Vat.: truth].

“Terrible as an army drawn up in battle array.” She is terrible to the airy [Cod. Vat.: aerial] powers through the unity of love, faith, and hope.

### Verse 11

“I went down to the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valley.” The garden of nuts is the Church of the present age [Cod. Vat.: the present Church], where we do not at all see one another’s consciences; but when the shell of the body has been broken through temptation, the taste of inward sweetness will appear. The fruit of the valley is the fruit of humility.

The holy Church descends through the holy teachers, who advance toward good fruits and who still need the watering of instruction.

“To see whether the vine had blossomed.” To see whether the pursuit of virtues had blossomed.

“And whether the pomegranates had put forth their flowers.” Whether any had been prepared, in imitation of the Lord’s passion, to pour out their blood.

### Verse 12

“I did not know; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Amminadab.” “I did not know that the gifts of spiritual grace were in you, O bride; but my soul troubled me because of the introduction [Cod. Vat.: induction] of the New Testament and the evangelical chariot by which Amminadab—who is interpreted as ‘the spontaneous one of my people’—that is, Christ, is carried throughout the whole world” [Cod. Vat.: “because”]. To him the Church immediately replies in consolation:

### Verse 13

“Return, return, O Shulammite; return, return, that we may look upon you.” Do not be troubled, but return to the knowledge of your Redeemer, who was promised to you so many times in the prophets and the Law. Return in purity of faith and perfection of works. O Shulammite, that is, captive, now that the bond of unbelief has been completely erased [the words “completely erased” are omitted in Cod. Vat.], return to your Redeemer, so that you may be saved.

## Chapter VII

### Verse 1

“What will you see in the Shulammite, except the choruses of armies?” You grieve over the hardened Synagogue; the time is near when you will see in her the choruses of those fighting against the evil spirits and praising God.

“How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of the prince!” Now the praises of the Church are spoken by the Bridegroom himself. First, the steadfastness of her works and the mortification of pleasures are praised; and he calls her the daughter of the prince, that is, of Christ, because of the grace of baptism and the nobility of virtues.

“The joints of your thighs” [Vulg.: “of the thighs”] “are like necklaces fashioned by the hand of an artisan.” The agreement of the two peoples, made fruitful by spiritual offspring, is signified in the joining of the thighs. They are like necklaces fashioned by the hand of an artisan, that is, strengthened by the ineffable generosity of our Creator. In the necklaces, good works are expressed.

### Verse 2

“Your navel is a turned-work bowl, never lacking cups.” The navel, that is, the frailty of our weakness, is understood as opposed to faith [Cod. Vat. omits the words “as opposed to faith”]. The bowl becomes turned work when, reminded of our mortality and weakness, we strive with ready minds to offer our neighbors the cup of the saving word.

“Your belly is like a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies.” A heap of wheat surrounded by lilies exists when an abundance of good works is gathered solely in hope of perpetual light. In the belly, memory is expressed; in the wheat, the multiplication of good works; in the lilies, the chastity of hope. Likewise, in the wheat bread is expressed, and in the bowl the drink given to the poor.

### Verse 3

“Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle.” This verse was discussed above. The two breasts are the teachers of both peoples; the twin fawns are the two Testaments agreeing with one another.

Cod. Vat.: “twin fawns because of their one agreement.”

### Verse 4

“Your neck is like an ivory tower” [Cod. Vat.: “an ivory tower”]. Here too the teachers are signified by the neck. They are compared to an ivory tower because of firmness [Cod. Vat.: because of firmness] and beauty, since they provide the city of God both strength and ornament.

“Your eyes are like the pools in Heshbon, which are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude.” Here too the eyes of the Church are the teachers because of foresight, just as the neck is understood because of nourishment. They are rightly compared to pools because they do not cease to provide streams of teaching to their hearers.

Heshbon is interpreted as “a belt of mourning,” because the saints are bound by the belt of abstinence instead of the empty joy of the flesh. And rightly they are at the gates of the daughter of the multitude, because of the abundance of peoples who converge through the gate of faith into the Church.

“Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon.” Here too the dispensers of God’s word are signified by the nose, on account of discernment. It is a tower because they occupy the most eminent place in the Church.

“Which looks toward Damascus.” That is, toward the bloodthirsty and impious, since Damascus is interpreted as “drinking blood.” It signifies the carnal and cruel, against whom the holy teachers continually keep watch in the tower of Lebanon, that is, in the firmness of the Church.

### Verse 5

“Your head is like Carmel, and the hair of your head is like purple, bound in channels by a king.” In the head, the mind is signified; in the hair, thoughts. Just as the head governs the members, so the mind governs thoughts, so that they may move in Carmel—interpreted as “conscience of circumcision” [the words enclosed in semicircles are omitted in Cod. Vat.]—that is, in sublime things and in passion, which is expressed by the name purple. The channels are the inmost hearts of the saints, in which such thoughts are bound.

### Verse 6

“How beautiful and how lovely you are, most beloved, among delights.” Beautiful in faith and lovely in works. “Most beloved among delights,” that is, among spiritual virtues.

### Verse 7

“Your stature is like a palm tree.” That is, the uprightness of good action always tends toward victory.

“And your breasts are like clusters of grapes.” The breasts are compared to the teachers of the Church because of the milk of initial instruction, and they are made equal to clusters of grapes because of the mysteries of the sweetest eternity [Cod. Vat.: sweetest eternity].

### Verse 8

“I said, ‘I will climb the palm tree; I will grasp its fruits,’ and your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine.” The victorious cross [Cod. Vat.: the most victorious cross] is aptly compared to a palm tree. Christ climbed it and grasped its fruits, that is, the gifts he bestowed upon the holy Church. From that time she began to produce clusters of the vine, that is, holy teachers who, after the Savior’s cross and resurrection, abounded in greater knowledge and grace.

“And the fragrance of your mouth is like apples” [Cod. Vat.: “and your fragrances are like apples”].

### Verse 9

“Your throat is like the finest wine for drinking.” In the throat, the voice of present teaching is signified; in fragrance, the fame of one who is absent. Therefore the former is compared to wine because of the fragrance of virtues, and the latter to apples because of the sweetness of an absent reputation.

“Worthy of my beloved.” The bride seized the word from the bridegroom’s mouth, because he compared her to the finest wine and subjected her to it. “Worthy of my beloved,” that is, the sublimity of evangelical preaching is so great that the beloved himself, appearing first in the flesh through it, opened the heavenly way to the world.

“And to be ruminated upon by his lips and teeth.” That is, he gave it especially to the apostles and preachers [Cod. Vat.: to the greatest apostles and preachers] for meditation.

### Verse 10

“[I am my beloved’s and not another’s, to whom I devote all the care of service and love].” “And his turning is toward me.” He alone loves me and helps me, so that I do not fail on the way.

### Verses 11–12

“Come, my beloved; let us go out into the field; let us stay in the villages. Let us rise early and go to the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has blossomed, whether the fruits are forming, whether the pomegranates have blossomed.”

The holy Church is in no way sufficient either to go out and advance toward good works, to remain steadfast in the practice of good action, to rise at least toward the purpose of doing good, or to discern how much the minds of her hearers have progressed, unless she is assisted by God’s grace, who said: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

Likewise, in the field Christians are signified; in the villages, pagans; in the vineyards, Churches; in the blossoms, faith; in the fruits, virtues; and in the pomegranates, martyrdom. In each of these the bride seeks the presence of her beloved.

“There I will give you my breasts.” That is, the instructors of my little ones, because the holy teachers advance in all these things.

### Verse 13

“The mandrakes have given their fragrance at our gates.” The mandrake, because of its many kinds of medicinal properties, is compared to the virtues of the saints. The gates of the Church are the holy teachers. At such gates the mandrakes give their fragrance when all spiritual people spread the fame [Cod. Vat.: palm] of their virtues far and wide.

“All new and old fruits, my beloved, I have kept for you.” The new and old fruits are the commandments or promises of the New and Old Testaments, all of which the Church refers to his grace.

## Chapter VIII

### Verse 1

“Who will grant me that you were my brother, nursing at the breasts of my mother?” This is the voice of the righteous of ancient times, desiring Christ’s coming in the flesh.

“Nursing at the breasts of my mother,” that is, being born and nourished in the synagogue according to the nature of human condition.

“That I might find you outside.” The beloved was within when “the Word was in the beginning”; outside, when “the Word became flesh.”

“And kiss you.” That is, see you face to face and speak mouth to mouth.

“And now no one would despise me.” Before Christ’s coming, the Church existed only within the narrow confines of Judea; after his ascension, she was extended throughout the whole world and became venerable.

### Verse 2

“I will take hold of you.” I will receive you as you come with ready and faithful devotion.

“And I will lead you to the house of my mother.” When you return after the dispensation of the flesh has been completed, I will lead you with joyful lights into the house of my mother, where the heavenly Jerusalem is our mother.

“There you will teach me.” You will make me hope for better gifts than those I had in the Law.

“And I will give you a cup of spiced wine.” That is, fervent love adorned with various spices of virtue.

“And the must [Cod. Vat.: mixed wine] of my pomegranates.” That is, the glorious triumph of the holy martyrs, who do not hesitate to pass over to you through iron and flames with the most fervent love.

### Verse 3

“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.” The left hand signifies the gifts of Christ’s incarnation; the right hand expresses the future joys of the saints with Christ.

### Verses 4–5

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not rouse or awaken [the beloved], until she herself wishes it.” Who is this who comes up from the desert, overflowing with delights?

This is the voice of the Synagogue wondering how the Church had suddenly risen from the desert of the Gentiles into the embraces of the bridegroom. “Overflowing with delights,” that is, with the beauty of all gifts.

“Leaning upon her beloved.” Referring all that she has to the grace of her beloved, relying upon him alone.

“Under the apple tree I awakened you.” The bridegroom himself answers the Synagogue on the bride’s behalf. “Under the apple tree I awakened you,” that is, under the tree of the cross I recalled you from perpetual death [Cod. Vat.: renewed you], as I did the apostles and the other elect from the Jews.

“There your mother was corrupted; there she who bore you was violated.” That is, the greater part of the people, by denying Christ and choosing Barabbas, was rejected at the cross.

### Verse 6

“Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm.” We bind a seal to the arm or finger in remembrance of something. By the heart, thought is signified; by the arm, action. If you wish to have me as your bridegroom, let love be inward, in sincere faith, and let devoted action be outward.

“For love is strong as death, jealousy hard as Sheol.” My love for you, O Synagogue, is strong even unto death; but your jealousy against me was hard as Sheol. Turn your jealousy into love, and you will be my bride, sister, and friend.

“Her lamps are lamps of fire and flames.” The lamps of love are the hearts of the faithful: fire because of the fervor of the heart; flames because of the effectiveness of action [Cod. Vat.: prayer].

### Verse 7

“Many waters could not extinguish love, nor will rivers overwhelm it.” By many waters and rivers he means the assaults of temptations, which do not cease to attack the souls of the faithful visibly or invisibly, but to which love does not yield.

“If a man were to give all the substance of his house for love [Cod. Vat.: affection], they would utterly despise him.” But the saints, who leave the substance of the whole world for the greatness of love, accomplish nothing unless they also reject themselves.

Cod. Vat.: “But the saints despised the substance of the whole world as nothing for the greatness of love.”

### Verse 8

“Our sister is little, and she has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she must be spoken to?” This signifies the first beginnings of the Church from the Gentiles, when she was still small in number and less suited to preach the word, as though the Bridegroom had said concerning her to the Synagogue:

“What shall we do for our sister on the day when she must be spoken to?” As though he openly said: “The Church of the Gentiles is indeed small in number and does not yet suffice to undertake the ministry [Cod. Vat.: mystery] of the word. What, then, do you think should be done for our sister, when she must be addressed—that is, led to faith through the ministry of the word?”

When the Synagogue remained silent, the Bridegroom himself replied what should be done:

### Verse 9

“If she is a wall, let us build upon her silver battlements.” As though he said: “If she has within her some who are strong in faith, or distinguished in intellect, or instructed in philosophy, let us add silver battlements to them—that is, knowledge of the divine Scriptures—so that they may more easily defend the weak and unlearned.

“If she is a door, let us join it with cedar boards.” If they are simple, yet eager for the zeal of teaching, let us set before them the examples of the righteous of former times, so that they may fulfill the work of teaching with greater certainty and effectiveness.

The cedars signify the virtues of the saints, and the boards the breadth of love. To this the Church herself replies:

### Verse 10

“I am a wall.” I am built from living stones, joined together by the glue of love, and constructed upon an immovable foundation.

“And my breasts are like a tower.” That is, I have the strongest teachers, like a tower, who know both how to nourish the little ones and how to drive away all the darts of the Evil One.

“And this happened to me from the time when Christ reconciled me [and I found peace through him].” As though finding peace. For he himself is true peace, making both one.

### Verse 11

“There was a vineyard belonging to the peaceful one, in which he has peoples.” The vineyard, that is, the Catholic Church, abounding in the fruit of faith, belonged to the peaceful one, that is, to Christ, who pacified all things in heaven and on earth, in that gathering which possessed many peoples from the whole world, not in Judea alone.

“He entrusted it to its keepers,” to the prophets and apostles, or to the angelic orders.

“A man brings a thousand silver coins for its fruit.” That is, for the eternal recompense of this vineyard he brings a thousand silver coins; that is, for the acquisition of the heavenly kingdom, which is the fruit of the vineyard, he has abandoned everything that belongs to the world. The number one thousand is used for perfection, that is, for the one who abandoned everything. Silver coins are understood as all money.

### Verse 12

“My vineyard is before me.” This too is the voice of the Bridegroom. Even if I commend you to other keepers, nevertheless I always have you in my presence, seeing and rewarding the devotion of your labor in all things.

“A thousand are yours, O peaceful one.” “A thousand of yours” means silver coins, as though he had said: “Those who abandon all that they possess for love of me have it reserved in peace.” He signifies the simpler members of the Church, who lose all their substance, designated by the number one thousand, for the love of God.

“And two hundred for those who guard its fruits.” That is, silver coins for those who guard its fruits. These are the holy teachers, who abandon everything worldly and do not cease to labor in preaching the word. They are given by me a twofold recompense, represented by the number two hundred.

### Verse 13

“You who dwell in the gardens, the friends are listening.” Since our speech must end, hear this final farewell from me. Dwell [Cod. Vat.: “dwell always”] in the gardens of virtues, and know that the friends—that is, the angelic spirits and the souls of the saints—always observe you and rejoice in your progress.

“Make me hear your voice.” That is, let the voice of preaching always be heard by me, as far as you are able.

To this the bride replied:

### Verse 14

“Flee, my beloved, and be like a gazelle and a young stag upon the mountains of spices.” As though she openly said: “Since you appeared in the flesh and brought me the commandments and gifts of life, now that these things have been accomplished, return into the bosom of the Father [O my beloved, be like a gazelle and a young stag upon the mountains of spices].”

“And let this be my consolation: since I cannot see you in continual vision, may you at least deign to console me with frequent visitation” [Cod. Vat.: “at least remember to console me with frequent vision”].

## Letter to Daphnin

### Concerning that passage from the Song of Songs

Cod. ms. Salisb. gives the title: “On the number sixty of the queens and the number eighty of the concubines: ‘There are sixty queens and eighty concubines’” (Song of Songs 6:7).

### Preliminary Notice

The present letter, or brief commentary on the cited passage from the Song of Songs, is believed to have been first published by Canisius in volume VI of *Lectiones Antiquae*, pages 366–368, or in volume II, part I, page 540, of Basnage’s edition, from the library of the most celebrated monastery of St. Gall. Nevertheless, Antonius Possevinus, in volume I of the *Apparatus Sacri*, page 35, records an earlier edition, produced in 1568, together with a commentary on the Psalms.

The distinguished Quercetanus followed Canisius’s edition and included it among the works of Blessed Flavius Alcuin on page 306. We too follow that edition, collated with an old manuscript codex from Salzburg, from which we have noted several differing readings.

“Young, if I am not mistaken,” Basnage says in the place cited, “he was still when he wrote this letter; for he wished to remain hidden among his intimates, feared the judgments of the learned, and did not dare to present himself to their view.” The writers of the *Literary History of France*, volume IV, page 305, note 6, likewise consider this letter to be of little importance.

Everything concerning Daphni or Daphnin is unknown to us, except that he was a disciple of Alcuin. To him Alcuin disclosed his grief concerning the perverse manner of life to which another disciple, named Cuculus, had given himself. Alcuin mourns him in a distinctive poem, which will also be presented in its proper place from the *Analecta* of the distinguished Mabillon.

To my most beloved son Daphnin [Ms.: Daphni], Father Albinus, greetings.

Since some time ago you discussed with me the nature of numbers, asking how, in the most excellent Song of Solomon, the number sixty corresponded to queens and the number eighty to concubines, and why the maidens were without number, therefore—even though I know that you have read the full explanation of this in the treatises of the holy Fathers—so as not to distress your anxious concern, I shall say what seems able to accord with my own incompetence, and what I wish to remain hidden only among the ears of intimate friends, because I do not dare to present myself publicly [Ms.: in public] to the judgment of great teachers.

For in the most subtle account of numbers, we read that some numbers are even and others odd; and likewise that among even numbers some are perfect and others imperfect; and again that among imperfect numbers some are abundant and others deficient. Even numbers are those that can be divided into two equal parts: for example, eight into twice four, and four into twice two. Odd numbers are those that cannot be divided into two equal parts, such as seven or nine; if you divide them, you cannot find two equal parts in them. Likewise, among even numbers themselves, some are perfect and others imperfect.

A perfect number is one that is filled out by its parts, is not broken by diminution, and does not exceed itself through the multiplication of its parts, such as the number six. For the number six has as its half three, as its third two, and as its sixth one; these, joined together, fill out that same six. For one, two, and three make six, by which it is filled out. It is neither broken by diminution nor increased beyond itself by excess. Therefore the most perfect Creator, who created all things very good, established the creatures of the original world in this number, to show that everything he created is perfect in its own kind.

Likewise, the number eight [Ed.: “eighty”], if divided according to the parts named after itself, is found to be less than itself. For it has as its half four, as its fourth two, and as its eighth one; and these, added together, do not fill out eight but seven: one, two, and four make seven, not eight. And {409} therefore the second origin of this kind [F.: of the human race] began to arise from the number eight. We read, namely, that eight souls were in the ark, from whom the multitude of the entire human race sprang forth, so that it might be shown that the second origin was more imperfect than the first, which was created according to the number six. Hence also our Redeemer and Restorer of the first perfection, just as Adam was created on the sixth day from virgin earth, was likewise made human in the sixth age from the Virgin Mary, so that by his coming he might consecrate the perfection of the number six, which he had displayed in the creation of the first man.

Likewise, we see the progression of numbers growing toward infinity through certain finite forms, arranged in stages as though by units. For the first progression of numbers is from one to ten; the second from ten to one hundred; the third from one hundred to one thousand. And the same rule of perfection [or imperfection] which [read: “that”] the first unit preserves in its numbers [Ms.: “under”] ten, the second must likewise preserve in its tens under one hundred. For just as the number six, set forth through its parts by means of the unit [Ms.: “units”], is perfect in itself, so the number sixty, through the placement of its parts, is known to be perfect by means of the ten. Thus the ten always occupies in sixty the place that the unit occupies in six, and its division through its parts is as follows: half of sixty is thirty, just as three is the half of six; its third is twenty, just as two is in six; and ten holds in it the place of the unit. When this sum is gathered together, it fills out the same sixty. Ten, therefore, and twenty, and thirty make sixty, just as three, and two, and one make six.

You can also examine for yourself, according to the same rule, the diminution of eighty. For forty is half of eighty, twenty is its fourth, and ten its eighth; these added together make seventy, not eighty. Thus ten, twenty, and forty make seventy [Ms.: “make”].

The sixty queens and eighty concubines, however, are rulers of the holy Church. Some of them teach solely because of the love of Christ; others, pursuing earthly advantages, labor in the Church—not with the labor [Ms.: ardor] of the heavenly homeland, but they toil in teaching for the sake of earthly profit. These, in their perfection [F.: imperfection], are compared with the number eighty; those, in perfect blessedness, are represented by the number sixty, so that they may become worthy of the name “queens,” because for love of the Bridegroom alone, and in order to multiply children for the heavenly homeland, they do not cease to beget spiritual offspring by baptizing or preaching, bringing forth a blessed progeny. The others are designated by the name “concubines,” because through worldly ambition or for the sake of temporal honor they often beget noble sons by preaching or baptizing, but those sons remain ignoble in themselves. Flee their companionship, dearest son, I beg you; and if at any time God’s mercy should deem you worthy to become a teacher, do not cease to labor for love of him who did not hesitate to pour out his blood for your salvation, so that your reward [Ms.: “rewards”] may be not perishable riches but everlasting glory in the heavenly bridal chamber of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be praise and glory throughout all ages. Amen.

{410}

# FOURTH OPUSCULUM: COMMENTARY ON ECCLESIASTES

## PRELIMINARY NOTICE

[Col. 0665D]

This commentary, so far as is known, was first published in print at Strasbourg or— as noted in the *Bibliotheca Baluziana*, volume II, page 603—at Basel by Johann Bebel, in 1531, in octavo. From there the distinguished Quercetanus transcribed it into his own collection. The compilers of the great *Ecclesiastical Library* also mention a Paris edition from the year 1589, though all other scholars are unaware of it.

We collated the edition of the distinguished Quercetanus with the manuscript codex of our own library, namely that of the monastery of Saint Emmeram. With its assistance we corrected the aforementioned edition in several places and recorded readings that differ or are lacking elsewhere; we also added the verses at the end of the epistle. The following title is prefixed to our codex: “Here begins Albinus’s Exposition of Ecclesiastes.” At the end, however, its last three or four pages have been cut out; we shall note this defect below in its proper place.

## PREFACE

To his dearest sons in Christ, Onia the priest, Candidus the presbyter, and Nathanael [Ms.: Nathahel] the deacon, Albinus sends greetings of perpetual prosperity in the Lord God.

After you flew forth from the nest of paternal affection into the open air of secular affairs, the concern of my mind has accompanied your occupations through almost every hour, wishing that, by God’s gracious gift, you might please God in perfect charity, live honorably before men, and display in noble conduct what you learned under the wings of paternal instruction. Nor would I wish the glory of wisdom that you possess in your hearts to be obscured by the vanities of the world; rather, amid them, may the religion of your way of life shine like the brightness of light in darkness.

Remember that you administer what belongs to others, rather than possess what is your own. Concerning these things Truth itself says: “If you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” (Luke 16:12). The possessions of this world are alien to us—that is, they are situated outside our nature. For there is no doubt that we brought nothing into this world, and that we can take nothing away (1 Tim. 6:7). Our possession, however, is the kingdom of heaven; our life is Christ; our riches are the fruits of spiritual works. I exhort you, dearest sons, to gather these with complete devotion, and not to place your hope in uncertain riches, which either abandon their possessor or are abandoned by their possessor.

The Holy Spirit forbade us through the Prophet to direct the intention of our minds toward these things, saying: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61:11). Their abundance is another person’s poverty. Concerning them the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity” (Luke 16:9). He called the riches of this world iniquitous—for *mammon* is a Syriac word and may be rendered in Latin as “riches”—because riches are either gathered through iniquity or unjustly taken away from the poor.

Of the vain possession of these riches, the almost supremely wise Solomon composed an entire book amid the delights of this world. Its title is *Ecclesiastes*, and at the beginning of the book he says: “Vanity of vanities, said Ecclesiastes, and all is vanity.” If all is vanity, what benefit is there in retaining fleeting riches? From the works of the holy Fathers, and especially from the commentary of blessed Jerome, I have composed a brief summary of this book for your sake, dearest sons, so that with paternal concern I might admonish your noble minds not to strive with excessive love after fleeting and quickly passing riches. They depart most swiftly, like flying shadows. I also wish you to distribute to the poor whatever remains from them after the necessary support of your life, because, as the same Solomon says: “The redemption of a man’s soul is his own riches” (Prov. 13:8).

Consider with attentive mind the holy command of the Lord himself, by which he admonished us to seek heavenly treasures rather than earthly ones, saying: “Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal; for where your treasure is, there also is your heart” (Matt. 6:20). Always keep this book mentioned above in your hands as a teacher, so that you may learn not to love earthly things but heavenly ones; to rule riches, not to serve them; not to seek earthly praise, but to hear from Christ the Judge, the consoler of the wretched, the gracious sentence among those to whom he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

@ [Col. 0667D] The distinguished Frobenius indicated that this poem, except for its last four verses, had been drawn from a very ancient manuscript and should be restored to its proper place among the Addenda to his edition:

> lest the troubled South Wind sink it,  
> let him voyage in his own skiff

> happily read our comments with a serene spirit,  
> drawn from the treasures that the hooked hand of the ancients brought forth.  
> Live for God always—so the manuscript reads—  
> for to live for this world is death;  
> true life is to live for God.

[Col. 0668C] May Christ’s grace, I ask, preserve you happy,  
> O beloved children, by the holy aid of salvation.

# CHAPTER ONE

## VERSE 1. “The words of Ecclesiastes, son of David, king of Jerusalem.”

@ [Col. 0668D] From Saint Jerome.

The Scriptures most clearly teach that Solomon was called by three names: Solomon, that is, “peaceful”; Jedidiah [Ms.: Edida], that is, “beloved of the Lord”; and what is now called Qoheleth, that is, “Ecclesiastes.” He is called *Ecclesiastes* in Greek because he gathers an assembly, that is, the Church. We may call him a preacher, one who speaks to the people, whose speech is directed not specifically to one person but generally to all.

He was called peaceful and beloved of the Lord because there was peace in his kingdom and because the Lord loved him. For the forty-fourth and seventy-first Psalms are also prefaced with the titles “of the beloved” and “of the peaceful.” Although these Psalms, insofar as they pertain to the prophecy of Christ and the Church, surpass Solomon’s happiness and strength, they were nevertheless written historically concerning Solomon.

Accordingly, in keeping with the number of his names, he produced three books: *Proverbs*, *Ecclesiastes*, and the *Song of Songs*. In *Proverbs*, teaching the little one and instructing him, as it were, concerning present duties [Jerome: “through maxims”], he frequently addresses his speech to a son. In *Ecclesiastes*, he instructs a man of mature age not to think that anything in worldly affairs is perpetual, but that all things we see are fleeting and brief. Finally, in the *Song of Songs*, he joins the perfected man, prepared after trampling upon the world, to the embraces of the bridegroom.

Unless we first abandon our vices and, renouncing the pomp [Ms.: “pomps”] of the world, prepare ourselves unencumbered for Christ’s coming, we cannot say: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1). Not far from this order of instruction, the followers of philosophy also educate their disciples: first teaching ethics, then interpreting physics, and leading to theology the one whom they perceive to have advanced in these subjects.

It should also be carefully noted that the titles differ among the author’s three books. In *Proverbs* it is written: “The Proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel.” In *Ecclesiastes*, however: “The words of Ecclesiastes, son of David, king of Jerusalem.” The word “Israel” is superfluous here, although it is found incorrectly in Greek and Latin manuscripts. In the *Song of Songs*, neither “son of David” nor “king of Israel” or “of Jerusalem” is written at the beginning, but only: “The Song of Songs, which is Solomon’s.”

Just as *Proverbs*, and elementary instruction, pertain to the twelve tribes and to all Israel, and just as contempt for the world is appropriate only to metropolitans—that is, to the inhabitants of Jerusalem—so the *Song of Songs* properly concerns those who desire only heavenly things. For beginners and those making progress, both paternal dignity and the authority of his own kingdom are rightly judged [Ms.: indicated; al.: vindicated]. But for the perfect, where the disciple is instructed not by fear but by love, the proper name is sufficient; he is an equal teacher and does not know himself to be a king.

{412}

This is sufficient for the literal sense for now. In spiritual understanding, however, Christ is the peaceful one, beloved of God the Father, and our Ecclesiastes. Having destroyed the dividing wall and abolished hostility in the flesh, he made both one, saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27). Concerning him the Father said to the disciples: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. 17:5). He is the head of the Church.

He speaks not at all to the synagogue of the Jews, but to the multitude of the Gentiles, built of living stones—not to that Jerusalem of which he himself says: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets,” and “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23:37–38), but to the one by which he forbids us to swear, because it is the city of the great King.

He is the son of David, to whom the blind cried out in the Gospel: “Have mercy on us, son of David” (Matt. 15:22); and the whole crowd joined in, answering with one voice: “Hosanna to the son of David” (Matt. 21:9). Finally, the word of God is not addressed to him as it is to Jeremiah and the other prophets. Rather, because he is rich and a powerful king, he himself is the Word, Wisdom, and the other virtues. He speaks words to the men of the Church and communicates his speech to the apostles, of whom it is sung in the Psalm: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5).

Some people are therefore mistaken in thinking that this book urges us toward pleasure and luxury, when on the contrary it teaches that everything we see in the world is vanity and that we ought not eagerly pursue those things which, while they are held, perish.

@ [Col. 0669D] Thus far from Saint Jerome.

The Hebrews report that this book, which we now have in our hands, is the work of Solomon as he was doing penance. Because he had offended God by trusting in wisdom and riches and through women, he now reflects within himself that all the pleasures of this world are vanity and that they plunge into utter misery those who place their hope in them.

But blessed Gregory, that wonderful teacher and most lucid expositor of Sacred Scripture, also explained extremely well, in the fourth book of the *Dialogues* (chapter 4), how this book should be read and understood. Concerning the title of the book, he says:

> “Ecclesiastes properly means ‘preacher.’ In a public address, a judgment is pronounced by which the sedition of a tumultuous crowd is restrained; and when many people hold different opinions, they are brought to one judgment through the reasoning of the preacher. This book is therefore called ‘Preacher’ because Solomon assumed in it the mind, as it were, of a tumultuous crowd, so that through inquiry he might say what perhaps an inexperienced mind feels through temptation. For as many judgments as he raises through inquiry, so many persons of different kinds he seems to assume within himself.
>
> “But the true preacher, as though extending his hand, quiets the tumult of all and recalls them to one judgment when, at the end of the same book, he says: ‘Let us all hear the conclusion of the matter together: Fear God and observe his commandments, for this is the whole human being’ (Eccles. 11:13). For if in the same book he did not assume, through his dialogue [Ms.: speech], the persons of many people [Ms.: ‘had assumed’], why would he exhort everyone together with himself to hear the conclusion of his speech?
>
> “Since, therefore, at the end of the book he says, ‘Let us all hear together,’ he himself bears witness that, assuming within himself the persons of many, he did not speak as though he were alone. Hence some things in the same book are raised through inquiry, while others provide an answer through reason; some are uttered from a mind under temptation and still devoted to the pleasures of this world, while others expound what belongs to reason and restrain the mind from pleasure.
>
> “There he says: ‘This therefore seemed good to me: that one should eat and drink and enjoy happiness from his labor’ (Eccles. 5:17). And much farther on he adds: ‘It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting’ (Eccles. 7:3). If eating and drinking are good, it would seem better to go to the house of feasting than to the house of mourning. From this it is shown that he introduced the former from the persona of the weak, but added the latter as a definition of reason. For immediately he explains the reasons belonging to reason and shows what benefit there is in the house of mourning, saying: ‘For in that house the end of all human beings is recalled, and the living person considers what will be’ (Eccles. 11:9–10).
>
> “Again, it is written there: ‘Rejoice, young man, in your youth.’ And shortly afterward it adds: ‘For youth and pleasure are vanity.’ By subsequently condemning as vain what he had earlier seemed to recommend, he plainly [Ms.: clearly] indicates that he introduced the former words as though from carnal desire, but added the latter from the truth of judgment.
>
> “Thus, after first expressing the pleasure of the flesh, he declares—setting cares aside—that it is good to eat and drink, but later condemns this according to the reasoning of judgment when he says that it is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting. Likewise, he proposes that the young man ought to rejoice in his youth, as though this were the deliberation of the flesh, yet later, by a definitive judgment, condemns youth and pleasure as vanity.
>
> “Similarly, this preacher, setting forth the various temptations of thought, says elsewhere: ‘One death [is] that of human beings and beasts, and the condition of both is equal; as a human being dies, so they die; all breathe alike, and a human being has nothing more than beasts’ (Eccles. 3:10). Yet afterward he brings forth his judgment according to the definition of reason, saying: ‘What more has the wise person than the fool? And what has the poor person, except that he should go there where there is life?’ (Eccles. 6:8). Thus the one who said, ‘A human being has nothing more than beasts,’ afterward defined that the wise person possesses something more not only than a beast but also than a foolish human being—namely, that he should go there where there is life. By these words he first indicates that human life is not here, since he testifies that it exists elsewhere.
>
> “A human being therefore has this advantage over beasts: they do not live after death, whereas a human being begins to live at the moment when, through the death of the flesh, he brings this visible life to an end. Farther on he also says: ‘Whatever your hand can do, perform it diligently, because there is neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge in the underworld, where you are going’ (Eccles. 9:10).
>
> “How, then, is the death of a human being and a beast one death, and the condition of both equal? Or how does a human being have nothing more than beasts, when beasts do not live after the death of the flesh, whereas the spirits of human beings, led to the underworld after the death of the flesh because of their evil works, do not die even in that death? Yet in these two sentences, so different from one another, it is shown that the true preacher introduced the former from carnal temptation, but later defined the latter from spiritual truth.”

Let the reader of this book therefore understand carefully these various opinions of the human mind, discerning which belongs to which persona. Let him beware lest, through reading this book without more careful examination of what this preacher says from the temptation of each persona, he fall into the doctrines of Epicurus.

## VERSE 2. “Vanity of vanities, said Ecclesiastes; vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.”

If, according to the judgment of the Psalmist, every living human being is vanity, how much more rightly are irrational creatures said to be subject to vanity, as the Apostle says: “For creation was subjected to vanity” (Rom. 8:20)? Whatever is changeable and cannot remain what it is may rightly be called vanity. For God alone is unchangeable, and he is always what he is, and not something else. Whatever changes in some way vanishes and is no longer what it was. Therefore, in comparison with the Creator, every creature may be called vanity, and everything contained within this cycle may be counted as nothing in comparison with eternal majesty.

## VERSE 3. “What remains for a human being in all his labor with which he labors under the sun?”

@ [Col. 0671D] From Saint Jerome, as are most of what follows.

After the general judgment, he turns his speech to the vain labors of human beings, who toil in vain at the labor of this world, gathering perishable riches and seeking honors, until they are suddenly told: “Fool, this night your life will be demanded of you; whose will the things be that you have gathered?”

## VERSE 4. “A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth remains forever.”

While some die, others are born; those whom you had seen you no longer see, and you begin to see people who previously did not exist but are suddenly born. What is more vain than this vanity: that the earth, which was made for the sake of human beings, should remain, while the human being himself, the lord of the earth, is suddenly dissolved into dust? He significantly said, “The earth remains forever,” not “for ever and ever,” because heaven and earth will pass away, and behold, all things will be made new.

## VERSE 5. “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place, so that it may rise again.”

The sun itself, which was given to mortals for light, demonstrates the world’s daily destruction through its rising and setting. It returns to us by unknown paths from setting to rising; and, when the cycle of night has been completed, it rises new from its chamber. He says all this in order to teach that, through the changes of the seasons and the rising and setting of the stars, human life slips away and perishes without knowing it.

{414}

## VERSE 6. “It goes toward the south and circles toward the north; circling and circling, the spirit goes through its circuits.”

He called the sun itself “spirit,” because it animates, breathes into, and gives life to all things, as we see each year in spring, which is thought to be the beginning of the world. For the line of the zodiacal circle is oblique, and the sun’s course follows that zone. Therefore in winter the sun inclines toward the southern regions along a descending course, and again in the summer circle it rises toward the northern regions, lest, if it moved in only one manner, heat consume some things and cold consume others.

Alternatively: the Sun, Christ God, gives life to and illuminates all things by the splendor and power of spiritual grace. In his wings there is healing. He rises for the one who believes in him and sets for every unbeliever.

## VERSE 7. “All the rivers enter the sea, and the sea does not overflow; they return to the place from which the rivers flow, so that they may flow again.”

Philosophers say that the fresh waters flowing into the sea are either consumed by the sun burning above or serve as nourishment for the sea’s salt. But our Ecclesiastes, that is, Christ, the creator of these waters, says [Ms.: leads] that he causes them to return through the hidden veins of the earth to the sources of the springs, and to boil perpetually from the womb of the abyss at their original sources.

Nevertheless, under the name of rivers and sea we can metaphorically understand human beings [Ms.: the human race], who return to the earth from which they were taken, after they heard in the first sinner: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go.” Yet the earth is not filled by the multitude of the dead.

## VERSE 8. “All things are difficult; a human being cannot explain them in speech. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.”

Speech is wholly unable to explain the causes and natures of things; nor can the eye be satisfied, so that it may contemplate the dignity of a thing [Ms.: “nor can the eye contemplate as the dignity of the thing demands”]; nor can the ear, under the instruction of a teacher, attain complete knowledge of things. For now all things are seen in a riddle and understood in part, until perfect knowledge comes—a knowledge that cannot exist in this mortal body.

Nevertheless, this judgment is directed especially against those who promise themselves knowledge of the Holy Scriptures without labor or a desire to learn, thinking themselves wise when they are foolish.

## VERSES 9–10. “What is that which was? The same as what will be. What is that which has been done? The same as what will be done. There is nothing new under the sun, nor can anyone say, ‘Behold, this is recent.’”

He seems to be speaking of the natures created at the beginning of the world and of their succession, how they come and how they pass away. For example, while one human being dies, another is born. The nature of the one who dies was the same as that which will exist in the one who is born. The same is to be understood of birds, fish, serpents, and all living creatures, as well as of herbs, trees, and the other natures of things: nothing new is found that did not exist before, and nothing perishes that does not later come to be [Ms.: “will come to be”].

Therefore Scripture says: “God rested on the seventh day from all his works”—that is, he ceased from creating new natures, not from governing them, concerning which Truth itself says: “My Father is working until now, and I am working.” Hence the entire course of the world’s time is carried out according to nature from the primordial seeds of creatures.

## VERSE 11. “For what has already gone before in the ages was before us. There is no memory of former things, nor will there be remembrance of things yet to come among those who will exist afterward.”

Just as oblivion has hidden from us the things of the past that once existed, so those who are destined to be born will be unable to know what is now taking place among us. For all things will perish in silence and be hidden as though they had never existed, and this sentence will be fulfilled: “Vanity of vanities; all is vanity.” [“Vanity of vanities”] because all things pass away, and go like flowing water, and do not return. The whole world bears witness to this judgment, and especially the human race.

## VERSE 12. “I, Ecclesiastes, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.”

Thus far the preface has discussed generally the vanities of this world. From here he returns to himself and shows who he was, or how he came to know and teach all things through experience. Therefore he immediately adds:

## VERSE 13. “And I applied my mind to seek and investigate wisely all that is done under the sun.”

[Col. 0674A] “God has given this most grievous occupation to the children of human beings, so that they may be occupied with it.” He says “given” in the manner of speech by which the Apostle says to the Romans: “God handed them over to a reprobate mind” (Rom. 1:6)—that is, because of their preceding sins, he permitted them to fall into a reprobate mind.

Ecclesiastes therefore first applied his heart to seeking wisdom; extending himself beyond what was permitted, he wished to know the causes and reasons why little children should be attacked by a demon, and why shipwrecks should swallow the pious and impious alike: whether these and similar things happened by chance [Ms.: “by circumstance”], or by the judgment and providence of God. If not by judgment, where is providence?

@ Read from Saint Jerome at this point:

> “And if by chance, where is providence? If by judgment, where is justice?”

“Desiring to know these things,” he says, “I understood that God had given human beings a needless concern and an anxiety tormenting them in various ways, so that they might desire to know what they were not permitted to know.” Because of the curiosity into which they had thrust themselves of their own accord, God permitted them to struggle [in them] amid the events of this life, in which they were unable to find any explanation.

## VERSE 14. “I saw all the things that are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and an affliction of spirit.”

Alternatively [omitted in the manuscript], the sense is: “I considered all that is in the world and discovered nothing other than vanity and evil”—that is, the miseries of the spirit, by which the mind is wearied with various thoughts. The wise person labors to know what human wisdom has not been granted to know.

## VERSE 15. “The crooked are difficult to correct, and the number of fools is infinite.”

The multitude of the saints is countable, but the gathering of fools is not worthy of being numbered. The Psalmist says something similar: “I will number them,” that is, the saints, “more than the sand of the sea” (Ps. 138:18)—that is, the fools who are compared with sand. As the Lord said to Abraham: “Your offspring will be like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea” (Gen. 22:17). In the stars understand the saints, of whom the Psalmist says: “He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name” (Ps. 146:4). In the sand, sinners, of whom it is said: “Sinners shall be destroyed from the earth.”

## VERSE 16. “I spoke in my heart, saying: ‘Behold, I have become great, and I surpassed in wisdom all who were before me in Jerusalem; and my mind contemplated and learned many things wisely.’”

We also read in the Books of Kings that Solomon possessed great wisdom and that he asked this as a special gift from God above all the other riches or honors of the world (1 Kings 3). The eye of a pure heart therefore beholds much wisdom and knowledge. Hence he did not say, “I spoke much wisdom and knowledge,” but “my heart saw [much wisdom and knowledge].” For we cannot express everything that we perceive; the understanding of the heart is broader than the interpretation of the mouth.

## VERSE 17. “I also applied my heart to know prudence and doctrine, error and folly, and I recognized that in these also there are labor and affliction of spirit.”

Contraries are understood through contraries, and the first form of wisdom is to be free from folly. No one can be free from folly unless he has understood it. Hence many harmful things have been created among existing things, so that, by avoiding them, we may be instructed in wisdom.

It was therefore Solomon’s equal concern to know wisdom, error, and folly, so that, by pursuing some things and avoiding others, wisdom might be tested more truly. And I recognized that in such thoughts there was affliction of spirit and disturbance of mind.

## VERSE 18. “For in much wisdom there is much indignation, and whoever increases knowledge increases pain.”

The more wisdom someone has attained, the more he is indignant at being subject to vices [Ms.: “at subjecting himself”] and at being far from the virtues he seeks. He grieves over ignorance while seeking knowledge. He understands that he knows only in part, and sees that he cannot reach the full light of understanding hidden things. Therefore whoever increases knowledge increases pain.

# CHAPTER TWO

## VERSE 1. “I said in my heart: ‘I will go and abound in delights, enjoy good things,’ and I saw that this too was vanity.”

Here, in the manner of a preacher, he speaks with the common judgment of the crowd, while nevertheless showing it to be vain. The sense is this: “After I understood that in the abundance of wisdom and increase of knowledge there were pain and labor, and nothing but empty labor and a futile struggle, I turned myself toward pleasure, so that I might indulge in luxury, gather wealth, abound in riches, and seize perishable pleasures before I died. But in this too I perceived vanity, since past pleasure does not help the present and, once exhausted, does not satisfy.” Therefore I understood that carnal luxury is vanity, and I added, saying:

{416}

## VERSE 2. “I considered laughter an error, and I said of joy: ‘Why are you deceived in vain?’”

This is what is read in the Gospel: “Woe to you who laugh, for you will mourn” (Luke 6:25). Those who pursue carnal desires in this world are deceived, living more carnally than spiritually. They think that what will pass most swiftly like a shadow is perpetual, and their labor will be punished with pain. This can also be understood of heretics, who, agreeing with false doctrines, promise themselves joy and prosperity, although they are children of everlasting destruction.

## VERSE 3. “I considered in my heart how to withdraw my flesh from wine, so that I might transfer my mind to wisdom and avoid folly, until I saw what would be useful for the children of human beings—what deed must be done [Ms.: “what”] under the sun during the number of the days of their life.”

He aptly compared pleasure with drunkenness, since drunkenness overturns the vigor of the mind. Whoever can exchange it for wisdom and, as some manuscripts have it, “obtain spiritual joy,” will be able to arrive at knowledge of this matter: what ought to be pursued in this life and what ought to be avoided.

## VERSES 4–14

I magnified my works, I built houses for myself, and planted vineyards; I made gardens and orchards, and sowed them with trees of every kind; I constructed pools of water for myself, to irrigate a forest of growing trees. [Col. 0676A] I acquired male and female slaves, and possessed a large household; also herds of cattle and great flocks of sheep, more than all who had been before me in Jerusalem. I heaped up silver and gold for myself, and the treasures of kings and provinces; I made singers and female singers for myself, and the delights of the sons of men—cups and pitchers for the service of pouring wine. I surpassed in wealth all who had been before me in Jerusalem. Wisdom, too, remained with me.

Whatever my eyes desired, I did not deny them; nor did I restrain my heart from enjoying every pleasure and delighting in the things I had prepared. I considered this my portion, if I made use of my labor. When I turned to all the works my hands had made, and to the labors over which I had sweated in vain, I saw in everything [Col. 0676B] vanity and affliction of spirit, and that nothing endures under the sun.

I turned to contemplate wisdom, and errors and folly. “What,” I said, “is a human being, that he should be able to follow the king who made him?” And I saw that wisdom surpassed folly as light differs from darkness. The wise person’s eyes are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. I also learned that the same fate awaited them both.

It seems useful to me, for the benefit of readers, to gather briefly all that Ecclesiastes adds here concerning his glory, and to reduce its meaning, as it were, into a single body, so that what is said may be understood more easily.

Thus, I possessed what are thought to be the good things of this age, like a king and a powerful man. I built palaces for myself; I planted hills and mountains with vines; and, so that nothing might be lacking in luxury or pleasure [Ms., “for luxury and pleasure”], I planted gardens [Col. 0676C] and orchards for myself, establishing trees of various kinds, which collected waters in pools would irrigate from above, so that their enduring greenery [Ms., “their more lasting vigor”] might be nourished by perpetual moisture.

I also possessed an innumerable multitude of servants—whether purchased slaves, female slaves, or household-born servants—and many herds of four-footed animals, namely oxen and sheep, as many as no other king before me had possessed in Jerusalem. Moreover, countless treasures of silver and gold were stored up, contributed by the tributes of various kings and nations. Hence it happened that, because of my excessive wealth, I was impelled toward still greater pleasures, and choirs of musicians sang to me with the sound of pipes [Apud Hier., “with pipe, lyre, and voice”], so that both sexes might serve me at banquets.

But the more these things increased, the more wisdom was lacking. For whatever pleasure desire had drawn me toward, I was carried headlong without restraint, and I thought that this was the fruit of my labors: that I should consume myself in the lust of luxury [Ms., “in luxury”].

At last I returned to myself, and, as though awakening from a deep sleep, I looked upon my hands and my works, and saw them full of vanity, full of filth, full of the spirit of error. For I could find nothing good that is considered good in the world.

Therefore, weighing what belonged to wisdom as good and what belonged to folly as evil, I proceeded to burst into praise of the person who, restraining himself after his vices, can become a follower of the virtues. For there is a great difference between wisdom and folly; and as far as day is separated from night, so far are virtues separated from vices.

It seems to me, then, that the person who follows wisdom always raises his eyes toward heaven, and holds his face lifted upward, contemplating the things that are above his head. But the person devoted to folly and vices dwells in darkness and rolls about in ignorance of reality. Since these things are so, there is this difference between the wise person and the fool: one is compared with day, the other with darkness. The former lifts his eyes toward heaven; the latter lowers them toward the earth.

Then this thought suddenly crept over me: why do the wise and the foolish perish by a common death? Why are they oppressed by the same blow, the same outcome, the same death? Why do the same afflictions belong to both?

There are some who attempt to interpret the Ecclesiastes’ words from the place where he says, “I magnified my works,” up to the place where he says, “The wise person’s eyes are in his head,” as referring to Christ.
