[Col. 0677B] But in certain passages the interpretation is difficult, unless perhaps they can be understood of his members. Therefore, in this place we are content with the historical understanding alone, especially since it is not our purpose to say everything that various authors are found to have said, but to touch briefly, in concise discourse, on those matters that seem to belong to a clearer meaning.

## VERSES 15–16

And I said in my heart: “If the fate of the fool and my own fate will be one, what benefit is there for me in having devoted greater effort to wisdom?” And speaking with my mind, I observed that this too was vanity. For the memory of the wise person will not endure forever any more than that of the fool; future times will cover everything equally with forgetfulness. The learned person dies just like the unlearned. [Col. 0677C]

Considering these things more carefully, I said: “The wise and the foolish, the just and the impious, die by an equal death” [Hier., “will die by an equal lot”], “and in this age will endure all evils with a similar outcome.” For just as the impious person suffers tribulations, so too does the just person. Nor will anyone’s justice help him in this age; everything is uncertain, and no one knows why one thing happens to one person and another to another.

“If this is so,” I said in my heart, “what benefit is there for me in having followed wisdom and labored more than the others, if my fate and the fool’s will be equal?”

But thinking again and considering the matter more carefully, I understood that the wise and the foolish will not have a similar memory in the future, when the consummation of all things comes; nor will the unjust and the just be judged with an equal outcome, because the one proceeds to refreshment and the other to punishment. Therefore I condemned my earlier judgment [Col. 0677D], and understood that I had spoken foolishly and had erred, because [Ms., “for”] I had earlier thought in this way.

## VERSES 17–19

Therefore life became wearisome to me, when I saw that everything under the sun was evil, and that all was vanity and affliction. Again I detested all my industry, with which I had labored most diligently under the sun, since I would have an heir after me whose character I do not know—whether he would be wise or foolish—and he would rule over the labors in which I had toiled and been anxious. And is anything so vain?

He seems indeed to be returning to the subject of riches and wealth, because, according to the Gospel, when we are suddenly taken away by death, we do not know what kind of heir will possess what we have left, whether wise or foolish, who will enjoy the fruit of our labor. The books of Kings testify that this evil befell Solomon, who left his labors to his foolish son Rehoboam. [Col. 0678A]

But it is better understood [Ms., “I think”] as referring to spiritual labor, in which a wise person meditates on the law of the Lord day and night, exerts himself in the interpretation of the Holy Scriptures, and composes many books so as to leave a memorial of himself to later generations [Ms., “to his descendants”]. Nevertheless, his labors come into the hands of fools, who frequently, according to the perversity of their hearts, seize seeds of heretical depravity from the sayings of the holy Fathers and malign the labors of others.

## VERSES 20–23

Therefore I ceased, and my heart renounced further labor under the sun. For when someone labors in wisdom, learning, and anxiety, he leaves what he has acquired to a person who is idle; and this too is vanity and a great evil. [Col. 0678B]

For what benefit will a person have from all his labor and from the affliction of spirit with which he has been tormented under the sun? All his days are full of pains and sorrows, and even at night his mind does not rest. And is this not vanity?

Here, as above, he speaks about the uncertainty of the heir—whether he will be foolish or wise—who will enjoy another’s labor; and the matter returns to the same circle, so that the labors of the dying become the pleasures of the living.

Yet he is speaking especially about the labor of wisdom, in which those who apply themselves—whether to spiritual or visible matters—labor day and night, not knowing into whose hands their little works will fall, whether learned people will discuss their writings or whether fools and idlers will do so. Is anything so vain? For he does not cease from labor by night or by day, and he does not know to what future benefit his labors will contribute. [Col. 0678C]

## VERSES 24–26

Is it not better to eat and drink and show one’s soul good things from one’s labors? This too is from the hand of God. Who will eat so greedily and abound in pleasures as I?

To the person who is good in his own sight, God has given wisdom, knowledge, and joy; but to the sinner he has given affliction and excessive care, so that he may add to his wealth, gather it, and hand it over to the one who pleases God. But this too is vanity and empty anxiety of mind.

It is one thing to argue from rational reflection, and another to speak from the temptation of the weak multitude. Here he seems to define what the unlearned crowd thinks. But when he says, “It is better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of feasting,” he shows, through rational discernment, that he is speaking.

Let us nevertheless speak according to the sequence of the preceding discussion. [Col. 0678D] After I had examined everything and understood that nothing in the labor of this world is lasting, and that a later generation enjoys the labors of an earlier one, it seemed to me that the most just arrangement in human affairs—and, as it were, a gift of God—was that a person should enjoy his own labor, drinking and eating, and using in due measure [Al., “nourishing himself with”] the wealth he had gathered.

This indeed is a gift [Ms., “a gift”] of God: that such a disposition should be given to a just man that he himself consumes what he acquired through cares and vigils. Conversely, it is God’s anger when a sinner gathers wealth day and night and, never using it, leaves it to those who are just in the sight of God. But, he says, carefully examining this too and seeing that everything ends in death, I judged it most vain.

For the present, this is enough concerning the literal text, lest we seem entirely to pass over the simple meaning while pursuing spiritual riches and despising the poverty of history. It is good, therefore, to receive true food and true drink, which we find in the divine books from the flesh and blood of the Lamb. Of these it is said in the Song of Songs: “Eat, my friends; drink and be intoxicated” (Song of Songs V, 1). Wisdom herself calls them, saying: “Come, eat my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you. Leave childishness and live, and walk in the ways of prudence” (Prov. IX, 5–6).

For who can eat, or, when necessary, exercise restraint [Al., “nourish himself”], without God, who commands that what is holy not be thrown to dogs and teaches how food is to be given at the proper time?

Beautifully, then, God gives the good person wisdom, [Col. 0679B] knowledge, and joy. For unless he is good and, with the help of God’s grace, has first corrected his conduct by his own free choice [Ms., “according to his choice”],

> [Col. 0679D] In Jerome’s text, at this point: “For unless he is good and has first corrected his conduct by his own free choice.” The venerable Father’s judgment, which might seem to give off some scent of Pelagian error, Alcuin tempered by his own ingenuity in accordance with the sense of Catholic doctrine, which after Jerome was defined more clearly throughout the world, as follows (the Veronese editor of the Works of St. Jerome): “He will not deserve wisdom, knowledge, and joy.” Thus, just as God gave wisdom and the rest to the good person in his own sight, so, abandoning the sinner to his own choice, he makes him gather riches and sew together, here and there, cushions of perverse doctrines. When the holy man, pleasing to God, sees these things, he understands that they are vain and composed through presumption of spirit. Nor is it surprising that he said that he gave care, and so forth, to the sinner: “gave” must be understood as “allowed.” Therefore he gives him care or affliction because he was a sinner; the cause of the affliction is not in God, but in the one who previously sinned of his own will.

# CHAPTER III

[Col. 0679C]

## VERSE 1

Everything has its season, and all things under heaven pass through their appointed intervals.

Above he taught the uncertain and fluctuating condition of human existence. Now he wishes to show that everything in the world is opposed to everything else, and that nothing endures forever—at least among those things that are under heaven and subject to time—for the other spiritual substances are contained neither by heaven nor by time.

## VERSES 2–8

A time to be born and a time to die; a time to plant and a time to uproot what has been planted; a time to kill and a time to heal; a time to destroy and a time to build; a time to weep and a time to laugh; a time to mourn and a time to dance; [Col. 0679D] a time to scatter stones and a time to gather them; a time to embrace and a time to withdraw from embraces; a time to acquire and a time to lose; a time to keep and a time to cast away; a time to tear and a time to sew; a time to be silent and a time to speak; a time for love and a time for hatred; a time for war and a time for peace.

No one doubts that the birth and death of human beings are known and predetermined by God, and that giving birth is the same as planting, while dying is the same as uprooting what has been planted.

The Hebrews understand everything written here about the opposition of times, up to the place where it says, “a time for war and a time for peace,” as referring to Israel. There was a time for the birth of God’s people in the patriarchs, and a time for their death in the days of Vespasian and Titus. There was a time for planting in the promised land under Joshua son of Nun, and a time for uprooting when they were led into captivity by the rulers mentioned above. There was a time for killing them in Egypt, and a time for liberating them from Egypt. There was a time for destroying [Add from Jerome: “the temple”] under Nebuchadnezzar, and a time for building under Darius. There was a time for mourning the destruction of the city, and a time for laughing and dancing under Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah.

There was a time for scattering Israel among various nations, and a time for gathering it together when those who had been taken captive were brought back to their homeland. There was a time for embracing, when they were surrounded by heavenly assistance; and a time for withdrawing from embraces, when they were abandoned by God because of their sins. There was a time for seeking them from the Babylonian captivity, and a time for losing them in the destruction of the city under the Romans. There was a time for keeping the legal commandments, and a time for casting away the ragged commandments of the law.

There was a time for tearing, when the people was divided into two kingdoms after Solomon, and a time for sewing during the Maccabees. There was a time for silencing the prophets, now in the Roman captivity, and a time for the apostles to speak, when the Lord said: “Go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. X, 6).

There was a time for love, when he loved them earlier under the patriarchs [Hier., “when he loved them”], and a time for hatred, when they laid hands upon Christ. There is now a time for war, while they do not repent; and there will be a time for peace in the future, when the fullness of the Gentiles enters and thus all Israel will be saved.

In another, more elevated sense:

A time to kill and a time to heal, as he says: “I kill, and I make alive” (Deut. XXXII, 39). He heals by calling to repentance; he kills according to the saying: “In the morning I killed all the sinners of the earth” (Ps. C, 8).

A time to destroy and a time to build. We cannot build good things unless we have first destroyed evil things.

A time to weep and a time to laugh: now is the time for weeping, and in the future the time for laughter, as the Lord says: “Blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh” (Luke VI, 21).

A time to mourn and a time to dance. The meaning is the same as above. We must mourn in the present, so that in the future age we may rejoice in spiritual dancing.

A time to scatter stones and a time to gather them, because there was a time for scattering the Gentile people, and a time for gathering it again into the Church.

A time to embrace, when it was said, “Be fruitful and multiply” (Gen. I, 28); and a time to withdraw from embraces, where it says, “I will give eunuchs a place in my house better than sons and daughters, an everlasting place.” Alternatively: there is a time to embrace wisdom—that is, to think about heavenly things—and there is again a time to care for the body.

A time to acquire a people from the Gentiles, and a time to lose the Jewish people. A time to preserve believers from the nations, and a time to cast away unbelievers from Israel.

A time to tear and a time to sew. Under different expressions, the meaning is the same as above, in what he says, “a time to destroy and a time to build,” and then, “a time to tear and a time to sew.” For now the Synagogue is being destroyed so that the Church may be built, and the legal rifts are being bound together so that they may be sewn into the glory of the Gospel [Ms., “so that the Gospels may be sewn together”]. This is what the evangelists individually accomplished, sewing together testimonies from the Law and the Prophets concerning the Lord’s coming.

A time to be silent, so that we may learn what ought to be taught; a time to speak, so that we may teach what we have rightly learned. Let us think nothing right except what we learn, so that after much silence we may become teachers from being disciples.

There is a time for loving the law and the things commanded by the law—circumcision, sacrifices, Sabbaths, and new moons—and a time for hating these things, when the grace of the Gospel succeeds them.

A time for war and a time for peace. As long as we are in this age, it is a time for war; but when we have departed from this age, the time of peace will come. In peace there is the praise of God [Hier., “the dwelling of God”], and our city, Jerusalem, received its name from peace.

Therefore let no one now think himself secure in a time of war, when one must struggle and take up apostolic weapons, so that after conquering we may one day rest in peace.

## VERSES 9–11

What greater thing does a person have from his labor? I saw the affliction that God gave to the sons of men. He made everything beautiful in its time, and he handed the world over to their disputation, so that a person may not discover the work that God has done from beginning to end. [Col. 0681C]

Most think that this was said about teachers, to whom God gave understanding so that they might seek the natures of things and praise the Creator through them, lest the idle mind grow sluggish and fall into vices. Earlier he discussed the diversity of times and the changing variety of things; now he says: What greater thing does a person have from his labor than to understand wisely and praise the Creator in his creatures, and not consider anything in this age everlasting?

For what greater thing can we possess in this age by laboring than to be instructed through the diversity of creatures to recognize the greatness of the Creator, and to understand that everything God made is good? He gave the world to human beings for habitation, so that they might enjoy it and understand the variations of times, not seeking to know how everything was created, or why he caused this or that to grow, remain, or change from the beginning of the world to its consummation. [Col. 0681D]

## VERSES 12–13

And I learned that there was nothing better than to rejoice and do good during one’s life. For every person who eats and drinks and sees good from his labor possesses this as a gift from God.

Therefore a person has been given as a tenant and guest of the world, so that he may enjoy the brief span of life and, with the hope of a longer existence cut short, regard everything he possesses as though he were soon to depart to other things; and, insofar as he can, do good during his life. He should not torment himself with thoughts by gathering great riches in vain, nor think that he can gain anything more from his labor than food and drink. And if he spends anything from his wealth on good works, this alone is the gift of God. [Col. 0682A]

This is not intended to urge us toward despair and luxury, but that, possessing food and clothing, we should be content with them, and that whatever exceeds the body’s necessities should be spent for the relief of the poor. For just as the flesh is nourished by food and drink, so the soul is nourished by alms for the poor and by consolations for the afflicted.

According to the allegorical sense, true food is Christ’s flesh, and true drink is his blood, as the Lord himself says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John VI, 57). In this spiritual delight of food and drink we ought to rejoice, not only in the mystery but also in the reading of the Holy Scriptures, where we are fed and given drink from the tree of life, which was planted beside streams of water.

## VERSE 14

I learned that all the works God has made endure forever. We cannot add anything to them or take anything away from them. God has made them so that he may be feared.

There is nothing new in the world. The course of the sun and the phases of the moon, and the dryness or greenness of the earth and the trees, were born and created together with the world itself. Therefore God has ordered all things according to a fixed plan and commanded the elements to serve human uses, so that when people see these things they may understand that God’s providence exists and may fear before God’s face. From the equality, course, order, and constancy of things, they understand the Creator.

He beautifully tempered his words by saying, “so that they may fear before him,” for “the face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (Ps. XXXIII, 17).

## VERSE 15

What has happened is what continues; what is to happen has already happened; and God restores what has gone away. Whether past, present, or future, all the things we see have been, are, and will be.

The sun that now rises existed in the world before we existed, and it will rise after we have died. What we have said about the sun must be understood about all creatures. Each year the earth dries up and then becomes green again in its growth. The sea flows and recedes so that it may flow back. Animals die and are born again according to the same kind. Human beings come to an end in death, and others arise in their place.

By this law of creatures, nothing new can be found; rather, through successive ages God restores everything that has existed.

## VERSES 16–17

And I saw under the sun, in the place of judgment, wickedness; and in the place of justice, iniquity. And I said in my heart: God will judge the just and the impious; there will then be a time for every matter. [Col. 0682D]

“Under this sun,” he says, “I sought truth and judgment, and I saw that in judgments it was not truth that prevailed, but bribes.”

Alternatively: I thought that some justice was being administered in the present age, so that either the devout person received what was due according to his present merit, or the impious person was condemned according to his crime. But afterward, speaking with my heart and reflecting, I understood that God does not always judge partially and individually, but reserves judgment for the future, so that all may be judged together and each may receive what is worthy of his merits, according to what he did in this age. Then I perceived that there is a time of judgment for every matter.

## VERSES 18–21

I said in my heart concerning the sons of men: God tests them and shows that they are like beasts. Therefore the end of human beings and animals is one, and the condition of both is equal. As a human being dies, so they die. All breathe alike, and a human being has no more than an animal. Everything is subject to vanity, and all proceed to one place. They were made from the earth, and together they will return to the earth. Who knows whether the spirit of the sons of Adam rises upward, and whether the spirit of animals descends downward?

It is not surprising that in the present life there is no distinction between the just and the impious, nor does virtue have any force [Hier., “nor do virtues have any force”], but everything is tossed about by uncertain chance, since even between animals and human beings, according to the lowliness of the body, there seems to be no difference.

As the condition of birth is the same, so the lot of death is one. We proceed alike into the light, and are equally dissolved into dust. But if this seems to be the distinction—that the human spirit rises into heaven while the spirit of the animal descends to earth—by what certain authority have we learned this? Who can know whether what we hope for is true or false?

He says this not because he thinks that the soul perishes with the body, or that one place is prepared for beasts and human beings, but because, before Christ’s coming, all descended together to the underworld [Ms., “were led down”]. Hence Jacob also says that he will descend to the underworld (Gen. XXXVI). Job too complains that the pious and the impious are held in the underworld (Job VII, 17).

Indeed, before Christ, together with the thief, opened that fiery wheel and fiery sword at the gates of paradise, the heavenly places were closed, and the equal lowliness of the human and animal spirits kept them confined. And although one seemed to be dissolved and the other reserved, there was not much difference between perishing with the body and being held in the darkness of the underworld.

When he says, “They were made from the earth, and they will return to the earth,” it is clear that he is speaking of the body, because the body was created from the earth, not the soul. This is why the sentence pronounced against the human being as the avenger of sin says: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 19).

This is enough for the literal meaning. As for the spiritual understanding, who knows whether the spirit worthy of being called human rises into heaven, and whether the sinner, who is called an animal, descends to earth? Because of the uncertainty and slippery condition of this life, both may happen: the just person may fall, and the sinner may rise. Sometimes it may happen that a person more rational and learned in the Scriptures—that is, a human being—does not live circumspectly or as his knowledge demands, and is led down to the underworld; while someone simpler and more rustic, who is called an animal by comparison with a human being, may live better and, crowned with martyrdom, become a citizen of paradise.

## VERSE 22

And I discovered that there is nothing better than for a person to rejoice in his work, and that this is his portion. For who will bring him to see what will happen after him?

Disturbed by my earlier error, in which I thought that there was no difference between human beings and beasts, I was led astray by a perverse opinion [Ms., “was brought”] into saying that nothing else was good except to seize present pleasure. For once death has dissolved us, we cannot enjoy the things from which we depart unwillingly.

But it is better understood, in a better sense, as referring to joy in good works. Nothing, then, is better in this life than for a person to rejoice in his work by giving alms and preparing future treasures for himself in the kingdom of heaven. This alone is truly our portion, which neither a thief nor a robber nor a tyrant can take away, and which alone will follow us after death.

# CHAPTER IV

## VERSE 1

I turned to other matters, and I saw the oppressions that are committed under the sun [Ms., “generated”], and the tears of the innocent, with no one to console them; deprived of every assistance, they could not resist the violence of their oppressors. [Col. 0684B]

After this reflection I turned my mind and eyes there, so that I might see the oppressors and those suffering oppression. And behold, I saw the tears of those who are oppressed by the more powerful—the only thing they can possess amid their calamities, protesting the injustice done to them, while unable to find a consoler.

And what makes the misery greater and the grief inconsolable [Ms., “what is the greater misery”] is that the oppressors see themselves stronger in their wickedness; and this is why they cannot console them. David examines this passage more fully in Psalm 72, and Jeremiah in his book.

## VERSES 2–3

And I praised the dead more than the living, and judged happier than either the one who has not yet been born and has not seen the evils that are done under the sun. [Col. 0684C]

In comparison with the miseries by which mortals are oppressed in this world, I judged the dead—freed from the labor of this misery—happier than the living. Better than these two, namely the living and the dead, is the one who has not yet been born; he is happier because he has not yet experienced the evil of the world.

He says this not because human souls exist, according to the error of some, before a human being is born into the world, but because it is altogether better not to exist and not to possess the awareness of being than to exist or live in misery. In the same way the Lord speaks about Judas, signifying his future torments: “It would have been better for that man not to have been born” (Matt. XXVI, 24). For it would have been better for him not to exist at all than to suffer eternal torments.

## VERSE 4

Again I considered all the labors of human beings, and I observed that their industry is exposed to the envy of their neighbor; and in this too there is vanity and excessive care. [Col. 0684D]

Again I turned to other matters, and I saw all the strength and glory of those who labor. I discovered that one person’s good is another person’s evil: the envious person is tormented by another’s happiness, while the celebrated person is exposed to plots.

For what is more vain than for people not to weep over their own miseries or mourn their own sins, but to judge others, forget themselves, envy only those who are better, and be tormented by the good deeds of others?

## VERSE 5

The fool folds his hands together and eats his own flesh.

Everything he says has this purpose: to show that the person who labors and possesses something in the world is exposed to envy, while the person who wishes to live in quiet is oppressed by poverty; and that both are miserable, since one is endangered because of his wealth and the other is consumed by want because of his poverty.

Alternatively: hands are often understood as works. The fool withdraws his hands from good work and does not wish to act manfully, but eats his own flesh—that is, he lives according to carnal desires, wasting away in his pleasures until they are consumed [Ms., “until he is consummated”].

## VERSE 6

Better is one handful with rest than both hands full with labor and affliction of spirit.

It is better for the just person to possess a little than for sinners to possess many riches. Justice elegantly has rest, while iniquity has labor. And because the singular number is always understood in connection with the good, and the dual with evil, one handful has rest, while both hands are full of labor. [Col. 0685B]

## VERSES 7–8

Considering this, I found another vanity under the sun: there is one person, and he has no second—not a son, not a brother—yet he does not cease laboring. His eyes are not satisfied with riches, nor does he reflect, saying, “For whom am I laboring and defrauding my soul of good things?” This too is vanity and a grievous affliction.

I turned to others and saw them laboring more than was necessary, gathering wealth by right and wrong, yet not using what they had gathered; possessing everything, clinging to riches, preserving them for others [Ms., “clinging to riches and preserving them for another”], and not enjoying the fruit of their own labor—especially since they had neither son nor brother nor relative, so that their pious labor might appear to have been reserved for those who needed it.

Therefore I discovered that nothing is more vain than the person who gathers riches without knowing for whom he will leave them. We can also understand this, according to the preceding interpretation, of those who write books and leave them to readers who find them tedious.

Some interpret this passage, from the words “there is one person, and there is no second,” as referring to the Savior: he descended alone and without any companion to save the world. Although there are many sons of God and many are called brothers by adoption, no one worthy was found to join him in this work.

His labors have no end: he bears our vices and sins and grieves for us; and his eye will not be satisfied with riches, since he always desires our salvation. The more people he sees sinning, the more he exhorts them to repentance [Ms., “presses them toward repentance”].

By this kind of expression we say, “He grieves,” in the sense in which the Apostle says: “The Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. VIII, 26)—that is, he causes us to groan. Thus Christ also grieves here, because he causes us to grieve over our sins.

### {423} VERSES 9–12

It is therefore better for two to be together than for one: for they have the benefit of their companionship. If one falls, the other will support him. Woe to the one who is alone, because when he falls he has no one to lift him up. And if two sleep together, they will be warmed by one another; how can one person keep warm? And if someone prevails against one, two resist him. A threefold cord is not easily broken.

After the anxieties and miseries in which the man who torments himself by gathering wealth without a certain heir has been corrupted, the discussion now turns to companionship, and it says what good there is in the fellowship of friends and in shared consolation: one person’s fall is raised up by the help of the other. It also says that one who has a faithful friend manages domestic concerns and even obtains the rest of the night better than one who broods over wealth acquired alone. If a stronger enemy rises against one person, it says that the weakness of the other is sustained by the comfort of his friend. And just as two, when joined by love, differ from one, so the fellowship of three is also stronger. For true charity, violated by no envy, grows in strength as its number increases. For the present, let these things be understood simply.

But since above we set forth the understanding of certain people concerning Christ [Manuscript: “also”], the remaining matters must likewise be discussed in that order. It is better for two to be together than for one: it is better to have Christ dwelling within oneself than to be alone [In Jerome: “to dwell alone and”] and exposed to the attacks of the adversary. The reward of companionship is immediately shown in the benefit of the fellowship itself. If one falls, Christ will raise up his companion. Woe to the one who, when he falls, does not have Christ within him to raise him up. [Col. 0686A–B]

And if one should sleep [Manuscript: “also”]—that is, if he should be dissolved by death—and should have Christ with him, being warmed he will quickly come back to life. And if the devil, stronger in attacking, should rise against a human being, the human being will stand, and Christ will also stand for his own man, for his companion. This is not because Christ’s power alone against the devil is weak, but because free choice is left [Manuscript: “be left”] to the human being, and, when we strive with him, he becomes stronger in battle. But if the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit should also come [Manuscript: “But if also”], this fellowship will not quickly be destroyed [Manuscript: “broken”]. [Col. 0686C]

Concerning this fellowship it is said in the Gospel: “And my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.” And shortly afterward: “But the Paraclete, the Spirit, will himself teach you everything” (John 14:23, 26). This signifies that the work of the three—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is one, and that there is one dwelling in the heart of the person who loves God.

What he said above—“If one should sleep, how will he be warmed?”—means that unless Christ sleeps with us and rests in death, we cannot receive the warmth of eternal life.

### VERSES 13–16

A poor and wise boy is better than an old and foolish king who does not know how to provide for the future. Sometimes someone also comes forth from prison and chains to a kingdom, while another, born in a kingdom, is consumed by poverty. I saw all the living who walk under the sun, together with the second youth who rises in his place. There is no end to all the people who were before him; and those who come afterward will not rejoice in him. Yet this too is vanity and an affliction of spirit.

The Hebrews explain this passage as follows: “The inner person, who arises within us after the fourteenth year of puberty, is better than the outer person, who is born from his mother’s womb [Manuscript: ‘belly’].” The outer person does not know how to depart from vice; he has come forth from the house of vices [Manuscript: “prisoners”—an uncertain reading], that is, from the maternal womb, for this purpose: to reign in vices. He has also been made poor in his nature, possessing no wisdom because he abandons [Manuscript: “desires”—an uncertain reading] all evil. [Col. 0686D–0687A]

“I saw those who lived in the former person and afterward conducted themselves in the second person,” namely, the one who was generated after the former had departed. I understood that human beings sinned in the former person before, when the second person was born, the two persons had come into being at the proper time: one carnal, the other spiritual. But those who have turned to better things and know how to submit themselves to the inner person—that is, to the second person—do not rejoice in the former person, who reigned in vices. The distinguished teacher used to call these two persons one inner and the other outer.

We, however, think that these matters are better understood of the devil, the foolish king, and of Christ, the poor and wise one. Christ came forth from the virginal womb into the world in order to crush and overthrow the rule of the foolish king, who showed him all the kingdoms of the world. After defeating him, Christ would seize his possessions and overthrow his house, and would lead captivity captive. [Col. 0687B]

He called Christ a boy by prophetic inspiration, and poor, as it is said: “Behold my servant whom I have chosen” (Matthew 12:18). Likewise the Apostle says: “Though he was rich, he became poor for our sake” (2 Corinthians 8:9). The Evangelist also bears witness that he was wise, saying: “And Jesus advanced in age and wisdom and grace before God [and human beings]” (Luke 2:52).

This excellent, poor, and wondrous boy was born in the kingdom of the old and foolish king, so that he might proceed from the house of prisoners into the kingdom, going away into a distant region, according to the Gospel parable, to receive a kingdom for himself and return. After some time he will condemn in judgment those who did not want him to reign over them. [Col. 0687C]

Nevertheless, there will be very many who will not rejoice in Christ, receiving Antichrist in his place. Nor do those rejoice in him who follow carnal desires—that is, the vices of the outer person—more than the wisdom of the inner person. These are people who are born into the kingdom through the grace of the Holy Spirit and the sacrament of baptism, but do not remain in it. Returning to vices, they waste away and perish in poverty.

### VERSE 17

Guard your foot when you enter the house of God, and draw near in order to hear. For obedience is much better than the sacrifices of fools, who do not know what evil they are doing.

He gives instructions for life and does not want to offend those who go to church. For it is not simply entering the house of God, but entering without offense, that is praiseworthy. And if it were the case that everyone who is in the church of God heard the word and the divine mysteries, he would never have added, “Draw near in order to hear.” Indeed, Moses alone drew near to hear God; the others could not draw near. [Col. 0687D]

Fools, not knowing that obedience is a remedy for sin and thinking that they can satisfy God by offering gifts, do not understand that it is evil and sinful to want to correct what they have done wickedly not through obedience to God’s commands [Edition: “not because of obedience”] [and] good works, but through gifts and sacrifices. To this agrees what Truth himself says in the Gospel: “Learn what this means: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13).

## CHAPTER V

### VERSES 1–2

Do not speak rashly, nor let your heart be quick to utter a word before God. For God is in heaven, and you are upon earth; therefore let your words be few. Many cares produce dreams, and in many words folly is found.

Most people think that these instructions are given for the present age [Jerome: “in the present passage”], so that we should not readily promise something before God and, without considering our strength, vow what we cannot fulfill. God is indeed present; and although he is in heaven and we seem to be on earth, he nevertheless hears what we say, and our foolishness is exposed by the multiplication of our words. [Col. 0688A]

Others, understanding the passage better, assert that it chiefly commands us not to think, whether speaking or reasoning, more about God than we are able to do, but to recognize our weakness. For as far as heaven is distant from earth, so far is our opinion separated from his nature; therefore our words ought to be measured. Just as a person occupied with many thoughts frequently dreams of the things about which he is thinking, so one who wishes to discuss too much about divinity falls into folly. [Col. 0688B]

Or certainly our words ought to be few for this reason: even what we think we know we see “through a mirror and in an enigma,” and we grasp it as though it were a dream, although we think that we hold it securely. When we have said more than seemed appropriate to us, the end of our discussion is folly; for through excessive speech we do not escape sin.

### VERSES 3–4

If you have made a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it; for an unfaithful and foolish promise displeases him. Whatever you vow, fulfill it. It is much better not to make a vow than, after making one, not to fulfill your promises.

The simple meaning requires no interpretation. It is better not to promise than not to do what one has promised, because the vows of unfaithful people who do not fulfill what they promise to God displease him [Manuscript: “are displeasing”]. God is truthful—indeed, he is truth—and he loves those who perform works of truth.

Let a person consider what he vows to God and whether he can fulfill what he is thinking of vowing. But every Christian is generally commanded to complete faith through works and not to resemble the Jews, who promised that they would do everything the Lord commanded, saying: “Everything that the Lord has commanded us, we will do” (Exodus 24:3). Later, however, they made calves and worshiped idols. [Col. 0688C–D]

### {425} VERSE 5

Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, nor say before the angel, “There is no providence,” lest perhaps God, angered by your words, destroy all the work of your hands.

The Hebrews understand it in this way: Do not promise what you cannot do. For words do not pass away into the wind; rather, they are immediately reported [Jerome: “carried”] to the Lord by the present angel who accompanies each person as a companion. And you, who think that God does not know what you have promised, provoke him to anger, so that all your works may be destroyed.

We, however, understand these words to rebuke those who claim that they sin out of the necessity of the flesh and nature, and who charge the Creator with having made them such that they are compelled to sin when overcome by carnal desire. This is what he means by: “Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin.” [Col. 0689A]

Therefore, do not seek empty excuses and give your flesh an occasion to sin, saying: “I am not the one who sins, but sin that dwells in my flesh.”

For if you say this, he says, you provoke God as the author of evil and sin, so that he becomes angry; and if you seem to have anything good, he will take it from your hands. Or rather, he will hand over to a reprobate mind the person who thinks such things, so that he may do what is improper.

### VERSE 6

Where there are many dreams, there are very many vanities and innumerable words. But you should fear God.

The Hebrews explain this passage as follows: Do not do the things mentioned above, about which he has already spoken, and do not readily believe dreams. When you see various things during the night’s rest and your soul has been shaken by different terrors or stirred by promises, disregard them, because they are dreams, and fear God alone. For whoever believes dreams will surrender himself to vanities and foolishness. [Col. 0689B]

Alternatively: Because I said and commanded, “Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin” and “Do not seek empty [Manuscript: “various”—an uncertain reading] excuses,” I now add this: in the sleep of this life and in the image of the cloud’s shadow in which we live, we can find many things that seem plausible to us and appear to excuse our sins. Therefore I warn you to beware of this in every way, so that you do not think that God is absent from your actions—or even from your perverse thoughts—but fear him and know that his providence is present in all your works. You were created with free choice [Manuscript: “of free will”]; you are not compelled, but will what you do. [Col. 0689C]

### VERSES 7–8

If you see the oppression of the poor, violent [Manuscript: “violated”] judgments, and justice overthrown in a province, do not be astonished at this matter, because one who is higher than the high exists, and there are others more eminent even above him, and the king over the whole earth rules the servant.

Let us preserve one continuous line of argument and follow the same meaning and order. Above he said: “Do not say before the angel, ‘There is no providence,’ lest perhaps God become angry at your voice,” and so forth. He was speaking against those who denied that human affairs are governed by God’s providence.

Here he understood that the following question could arise: If human affairs are governed by God as their author, why do the righteous suffer oppression? Why are judges wicked? Why does God not take vengeance on those who do and judge unjustly? [Col. 0689D]

Now he introduces and resolves the question that could be raised, saying: If you see the oppression of the poor man, who is proclaimed blessed in the Gospel, and affairs flourishing without justice [Jerome: “affairs flourishing, not justice”], do not be astonished, and do not regard it as something strange, because one higher than the high exists. God sees everything, and he has placed his angels over the judges and kings of the earth. They can certainly prevent injustice and prevail on earth more than any human power [Manuscript: “powers”].

But because he reserves judgment for the end and for the consummation of the world, when he will command reapers to come to the ripened crops so that the wheat may be separated and stored in the granary of the heavenly kingdom, while the darnel is handed over to eternal fire, he now waits and delays the sentence, until at the end of the world the wicked are punished and the righteous receive the crown of righteousness. [Col. 0690A]

### VERSES 9–10

The miser will not be satisfied with money, and the one who loves wealth will gain no fruit from it; this too is vanity. Where there are many riches, there are also many who consume them. And what benefit does the owner have, except that he sees his riches with his eyes?

Here the miser is described, one who is never satisfied with wealth: the more he acquires, the more he desires, like a dropsical person, for the more he drinks, the more his thirst increases.

The opinion of Flaccus also agrees with this; he says (*Letter 1 to Lollius*): [Col. 0690B]

> The miser is always in need . . . .

“Therefore,” says Ecclesiastes, “wealth benefits its owner in no way except that he sees what he possesses.” For the greater his estate, the more servants he will have to devour the wealth that has been gathered; but its master merely sees what he has and cannot consume more than one person’s food.

### VERSE 11

Sleep is sweet to the laborer, whether he eats little or much; but the abundance of the rich does not allow him to sleep.

The discussion is still about the rich and the miser, and they are compared with the laborer who sleeps without anxiety, whether he has eaten little or much. Through the labor of his work and the sweat he has expended, he digests any food and enjoys sweet sleep. But the rich man, distended by lavish meals and torn by conflicting concerns, cannot sleep: excess food overflows, while undigested food burns within the narrow confines of his stomach. [Col. 0690C]

Moreover, since sleep is called the common departure from this life, the rest of the person who works in the present and lives according to his strength in good works will be better than the wealth of those about whom it is written: “Woe to you who are rich, because you have received your consolation” (Luke 6:24).

### VERSES 12–16

There is also another very serious infirmity that I saw under the sun: riches preserved to the harm of their owner. For they perish in grievous misery. He has begotten a son who will be in extreme poverty. As he came forth naked from his mother’s womb, so he will return, and he will take nothing with him from his labor. This is truly a miserable infirmity: as he came, so he will return. What benefit is there, then, for him who has labored for the wind? All the days of his life he eats in darkness, amid many cares, misery, and sorrow. [Col. 0690D]

Join what follows with the preceding passage. Ecclesiastes describes the rich man as unable to enjoy his own wealth, as repeatedly coming into danger because of it, and as leaving what he has gathered neither to an heir nor to anyone else. Both he and his son, just as they came naked, will return naked to the earth, and none of their labors will accompany them; nor will he leave to an heir what he has gathered.

Is it not the most grievous sickness to be tormented by thoughts on account of wealth, and to gather with sorrow, groaning, indignation, quarrels, and futile labor riches that will perish and that we cannot take away with us when we die?

We can understand these same words of the teachings of philosophers or the perverse doctrines of heretics. They gather, to their own harm, the riches of various doctrines, but derive no benefit from them [Manuscript: “will derive no benefit”]. Nor do they leave lasting fruit to their followers; rather, both they and their disciples will return naked, without any merits [Manuscript: “good merits”], to the earth. They will possess not the light of true wisdom, but the darkness of ignorance, and, deprived of the true light, will lose all their labors at the judgment of him who says: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the intelligent” (1 Corinthians 1:19). [Col. 0691A]

### VERSES 17–19

This, then, seemed good to me: that a person should eat and drink and enjoy gladness from his labor, with which he himself has labored under the sun, during the number of the days of his life that God has given him. This is his portion, and it is also the portion of every person to whom God has given riches and possessions and granted power to eat from them, to enjoy his portion, and to rejoice in his labor. This is the gift of God. [Col. 0691B]

For he will not remember the days of his life very much, because God occupies his heart with delights.

He who feeds upon his labors in the darkness of cares and, with great weariness of life, gathers things destined to perish is said to be worse off than the one who enjoys present goods in gladness and pleasure. In the one case there is at least a small pleasure in enjoyment; in the other there is only the magnitude of anxiety.

He gives the reasons why being able to enjoy wealth is a gift of God: because the person will not remember his days of labor very much and therefore will not be in sorrow or tormented by thought, being carried away by present joy and pleasure.

But it is better, according to the Apostle (1 Corinthians 10:3), to understand this as referring to spiritual food, spiritual drink, and spiritual joy given by God; to see the goodness of God and the delight of one’s heart in all one’s labor, by which one labors spiritually in good works, comforted by the hope of future recompense. [Col. 0691C]

This is our portion: to rejoice in devotion to good works. Although this joy is good, it is not yet fully good until Christ is revealed, whose vision is perfect goodness and delight.

It should also be noted that “occupation” in this passage ought to be understood in a good sense, as spiritual devotion and true joy, which divine grace inspires here in those who labor under God’s commands.

## CHAPTER VI

### VERSES 1–6

There is another evil that I saw under the sun, and it is indeed common among human beings. There is a man to whom God has given riches, possessions, and honor, and nothing is lacking from his soul of all that he desires; yet God has not given him the power to eat from them, and a stranger will consume them. This is vanity and a great misery. [Col. 0691D]

If someone begets a hundred children, lives many years, and has many days of life, but his soul does not use the good things of his possessions and he lacks burial, I declare that an untimely birth is better than he. For it comes in vain and goes away into darkness, and its name will be erased by oblivion. It has not seen the sun or known the distinction between good and evil. And if he should live for two thousand years and not enjoy good things, do not all go to one place?

He describes the avaricious rich man and asserts that this evil is common among human beings: nothing that is thought good in the world is lacking to him, yet by the most foolish frugality he torments himself, preserving things for others to devour [Jerome: “things to be devoured”]. [Col. 0692A]

He adds hyperbolically that even if he has begotten a hundred children—not, like Adam, nearly a thousand—and has lived not merely one thousand but two thousand years, if his soul wastes away in desire and avarice, he is in a much worse condition than that untimely birth which perished as soon as it was born. The latter saw neither evil nor good; the former, although he possessed good things, was always sorrowful and tormented by thought. The untimely birth will therefore have more rest than that long-lived miser. Yet both will be carried away to an equal end, since both are removed by a similar death.

This can also be understood of Israel, to whom God gave the law and the prophets, the covenant and the promise, while the Savior said: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew 21:43). All these things have been transferred to another and foreign people, the nations, so that Israel may see its good things and not enjoy them. [Col. 0692B]

We are in a much better condition than they, although we were regarded by them as untimely and newly born, while they applauded themselves in their antiquity, boasting of their ancestors and saying: “Our father is Abraham” (John 8:39). Yet both they and we hasten to one place—that is, to the judgment of God.

As for what he says in the middle, “And indeed he had no burial,” this may mean either that the rich man does not think about his death and, although he possesses everything, is miserly even in building a tomb; or that he is often killed through ambushes because of these riches and is cast away unburied; or, as I think better, that he has done nothing good or honorable [Manuscript: “nothing good or worthy of honor”] by which he might obtain a memorial among posterity. He passes through life silently like an animal, although he possessed the means by which it could have become evident that he had lived. [Col. 0692C]

### VERSES 7–8

All a person’s labor is for his mouth, but his soul will not be filled with good things. What more does the wise person have than the fool? And what does the poor person have except to proceed to the place where there is life?

Everything people labor for in this world is consumed by the mouth, worn down by the teeth, and handed over to the stomach for digestion. Yet the soul of the person eating will not be filled, because it desires again what it has eaten.

And since neither the wise nor the foolish can live without food, and the poor person seeks nothing else except how he can sustain the organ of his little body, therefore the poor person hastens to the place where he sees that wealth exists. [Col. 0692D]

But it is better to understand this of the churchman who, instructed in the heavenly Scriptures, has all his labor in his mouth—that is, in spiritual teaching. His soul will not be filled, since he always desires to learn what he may teach. In this respect the wise person has more than the foolish: together with that poor person who is called blessed in the Gospel, he hastens to grasp the things that belong to life and walks along the narrow and constricted way that leads to life. The poor man is adorned with works [Manuscript: “and the poor man is poor in evil works”], and he knows where Christ, who is life, dwells.

### VERSE 9

It is better to see what you desire than to desire what you do not know. Yet this too is vanity and presumption of spirit.

It is better to act according to understanding and providence, because understanding is the eye of the soul, than to follow the will of the flesh, which leads the ignorant person to destruction.

Or certainly he rebukes the proud person who pleases himself and says that the one who has provided for everything is better than the one for whom nothing is useful [Jerome: “nothing is pleasing”] except what he himself has done. For this is an evil affliction of the mind and the worst presumption, since God scatters the bones of those who please themselves [Manuscript: “despises the bones”—an uncertain reading]. [Col. 0693A]

### {428} VERSE 10

He who is to come has already been called by his name, and it is known that he is a human being and cannot contend in judgment against one stronger than himself.

This openly proclaims the coming of the Savior, because the one who was to come, before he was seen in the body, had already been named in the Scriptures. It was known to the prophets and saints of God that he would be human, and, insofar as he is human, he cannot compare himself with the Father, as he himself says in the Gospel: “The Father who sent me is greater than I” (John 14:28). [Col. 0693B]

There are very many words here, and they contain much vanity in argument.

## CHAPTER VII

### VERSE 1

What need is there for a person to seek things greater than himself, when he does not know what benefits him during his life, through the number of the days of his pilgrimage and the time that has passed like a shadow? Or who will be able to tell him what will happen after him under the sun?

He seems still to be speaking about the Savior and forbidding us to inquire curiously what kind of person he was, how great he was, or how he would come, but only to believe what Holy Scripture bears witness about him. [Col. 0693C]

Since we do not know our own condition, our life passes like a shadow, and the future is uncertain, it is not advantageous for us to investigate things greater than we are able to comprehend. Rather, we should impose silence upon our mouth, believing that the one who was foretold has come.

### VERSE 2

A good name is better than precious perfumes, and the day of death than the day of birth.

Consider, he says, O human being, that your days are short and that, soon removed from the flesh, you will cease to exist in this life. Make a reputation for yourself through good works that will last longer, so that, just as noses are delighted by the fragrance of perfumes, so all posterity may be delighted by your name [Manuscript: “designation”].

This is what is said in Proverbs: “The memory of the righteous is with praise, but the name of the wicked rots” (Proverbs 10:7).

When he says, “And the day of death is better than the day of birth,” he shows that it is better to depart from this world and be free from the labors of this life than to be born merely for tribulations and labors and to endure all the evils that seem to come upon people in this world. [Col. 0693D]

Or certainly it is because, at death, what sort of people we are is known, whereas at the beginning of our birth it is unknown what sort of people we will become.

### VERSE 3

It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting; for in it the end of all human beings is recalled, and the living person considers what will happen.

It is more useful to go to a funeral than to a banquet, because there, through the remembrance of our condition and human fragility, we are admonished by the corpse present before us. At banquets, however, amid pleasure and rejoicing, even if we seem to retain some fear or compunction in our heart, we lose it and do not consider what we will become. [Col. 0694A]

### VERSE 4

Anger is better than laughter, because through a sorrowful expression the mind of the offender is corrected.

Laughter dissolves the wise person; anger rebukes and corrects the sinner. Let us be angry with ourselves because we have sinned; let us also be angry with other sinners, for their correction, not for our revenge.

### VERSE 5

The heart of the wise is where there is sadness, and the heart of fools is where there is joy.

“Blessed,” says the Savior, “are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5:5). Therefore let the wise person go to the house of one who mourns, who corrects himself and admonishes others to lament their sins, not to the house of the flatterer, who seeks the applause of his listeners rather than the tears of those who offend.

Such a teacher is to be lamented: rich in speech, not rich in action. Therefore he immediately adds in the following verse: [Col. 0694B]

### VERSES 6–7

It is better to be corrected by a wise person than to be deceived by the flattery of fools, because as the crackling of burning thorns beneath a pot is, so is the laughter of a fool. Yet this too is vanity.

Similar to this statement is the following: “The wounds of a friend are better than the deceitful kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27:6).

For just as burning thorns beneath a pot produce an unpleasant crackling, so the words of a flattering teacher will not benefit the listener—whether he is encouraging his hearers toward worldly cares, which are interpreted as thorns, or preparing them for future fire.

### VERSE 8

Calumny troubles the wise person and destroys the strength of his heart.

Let us use this verse if we see some righteous and wise man suffering calumnies and being troubled by the injustice of a judge, while God does not [immediately] come present to the aid of the person in danger. [Col. 0694C]

There are many tribulations of the righteous, because the love of many grows cold and iniquity abounds. For this the heart of the wise person who fears God will be troubled.

### {429} VERSE 9

The end of a speech is better than its beginning.

Epilogues in speaking are better than beginnings, because in the latter there is the start of speech, while in the former there is its completion. A person who goes to a teacher understands what is being said better at the end of the lesson than at the beginning. So completed righteousness is better than righteousness begun: the former grants victory, while the latter begins to fight.

Here we know only in part; but when what is perfect has come, what is partial will no longer be necessary.

The patient person is better than the arrogant. [Col. 0694D]

Since above he had permitted anger, saying that anger is better than laughter, lest we think that the anger arising from passion is being praised, he now commands that anger be removed through patience. There you placed anger for the correction of sinners and the instruction of those inferior to you [Manuscript: “he placed it”]; here, however, you placed patience, which is necessary not only in difficulties but also in more joyful circumstances, so that we may not become more exalted than is fitting.

### VERSE 10

Do not be quick to become angry, because anger rests in the bosom of a fool.

He forbids inconsiderate anger, because sudden fury has no counsel, and nothing should be done by a wise man without reason. Therefore a certain comic poet says: “Nothing in excess,” because every lack of moderation falls into vice.

Anger rests in the bosom of a fool. Anger is always joined to pride and seeks revenge. For although someone may seem powerful and be considered wise, if he is angry without reason, he is exposed as foolish. [Col. 0695A]

And in the Gospel: “Whoever is angry with his brother” will be judged worthy according to that or another assessment of judgment [Manuscript: “that assessment”].

### VERSE 11

Do not say, “Why do you think the former times were better than the present?”

Such a question is foolish. Therefore do not say that the days under Moses and under Christ were better than those of the present. For even at that time there were many unbelievers, and their days became evil; and now many believers are found, concerning whom the Savior said: “More blessed are those who have not seen me and have believed” (John 20:29).

Alternatively: You ought to live in such a way that the present days are always better for you than those that have passed, lest, when you gradually begin to decline, it be said to you: “You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth?” (Galatians 5:7). [Col. 0695B]

### VERSES 12–13

Wisdom is more useful than riches, and it benefits those who see the sun more greatly. For just as wisdom protects, so money also protects. But learning and wisdom have this further advantage: they give life to their possessor.

Wisdom with riches possesses greater glory. Some people need wisdom, others resources; and the better person is the one who provides both to the person lacking both.

One who is wise but not rich can indeed teach what is good, but sometimes cannot provide what is requested. Therefore he says: Just as wisdom protects, so money also protects. But wisdom is greater than riches in this respect: without any resources of this world, it gives life to the person who possesses it.

Nevertheless, it must be understood that this is said of true wisdom, which leads toward eternal life and guides the person who follows it to the sun of righteousness. Hence he says, “those who see the sun,” that is, those who understand what the sun of righteousness is and how one must reach it. [Col. 0695C]

### VERSE 14

Consider the works of God, for no one can correct the one whom he has rejected.

In this verse he clearly urges us to pursue wisdom and knowledge, so that we may consider how great and wondrous the works of God are, and how he has chosen one through gratuitous mercy and rejected another by a just judgment, as it is said concerning Jacob and Esau: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Romans 9:13).

It is also said in the Psalm: “All your ways are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10).

### VERSE 15

On a good day enjoy good things, and beware of an evil day. For God made the one as well as the other, so that a person may not find just complaints against him. [Col. 0695D]

By this he signifies that retribution belongs to everyone; therefore he warns us to beware of the evil day, that is, the day of vengeance. For to the person who acts well, the day of this life is good, as an opportunity to earn the day of eternal blessedness. Just as God made this day so that we might live well in it, so he also made that day for those who do evil.

Alternatively: Good and evil—that is, prosperity and adversity—should be endured courageously as they come to you, O man, because both always come by God’s judgment, which is just although often hidden. He forbids complaints against God about why some have happiness and others misery in this world.

### {430} VERSE 16

I have also seen this in the days of my vanity: a righteous person perishing in his righteousness, and a wicked person living for a long time in his wickedness.

The Prophet also marveled at and abhorred this in the seventy-second Psalm. The prophet Habakkuk likewise laments in his prophecy why the wicked have prosperous times while the righteous are tormented by many adversities.

God’s patience is hidden in this: the holy are afflicted now so that they may receive evils in their lifetime, while sinners are not punished for their crimes in the present age; thus he can restore eternal good to the former and inflict eternal [Manuscript: “perpetual”] evil upon the latter, as is read concerning Lazarus and the rich man.

Therefore the Psalmist mentioned above, looking toward the end of those who live prosperously here, exclaimed: “I thought that I might understand this; it is labor before me, until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand their end” (Psalm 72:16).

### Verse 17

Do not be excessively righteous, nor be wiser than necessary, lest you become stupefied. But whoever is unwilling ever to forgive the sins of his brothers, and wishes to exact vengeance for everything according to the fury of his own spirit, is more righteous than is fitting. For when the Savior says, “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged” (Luke 6:37), and, “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offenses” (Matthew 6:14), a teacher ought to be neither excessively rigid nor excessively lax in spirit, but should proceed along the royal road and carefully consider what is appropriate for each person’s salvation.

But when he says, “Do not seek more, lest you become stupefied,” he knows that our mind cannot comprehend perfect wisdom, and he commands us to recognize the measure of our frailty.

### Verse 18

Do not act very wickedly, and do not be foolish, lest you die at a time not your own. Since the Lord says, “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he return and live” (Ezekiel 18:32), it is enough to have sinned once; after a fall, we ought to raise ourselves up again. For if, according to those who discuss natural science, the swallow knows the herb chelidonium with which to restore sight to its young, and wounded she-goats seek dittany, why should we be unaware that the medicine of repentance has been appointed for sinners?

But when he says, “Lest you die at a time not your own,” we know that Korah, Dathan, and Abiram were swallowed by a sudden opening of the earth because of their rebellion against Moses and Aaron (Numbers 16), and that, for the correction of others before the day of judgment, very many have also been judged in this life before their time.

What he says, therefore, amounts to this: Do not add sins to sins, lest you provoke God and he inflict punishment upon you here.

### Verse 19

It is good for you to support the righteous, but do not withdraw your hand from him, because whoever fears the Lord neglects nothing. It is good to do good to the righteous; it is not unjust merely to support those who are members of the household of faith.

**[Note on the text, with reference to Col. 0695D and 0696D:]** These words from Saint Jerome should be supplied as follows: “It is good to do good to the righteous, but it is also not unjust to do good to sinners. It is good to support those who are members of the household of faith,” and so forth. But it is also commanded that one give to everyone who asks.

For the person who fears the Lord, and imitates his Creator, who makes his rain fall upon the righteous and the unrighteous, hastens to do good to everyone without respect of persons.

Alternatively: Since this miserable life is daily changed by various events, the mind of the righteous person should be prepared both for adversity and prosperity, and should ask for God’s mercy, so that whatever happens he may endure it with a free mind. For whoever fears the Lord is neither lifted up by prosperity [Ms., by what comes later] nor crushed by adversity.

### Verses 20–21

Wisdom strengthened the wise man more than ten rulers of the city. For there is no human being who does good and does not sin.

Wisdom, as is read elsewhere, is better than strength; here it says that it is stronger than ten rulers in one wise man.

Alternatively: The ten who have authority and dwell in the city are angels, who can attain the perfect number of ten [Jerome: “who attained the number ten”], and who assist the human race. But if one considers all forms of assistance, the assistance of wisdom—that is, of our Lord Jesus Christ—is greater than that of all the angels, because none of the angels was able to redeem the human race, which was subject to sins.

Then the Lord of the angels descended and healed us, sprinkled with his blood, from every infirmity of our sins. For just as through one human being death entered the world (Romans 5:12), so through one—namely, Jesus Christ—redemption came into the world.

### Verses 22–23

Also, do not set your heart upon all the words that are spoken, lest you happen to hear your servant cursing you. For your conscience knows that you too have often cursed others.

He therefore teaches the wise person not to listen to the tongues of those who curse, but, strengthened by the help of wisdom, to regard vain behavior as of little account and to rejoice more in the goodness of his conscience than to be saddened by the curses of others—especially one who knows that he himself has sometimes spoken against others. And if he wishes to be forgiven when he reproves another, let him also forgive others when they reprove him.

For if someone is curious about what others say and judge concerning him, he will always be in distress, since he is completely unable to restrain even the mutterings of his servants. At the same time, the passage teaches that one should not judge hastily, and that a person who has a beam in his own eye should not speak of the splinter in another’s.

### Verses 24–25

I tested everything through wisdom. I said, “I will become wise,” but it withdrew farther from me, much farther than it had been; and the depth is profound—who can find it?

He says that, as the books of Kings also testify, he sought wisdom beyond all other human beings and attempted to reach its end; but the more he sought it, the less he found it, being submerged in the midst of darkness and surrounded by the gloom of ignorance.

But alternatively: Whoever has been instructed in the Scriptures, the more he begins to rise—in Jerome’s text, “the more he begins to know”—the greater the obscurity that arises for him in them day by day. For we see in a mirror and in an image until what is perfect comes; therefore this wisdom of mortals is small in comparison with that wisdom which is given to the saints in the future kingdom of God.

### Verses 26–27

I examined everything in my mind, to know, consider, and seek wisdom and reason, and to understand the wickedness of the fool and the error of the senseless. And I found woman more bitter than death: she is the hunters’ snare, and her heart is a net; her hands are bonds. Whoever pleases the Lord will escape her, but the sinner will be captured by her.

Since Ecclesiastes had said above that he had tested everything through wisdom, and that the more he sought it, the farther it withdrew from him, he now says that he also found in his wisdom this evil which surpassed every evil in human affairs: namely, that woman is the source of all evils, because through her death entered the world, and she captures the precious souls of men. When she falls into the mind of a wretched lover, she drags him headlong and does not allow him to look before his feet, but fastens the young man’s heart like a snare and a net.

“Her hands are bonds”—that is, she can persuade but cannot use force, nor compel those unwilling to come to her. The righteous person who is good before God will be rescued from her; but the sinner, once captured, will be led away to death.

Let us not think that Solomon pronounced this judgment concerning every kind of woman. He speaks of what he experienced; for this reason he offended God, because he was captured by women.

This is the literal interpretation. But according to the spiritual understanding, heretical perversity is signified under the name of woman. She often binds the unwary with soft words, because hidden bread and stolen waters are usually sweeter to the foolish.

### Verses 28–30

“Behold, this I found,” says Ecclesiastes, “one thing and another, in order to discover the explanation that my soul is still seeking, but I did not find it. I found one man among a thousand, but among all women I did not find one. Only this I found: God made human beings upright, but they themselves became involved in innumerable questions.”

By treating everything carefully, I considered how I might find the explanation of one thing or another—that is, of any matter—or even discern, among human beings and their customs, who might be perfectly good. But among all men I found one who was perfectly good: Christ. As the Prophet says, “There is none who does good, not even one” (Psalm 13:1, 3). Christ alone was found to be good, without any stain of sin.

The number one thousand is placed here to distinguish the saints from sinners, who are signified by the name “woman.” Thus “man” is derived from virtue, and “woman” from softness. Woman may also be understood as carnal works, while man, who is named from virtue, may signify the excellence of the rational mind.

But lest he appear by these words to condemn the common nature of the human race and to make God the author of evil—since he would then be the creator of those who cannot avoid evil—he prudently anticipates this objection and says that we know ourselves to have been created good by God, but that, having been left with free will, we slide into worse things through our own fault while seeking greater things and thinking various thoughts beyond our strength.

## Chapter 8

### Verse 1

Who is like the wise man, and who knows the interpretation of a word? A person’s wisdom shines upon his face, and the strength of his countenance is changed.

Above he had taught that it is difficult to find a good person, and he had forestalled the question that arose against him by saying that God created human beings good, but that they had voluntarily fallen into sin.

Now, as though boasting, he enumerates what God has given to a good person: wisdom, the reasoning of prudence, knowledge of God’s hidden mysteries, and entrance into his secrets through the understanding of the heart.

Indirectly, however, he speaks about himself, saying that no one was as wise as he, and that no one knew problems and their solutions in the same way. His wisdom was praised by the entire people; it did not remain hidden only within, but also shone on the surface of his body and in the mirror of his face, and he portrayed the prudence of his mind upon his countenance beyond all other human beings.

Many promise that they possess wisdom and know the solution of divine Scripture, but few discover the true solution. It should also be understood that a wise person is often recognized by honorable conduct and distinguished from a fool by his appearance.

### Verses 2–4

I observe the king’s mouth and the commands of God’s oath. Do not hasten to withdraw from his presence, and do not persist in an evil action, because he will do whatever he wishes, and his word is full of authority. No one can say, “Why are you doing this?”

He seems to be speaking of the one of whom it is sung in the Psalm, “The king will rejoice in your strength, O Lord” (Psalm 20:1). And elsewhere, to signify that the kingdom of the Father and the Son is one, Scripture recalls: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Psalm 72:1). For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22). The Son who is king is the Son of God the Father, who is king.

His commandments, therefore, must be kept, since he says, “If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments” (Matthew 19:17). He also warns that God’s commandments should not be subjected to examination—asking why he commanded this or that—but that whatever he sees to have been commanded, the devout mind of a human being should hasten to fulfill, so that his delight may be in the law of the Lord day and night.

“God’s oath” is said in place of the affirmation of his judgment, which can in no way be changed. Therefore he counsels us not to remain in an evil action, because no one knows what the coming day may bring. Forgiveness has been promised to the repentant, but tomorrow is certain for no one. Hence Scripture says, “Do not delay turning to the Lord” (Sirach 5:8).

### Verse 5

Whoever keeps the commandment [Ms., “precept”] will experience no evil in the future.

Whoever keeps the Lord’s precept in this world will experience no evil. The wise heart understands the time and the answer. He commands that the king’s authority—that is, Christ’s—also be preserved, and that one should know what he commands, why he commands it, and at what time.

### Verses 6–7

There is a time and an occasion for every matter, and there is much affliction for a human being, because he does not know what has happened, and no messenger can tell him what will happen.

“There is a time for every matter,” he says—that is the same as what he said above, that everything has its proper occasion. Once there was a time for circumcision, but now there is a time of grace.

Indeed, there is great affliction for the human race, because a human being is born for labor and is afflicted by various tribulations. Often something different happens to him from what he hopes; he guards against one thing as though from an enemy, and is wounded by another’s dart, because he does not know the future, as the poet says:

> The human mind is ignorant of fate and of what the future lot will bring.  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid* 10
