Although no one is conscious of the future, he should nevertheless know that everything is done by God for the benefit of human beings and is ordered not without his will. Without his ordering, not even one sparrow falls into a snare.

### Verse 8

It is not within human power to restrain the spirit, nor does he have authority over the day of death. He is not permitted to rest when war breaks out, and wickedness will not save the wicked.

There is therefore no reason to grieve if we cannot know the future, or if we are often oppressed by more powerful wicked people, since everything ends in death. The proud and powerful person who has plundered everything cannot retain his soul when he is ordered to leave the body. His wickedness will not save him; rather, it increases his burden on the day of his departure, when he receives what corresponds to his deeds. When the misery of his sins wages war against him, he cannot be saved, because he has neglected the time of repentance [Ms., “because he neglected”].

### Verses 9–11

I considered all these things and gave my heart to every work that is done under the sun. Sometimes a human being rules over another for his own harm. I saw the wicked buried—those who, while they were still alive, had been in a holy place and had been praised in the city as though for righteous deeds. But this too is vanity. Because sentence against evil deeds is not quickly pronounced, the children of men commit evil without any fear.

Blessed Jerome interpreted this passage as follows:

“I gave my heart,” he says, “so that I might observe everything that is done under the sun, and especially this: that a human being receives power over other human beings, so that he may afflict and condemn whomever he wishes. When, therefore, I directed my mind to observing these matters, I saw the wicked die with such a reputation and be buried in such a way that they were considered holy on earth. While they were alive, they were thought worthy to be leaders of the Church and of the temple of God. Moreover, as they walked about arrogantly, they were praised in their evil deeds, as it is written: ‘The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who commits iniquity is blessed’” (Psalm 9:24).

This happens because no one dares contradict bishops when they sin. God does not immediately avenge the crime, but delays punishment while he awaits repentance. Sinners who are not immediately reproved and corrected, thinking that judgment will never come, persist in their crime.

We can take this testimony as directed against bishops who have received power in the Church and scandalize those whom they ought to teach and encourage toward better things. Such men are often praised in the Church after death [Ms., “in the world”], and are proclaimed blessed for deeds that they did not perform honorably, whether by their successors or by the peoples. This is indeed vanity: they do not hear what they did in the same way as they did it, nor are they immediately corrected for their sin. No one dares accuse a superior. Therefore, as though holy and blessed and walking in the commandments of the Lord, they increase sins with sins.

It is difficult to bring an accusation against a bishop: if he has sinned, no one believes it; and if he has been convicted, he is not punished.

### Verse 12

Nevertheless, because a sinner commits evil a hundred times and is sustained by patience, I know that it will be well with those who fear the Lord and revere his face.

Because the wicked sin very often—for this is what “a hundred times” signifies—God gives them an opportunity for repentance. He does not immediately punish them in their crime, but waits for them to turn from their iniquity and repent, because God does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live.

I understand, therefore, that God will be kind and merciful toward those who fear him, tremble at his word, repent of the past, and begin to guard themselves against the future. For after repentance, if a sinner returns again to his former sins, he is compared to a dog returning to its vomit.

### Verse 13

May it not be well with the wicked, and may their days not be prolonged; may they pass away like a shadow, those who do not fear the face of God.

He invokes evil upon those who do not fear God and wishes that their punishment not be long delayed, but that, removed immediately by death, they may receive the sufferings they deserve.

The Apostle says something similar: “Would that those who trouble us were cut off!” (Galatians 5:12). And elsewhere: “Alexander the coppersmith showed me much evil; may God repay him according to his deeds” (2 Timothy 4:14).

For evil people who do not wish to convert but remain in their wickedness, it is better to die than to live. The more days they live, the more atrocious a punishment they prepare for themselves. Hence the comic poet says:

> What evil should I wish upon a man, except that he live a long time?

### Verse 14

There is also another vanity that occurs upon the earth: there are righteous people to whom things happen that should happen to the wicked, as though they had done the deeds of the wicked; and there are wicked people who are so secure, as though they possessed the deeds of the righteous. But this too I judge to be the greatest vanity.

Among the other vanities that occur in the world through varied events, I also discovered this: things that ought to happen to the wicked frequently happen to the righteous, while the wicked live so happily in this world that you would think them perfectly righteous. The same is read in the Gospel concerning the rich man dressed in purple and the beggar Lazarus (Luke 16).

Psalm 72 also discusses why evil sometimes happens to the righteous and good to the wicked. But the Hebrews understand this passage as referring to the sons of Aaron, who perished while sacrificing to God, and to Manasseh, who, after so many evils, was brought back from captivity and restored to the kingdom, so that he might end his days happily.

### Verse 15

Therefore I praised joy, because there is no good for a human being under the sun except to eat, drink, and rejoice, and because this alone he may take with him from his labor during the days of his life that God has given him under the sun.

Our Preacher, who assumes many different persons, now gives voice to the words of the common people. They consider nothing else good except to rejoice by eating and drinking, to serve the pleasures of the age, and to attain the highest happiness.

But if this opinion is understood as it is written, it approves the miserable people whom the Lord in the Gospel declares blessed (Matthew 5)—namely, the poor, to whom he says the kingdom of heaven belongs—and likewise declares the hungry and thirsty blessed.

It is better, however, to understand these words spiritually, of the food and drink of wisdom, concerning which it is also read in the Psalm: “Wine gladdens the heart of man, and bread strengthens him” (Psalm 103:15). That these things are to be understood spiritually is shown by the following verse, where he says:

### Verses 16–17

I applied my heart to know wisdom and to understand the matter [Ms., “the extension”] that takes place upon the earth. There is a man who does not allow sleep to come to his eyes by day or by night, and I understood that, of all the works of God, a human being can find no explanation for what is done under the sun. The more he labors to seek, the less he will find; and even if he says that he is wise and knows, he will not be able to discover it.

He testifies, then, that it is better to spend day and night in meditation upon Holy Scripture than to waste in bodily banquets the time given by God for advancement in the study of wisdom, so that one may know God’s wonders and praise the Creator in his works. Although God’s judgments are hidden, they are nevertheless wonderful, and the Creator is to be praised in them.

What, then, should be said about the fool, when even the diligent investigator of wisdom cannot discover why this or that has happened, why the world is governed by various events, or why one person is born blind, another weak, and another seeing and healthy; why one has poverty and another riches; why one is noble and another without honor?

By these words he intimates that there are rational causes for everything, grounded in God’s justice, explaining why each thing occurs, but that these causes lie hidden and cannot be comprehended by human beings.

## Chapter 9

### Verses 1–2

I considered all these things in my heart, in order to understand them carefully. There are righteous and wise people, and their works are in the hand of God; yet no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but everything is kept uncertain for the future, since all things happen alike.

The sense of this statement is as follows: I applied my heart to this and wished to know whom God loved and whom he hated. I found that the works of the righteous are in God’s hand; yet I cannot know whether they are loved by God or not. I remain uncertain and wavering in my thoughts as to whether, like Job, they endure tribulations in this world for the testing of their righteousness, or whether they endure them through hatred, like very many sinners. This is now entirely uncertain.

### Verse 3

The same thing happens to the righteous and the wicked, to the good and the evil, to the clean and the unclean, to the one who sacrifices victims and the one who despises sacrifices. As with the good, so with the sinner; as with the one who swears falsely [Edit., “the one who is destined to perish”], so with the one who swears truly.

This is the worst thing among all that happen under the sun: that the same things happen to everyone. Matters that in themselves are neither good nor evil, and that the wise people of this age call “indifferent,” because they happen equally to the righteous and the unrighteous, disturb simple people, who ask why such things happen. Consequently, they do not believe that there is a judgment, although there will be a distinction among all things in the future.

The Lord himself says something similar in the Gospel: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the righteous and the unrighteous” (Matthew 5:45, 48).

When he says that the outcome is one for everyone, for the righteous and the wicked alike, he means the outcome either of distress or of death. Therefore they do not understand themselves to be worthy either of God’s love or of his hatred. He said that this was the worst of all things under the sun because here no distinction appears to exist between the good and the evil—at least among those who, with the Prophet, will not enter the sanctuary of God to understand their final destiny.

### Verse 4

Hence the hearts of the children of men are filled with wickedness and contempt during their life, and afterward they are led down to the underworld. No one lives forever, nor does anyone possess certainty of this.

He repeats the same meaning that he expressed earlier: common distress presses upon the righteous and the unrighteous alike. Therefore people do not fear committing sins, since they do not see God’s judgment in the present against the wicked, who are suddenly carried away to the underworld for their sins. They are not granted power to live forever, nor is anyone in this world so powerful that he can possess the ability to live without death.

Thus he immediately adds what follows:

### Verses 5–6

A living dog is better than a dead lion. For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing more, nor do they have any further reward, because the memory of them has been forgotten. Their love, hatred, and envy have likewise perished, and they have no share forever in anything that is done under the sun.

What he had said above—that the hearts of the children of men are filled with wickedness and iniquity, and that afterward everything ends in death—he now completes and repeats. As long as human beings live, they can become righteous; after death, no opportunity for a good work is given.

The living sinner, whom he compares to a dog, can become better than the dead righteous person, whom he calls a lion, because the living person can advance in good works, whereas the dead can add nothing to his merits.

We may also understand the living poor dog as the righteous person, and the dead lion as the powerful man of this age, who carried no good merits with him when he departed from this world. Their love, hatred, sacrifice, and everything else they could possess in this world also come to an end with the arrival of death. They can neither do anything just nor sin; neither add virtues nor vices.

Spiritually, let us also understand that Canaanite woman to whom it was said, “Your faith has saved you” (Matthew 9:22), as the dog according to the Gospel, and the dead lion as the circumcised people, as the prophet Balaam says: “Behold, the people will rise up like a lion’s cub, and like a lion exulting” (Numbers 23:24).

The living dog is us, from the nations; the dead lion is the Jewish people, abandoned by God. This living dog is better before the Lord [Ms., “before God”] than that dead lion.

We who are living know the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; but those who are dead know nothing, nor do they regard any promise or reward. Their memory has come to an end: they themselves do not remember what they ought to have known, nor does their Lord now remember them, since they perished in their crime. Their zeal, envy, and rivalry against Christ and the apostles have likewise perished.

### Verse 7

Go, then, eat your bread with joy and drink your wine with gladness, because your works please God.

As we have often said, all these things are better understood spiritually than carnally, lest we fall into the doctrine of Epicurus, who considered life blessed when it enjoyed bodily pleasures. Unless, perhaps, in the manner of a preacher, we suppose that Solomon is presenting the words of the common people and expressing their sentiments in their own person.

Let us speak according to a higher sense: Because you have learned from the preceding statement that everything ends in death, that in the underworld repentance is not fruitful, and that there is no return to virtue, hasten, strive, and repent while you are in this world. While you have time, labor. For God willingly receives repentance.

Eat the bread of charity and drink the wine of wisdom, so that your works may please God, as the true Ecclesiastes says in the Gospel: “Whoever thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). And in Proverbs: “Come, eat my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you” (Proverbs 9:5).

### Verse 8

At all times let your garments be white, and let oil not fail from your head.

“Have,” he says, “a clean and chaste body, and be merciful.” This is what the Truth himself says in the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12:35).

By the girding he signifies chastity of the body; by the burning lamps, which are nourished by the oil of good works, he signifies purity and the light of preaching. Our face is to be made cheerful by this oil. Let those who fast have this ointment upon their heads—something sinners cannot possess. The righteous person detests their oil when he says: “Let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” (Psalm 141:5).

Heretics commonly possess this oil with which they pour over the heads of the deceived—that is, smooth words full of deceit.

### Verse 9

Enjoy life with the wife whom you love, all the days of your unstable life that have been given to you under the sun, throughout all the days of your vanity. For this is your portion in life and in your labor with which you labor under the sun.

Follow wisdom and knowledge of the Scriptures, and join this wisdom to yourself as a wife. Concerning her it is said in Proverbs: “Love her, and she will preserve you; embrace her, and she will surround you” (Proverbs 4:8).

The days of vanity signify the days of this wicked age, about which the Apostle also does not remain silent. Beautifully, he commands us to seek true life during the days of our vanity together with wisdom as our wife. For this is our portion and the fruit of our labor: if, in this shadow-like life, we are able to find true wisdom that may lead us to eternal life.

### Verse 10

Whatever your hand is able to do, perform it diligently, because there is no work, reasoning, knowledge, or wisdom in the underworld, where you are going.

Do whatever good work you are able to do; now is the time to labor [Ms., “labor”]. You have time for labor, because death, signified by the name “underworld,” will take away your time for advancement. The Prophet says: “Will you work wonders for the dead, or will anyone in the underworld confess to you? Will anyone in the grave declare your mercy?” (Psalms 6:6; 88:11–12).

The Savior says something similar in the Gospel: “Work while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work” (John 9:4).

### Verse 11

I turned to something else and saw under the sun that the race does not belong to the swift, nor battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the learned, nor favor to the craftsmen, but time and chance belong to all.

The Epistle to the Romans agrees with this passage, where it says that it depends “not on him who wills or on him who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Romans 9:16). For without God’s grace, there is not even a good will in a human being, nor can a course of good works be completed without God.

This passage thoroughly overthrows the Pelagian sect. Whoever is weighed down by the great burden of sins is not fit for that race of which it is said: “I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7). But whoever is light and whose soul is not burdened cannot nevertheless reach heaven without the Lord’s help, because as long as the soul is weighed down by the burden of the flesh, a war remains for it against the powers of the air.

Even if it is strong [Ms., “whom, although he is strong”], it cannot conquer by its own powers, nor can it possess the heavenly and living bread except through wisdom, which urges: “Come, eat my breads” (Proverbs 9:5).

It should also be understood that a prudent person cannot possess the riches of salvation and wisdom unless he has received them from God, since they are God’s own riches. Elsewhere it is written: “The redemption of a man’s soul is his own riches” (Proverbs 13:8).

Nor can anyone learned find favor unless it is accompanied by knowledge and granted by God.

**[Manuscript and Jerome’s reading:]** “Nor can anyone learned find it if grace has not been accompanied by knowledge and granted by God.” [The supplied text marks the reading with uncertainty and a doubled question mark.]

Paul knew this when he said, “I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God that is with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10). And again: “His grace toward me was not in vain.”

Finally, no one knows when the time will come in which varied events and the end of all things will follow.

### Verse 12

A human being does not know his end. Just as fish are caught on a hook, and just as birds are seized in a snare, so human beings are caught at an evil time when it suddenly overtakes them.

As was said above, people do not know the tribulations or sudden miseries that come upon them by God’s uncertain judgment—often hidden, but never unjust. Nor can they know the hour of death itself, which will come like a thief to devastate the house of our pilgrimage.

As fish are caught in a net and birds in a snare, so sudden troubles will entangle the children of men.

According to the allegory, it should be understood that the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea—that is, like evangelical preaching cast into the stormy waves of this world. Hence the Lord says at the calling of the apostles: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4:19).

By contrast, heretics possess the net of evil preaching, by which they capture innocent souls for destruction. Their net is agreeable speech, flattering eloquence, false or forced fasts, humble clothing, and imitation of virtues. Through these things they set a snare for simple souls in order to capture them, just as fish are caught in a net and birds in a snare.

It should also be understood that ecclesiastical men, who are called “children of men” and are of little faith, can quickly fall.

It should be noted [Ms., “also”] that throughout the book, wherever “children of men” occurs, the Hebrew has “sons of man,” that is, “sons of Adam.” Nearly all Scripture is full of this idiom, calling the entire human race the children of Adam.

### Verses 13–15

I also saw this wisdom and considered it very great. There was a small city with few men in it. A great king came against it, surrounded it, and built siegeworks around it. The siege was completed, and a poor man was found within it. By his wisdom he delivered the city, but afterward no one remembered that poor man.

While others say that everything is uncertain and that the righteous have nothing more than the unrighteous, I judged wisdom to be very great in this respect: it often happens that a city is small, its inhabitants few, and it is surrounded by an army of innumerable enemies; the people within are killed by siege and famine; and suddenly, contrary to everyone’s expectation, a humble and poor man is found who possesses greater wisdom than all the rich, great, and powerful.

While the proud are endangered and terrified by the siege, he thinks and investigates how he may rescue the city from its evils.

But human forgetfulness is ungrateful. Once they have been delivered to freedom, the captivity dissolved, and liberty restored to their homeland, no one remembers that wise poor man. No one gives thanks to the poor man for their salvation; instead, everyone honors the rich, who were able to provide no assistance in the danger.

Alternatively: The small city with few men in it, in comparison with the whole world, is the Church. Against it the great king, the devil, often rises—not because he is great, but because he boasts that he is great—and surrounds it with a siege, whether persecution or some other kind of distress.

Within it he finds a poor and wise man, our Lord Jesus Christ, who became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9), and who delivers the city by his wisdom.

But, alas, when the city has been delivered by this poor wise man, scarcely anyone remembers him, and scarcely anyone considers his commandments. Instead, giving themselves wholly to luxury and pleasures, they seek riches, which cannot deliver them in a time of necessity and distress.

## VERSE 16

And I said that wisdom is better than strength. How, then, has the wisdom of the poor man been despised, and his words not been heard? When everything is prosperous, no one remembers that poor wise man, but everyone admires wealth and power [Manuscript: “although … may remember … may admire”]. Yet, throughout all the interpretations given above, I honor more highly the despised wisdom and the words that no one deigns to hear.

## VERSE 17

The words of the wise are heard in silence, more than the shouting of a ruler among fools. For the words of the wise are heard in quiet and measured silence; they do not seek to arouse the applause of the crowd, but desire the salvation of their hearers. Whoever is foolish, however powerful he may be, and whether he possesses the shouting of his own voice or the acclamation of the people, is counted among the senseless, since he seeks human praise rather than the improvement of the people who listen.

## VERSE 18

Wisdom is better than weapons of war, and whoever sins in one thing will lose many good things. Here too he prefers wisdom to strength, saying that it is more effective in battles than the weapons of combatants. It frequently happens that, through the foolishness of one person, great resources and riches perish.

But when he says, “Whoever sins in one thing will lose many good things,” the apostle James makes a similar statement when he says: “Whoever [but] sins in one thing has become guilty of all” (James 2:10). Whoever sins against charity alone will be found deprived of every good.

# CHAPTER 10

## VERSE 1

Dead flies spoil the sweetness of perfume; wisdom and a little glory are more precious than the folly of a short time. He has given an example of the preceding meaning, in which he said that through one fool many good things can be overturned: just as an evil element mixed with good contaminates many, so flies, if they die in perfume, destroy [and] both its fragrance and its flavor.

And because cunning is often mixed with wisdom, and malice with prudence, he commands us to seek simple wisdom, and to combine the prudence of serpents with the innocence of doves, so that we may be prudent toward the good but simple toward evil.

Alternatively: Humble glory is more precious than proud exaltation; and it is better to appear foolish for a time—that is, simple—than glorious and proud.

{438}

## VERSES 2–3

The heart of the wise man is in his right hand, but the heart of the fool is in his left. Yet, when the fool walks along the road, although he himself is senseless, he considers everyone else foolish. In the Gospel it is commanded that the left hand of the wise man should not know what his right hand is doing (Matthew 5:39; 6:3). And when we are struck on the right cheek, we are not commanded to offer the left cheek to the one striking us, but the other one. The righteous person, however [Manuscript: “indeed”], has no left side in himself; everything in him is right.

Whoever is wise always thinks about the age to come, which leads to the right; whoever is foolish always seeks the present, which is placed on the left.

The following verse, in which he says, “Yet, when the fool walks along the road, although he himself is senseless, he considers everyone else foolish,” has this meaning: Because the fool sins himself, he hopes that everyone sins in the same way, and he judges everyone according to his own character.

## VERSE 4

If the spirit of one who has power rises against you, do not leave your place, because healing will cause great sins to cease [Manuscript: “if it should rise”]. Scripture now signifies the ruler of this world, the governor of these darknesses, and the one working in the sons of disbelief, whom the Apostle also mentions. If he rises into our heart and the mind receives the wound of an evil thought, we must not voluntarily give it room, but fight against the most wicked thought and be freed from the greatest sin—namely, lest we complete the thought in deed. For it is one thing to sin in thought and another to sin in deed.

Concerning this great sin it is written in the Psalm: “If they do not rule over me, then I shall be blameless, and I shall be cleansed from the greatest offense” (Psalm 18:14).

## VERSES 5–7

There is also an evil that I have seen under the sun, as though proceeding by mistake from the presence of a ruler: a fool placed in high dignity, while the rich sit below. I have seen slaves on horses and princes walking on the ground like slaves.

He therefore recalls having observed this injustice in the world: that the wicked rule over the righteous, and that those who are worse are often made higher [have been made] than those who are better. This occurs not only in secular powers but also frequently in the dignity of the Church. Priests are chosen not for the merits of their virtues but through the favor of the people and the will of rulers, by the prompting of the devil’s deceit and the permission of God’s just judgment, on account of the merits of the people. As it is said in the Prophet: “Wicked priests are the sins of the people,” so that they may have blind leaders who are themselves blind, until they fall together into the pit of destruction.

The following statement also suits this meaning: “I have seen slaves on horses and princes walking like slaves on the ground.” Those who are slaves of vices and sin—or so lowly that they are reckoned slaves by men—may, through public crimes and a sudden dignity bestowed by the devil, appear to be exalted; while good teachers who fear God are oppressed and humbled [Manuscript: “made humble”] by the office of slaves.

## VERSE 8

Whoever digs a pit will fall into it himself, and whoever tears down a hedge will be bitten by a snake. The meaning is partly simple and partly mystical.

Solomon himself says elsewhere: “Whoever sets a snare will be caught in it” (Ecclesiasticus 27:29). And in the seventh Psalm: “He opened a pit and dug it out, and he fell into the pit that he made” (Psalm 7:16).

The strengthening of the hedge [Manuscript: “weakening”] consists in ecclesiastical and apostolic doctrines. Whoever dissolves them and wishes to pass beyond them is struck by the serpent in the very thing that he neglects—the statutes of the holy Fathers—that is, he is wounded by the devil. Concerning this serpent it is written in Amos: “If he descends into hell, I will command the serpent, and it will bite him” (Amos 9:3).

## VERSE 9

Whoever moves stones will be hurt by them, and whoever splits wood will be wounded by it. Holy stones are also rolled over the earth in Zechariah (Zechariah 9:16); for they do not stand firm with steadfast purpose, but pass away, always striving toward higher things and hastening to depart from here.

From these living stones the Savior’s city is built in the Apocalypse (Revelation 21:18), and the Apostle mentions that the Church is built from them [Manuscript: “does not fail to mention it”]. Whoever removes these living stones from the building [Manuscript: “structure”] of the Church through any heretical perversity will be afflicted with eternal pain on their account. In splitting the wood, he too will suffer danger from it.

Heretics are fruitless wood and a forest without useful fruit. On account of their schismatic division, the prudent and ecclesiastical teacher will be wounded in spirit, as the Apostle says: “Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (2 Corinthians 11:29).

## VERSE 10

If the iron has become blunt, and is not as it was before but has grown dull, it will be sharpened with much labor; and after diligence will come wisdom.

“If,” he says, “someone sees that through negligence in learning the holy Scriptures he has a dull understanding, and does not understand himself [to have remained] such as he was before, when he diligently acquired spiritual meanings in the divine books”—for it sometimes happens that, possessing a little wisdom, a person is lifted up in pride and stops learning. Gradually, however, what he knew is diminished because nothing is added to it, and his breast remains empty of learning. Iron that had been sharp becomes blunted through idleness, and through sloth it suffers, as it were, a kind of rust of wisdom.

If someone has suffered this, he should not despair of a remedy for his recovery. Let him go to a teacher and be instructed by him again; after labor and diligence, through great exertion he will be able to recover the wisdom he had lost.

{439}

## VERSE 11

If a serpent bites in silence, the one who secretly slanders is no less harmful. The meaning here is simple. The serpent and the slanderer are equals. Just as the serpent, biting secretly, injects poison, so the person who secretly slanders pours the venom of his heart into his brother, and is no less than a serpent. Since the human tongue was created for blessing and for the building up of one’s neighbor, this person makes it equal to a serpent by perversely abusing its powers.

Alternatively: If the devil-serpent bites someone secretly and, without anyone knowing, infects him with the poison of sin, then, if the one who has been struck remains silent, does not repent, and refuses to confess his wound to a teacher, the teacher—who possesses a tongue for healing—will not easily be able to help him.

## VERSE 12

The words of the mouth of the wise are gracious, but the lips of the fool will bring him down. If folly were content with its own rusticity, it would possess somewhat less evil. But now it wages war against wisdom, and whatever prudence it sees in a learned man, it refuses to accept, goaded by jealousy.

The wise man speaks words of knowledge, words of grace, which can provide benefit to those who hear. The fool’s ears, however, do not hear what is said in the way it is said. On the contrary, the fool tries to undermine the prudent man and make him like himself. Indeed, the wise man is brought down when he speaks into the ear of an imprudent person, and his words perish in a deep abyss, so to speak. Hence blessed is the one who speaks into the ear of someone willing to hear.

[Col. 0709D]

## VERSES 13–14

The beginning of his words is folly, and the end of his mouth is the worst error. The fool multiplies words. A person does not know what has been before him; and who can tell him what will be after him?

He is still discussing the fool, whose lips bring down the wise man. Or, according to another interpretation, they cause the fool himself to fall. The beginning and end of his speech are folly and the worst error, because the fool does not remain in the judgment of the prudent, but thinks that through multiplying words he has become learned and can escape sin.

Since he remembers neither the past [Manuscript: “may remember”] nor knows the future, wrapped in the darkness of ignorance and promising knowledge to himself alone, he thinks himself learned and wise if he multiplies words.

This may be understood of heretics, who do not grasp the statements of prudent men but prepare themselves for contrary disputes, accumulating vanity and great error both at the beginning and at the end of their speech. Although they know nothing, they say more than they understand.

## VERSE 15

The labor of fools will weary those who do not know how to go to the city. Reader, join these verses also with the preceding ones.

Understand them either generally of all fools who do not know God and do not know how to go to the city of Catholic peace, or specifically of heretics engaged in disputation, who have gone out from the city of God into perverse strongholds, whose city the Lord destroys, in the words of the Psalmist.

Whoever reads the vain labors of the philosophers will be able to prove the truth of what is said: “The labor of fools will weary them.” They sought the truth with every effort, but because they had neither a guide nor a forerunner on the way, and [having thought] through human senses that they could grasp the height of wisdom, they did not reach the city of God.

Concerning it and its inhabitants it is written in the Psalm: “Lord, in your city you will reduce their images to nothing” (Psalm 72:20). Concerning this city the prophet Isaiah likewise says: “I am a fortified city, a city that is attacked” [Manuscript: “a city that is not attacked”] (Isaiah 27:3, according to the Septuagint).

This city of truth and wisdom, although firm and strong, is known to be attacked [Manuscript: “they strive to attack it”] by all the wise men of the world and by heretics. What we have said of philosophers we understand in the same way of heretics: they labor and weary themselves in the study of the Scriptures in vain, since they are unable to find the truth.

{440}

## VERSES 16–17

Woe to you, land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning. Blessed is the land whose king is noble and whose princes eat at the proper time for refreshment, and not for luxury.

He seems to condemn the rule of the young and to judge luxurious rulers, since in the one case wisdom is weakened by age, while in others mature age is enervated by pleasures. Conversely, he approves a ruler liberally trained in good works, and praises those rulers who in no way put their own pleasure [Perhaps: “will”] before the affairs of the citizens, but take food after much labor and administration of the commonwealth, as though compelled by necessity and not driven by luxury.

Alternatively: “Woe to the land”—that is, to the carnal person—whose king is the devil, who is always desirous of new things, and who has as judges and rulers those who love the pleasures of this age. They are accustomed to say, or even to fulfill in deed: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” (Wisdom 2:6; Isaiah 22:13).

Conversely, the blessed Church is the one whose king is Christ, the son of noble and holy parents—namely, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—and descended from the line of David. Sin had not ruled over them, and for that reason they were truly free and noble. From them was born the blessed Virgin Mary, who had no offshoot and no shoot springing from her side; rather, all her fruit burst forth into a speaking flower in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs 2:1).

Her princes are also the apostles and all the saints, who have as king the son of noble parents—namely, one born from Abraham, not from the slave woman Hagar, but from free Sarah [Manuscript: “born through Sarah’s freedom”]. They neither eat in the morning nor hastily; for in the present age they do not seek their pleasure, but they will eat at the proper time, when the time of reward has arrived. Concerning them the Savior himself says in the Gospel: “And I appoint for you a kingdom, so that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22:29–30).

## VERSE 18

Through sloth the framework will collapse, and through the weakness of the hands the house will drip. Our house, which was created together with the condition of the human being, or the dwelling that we have in the heavens, will collapse because we are lazy and slow toward good works. Every framework that ought to carry the roof upward falls to the ground and crushes its inhabitant. When the help of hands and virtues grows numb, every force above us and the storm of the clouds breaks forth upon us.

What we have interpreted of one human being can better be understood of the Church: through the negligence of its rulers all its height collapses, and the allurements of vices are found where the covering of virtues was thought to be.

## VERSE 19

They make bread and wine for laughter, so that those who drink may feast; and money obeys everything.

The meaning of this statement depends on what came before. In speaking of laziness and the negligence of teachers, he said that the Church would be humbled, its summit would fall, and its beams would be drenched [Manuscript: “would flow through”].

Now he speaks of those same teachers, accusing them of serving the pleasures and luxury of the world, and banquets more than the salvation of the flock entrusted to them through the preaching of God’s word. Bishops and presbyters established in the Church do not labor in speech and teaching; or they teach what is pleasing for the people to hear, so that they may have the favor of their listeners rather than their improvement.

Thus, in laughter, they serve the people the bread of eternal life and the wine of wisdom—not for salvation but for destruction. The teachers themselves seek riches, wealth, and food through promises of pleasure, and attain secular honors; those who are subject to them often lose the heavenly honors.

[Col. 0711D]

## VERSE 20

In your thought do not slander the king, and in the secret chamber of your bedroom do not curse the rich, because the birds of heaven will carry your voice, and the winged creature will announce the judgment.

This is a simple command, building up those who hear it, lest, overcome by anger and fury, we burst into cursing and slander against kings and rulers. For contrary to expectation, it sometimes happens that, if what we have said against them is reported to them, we incur danger through the unrestrained use of our tongue.

When he says, “The birds of heaven will carry away the voice, and the winged creature will announce the word,” this is to be understood hyperbolically. We are accustomed to say that even the walls themselves, in whose presence we speak, will not conceal what they have heard. But it is better to understand the command in this way: we should know that we are commanded not only to say nothing rash against Christ, but also, in the secret places of the heart, even when we are constrained by various tribulations, to think nothing blasphemous or impious.

And because the love we show to Christ must also be shown to our neighbor—“Love the Lord your God, and also your neighbor as yourself”—he now commands that after the king we should not easily slander even the saints, nor disparage with a biting tongue [Manuscript: “with the sharpness of the tongue”] those whom we see enriched with wisdom, knowledge, and virtues.

The angels who travel around the earth and are ministering spirits, and who speak in Zechariah—“We have traveled around the earth, and behold, the whole earth is inhabited and at rest” (Zechariah 1:11)—may carry our words to heaven like birds, along with our thoughts. What we think secretly is not hidden from the knowledge of God.

# CHAPTER 11

## VERSE 1

Cast your bread upon the passing waters, for after many days you will find it. He exhorts us to almsgiving: everything should be given to whoever asks, and good should be done without distinction [Manuscript: “with distinction”].

Just as one who sows upon irrigated ground awaits the fruit of his sowing, so the person who gives to the needy sows not a grain of seed but bread itself, awaiting its multiplication as though at interest, and, when the day of judgment comes, receiving much more than he gave.

Alternatively: In whatever person you see that water of which it is said, “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38), do not be reluctant to provide the bread of wisdom, the rational bread of speech. And “after many days you will find it”—that is, in the heavenly recompense you will find the length of the days of eternal life. If you do this frequently, you will find that you have not sown the seed of teaching in vain.

I think something similar is said in Isaiah: “Blessed is the one who sows beside the water, where the ox and the donkey tread” (Isaiah 32:20). That teacher is worthy of blessedness who sows upon the well-watered breast of his hearers, gathering a people both from Jews and from the nations.

## VERSE 2

Give a portion to seven, and also to eight, because you do not know what evil will be upon the earth. He therefore commands that both Testaments—the Old, signified by the number seven, and the New, understood in the number eight—be held in worthy and holy reverence.

The Jews gave a portion to seven, believing in the Sabbath, but did not give one to eight, denying the resurrection of Christ on the Lord’s Day [Manuscript: “of the Lord’s Day”]. Conversely, the heretics Marcion and Manichaeus, and all who tear the old law apart with savage mouths, give a portion to eight, accepting the Gospel; but they do not assign the same honor to the number seven, rejecting the old law.

We, however, should believe both things that he sets forth and venerate both. We cannot yet comprehend in our minds the torments and deserved punishment reserved for those who dwell upon the earth of unbelief—namely, Jews and heretics—who deny one of the two.

The Hebrews therefore understand this passage as follows: “Observe both the Sabbath and circumcision” [Manuscript: “Observe the Sabbath and circumcision”], lest, if you should fail to do this, unexpected evil come upon you.

## VERSE 3

If the clouds are filled, they will pour rain upon the earth. If a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, in whatever place it falls, there it will remain.

Observe the commandments that were prescribed to you above, so that the clouds may pour their rain upon you in God’s blessing. For wherever you prepare a place and future dwelling for yourself, whether toward the south or toward the north, there you will remain when you have died.

Alternatively: For this reason we said above, “Cast your bread upon the face of the water, and give to everyone who asks,” because clouds too, when they are full, distribute their riches to mortals. And [you], like a fruitful tree, although you may live long, will not exist forever. Overthrown by the sudden force of the winds, as by a storm of death, wherever you fall, there you will remain forever—whether your final hour finds you harsh and severe, or gentle and merciful.

Alternatively: The clouds are the prophets and teachers. When they possess many meanings of sacred Scripture in their hearts, they are then able to rain down the commandments of teaching and to say: “Let my speech be awaited like rain” (Deuteronomy 32:2).

When he says that the tree will fall either toward the south or toward the north, as I judge, the south is always understood in a good sense and the north in a bad one. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: “Arise, north wind”—that is, “Depart and go away”—“and come, south wind” (Song of Songs 4:16). There is no tree that is not either toward the north or toward the south, because every person, good or evil, will die.

[Col. 0713C]

{442}

## VERSE 4

Whoever watches the wind will not sow, and whoever considers the clouds will never reap. Whoever considers whom he should benefit, and does not give to everyone who asks, often passes by the person who deserves either the consolation of mercy or the seed of God’s word.

For even amid prosperity, adversities arise while we are unaware. Therefore the word of God must be preached in season and out of season. The good sower, frightened neither by the wind of adversaries nor overshadowed by the clouds of flatterers, must not cease sowing the seed of preaching.

Without considering the clouds or fearing the winds, we must therefore sow in the midst of storms. We must not say, “That time is favorable, this one useless,” since we do not know what is the way and will of the Spirit who disposes all things. Hence it follows:

## VERSE 5

Just as you do not know what is the way of the spirit, or how the bones are joined together in the womb of a pregnant woman, so you do not know the work of God, who is the governor of all things.

Just as you do not know the way of the spirit and of the soul entering the little one, and do not know the variety of bones and veins in the womb of a pregnant woman—how, from a lowly element, the human body is shaped into various forms and limbs; how from the same seed one thing softens into flesh, another hardens into bones, another pulses in veins, and another is bound in sinews—so you will not be able to know the works of God, who is the maker of all things.

From this he teaches that we should not fear contrary circumstances, nor rashly judge concerning the winds and clouds mentioned above, since the sower must scatter seed in its proper time and leave the outcome to the Lord’s judgment. For it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy (Romans 9:16).

## VERSES 6–8

In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not let your hand cease, because you do not know which will rise, this or that; and if both together, it will be better.

Light is sweet, and it is pleasant for the eyes to see the sun. If a person lives for many years and rejoices in all of them, he should remember the dark time and the many days; when they come, they will convict the past of vanity.

He exhorts us to do good to everyone and not to choose the person to whom we should do good or the time at which we should do it. He never wants you to cease from good work; rather, let the evening find the justice of the morning, and let the rising sun increase the mercy of the evenings.

It is uncertain which work may please God more and from which the fruit of righteousness may be prepared for you. It can happen that not one but both please God.

Alternatively, this may be understood of the ages of a person’s life, so that we do good equally in youth and in old age, because you do not know whether you will please God more in youth or in prolonged old age.

Youth is of no benefit—

@ [Col. 0713D] End of the manuscript codex: “frugality,”

—if old age is spent in luxury. For on whatever day the righteous person goes astray, his former righteousness will not be able to deliver him from death.

But if, according to both interpretations, you have always done good and maintained an equal course throughout every age, you will see God the Father as the sweetest light; you will see Christ, the sun of righteousness.

Moreover, if you live many years, possess all good things, or perform good works, and know that you will always die, and if the coming of darkness—that is, death—is always before your eyes, you will despise present things as fleeting, fragile, and perishable. Whoever does this will see Christ, the sun of righteousness, always and forever.

Alternatively: Light is the teaching of heavenly wisdom, and it is good for the eyes to see the sun—that is, for the senses of the heart to see Christ.

## VERSES 9–10

Rejoice, therefore, young man, in your youth, and let your heart be in goodness.

From this point to the end of the little book, the teachers offer various interpretations. The Hebrews think that these words were spoken to the people of Israel, who are commanded to enjoy their riches before the time of captivity comes upon them or changes youth into old age—yet in such a way that their heart is in goodness, that is, in the law of God.

He also admonishes them to walk, in days of prosperity and salvation, in the ways of their heart and in the sight of their eyes—that is, in consideration of God’s commandments—rather than in carnal desires. He tells them to know that God will judge them for everything they have done, whether good or evil, and to remove anger from their heart and wickedness from their flesh—that is, evil thoughts and the lusts of their flesh. For the desires of the flesh, of youth, and of carnal pleasures are vain.

He also tells them always to remember their Creator before the day of tribulation arrives—that is, the misery of Babylonian or Roman captivity—in which they will be unable to exercise their will.

They explain the whole passage in which he says, “Before the sun, the moon, and the stars grow dark,” through the passage where Scripture says, “The dust will return to the earth from which it came, and the spirit will return to God who gave it” (Ecclesiastes 12:2, 7), as referring to the condition of Israel’s existence. They say that Solomon diligently urges the people of God to do all these things before all their honor and glory are taken from them: their leaders and judges, priests, temple and sacrifices, power and kingdom, and the saints whom they wish to understand as the sun, moon, and stars.

All these will be removed before Nebuchadnezzar comes, or Titus, the son of Vespasian, summoned by the prophets so that their predictions might be fulfilled. This will be on the day when the angels who preside over the temple withdraw; when the strongest men in Israel’s army will bend; when the words of the teachers will become idle; and when the prophets, who used to receive from heaven the light of their visions, will grow dark.

It will be when the doors of the temple are closed, Jerusalem is humbled, and the Chaldean comes, prophesied in the words of Jeremiah as though by the song of a bird. The daughters of the Song and the choirs of those singing psalms will fall silent.

It will be the time when, on arriving at Jerusalem, even the enemies of God will fear its greatness, and will be afraid on the road when they hear of the destruction of Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, and of his army (Isaiah 37). They think that this is what is meant: “From the Exalted One”—that is, from the God of the Hebrews—“they will be afraid.”

In those days the almond tree will blossom—that staff and rod which Jeremiah saw at the beginning of his prophecy (Jeremiah 1:11). The locust will grow fat: Nebuchadnezzar with his army. The caper plant will be scattered: God’s friendship with Israel.

All this happened to Israel, because the man went into his eternal house and, under God’s protection, returned to the heavenly things. While he dwells in his tabernacle, they will go about the street mourning and weeping, surrounded by the siege of their enemies.

Rejoice, therefore, Israel, in the youth of your prosperity, before the silver cord is broken—that is, while your glory is still with you. Before the golden band returns—that is, before the ark of the covenant is taken away. Before the pitcher is shattered at the fountain and the wheel is rolled over the cistern—that is, while the precepts of the law and the grace of the Holy Spirit remain in the Holy of Holies. And before you return to Babylon, from which you came forth in the loins of Abraham; before you begin to be crushed in Mesopotamia, from which you once departed; and before all the grace of prophecy, with which you were once inspired, returns to its giver.

We, however, returning more appropriately to the discussion in the preceding order, will try to explain each point individually.

According to the tropological interpretation, the meaning of this chapter looks back to what was said above: “In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not let your hand cease.” This is to be understood as meaning that good must be done at every age and that God’s judgment must be feared in all our works.

For he says here: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth,” and immediately adds: “And let your heart be in goodness,” lest he appear to exhort us to the luxury of the flesh. The Apostle says something similar: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Philippians 4:4).

Blessed is the person who does good with a joyful spirit and rejoices to exercise his heart in goodness rather than in evil. “Let your heart be in goodness in the days of your youth.” He wishes the flourishing age to flourish with the beauty of virtues, and to walk in contemplation of the heart—that is, in wisdom, which he designates by the name of the eyes—rather than follow the desires of the flesh, because “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Galatians 5:17), whose works the Apostle distinguished.

He admonishes us to do these things before the night of eternal death comes, in which no one will be able to work. Thus Truth itself says in the Gospel: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John 12:35). In this passage Scripture continually admonishes us, while we live, to think about the future judgment, in which everything we have done will be judged.

## VERSE 10

Remove anger from your heart, and take wickedness away from your flesh, because youth and pleasure are vain.

By anger he includes all the disturbances of the mind; by wickedness of the flesh he signifies all bodily pleasures. He urges us to abandon the vices of youth, because youth is joined to folly and commonly gives birth to harmful pleasures.

# CHAPTER 12

{444}

## VERSES 1–3

Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the time of your affliction comes and the years approach of which you will say, “They do not please me”; before the sun, the light, the stars, and the moon grow dark, and the clouds return after the rain; when the guardians of the house will tremble, the strongest men will be changed, the women grinding will cease because they have become few, and those who see through the openings will grow dark.

Always remember your Creator, and walk the path of youth in such a way that you remember that your path will end in death and that everything you have done will be judged.

Remember your Creator before the time of sadness and old age comes upon you, and the years that will not please you; before the sun, the light, the moon, and the stars grow dark, and the clouds return after the rain.

Some adapt the sun, moon, and stars to the eyes, ears, and senses of the head, all of which are weakened by the troubles of old age. They think that the passage below speaks of the limbs of the human body. They believe that the guardians of the house signify the ribs, since the intestines are enclosed by them and the entire softness of the belly is protected; they consider the strongest men to be the legs.

When he says, “The women grinding will cease because they have become few,” they refer this to the work of the teeth. When extreme old age arrives, the teeth are either worn down or fall out; by them food is ground and sent into the stomach. They are idle because they do not supply strength to the body, but seem merely to sustain life for a short time that will quickly perish.

They think that “those who see through the openings will grow dark” refers to the eyes, since it is beyond doubt that in extreme old age the sharpness of vision grows dim and the sight becomes clouded.

## VERSES 4–5

And the doors in the street will be closed when the sound of grinding is low; they will rise at the sound of a bird, and all the daughters of song will fall silent. They will fear what is high and be afraid on the road.

They wish the doors closed in the streets to be understood of the weakened steps of the elderly: they always sit and cannot walk, nor do they share in the games of the young, which usually take place in the streets; instead, with the door closed, they avoid seeing them.

They interpret “when the sound of grinding is low” as referring to the hands [Jerome: “jaws”], because the elderly cannot obtain food through their own labor, and, with their breath constricted, the voice is scarcely heard, faint in the aged body.

Moreover, his rising at the sound of a bird shows that, when the blood grows cold and the moisture dries up—by which the substance of sleep is nourished [Jerome: “by which substances sleep is nourished”]—he awakens at a light sound. In the middle of the night, when the rooster has crowed, he quickly rises, unable to turn his limbs frequently in bed.

The falling silent—or, as it is better rendered in Hebrew, the becoming deaf—of the daughters of song signifies the ears: hearing becomes heavier for the old person, who can no longer distinguish among voices or take pleasure in songs.

“They will fear what is high and be afraid on the road” means that they will be unable to walk along steep places. With weary knees and trembling steps, they will falter even on level ground and fear stumbling because of the weakness of their gait [Jerome: “fear the stumbling of their steps”].

The almond tree will blossom, the locust will grow fat, and the caper plant will be dispersed, because a man will go to his everlasting home, and mourners will go about in the street. By metaphor, Ecclesiastes’ discourse now concerns our limbs: when old age has come, the hair has turned white, the feet have swollen, desire has grown cold, and the man has been dissolved, then he will return to his own everlasting earth, to the grave, after the funeral rites have duly been performed and completed, with a crowd of mourners preceding him around the grave. These names—almond tree, locust, and caper plant—also suit an old man figuratively: the almond tree for gray hair, the locust for pain in the legs and swelling of the feet, and the caper plant for desire growing cold, according to the etymology of the Hebrew interpretation, as we have said, and so they suit old age. Having thus pursued at length the many evils of old age, Ecclesiastes speaks of the end of every human being:

**VERSES 6–8.**—Before the silver cord is severed, and the golden band returns, and the pitcher is broken at the spring, and the wheel is shattered above the cistern, and the dust returns to its earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it. “Vanity of vanities,” says Ecclesiastes; “all is vanity.”

He returns to the matters discussed above and, after the great hyperbaton (which he had inserted after the passage where he says, “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come, and before the sun and moon and stars are darkened,” and so forth, “on the day when the keepers of the house will tremble”), now concludes the sentence he had begun with a similar ending, saying: “Before the cord of silver is severed, let this or that happen.” The silver cord signifies this bright life and the breath granted to us from heaven; the return of the golden band signifies the soul, which returns there from which it had descended. The two things that follow—the breaking of the pitcher at the spring and the shattering of the wheel above the cistern—are likewise, metaphorically, enigmas of death. For just as a pitcher, once broken, ceases to draw water, and when the wheel by which water is raised from wells in the cistern has been broken, its use is interrupted, so, when the silver cord has been cut and the stream of the soul returns to the spring, the human being will perish. As the text more plainly continues, the dust will return to its own earth, from which it was taken, and the spirit will return to God who gave it.

From this it is sufficiently clear that those who think that souls are sown together with bodies and generated not by God but by the parents of bodies deserve ridicule. For when the flesh returns to its own earth and the spirit returns to God who gave it, it is evident that the Lord is the Father of souls, not human beings. After describing human destruction, he beautifully takes up again the beginning of his book and says: “Vanity of vanities,” says Ecclesiastes; “all is vanity.” Since all the labor of mortals, about which he has argued throughout the entire volume, comes to this—that the dust returns to its own earth and the soul returns there from which it was taken—it seems a great vanity to labor with one’s whole attention amid the pleasures of the world and the indulgence of the flesh, which end in the swiftest death; and the human being hastens to judgment for all the errors of his vanity. He then added a statement about himself, saying who he was:

**VERSES 9–10.**—And because Ecclesiastes was exceedingly wise, he taught the people and recounted what he had done; and, investigating, he composed many proverbs, sought useful words, and wrote down very upright sayings, full of truth.

By these words also he now urges the reader to seek allegory in his books rather than simple history, and indicates that his teaching benefits the people if the proverbs are understood mystically, since they promise one thing on the surface and contain another in their inner substance. We are taught in the Gospel that proverbs do not mean merely what is written, for the Lord spoke to the people in parables and proverbs, but explained them privately to the apostles (Matt. 13:15). Hence it is evident that the book of Proverbs does not contain, as simple people suppose, obvious instructions; rather, just as gold is sought in the earth, a kernel in a nut, and hidden fruit beneath the hairy coverings of chestnuts, so the divine meaning must be searched out more deeply in them. After this he also added the causes and natures of things, the disposition of God, and the wisdom explaining why each thing exists or how it came to be, saying that he had wished to know these matters.

**VERSE 11.**—The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deep; they are given through the counsel of teachers by one shepherd.

Lest he seem, after God’s law, rashly to break into a commandment and claim authority for teaching (*quod*, “which”; Jerome: *quam*, “which”)—a role which Moses had undertaken not so much on his own initiative as first at God’s command and then by his inspiration—he says that his words are truly the words of the wise. Like goads, they correct those who do wrong and stir the sluggish steps of mortals by the piercing of their points. Thus they are firm, like nails driven deep into solid ground, and are not put forward on the authority of one person but through the counsel and agreement of all the teachers. And lest human learning be despised, he says that it was granted by one shepherd: although many teach, the Lord is nevertheless the author of this teaching.

At the same time, it should be observed that the words of the wise are said to pierce, not to flatter; they do not caress wantonness with a gentle hand, but inflict the pains and wound of repentance upon those who stray and, as we said above, upon the sluggish. Therefore, if someone’s speech does not pierce but gives pleasure to its hearers, it is not the speech of a wise man. “The words of the wise are like goads,” because they summon the sinner to conversion; they are strengthened, given through the counsel of the saints, granted by one shepherd, and founded on a solid root.

**VERSE 12.**—Beyond these, my son, do not seek more. There is no end to the making of many books, and much study is a weariness of the flesh.

Except for these words, which were given by one shepherd and through the counsel and agreement of the wise, do nothing and claim nothing for yourself. Follow the footsteps of your elders and do not depart from their authority; otherwise, if you seek many things, an endless number of books will confront you, dragging you into error and making your labor in reading fruitless.

Or certainly he teaches the pursuit of brevity and that one should follow meaning rather than words, in opposition to the philosophers and rulers [Jerome: “teachers”] of this age, who attempt to establish the falsehoods of their doctrines through the variety and multitude of their arguments. Divine Scripture, by contrast, is compressed within a brief compass; and the more it expands in meaning, the more it is contracted in expression. The Lord makes a brief and concise word upon the earth, and his word is near, in our mouth and in our heart (Deut. 30:14).

I therefore think that this is the meaning of the present commandment: that many books should not be made. For whatever you say, if it is referred to him who in the beginning was the Word with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1), there was one volume, though there are innumerable books; one Law, one Gospel. But if you argue about diverse and contradictory matters, and through excessive curiosity draw your mind here and there, then even in one book there are many books. Hence it is said: “You will not escape sin through much speaking” (Prov. 10:19).

Such books, therefore, have no end. For what is good and every truth are enclosed within a definite limit, whereas wickedness and falsehood are without end. Such study is indeed a weariness of the flesh—that is, of the carnal, not the spiritual, understanding.

**VERSES 13–14.**—Let us all hear the conclusion of the matter together: Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole human being. And God will bring everything that is done into judgment, concerning every error, whether it is good or evil.

The Hebrews say that, although among Solomon’s other writings—works that have become obsolete and have not remained in memory—this book also seemed destined to be forgotten because it asserted that God’s creatures are vain and that everything is nothing, and because it preferred passing food, drink, and pleasures above all else, it nevertheless deserved authority from a single chapter and was placed among the divine books because it compressed his entire argument and his whole catalogue into this very brief recapitulation. He said that the whole meaning of his words is most accessible and contains nothing difficult: namely, that we should fear God and do his commandments.

For this is the purpose for which the human being was created: that, understanding the Creator, he should revere him through fear, honor, and the performance of his commandments. For when the time of judgment arrives, whatever we have done will stand before the Judge; we shall await the Lord’s twofold sentence, and each person will receive according to his work, whether he has done evil or good. The equity of judgment will remain forever.

[Col. 0719D] **Editorial note:** The learned reader will have observed that Alcuin, in this Exposition, copied almost word for word St. Jerome’s commentary on Ecclesiastes and transferred it into his own work, very rarely making use of his own lights. This, however, was the custom of his age, when the study of sacred Scripture, like that of the other sciences, had begun to be reformed but had not yet reached such perfection that learned men, in explaining the sacred books, readily trusted their own learning. Rather, they preferred to rely on the teachings and expositions of the ancient Fathers approved in the Church, so that in this way they might avoid every danger of novelty, which has always been harmful to the Church. The most learned Vallarsius, the latest editor of St. Jerome’s works, in volume III, page 381, note, declares that he compared this holy Father’s commentary on Ecclesiastes in its entirety with Alcuin’s work, and that the better readings found here should generally be attributed to it.

**The end of Albinus’s little commentary on Ecclesiastes.**

## BY THE SAME AUTHOR, TO THE READER

This book, in speech of varied meaning, lays open  
the differing desires of human beings, and what pleases each.  
May your understanding, O young man, read it through  
with such moderation that it may not fall into Epicurus’ pit.

Albinus, walking through the meadows of the pious Fathers,  
would pluck flowers through the holy fields,  
wishing to fashion [perhaps “encircle with”] garlands suited to the brows of boys,  
whose age cannot bear great burdens.

I ask you, my children, learn these little letters of ours  
and keep them in your whole mind through all the eternal days.  
All the fleeting joys of the ages flow far away  
and do not return again, like flowing water.

Do not assail your hearts too much with empty affairs,  
but always strengthen them through the love of God.  
Death hastens through all hours and moments  
to snatch us away before the face of the Judge.

By this there is established for our deeds  
a sure and decisive judgment for all, as this book sings.  
The rich and the poor, the young and the old alike should fear it;  
then each receives the rewards corresponding to his merits—  
rewards that will always remain through everlasting days.

Soon each good person receives good, each wicked person evil:  
the impious is driven with the demon into dark shadows,  
while the good reigns with Christ in the citadel of light.

Receive these Easter gifts with joyful hearts;  
be mindful of the sender, and with devout speech.  
This work, still raw, was snatched by its bearer from the fire,  
baked in a fire-breathing oven, but not properly beneath the kiln.

I beg you, my son, let your piety cleanse its errors;  
may no rotten tooth be able to gnaw it,  
nor an eye suffused with black bile  
strive through the open air to scatter it in its accustomed manner.

# THE PRAYER OF SOLOMON, WHICH HE SPOKE AT THE DEDICATION OF THE TEMPLE  
*(2 Chron. 6:14 ff.)*

Lord God of Israel, there is no god like you in heaven above or on earth below, keeping the covenant and mercy with your servants who walk before you with all their heart. You have kept for your servant David, my father, what you spoke to him. You spoke with your mouth and fulfilled it with your hands, as this day proves.

Now therefore, Lord God of Israel, preserve for your servant David, my father, what you spoke to him, saying: “There shall not fail you before me a man to sit upon the throne of Israel,” provided only that your sons guard their way, walking before me as you have walked in my sight.

And now, Lord God of Israel, let your words be confirmed which you spoke to your servant David, my father. Can it really be thought that God dwells upon the earth? If the heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you, how much less this house which I have built! Yet regard the prayer of your servant and his supplication, Lord my God. Hear the hymn and the prayer which your servant prays before you today, that your eyes may be open over this house day and night, over the house concerning which you said: “My name will be there.” Hear the prayer which your servant prays to you in this place; hear the supplication of your servant and of your people Israel, whatever they pray for in this place. Hear from your dwelling-place in heaven, and when you hear, be merciful.

If a man sins against his neighbor and is bound by some oath, and comes on account of the oath before your altar in this house, hear in heaven, act, and judge your servants, condemning the wicked and bringing his way back upon his own head, while justifying the just and repaying him according to his righteousness.

If your people Israel flee before their enemies because they have sinned against you, and then, repenting and confessing your name, come and worship and beseech you in this house, hear in heaven, forgive the sin of your people Israel, and bring them back to the land which you gave to their fathers.

If heaven is shut and there is no rain because of their sins, and, praying in this place, they repent before your name and turn from their sins because of their affliction, hear them in heaven, forgive the sins of your servants and of your people Israel, and show them the good way in which they should walk; give rain upon the land which you gave to your people as a possession.

If famine arises in the land, or pestilence, or corrupted air, or blight, or locust, or mildew, and their enemy afflicts them by besieging their gates—whatever plague, whatever sickness, whatever prayer or imprecation may befall any person among your people Israel—if anyone recognizes the plague in his heart and spreads out his hands in this house, hear in heaven, in the place of your dwelling; be reconciled and act, giving to each according to all his ways, as you see his heart, for you alone know the hearts of all the children of human beings. Thus may they fear you all the days that they live upon the face of the land which you gave to our fathers.

Moreover, when a foreigner who is not of your people Israel comes from a distant land for the sake of your name—for they will hear of your great name, your strong hand, and your outstretched arm everywhere—when he comes and prays in this place, hear in heaven, in the firmament of your dwelling, and do everything for which the foreigner calls upon you, so that all the peoples of the earth may learn to fear your name as your people Israel does, and may know that your name has been invoked over this house which I have built.

If your people go out to war against their enemies by the way wherever you send them, and pray to you toward the direction of the city which you have chosen and of the house which I have built for your name, hear their prayers and supplications in heaven, and execute their judgment.

But if they sin against you—for there is no one who does not sin—and, being angry, you deliver them to their enemies, and they are taken captive to the land of their enemies, whether far or near, and repent in their heart in the place of their captivity, and, turning back to you, beseech you in their captivity, saying, “We have sinned, we have acted unjustly, we have behaved wickedly,” and return to you with all their heart and all their soul in the land of their enemies to which they were taken captive, and pray to you toward the direction of their land which you gave to their fathers, and of the city which you chose, and of the temple which I built for your name, hear in heaven, in the firmament of your throne, their prayers and supplications; execute their judgment, and be merciful to your people who sinned against you and to all their iniquities by which they transgressed against you. Grant them mercy before those who took them captive, so that they may show them mercy.

For they are your people and your inheritance, whom you brought out of the land of Egypt, from the midst of the iron furnace. Let your eyes be open to the supplication of your servant and of your people Israel, and hear them in everything for which they call upon you. For you separated them for yourself as an inheritance from all the peoples of the earth, as you spoke through Moses your servant when you brought our fathers out of Egypt, Lord God.

# FIFTH WORK: INTERPRETATIONS OF THE HEBREW NAMES OF THE ANCESTORS OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST

*From chapter 1 of the Gospel of St. Matthew.*

## PRELIMINARY NOTICE

We have transcribed the present little work, in which Alcuin interprets the Hebrew names of the ancestors of our Savior Jesus Christ according to a threefold sense—literal, allegorical, and moral—from an ancient manuscript codex of the library of the monastery of St. Emmeram, no later than the ninth century, and now publish it for the first time.

The verses placed beneath it do not allow us to doubt its author. For Alcuin, following his customary practice, sings there, discloses his name, and offers this writing as a gift to the king, plainly Charlemagne. Nor do I doubt that he inscribed the same little commentary to that king with a dedicatory letter prefixed to it, as he was accustomed to do; that letter, however, is absent from our codex and has appeared nowhere else.

This writing agrees with the homily on the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary among the summer homilies of the Venerable Bede, volume VII of the Basel edition of 1563, page 183 (Patrologia, volume XCIV), and among the works of Alcuin edited by Quercetanus, page 1197. The writers of the *Literary History of France*, volume IV, page 341, rejected it among the works falsely attributed to Alcuin because they had no evidence in its favor, not yet having seen the poem now being published for the first time.

Whether it likewise agrees with the little work which John Albert Fabricius records that Alcuin wrote, *On the Genealogy of Christ’s Humanity*, cannot be decided until that work itself is someday found and published from the Menarsian Library, where it is listed on page 157.

Moreover, in the cited manuscript codex of St. Emmeram at Regensburg, after those interpretations of the Hebrew names—with the blank space of one page inserted—the commentary continues through the entire Gospel of St. Matthew as follows:

> “Now the generation of Christ was as follows. As he foretold, he will speak next. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph. Why does he here call him a betrothed man when above he called him a husband? And how is he called a husband when he did not know her? Because it is the custom of Scripture to call a betrothed man a husband and to call betrothed women wives, just as we read in Genesis concerning the sons of Noah and their wives [manuscript: *et uxores*, “and wives”; read: *uxoribus*, “with wives”]. Alternatively: ‘When she had been betrothed.’ Why was Mary betrothed? What need was there for her to be betrothed? For two reasons: so that Mary’s ancestry might be shown through the man Joseph, and so that it might not conflict with the text of the Law, which says, ‘No one shall enter into marriage except within his own tribe,’ and so forth.”

And so on through the entire Gospel.
