In the aforementioned codex this work is attributed to Alcuin by a later fifteenth-century hand and in the older catalogue of our library, compiled in the year 1300, in these words: “Albinus on Matthew.” Therefore someone might not rashly suppose that not only these interpretations, which we publish here, but also this entire commentary, is genuinely Alcuin’s work. Indeed, who else would have wished to borrow from Alcuin only the brief beginning of this labor and not also add something of his own?

The style, too, does not differ from Alcuin’s style, although it is not so carefully composed, elegant, and polished as in his commentaries on the Gospel of St. John. Perhaps this happened because Alcuin did not put the finishing hand to it but, hindered by various other labors, old age, and illnesses, left it unfinished. Nevertheless, I would not wish to prejudge the matter, being well aware how easily one may err when forming an opinion about the true author of an ancient work lacking the proper characteristics or suitable testimony.

Although, therefore, I think that the commentary on the Hebrew names of the patriarchs, or ancestors, of Christ should be counted among Alcuin’s genuine little works, the following consideration prevents us from making the same judgment about the remainder of the commentary that follows it in the same codex.

First, the conclusion of that commentary, or the poem appended to it, seems to imply that Alcuin’s entire labor was completed with that interpretation. Second, in Bales’s *Second Century of the Writers of Britain* and in the Menarsian Library, only a commentary on the Genealogy of Christ, not any complete commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, is listed among Alcuin’s works. Third, there is the silence both of the author of Alcuin’s Life and of the learned men who devoted the greatest care to collecting and publishing Alcuin’s little works.

But, you say, there is clear testimony that Alcuin commented on the entire Gospel of St. Matthew: St. Anselm of Lucca, in his treatise against the antipope Guibert, cites two passages from book II of Albinus on Matthew to demonstrate, as Canisius says (*Ancient Monuments*, edited by D. Basnagius, volume III, part I, pages 389–491), that the Church’s resources are not in the power of the king or emperor. Alcuin therefore wrote on Matthew, and this work, divided into several books, still existed in the time of St. Anselm of Lucca—that is, toward the end of the eleventh century. This indeed is the judgment of the celebrated authors of the *Literary History of France*, volume VI, page IX.

Yet I am certain that these otherwise very learned men were deceived in this judgment. First, the passages mentioned above from Alcuin are not found in St. Anselm’s treatise against Guibert, but in collections appended to that treatise. Canisius himself doubts whether these collections belong to Anselm of Lucca, warning the reader in these words:

> “In the manuscript codex which we used, the following sentences were appended, apparently collected by Anselm himself from various authors.”

Second, the passages cited from Alcuin in those collections are found in full and word for word in book II of his commentary on John, chapter II, verses 14–17. It is therefore clear that, through the carelessness of the compiler of those collections, this was written: “Albinus in book II on Matthew,” when he should have written: “Albinus in book II on John.”

Consequently, this testimony attributed to St. Anselm of Lucca is entirely without force as evidence for attributing some commentary on the Gospel of St. Matthew to Alcuin. We therefore leave the matter uncertain and refrain here from publishing that work from our codex. Nor do we wish at present to assign it a place among the doubtful works until, perhaps with the help of another codex that may in due time be discovered, it can be cleansed of the many errors that often arouse nausea in readers and can emerge in a more corrected form, as we hope.

For the present, therefore, we publish here only the interpretations of the names of Christ’s ancestors from the cited codex, together with the additions and variant readings of the aforementioned homily on the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, which we have inserted in the text within brackets or placed among the notes.

# THE BOOK OF THE GENERATION OF JESUS CHRIST, SON OF DAVID, SON OF ABRAHAM, ETC.

[Col. 0725D] **From the homily on the Nativity of the blessed Virgin Mary, in the Venerable Bede:** Blessed Matthew the Evangelist, dearly beloved, is not without reason described among the other creatures of the heavenly mysteries with the face of a human being, because, beginning his Gospel far back among the ancient Fathers, he set forth the genealogy of the Lord’s humanity more clearly than the others. But it must be understood that all these names fully contain within themselves meanings belonging to the allegorical and moral senses.

## LITERAL INTERPRETATION

Abraham: father of many [nations]. Isaac: joy. Jacob: supplanter. Judah: confession [is interpreted]. Phares: division. Zara: rising. Esrom: seeing an arrow. Thamar: she is called “palm.” Aram: chosen. Aminadab: willing people. Naasson: strong diviner. Salmon: understood as “perceptive.” Booz: in him is strength. Raab: breadth. Obed: serving. Ruth: hastening [is understood]. Jesse: incense [the edition reads “fire”]. David: strong of hand, or desirable. Solomon: peaceful. Urias: my light is God. Bersabee: son of the oath [is understood]. Roboam: breadth of the people. Abia: the Lord is Father. Asa: lifting up. Josaphat: the Lord has judged [is expressed]. Joram: exalted. Amasias: elevated people [the edition omits “Amasias” and what follows]. Ozias: strong of the Lord. Joathan: perfect. Achaz: apprehended [Bede: apprehending] [is said]. Ezechias: the Lord is strong. Manasses: forgetful. Amon: faithful. Josias: salvation of the Lord [is interpreted]. Jechonias: preparation of the Lord. Salathiel: God is my petition. Zorobabel: this is the teacher. Abiuth: this is my father [is understood]. Eliachim: resurrection of God. Azor: helped. Sadoc: just. Jochim [read: Achim]: my brother [is understood]. Heliuth: my God. Eleazar: God is my helper. Mathan: gift. Jacob: supplanter [is expressed]. Joseph: added, or increased. Maria: illuminatrix, or star of the sea. Jesus: Savior. Christ: anointed [is interpreted].

## ALLEGORICAL INTERPRETATION

Through these patriarchs Christ [the Lord our God] was coming into the world, and in himself he allegorically performed the office of them all; through the interpretation of their names he wished to signify our salvation.

In Abraham, he is the father of all believers, to whom all are permitted to cry out and say: “Abba, Father!” (Rom. 8:15).

In Isaac, the joy of all the faithful, of whom the angel sang: “Behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people” (Luke 2:10).

In Jacob, the supplanter, because he disabled and crushed the devil, the despoiler of the human race, and plundered his vessels.

In Judah, confession, who said: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth” (Matt. 11:25).

In Phares, division, who separates the sheep from the goats (Matt. 25:33)—that is, the good from the wicked, the chosen from the rejected.

In Zara, the rising for our salvation, as it is said: “For those who fear the name of the Lord, the sun of righteousness will rise” (Mal. 4:2). [The edition reads: “He has visited us, the rising from on high.”]

In Esrom, the arrow of the Lord’s salvation, as it is said: “The arrows of the mighty are sharp” (Ps. 119:4).

In Thamar, the palm of victory, [as he himself said: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16:33)].

In Aram, the chosen one, of whom the Father speaks: “Behold my servant, whom I have chosen, my chosen one; I have placed my Spirit upon him” (Isa. 42:1).

In Aminadab, a willing people, because he willingly laid down his life for our salvation, so that he might make us a willing people for himself and acceptable to God.

In Naasson, a diviner—that is, a prophet—strong, when he says: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, then he will sit upon the seat of his majesty” (Matt. 25:31), to judge the world with equity.

In Salmone, perceptive—that is, intellectual—of whom it is written: “But he, seeing their thoughts” (Luke 11:17), and again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings” (Ps. 93:11), and: “God, who searches hearts and kidneys” (Ps. 7:10). He said to the Jews: “Why are you thinking these things in your hearts?” (Luke 5:22). He recognizes past and future as though they were present.

In Booz, the strength of his virtue is expressed, as he says: “I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:22).

[Col. 0725D] **Editorial note:** “In Booz, strength is in him, because he received strength from no one. Concerning him it is said: ‘The Lord is strong and mighty; the Lord is mighty in battle’” (Ps. 23:8).

In Raab, the breadth of his dominion in the Church is signified.

[Col. 0726D] **Editorial note:** “In Raab, the breadth of his power is expressed: the whole world cannot contain him, and there will be no end to his kingdom.”

In Obeth, serving, because he did not come to be served but to serve, as the Apostle said: “Taking the form of a servant.”

In Ruth, hastening to our salvation, [because he hastens to wish all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, saying in the Gospel: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is drawing near” (Matt. 4:17)].

In Jesse, incense [the edition reads “fire”], he is recognized who says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12:49). John likewise said of him: “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3:11).

In David, desirable, because it is said: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44:3). [In the same name, strong of hand, when, holding a whip of cords in his hand, he drove an immense multitude of sellers and buyers from the temple (John 2:15).] Likewise, a strong warrior, when he overcame the devil and humbled [the edition reads “conquered and crushed”] our accuser.

In Solomon, peaceful, as he said: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14:27). And the Apostle says: “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2:14).

In Bethsabea, son of the oath, of whom it is said: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever” (Ps. 109:4).

In Roboam, the breadth of the faithful people, when he says: “Many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 8:11).

In Abia, the Lord is Father, who says: “Do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. 23:9).

In Aza, lifting up, of whom John says: “Behold the Lamb of God,” he says, “who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

In Josaphat, judge, because he himself will judge the world with equity (Ps. 95:13) [and he himself is the judge of the living and the dead]. He likewise says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to his Son” (John 5:22).

In Joram, exalted, because he himself ascended above the heavens of heavens [the edition reads “above all the heavens”], [“to fulfill all things”; and as the Psalmist says: “He is exalted above all nations, and his glory is above the heavens” (Ps. 112:4)].

[Col. 0727D] **The edition omits:** “In Amasias … and loosing.” In Amasias, elevated people, because through him the Church of God was elevated, to which he gave the power of binding and loosing.

In Ozia, strong of the Lord, because he freed the captive human race [with a strong hand] from captivity [the edition reads “the captivity of the human race”] and led it to the heights of heaven.

In Joathan, perfect, as he says in the Gospel: “For it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. 3:15).

In Achaz, apprehending, who weighed the heavens with a span (Isa. 40:12) and enclosed the earth in a handful [the edition reads “enclosed it”].

In Ezechia, strength of the Lord, who says: “Take courage, for I have conquered the world” (John 16:33). Likewise, according to the Apostle: “Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24).

In Manasse, forgetful of our iniquity, as it is read in Ezekiel: “On whatever day the sinner turns from his injustice, all his iniquities will be consigned to forgetfulness” [the edition reads “I will remember none of all his iniquities”] (Ezek. 18:21–22).

In Amon, faithful, who says: “Ask, and it will be given to you.” Likewise Paul: “so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God” (Heb. 9). Likewise John: “He who is the faithful witness” (Rev. 1:5).

In Josias, salvation of the Lord, because everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.

In Jechonia, preparation of the Lord, who says: “If I go, I will prepare a place for you” (John 14:3).

In Salathiel, God is my petition, who says: “Holy Father, preserve those whom you have given me” (John 17:11).

In Zorobabel, teacher of sinners and publicans, so that he might call them back from the error of their life [the edition reads “of their way”]. [And as he himself says: “Do not be called teachers, for one is your teacher, Christ” (Matt. 23:10).]

In Abiuth, this is my father, because he said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and he is the Father and head of all believers.

In Eliachim, resurrection of the Lord, as he says: [“I am the resurrection and the life;”] “who believes in me will not die forever, but I will raise him on the last day” (John 11:25).

In Azur [Azor], helped, as he says: “I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 8:16, 29); he himself is the helper of all who hope in him. [And: “He who sent me is with me, and he has not left me alone.”] And again: “The works that I do, I do not do from myself; but the Father who is with me, he himself does the works” (John 14:10).

In Sadoch, just, as it is written: “That he himself might be just and justifying those who are of the faith of Abraham” (Rom. 3:26).

In Jochim [read: Achim], my brother, as he says: “Whoever does the will of my Father is my brother, and my mother, and my sister” (Matt. 12:50).

In Eliuth, my God, who from our weakness said to the Father: “God, my God, I keep vigil for you from the dawn, so that I may rise again to you.”

[Col. 0727D] **Editor’s reading:** “In Eliud, ‘my God,’ because he himself is God, begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages; he said upon the cross of the gibbet: ‘Eli, Eli,’ that is, ‘My God, my God’ (Matthew 27).” In Eleazar, “God my helper,” and protector of all who believe in him, who said: “The Father who sent me is with me and has not left me alone.”

[Col. 0728D] **Editor’s reading:** “In Eleasar, ‘God my helper,’ because he himself is a helper in time of need and in tribulation, and the protector of all who hope in him (Psalm 9).” (John 8:29.)

In Mathan, “gift,” because through him God the Father forgave us all our debts; and, ascending on high, “he led captivity captive” and “gave gifts to human beings” (Psalm 67:19; Ephesians 4:8).

In Jacob, as I said earlier, “supplanter” of our ancient enemy, because he gave his faithful ones power “to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19).

In Joseph, “increased”—[“to whom the Father gave the nations as his inheritance and the ends of the earth as his possession” (Psalm 2:8)]—or “increase of eternal life,” as he himself said: “I came that they may have life, and have it more abundantly” (John 10:10).

But in the holy and perpetual virgin Mary, from whom he was born, “star of the sea” and “light of this age”—[“he himself is,” as he said, “the light of the world” (John 8:12)]—who illuminates every human being coming into this world (John 1:9).

In his proper name, Jesus is “salutary” or “Savior,” as the angel explained when he said: “For he himself will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21).

This same Christ—that is, “anointed”—was so called because God anointed him in his humanity with the oil of gladness, that is, with the anointing of the Holy Spirit, as eternal priest and king: so that he might save Christians, called by his name, from their sins insofar as he is Savior; reconcile them to God the Father insofar as he is priest; and place them in the eternal kingdom insofar as he is king.

For he himself came into the world through these forty-two encampments, so that through these same encampments he might lead us into the land of the living and of eternal promise, where, rejoicing in perpetual peace in the heavenly Jerusalem, we shall reign for ever and ever. Amen.

[The passage beginning “For he himself,” and continuing through “Amen,” is omitted in Quercetanus’s edition.]

{453} **MORAL INTERPRETATION**

Morally, these interpretations of the names are also understood to contribute in many ways to our edification. Just as Christ everywhere carried out the work of our salvation, so too the names of the patriarchs signify our progress.

In Abraham, that we may be fathers of many virtues and, by right of inheritance, possess an increase of good works.

In Isaac, that we may have joy in the Lord [and not in this world, in accordance with what he himself said: “Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20)]. And, according to the Apostle: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Philippians 4:4).

In Jacob, that we may be supplanters of our vices and carnal desires, and trample the devil’s power beneath our victorious feet [Editor’s reading: “and trample carnal desire beneath a vigorous foot, rescuing it from the devil’s power”].

In Judah, that [according to the Psalmist] we may go before the face of the Lord in confession, confess his holy name, and praise him for ever and ever (Psalm 94:2).

In Phares, that we may separate ourselves from the ungodly, distinguishing our actions from their fellowship [and withdrawing ourselves from every brother who walks disorderly, and not sharing in his evil works].

In Zara, that the true Lucifer may arise in our hearts, and that the Sun of Justice may shine everywhere in our hearts [Editor’s reading: “everywhere in us”], [and that our light may shine before human beings, so that they may see our good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven (Matthew 5:16)].

In Esrom, that we may be arrows of the Lord’s salvation, so that it may be said of us: “The sharp arrows of the mighty one” (Psalm 119:4).

[In Thamar, that with the palm of victory we may overcome the devil’s pomp and the desires of the world, for the sake of him who loved us.]

In Aram, that we may be God’s chosen ones and be a chosen race [“a holy nation, a people for his possession; and that we may proclaim the virtues of him who called us out of darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Peter 2:9)]; a royal priesthood for Christ, and exalted in merits.

In Aminadab, that we may be the Lord’s willing people in the building up of his body [Editor’s reading: “the body of Christ”].

In Naasson, that, abandoning the worldly omens of the gentiles, we may place our faith in the divine promises.

In Salmon, that we may be found perceptive—that is, intellectually discerning—of God’s truth, and teachable [and doers], [because it is not the hearers of the law but the doers who will be justified (Romans 2:13)].

In Booz, that we may confess God [Col. 0730A] and act courageously, triumphing in Christ over the aerial powers.

[Col. 0729C] **Editor’s reading:** “In Booz, that, according to the Apostle, we may be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might; girding our loins with truth; putting on the breastplate of righteousness; taking up the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:10).

[In Rahab, that, observing with the greatest care the Lord’s broad commandment, we may love the Lord God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength, and embrace our neighbor as ourselves.]

In Obeth, that we may serve with joy through the spirit of love and holy devotion.

[Col. 0729D] **Editor’s reading:** “In Obeth, that we may serve the Lord through the spirit of fear and holy love, so that our service may be rational and our sacrifice may become acceptable.”

[In Ruth, that, hastening to enter that rest—that is, the heavenly Jerusalem—while we have time, we may do good to all (Galatians 6:10), because here we have no lasting city, but seek the one that is to come (Hebrews 13:14).]

In Jesse, that we may offer the incense of our prayers upon the altar of our heart [“in a contrite and humbled spirit”] to God, as the Prophet says [Editor’s reading: “as the Psalmist says”]: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your presence” (Psalm 140:2).

In David, that we may become desirable to our God and be strong-handed, fighting against the spiritual Goliath.

[Col. 0729D] **Editor’s reading:** “In David, that, strong-handed, we may fight against the spiritual Goliath and, presenting our bodies as a living, holy sacrifice pleasing to God (Romans 12:1), become a desirable temple for the Holy Spirit.”

In Solomon, that, insofar as it depends on us, we may have peace with all people [keeping in mind the Lord’s saying], because “blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9).

[In Bathsheba, that we may guard every oath, lest we fall into the devil’s snare through perjury. In Uriah, that God may be our light, so that, following him, we may not walk in the darkness of death, but have the light of life.]

In Roboam, that, fulfilling the broad commandment of charity, we may rejoice in the breadth of spiritual gifts.

{454} [Col. 0729D] **Editor’s reading:** “In Roboam, that, though the people are dispersed far and wide throughout the world, we may possess unity of spirit in the bond of peace and charity; and profess one Lord, one faith, and one baptism, with a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (Ephesians 4).

In Abia, that we may be brothers, having God as our Father, and heirs of God—indeed, coheirs with Christ.

[Col. 0729D] **Editor’s reading:** “In Abia, that, loving one another with brotherly charity, we may have one Father, the Lord in heaven, who begot us willingly through the word of truth, so that we might be a kind of firstfruits of his creation (James 1:18); and that we may possess the blessing as an inheritance and glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God” (Romans 5:12).

In Asaph [read: Asa], that we may turn our attention from vices to virtues, from earthly things to heavenly things.

[Col. 0730D] **Editor’s reading:** “In Asa, that we may lift our members out of the mud and dung of vices, so that they may not serve uncleanness and iniquity leading to iniquity, but righteousness leading to sanctification; for God did not call us to uncleanness but to sanctification” (Romans 6:19).

In Josaphat, that we may judge every person rightly [as it is written: “Judge rightly, you sons of men” (Psalm 57:2)]; and whatever we wish people to do for us, that we may likewise do for them, knowing that with the measure with which we measure, it will be measured back to us (Matthew 7:2).

In Joram, that we may set our minds on heavenly things, made exalted in the Lord and having our manner of life in heaven.

[Col. 0730D] **Editor’s reading:** “In Joram, that, made lofty and exalted, we may seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; that we may set our minds on the things above, not on those upon the earth (Colossians 3:2), because every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James 1:17).

In Ozia, that we may be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might.

[Col. 0730D] **Editor’s reading:** “In Ozia, that, made strong in the Lord amid all our persecutions and tribulations that we endure, we may take as an example the labor and patience of the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord Jesus” (James 5:10).

In Joathan, that, doing perfect works, we may follow the Gospel: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5:48) [presenting ourselves as examples in all things and teaching everyone in all wisdom, so that we may present everyone perfect].

In Achaz, that we may grasp the way of our salvation, which is Christ, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.”

[Col. 0731B] **Editor’s reading:** “In Achaz, that we may take hold of discipline, lest the Lord become angry and we perish from the righteous way (Psalm 2:12), which is Christ, who said: ‘I am the way, the truth, and the life’” (John 14:6).

In Hezekiah, that we may praise the strength of the Lord who fights for us, and ask that he strengthen us.

[Col. 0731C] **Editor’s reading:** “In Hezekiah, that we may stand strong in the Lord against our adversary, the devil, who, like a roaring lion, prowls around seeking someone to devour; not trusting in our own strength, but praising with the Psalmist the Lord’s strength: ‘The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation’” (Psalm 117:14).

In Manasseh, that we may forget our injuries.

[Col. 0731C] **The editions continue:** “and forgive those who act against us for the Lord’s name, lest we incur that curse: ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.’” And, forgetting the past, let us always press forward.

In Amon, that we may stand in the faith, in which we can extinguish all the flaming darts of the devil’s deceit.

[Col. 0731C] **Editor’s reading:** “In Ammon, that, faithful and rooted and grounded in faith, we may take up the shield of faith in all things, by which we can extinguish the flaming darts of the wicked one” (Ephesians 6:16).

In Josiah, that with all our strength and courage we may follow the Lord’s salvation, which he has deigned to grant us.

[Col. 0731C] **Editor’s reading:** “In Josiah, that we may continually ask for the Lord’s salvation and the salvation of our souls, lest we be blinded in unbelief, stumble on the paths of his commandments, become deaf to hearing the word of God, or die in sins; but that we may always be saved by him who saves those who hope in him.”

In Jechoniah, that at the Lord’s [second] coming we may be prepared, watching and praying, lest we fall into temptation [but may deserve to enter the wedding feast with those of whom he says: “Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, will find watching” (Luke 12:37)].

In Salathiel, that we may ask for one petition: namely, that we may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of our life.

[Col. 0731D] **Editor’s reading:** “In Salathiel, so that our petition may always be directed to God, that our joy may be full—not mingled with the sorrow of this age, but eternal in infinite blessedness—and this in the name of the Savior, so that we may obtain what we ask.”

In Zorobabel, that we may be teachers of truth, restraining doctrinal pretensions and the confusions of heretics [and commending by our examples what we teach in words, lest God say of us: “Why do you recite my statutes and take my covenant upon your mouth, while you hate discipline and cast my words behind you?” (Psalm 49:16–17)].

In Abiuth, that God may be our Father and we may be his sons and daughters, [having the spirit of adoption, by which we cry, “Abba, Father!” And if sons, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and coheirs with Christ (Romans 8:15, 17)].

In Eliachim, that we may rise from the death of sin and live to God in the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0731D] **Editor’s reading:** “In Eliachim, that we may rise from the tombs of vices to the height of virtues, from earthly things to heavenly, from death to life, from Gaza to Galilee—that is, from hell to eternal translation—where the saints shall go from strength to strength, until the God of gods is seen in Zion” (Psalm 83:8).

In Azur, that, with God’s help, we may conquer the enemies of our salvation.

[Col. 0731D] **Editor’s reading:** “In Azor, that, aided by divine grace, we may patiently endure everything opposed to us, and praise our helper, the Lord, with the Psalmist, saying: ‘The Lord is my helper and protector; in him my heart hoped, and I was helped’” (Psalm 27:7).

In Sadoch, that we may deserve to be justified by him who justifies the ungodly.

[Col. 0732C] **Editor’s reading:** “In Sadoch, that we may appear righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord, so that with the righteous we may deserve to hear the voice of him who says: ‘Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world’” (Matthew 25:34).

In Joachim, that we may be brothers, mothers, and sisters of Christ, insofar as we do his will.

[Col. 0732C] **Editor’s reading:** “In Joachim, that we may deserve to be called brothers of Jesus Christ—not through kinship of the flesh, but through the anointing of the Holy Spirit, which he poured out abundantly upon us—so that, doing his will by living temperately, righteously, and devoutly in this age, we may hereafter ascend to his Father and our Father, his God and our God.”

In Eliuth, that we may have no God except the Lord Jesus Christ, [to whom every knee bows and every tongue confesses (Philippians 2:10–11); and that to him alone we may offer the sacrifice of praise, fulfill our vows, and worship him alone, who must be worshiped in spirit and truth (John 4:23)].

In Eleazar, that we may confess that our salvation rests solely in the Lord Jesus.

[Col. 0732C] **Editor’s reading:** “In Eleazar, that we may seek no helper except our Lord Jesus Christ, who is able to do all things more abundantly than we ask or understand; and that whatever we do in word or deed, we may do everything in the name of the Lord (Colossians 3:17), saying with the Prophet: ‘Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth’” (Psalm 123:8).

In Mathan, that, receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit, we may not be desiring evil things like the gentiles.

[Col. 0732D] **Editor’s reading:** “In Mathan, that, retaining the gift of heavenly grace—namely, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isaiah 11:2–3)—we may possess discernment between good and evil, which is the mother of all virtues.”

In Jacob, that with spiritual strength we may supplant the rulers of this darkness together with our vices.

[Col. 0732D] **Editor’s reading:** “In Jacob, that we may uproot from ourselves the weeds of vices and plant within us the spices of virtues, so that, fragrant like cinnamon and balsam, and like choice myrrh, we may give off a pleasing odor; and, planted in the house of the Lord, may flourish for ever before the Lord.”

In Joseph, that as the outer person fails, the inner person may be renewed day by day, until Christ is spiritually strengthened within us.

{456} [Col. 0732D] **Editor’s reading:** “In Joseph, that, adding virtue to virtue and sanctification to sanctification from day to day, we may increase in merit and number, and grow in him unto salvation; and that, by the ladder erected into heaven, we may ascend daily from step to step, until Christ is spiritually formed in us” (Galatians 4).

In the holy and perpetual virgin Mary, whose name is interpreted as “star of the sea” or “illuminatrix”: that we may be illuminators of the world—that is, teachers of the holy Church—and through the teaching of truth and examples of holiness cause the light of faith and love of Christ to arise in the hearts of believers, preparing a dwelling place for God.

In Jesus our Lord, that we may be able to become saviors of our souls, is plainly declared. For whoever perseveres to the end in faith, hope, and charity; in vigils, fasts, and prayers; in chastity, sobriety, generosity in almsgiving, and love of God and neighbor; and converts a sinner from the error of his way, will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins (James 5:10).

But in Christ, that we may be Christians in such a way that, just as he walked, we too may walk; and just as he laid down his life for us, so we too may lay down our lives for our brothers (1 John 2; 3); and just as he naturally bore within himself the meanings of these names, so we too may recall them spiritually in every active and contemplative life, as has been said.

For Christ suffered for this purpose, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps (1 Peter 2:21); deny ourselves, take up our cross, and follow him (Luke 9), as he leads us to the eternal glory “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9).

To him be honor, praise, and dominion for infinite ages of ages. Amen.” (End of the homily so called in Quercetanus and Bede.)

And through Mary—that is, through the light of faith and divine grace—may we be led to the ineffable vision of almighty God, in which, rejoicing and freed from every sorrow of this age, we shall reign with Christ in eternal blessedness.

Receive, O king, this small gift of great love,  
which your Albinus has offered here to you.  
The mighty bring great gifts of the world’s treasures;  
my poverty brings these two little things.

[Col. 0734A] So that my right hand might not come empty on sacred days  
before your holy face, revered king:  
I have marked the sacred Hebrew names of the holy fathers,  
rendering them in Latin speech for you.

(End in the manuscript of Saint-Emmeram.)

{457}

**SIXTH LITTLE WORK. COMMENTARIES ON THE HOLY GOSPEL OF JOHN**

[Col. 0733D] In the manuscript of the Royal Vatican Library the title is: *Selections of Master Albinus from the sayings of the Fathers on John the Evangelist.* In our Saint-Emmeram manuscript it is inscribed as follows: *Master Albinus’s Exposition of John.*

**PRELIMINARY NOTICE**

[Col. 0733B]

This exposition of the holy Gospel of John, which among Alcuin’s exegetical works deserves first place because of its more expansive style and its selection of doctrines collected from the earlier Fathers, first appeared in print, so far as we know, at Strasbourg under the following title: *Seven Books of Commentaries on the Gospel of St. John by Albinus, an English Deacon, Filled with Christian Fruitfulness.* Strasbourg, Johann Hervagius, January 1527, octavo.

The distinguished Quercetanus used this edition in his collection of Alcuin’s works; nevertheless, as he himself testifies, he corrected it with the aid of an ancient manuscript belonging to the library of the illustrious and highly cultivated man Jacques-Auguste de Thou and made it more complete. We too had that Strasbourg edition at hand for our present edition, having received it graciously from the distinguished man of varied learning, D. Felix Oefelius of Munich, from the Bavarian Electoral Library. In addition, we received from Rome several variant readings of the Royal Vatican manuscript, written in the thirteenth century and noted at the command of the late eminent cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Domenico Passionei.

[Col. 0733D] Yet in restoring the true reading and correcting the remaining errors, the manuscript of our library of Saint Emmeram gave us better assistance than the others. It is of excellent quality and was written fully nine hundred years ago, during the episcopate of Baturicus, bishop of Regensburg, who held that see from 817 to 843 and was thus a contemporary of our Alcuin.

At the end of the manuscript, in the same hand in which the entire volume was written, these words may be read:

“Isanbertus completed this book by writing it on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of August, entreating those who read it” (so the manuscript reads) “to remember him as is fitting, since they are refreshed by another’s labor.”

“Patericus the bishop gave it to Saint Emmeram, for the remedy of his soul.”

[Col. 0734B] Through the benefit of these manuscripts, therefore, we have made these commentaries, carefully collated with the printed editions, more accurate in many places. A letter of Alcuin to Lucia and Columba is now newly added. He wrote it when he had completed the entire work, of which he had previously sent only a part, and addressed it to the same virgins.

We owe this precious literary monument to the industry and generosity of the most learned man, D. Brequigny, associate of the Royal Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres of Paris. He recovered it, together with many other letters of Alcuin, which we presented in Part I of the works of the blessed Father, from a manuscript in the Harleian Library in England, and most graciously allowed us to publish it.

We therefore thought that this letter should be placed at the head of the entire commentary, before the letters of Gisla and Richtrudis to Alcuin and of Alcuin to them, following the order that Alcuin himself established there.

From this letter we first learn that Alcuin had begun thirty years earlier—and therefore while he was still living in England—to plan the completion of this work, but that his pen had rested because there was no one to stir it, until the good intention of the aforementioned virgins recalled him to the labor of writing.

Second, we learn that this work was finally completed and sent to the same virgins at the time when he received news of the elevation of their excellent lord David; of the prosperity of the apostolic man, namely Pope Leo III; and of the embassy from the holy city of Jerusalem. All these events belong to the year 800: in that year Pope Leo was freed from the plots and unjust persecutions of his enemies and restored to his see; Charles the Great was invested with imperial majesty; and Zacharias the priest, with two monks sent by the patriarch of Jerusalem, came to Rome carrying the keys of the Lord’s sepulchre, the city and Mount Zion, together with the city’s banner, as the Frankish Annals, those of Petavius, Loisellus, and Moissac, Einhard, and others relate under that same year.

[Col. 0735A] From this same letter we learn, third, that in the preceding year, or 799, Alcuin had sent part of this commentary beforehand to those virgins. We think that this was the portion contained in the final two books, where, in the short letter prefixed to them, Alcuin declares that he had wished to send them an exposition of the whole Gospel, but had been occupied by the labor assigned to him by the king, namely, the correction of the Old and New Testaments.

{458} We are certainly not unaware that the most distinguished men D. Rivet (*History of French Literature*, vol. 4, p. 307), D. Remigius Ceillier (*General History of Sacred Authors*, vol. 18, p. 289), and others hold that the first five books of this commentary were initially sent to the aforementioned virgins, and that the remaining two were later added as the Easter festivals approached.

This opinion, however, has never been convincing to us. Alcuin does not mention even a word of the books previously sent in the introductory letter prefixed to the two later books; and, from the very context of that introduction, it seemed sufficiently clear to us that he had not yet completed the entire exposition of the Gospel. For there he says that he would have sent them an exposition of the whole Gospel, but, occupied with the king’s command to correct the Old and New Testaments, he had not yet been able to complete the work he had begun. Meanwhile, because the sacred season of Easter was approaching, he was sending this portion so that they might exercise their devotion during those holy days by reading it. He also promises to send them the complete exposition after he had completed and finished it as the opportunity of the time allowed.

We know that the learned men mentioned above interpret Alcuin’s words, “I would perhaps have sent you an exposition of the whole Gospel,” as referring not only to an exposition of the holy Gospel of John but also to those of the other evangelists. Yet no necessity compels us to draw the words in that direction; they are far more naturally understood of the complete Gospel of John alone, since it is certain that Alcuin did not send this commentary all at once in its entirety, but successively and in parts.

And certainly, now that this letter to Lucia and Columba has been discovered, that conjecture can no longer be maintained. If Alcuin had sent the final two books as the final portion of a commentary already completed, he would have prefixed to them not that brief letter but the present letter, since the work would by then have been complete.

Fourth and finally, this new letter makes it known that the names Gisla and Lucia, Richtrudis and Columba, belong not to different persons but to the same persons. For to the same virgins—who, in the immediately following letter requesting the commentary on the holy Gospel of John, address themselves by their proper and family names, Gisla and Richtrudis—Alcuin sends the requested commentary and, in his customary manner, calls them by the Latin and adopted names Lucia and Columba.

Concerning these virgins, their condition, and their lineage, see what we say in the general preface, where we also show that they were not of English, as Alfortus asserted, but of Frankish and indeed illustrious origin; and that, by profession, they appear to have been religious women.

One further matter remains to be noted here, which, in our opinion, no one has yet observed: namely, that among the works of the venerable priest Bede, volume 5 of the Basel edition of 1563, pages 519 and following (volume 92 of the *Patrologia*), there is published a commentary on the Gospel of John which, from the beginning of chapter 1 through the end of chapter 12, agrees completely with this commentary attributed to Alcuin—not only in its sense but even in its very words—so that there is no difference except in certain variant readings.

From chapter 13, however, which is where Book 6 begins in Alcuin, to the end, there is a great difference between the two. Bede’s exposition is much more expansive there, and the Gospel text is explained more through his own study than through the words of other Fathers. The homilies of Bede himself and of Saint Gregory the Great, which are inserted in full in the same final two books of Alcuin, are also absent there, and other expositions have been substituted in their place. Nevertheless, even in this edition of Bede, one often encounters sentences that Alcuin brought forward in the same passage.

[Col. 0736A] Although this is so, we do not think that any learned man would wish to raise a question concerning the true and genuine author or compiler of this commentary, deprive Alcuin of the work of his industry, or attribute it to the venerable Bede.

Indeed, we are convinced by the most certain arguments that this commentary is genuinely the work of Alcuin and was falsely ascribed to Bede through some error. We think it unnecessary to demonstrate this at length to learned readers, for the work bears marks by which no one could demand clearer evidence for recognizing its true author—namely, Alcuin’s own letters prefixed to this commentary. There he openly declares that, through his own labor and industry, he gathered in complete good faith and according to the integrity of his memory whatever he could find in the storehouses of the holy Fathers, especially Augustine, Gregory, and the venerable Bede himself.

Moreover, the fact that this commentary cannot in any way be attributed to Bede is demonstrated most clearly by its condemnation, in chapter 7, verse 13; chapter 10, verses 1–6; and chapter 20, verse 31, of the error of the Adoptionists. That error arose in Spain only after the death of the venerable Bede and later began to spread into Gaul.

The testimony of Jonas of Orléans, a contemporary of Louis the Pious, should therefore not move anyone in favor of Bede. In Book 1 of *On the Institution of the Laity*, chapter 13, in d᾽Achery’s *Spicilegium*, volume 1, page 270, Paris edition of 1723, Jonas quotes several verses from Bede’s twentieth homily on the Gospel, which are found in the aforementioned commentary in chapter 2. For this reason Mabillon suspects that Jonas should be read as citing not the twentieth homily but the second.

The passages cited by Jonas of Orléans are indeed Bede’s, but they were not taken from any complete commentary by him on John. Rather, they come from one of his homilies on that passage in chapter 2 of John concerning those buying and selling in the Temple, whom Christ expelled.

This homily is absent from the collections of Bede’s works and could therefore have been unknown to the distinguished Mabillon. It has now been published from a manuscript of Tours in D. Martène’s *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, volume 5, page 343. It is precisely the homily listed as the twenty-second in the capitulation of Bede’s Book of Fifty Homilies in Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, third century, part 1, page 556. This reading seems therefore to require restoration in Jonas of Orléans.

That commentary on the Gospel of John must therefore be entirely removed from the catalogue of the works of the venerable Bede. Bede himself makes no mention of it in the list of his little works, which he composed four years before his death, namely in 731. Alcuin, however, transferred into his commentary all the homilies of the venerable Bede in which Bede expounded certain chapters of Saint John.

As for the author of the final part of the commentary published under Bede’s name—that is, from chapter 13 of John to the end—which, as we said above, differs greatly from Alcuin’s exposition, it is difficult to determine. It does not seem unlikely to us that this part too belongs to Alcuin and that he reworked it in a second revision, if the words of his letter to Lucia and Columba are carefully considered. He writes:

“I ask that, if you deem it worthwhile, you order this portion”—namely, the first five books—“which I have just sent, to be copied . . . and sent back to us as soon as possible; and likewise that portion”—the final two books—“which I sent you last year, so that it may be arranged by numbers, chapters, and beginnings of books; and, if anything ought to be added at the end, so that it may be completed. I have considered adding something further that is scarcely found in other little works.”

Here Alcuin asks that both portions, sent separately, be copied and returned to him, so that something may be added at the end—or, as we interpret it, in the final portion of his commentary—which is not found in the other little works either of the holy Fathers or in those previously sent.

It is therefore easy to conjecture that Alcuin devoted renewed attention to the second part of his commentary and recast it into the form in which it appears among Bede’s works. This is our conjecture, arising from the words cited above; we willingly submit it, however, to the more refined judgment of learned men.

Moreover, Alcuin himself, with his customary candor, openly admits in his letter to Gisla and Richtrudis that he does not bring forth flowers from his own meadow. Conscious of his own insignificance, and wishing to satisfy the will of the aforementioned virgins without risking his reputation, he says that he wandered through the flowering fields of many Fathers and gathered the flowers he found there in scattered form:

“After the example of physicians, who customarily compose for the health of one who asks it a certain kind of medicine from the ingredients of many remedies, and do not dare to declare themselves creators of the herbs or other ingredients from whose composition the sick receive health, but acknowledge themselves to be servants in gathering them and in combining them into one body with the apothecary’s art.”

Later he also identifies the sources from which he drew almost everything: the treatises of Saint Augustine and the homilies of Saint Gregory and the venerable Bede, as well as the little works of Saint Ambrose and the other holy Fathers. He says that he used “the meanings and words of all these men more than committing anything to the presumption of my own judgment,” so that the curiosity of readers can easily test this, and that he carefully guarded his style lest he place anything contrary to the meanings of the holy Fathers.

We have included these remarks so that no one, surveying this commentary, which from beginning to end is compiled almost entirely from the judgments and words of other Fathers, might think that Alcuin passed off another’s work as his own. We identify in their proper places what has been drawn from Augustine, Gregory, and Bede.

**LETTER TO A SISTER AND DAUGHTER. (Year 800.) From a manuscript of the Harleian Library.**

[Col. 0737C]

To the beloved persons in Christ, Lucia and Columba, Albinus, brother and father, sends greetings in the consolation of the Holy Spirit.

Remembering your request and my promise, although I fulfilled it later than I should have because of my many occupations, I never at all forgot what I recalled having pledged to you. You imposed upon me a difficult and arduous task, presumptuous for my small abilities; but I considered it established that I should refuse nothing to charity, because I knew very well that nothing is impossible to him [F., in him] who is true charity. Devotedly traversing the storerooms of the holy Fathers, whatever I was able to find in them I have brought to you for tasting, so that you may judge whether it has a catholic flavor—or otherwise, which God forbid. What I read I have presented in full faith, according to the integrity of my memory. I have also placed before this work the letter containing your request, so that future readers might recognize your devotional zeal and the occasion of my obedience.

{460} I have likewise added a letter assenting to your desire, which I have also placed before our little work as a kind of prologue; and I have included the evangelist’s account of the necessity that compelled him to write the Gospel, together with the other matters that you can read and recognize in that letter, and how necessary it appears to be. Indeed, I confess that nearly thirty years ago I had the desire to undertake this work; but my pen rested, because there was no one to rouse it, until your good intention recalled it to the practice of writing. If you find anything worthy to have been produced by my labor, give glory to God, who gave it, and hope for a reward yourselves, since you stirred up my sluggish talent to put its hand into Christ’s treasury, so that it might bring something out of it for the consolation of his handmaids. I know that to everyone who has, something must be given; likewise, to whoever has the desire to learn, the grace of understanding will be given. But there are some who are more ready to bite the words of others than to bring their own into public view; their teeth should be avoided, or at least held in little account. For dove-like charity easily disregards a serpent’s tooth. Often, where charity advances, envy languishes; and it stains milky sweetness with black poison. May your prudence disregard such people, striving more to make progress than to concern yourselves with those who envy.

I ask you, if you deem it worthwhile, to have this portion that I have now sent you transcribed, and to mark the chapters of each section with their numbers; carefully distinguish the beginnings of the books, and send the written copy back to me as soon as possible. At the same time, send also the portion that I sent you last year, so that it may be arranged by numbers and chapters, with the beginnings of the books. And if anything ought to be added at the end, so that it may be complete, I have thought of adding something further, which is scarcely found in other little works.

As for the letter that you sent me [F., direxistis, “you sent” (plural)], I received it kindly, giving thanks to God for the exaltation of my most excellent lord David; for the prosperity of the apostolic man; and for the honorable embassy to the holy city, in which our Savior deigned to redeem [redemere; for redimere] the world by his blood and to be crowned and exalted by the glory of his resurrection and ascension. But you, my dearest daughters, always keep his charity in your hearts, praise upon your lips, and his work in your hands. Prepare for yourselves a place among the brides of that eternal King, so that he may deign to show himself to you—he who promised that he would show himself to those who love him. In the vision of him there is blessed eternity and eternal blessedness. Remember me in your sacred prayers and in those of the handmaids of Christ who serve God with you, so that the blessing of our Lord Jesus Christ may enable me, his servant, to prosper in his house, and may he deign to grant pardon for my sins. May God, the Son of God, Jesus Christ our Lord, make you flourish and grow strong for a long and blessed time in every pursuit of holiness and in the understanding of wisdom, my dearest daughters.

## LETTER OF CHRIST’S HANDMAIDS GISLA AND RECTRUDA TO ALBINUS, THEIR TEACHER

To the venerable Father Albinus, our teacher, whom we embrace with the greatest honor [Al., devotion], the most humble handmaids of Christ, Gisla and Rectruda [Ms., Richtruda], send greetings of everlasting blessedness.

After we had drawn from your exposition something of the honey-sweet knowledge of Holy Scripture, venerable teacher, our desire for this most sacred reading, as we confess, burned in us more intensely from day to day. In it there is the purification of the soul, the consolation of our mortality, and the hope of everlasting blessedness. In it the blessed man, according to the Psalmist, exercises himself in daily meditation, understanding that knowledge of it [Ms., cognitionem, “knowledge”] must be preferred to all the riches of the world, and that there is no other true wisdom except that which, according to the dispensation of divine providence, heavenly grace has administered to the human race. This is the manna that satisfies without weariness and nourishes without failing. These are the grains of the divine harvest, which, rubbed by apostolic hands and set before the banquets of the faithful, have been offered to their souls.

But two things greatly opposed to us weary our small minds with daily sadness. One is that we took up the diligent study of this excellent subject too late; the other is that now, while we possess great devotion, your distance sufficiently obstructs our desire. Therefore, dearest teacher, we implore your goodness not to deprive us of the consolation of your letters. You can show yourself to us who seek you through the service of letters, so that your voice may be understood in the hidden desire of our hearts. For just as the tongue of one speaking benefits the ear of the listener, so the pen of one writing benefits the eye of the reader; and the thought of the one who directs reaches the inner parts of the heart, just as the words of one who instructs do. Therefore, most blessed Father, do not deny us this. Water the breasts of our smallness, dried up, with the stream of a saving [Al., salutary] fountain. We know that in you there is a fountain of living water which, as the Lord says, will spring up into eternal life (John 4:14). We do not wish what Solomon says about those who are accustomed to conceal their wisdom to apply to you:

> A treasure hidden and wisdom concealed: what use are either? (Ecclesiasticus 41:17)

Rather, let what the Lord says through the Prophet apply:

> Open your mouth, and I will fill it (Psalm 80:11).

Open your mouth confidently, with the Holy Spirit inspiring you, upon the most sacred exposition of the blessed evangelist John, and unfold for us the venerable thoughts of the holy Fathers. Gather the pearls of many writers into the chamber of your spiritual treasury, and feed Christ’s poor from it. Do not send us away hungry, lest we fail on the road.

We do indeed possess the explanations of the most illustrious teacher Augustine, in homiletic [Al., homiletical] discourse, on this same evangelist; but in certain places they are much more obscure and adorned with greater circumlocution than the little intellect of our smallness can penetrate. It is enough for us to drink from the rivulets of your devotion’s sweetest water; do not launch our little boats upon the deepest whirlpools of the rivers [Al., rather, it is enough for our devotion]. For you know very well that little things suffice for the small, and that a poor crowd cannot approach the table of the great.

Nor is it our task to climb the highest peaks of the cedars; rather, because of the shortness of our stature, let us stand with Zacchaeus in the sycamore and see Jesus passing by (Luke 19:4), continually entreating in our prayers that he may make us worthy of his banquets, and singing with you the sweetest model of a wedding song:

> The King has brought us into his chambers; we will exult and rejoice in him (Song of Songs 1:3).

Remember the most illustrious teacher of divine Scripture in the holy Church, the most blessed Jerome. He did not in any way disdain the prayers of noble women, but devoted many little works to their names in explanation of prophetic obscurities. Often, too, from the little town of Bethlehem, consecrated to the nativity of Christ our Lord, he sent letters flying to the Roman citadels at the request of the women who sought this from him [Al., “epistolary letters”]; nor was he frightened by the distance of the lands or by the stormy waves of the Adriatic Sea, so as not to grant the requests of holy virgins.

The shallow river Loire is navigated with less danger than the breadth of the Tyrrhenian Sea. And the bearer [Ms., carrier] of your letters will be able to reach the city of Paris from Tours much more easily than his letter-bearer could travel from Bethlehem to Rome.

@ [Col. 0739D] Here the Vatican manuscript ends, omitting what follows.

Do not withhold from us the knowledge of your devotion; do not place the lamp burning within you under a bushel (Matthew 5:15), or hide it in the repose of a sluggish bed. Rather, set it upon a lofty lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house of God. Enter the treasuries of the holy teachers, and bring forth for us, like a most learned scribe and one praised by the Lord, things new and old (Matthew 13:52). His grace will assist you on the journey of this labor: he who, when two disciples were walking along the road, added himself as a third companion and opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Holy Scriptures. How will you be able to excuse yourself for the fault of silence before him who says, “Give to everyone who asks you” (Luke 24:32 and following), especially when what you give will in no way be diminished for you, but rather increase by being given? May the Paraclete Spirit fill your breasts with every teaching of truth and knowledge of perfect charity, sweetest teacher.

{462} ## LETTER OF ALBINUS, THE TEACHER, TO GISLA AND RICHTRUDA

To the most noble virgins devoted to the sanctity of the Christian religion and to the study of wisdom, and dedicated to God, Gisla my sister and Richtruda my daughter [Al., Gisla and Richtruda, my daughters], the humble brother and father Albinus sends greetings of everlasting blessedness.

As much as I praise in you your excellent devotion to the most sacred study of wisdom, so much do I lament my own ignorance [Ms., that of myself], and I recognize that I am far unequal to your praiseworthy devotion. Would that the ability to write in my breast were as great as the desire to read in yours [Ms., as great as your desire]. Therefore I am hemmed in by two difficulties: on the one side, to deny anything to charity, to which I am bound to offer everything; on the other, to seek higher things and to exceed the measure of my smallness, since Scripture says:

> Do not seek what is above you (Ecclesiasticus 3:22).

Unless perhaps the fault lies in you, because you asked for difficult things, and I have a just ground for excusing myself, since, considering my weaknesses, I have resolved to restrain my pen from a work too lofty for me [Ms., my highest work].

You ought to know that among all the pages of divine Scripture the authority of the Gospel rightly excels, because what the Law and the Prophets foretold would happen is shown in the Gospel as given and fulfilled. Among the evangelists themselves, the blessed John is greatly distinguished as more eminent in the depth of divine mysteries. It is also related of him, as we read in ecclesiastical history, that almost until the very end of his life he preached the Gospel in pure speech, without the aid of any written Scripture. For from the time of the Lord’s passion, resurrection, and ascension until the final years of the reign of Domitian, about sixty-five years, he preached the word of God without any writing to assist him.

But when Domitian, who became the second persecutor of Christians after Nero, sent him into exile on Patmos [Beda, exiled on Patmos], the opportunity created by the absence of that devout Father was seized by heretics who broke into the Church like wolves into sheepfolds abandoned by their shepherd: Marcion, Cerinthus, Hebion, and the other Antichrists, who denied that Christ existed before Mary. By their perverse doctrine they stained the simplicity of evangelical faith.

But after Domitian’s killing [Edit., opportunity], when the devout emperor Nerva permitted him to return to Ephesus, almost all the bishops of Asia at that time and delegations from many churches compelled him to speak more profoundly about Christ’s divinity, coeternal with the Father. They believed that in the writings of the three evangelists—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—they already had sufficient testimony concerning his humility [Ms., humanity] and concerning what he had done as a human being.

John replied that he would do this only if, after proclaiming a fast, they all prayed together to the Lord, so that, by his gift, he might be able to write what was worthy. When this had been done, instructed by heavenly revelation and filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, he suddenly dispelled all the darkness of the heretics by the light of truth revealed, saying:

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1).

When knowledge of the three Gospels—those of Matthew, Mark, and Luke—reached him, he is said to have approved the faith and truth of their statements. Yet he saw that something was lacking from the history of the events, especially those that the Lord had done at the beginning of his preaching. For it is certain that in the three earlier Gospels only those events seem to be contained that took place after John the Baptist had been handed over and confined in prison.

Indeed, if you observe the narrative at its beginning, after Matthew reports the forty-day fast and Christ’s temptation, he immediately adds:

> But when he heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew from Judea and came into Galilee (Matthew 4:12).

Mark likewise says:

> After John had been handed over, Jesus came into Galilee (Mark 1:14).

Luke, even before he begins to report anything about Jesus’ deeds, says:

> Herod added this also to all the evils that he had done, and shut John up in prison (Luke 3:20).

Since these matters appeared to have been omitted by the others, the apostle John is said to have been asked to describe what the earlier evangelists had passed over—namely, what the Savior had done before John was handed over. Therefore he says in his Gospel:

> This was the beginning of Jesus’ signs (John 2:11).

And again, in another place, he indicates:

> For John had not yet been sent to prison (John 3:24).

From this it is clear that he describes what Jesus had done before John was handed over.

But beyond doubt he intended especially to make known the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which he is equal to the Father, and he took care to commend this above all in his Gospel, as far as he judged sufficient among human beings. Thus he rose far higher than the three earlier evangelists, so that you seem to see them, in a certain sense, walking upon the earth with Christ as man, while he has transcended the cloud that covers all the earth and reached the clear light of heaven. From there, with the sharpest and most steadfast vision of the mind, he saw in the beginning the Word, God from God, light from light, through whom all things were made; and he recognized that the Word himself had been made flesh so that he might dwell among us—not that he had been changed into flesh, but that he had assumed flesh.

For unless the assumption of flesh had taken place while his divinity remained unchangeable, it would not have been said:

> I and the Father are one (John 10:30).

For the Father and flesh are not one. The same John alone also recalled the Lord’s testimony about himself:

> Whoever sees me sees the Father.

And:

> I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.

And:

> That they may be one, just as we also are one.

And:

> Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does the same (John 14:9–10).

And whatever other statements rightly disclose to those who understand them Christ’s divinity, in which he is equal to the Father, John alone set forth more fully in his Gospel, as though he had drunk more abundantly and, in a certain way, more intimately from the Lord’s own breast the secret of his divinity—the breast upon which he was accustomed to recline at the Lord’s banquet.

Accordingly, since two virtues have been set before the human soul, one active and the other contemplative—the one by which we travel, the other by which we arrive; the one by which we labor so that the heart may be cleansed for seeing God, the other by which God is called and seen—the former belongs to the commandments governing this temporal life, the latter to the teaching of that everlasting life. Hence the one works, while the other rests: the one is concerned with the cleansing of sins, the other with the light of those who have been cleansed. Thus, in this mortal life, the one is expressed in the practice of good conduct, while the other is found more in faith, and among very few in a partial vision of unchanging Truth, through a mirror and in an enigma.

From this, if you attend carefully, it may be understood that the three evangelists, who more abundantly pursued the Lord’s temporal deeds and words—those especially useful for forming the conduct of the present life—were occupied with the active virtue. John, however, narrating far fewer of the Lord’s deeds but writing his words more carefully and abundantly, especially those that suggested the unity of the Trinity and the blessedness of eternal life, maintained his course [Ms., intention] and preaching in commending the contemplative virtue.

This is John, one of Christ’s disciples, whom the Lord called a virgin from the stormy upheaval of marriage. Two testimonies to his virginity are given in the Gospel: he is said to have been loved by God above the others, and the Lord entrusted his mother to him from the throne of the cross, saying [Beda, God entrusted her], so that a virgin might preserve a virgin. By the singular privilege of chastity he deserved, above all the other writers of Christ’s miracles, both to grasp and to disclose more profoundly the mystery of divine majesty.

For it is not without reason that he is said to have reclined upon Jesus’ breast at the mystical supper. By this it is most truly taught that he drank more excellently than the others from the most sacred fountain of that same breast the draught of heavenly wisdom. Therefore, in the figure of the four living creatures, he is rightly compared to a flying eagle (Ezekiel 1). The eagle is accustomed to fly higher than all birds and to fix its gaze more clearly than all living creatures upon the rays of the sun. Thus the blessed John saw more sublimely the mysteries of Christ’s eternal birth.

He was the first [before Peter] of the disciples laboring at fishing to recognize Christ standing on the shore and commanding them to cast the net on the right side of the boat. He said to Peter:

> It is the Lord.

He is one of those of whom the Prophet foretold:

> The heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 18:1).

Therefore he was called by the Lord himself the son of thunder, because from heavenly brightness he thundered forth this marvelous preface, unheard throughout all the ages:

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1).

These words must always be revered with pure faith and cultivated with perpetual religious devotion; they must not be excessively dissected by the petty arguments of human conjecture, which is often deceived when it thinks it recognizes what surpasses the investigation of human understanding.

Nevertheless, whatever devout charity and humble inquiry have been able to understand from them is found expressed in the most sacred writings of the holy Fathers, although scattered in different places. Likewise, throughout the entire text of this same Gospel, many passages are read as expounded by catholic teachers according to the needs of the place or time, both for the confirmation of orthodox faith and in opposition to heretical perversities, in defense of apostolic tradition.

Therefore I think I may perhaps find a certain middle course between my refusal and your request, so that neither your charity may be wholly disregarded through my silence nor my presumption be reproved in complying with your request. Physicians commonly compose a kind of medicine from many kinds of pigments for the healing of the person who asks for it. They do not presume to call themselves creators of the herbs or other ingredients from whose composition the health of the sick is produced, but only ministers in gathering them and forming them into one body with the apothecary’s art. So also, if perhaps the labor of my devotion can contribute something to your charity, I do not think that I ought to gather flowers from just any meadow of my father’s inheritance. Rather, I see that I must traverse, with humble heart and bowed neck, the flowering fields of many Fathers, so that I may satisfy your most sacred desire without danger to my own reputation.

First of all I seek the assistance of Saint Augustine, who labored with the greatest zeal to expound the sacred words of this holy Gospel. Then I draw certain things from the little works of the most holy teacher Saint Ambrose; likewise, I take much from the homilies of the distinguished Father, Pope Gregory, and from the homilies of the blessed priest Bede. I have also set down the interpretations of other holy Fathers as I was able to find them, using the thoughts and words of all these men more than committing anything to my own presumption, as the curiosity of readers will easily be able to prove. With the greatest care, plainly, and with the help of divine grace, I have taken precautions not to place anything contrary to the thoughts of the holy Fathers.

Accordingly, I have divided the whole work according to the chapters of this same Gospel and completed it in the numbering of seven books. I pray that, with the grace of the sevenfold Spirit inspiring your hearts, you may flourish in the varied delights of Christ’s Church and walk each day with the saints from virtue to virtue, until the God of gods is seen in Zion, where, amid the choirs of the heavenly hosts, you may say in perpetual sweetness:

> Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; they will praise you for ever and ever.

Amen.

{467} ## BOOK ONE OF THE COMMENTARIES ON JOHN

### CHAPTER ONE

In the beginning was the Word with God, through whom all things were made. John was sent before him, who makes those who receive him sons of God by grace.

### VERSE 1

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

@ [Col. 0743D] From the homily of the Venerable Bede on the Nativity of the Lord.—NOTE. In this work I have marked with this sign «» the words of the Venerable Bede, and likewise those of Saints Augustine and Gregory, from the point at which they begin to the point at which they end.

«For it is not without reason that the blessed John, the Lord’s beloved disciple, is said to have reclined upon Jesus’ breast at the supper. Through this it is taught figuratively that he drank more deeply than the others from the most sacred fountain of that same breast the draught of heavenly wisdom. Hence he is rightly compared, in the figure of the four living creatures, to a flying eagle (Ezekiel 1). The eagle is accustomed to fly higher than all birds and to fix its gaze more clearly than all living creatures upon the rays of the sun.

The other evangelists are, as it were, walking upon the earth with the Lord. Since they adequately explain both his temporal birth and his temporal deeds, they say little about his divinity. But this one, as it were, flies to heaven with the Lord. Explaining very little about his temporal actions, he recognized more sublimely and contemplated more clearly, by flying in the mind, the eternal power of his divinity, through whom all things were made; and by writing, he handed it down to us to be known. Thus the other evangelists describe Christ as born in time, while John testifies, teaching that he already existed in the beginning, saying:»

@ In the Strasbourg edition this first chapter is inserted.

“In the beginning was the Word.” This can be understood in two ways. For the Father is the beginning, as though he had said, “In the Father.” The Son is in the Father, and this evangelist called him the Word. Nor should we be troubled by the fact that later in this Gospel, when the Jews asked who he himself was, the Son of God replied, “The Beginning, who also speaks to you” (John 8:25). For if the Son is the beginning [Al., If the Son, begotten, had not been from the Father], who has a Father, how much more readily must God the Father be understood to be the beginning, since he has a Son for whom he is Father? The Son is the Father’s Son; and the Father is certainly the Son’s Father. The Father is God, but not God from God; the Son is true God from God.

The Father is called light, but not light from light; the Son is called light, but light from light. Thus the Father is the beginning, but not beginning from beginning; the Son is the beginning, but beginning from the beginning. What was in the beginning is not ended by time, nor begun from a beginning [Ms. and Beda, nor preceded by a beginning; the following line is omitted]. The Son, as beginning, is not ended by time and is not preceded by a beginning, whether you wish to refer the statement “In the beginning was the Word” to the beginning of creatures, or to the beginning of times. Whatever creature had a beginning in order to exist, the Word of God, through whom all things were made, already was. Therefore the evangelist says four times, “was, was, was, was,” so that you might understand that the Word, coeternal with God the Father, preceded every time [Ms., all times].

«The other evangelists show that the Son of God suddenly appeared among human beings; the blessed John declares that he had always been with God, saying, “And the Word was with God.” The others confirm that he was a true human being; this one confirms that he himself was true God, saying, “And the Word was God.” The others show him dwelling temporally as a human being among human beings; this one shows God remaining with God in the beginning, saying (verse 2), “He was in the beginning with God.”»

If it is also pleasing to refer the earlier “beginning” to the Father, and this subsequent beginning to creatures, the meaning is that the Word, that is, the Son, was eternally in the Father, and that by his essence he preceded every beginning of creatures.

«The others report the great things he did as a human being; this one teaches that God made every visible and invisible creature through him, saying (verse 3): “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” For if no creature was made without him, it is plainly evident that he himself is not a creature, through whom every creature was made.

And lest anyone, hearing that the creature was made through the Son of God, should believe that his will is changeable—as though he suddenly wished to make a creature that he had never before made from eternity—the Evangelist clearly teaches that the creature was indeed made in time, but that in the eternal wisdom of the Creator it had always been determined when and what it would be created. This is what he says:

### VERSE 4

“What was made, in him was life.”

That is, whatever appeared as having been made in time, whether living or lacking life, all of it had always lived, as it were, in the spiritual reasoning of the Creator, and lives there. This is not because what he created is coeternal with the Creator, but because the reasoning of his will is coeternal with him. In that reasoning, from eternity, he had and has knowledge of what he created and when; how he should govern what was created, so that it might remain; and to what end he should lead each thing he created.» [Ms., crearet, “might create”]

Therefore it should be punctuated and understood as a separate statement, with a different voice: “In him was life.” For whatever was made through him also lives in him. Just as an art lives in the mind of an artist, although the chest or some other object made by him may perish.

«And life was the light of human beings.» By this word it is plainly taught that the living reasoning through which all things have been ordered and are governed enlightens not every creature, but only the rational creature, so that it may be capable of understanding. Human beings, who were made in the image of God, can receive wisdom; animals cannot. Moreover, any human being who is merely animal does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 2:14). Therefore, after he had said, “And life was the light of human beings,” he appropriately added something about those who, withdrawing far from the honor of human nature, have been compared to foolish beasts and made like them, and therefore are rightly deprived of the light of truth.

### VERSE 5

“And the light,” he says, “shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.”

Christ is indeed the light of human beings, because by the presence of his knowledge he illuminates all human hearts that deserve to be enlightened. The darkness, however, consists of the foolish and the wicked. The light of eternal wisdom clearly knows what their blind hearts are like, although they themselves are entirely unable to grasp the rays of that same light through understanding. It is as if a blind person were covered with the brightness of the sun but could not see the sun itself, even though he were flooded with its light.»

Divine mercy therefore provided such people with a way by which they might reach the point of seeing the true light and becoming sons of light, although they had been sons of darkness. The beginning of this knowledge was what follows:

### VERSES 6–7
