«“There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. He came for testimony, to bear testimony concerning the light, so that all might believe through him.”

He did not say, “so that all might believe in him.” For:

> Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm (Jeremiah 17:5).

But he says, “so that all might believe through him,” that is, so that through John’s testimony they might believe in the light, which they did not yet know how to see—namely, the Lord Jesus Christ, who testifies about himself:

> I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life (John 8:12).

It follows:

### VERSES 8–9

“‘He was not the light, but to bear testimony concerning the light. He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into [this] world.’

Holy human beings are also rightly called light, since the Lord says to them:

> You are the light of the world (Matthew 5:14).

And the apostle Paul says:

> Once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord (Ephesians 5:8).

But there is a great difference between the light that is enlightened and the light that enlightens; between those who receive a share in the true light so that they may shine, and the everlasting light itself, which is sufficient not only to shine in itself but also to illuminate by its presence whoever it touches.

In comparison with this true light, not only any of the lesser elect, but even John himself—than whom no one has arisen among those born of women—is said not to be light, so that it might plainly be shown that Christ was not what he was thought to be. For John, as it is written:

> Was a burning and shining lamp (John 5:35).

Burning, that is, with faith and love; shining with word and action.

But to pour the grace of light into breasts belongs only to him of whom it says:

> He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into [this] world.

That means everyone who is enlightened, whether by natural intelligence or by divine wisdom. For just as no one can exist from himself, so no one can be wise from himself; rather, wisdom comes from the one who enlightens, of whom it is written:

> All wisdom is from the Lord God (Ecclesiasticus 1:1).

The Evangelist then described both of his natures: his divine nature, by which he always remains wholly present everywhere, and his human nature, from which he was born in time and appeared enclosed in a place, saying:

### VERSES 10–11

“‘He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. He came among his own, and his own did not receive him.’

He was in the world, and the world was made through him, because he was God, because he was wholly everywhere, because by the presence of his majesty he governs without labor and sustains without burden what he made.

And the world did not know him, because the light shines in the darkness and the darkness did not comprehend it. In this place, by “the world” he means human beings deceived by love of the world and, by clinging to the creature, turned away from recognizing the majesty of their Creator.

He came among his own, because in the world that he made through his divinity he was born and appeared through his humanity. He came among his own, because he deigned to be incarnate among the Jewish people, whom he had joined to himself by special grace above all other nations.

Thus he was in the world and came into the world. He was in the world through his divinity; he came into the world through the incarnation. To come and to depart belong to humanity; to remain and to exist belong to divinity. Therefore, because, while he was in the world through his divinity, the world did not know him, he deigned to come into the world through his humanity, so that in this way the world might at least recognize him.

But let us see what follows:

‘He came among his own, and his own did not receive him.’

They had known him creating and governing all things in the power of his divinity [Bede and Ms., they did not know him], but they did not wish to receive him shining forth in miracles in the weakness of flesh.

And what is more serious, his own did not receive him: human beings whom he himself had created; the Jews, whom he had specially chosen for himself as a people; to whom he had revealed the mystery of his knowledge; whom he had glorified through the wondrous deeds of their fathers; to whom he had given the teaching of his law; from whom he had promised that he would take flesh; and among whom he showed himself incarnate, as he had promised. They, for the most part, refused to receive him when he came.

For not all refused him; otherwise no one would be saved and his incarnation would have been in vain. But now many from both peoples received him by not believing [variant: rejected him; many received him by believing]. Concerning them the Evangelist next says:»
{470} **VERSE 12.**—But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name. Let us consider, dearest brothers, how great is the grace of our Redeemer, how immense is the abundance of his sweetness. He was born One and Only from the Father, and he did not wish to remain alone. He descended to earth, [Col. 0748B] where he might acquire brothers for himself to whom he could give the kingdom of his Father. God was born from God, and he did not wish to remain only the Son of God; he also deigned to become the son of man, not losing what he was, but assuming what he was not, so that through this he might transfer human beings into the sons of God and make them coheirs of his glory—those who would begin to possess by grace what he himself had always possessed by nature.

Let us consider how great is the power of faith, by whose merit human beings are given the power to become children of God. Hence it is well written: “The righteous man lives by faith” (Heb. II, 4; Rom. I, 17). The righteous man lives by faith—not by that which is expressed merely by a confession of the lips, but by that which works through love. Otherwise, “if faith does not have works, it is dead in itself” (James II, 17). Let no one despise himself; let no one despair of his salvation. Let us all run—let each of us run—so that we who were far away may deserve to be brought near through the blood of Christ. Let us see what is said: “To all who received him he gave power to become children of God.” “To all,” he says, “who received him.” For God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears him and practices righteousness is acceptable to him. The evangelist next indicates in what order believers can become children of God, and how greatly this generation differs from carnal generation.

**VERSE 13.**—“Who were born,” he says, “not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.” Our carnal generation as individuals originated from “bloods,” that is, from the seed of male and female, through the union of marriage. But spiritual generation is supplied by the grace of the Holy Spirit. Distinguishing it from carnal generation, the Lord says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit” (John III, 5–6). Yet, lest anyone doubt that human beings can become sons of God and coheirs of Christ, the evangelist provides an example: the Son of God himself deigned to become man and dwell among human beings, so that, by sharing in human frailty, he might grant human beings a share in his divine power.

**VERSE 14.**—“And the Word,” he says, “became flesh and dwelt among us.” This means that the Son of God became man and lived among human beings. Scripture commonly designates the whole human being sometimes by the term “soul,” sometimes by the term “flesh”: by “soul,” as it is written, “Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy souls” (Deut. X, 22); by “flesh,” as it is written again, “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke III, 6). For neither can souls descend into Egypt without bodies, nor can flesh see anything without a soul; rather, in the former passage the whole human being is signified by “soul,” and in the latter by “flesh.”

Thus, in this passage, when it is said, “The Word became flesh,” nothing else should be understood than if it had been said, “God became man,” by putting on flesh and a soul. Just as each of us is one human being composed of flesh and soul, so, from the time of the incarnation, the one Christ consists of divinity, flesh, and soul: truly God, existing from eternity to eternity as he was, assuming in time a true man whom he had not previously possessed, into the unity of his person. It follows:

“And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.” The glory of Christ, which human beings could not see before the incarnation, they saw after the incarnation, beholding his humanity shining with miracles and understanding the divinity concealed within. This was especially true of those who deserved to contemplate his splendor when he was transfigured on the holy mountain, and who heard a voice descending to him from the magnificent glory: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. XVII, 5). After the passion, when they had seen the glory of his resurrection and ascension, they were wonderfully refreshed by the gift of his Spirit. [Col. 0749C] Through all these things they clearly recognized that such glory belonged not to just any saint, but only to that man who, in his divinity, was the Only-begotten from the Father.

As for what follows, “Full of grace and truth”: Christ Jesus as man was and is full of grace. By a singular gift he was granted, above all other mortals, that from the very moment he began to be conceived in the Virgin’s womb and to become man, he should be truly God. Hence that same glorious ever-virgin Mary must rightly be believed and confessed to be not only the mother of the man Christ, but also the Mother of God.

He was and is likewise full of truth—namely, through the very divinity of the Word, which deigned to assume that uniquely chosen man with whom there was one person of Christ. It did not, as heretics claim, transform something of its divine substance into the making of human nature; rather, remaining what it was with the Father, it assumed the whole nature of a true man from the seed of David, a nature it had not possessed.

@ [Col. 0749D] Thus far from Bede’s cited homily.»**

**VERSE 15.**—«

@ [Col. 0750D] From Bede’s Homily 2. John bears witness concerning him. The witness of our Redeemer’s forerunner, bearing testimony concerning him, proclaims with a clear voice both the loftiness of his humanity and the eternity of his divinity. For he cries out, saying: “This was he of whom I said to you, ‘He who comes after me has been placed before me, because he was before me’” (John I, 15).

In the statement, “He who comes after me,” he indicates the order of the human dispensation: Christ was born after John, and was also to preach, baptize, perform signs, and suffer death after him. In what he adds, “He has been placed before me,” he designates the sublimity of that same humanity, by which he was rightly to be preferred to all other creatures.

The expression “before me” does not refer to the order of time, but to a difference of dignity, in accordance with what is written of Jacob when he blessed Joseph’s sons: “He placed Ephraim before Manasseh” (Gen. XLVIII, 20). There Manasseh could rightly have said, “He who comes after me has been placed before me”—that is, “He who was born after me has surpassed me in royal power.” In the same way John says of the Lord, “He who comes after me has been placed before me”—that is, “He who will come after me to preach surpasses me in the dignity of an enduring kingdom and priesthood.”

He explains why the one who was to come after him would surpass him in dignity when he adds: “Because he was before me.” That is: because he was God eternal before the ages, therefore, although born later than I, he will precede me in the glory of his majesty, even in the humanity he assumed.

After the evangelist has set forth the testimony that the Lord’s forerunner had given concerning him, he immediately resumes the testimony that he himself had begun to give. For it follows:

**VERSE 16.**—“And from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace.” Above he had said: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.” After confirming this also by the testimony of his forerunner, who said, “This was he of whom I said to you, ‘He who comes after me has been placed before me, because he was before me,’” he again continues what he had begun, saying: “And from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace.”

The Lord was full of the Holy Spirit, full of grace and truth, because, as the Apostle says, “In him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II, 9). From his fullness we have all received, according to the measure of our capacity, because grace has been given to each of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift (Eph. IV, 7).

Of the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, it could truly be said: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. XI, 2). All the saints, however, do not receive the fullness of his Spirit, but receive from his fullness as much as he grants.

“To one,” indeed, “through the Spirit is given the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge, according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, the grace of healings in one Spirit; to another, the working of miracles; to another, prophecy [Ms., prophetia, ‘prophecy’]; to another, the discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, the interpretation of utterances. But all these things one and the same Spirit brings about, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. XII, 8–11).

Since, therefore, from the fullness of our Creator we possess whatever good we have received—not some of us, but all—it must be guarded with the greatest care that no one thoughtlessly exalts himself on account of a good action or thought, lest, if he remains ungrateful to the giver, he lose the good he received.

When the evangelist had said that we all received from Christ’s fullness, he immediately added: “Grace upon grace.” Thus he testifies that we have received a twofold grace: one in the present and another in the future. In the present, faith that works through love; in the future, eternal life.

Faith that works through love is itself the grace of God, because we have received both that we believe and that we may love and do the good things we know—not from any preceding merits of our own, but from him who gives [Ms., “because in order that we might believe, that we may”], who says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit” (John XV, 16).

And that we may receive eternal life on account of faith and love, through good works, is also the grace of God, because in order not to stray from the good path we always need him as our guide. To him it is said: “Lead me, Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth” (Ps. LXXXV, 11).»

It should be noted that some books read: “We have all received from his fullness, and grace upon grace.” First we received something from his fullness; and afterward, grace upon grace—that is, from his fullness we received remission of sins, and “grace,” namely eternal life, in exchange for the grace of faith that works through love. It is entirely certain that all these things come to us from the one source of Christ’s fullness.

What, then, did we receive from the fullness of his goodness? Namely, remission of sins, so that we might be justified by faith. What more? “And grace upon grace”—that is, in exchange for the grace by which we live from faith, we shall receive another. Yet what else can it be but grace? That is, eternal life. It follows:

**VERSE 17.**—«

@ [Col. 0751D] Bede, at the cited passage. “Because the law was given through Moses, grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” The law was indeed given through Moses, in which heavenly law determines what must be done and what must be avoided. But what it commands is fulfilled only through the grace of Christ. For the law was able to display sin, teach righteousness, and show transgressors to be guilty before it. The grace of Christ, spread through the spirit of love in the hearts of the faithful, causes what the law commands to be fulfilled.

Hence the commandment that is written, “You shall not covet,” belongs to the law given through Moses, which commands it [Al., “because it is commanded”]; but grace comes through Christ when what is commanded is fulfilled.

Truth, however, came through Christ because the law had a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of those things. As the Apostle says elsewhere: “All these things happened to them in figure” (1 Cor. X, 11). But in place of the shadow Christ brought the light of truth; in place of the figure of the law, he brought the very image of the things represented, when, having given the grace of the Spirit, he opened the understanding of his disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures.

The law was given through Moses when the people were commanded to be cleansed by the sprinkling of the blood of a lamb. The grace and truth prefigured in the law came through Jesus Christ when, having suffered on the cross, he washed us from our sins in his blood.

The law was given through Moses because he instructed the people in saving commandments, promising that if they kept them they would enter the promised land and live in it forever; but if they did otherwise, he foretold that they would be struck down by their enemies. Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ because, after giving the gift of his Spirit, he also granted the ability to understand and keep the law spiritually; and he brings those who keep it into the true blessedness of heavenly life, which the promised land signified.

The evangelist makes clear what is the sum of the grace and truth that came through Jesus Christ by adding:

**VERSE 18.**—“No one has ever seen God; the Only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he himself has declared him.” No greater grace can be given to human beings, and no higher truth can be known by them, than that concerning which the Only-begotten Son of God, teaching his faithful, says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8). And concerning which, praying to the Father, he says: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the true and one God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII, 3).

Since this most blessed perception of grace and truth cannot take place in the life of the present age, it is rightly said: “No one has ever seen God” (1 John IV, 2)—that is, no one still enclosed in corruptible and mortal flesh can gaze upon the unbounded light of divinity. Hence the Apostle says more explicitly: “Whom no human being has seen, nor can see” (1 Tim. VI, 16). No human being, that is, no one still weighed down by human condition and subject to frailty in human conduct, is meant.

For this reason Moses, desiring to see in God’s very nature the one whom he saw in an angel, prayed: “If I have found grace in your sight, show me your glory.” He heard: “You cannot see my face, for no human being shall see me and live” (Exod. XX, 18–20).

The evangelist next explains by what means one must reach the vision of the unchangeable and eternal light, saying:

{473} “The Only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he himself has declared him.” To this is similar what the Lord says: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV, 6); and elsewhere: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matt. XI, 27).

Under his guidance we must come to the Father; through his teaching we must know the Father and the Son, and also the Holy Spirit, one God and Lord. For he himself, having become man for us and speaking to us in human form, clearly revealed what should rightly be believed concerning the unity of the Holy Trinity, how the faithful should hasten toward its contemplation, and by what actions it must be reached.

By instructing us in the sacraments of his incarnation and sanctifying us with the gifts of his Spirit, he helps us to reach it. After completing judgment in human form, he will finally raise us into the vision of the divine majesty and wonderfully declare to us the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom [Ms., “declared them”].

In saying, “who is in the bosom of the Father,” he signifies “in the Father’s secret.” The bosom of the Father must not be understood childishly, after the likeness of our bosom, which we have in our garments; nor should God, who is not composed in the form of human limbs, be thought to sit in the way that we do. But because our bosom is within, Scripture, speaking according to our manner of expression, says that he is in the bosom of the Father—meaning that he continually remains in the Father’s secret, to which human sight cannot reach.

The Only-begotten Son will not declare God—that is, manifest to human beings the glory of the holy and undivided Trinity, which is one God—only when, after the universal judgment, he leads all the elect together into the vision of his glory. He also declares him daily, when he begins to fulfill for each of the perfected faithful, as soon as they have been released from the corruption of the flesh [Edit., “incorruption”], what he promised: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.” “I will manifest myself,” he says, “to those who love me,” so that they who knew him as mortal in his own nature may nevertheless see him, in my nature, equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit.»

**CHAPTER II**

John denies that he is the Christ, but declares that he was sent before him and proclaims, according to Isaiah, the voice of one crying in the wilderness.

**VERSE 19.**—“This is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to him to ask him, ‘Who are you?’ etc.” «

@ [Col. 0753D] From Book I, Homily 7, of the holy Pope Gregory. These words commend John’s humility. Although he possessed such great virtue that he could have been believed to be the Christ, he chose to remain firmly within himself, lest he be vainly carried beyond himself by human opinion.

**VERSE 20.**—“And he confessed, and did not deny; and he confessed: ‘I am not the Christ.’” Since he said, “I am not,” he plainly denied what he was not, but he did not deny what he was. Speaking the truth, he became a member of the one whose name he did not falsely claim for himself. When, therefore, he did not wish to seek the name of Christ, he became a member of Christ; for while he humbly strove to acknowledge his own lowliness, he deserved truly to possess Christ’s exalted dignity.

He immediately declares who he is when he adds:

**VERSE 23.**—“I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness.” You know that the Only-begotten Son, the Word of the Father, is called the Word, as John testifies when he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word.” From your own speech you know that the voice sounds first, so that the word may afterward be heard.

John therefore asserts that he is the voice because he precedes the Word. The voice that goes before the Lord’s coming is so called because through his ministry the Father’s Word is heard by human beings [Ms., “by all”]. He also cries in the wilderness because he announces the consolation of the Redeemer to forsaken and desolate Judea.

He indicates what he cries when he adds:

“Make straight the way of the Lord, as the prophet Isaiah said.” The Lord’s way is made straight to the heart when the word of truth is heard humbly. The Lord’s way is made straight to the heart when life is prepared for obedience to the commandment. Hence it is written: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV, 23).

Whoever therefore raises his mind in pride, whoever pants in the heat of greed, whoever defiles himself with the pollution of lust, closes the door of his heart against the truth; and, lest the Lord come to him, he fastens the locks of his soul with the bolts of vices. But those who had been sent continue to question him.

**VERSE 25.**—“Why then do you baptize, if you are not Elijah, nor the Christ, nor the prophet?” The evangelist quietly indicates that this was said not from a desire to learn the truth, but from the malice of rivalry, when he adds [saying]:

**VERSE 24.**—“And those who had been sent were from the Pharisees.” It is as though he openly said: Those who do not know how to seek doctrine, but only how to envy, inquire of John concerning his deeds. Yet every holy person, even when questioned with a perverse mind, is not diverted from the pursuit of goodness. Accordingly, John also responds to words of envy with commendations of life. For he immediately adds:

**VERSE 26.**—“I baptize in water; but one stands among you whom you do not know.” John baptizes not with the Spirit but with water, because, unable to release sins, he washes the bodies of those baptized with water, but nevertheless does not wash by forgiveness [Gregory, “does not wash the mind through forgiveness”].

Why, then, does he baptize if he does not remit sins through baptism? He does so in order that, preserving the order of his forerunning, he might, by baptizing, precede the Lord who was to baptize, just as by being born he had preceded the one who was to be born. Having become Christ’s forerunner by preaching, he might also become his forerunner through baptism, in imitation of the sacrament.

Meanwhile, announcing the mystery of our Redeemer, he asserts that the Lord both stood among human beings and was not known: appearing in the flesh, the Lord stood visibly in the body and invisibly in majesty. Concerning him he also adds: “He who comes after me has been placed before me.” Thus it is said, “He has been placed before me,” as though it were said, “He has been set before me.” He came after me because he was born later; but he was placed before me because he was preferred to me.

A little earlier, in saying this, he also disclosed the reasons for his precedence when he added: “Because he was before me.” It is as though he openly said: He surpasses me, though born after me, because the times of his birth do not confine him. He who is born in time through his mother was generated without time by the Father. John reveals what humility of reverence he owes him when he says:

**VERSE 27.**—“Whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie.” It was customary among the ancients that if someone did not wish to take as his wife the woman who was rightfully his, the man who came as bridegroom to her by right of kinship would untie his sandal.

What, then, did Christ appear among human beings to be, if not the Bridegroom of the holy Church? Of him the same John says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John III, 29). But because people thought John was the Christ—a claim John himself denies—he rightly declares that he is unworthy to untie the strap of Christ’s sandal.

It is as though he openly said: “I am unable to uncover the Redeemer’s footprints, because I unworthily do not claim for myself the name of bridegroom.”

This can nevertheless be understood in another way. Who does not know that sandals are made from dead animals? The incarnate Lord, coming among us, appeared as though shod, since in his divinity he assumed the dead matter of our corruption. Hence he says through the Prophet: “I will extend my sandal over Edom” (Ps. LIX, 10). Edom signifies the Gentiles. The Lord therefore declares that he will extend his sandal over Edom because, when he became known to the Gentiles through the flesh, the divinity came to us as though shod.

But the human eye is not sufficient to penetrate the mystery of this incarnation. For it cannot in any way investigate how the Word became embodied; how the highest and life-giving Spirit was enlivened within the womb of a mother; or how the one who has no beginning both exists and is conceived.

The strap of the sandal is the bond of the mystery. John therefore cannot untie the strap of his sandal, because even he, who recognized the incarnation through the spirit of prophecy, is not sufficient to investigate its mystery.

What, then, does it mean to say, “I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal,” except openly and humbly to confess his ignorance? It is as though he clearly said: “Why should it be surprising that he has been placed before me, when I consider that he was born after me but do not comprehend the mystery of his birth?”

@ [Col. 0755D] Thus far from Gregory.»**

[Col. 0755C] {475} **VERSE 28.**—“These things took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.” It is fitting that our Lord’s forerunner is said to have baptized in Bethany, for Bethany is interpreted as “house of obedience,” so that it might show that all must come to Christ’s baptism through the obedience of faith.

Just as the Magi were commanded to return to their homeland by another way, so we are commanded to reach the joys of paradise by another way. Our parents were expelled from there through the guilt of disobedience; we, however, must reach the paradise of eternal blessedness through the goodness of obedience and observance of God’s commandments.

**VERSE 29.**—“The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him.” John is interpreted as “grace of God.” The next day is the Christian people under grace, redeemed by Christ’s precious blood. The former people also had a next day under the law: they were mystically redeemed from Egyptian slavery by the blood of a lamb. That lamb signified this Lamb, whom the blessed Baptist, present before him, pointed out with his finger, saying: «

@ [Col. 0756D] Bede, Homily on the Epiphany of the Lord. “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” Behold the Lamb of God; behold the innocent one, free from every sin, since he indeed has bone from Adam’s bones and flesh [Bede, “and flesh”] from Adam’s flesh, but drew no stain of guilt from sinful flesh.

Behold him who takes away the sins of the world: behold him who, righteous among sinners and meek among the impious—that is, appearing as a lamb among wolves—also possesses the power to justify sinners and the impious. The Apostle Peter shows how he takes away the sins of the world and by what order he justifies the impious, saying: “You were not redeemed with corruptible things, silver or gold, from your futile way of life handed down from your fathers, but with the precious blood, as of an unblemished and spotless lamb, Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. I, 18–19).

It follows:

**VERSE 30.**—“John bears witness concerning the Lord: ‘This is he of whom I said, “After me comes a man who has been placed before me, because he was before me.”’”

“After me comes a man”: he was born into the world after me, and after me he will begin to preach to the world. “He has been placed before me”: he surpasses me in the power of majesty as much as a judge surpasses a herald, and the sun surpasses Lucifer, although appearing later.

“Because he was before me”: because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word.”

“After me comes a man”: understand the time of human birth, in which Christ is later than John. “He has been placed before me”: contemplate the primacy of royal power, by which he presides even over the angels. “Because he was before me”: understand the eternity of divine majesty, by which he is equal to the Father.

“After me comes a man who has been placed before me, because he was before me.” He came after me in humanity, and for this reason surpasses me in dignity: because he was before me in divinity.

**VERSE 31.**—“And I did not know him,” he says. It is certain that John knew the Lord, since he was sent to bear witness to him and proclaimed that he would come as judge of all, saying: “His winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor” (Matt. III, 12). He testified that the Holy Spirit would be given by him, saying: “He himself will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.” He desired to be cleansed by him, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?”

How, then, does he say, “I did not know him”? Only because, although he had known him previously, he recognized him more perfectly when he was baptized. He knew him as the Savior and judge of the world, but when the Holy Spirit descended upon him he recognized more profoundly the power of his majesty.

There is no doubt that, when the blessed John was permitted to see the Holy Spirit—even in bodily form—and to hear the Father’s voice—even though it sounded bodily—he greatly profited from this sight and hearing and, with the eyes of his mind opened, received great knowledge of the excellence of divine power. Indeed, in comparison with the understanding with which he then began to be illumined, it seemed to him that up to that point he had been utterly ignorant of how great Christ was [Bede, “he received from God, so that…”].

Bearing diligent witness to the Lord concerning whom he had been sent, he adds:

“But that he might be revealed to Israel, for this reason I came baptizing in water.” This is to say openly: “I did not come baptizing in water because I am able, by baptizing, to take away the sins of the world, but so that by baptizing and preaching I might reveal him to the people of Israel. He baptizes in the Holy Spirit and is able to take away the sins not only of Israel but of the whole world, if it is willing to believe in him.”

“For this reason I came baptizing in water” [Al., “in repentance”], so that by baptizing in this way I might prepare the way for him who would baptize for the remission of sins.

**VERSE 32.**—“And John bore witness, saying: ‘I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it remained upon him.’” It was fitting that the Spirit descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove, so that the faithful might learn that they can become his members and be filled with his Spirit only if they are simple and maintain true peace with their brothers, which the kisses of doves signify.

Ravens also have kisses, but they tear apart, whereas doves do so in no way. They signify those who “speak peace with their neighbor, but evil is in their hearts” (Ps. XXVII, 3). The nature of the dove, which is innocent of tearing, most aptly corresponds to those who pursue peace with all and holiness, striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. IV, 3).

Therefore, by descending in the form of a dove, the Spirit signifies not only his own innocence and simplicity, or those of the one upon whom he descended, but equally those who think of him in goodness and seek him in simplicity of heart (Wis. I).

“And I,” he says, “did not know him.” Supply: “I did not know him so subtly as I came to know him when the Spirit descended upon him” [Bede, “the Spirit . . . descending”].

**VERSE 33.**—“But the one who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’”

The Lord baptizes in the Holy Spirit by forgiving sins through the grace of the Holy Spirit. Whether he himself first baptized certain of his disciples with water, through whom the stream of baptism would flow to the other faithful, he also baptized those same people with the Spirit, forgiving their sins and supplying the gifts of the Holy Spirit; or whether his faithful, invoking his name, baptize the elect with water and anoint them with holy chrism, he nevertheless himself baptizes those same people with the Holy Spirit. For no one except him can loose the bonds of sins or bestow the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

But we must examine carefully that, after saying, “Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending,” he added, “and remaining upon him.” The Spirit also descends upon his saints. Yet, as long as they are in the body, they cannot be free from sin, because they are not always able to direct the eye of the mind toward contemplation of heavenly things; rather, they often turn it toward the care of earthly conduct. In their hearts, therefore, the Spirit undoubtedly comes at times and withdraws at times.

Hence it is said: “The Spirit blows where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes” (John III, 8). The Spirit comes to the saints and goes away from the saints, so that those who are not capable of possessing him continually may be refreshed by the frequent light of his returning presence.

But in the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, the Spirit truly remains perpetually. In him he finds no stain of an impure thought from which he would withdraw. The Spirit remained wholly in him, not only from the time when John saw him descend upon him, but from the moment when, beginning to become man, he was conceived through the Spirit’s ministry and work.

For this reason the Spirit is shown descending upon him at his baptism, although he always remained in him: so that the Baptist himself might recognize more clearly the one whom he was to preach, and so that believers might receive an indication that they cannot attain the baptism of that same Spirit unless they have first been baptized with water.

Meanwhile, it must be asked how it could have been a special sign by which the Son of God was recognized that the Spirit descended upon him and remained in him, when he himself also promises his disciples, saying: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you forever, the Spirit of truth” (John XIV, 15). And shortly afterward: “For he will remain with you and will be in you.” If the Spirit remains with God’s chosen servants and will be in them, what great thing is it for the Son of God that the Spirit is affirmed to remain in him?

It should also be noted that the Holy Spirit has always remained in the Lord; but in holy human beings, as long as they bear a mortal body, he partly remains forever and partly withdraws in order to return.

He remains with them so that they may devote themselves to good works, love voluntary poverty, pursue meekness, grieve for the desire of eternal things, hunger and thirst for righteousness, and embrace mercy, purity of heart, and the tranquility of peace. They should also not fear suffering persecution for the observance of righteousness, and should desire to persist in almsgiving, prayers, fasts, and the other spiritual [Ms. and Bede, “of the Spirit”] fruits. {477}

He withdraws for a time so that they may not always possess the power to heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons, or even prophesy. He remains forever so that they may themselves live wondrously.

@ Bede: “He remains forever so that they may possess the power by which they themselves live wondrously; he comes for a time so that, through signs of miracles, they may also shine before others as the kind of people they are within.”

**VERSE 34.**—“I,” he says, “saw and bore witness, because this is the Son of God.” Above he had said: “After me comes a man who has been made before me”; now he bears witness that “this is the Son of God,” clearly designating the truth of both natures—namely, the human and the divine—in one and the same person of Christ. Let Manichaeus blush when he hears: “A man has come.” Let Photinus fall silent when he hears: “This is the Son of God.” Let the meek hear and rejoice, because a man has come after John, stronger than John, who baptizes in the Holy Spirit, and because this is the Son of God.

Because through pride we all withdrew from God, the Son of God, through mercy, became man, so that he himself might correspond both to the Father through divinity and to us through humanity; and so that, through a humanity like ours, he might contend against the enemy for us, while, being consubstantial with the Father through divinity, he might worthily restore in us the image and likeness of God, which we had lost through sin; and so that, through the death of our frailty, he might destroy him who held the power of death, and through the impassible power of his divinity reconcile us to God the Father.

[Col. 0759D] **Up to this point from Bede.**»

**VERSE 35.**—John was standing, and two of his disciples. John was standing because he believed in the Lord, and two of his disciples likewise; for they immediately believed and followed Jesus as he walked.

**VERSE 36.**—And looking upon Jesus as he walked. We ought to examine each word of Scripture, asking why John is said to be standing and Jesus to be walking: “And looking upon Jesus as he walked, he says: Behold the Lamb of God.” The Law bears witness: behold the Lamb of God, the spotless Lamb, the year-old Lamb, the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, the Lamb who does not allow the destroyer to strike the people of Israel in Egypt. Behold the Lamb of God.

[Col. 0759B] **VERSE 37.**—And the disciples heard him. Why did he wish to say, “Behold”? When “behold” is said, the one who is being shown is, in a certain manner, pointed out with a finger. Therefore he says to his disciples: “Why are you following me? Why do you suppose that you should have me as your teacher? Behold the Lamb of God. Follow him; he ought to increase, but I must decrease.” No prudent person follows the one who is decreasing and abandons the one who is increasing.

And the two disciples heard their teacher John speaking. They followed the command of the teacher. John’s testimony is the faith of the disciples. And they followed Jesus. In following Jesus, they left John; in following the Gospel, they lost the Law. Yet they followed the Gospel in such a way that they made use of the testimony of the Law.

But Jesus, turning and seeing them—John’s disciples could not see Jesus from close by, face to face, or from in front; rather, they followed his back in order to see. Therefore those disciples could not see the Lord’s face. He turned, and in a certain sense descended from his majesty, so that the disciples could contemplate his face; he turned so that he might be seen by the disciples as the one signified by the Law.

**VERSE 38.**—But turning and seeing them following, he said: “What are you seeking?” He does not ask as though ignorant; rather, he asks so that those who answer may receive their reward. “What are you seeking?” He did not say, “Whom are you seeking,” lest he seem to point to himself. “What are you seeking?” He asks about the matter, so that they may indicate the person.

“What are you seeking?” They said to him: “Rabbi.” The very form of address is an indication of their response and faith. For when they say “Rabbi,” which means “teacher,” and follow him, they plainly follow a teacher and say:

**VERSE 39.**—“Where do you dwell?” He says to them: “Come and see.” They wish to know Jesus’ dwelling; they wish the Savior to show them what sort of dwelling he has, so that, when he has shown in whom Christ dwells, they may present themselves as those in whom the Lord can dwell.

And he said to them: “Come and see. Do you wish to see my dwelling? It cannot be explained in words; it is demonstrated by works. Come and see.”

These men, since they had come from the testimony of the Law, immediately confess him in the very name they use, saying: “Rabbi,” which is interpreted as “teacher.” [Perhaps: “These, who had come from the testimony . . . immediately.”] But Jesus answered them and said: “You, who are John’s disciples, who demonstrate your confession from the very name you use and say, ‘Rabbi,’ come and see [the manuscript adds: ‘where I dwell’].”

They came and saw where he was dwelling, and they remained with him that day. Because they believed, they did not remain in the night but in the day. That night had no darkness, because there was faith in the true light. And they remained with him that day. It was about the tenth hour. They were coming from the Law to the Gospel; the Law’s Decalogue, signified by John, was sending them on to faith in Christ.

**CHAPTER III**

How, from the two disciples of John who had followed the Lord, one—Andrew—brought his brother to Jesus, who was then called Peter by him. Philip also, when called, announced him to Nathanael. The latter immediately confessed, among other things, that he was the Son of God. From this point Jesus changed water into wine, and his disciples believed in him. [Col. 0760B]

**VERSE 40.**—Now Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, was one of the two who had heard John and followed him. In faith there is no order: wherever the soul is faithful, neither a multitude nor a small number of years is sought. Andrew was younger than Simon Peter, and yet the order of age is not considered but that of faith: he found Jesus first.

“Now Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, was one of the two.” Unless perhaps this too is Andrew’s distinction: that he is called Peter’s brother, upon whom the Church was founded [the manuscript: “was later to be founded”]. They had heard John and followed the Lord.

**VERSE 41.**—He first finds his own brother. O true devotion! As soon as he found Jesus, as soon as he found the pearl, as soon as he found the treasure, he announces it to his brother. He calls Simon his brother—not so much by blood as by the Spirit. He had him as a brother by kinship and blood, and he wished to have him as a brother also in faith.

And he says to him: “We have found the Messiah.” No one finds unless he seeks. This man, who says that he has found, shows that he had sought for a long time. “We have found the Messiah,” which is translated “Christ.” For a long time we sought Christ in Moses and in all the prophets; and the one whom we desired to find found us, and, having been found, we found him.

**VERSE 42.**—And he brought him to Jesus. The elder does not disdain to follow the younger, because there was no order of age where there was the merit of faith.

But Jesus, looking upon him, said: “You are Simon, the son of Jonah; you shall be called Cephas,” which is translated “Peter.” Peter had not yet done anything, and already he had earned a change of name [the manuscript: “to change his name”]. Had he believed more than Andrew? What greater thing had he done, so as to receive more from his brother? [“What greater thing had he done?”] He followed his younger brother and did not disdain to have as his teacher the one whom he had as a disciple.

“You are Simon, the son of Jonah.” In our language, Jonah means “dove.” You are therefore the son of Jonah; you are the son of the Holy Spirit. He is called the son of the Holy Spirit because he had received humility from the Holy Spirit.

**VERSE 43.**—On the following day he wished to go out into Galilee. “On the following day,” he says, “Jesus wished to go out into Galilee,” and he found Philip and said to him: “Follow me.”»

[Col. 0761D] **Bede, Homily 4.** It is now clear from what precedes from where Jesus wished to go out into Galilee—namely, from Judea, where John was baptizing and bearing witness to him that he was the Lamb of God. He urged two of his disciples to follow him, one of whom, Andrew, also brought his brother Peter to him.

It is clear, and through frequent exposition it is already known to your fraternity according to the spiritual sense, what it means to follow the Lord [the manuscript: “what follows the Lord?”]. For the one who imitates him follows the Lord; the one who, insofar as human frailty permits, does not abandon the examples of humility that the Son of God displays in humanity follows the Lord; and the one who, by becoming a companion of his sufferings, earnestly longs to attain participation in his resurrection and ascension follows the Lord.

But it is not without a definite mystical reason that it is related that Jesus was going to say to Philip, “Follow me.” He wished to go out into Galilee. Galilee is interpreted as “a transmigration accomplished,” or “revelation.” In the sense that it is called “a transmigration accomplished,” it designates the progress of the faithful: namely, that they strive either to migrate from vices to the heights of virtues, or gradually to advance within the virtues themselves, and daily to pass from lesser things to greater, until, with the Lord’s help, they reach from this valley of tears the citadel of heavenly joy. In the sense that it signifies “revelation,” it indicates the blessedness of eternal life itself, for which the saints labor in the present.

The Psalmist includes both interpretations of the name in one verse, where he says: “They will go from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion” (Ps. 83:8). This is the vision of which the Apostle says: “But we, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” [variant: “as by the present Lord”] (2 Cor. 3:18).

Therefore, when Jesus wished to call a disciple to follow him, he rightly wished to go out into Galilee—that is, into an accomplished transmigration, or revelation—so that, just as, according to the Gospel, he advanced in wisdom and age and grace with God and human beings (Luke 2:52), and just as he suffered and rose again and thus entered into his glory, so also he might show that his followers must advance in virtues and, through passing sufferings, migrate to the gifts of eternal joys.

It follows:

**VERSE 44.**—Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter. We must not suppose that the evangelist wished to mention by chance and without mystical reason the name of the city from which Philip came, and that it also belonged to Andrew and Peter. Rather, through the name of the city he wished typically to show what Philip already was in spirit and what he would be in office, and what Peter and Andrew would likewise be.

Bethsaida is said to mean “house of hunters.” Certainly, those who heard the Lord say, “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of men” (Matt. 4:19), were destined to be hunters. The one who, even before he was ordained by the Lord for the office of preaching, immediately showed by voluntary preaching how intent he would be on capturing souls for life was also a hunter.

**VERSE 45.**—For Philip finds Nathanael and says to him: “We have found Jesus, the son of Joseph, from Nazareth, whom Moses in the Law and the prophets wrote about.”

Let us see how great a net of faith he spreads around his brother, whom he wisely desires to catch for eternal salvation, a net woven with the spacious marvels of devoted preaching [the manuscript: “stains”]. He says that he has found the one whom Moses and the prophets marked out in their writings as the one who would come, so that all who follow may understand that he is the one whose coming all the ancient writings serve by proclaiming it [variant: “served”].

He calls him Jesus, the name whose future bearing by Christ the prophetic oracles proclaimed. He calls him the son of Joseph—not to assert that he was born from the union of man and woman, since he had learned from the prophets that he would be born of a virgin, but to teach that, according to the prophecies of the prophets, he came from the house and family of David, from whom he knew Joseph to have descended.

Nor is it surprising if Philip calls him the son of Joseph, since even his undefiled mother, the ever-virgin Mary, who had not known a man, is read as speaking according to common usage: “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been seeking you in sorrow” (Luke 2:48).

He adds his homeland, “from Nazareth,” in order to identify him as the one of whom he had read in the prophets: “He shall be called a Nazarean.” It is therefore not surprising that Philip immediately won Nathanael over to consent to believe and come to Christ, for he presented such great nets of truth to him from every side.

“We have found Jesus, the son of Joseph, from Nazareth, whom Moses in the Law and the prophets wrote about.” Nor is it without reason that he is asserted to have originated from Bethsaida—that is, from the house of hunters—since he is shown to have received, at the same time, such care and grace for the hunt beloved by God.

For it follows:

**VERSE 46.**—And Nathanael said to him: “Something good can come from Nazareth.”

Nazareth is interpreted as “purity,” or “its flower,” or “separated.” Therefore Nathanael, assenting to Philip’s words as he evangelized him, says: “Something good can come from Nazareth.” As though he were plainly saying: “Can it happen that something of supreme grace should arise for us from a city of such a name”—namely, the Lord, the Savior of the world, who is uniquely holy, innocent, undefiled, and separated from sinners, and who says in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:1).

Or certainly, he might mean some outstanding teacher who was sent to preach to us the flower of virtues and purity of holiness. We can also correctly understand this passage in the following way: when Philip said, “We have found Jesus, the son of Joseph, from Nazareth, whom Moses in the Law and the prophets wrote about,” Nathanael understood everything else correctly, but wondered how Philip could say that Christ had come from Nazareth, since the prophets sang that he would come from the house of David and from Bethlehem, the city of David. Therefore, in his wonder, he answered: “From Nazareth?” But immediately, recalling how much even the name Nazareth corresponded to the mysteries of Christ, he cautiously assented to the preacher, saying: “Something good can come from there.”

The following can suit either interpretation:

Philip says to him: “Come and see.” He urged him to come and see in person, so that, if anything doubtful about the preacher’s word had remained in his heart, the sight and present conversation with the one whom he proclaimed might remove it all. Nor did the devout hearer delay in diligently seeking and piously knocking for the truth proclaimed to him, so that he might deserve to receive it and persevere in it.

Therefore the Lord, hastening to satisfy his desire for good things, soon rewards his salutary beginning with prudent praise, so that he might gradually advance him both to seek and to grasp higher things.

**VERSE 47.**—For he saw him coming to him and said of him: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit.”

Here it must be noted that God, who knows hearts, when praising a human being, confirms not that he existed without sin but that he existed without deceit. For there is no just person on earth who does good and does not sin. Many, however, are read to have walked without deceit—that is, to have lived with a simple and pure heart. Indeed, all the faithful are taught to live in this way, as Scripture says: “Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wis. 1:1). The Lord himself says: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16).

Such was Job, an example of patience, of whom it is written: “That man was simple and upright” (Job 1:1). Such was the patriarch Jacob, of whom it is written: “Jacob was a simple man, dwelling in tents” (Gen. 25:27). Because he deserved to see God through the purity of a simple conscience, he was also called Israel—that is, “a man seeing God.”

Such was this Nathanael, whom the Lord, because of the likeness of his blameless conduct, deemed worthy of the merits and name of that same patriarch. “Behold,” he says, “truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit.” Behold one who truly derives his origin from the patriarch who saw God, in whom, as in that patriarch himself, no duplicity of deceit is shown to exist.

O how beautiful a beginning for one coming to the Lord [Bede: “for coming”] and desiring to see him: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit.” “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). Desiring to see God, this man is praised by God himself, who searches the kidneys and hearts, as pure in heart; and he is affirmed to be an Israelite—that is, generated from a man who sees God.

O how great a spirit of salvation is opened in this statement of our Redeemer also for us, who have come to faith from the Gentiles [Bede: “how great a hope”]. For if the one who walks without knowing deceit is truly an Israelite, then the Jews have already lost the name of Israelites, although they were born carnally from Israel, insofar as all who degenerated through deceitful hearts from the simplicity of their patriarch have lost it. And we ourselves have been admitted into the seed of the Israelites, although we have the descent of the flesh from other nations, because in faith in the truth and in purity of body and mind we follow the footsteps of Israel, according to the Apostle’s statement: “For not all who are from Israel are Israelites; nor are all who are Abraham’s seed his children; but ‘in Isaac shall your seed be called’” (Rom. 9:6).

That is: those who are children of the flesh are not the children of God; rather, those who are children of the promise are reckoned as the seed.

It follows:

**VERSES 48, 49.**—Nathanael says to him: “From where do you know me?” Jesus answered and said to him: “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.” Nathanael answered him and said: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the king of Israel.”

Because Nathanael recognized that God had seen and known things being done elsewhere—that is, how and where he had been called by Philip, although Jesus himself was not bodily present there—he considered the gaze of the divine majesty and immediately confessed him not only as Rabbi, that is, teacher, but also as the Son of God and king of Israel, that is, Christ.

And it is pleasing to observe how wisely the confession of the servant who praises corresponds to the Lord [the manuscript and Bede: “how the confession of the servant corresponds to the Lord who praises”]. The Lord affirmed that this man was truly an Israelite—that is, a man who could see God—because he had no deceit at all. Nathanael, for his part, religiously confesses him not merely as a teacher who gives useful commands, but also as the Son of God, who bestows heavenly gifts, and as the king of Israel, that is, of the people who see God. By this confession he signifies that this one is also his king and that he himself is a soldier of his kingdom.

This statement of the Lord, in which he said that he had seen Nathanael under the fig tree before Philip called him, can also be understood mystically concerning the election of spiritual Israel, that is, the Christian people. Before this people saw the Lord, before it was called through his apostles to the grace of faith, while it was still hidden under the covering of pressing sin, the Lord mercifully deigned to see it. Paul bears witness to this when he says: “He blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and undefiled before him in love” (Eph. 1:3).

Indeed, the fig tree sometimes signifies in Scripture the sweetness of heavenly love. Hence it is written: “Whoever guards a fig tree will eat its fruit, and whoever is the guardian of his lord will be honored” (Prov. 27:18). But because our first parents, confused by the guilt of transgression, made themselves girdles from fig leaves (Gen. 3), the fig tree can not inappropriately signify the badly sweetened habit of sinning among the human race. While his elect are still placed beneath this habit, not yet recognizing the grace of their election, the Lord sees Nathanael as though placed beneath the fig tree, Nathanael not yet seeing him. For “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19).

The name Nathanael itself most aptly suits their salvation. Nathanael is interpreted as “gift of God,” and unless each person is called by the gift of God, he will never escape the guilt of the first transgression or the shadows of sins that daily grow and flatter him; nor will he ever deserve, once destined for salvation, to come to Christ.

Therefore the Apostle says: “For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God—not from works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. 2:8–9).

It follows:

**VERSE 50.**—Jesus answered and said to him: “Because I said to you, ‘I saw you under the fig tree,’ you believe; you will see greater things than these.”

What he means by “greater” he himself subsequently makes clear, promising believers the future opening of the kingdom of heaven and the proclamation to the world of both natures in the one person of Christ. This is truly a much more excellent mystery than the fact that, while we were still placed in the shadow of sin, he foresaw that we would be illuminated by him.

For greater is the fact that he fills us, once saved, with the knowledge of his grace; that he opens to us the joys of heaven; and that he scatters throughout the world preachers of his faith, than the fact that, before the ages, he foreknew that we would be saved by the power of his majesty.

**VERSE 51.**—“Amen, amen, I say to you: you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending above the Son of Man.”

We now see the fulfillment of this promise. For we see heaven opened, because, after God made man had entered heaven, we recognize that the entrance to the heavenly homeland has also been opened to us who believe in him [variant: “the way in”].

We see the angels of God ascending and descending above the Son of Man, because we know that the holy preachers announce both the sublimity of Christ’s divinity and the weakness of his humanity.

The angels ascend above the Son of Man when the preachers teach that “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John 1:1). The angels descend above the Son of Man when those same preachers add that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

Nor is it without reason that the holy preachers are figuratively called angels, to whom the name “evangelists,” derived from angels, is customarily applied, so that, just as the former are messengers, so the latter, because of the same office of supreme proclamation, may be called bearers of good news.

It must also be noted that the Lord calls himself the Son of Man, while Nathanael proclaims him to be the Son of God. The same thing occurs when, in the other Evangelists, he himself asks the disciples: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” They said: “Some John the Baptist, others Elijah, and so on.” Jesus says to them: “But who do you say that I am?” Simon Peter answered: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:13–16).

It was done by a proper ordering of divine dispensation that, when both substances of the same mediator, our God and Lord, had to be mentioned either by the Lord himself or by a human being, God made man should affirm the weakness of the humanity he had assumed, while a pure human being should affirm the power of the eternal divinity in him: he should confess his own humility, and the other should confess his exalted nature.

It must also be noted that the Lord, who calls blessed Nathanael truly an Israelite, recalls in the words “You will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending above the Son of Man” (John 1:33) the vision of the patriarch Jacob (Gen. 28), who was called Israel through the blessing.

When Jacob wished to rest in a certain place, he placed a stone under his head and saw in a dream a ladder standing on the earth, with its top touching heaven; he also saw the angels of God ascending and descending upon it, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder and saying to him: “I am the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac.” Rising in the morning, and offering due praise to the Lord with fear, he took the stone and raised it as a pillar, pouring oil over it.

The Lord therefore makes mention of this passage and most clearly testifies that it was figured with reference to himself and his faithful.

[Col. 0765D] **Up to this point from the cited homily of Bede.**»

**CHAPTER II, VERSE 1**

And on the third day there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there.

[Col. 0766A] **From Bede’s homily on the Second Sunday after Epiphany.** «It is not without mystery that the wedding is said to have taken place on the third day, after the things that the preceding discourse of the Gospel had described. It signifies that the Lord came, in the third age of the world, to unite the Church to himself.

The first age of the world, before the Law, shone upon the world through the examples of the patriarchs; the second, under the Law, through the writings of the prophets; and the third, under grace, through the proclamations of the evangelists, like the third light of day. In this third age our Lord and Savior appeared, born in the flesh for the redemption of the human race.

Likewise, the fact that the same wedding is said to have taken place at Cana of Galilee—that is, in the zeal of accomplished transmigration—announces figuratively that those are especially worthy of Christ’s grace who know how, through the zeal of fervor and devout devotion, to strive for greater spiritual gifts, and, by doing good, to migrate from vices to virtues, and from earthly things to eternal things through hope and love [Bede: “who know how to burn with the zeal of devout devotion”].

While the Lord was reclining at the wedding, the wine ran out, so that, when better wine had been miraculously made through him, the glory of God hidden in the man might be revealed and the faith of those who believed in him might be strengthened and advance.

But if we know the mystery [the manuscript and Bede: “if we seek the mystery”], then, when the Lord appeared in the flesh, that pure savor of the Law’s meaning had gradually begun to fail from its ancient strength because of the Pharisees’ carnal interpretation. He immediately transformed those commandments that seemed carnal into spiritual teaching, and changed the entire surface of the letter of the Law through the power of evangelical heavenly grace. This is what it means to have made wine from water.

But first let us see what it means that, when the wine had run out, the mother of Jesus says to him:

**VERSES 3, 4.**—“They have no wine.” He replied: “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.”

For he did not dishonor his mother, who commands us to honor father and mother; nor did he deny that she was his mother, from whose virginal flesh he did not disdain to assume flesh. The Apostle also bears witness to this when he says: “Who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:3).

For how could he be from the seed of David according to the flesh unless he was from the body of Mary according to the flesh, she who descended from the seed of David?

But in saying, as he was about to perform a miracle, “What is there between me and you, woman?” he signifies that he did not temporally receive from his mother the beginning of his divinity, by which the miracle was to be performed, but always possessed eternity from the Father.

“What is there,” he says, “between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.” What does the divinity that I have always had from the Father share with your flesh, from which I assumed flesh? The hour has not yet come for me to demonstrate by dying the frailty of the humanity assumed from you. First it is necessary for me to reveal the power of eternal divinity by performing mighty works.

But the hour will come when he will show what he shares with his mother, when, as he was about to die on the cross, he took care to commend the virgin mother to the virgin disciple. Having endured the weakness of the flesh, he piously entrusted to the disciple whom he loved most the mother from whom he had received that flesh. But when about to perform divine works, he pretends not to know her, as though she were unknown, because he recognizes that she was not the author of his divine birth.»

The Lord recalls this hour [alternative: “therefore”] while hanging on the cross, when he said to his mother: “Mother, behold your son”—as though he had said: “Behold, what I took from you is now being revealed through dying, although this nature was afterward to be glorified in the glory of the resurrection.”

**VERSE 5.**—His mother said to the servants: “Whatever he tells you, do.”

His mother knew the humanity of her Son. Although, in some way, it seemed that what she requested had been refused, she nevertheless knew the Son’s compassion, that he would not refuse what was being asked [the manuscript: “that he did not wish to refuse”]. Therefore she confidently instructed the servants to carry out the commands of the Son who was giving orders.

[Col. 0767C] **VERSE 6.**—Now six stone water jars had been set there, in accordance with the purification custom of the Jews, each holding two or three measures. “Water jars are vessels prepared for receiving water, for in Greek water is called ὕδωρ (*hydōr*). Water, moreover, signifies the knowledge of Holy Scripture, which is accustomed both to wash its hearers from the filth of sins and to give them drink from the fountain of divine knowledge. The six vessels in which the water was contained are the devoted hearts of the saints, whose perfection of life and faith has been set before the human race as an example of right belief and conduct through the six ages of the passing world, that is, up to the time of the Lord’s preaching [Beda, passion]. And rightly the vessels are made of stone, because the inmost hearts of the righteous are strong, being solidified by faith in and love of that stone which Daniel saw cut from the mountain without hands and made into a great mountain, filling the whole earth (Dan. II, 34). And concerning it Zechariah says: ‘In one stone there are seven eyes’ (Zech. III, 9), that is, in Christ the fullness of spiritual knowledge dwells. The apostle Peter also remembers him, saying: ‘Approaching him, a living stone, you yourselves also, as living stones, are built upon him’ (I Pet. II, 4). Rightly the water jars had been set there only for the purification of the Jews [Beda adds *tantum*], because the law was given through Moses to the Jewish people alone; but the grace and truth of the Gospel were given through Jesus Christ no less to the Gentiles than to the Jews.

“Each holding,” he says, “two or three measures.” For the authors and ministers of Holy Scripture, the prophets, sometimes speak only of the Father and the Son, as in the passage: ‘You have made all things in wisdom’ (Ps. CIII, 24), for Christ is the power and wisdom of God; sometimes they also mention the Holy Spirit, as in the saying of that same Psalmist: ‘By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their power’ (Ps. XXXII, 6). ‘The Word, the Lord, and the Spirit’—the whole is to be understood as one God in the Trinity [Ms. and Beda: ‘Understand the Word, the Lord, and the Spirit as the whole Trinity, which is one God’].

“But as far as water differs from wine, so far does that meaning differ by which the Scriptures were understood before the Savior’s coming from that which he himself, when he came, revealed to the apostles and left to their disciples for perpetual observance. Indeed, the Lord could have filled the empty water jars with wine, for at the beginning of the world’s creation he created all things from nothing; but he preferred to make wine from water, thereby teaching figuratively that he had come not to abolish or condemn the law and the prophets, but rather to fulfill them, and that through evangelical grace he neither did nor taught anything other than what the legal and prophetic Scriptures had indicated that he would do and teach [Beda: “that he himself, through evangelical grace, did and taught nothing other than …”].

“Let us therefore see the six water jars filled with the saving water of Scripture; let us see that same water changed into the most pleasing fragrance and taste of wine. In the first age of the world, a brother, envious of righteous Abel, killed him (Gen. IV); for this reason Abel himself, blessed with the perpetual glory of martyrdom, also received praise for righteousness in the Gospel and apostolic writings (Matt. XXIII; Luke XI). But the impious fratricide paid the penalties of eternal condemnation. Whoever, having heard these things, fears [Beda: *metuunt*, “they fear”] being condemned with the wicked and desires to be blessed with the righteous, casts away every tinder of hatred and envy and takes care to please God through the sacrifice of righteousness, by the virtue of moderation and innocence, and by the strength of patience [Ms.: *modestiam, innocentiam, virtutem*, “moderation, innocence, and virtue”]: he has certainly found in Scripture a vessel of water from which he may rejoice to be healthfully washed and refreshed.

“But if he understands that Cain the murderer signifies the faithlessness of the Jews; that Abel’s killing signifies the passion of the Lord the Savior; that the earth which opened its mouth and received his blood from Cain’s hand signifies the Church, which received Christ’s blood, poured out by the Jews, into the mystery of her redemption—then surely he finds water changed into wine [Beda: “found”], because he understands the sayings of the sacred law in a more sacred sense.”

[Col. 0768D] “At the beginning of the second age of the world, the world was destroyed by the waters of the Flood because of the magnitude of its sins; but Noah alone, together with his household, was saved through righteousness in the ark (Gen. VII). Whoever, having heard of the horrifying devastation of this punishment and the wondrous deliverance of the few, begins to live more carefully, desiring to be saved with the elect and fearing to be destroyed with the reprobate, has certainly received a water jar by which he may be cleansed and refreshed. But when he begins to understand more deeply [Beda: ‘to contemplate more deeply’], and recognizes in the ark the Church, in Noah Christ, in the water that washed away sinners the water of baptism that washes away sins, in the human beings and animals contained in the ark the manifold distinction among the baptized, and in the dove that brought an olive branch into the ark after the Flood the anointing of the Holy Spirit with which the baptized are imbued, he surely tastes wine made from water [Beda: ‘he marvels at wine made from water’], because in the history of an ancient event [Ms.: *historiae factis*, “in the events of history”] he contemplates the prophecy of his own washing, sanctification, and justification.”

“In the third age of the world, God, testing Abraham’s obedience, commanded him to offer as a burnt offering his only son, whom he loved (Gen. XXII). Abraham does not delay to do what he is commanded, but a ram is sacrificed in place of the son; nevertheless, because of the exceptional virtue of his obedience, he is granted the inheritance of perpetual blessing. Behold, you have the third water jar. Hearing how great [source: *quanta*, “how great”] is the virtue of obedience and with what reward it is recompensed, you too strive to learn and possess obedience. And if, in the sacrifice of the beloved only son, you understand the passion of him of whom the Father says, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’ (Matt. XVII, 5)—in which, while the divinity remained incapable of suffering, humanity alone underwent death and pain—then the son is offered, as it were, but the ram is slain. If you understand that the blessing promised to Abraham has been fulfilled in you, who believe from the Gentiles, surely he has made wine from water for you, because he has opened the spiritual meaning, by whose new fragrance you are intoxicated [Ms., ‘you become drunk’; Beda, ‘you are inebriated’].”

“At the beginning of the fourth age, David obtained the kingdom of the Israelite people in place of Saul: humble, innocent, and gentle, he was an exile; but Saul, by whose unjust persecution he had long been tormented, was rejected [Beda: ‘he was an exile in place of him by whose unjust persecution he had long been tormented’]. Behold the fourth water jar, filled from the saving fountain. Whoever, hearing these things, begins to pursue humility and innocence and to drive pride and envy from his heart has found, as it were, a drink of the clearest water by which he may be refreshed. But if he recognizes that Saul signifies the Jews who persecute, and David Christ and the Church, and that through their faithlessness both their carnal and spiritual rule were destroyed, while the kingdom of Christ and the Church would endure forever, he will surely perceive a cup of wine [Ms.: “not merely wine”] made from water, because he knows that he is reading there about himself, his own life and kingdom, and even the king himself, where previously he had been reading an ancient history as though it concerned others.”

“In the fifth age of the world, the sinful people, when Nabuchodonosor took them captive [Beda: “in the captivity of Nabuchodonosor”], migrated to Babylonia. But after seventy years, having repented and been corrected, they were led back to their homeland by Jesus the great priest, where they rebuilt the house of God, which had been burned, and the holy city, which had been destroyed. Whoever reads or hears this is seized by fear of sinning and flees to the remedy of repentance; he has been washed with the water of a purifying jar. But if he has learned to understand Jerusalem and the temple of God as the Church of Christ, Babylon as the confusion of sins, Nabuchodonosor as the devil, Jesus the great priest as Jesus Christ, the true and eternal high priest, and the seventy years as the fullness of good works bestowed through the gifts of the Holy Spirit—that is, because of the Decalogue and the sevenfold grace of that same Spirit—and if he sees this happening daily, namely, some being snatched from the Church by the devil through sin, while others are reconciled by the grace of the Holy Spirit through Jesus as they regain their senses and repent [Beda: ‘with some snatched away … and others reconciled’], then he possesses wine made from water. For, understanding that what has been written pertains to him, he soon grows hot, as though with the must of deep compunction, and whatever sin of captivity he discovers [Al.: “understands”] to be present in himself, he begs to have liberated through Christ’s grace.”

“At the beginning of the sixth age of the world, when the Lord appeared in the flesh, he was circumcised according to the law on the eighth day of his birth.
