After this, on the thirty-third day, he was brought to the temple, and the prescribed offerings were made for him. Considering these things literally, we plainly learn with what diligence we must undertake the mysteries of evangelical faith, since he himself, bringing the blessing of grace, who gave the law of the letter, first took care to be consecrated by the ancient rite of ceremonies, he through whom all things are divinely consecrated [Beda: ‘by which’], and thus both to receive and to hand on the new sacraments of grace.

“Behold the sixth water jar, bringing a purer stream than the others for washing away the contagion of sin and drinking the joys of life. But if in the circumcision of the eighth [Beda: ‘of the eighth day’] day you understand baptism, which, as a mystery of the Lord’s resurrection, redeemed us from the death of sins; and if in the bringing into the temple and the offering you recognize the figure of the offering of a purifying sacrifice, you understand that all the faithful must enter from the baptistery into the holy altar and be consecrated by the singular sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood [Ms.: ‘in the bringing into the temple and the offering of the purifying sacrifice you recognize the figure, and understand that all the faithful…’]. Then indeed you have been given wine made from water, and the purest wine at that.

“Moreover, if you interpret the day of circumcision as referring to the general resurrection of the human race, when mortal offspring will cease and all mortality will be changed into immortality; and if you understand the circumcised being brought into the temple with offerings as referring to the time when, after the resurrection and the completion of universal judgment, the saints, now made incorruptible, will enter with the gifts of good works to contemplate forever the form of the divine majesty, then surely you will see wine being made from water, and you will rightly proclaim to its creator and say: ‘And how excellent is your cup, making drunk!’ (Ps. XXII, 5).”

“Therefore the Lord did not wish to make wine for the wedding from water [Al., ‘into joy’; Ms. and Beda, ‘into joys’] out of nothing, but, commanding the six water jars to be filled with water, he wonderfully changed it into wine, because he bestowed the six ages of the world with the abundance of saving wisdom, which, when he himself came, he enriched with the power of a higher meaning. For [Beda: *Nam quo*, materially uncertain] while carnal people understood only carnal things, he disclosed to spiritual people the things that were to be understood spiritually.

“Do you wish to know how he made wine from water? After his resurrection he appeared to two disciples walking on the road; he went along with them and, beginning with Moses and all the prophets, interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke XXIV). Do you wish again to hear how they were intoxicated with that same wine? Later, when they recognized who it was that had been offering them the word of life, they said to one another: ‘Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?’”

**VERSE 7.**—Therefore Jesus says to the servants: “Fill the water jars with water.” And they filled them to the brim. What are signified by the servants who are commanded to do these things, if not Christ’s disciples, who filled the water jars with water? They did not fill the past ages of the world with legal and prophetic writings, but they did so by understanding them wisely and opening them faithfully, because Scripture, which was ministered by the prophets, was both healthful for drinking the wisdom of heaven and useful for correcting conduct. They filled them to the brim, because they rightly understood that there had been no age of the world alien to holy teachers who, whether by words, examples, or writings, opened the way of life to mortals.

**VERSE 8.**—And Jesus says to them: “Draw some out now and take it to the master of the feast.” And they took it. The master of the feast is some learned interpreter of the law from that time, perhaps Nicodemus or Gamaliel, or Saul, then his disciple but now Paul the apostle, teacher of the whole Church. And when the word of the Gospel is entrusted to such men—what had lain hidden in the letter of the law and the prophets [Ms., ‘prophecy’; Al., ‘the prophecy’]—wine made from water is offered to the master of the feast.

[Col. 0771C] **Thus far Bede.**” And rightly in the house of this wedding, which symbolized the mysteries of Christ and the Church, a dining hall—that is, three orders of reclining guests, distinguished by height [Al., “distinguished”]—is described as present, because there are plainly three orders of the faithful of which the Church consists: married people, continent persons, and teachers.

The first order of those reclining at the wedding of the heavenly Bridegroom—that is, in the Church, those who rejoice in faith and works—is the rank of faithful married people. The second is that of the continent. The highest is that of preachers. “”

[Col. 0771C] **Bede again.** Accordingly, it is fittingly reported that the master of the feast, after calling the bridegroom, said: **(VERSE 10)** “Everyone first sets out the good wine, and when they have become drunk, then the inferior. But you have kept the good wine until now.” For it belongs to teachers to recognize the difference between the Law and the Gospel, between truth and shadow, and to prefer the new grace of evangelical faith and the eternal gifts of the heavenly homeland to all ancient institutions and all promises of an earthly kingdom [Beda, “to proclaim”].

**VERSE 11.**—Jesus performed this beginning of signs at Cana of Galilee and manifested his glory. By this sign he manifested that he was himself the king of glory and therefore the Bridegroom of the Church, who came to the wedding as an ordinary human being but, as Lord of heaven and earth, changed the elements as he wished. There is, moreover, a beautiful correspondence among these things. He who at the beginning of the signs that, while still mortal, he was to show to mortals changed water into wine—he himself, at the beginning of the signs that, having already been made immortal through the resurrection, he would show to those pursuing only the concerns of immortal life, imbued their previously carnal and, as it were, tasteless minds with the flavor of heavenly knowledge:

[Col. 0772C] “Thus far from Bede.” After the glory of the true resurrection, he was to fill them with a greater gift of spiritual grace [Al., “after the true…”].

# BOOK TWO

## CHAPTER IV

**As the Passover of the Jews approached, he drove the sellers and buyers from the temple.** [Col. 0771C]

For there follows the marvelous mystery of the sign mentioned above: how Jesus himself, having gone up to Jerusalem with his mother and brothers, found sellers and buyers in the temple, and how he drove them out, as the Evangelist says:

[Col. 0771D] **VERSES 12, 13.**—Jesus went down to Capernaum, he and his mother, his brothers, and his disciples; and they remained there not many days. The Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. The Evangelist rightly says that Jesus went down to Capernaum. Capernaum is interpreted as “most beautiful village,” signifying this world, to which our Lord Jesus Christ is said to have descended for the salvation of the human race, never departing from his Father’s dwelling. “”

[Col. 0771D] **From Homily 6 of the Venerable Bede.** Some are accustomed to be troubled by the fact that at the beginning of this Gospel reading it was said that, when the Lord descended to Capernaum, not only his mother and disciples but also his brothers followed him. Nor were there lacking heretics who thought that Joseph, the husband of the blessed perpetual virgin Mary, had fathered with another wife those whom Scripture calls the Lord’s brothers. Others, with greater impiety, thought that he had fathered them with Mary herself after the Lord’s birth. But we, dearest brothers, ought to know and confess without any scruple of doubt that not only the blessed Mother of God, but also Joseph, the most blessed witness and guardian of her chastity, always remained entirely free from every conjugal act; and that they were not her children but their relatives, who, according to the customary usage of Scripture, are called the Savior’s brothers and sisters.

Thus Abraham speaks to Lot in this way: “Please let there be no quarrel between me and you, and between my shepherds and your shepherds, for we are brothers” (Gen. XIII, 8). And Laban says to Jacob: “Because you are my brother, will you serve me for nothing?” (Gen. XXIX, 15). It is in fact established that Lot was the son of Haran, Abraham’s brother, and Jacob the son of Rebekah, Laban’s sister. Yet because of their kinship they were called brothers. According to this rule, which, as I have said, is extremely common in Holy Scripture, Mary’s or Joseph’s relatives also must be understood to have been called the Lord’s brothers.

That Jesus went up to Jerusalem as the Passover approached gives us a clear example of how vigilantly we must submit to the Lord’s commands, since he himself, appearing in human weakness, observed the same decrees that he had established by the authority of his divinity. To prevent servants from thinking that they could escape punishments or receive rewards without frequent offerings of prayers and good works, the Son himself went up among the servants to worship [Beda, “to pray”] and sacrifice to God. Let us see what he found them doing when he came to Jerusalem, and what he himself did there.

**VERSES 14, 15.**—

[Col. 0773D] The following passages are cited and transcribed in Anselm of Lucca’s *Collectanea*, in Canisius’s *Lectio Antiqua*, Basnage’s edition, vol. III, part I, p. 389, from Book II of Albinus on Matthew; however, we have already noted in the preliminary notice that the title should read “on John.” “And he found,” he says, “in the temple those selling sheep, oxen, and doves, and the moneychangers sitting. And when he had made something like a whip from cords, he drove them all from the temple, the sheep and the oxen as well, and poured out the money of the moneychangers and overturned the tables.”

Oxen, sheep, and doves were bought for the purpose of being offered in the temple. The moneychangers sat at the tables so that the price of the sacrifices might readily be assessed between the buyers and sellers. Thus the things that were being bought in order to be offered to the Lord in that same temple appeared to be sold lawfully in the temple. But the Lord himself, unwilling that anything belonging to earthly commerce—even commerce thought honorable—should be displayed in his house, drove out the unjust traders and expelled everyone together with the things in which they traded.

What, then, my brothers, what do we think the Lord would do if he found people quarreling, indulging in idle talk, dissolved in laughter, or entangled in any other crime? He saw people buying sacrifices to be offered to him in the temple and hastened to drive them out. We have said this for the sake of those who enter the church and not only neglect the intention of praying, but even increase the very things for which they ought to have prayed. Moreover, they pursue those who rebuke them for such folly with insults and hatred, or even slander, adding sins to sins and, as it were, weaving for themselves a very long cord by their careless accumulation of them, without fearing that they will be condemned by the examination of the strict Judge.

For twice in the holy Gospel we read that the Lord came to the temple and drove out such traders: here, namely, in the third year before his passion, as we recognize from what follows in this Evangelist’s writings; and in the very year in which he suffered, when five days before Passover he came to Jerusalem seated on a donkey. Everyone who thinks rightly understands that he also does this same thing in the temple of the holy Church through his daily visitation and judgment. Therefore these things are greatly to be dreaded, beloved, and feared with fitting terror; and we must take diligent care lest, when he comes unexpectedly, he find anything perverse in us for which we ought deservedly to be scourged and cast out of the Church.

And especially in that place which is specifically called a house of prayer, we must beware of doing anything foolish, lest we hear from the Apostle, together with the Corinthians: “Do you not have houses for conducting or discussing worldly affairs?” (I Cor. XI, 22), or, “Do you despise the Church of God?” And from the Prophet, together with the Jews: “My beloved has committed many crimes in my house” (Jer. XI, 15).

Indeed, we should rejoice because in baptism we ourselves have become the temple of God, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (I Cor. III, 17). We ourselves are the city of the great King, of which it is sung: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI, 1), that is, the foundations of the Church are established in the firmness of the faith of the apostles and prophets. But it is no less—or rather, very greatly—to be feared, because the Apostle first says: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (I Cor. III, 17). And the just Judge himself says: “I will destroy from the city of the Lord all who practice iniquity” (Ps. C, 8).

We should rejoice because the solemnity of Passover is enacted in us when we strive to pass from vices to virtues. For *Pascha* means “passing over.” We should rejoice because the Lord deigns to visit our hearts—his own city, so to speak—and to illuminate that same Passover of our good action with the presence of his mercy. But we must greatly fear lest he find us doing in his city something other than what he loves, and lest he show himself to us as a strict exactor in a form that we do not love; lest, finding us moneychangers in his temple, or sellers of oxen, sheep, or doves, he condemn us (Matt. XXII).

Oxen signify the teaching of heavenly life; sheep, works of purity and devotion; doves, the gifts of the Holy Spirit. The field is accustomed to be cultivated with the help of oxen; the field, however, is the Lord’s, and it is the heart cultivated by heavenly teaching and properly prepared to receive the seeds of God’s word. Sheep innocently provide their fleeces for clothing human beings. The Spirit descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove.

They sell oxen who offer the word of the Gospel to their hearers not out of divine love but for the sake of earthly gain; the Apostle rebukes such men because they proclaim Christ insincerely. They sell sheep who perform works of devotion for the sake of human praise; concerning them the Lord says: “They have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 2). They sell doves who give the grace of the Spirit that they have received not freely, as commanded, but in exchange for a reward; who confer the laying on of hands, through which the Spirit is received, not for money but nevertheless for popular approval; who bestow sacred orders not for the merit of life but for favor.

They lend money in the temple who serve heavenly things only pretendedly but earthly affairs openly in the Church, seeking their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ (Phil. II, 21). But the Lord shows what reward awaits such fraudulent workers when, having made a whip of cords, he drives them all from the temple.

Those are expelled [Ms.: “are, however, expelled”] from the portion of the lot of the saints who, placed among the saints, either falsely perform good works or openly perform evil ones. He also expelled the sheep and oxen, showing that the life and teaching of such people alike are rejected. The cords with which he scourged the impious and drove them from the temple are the dreadful accumulation [Ms. and Beda, “growth”] of evil actions, from which the strict Judge receives the material for condemning the reprobate.

For Isaiah says: “Woe to those who drag iniquity with cords of vanity” (Isa. V, 18). And Solomon says in Proverbs: “The iniquities of the wicked ensnare him, and he is bound by the cords of his sins” (Prov. V, 22). Whoever heaps sin upon sin, for which he will be condemned more severely, gradually lengthens, as it were, the cords by which he will be bound and scourged.

He also poured out the copper of the moneychangers whom he had expelled [Beda, “expels”] and overturned their tables, because at the end, when the reprobate have been condemned, he will also remove the form of the very things they loved, in accordance with what is written: “The world will pass away, and its desire” (I John II, 17).

[Col. 0775B] **VERSE 16.**—And to those who were selling doves he said: “Take these things away from here; do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce.” He commands the selling of doves to be removed from the temple, because the grace of the Spirit ought to be received freely and given freely.

[Col. 0775D] **Bede:** “Whoever has received the grace of the Spirit freely ought to give it freely” (Matt. X). Hence Simon the magician, because he wished to buy it with money in order to sell it at a higher price, heard: “May your money be with you unto perdition, because you have neither part nor lot in this word” (Acts VIII, 20–21).

It should be noted, however, that not only are those sellers of doves and makers of God’s house into a house of commerce who, by granting sacred orders [Beda, “by granting”], seek a price in money, praise, or even honor. So too are those who exercise a spiritual rank or grace in the Church, which they received through the Lord’s generosity, not with a simple intention but for the sake of some human recompense, contrary to the words of the Apostle Peter: “Whoever speaks, as the words of God; whoever ministers, as from the strength which God supplies, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ” (I Pet. IV, 11).

Therefore, whoever is such a person, if he does not wish to be removed from the Church when the Lord comes, must remove these things from his actions, lest he make God’s house a house of commerce. It must also not be passed over that Scripture carefully commends both natures of our Savior, namely, the human and the divine. So that he may be understood to be the true Son of God, let us hear him say: “Do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce.” For he plainly shows himself to be the Son of God the Father when he calls the temple of God the house of his Father. And so that he may again be understood to be the true son of man, let us recall that at the beginning of this reading he is said to have descended into Capernaum with his mother as his companion [Beda omits “as his companion”]. It follows:

**VERSE 17.**—But his disciples remembered that it was written: “Zeal for your house has consumed me.” Because of his zeal for the house of the Father, the Savior drove the impious from the temple. Let us also be zealous, dearest brothers, for the house of God, and, as far as we can, let us strive to prevent anything wicked from being done in it.

If we see a brother who belongs to the house of God swollen with pride, accustomed to slander, enslaved to drunkenness, weakened by lust, disturbed by anger, or subject to any other vice, let us strive, insofar as our ability permits, to correct him and set right what has been polluted and perverted. If we cannot amend anything in such people [Beda, “if we are unable”], let us nevertheless endure it with the sharpest grief of heart.

And especially in the house of prayer itself, where the Lord’s body is consecrated and where the presence of the angels is always believed to be present, let us act with all our strength so that nothing foolish may occur and nothing may be done that impedes our prayer or that of our brother.

[Col. 0776D] **Thus far Anselm of Lucca.** It follows:

**VERSES 18, 19.**—Then the Jews answered and said to him: “What sign do you show us, since you do these things?” Jesus answered and said to them: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”

The Evangelist later explained which temple he meant: namely, the temple of his body, which, after they had destroyed it by his passion, he himself raised from the dead after three days. Since they were asking the Lord for a sign—why he ought to have cast the customary commerce out of the temple [Ms. and Beda, “why he should have”]—he replied that he was therefore entirely right to drive the impious from the temple, because that temple signified the temple of his body, in which there was absolutely no stain of sin. Nor was it without reason that he cleansed the figurative temple from crimes, since he could, by the power of his divine majesty, raise from the dead the true temple of God, destroyed by human beings through death.

**VERSE 20.**—Then the Jews said: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and you will raise it up in three days?” They answered according to how they understood. But so that we too might not understand the Lord’s spiritual saying carnally, the Evangelist subsequently explained which temple he was speaking about.

When they say that the temple was built in forty-six years, they indicate not its first but its second construction. Solomon first completed the temple, with the greatest peace in his kingdom and in a most splendid [Beda, “most rapid”] work of seven years [Ms., “twenty-seven years”]. After it had been destroyed by the Chaldeans, its rebuilding began after seventy years, when the captivity was released at the command of Cyrus the Persian. But the children of the transmigration could not complete the work they were carrying out under the leaders Zerubbabel and Jesus before forty-six years, because of the opposition of the neighboring peoples.

This number of years also corresponds most aptly to the perfection of the Lord’s body. For writers of natural history report that the form of the human body is perfected over this many days: during the first six days after conception it has the likeness of milk; during the following nine it is changed into blood; then during twelve it becomes solid; during the remaining eighteen it is formed until all the limbs have their complete contours; and from then on, during the remaining period up to the time of birth, it increases in size.

Six, nine, twelve, and eighteen make forty-five; if we add one to these—that is, the very day on which the body, divided among its limbs, begins to grow—we find the same number of days in the construction of the Lord’s body as we find years in the construction of the temple.

And because that man-made temple prefigured the Lord’s most holy flesh, which he took from the Virgin, as we learn from this passage, it also signified his body, which is the Church, and the body and soul of each of the faithful, as we find in many passages of Scripture.

[Col. 0777D] **Thus far from the cited homily of Bede.**” But the first Adam, after sin, heard: “You are earth, and into earth you will go” (Gen. III). The second Adam said of himself: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”

The first Adam was scattered throughout the whole world, while in the second he was gathered together. This is signified by the name *Adam*, which is written with four letters: Alpha, Delta, Alpha again, and My. These four letters signify the four parts of the world into which Adam was scattered in his descendants.

Therefore these four letters are found at the beginnings of the names of the parts of the world. For ἄρκτος, which is “the North,” begins with Alpha; and δυσις, which is “the West,” begins with Delta; and ἀνατολή, which is “the East,” begins with Alpha; and μεσημβρίος, which is “the South,” begins with My. These are the four parts of the world, beginning with these four letters.

If these letters are considered according to Greek numeration, they make forty-six. Alpha is one, Delta four, Alpha again one, and My forty; together they make forty-six. This number mystically signifies the forty-six days during which the temple of Christ’s body was built in the Virgin’s womb, as we said above.

But Christ’s flesh, which was taken from Adam, was destroyed by the Jews and rebuilt by him from himself according to the Scriptures of the prophets. Therefore the Evangelist says: “For he was speaking about the temple of his body.”

**VERSES 21, 22.**—When therefore he had risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture—that is, the prophets, who foretold that Christ would rise on the third day—and the word that Jesus had spoken, namely, when he said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” That is: “On the third day I will raise up what you will destroy on the cross.” It follows:

**VERSES 23, 24.**—When Jesus was in Jerusalem at Passover, on the feast day, many believed in him; but Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them, because he knew what was in man.

For they did not believe in him in such a way as to be worthy for Christ to dwell in them. Their faith can be compared with that of catechumens, who believe in Christ, but to whom Christ does not entrust himself, because unless someone has been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. Christ entrusts himself to no one except one who is worthy to enter the kingdom of God; and no one is worthy to enter the kingdom of God except one who has been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit.

For this reason ecclesiastical custom does not give catechumens communion of Christ’s body and blood, because they have not been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit; only to those who have been so reborn is participation in Christ’s body and blood entrusted.

Among these many who believed in Jesus was this Nicodemus; and therefore he came by night, not by day, because he came not yet enlightened by the light of heavenly grace.

# CHAPTER V

**To Nicodemus he says among other things that no one can enter the kingdom of God unless reborn, and that he came not to judge but to save the world. He also says that the works done in God are made manifest.**

# CHAPTER III. VERSES 1, 2

—There was a man from the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. He came to Jesus by night. “
@ [Col. 0778D] From Bede, homily on the feast of the Finding of the Holy Cross. The ruler of the Jews came to Jesus by night, wishing through a private conversation with him to learn more fully the mysteries of the faith, of which he had already acquired some rudiments through the open display of signs. Since he wisely sought to understand what he saw being done by him, he deserved to investigate subtly what he was asking of him. “Rabbi,” he said, “we know that you have come from God as a teacher; for no one can perform these signs that you perform unless God is with him.” He therefore confessed that Jesus had come from God to offer the world heavenly instruction; he understood from the miracles that God was with him [Al., “more prudently”], but he did not yet recognize that he himself was God. Yet because he approached the teacher whom he knew for instruction in the pursuit of truth, he deserved to be perfectly instructed and brought to knowledge [Beda, “recognition”] of his divinity; he deserved to grasp the mysteries of both his births—namely, the divine and the human—as well as of his passion and ascension; and he also learned from the Lord’s revelation the manner of the second generation, entry into the heavenly kingdom, and many other sacraments of evangelical teaching.

**VERSE 3.**—“Jesus answered and said to him: Truly, truly, I say to you: Unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” This statement shines all the more clearly upon all the faithful, since it is certain that without its light the faithful cannot exist. For who can obtain remission of sins and enter the kingdom of heaven without the washing of regeneration? But Nicodemus, who came to Jesus by night, did not yet know how to grasp the mysteries of the light; for the night in which he came signifies the very ignorance by which he was oppressed. He had not yet been joined to the number of those to whom the Apostle says: “Once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians V, 8); rather, he remained among those to whom Isaiah speaks: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, because your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen over you” (Isaiah LX, 1). He therefore answered the Lord and said:

**VERSE 4.**—“How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter again into his mother’s womb and be born?” Since he still did not know about the second birth, but had already become concerned about his salvation, he necessarily asked whether the one birth he knew could be repeated, or by what procedure regeneration could be accomplished, lest, remaining without it, he should be unable to share in heavenly life. It should be noted, however, that what he said concerning the carnal birth must also be understood of spiritual regeneration: namely, that once it has been accomplished, it cannot be repeated. Whether a heretic, a schismatic, or any criminal person baptizes in confession of the holy Trinity, the one who has thus been baptized cannot be baptized again by good Catholics, lest the confession or invocation of so great a name appear to be annulled. And because Nicodemus, anxious about the Lord’s first answer, carefully inquires how it should be understood, he deserves now to be instructed more plainly and to hear that the second birth is not carnal but spiritual. Jesus therefore answered him:

{491}

**VERSE 5.**—“Truly, truly, I say to you, unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” Explaining the manner of this birth afterward and thoroughly distinguishing it from the carnal birth, he says:

**VERSE 6.**—“What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.” The nature of the spirit is invisible, while that of the flesh is visible; and therefore carnal generation is visibly brought about through visible growth. Whoever is born in the flesh advances through the stages of life; spiritual generation, however, takes place entirely invisibly. For the baptized person [Beda, “the person about to be baptized”] is indeed seen to descend into the font, is seen to be immersed in the waters, and is seen to rise from the waters; but the one who has undergone the washing of regeneration in him cannot be seen at all. Only the devotion of the faithful knows that a sinner descends into the font but rises purified. A son of transgression descends, but a son of reconciliation rises; a son of death descends, but a son of resurrection rises; a son of wrath descends, but a son of mercy rises; a son of the devil descends, but a son of God rises. Only this mother Church, which gives birth, knows it. To the eyes of the foolish, however, such a person appears to come out of the font exactly as he entered it, and everything being done seems to be mere play. Hence, at the end, when they see the glory of the saints, they will say, groaning in their torments: “These are the ones whom we once held in derision and as a reproach; how have they been counted among the sons of God?” (Wisdom V, 3). The Apostle John says, “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (1 John III, 2).

“What is born of the Spirit is spirit,” because whoever is regenerated from water and the Spirit is invisibly changed into a new person and from being carnal becomes spiritual. For this reason he is rightly called not only spiritual but also spirit: just as the substance of the spirit is invisible to our eyes, so the person who is renewed by God’s grace becomes invisibly spiritual and a child of God, although visibly he appears to everyone as flesh and a human being. It follows:

**VERSES 7, 8.**—“Do not marvel that I said to you, You must be born again. The Spirit breathes where it wills, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.”

“The Spirit breathes where it wills,” because he himself has authority over whose heart he may enlighten with the grace of his visitation. “And you hear his voice,” when, in your presence, someone who is filled with the Holy Spirit speaks; “but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes,” because even if the Spirit fills someone for a time in your presence, you cannot see [Al., “you are unable to see”] how he entered that person or how he departed again, since his nature is invisible.

“So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit”: for, with the Spirit acting invisibly, he begins to be what he was not, so that unbelievers do not know where he comes from or where he goes—that is, he comes from the grace of regeneration into adoption as the children of God, and he goes toward the reception of the heavenly kingdom.

While Nicodemus was still asking how these things could happen (**VERSE 9**), the Lord adds, saying:

**VERSE 10.**—“You are a teacher in Israel, and you do not know these things?” He does not say this as though he wished to insult the one called a teacher because he was ignorant of the heavenly sacraments, but to summon him to the path of humility, without which the heavenly door cannot be found.

**VERSE 12.**—“If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” He told them earthly things, as we found in the preceding lesson, when he was speaking of the passion and resurrection of his body, which he had taken from the earth, saying: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II, 19). Yet they did not believe the word he spoke, and were not even able [Beda, “were not willing”] to understand that he was speaking of any temple other than the temple of his body. Therefore, if they did not grasp earthly things when they heard them, how much less are they capable of grasping heavenly things—that is, the mysteries of divine generation [Ms., “regeneration”]?

The Lord continues to instruct him both in heavenly sacraments and in earthly matters, since he saw that Nicodemus was wisely and diligently attentive to what he heard. His ascension to eternal life is heavenly; his exaltation to temporal death is earthly. Thus he speaks of the heavenly things:

**VERSE 13.**—“And no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.”

He then adds concerning the earthly things:

**VERSE 14.**—“And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.”

It is rightly asked how the Son of Man is said either to have descended from heaven or already to have been in heaven at the time when he spoke these things on earth. The confession of the Catholic faith is well known: the Son of God, descending from heaven, assumed the Son of Man in the virgin’s womb; after completing the dispensation of his passion, he raised him from the dead and took him into heaven. Therefore Christ’s flesh did not descend from heaven, nor was it in heaven before the time of his ascension.

Why, then, is it said, “Unless the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven”? It is because Christ is one person existing in two natures. For this reason the Son of Man is rightly said both to have descended from heaven and to have been in heaven before the passion: what he could not possess in his own nature, he possessed in the Son of God by whom he was assumed.

For the same reason—that the one Christ exists in two natures—the Apostle says: “The Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood” (Acts XX, 28). For God did not possess blood in his own substance, but in the man he assumed he possessed blood to be poured out for the Church [Beda, “which he would pour out”].

For this reason the Psalmist says: “God has ascended amid jubilation” (Psalm XLVI, 6). For how could God ascend except in the man, since in the majesty of his own nature he is always and everywhere present?

But it must also be asked how it was said, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven,” when all the elect truly trust that they will ascend into heaven, since the Lord promises them: “Where I am, there my servant will also be.” The clearest reasoning resolves the difficulty: the mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, is the head of all the elect. Likewise, all the elect are members of that same head, as the Apostle says: “He gave him as head over all things to the Church” [Ms. and Beda, “over the whole Church”] (Ephesians I, 22). And again: “You are the body of Christ and members from a member” (1 Corinthians XII, 27).

Therefore, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven” means plainly: no one ascends into heaven except Christ in his body, which is the Church. He first ascended in himself, before the eyes of the apostles, who were his more eminent members; and from that point onward he ascends daily in his members and gathers himself into heaven.

This is why his body, caught amid the adversities of the present age, boasts and says: “Now he has exalted my head above my enemies” (Psalm XXVI, 6). It is as though it openly said: “He who raised Christ, my head, whom the Jews killed, from the dead, and, frustrating all the plots of my enemies, lifted him into heaven—I hope that, rescuing me also from present dangers, he will join me to my head in his kingdom.”

Since, then, no one ascends into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, whoever desires to ascend into heaven must be joined to the one who descended from heaven and is in heaven by the true unity of faith and love, clearly understanding that he can ascend into heaven by no other order than through the one who descended from heaven. Hence he says elsewhere: “No one comes to the Father except through me.”

These things are said to Nicodemus and to all catechumens so that they may learn to be incorporated by rebirth into the members of the one through whom they can ascend into the kingdom of God. And because ascent or entry into the kingdom cannot take place without faith and the sacraments of the Lord’s passion, it is rightly added:

“And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.”

**VERSE 15.**—“So that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

With remarkable skill in heavenly instruction, the Lord leads the teacher of the Mosaic law toward the spiritual meaning of that same law, recalling the history of old and explaining that it was made as a figure of his passion and of human salvation.

The Book of Numbers relates that the people of Israel, wearied in the wilderness by the length and hardship of the journey, murmured against the Lord and Moses. Therefore the Lord sent fiery serpents among them. When many were being wounded and dying from their attacks, they cried out to Moses, and he prayed for them. The Lord commanded him to make a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign. “Whoever,” he said, “has been bitten and looks upon it shall live.” And so it happened (Numbers XXI).

The wound [Ms. and Beda, “wounds”] of the fiery serpents therefore represents the poisons and incitements of vices, which kill the soul they touch with spiritual death. And rightly, when the people murmured against the Lord, they were struck down by the bites of serpents, so that through the outward order of the scourge they might recognize what inward destruction they were suffering by their murmuring.

The lifting up of the bronze serpent, by looking upon which those who had been bitten were healed, is the passion of our Redeemer on the cross; by faith in him alone the kingdom of death and sin is overcome.

Sins are rightly represented by serpents, since they drag both soul and body to destruction—not only because serpents are fiery, venomous, and cunning in killing, but also because our first parents were persuaded to sin through a serpent and, by sinning, were changed from immortal to mortal.

The Lord is rightly shown by the bronze serpent, since he came in the likeness of sinful flesh (*in similitudinem carnis peccati*; Beda, *in similitudine carnis peccati*). Just as the bronze serpent had an appearance resembling that of the fiery serpents but possessed no burning of harmful poison in its members, and by being lifted up healed those who had been bitten by serpents, so, precisely so, the Redeemer of the human race did not assume sinful flesh but the likeness of sinful flesh, in which, by suffering the death of the cross, he would free those who believed in him from every sin and even from death itself.

“Therefore, just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert,” he says, “so must the Son of Man be lifted up.” Just as those who looked upon the bronze serpent lifted up as a sign were temporarily healed from the temporal death and wound inflicted by the serpents’ bites, so those who by believing, confessing, and sincerely imitating look upon the mystery of the Lord’s passion are saved forever from every death that they had brought upon soul and body alike by sinning.

Hence it is rightly added:

“So that everyone who believes in him” (*in ipsum*; Beda, *in ipso*) “may not perish but have eternal life.”

The meaning of this statement is clear: whoever believes in Christ not only escapes the destruction of punishments but also receives eternal life. The difference between the figure and the reality is that through the former temporal life is prolonged (*protelatur*; Beda, “was prolonged” [*protelabatur*]), whereas through the latter life is granted that endures without end.

But careful effort is needed so that what the understanding rightly perceives may be fulfilled by conduct worthy of it, so that our confession of the true faith, through pious and sober living, may deserve to attain the perfection [Beda, “reception”] of the life promised to us.

Yet because these things are said of the Son of Man, who could be lifted up on the cross and suffer death, lest Nicodemus think that he was merely the Son of Man, from whom perpetual life was to be expected, the Lord also took care to reveal to him the mystery of his divinity and to show that one and the same person, the Son of God and the Son of Man, is the Savior of the world. For it follows:

**VERSE 16.**—“For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

It should be noted that he repeats concerning the only-begotten Son of God the same things that he had previously said concerning the Son of Man lifted up on the cross, saying: “So that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

For our same Redeemer and Creator, existing as the Son of God before the ages, became the Son of Man at the end of the ages, so that he who by the power of his divinity had created us to enjoy the blessedness of eternal life might by the weakness of our humanity restore us to receive the life we had lost.

@ [Col. 0783D] “Up to this point from the cited homily of Bede.” It follows:

**VERSE 17.**—“For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him.”

@ [Col. 0783D] From Saint Augustine, *Tractate XII on John*, nos. 12–13.

Therefore, insofar as it depends upon the physician, he came to heal the sick person. The one who does not wish to observe the physician’s instructions kills himself. The Savior came into the world. Why is he called the Savior of the world, unless to save the world and not to judge the world? You do not wish to be saved by him; you will be judged by yourself. And what shall I say—“you will be judged”? See what he says: “Whoever believes in him will not be judged” [Al., “is not judged”]. But whoever does not believe—what did you expect him to say, except “is judged”? “He has already been judged,” he says. Judgment has not yet appeared, but judgment has already taken place. For “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy II, 19); he knows who will remain for the crown and who will remain for the flame; he knows his wheat on his threshing floor, and he knows the chaff; he knows the crop, and he knows the weeds.

The one who does not believe has already been judged. Why has he been judged? Because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.

**VERSE 19.**—“This is the judgment: that the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than the light, for their works were evil.”

My brothers, whose works did the Lord find good? No one’s. For he found all their works evil [Augustine, “the works of all”]. How, then, did some do the truth and come to the light? For what follows is:

**VERSE 21.**—“But whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be revealed, because they have been done in God.”

How, then, did some perform a good work so as to come to the light—that is, to Christ? And how did some love darkness? If he found all people to be sinners, and heals all from sin; and if that serpent in which the Lord’s death was prefigured heals those who had been bitten; and if the serpent was raised up because of the bites of the serpent—that is, the Lord’s death because of mortal human beings whom he found unrighteous—how is this understood: “This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than the light, for their works were evil”?

What does this mean? Whose works were good? Did you not come to justify the ungodly? But “they loved darkness,” he says, “more than the light.” There he placed the force of the statement. For many loved their sins; [many confessed their sins]. Whoever confesses his sins and accuses his sins is already acting together with God. God accuses your sins; if you also accuse them, you are joined to God.

There are, as it were, two things: the human being and the sinner. When you hear “human being,” God made that; when you hear “sinner,” that human being made it. Destroy what you have made, so that God may save what he made. You must hate in yourself what you have done, and love in yourself what God has done.

When what you have done begins to displease you, your good works begin there, because you accuse your evil works. Confession of evil works is the beginning of good works. You do the truth and come to the light.

What does it mean, “You do the truth”? You do not flatter yourself, you do not indulge yourself, you do not praise yourself; you do not say, “I am righteous,” when you are unrighteous. Thus you begin to do the truth. You come to the light so that your works may be revealed, because they have been done in God. For the very fact that your sin displeased you would not displease you unless God shone upon you and his truth showed you the light [In Augustine, “the light” is absent].

But the person who, even when admonished, loves his sins hates the light that admonishes him and flees from it, so that his evil works, which he loves, may not be exposed.

Whoever does the truth accuses his own evils, does not spare himself, and does not forgive himself, so that God may forgive him. For what he wants God to forgive, he himself acknowledges; and he comes to the light, giving thanks to it because it has shown him what he should hate in himself.

He says to the Lord: “Turn your face away from my sins.” And with what face does he say this unless he also says again: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Psalm L, 5, 11)? Let what you do not want to be before the Lord be before you.

But if you put your sin behind you, God turns it back before your eyes; and he turns it back when there will no longer be any fruit of repentance. Run while you have the light, lest the darkness of death overtake you.

It follows:

**VERSE 22.**—“After this, Jesus and his disciples came into the land of Judea. There he stayed with them, and there he was baptizing.”

@ [Col. 0784D] From Saint Augustine, *Tractate XIII*, no. 4, 6.

The baptized person baptizes, but he does not baptize with the baptism with which he himself was baptized. The Lord, baptized by a servant, gives baptism [Ms., “baptism”], showing the way of humility and leading to the Lord’s baptism. This is his baptism: by offering an example of humility, he himself did not reject the baptism of a servant. Through the servant’s baptism, the way was prepared for the Lord; and, having been baptized, the Lord made himself the way to himself for those coming [“to him”].

Let us hear him himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6). If you seek the truth, hold to the way; for the one who is the truth is himself the way.

Let us hear John: “Jesus was baptizing.” We have said that Jesus baptizes. How, he says, Jesus? How, the Lord? How, the Son of God? How, the Word? But “the Word became flesh.”

## CHAPTER VI

When John was baptizing at Aenon, his disciples told him that the one to whom he had borne witness was baptizing and that everyone was coming to him. John declares that the other is the bridegroom and that he himself must decrease, while the other must increase; that the other is from above and is above all; and that the believer in him has eternal life, whereas wrath remains upon the unbeliever. [Col. 0785A]

**VERSE 23.**—“John was also baptizing at Aenon, near Salim.”

The place is indeed identified from its name, because there were many waters there [Perhaps: “a certain lake”]. Aenon near Salim is the place where John baptized, and it is still shown today at the eighth milestone south of Scythopolis, near Salim and the Jordan.

**VERSE 24.**—“For John had not yet been thrown into prison.”

Why was John baptizing? Because it was necessary for the Lord to be baptized. Why was it necessary for the Lord to be baptized? So that no one, however endowed with great grace or power, might disdain to be baptized. The Lord himself did not disdain the sacrament of baptism, although there was nothing in him to be cleansed by baptism, since he had no sin to be forgiven in the washing of baptism. The Lord was baptized by a servant so that the servant of the Lord would not despise baptism.

“For John had not yet been thrown into prison.” The evangelist said this so that it might be understood that [these miracles], which he had mentioned earlier, were performed in the first year of the teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ, which began with his baptism; the other evangelists, he understood, were especially silent about the events of that year.

**VERSE 25.**—“A dispute arose between John’s disciples and the Jews concerning purification.”

John’s disciples were jealous of their teacher because they heard that more people were flocking to Christ’s baptism and that the Jews were preferring Christ’s baptism to John’s. At last they came to John himself, so that he might resolve the dispute that his disciples had had with the Jews concerning the distinction between Christ’s baptism and John’s baptism. They said to him:

**VERSE 26.**—“Rabbi, the one who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you bore witness—behold, he is baptizing, and everyone is coming to him.”

As though indignant that more people had come to Christ’s baptism, they said: “Everyone is coming to him and abandoning you, although he was baptized with your baptism—the one to whose baptism everyone is now flocking.”

**VERSE 27.**—“John answered and said: A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven.”

“You yourselves bear witness to me that I said: ‘I am not the Christ.’ If you believe my testimony, know that I am not the Christ, but he is; and that his is the baptism in which there is remission of sins and the Holy Spirit is given—not mine, in which only repentance was given, together with faith in the one about whom [Ms., ‘concerning whom’] you now complain.

“A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven. I have received the ministry that was given to me from heaven. I am the herald; he is the judge. I am the servant; he is the Lord. He is the bridegroom; I am the friend of the bridegroom. He must increase, but I must decrease. I came to prepare his way, not to exalt myself. I am the voice of one crying out; he is the Father’s Word. The one who comes after me was made before me—that is, he was placed above me in dignity. I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal [‘his’], that is, to explain the mystery of his birth, by which he was born from a virgin and came into the world.

“You have heard my testimony; believe my testimony. Flock to the one whose baptism contains the remission of sins.

“This John was held in such great authority that he was thought by the people to be the Christ. But he rejected the false honor so that he might possess the solid truth. He did not wish to boast of himself that he was what he was not, lest he be without the one who always was.”

**VERSE 29.**—“Whoever has the bride is the bridegroom. I am not the bridegroom. But what am I? The friend of the bridegroom, rejoicing at the bridegroom’s voice.”

Who is the bridegroom? The one of whom it is said: “God is King of the whole earth, and all the kings of the earth will adore him; all nations will serve him” (Psalm LXXI, 11). He is the true bridegroom. The bride is the holy Church, gathered from all nations, of whom the Apostle says: “I have betrothed you to one man, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians XI, 2).

She is a virgin and has a bridegroom; she gives birth daily and remains perpetually a virgin. This virginity is integrity of mind, perfection of love, unity of the Catholic faith, harmony of peace, and purity in heart and soul, because bodily chastity is worthless without the integrity of the Catholic faith. The friends of this virgin—that is, of the universal Church—are the preachers of evangelical truth.

Therefore this John, the friend of the bridegroom, says: “The one who stands and hears him rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice.” He stands who remains in the right faith and preaches what he believes.

@ [Col. 0785D] Saint Augustine, in the cited passage, no. 12.

Why does he stand? Because he does not fall. Why does he not fall? Because he is humble. This forerunner of the Lord stood upon the solid rock when he said: “I am not the Christ; I am not the bridegroom, but the friend of the bridegroom.”

Whoever seeks the glory of the one who sent him rightly does not fall, rightly stands, rightly hears the bridegroom’s voice, and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice.

The bridegroom’s voice is therefore: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

{496}

@ [Col. 0786D] Saint Augustine, *Tractate XIV*, nos. 2, 3, 5.

As you heard above, John confessed: “I am not the Christ.” When Jesus was making many disciples and the report was brought to John, as though [or: “so that”] he might be provoked—indeed, they told him this as if he were jealous—he confessed what he was. By this he deserved to belong to Christ, because he did not dare to say that he was what Christ is.

John therefore says: “A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven.” Thus Christ gives, and a human being receives.

[Col. 0786D]

**VERSES 28, 29.**—“You yourselves bear witness to me that I said: ‘I am not the Christ,’ but that I was sent before him. Whoever has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice.”

He does not make joy for himself from himself. Whoever wishes to rejoice in himself will be sad; but whoever wishes to rejoice in God will always rejoice, because God is eternal. Do you wish, then, to have eternal joy? Cling to the one who is eternal.

John described himself in this way. “The friend of the bridegroom rejoices because of the bridegroom’s voice,” he says, not because of his own voice; and he stands and hears him. Therefore, if he falls, he does not hear him. Of the one who once fell it was said: “He did not stand in the truth” (John VIII, 44). This was said of the devil.

The friend of the bridegroom must therefore stand and hear. What does it mean to stand? To remain in the grace that he has received and to hear the voice at which he may rejoice.

This is how John was. He knew from where his joy came. He did not claim for himself what he knew [Augustine, “what he was not”]. He knew that he had been enlightened, not that he was the enlightener. For the evangelist says: “He was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John I, 9). If every human being, then John also, since he too was one of the human beings.

John continues and says: “Therefore this joy of mine has been fulfilled.” What is his joy? That he may rejoice at the bridegroom’s voice.

Many became foolish for this reason: they said that they were wise. The Apostle rebukes them in his Epistle to the Romans, saying: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Romans I, 20). Thus God took away from those who do not give thanks what he gives to those who do give thanks.

John did not wish to be like this; he wished to be grateful. He confessed that he had received, said that he rejoiced because of the bridegroom’s voice, and said:

**VERSE 30.**—“Therefore this joy of mine has been fulfilled. He must increase, but I must decrease.”

What does this mean? He must be exalted, but I must be humbled. This is a great mystery. Before the Lord Jesus came, human beings gloried in themselves. He came as a human being so that his glory [Ms., “the human being’s glory”] might decrease and the glory of God increase.

For he came without sin and found everyone with sin. If he came to forgive sins, let God give and let the human being confess. The confession of the human being is the human being’s humility; the mercy of God is the exaltation of God.

If he came to forgive sins [Augustine, “to forgive sins to the human being,”], let the human being acknowledge his humility, and God will show his mercy.

“He must increase, but I must decrease”: that is, he must give, and I must receive; he must be glorified, and I must confess.

Let the human being understand his place and confess to God, and let him hear the Apostle speaking to the proud and haughty person who wishes to exalt himself: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians IV, 7).

Let the human being therefore understand that he has received. He wanted to call his what is not his, and he must decrease. It is good for him that God be glorified in him; let him decrease in himself, so that he may increase in God.

Christ and John signified these testimonies and this [Aug., “and this”] truth even by their sufferings. John was diminished by the loss of his head, while Christ was exalted on the cross, so that there too it might be revealed what is meant by “He must increase, but I must decrease”—that is, “He must be exalted, but I must be humbled.”

The very creation of light signifies this. Christ was born during the days that were increasing, while John was born during the days that were decreasing, to show what Christ is—namely, the true light—and what John is—namely, one enlightened by him.

Let us [we] grow in him and through him, so that he may grow in us, until we reach the perfect day.

Let us hear further what John said about Christ, and what he said about himself. For he says:

[Col. 0788A] {497}

**VERSE 31.**—“”

@ [Col. 0787D] Saint Augustine, in the cited passage, nos. 6, 7, 8.

“The one who comes from above is above all, and the one who is from the earth is of the earth and speaks from the earth.”

“The one who comes from above is above all”—that is, Christ. “But the one who is from the earth is earth and speaks from the earth”—that is, John.

How, then, does he speak from the earth? Every human being is earthly, and while he speaks earthly things, he speaks from the earth. But whoever has been enlightened by the one who is the true light speaks of divine things.

Thus the grace of God is distinct [Ms., “above”] from human nature. The carnal person judges carnally and suspects carnally. When the grace of God comes, enlightening the human being, he speaks of heavenly things, as it is said: “You who enlighten my lamp, Lord my God, enlighten my darkness” (Psalm XVII, 29).

“This is what is meant by ‘He must increase, but I must decrease.’ Therefore, insofar as John is concerned, John is from the earth and speaks from the earth. If you have heard anything divine from John, it comes from the one who enlightens, not from the one who receives.”

**VERSE 32.**—“The one who comes from heaven is above all; and what he has seen and heard, that he testifies, and no one has accepted his testimony.”

The one who comes from heaven is above all—our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom it was said above: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.”

He is above all, and he speaks what he has seen and heard. For that Son of God also has a Father; he also has a mother [Augustine, “and a Father”], and he has heard from the Father.

And what is it that he heard from the Father? Who could explain this? When could my tongue, when could my heart, suffice—my heart for understanding, or my tongue for expressing it?

What is it that the Son heard from the Father? Perhaps the Son heard the Father’s Word? No; the Son is the Father’s Word. Since the Son is the Word of God, and the Son spoke to us, he wished to speak to us not his own word but the Father’s Word, because he was speaking the Father’s Word.

John therefore said this as was fitting and necessary: “The one who comes from heaven is above all, and he testifies to what he has seen and heard, and no one has accepted his testimony.”

If no one accepted it, why did he come? “No one” means, for [Al., “therefore”], none among a certain people: a people prepared for God’s wrath and to be condemned with the devil; none of these accepted Christ’s testimony [Augustine, “accepts it”]. For if absolutely no one—if no human being accepted it—what, then, is the meaning of what follows?

### VERSE 33 [Col. 0788D]

“He who accepted his testimony set his seal to it, because God is truthful.”

Certainly, then, no one—but you yourself say [Augustine: “not ‘no one,’ if you yourself say”]: “He who accepted his testimony set his seal to it, because God is truthful.” Perhaps John, if questioned, would answer and tell us what he had said [Augustine: “I know what I said: ‘no one’”]—“no one” [Manuscript: “Certainly then no one, if you yourself say, ‘He who accepted,’ etc. . . . And he would say: ‘I know what I said: no one is a certain people’”].

There is a certain people born for the wrath of God and foreknown for this purpose. For the Lord knows who will believe and who will not believe; God knows who will persevere in what they have believed and who will fall away; and all who will come to eternal life are numbered before God.

“No one accepted the testimony of him who came from heaven; but he who accepted his testimony set his seal to it, because God is truthful” [Col. 0789A]. He said, “set his seal”—that is, he placed a sign in his heart, as though affirming that this one, who was sent for the salvation of the human race, is uniquely and especially the true God.

“What is ‘he set his seal to it, because God is truthful,’ except that every human being is a liar, whereas God is truthful? For no human being can say what truth is [Augustine: ‘of truth’] unless he is enlightened by him who cannot lie. God, therefore, is truthful, and Christ is God. Do you wish to prove it? Accept his testimony, and you will find it so. For he who accepted his testimony set his seal to it, because God is truthful. Who is this? He who came from heaven and descended, and is above all: he is the true God” [Col. 0789B].

“He whom God sent speaks the words of God”; he is the true God, he is God, and he is our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law” (Galatians 4:4).

### VERSE 34 [Col. 0789D]

“[He whom God sent speaks the words of God.]”

**Saint Augustine, same passage, no. 10.** “He whom God sent speaks the words of God.” He was certainly speaking this about Christ in order to distinguish himself from him. What then? Did God not send John? Did he not himself say, “I have been sent before him,” and, “He who sent me to baptize in water”? And it was said of him: “Behold, I send my messenger before you, and he will prepare your way” (Malachi 3:1). Does he not also speak the words of God, of whom it was even said that he is greater than a prophet? If God sent him as well, and he speaks the words of God, how are we to understand that he said this about Christ by way of distinction: “He whom God sent speaks the words of God” [Col. 0789C]? But see what he adds:

{498}

“For God does not give the Spirit by measure.”

Hear the Apostle saying: “According to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Ephesians 4:7). He gives to human beings by measure; to the only-begotten Son he does not give by measure.

How does he give to human beings by measure? “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another prophecy; to another discernment [Augustine: judgment] of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another gifts of healings” (1 Corinthians 12:8). [Augustine: “Are all apostles?”] “Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all possess powers? Do all have gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret?” [Col. 0789D]

One person has one gift, another has another; and what one has, the other does not have. The measure is a certain distribution of gifts.

Thus, measure is given to human beings, and concord there makes one body. Just as the hand receives one function, so that it may work; the eye another, so that it may see; the ear another, so that it may hear; and the foot another [same author: “the eye, the ear, the foot”], so that it may walk—yet the soul is one, acting through everything: in the hand, so that it may work; in the foot, so that it may walk; in the ear, so that it may hear; in the eye, so that it may see—so also there are diverse gifts among the faithful, distributed to each according to his proper measure, as to members. But Christ, who gives, does not receive by measure [Col. 0790A].

**The same author, cited passage, no. 11.** Hear further what follows, since he had said of the Son: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure.”

### VERSE 35

“The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand.”

He added, “and has given all things into his hand,” so that here too you might recognize how distinctly [Augustine: “with what distinction”] it was said: “The Father loves the Son.” Why? Does the Father, then, not love John—and yet he has not given all things into his hand? Does the Father not love Paul—and yet he has not given all things into his hand?

“The Father loves the Son”—but as the Father loves the Son, not as the Lord loves a servant; as he loves the only-begotten, not as he loves an adopted son. Therefore he has given all things into his hand. What does “all things” mean? It means that the Son is as great as the Father. It follows:

## CHAPTER IV

### VERSES 1–3 [Col. 0790B]

“Therefore, when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John—although Jesus himself was not baptizing, but his disciples—he left the land of Judea and went into Galilee.”

**Saint Augustine, Treatise 15 on John, nos. 2–4 [Col. 0790D].** Certainly, if the Lord had known that the Pharisees had learned about him—that he was making more disciples and baptizing more people—in such a way that this knowledge concerned their salvation, namely, that they should follow him, become disciples themselves, and wish to be baptized by him, he would not have left the land of Judea; rather, he would have remained there for their sake. But because he knew their knowledge, he also knew their envy: they had not learned this in order to follow him, but in order to persecute him; therefore he departed.

Certainly, even while present, he could not have been seized by them if he had not wished it, nor killed if he had not wished it—he who could also have chosen not to be born if he had not wished it [Augustine: “because he could”]. But because in everything he did as a human being he offered an example of himself to human beings who would believe in him—for no servant of God sins by withdrawing to another place when he sees the violent rage [Augustine: “perhaps”] of those pursuing him or seeking his life for evil purposes; yet a servant of God might think that he was sinning by doing so unless the Lord had gone before him in doing it—the good teacher did this to teach, not because he was afraid [Col. 0790C].

Perhaps another question may arise: why is it said, “Jesus was baptizing more than John,” and after the statement “he baptizes” there is added, “although Jesus himself was not baptizing, but his disciples” [Manuscript: “was baptizing”]? What then? Was the first statement false and corrected when it was added that Jesus himself was not baptizing, but his disciples? Or are both true, because Jesus both baptized and did not baptize?

He baptized, because he himself cleansed; he did not baptize, because he himself did not immerse. The disciples supplied the ministry of the body; he supplied the assistance of majesty. For when would he cease baptizing who does not cease cleansing—he of whom the same John said, speaking through the person of John the Baptist: “This is he who baptizes”? Therefore Jesus still baptizes; and as long as those who are to be baptized are being baptized, Jesus baptizes [Augustine: “as long as we are to be baptized”]. Let a person approach the lower minister without fear, for he has a higher teacher.

But perhaps someone will say: “Christ baptizes in the Spirit, not in the body.” As though anyone were initiated into the sacrament of bodily and visible baptism by the gift of anyone other than him! Do you wish to know that he himself baptizes not only in the Spirit but also with water? Hear the Apostle: “Christ,” he says {499}, “loved the Church and gave himself for her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word, so that he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind” (Ephesians 5:25).

“Cleansing her”—by what? “By the washing of water in the word.” Take away the water, and there is no baptism. Likewise, if you take away the word, baptism does not take place [Manuscript: “baptism; take away the word, and there is no baptism”] [Col. 0791A].

**“Thus far Augustine.”** It is often asked whether the Holy Spirit was given in this baptism administered by Christ’s disciples, because of the words that occur later in this Gospel, where it is said: “The Holy Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39) [Col. 0791B].

Certainly, the Holy Spirit was given in this baptism administered by Christ’s disciples, although not with that manifestation in which, ten days after Christ’s ascension, he was given in tongues of fire. The fact that God accomplishes some things secretly and others visibly by means of a visible creature belongs to the governance of his wisdom, because all divine actions are carried out with the most beautiful distinction of order according to places and times.

How, then, did the Lord himself have the Holy Spirit with him in the very human nature that he bore when he came to the Jordan to be baptized [Manuscript: “the river”]—and yet, after he had been baptized, the same Holy Spirit was seen descending upon him in the form of a dove? In the same way, we should understand that before the Spirit’s manifest and visible coming, any holy people could have possessed him secretly [Col. 0791C].

We have said this in such a way that we may also understand that, through the visible manifestation of the Holy Spirit—an event called his coming—the fullness of the Spirit was poured into human hearts in an ineffable, indeed inconceivable, manner with greater abundance.

It follows: “He left Judea and went again into Galilee.” What does “he left Judea” mean except that he left the unbelief of those who refused to receive him, and that they rejected the stone which they ought to have built upon? And he went through the apostles into Galilee, that is, into the changing condition of this world, commanding the apostles: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

### VERSE 4 [Col. 0791D]

“For it was necessary for him to pass through Samaria.”

In the reading of the Gospel, the holy evangelist has shown us most fully that the Lord Jesus Christ assumed the weakness of the human race. For after saying that the Lord had come to the city of Samaria called Sychar, near the estate that Jacob gave to his son Joseph—on which estate was Jacob’s well—he added: “Jesus, wearied from the journey, was sitting thus above the well” [Manuscript: “above the cistern”].

## CHAPTER VII

Christ reveals himself to the Samaritan woman at Jacob’s well and speaks many things mystically; and many Samaritans believe in him, saying: “Truly, this is the Savior of the world” [Col. 0792A].

### VERSES 5–6

“Jesus came to a city of Samaria called Sychar, near the estate that Jacob gave to his son Joseph. Jacob’s well was there. Jesus,” he says, “wearied from the journey, was sitting thus above the well.”

He was sitting above the well, that is, above the cistern [which was on the estate that] holy Jacob had left to his son Joseph. I think that this estate was left not so much to Joseph as to Christ, whose figure the holy patriarch Joseph bore—he whom truly the sun worships, the moon worships, and all the stars bless.

The Lord came to this estate so that the Samaritans, who wished to claim for themselves the inheritance of the patriarch of Israel, might recognize their possessor and be converted to Christ, who has become the legitimate heir of the patriarch [Col. 0792B].

The evangelist says: “Jesus, wearied from the journey, was sitting thus above the well” [Manuscript: “above the cistern”]. The mysteries of the Gospel, signified by the words and deeds of our Lord Jesus Christ, are not open to everyone; and some people, interpreting them less carefully and less soberly, often bring destruction instead of salvation and error instead of knowledge of the truth.

Among these is the mystery written here: that the Lord came to Jacob’s well at the sixth hour of the day, sat down exhausted from the journey, asked the Samaritan woman for a drink, and the other things that are said to require examination and discussion in this passage of Scripture.

Regarding this matter, we must first hold firmly {500} to the principle that throughout all the Scriptures we must guard with the utmost vigilance that the exposition of the divine mystery be in accordance with the faith [Col. 0792C].

Our Lord therefore came to the well at the sixth hour. I see in the well a dark depth. I therefore suggest that it be understood as signifying the weak parts of this world, that is, the earthly parts, to which the Lord Jesus came at the sixth hour—that is, in the sixth age of the human race—as though in the old man’s old age. We are commanded to strip off this old man so that we may put on the new man, who was created according to God (Ephesians 4:24).

For the sixth age is old age: the first is infancy, the second childhood, the third adolescence, the fourth youth, and the fifth maturity. The life of the old man, therefore, which is lived according to the flesh under temporal conditions, is brought to an end in the sixth age, that is, in old age. For, as I have said, our Lord, the creator and restorer of the human race, came in the old age of humanity, so that, with the old man dying, he might establish the new man in himself and transfer him, stripped of earthly clay, into the heavenly kingdoms [Col. 0792D].

Thus the well, as has been said, signifies by its dark depth the earthly labor and error of this world. And because the outer man is the old man, while the new man is inward, the Apostle says: “Even if our outer man is being corrupted, the inner man is being renewed day by day.” This is altogether most fitting, since all visible things belong to the outer man, and Christian discipline renounces them.

The Lord came to the well at the sixth hour, that is, at midday, when this visible sun is already beginning to decline toward sunset [Col. 0793A]. So may the inner man, recreated in us who have been called by Christ to love invisible things, return to the inner light that never sets, according to the apostolic discipline—not seeking the things that are seen, but the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal.

That he came wearied to the well signifies the weakness of the flesh; that he sat signifies humility. For he assumed the weakness of the flesh for us, and he deigned to appear as a human being to human beings with such humility.

Concerning this weakness of the flesh the Prophet says: “A man placed in affliction and knowing how to bear weakness”; concerning humility the Apostle speaks, saying: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Philippians 2:8).

Yet the fact that he sat—since teachers are accustomed to sit—can also be understood in another way, not as indicating the modesty of humility but the person of a teacher [Col. 0793B].

But one may ask why he asked the Samaritan woman, who had come to draw water, for a drink, since he later proclaimed that he himself could give the abundance of a spiritual fountain to those who asked him.

Clearly, God thirsted for the faith of that woman, because she was a Samaritan, and Samaria commonly represents the image of idolatry. For they, separated from the Jewish people, had brought disgrace upon their souls through images of mute animals, that is, golden calves [Manuscript: “they had assigned honor”].

Our Lord Jesus had come to lead the multitude of the nations, which had served images, to the stronghold of Christian faith and incorrupt religion. For he says: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” [Col. 0793C]. Therefore he thirsts for the faith of those for whom he shed his blood.

### VERSE 7

“Jesus therefore said to her: Woman, give me a drink.”

And so that you may know what our Lord thirsted for, shortly afterward his disciples came. They had gone into the city to buy food, and they said to him: “Rabbi, eat.” But he said to them: “I have another food to eat, which you do not know.”

His disciples therefore said to one another: “Has someone brought him something to eat?” Jesus said to them: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work.”
