Can any other will of the Father who sent him, and any other work which he said he wished to complete, be understood here except that he should convert us from the destructive error of the world to faith in him?

Therefore, as his food is, so also is his drink. For this reason he thirsted in that woman: to do the Father’s will in her and to complete his work.

But she, understanding him in a carnal way, replied [Col. 0793D]:

### VERSE 9

“You, though you are a Jew, how can you ask me for a drink, since I am a Samaritan woman?” For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.

Our Lord said to her:

### VERSE 10

“If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would rather have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”

By this he showed her that he had not asked for the kind of {501} water that she had understood, but that, because he himself thirsted for her faith, he desired to give the Holy Spirit to her in her thirst [Col. 0794A].

We rightly understand this living water to be the gift of God, as he himself says: “If you knew the gift of God”; and as the same John testifies elsewhere, saying: “Jesus stood and cried out: ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come [to me] and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly’” (John 8:37–38).

Entirely fittingly he says, “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly,” because we first believe in order to become worthy of these gifts. These rivers of living water, therefore, which he wished to give that woman, are the reward of the faith for which he first thirsted.

He then adds the interpretation of this living water: “He said this,” he says, “about the Spirit whom those who were to believe in him would receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” [Col. 0794B].

This gift, then, is the Holy Spirit, whom he gave to the Church after his glorification, as another Scripture says: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings” (Ephesians 4:8).

But the woman still thinks in a carnal way. For she replied:

### VERSES 11–12

“Lord, you do not even have a drawing-vessel, and the well is deep. From where, then, do you have living water to give me? Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well and drank from it himself, along with his sons and his livestock?”

Now the Lord explains what he had said:

### VERSES 13–14

“Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again. But whoever drinks from the water that I will give will never thirst forever. Rather, the water that I will give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” [Col. 0794C].

But the woman still embraces the wisdom of the flesh. What did she reply?

### VERSES 15–16

“Lord, give me this water, so that I may neither thirst nor come here to draw water.”

Jesus said to her: “Go, call your husband, and come here.”

Since he knew that she had no husband, the question is why he said this. For when the woman said, “I have no husband,” Jesus said to her:

### VERSE 18

“You have spoken well in saying, ‘I have no husband.’ For you have had five husbands, and the one whom you now have is not your husband. You have truly said this” [Manuscript: “You have spoken the truth”].

But these matters must not be understood carnally, lest we appear to be like this same Samaritan woman. Rather, if we have already tasted something of that gift of God, let us treat these matters spiritually.

**See Saint Ambrose, On Luke, chapters 14 and 20 [Col. 0794D].** Some understand the five husbands to be the five books that were administered through Moses. They understand the statement, “And the one whom you now have is not your husband,” as spoken by the Lord about himself, so that its meaning is: “At first you served the five books of Moses as though they were five husbands; but now the one whom you have—that is, the one whom you hear—is not your husband, because you have not yet believed in him.”

But since, before believing in Christ, she was certainly still held by the union of those five husbands, that is, the five books, it may be asked how it could be said, “You have had five husbands,” as though she no longer had them, when she was still living subject to them.

Furthermore, since the five books of Moses proclaim nothing other than Christ—as he himself says: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46)—how can it be understood that a person withdraws from those five books in order to pass over to Christ, when the person who believes in Christ does not abandon those five books but embraces them much more blessedly through spiritual understanding [Col. 0795A]?

**See Saint Augustine, Treatise 15, no. 21 [Col. 0795D].** There is therefore another interpretation: the five husbands may be understood as the five bodily senses.

The first belongs to the eyes, by which we see this visible light and the various colors and forms of bodies. The second belongs to the ears, by which we perceive the movements of voices and every kind of sound. The third belongs to the nostrils, by which we delight in the various fragrances of odors. The fourth is taste in the mouth, which perceives sweet and bitter and examines every kind of flavor. The fifth, extending throughout the body by touch, distinguishes hot and cold, soft and hard, smooth and rough, and everything else that we perceive by touch [Col. 0795B].

The first five ages of human life are therefore imbued with these bodily senses, by the necessity of our mortal nature. After the sin of the first human being we were born in such a way that, before the light of the mind had been restored, we passed through carnal life subject to bodily senses and without any understanding of the truth.

Infants and very young children must necessarily be like this, since they are not yet able to receive reason. And because these senses are natural, govern the first age, and have been bestowed upon us by God the creator, they are rightly called “men,” that is, husbands {502}, as though they were legitimate. Nature contributed them not through the fault of error, but through the workmanship of God [Col. 0795C].

When a person reaches the age at which life can become capable of reason, if he is immediately able to grasp the truth, he no longer uses those senses as rulers. Rather, he will have a rational spirit as his husband, reducing those senses to service and subjecting his body to servitude.

The soul is no longer subject to five men, that is, the five bodily senses; instead, it has the divine Word as its legitimate husband. Joined and clinging to him, and with the human spirit itself clinging to Christ—for “Christ is the head of man” (1 Corinthians 11:3)—it embraces spiritual things and enjoys eternal life without fear of separation. For who could separate us from the love of Christ? (Romans 8:35).

But because that woman was held by error, signifying the multitude of the world subjected to empty superstitions [Manuscript: “to be subjected”], after those five periods of the bodily senses by which, as we have said, the first age is governed, the Word of God had not taken her in marriage; rather, the devil held her in an adulterous embrace [Col. 0795D].

Therefore the Lord, seeing that she was carnal—that is, thinking carnally—said to her: “Go, call your husband, and come here.” That is: “Remove yourself from the carnal affection in which you are now established, because you cannot understand what I am saying. And call your husband”—that is, “Be present in spirit and understanding.”

For the spirit of a human being is, in a certain sense, the husband of the soul; it governs the animal affection as a spouse. This is not the Holy Spirit, who is given unchangeably with the Father and the Son, but the spirit of the human being, of whom the Apostle says: “No one knows what is in a person except the spirit of the person.” For the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of God, of whom he says again: “So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” [Col. 0796A].

When this human spirit is present—that is, attentive and submitting itself to God in reverence—the human being understands what is said spiritually. But when the devil’s error dominates the soul, as though understanding were absent, it is an adulterer.

“Call,” he says, “your husband”—that is, the spirit that is in you, by which a human being can understand spiritual things if the light of truth illumines it. Let it be present when I speak to you, so that you may receive spiritual water.

And when she said, “I have no husband,” he said, “You have spoken well. For you have had five husbands”—that is, the five senses of the flesh ruled you in your first age—“and the one whom you now have is not your husband,” because you do not possess within yourself a spirit that understands God, with whom you could have a legitimate marriage. Rather, the devil’s error dominates you and corrupts you with adulterous contamination [Col. 0796B].

Perhaps, in order to indicate to those who understand that the five bodily senses are signified by the name of five husbands, the woman names Christ in her sixth response, after five carnal responses.

Her first response was: “Although you are a Jew, how can you ask me for a drink?” The second: “Lord, you do not have anything with which to draw, and the well is deep.” The third: “Lord, give me this water, so that I may neither thirst nor come here to draw.” The fourth: “I have no husband.” The fifth: “I see that you are a prophet. Our fathers worshiped on this mountain.”

For this response is carnal: a physical earthly place had been given to carnal people in which they should pray. But the Lord had said that spiritual people would worship in spirit and truth [Col. 0796C].

After he had spoken, the woman’s sixth response confesses that Christ is the teacher of all these things. For she says: “I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ. When he comes, he will announce everything to us.”

But she is still in error, because she does not see that the one whose coming she hopes for has already come. Nevertheless, by the Lord’s mercy this error is now expelled like an adulterer. For Jesus says to her:

“I am he, the one speaking with you.”

After hearing this, she did not reply. Instead, immediately leaving her water jar, she hurried into the city, so that she might not only believe the gospel and the Lord’s coming but also proclaim it.

Nor should the fact that she left her water jar and departed be passed over carelessly. The water jar perhaps signifies the love of this world, that is, desire, by which people draw pleasure for themselves from the dark depth whose image is borne by the well—that is, from earthly conduct. After experiencing this pleasure, they burn again with desire for it, just as one who drinks that water will thirst again.

It was necessary that, by believing in Christ, she renounce the world; and by leaving the water jar behind, she should show that she had abandoned worldly desire {503}—not only believing in her heart for righteousness, but also confessing with her mouth for salvation and proclaiming what she had believed [Col. 0797A].

### VERSE 19

The woman said to him: “Lord, I see that you are a prophet.”

**Saint Augustine, cited passage, nos. 23–24 [Col. 0797D].** The husband began to come, but he had not yet come fully. She thought the Lord was a prophet. Indeed, he was also a prophet, for he said of himself: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (Luke 4:24).

It was also said of him to Moses: “I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like you” (Deuteronomy 18:18)—like him in the form of the flesh, not in the eminence of majesty.

Thus we find that the Lord Jesus was called a prophet. Therefore this woman was no longer greatly in error when she said: “I see that you are a prophet.” She began to exclude the adulterous husband when she said, “I see that you are a prophet,” and she began to seek what had usually troubled her.

There had been a dispute between the Samaritans and the Jews. The Jews worshiped God in the temple built by Solomon; the Samaritans, living far away, did not worship in it. The Jews rejoiced that they were superior because they worshiped God in the temple [Col. 0797B].

The Samaritans said to them: “Why do you boast—and therefore declare yourselves better than us—because you have a temple that we do not have? Did our fathers, who pleased God, worship in that temple? Did they not worship on this mountain, where we are? We therefore pray to God more rightly on this mountain, where our fathers prayed.”

Both groups contended in ignorance. Since neither had a husband, the one group became inflamed against the other on behalf of the temple, the other on behalf of the mountain [Manuscript and Augustine: “were puffed up against one another”].

What, then, does the Lord now teach the woman, as though her husband had begun to be present? The woman says to him: “Lord, I see that you are a prophet” [Col. 0797C].

### VERSES 20–21

“Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, and you say that Jerusalem is the place where one must worship.”

Jesus said to her: “Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.”

The Church will come, as it is said in the Song of Songs:

“My beloved speaks to me:

‘Arise, hasten, my beloved,  
my bride, my dove, my undefiled one, and come.  
For now the winter has passed;  
the rain has gone and departed;  
the flowers have appeared on the earth;  
the time of pruning has come;  
the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land’”

(Song of Songs 2:10, 12).

Rightly, now that her husband is present, she hears: “Woman, believe me.” For there is already within you one who believes, because your husband is present. You began to be present in understanding when you called me a prophet [Col. 0797D].

“Woman, believe me,” because “unless you believe, you will not understand.” Therefore, woman, believe me: “the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.”

### VERSES 22–23

“You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, because salvation is from the Jews.

But the hour is coming [when?]—and now is [what hour, then?]—when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. Not on this mountain, not in the temple, but in spirit and truth.”

### VERSE 24 [Col. 0798A]

“God is spirit. If God were corporeal, he ought to be worshiped on a mountain, because a mountain is corporeal; he ought to be worshiped in a temple, because a temple is corporeal. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit.

We worship what we know; you worship what you do not know, because salvation is from the Jews.”

**Same passage, nos. 26–33 [Col. 0798D].** He gave much to the Jews; but do not understand these as the rejected Jews. Understand that wall to which another wall has been joined, so that the two might be united in peace in the cornerstone, which is Christ.

One wall was from the Jews, one from the Gentiles. These walls were far apart from one another until they were joined at the corner [variant: “in Christ”]. The Gentiles were foreigners and strangers, outsiders to the covenant [Manuscript: “covenants”] of God [Col. 0798B].

Accordingly, the statement “We worship what we know” was spoken from the perspective of the Jews, but not of all Jews and not of the rejected Jews. It was spoken of those such as the apostles were, such as the prophets were, and such as all those holy people were who sold all their possessions and placed the proceeds of their property at the apostles’ feet (Acts 4:34).

For God did not reject his people whom he foreknew.

The woman heard this and added to it. A little earlier she had called him a prophet; now she saw him, the one with whom she was speaking, saying other things [Augustine: “such things”], and that he was even more than a prophet. And observe what she answered:

The woman said: “I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ. When he comes, he will announce everything to us.”

What does this mean? “At present,” she says, “the Jews are contending about the temple, and we are {504} contending about the mountain. When he comes, he will reject the mountain and overturn the temple. He will teach us everything, so that we may know that we must worship in spirit and truth” [Manuscript: “so that we must worship in spirit and truth”] [Col. 0798C].

She knew who could teach her, but she did not yet recognize him as the one teaching. She was therefore already worthy that he should reveal himself to her.

“Messiah” means “anointed”; for the anointed one is called *Christus* in Greek and *Messias* in Hebrew. Therefore the woman says to him:

### VERSE 25

“I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ. When he comes, he will announce everything to us.”

### VERSE 26

Jesus said to her: “I am he, the one speaking with you.”

He called her husband; the man became the head of the woman; Christ became the head of the man. The woman is now being ordered in faith and governed so that she may live well [variant: “lead her life well”].

After she heard, “I am he, the one speaking with you,” what more could she say, when Christ the Lord wished to reveal himself to the woman to whom he had said, “Believe me”?

### VERSE 27 [Col. 0798D]

“And immediately his disciples came, and they were amazed that he was speaking with a woman.”

They were amazed because the one who had come to seek what was lost was seeking the lost woman. They marveled at something good; they did not suspect anything evil.

Yet no one said: “What are you seeking?” or “Why are you speaking with her?”

The woman therefore left her water jar and went into the city. After hearing, “I am he, the one speaking with you,” and receiving Christ the Lord into her heart, what could she do except now abandon her water jar and run to evangelize?

She cast away desire and hastened to announce the truth. Let those who wish to evangelize learn: let them cast the water jar down beside the well. Recall what I said above about the water jar [Col. 0799A].

The water jar was a vessel from which water was drawn. It is called *hydria* in Greek, because in Greek “water” is called ὕδωρ (*hydōr*), as though one were to say “water-vessel.”

She therefore cast away the water jar, which was no longer useful but had become a burden. For she eagerly desired to be satisfied with that water. In order to announce Christ, she threw off the burden, ran into the city, and said to those people:

### VERSE 29

“Come and see a man who told me everything I have ever done. Could this be the Christ?”

She cast away the water jar, went away, and gradually announced him to the city, lest they should immediately become angry, resentful, and persecute her. For she said: “Come and see a man who told me everything I have ever done. Could this be the Christ?”

### Verses 30, 33

They went out of the city and were coming to him, and the disciples were asking him, saying: “Rabbi, eat.” For they had gone to buy food and had returned. But he said to them: “I have food to eat of which you do not know.”

The disciples therefore said to one another: “Could someone have brought him something to eat?” What wonder is it if that woman did not understand the water? Behold, the disciples still do not understand the food.

But he heard their thoughts and now instructs them as a teacher—not indirectly, as he had instructed the woman who was still seeking her husband, but Jesus now says openly to them:

### Verse 34

“My food,” he said, “is to do the will of him who sent me.”

Therefore that drink was also present in the woman, so that she might do the will of him who sent him. For this reason he said: “I thirst; give me something to drink”—namely, so that he might produce faith in her, drink her faith, and transfer her into his body; for his body is the Church.

### Verse 35

“Therefore,” he said, “my food is to do the will of him who sent me. Do you not say that there are still four months and the harvest [will come]?”

He was fervently engaged in the work and was preparing to send laborers. You reckon four months until the harvest; I show you another harvest, white and ready. Behold, I tell you: lift up your eyes and see that the fields are already white for harvest.

Therefore he is about to send reapers [Ms.: “I am about to send”]. For in this the saying is true: one is he who reaps, and another he who sows, so that the one who sows may rejoice together with the one who reaps.

### Verse 38

“I sent you to reap what you did not labor for. Others labored, and you entered into their labor.”

What, then? He sent reapers, not sowers. Where were the reapers sent? Where others had already labored. For where labor had already been done, certainly sowing had taken place; and what had been sown, having now matured, required the sickle and the threshing floor.

Where, then, were the reapers to be sent? Where the prophets had already preached—for they were the sowers. For if they were not sowers but reapers, how had the woman come to say: “I know that the Messiah is coming”?

That woman was already a mature fruit, and the harvests were white and were seeking the sickle. “I sent you”—where? “To reap what you did not sow: others sowed, and you entered into their labors.”

Who labored? Abraham himself, Isaac, and Jacob. Read their labors: in all their labors there is prophecy of Christ; and therefore they were sowers.

Moses and the other patriarchs, and all the prophets—how much they endured in that cold season when they were sowing! Therefore the harvest was already prepared in Judea. Rightly, it was like a ripe crop there when many thousands of people were bringing the proceeds of their possessions and, laying them at the apostles’ feet, with their shoulders freed from worldly burdens, were following the Lord Christ (Acts 4:35). Truly a ripe harvest!

What came of it? From that very harvest a few grains were cast out and sowed throughout the world, and another harvest arose, which is to be reaped at the end of the age. Of that harvest it is said: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psalm 125:5).

To this harvest, then, it is not apostles but angels who are sent. “The reapers,” he says, “are angels” (Matthew 13:39). This harvest therefore grows among the weeds and awaits purification in faith.

That harvest, then, was already ripe—the harvest to which the disciples were first sent, where the prophets had labored. Nevertheless, brothers, observe what is said: “So that the one who sows and the one who reaps may rejoice together.” They had labors belonging to different times, but they will enjoy the same joy; together they will receive the reward, eternal life.

### Verses 39–42

Many from that city believed in him because of the woman’s word, as she bore witness: “He told me everything I have done.”

When the Samaritans had come to him, they asked him to remain with them; and he stayed there two days, and many more believed because of his words. And they were saying to the woman: “We no longer believe because of what you said; for we ourselves have heard and know that this man is truly the Savior of the world.”

This too should be observed briefly, since the reading has come to an end. The woman first announced him, and at the woman’s testimony the Samaritans believed and asked him to remain with them. He stayed there two days, and more believed. And when they had believed, they said to the woman: “We no longer believe because of your word, but we ourselves have come to know and know that this man is truly the Savior of the world.”

First through report, afterward through presence. This is what happens today with those who are outside and are not yet Christians. Christ is announced through Christian friends; as through that woman—that is, through the Church announcing him—they come to Christ. They believe through this report; he remains with them for two days—that is, he gives them the two commandments of charity—and many more believe in him more firmly, because he truly is the Savior of the world.

[Col. 0799D] Thus far from Saint Augustine.

### Verses 43–44

After the two days he departed from there and went into Galilee. For Jesus himself testified that a prophet has no honor in his own country.

Having confirmed the Samaritans—that is, the Gentiles—in faith and charity, he returns in the last days of this age to his homeland, in which he had not yet received honor. Of it he himself testifies in this passage: “A prophet has no honor in his own country.”

In his homeland he performed miracles, and they did not believe in him; in Samaria he performed none, yet they believed, moved by the testimony of a single woman. The world believed, moved by the preaching of the apostolic Church, which is one dove; but in his earthly homeland, even when Christ himself preached, only a few believed.

This is also what he says elsewhere in the same [Ms.: “this”] Gospel: “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these” (John 14:12).

The greater works were the faith of the whole world through apostolic preaching, greater than that effected by Christ; for in Judea he saved very few—so very few that nearly all his disciples, apart from the Twelve, abandoned him, as it is said: “From that time many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him” (John 6:67).

### Verse 45

When he had therefore come into Galilee, the Galileans received him, having seen everything that he had done in Jerusalem at the feast; for they too had gone up to the feast—perhaps moved by curiosity about the miracles, not by a desire to hear the preaching.

### Verse 46

Jesus therefore came again to Cana of Galilee, where he had made water into wine.

It is as though he were saying: Although the house was full of those reclining at table, where Christ performed the miracle in their presence, nevertheless few believed in him, as the evangelist says: “And his disciples believed in him.”

Perhaps this was said to the shame of his fellow citizens and to the praise of foreigners; for the Galileans were Christ’s fellow citizens, while the Samaritans were foreigners, as is read in sacred history.

{506}

## Chapter VIII

### The Son of a Certain Royal Official, Sick in the Lord’s Absence, Is Healed by His Word

[Col. 0801C]

### Verse 46

There was a certain royal official whose son was ill at Capernaum.

“Royal official” is a diminutive name derived from “king”; and perhaps this man is called a royal official because he asked for health for his son without possessing complete faith. He had faith and did not have faith; therefore he heard:

### Verse 48

“Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.”

[Col. 0801D] From Saint Gregory, Homily 28, nos. 1–2.

The man who was seeking health for his son undoubtedly believed; for he would not have sought health from one whom he did not believe to be the Savior. Why, then, is it said, “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe,” when he believed before seeing the sign?

But remember what he asked, and you will clearly recognize that he doubted in faith. For he asked him to come down and heal his son. He was therefore seeking the Lord’s bodily presence, though the Lord was nowhere absent in spirit.

He therefore believed less in him, since he thought that he could not give health unless he were present bodily. For if he had believed perfectly, he would undoubtedly have known that there was no place where God was not.

He therefore distrusted [Ms.: “doubted”] to a considerable extent, because he did not honor majesty but bodily presence. Thus he both asked health for his son and nevertheless doubted in faith: he believed that the one to whom he had come was powerful enough to heal, yet he thought that God was absent from his dying son [Gregory omits “God”].

But the Lord, who is asked to go because he is not absent from the place where he is invited, indicates this: by a mere command he restored health, he who by his will created all things.

In this matter we must observe attentively that, as we learn from the testimony of another evangelist, a centurion came to the Lord saying: “Lord, my servant is lying paralyzed in the house and is suffering terribly.” Jesus immediately answered him: “I will come and heal him” (Matthew 8:6–7).

What does it mean that the royal official asks him to come to his son, and yet he refuses to go bodily, whereas the centurion does not invite him to his servant and yet he promises to go bodily? He does not deem it fitting to be bodily present with the royal official’s son, while he does not disdain to go to the centurion’s servant.

What does this mean except that our pride is rebuked? We honor in human beings not the nature by which they were made in the image of God, but honors and riches. And when we consider what surrounds them, we utterly fail to see their interior reality. While we consider what is despised in their bodies, we neglect to consider what they are.

Our Redeemer, therefore, to show that what is exalted among human beings is to be despised by the saints, and that what is despised among human beings is not to be despised by the saints, did not wish to go to the royal official’s son but was ready to go to the centurion’s servant.

Our pride, then, was rebuked—a pride that does not know how to value human beings for their humanity. It values only what surrounds human beings; it does not look upon their nature and does not recognize the honor of God in human beings.

Behold, the Son of God does not wish to go to the royal official’s son, and yet he is ready to come for the salvation of the servant—

[Col. 0802D] Thus far from Saint Gregory.

This is what the Apostle says: “God chose the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27).

### Verses 50–52

The man believed the word that Jesus had spoken to him, and he went away.

He was beginning already to have faith in Jesus’ word, and therefore he merited the healing of his son. The man who had come partly doubtful departed faithful, and therefore he merited the healing of his son.

As he was now going down, his servants met him, announcing that his son was alive. He therefore asked them at what hour he had begun to improve. They said to him: “Yesterday, at the seventh hour, the fever left him.”

The number seven is sanctified in the gifts of the Holy Spirit. In it the health of all believers is established, because in the Holy Spirit, who is the gift of God, there is forgiveness of all sins for believers.

The number seven, moreover, when divided into three and four, signifies the holy Trinity in the number three and the perfection of all creatures in the number four—because of the four complete [Ms.: “full”] elements, the four regions of the world, and the four seasons of the year. All these things were created from him, through him, and in him; they subsist and are governed, just as “in him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28).

{507}

### Verse 53

The father therefore knew that it was the hour at which Jesus had said to him: “Your son lives.” And he himself believed, and his entire household, because the announcement had been made to him that his son was well.

Thus many Samaritans believed at the mere word, but at that miracle only that household believed. This fact foreshadows the faith of the Gentiles in the multitude and the faith of the Jews in the few.

The Gentiles believed through the word alone—that is, through apostolic preaching; but the Jews saw the Son of God himself performing signs, and nevertheless only a few of them believed.

## Book Three

[Col. 0803A]

The delight [Bed.: “love”] of the divine utterances and the sweetness of understanding Holy Scripture—and especially of the humble truth of the Gospel, in which an honorable simplicity of words is open and a profound depth of meanings lies hidden—encourage us to speak and you to listen, with the Lord himself helping, who gives sweetness so that our land may yield its fruit.

Would that the power of our understanding in speaking were as effective as the diligence given to you in your eagerness [Ms.: “eagerly”] to listen! I see you listening without weariness, and I rejoice in the palate of your heart, which does not reject what is wholesome but receives it eagerly and retains it profitably.

Let us therefore speak to you now also about the Gospel reading in which two miracles of human healing are read together: one invisibly accomplished through angelic ministry, the other visibly exhibited through the Lord’s presence.

The mysteries of both must be explained briefly, lest a lengthy explanation of a lengthy reading perhaps become burdensome to anyone.

## Chapter IX

### Jesus Healed on the Sabbath a Man Who Had Been Ill for Thirty-Eight Years, Saying, “Take Up Your Pallet and Walk,” Thereby Making Himself Equal to God

[Col. 0803C]

## Chapter V

### Verses 1–4

After this there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Now there is in Jerusalem a pool called in Hebrew Bethesda, having five porticoes. In these lay a great multitude of the sick, the blind, the lame, and the withered, waiting for the movement of the water.

For an angel of the Lord descended into the pool at a certain time, and the water was stirred. And whoever descended first into the pool after the stirring of the water became well from whatever illness afflicted him.”

[Col. 0803D] From Bede’s Homily 7.

The pool surrounded by five porticoes is the Jewish people, fortified on every side by the guardianship of the Law so that they ought not to sin. For rightly the Law, which is described in the five books of Moses, is represented by the number five.

Rightly, too, the people—who were accustomed in some respects to preserve purity of life but in others to be troubled by the temptations of unclean spirits—are signified by the water of the pool, which was accustomed at one time to stand peacefully in the wind and at another to be disturbed when the winds rushed upon it.

The same pool is appropriately called *probatica*; for in Greek, “sheep” are called *probata*. There were clearly among that people those who knew how to say to the Lord: “But we are your people and the sheep of your pasture; we will give you thanks forever” (Psalm 78:13).

In common usage, however, it is said to have been called *probatica*, that is, the “animal pool,” because the priests were accustomed to wash sacrifices in it.

The multitude of the sick lying in the porticoes just mentioned, awaiting the movement of the water, signifies the crowds of those who, hearing the words of the Law, lamented that they could not fulfill it by their own strength, and therefore implored the help of the Lord’s grace with the full longing of their souls.

They were blind who did not yet possess the perfect light of faith. They were lame who could not fulfill through the steps of their actions the good things they knew. They were withered who, although they possessed some measure of the eye of knowledge, nevertheless lacked the richness of hope and love.

Such people lay in the five porticoes, but they were not healed except when the angel came into the pool; for through the Law came knowledge of sin, but the grace of remission came only through Jesus Christ (Romans 3:21 ff.).

The angel signifies him: descending invisibly into the pool, he stirred the water to suggest its healing power. For the angel of great counsel, clothed in flesh (Isaiah 9:6)—that is, the messenger of the Father’s will—descended into the Jewish people and moved sinners by his deeds and teaching, so that he himself might be killed, though by his bodily death he was able not only to heal those spiritually sick but also to give life to the dead.

The movement of the water therefore signifies the Lord’s Passion, through which, when the Jewish people were stirred, a tumult arose. Since, through that same Passion, believers were redeemed from the curse of the Law, those who had until then lain sick in the porticoes were healed as though by descending into the troubled water of the pool.

The letter of the Law taught those who did not know what ought to be done and what ought to be avoided, but it did not help those who had been taught to fulfill its decrees. Like people brought out from their former dwelling places of ignorance, it held them within its porticoes, but it did not heal the sick.

The grace of the Gospel, however, which through faith and the mystery of the Lord’s Passion heals all the diseases of our iniquities—diseases from which we could not be justified by the Law of Moses—brings the sick, chosen from the porticoes of the Law, into the troubled water of the pool so that they may be healed.

For through the water of baptism it washes away the sins that the Law had revealed, as the Apostle testifies: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:3).

It is rightly said that whoever descended first after the movement of the water was healed from whatever illness afflicted him, because there is “one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God” (Ephesians 4:5).

Whoever is instructed in the mysteries of Christ within Catholic unity is healed from whatever sickness of sins held him; but whoever separates himself from unity cannot attain the salvation that comes from the One.

Having spoken to your fraternity about the first miracle of the Gospel reading, which the Lord performed, let us now speak about the second, which he also performed. In this second miracle, too, only one man is commended as healed—not because the omnipotent mercy of the Savior was unable to heal all whom it found lying sick there, but so that it might teach that, apart from the unity of the Catholic faith, no place of salvation is open to anyone.

### Verse 5

“But there was a certain man there,” he says, “who had been in his illness for thirty-eight years.”

This man, held by an illness of many years, signifies any sinner weighed down by the enormity or multitude of his crimes. The period of time during which he languished corresponds appropriately to the guilt signified by him.

For he had been ill for thirty-eight years. The number forty, which is formed by multiplying ten by four, is usually taken in Scripture to signify the perfection of right conduct. Whoever has practiced perfect conduct fulfills the Law’s Decalogue through the four books of the Holy Gospel.

The man who walks empty of the love of God and neighbor—which the Scripture of both Law and Gospel commends—falls short of that perfection by two.

The Lord also taught this mystically when, healing the sick man, he said:

### Verse 8

“Rise, take up your pallet, and walk.”

“Rise” means: shake off the sluggishness of the vices in which you have long languished, and raise yourself for the exercise of the virtues by which you may be saved forever.

“Take up your pallet”—that is, carry it. Do you love your neighbor? Carry him patiently by bearing with his weaknesses.

[Bede and Ms.: “Take up your pallet; carry your neighbor, loving him, patiently bearing with his weaknesses, the one who…”]

The one who patiently and for a long time sustained you, still weighed down by the burden of temptations. “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). And as it is said elsewhere: “Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:2).

“Walk,” however: love God with your whole heart, your whole soul, and your whole strength. And, so that you may deserve to reach the vision of him, advance daily from virtue to virtue by the steps of good works.

Do not abandon the brother whom, by bearing with him, you lead for love of the one toward whom you are journeying; nor, for love of your brother, turn aside from the purpose of your right progress by seeking the one with whom you desire to remain.

Rather, so that you may be saved perfectly, rise, take up your pallet, and walk—that is, abandon your former sins, assist your brothers in their needs, and in all that you do, take care not to fix your mind in this age, but hasten to see the face of your Redeemer.

Rise by doing good; carry your pallet by loving your neighbor; and walk by awaiting the blessed hope and the appearance of the glory of the great God (Titus 2:13).

But what astonishing madness of the unbelieving! They ought to have believed and to have been spiritually healed at the unexpected healing of one who had long been sick; instead, they are scandalized and bring accusations both against the man who was saved and against the Savior.

Against the man who was saved, because he had carried his pallet on the Sabbath; against the Savior, because he had commanded him to be saved on the Sabbath and to take up his pallet—as though he himself knew the Sabbath day better than such great divine power.

### Verse 10

“The Jews,” he says, “were saying to the man who had been healed [Ms.: ‘who had been made well’]: ‘It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to take up your pallet.’”

They foolishly defended the letter of the Law, ignorant of the dispensation of the one who had once decreed the Law’s ordinances through a servant and who, now coming himself, had determined to change that same Law by grace, so that what carnal people had long observed carnally according to the letter, spiritual people might thereafter recognize as something to be observed spiritually.

On the carnal Sabbath, which was kept according to the letter, the people were commanded to abstain from every servile work on the seventh day. The spiritual Sabbath, however, consists in the light of spiritual grace, which is understood as sevenfold; for we ought to remain free from the restlessness of vices not on one day only but on every day.

For if, according to the Lord’s saying, “everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34), it is perfectly clear that sins are rightly understood as servile works. From these we are commanded to walk free, as though on the seventh day, through the reception [Bede: “perception”] of spiritual grace—not only to abstain from evil but also to persist in good works.

The Lord showed this typologically in this reading as well when he commanded the man who had been ill for thirty-eight years on the Sabbath not only to rise but also to take up his pallet and walk.

He was indicating, namely, that those who waste away in the long sickness of vices, empty of the love of God and neighbor and therefore two short of the complete sum of virtue, can already rise from their vices through the gift of the Holy Spirit; and, once their sluggishness has been shaken off, they ought to hasten toward the vision of their Creator by bearing the burden of brotherly love.

For it follows:

### Verse 14

Afterward Jesus found him in the temple and said to him: “Behold, you have been healed; now do not sin anymore, lest something worse happen to you.”

The fact that the man who had been healed recognized Jesus in the temple—not while he was still in the crowd but afterward—teaches us mystically that, if we truly desire to recognize the grace of our Creator, to be strengthened by his love, and to reach his vision, we must carefully flee the crowd.

This means not only the crowd of evil thoughts and affections that trouble us, but also wicked people who can obstruct the purpose of our sincerity, either by showing evil through their example, or by ridiculing, or even by prohibiting, our good works.

Let us diligently flee to the house of prayer, where, invoking the Lord in secret freedom, we may give thanks for the benefits received from him and pray with humble devotion for their reception [Ms. and Bede: “for those yet to be received”].

Indeed, let us take care to be ourselves a holy temple of God, in which he may deign to come and make his dwelling, hearing the Apostle: “Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you” (1 Corinthians 6:19).

Among these matters, my brothers, we must observe especially that, when the Lord found in the temple the man whom he had healed, he said to him: “Behold, you have been healed; now do not sin anymore, lest something worse happen to you.”

These words clearly show that he had been ill because of sins and could not be healed except after those sins had been forgiven; but the one whom he healed outwardly from illness, he also saved inwardly from crime. Hence he carefully warned him not to incur the sentence of a heavier condemnation by sinning again.

This must not be understood as though everyone who becomes ill becomes ill because of sins.”

Often a person becomes ill so that he may not become proud of God’s gifts, as we read concerning the Apostle Paul (2 Corinthians 12:7). Often he is afflicted so that he may be tested, as blessed Job’s patience was afflicted and tested. Often illness is given as chastisement, as in the saying: “God scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6). To some, however, illness is given for the glory of God, as is read concerning the man born blind or concerning Lazarus.

The Lord knows why he commands anyone to be ill or permits it; this is often hidden from human judgment, but it is never unjust.

“Thus let us learn humbly to submit to the scourges of our most merciful Redeemer, judging that we suffer less than we deserve, always mindful of that saying: ‘Blessed is the man whom the Lord reproves’” (Job 5:17).

And he himself says in the Apocalypse: “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline” (Revelation 3:19).

But while the man who had long been ill was healed inwardly and outwardly—that is, rescued both from the scourges of manifest chastisement and from the sins by which he had deserved them—the Jews, sick inwardly in the opposite way, began to suffer a worse illness by persecuting Jesus, who had done this on the Sabbath.

They persecuted him as though they were following both the authority of the Law and the examples of divine action. For the Lord completed the creation of the world in six days and rested on the seventh from all his works [Bede: “rested”]; and he commanded the people to work for six days and rest on the seventh.

They did not understand that the carnal decrees of the Law were gradually to be changed by spiritual interpretation, when he appeared who is not only the Lawgiver but also the end of the Law, Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10:4).

Nor did they observe that the Creator, on the seventh day, ceased not from the work of governing the world and from the annual—or rather daily [Ms.: “daily…”—the continuation is uncertain]—replacement of created things, but from the institution of a new creation.

[Col. 0807D] Here Bede, with Alcuin apparently not contradicting him, seems plainly to deny the daily creation of souls; a little later he explains this more clearly in these words: “Not by instituting a new kind of creature, but by propagating what he had created from the beginning, so that they might not perish.”

[Col. 0808D] Martene.

What is said—that God rested on the seventh day from all his works—is therefore to be understood as meaning that God ceased from the creation of new creatures.

But what does Truth itself say here?

### Verse 17

“My Father is working until now, and I am working.”

The Father and the Son are working so that the diversity of the natures created in the world’s first formation may continue. Therefore it is said in the Psalm: “He formed their hearts one by one” (Psalm 32:15). He does not create unknown kinds of souls, but reforms souls of the same substance that was created in the first man.”

[Col. 0808D] From the same homily of Bede.

Therefore, since the Psalmist referred not only the primordial creation of the world but also the daily governance of creation to the praise of the Creator, he said among other things: “You made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 103:24).

If we rightly confess Christ as the power of God and the wisdom of God, and if God made and governs all things in wisdom, it is certainly established that the Father is working until now, and the Son is working as well.

Therefore, he says, “My Father”—not only did he work, as you think, during the first six days, but he is working until now—not by instituting a new kind of creature, but by propagating what he created in the beginning so that it may not perish.

“And I am working,” that is understood to mean, “until now,” arranging, governing, and increasing all things with him.

It is as though he were saying openly: “Why do you envy me? Why do you reproach me, blind readers [Bede: ‘legislators’] of the Law, because in the form of a human being I have worked the salvation of one man on the Sabbath, when in the nature of divinity, together with God the Father, I am always quietly working the whole human race—indeed, the entire structure of the world—and all things visible and invisible?”

But they, being less capable of such a great mystery, sought all the more to kill him because he not only was breaking the Sabbath but also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God.

They were especially distressed because the one whom they had recognized as truly human through the weakness of the flesh wanted to be believed to be truly the Son of God—not adopted by grace, like the other saints, to whom the Prophet says: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’” (Psalm 81:6), but equal to the Father in every respect by nature.

[Col. 0808D] Thus far from Bede’s Homily 7.

It should certainly be noted that the phrase “making himself equal to God” is spoken from the perspective of the Jews, who thought that the Lord Jesus was claiming through his preaching to be what he was not, rather than truthfully declaring what he was.”

[Col. 0808D] Saint Augustine, *Tractate XVIII on John*, no. 2.

The Jews were therefore moved and indignant. Rightly so, because a man dared to make himself equal to God; but wrongly, because they did not understand God in the man.

They saw the flesh but did not know God; they beheld the dwelling but did not recognize its inhabitant. For that flesh was a temple, and God dwelt within.

Jesus therefore did not make the flesh equal to the Father, nor did he compare the form of a servant with the Lord—not what was made for our sake, but what he was when he made us.

Who Christ is, I speak to Catholics—you know, because you have believed rightly: he is not the Word alone, nor flesh alone; but the Word became flesh and dwelt [Augustine: “so that he might dwell”] among us.

Recall what you know concerning the Word: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Here there is equality with the Father.

“But the Word became flesh and dwelt among us”: in this respect the Father is greater than he. Thus the Father is both equal and greater: equal to the Word, greater than the flesh; equal to him through whom he made us, greater than him who was made for our sake.

When the Jews were moved and troubled because Christ made himself equal to the Father—since they understood only a human being and not God, saw the flesh but did not believe in the divinity—he said:

### Verse 19

“The Son can do nothing of himself unless he sees the Father doing it.”

[Col. 0809D] Saint Augustine, in the same work, no. 8.

The Father does not do some works that the Son sees, while the Son does other works when he has seen the Father doing them. Rather, the Father himself and the Son perform the same works.

For he continues [Ms.: “for he then says”]: “Whatever he does, the Son also does likewise.”

He does not mean: “When he has done something, the Son likewise does something else”; rather: “Whatever he does, the Son also does likewise.”

If the Son does what the Father does, the Father does it through the Son. If the Father does through the Son what he does, the Father does not perform one set of works and the Son another; rather, the works of the Father and the Son are the same.

And how does the Son perform the same works, and the Father likewise—

[Col. 0809D] Manuscript and Augustine: “And how does the Son also perform the same works? The same, and likewise.” Lest someone think that they are the same but performed differently: “The same,” he says, “and likewise.” And how could they be the same without being performed likewise—

[Col. 0809D] Thus far Saint Augustine, at the cited passage.

—since the Father does everything through the Son? As it is said: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.”

Therefore he said “likewise,” because the Son performs the same works that the Father performs: for the substance and operation of the Father and the Son in divinity are one [Ms.: “one substance and operation”], their will and power are one, their life and essence are one, and everything in the Father and the Son is equal, except that the Father is Father and the Son is Son.

There is distinction in the persons, but unity in nature. For the Son cannot do anything of himself unless he sees the Father doing it.

We must not understand this saying carnally—

[Col. 0810D] From Saint Augustine, *Tractate XIX*, no. 1.

—as though the Father and the Son were two human beings, one showing and the other seeing, one speaking and the other hearing; all such notions are fantasies of the heart.”

Such a thought must be driven far from Christian breasts. Therefore the example of the present reading teaches concerning the Son and the Father that the Father does not have a lesser person than the Son, nor does the Son of God have a greater person than the Father.

[Col. 0810D] Manuscript: “For neither does the Father have a lesser one, nor does the Son of God have a greater one: since …,” since there is no difference of divinity between the Father and the Son, but one majesty. For when he says that the Son can do nothing except what he has seen the Father doing, this is not to be understood bodily, since God does not see in bodily ways; rather, all his seeing is in the power of his nature. Nor can there be division in the simple nature of divinity. Rather, for the Son to see the Father’s works is for him to do them equally with the Father, because for the Son seeing and being are the same thing. Therefore he added: “For whatever the Father does, the Son also does in the same way.” He shows the identity of one nature and one operation, because the operation of the Father and the Son is common to them, whose nature is one and whose operation likewise is one. Therefore he subsequently added [Col. 0810A]: “For the Father loves the Son and shows him everything that he himself does.” He wished to show that this entire showing by the Father is instruction for our faith: namely, that the Father and the Son alike should be confessed by us; and lest any ignorance should be understood in the Son, to whom the Father would show all the works that he himself was doing, he immediately said: “And he will show him works greater than these, so that you may marvel.”

## CHAPTER X

That just as the Father raises the dead, so also does the Son; and that he is to be honored equally with the Father; and that believers pass from death to life. He also declares that an hour will come when the good and the evil will rise from their tombs.

[Col. 0810B] VERSE 21.—“For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes.” He says that the Father will show the Son things at which they will marvel. And he soon teaches what those same things are: “For just as the Father raises the dead, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes.” Equal power is not dissimilar through the unity of nature [Manuscript: “through [the unity] of the undissimilar nature”], and the demonstration of works is not instruction for one ignorant, but for our faith, which has introduced not knowledge of unknown things to the Son, but confession of his birth to us. For the Father’s showing means that he does through the Son what he is going to do. For the greater works are the resurrection of the dead that will take place on the last day, greater than the healing of this sick man who was healed by Christ’s word. From this the entire occasion of the discourse arose; for he says: “So that you may marvel.”

[Col. 0810D] From St. Augustine, Treatise XIX, §§4–5. “And it is difficult to see how the eternal Father could, as though in time, show anything to the co-eternal Son, who knows everything that is with the Father. What, then, are those greater works? This is easy to understand. ‘For just as the Father,’ he says, ‘raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes.’ The greater works, therefore, are to raise the dead rather than to heal the sick. But just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes. The Father, then, does not give life to some and the Son to others; rather, everything is through him. Therefore the Son gives life to the very ones whom the Father does, because the Son does not do other things or do them otherwise, but does these things in the same way. This must plainly be understood and firmly held. But remember that the Son gives life to whomever he wishes. Here, then, hold not only the Son’s power but also his will [Manuscript: ‘and the Father’s will’]. The Son gives life to whomever he wishes, and the Father gives life to whomever he wishes; and the Son gives life to the very ones whom the Father does. Accordingly, the power and will of the Father and the Son are the same, as are also their life and the giving of life to the dead. And therefore he says: ‘Just as the Father raises the dead and gives life to whomever he wishes, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes.’ For the Father does not give life to some and the Son to others; rather, one power produces one giving of life. This power is also to be honored with one honor [Alternative: revered].” And consequently he added:

VERSES 22–23.—“For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Father does not honor the Son.”

The Father judges no one because the person of the Father did not assume humanity and will not be seen in the judgment; rather, only the person of the Son will judge, in that form which was unjustly judged and will justly judge the living and the dead. For the Son will not be seen in the judgment in the nature in which he is consubstantial with God the Father, but in that in which he is consubstantial with his mother and became human. This is to be understood as follows: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son,” as though it were said: No one will see the Father in the judgment of the living and the dead, but everyone will see the Son, because he is also the Son of Man, so that he may be seen even by the ungodly, when they too will see him whom they pierced. And lest we seem to be making an inference rather than presenting an explicit demonstration, we bring forward the Lord’s own certain and clear statement, by which we show that this was the reason he said, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son”: the judge will appear in the form of the Son of Man. This form is not the Father’s, but the Son’s; nor is it the Son’s form in which he is equal to the Father, but that in which he is lesser than the Father, so that he may be visible in the judgment to the good and the evil.

“So that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Father does not honor the Son.”

[Col. 0811D] St. Augustine, cited passage, §§6–7. “For what is it to honor the Father except to acknowledge that he has a Son? It is one thing when God is commended to you because he is God, and another when God is commended to you because he is Father. When God is commended to you because he is God, the Creator is commended to you; the Almighty is commended to you; the highest spirit—eternal, invisible, unchangeable—is commended to you. But when the Father is commended to you because he is Father, nothing other than the Son is commended to you also, because he cannot be called Father if he does not have a Son, just as the Son cannot be called Son if he does not have a Father.

“But perhaps you honor the Father as the greater and the Son as the lesser, saying to me: ‘I honor the Father; for I know that he has a Son, and I do not err in the name Father—I do not understand the Father without the Son—but nevertheless I honor the Son as the lesser.’ The Son himself corrects you and recalls you, saying: ‘So that all may honor the Son,’ not less, but ‘just as they honor the Father.’ Therefore whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father [Col. 0811D] who sent him.

“‘I want,’ you say, ‘to give the Father greater honor and the Son lesser honor.’ You take honor away from the Father precisely where you give lesser honor to the Son. For what else does this opinion of yours seem to imply [Augustine: ‘this way of thinking’] than that the Father either did not wish or was unable to beget a Son equal to himself? If he did not wish to, he was envious; if he was unable to, he failed. Do you not see, therefore, that this is how one must think? Where you wish to give greater honor to the Father, there you are insulting the Father. Accordingly, honor the Son as you honor the Father, if you wish to honor both the Son and the Father.”

[Col. 0812A] VERSE 24.—“Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life and will not come into judgment, but passes from death to life.”

He does not now pass over; he has already passed from death into life. And pay attention to this: “whoever hears my word.” He did not say, “believes me,” but “believes him who sent me.” Let him hear the Son’s word; let him believe in the Father [Manuscript and Augustine: “so that he may believe the Father”]. Why do you hear your word and believe another? When we hear someone’s word, do we not believe the very one speaking the word, lending our trust to his speech? What, then, did he wish to say by “whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me,” except that his word is in me? And who is the one who hears my word except the one who hears me? [Augustine: “And what is ‘hears my word’ except ‘hears me’?”] Whoever believes in me also believes him who sent me, because when he believes him, he believes his word; and when he believes his word, he believes me, because I am the Word of the Father.

[Col. 0811D] From St. Augustine, cited passage, §8. “For he would not pass from death to life unless he were first in death and were not in life. When, therefore, he has passed into life, he will not be in death. He was therefore dead and came to life again; he had perished and was found again (Luke XV, 32). Thus a certain resurrection already takes place, and people pass from one kind of death to one kind of life: from the death of unbelief to the life of faith; from the death of falsehood to the life of truth; from the death of iniquity to the life of righteousness. This, too, is a resurrection of the dead. Let him open it more fully, and let it shine upon us, as it has begun to do.”

[Col. 0812C] VERSE 25.—“Amen, amen, I say to you: the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.”

This is proper to the devout: they hear about his incarnation in such a way that they believe he is the Son of God. That is, they receive him as having been made lesser than the Father for their sake in the form of a servant, while believing that he is equal to the Father in the form of God. Therefore it follows—and, commending this very point, he says:

VERSE 26.—“For just as the Father has life in himself, so also he has granted the Son to have life in himself” [Manuscript: “life”].

[Col. 0812D] From the same author, §13. “Therefore, when he says, ‘He granted the Son to have life in himself,’ I shall say it briefly: He begot the Son as having life in himself. For he was not without life and received life; rather, by being born he is life. The Father is life without being born; the Son is life by being born. The Father is from no father; the Son is from God the Father. The Father is Father because of the Son, while the Son, both in what he is [Son] and in the fact that he is, is because of the Father; and what he is, he is from the Father.

“Thus he said: ‘I gave the Son to have life in himself,’ as though he were saying: ‘The Father who is life in himself begot the Son who would be life in himself.’ He wished ‘gave’ to be understood in place of ‘begot,’ because he begot him. It is as if we were to say to someone: ‘God gave you being.’” For it follows and says:

VERSE 27.—“And he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.”

I think nothing could be clearer. Because he is the Son of God, he is equal to the Father; he does not receive this authority to execute judgment, but has it with the Father in secret. He receives it, however, so that the good and the evil may see him judging, because he is the Son of Man. The vision of the Son of Man is indeed displayed even to the evil. But the vision of the form of God is granted only to the pure in heart, because “they shall see God” (Matthew V, 8)—that is, only to the devout, to whose love he promises this very thing, that he will show himself to them.

And therefore see what follows:

VERSE 28.—“Do not marvel at this,” he says.

What prevents us from marveling except that which truly astonishes everyone who does not understand? He therefore said that the Father had given him authority to execute judgment because he is the Son of Man, when one might rather have expected him to say [Alternative: “judge”], “because he is the Son of God.” But because the wicked cannot see the Son of God according to that in which he is equal to the Father in the form of God, while it is necessary that both the righteous and the wicked see the judge of the living and the dead when they are judged before him, he says: “Do not marvel at this.”

VERSE 29.—“For the hour will come in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice, and they will come forth: those who have done good, to a resurrection of life, but those who have done evil, to a resurrection of judgment.”

It was therefore necessary that he receive that authority because he is the Son of Man, so that, when all rise, they might see him in the form in which he can be seen by everyone—some for condemnation, others for eternal life.

And what is eternal life except that vision which is not granted to the ungodly? “That they may know you,” he says, “the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII, 3). And how will they know Jesus Christ himself except as the one true God, who will show himself to them—not in the way in which he will also show himself to those who are to be punished, in the form of the Son of Man?

According to that vision he is good, according to which vision God appears to the pure in heart, although “God is good to Israel, to those who are upright in heart.” But when the evil see the judge, he will not appear good to them, because they will not rejoice in him in their hearts; rather, then “all the tribes of the earth will mourn”—that is, the whole number of the evil and unbelieving.

For this reason also, when the man who had called him “Good Teacher” asked him for advice about attaining eternal life, he replied: “Why do you ask me about the good? No one is good except the one God” (Luke XVIII, 19). Yet elsewhere the Lord himself calls a human being good: “The good man,” he says, “out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth good things, and the evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings forth evil things” (Matthew XII, 35).

But because that man was seeking eternal life, and eternal life exists in that contemplation in which God is seen not for punishment but for heavenly joy [Manuscript: “everlasting joy,”] the Lord Christ here shows us two resurrections in these words.

The first is the resurrection that exists in faith, when one rises from sins, of which he says: “Amen, amen, I say to you: the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God.”

The second is the one he indicates when he says: “Amen, amen, I say to you: the hour will come in which all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God.”

The former is the resurrection of souls; the latter, which follows, will be the resurrection of bodies. Whoever rises in this first resurrection will rise in the second to glory. Whoever does not rise in this first resurrection will nevertheless rise in the second, but to punishment. God accomplishes both through Christ. Whoever rises here through him will rise there to him. Whoever does not rise here through him will not rise there to him.”

[Col. 0813D] St. Augustine, cited passage, §16. “Now is the hour for the dead to rise; at the end of the age there will be an hour for the dead to rise. But now they rise in mind; then they will rise in the flesh. Now let them rise in mind through the word of God, the Son of God; then they will rise in the flesh through the Word of God, the Son of Man made flesh.

“For the Father himself will not come to judge the living and the dead; yet the Father does not depart from the Son. How, then, will he not himself come? Because he himself will not be seen in the judgment. ‘They will see him whom they pierced’ (John XIX, 37). That form will be the judge which stood under judgment; it will judge which was judged. It was judged unjustly; it will judge justly. Such will the judge appear as can be seen both by those whom he is going to crown and by those whom he is going to condemn.”

There is a distinction between the word he said above, that the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and what he says here: “The hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God.”

In the former passage he said “they will hear,” that is, “they will obey.” Therefore that resurrection is to life. But of the future resurrection, concerning which he says that they will hear the voice of the Son of God, they will hear in order to rise to judgment. He does not add here “to life,” because not all will rise to glory, but many to punishment.

Therefore, concerning the future resurrection, he added: “Those who have done good, to a resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to a resurrection of judgment”—that is, of condemnation, because here he used “judgment” for punishment.

Then will be the final winnowing-shovel [Manuscript: “chaff”] that separates the good from the evil, the wheat from the chaff. Then the ungodly will go into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life. It follows:

VERSE 30.—“I can do nothing of myself, but as I hear, I judge; and my judgment is just.”

Perhaps he said, “I can do nothing of myself,” as though he had said: “I am not from myself, but from the Father.” For the Father is from no other; the Son is from the Father.

Therefore he said: “As I hear, I judge,” because the work of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one. As he hears, he judges—he hears, that is, through the unity of substance and the proper possession of knowledge. He does not judge from himself because he is not from himself. For the Father alone is from no other; the Son was begotten from the Father, as we have said. He hears from the one from whom he was begotten, because he is not from himself but from the one by whom he was begotten. From the one from whom he has understanding, he also has knowledge. From him, therefore, comes hearing, which is nothing other than knowledge.

This same statement, “As I hear, I judge,” can also be understood of the nature of his humanity, which the Son of God took from the Virgin. When he was speaking about the resurrection of souls, he did not say, “I hear,” but “I judge.” “I hear,” as though referring to the command of the Father who gives orders. Thus he is now acting as a human being, as one for whom the Father is greater; now from the form of a servant, not from the form of God.

“As I hear, I judge; and my judgment is just.” From what does a human being’s judgment become just? Because it follows: “I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me.”

This sending is Christ’s incarnation, which took place so that the Father’s will might be accomplished through him for the salvation of the human race. In this passage, from the words of our Savior, he appears to wish to indicate that there are two natures in him and that he truly possesses a soul, in which alone there is will [Manuscript: “in which there is usually will”]. This soul has also been so closely mingled with the divinity that its whole will was spiritual, not animal—that is, not carnal. For he subsequently added:

[Col. 0815B] VERSE 31.—“If I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is not true.”

As he said later: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing; but the Father who sent me is the one who glorifies me,” so here too it is said: “If I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is not true.” And shortly afterward: “The Father who sent me is himself the one who bears witness concerning me.”

Now he demonstrates the nature of a human being; now he signifies himself as equal to the Father in the majesty of God; now, claiming for himself unity of divinity with God the Father; now, displaying the frailty of human flesh; now, signifying that he does not speak his own teaching; now, that he does not seek his own will; now, that his testimony is not true; now, that it is true.

For here he says: “If I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is not true”; and shortly afterward: “Even if I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is true.”

How, then, is your testimony not true, Lord, except according to the frailty of the flesh? Likewise, what he said—“I did not come to do my own will,” and “the Son can do nothing from himself,” and many other statements of this kind—does not weaken the Son, diminish his worth, or separate him from the Father. Indeed, these things were stated so that the truth of the incarnation might be recognized.

For when he says: “I came forth from the Father; I am in the Father, and the Father is in me; I and the Father are one; whoever sees me sees the Father; and just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes,” his true divinity is affirmed. For the will of the Father and the Son is one, their operation is one, their grace ultimately one, and their governance likewise one, as the apostle to the nations teaches when he writes: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans I, 7).

VERSE 32.—“There is another who bears witness concerning me.”

In what follows he shows who that other one is who bears witness concerning him, when he says: “The Father who sent me is himself the one who bears witness concerning me” (John V, 37).

The Father’s testimony concerning the Son was given at the baptism, when a voice came from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” [Manuscript: “in whom I have been well pleased”] (Matthew XVII, 5). The Father also gave similar testimony on the holy mountain, in the hearing of the three disciples, concerning his Son.

“And I know that his testimony is true.” Everything true is true from the truth, for God is truth. And whatever is true is true from God.

[Col. 0815D] St. Augustine, Treatise XXIII, §§2–3. “And he said what that testimony is: ‘The works,’ he says, ‘which I do bear witness concerning me.’ Then he added: ‘And the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me.’ He says that the very works he does he received from the Father.

“The works, therefore, bear witness; the Father who sent him bears witness. John bore witness concerning Christ like a lamp—not to heal [Augustine: ‘to satisfy’] friends, but to confound enemies. It had already been foretold by the person of the Father: ‘I have prepared a lamp for my Christ; I will clothe his enemies with shame, but upon him my sanctification will flourish’ (Psalm CXXXI, 17–18).

“Suppose you are placed as though in the night: you have fixed your attention on a lamp, marveled at the lamp, and rejoiced at the lamp’s light. But that lamp tells you that there is a sun in which you ought to rejoice; and although it burns in the night, it commands you to await the day.

“Therefore it is not because the testimony of that man was unnecessary [Augustine: ‘the testimony of that man’]. For why would he have been sent if he were unnecessary? But lest a person remain with the lamp and suppose that the lamp’s light is sufficient for him, the Lord neither says that the lamp was superfluous nor says that one ought to remain with the lamp. He points to another testimony: the Scripture of God, in which God certainly bore witness to his Son.

“And in that Scripture the Jews had placed their hope, namely, in the law of God administered to them through Moses, the servant of God. ‘Search the Scripture,’ he says (John III, 39–40), ‘in which you think you have eternal life. It is that Scripture which bears witness concerning me, and you do not wish to come to me so that you may have life.’

“Why do you think you have eternal life in the Scripture? Ask the one to whom it bears witness, and understand what eternal life is.

“And because, on account of Moses, they seemed [Augustine: ‘wanted’] to reject Christ as an opponent of the institutions and commandments that Moses had handed down, he again refutes them as though by reference to another lamp, saying:

## CHAPTER XI

He calls John a lamp. The Father and the Scriptures also bear witness concerning him. The Jews, who do not receive him when he comes in the name of the Father, will receive another who will come in his own name. He testifies that Moses wrote about him.

[Col. 0816D] VERSES 33–36.—“You sent to John, and he bore witness to the truth. But I do not receive testimony from a human being; rather, I say these things so that you may be saved. He was a burning and shining lamp. You wished for a time to rejoice in his light.

“But I have testimony greater than John’s. For all human beings are lamps, because they can both be kindled [Augustine: ‘lit’] and extinguished. And lamps, when they possess wisdom, shine and burn with the Spirit. For even if they burned and were extinguished, they can also become foul-smelling. But the servants of God remained good lamps from the oil of his mercy, not from their own strength.

“For the free gift of God is the oil of the lamps. ‘I labored more than all of them’ (1 Corinthians XV, 10), says one lamp; and lest he seem to burn by his own strength, he added: ‘Yet not I, but the grace of God with me.’

“Every prophet, therefore, before the Lord’s coming, is a lamp. The apostle Peter says of him: ‘We have the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts’ (2 Peter I, 19).
