“The prophets, then, are lamps, and all prophecy is one great lamp. What of the apostles—are they not lamps? They are certainly lamps as well. The sun alone is not a lamp. It is not lit and extinguished, but is the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world.

“It is said of John: ‘He was not the light, but came to bear witness to the light’ (John I, 8–9). But of Christ: ‘He was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world.’

“What is it that the Truth itself says about the apostles? ‘You are the light of the world’ (Matthew V, 14). And the evangelist John says: ‘He was not the light.’ John was not a lamp by himself, nor were the apostles light by themselves; rather, John was a lamp from the light, Christ, and they were illuminated by him, who is the true sun rising in the hearts of the faithful [Alternative: believers].

“But I have testimony greater than John’s. The works that the Father gave me—the very works that I do—bear witness concerning me, because the Father sent me.

“VERSE 37.—And the Father who sent me himself bore witness concerning me.”

Above he said: “I do not receive testimony from a human being.” Here he gives the reason why he did not receive testimony from a human being: because he has the testimony of the Father and the testimonies of the works, which are greater than those of human beings.

Therefore this sending is Christ’s incarnation; Christ’s incarnation is our redemption; and our redemption is the Truth itself, which says: “I came so that they may have life, and have it more abundantly.”

He added to this testimony of the Father concerning him a statement about the Father himself, because the Jews—or the magicians, and all unbelievers—cannot, with minds blinded, receive the truth of his divinity. He says:

VERSE 38.—“Nor have you ever heard his voice, nor seen his form; and you do not have his word remaining in you.”

The apostle says: “It is not the hearers of the law who are justified, but the doers of the word of God” (Romans II, 13). That is, the Son of God does not remain in their hearts because they do not keep what they hear.

But when he says, “You have neither heard his voice nor seen his form,” he shows that the substance of divinity is incomprehensible and invisible, and that his voice could not be heard by carnal ears; rather, it must be understood or loved through spiritual understanding by the grace of the Holy Spirit, according to what will be given to each person.

VERSE 39.—“Because you do not believe the one whom he sent. Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life, and they are the ones that bear witness concerning me.

VERSE 40.—And you do not wish to come to me so that you may have life.”

“You do not wish to come,” that is, “you do not wish to believe,” because it is impossible to please God without faith (Hebrews XI, 6). Our coming to Christ means believing that he is the true Son of God and that through him we truly have salvation.

For every sacred Scripture bore witness to Christ, whether through figures, through prophets, or through the ministries of angels. Thus Moses also bore witness to Christ; John bore witness to Christ; the other prophets and the apostles bore witness to Christ.

He places the testimony of his works above all these testimonies, because through those works none other than God bore witness to his Son.

VERSE 41.—“I do not receive glory from human beings.”

That is, I do not seek human praise, because I did not come to be served but to serve. That is, I did not come to receive carnal honor from human beings, but to give spiritual honor to human beings.

VERSE 42.—“But I know you, that you do not have the love of God in yourselves.”

They did not have the love of God because they did not believe in him [Manuscript: “in it”], who did not come to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him.

Therefore he added:

VERSE 43.—“I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me.”

That is, you did not believe in me, because I came into the world for this reason: that the name of the Father might be glorified.

“If another comes in his own name, you will receive him.” Who is the one who comes in his own name except the one who seeks his own glory and not the glory of the one who sent him? Who is the one whom the Jews will receive except the Antichrist, who is to come seeking his own glory?

And this will be the punishment for their sin, because they did not wish to believe the truth, so that they might believe falsehood [Manuscript: “and they will believe the lie”] (2 Thessalonians II).

[Col. 0818C] VERSE 44.—“How can you believe, who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that is from God alone?”

We must consider more attentively how great an evil vainglory and the pursuit of human praise are, since the Truth itself says that some cannot believe because they were desirous of worldly glory.

What is the desire for human praise except the exaltation of a proud mind? A person wishes to be thought to possess what he does not strive to have within himself. He is one person inwardly and desires to appear another outwardly.

Humility seeks glory from God alone; pride seeks it from human beings.

For this reason John the Baptist was praised so remarkably by the Truth itself, so that he was not a reed shaken by the wind (Matthew XI, 7), because he was not pliable when the breeze of human praise or of hateful reproach blew.

Therefore he had glory from God Christ because he did not seek human glory.

VERSES 45–46.—“Do not think that I will accuse you before the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, in whom you place your greatest hope. For if you believed Moses, you would perhaps also believe me, for he wrote about me.”

Therefore I do not accuse you, because I did not come to condemn but to save. Moses, however, accuses you because you are unbelieving toward his voice.

He wrote about me when he said: “The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him as to me” (Deuteronomy XVIII, 15; Acts III, 22–23).

But pay attention to what follows: “And every soul that does not obey that prophet shall be exterminated from the people of God.”

VERSE 47.—“But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?”

For whatever the law and the prophets wrote, everything indicated that Christ would come. If the Jews had believed the law or the prophets, they would certainly also have believed Christ.

After these mystical words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the deepest understanding, by which he wished to reveal the hidden mysteries both of his divinity and of his humanity to those who were then hearing and to those who now read, he undertook to show by the miracle of the five loaves who he was. Therefore the evangelist subsequently added:

{518}

## CHAPTER XII

As the Passover of the Jews approached, he satisfied five thousand men with five loaves and two fish. When they wished to make him king because of this sign, he fled into the mountain. Then, walking upon the sea, while the disciples were afraid, he said to them: “It is I; do not be afraid.”

[Col. 0819B]

## CHAPTER VI, VERSES 1–2

After these things Jesus went across the Sea of Galilee, which is that of Tiberias, and a very great multitude followed him, because they saw the signs that were being performed upon those who were sick [Manuscript: “which he performed upon the sick”].

“Jesus went across the Sea of Galilee, which is that of Tiberias.”

From Bede’s Homily 21, on Lent, Patrologia, volume XCIV, column 110. First, according to the historical sense, it must be said that the Sea of Galilee, which is distinguished by many names according to the variety of the surrounding regions, was called the Sea of Tiberias only in those places where, on the western side, it displayed the city of Tiberias, which, as they say, was a healthy dwelling because of its warm waters [Manuscript: “is a healthy dwelling”]. For with the Jordan flowing through it, it extends twenty-two thousand paces in length and five in width.

Mystically, however, the sea signifies the turbid and swelling currents of this present age. In them, all the wicked who take unlawful delight, like fish devoted to the depths, do not direct their minds toward the joys above.

Hence that same sea is appropriately called Galilee, that is, “wheel,” because the love of the passing age casts hearts, as it were, into a whirlpool [Alternative: abyss] and does not allow them to rise toward the desires of everlasting life.

Of such people the Psalmist says: “The ungodly walk around” (Psalm XI, 9).

But as Jesus went away across the Sea of Galilee, a very great multitude followed him, so that from him they might receive the greatest gifts of heavenly instruction, healing, and nourishment [Bede: “great gifts”].

For before the Lord appeared in the flesh, only the Jewish people followed him by believing. But after, through the dispensation of his incarnation, he approached, trod upon, and crossed the waves of corruptible life, a very great multitude of believing nations immediately followed him, desiring to be instructed, healed, and satisfied spiritually, and praying with the Psalmist:

“Lord, I have taken refuge in you; teach me to do your will” (Psalm CXLII, 9–10).

And again:

“Have mercy on me [Alternative: on us], Lord, for I am weak; heal me, Lord, for all my bones are troubled” (Psalm VI, 3).

And again, trusting that they would receive from him the nourishment of perpetual life:

“The Lord,” he says, “feeds me, and I shall lack nothing; he has settled me in a place of pasture” (Psalm XXII, 1–2).

## Verses 3–4

Jesus therefore went up onto the mountain, and there he was sitting with his disciples. Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was near.

Let us not believe that the fact that Jesus went up onto the mountain and sat there with his disciples, but, when the crowd came to him, descended and fed it in the lower places—the same crowd whom shortly before he had healed in the lower places—was done without purpose. Rather, it mystically signifies that the Lord distributes his teaching and gifts according to the capacity of those who receive them. To minds still weak and spiritually childlike he entrusts simpler instructions and reveals more accessible mysteries; but to those who are loftier and more mature in understanding he discloses the more hidden secrets of his majesty, suggests the narrower paths of devoted conduct, and promises the higher gifts of heavenly rewards.

Accordingly, when a certain man asked what he should do in order to possess eternal life, as though he were still placed below, he bestowed the common gifts of his generosity, saying: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; honor your father and your mother.” But when the man afterward sought greater things, and, as it were, desired to climb the mountain of virtues, he said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matthew 19:18–19, 21).

The Lord displayed this discerning moderation not only when teaching in the flesh, but even now he does not cease to display it through the ministers of his word. Thus, concerning these ministers, he testifies under the persona of one good servant that they ought to give their fellow servants their measure of grain at the proper time—that is, according to the capacity of their hearers, they should seasonably and proportionately provide the nourishment of the word (Luke 12:42).

That the Lord teaches, heals, and feeds the crowds as Passover approaches may be interpreted mystically in this way: Passover is called a passing-over; and all whom the Lord restores on earth through the sweetness of his gifts he prepares for a healthy passage, so that they may transcend carnal desires by the elevation of their minds; trample underfoot the lowest desires of the world, both prosperity and adversity, through heavenly hope and love; and, even if they are not yet able to reach the heights in soul or body—for this is plainly promised in the future—nevertheless, whatever they see carnal people embracing as something lofty, they may despise as almost nothing in comparison with eternal things.

This is according to the example of the one who, seeing the wicked exalted and raised above the cedars of Lebanon, passed beyond temporal things by contemplating eternal ones and regarded as though already nonexistent the man whom he foresaw would soon be taken away (Psalm 36:35).

## Verses 5–7

When Jesus therefore had lifted up his eyes and had seen that a very large crowd was coming to him, he said to Philip: “Where shall we buy bread, so that these people may eat?” He said this to test him; for he himself knew what he was going to do.

Philip answered him: “Bread worth two hundred denarii would not be enough for them, so that each might receive even a little.”

That Jesus is said to have lifted up his eyes and seen the crowd coming to him is an indication of divine compassion: for, whenever all who seek to come to him approach, the grace of heavenly mercy is accustomed to meet them; and, lest they should be able to go astray while seeking, he opens the light of his Spirit to those who hasten [manuscript: “to those who seek”].

That the eyes of Jesus mystically signify the gifts of his Spirit is attested by John in the Apocalypse. Speaking figuratively about him, he says: “And I saw a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven Spirits of God sent into all the earth” (Revelation 5:6).

When the Lord tested Philip by saying, “Where shall we buy bread, so that these people may eat?”, he acted according to a provident dispensation—not so that he himself might learn what he did not know, but so that Philip, when tested, might recognize the sluggishness of his faith, which he himself did not know although the Teacher knew it, and might correct it through the miracle.

For he ought not to have doubted, in the presence of the Creator of all things, who “brings forth bread from the earth and wine that gladdens the heart of man” (Psalm 104:15), that bread costing only a few denarii could suffice for many thousands of people, so that each might receive enough and go away already satisfied.

## Verses 8–11

One of his disciples, Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, said to him: “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are these among so many?”

Jesus therefore said to them: “Have the people sit down.”

Now there was much grass in the place. So the men sat down, about five thousand in number. Jesus therefore took the loaves and, after giving thanks, distributed them to those who were seated. Likewise also of the fish, as much as they wanted.

The five loaves with which he satisfied the multitude signify the five books of Moses. When these are opened to spiritual understanding and multiplied through a now more abundant sense, they daily refresh the hearts of faithful hearers.

They are appropriately reported to have been barley loaves, because of the more austere commands of the Law and the coarser coverings of the letter [Bede: “of the coarser letter”], which concealed the inner understanding like the marrow of spiritual meaning.

The two fish that he added suitably signify the writings of the psalmists and the prophets. The former by singing, the latter by speaking, narrated to their hearers the future mysteries of Christ and of the Church [Bede: “the one by singing, the other by speaking”].

And rightly are the heralds of that age represented by aquatic creatures, since in that age the people of the faithful could in no way live without the waters of baptism.”

There are some who think that the two fish, which gave a pleasant flavor to the bread, signify the two persons by whom that people was governed, so that through them it might receive direction in counsel: namely, the royal and the priestly persons. The sacred anointing also belonged to them. Their duty was never to be broken or corrupted by the stormy waves of the people, but often to break through the violent contradictions of the crowds like opposing waves, and sometimes to yield to them while preserving their integrity—altogether, after the manner of fish, to move about in the turbulent administration of the people as in a stormy sea.

These two persons, however, prefigured our Lord: he alone bore both offices, and he alone fulfilled them not figuratively but in reality.

“The boy who had the five loaves and two fish, yet did not distribute them to the hungry crowds but offered them to the Lord to distribute, is the Jewish people, childish in its literal understanding. It kept within itself the sayings of Scripture in a closed form; yet the Lord, appearing in the flesh, received them and showed what usefulness and sweetness they contained. He disclosed how greatly those things that had seemed few and contemptible overflowed through the manifold grace of the Spirit, and he presented them to be served to all nations through his apostles and the successors of his apostles.

Hence the other evangelists rightly report that the Lord gave the loaves and fish to the disciples, while the disciples served them to the crowds (Matthew 14; Luke 9; Mark 6). For when the ministry of human salvation had begun to be proclaimed by the Lord, it was confirmed to us by those who heard him.

He broke the five loaves and two fish and distributed them to the disciples when he opened their understanding, so that they might understand everything written about him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms (Luke 24). The disciples set them before the crowds when they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word by the signs that followed (Mark 16:20).

The grass on which the crowd reclines while being fed signifies carnal desire, which everyone who wishes to be satisfied with spiritual nourishment ought to trample and suppress. For ‘all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass’ (Isaiah 40:6).

Let him therefore recline upon the grass and crush the flower of grass—that is, let him chastise his body and bring it into subjection (1 Corinthians 9:27). Whoever desires to be refreshed by the sweetness of living bread, whoever wishes to be renewed by the banquets of heavenly grace lest he fail through the decay of what is earthly, must subdue the pleasures of the flesh and restrain the excesses of luxury.

The five thousand men who ate signify the perfection of the life of those who are refreshed by the word [Bede: “the perfection of those who are refreshed by the word of life”]. In Scripture, the name ‘men’ commonly represents those who are more perfect, whom no feminine softness corrupts—such as the apostle wishes those to be to whom he says: ‘Watch, stand firm in the faith, act manfully, and be strong’ (1 Corinthians 16:13).

The number one thousand, beyond which our counting does not increase, is accustomed to indicate the fullness of the matters under discussion.

By the number five, the five well-known senses of our body are expressed: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. Whoever in each of these strives to act manfully and be strengthened—living soberly, justly, and piously, so that he may deserve to be refreshed by the sweetness of heavenly wisdom—is represented by those five thousand men whom the Lord satisfied with mystical food.

Nor should it be passed over that, when he was about to feed the multitude, he gave thanks. He gave thanks both to teach us always to give thanks for gifts received from heaven and to indicate how much he rejoices in our progress, how much he delights in our spiritual nourishment.

Do you wish to know, brothers, how much our Savior rejoices in our salvation? The evangelist Luke tells us that he gave the disciples power to tread upon all the strength of the enemy and declared that their names were written in heaven (Luke 10:19–20). He immediately adds: “At that very hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said: ‘I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones’” (Luke 10:21; Matthew 11:25).

It is therefore clear that he rejoices with the salvation and life of the faithful: he praises the Father with thanksgiving because he has revealed to the humble in spirit the mysteries that he hid from the proud.

## Verse 12

When they had been filled, he said to his disciples: “Gather up the fragments that remain, so that they do not perish.”

That, after the crowd had been satisfied, he ordered the disciples to gather the fragments that remained so that they would not perish clearly signifies that there are many mysteries of the divine utterances that the understanding of the common people does not grasp. There are also things that the less learned cannot attain by themselves, but which they can quickly understand when explained by teachers.

Those who are capable must therefore gather these things carefully by searching them out, and by word or writing cause them to reach the instruction of the less mature, lest the nourishment of the word perish through their negligence and be taken away from the peoples who, by the Lord’s gift, know how to gather it through interpretation.

It follows:

## Verse 13

“So they gathered them,” he says, “and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves that remained after those who had eaten.”

Since the fullness of any perfection is commonly represented by the number twelve, the entire chorus of spiritual teachers is rightly expressed by the twelve baskets full of fragments. They are commanded to gather through meditation the obscure things of Scripture, which the crowds cannot gather even by meditation [the words “by themselves” are supplied], and, having meditated upon them, to preserve them in writing both for their own use and for the use of the crowds.

The apostles and evangelists themselves did this by inserting into their works many sayings of the Law and the Prophets, adding their mystical interpretation. The teachers who followed them throughout the world did the same, and some of them examined entire books of both Testaments through more diligent explanation. Though these books may be despised by human beings, they are nevertheless fruitful with the bread of heavenly grace.

For servile tasks are commonly performed with baskets. Thus, concerning the people who served in mud and bricks in Egypt, the Psalmist says: “His hands served in the basket” (Psalm 81:7).

## Verse 14

When those men had seen the sign that he had performed, they said: “This truly is the prophet who is to come into the world.”

They were right to call the Lord a great prophet, already destined to be the herald of great salvation for the world. For he himself also deigned to call himself a prophet when he said: “It cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke 13:33).

But they were not yet advancing in full faith, since they did not know how to call him God as well. Therefore, when they saw the sign Jesus had performed, they said: “This truly is the prophet who is to come into the world.”

Let us, with a more certain recognition of truth and faith, seeing the world that Jesus made and the signs with which he filled it, say: “This truly is the mediator between God and human beings” (1 Timothy 2:5)—he who was in the world through his divinity, and through whom the world was made; who came in his own humanity to seek and save what had perished (John 1), and to restore the world he had made; who, through the presence of his divinity, is in the world with his faithful “all days, until the consummation of the age.”

*Thus far Bede.*

## Verse 15

When Jesus therefore realized that they were about to come and seize him and make him king, he withdrew again to the mountain by himself alone.

### Augustine, Tractate 25, sections 1–2

It is therefore to be understood that, when the Lord was sitting on the mountain with his disciples and saw the crowds coming to him, he had descended from the mountain and fed the crowds in the lower places. For how could he flee there again unless he had first descended from the mountain?

This signifies something: the Lord descended from on high in order to feed the crowds. He fed them and ascended.

Why did he ascend when he knew that they wanted to seize him and make him king? What then? Was he not a king, since he feared becoming a king? He certainly was—but not such a king as would be made by human beings, rather one who would give a kingdom to human beings.

Perhaps Jesus, whose deeds are words, signifies something to us here as well. When they wanted to seize him and make him king, and for that reason he fled alone to the mountain, was what happened in him silent, without speech or significance? Or perhaps “to seize him” meant to wish to anticipate the time of his kingdom.

For he had come at that time, not yet to reign in the way in which he will reign when we say: “Your kingdom come.” He always reigns with the Father insofar as he is the Son of God, the Word of God, the Word through whom all things were made.

But the prophets foretold his kingdom also according to the fact that Christ became human and made his faithful into Christians. There will therefore be a kingdom of Christians—the kingdom that is now being gathered, now dwelling among us, now purchased by the blood of Christ. At some time it will become manifest, when the glory of his saints is revealed openly, after the judgment carried out by him. He himself said above that the Son of Man would carry out this judgment. Concerning this kingdom the apostle also says: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father” (1 Corinthians 15:24).

Hence he himself also says: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34).

The disciples and the crowds who believed in him thought that he had come in order already to reign. This was what it meant to wish to seize him and make him king: they wished to anticipate the time that he himself kept hidden within himself, so that he might reveal it at the proper time and declare it openly at the end of the age.

### Augustine, same work, section 4

Why, then, was it said that he fled? For if he did not wish to be held, he would not be held; if he did not wish to be seized, he would not be seized. If he did not wish it, he would not even be recognized.

But this was done symbolically. He fled alone so that he would not reign in a carnal manner, because he ascended into heaven alone, from where he would reign spiritually in his saints (Hebrews 9).

“He fled alone to the mountain”—the firstborn from the dead, ascending above all the heavens and interceding for us. The priest represents him when he enters the Holy of Holies once a year, not without blood, to intercede for the people.

Thus again he is placed alone on high on the great mountain, having entered within the veil, while the people remains outside. But let us see what the disciples were suffering in the little boat while he remained within the veil of heavenly height.

What is the boat tossed by the waves except the Church, which is wearied by persecutions both outside and within? Outside, by open persecution from the pagans; within, by hidden dissension from false brothers.

For this reason he added:

## Verses 16–17

When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea, and after getting into a boat, they came across the sea toward Capernaum.

### Augustine, same work, section 5

He quickly stated as completed what happened afterward: “They came across the sea to Capernaum.” Then he returns to explain how they came, because they crossed by sailing on the lake.

While they were sailing toward the place to which he had already said they had come, he explains by recapitulation what happened:

## Verse 18

It was already dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them. The sea was stirred up because a strong wind was blowing.

It was rightly dark, because the light had not come. “It was already dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them,” because the nearer the end of the world approaches, the more errors grow, terrors multiply, iniquity increases, and unbelief increases.

The light—which in John the evangelist himself is clearly shown to be love, so that he says, “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness” (1 John 2:11)—is very frequently extinguished when love grows cold and iniquity abounds.

These are the waves that disturb the boat; the storm and winds are the cries of curses. From this love grows cold; from this the waves increase.

The boat was being troubled; as a strong wind blew, the sea rose up. Darkness increased, understanding diminished, and iniquity increased. Yet amid all these things the boat was moving toward land, hurrying, seeking a harbor.

So, amid every kind of temptation, the Church makes progress. She labors but is not drowned. She awaits Christ, so that through him she may reach the harbor of tranquility.

## Verses 19–20

When they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia, they saw Jesus walking upon the sea and drawing near to the boat. And they were afraid.

But he said to them: “I am he; do not be afraid.”

### Augustine, same work, section 6

The waves grow, darkness increases, storms rage; yet the boat continues, because “whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22).

Nor does the number of stadia seem to be without significance. Why did the evangelist say, “about twenty-five or thirty stadia”? It would have been enough to say “twenty-five or thirty,” except that the evangelist uttered these numbers as an estimate, not as an affirmation.

Let us therefore examine the number. From what does twenty-five consist? From what is it made? From five. That number five pertains to the Law: the five books of Moses, the five porticoes containing the sick, and the five loaves feeding the five thousand.

The number twenty-five therefore signifies the Law, because five times five—that is, five multiplied by five—makes twenty-five, a square number, with five added [manuscript and Augustine: “they make twenty-five, the square of five”].

But before the Gospel came, this Law lacked perfection. Perfection, however, is comprehended in the number six. For six is a perfect number, and it is completed by its parts [manuscript: “is completed”]—that is, one, two, and three. No other parts can be found in it, nor can those parts joined together produce anything other than the number six.

For this reason God completed the world in six days. The five are multiplied by six so that the Law may be fulfilled through the Gospel: six times five makes thirty.

Jesus therefore comes to those who fulfill the Law. And how does he come? Treading upon the waves, holding all the world’s swellings beneath his feet, pressing down all the heights of the age.

### Augustine, same work, section 7

Yet the tribulations are so great that even those who have believed in Jesus and strive to persevere become afraid lest they fail, while Christ treads upon the waves of the age.

Why does the Christian fear while Christ is speaking? “I am he; do not be afraid. Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16).

## Verse 21

So they wanted to receive him into the boat. Recognizing him and rejoicing, they became secure. And immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going.

The journey had reached its end at the shore: from the wet to the solid, from what was troubled to what was firm, from the journey to the destination—that is, to perfect tranquility, which will exist only in the harbor of eternal serenity.

There will be complete love and no iniquity, complete happiness and no disturbance. There those will reign without end who here labor courageously to the end of their lives.

## Verses 22–23

The next day, the crowd that stood on the other side of the sea saw that there was no other boat there except one, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples alone had departed.

Other boats, however, came from Tiberias, near the place where they had eaten the bread after thanks had been given to God.

## Chapter 13

Sought by the crowds and found, he says: “Work for the food not that perishes, but that which remains unto eternal life.” And he declares himself to be the true bread from heaven and the life of the world.

## Verse 24

When the crowd therefore saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they got into the boats and came to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.

### Augustine, same work, sections 8–10

Nevertheless, so great a miracle had been intimated to them. For they saw that the disciples alone had entered the boat and that the boat was not there.

They came from that place, however, and boats were near the place where they had eaten the bread, in which the crowds had followed him. He had not gone up with the disciples; no other boat was there.

How, then, did Jesus suddenly come across the sea, unless he walked upon the sea in order to display the miracle?

And when the crowds had found him, behold, he presents himself to the crowds from whom he had feared being seized and had fled to the mountain—clearly confirming and suggesting to us that all those words had been spoken mystically and that the deeds had taken place in a great mystery, so that they might signify something.

Behold, he is present who had fled from the crowds to the mountain. Does he not now speak with those very crowds? Let them seize him now; let them now make him king.

## Verse 25

When they had found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him: “Rabbi, when did you come here?”

After the mystery of the miracle, he introduces his discourse, so that, if possible, those who had been fed might themselves be fed, and that he whose bread had filled their stomachs might satisfy their minds with his words—but in such a way that they could grasp them; and if they did not grasp them, they might take what they could grasp [Augustine: “let what they do not grasp be taken”], lest the fragments perish.

Let the Lord therefore speak, and let us hear what follows:

## Verse 26

Jesus answered and said to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate from my loaves and were satisfied.”

You seek me for the sake of the flesh, not for the sake of the spirit.

How many do not seek Jesus except so that he may make things go well for them in this present life? One has a business matter and seeks the intercession of the clergy; another is oppressed by a powerful person and flees to the Church; another wants someone to intervene for him with one against whom he has little influence. One acts this way, another that way; the Church is filled daily with such people. Jesus is scarcely sought for Jesus’ sake.

“You are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate from my loaves and were satisfied.”

## Verse 27

“Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which remains unto eternal life.”

You seek me for another reason; seek me for my own sake. He indicates himself as this food, which shines forth in what follows, and which the Son of Man will give you.

You were expecting, I suppose, to eat bread again, recline again, and be filled again. But he himself had said [variant: “himself”]: “Food not that perishes, but that which remains unto eternal life.”

Above we said that the boat signifies the Church of Christ, which is troubled by the storms of this age and carries within it those who labor, urging them to labor courageously until Christ suppresses the waves of persecution and restores serenity.

Here, however, he says: “The next day the crowd that stood on the other side of the sea saw that there was no other boat there except one.”

What does it mean for the crowd to stand upon the sea on the next day except that, after Christ’s ascension, the crowd stands in good works—not lying prostrate in earthly mire, but awaiting the coming of Jesus to them?

Here also one boat is mentioned, just as previously there was one Church of Christ, in which he was bodily present. Now also there is one Church, which similarly awaits his coming in hope.

But what does it mean that other boats came from Tiberias except the gatherings of heretics, who do not seek Jesus with sincere faith? Under the deceit of cunning they seek their own interests, not the things of Jesus Christ (Philippians 2:21).

Accordingly, Jesus answered them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate from the loaves and were satisfied.”

Of those who have been satisfied he says in another Gospel: “Woe to you who are satisfied” (Luke 6:25).

But concerning those who hunger for the bread of life and knowledge of righteousness, it is said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matthew 5:6).

It was to this food that Christ immediately exhorted them in the following discourse, saying: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which remains unto eternal life.”

Carnal food perishes, but spiritual food remains—the food that the Son of Man will give you.

This one God the Father has signified [variant: “sealed”].

### Augustine, same work, section 11

Do not understand this Son of Man as though he were one of the other sons of men, concerning whom it is said: “But the sons of men will hope in the protection of your wings” (Psalm 36:8).

This Son of Man has been set apart from the other sons of men by a certain grace of God. This Son of Man, distinguished from the number of human beings, is Son of Man. This Son of Man is also Son of God; this human being is also God.

Therefore the Truth itself, which was then speaking to the Jews and now speaks to all through the words of evangelical preaching, indicates who he is—not what many then judged him to be, or even now judge him to be.

He added: “For God the Father has signified him” [manuscript: “sealed him”].

What does “to seal” mean except to assign something as distinctive? To seal is to place something that will not be confused with other things. To seal is to place the sign of a thing. Whenever you place a sign on something, you do so so that it may not be confused with other things and become unrecognizable to you.

The Father therefore sealed him. What does “he sealed him” mean? He gave him something distinctive, so that he would not be compared with other human beings. Hence it is said: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 45:8).

What, then, does “to seal” mean? To hold as distinguished; this is what “above your companions” means.

Therefore, he says, do not despise me because I am Son of Man, but ask me for food—not food that perishes, but food that remains unto eternal life.

For I am Son of Man in such a way that I am not one of you. I am Son of Man in such a way that God the Father sealed me.

What does “to seal” mean? To give me something distinctive, so that I would not be confused with the human race, but so that through me the human race might be liberated.

## Verse 28

Therefore they said to him: “What shall we do, so that we may perform the works of God?”

### Augustine, same work, sections 12–13

For he had said to them: “Work for food not that which perishes, but that which remains unto eternal life.”

“What shall we do?” they said. “By observing what command will we be able to fulfill this?”

## Verse 29

Jesus answered and said to them: “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent.”

This, then, is to eat food not that perishes, but that remains forever [manuscript: “unto eternal life”].

Why prepare your teeth and your stomach? Believe, and you have eaten.

Faith is indeed distinguished from works, as the apostle says, that a person is justified by faith without the works of the Law (Romans 3:28).

There are works that appear good without faith in Christ, yet are not good, because they are not referred to the end from which all good things proceed. For “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4).

Therefore he did not distinguish faith from the work, but said that faith itself is the work. For it is faith that works through love (Galatians 5:6).

Nor did he say, “This is your work”; rather, he said: “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent,” so that “whoever boasts may boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31).

Because he was inviting them to faith, they still sought signs by which they might believe.

See whether the Jews are not asking for signs.

## Verse 30

Therefore they said to him: “What sign are you going to perform, so that we may see and believe you? What work are you doing?”

Was it not enough that they had been fed from the five loaves? They knew this indeed, but they preferred manna from heaven to this food.

The Lord Jesus, however, was declaring himself to be such that he should be preferred to Moses. Moses did not dare to say of himself that he would give food not that perishes, but that has eternal life [Augustine: “that remains unto eternal life”].

The Lord was promising something greater than Moses. Through Moses, a kingdom and a land flowing with milk and honey, temporal peace, an abundance of children, bodily health, and all the other temporal things were promised—though in a figure they were spiritual things, since they were promised to the old person in the old covenant [manuscript: “and because they were promised”].

They were considering what had been promised through Moses [variant: “through Christ concerning Moses”], and they were considering what was promised through Jesus.

Moses promised a full stomach on earth, but with food that perishes; this one promised food not that perishes, but that remains unto eternal life.

They were considering one who promised more, yet seemed not to see him doing greater things. They were certainly considering the kinds of things Moses had done, and still wanted some greater things to be performed by the one who promised such great things.

“What are you doing,” they said, “so that we may believe you?”

And so that you may know that they were comparing those miracles with this miracle, and therefore judged these to be greater than the things Jesus was doing—or, according to the manuscript and Augustine, “judged these to be lesser than the things he was doing”—

## Verse 31

“Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness,” they said. But what is manna? Perhaps you despise it, as it is written: “He gave them manna to eat.”

Through Moses our fathers received bread from heaven, and Moses was not told: “Work for food that does not perish, but that remains unto eternal life.” Yet you do not perform such works as Moses did.

He did not give barley loaves, but manna from heaven.

## Verses 32–33

Jesus therefore said to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gave you bread from heaven. For the true bread is the one who descends from heaven and gives life to the world.”

The true bread, then, is the one who gives life to the world, and he himself is the food of which I spoke shortly before: “Work for the food that does not perish, but that remains unto eternal life.”

Therefore that manna also signified this, and all those things were my signs. You loved my signs; you despise what they signified.

Moses therefore did not give the bread from heaven. God gives the bread. But what bread? Perhaps manna? No, but the bread signified by manna—namely, the Lord Jesus himself.

“My Father gives you the true bread.” The true bread of God is the one who descends from heaven and gives life to the world.

## Verse 34

Therefore they said to him: “Lord, always give us this bread.”

Just as the Samaritan woman, to whom he said, “Whoever drinks from this water will never thirst,” immediately understood it according to the body, yet desired to be free from need, and said, “Lord, give me this water”; so these people also said: “Lord, give us this bread, which will refresh us and never fail.”

## Chapter 14

He declares himself to be the bread of life, and that believers in him will rise on the last day.

## Verse 35

Jesus therefore said to them: “I am the bread of life” [manuscript: “the living bread”]. “Whoever comes to me will not hunger, and whoever believes in me will never thirst.”

@ [Col. 0829D] See St. Augustine, the cited passage, nos. 14, 15, 16, 18, and 19. “He who comes to me”—this is what he means by “and he who believes in me”; and what he said, “shall not hunger,” is to be understood as “shall never thirst.” By both expressions eternal satisfaction is signified, where there is no want. You desire bread from heaven; you have it before you, and you do not eat it.

(VERS. 36.) “But I told you that you have both seen me and have not believed” (Rom. III, [Col. 0830B] 3). “But it is not for that reason that I have lost the people. Has your unbelief, then, annulled the faithfulness of God? Let us see what follows:

(VERS. 37.) ‘Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will certainly not cast out.’ What is that interior place from which one does not go out? A great inner chamber and a sweet secret place. O secret place without weariness, without the bitterness of evil thoughts, without the interruption of temptations and sorrows! Is it not that secret place into which the one will enter to whom God will say: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord’ (Matt. XXV, 23)? And: ‘Whoever comes to me I will certainly not cast out.’

(VERS. 38.) ‘Because I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.’ Therefore you will not cast out the one who comes to you, because you have come down from heaven not to do your own will, but the will of him who sent you. It is a great mystery that he says: ‘Whoever comes to me I will certainly not cast out.’ Immediately adding the reason why he would not cast out the one who comes to him—that is, the one who believes in him—he says [Ms., *saying*]: ‘Because I did not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.’”

Who is cast out from that sweet and most delightful secret place into which the servant who does his lord’s will is commanded to enter, except the proud person, except the soul that trusts in itself and seeks to belong to its own power, not having with the prophet the words: “Is not my soul subject to God?” (Ps. LXI). But the soul subjected through humility to God’s grace will never be cast out; rather, it enters into the joy of the Lord its God.

“Therefore, in order that the cause of all diseases—namely, pride—might be cured, humility descended; that is, the Son of God humbled himself. Why are you proud, O human being? God became humble for your sake. Perhaps you would be ashamed to imitate a humble human being; at least imitate the humble God. The Son of God came in human form and became humble: you are commanded to be humble, not commanded to turn from a human being into a beast. He, God, became human; you, a human being, recognize that you are human. Your entire humility consists in recognizing yourself. Therefore, because God teaches humility, he said: ‘I did not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.’ This is indeed a commendation of humility. Pride does its own will; humility does the will of God.

[Col. 0831A] “Therefore, whoever comes to me I will not cast out. Why? Because I did not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me. I came in humility; I came to teach humility; I came as the teacher of humility. Whoever comes to me is incorporated into me; whoever comes to me becomes humble; whoever clings to me [Al., *who will be present*; Ms., *clings*] will be humble, because he will not do his own will, but God’s. And therefore he will not be cast out, because Adam, when he was proud, was cast out.”

But Christ, having become humble, was exalted above every name that is named either in heaven or on earth (Phil. II). “He came as the teacher of humility, not to do his own will, but the will of him who sent him. Let us come to him, let us enter into him, let us be incorporated into him, so that we too may do not our own will, but the will of God; and he will not cast us out, because we are his members, since he chose to be our head by teaching humility.” No one can come to him except the humble; and no one is sent away by him except the proud.

(VERS. 39.) “This is the will of the Father who sent me: that I should lose nothing of everything that he has given me, but should raise it up on the last day.”

“He himself is the one who was given. Whoever preserves humility receives this; whoever does not preserve [Aug., ‘He himself was given to the one who preserves humility; he receives him; whoever does not preserve’] humility is far from the teacher of humility. ‘That I should lose nothing of everything that the Father has given me.’ Thus it is not the will of your Father that one of these little ones should perish. Something may perish of those who are swollen with pride; nothing perishes of the little ones, because unless you become like this little one, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XVIII, 4). ‘Everything that the Father has given me I will not lose, but I myself will raise it up on the last day.’ See how here too he delineates [Ms., *will delineate*; Aug., *may delineate*] that twofold resurrection. Whoever comes to me now rises, having become humble among my members; but I will raise him up on the last day according to the flesh.”

(VERS. 40.) “For this is the will of my Father who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life. And I will raise him up on the last day.”

Above he said: “Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me”; but now: “Whoever sees the Son and believes in him.” He did not say, “sees the Son and believes in the Father”; for to believe in the Son is the same as to believe in the Father. “For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John V, 26). “That everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life”—by believing and passing over into life, as through that first resurrection [Aug., *by that first resurrection*]. And because it is not the only one, he says, “I will raise him up on the last day.”

It follows: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.” Therefore he is bread because he is life; and therefore life because he came down from heaven, as he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” He is the supersubstantial bread which we are commanded to ask to be given to us daily, when our Lord Jesus Christ said that he had come down from heaven as bread.

## CHAPTER XV

The Pharisees murmur and call him the son of Joseph. And among many other things he says that he will give his flesh as bread for the life of the world. He bears witness to many other similar things concerning his bread and flesh. [Col. 0832A]

(VERS. 41, 42.) “The Jews murmured, and said to him: ‘Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then does he say, “I have come down from heaven”?’”

They murmured because they did not understand this bread, did not hunger for this bread, and did not love this bread. If they had loved it, surely they would not have murmured.

@ In Saint Augustine, *Tractate XXVI on John*, nos. 1, 5, 6, 7, 9–13, 15–20. “Therefore they were far from the heavenly bread and did not know how to hunger for it. They had languid throats of the heart; with open ears they were deaf; they saw, and yet stood blind. For this bread seeks the hunger of the inner person [Col. 0832B]; hence elsewhere he says: ‘Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied’ (Matt. V, 6).”

They said: “Whose father and mother we know.” They knew an earthly mother; they did not know a heavenly Father, because they had not been drawn by the heavenly Father. The Lord himself soon made this known in the following words, saying:

(VERS. 43, 44.) “Do not murmur among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.”

What does “No one can come to me” mean, except that no one can believe in me unless the Father who sent me draws him? He comes whom the grace of God has preceded, to whom we say with the Prophet: “His mercy will go before me” (Ps. LVIII). And again: “His mercy will follow me” (Ps. XXII). It precedes the willing and follows through to completion.

“The Father draws to the Son those who therefore believe in the Son because they think that he has God as his Father. For God the Father begot a Son equal to himself; and whoever thinks, senses in faith, and meditates that the one in whom he believes is equal to the Father—the Father himself draws that person to the Son.”

For whoever says of Christ, “He is not the true God,” is not drawn by the Father; rather, his perverse thought draws him not to consent to the truth.

“He is drawn by the Father who says: ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.’ To him the Lord says: ‘Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven’ (Matt. XVI, 16–17). This revelation is itself the drawing. For when he said, ‘No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him,’ he immediately added: ‘And I will raise him up on the last day.’ Believing what he hopes for, he will see what, while not yet seeing it, he has believed; he will eat what he hungered for and be satisfied with what he thirsts for. Where? In the resurrection of the dead. Because I will raise him up on the last day.

(VERS. 45.) “For it is written in the prophets: ‘And they shall all be taught by God.’ Why does he say this, O Jews? The Father has not taught you; how can you know me? All the people of that kingdom will be taught by God. They do not hear from human beings; and if they hear from human beings, nevertheless what they understand is given inwardly, flashes inwardly, and is revealed inwardly.”

Human beings can make the word resound outwardly, but they labor in vain unless God, teaching inwardly, opens the senses. That person is taught by God whom God inwardly instructs in the recognition and love of the truth.

“Everyone who hears from the Father and learns comes to me.” How does the Father draw? By teaching and giving delight, not by imposing necessity, because no one believes under compulsion, but willingly. The Son was speaking; the Father was teaching. The human being who was visible was speaking, but God, as the one teaching within the heart of the hearer, was instructing inwardly. Therefore he added:

(VERS. 46.) “Not that anyone has seen the Father, except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father.”

Do not suppose that the Father is visible to you. No one has seen the Father except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father. I am from the Father, and therefore I see the Father.

“What, then, does it mean that you are drawn by the Father, except that you learn from the Father? What does it mean to learn from the Father, except to hear the Father? And what does it mean to hear from the Father, except to hear the Word of the Father—that is, me? Lest, therefore, when I say to you, ‘Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned,’ you say among yourselves, ‘But we have never seen the Father; how, then, could we learn from the Father?’ Hear from me: ‘Not that anyone has seen the Father, but the one who is from God has seen the Father.’ I know the Father; I am from him. But how does the word come from the one whose word it is? Not like a sound that is uttered and passes away, but as that which remains with the speaker and draws the hearer.

“It follows:

(VERS. 47.) ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever believes in me has eternal life.’ He wished to reveal what he was; for he could have said briefly: ‘Whoever believes in me has me.’ For Christ himself is the true God and eternal life. Whoever therefore believes in me, he says, comes to me; and whoever comes to me has me. But what does it mean to have me? To have eternal life. Eternal life assumed death and was willing to die, but from what belonged to you, O human being, not from what belonged to itself: it received from you that in which it would die for you. Eternal life therefore assumed death, so that life might kill death. For whoever believes, he says, has eternal life—not the life that is manifest, but the life that is hidden. For eternal life was the Word in the beginning with God, and the Word was God, and it was life, the light of human beings. He came to die, but on the third day he rose again.

(VERS. 48, 49.) ‘I am,’ he says, ‘the bread of life.’ And why should they be proud? ‘Your fathers,’ he says, ‘ate manna and died.’ Why did they eat and die? Because they believed what they saw; what they did not see, they did not understand. Therefore they are called your fathers, because you are like them. Moses and Aaron [Col. 0833D] and the other holy people who were among the people ate manna, and they did not die, because they understood the visible food spiritually; they hunger spiritually [Ms., *they hungered spiritually*].” Others, however, ate and remained in unbelief, just as the Jews heard Christ speaking but did not understand his words spiritually. Therefore he said to them: “Your fathers ate manna in the desert and died.” By what death, except the death of unbelief? For the holy people who were among them also died the common death. Therefore by these words the Lord signified spiritual death, not bodily death.

“The fathers of these people, then—that is, evil fathers of evil people, unbelieving fathers, unbelieving murmurers, fathers of murmurers [Ms. and Aug., ‘unbelieving fathers of unbelievers; murmurers, fathers of murmurers’]. For this people is said to have offended God in no matter more than by murmuring against God. Therefore, wishing to show that they were children of such people, the Lord began from this point with them: ‘Why do you murmur among yourselves, murmurers, children of murmurers? Your fathers ate manna and died—not because the manna was bad, but because they ate it badly.’”

(VERS. 50.) “This is the bread that came down from heaven.”

“This bread was signified by the manna; this bread is signified by the altar of God. The sacraments existed there; they differ in their signs, but in the reality signified they are equal. Hear the Apostle: ‘For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food’ (1 Cor. X, 1 ff.). Certainly spiritual, not bodily. Another [Aug., ‘certainly the same spiritually; for bodily, another’], because they had manna and we have something else; but the spiritual food was the same as ours; and they were our fathers, not the fathers of those to whom we are like, but of those to whom they themselves were like.

“This, then, is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he will not die. But this concerns the power of the sacrament, not the visible sacrament; the one who eats inwardly, not outwardly; the one who eats in the heart, not the one who presses with the tooth.

(VERS. 51.) ‘I am the living bread that came down from heaven.’” [Col. 0834C] He is living, therefore, because he came down from heaven. Manna also came down from heaven, but manna was a shadow; this is the truth.

(VERS. 52.) “‘If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever; and the bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world.’ When would flesh comprehend what he said—that bread is flesh? What flesh does not comprehend is called flesh; and for that very reason flesh comprehends it even less, because it is called flesh. This is what they recoiled from; this they said was feigned [Ms., *made similar*; Aug., *too much for themselves*]; this they thought could not happen. ‘My flesh,’ he says, ‘is for the life of the world.’

“The faithful know the body of Christ, if they do not neglect to be the body of Christ. Let them become the body of Christ if they wish to live by the Spirit of Christ. No one lives by the Spirit of Christ except the body of Christ.” Whoever wishes to live should believe in Christ and eat spiritual, spiritually understood food. Let him be incorporated into the body of Christ, and let him not be a rotten member deserving to be cut off [Al., *which ought to be cut off*]. Let him be beautiful, healthy, and suited to his head.

(VERS. 53.) “The Jews therefore disputed among themselves, saying: ‘How can this man give us his flesh to eat?’”

“They disputed among themselves because they did not understand the bread of concord, nor did they wish to receive it. For those who eat such bread do not dispute among themselves, since ‘we, though many, are one bread and one body,’ and through this God causes people of one disposition to dwell in a house (1 Cor. X, 17; Ps. LXVII, 7). But when, disputing among themselves, they ask how the Lord can give his flesh to eat, they do not immediately eat [Aug., *hear*]; rather, they are still told:

[Col. 0835A] (VERS. 54.) ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.’ You do not know how it is given [Aug., *eaten*], nor what the manner of eating this bread is; nevertheless, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you do not have life in yourselves.”

@ [Col. 0835D] The Strasbourg edition of 1527 continues as follows:

“Thus he wishes this flesh, this food and drink, to be understood as the fellowship of his body and members, which is the holy Church, which is the body of Christ; and on this matter they disputed. He followed by adding, and so forth.”

But this sentence is wholly irrelevant here. It is found neither in the manuscript codices that I consulted, nor in the edition of the distinguished Quercetanus, [Col. 0836D] nor in Augustine, whom Alcuin transcribed. It was therefore inserted by some malicious person in order stealthily to corrupt Alcuin’s understanding of the truth of Christ’s body and blood in the Eucharist; and other heretics have attempted the same thing in the writings of other Fathers.

These words, then, were not spoken to corpses but to living people. Therefore, lest those who understood this life should dispute about the matter, he continued:

{529} (VERS. 55.) “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.”

“He therefore does not have this life who does not eat this bread and drink this blood. For people who are not in his body through faith can, in whatever way, have temporal life without him in this world; but eternal life, which is promised to the saints, they can never have. But lest they should suppose that eternal life was promised in this food and drink in such a way that those who received it would no longer die bodily—those who take it carnally [Ms., ‘of which they take carnally’; Al., ‘understand carnally’] and do not understand it spiritually in faith—he deigned to address this thought as well.

“For after saying, ‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life,’ he immediately added and said: ‘And I will raise him up on the last day.’ Thus he may meanwhile have eternal life according to the spirit, in the rest that receives the spirits of the saints; but as regards the body, his life is not deprived of eternity [Ms., ‘nor does it deprive them . . .’]; rather, on the resurrection of the dead, on the last day, the flesh” [Col. 0835C] “will rise alive” [Ms., “the flesh will be raised up”].

(VERS. 56.) “For my flesh,” he says, “is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.”

“For when people desire food and drink so that they may not hunger or thirst, this is truly provided by no food and drink except that which makes those who partake of it immortal and incorruptible—that is, the fellowship itself of the saints, where there will be peace and complete and perfect unity.

“For this reason, as people of God before us also understood, our Lord Jesus Christ commended his body and blood to us under those things that are brought together from many into one. For one thing is made and composed into one from many grains; another flows together into one from many clusters [Al., *berries*]. Finally, he now explains how what he says comes about, and what it means to eat his body and drink his blood.

(VERS. 57.) ‘And whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood,’ he says, ‘remains in me, and I in him.’ To eat that food and drink that drink, then, is to remain in Christ and to have him remain in oneself. Accordingly, whoever does not remain in Christ, and in whom Christ does not remain, undoubtedly does not eat his flesh spiritually, even though carnally and visibly he presses the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood with his teeth. Rather, he eats and drinks the sacrament of so great a reality to his own judgment, because, being unclean, he presumptuously approaches Christ’s sacraments, which no one receives worthily unless he is clean. Of such people it is said: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’ (Matt. V, 8).

(VERS. 58.) ‘As the living Father sent me,’ he says, ‘and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will live because of me.’ The Son does not become better through participation in the Father, since he was born equal to him; but our participation in the Son through the unity of his body and blood—which that eating and drinking signifies—makes us better.

“We therefore live because of him, eating him—that is, receiving from him the eternal life that we do not have from ourselves. But he lives because of the Father, having been sent by him, because he emptied himself, becoming obedient unto the sign [Al., *death*] of the cross (Phil. II, 8).

“‘As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, and whoever eats me will live because of me’—as if he were saying: In order that I might live because of the Father, that is, in order that I might refer my life to him as to one greater, my self-emptying brought this about, in which he sent me; but in order that anyone might live because of me, participation brings this about, by which he eats me. I, having been humbled, live because of the Father; he, being upright [Aug., *raised up*], lives because of me.”

He did not speak of that nature by which he is always equal to the Father, but of that nature in which he was made lower than the Father. For above also he had said: “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son to have life in himself”—that is, he begot the Son having life in himself.

(VERS. 59.) “This is the bread that came down from heaven, ‘so that by eating it we may live, because we cannot have eternal life from ourselves. Not as your fathers ate,’ he says, ‘and died: whoever eats this bread will live forever.’ That they died is therefore to be understood as meaning that they do not live forever. Certainly those who eat Christ will also die temporally; but they will live forever because Christ is eternal life.”

@ [Col. 0836D] From St. Augustine, *Tractate XXVII on John*, nos. 1–5.

“The sign that he has eaten and drunk is this: that he remains and is remained in, that he dwells and is dwelt in, that he clings in such a way that he is not abandoned. This, then, he taught and admonished us through mystical words: that we should be in his body, under the head, as his members, eating his flesh and not abandoning his unity.

“But many of those who were present were scandalized because they did not understand; for when they heard these things, they thought only of flesh, which is what they themselves were. But the Apostle speaks truly when he says: ‘To think according to the flesh is death’ (Rom. VIII, 6). The Lord gives us his flesh to eat, and yet to think according to the flesh is death, although he says of his flesh that eternal life is there.

“Therefore we must not think of the flesh according to the flesh, as in these words:

(VERS. 61.) ‘Many therefore, when they heard this—not enemies, but his disciples—said: “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?”’ If the disciples found this saying hard, what did the enemies think? And yet it was necessary that what would not be understood by all people should be said. The secret of God ought to make people attentive, not turn them away [Ms. and Aug., *adverse*].

“These people, however, soon failed while the Lord Jesus was speaking such things. They did not believe him when he spoke something great and concealed some grace in his word [Aug., ‘they did not believe him speaking something great and concealing some grace in those words’]. They understood it according to their own wishes and, in the human manner, because Jesus was present among them, or because Jesus was arranging this [Ms., ‘and in the human manner, because Jesus had asserted this’; Aug., ‘and in the human manner, because Jesus was able’], they supposed that he would distribute among believers in him, as though it were cut up, the flesh with which the Word was clothed.

“‘This is a hard saying,’ they said; ‘who can hear it?’

(VERS. 62.) “But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were murmuring about this [Aug. and Ms., *about him*], said: ‘Does this scandalize you?’ Because I said, ‘I give you my flesh to eat and my blood to drink,’ this is what scandalizes you.

(VERS. 63.) “‘Then what if you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?’ What does this mean? Does he thereby resolve what had disturbed them? Does he thereby disclose the source of their scandal? Certainly—if they understood. For they thought that he would distribute his body, but he said that he would ascend into heaven, whole and entire. When you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before, then certainly you will see that he does not distribute his body in the manner you suppose. Then certainly you will understand that his grace is not consumed by bites.”

In these words it is clearly understood that Christ is one person, since he said that the Son of Man had previously been in heaven.

“He was speaking on earth and said that he was in heaven. What does this imply except that we should understand Christ God and man to be one person, not two, lest our faith be not a Trinity but a Quaternity? Christ, therefore, is one: Word, soul, and flesh are one Christ; Son of God and Son of Man are one Christ. Son of God eternally, Son of Man in time; nevertheless one Christ according to the unity of person. He was in heaven when he was speaking on earth. The Son of Man was in heaven in the same way that the Son of God was on earth. The Son of God was on earth in the flesh he had assumed; the Son of God [Ms. and Aug., *Son of Man*] was in heaven in the unity of person.”

He immediately explains more broadly the difference between spirit and flesh, and between wishing to eat Christ carnally and receiving him spiritually. For he says:

(VERS. 64.) “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is of no benefit at all.”

A little earlier he said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves”; but now he says: “The flesh is of no benefit at all”—that is, if you wish to understand what I say carnally, the flesh is of no benefit at all; if you understand the flesh as something to be eaten in the same way as other food, like meat purchased in butcher shops, the flesh is of no benefit at all.

“It is therefore the Spirit who gives life. Through the Spirit the flesh is beneficial, although by itself it is not beneficial, because the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

“For through the flesh the Spirit accomplished something for our salvation. The flesh was a vessel; through it the Spirit saved [Ms., *saved*] us, using the instrument of the flesh for the salvation of the human race, just as the devil used the serpent as an instrument for the overthrow of our first parent.

“‘It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is of no benefit at all.’ I do not give my flesh to be eaten in the way they understood flesh.”

{531}

## CHAPTER XVI

He declares that his words are spirit and life, and calls one of the Twelve a devil.

@

From St. Augustine, *Tractate XXVII on John*, nos. 6, 7, 9, 10.

“Therefore the words,” he says, “that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. For we have said, brothers, that in the eating of his flesh and the drinking of his blood the Lord commended this to us: that we should remain in him, and he in us. We remain in him when we are his members; and he remains in us when we are his temple.

“But in order that we may be his members, unity must join us together; and in order that unity may join us together, what brings this about except the love of God? From where does this come? Ask the Apostle: ‘The love of God,’ he says, ‘has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us’ (Rom. V, 5).

“Therefore it is the Spirit who gives life. For the Spirit makes the members living; and the Spirit does not make living members except those whom Christ himself finds in the body that he animates [Aug., *the Spirit himself*]. For the spirit that is in you, O human being, by which you exist as a human being—does it give life to a member that it finds separated from your flesh? I mean your spirit, your soul. Your soul gives life only to the members that are in your flesh; if you remove one, it is no longer given life by your soul, because it is not joined to the unity of your body.

“These things are said so that we may love unity and fear separation. For a Christian ought to fear nothing so much as being separated from the body of Christ. If he is separated from the body of Christ, he is not his member; if he is not his member, he is not animated by his Spirit. ‘Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ,’ the Apostle says, ‘does not belong to him’ (Rom. VIII, 9).

“Therefore it is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is of no benefit at all. ‘The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.’ What does ‘they are spirit and life’ mean except that they are to be understood spiritually? Did you understand them spiritually? They are spirit and life. Did you understand them carnally? Even then they are spirit and life, but they are not so for you, O human being, if you do not understand them spiritually and do not know how to venerate them in faith.”

(VERS. 65.) “For there are some among you who do not believe; and therefore they do not understand, because they do not believe. For the Prophet said: ‘Unless you believe, you will not understand’ (Isa. VII, 9, according to the Septuagint). We are joined together through faith; through understanding we are given life. Let us first cling through faith, so that afterward there may be something to receive life through understanding [Aug., ‘so that there may be something to receive life’].

“For Jesus knew from the beginning who the believers were and who would betray him. For Judas was among those who were scandalized; Christ neither remained silent about him nor openly pointed him out, so that all might fear, although one would perish. But after he had spoken of and distinguished believers from unbelievers, he expressed the reason why they did not believe.”

(VERS. 66.) “Therefore I said to you,” he says, “that no one can come to me unless it has been granted to him by my Father. For faith will be given by the Father to believers, so that no one may boast in his faith, as though it came from himself and were his own, but may recognize it as given by God, as grace.”

(VERS. 67.) “From that time many of his disciples went back and no longer walked with him.” They went back—not after Christ, but after Satan. They went back in such a way that they were cut off from the body of Christ and did not thereafter return to him, because they had not been steadfastly faithful in his body [Ms., *perhaps*]. And they were not few, but many.

“Let us hear, then, what he said to the few who remained.

(VERS. 68.) “Jesus therefore said to the Twelve: ‘Do you also want to leave?’ Judas did not depart either; but why he remained with the Lord was later revealed to us. Peter answered for all: one for many, unity for the united [Aug., *for all*].

“Simon Peter therefore answered: ‘Lord, to whom shall we go? Give us another like you, to whom we may go. If we depart from you, to whom shall we go?’ [Aug.: ‘Give us another you. To whom shall we go? If we depart from you, to whom shall we go?’]

(VERS. 69.) “You have the words of eternal life.” See how Peter, by the Lord’s gift and the Holy Spirit’s renewal, understood. From where, except because he believed the words of eternal life? You have eternal life in the ministry of your body and blood.

[Col. 0839D] (VERS. 70.) “And we have believed, and we have known.” He did not say, “We have known and believed,” but “We have believed and known.” For we believed in order to know; if we had wished first to know and then to believe, we would have been able neither to know nor to believe.

“What have we believed and what have we known? That you are the Christ, the Son of God. That is, that you yourself are eternal life, and that in your flesh and blood you give nothing except what you are.”

(VERS. 71, 72.) “Jesus answered them: ‘Did I not choose you Twelve, and one of you is a devil?’ He was speaking of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot. For he was going to betray him, although he was one of the Twelve.”

He was one of the Twelve not in faith but in number, not in truth but in pretense. But how should we understand “Did I not choose you Twelve,” when that one is said to be a son of the devil, unless the eleven were chosen in one way and that one in another?

“They were chosen so that they might remain in Christ and so that their sound might go out through the whole world; that one was chosen so that through him the dispensation of divine mercy might be fulfilled for the salvation of the human race. Thus God’s goodness made good use of his wickedness, just as God made good use of the wickedness of Joseph’s brothers in selling him (Gen. XXXVII), so that from their evil deed the goodness of God might be shown for the salvation [Ms., *in the salvation*] of many. Thus Judas’s evil was turned into our good. What the evil person does by misusing God’s good gifts harms himself; he cannot destroy God’s goodness.

“Why did Christ choose twelve? ‘The number twelve is sacred. It was not, therefore, because one of that number perished that the honor of the number was taken away; for another was substituted in the place of the one who perished. The consecrated number remained—that is, the number twelve—because he was going to announce the Trinity throughout the whole world, that is, through the four quarters of the world. Therefore three groups of four’ were chosen, so that the Holy Trinity might be preached throughout the four parts of the world.

“For the year also proceeds according to the number twelve, and the order of the signs in heaven, through which the moon is accustomed to travel, is known to be divided according to the number twelve.
