Therefore Christ God sent the first preachers into the world according to this number. The number was not violated when Judas perished; another was substituted in his place.

“Concerning the most sacred significance of this number, Christ himself says in the Gospel, speaking of the highest glory of the saints: ‘When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel’ (Matt. XIX, 28).”

## BOOK FOUR

## CHAPTER XVII

When the Jews sought to kill him, he went up secretly to the feast of Booths, where various things are said about him and by him. And when they sought to seize him, they could not, because his hour had not yet come.

[Col. 0839D]

## CHAPTER VII, VERSE 1

“After these things,” the evangelist says, “Jesus went about in Galilee. For he did not wish to go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him.” «
[Col. 0839D] Saint Augustine, *Tractate* XXVIII, nos. 2–4, 6, 8, 10–12.

“This he offered as an example to our weakness. He had not himself lost power, but was consoling our frailty. For it was going to happen, as I have said, that one of his faithful would hide himself lest he be found by persecutors; and lest hiding be charged against him as a crime, he went before us in the Head, so that it might be confirmed in the members.” Christ could indeed go into Judea [Ms., “among the Jews”] and not be killed, since he said: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18). He displayed this power when he wished, when those who came to seize him with weapons fell backward at his voice.

**(Verse 2.)** “Now the Jewish feast of Booths was near” [Ms., “of the construction of booths”]. *Scenopegia* is the feast on which the Jews were commanded, in the seventh month, to live for seven days in tents beneath the branches of trees, in remembrance of their dwelling in the wilderness. This was the feast which the Jews celebrated with great solemnity, as though recalling the Lord’s benefits, who had led them out of the land of Egypt. The feast is called a “day” according to Jewish usage—not one day only, but all the days belonging to that festival; they customarily called them one feast-day because of the unity of the celebration.

**(Verse 3.)** “His brothers therefore said to him: ‘Leave here and go into Judea.’” The Lord’s “brothers” were called his relatives according to the very common usage of Holy Scripture concerning the ever-virgin holy Mary. Thus Abraham and Lot are called brothers, although Abraham was Lot’s uncle; and Laban and Jacob are called brothers, although Laban was Jacob’s maternal uncle (Gen. 14:14; 29:15). Whenever, then, you hear of the Lord’s brothers, understand Mary’s relatives, not any further offspring of one who bore another child.

“We have said who these brothers were; let us hear what they said: ‘Leave here and go into Judea, so that your disciples also may see the works that you do.’” The Lord’s works were not hidden from his disciples, but they were hidden from these men. These brothers—that is, Christ’s relatives—were able to have Christ as their kinsman, but because of that very closeness they disdained to believe in him. Therefore the Evangelist immediately continued:

**(Verse 4.)** “For neither did his brothers believe in him.” Why did they not believe in him? Because they sought human glory, saying to him:

**(Verse 5.)** “For no one does anything in secret while seeking himself to be known openly. If you do these things, show yourself to the world.” These words show that they were seeking his glory in a carnal manner, as though they had said: “You perform miracles, but you hide yourself. Go into Judea, so that the rulers of the nation and the capital city of the kingdom [Col. 0841D] may see your wonders. Make yourself known; appear to everyone, so that everyone may praise you.”

What, then, does the Lord Jesus say to this?

**(Verse 6.)** “My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready.” The Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Gal. 4:4). But the time of Christ’s glory had not yet come when he said these things. That was what those men appeared to be seeking when they urged him to go into Judea, perform a miracle, and make himself known to the world, lest he be thought insignificant because he remained hidden. But he wished to precede exaltation by humility and to reach that very height by the way of humility.

“Your time,” that is, the glory of the world, “is always ready.” There will indeed be a time of glory, because he who came in humility will come in exaltation; he who came to be judged will come to judge; he who came to be killed by the dead will come to judge the living and the dead.

**(Verse 8.)** “Go up to this feast.” What does “this” mean? The place where you seek human glory. What does “this” mean? The place where you wish to extend carnal joys and do not think of eternal ones. “I am not going up to this feast, because my time has not yet been fulfilled.” At this feast you seek human glory; but my time—that is, the time of my glory—has not yet come. My feast will be that day—not one that runs through (*percurrens*) [Aug., “runs before,” *praecurrens*] and passes away in these days, but one that remains forever. That will be festivity: endless joy, eternity without stain, serenity without cloud.

**(Verse 9.)** “When he had said these things, he remained in Galilee.” But when his brothers had gone up, then he too went up to the feast, not openly, but as though in secret. He did not go up to “this” feast because he did not desire temporal glory [Ms., “to glory temporally”], but wished beneficially to teach something, correct people, warn them about the eternal feast, turn their love away from this world, and direct it toward God. What does it mean that he went up to the feast as though secretly? This too is not without meaning and is not an empty work of God [Ms., “of the Lord”]. All the Jewish feasts were figures. Therefore Christ went up to them secretly, because Christ was hidden within them. He was hidden from the earlier people, but is now manifest to the better people, because that people acted in shadow, whereas we act in manifest light.

Some may wish to understand the Lord’s reply—“I am not going up to this feast”—as referring to his Passion, in which [Ms., “because”] Christ did not ascend the cross at the feast of Booths, but at the Passover feast, at which the lamb was accustomed to be killed.

**(Verse 11.)** “The Jews were seeking him at the feast, before he had gone up.” His brothers went up first, and he did not go up at the time when they thought and wished him to do so. Thus this too was fulfilled: “Not to this”—that is, not on the first or second day to which you wish me to go. Later, as the Gospel says, he went up in the middle of the feast [Aug. and Ms., “when the feast was halfway through”], that is, when as many days of the feast had already passed as remained. For, so far as can be understood, they celebrated that festival for many days.

[Col. 0842D]

**(Verse 12.)** “Therefore they were saying: ‘Where is he?’ And there was much murmuring about him among the crowd.” Why the murmuring? Because of disagreement. What disagreement? Some were saying: “He is good.” Others were saying: “No, but he is misleading the crowds.” This is said in the same way about all his servants who excel in some grace: some say, “He is good”; others, “No, but he misleads the crowds.” Why is this so? Because “our life is hidden with Christ in God.”

Christ [Ms., “the body of Christ”] suffers this from the lovers of the world until the end of the age—what he then suffered from the murmuring Jews. The grain has not yet been separated from the chaff, so that the grains of wheat may be gathered into the granary and the chaff burned in eternal fire. What was said about the Lord, therefore, serves for the consolation of any Christian about whom the same thing is said.

**(Verse 13.)** “Yet no one spoke openly about him because of fear of the Jews,” who said, “He is good,” not [Ms., “for”] those who said, “He misleads the crowds.” The sound of those who said “He misleads the crowds” was like the sound of dry leaves; they spoke more loudly, whereas “He is good” was whispered more quietly. But now, brothers, although that glory of Christ which will make us eternal has not yet come, his Church is nevertheless growing so greatly, and he has deigned to spread it throughout the whole world, that it is even whispered, “He misleads the crowds”; but “He is good” resounds more loudly.

For a new heresy whispers secretly in corners: “Christ is adopted.” But the voice of the universal holy Church rings out more clearly: “Christ is the proper Son of God.” They also hiss with serpent-like mouths: “Christ is a named [Ms., ‘nominal’] God.” But the closer and firmer unanimity of all the faithful cries out: “Christ is a good God; he is true God,” as the outstanding preacher testifies: “Their fathers are theirs, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5).

**(Verse 15.)** “The Lord therefore went up to the feast in the middle of the feast, and he was teaching. And the Jews were amazed, saying: ‘How does this man know letters, since he has not studied?’”

[Col. 0843D] From Saint Augustine, *Tractate* XXIX, nos. 2, 3, 5, 6, 8.

“He, because he was hidden [Al., “who was hidden”], was teaching; he spoke openly and was not seized. His being hidden was an example; the latter was an exercise of power. But when he was teaching, the Jews were amazed—all of them, I think, were amazed, but not all were converted. Why were they amazed? Many knew where he had been born and how he had been brought up; they had never seen him studying letters, yet they heard him discussing the Law and producing testimonies from the Law—things no one could produce unless he had read, and no one could read unless he had learned letters. Therefore they were amazed. Their amazement became for the Teacher an opportunity to introduce the truth more deeply. From their amazement and their words, the Lord said something profound and worthy of careful examination.”

What, then, did the Lord answer those who were amazed at how he knew letters which he had not studied?

**(Verse 16.)** “My teaching,” he said, “is not mine, but his who sent me.” This is the first depth [Ms. and Augustine: “This is a first depth”]; for he seems, in a few words, to have said something apparently contradictory. He did not say, “This teaching is not mine,” but “My teaching is not mine.” How is it mine and not mine? The question is how both can be true: mine and not mine.

If we carefully consider what the holy Evangelist says at the beginning—“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”—the solution to this question depends upon it. What, then, is the Father’s teaching, if not the Father’s Word? Christ himself, therefore, is the Father’s teaching, if he is the Father’s Word. But because a word cannot belong to no one, but must belong to someone, he called it his teaching, meaning himself; and he called it not his, because it is the Father’s Word.

The Lord Christ seems to have said: “My teaching is not mine,” as if he were saying: “I am not from myself.” Although we call and believe the Son equal to the Father, and although there is no difference of nature or substance between them, and no interval separating the Begetter from the Begotten [Augustine, “no interval of time”], nevertheless, while preserving and maintaining this, we say that the one is the Father and the other the Son. The Father is not Father if he does not have a Son; the Son is not Son if he does not have a Father. Yet the Son is God from the Father, while the Father is God, but not from the Son. The Father is not God from God, but the Son is God from God, light from light. The Father is light, the Son is light—not two lights, but one light.

The Father is God, the Son is God—not two gods, but one God, Father and Son. The Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, is also God. As the Father is God, and as the Son is God, so also the Holy Spirit is God. Not three gods, but one God: one light, one substance, one nature, one majesty, one eternity, one greatness, one power, one goodness.

The Lord Christ, the Wisdom of God, saw that not everyone would understand this profound mystery. He therefore offered a direction in what followed. Do you wish to understand? Believe. For God said through the prophet: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9, according to the Septuagint). To this belongs what the Lord also added next:

**(Verse 17.)** “If anyone wishes to do his will, he will know about my teaching, whether it is from God or whether I speak from myself.”

What does “If anyone wishes to do his will” mean? But I had said, “If anyone believes,” and had given this advice: “If you do not understand, believe.” Understanding is the reward of faith. Therefore do not seek to understand in order to believe; believe in order to understand, since unless you believe, you will not understand.

Since I had given obedience in believing as the means of attaining understanding, and had said that the Lord Jesus Christ himself joined [Aug., “added”] this to the matter, in the following sentence we find him saying: “If anyone wishes to do his will”—that is, to believe—“he will know about the teaching.” What does “he will know” mean? It means “he will understand.” Because “he will know” means “he will understand,” everyone understands this. But because he says, “If anyone wishes to do his will,” and this pertains to believing, we need the Lord himself as our interpreter, so that he may show us whether doing the will of his Father truly pertains to believing.

Who does not know that doing God’s will means working his work—that is, doing what pleases him? Yet the Lord himself clearly says elsewhere: “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent” (John 6:29). He says, “that you believe in him,” not merely “that you believe him.” But whoever believes him does not immediately believe in him. The demons also believed him, but did not believe in him. Again, we can say concerning his apostles: “We believe Paul,” but we do not believe in Paul; “we believe Peter,” but we do not believe in Peter.

“To the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness” (Rom. 4:5). What, then, does it mean to believe in him? It means to love by believing, to cherish by believing, to go to him by believing [Augustine, “to go into him”], and to be incorporated into his members. This, then, is the faith that God requires of us—the faith that works through love.

If you understand the words of God, understand that Christ is the Son of God, who is the Father’s teaching—not from himself, but the Father’s Son; not from nothing, nor from other subsistent beings, but from the Father alone, remaining in the Father equal to the Father.

**(Verse 18.)** “Whoever speaks from himself seeks his own glory.” This will be [Ms., “seeks”] the one called Antichrist, exalting himself, as the Apostle says, “above everything that is called God or worshiped” (2 Thess. 2:4). The Lord, announcing that he would seek his own glory rather than the Father’s glory, said to the Jews: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me. Another will come in his own name, and him you will receive” (John 5:43). He signified that they would receive Antichrist, who will seek the glory of his own name—puffed up, not substantial; and therefore unstable and destined to ruin.

But our Lord Jesus Christ gave us a great example of humility: he is equal to the Father; “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” He himself said, and said most truly: “I have been with you for so long, and you have not known me. Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14:8). He himself said, and said most truly: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

If, then, he is one with the Father, God equal to the Father, God from God, God with God, coeternal, immortal, equally immutable, equally [without time, equally] Creator and disposer of times; nevertheless, because he came in time, received the form of a servant, and was found in appearance as a man, he seeks the glory of the Father, not his own. What ought you, a human being, to do, when you seek your own glory whenever you do something good, but contrive accusations against God whenever you do something evil?

Pay attention to yourself: you are a creature; acknowledge the Creator. You are a servant; do not despise the Lord. You have been adopted, but not through your own merits. Seek the glory of him from whom you have received this grace, adopted human being, whose glory was sought by the one who was uniquely born from him.

“But whoever seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and there is no injustice in him.” In Antichrist there is injustice, and he is not true, because he will seek his own glory, not the glory of him by whom he was sent. For he was not sent, but permitted to come.

Therefore all who belong to the body of Christ, lest we be caught in the snare of Antichrist, let us not seek our own glory. If he sought the glory of him who sent him to us, how much more ought we to seek the glory of him who made us?

The text continues:

**(Verses 19–20.)** “‘Did not Moses,’ he says, ‘give you the Law, and none of you keeps the Law? Why do you seek to kill me?’”

[Col. 0845D] From Saint Augustine, *Tractate* XXX, nos. 2–7.

“You seek to kill me because none of you keeps the Law. For if you kept the Law, you would recognize Christ in the very letters of the Law and would not kill him when present.”

“And they answered: ‘The crowd answered and said.’ It answered as a crowd—not according to order, but according to disturbance. Finally, since the crowd was disturbed, see what it answered: ‘You have a demon; who is seeking to kill you?’ It was surely worse to say, ‘You have a demon,’ than to kill him. For they said ‘You have a demon’ to the one who was casting demons out. What else could a turbulent crowd say? What else could stirred-up mud smell like except foulness?

“Why is the crowd disturbed? By the truth. The brightness of the light disturbed the crowd’s diseased eyes. Eyes that are not healthy cannot endure the brightness of the light.

“But the Lord was not really disturbed. Tranquil in his truth, he did not return evil for evil or insult for insult. If he had said to them, ‘You have a demon,’ he would certainly have spoken truly. Why would they dare to say to the Truth, ‘You have a demon,’ unless the devil’s falsehood provoked them? Let us hear, then, what the tranquil one answered, and let us live tranquilly [Augustine, in the cited passage: ‘What, then, did he answer? Let us hear tranquilly, and drink what is tranquil’].”

**(Verse 21.)** “I performed one work, and you are all amazed.” It was as though he said: “What would you do if you saw all my works?” The works they saw in the world were his works, but they did not see him who made all things. He performed one deed, and they were disturbed because he had made a man well on the Sabbath.

They did not understand that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath, who established the Sabbath for man, not man for the Sabbath. Nor did he destroy the Sabbath when he made a man well on the Sabbath, because the observance of the Sabbath was given to human beings for their salvation.

**(Verse 22.)** “For this reason Moses gave you circumcision.” It was rightly done that you should receive circumcision from Moses—not because it originated with Moses, but because it came from the patriarchs. Abraham was the first to receive circumcision from the Lord (Gen. 17:10). “And you circumcise a man on the Sabbath.” Moses refutes you. In the Law you received the command to circumcise on the eighth day; in the Law you received the command to rest on the seventh day. If the eighth day of the one who was born falls on the seventh day, the Sabbath, what will you do? Will you rest in order to keep the Sabbath, or will you circumcise in order to fulfill the sacrament of the eighth day?

“But I know,” he says, “what you will do: you will circumcise the man.” Why? Because circumcision pertains to a sign of salvation, and people ought not to rest from salvation on the Sabbath. Therefore do not be angry with me because I made the whole man well on the Sabbath.

**(Verse 23.)** “If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath so that the Law of Moses may not be broken”—for something salutary was established through Moses in that ordinance of circumcision—“why are you angry with me because I made a man entirely well on the Sabbath?”

Perhaps that circumcision signified the Lord himself, at whose healing and restoration they were angry. It was commanded to be performed on the eighth day; and what is circumcision except the stripping away of the flesh? Thus circumcision signifies the stripping away from the heart of carnal desires.

It was not given without reason, nor commanded to be performed on that member, since through that member the mortal human race is propagated. Through one man came death, just as through one man came the resurrection of the dead (1 Cor. 15:21); and through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death (Rom. 5:12).

Therefore everyone is born with a foreskin, because every person is born with the defect of inherited origin. God cleanses no one—whether from the defect with which we are born or from the faults we add by evil living—except by the stone knife, that is, the Lord Jesus Christ. For “the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). They circumcised with stone knives, and by the name of the rock they represented Christ; yet they did not recognize him when present, and even desired to kill him.

But when you circumcise a man on the Sabbath, understand that this signifies the good work which I performed in making the whole man well on the Sabbath: he was healed so that he might be sound in body, and he believed so that he might be sound in mind [Al., “in soul”].

**(Verse 24.)** “Do not judge according to appearance, but judge a righteous judgment.” What does this mean? When you circumcise according to the Law of Moses on the Sabbath, you are not angry with Moses; but because I made a man well on the Sabbath, you are angry with me. You judge according to appearance. Pay attention to the truth and judge a just judgment. If you judge according to truth, you will condemn neither Moses nor me; and once you know the truth, you will know me, because I am the truth.

This vice which the Lord marked here—judging according to persons rather than retaining righteous judgment—is difficult to escape in this world. The Lord admonished the Jews, but he warned us; he convicted them, but instructed us; he rebuked them, but sharpened us. Let us not think that this was not said to us because we were not there at that time.

Let us therefore hear the Gospel as though the Lord were present. Let us not say, “How fortunate were those who were able to see him!” Many among those who saw him physically killed him; many among us who have not seen him believed. Of these it was said: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”

Who is the one who does not judge according to appearance, except the one who loves equally? Whoever loves everyone equally judges equally concerning everyone. Nor should we think that this was said about those whom we honor differently on account of the differing dignity of their ranks, but about those whose cases we are commanded to discern.

[Col. 0847D] From Saint Augustine, *Tractate* XXXI, nos. 1–4.

“The Lord Jesus therefore went up to the feast, not openly but secretly—not because he feared lest [Ms., “that”] he be seized, since he had the power not to be seized, but to signify that already [Ms., “even”] in the very feast celebrated by the Jews, his mystery was to be hidden [Augustine, ‘that he himself was to be hidden’]. But soon the power that had been thought to be timidity became evident. For he spoke openly at the feast, so that the crowds were amazed and said what we heard when the reading was read:”

**(Verses 25–26.)** “Is this not the one whom they were seeking to kill? And behold, he speaks openly, and they say nothing to him. Have the rulers now recognized that this is the Christ?”

Those who knew with what savagery he was being sought were amazed at the power by which he was not seized. Then, not fully [Ms., “plainly”] understanding his power, they thought it was the rulers’ knowledge—that the rulers themselves had recognized him as the Christ—and therefore that they had spared the one whom they had sought for so long to kill.

Then those very men who had said among themselves, “Have the rulers recognized that this is the Christ?” raised for themselves a question by which they concluded that he was not the Christ. They added:

**(Verse 27.)** “But we know where this man is from; when the Christ comes, no one knows where he is from.”

What did the Jews mean by saying, “When the Christ comes, no one knows where he is from,” when, upon Herod’s questioning about the place of his birth, they had indicated it according to the prophecy of the prophet Micah? From this it is certain that they knew the place of his birth. But we must consider what they thought they knew and what they said they did not know. They knew the place of his birth through the words of the prophets, but because of the impiety of their hearts they did not know his divine birth, by which he was eternally born from God the Father. Isaiah says: “Who will recount his generation?” (Isa. 53:8).

Finally, the Lord himself answered both points, speaking both of the weakness of his humility and of the majesty of his birth [Ms., “of the majesty of his divinity”]:

**(Verse 28.)** “Jesus therefore cried out as he taught in the temple: ‘You know me, and you know where I am from.’” He rightly said, “You know me, and you know where I am from.” That is, you know my birth according to the flesh, the nobility of my parents, and the appearance of my face; but according to my divinity you do not know me, because I did not come from myself. Rather, the one who sent me is true, and you do not know him.

But in order that you may know him, believe in the one he sent, and you will know that no one has ever seen God except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, and he has declared him; and no one has known the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son has wished to reveal him.

Finally, after saying, “But the one who sent me is true, and you do not know him,” he added, in order to show them how they could know what they did not know:

**(Verse 29.)** “I know him.” Therefore ask me, so that you may know him. Why do I know him? “Because I am from him, and he sent me.”

Magnificently he showed both things. “I am from him,” he says, because the Son is from the Father; and whatever the Son is, he is from the one whose Son he is. Therefore we call the Lord Jesus “God from God,” whereas we do not call the Father “God from God,” but simply God. We call the Lord Jesus “light from light,” whereas we do not call the Father “light from light,” but simply light.

This, then, is the meaning of “I am from him.” But when you hear, “He sent me,” referring to the fact that you see me in the flesh, do not understand a difference of nature, but the authority of the Begetter.

**(Verse 30.)** “Therefore they sought to seize him, and no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come”—that is, because he did not wish it. He who was born by his will also suffered by his will. Just as he foresaw the hour of his birth, so he predestined the hour of his Passion. If the hour of our death [Al., “his death”] depends on his will, how much more did the hour of his Passion come according to the decision of his will?

Great, then, is the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ: he was made for us in time, through whom the times were made; he was made among all things, through whom all things were made; he was made what he made [Ms., “what was made”], in order to save what he had made. The man-maker was made man, so that what he had made might not perish.

According to this dispensation, the hour of his birth had already come, and he had been born; but the hour of his Passion had not yet come, and therefore he had not yet suffered, because the hour had not yet come at which he wished to suffer. Hence it is read that on the cross, when everything had been completed according to the Scriptures of the prophets, he said: “It is finished.” And, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit (John 19:30). When he wished, the things written about him were completed; and when all had been completed, he released his spirit by his own power.

**CHAPTER XVIII**

He speaks at length to many from the crowd who believe, among other things saying: “Whoever thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” Nicodemus is also resisted by the Pharisees because of his hearing of the Lord.

[Col. 0849D] Saint Augustine, cited passage, nos. 7–10.

“Many from the crowd believed in him. The Lord was saving the humble and the poor; the rulers were raging, and therefore not only did they fail to recognize the physician, but they also desired to kill him. There was a certain crowd which quickly saw its own illness and recognized his medicine without delay.” It believed, moved by the miracles, while the rulers remained in unbelief.

**(Verse 32.)** “And the Pharisees heard the crowd murmuring these things about him.” They murmured because they heard the multitude’s faith, since Christ was being glorified. They quickly sent officers to seize him—the one whom they had not yet been able to seize because he did not wish to be seized—but they heard him teaching, although they had come to seize him.

**(Verse 33.)** Jesus therefore said: “I am with you for a little while longer, and I am going to him who sent me.” What you wish to do now, you will do, but not now, because now I do not wish it. Why do I not wish it yet? Because I am with you for a little while longer, and then I go to him who sent me. I must complete my dispensation and [so] reach my Passion.

**(Verse 34.)** “You will seek me and will not find me, and where I am, you cannot come.”

Here he already foretold his resurrection. They did not wish to recognize him when he was present, and afterward they sought him when they saw that a multitude already believed. Great signs were performed even when the Lord rose and ascended into heaven. Then great things were done through the disciples—but he did them through them, as well as through himself. For he himself had said to them: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

Why could they not come? Because they did not wish to believe, since no one can be saved without faith.

**(Verse 35.)** “The Jews therefore said—not to him, but to themselves: ‘Where is this man going, that we shall not find him? Is he perhaps going to the dispersion of the nations and going to teach the Gentiles?’”

They did not know what they were saying; but because he wished it, they prophesied. The Lord was going to the Gentiles—not by the presence of his body, but by divine power in his disciples, of whom the Prophet said: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things” (Rom. 10:15).

On these feet Christ was going to go to the Gentiles and through them teach the Gentiles, so that the Gentiles might receive the faith which the Jews rejected. Not knowing the truth, they prophesied; and they did not understand Christ saying: “Where I am, you cannot come.” Why can you not come? Because you do not wish to believe.

What does “where I am” mean except “in the bosom of the Father”? I am coeternal with the Father. He was speaking on earth, but was showing that he was in the bosom of the Father.

[Col. 0850D] From Saint Augustine, *Tractate* XXXII, nos. 1, 8.

“Among the other dispensations of our Lord, the teachings of our salvation, and the Jews’ doubts concerning the Lord Jesus Christ—things he said by which some might be confounded and others instructed—on the last day of that feast (for these things were then taking place, and the feast was called *Scenopegia*, that is, the construction of booths), a feast which, as your charity remembers, was discussed previously, the Lord Christ called out—not speaking in an ordinary manner, but crying out—so that whoever thirsts might come to him.

“If we thirst, let us come; not with our feet, but with our affections; not by moving away, but by loving, let us come. Nevertheless, according to the inner person, the one who loves also moves away. But it is one thing to move away bodily and another to move away in the heart. One moves away bodily who changes place by bodily motion; one moves away in the heart who changes affection by movement of the heart. If you love one thing now and loved another before, you are no longer where you were.

“The Lord therefore cried out to us. He stood and cried out:”

## VERSES 38–39

“If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

“We need not linger over what this means, since the Evangelist explained it. For after the Lord had said, ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink,’ and, ‘Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly,’ the Evangelist consequently explained, saying: ‘Now he said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were going to receive.’ Let us know only this: the Lord Jesus cried out about charity.

“He therefore cries out and says that we should come and drink, if the soul thirsts within [Augustine: ‘if we thirst within’], because when we have drunk, rivers of living water will flow from our belly. The belly of the inner person is the conscience of the heart [Manuscript: ‘his’]. After drinking this liquid, the cleansed conscience comes to life again; and, drawing from the spring, it will possess one—it will itself even become a spring. What is the spring, or what is the river that flows from the belly of the inner person? Goodwill, by which one wishes to benefit one’s neighbor. For if someone thinks that what he has drunk ought to suffice for himself alone, living water does not flow from his belly. But if he hastens to benefit his neighbor, it does not dry up for that reason, because it flows forth.

“We shall see now what those who believe in God are drinking, since we are certainly Christians, and, if we believe, we drink. [Col. 0851A] Each person ought to recognize in himself whether he is drinking. And if he is drinking, let him distribute what he drinks [Augustine: ‘and if he lives from what he drinks’]; for the spring does not abandon us if we do not abandon the spring.

“The Evangelist explained and said from where the Lord had cried out, to what kind of drink he had invited them, and what he had supplied from those drinking [Manuscript: ‘what he supplied to those drinking’], saying: ‘Now he was speaking about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were going to receive.’ For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.

“What spirit does he mean, except the Holy Spirit? For every human being has his own spirit within him, that is, his soul. For each person’s *anima* (‘soul’) is his spirit [Manuscript: *animum* (‘mind’); *animus* (‘mind’)]. Of this the apostle Paul says: ‘For who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him?’ (1 Cor. 2:11).

“But what does he mean by saying, ‘For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified’? Was there not a spirit in the holy prophets and patriarchs of God, who foretold many future things through the Holy Spirit? Thus Elizabeth also is read to have been filled with the Holy Spirit, and likewise Zechariah, as the Evangelist says: ‘And Zechariah his father was filled with the Holy Spirit, and he prophesied’ (Luke 1:67). What, then, does he mean by saying that the Holy Spirit had not yet been given?

“We have, therefore, many indications of the Holy Spirit’s prior presence [Augustine: ‘preceding manifestations’] before the Lord was glorified by the resurrection of his flesh. For the prophets who foretold the coming Christ possessed no other spirit. But a certain future mode of this giving [Augustine: ‘of this gift’] was to come, one that had not appeared previously at all; it is of this that he speaks here.

“For nowhere do we read that, before this, people gathered together after receiving the Holy Spirit had spoken in the languages of all nations. But after his resurrection, when he first appeared to his disciples, he said to them: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John 20:22). Thus it was of this that he said: ‘The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.’

“And he breathed into their face (Gen. 2:7). By that breath he first gave life to the human being whom he had made, and raised him from the clay; by that breath he gave a soul to his limbs. He was signifying that he himself is the same one who breathed into their face [Augustine: ‘signifying that he is the one who breathed into their face’], so that they might rise from the mud and renounce works of clay.

“Then, for the first time after his resurrection—the glorification that the Evangelist mentions—the Lord gave his disciples the Holy Spirit. Afterwards, having remained with them for forty days, as the book of the Acts of the Apostles demonstrates, he ascended into heaven while they watched and followed him with their sight (Acts 1:3, 9). After ten days had been completed there, on the day of Pentecost he sent the Holy Spirit from above upon those who, as I said, had been gathered together in one place. Having received the Holy Spirit, they spoke in the languages of all nations.

“Perhaps someone asks: If those who have been baptized in Christ and live in the charity of his commandments have certainly received the Holy Spirit, why do they not speak in the languages of all nations? Because the Church itself, which is Christ’s body, speaks in the languages of all nations. This was signified beforehand at that time in the primitive Church, which was begun in Judea among one nation alone but is now gathered from all nations. And just as one person then spoke in all languages, so now the unity of the holy Church speaks in all languages.

“Therefore we too receive the Holy Spirit if we love the Church, if we are joined together by charity, and if we rejoice in the catholic name and faith. Accordingly, the more each person loves Christ’s Church, the more he possesses the Holy Spirit. We possess the Holy Spirit, then, if we love the Church; and we love it if we agree [Manuscript: ‘remain’] in its bond and charity, which the Apostle confidently placed before all virtues. Whoever possesses this will possess every good, because without it whatever a human being may possess will profit him nothing” (1 Cor. 13).

Of this the blessed apostle James says: “Whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all” (James 2:10). Concerning this also Truth itself says: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

“When Christ was saying these things on the last day of the festival that we have now proposed and, as best we could, expounded—”

## VERSES 40–41

“Then some of the crowd, when they had heard the words of Jesus, were saying: ‘This is truly the prophet.’ Others were saying: ‘This is the Christ.’”

[Col. 0851D] This passage is omitted in the manuscript codex and in other editions, and the preceding words are joined in the same sense to what follows [Col. 0852D] as follows: “we expounded; there arose, etc.”

[Col. 0852D] From Saint Augustine, *Tractate XXXIII*, nos. 1–2.

“There arose, then, a dissension among the crowd: some thinking that he was the Christ, others saying that the Christ would not arise from Galilee. But those who had been sent to seize him returned free from guilt and full of admiration. For they also bore witness to his divine teaching when they said to those by whom they had been sent: ‘Why did you not bring him?’ (v. 45). For they replied that they had never heard a human being speak in this way. ‘No human being ever spoke in this way’ (v. 46). But he spoke in this way because he was God and human being.

“Nevertheless, rejecting their testimony, the Pharisees said to them: ‘Have you too been led astray?’ (vv. 47–48). For we see that you have been delighted by his words. ‘Has any one of the rulers believed in him, or any of the Pharisees? But this crowd, which does not know the law, is accursed.’

“Those who did not know the law were the ones who believed in him; and those who taught the law were scorning the one who had given the law, so that what the Lord himself had said might be fulfilled: ‘I came so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.’ For the Pharisees, who were teachers, became blind; the peoples who did not know the law were enlightened and believed in the author of the law.

“Yet Nicodemus, one of the Pharisees, who had come to the Lord by night—and he was not unbelieving, but timid; for that is why he had come to the light by night: because he wanted to be enlightened but feared being known—answered [the Jews]: ‘Does our law judge a person unless it has first heard him and learned what he does?’ (v. 51). For those perverse men wanted to be condemn­ers before they were investigators.

“Nicodemus knew, or rather believed, that if they would only patiently hear him, they might perhaps become like those who had been sent to seize him but had preferred to believe him rather than seize him.

“They answered out of the prejudice of their hearts, saying to him what they had also said to the others: ‘Are you a Galilean too?’ (v. 52)—that is, as though you had been led astray by a Galilean. For the Lord was called a Galilean because his parents were from the city of Nazareth. I said ‘parents’ with respect to Mary, not with respect to male seed; for he who already had a Father above sought on earth only a mother. Both of his births were wondrous: divine birth without a mother, human birth without a human father.

“What, then, did they say to Nicodemus, as though they were teachers of the law? ‘Search the Scriptures and see that no prophet will arise from Galilee.’ But the Lord of the prophets arose from there.

“The Evangelist says: ‘Each of them went to his own house.’”

# CHAPTER XIX

He absolved the woman caught in adultery and brought before him, whom the accusers themselves did not condemn, on the condition that she would sin no further.

## CHAPTER VIII, VERSES 1–2

“From there Jesus went to the Mount of Olives, and at dawn he came again into the temple.”

[Col. 0853D] From Homily 5 of the Venerable Bede.

“The Mount of Olives signifies the sublimity of the Lord’s compassion and mercy. For in Greek, *eleos* (ἔλεος) means ‘mercy,’ while an olive grove is called *elaion* (ἐλαιών); and the anointing of oil commonly brings relief to weary and suffering limbs. Moreover, because oil surpasses other liquids in both power and purity, and because whatever liquid one wishes to pour over it immediately rises above it and lies upon it, it aptly signifies the grace of heavenly mercy, of which it is written: ‘The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works’ (Ps. 144:9).

“The time of dawn also indicates the rising of that same grace [Another reading: ‘indicates that same grace having arisen’], by which, once the shadow of the law had been removed, the light of evangelical truth was to be revealed.

“Jesus therefore goes to the Mount of Olives in order to declare that the stronghold of mercy resides in him. He comes again at dawn into the temple in order to signify that the same mercy was to be revealed and offered to the faithful, namely, to his temple, when the light of the New Testament began.

“And all the people,” he says, “came to him, and he sat down and taught them.” The Lord’s sitting signifies the humility of his incarnation, through which he deigned to have mercy on us. It is rightly said that when Jesus sat and taught, all the people came to him, because after he became near to human beings through the humility of his incarnation, his word was more willingly received by many. By many, I say, his word was received; for by more people it was rejected in proud impiety. “The meek heard and rejoiced” (Ps. 33:3).

“Finally, the Jews, testing him, brought a woman caught in adultery and asked what he commanded should be done with her. For Moses had commanded that such a woman be stoned (Lev. 20), so that if he too decided that she should be stoned, they might mock him as though he had forgotten the mercy he always taught; but if he forbade her to be stoned, they would gnash their teeth at him and condemn him, as though rightly, as an accomplice of crimes and an opponent of the law.

## VERSE 6

“But Jesus, bending down, was writing on the ground with his finger.”

“Through Jesus’ bending is expressed humility; through the finger, which is flexible because of the articulation of its joints, is expressed the subtlety of discernment; and through the ground is shown the human heart, which habitually produces the fruits of either good or evil actions.

“When the Lord was asked to judge the sinful woman, he did not immediately give judgment. Rather, first bending down, he wrote on the ground, and only then judged what he was earnestly asked to judge [Manuscript: ‘what he was urgently asked’]. In this he teaches us figuratively that when we observe any faults of our neighbors, we should not judge them by reproving them before we have humbly returned to our own conscience and carefully examined it with the finger of discernment, distinguishing through diligent examination what pleases and what displeases the Creator.

“This accords with the Apostle’s words: ‘Brothers, if anyone is overtaken in any trespass, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, keeping watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted’ (Gal. 6:1).”

## VERSE 7

“When they continued asking him, he stood up and said to them: ‘Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.’”

“Because the scribes and Pharisees were stretching the snares of their ambushes toward the Lord from both sides, thinking that he would be either lacking in mercy when judging or unjust, he foresaw their deceit, as though passing through a spider’s threads, and displayed in every respect both the judgment of justice and the gentleness of compassion.

“Behold the moderation of mercy: ‘Let the one among you who is without sin’—behold again the justice of judgment: ‘let him be the first to throw a stone at her.’ It is as though he had said: ‘If Moses commanded you to stone such a woman, see that he commanded not sinners but righteous people to do this. First fulfill the justice of the law yourselves, and then, with innocent hands and a pure heart, come together to stone the guilty woman. First perfect the spiritual decrees of the law—faith, mercy, and charity—and then turn to judging carnal matters.’

“After giving this judgment, the Lord again bent down and wrote on the ground. In accordance with ordinary human custom, it may be understood that the Lord wished to bend down before those wicked tempters and write on the ground in order to give them freedom to leave by directing his face elsewhere. He foresaw that, struck by his answer, they would depart more quickly than they would ask further questions [Another reading: ‘he gave them a free exit’; Bede: ‘the discretion to leave’].”

## VERSE 9

“Finally, after hearing this, they went out one by one, beginning with the elders.”

“But he admonishes us figuratively by the fact that, both before and after giving judgment, he bent down and wrote on the ground: both before we rebuke a sinning neighbor and after we have rendered him the service of deserved correction, we should examine ourselves with a fitting investigation of humility, lest perhaps we be entangled either in the same crimes that we condemn in them or in any others.

“For it may happen that the very person who judges a murderer guilty and deserving death may himself be found guilty before the eyes of the Creator, through hatred, of his brother’s death. Similarly, one who accuses a brother of the crime of fornication may fail to see in himself the crime of pride. Therefore the judge of another’s crime is commanded to describe it with the finger of discernment in his own heart, lest he be found guilty in himself.

“What remedy, then, do we have in such dangers; what salvation remains for us, except that whenever we see another sinning, we immediately bend down—that is, humbly examine how cast down we are by the condition of our frailty if divine mercy does not sustain us [Another reading: ‘support us’]? Let us write on the ground—that is, carefully weigh by discernment whether we can say with blessed Job: ‘My heart does not reproach me for any of my days’ (Job 27:6).

“It is fitting that the one who bent down and wrote on the ground brings forth words of mercy when he rises, because what he promised through participation in human weakness he bestows on human beings as a gift of compassion through the power of divine strength.”

## VERSES 10–11

“Jesus, raising himself, said to her: ‘Woman, where are they who accused you? Has no one condemned you?’ She said: ‘No one, Lord.’”

“No one dared condemn the sinful woman, because each of them had begun to perceive in himself what he recognized as more deserving of condemnation. But since he drove away the crowd of accusers by bringing forth the weight of justice, let us see by how great a gift of mercy he lifts up the accused woman.”

It follows: “Jesus said: ‘Neither will I condemn you. Go, and sin no more.’” Because he is merciful and compassionate, he releases past sins. Because he is just and loves justice, he forbids her to sin any further.

“But because some might doubt whether Jesus, whom they knew to be truly human, could forgive sins, he deigned to show more openly what he could accomplish by divine power. After repelling the wickedness of the tempters and releasing the sinful woman from her guilt, he spoke again.”

# CHAPTER XX

He declares himself to be the light of the world. Refuting the Pharisees concerning his own testimony, he rebukes them. He confirms that his judgment is true.

[Col. 0855D] ## VERSE 12

“I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.”

“Here he clearly teaches not only by what authority he forgave the woman’s sins, but also that he himself is the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world. Human frailty could not have seen his perpetual radiance unless it had been covered by the cloud of flesh, through which, as through a certain most luminous mirror, the brilliance of divine light might become known to human minds. The human mind must be purified by faith, so that it may be made worthy of beholding so great a light.

“Therefore he continues [Col. 0856A]: ‘Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light [Manuscript: *lumen* (‘light’); printed *lucem* (‘light’)] of life.’ Whoever now obeys my commands and examples will not fear the darkness of condemnation in the future, but will possess the light of life, where he will never die at all.”

[Col. 0855D] Thus far from a homily of the Venerable Bede.

[Col. 0855D] From Saint Augustine, *Tractate XXXV on John*, nos. 1–2, 4–6.

“Therefore, my brothers, let us follow Christ, the light of the world, so that we may not walk in darkness. The darkness to be feared is that of conduct, not of the eyes; and if of the eyes, it is not that of the outward eyes but of the inward, by which one distinguishes not white and black but just and unjust.

“When our Lord Jesus Christ had said this, the Jews answered: ‘You bear witness about yourself; your testimony is not true’ [Another reading: ‘you give testimony’] (v. 13).

“Before our Lord Jesus Christ came, he lit and sent many prophetic lamps before him. Among these was John the Baptist, to whom the great light itself, which is Christ, bore witness—such a testimony as he bore to no human being. For he said: ‘Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist’ (Matt. 11:11).

“Yet this man, than whom no one born of women was greater, says of our Lord Jesus Christ: ‘I indeed baptize you with water, but the one who comes after me is mightier than I, and I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal’ (John 1:26). See how he submits himself as the lamp of God [Another reading: ‘of the day’].

“The Lord himself testifies that John was a lamp: ‘He was,’ he says, ‘a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing for a time to rejoice in his light’ (John 5:35).

“The Jews therefore answered: ‘You bear witness about yourself; your testimony is not true.’ Let us see what they hear; let us also hear, but not as they do: they in contempt, we in belief; they wishing to kill Christ, we wishing to live through Christ. In the meantime, let this difference distinguish our ears and minds, and let us hear what the Lord answered the Jews.”

## VERSE 14

“Jesus answered and said to them: ‘Even if I bear witness about myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I am going.’

“Light reveals both other things and itself. Christ reveals both himself and the Father, and what was going to happen to the Jews. Therefore the Lord says—and says truly: ‘Even if I bear witness about myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I am going.’

“He wanted the Father to be understood; the Son gave glory to the Father. The equal glorified the one by whom he was sent. How much, then, ought a human being to glorify the one by whom he was created? ‘I know where I came from and where I am going.’

“This one who is now speaking to you possesses what he did not abandon, yet he came. For by coming he did not depart from there, nor by returning did he leave us. Why are you amazed? He is God. This cannot happen by a human being; it cannot happen even to the sun itself when it rises.

“The rising sun proceeds toward the west and abandons the east. Our Lord Jesus Christ does not act in that way.”

[Col. 0856D] Augustine: “This cannot happen by a human being; it cannot happen even to the sun itself. When it proceeds toward the west, it abandons the east, and until it returns to the east in order to rise, it is not in the east. But our Lord Jesus Christ both came, etc.” For he came, and he is there; he returned, and he is here.

“Hear the Evangelist himself saying elsewhere, and if you can, grasp it; if you cannot, believe it: ‘No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known’ (John 1:18). He did not say, ‘who was in the bosom of the Father.’ He was speaking here and saying that he was there. And when he was about to depart from here, he said: ‘Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age’ (Matt. 28:20).

“Therefore the testimony of the light is true, whether it reveals itself or other things, because without light the light cannot be seen, and without light nothing else that is not light can be seen.”

Thus light reveals both itself and the things around it. So also Christ both reveals himself and enlightens others who are around him in charity and follow him—not by the steps of their feet but by deeds of charity.

[Col. 0857B] We read in the holy Scriptures that two comings of our Lord Jesus Christ were foretold by the prophets: one of mercy, which has been accomplished, and the other of judgment, which is to come.

[Col. 0858D] From Saint Augustine, *Tractate XXXVI*, nos. 4–5, 9–10.

“The first dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ was medicinal, not judicial. For if he had first come to judge, he would have found no one to whom he could repay the rewards of justice. Since, therefore, he saw that all were sinners and that absolutely no one was free from the death of sin, his mercy had first to be brought forward, and afterward judgment had to be exercised, because the Psalm had sung of him: ‘I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, Lord’ (Ps. 100:1).

“For it is not first judgment and afterward mercy. If judgment came first, there would be no mercy; rather, mercy came first, and afterward judgment.

“What is the first mercy? The Creator of the human being deigned to become a human being, becoming what he had made, so that what he had made might not perish. What can be added to this mercy? Yet he added to it.”

For he was rejected by all [Another reading: ‘by human beings’] for whose salvation he had come into the world. He endured mockery, scourging, spitting, the insults of enemies, and the most shameful death of the cross. He endured all these things because he wished to save the human being whom he had created.

“No kind of death was more intolerable than the cross, because of its prolonged tortures; yet nothing is now more glorious than to bear the sign of the cross on one’s forehead. Hence the Apostle, proclaiming the glory of the cross, says: ‘But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world’ (Gal. 6:14).”

[Col. 0857D] ## VERSE 15

“Because he came to judge no one,” he consequently replied to the Jews: “You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one.”

“He endured an unjust judgment in order to carry out a just one. Yet in enduring what was unjust there was mercy. Finally, he was made so humble that he reached the cross. He delayed the display of his power but made his mercy public.

“Where did he delay his power? Because he did not wish to descend from the cross, although he was able to rise from the tomb. Where did he make his mercy public? Because, hanging on the cross, he said: ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing’ (Luke 23:24).

“Therefore, either because he had not come to judge the world but to save the world, he said, ‘I judge no one’; or, as I recalled, because he had said, ‘You judge according to the flesh,’ he added, ‘I judge no one,’ so that we may understand that Christ does not judge according to the flesh, just as he was judged by human beings.”

“For you may already recognize Christ as judge; hear what follows:

## VERSE 16

“‘And if I do judge, my judgment is true.’

“Behold, he possesses judgment as well [Augustine: ‘and a judge as well—do not fail to recognize the judge’]. But recognize the Savior, so that you may not experience the judgment. Why did he say that his judgment was true? ‘Because,’ he says, ‘I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.’”

“What is Christ’s mission except his incarnation? ‘Christ was sent’ means the same as ‘Christ was incarnate.’ He was sent by the Father, yet he never departed from the Father; he was here through his incarnation, and he is here now through his divinity.

“Therefore let faith cleanse our hearts, and let understanding fill our hearts, so that we may understand the mystery of our salvation. It is lofty, deep, and secret. The Father and the Son have one substance, one divinity, one majesty. The Father did not suffer; only the Son did.

“Therefore let us understand that the Son’s mission is called the Son’s incarnation; but let us not believe that the Father was incarnate. How, then, is his judgment true, except because he is truly the Father’s Son? Therefore he said: ‘My judgment is true, because I am not alone,’ he says, ‘but I and the Father who sent me.’

“The same thing he said elsewhere: ‘I and the Father are one’—one in substance, two in person. He said ‘one’ because of the unity of substance; he said ‘are’ because of the distinction of persons.

“Hear [recognize] what he said: ‘I and the Father who sent me.’ Distinguish the persons and recognize that the Father is Father and the Son is Son, lest you fall into the abyss of Sabellius. And do not say ‘one thing and another,’ but say ‘one person and another.’ Not another thing in substance, but another person. The Father is not greater, nor the Son lesser, in the glory of divinity; rather, believe: ‘We are one.’

“In saying ‘one,’ Truth itself frees you from Arius; in saying ‘are,’ it frees you from Sabellius. If ‘one,’ then not different; if ‘are,’ then not one person.”

“He had spoken of judgment when he said, ‘I judge no one’; now he wishes to speak of testimony, so that understanding may fill our hearts.”

## VERSE 17

“‘In your law,’ he says, ‘it is written.’ He said ‘your law’ as though he were saying: ‘In the law that God gave you,’ just as we say, ‘our daily bread,’ which we ask God to give us.

“What does it mean that it is written in your law that the testimony of two people is true? Do two people always give true testimony? Did not two false witnesses give false testimony against Susanna (Dan. 13:36)? And when the Jews sought false testimony against Christ, the Evangelist says: ‘Finally two false witnesses came forward.’

“Were they not false witnesses because there were two of them? What shall we say about two or three? The entire people lied against Christ. If, then, the entire people, consisting of a great multitude of human beings, was found to give false testimony, how should we understand: ‘By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand’? It means that, through a mystery, the Trinity was commended in this way, in which there is the perpetual stability of truth.

“If you wish to have a good case, have two or three witnesses: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Finally, when Susanna, a chaste woman and faithful wife, was pressed by two false witnesses, the Trinity supported her in her conscience and in secret. That Trinity raised up one witness, Daniel, from secrecy, and convicted the two.

“Therefore, because it is written in your law that the testimony of two people is true, receive true testimony, so that you may not experience judgment. ‘For I,’ he says, ‘judge no one, but I bear witness about myself; I postpone judgment, but I do not postpone testimony.’

“Let us choose, brothers, the testimony of God, because God’s testimony is true. The one who is now witness of everything we do will be judge of everything we have done. He seeks no other witness than himself, because he considers all the secrets of our hearts, both what proceeds from them and from what source it proceeds. He is a witness because he does not need another from whom to learn who or what sort of person you are; he will repay each person according to his works.”

The Jews therefore answered the Lord, who was speaking about his Father, and said:

## VERSE 19

“‘Where is your father?’”

“They understood Christ’s Father carnally because they judged Christ’s words according to the flesh. The one who was speaking was flesh openly and the Word secretly; a manifest human being, a hidden God. They saw the garment and despised the one clothed in it.

“Let us therefore see what the Lord answered them. They say: ‘Where is your father?’ For we heard you say: ‘I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.’ We see only you; we do not see your Father with you. How, then, do you say that you are not alone but are with your Father? Or show us that your Father is with you.

“And the Lord: ‘Do you see me and not see my Father?’ [Augustine: ‘so that I might show you the Father’]. This is what follows; this is what he himself answered in his own words, whose exposition we gave earlier.

“See what he said: ‘You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, perhaps you would know my Father also.’ You say, then, ‘Where is your Father?’ as though you already knew me, as though I were entirely what you see. Since you do not know me, therefore I do not show you my Father.

“You think I am a human being; therefore you seek my human father, because you judge according to the flesh. But because, according to what you see, I am one thing, and according to what you do not see, another, I speak of my Father as hidden [Augustine: ‘the hidden one, hidden’]. First you must know me; then you will know my Father also.”

“For if you knew me, perhaps you would know my Father also. He who knows everything does not doubt when he says ‘perhaps,’ but rebukes. Consider how the word ‘perhaps,’ which appears to be a word of doubt, is spoken as a rebuke.

“It is a word of doubt when spoken by a human being, who doubts because he does not know. But when a word of doubt is spoken by God, from whom nothing is hidden, that doubt rebukes unbelief; it does not express divine uncertainty.

“Human beings sometimes, by way of rebuke, express doubt about things they actually regard as certain. For example, if you become angry with your servant and say: ‘You despise me; consider that perhaps I am your master.’ Likewise the Apostle, speaking to certain people who despised him, says: ‘I think that I too have the Spirit of God’ (1 Cor. 7:40). The one who says ‘I think’ appears to doubt, but he was rebuking, not doubting.

“And the Lord Jesus Christ, rebuking the future unbelief of the human race, says elsewhere: ‘When the Son of Man comes, do you suppose he will find faith on earth?’ (Luke 18:8).

“He therefore knows everything, through whom everything was made, and yet he rebuked by expressing doubt. ‘If you knew me, perhaps you would know my Father also.’ He rebuked unbelievers and admonished believers, so that they might know that the Father and the Son have one thought, and thus know that knowledge of the Son is also knowledge of the Father.

“Therefore, when the chosen disciple asked him to show them the Father, he answered: ‘I have been with you for so long, and you have not known me, Philip? Whoever sees me sees the Father also’ (John 14:8). If the Son were unlike the Father, would he have said to his disciples, ‘Whoever sees me sees the Father’? Would he have said to the Jews, ‘If you knew me, perhaps you would know my Father also’?”

## VERSE 20

“These words Jesus spoke in the treasury while teaching in the temple.”

“Great confidence, without fear. For he would not suffer if he did not wish to; nor would he be born if he did not wish to be born.”

“What does it mean that Jesus spoke these words while teaching in the treasury in the temple? The treasury is the place where treasures are stored. Jesus was speaking to the Jews in the treasury, whereas he spoke to the crowds in parables. For Christ was the treasury in which all the mysteries were hidden, to be opened at that time, when he himself, who had been hidden in the letter, spoke—not in riddles, but openly explaining everything to his faithful.

“The treasuries were also attached to the temple, because Christ himself is the temple, concerning which he said: ‘Destroy this temple’ (John 2:19). All the mysteries of the Old Law were attached to him and looked toward him, until he came to open each treasury of the mysteries, opening the understanding of his faithful so that they might understand what had been hidden, as the Evangelist says: ‘Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures’ (Luke 24:45).

“Finally, what follows? ‘No one seized him, because his hour had not yet come.’ That is, everything occurred according to his own disposition and according to his will. For he who was born by his will also suffered by his will.

“If, then, he had not wished to suffer, he would not have suffered; if he had not suffered, that blood would not have been poured out, and the world would not have been redeemed. Let us therefore give thanks both for the power of his divinity and for the compassion of his weakness: for the hidden power that the Jews did not know, concerning which it was said to them, ‘You know neither me nor my Father’ (John 8:19), and for the flesh he assumed, which the Jews did know and whose homeland they knew. For elsewhere he said to them: ‘You know me, and you know where I am from’ (John 7:28).

“Let us know both things in Christ: from what standpoint he is equal to the Father, and from what standpoint the Father is greater than he. The one is the Word; the other is flesh. The one is God; the other is human being. Yet there is one Christ, God and human being.”

“Now let us hear what Christ says about his passion.”

# CHAPTER XXI

He tells the Jews that they will die in their sin. When they ask him who he is, he replies that he is the beginning, adding this: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am.”

## VERSE 21

“
@ [Col. 0861D] St. Augustine, Tractate XXXVIII, §§ 2–8, 11. “I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin. Where I am going, you cannot come.” “I am going away,” he says, “and you will seek me”—not out of desire, but out of hatred. For after he had withdrawn from human eyes, both those who hated him [Col. 0861B] and those who loved him sought him: the former by persecuting him, the latter by desiring to possess him. It is good to seek Christ’s soul, but in the way the disciples sought it; and it is evil to seek Christ’s soul, but in the way the Jews sought it: the former sought it in order to possess it, the latter in order to destroy it. Finally, because they sought him in this evil manner, with a perverse heart, what did he add? “You will seek me; and lest you think that you will seek me rightly, you will die in your sin”—that is, to seek Christ wrongly is to die in one’s sin.”

He dies in his sin who remains in sin until death. He does not seek Christ who does not seek the salvation of his soul through repentance. To him the Prophet cries: “Seek the Lord while he may be found” (Isa. 55:6). Whoever does not seek the merciful one while he has the opportunity will find him angry [Col. 0861C]. He said to the Jews, “You will die in your sin,” because he foreknew that they would remain in their sin. He said “in sin” in the singular, but “you will die” in the plural, because he knew that all those to whom he was speaking had one will and an equal wickedness in seeking to destroy him who had come to save them.

“But elsewhere he said to his disciples: ‘Where I am going, you cannot come now’ (John 21:22). He did not take away their hope, but foretold a delay. For when the Lord was speaking this to the disciples, they could not then come where he was going, but they were going to come afterward; these, however, would never come—those to whom, in his foreknowledge, he said: ‘You will die in your sin.’

“After hearing these words, they responded as those usually do who think carnally, judge according to the flesh, and hear and understand everything in a carnal way. They said: (VERSE 22) ‘Will he perhaps kill himself, because he says: “Where I am going, you cannot come”?’ Foolish words, utterly full of stupidity. What then? Could they not come where he would have gone if he had killed himself? Were they themselves not going to die? What, then, does ‘Will he perhaps kill himself, because he said: “Where I am going, you cannot come”?’ mean? If he were speaking of a man’s death, what human being does not die? Therefore, when he said, [Col. 0862A] ‘Where I am going,’ he meant not the place to which one goes for death, but the place where he himself was going after death, in order to kill death.”

“Since they did not understand these things, the Lord answered them” [Col. 0861D].

@ [Col. 0861D] Another edition: “Since they did not understand these things, the Lord answered them, who savored earthly things. What does he say? He said to them: ‘You are from below,’ etc.”: “You are from below. Therefore you savor earthly things, because, like the serpent, you eat earth. What does ‘you eat earth’ mean except that you feed on earthly things, delight in earthly things, and gape after earthly things, having no heart above? You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world.”

How, then, was he not of this world, through whom the world was made and who is always everywhere? Yet all are from the world: first there was the world, and afterward man. But Christ existed before the world; before Christ there was nothing. For “in the beginning was the Word, and all things were made through him.” Thus he was from above. From which above was [Col. 0862B] Christ? From the Father himself; there is nothing higher than he, because the Father begot the Word equal to himself, coeternal with himself, his only-begotten Son, without time, through whom he established time.

Therefore Christ is before all creatures and before all times, because he was begotten from the Father as coeternal with the Father. “I am from above; you are from this world; I am not of this world.”

VERSE 24.—“Therefore I said to you that you will die in your sins.” He explained to us, brothers, what he wished “You are of this world” to mean. For he said, “You are of this world,” because they were sinners, because they were unrighteous, because they were unbelievers, because they savored earthly things.

Were the apostles and the saints of God not of this world? They certainly were, because they were born from Adam; but Truth himself says of them: “I [Col. 0862C] chose you out of the world” (John 15:19)—that is, out of the carnal way of life, which seems to be signified here by the name “world.”

“Those, therefore, who were of the world became not of the world, and began to belong to him through whom the world was made. But these remained in the world, to whom it was said: ‘You will die in your sins.’

“Let no one say, ‘I am not of this world.’ Whoever you are, O man, you are of this world. But he who made the world came to you and freed you from this world. If the world delights you, you always wish to be in the world [Augustine and the manuscript: ‘unclean’]. But if this world no longer delights you, you will no longer be clean [manuscript: ‘you will now be clean’].”

@ [Col. 0861D] St. Augustine: “If the world delights you, you always wish to be [Col. 0862D] unclean; but if this world no longer delights you, you are now clean. Nevertheless, if through some weakness the world still delights you, let him who cleanses dwell in you, and you will be clean. But if you are clean, you will not remain in the world, nor will you hear, etc.” And you will not hear what the Jews heard: “You will die in your sin.”

And the more someone sins, the more he is [in the world and the more] unclean; and the more anyone cleanses himself from sin, the more he rises above belonging to the world.

“Justly did the Jews hear: ‘You will die in your sins,’ because you could in no way have been without sin, since you were born with sin. Yet, if you believe in me,” he says, “although you were born with sin, you will not die in your sin. The whole misery, therefore, consisted not in having sin, but in dying in sins. This is what every Christian ought to flee. For this reason one runs to baptism [Col. 0863A]; for this reason whoever is endangered by illness or by some other circumstance desires help for himself; for this reason even a nursing infant is carried by a mother’s pious hands to the Church, so that he may not depart without baptism and die in the sin in which he was born [Augustine and the manuscript: ‘die in that in which he was born’].”

For he added, saying: “If you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sins.” Therefore, if you believe that I am, you will not die in your sins.

“Hope was restored to the despairing; those who slept were roused; hearts awoke. As a result many believed, as the continuation of the Gospel itself bears witness, where it says: ‘As he was saying these things, many believed in him.’ Thus in that crowd to which the Lord was speaking there were those who were going to die in their sin, and there were also those who were going to believe in the one who was speaking [Col. 0863B] and be freed from every sin.

“Nevertheless, observe what the Lord Christ says: ‘If you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sin.’ What does ‘if you do not believe that I am’ mean? What? He added nothing. Great is what he commended.” He said, “I am,” and did not add what he was—whether Christ, or the Son of God, or the one whom the prophets foretold, or the Savior of the world, or [some] other thing that is read about him in the Scriptures. Great is what he said: ipse, “I am” [manuscript: ipsum].

For God had said to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14). And here he now used the same word of eternal being before the Jewish people that he had then used before Moses through the angel in the flaming bush of fire, whom he was going to send to liberate his people [Col. 0863C]. What does he mean here by saying, “I am,” except that he is the very one who then came in the angel to send Moses his servant to liberate his people? “I myself have now come in person, incarnate, made man, to free the human beings whom I created and save those who had been lost.”

For whatever can in any way be changed, whether for the better or for the worse, in a certain sense dies with regard to what it was before, while it begins to be something else or to be otherwise than it was. God alone is always the same: unchanging truth, unchanging goodness, unchanging eternity, unchanging nature, unchanging substance. And whatever can be said of him is always the same as what it was and what it will be.

Nothing else seems properly to be understood in [Col. 0863D] this word which the Lord said, “I am,” except “I am God.” “You will die in your sin.”

“But those who always savored earthly things and always heard and answered according to the flesh—what did they say to him?”

VERSE 25.—“Who are you?” For when you said, “Unless you believe that I am,” you did not add who you were [Augustine: “what you were”]. “Who are you, that we should believe?” And he replied: “The Beginning.” Behold what it means to be. The Beginning cannot be changed; the Beginning remains in itself and renews all things. It is the Beginning to which it was said: “But you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Ps. 101:28).

“‘The Beginning,’ he says, ‘who also speaks to you.’ Believe me to be the Beginning, lest you die in your sins.” [Col. 0864A] For, as though in saying “Who are you?” they had said nothing other than, “What are we to believe you to be?” he replied: “Believe me to be the Beginning,” and he added, “who also speaks to you.” That is, because I became humble for your sake, I descended to these words.

For if the Beginning had remained with the Father as it is, without taking the form of a servant and speaking as man to men, how could they have believed in him, when their weak hearts could not hear the intelligible Word without a sensible voice [another edition: “could not see it without a voice, but through the sensible”]? Therefore, he says, believe me to be the Beginning, because, in order that you may believe, I not only am, but also speak to you.”

«

@ [Col. 0863D] From St. Augustine, Tractate XXXIX, §§ 1, 6, 7. “The words of our Lord Jesus Christ that he spoke with the Jews, regulating his speech in such a way that the blind would not see and the faithful would open their eyes [Add: ‘these [Col. 0864B] are’].
