The Jews were therefore saying: ‘Who are you?’ because the Lord had said above: ‘Unless you believe that I am, you will die in your sins.’ To this they replied: ‘Who are you?’ as though asking to know in whom they ought to believe, lest they die in their sin. He answered those who said, ‘Who are you?’ and said: ‘The Beginning, who also speaks to you.’”

Why does the Lord Jesus call himself the Beginning? Because all things were made through him, as the Psalm says [manuscript: “the Psalmist says”]: “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24). If, therefore, God made all things in wisdom—that is, in his Son, coeternal and consubstantial with him—the Son is certainly the Beginning of all things.

Can the Father also be called the Beginning? Certainly. The Father is rightly called the Beginning, and the Son the Beginning; yet they are not two beginnings. Just as the Father is God [Col. 0864C] and the Son is God, yet they are not two gods but must be called one God, so the Father is the Beginning and the Son is the Beginning, yet they are not two beginnings but one Beginning must be confessed.

Therefore the Holy Spirit also is the Beginning; yet there are not three beginnings—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—but one Beginning. Just as the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, yet there are not three gods but one God; and the Father is almighty, the Son is almighty, and the Holy Spirit is almighty, yet there are not three almighty ones but one Almighty.

What the Father is in relation to himself, he is God; what he is in relation to the Son, he is Father. What the Son is in relation to himself, he is God; what he is from the Father, he is Son. And what the Holy Spirit is in relation to himself, he is God; what he is from the Father and the Son, he is the Holy Spirit, because he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, proceeding from the Father and the Son, of one substance, power, and majesty with the Father and the Son.

[Col. 0864D] Let us therefore hear the Beginning who speaks to us.

VERSE 25.—“I have many things to say and judge concerning you,” he says. Elsewhere he said: “I judge no one,” indicating his present coming, in which he came to save, not to judge, because he had come to save the world, not to judge the world.

“But when it is now said, ‘I have many things to say and judge concerning you,’ he is speaking of the future judgment. For he ascended in order to come to judge the living and the dead. No one will judge more justly than he who was judged unjustly. [Col. 0865A]

“‘I have many things,’ he says, ‘to say and judge concerning you; but the one who sent me is true.’ See how the Son, equal to the Father, gives glory to the Father [manuscript: ‘gives’].” For he gives us an example of giving glory to God and seeking God’s glory, not our own, as though he were saying: “O faithful man, if I, the Son of the Father, equal to the Father, consubstantial with the Father, coeternal with the Father, give glory to him from whom I am, how are you proud before the one whose servant you are?”

“‘I have many things,’ he says, ‘to say and judge concerning you, but the one who sent me is true,’” as though he were saying: “I speak the truth because I am the Son of the truthful one, I am the Truth.” The Father is truthful; the Son is Truth.

“For the Lord himself says most openly: ‘I am the way, and the truth, and the life.’ Therefore, if the Son is Truth, what is the Father except what Truth says: ‘The one who sent me is truthful’? The Son is Truth; the Father is truthful” [Col. 0865B]. Just as the Son is from the Father, so Truth is from the truthful one. The Father is truthful, but not from Truth; the Son is Truth, but from the Father, as [another edition: ‘because’] the Son is from the Father and not from himself.

Therefore he says elsewhere: “I did not come from myself,” that is, “I am not from myself.” The Father is truthful, not by sharing in truth [manuscript: “truth”], but by begetting Truth, because the Father begot the Son, who says of himself: “I am the way and the truth.”

When the Lord Jesus had said, “The one who sent me is truthful,” they did not understand that he was speaking to them about the Father. They did not yet have the eyes of their hearts opened, so that they could understand the equality of the truthful one and Truth.

VERSE 28.—Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am, and that I do nothing from myself, but just as the Father taught me, I speak these things” [Col. 0865C].

«

@ [Col. 0865D] From St. Augustine, Tractate XL, §§ 2, 5, 6, 8, 9. “What does this mean? For he seems to have said nothing other than that after his passion they would come to know what he was [Augustine: ‘who he was’]. Without doubt, therefore, he saw there some whom he himself knew and whom, together with all his other saints, he had foreknown and chosen before the foundation of the world, and who were going to believe after his passion.

“These are the ones whom we constantly commend and set before others for imitation with great exhortation. After the Holy Spirit had been sent from above, following the Lord’s passion, resurrection, and ascension, miracles were performed in the name of the one whom the Jews, persecuting him as though he were dead, had despised. They were pierced to the heart (Acts 2:37); those who had killed him in their rage were changed and believed; and by believing they drank the blood which they had shed in their rage [Col. 0865D] (Acts 4:4). Those three thousand and those five thousand Jews whom he saw there when he said, ‘When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am’—it was as though he were saying: ‘I defer your recognition until I have completed my passion; in due course you will know who I am.’

“Not all who were listening were then going to believe—that is, after the Lord’s passion. For a little earlier [reading: ‘a little later’] he says: ‘As he was saying these things, many believed in him’; and the Son of Man had not yet been lifted up.

“For by ‘lifting up’ he means the lifting up of the passion, not of glorification; of the cross, not of heaven. For he was lifted up there when he hung upon the wood [Col. 0866A]; but that lifting up was a humiliation. Then he became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2:8). Therefore God exalted him.”

There was another exaltation when he was raised upon the cross, and another when he ascended into heaven. The former was an exaltation of humiliation; the latter, of glorification.

“The exaltation of the cross had to be accomplished through the hands of those who would afterward believe, to whom he says: ‘When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am.’ Why was this done except so that no one might despair, however conscious of an evil crime, when he saw that forgiveness was granted to those who had committed the murder of Christ [to themselves]?”

He added: “Then you will know that I am.” What is “I am” except “of one substance with the Father”? As we said above concerning Moses, it was said: “I am who I am.” The Lord uses of himself a substantial word [Col. 0866B], so that it may be understood that his substance is eternal and that the substance of the Father and the Son is one.

Yet, lest he himself be understood to be the Father, he immediately added: “And I do nothing from myself, but just as the Father taught me, I speak these things.”

What does he mean when he says, “I do nothing from myself”? That is, “I am not from myself.” But what he added—“Just as the Father taught me, I speak these things”—has a very profound meaning. The heart must be cleansed in order to understand what he says: “Just as the Father taught me, so I speak.” It must not be understood as though the Father, being a man, spoke to the Son as man, but in a more exalted and sacred sense.

One thing is meant by what the Evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word,” and another by: “The Word became flesh.” One meaning concerns Christ’s divinity, in which he is equal to God the Father [Col. 0866C]; another concerns his humanity, in which he is like us. We must consider that the Lord’s words “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30) must not be understood in the same way as his statement “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

“Let the Father be thought of as speaking to the Son incorporeally, because the Father incorporeally begot the Son. He did not teach him as though he had begotten him ignorant; rather, to teach him is to beget him knowing, and ‘the Father taught me’ means ‘the Father begot me knowing.’

“For if, as few understand, the nature of Truth is simple, then for the Son to be is the same as for him to know. Therefore he has knowledge from the one from whom he has being—not in such a way that he first existed from him and afterward knew from him, but just as by begetting he gave him being, so by begetting he gave him knowledge, because it is characteristic of the simple nature of truth [another edition: ‘because the truth of the simple nature’]” [Col. 0866D].

@ [Col. 0865D] Manuscript: “Because, as has been said, the truth of a simple nature is [Col. 0866D].” Augustine: “Because, as has been said, for the simple nature of truth, being and knowing are not different,” etc.—“being and knowing are not one thing and another, but the very same thing.”

“He therefore said these things to the Jews and added: (VERSE 29) ‘And the one who sent me is with me.’ He had already said this earlier, but he repeatedly recalls a great truth: ‘He sent me, and he is with me.’

“If he is with you, O Lord, then one was not sent by another, but both of you came. And yet, although both are together, one was sent and the other sent, because being sent is incarnation; and the incarnation belongs to the Son alone, not to the Father. The Father therefore sent the Son, but did not depart from the Son.

“Therefore,” he says, “the one who sent me did not leave me alone. By whose authority—as by the Father’s [Col. 0867A]—I was made incarnate, he is with me; he did not abandon me.”

Why did he not abandon me? “He did not leave me alone,” he says, “because I always do what pleases him.” This is the equality that is always present, not from some beginning and afterward, but without beginning and without end. For God’s generation has no beginning in time, because through the begotten one time itself was made.

VERSE 30.—“As he was saying these things, many believed in him.” Many believed; the sound of their preaching had not yet gone out into all the earth, nor had it yet been proclaimed to all, nor had it yet been said: “Go, teach all nations.”

Therefore the Lord said to the Jews who believed in him:

CHAPTER XXII

To the Jews who believed he said: “If you remain in my word, the truth will set you free.” When they answered that they were free, he said: “Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin.”

[Col. 0867B]

VERSE 31.—“If you remain in my word.” He says “remain” because you have been initiated, because you have begun to be there. If you remain—that is, in the faith that has begun to exist in you who believe—where will you arrive? See what a beginning it is, and to what it leads [another edition: “what it leads to”]. You have loved the foundation; look toward the summit, and from this humility seek another elevation.

Faith has humility; knowledge, immortality, and eternity do not have humility, but elevation and uprightness, no falling away, eternal stability, no assault by the enemy, and no fear of failing. “Great is what begins from faith,” but greater is that to which one arrives through faith.

Hear, then, where it leads, and see how great faith is.

VERSE 32.—“Therefore,” he says, “if you remain in my word [Col. 0867C] in which you have believed, you will truly be my disciples.” He also added where it leads: “And you will know the truth.”

Whoever knows the truth knows God, because God is truth, as the Lord himself says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). Let us therefore believe so that we may know the truth, because without faith no one can arrive at knowledge of the truth.

“What will we come to know? That which ‘eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and has not entered the human heart’ (Isa. 64:4; 1 Cor. 2:9). What is faith, then, except believing what you do not see? Faith, therefore, is believing what you do not see; truth is seeing what you believed.

“What is it that we are promised we shall see? For the Lord says elsewhere what it is that we shall see: ‘Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself [Col. 0867D] to him’ (John 14:21).”

This is the promise; this is the reward of faith that works through love. This is the satisfaction for which the Psalmist prayed, saying: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. 16:15).

O Lord, make us worthy to love you and not love the world, so that we may be able to arrive at that freedom which is reached through knowledge of the truth. Concerning it you added, saying:

“‘And the truth will set you free.’ What does ‘it will set you free’ mean? It will make you free. Finally, the carnal Jews, judging according to the flesh—not those who had believed, but those in the crowd who did not believe—thought that an insult had been directed at them because he said [Col. 0868A] to them, ‘The truth will set you free.’ They were indignant that they had been signified as slaves. And indeed they were slaves. He explains to them what this slavery is and what the future freedom is that he promises.”

For to say “The truth will set you free” means nothing other than “It will make you free,” just as “it will save” means nothing other than “it will make you safe.”

We have heard what liberating Truth said; let us hear what arrogant falsehood answered.

The Jews therefore said: (VERSE 33)

«

@ [Col. 0867D] From St. Augustine, Tractate XLI, §§ 2, 3, 4, 8. “We are Abraham’s offspring, and we have never served anyone. How can you say, ‘You will [Col. 0868B] be free’?”

For the Lord had not said, “You will be free,” but, “The truth will set you free.” Yet in this statement they understood nothing other than carnal freedom. They exalted themselves because they were Abraham’s offspring and said: “We are Abraham’s offspring, and we have never served anyone. How can you say, ‘You will be free’?”

O empty pride! O false boasting! How could you truly say, “We have never served anyone”? Was Joseph not sold? Were the holy prophets not led into captivity? Finally, was it not that very people who made bricks in Egypt and served under harsh labor—not even in silver or gold, but in clay?

If you have never served anyone, O ungrateful people, what is the meaning of God’s constant reminder of how he freed you from the house of slavery? Or perhaps your fathers served, but you who are speaking have never served anyone? How, then, did you pay tribute to the Romans?

And from this you yourselves set a snare of entrapment for Truth, so that you might say: “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar?” If he had said that it was lawful, you would have seized him, as though he had wished an evil freedom upon Abraham’s [Col. 0868C] offspring [Augustine: “as though he had wished evil upon the freedom of Abraham’s offspring”]. But if he had said that it was not lawful, you would have accused him before the rulers of the earth of forbidding tribute to be paid to kings.

Then, when the coin was produced, you were defeated, and you yourselves were compelled to answer your own trap. For there it was said to you: “Give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s” (Matt. 22:21), when you yourselves had answered that the coin bears Caesar’s image. For just as Caesar seeks his image on the coin, so God seeks his image in man.”

God does not seek from man something alien, but what he established in man. For this reason God became man: to restore in man what he had formed in man.

Let us therefore hear what the Lord answered the Jews who were lying and swelling with empty claims of freedom.

[Col. 0868D] VERSE 34.—“Amen, amen, I say to you: everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin.”

Who would not tremble at these words? If every human being is a sinner, every human being is a slave of sin. But let us listen more attentively to how we may be freed from this slavery. He instills terror and applies medicine.

For the Lord says: “Amen, amen, I say to you.” What is “amen, amen” except “truly, truly I say to you”? Neither the Greek translator nor the Latin one dared to transfer this word into another language, so that, under the veil of secrecy, the testimony of truth in Christ might retain its honor.

Truth says: “Truly, truly I say to you.” He repeats and reiterates the word of truth, so that he might awaken those who sleep, make those listening attentive [Col. 0869A] [manuscript and Augustine: “intent”] within, and prevent contempt for the one who says: “Amen, amen, I say to you: everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin.”

“O wondrous [Augustine: ‘wretched’] slavery—to serve sin, to serve the devil, who is the author of sin! Often, when people suffer wicked masters, they ask to be sold, not seeking to have no master, but at least to change masters. What can the slave of sin do? Whom can he call upon? Before whom can he plead? To whom can he ask to be sold?”

People often flee wicked masters so as not to serve evil men, but they do not flee sin, whose slave is the sinner. And how much more fortunate it would be to flee sin and serve a human being with a free conscience!

“Furthermore, a human slave, at times worn out by his master’s harsh commands, finds rest by fleeing [Col. 0869B]. Where can the slave of sin flee? Wherever he flees, he drags sin with him. An evil conscience does not flee from itself; it has nowhere to go; it follows itself—indeed, it does not depart from itself, for the sin it commits is within.

“He committed sin in order to obtain some bodily desire (voluntas); the desire (voluntas) [manuscript: pleasure (voluptas): delight (voluptas)] passed away, but the sin remains. What delighted him has gone by; what pricks him remains. Evil slavery. At times people flee wicked masters, wishing to be rid of masters, while they do not wish to be rid of sins.”

How much happier it would be if a person abandoned sin, fled to Christ, and called upon God the Liberator! Therefore only the Lord frees from this slavery of sin—the one who did not possess it, who alone came into the world without sin. Only he who came without sin and became a sacrifice for sin can free from sin [Col. 0869C].

“Since, then, everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin, hear what hope we have of freedom: (VERSE 35) ‘A slave,’ he says, ‘does not remain in the house forever.’ The house is the Church; the sinner is the slave.”

Let a person not remain in sin, and let him not be a slave of sin, so that he may be able to remain in the house—that is, in the Church. Let him remain in the body of his head, so that he may be a son, not a slave.

It is one thing to sin, and another to remain in sin. Whoever remains in sin is the slave of sin; whoever flees from sin will be the slave of righteousness.

“He therefore terrified and gave hope: he terrified us so that we would not love sin; he gave hope so that we would not despair of release from sin. ‘Everyone,’ he says, ‘who commits sin is a slave of sin. A slave does not remain [in the house] forever.’ What hope, then, is there for us, who are not without sin? Hear [Col. 0869D] your hope: ‘The Son remains forever.’”

VERSE 36.—“Therefore, if the Son sets you free, you will truly be free.”

This is our hope, brothers: that we may be freed by the Free One, and that by freeing us he may make us servants. For we were slaves of desire; once freed, we become servants of love.

The first freedom is not to remain in sin, but to serve righteousness, as the Apostle says: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free with regard to righteousness” (Rom. 6:20). But now you have your fruit in sanctification, and the end is eternal life.

Perfect freedom, however, is to serve Christ [God], to love him who truly freed us, who is the true Son of God and Lord in the form of a servant [Col. 0870A].

@ [Col. 0869D] From St. Augustine, Tractate XLII, §§ 1–14. “Not a slave, but the Lord in the form of a slave. For that form of the flesh was indeed servile; but although it was the likeness of sinful flesh, it was not sinful flesh.

“He promised freedom to those who believed in him. But the Jews, as though proud of their freedom, disdained to be made free, although they were slaves of sin. They said that they were free because they were Abraham’s offspring.

“What, then, did the Lord answer them? Let us hear:

VERSE 37.—‘I know,’ he says, ‘that you are Abraham’s children, but you seek to kill me.’ I acknowledge the origin of your flesh, not the faith of your heart. You are Abraham’s children, but according to the flesh. Therefore, he says, you seek to kill me; for my word has no place in you.

“If my word had a place in you, it would certainly possess you. What, then, does ‘it has no place in you’ mean? It means that it does not possess your heart [Col. 0870B], because it is not received by your heart.”

You have certainly heard the Lord saying: “I know that you are Abraham’s children.” Hear what he says afterward: “I speak what I have seen with my Father; and you do what you have heard from your father.”

What do they do? What he told them: “You seek to kill me.” They never saw this in Abraham.

He says: “I speak what I have seen with my Father.” I saw truth; I speak truth, because I am Truth. For if the Lord speaks truth because he himself is the Father’s Truth, whom he saw with the Father [“he saw himself, he speaks himself, because he himself is the Father’s Truth, whom he saw with the Father”].

For he is the Word, and the Word was with God. Where, then, did these people see the evil they do, which the Lord rebukes and censures? With their father.

When we hear [Col. 0870C] more clearly in what follows who their father is, then we shall understand what sort of things they saw with such a father. For he has not yet named their father.

A little earlier he mentioned Abraham, but in terms of the origin of the flesh, not similarity of life. He was going to name another father of theirs, who neither begot them nor created them so that they might be human beings; yet they were his children insofar as they were evil, not insofar as they were human beings [“were”]. They were his children in what they imitated, not in what they were created.

**VERSE 39.**—They answered and said to him: “Our father is Abraham.” As if to say: “What are you going to say against Abraham? Or, if you dare anything, criticize Abraham” [Augustine: “dare to criticize Abraham”]. Not that the Lord did not dare to criticize Abraham, but Abraham was such a man that he would not be criticized by the Lord, but rather praised. Nevertheless, these people seemed to be provoking him to say something evil about Abraham, so that there might be an opportunity to do what they were planning. “Our father is Abraham.”

“Let us hear how the Lord answered them, praising Abraham while condemning them.” **(VERSE 40.)** Jesus says to them: “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham. But now you are seeking to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth that I heard from God. Abraham did not do this.” Behold: he is praised, while they are condemned. Abraham was not a murderer. “I am not saying,” he says, “that I am the God of Abraham” [Augustine: “I am the Lord of Abraham”]; for if I said that, I would be speaking the truth. For he said elsewhere: “Before Abraham was, I am.” Then they wanted to stone him. He did not say this. For the moment, what you see, what you behold, what you think I am alone—I am a man. Why do you wish to kill a man telling you what he heard from God, unless because you are not Abraham’s children? And yet above he said: “I know that you are Abraham’s children.” He did not deny their origin, but condemned their deeds: their flesh was descended from him, but their life was not.

“Therefore Christians have become Abraham’s seed by the grace of God. They did not become co-heirs through the flesh of Abraham: God disinherited those people and adopted these.” These are the ones of whom John the Baptist said elsewhere: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matthew 3:9). Those who imitate Abraham’s faith will be Abraham’s children. Therefore the Lord added, saying: “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham.” Prove your nobility by deeds, not by words. “But you are seeking to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth that I heard from God; Abraham did not do this.” “You are doing the works of your father,” and even then he does not say who their father is.

“What did they answer him at that point? They had begun, in some fashion, to understand that the Lord was not speaking of carnal generation but of the formation of one’s life. And since it was the custom of the Scriptures they were reading to call subjection to many and false gods ‘prostitution’ spiritually, when the soul is subjected to them as though prostituted, they answered accordingly: **(VERSE 41.)** They therefore said to him: ‘We were not born of prostitution; we have one Father, God.’”

Abraham had now become worthless in their eyes. They had been repelled, as they deserved to be repelled by the truthful mouth, because Abraham was such a man whose deed they did not imitate, while they gloried in his lineage. And they changed their answer, thinking among themselves—[Augustine and the manuscript: “I think”]—“Whenever we mention Abraham, he will say to us: ‘Why do you not imitate the one whose lineage you boast of?’ We cannot imitate that holy, just, innocent, and extraordinary man. Let us call God our Father; let us see what he will say to us.”

“If falsehood found something to say, would truth not find something to answer? Let us hear what they say; let us hear what they hear: ‘We have one Father, God.’ **(VERSE 42.)** Jesus therefore said to them: ‘If God were your Father, you would certainly love me, for I proceeded from God and came. For I did not come of myself, but he sent me.’”

You call God your Father; recognize at least your brother [Augustine: “recognize me as your brother”]. Here he touched upon what he often says: “I did not come of myself, but he sent me; I proceeded from God and came.” Christ’s being sent, therefore, is his incarnation. But that the Word proceeded from God is an eternal procession, not having a temporal beginning through which time itself was made. Thus he proceeded from him as God, as equal, as the only Son, as the Word of the Father; he came to us because the Word became flesh, so that he might dwell among us. His coming is his humanity; his dwelling is his divinity.

**VERSE 43.**—“Why,” he says, “do you not understand my speech? Because you cannot hear my word.” They could not understand because they could not hear. But why could they not hear, unless because they were unwilling to be corrected by believing? And where did this come from? “You are from your father the devil.” How long will you keep mentioning a father? How long will you keep changing fathers—now Abraham, now God? Hear it from the Son of God, whose children you are: “You are from your father the devil.”

God, therefore, the Creator of all creatures, created the human being. How, then, does he say here: “You are from your father the devil”? Whatever has been created by God is good, and every human being, insofar as he is God’s creature, is good; but insofar as he submits himself through free choice to the devil, he is from the devil as father.

“For human nature is good, but it was corrupted by an evil will, and from this corruption he was from the devil as father. What God made cannot be evil, unless the human being himself is evil to himself. Therefore the Jews are called children of the devil, not by being born, but by imitating. It is the custom of Holy Scripture often to call people children on the basis of imitation or similarity of deeds, as the Prophet says to the Jews: ‘Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite’ (Ezekiel 16:3). The Amorites were a certain nation, from which the Jews did not derive their origin; the Hittites likewise had their own nation, entirely alien to the race of the Jews. But because the Amorites and Hittites were impious, while the Jews imitated their impieties, they had found parents—not those from whom they had been born, but those whose ways they followed and by whose likeness they were likewise condemned.”

You may perhaps ask: “From where did the devil himself come?” From the same source as the other angels, certainly. The other angels remained in their obedience; he fell through disobedience and pride, and the angel became the devil.

“But now hear what the Lord says: ‘You are from your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father. You are seeking to kill me, a man who tells you the truth.’ He envied the human being and killed the human being. When the devil envied the human being, he clothed himself in a serpent, spoke to the woman, and through the woman poisoned the man as well. They died by listening to the devil, whom they would not have listened to if they had wished to listen to God—for the human being had been placed between God, who created him and whom he ought to have obeyed, and the deceiver [Augustine adds: ‘and him who had fallen’]. Therefore he was a murderer from the beginning.”

Observe the kind of murder involved, brothers. The devil is called a murderer, not because he was armed with a sword or girded with iron. He came to the human being, sowed an evil word, and killed him. Therefore do not think that you are not a murderer when you persuade your brother to do evil: if you persuade your brother to do evil, you kill him. Hear the Psalmist: “The teeth of human beings are their weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Psalm 56:5).

You therefore wish to do the desires of your father; that is why you rage against the flesh, because you cannot rage against the mind. He was a murderer from the beginning—certainly in the first human being. From that time he was a murderer when murder could come to be [Augustine adds: “from that time murder could come to be”], from the time the human being was made. For the human being could not be killed unless he had first been made. He was therefore a murderer from the beginning.

And from where was he a murderer? “And he did not stand in the truth, because the truth is not in him.” Not in the way that truth is in Christ, so that Christ himself is the truth. If he had stood in the truth, he would have stood in Christ. But he did not stand in the truth, because the truth is not in him.

**VERSE 44.**—“When he speaks falsehood, he speaks from what is his own, because he is a liar and its father.”

What does this mean? You heard the words of the Gospel and received them attentively. Behold, I repeat them, so that you may recognize what you should demand. The Lord was speaking about the devil what the devil deserved [Augustine: “what ought to have been said about the devil by the Lord”]. “He was a murderer from the beginning.” It is true: for he killed the first human being. “And he did not stand in the truth,” because he fell away from the truth. “When he speaks falsehood”—the devil himself, certainly—“he speaks from what is his own, because he is a liar and its father.”

“But the devil was a liar from himself, and he himself generated his falsehood; he had previously heard falsehood from no one. Just as God the Father begot the Son, the truth, so the devil begot, as it were, falsehood as a son.” He generated falsehood because he did not stand in the truth. For everyone who remains in God remains in the truth, because God is truth. But whoever withdraws from God will be a liar, as the Psalmist says: “Every human being is a liar” (Psalm 116). Insofar as a human being withdraws from God, he will be a liar, insofar as he turns away from the truth, and for this reason he will be a sinner: for every sin is not truth but falsehood, because, by withdrawing from God, it does not possess truth.

The devil, however, was created good, but became evil through himself, by turning away from the highest good. Therefore he spoke falsehood from what was his own, because he found in himself the source of his being a liar. The human being, deceived by the devil, became a liar through the devil. And therefore he is the devil’s son, not by nature but by imitation.

Let us therefore withdraw from the father of falsehood and run to the Father of truth. Let us embrace the truth, so that we may receive true freedom.

“The Jews had seen with their father what they were saying. What was it except falsehood? But the Lord had seen with his Father what he should say. What was it except himself? What was it except the eternal Word of the Father, coeternal with the Father?”

Therefore he added: **(VERSE 45.)** “I speak the truth to you, and you do not believe me.” For a liar speaks falsehood, but the truth brings forth truth. The devil is a liar, whereas Christ is the truth and the defender of truth, because from the mouth of truth nothing other than truth can proceed. It follows, therefore:

## CHAPTER XXIII

He says that the one who keeps his word will never see death. And, among many other things, affirming that he existed before Abraham, he departed from the Temple.

**VERSE 46.**—“Which of you will convict me of sin, as I convict you and your father of sin and falsehood? Behold the gentleness of Christ.”

> **[Column 873D] From Saint Gregory, Homily 18, no. 1.**  
> He had come to release people from sins, and he said: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” He does not disdain to show by reason that he is not a sinner, although by the power of his divinity he could justify sinners.

He asks them why they do not wish to believe the one speaking the truth: “If I have spoken the truth to you, why do you not believe me?”—unless because you are children of the devil and not of truth; children of the devil not by nature, but by imitation. He gave the reason why they did not believe the truth when he said: **(VERSE 47.)**

> **[Column 873D] From Saint Augustine, Treatise 42, nos. 15–16.**  
> “For this reason you do not hear, because you are not from God.” Again, do not consider nature, but vice. In this way these people are from God and are not from God: by nature they are from God, but by vice they are not from God. The good nature that is from God sinned by the will, believing what the devil persuaded it to believe, and was corrupted; therefore it must seek a physician, because it is not healthy. Let nature be acknowledged, so that the Creator may be praised; let vice be acknowledged, because of which a physician must be summoned. Terrible is what he adds:

> **[Column 874D] From Saint Gregory, the passage cited, no. 2.**  
> “Whoever is from God hears the words of God. For this reason you do not hear, because you are not from God.” If the one who is from God hears the words of God, and whoever is not from him cannot hear his words, let each person ask himself whether he perceives the words of God in the ear of his heart, and understand from whom he is. Truth commands us to desire the heavenly homeland, to crush the desires of the flesh, to turn away from the glory of the world, not to seize what belongs to others, and to give away what belongs to us. Let each of you therefore consider within himself whether this voice of God has grown strong in the ear of his heart, and recognize that he is now from God.

The Jews therefore said: **(VERSE 48.)** “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?”

After receiving such a great insult, let us hear what the Lord answers: **(VERSE 49.)** “I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you dishonor me.”

Since “Samaritan” means “guardian,” and he himself is truly a guardian, of whom the Psalmist says: “Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain” (Psalm 127:1), and to whom Isaiah says: “Guardian, what of the night? Guardian, what of the night?” (Isaiah 21:11), the Lord did not wish to answer, “I am not a Samaritan,” but said: “I do not have a demon.”

Two charges had been brought against him: he denied one and, by remaining silent, accepted the other. For he had come as the guardian of the human race; and if he had said that he was not a Samaritan, he would have denied that he was its guardian. Thus he kept silent about what he acknowledged and patiently rejected what he heard falsely said, declaring: “I do not have a demon.”

Here the Lord offered us in himself an example of patience. If he had wished to answer the Jews, “You have a demon,” he would certainly have spoken the truth, since they could not speak so perversely about God unless they were filled with a demon. But after receiving the insult, the Truth did not wish to say even what was true, lest he appear not to have spoken the truth but to have returned an insult because he had been provoked.

What, then, is suggested to you by this, except that when we receive insults from our neighbors on the basis of falsehood, we should also keep silent about their true faults, lest we turn the ministry of just correction into weapons of rage?

But he still instructs us by his example concerning what we should do in such circumstances, when he adds: **(VERSE 50.)** “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges.”

We certainly know what is written: “The Father has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). And yet behold, the same Son, receiving insults, does not seek his own glory. He reserves the insults inflicted upon him for the Father’s judgment, clearly indicating to us how patient we ought to be, while even the one who judges does not yet wish to avenge himself.

But when the perversity of the wicked increases, preaching ought not merely to be broken off; it ought also to be increased. The Lord teaches us this by his own example. After he had been called demon-possessed, he bestowed the benefits of his preaching more abundantly, saying: **(VERSE 51.)** “Amen, amen, I say to you: if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.”

But just as it is necessary for the good to become still better even through insults, so the reprobate always become worse through a benefit. For after receiving this preaching, they again say: **(VERSE 52.)** “Now we know that you have a demon.”

Because they had clung to eternal death, and did not see the same death to which they had clung, since they looked only upon the death of the flesh [others: “the death of the flesh”], they became blind to the word of truth, saying: “Abraham died, and the prophets, and you say: ‘If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death forever.’”

Thus they themselves, as though venerating Abraham and the prophets, place them before the Truth himself. But the reason is made clear to us: those who do not know God also falsely venerate God’s servants.

“You say,” he says, “that I have a demon. I call you to life: keep my word, and you will not die.” They heard that the one who kept his word would never see death, and they were angry because they were already dead by the death that ought to have been avoided. For they could not avoid the death by which Abraham and the prophets died—that is, the death of the flesh. Abraham, however, lived in spirit; and therefore the Truth himself says of him elsewhere: “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.”

> **[Column 875D] See Saint Augustine, Treatise 43, nos. 13 and 15.**  
> What does he mean when he says, “He will never see death forever”? (Matthew 22.) He means the death of condemnation with the devil and his angels. For the death of the body is a kind of departure for the saints into a better life, but for the impious it is a departure into everlasting punishments. It is this that the Truth wished to designate here by the name of death. But by this death, which the Lord wished to be understood, neither Abraham died nor did the prophets die. They died and live; these lived and were dead.

**VERSE 53.**—“They say: ‘Whom do you make yourself out to be, that you say, “The one who keeps my word will never see death,” when you know that Abraham died and the prophets died?’”

Jesus answered: **(VERSE 54.)** “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me.”

He said this because of what they had said: “Whom do you make yourself out to be?” For he refers his glory to the Father, from whom he has his being as God. The Lord Jesus Christ calls him his Father, whom they called their God but did not know. For if they had known him, they would have received his Son.

**(VERSE 55.)** “But I know him,” he says. To those judging according to the flesh, he might also have seemed arrogant because he said: “I know him.” But observe what follows: “If I say that I do not know him, I shall be like you, a liar.” Therefore arrogance is not to be avoided in such a way that the truth is abandoned. Rather, “I know him, and I keep his word.” He was speaking the Father’s word as the Son, and he himself was the Father’s Word speaking to human beings.

**VERSE 56.**

> **[Column 875D] Saint Gregory, the passage cited, nos. 3–4.**  
> It should be noted that the Lord saw them resisting him with open hostility, yet he did not cease to preach to them with repeated speech, saying: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad.”

Abraham saw the Lord’s day when, as a figure of the highest Trinity, he received three angels as guests. After receiving them, he spoke to the three as though to one, because although there is a number of persons in the Trinity, there is unity of divinity in nature.

But the carnal minds of his hearers do not lift their eyes from the flesh; they consider only the age of his flesh, saying: **(VERSE 57.)** “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?”

Our gracious Redeemer removes them from contemplating his flesh and draws them toward contemplation of his divinity, saying: **(VERSE 58.)** “Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am.”

“Before” belongs to past time; “I am” belongs to the present. And because divinity does not possess past or future time, but always possesses being, he did not say, “Before Abraham, I was,” but, “Before Abraham, I am.”

Hence it is said to Moses: “I am who I am”; and, “You shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exodus 3:14). Before or after Abraham belongs to one who could approach through the manifestation of presence and withdraw through the course of life. But the Truth always possesses being, because nothing begins for him in an earlier time, nor is anything brought to an end in a later one.

But since the minds of the unbelieving were unable to endure these words of eternity, they ran to stones and sought to bury the one whom they could not understand. What the Lord did in response to the fury of those who were stoning him is shown immediately afterward: **(VERSE 59.)** “But Jesus hid himself and went out of the Temple.”

It is exceedingly astonishing, dearly beloved brothers, why the Lord avoided his persecutors by hiding himself, since, if he had wished to exercise the power of his divinity, by a silent movement of his will he could have bound them in the act of striking him, or overwhelmed them with the punishment of sudden death. But because he had come to suffer, he did not wish to exercise judgment.

Certainly, at the very time of his Passion, he both showed how much he could do and nevertheless endured that for which he had come. For when he said to his persecutors who were seeking him, “I am he,” with this single utterance he struck down their pride and cast them all to the ground (John 18:6).

Since, then, he could here have escaped the hands of those who were stoning him without hiding himself, why did he hide himself, unless because our Redeemer, made human among human beings, speaks one thing to us by word and another by example? What does he speak to us by this example except that, even when we are able to resist, we should humbly avoid the anger of the proud?

> **[Column 876D] Thus far Saint Gregory.**

# BOOK FIVE

## CHAPTER XXIV

The man blind from birth is given sight, while the Pharisees are greatly troubled; he declares himself to be the light of the world. Later, the man who had been enlightened recognizes him and worships him.

## CHAPTER IX, VERSE 1

After the Lord had gone out from the Temple of the Jews, let us hear what he did among the Gentile people—or rather, among the whole human race.

For the Evangelist continues and says: “As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth.”

> **[Column 877D] From Saint Augustine, Treatise 44, nos. 1–17.**  
> The things our Lord Jesus Christ did, things astonishing and wondrous, are both deeds and words: deeds because they were performed, words because they are signs. If, then, we consider what this event signifies, this blind man is the human race. This blindness occurred in the first human being through sin, from whom we all derived our origin—not only of death but also of iniquity. For if blindness is unbelief and illumination is faith, whom did Christ find faithful when he came?

Therefore the Evangelist says of Christ: “And as he passed by.” For Christ passed by in such a way that he did not stand in the way of our sins, just as the Lord himself says in a certain parable: “A Samaritan came along the road” (Luke 10:33), the one who came to heal the wounded man who was half-dead. He passed by to illuminate the blind [in Bede: “passing by, he illuminates the blind”]; the man who is called wounded in the parable is here, in the actual event, given sight.

“He therefore saw a blind man—not merely blind, but blind from birth.” For all human beings except the one who was born from a virgin were blind through original sin; that is, they were born with the sin that their first parents drew from a sinful root.

**(VERSE 2.)** His disciples asked him:

“Rabbi”—you know that “Rabbi” means “teacher.” They called him Teacher because they desired to learn. They put a question to the Lord as to a teacher:

**VERSE 3.** “Who sinned, this man or his parents, that he should be born blind?”

Jesus answered: “Neither this man sinned nor his parents” [“so that he should be born blind”]. What does this mean? If no human being is without sin, were the parents of this blind man without sin? Was he himself born without original sin, or had he added nothing through his manner of life?

If, then, both his parents had sin and he himself had sin, why did the Lord say, “Neither this man sinned nor his parents,” unless he answered with regard to the matter about which he had been asked—why he had been born blind? His parents did have sin, but it was not because of that sin that he was born blind.

If it was not because of the sin of his parents that he was born blind, why was he born blind? Hear the teacher teaching: he seeks one who believes, so that he may make him understand. He himself gives the reason why that man was born blind: “Neither this man sinned,” he says, “nor his parents, but so that the works of God might be manifested in him.”

Not only so that I might do something in this particular blind man, but so that it might be manifested what must be done through me in the blindness of the entire human race. [Then he continued and added:] “I must work the works of the one who sent me while it is day.”

“Remember how he assigns all glory to the one from whom he is, because that one has a Son who is from him, while he himself does not have one from whom he is.”

What are the works of the Lord for which the Son of God came into the world, except to illuminate the blindness of the human race, to heal the wounded, to seek the lost, and to restore what was deformed?

But what does he mean when he says: **(VERSE 4.)** “I must work the works of the one who sent me while it is day. Night is coming, when no one can work”?

“It is clear that in this passage the Lord mentioned an actual and determined day, namely, himself, the light of the world. **(VERSE 5.)** ‘As long as I am in the world,’ he says, ‘I am the light of the world.’ Therefore he himself works.

“But how long is he in this world? Do we think, brothers, that he was here then and is not here now? If we think this, then after the Lord’s Ascension this fearful night has already come, in which no one can work.”

If this night came after the Ascension, what is the meaning of what he said to his disciples as he ascended into heaven: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20)? Then he was in the world by bodily presence; now he is present everywhere in the world by divine power.

We have heard about the day; let us hear what this night is. “What, then? What shall we say about this night? When will it be, when no one will be able to work? This night will belong to the impious; this night will belong to those to whom it will finally be said: ‘Go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels’ (Matthew 25:41).

“But it is called night, not flame or fire. Hear that it is also night. It is said of a certain servant: ‘Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the outer darkness’ (Matthew 22:13). Let the human being therefore work while he lives [Augustine adds: “while he lives”], lest he be overtaken by that night in which no one can work.

“Now is the time for faith to work through love; and if we work now, this is the day, this is Christ. Hear him promising, and do not suppose that he is absent: ‘Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age.’ There will be night there, where no one can work, but only receive what he has worked for. The time of working is one thing, the time of receiving another; for he will repay each person according to his works.”

Let us hear the Apostle exhorting us with attentive concern to work while we have time. For he says: “While we have time, let us do good to all” (Galatians 6:10).

We have heard what Christ said, admonishing the good and frightening the wicked; but let us see what he did. **(VERSES 6–7.)** When he had said these things, he spat on the ground, made clay from the spittle, and spread the clay over his eyes. Then he said to him: “Go and wash in the pool of Siloam,” which is interpreted as “Sent.”

What the Lord did is clear. Illumination was given to the blind man, but a great mystery is commended to us concerning the human race.

“He spat on the ground and made clay from his saliva, because the Word became flesh. And he anointed the blind man’s eyes. He had been anointed, but he did not yet see. He sent him to the pool called Siloam. It was relevant to the Evangelist to make known to us the name of this pool, and he said: ‘which is interpreted as Sent.’

“Now you recognize who was sent: unless he had been sent, none of us would have been released from iniquity. He therefore washed his eyes in the pool that is interpreted as ‘Sent’; he was baptized in Christ.

“If, then, he illuminated him when he baptized him, in a certain sense, in himself, perhaps when he anointed him he made him a catechumen. The depth of so great a sacrament can indeed be explained and treated in various ways, but let this suffice for your charity.”

The catechumen is anointed—that is, he is taught to believe in Christ. He is sent to the pool of baptism, so that he may be illuminated, recognize the true light, receive the remission of sins, be made from a son of wrath a son of God, and come enlightened to preach Christ.

**VERSES 8–9.** Accordingly, the neighbors and those who had previously seen him, because he was a beggar, were saying: “Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?” Others were saying: “It is he”; others, however: “No, but he resembles him.”

“The opening of his eyes had changed his face. He said: ‘It is I.’ A pleasing voice, lest it be judged displeasing.”

**(VERSES 10–11.)** They therefore said to him: “How were your eyes opened?” He answered: “The man who is called Jesus” [the manuscript: “Christ”] “made clay and anointed my eyes, and said to me: ‘Go to the pool of Siloam and wash.’ I went, washed, and saw.”

Behold, he has become a messenger of grace; behold, he evangelizes and, seeing, confesses. The blind man confessed him, while the hearts of the impious writhed [others: “were constricted”; Augustine: “were broken”], because they did not have in their heart what he already had in his face.

**(VERSE 12.)** They said to him: “Where is he?” He replied: “I do not know.”

In these words his mind was still like that of one who had been anointed but did not yet see. But let us suppose, brothers, that he had that anointing in his soul. He preaches and does not know whom he preaches.

**(VERSES 13, 15.)** “They bring to the Pharisees the man who had been blind. Now it was the Sabbath when Jesus made the clay and opened his eyes. Again the Pharisees asked him how he had received his sight. But he said to them: ‘He put clay on my eyes, and I washed, and I see.’

“Some of the Pharisees were saying”—not all, but some, for certain people were already being anointed—“‘This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath.’”

Rather, the one who was without sin was keeping it. For the spiritual Sabbath is not having sin. Finally, brothers, this is what God indicates when he commends the Sabbath: “You shall do no servile work” (Leviticus 23:8). These are the words of God commending the Sabbath: “You shall do no servile work.”

Ask the earlier readings what servile work is, and hear the Lord: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). But these people, neither seeing, as I said, nor anointed, observed the Sabbath carnally and violated it spiritually.

Others were saying: “How can a sinful man perform such signs?” Behold, these are the anointed. And there was a division among them. That day had been divided [Augustine: “had divided”] between light and darkness.

**VERSE 17.** They therefore said to the blind man again: “What do you say about him who opened your eyes? What do you think about him? What is your judgment concerning him?”

They were looking for a way to bring an accusation against the man, so that he might be expelled from the synagogue but found by Christ. But he firmly expressed what he thought. For he said: “He is a prophet.”

He was still anointed in heart and did not yet confess the Son of God, but he was not lying. The Lord himself said of himself: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (Matthew 13:57).

**VERSE 18.** “The Jews therefore did not believe concerning him that he had been blind [and had received his sight], until they called the parents of the man who had received his sight”—that is, who had been blind and had received his sight.

**(VERSES 19–21.)** And they questioned them, saying: “Is this your son, whom you say was born blind? How, then, does he now see?”

His parents answered them and said: “We know that this is our son and that he was born blind. But how he now sees, we do not know. Ask him himself; he is of age; let him speak for himself.”

“We know that he is our son; but we would rightly be compelled to speak for an infant, because he could not speak for himself. He has long been able to speak; now he sees. We know him as blind from birth; we have long known him speaking; now we see him seeing. Ask him himself, so that you may be informed.”

**(VERSE 22.)** His parents said these things because they feared the Jews. For the Jews had already agreed that if anyone confessed him to be Christ, he should be expelled from the synagogue.

It was no longer an evil to be outside the synagogue. They expelled him, but Christ received him.

**VERSES 23–24.** For this reason his parents said: “He is of age; ask him himself.”

So they called again the man who had been blind and said to him: “Give glory to God.”

“What does ‘Give glory to God’ mean? Deny what you received. This certainly is not to give glory to God, but rather to blaspheme God.”

“Give glory to God,” they say. “We know that this man is a sinner.”

**(VERSES 25–26.)** The man therefore said: “Whether he is a sinner, I do not know. One thing I know: though I was blind, now I see.”

Then they said to him: “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?”

And he, already becoming irritated at the hardness of the Jews, seeing though he had been blind and unable to tolerate the blind, answered them: **(VERSE 27.)** “I have already told you, and you heard. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?”

What does “Do you also” mean, except: “I am one already”? “Do you also want to become his disciples?” “I see already, but I do not see you seeing” [Augustine: “but I do not envy you”].

**(VERSE 28.)** “They cursed him and said: ‘You are his disciple.’”

Let such a curse fall upon us and upon our children. It is a curse if you examine the heart, not if you weigh the words.

**(VERSE 29.)** “But we are disciples of Moses. We know that God spoke to Moses.”

Would that you knew that God spoke to Moses! Then you would know that God was preached through Moses. For you have God saying: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46).

Do you follow the servant and turn your back upon the Lord? But you do not even follow the servant, for through him you would be led to the Lord.

**VERSES 30–31.** The man answered and said to them: “This is astonishing: you do not know where he is from, and yet he opened my eyes. We know that God does not hear sinners, but that if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God hears him” [the manuscript: “but the one who is a worshiper of God…”].

He is still speaking as one who has been anointed. For God also hears sinners. If God did not hear sinners, that publican would have looked down at the ground in vain, struck his breast, and said: “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13). By this confession he deserved justification, just as this blind man deserved illumination.

But the hearts of sinners must be washed by the tears of repentance, so that they may be heard. Then what was done in the face of this blind man will be done in their hearts, and they will perceive that God hears them—the God who came into this world to save sinners.

## Verses 32–33

“From the beginning of the world it has never been heard that anyone opened the eyes of one born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.”

He openly and steadfastly confessed the truth. For these things that were done by the Lord—by whom could they have been done except by God? Or when could such things have been done by the disciples, unless the Lord dwelt in them?

### Verse 34

“They answered and said to him: ‘You were born entirely in sins.’” What does “entirely” mean? With his eyes closed. But the one who opened his eyes also saves him entirely: the same one who gave illumination to his face will give resurrection in his heart.

“You were born entirely in sins, and you teach us?” And they cast him out. They themselves had made him a teacher, so that they might learn; they had questioned him so many times, and, ungrateful toward their teacher, they threw him out. But, as I said a little earlier, brothers: they drive him away, but the Lord receives him. Indeed, because he was expelled, he became a Christian. [Col. 0881C]

Certainly this man was cast out of the synagogue. Jesus heard of it, found him, and said to him:

### Verses 35–36

“Do you believe in the Son of God?”

And he replied: “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?”

He was seeing, and yet he was not seeing. He saw only with his eyes; in his heart he still did not see. The Lord said to him: “You have seen him”—when you were enlightened, that is, with your eyes—“and the one who speaks with you is he.”

“When Jesus therefore heard that they had cast him out, and when he had found him, he said to him: ‘Do you believe in the Son of God?’ Now he washes the face of his heart. He answered and said, as though still anointed: ‘Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?’ [Col. 0881D]

### Verse 37

“And Jesus said to him: ‘You have seen him, and the one who speaks with you is he.’”

Then he fell down and worshiped him. Then [variant: “Now”] he washed the face of his heart. Finally, with the face of his heart washed and his conscience cleansed, recognizing him not merely as the Son of Man, as he had previously believed, but now as the Son of God whom he saw [Augustine: “the Son of God who had assumed flesh”], he said:

### Verse 38

“I believe, Lord.”

But it is too little merely to say, “I believe.” Do you want to see what sort of belief he had? Falling down, he worshiped him.

If he had not believed that the Lord whom he saw was the Son of God, he would certainly not have worshiped him.

Therefore, sinners, devote yourselves to prayer; confess your sins; pray that they may be blotted out; pray that they may be diminished; pray that, as you make progress, they themselves may decrease. [Col. 0882A] Yet do not despair, and pray even as sinners. For who has not sinned? Begin with the priests. It was said to the priests: “First offer sacrifices for your own sins, and then for the people” (Hebrews 7:27).

The text continues:

### Verse 39

“I came into this world for judgment, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”

What does he mean by saying, “I came into this world for judgment,” when elsewhere he says, “I did not come to judge the world” (John 3:17–18)? It means that one kind of judgment is the judgment of discernment, and another is the judgment of condemnation. Concerning the latter the Lord himself says elsewhere: “The one who does not believe in me has already been judged,” that is, condemned.

Here, as is clear from the words that follow, he means the judgment of discernment, when he says: “So that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.” [Col. 0882B]

“What does ‘so that those who do not see may see’ mean? Those who confess that they do not see and seek a physician in order to see. And what does ‘those who see may become blind’ mean? That is, those who think that they see and do not seek a physician, but remain in their blindness” [Augustine: “may remain”].

Therefore he called this discernment “judgment,” because it distinguishes the humble from the proud, believers from unbelievers, and those who seek a physician from those who disdain to seek one.

O Lord, you came so that those who do not see may see—rightly, because you are light; rightly, because you are day; rightly, because you free human beings from darkness. May every soul receive this; may every soul understand it, so that it may not remain in darkness but be illuminated by the one who enlightens every person coming into this world.

[Col. 0882C]

### Verse 40

For some of the Pharisees were disturbed by these words and said to him:

“Are we blind too?”

Let them hear what it was that disturbed them: “And those who see may become blind.”

### Verse 41

Jesus said to them:

“If you were blind, you would not have sin. But blindness itself is sin. If you were blind—that is, if you recognized yourselves as blind and ran to the physician—then, if you were blind in that way, you would not have sin. But now you say, ‘We see’; therefore your sin remains. Why? Because by saying, ‘We see,’ you do not seek the physician, but remain in your blindness.”

The text continues:

# Chapter XXV

He says that the one who does not enter the sheepfold through the door is a thief; he also says that he himself is the door and the shepherd of the sheep, for which he will lay down his life, and that he will bring in other sheep so that there may be one sheepfold and one shepherd. [Col. 0882D]

## Chapter 10, verses 1–6

“Amen, amen, I say to you: the one who does not enter the sheepfold through the door but climbs in by another way is a thief and a robber” [up to the place]: “Jesus spoke this proverb to them, but they did not understand what he was saying to them.”

### From Saint Augustine, *Tractates on John* 45.2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 14, 15

“Because of the Pharisees’ poisonous, proud, and incurable arrogance—for they boasted that they saw while they were blind—the Lord Jesus composed these sayings,” which are read in this parable. He graciously explained the parable to them, although they did not understand it. In it he salutarily warned us, if we pay attention, not to glory in human wisdom or in moral respectability if the humility of Catholic faith in Christ is absent. [Col. 0883A]

“For there are many pagans who, according to a certain manner of life in this world, are called good and innocent people, honoring their parents, not committing adultery, not committing murder, not stealing, not giving false testimony against anyone, and, as it were, observing the other things commanded in the law [main text: *velut observant*; manuscript: *velut observantes*, “as though observing”]—and yet they are not Christians. They often boast, like these Pharisees, saying: ‘Are we blind too?’”

But they do all these things in vain, because they do not enter through the door; rather, in their swollen arrogance, they seek to climb in by another way, as though they could ascend by their own power.

“Therefore the Lord proposed a comparison concerning his flock and the door through which one enters the sheepfold.” [Col. 0883B]

For what benefit is there in the empty inflation of those who boast about living well, if their life does not reach the end by living well forever?

“For this reason living well ought to benefit each person: so that he may be granted to live well forever. For if someone is not granted to live well forever, what benefit is it for him to live well for a time? Therefore those too should not be called people who live well who, whether through blindness they do not know the end of good living, or through vanity despise it. No one has a true and certain hope of living forever unless he acknowledges the life that is Christ and enters the sheepfold through the door.”

There are certain people who glory in their own morals and seek to draw others after them, not instructing their followers in Christ’s commands but persuading them to live according to their own examples. Concerning such people the Truth says elsewhere: “Teaching human doctrines” (Matthew 15:9), while despising the commandments of God. [Col. 0883C]

“These seek to climb in by another way, to rob and kill—not, like the shepherd, to save and preserve.”

It is of such people that this passage says: “But he climbs in by another way; he is a thief and a robber.”

Such teachers are found not only among those who are without the name of Christ—for example, among the many philosophers who loudly proclaimed their wisdom and promised a blessed life to [*suis*, inserted: “their”] followers—but also among very many who were reckoned under the Christian name and boasted that they had been enlightened by Christ, giving themselves every sort of novel designation derived from Christ and contrary to the Catholic faith, as countless heretics did. They falsely supposed that, under a false name, they entered through the door, which is Christ. [Col. 0883D]

“Sabellius says: ‘The one who is Son is himself the Father.’ But the Son [Augustine: “if he is Son”] is not the Father. The one who says that the Son is the Father does not enter through the door.

“An Arian [manuscript: Arius] says: ‘The Father is one thing, and the Son another.’ He would speak correctly if he said ‘another person,’ not ‘another thing.’ For when he says ‘another thing,’ he contradicts the one from whom he hears: ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30). Therefore he too does not enter through the door. He preaches Christ as he imagines him, not as the truth possesses [Augustine: ‘declares’] him.

“Photinus says: ‘Christ is merely human, not God.’ He too does not enter through the door, because Christ is both human and God.”

A new heresy that has arisen in our own times appears to agree with this when it asserts and preaches: “Christ, like any holy person, is God only in name [*nuncupativus Deus*], and not true God.” [Col. 0884A]

“What need is there to run through many things and enumerate the many vain heresies? Hold fast to this: the Catholic Church is in Christ’s sheepfold; believe this [Augustine: ‘Hold fast to this: the sheepfold of Christ is the Catholic Church’]. Whoever wishes to enter the sheepfold should enter through the door—that is, through Christ—and should preach Christ as true God and true Son of God.

“Let him not merely preach Christ, but seek Christ’s glory, not his own. For many, by seeking their own glory, scattered Christ’s sheep rather than gathered them. Christ the Lord our God is a humble door. Whoever enters through this door must humble himself so that he may enter with a sound head.”

These are the ones who hear the voice of the true shepherd; these are the ones whom the true shepherd calls by name as his own sheep. Concerning them it is said: “Rejoice and be glad, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). For this is how he calls them by name. [Col. 0884B]

“And who else sends them out except the one who forgives their sins, so that, freed from their harsh bonds, they may be able to follow him? And who has gone before them for them to follow except the one who, having risen from the dead, no longer dies, and death no longer rules over him” (Romans 6:9)?

He leads these sheep from faith to sight, and goes before them because he was the first of all to ascend into heaven. Those who are his sheep follow him because they know the voice of his teaching; but they do not follow alien teachers. Rather, they flee from them because they do not know the voice—that is, the teaching—of strangers.

But when the Lord Jesus was speaking, those who heard him did not understand. Their heart had grown fat, and they heard with difficulty.

“He names the door, he names the sheepfold, he names the sheep; he commends all these things, but does not yet explain them. Let us therefore read on, because he will come to those words in which he may graciously explain to us some of what he has said. From his explanation he may perhaps also enable us to understand what he did not explain. For he feeds us with what is clear and exercises us with what is obscure.

“Let us listen to the one explaining, since we have heard the one making the proposal.” [Col. 0884C]

### Verse 7

Therefore Jesus said to them again:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: I am the door of the sheep.”

Behold, he has opened the very door that he had presented as closed. He is the door. We have recognized it; let us enter, so that we may rejoice that we have entered.

### Verse 8

“All who came are thieves and robbers.”

“What does this mean, Lord—‘All who came’? What then? Did you not come?”

But understand: when he said, “All who came,” he meant all apart from him [Augustine: “I said, ‘all who came,’ certainly apart from me”].

Let us recall the matter. Before his coming, the prophets came. Were they thieves and robbers? Certainly not. They did not come apart from him, but came with him. He sent heralds announcing that he would come, but he possessed the hearts of those whom he sent. They came with him, therefore, because they came with the word of God. [Col. 0884D]

“I am,” he says, “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). He is the truth. They came with him because they were truthful and preached the truth.

But all who came apart from him were thieves and robbers.

They came by themselves because they had not been sent through him, as the Apostle says: “How will they preach unless they are sent?” (Romans 10:15). Those who came by themselves and were not sent by him are thieves and robbers.

Before Christ’s coming there were false prophets among God’s people and false teachers. Likewise, after his coming, very many false teachers arose under the Christian name—not teachers but seducers, not preachers but false preachers [manuscript: “plunderers”], practicing robbery and not adhering to sound doctrine. [Col. 0885A]

Of such people it is said: “They are thieves and robbers,” that is, they came to steal and kill.

But the true sheep did not listen to them; they did not hide a wolf’s heart beneath a sheep’s skin.

Therefore those who preached before Christ’s coming preached by the same Spirit by whom the apostles and holy teachers preached after Christ’s coming, showing the way of truth to the world.

“But all those who at that time believed—whether Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, or the other patriarchs and prophets who foretold Christ—were sheep, and they heard Christ. They heard not a strange voice but Christ’s own voice. For the judge cries out in the herald, while the herald announces that the judge is coming. [Col. 0885B]

“There are others, therefore, whom the sheep did not hear, because Christ’s voice was not in them: they wandered, spoke falsehoods, chattered empty things, invented vanities, and deceived the wretched—such as the false prophets and the scribes and Pharisees in the time of the Lord himself. These are the ones who came by themselves and were not sent by the judge.”

Now that these people and their teachings have been driven far away, let us see where the good shepherd calls us.

### Verse 9

“I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved; he will enter and go out and find pasture.”

“This plainly shows that not only the shepherd but also the sheep enter through the door. But what does ‘he will enter and go out and find pasture’ mean?

“To enter the Church through Christ the door is exceedingly good. But to leave the Church, as the evangelist John himself says in his letter, ‘They went out from us, but they were not of us’ (1 John 2:20), is certainly not good.

“Such an exit, therefore, could not be praised by the good shepherd, so that he would say: ‘He will enter and go out and find pasture.’ There is, then, not only a good entrance but also a good exit through the good door, which is Christ.

“But what is that praiseworthy and blessed exit? I could say that we enter when we think something inwardly, but go out when we perform something outwardly. And since, as the Apostle says, Christ dwells in our hearts through faith (Ephesians 3:17), to enter through Christ would be to think according to that faith, while to go out through Christ would be, according to that same faith, also to act outwardly, that is, before human beings.

“Therefore it is said in the Psalm: ‘A person goes out to his work’ (Psalm 103:23). The Lord himself also says: ‘Let your works shine before human beings’ (Matthew 5:16).

“But I am more pleased by what the Truth itself, as the good shepherd and therefore the good teacher, in a certain way admonished us to understand concerning the words: ‘He will enter and go out and find pasture.’ Then he immediately added: [Col. 0885D]

### Verse 10

‘The thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy. I came so that they may have life, and have it more abundantly.’”

He seems to have said that they may have life as they enter [Augustine adds: “and have it more abundantly as they go out”].

No one can go out through the door—that is, through Christ—to eternal life, which will be in sight, unless through that same door, namely Christ, he has entered into Christ’s Church, which is his sheepfold, for the temporal life that exists in faith [variant: “unto the end”]. [Col. 0886A]

Therefore he says: “I came so that they may have life,” that is, the faith that works through love (Galatians 5:6), through which faith they enter the sheepfold so that they may live, because “the righteous person lives by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4).

“And have it more abundantly”: those who persevere to the end go out through that door, namely through faith in Christ. For true believers die, and they will have life more abundantly when they come to the place where that shepherd has gone before them, where they will never again die. [Col. 0886B]

Although even here, in the sheepfold itself, pasture is not lacking—for we can understand the saying, “and will find pasture” in relation both to entrance and to exit [manuscript: *pascuae*, an inflectional variant; manuscript: *pascuam*, “pasture,” and likewise elsewhere]—nevertheless they will truly find pasture where those who hunger and thirst for righteousness will be satisfied (Matthew 5:6).

What sort of pasture did the one find to whom it was said: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43)?

The Lord’s saying concerning the perfection of the good shepherd and the flight of the evil shepherd, whom he calls a hired man, follows.

### Verses 11–12

“I am the good shepherd,” he says. “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep. But the hired man flees, because he is a hired man and does not care about the sheep.”

### From Saint Augustine, *Tractate on John* 46.1, 2, 4

The Lord Jesus was speaking to his sheep, both present and future, who were there at that time [manuscript: “who were present”]. Already in the present [*in praesentia*] they were his sheep, though they were to become his sheep. [Col. 0885D]

### According to Augustine

“The Lord Jesus was speaking to his sheep, both present and future, because those who were to become his sheep were already there, where his sheep already were. Again: to the present and future sheep—to them and to us, and to all who will be his sheep after us—he showed them as already his own [inserted: *suas jam*]. [Col. 0886D]

“Therefore let all hear the voice of their shepherd saying: ‘I am the good shepherd.’ He would not have added ‘good’ unless there were bad shepherds. But the bad shepherds are the thieves and robbers—or, at any rate, the hired men.

“We must examine, distinguish, and recognize all the persons whom he has introduced here. The Lord has already disclosed two things that he had presented in a way as though they were hidden. We now know that he himself is the door; we know that he himself is the shepherd.

“Who the thieves and robbers are was revealed in the preceding saying. But now we have heard of the hired man; we have heard of the wolf; and the doorkeeper has also been named.

“Among the good, therefore, there are the door, the doorkeeper, the shepherd, and the sheep; among the bad, there are thieves and robbers, the hired man, and the wolf.

“We understand the door to be the Lord Christ, and the shepherd to be Christ himself. Who is the doorkeeper? For he himself explained these two things and left us to seek the doorkeeper.

“And what does he say about the doorkeeper? ‘To him,’ he says, ‘the doorkeeper opens.’ To whom does he open? To the shepherd. What does he open to the shepherd? The door. And what is the door itself? The shepherd himself also.” [Col. 0887A]

The names are different—shepherd, [door], and sheep—but they signify one reality. For shortly before we heard the Lord’s own words: “I am the door”; and now we have read: “I am the shepherd.”

He is also called the Lamb by the friend of the bridegroom, as we heard in this present Gospel: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold the one who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).
