Long before, the Prophet foretold of him: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Isaiah 53:7), although his entire body is understood as his sheep.

The doorkeeper may also be understood as Christ, because no one enters or leaves unless he opens—the one who holds the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens (Revelation 3:7).

“Let us not hesitate, therefore, to understand the same person as both the doorkeeper and the door, according to a certain comparison. Who is the doorkeeper except the one who opens? And who opens except the one who reveals himself? For he says of himself: ‘I am the way, and the truth, and the life.’ [Col. 0887B]

“If perhaps you wish to seek another person as the doorkeeper, it is the Holy Spirit, of whom the Lord himself said to his disciples: ‘He will teach you all truth’ (John 16:13). What is the door? Christ. What is Christ? The truth. Who opens the door except the one who teaches all truth?”

When the Lord wished to show the work of the good shepherd, he set himself forth as an example, saying: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep.”

He did what he commanded; he demonstrated what he ordered. He laid down his life for his sheep. He showed us the way of despising death, and provided a model after which we should be formed.

First, we must mercifully expend our external possessions for his sheep; finally, if necessary, we must even offer our own death for those same sheep. [Col. 0887C]

Whoever does not give his possessions for the sheep—when will he give his life for them?

We have explained—or rather, with the Lord teaching us, we have understood—who the shepherd is, who the door is, who the doorkeeper is, and who the sheep is. We have also learned who the thieves and robbers are.

But now let us consider the hired man and the wolf, concerning whom the Lord himself said:

“But the hired man, who is not the shepherd and whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and flees.”

### From Saint Gregory, *Homilies*, Book I, Homily 14.2–5

He is called not a shepherd but a hired man who feeds the Lord’s sheep not out of intimate love but for temporal rewards.

For a hired man is one who indeed occupies the place of a shepherd but does not seek the profit of souls. He craves earthly advantages, rejoices in the honor of authority, feeds on temporal gains, and delights in the reverence shown to him by human beings. [Col. 0887D]

These are the hired man’s wages: that, for the very labor he performs in governance, he finds here what he seeks, while in the future he remains alien to the inheritance of the flock.

The wolf comes upon the sheep when any unjust and rapacious person oppresses the faithful and humble.

But the one who seemed to be a shepherd and was not one abandons the sheep and flees, because, fearing danger for himself, he does not dare to resist the other’s injustice.

He flees not by changing his location but by withdrawing his assistance. He flees who sees injustice and remains silent; he flees who hides himself in silence.

“But there is another wolf who daily, without ceasing, tears apart not bodies but minds: namely, the evil spirit, who prowls around the folds of the faithful, lying in wait and seeking the deaths of souls. [Col. 0888A]

“Concerning this wolf it is immediately added: ‘The wolf seizes and scatters the sheep.’

“The wolf comes and the hired man flees, because the evil spirit tears apart the minds of the faithful in temptation, while the one who occupies the shepherd’s place does not exercise watchful care. Souls perish, and he rejoices in earthly advantages.

“The wolf seizes and scatters the sheep when he draws one person into lust, inflames another with greed, raises another up in pride, divides another through anger, goads this one with envy, and trips that one through deceit.

“Thus the wolf scatters the flock when the devil kills the faithful people through temptations.

“But the hired man is not set on fire by zeal against these things; he is not stirred by the fervor of love. Because he seeks only external advantages, he carelessly allows the internal losses of the flock.

“Hence it is immediately added: [Col. 0888B]

### Verse 13

‘But the hired man flees, because he is a hired man and does not care about the sheep.’

“The sole reason the hired man flees is that he is a hired man. It is as though it were plainly said: He cannot stand in danger for the sheep who, in presiding over the sheep, does not love the sheep but seeks earthly profit.

“For while he embraces honor and rejoices in temporal advantages, he trembles to oppose himself to danger, lest he lose what he loves.

“But because our Redeemer has made known the faults of the false shepherd, he again showed the model after which we ought to be formed, saying: [Col. 0888C]

### Verse 14

‘I am the good shepherd.’

And he adds: “I know my own”—that is, I love them—“and my own know me.”

It is as though he plainly said: “Those who love obey.”

### Verse 15

He immediately added:

“Just as the Father knows me, and I know the Father, and I lay down my life for the sheep.”

It is as though he plainly said: This is how it is shown that I know the Father and am known by the Father: I lay down my life for my sheep. That is, by the love with which I die for the sheep, I show how greatly I love the Father.

Because he had come to redeem not only Judea but also the Gentiles, he added:

### Verse 16

“And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one sheepfold and one shepherd.” [Col. 0888D]

The Lord had foreseen our redemption—we who have come from the Gentile people—when he said that he would bring in other sheep.

“You see this happening daily, brothers; today you see it accomplished in the reconciliation of the nations. He makes one sheepfold out of two flocks because he joins the Jewish and Gentile peoples in one faith, as Paul testifies when he says: ‘He himself is our peace, who made both one’ (Ephesians 2:14).

“For choosing the simple from both nations for eternal life, he leads the sheep into his own sheepfold.

“Concerning these sheep he said again:

‘My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life.’

“Of these he also said shortly before:

‘If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will enter and go out and find pasture.’

“He will enter into faith; he will go out from faith to sight, from belief to contemplation; and he will find pasture in eternal refreshment.

“His sheep will find pasture because whoever follows him with a simple heart is nourished by the food of eternal verdure.

“And what is the pasture of these sheep except the eternal joys of the ever-green paradise? The pasture of the elect is the present face of God: while it is gazed upon without failing, the mind is satisfied forever with the food of life.” [Col. 0889A]

### Thus far Saint Gregory. The text continues:

## Verse 17

### From Saint Augustine, *Tractate on John* 47.7, 9

“Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, and I take it up again.”

“What does he say—”

### In the Rheims manuscript this begins Chapter 27

“Therefore the Father loves me? Because I die so that I may rise again.”

He spoke with great emphasis when he said: “I.” “Because I,” he says, “lay down my life. I lay it down.”

What does “I lay it down” mean? “I,” he says, “lay it down.”

Let the Jews not boast. They were able to rage; they were not able to exercise power. Let them rage as much as they can: if I do not wish to lay down my life, what will they accomplish by raging?

They were struck down by a single answer when he said to them: “Whom are you seeking?” (John 18:6). They said, “Jesus,” and he said to them, “I am.” They drew back and fell. [Col. 0889B]

Those who were about to die fell at the one voice of Christ. What will they do at the voice of the judge?

“I,” he says, “lay down my life.”

Let the Jews not boast as though they had prevailed. He himself laid down his life.

Just as he had the power to lay it down, so he had the power to take it up again.

He showed this in other words in this same Gospel when he said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19, 21). The evangelist followed this with an explanation: “He was speaking about the temple of his body.” He added that the disciples remembered these words when Christ had risen from the dead. [Col. 0889C]

What was raised was what had died; for the Word could not die, nor was that soul dead. Only the flesh died, and it rose on the third day.

But it must be asked what he meant when he said: “I lay down my life.”

Who laid it down? What did he lay down? Who is the one who laid it down?

What is Christ? The Word and the human being. Yet not a human being in such a way as to be flesh alone: since a human being consists of flesh and soul, and the whole human being is in Christ.

For he would not have assumed the inferior part and abandoned the better part; the soul is the better part of a human being than the body.

Since, therefore, the whole human being is in Christ, what is Christ? The Word, I say, and the human being. “The Word became flesh,” that is, God became human. For he says:

# Chapter XXVI

He says that he has the power to lay down and take up his life again. After the Dedication had taken place in Jerusalem, and while the Pharisees were questioning him amid many other matters, he said: “I and the Father are one.” And many believed in him. [Col. 0889D]

### Verse 18

“I have the power to lay down my life, and I have the power to take it up again.”

### Saint Augustine, in the cited passage, sections 11–14

Christ laid down his life for us and, when he wished, laid it down; when he wished, he took it up again.

Therefore to lay down one’s life is to die. As the Apostle Peter said to the Lord: “I will lay down my life for you” (John 13:37), that is, “I will die in the flesh for you.” [Col. 0890A]

The flesh laid down its life, and the flesh again took up its life—not, however, by the flesh’s own power, but by the power of the indwelling Word of God.

The Word of God never laid down the soul after he had assumed it into unity with himself in person. Rather, the soul was laid down by the flesh and taken up again through the power of the divinity.

The flesh therefore lays down its life by expiring.

Look at the Lord himself on the cross. What did he say? “I thirst” (John 19:28 and following). Those standing nearby dipped a sponge in vinegar, fastened it to a reed, and brought it to his mouth. When he had received it, he said: “It is finished.”

What does “It is finished” mean? Everything that had been prophesied beforehand as destined to occur before my death [inserted: *de me*, “concerning me”] has been fulfilled.

And because he had the power to lay down his life whenever he wished, after he said “It is finished,” the evangelist says: “And bowing his head, he gave up his spirit.” [Col. 0890B]

What is called there “he gave up” is called here “he lays down,” because to give up and to lay down are one thing.

“Who gave it up? What did he give up? He gave up the spirit; the flesh gave it up.

“What does ‘the flesh gave it up’ mean? The flesh sent it out; the flesh expired it. For this is why one is said to ‘expire’: to become outside the spirit, just as ‘to be exiled’ means to be outside one’s soil.”

What is said here—“I have the power to lay down my life”—is said there as “Bowing his head, he gave up his spirit,” because the spirit is the soul. [Col. 0890C]

“When the soul leaves the flesh and the flesh remains without the soul, then a human being is said to lay down his life.

“When did Christ lay down his life? When the Word willed it. Sovereignty was in the Word; there was the power to determine when the flesh should lay down its life and when it should take it up again.

“For just as one human being consists of soul and body, so one Christ consists of the Word and the human being. Soul and body are two things, but one human being. The Word and the human being are two things, but one Christ.

“Let no one waver in faith when he hears the Lord say: ‘I have the power to lay down my life.’ The flesh lays it down, but by the power of the Word; the flesh takes it up, but by the power of the Word.”

The Word, soul, and flesh are one Christ. When the flesh was killed, Christ was killed; when the flesh took up the soul again, Christ took up the soul again.

For whatever was accomplished there in the dispensation of human salvation, the one Christ accomplished it all: one proper and perfect Son of God, one true and almighty God; the human being is God because of the Word; God is a human being because of the human being, as it is said: “The Word became flesh.” [Col. 0890D]

But how all these things were to be fulfilled, he showed in the following words.

“This commandment,” he says, “I received from my Father.”

The Word did not receive a commandment through a word; rather, in the only-begotten Word of the Father there is every commandment.

But when the Son is said to receive from the Father what he possesses substantially, how is it said: “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son to have life in himself” (John 5:26), when the Son himself is life?

The power is not diminished; rather, generation is being shown. For the Father did not add something to the Son as though he had been born imperfect, but by begetting gave everything to the one whom he begot perfect. [Col. 0891A]

Thus he gave his equality to the one whom he did not beget unequal.

But while the Lord was speaking these things, the light was shining in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.

### Verses 19–20

A division arose again among the Jews because of these words. Many of them were saying:

“He has a demon; he is insane. Why do you listen to him?”

These were the densest darkness.

### Verse 21

Others were saying:

“These words are not those of one who has a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?”

The eyes of these people [manuscript: “of these just people”] were beginning to be opened.

### Thus far from Saint Augustine

They had begun to see some light and to recognize the truth.

We have heard of God’s patience [manuscript: “the Lord’s patience”], and, amid the Jews’ insults, of the preaching of salvation. But they, hardened, began rather to test him than to obey his words. [Col. 0891B]

### Verse 22

The evangelist says:

“The Dedication took place in Jerusalem. It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the portico of Solomon.”

### From Bede’s Homily on the Dedication of the Church

The Dedication was the solemnity of the temple’s dedication, which the people of God had been accustomed to celebrate every year according to the ancient tradition of the Fathers.

But it should be noted that the Dedication mentioned here does not concern the temple’s first dedication but its final one. This can easily be gathered from the fact that it is reported as having taken place in winter.

The first dedication of that temple was carried out by Solomon in autumn (2 Chronicles 7); the second, by Zerubbabel and Joshua the priest, in spring (Ezra 6); the third was carried out by Judas Maccabaeus in winter, when it is specifically recorded that the Dedication was established to be renewed every year through solemn observances as a memorial (Maccabees 4). [Col. 0891C]

We heard when the Gospel was read that this observance was maintained even until the time of the Lord’s incarnation.

This dedication too is recognized as being maintained in the churches of Christ in the present day by salutary custom.

It must be considered why the evangelist said that this Dedication took place in winter. It was entirely because of the Jews’ hardness and unbelief, which, as we often read, are signified by the name of cold.

### Verse 23

“And Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s colonnade” [Col. 0891D].

“If, then, the Son of God wished to walk in the temple where the flesh and blood of brute animals were offered, how much more gladly will he visit our house of prayer, where the sacraments of his own flesh and blood are celebrated. If he did not disdain to walk through the colonnade in which a once-mortal and earthly king, although most powerful and wisest, used to stand in prayer, how much more does he desire to visit and enlighten the inner chambers of our hearts—provided, however, that he sees them to be Solomon’s colonnade, that is, to possess his fear, which is the beginning of wisdom?

“For it must not be thought that only the house in which we gather for prayer or for the celebration of the mysteries is the Lord’s temple, and that we ourselves, who gather in the Lord’s name, are not called and are not, much more truly, his temple, since the Apostle plainly says: ‘You are the temple of the living God, as God says: I will dwell in them, and I will walk among them’” (II Corinthians 6:16) [Col. 0892A].

The Evangelist shows why he had said, “in wintertime.”

### Verse 24

“Then,” he says, “the Jews surrounded him.” They surrounded him, therefore, in order to test him, not with the desire to recognize the truth, and they said: “How long will you keep our soul in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us openly” [Col. 0892C].

#### From Bede, at the cited passage [Col. 0892D]

“They said this not by seeking the truth of faith, but by plotting against the one whom they questioned and preparing an accusation against him, so that they might find a way to accuse him. They refused to believe that he was God, intending him merely to be a human being and to come as a king superior to all others. In this same madness later generations [Bede: ‘their descendants’] have continued to err down to the present day, and will continue until they receive the Antichrist in place of Christ” [Col. 0892B].

“And if the Lord Jesus had answered that he was the Christ, they were planning to hand him over to the governor’s power for punishment, as though, resisting Augustus, he were illicitly claiming imperial authority. But, taking thought for our salvation—for whose sake these things had to be written—he tempered his answer in such a way that he both closed the mouths of his accusers and openly declared to the faithful that he is the Christ [manuscript: ‘that he was’]. For they were asking about Christ as a man; but he himself openly declares the mysteries of his divinity, by which he is equal to the Father” [Col. 0892D].

Let us see, then, what the Jews surrounding the Lord said: “How long will you keep our soul in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us openly” [Col. 0892C].

Christ did not come to take away the soul of those who believe in him, but to give the soul life. The Jews, however, took away their own souls through unbelief, for they gathered to test Christ, not to believe in Christ.

### Verse 25

“Jesus answered them: ‘I speak to you, and you do not believe.’”

He expressly showed who he was when he said, “I speak to you”—that is, “I am the Word of God, coeternal with the Father.” For the works that he does in the Father’s name bear witness that he is the Son of God. He did not seek his own glory, but the glory of the one who sent him, because the glory of the Father and of the Son is one. But the hearts of unbelievers could not receive this faith. Of them he says:

### Verse 26

“But you do not believe,” and he gives the reason why they did not believe: “because you are not of my sheep.”

#### From Saint Augustine, Treatise 48, sections 4 and 6 [Col. 0892D]

“Sheep are sheep by believing; sheep are sheep by following the shepherd; sheep are sheep by not despising the Redeemer. Sheep are sheep by entering through the door; sheep are sheep by going out and finding pasture.

“How, then, did he say to these people, ‘You are not of my sheep’? Because he saw that they were destined for everlasting destruction [Augustine: ‘predestined to everlasting ruin’], not purchased for eternal life by the price of his blood” [Col. 0892D].

### Verses 27–28

“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life” [Col. 0892D].

He says, “I know them.” It is the custom of Holy Scripture to say that the Lord knows whatever he has chosen, as the Apostle says: “The Lord knows those who are his” (II Timothy 2:19); and to say that he does not know what he does not approve as worthy of eternal life. Hence he will also say to the ungodly: “I do not know you” (Matthew 7:23) [Col. 0893A].

He continues concerning the sheep: “And I give them eternal life.” These are the pastures that he previously promised to his sheep, where no grass withers, where everything remains green, everything flourishes, and everything remains whole; and whatever is once received is possessed forever.

“And they will never perish.” Here one must understand: “as you will perish, because you are not of my sheep.”

“And no one will snatch them from my hand”—that is, from my power.

### Verse 29

“What my Father gave me is greater than all” [Col. 0893A].

What the Father gave to the Son is greater than all: namely, that he should be his only-begotten Son, equal and consubstantial with him. What is it that he gave? Certainly, he gave it by begetting, because he did not beget one inferior to himself, nor one later in time, but one coeternal with him, always God, without a beginning in time [Col. 0893B].

“It must not be said: ‘He did not exist before he was born.’ For he was never not-born who was coeternal with the Father. Whoever understands, grasps this; whoever does not grasp it, let him believe. Let him be nourished by faith so that he may be able to grasp the Word of God, because the Word is the Son.

“Thus the Son is always Son and always equal. He is not equal by growing, but by being born: he who is always born from the Father, God from God, coeternal from the eternal. The Father, however, is not God from the Son; the Son is God from the Father. Therefore, by begetting, the Father gave to the Son that he should be God; by begetting, he gave him that he should be equal. This is what is greater than all” [Col. 0893B].

Therefore this John rises above all the heights of created things, above the thousands of angelic hosts and all great things, “and he reaches what is greater than all and says: ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God’” (John 1:1) [Col. 0893C].

“This is what is greater than all: that I should be his Word, that I should be his only-begotten Son, that I should be the radiance of his light. Therefore no one will snatch the sheep from my hand, and no one can snatch them from the hand of my Father.”

The Father’s hand and the Son’s hand are one hand, that is, one power, because there is one divinity, one majesty, one eternity, and one equality. This equality the Lord possessed in his divinity with the Father before the world existed; in his humility [manuscript: “humanity”], from the time of the incarnation, he assumed.

“And no one can snatch them from the hand of my Father.”

#### From Bede, at the cited homily [Col. 0893D]

“He clearly shows that his hand—that is, his power—and the Father’s are one and indistinguishable. Therefore it must be believed that he is Christ, because he was not, like the other saints, made [Bede: ‘sanctified’] by grace at a particular time, but has always existed as the true Son of God” [Col. 0893D].

“He makes this even clearer in the following sentence when he says:

### Verse 30

‘I and the Father are one.’

“‘We are one,’ he says: we have one substance, one divinity, one eternity, perfect equality, and no dissimilarity. In these words he explained not only the Jews’ present question, in which they asked whether he was the Christ, but also showed how utterly detestable is the perfidy of the heretics whose future coming he foresaw” [Col. 0894A].

Let Sabellius be silent when he hears, “I and the Father,” for by his perverse teaching he asserted that the Father and the Son were one person; but “I and the Father” refers to two persons.

Let Arius likewise be ashamed when he hears, “We are one.” He asserts two natures in the Father and the Son, whereas “one” signifies one nature, just as “we are” signifies two persons.

Let us follow the apostolic faith confessed by blessed Peter, chief of the apostles: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16) [Col. 0894C].

#### Saint Augustine, at the cited passage, sections 8–12 [Col. 0894D]

“The Jews, hearing the Lord’s words, endured them up to this point. But when he said, ‘I and the Father are one,’ they could bear it no longer. In their customary hardness they ran for stones, as the Evangelist says:

‘They took up stones to stone him’” [Col. 0894B].

“The Lord, who [manuscript: ‘because’] did not suffer what he did not wish to suffer, and suffered only what he wished to suffer, addressed them while they still desired to stone him. The Jews picked up stones to stone him.

### Verses 32–33

“Jesus answered them: ‘I have shown you many good works from my Father. For which of these works are you stoning me?’

“They answered him: ‘We are not stoning you for a good work, but for blasphemy, because you, although you are a man, make yourself God.’

“They answered this because he had said, ‘I and the Father are one.’ Behold, the Jews understood what the Arians do not understand. They became angry because they realized that ‘I and the Father are one’ could not be said except where there is equality between the Father and the Son.

“But the Lord saw what he should answer the wicked. He saw that they could not endure the splendor of the truth, and he tested them in his words [Augustine: ‘and tempered him in his words’]” [Col. 0894C].

“‘Is it not written in your law’—that is, the law given to you—‘I said, You are gods’? God says through the Prophet in the Psalm to human beings: ‘I said, You are gods’ (Psalm 81:6).

“The Lord called all those Scriptures ‘the law’ in a general sense, although elsewhere he specifically calls it the law, distinguishing it from the prophets, as when he says: ‘The law and the prophets were until John’ (Luke 16:16). And: ‘On these two commandments depend the whole law and the prophets’ (Matthew 22:40).

“At times he divides those same Scriptures into three parts, when he says: ‘Everything written about me in the law, the prophets, and the psalms had to be fulfilled’ (Luke 24:44).

“But here he also calls the Psalms ‘the law,’ where it is written: ‘I said, You are gods.’

### Verses 35–36

“If he called those gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be annulled—do you say that the one whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world is blaspheming because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?

“If the word of God came to human beings so that they might be called gods, how is the Word of God himself, who is with God, not God? If human beings become gods through the word of God, if they become gods by participation, then [how] is the one from whom they receive participation not God? If illuminated lights are gods, how is the light that illuminates them not God? If those who are warmed, as it were, by a saving fire become gods, how is the one from whom they are warmed not God?

“You draw near to the light, you are illuminated, and you are numbered among the children of God. If you withdraw from the light, you become dark and are counted among the darkness. Yet that [light] does not draw near to itself, because it does not withdraw from itself.

“If, then, the Word of God makes you gods, how is the Word of God not God?

“Therefore the Father sanctified his Son and sent him into the world. Perhaps someone may say: ‘If the Father sanctified him, was he at some time not holy?’ He sanctified him in the same way as he begot him. He gave him holiness by begetting him, because he begot him holy. For if what is sanctified was previously not holy, how can we say to God the Father, ‘Hallowed be your name’?” [Col. 0894D–0895A].

### Verses 37–38

“If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me. But if I do them, and if you do not wish to believe me, believe the works, so that you may recognize and believe that the Father is in me and I am in him” [Col. 0895B].

#### Here supply the omission from Augustine [Col. 0895D]

“The Son does not say, ‘The Father is in me and I am in him,’ in the same way that human beings can say this.

“For if we think rightly, we are in God; and if we live rightly, God is in us. We, the faithful, participating in his grace and illuminated by him, are in him, and he is in us.

“But the only-begotten Son is not so. He is in the Father, and the Father is in him, as an equal in the one to whom he is equal.

“After all, we can sometimes say, ‘We are in God, and God is in us.’ But can we say, ‘I and God are one’? You are in God because God contains you; God is in you because you have become God’s temple. But because you are in God and God is in you, can you say, ‘Whoever sees me sees God’? How, then, did the only-begotten Son say, ‘Whoever sees me sees the Father’? ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 14:9).

“Recognize what belongs properly to the Lord and what is the servant’s gift. The Lord’s proper possession is equality with the Father; the servant’s gift is participation in the Savior.”

### Verse 39

“Therefore they sought to seize him.”

Would that they had seized him by believing and understanding, not by raging and killing.

“They sought to seize him. When they wished to seize him, what did he do to them? He went out of their hands. They did not seize him because they did not have the hands of faith. And because the one who had power to lay down his life did not wish it, they did not seize him. But when he wished, he was seized by the hands of iniquity” [Col. 0895C].

### Verses 40–41

“And he went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had first been baptizing. He remained there, and many came to him and said: ‘John indeed performed no sign’” [Col. 0895D].

“You remember that it was said of John that he was a lamp (John 5:35) and bore witness to the day.

“What, then, did these people say among themselves? ‘John showed no miracle. He did not drive out demons, he did not remove a fever, he did not give sight to the blind, he did not raise the dead, he did not feed so many thousands of people with five or seven loaves, he did not walk upon the sea, and he did not command the winds and waves. John did none of these things.’

“Yet everything he said bore witness to this man. Let us come to the day through the lamp. John performed no sign” [Col. 0895D].

### Verse 42

“For everything that John said about this man was true.”

Behold what they seized—not in the way the Jews wished [Col. 0896D].

#### In Augustine [Col. 0896D]

“Behold those who seized him, not as the Jews did. The Jews wished to seize him while he was departing; these seized him while he remained” [Col. 0896A].

What follows, finally? “And many believed in him.”

## Chapter 27

He says that Lazarus, his friend, who had been dead for four days, was sleeping. Calling out in a loud voice, he raised him and commanded him at once to be released and go away; and many of the Jews believed.

## Chapter 11, verse 1

“Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, from the village of Mary and Martha.”

#### From Saint Augustine, Treatise 49, sections 4–25 [Col. 0896D]

“Many things are evident in this miracle of Lazarus’s resurrection. Let us not seek an explanation for every detail, so that we may deal more freely with what is necessary.

“In the preceding reading you remember that the Lord went out from the hands of those who had wished to stone him and departed across the Jordan, where John was baptizing. While the Lord was there, Lazarus was sick in Bethany, a village near Jerusalem” [Col. 0896B].

### Verses 2–3

“Mary was the one who had anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair; her brother Lazarus was ill. Therefore his sisters sent to him, saying—”

We now understand where they sent the message, namely, to the place where the Lord was, since he was absent across the Jordan. They sent to the Lord to announce that their brother was ill, so that, if he deemed it worthy, he might come and free him from his illness.

He delayed healing him so that he might raise him.

What, then, did his sisters announce? “Lord, behold, the one whom you love is ill.” They did not say, “Come,” for only the fact was announced to the one who loved him.

They did not dare to say, “Come and heal him.” They did not dare to say, “Give the command there, and it will happen here.” Why indeed did they not say this (istud) [alternative reading: “these women” (istae)], if the faith of the centurion is praised for precisely that? He said: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed” (Matthew 8:8).

They said none of these things, but only: “Lord, behold, the one whom you love is ill.” It is enough that you know; for you do not love and abandon.

Someone may say: How was Lazarus a symbol of the sinner, and how was he loved by the Lord in this way? Let him hear the Lord saying: “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matthew 9:13). For if the Lord did not love sinners, he would not have descended from heaven to earth [manuscript: “he would by no means have called them”; another reading: “he would not have come to call them”] [Col. 0896C].

### Verse 4

“But when Jesus heard it, he said to them: ‘This illness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it’” [Col. 0896D–0897A].

“Such glorification did not increase him, but benefited us. This is why he said, ‘It is not unto death’: that death itself is not unto death, but rather for a miracle through which people would believe in Christ and avoid true death.

“Observe carefully how, as though indirectly, the Lord called himself God, because of certain people who deny it. There are heretics who deny that the Lord is the Son of God [manuscript: ‘God’]. Let them hear: ‘This illness,’ he says, ‘is not unto death, but for the glory of God.’

“Whose glory? Of what God? Hear what follows: ‘So that the Son of God may be glorified through it.’ This illness, then, he says, is not unto death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it. Through what? Through that illness.”

### Verse 5

“Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister Mary and Lazarus.”

“He was ill, they were sorrowful, and all were beloved. But he loved them as the savior of the sick, indeed as the raiser of the dead and the comforter of the sorrowful.”

### Verse 6

“When, therefore, he heard that he was ill, he then remained in the same place for two days.”

They announced it: “He remained there.” The time was prolonged until the four days were completed. This was not without reason, unless perhaps—indeed, certainly—the number of days itself indicates some mystery [Col. 0897A].

### Verse 7

“Then after this he said to his disciples: ‘Let us go again into Judea,’” where he had almost been stoned. For this reason he seemed to have departed from there, lest he be stoned.

He departed as a man, but in returning, as though he had forgotten the illness, he displayed his power. “Let us go,” he said, “into Judea.”

After he had said this, observe how frightened the disciples became [Col. 0897B].

### Verses 8–9

“The disciples said to him: ‘Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?’

“Jesus answered: ‘Are there not twelve hours of the day?’”

What does this answer mean? They had said: “The Jews just now wished to stone you, and are you going there again so that they may stone you?” And the Lord answered: “Are there not twelve hours of the day?”

### Verse 10

“If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him” [Col. 0897C].

“He spoke about the day, but for our understanding [Augustine: ‘in our understanding’] it is as though it were still night. Let us call upon the day to drive away the night and illuminate the heart with light.

“What did the Lord intend to say? As far as I can see, as far as the height and depth of the saying lie before us [Augustine: ‘shine forth’], he wished to rebuke their hesitation and unbelief. They wished to advise the Lord not to die, although he had come to die so that they themselves would not die.

“Likewise, in another passage, holy Peter loved the Lord but did not yet fully understand why he had come. He feared that he would die and objected to life—that is, he objected to the Lord himself (Matthew 16:22).

“When human beings therefore wished to give advice to God, disciples to their teacher, servants to their lord, and the sick to their physician, he rebuked them and said: ‘Are there not twelve hours of the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble’ [Col. 0897D].

“Follow me, if you do not wish to stumble. Do not give advice to me, when you ought to receive advice from me.

“What, then, does ‘Are there not twelve hours of the day?’ signify? It signifies that, to show himself to be the day, he chose twelve disciples.

“If I am the day,” he says, “and you are the hours, do the hours give advice to the day? The hours follow the day; the day does not follow the hours.

“If they are the hours, what of Judas—and he himself among the twelve hours? If he was an hour, he was shining; and if he was shining, how could he hand the day over to death?

“But in this saying the Lord was foreseeing not Judas himself, but his successor. When Judas fell, Matthias succeeded him, and the number twelve remained (Acts 1:26) [Col. 0898A].

“For he did not choose twelve disciples without reason, but because he himself is the spiritual day. Let the hours, then, follow the day; let the hours preach the day; let the hours be enlightened by the day; let the hours receive light from the day; and through the preaching of the hours let the world believe in the day.

“This, then, is what he said in brief: ‘Follow me, if you do not wish to go astray.’”

### Verse 11

“And after this he said to them: ‘Lazarus our friend is sleeping, but I am going to awaken him from sleep’” [Col. 0898A].

He spoke truly. To the sisters he was dead; to the Lord he was sleeping. To human beings he was dead, because they could not raise him; but the Lord raised him from the tomb as easily as you awaken someone sleeping in bed.

Therefore he called him sleeping according to his power, because other dead people are also frequently called sleeping in Scripture, as the Apostle says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope” (I Thessalonians 4:22) [Col. 0898B].

For this reason he himself called them sleeping, because he foretold that they would rise [Augustine: “he announced beforehand that they would rise”].

And elsewhere: “We will all sleep, but we will not all rise.”

#### In the Vulgate [Col. 0897D]

The Vulgate reads: “We will all rise, but we will not all be changed.” Alcuin seems here to have followed certain Greek and Latin manuscripts in which, instead of “we will all rise,” one also finds, “We will all sleep.” See Jerome, Letter 119 to Minervius and Alexander, and Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 20, chapter 20 [Col. 0898D].

There is nevertheless an error here in the words, “We will not all rise.” The reading should be, “We will not all be changed” (I Corinthians 15:51), signifying our death by the term “sleep.”

For when the body is abandoned by the soul, it sleeps in the grave, to be raised on the last day. “But souls, when they leave their bodies, have different destinations: joy for the good and torments for the wicked. When the resurrection has taken place, however, the joy of the good will be greater and the torments of the wicked more severe, when they will be tormented together with their bodies” [Col. 0898C].

While the Lord had spoken to his disciples about the friend’s sleep, “they answered according to the way they understood him.”

### Verses 12–15

“‘Lord, if he is sleeping, he will be saved.’ For sleep is ordinarily an indication of recovery for the sick.

“But Jesus had spoken about his death, while they thought that he was speaking about ordinary sleep. Then Jesus said to them plainly. He had said obscurely, ‘He is sleeping.’ Therefore he said plainly: ‘Lazarus has died, and I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe, because I was not there; but I know that he has died.’

“He had been reported ill, not dead. But what could be hidden from the one who had created him, and into whose hands the soul of the dying man had departed?

“This is what he said: ‘I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe because I was not there,’ so that they might begin to wonder that the Lord could say he was dead although he had neither seen nor heard it [the source supplies quod, “which” or “that”].

“Here we must remember that even the faith of the disciples themselves, who already believed in him, was still being built up by miracles—not so that faith, which did not yet exist, might begin to exist, but so that what had already begun to exist might grow. Nevertheless, he used a word as though they were then beginning to believe.

“For he did not say, ‘I rejoice for your sake so that your faith may be increased or strengthened,’ but, ‘so that you may believe.’ This must be understood as meaning, ‘so that you may believe more fully and more firmly’” [Col. 0898D–0899A].

### Verses 16–17

“‘But let us go to him.’

“Then Thomas, who is called Didymus, said to his fellow disciples: ‘Let us also go, so that [alternative reading: ‘and’] we may die with him.’

“Therefore Jesus came and found that he had already been four days in the tomb” [Col. 0899A].

Many things can be said about the four days, in accordance with the obscure passages of Scripture, which produce many interpretations according to the diversity of those who understand them.

“Let us also say what seems to us to be signified by the dead man who had been four days in the tomb. Just as in the case of the blind man we understand the human race in some sense, so perhaps in this dead man also we shall understand many things. For one reality can be signified in different ways.

“When a human being is born, he is born already with death, because he draws sin from Adam. Hence the Apostle says: ‘Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned’ (Romans 5:12).

“Behold one day of death: sin, which a person draws from the lineage of death.

“Then he grows and begins to approach the years of reason, so that he may recognize the natural law, which people [manuscript: ‘all’] have fixed in their hearts: ‘What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.’

“Is this said of the pagans [Augustine: ‘learned from the pages’], and is it not, in a certain way, read in nature itself? Do you wish to suffer theft? Certainly not. Behold the law in your heart: what you do not wish to suffer, do not do.

“And people transgress this law. Behold the second day of death.

“There was also a law given divinely through God’s servant Moses. It was said to them [Augustine and manuscript: ‘there’]: ‘You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not bear false witness; honor your father and your mother; you shall not covet your neighbor’s property’ (Exodus 20:13 ff.).

“Behold, the law is written, and it too is despised. Add [Augustine: ‘behold’] the third day of death.

“What remains? He comes to the Gospel; the kingdom of heaven is preached; Christ is proclaimed everywhere; Gehenna is threatened; eternal life is promised—and he himself is despised.

“People transgress the Gospel. Behold the fourth day of death. It is rightly thought that he now stinks.

“Yet is mercy to be denied even to such people? Certainly not. The Lord does not disdain to approach even such people in order to raise them” [Col. 0899B–C].

### Verses 19–20

“Many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother. Therefore Martha, when she learned that Jesus had come, went to meet him; but Mary was sitting at home” [Col. 0899C–D].

### Verses 21–22

“Martha therefore said to Jesus: ‘Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you’” [Col. 0899D].

She did not say, “Even now I ask you to raise my brother.” For how did she know whether it would be useful for her brother to rise [alternative reading: “if he had been present”; Augustine: “if it would be useful for her brother to rise”]?

She said only this: “I know that you can; if you wish, you do it. Whether you will do it, however, is a matter of your judgment, not of my presumption.”

“But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you.”

### Verses 23–25

“Jesus said to her: ‘Your brother will rise.’

“Martha said to him: ‘I know that he will rise in the resurrection on the last day.’

“I am certain about that resurrection; I am uncertain about this one.

“Jesus said to her: ‘I am the resurrection and the life.’

“You say: ‘My brother will rise on the last day.’ That is true. But through whom will he rise then? He can also rise now, because I am the resurrection and the life.

“Therefore he is the resurrection because he is life: [because] ‘Whoever believes in me will not die forever’” [Col. 0900A].

What does this mean? Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live, just as Lazarus died and lives, because God is not the God of the dead but of the living.

He gave this answer to the Jews concerning the fathers who had died long ago, that is, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: “I am the God of Abraham, [and the God of Isaac,] and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:6). “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22:32). For all those people live [Col. 0900B].

Believe, then, and even if you have died, you will live. But if you do not believe, although you are alive, you are dead.

Where, then, does death exist in the soul? Because faith is not in it. Where does death exist in the body? Because the soul is not there. Therefore the life of your soul is faith [manuscript: “the soul”].

“As the soul is the life of the body, so faith is the life of the soul.

“‘Whoever believes in me,’ he says, ‘even if he has died in the flesh, will live in the soul until the flesh rises, never afterward to die. This is what he means: whoever believes in me, even if he dies, will live. And everyone who lives in the flesh and believes in me, even if he dies for a time because of the death of the flesh, will not die forever because of the life of the spirit and the immortality of the resurrection.’”

This is what he says:

### Verse 26

“And everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” [Col. 0900C].

### Verse 27

“‘Do you believe this?’

“She said to him: ‘Certainly, Lord. I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who has come into this world.’

“When I believed this, [I believed] that you are the resurrection; I believed that you are life; I believed that whoever believes in you, even if he dies, will live; and that whoever lives and believes [in you] will never die.” [Augustine repeats credidi, “I believed,” after “When I believed this.”]

### Verse 28

“When she had said this, she went away and secretly called her sister Mary, saying: ‘The Teacher is here and is calling you’” [Col. 0900D].

We should observe how she called “silence” a suppressed voice. For how was she silent when she said, “The Teacher is here and is calling you”?

We should also observe how the Evangelist did not say where, when, or how the Lord called Mary. He preserves the truth of the narrative (narrationis veritatem servat) [manuscript: veritate, “with truth”; Augustine: brevitate servata, “with brevity preserved”] so that this might rather be understood in Martha’s words.

### Verses 29–31

“When she heard this, she rose quickly and came to him. Jesus had not yet entered the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him.

“Therefore the Jews who were with her in the house and were consoling her, when they saw Mary rise quickly and go out, followed her, saying: ‘Because she is going to the tomb to weep there’” [Col. 0900D].

Why did the Evangelist consider it important to relate this? [So that] we may see what caused there to be many people present when Lazarus was raised. [The source supplies ad, “to” or “for,” before “the Evangelist,” and Ut, “so that.”] The Jews thought that she was hurrying there to seek consolation for her grief through tears, and therefore followed her, so that the great miracle of a man dead for four days rising again might have many witnesses [Col. 0901A].

### Verses 32–34

“Mary, therefore, when she came to where Jesus was, seeing him, fell at his feet and said to him: ‘Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.’

“Jesus, therefore, when he saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, groaned in spirit and troubled himself, and said: ‘Where have you laid him?’” [Col. 0901A].

By groaning in spirit and troubling himself he conveyed something to us. For who could trouble him except he himself (ipse) [manuscript: “himself” (seipsum)]?

First, then, attend to his power, and afterward seek the meaning. You are troubled unwillingly; Christ is troubled because he willed it. Jesus hungered—it is true, because he willed it. Jesus slept—it is true, because he willed it. Jesus was sorrowful—it is true, but because he willed it. Jesus died—it is true, but because he willed it.

It was in his power to be affected in this way or that—or not to be affected in this way [or not to be so affected]. For the Word assumed a soul [alternative reading: “He assumed a true soul”] and flesh, joining to himself the nature of the whole human being in the unity of his person.

For the souls of the apostles Paul and Peter were enlightened by the Word.

#### Manuscript reading [Col. 0901B]

“For the Apostle’s soul was enlightened by the Word; the soul of Paul and the soul of Peter were enlightened by the Word.”

The souls of the other apostles, of the saints, and of the prophets were enlightened by the Word. But of none of them was it said, “The Word became flesh,” nor of any was it said, “I and the Father are one.”

The soul of Christ and the flesh of Christ, together with the Word of God, are one person, one Christ. Therefore, where supreme power exists, weakness is troubled according to the inclination of the will.

This is what is meant by, “He troubled himself.”

I have spoken of his power; attend now to the meaning. The four-day burial signifies a great guilt [Augustine: “He is a great guilty man whom the four days of death and that burial signify”] [Col. 0901C].

What, then, does Christ’s troubling himself signify, except that it shows you how you ought to be troubled when you are burdened and weighed down by such a mass of sin?

You examined yourself; you saw yourself guilty; you reckoned up your deeds: “I did that, and God showed patience; I committed that, and he deferred me; I heard the Gospel, and I despised it.”

Say it—say it with tears: “I was baptized, and I have returned again to the same things. What shall I do? Where shall I go? Where shall I escape?”

When you say these things, Christ already groans, because faith groans. In the voice of the one who groans, hope of resurrection appears. Where faith itself is within, there is Christ groaning; if faith is in us, Christ is in us.

For what else does the Apostle say? “That Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith” (Ephesians 3:17).

Therefore, if your faith is in Christ [manuscript: “from Christ”], Christ is in your heart [Col. 0901D].

Let Christ, then, groan in your heart.

Thus Christ wept for his dead friend, whom he had come to raise. Why did he weep, except to teach a human being, oppressed by the weight of sins, to weep?

“Why did he groan and trouble himself, except because the faith of a person rightly displeased with himself ought to groan in accusation of evil works, so that the habit of sinning may yield to the urgency of the penitent” [Augustine: “to the urgency of repenting”]?

And he said: “Where have you laid him?”

You know that he is dead, and do you not know where he was buried? This too is a symbolic expression. I do not dare say that he does not know—for what does he not know?—but that he acts as though he does not know.

How do we prove this? Hear the Lord saying at the judgment: “I do not know you; depart from me” (Matthew 7:23).

What does “I do not know you” mean? “I do not see you in my light; I do not see you in that righteousness which I know.”

So here, as though he did not know such a sinner, he said: “Where have you laid him?”

Such is the voice of God in paradise after Adam sinned: “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9).

They say to him, “Lord, come and see.” What does “see” mean? Have mercy. For the Lord sees when he has mercy. Hence it is said to him: “See my humiliation and my labor, and forgive all my sins” (Psalm 24:18).

**Verses 35–36.** Jesus wept. Therefore the Jews said, “See how he loved him.” What does “he loved him” mean? “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”

**Verse 37.** But some of them said, “Could not this man, who opened the eyes of the blind man, have made it so that this man would not die?” He who did not wish to make him not die is about to do something greater: raise him from the dead.

**Verse 38.** Jesus, therefore, again groaning within himself, came to the tomb. He groans also within you, if you are resolved to come back to life. To every person weighed down by a most evil habit it is said: “He came to the tomb.” Now it was a cave, and a stone had been placed over it. The dead man is beneath the stone; the guilty person is beneath the Law. For you know that the Law given to the Jews was written on stone (Exodus 31:18). But all the guilty are under the Law; those who live rightly are not in the Law [Augustine: “are with the Law”]. “The Law was not laid down for the righteous” (1 Timothy 1:9).

What, then, does it mean to remove the stone? To preach grace. For the apostle Paul says that he is a minister of the new covenant, “not of the letter but of the Spirit.” For “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6). The killing letter is like a stone that presses down.

**Verses 39–40.** “Remove the stone,” he says. Remove the burden of the Law; preach grace. Martha, the sister of the one who had died, says to him, “Lord, by now there is an odor, for he has been dead four days.” Jesus says to her, “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?” What does “you would see the glory of God” mean? That he raises even one who is stinking and four days dead. For “all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). And “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20).

**Verses 41–43.** Therefore they removed the stone. But Jesus, raising his eyes upward, said, “Father, I give you thanks because you have heard me. I knew, however, that you always hear me; but because of the people standing around I said this, so that they may believe that you sent me.” When he had said this, he cried out with a loud voice.

He groaned, he wept, he cried out with a loud voice. How difficult it is for one whom the weight of an evil habit oppresses to rise. Yet he rises, inwardly brought to life by hidden grace; he rises after the loud voice. What happened?

**Verse 44.** “He cried out with a loud voice: Lazarus, come out!” And immediately the one who had been dead came out, his feet and hands bound with wrappings, and his face bound with a cloth. You marvel that he came out with bound feet, and do not marvel that he rose after four days? In both cases the Lord’s power was at work, not the dead man’s strength. He came out, and he is still bound; still wrapped, yet he has already come out.

What does this signify? When you despise, you lie dead; and if you despise things as great as I have said, you lie buried. When you confess [alternative reading: “you rise”], then you come out. For what is it to come out except to become manifest, as though emerging from hidden places? But so that you may confess, God brings this about by crying out with a loud voice—that is, by calling with great grace.

Therefore, when the dead man had come out still bound—confessing and still guilty, so that his sins might be loosed—the Lord said this to the ministers: “Loose him, and let him go.” What does “Loose him, and let him go” mean? “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.”

For he who raised the dead could have loosed the bonds; but, on account of the unity of the holy Church of God and indivisible charity, he says to the ministers, that is, to Christ’s disciples, “Loose him,” because sins are not loosed without the unity of the catholic faith and the charity of ecclesial holiness.

**Verses 45–46.** Many of the Jews who had come to Mary, and had seen what Jesus did, believed in him. But some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.

Not all the Jews who had gathered to Mary believed, but many did. Some of them—whether from among the Jews who had gathered, or from among those who had believed—went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done: either announcing it so that they too might believe, or rather betraying him so that they might rage against him. In any event, and whoever they were, this report was brought to the Pharisees.

## CHAPTER 28

The chief priests gather a council against him. In it Caiaphas prophesies that one man ought to die for the people, lest all perish. And six days before Passover, Judas is rebuked for grumbling at the price of the ointment poured over the Lord’s feet.

**Verse 47.** Therefore the chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council and said, “What shall we do?”

Yet they did not say, “Let us believe.” For these utterly lost men were thinking more about how they might harm him and destroy him than about how they might take care of themselves so that they would not perish; and yet they were afraid, and seemed to be consulting together.

**Verse 48.** For they said, “What shall we do? For this man performs many signs. If we leave him alone in this way, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”

They did not wish to lose temporal things [Augustine: “they feared losing them”], and they did not consider eternal life; thus they lost both. For after the Lord’s passion and glorification, the Romans did take away their place and their nation, both by fighting [Augustine: “by conquering”] and by transferring them. And what was said elsewhere follows them: “But the sons of the kingdom will go into the outer darkness” (Matthew 8:12).

They feared that, if everyone believed in Christ, no one would remain to defend the city of God and the temple against the Romans, because they perceived Christ’s teaching to be directed against that very temple and against their ancestral laws.

**Verses 49–51.** But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all, nor do you consider that it is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish.”

He did not say this from himself; but, because he was high priest that year, he prophesied. Here he also taught that the spirit of prophecy can proclaim future things through evil men. Yet the evangelist attributes this to a divine sacrament, because he was the high priest, that is, the chief priest.

It may, however, cause difficulty that he is called the high priest of that year, when the Lord had established one chief priest, with one successor appointed after his death. But it must be understood that afterward, through ambitions and rivalries among the Jews, it was established that there should be several, serving in rotation year by year. For this is said of Zechariah: “It happened that, while he was serving as priest in the order of his division before God, according to the regulation [another reading: custom] of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense” (Luke 1:8–9).

From this it is clear that there were several of them and that they had their turns; for no one was permitted to offer incense except the high priest. Perhaps several served during one year [manuscript: *uno anno*, rather than *unum annum*], while others succeeded them in another year, and the one who was to offer incense was selected by lot.

What, then, did Caiaphas prophesy? That Jesus was going to die for the nation—not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad. The evangelist added this; Caiaphas prophesied concerning only the Jewish nation, in which were the sheep of whom the Lord himself said: “I was sent only to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24).

But the evangelist knew of other sheep that were not of this fold, which had to be brought in, so that there might be “one fold and one shepherd” [manuscript: “there might be” in the plural]. These things were said according to predestination, because those who had not yet believed were not yet his sheep or the children of God.

**Verses 53–54.** From that day, therefore, they resolved to kill him. Jesus, therefore, no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went away into the region near the wilderness, to a city called Ephraim, and there remained with his disciples.

This was not because his power had failed—since, if he had wished, he could certainly have continued openly among the Jews, and they could have done nothing to him—but in the weakness of human life he was displaying to his disciples an example of how to live. From this it is evident that it is not sinful if his faithful, who are his members, withdraw themselves from the eyes of their persecutors and avoid the fury of criminals by hiding rather than confronting it.

Jesus knew that the time of his passion and our redemption was approaching. As the time approached in which he had resolved to suffer, he drew near also to the place where he wished to accomplish the dispensation of that passion. For the evangelist says:

**Verse 55.** “Now the Passover of the Jews was near.”

> **[Column 0903D] From Saint Augustine, Treatise 50, no. 2.** The Passover of the Jews was near. The Jews wished to make that feast-day bloody with the Lord’s blood. On that feast-day the Lamb was slain, who consecrated that same feast-day for us with his blood. There was a plot among the Jews to kill Jesus; he who had come from heaven [to suffer] wished to draw near to the place of his passion, because the hour of his passion was imminent.
>
> Many therefore went up to Jerusalem from the region before Passover, in order to sanctify themselves. The Jews did this according to the command of the Lord, given through holy Moses in the Law: on the feast-day of Passover, everyone was to gather from all sides and be sanctified by celebrating that day. But that celebration was a shadow of things to come.
>
> What is “a shadow of things to come”? It is a prophecy of Christ who was to come, a prophecy of the one who was to suffer for us on that day: so that the shadow might pass away and the light might come; so that the sign might pass away and the reality might be grasped. The Jews therefore had Passover in shadow; we have it in the light.
>
> For why would the Lord have commanded them to slaughter a sheep on that very feast-day, unless it was because he was the one of whom it was prophesied: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Isaiah 53:7)? The doorposts of the Jews were marked with the blood of the slaughtered animal (Exodus 12:22); our foreheads are marked with Christ’s blood. That marking—which was itself a sign—was said to keep the destroyer away from the marked houses. The sign of Christ drives the destroyer away from us if our heart receives the Savior.

> **[Column 0905D] Thus far from Augustine.**  
> **Verse 56.** “They were seeking Jesus,” says the evangelist, “and they were saying to one another as they stood in the temple, ‘What do you think? Surely he will not come to the feast?’”

> **[Column 0905D] From a homily of Bede, Monday after Palm Sunday.** The Jews were seeking Jesus, but wrongly: they were seeking him in order to kill him when he came to the feast. Let us, however, seek him as we stand in the temple of God, persevering together in prayer, and let us speak to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs (Ephesians 5:19), asking him in grace that he may deign to come to our feast, to enlighten us by his presence, and himself to sanctify his gifts for us.

The chief priests and Pharisees had also given orders that, if anyone knew where he was, he should report it, so that they might seize him. The command of the Jews is therefore their sin. They sought to kill Christ, not to live in Christ. Let us seek to live in Christ, whom they sought to kill. They sought wrongly; let us seek rightly. For now is the time to seek the Lord, as the Prophet says: “Seek the Lord while he may be found” (Isaiah 55:6). Whoever wishes to find him merciful in judgment should seek him now in the duty of humility and charity.

## CHAPTER 12, VERSE 1

Six days before Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus had been dead, whom he had raised.

> **[Column 0905D] Again from Bede, the homily cited above.** Knowing that the Jews had conspired to kill him, the Lord did not flee the hands of those lying in wait. Certain of the glory of the resurrection, he first came to Bethany, the city near Jerusalem, where he had raised Lazarus from the dead; then he also came to Jerusalem, where he himself was to suffer and rise from the dead. He came to Jerusalem so that he himself might die there; but to Bethany so that the raising of Lazarus might be more firmly impressed on everyone’s memory, and so that the impious rulers might be increasingly confounded and proved inexcusable—those who were not afraid to kill one who could raise the dead [alternative reading: “could be raised from the dead”], and who, neither moved by the benefits of the resurrection nor terrified by the divine power of the one who raised him, would not withdraw their minds from their unjust slaughter.

It should not be read superficially why Jesus came to Bethany six days before Passover. The number six has great significance in the holy Scriptures, and many works of the Lord our God are shown to have been completed in the number six, because the number six, divided or combined according to its own proper parts, is acknowledged to be most perfect. For it has three parts named within itself: one, two, and three. Its sixth part is one; its third part is two; and its half is three. One, two, and three are recognized to amount to six; nothing else can be produced from these three parts when combined except six, nor can the number six be divided into other parts except these three: one, two, and three.

For it is well known that the Lord, the Creator of all, completed the creatures of this world in six days, and that he made the human being on the sixth day. When that human being had been destroyed by the serpent’s deceit, the Son of God himself, through whom he was created, came to Bethany six days before Passover to set him free. Thus the one who was created on the sixth day was freed on the sixth day of the week; for I think no one is unaware that Christ suffered on the sixth day of the week.

Likewise, in the sixth month, when the archangel announced it, the holy Virgin is read to have conceived our same Redeemer through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. He also, at the sixth hour, in the fullness of his age, sitting beside a well, deigned to open to the Samaritan woman the streams of the divine fountain. Likewise, in the sixth age of the world, the Creator himself is now read, according to the faith of sacred history, to have come for the redemption of the world.

These three parts—one, two, and three—from which, as we have said, six is constituted, also contain a mystery in the dispensation of human salvation. In the first period, under the law of nature, the holy Fathers served God as though in a kind of unity. In the second period, the Law was added to nature, so that what evil habit had corrupted in nature, the Law might reform in the letter; and there were two: nature and Law. In the third period, heavenly grace came through Jesus Christ; and there are three: nature, Law, and grace.

Just as the Law of nature does not destroy what is good, and grace does not abolish the Law but fulfills it and restores nature to its former nobility, nevertheless neither nature nor Law could be fulfilled without grace. Nor was free will given to humanity in such a way that, by the commandment of the Law, it [manuscript: “or the commandment of the Law”] would not need grace, as the Pelagian heresy asserts.

> **[Column 0906D] Again from Bede, the homily cited above.** And so that the contrivers of slanders might not say that Lazarus had been raised in an apparition, a meal was made there for the Lord, and Lazarus himself was one of those reclining with him. Thus, when they saw or heard him alive, speaking, eating, and familiarly associating with his own people, they might at least in this way recognize the power of the one who had raised him and receive grace.
>
> Mystically, however, this Lord’s supper, at which Martha served and Lazarus reclined among the others, is the faith of the Church, which works through love. At this supper Martha serves when every faithful soul offers the Lord the work of its devotion.
>
> Lazarus becomes one of those reclining with the Lord when those who have been raised to righteousness after the first death of sins rejoice in the presence of truth together with those who have remained in their righteousness; the penitents are nourished together with the innocent by the gifts of heavenly grace.
>
> This supper is fittingly celebrated in Bethany, which is a city on the side of the Mount of Olives and is interpreted as “house of obedience.” For the house of obedience is the Church, which faithfully obeys the Lord’s commands. It is also the city established upon the mountain of mercy, which can never be hidden. It was built from the side of its Redeemer—that is, it was imbued with the water of cleansing and the blood of sanctification that came forth from his side as he died for it [Bede: “came forth”].
>
> There also, Mary, Lazarus’s other sister, as the following Gospel reading shows, received [the supplied editorial reading: “first”] a pound of costly ointment of genuine nard as a sign of great love, and anointed Jesus’ feet and wiped his feet with her hair. By this action she not only gives a sign of her own devotion, but also signifies the pious service of other faithful souls to God.

**Verse 3.** Mary, therefore, took a pound of costly ointment of genuine nard.

What is expressed by a pound of ointment except the perfection of righteousness? This ointment is said to have been made from genuine nard. What is suggested by ointment except the good odor of reputation? And this ointment is made from *nardo pistico* [alternative reading: *pistica*], that is, faithful nard. For *pistis* is Greek and *fides* is Latin for “faith”; without faith it is impossible to please God, and good reputation cannot exist without catholic faith.

> **[Column 0907D] From Saint Augustine, Treatise 50, no. 6.** O man, anoint Jesus’ feet by living well; follow the Lord’s footsteps, and wipe them with your hair, as though you had surplus goods, and give them to the poor. This is to wipe Jesus’ feet with your hair. What is surplus for you is necessary for the Lord’s feet—that is, for the least members in the Church. Concerning them the Lord will say at the end: “As long as you did it to one of these least ones, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40).
>
> “The house was filled with the odor,” that is, the Church was filled with the reputation of religious life [good]. For a good odor is a good life. Hear the Apostle: “We are the good odor of Christ,” he says, “in every place” (2 Corinthians 2:15); and in the Song of Songs: “Your name is poured-out ointment” (Song of Songs 1:2). Likewise: “While the king was at his banquet, my nard gave forth its fragrance.” Here it is clearly shown what Mary did once [manuscript: “has done”], and typologically what the whole Church and every perfected soul continually do.

**Verses 4–5.** Therefore one of his disciples, Judas Iscariot, who was going to betray him, said, “Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?”

> **[Column 0908D] From a homily of the Venerable Bede, Monday after Palm Sunday.** Woe to the impious betrayer! Woe to his accomplices in wickedness, who even now persecute Christ’s members and do not cease to envy their neighbors for possessing the reputation of virtue that they themselves do not deserve to have!
>
> We might indeed think that Judas had spoken this out of concern for the poor, but the truthful witness exposes his mind when he says:
>
> **Verse 6.** “He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and, having the money-box, he used to carry what was put into it.”
>
> Judas did not perish then, when, corrupted by money, he destroyed [another reading: betrayed] the Lord; rather, he was already lost when he followed the Lord. Having the Lord’s money-box, he carried what was put into it for the service of the poor, though with his faithless mind he was accustomed to steal it.
>
> Therefore, seeing that his heart was already stained by greed and foreseeing that it would be stained by the worse filth of betrayal, the Lord entrusted to his keeping whatever they had [Bede: whatever he had] in the money-bag, and allowed him to do with it whatever he wished, so that either the honor conferred or the remembrance of the money he had received might turn his mind away from selling him.
>
> But because the greedy person is always in need, and the faithless never remembers benefits, the impious man proceeded from stealing the money he carried to betraying the Lord, who had entrusted the money to him for safekeeping.

**Verse 7.** Therefore Jesus said, “Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial.”

As though Judas had asked an innocent question, the Lord simply and gently explained what Mary’s service signified: namely, that he was going to die and would be anointed with spices for burial. Therefore Mary, although she greatly desired to reach the anointing of his dead body and would not be permitted to do so, was granted the opportunity to offer him while he was still alive the service that, after his death, she would have sought [manuscript and Bede: “would have been unable to do so”], had she not been forestalled by his swift resurrection.

Hence Mark rightly testifies that the Lord said of her: “She has done what she could; she has anticipated anointing my body for burial” (Mark 14:8). This is plainly to say: Since she will not be able to touch my body once I am dead, she has done the only thing she could. She has anticipated the act of burial by giving it to me while I am still alive.

**Verse 8.** “For you will always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me.”

Here also, with great restraint and patience, the Lord does not accuse Judas of greed or of speaking about the money without concern for the poor. Rather, he demonstrates by reason that those who ministered to him from their possessions while he lived among human beings were not to be blamed, since he himself would remain bodily with the Church for only a short time, whereas the poor, to whom alms could be given, would always be present in it.

**Verse 9.** Therefore the great crowd of Jews learned that he was there, and they came, not only because of Jesus, but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead.

Curiosity, not love, brought these people to Jesus. But let us, dearest brothers, reverse the situation: if we learn where Jesus is, where he makes his dwelling, where he finds a Bethany—that is, a house of the obedient soul—in which he may dwell, let us come there in contemplation, not merely because of the man whom he raised from the death of the soul and granted spiritual life, but so that, by imitating the man’s good life, we may thereby deserve to reach the vision of Jesus.

For we know with certainty where Jesus is: he rose after death and ascended into heaven, where he has an everlasting dwelling. That is the true Bethany, the heavenly city, which no one can enter except the obedient.

**Verses 10–11.** But the chief priests resolved to kill Lazarus also, because many of the Jews were leaving on his account and believing in Jesus.

O blind cunning of the blind—to wish to kill one who had been raised, as though the one who could raise the dead could not raise the slain! Indeed, he taught that he could do both, for he raised Lazarus who had died and himself who had been killed.

> **[Column 0909D] Thus far from the cited homily of Bede.**

After the Lord had raised the four-days-dead man, while some Jews were astonished and, seeing, came to believe, and others, through envy, were perishing, Jesus reclined at table in the house, and Lazarus, who had been raised from death, also reclined with him. After the ointment had been poured over his feet, filling the house with its fragrance, concerning which we have treated above as far as we could, we must now consider what took place before the Lord’s passion. For the evangelist says:

## CHAPTER 29

The crowd, coming to meet him with palm branches, cries, “Hosanna.” He himself sits upon a young donkey, while the Pharisees say, “The whole world has gone after him.”

**Verses 12–13.** On the following day the great crowd that had come to the feast, when they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, took palm branches and went out to meet him, crying, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.”

> **[Column 0910D] From Saint Augustine, Treatise 51, nos. 2–13.** Palm branches are praises, signifying the victory by which the Lord was about to overcome death by dying and to triumph over the devil, the prince of death, by the trophy of the cross [manuscript: “to triumph over the devil … the prince”].
>
> “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” It should certainly be noted that *Hosanna*, a Hebrew word, is composed of two elements, one corrupted and one intact. Among them *osi* means “save” or “saving”; but *anna* is an interjection of one making a plea, just as among Latins *heu!* is the interjection of one grieving, and *papae!* the interjection of one expressing astonishment.
>
> Thus, in the Psalm where the Seventy translated, “O Lord, save me,” the Hebrew has written, “Anna, Adonai, Hosanna” [manuscript: “Osianna”]. Our translator Jerome, explaining this more carefully, translated it: “I beseech you, Lord, save; I beseech you.” “O Lord” by the interjection of one pleading means the same as “I beseech you, Lord” by the very word of entreaty.
>
