> Thus *Hosanna* means “Save, I beseech you,” with the vowel *i* consumed—the letter that ends the first word when it is pronounced fully as *osi*—through the force of the vowel letter *aleph*, with which the following word *anna* begins. This is what grammarians call *synaloepha* when scanning verse, although in scanning they pass over the written letter. In the word *Hosanna*, however, the letter *iota* is not even written [manuscript: *saltim* for *saltem*], but is completely omitted while the meaning intended by the speakers remains intact.

“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.”

This should be understood so that “in the name of the Lord” means “in the name of God the Father,” although it can also be understood as “in his own name,” since he too is Lord. Hence it is written elsewhere: “The Lord rained from the Lord” (Genesis 19:24).

His own words direct our understanding more accurately. He says: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me. Another will come in his own name; him you will receive” (John 5:43).

Christ is the teacher of humility, who “humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:8). He does not therefore lose his divinity when he teaches us humility. In the former he is equal to the Father; in the latter he is like us. By that in which he is equal to the Father, he created us to exist; by that in which he is like us, he redeemed us so that we would not perish.

The crowd praised him with these words: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.” The rulers of the Jews, blinded by envy, could not endure this voice, when such a great multitude proclaimed Christ their king [Augustine: “What cross could the envy of the rulers of the Jews endure?”].

But what great thing was it for the Lord to be King of Israel? What great thing was it for the King of the ages to become king of human beings? Christ was not King of Israel in order to exact tribute, arm an army with iron, and conquer enemies. Rather, he was King of Israel in order to rule the mind, to provide for it eternally, and to lead believers, those who hope and love, into the kingdom of heaven.

The Son of God, therefore, equal to the Father, the Word through whom all things were made, chose to be King of Israel. This was condescension, not promotion; a sign of mercy, not an increase of power. For the one who was called King of the Jews is Lord of the angels in heaven.

**Verse 14.** Jesus found a young donkey and sat upon it.

This is stated briefly here; how it happened is read in full in the other evangelists. Prophetic testimony is applied to this deed, so that it might be evident that the wicked rulers of the Jews did not understand the one in whom the things they read were being fulfilled: “Jesus found a young donkey and sat upon it.”

**Verse 15.** As it is written: “Do not fear, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, seated upon a donkey’s colt” (Zechariah 9:9).

This daughter of Zion, to whom these things are divinely spoken, was among those sheep who heard the Shepherd’s voice; she was among that multitude which praised the approaching Lord with such devotion and escorted him in such a great procession.

It was said to her, “Do not fear.” Recognize the one who is now praised [manuscript: “who is praised by you”]; and do not tremble when he suffers, because that blood will be poured out by which your sin will be erased and your life redeemed [Augustine: “restored”].

The donkey’s colt, on which no one had sat—for this is found in the other evangelists—we understand as the people of the Gentiles, who had not received the Law of the Lord. The donkey itself—for both animals were brought to the Lord—we understand as his people coming from the people of Israel, not unruly, but a people that recognized the Lord’s manger.

**Verse 16.** His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified—that is, when he displayed the power of his resurrection—they remembered that these things had been written about him. Recalling, according to Scripture, the things fulfilled before the passion and during the Lord’s passion, they found this also: that, in accordance with the prophetic words, he would sit upon a donkey’s colt.

**Verses 17–19.** The crowd that was with him therefore bore witness that he had called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead. For this reason the crowd also came to meet him, because they had heard that he had performed this sign.

The Pharisees therefore said to one another, “You see that we are accomplishing nothing. Look, the whole world has gone after him.”

One crowd disturbed another. Why do you envy this, blind crowd—that the world follows the one through whom the world was made?

## CHAPTER 30

When Gentiles announce that they wish to see him, he says that the hour of his glorification has come, and declares that a grain of wheat, once dead, will produce much fruit. He also promises that the one who ministers to him will be honored.

**Verses 20–22.** Now there were some Gentiles among those who had gone up to worship at the feast. These approached Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee, and asked him, saying, “Lord, we wish to see Jesus.” Philip came and told Andrew. Andrew and Philip in turn told Jesus.

Let us see what the Lord answered them. The Jews wished to kill him; the Gentiles wished to see him. Yet those Jews also included the ones who cried, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.” Here are those from the circumcision and those from the uncircumcision, like walls coming from opposite directions and converging in the one faith of Christ with the kiss of peace. Let us therefore hear the voice of the cornerstone.

**Verse 23.** “Jesus,” he says, “answered them: The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.”

Perhaps someone thinks that he said he was glorified because the Gentiles wished to see him. It is not so. Rather, he saw that these Gentiles would believe in him after his passion and resurrection among all the nations, because, as the Apostle says, “A partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters” (Romans 11:25).

Taking occasion, therefore, from these Gentiles who desired to see him, he announces the future fullness of the Gentiles, and declares that the hour of his glorification is already approaching—the hour in which, once his glorification had taken place in heaven, the Gentiles would believe. Hence it was foretold: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth” (Psalm 107:7).

This is the fullness of the Gentiles of which the Apostle says: “A partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters.” But the humility of the passion had to precede the height of glorification. Therefore he immediately added:

**Verses 24–25.** “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.”

He was saying that he himself was the grain that had to die and multiply: to be put to death through the unbelief of the Jews, and to multiply through the faith of all peoples.

Now, exhorting them to follow the footsteps of his passion, he says: “Whoever loves his life will lose it.” This can be understood in two ways. “Whoever loves it will lose it”—that is, if you love it, you will lose it [manuscript and Augustine: “lose it!”]. If you wish to preserve life in Christ, do not fear dying for Christ.

Or, in another way: “Whoever loves his life will lose it.” Do not love it in this life, lest you lose it in eternal life. This latter interpretation seems to accord more closely with the Gospel sense, for it follows: “And whoever hates his life in this world will preserve it for eternal life.” Therefore, where it was said above, “Whoever loves,” it is understood: “Whoever loves in this world”—he will indeed lose it. But whoever hates it, certainly in this world, will himself preserve it for eternal life.

Great and wonderful is the saying: how can love for one’s own life cause a human being to perish, while hatred keeps him from perishing? If you love wrongly, then you have hated; if you hate rightly, then you have loved.

Blessed are those who hate in order to preserve, lest they lose by loving.

Here “soul” designates the present life, or even the enjoyment of this life, which must be abandoned so that you may happily find in the kingdom of God the will you have courageously overcome in this world. For the holy martyrs hated this present life for Christ’s name, preferring to lose this present life rather than deny Christ, fulfilling what follows:

### Verse 26

“If anyone serves me, let him follow me.”

“What does ‘let him follow me’ mean except ‘let him imitate me’? For Christ suffered for us, the Apostle Peter says, leaving us an example so that we might follow in his footsteps (1 Peter 2:21). Behold what was said: ‘If anyone serves me, let him follow me.’ With what fruit, what reward, what recompense? ‘And where I am,’ he says, ‘there also my servant will be.’”

The reward of love, and the compensation for the work by which Christ is served, is to be with the one whom one serves. “For where can it be well without him? Or how [Augustine: when] could it be possible to be ill with him?” Listen more clearly: “And if anyone serves me, my Father will honor him.” With what honor, except that he should be with his Son? For what he said above—“Where I am, there also my servant will be”—he is understood to have explained when he says, “My Father will honor him.” For what greater honor could an adopted son receive than to be where the Only-Begotten is—not made equal to the Godhead, but associated with eternity [Manuscript: consocius, ‘a companion’ of eternity]?

What it means to serve Christ, for which such a great reward is promised, must be considered: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me.” He intended this to be understood as though he were saying: “If anyone does not follow me, he does not serve me.” Those, therefore, serve Jesus Christ who seek not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ (Philippians 2:21). For “let him follow me” means: let him walk in my ways, not his own; as it is written elsewhere: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk just as he walked” (1 John 2:6).

Even if he offers bread to one who is hungry, he ought to do so out of mercy, not ostentation; he should seek nothing else there except the good work, with his left hand unaware of what his right hand is doing (Matthew 6:3)—that is, so that the intention of greed may be removed from the work of charity. To him it is said: “What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40).

And not only those things that pertain to bodily mercy, but, doing all works for Christ—for then they will be good, since Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10:4)—the believer [Augustine omits: “the believer”] is Christ’s servant, even unto that great work of charity which consists in laying down one’s life for one’s brothers. This is also to lay it down for Christ, because he will say this concerning his members as well: “When you did it for these, you did it for me.”

Concerning such a work he also deigned to make and call himself a servant, when he said: “The Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to lay down his life for many” (Matthew 20:28). Hence each person is Christ’s servant in the same way that Christ is a servant. The Father honors one who thus serves Christ with that great honor: that he may be with his Son, and that his faith [Augustine: his blessedness] may never fail.”

He speaks generally of everyone when he says: “If anyone serves me”; for everyone who acts well serves Christ. “Therefore let each person serve Christ according to his measure, by living well, giving alms, and preaching his name and teaching to those whom he can.”

Whoever exhorts those who live well to persevere in living well serves Christ; whoever humbly obeys one who admonishes him serves Christ; and whoever faithfully serves Christ in this present age will happily reign with Christ in the age to come.

### Chapter XXXI

When the Lord Jesus had foretold his passion in the grain of wheat [Manuscript: mustard] and urged his servants to follow him, he again accommodated his own feeling to our weakness and said:

To him who said that his soul was troubled and asked the Father to glorify him, a voice from heaven said: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.” After this he continues with many things, among which he testifies that he came not to judge the world but to save it.

### Verse 27

“Now my soul is troubled.”

Why is your soul troubled, Lord Jesus? Did you not for this reason receive a soul and become a complete man, so that you might suffer in it? I see, Lord, that you transfer our weakness into yourself and take up our cause in yourself. You were troubled because you willed it, just as you were born because you willed it.

For shortly before this it was said of you, when you raised Lazarus: “He troubled himself.” By these words he drew us from our weakness to his own weakness. For it is the voice of the Lord’s strength when he says: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified”; but it is the voice of our weakness when he says: “Now my soul is troubled.”

@ [Col. 0913D] From Saint Augustine, Treatise 52, §§2–14.

O Lord, Mediator, God above us, man for our sake, I recognize your mercy. For by the fact that you, so great, are troubled by the will of your love, you console many in your body who are troubled by the necessity of their weakness, lest they perish through despair.

Listen, therefore, soldier of Christ, to what he adds next after saying, “Now my soul is troubled.” “And what shall I say?” he asks. “Father, save me from this hour. But for this reason I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name.”

He taught you what to think; he taught you what to say, whom to call upon, in whom to hope; and he taught you to set the certain and divine will of the one you invoke before your own human and weak will [Augustine: to place it before]. Do not therefore think that he is failing from above because he wishes you to look upward from below [Augustine: to advance from below].

He also deigned to be tempted by the devil, by whom he certainly would not have been tempted if he had not wished it. And he gave the devil those answers which you ought to give in temptations. He was tempted, indeed, but he was not endangered, so that he might teach you, when endangered in temptation, to answer the tempter and, after temptation, not to follow [Manuscript and Augustine: to answer and not to follow the tempter], but to emerge from the danger of temptation.

As he said here, “Now my soul is troubled,” so there also he says: “My soul is sorrowful unto death.” And: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” He took upon himself the weakness of man in order to teach the one who is thus saddened and troubled to say what follows: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will, Father” (Matthew 26:38–39).

Thus man is directed from human things to divine things when the divine will is placed before the human will. What else is meant by “Glorify your name” except in his passion and resurrection? What else, then, does it mean except that the Father glorifies the Son, who glorifies his name even in the similar sufferings of his servants?

### Verse 28

Then a voice came from heaven saying: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”

“I have glorified it” before I made the world; “and I will glorify it again” when he rises from the dead and ascends into heaven.

It can also be understood in another way: “I have glorified it” when he was born of a virgin; when, with a star as herald from heaven, he was adored by the Magi; when he was recognized by holy men filled with the Holy Spirit; when he was declared by the Spirit descending in the form of a dove; when he was manifested by a voice sounding from heaven; when he was transfigured on the mountain; when he performed many miracles; when he healed and cleansed many; when he fed such a multitude with a few loaves; when he commanded the winds and waves; when he raised the dead.

“And I will glorify it again” when he rises from the dead; when death will no longer rule over him; when God will be exalted above the heavens and his glory above all the earth.

### Verses 29–30

The crowd standing there and listening said that there had been thunder; others said, “An angel has spoken to him.”

Jesus answered and said: “This voice came not for me but for you.”

Here he shows that by that voice it was not announced to him what he already knew, but to those to whom it was necessary that it be announced. Just as that voice was produced by the divine power not for him but for them, so his soul was troubled, by his will, not for him but for others.

### Verse 31

“Now is the judgment of the world.”

Let us not think that this was said about the future judgment that will take place at the end of the world, when the good and the wicked will be separated by an eternal division, but about the judgment that ordinarily takes place daily in the holy Church of God.

“The devil therefore possessed the human race and held the guilty liable to punishment by the record of their sins. He ruled in the hearts of unbelievers, dragging the deceived and captive into worship of the creature while abandoning the Creator. But through faith in Christ, established by his death and resurrection; through his blood, poured out for the remission of sins, thousands of believers are freed from the devil’s dominion, joined to Christ’s body, and, under so great a head, his weak [Augustine: faithful] members are invigorated by one Spirit.

“This he called the judgment, this the separation, this the expulsion of the devil from those redeemed by him. Finally, observe what he says, as though we were asking what he meant by ‘Now is the judgment of the world.’ He explains it by adding: ‘Now the prince of this world will be cast out.’

“We have heard what sort of judgment he said it was. It is not therefore that judgment which will come at the end, when the living and the dead will be judged, some being separated to the left and others to the right; it is the judgment by which the prince of this world will be cast out.

“How, then, was he inside? Where did he say that he would be cast out? ‘Now,’ he says, ‘the prince of this world will be cast out.’ This must be understood as what is now taking place, not merely what will happen later [Augustine: tanto, “so much later”] on the last day.

“The Lord therefore foresaw [Augustine: foretold] what he knew would happen: after his passion and glorification, many peoples throughout the world would believe, in whose hearts the devil was within. Whenever they renounce him through faith, he is cast out.

“But someone may say: ‘Was he not cast out from the hearts of the patriarchs and prophets and the ancient righteous as well?’ Certainly he was [the text’s reading is uncertain: “out”? “Cast out”]. How, then, was it said, ‘Now he will be cast out’? How are we to understand it except that what was then done in a very few people was now foretold as about to happen among many and great peoples?

“The same question and solution can apply to what was said: ‘The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified’ (John 7:39). The prophets did not foretell future things without the Holy Spirit; nor did the aged Simeon and the widow Anna recognize the infant Lord in the Holy Spirit; nor did Zechariah and Elizabeth, before he was born but after he had been conceived, foretell so many things about him through the Holy Spirit.

“But ‘the Spirit had not yet been given’ means that abundance of spiritual grace had not yet been given by which those gathered together would speak in all languages, as though the Church destined for all the languages of the nations were being foretold; by which peoples would be gathered spiritually; by which sins would be forgiven far and wide; and by which thousands upon thousands would be reconciled to God.

“What then? someone may ask. Since the devil is cast out from the hearts of believers, does he now tempt no believer? On the contrary, he does not cease to tempt. But it is one thing to reign within, another to attack from without; one thing to wound, another to kill. But if he wounds, there is one who heals.

“For just as it was said to those who fight, ‘I write these things to you so that you may not sin,’ so those who are wounded hear what follows: ‘And if you sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; he is the propitiation for our sins’ (1 John 2:1).

“For what do we pray when we say, ‘Forgive us our debts’ (Matthew 6:12), except that our wounds may be healed? And what else do we ask when we say, ‘Do not bring us into temptation,’ except that the one who lies in wait, or struggles from without, may not break in from any side, deceive us by any fraud, or overthrow us by any contrivances?

“When he does not occupy the place of the heart where faith dwells, he has been cast out. But ‘unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain’ (Psalm 126:1). Do not therefore presume upon yourselves if you do not wish to call the devil, once cast out, back inside.

“Let us not imagine that the devil is called the prince of the world in such a way that we believe he can rule heaven and earth. Rather, the wicked people dispersed throughout the whole earth are called ‘the world,’ just as a house is named from those who inhabit it, according to the way we say, ‘It is a good house’ or ‘It is a bad house’—not when we criticize or praise the structure of its walls and roofs, but when we speak of the conduct of good or wicked people.

“Thus he is called ‘the prince of this world,’ that is, the prince of wicked people [Augustine: of all the wicked] who inhabit the world.

“The good are also called ‘the world,’ since they likewise are dispersed throughout the whole earth. Thus the Apostle says: ‘God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself’ (2 Corinthians 5:19). These are the people from whose hearts the prince of the world is cast out.

“After he had said, ‘Now the prince of this world will be cast out’:

### Verse 32

‘And I,’ he says, ‘if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things after me.’

“What are ‘all things’ except those from whom he is cast out? He did not say ‘all people,’ but ‘all things,’ for faith does not belong to everyone (2 Thessalonians 3:2).

“He did not therefore refer this to the totality of human beings, but to the integrity of the creature: spirit, soul, and body; “that which” (quod; Augustine: quo, “by which”) we understand, and “that which” (quod; Augustine: quo, “by which”) we see; and “that which” (quod; Augustine: quo, “by which”) we are visible and tangible.

“For he who said, ‘Not a hair of your head will perish’ (Luke 21:18), draws all things after him.

“Or, if ‘all things’ is to be understood as human beings themselves, we can say that all who are predestined for salvation are meant; concerning all of these he said that nothing would perish, when above he was speaking of his sheep (John 10:28).

“Or certainly it means every kind of human being: in every language, every age, every rank of honor, every variety of intelligence, every profession of lawful and useful arts, and whatever else may be said according to the countless differences by which human beings differ from one another, apart from sins alone—from the highest to the lowest, from the king to the beggar. ‘I will draw all things after me,’ he says, so that he may be their head and they his members.

“But when he says, ‘If I am lifted up from the earth,’ this means, ‘when I have been lifted up.’ For he does not doubt that what he came to fulfill will happen.

“This refers to what he said above: ‘But if the grain has died, it bears much fruit’ (John 12:24). For what else did he call his exaltation than his passion on the cross? The evangelist himself did not leave this unsaid; he added:

### Verses 33–34

“He said this to signify by what death he was going to die.”

The crowd answered him: “We have heard from the law that the Christ remains forever. How then do you say, ‘The Son of Man must be lifted up’? Who is this Son of Man?”

They remembered well that the Lord was continually saying that he was the Son of Man. For here he did not say, “If the Son of Man is lifted up from the earth,” but, as he had said above when the Gentiles who wished to see him were announced: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.”

Keeping this in mind, and understanding his present words—“When I have been lifted up from the earth”—as referring to the death of the cross, they asked him: “We have heard from the law that the Christ remains forever. How then do you say, ‘The Son of Man must be lifted up’?”

“If he is the Christ,” they said, “he remains forever; if he remains forever, how will he be lifted up from the earth?” That is: how will he die through the passion of the cross? For they understood that this was what he had said, and what they were plotting to do.

The wisdom poured into them did not reveal the obscurity of these words to them; rather, their conscience was goaded.

### Verse 35

Jesus therefore said to them: “The light is with you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, lest the darkness seize you.”

This is why you understand [Manuscript: “will understand”] that the Christ remains forever. Therefore walk while you have the light, so that the darkness may not seize you.

Walk; draw near; understand the whole: both the Christ who would die and the one who would live forever; both the one who would pour out his blood to redeem and the one who would ascend into the heights to lead you there.

The darkness will seize you if you believe in Christ’s eternity in such a way that you deny in him the lowliness of death. And whoever walks in darkness does not know where he is going.

Thus one can stumble over the stone of stumbling and rock of offense, which the Lord became for the blind Jews (1 Peter 2:8), just as for believers the stone which the builders rejected became the cornerstone (Psalm 117:22).

For this reason they were indignant at believing in Christ: their ungodliness despised the dead and mocked the slain. Yet this was the death of the grain destined to multiply, and the exaltation of the one who draws all things after himself.

### Verse 36

“While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may be sons of light.”

When you hear something true, believe in the truth, so that you may be reborn in the truth.

Jesus said these things and withdrew from them. Not from those who had begun to believe and love; not from those who had come to meet him with palm branches and praises; but from those who saw and envied, because they did not truly see, but, blinded [Augustine: “through blindness”], stumbled over that stone.

When Jesus hid himself from those who wanted to kill him—a point you are often reminded of because of forgetfulness—he took care of our weakness; he did not diminish his own power.

[Col. 0918A] After the Lord Christ had foretold his passion in the exaltation of the cross—when the Jews, understanding this, raised the question of how he could say that he would die, since they had heard from the law that the Christ remains forever—the evangelist then continued and said:

### Verses 37–38

“Although he had performed so many signs before them, they did not believe in him, so that the word of the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, which he said:

‘Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?’” (Isaiah 53:1)

He used “who?” because of the rarity: very few believed what the holy prophets had heard from God and proclaimed to the people.

In the words, “To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”

@ [Col. 0917D] From Saint Augustine, Treatise 53, §§2–13.

He sufficiently demonstrates that the arm of the Lord is the name given to the Son of God—not because God the Father is defined by the form of human flesh, with the Son attached to him like a bodily limb, but because all things were made through him; for this reason he is called the arm of the Lord.

Just as your arm, through which you work, is called your arm, so the Word of God is called the arm of God, because God made the world through the Word. For why does a human being extend an arm in order to accomplish something, except because what he has said does not happen immediately? But if he possessed such great power that what he said came to be without any movement of his body, his word would be his arm.

But the Lord Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God the Father, just as he is not a member of the Father’s body, so he is not a word that can be conceived, sounded, and pass away; for since all things were made through him, “the Word was God” [Augustine: “the Word of God was”].

The evangelist called him the Word who was with God; the prophet called him the arm of the Lord. When we hear “the arm of the Lord,” let us recognize Christ as the power and wisdom of God, through whom all things were made. “You made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 103:24), says the Psalmist.

“He is not the Father himself, but he and the Father are one, and he is equal to the Father, wholly present everywhere.”

Here a difficult question arises: What had the wicked Jews done? Or what was their guilt, if they did not believe because it was necessary that the word of the prophet Isaiah be fulfilled, who said: “Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”

We answer this question by saying that the Lord, who knows the future, foretold through the prophet the unbelief of the Jews; yet he foretold it, he did not cause it. For God does not compel anyone to sin merely because he already knows the future sins of human beings. He foresaw their sins, not his own; not another’s, but theirs. Therefore, if the things he foresaw are not theirs, he did not truly foresee them.

@ [Col. 0917D] In Augustine these words are punctuated as follows: [Col. 0918D] “Therefore, if those things which he foresaw as theirs are not theirs, he did not truly foresee them.”

But because his foreknowledge cannot be deceived, beyond doubt it is not someone else but those whom God foresaw as sinners who sin. The Jews therefore committed the sin which he, to whom no secret is hidden, had foretold they would commit, but did not compel them to commit, since he does not approve of sin.

But the words of the Gospel that follow press the matter further and make the question more profound. For it is said here as though God were the cause of their unbelief, since he blinded their eyes and hardened their heart. This is stated altogether of God, not of the devil.

The reason must therefore be sought why the prophet said that God had done this. With his granting, we shall explain it as far as we are able.

They could not believe because the prophet foretold this. But the prophet foretold it because God foresaw that it would happen. If I am asked why they could not, I answer quickly: because they were unwilling. God foresaw their evil will and foretold it through the prophet, to whom future things cannot be hidden; and their evil will deserved this blindness or hardening [Manuscript: their evil … will].

Thus God blinds and hardens by abandoning and not helping, which he does by a judgment hidden from us but never unjust. When the Apostle was treating this very difficult question, he said: “Is there injustice with God?” (Romans 9:14) Certainly not.

If, then, it is impossible that there be injustice with God, whether he helps or does so mercifully, or whether he does not help and does so justly, because he does everything not rashly but by a just judgment: if the judgments of the saints are just, how much more so the judgments of God, who sanctifies and justifies?

They are therefore just, but hidden. For this reason, when questions of this kind arise—why one person is judged in one way and another in another; why one is blinded when God abandons him, while another is enlightened when God helps him—let us not usurp judgment over the judgment of so great a Judge. Rather, trembling, let us exclaim with the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Romans 11:33)

Concerning such questions or judgments of God, let us listen to Scripture when it admonishes us and says: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not investigate what is too strong for you” (Ecclesiasticus 3:22).

Let us therefore enter upon the way of faith and hold to it with the greatest perseverance. It leads to the king’s chamber, in which all the treasures of wisdom are hidden.

For the Lord Jesus Christ himself did not begrudge those great and especially chosen disciples of his when he said: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12).

We must walk, advance, and grow, so that our hearts may become capable of those things which we cannot presently contain. And if the final day finds us advancing, there we shall learn what we could not learn here.

It is therefore no wonder that they could not believe, since their will was so proud that, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own [Manuscript: vellent statuere, “wishing to set up their own”], as the Apostle says concerning them, they were not subject to God’s righteousness (Romans 10:3).

Because they swelled with pride, not from faith but as though from works, they were blinded by that very swelling and stumbled over the stone of stumbling.

Thus it was said, “They could not believe,” where it must be understood that they were unwilling—just as it was said of the Lord God: “If we do not believe, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself” (2 Timothy 2:13).

As the salvation of those people was an expression of the divine will [that he wished them to be saved], so the fact that they could not believe was the fault of the human will.

God foresaw this concerning the Jews who were blinded and hardened, and the prophet foretold it in God’s Spirit.

But when he added, “And let them turn, and I will heal them,” should “not” [Augustine adds: non] be understood—that is, “let them not turn”—the preceding sentence being connected to it, where it was said, “So that they may not see with their eyes and understand with their heart”? For here too it was said, “so that they may not understand”; and conversion itself comes from the grace of the one to whom it is said: “God of hosts, restore us” (Psalm 79:4).

Or should this also perhaps be understood as having been done through the mercy of heavenly healing? Since they were of a perverse and proud will and wished to establish their own righteousness, for this reason [Manuscript: ad hoc, “for this purpose”] they were abandoned, so that they might be blinded; they were blinded for this purpose, so that they might stumble over the stone of stumbling and their faces be filled with disgrace. Thus humbled, they might seek the name of the Lord, not their own righteousness by which the proud are inflated, but the righteousness of God by which the ungodly is justified.

For this benefited many of them for their good: stricken by remorse over their crime, they afterward believed in Christ, for whom he himself had also prayed, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

The text continues:

### Verses 42–43

“Nevertheless, many even of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, so that they would not be expelled from the synagogue; for they loved the glory of human beings more than the glory of God.”

“See how the evangelist marked out and condemned [some of] those whom he nevertheless said had believed in him. If they progressed in this beginning of faith, they would also, by advancing, overcome their love of human glory. The Apostle had overcome it when he said: ‘Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world’ (Galatians 6:14).

“For this reason the Lord himself also fixed his cross—where the madness of proud ungodliness mocked him—upon the foreheads of those who believe in him, where the seat of shame is, so to speak, so that faith would not be ashamed of his name, and so that they would love the glory of God more than that of human beings.”

@ [Col. 0919D] From Saint Augustine, Treatise 54, §§1–8.

While the Lord Jesus Christ was speaking among the Jews and performing such great signs of miracles, some believed, predestined to eternal life, whom he also called his sheep; others, however, did not believe and could not believe, because by the hidden yet not unjust judgment of God they had been blinded.

Others believed openly and came to meet him with palm branches; still others believed secretly but did not confess him because of the Pharisees. The evangelist marked them out when he said: “They loved the glory of human beings more than the glory of God.”

The glory of God is to confess Christ publicly, as the holy martyrs did. Concerning them the Lord himself says elsewhere: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I too will confess him before my Father” (Matthew 10:32).

Whoever confesses Christ in a confession of praise will confess him—that is, he will be praised by Christ before God the Father.

These things having been established, and his passion now drawing near:

### Verses 44–45

Jesus cried out and said: “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in him who sent me; and whoever sees me sees him who sent me.”

“He had already said in one place: ‘My teaching is not mine but his who sent me’ (John 7:16). There we understood him to have called his teaching the Word of the Father, which is himself; and by saying, ‘My teaching is not mine but his who sent me,’ he signified that he was not from himself but had one from whom he was.

“God is God from God, the Son of the Father; but the Father is not God from God, but God the Father of the Son.

“Now, when he says, ‘Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in him who sent me,’ how are we to understand this except that he appeared as a human being to human beings while God remained hidden?

“And lest they think that he was only what they saw, he wished them to believe him to be such and so great as the Father is. ‘Whoever believes in me,’ he says, ‘does not believe in me’—that is, in what he sees—but ‘in him who sent me’—that is, in the Father.

“But whoever believes in the Father must necessarily believe that he has a Son. And while believing the Father to be eternal, he must also believe that he has a Son coeternal with himself and consubstantial with himself.

“For this reason he said: ‘Whoever believes in me does not believe in me,’ wishing that everything believed about Christ should not be believed according to his humanity.

“He believes rightly in me who, according to what he sees in me, does not believe only in me, but according to what he sees in me believes me to be equal to the Father.

“And lest he be thought to have intended the Father to be understood as the father of many sons regenerated by grace, rather than as the Father of the only and equal Word, he immediately added: ‘And whoever sees me sees him who sent me.’

“So completely is there no difference between him and me that whoever sees me sees him who sent me.

“This vision must be understood as intellectual, not bodily. For now it belongs to the praise of the saints; after the day of the final resurrection it will exist in the appearance (species) [Manuscript: reality, res] of eternal blessedness. Concerning it he says elsewhere: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’ (Matthew 5:8).

“Let us attend to the remaining words.”

### Verse 46

“I have come into the world as light, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness.”

In one place he said to his disciples: “You are the light of the world. A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden. Nor do they light a lamp and place it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house. Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:14).

Yet he did not say: “You have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in you may not remain in darkness.” I affirm that this cannot be read anywhere.

All the saints, therefore, are lights; but by believing they are illuminated by him. If anyone withdraws from him, he will become darkened. But that light which illuminates cannot withdraw from itself, because it is altogether unchangeable.

When he says, “Everyone who believes in me will not remain in darkness,” he sufficiently reveals that all people found themselves in darkness. But so that they may not remain in the darkness in which they were found, they ought to believe in the light that came into this world, because through it the world was made.

### Verse 47

“And if anyone hears my words,” he says, “and does not keep them, I do not judge him.”

“Listen to how the Son says, ‘I do not judge him,’ although he says elsewhere: ‘The Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son’ (John 5:22). This must be understood in light of what follows: ‘For I did not come,’ he says, ‘to judge the world but to save the world.’

“Now is the time of mercy; afterward will be the time of judgment. For ‘I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, Lord’ (Psalm 100:1).

“But concerning that final judgment also, observe what he says:

### Verse 48

“Whoever rejects me and does not accept my words has one who judges him. The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day.”

He does not say: “Whoever rejects me and does not accept my words, I will not judge him on the last day.”

For the Son of God came to save, not to judge. Therefore he said, “I do not judge him”—that is, now, in the present—but I judge him on the last day.

“When he had said, ‘Whoever rejects me and does not accept my words has one who judges him,’ and those listening were waiting to know who that judge might be, he immediately added: ‘The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day.’ He clearly showed that he himself would judge on the last day.

“For he spoke himself, announced himself, and set himself as the door through which he himself, as shepherd, would enter to the sheep.

“Those who did not hear will therefore be judged in one way, and those who heard and despised will be judged in another. For the Apostle says: ‘Those who sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and those who sinned under the law will be judged by the law’ (Romans 2:12).

### Verse 49

“Because I,” he says, “have not spoken from myself.”

For this reason he says that he did not speak from himself: because he is not from himself. We have often said this already: the Son is not from himself but from the Father.

Therefore he adds: “But the Father who sent me himself gave me a commandment—what I should say and what I should speak.”

The Father does not speak to the Son through spatial distance, through the utterance of syllables, or through vocal sound, as though the Son heard the Father’s command in the way a human son ordinarily hears from a human being what his father commands him.

@ [Col. 0921D] Augustine: “So that he would have to receive in time what he previously did not have. For he received from the Father what he has in such a way that he received it by being born, and the Father gave it to him by begetting him”—something which he would not otherwise have had—but the Father begot him possessing life.

“But the only Son is the Word of the Father and the wisdom of the Father; in him are all the Father’s commandments. For the Son never at any time did not know the Father’s commandment, so that he would have needed to receive in time what he obtained, as though by being born he received it and the Father gave it to him by begetting him.

“As he said above, ‘As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself’—that is, he begot the Son possessing life in himself—so here he says, ‘As the Father gave me a commandment.’

“And because that birth itself is eternal, the Son, who is life, never did not exist; and just as he is eternal life, so the one who was born is eternal life.

“Likewise, the commandment was not given because the Son did not possess it; rather, as I have said, in the wisdom of the Father, which is the Word of the Father, all the Father’s commandments are present.

“For the text continues:

[Col. 0923A] **VERSE 50.**—“And I know that his commandment is eternal life.” If, then, the Son himself is eternal life, and the Father’s commandment is eternal life, what else has been said than, “I am the Father’s commandment”? Accordingly, when he adds and says, “What I speak, as the Father has said to me, so I speak,” let us not understand “he has said to me” as though he spoke through words [Ms.: “as though by a word”; Augustine: “as though the Father spoke words”] to the one Word, or as though God’s Word needed God’s words. The Father therefore said to the Son, just as he gave life to the Son—not something the Son did not know or possess, but what the Son himself was. What, then, is “As he has said to me, so I speak,” except “I speak the Word”? He spoke as the truthful one; the Son speaks as the Truth. The truthful one begot the Truth. What, then, would he already say to the Truth? The Truth was not imperfect, such that something true could be added to it. [Col. 0923B] He therefore “said” to the Truth because he begot the Truth.

Moreover, the Truth itself speaks as it was told to speak—but to those who understand, whom it teaches, as it has obtained [Augustine and others: “as it was born”]. But so that human beings might believe what they were not yet able to understand, words sounded from the mouth of flesh and passed away as the sounds flew by; they resounded [Augustine: “the passing sounds resounded”] as the brief intervals of their appointed times elapsed. {591} Yet the realities whose signs those sounds are were, in a certain way, drawn into the memory of those who heard them and have reached us also through letters, which are visible signs. The Truth does not speak in this manner: it speaks inwardly to understanding minds, instructs without sound, and floods them with an intelligible voice. Whoever, therefore, can see in it the eternity of its birth hears it speaking in the manner in which the Father told it to speak. It has awakened us to a great desire for its inward sweetness; but let us grasp it as we grow, grow as we walk, and walk as we advance, so that we may be able to arrive “through himself at himself, with him himself teaching us and promising us: ‘I am the way, and the truth, and the life.’ The way for those who seek, the truth for those who find, the life for those who remain.”

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0923B] To Gisla, the dearest sister in Christ [Al.: “Gislana”], and to Columba, a daughter devoted to God, Alcuin, a humble levite, sends greetings.

[Col. 0923D] Concerning this letter and the time when it was written, recall what we said in the prefatory notice placed before these commentaries. [Col. 0924D] The manuscript codex of St Emmeram does not contain this.

For the consolation of your holiness I have sent this little book, composed in a commatic (*comatico*) style, so that you may have it during these days to exercise your holy devotion through it. For it is most fitting, in such a study, to pass these most holy days, especially in the Gospel of the blessed evangelist John, in which are the higher mysteries of the Divinity, and also in the most holy words of our Lord Jesus Christ from that Gospel—words that he spoke on the night when he chose to be handed over for the salvation of the world.

I might perhaps have sent you an exposition of the whole Gospel [I would have sent], if the command of my lord the king had not occupied me with correcting the Old and New Testaments. Nevertheless, with God’s help and with life accompanying me, I shall complete the work I have begun as time permits and dedicate it, when finished, to your name.

But for the present I ask that you remember our name in your holy and sacred [perhaps: “most sacred”] prayers, and that you pass this most holy season prosperously in the service of holiness, in the religious practice of a most chaste life, and in the study of reading, so that, arriving at holy Easter, you may be able to celebrate the resurrection of our Lord with worthy praises. I wish you always to be well and to flourish in every exercise of piety, dearest ladies.

# CHAPTER THIRTY-TWO

Having risen from supper, he washed the disciples’ feet, saying that he had given them an example, so that they too might do for their fellow servants what he, the Lord of all, was shown to have done.

## CHAPTER 13, VERSE 1

“Before the feast of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father.” [Col. 0924B]

[Col. 0924D] From St Augustine, Tractate 55, sections 1–7. “Passover, brothers, is not, as some think, a Greek name, but a Hebrew one. In its own language, *Pascha* means ‘passage,’ because at that time the people of God first celebrated Passover, when, fleeing from Egypt, they crossed the Red Sea” (Exodus 14:29). This figure was fulfilled in Christ according to the truth, when through the passion of the cross he passed from this world to the Father. Thus we too must pass from this world to the Father, from temporal things to eternal things, from iniquity to righteousness, and from the deceitful devil to Christ the Savior.

“Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.” Certainly, so that they too might pass through his love from this world, where they were, to their Head, who had passed from here.” “To the end,” that is, he loved them eternally. “Or ‘to the end,’ that is, to Christ, because Christ is the end of the law.”

**VERSE 2.**—“And supper having been made.” We must not understand this to mean that supper had already been consumed [Augustine: “completed”] and finished; for they were still dining when the Lord rose and washed his disciples’ feet. Afterwards he reclined again and gave the morsel to his betrayer. Thus “supper having been made” means “supper having been prepared” [Ms.: “supper having been said”], with the disciples dining together with their master.

“When the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot to betray him.” “If you ask what was put into Judas’s heart, it was this: that he should betray him. This putting is a spiritual suggestion,” not into the ears through bodily sounds, but into the heart of one consenting to iniquity. For just as the good Spirit, in his kindness, introduces good thoughts, so the evil spirit suggests evil thoughts. “But it matters to which of these the human mind gives consent—whether it has been abandoned through merit or aided through grace by divine assistance.”

This betrayer came to the meal without faith, not believing that the one he was planning to betray was God. “He appeared and was tolerated; in the one whom he supposed could be deceived, he himself was deceived”; and God’s goodness made use of his wickedness for the salvation of others.

**VERSE 3.**—“Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands.” Therefore, even the betrayer himself. For if he did not hold him in his hands, he certainly could not use him as he wished. The Lord knew what he was doing for his friends, since he patiently made use of his enemies. He also knew that he had come forth from God and was going to God: he neither abandoned God when he came forth from him nor abandoned us when he returned.

**VERSE 4.**—“He rises from supper and lays aside his garments.” The evangelist, about to speak of the Lord’s great humility, first wished to commend his exaltedness. This is the point of what he says: “Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands.” Although the Father had therefore given all things into his hands, he fulfilled not the office of God the Lord but of a servant human being. For the usefulness of human humility is so great that even divine majesty commended it by its own example.

“He rises from supper”: he descended from the heavenly places. “He laid aside his garments”: that is, he emptied himself.

**VERSE 5.**—“When he had taken a towel, he girded himself,” putting on the form of a servant. “He poured water into a basin”: that is, he poured out his blood upon the earth, so that he might cleanse in himself the footsteps of believers, which had been soiled by earthly sins; and with the towel with which he was girded—that is, with the towel of his body with which he was girded—he wiped and cleansed them, because his entire passion is our purification. When he took the form of a servant, he did not abandon what he had, but assumed what he did not have.

**VERSE 6.**—“He came, then, to Simon Peter.” [Col. 0925C]

[Col. 0925D] From St Augustine, Tractate 56, sections 1–4. “This should not be understood as though, after washing the feet of the others, he came to the first of the apostles, but because he began there first.” Therefore Peter is terrified that the Son of God should wash his feet—the Lord those of a servant, God those of a human being.

“When he began to wash the disciples’ feet, he came to the one with whom he had begun, that is, to Peter. Then Peter, as any of them would have been terrified, was terrified and said: ‘Lord, do you wash my feet?’” You are God; I am human. You are Lord; I am a servant. You are Redeemer; I am a sinner.

**VERSE 7.**—“What I am doing, you do not know now; but afterward you will know.” You do not yet understand the mystery of this deed, but afterward you will understand, because “if I do not wash you, you will have no part with me.”

**VERSE 8.**—“Peter said to him: You shall never wash my feet.” He used “never” to mean “not ever.” But, terrified by the Lord’s response, he added:

**VERSE 9.**—“Lord, not only my feet, but also my head and my hands.” “Since you threaten in this way that my limbs must be washed, I not only do not withhold the lower parts, but also place the uppermost beneath you. Do not deny me a share with you; I deny you no part of my body to be washed.”

Jesus answered:

**VERSE 10.**—“He who has been washed has no need except to wash his feet, but is entirely clean.” [Col. 0926A] How can he be both entirely clean and still need his feet washed, unless he is entirely clean in the washing of holy baptism but is again soiled by the dust of earthly dwelling? Therefore he needs to be washed again through the grace [of the washing] of divine mercy, although previously he had been entirely cleansed by that same grace, as the apostle John testifies: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

“Therefore he washes our feet daily, he who intercedes for us; and that we daily need to wash our feet we confess in the Lord’s Prayer itself, when we say: ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors’” (Matthew 6:12).

“And you are clean, but not all.” The evangelist explained this in the words that follow. Let us therefore proceed [Col. 0926B] to the rest.

**VERSE 12.**—After he had washed their feet—that is, after the cleansing of our redemption had been accomplished through the shedding of his blood—he took his garments, rising on the third day from the tomb, and, in the same body in which he had died on the cross, he became immortal and clothed himself. And after reclining again, he ascended into heaven, sitting at the right hand of God and reclining in the majesty of the Father’s divinity. From there he will come again to judge the living and the dead.

For it follows: “He said to them: Do you know what I have done for you?” He says this concerning what he had previously announced [Ms.: “promised”] when he answered the apostle Peter: “What I am doing, you do not know now; but afterward you will know.” Now is that “afterward” which he promised earlier.

**VERSE 13.**—“You call me Lord and Teacher, and you speak rightly.” Certainly, because you speak the truth: that is what I am. He said “I am” not in the guise of arrogance, but in obedience to the truth.

**VERSE 14.**—“If I, then, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.” If I, God and Lord, have forgiven your sins, how much more ought you also to forgive one another’s sins?”

[Col. 0926D] From St Augustine, Tractate 58, section 5. “This is what the Apostle says: ‘Forgiving one another, if anyone has a grievance against another’ (Colossians 3:13), just as the Lord forgave us, so let us also [Augustine: ‘forgave you, and so you too’]. Let us therefore forgive one another’s offenses, and pray for one another concerning our offenses; and in this way, as it were, let us wash one another’s feet” [Ms. and Augustine: “let us wash”].

Although some may find it useful to do this bodily as an act of charity and an example of humility, nevertheless all must do it spiritually in the heart, so that we forgive one another our debts, just as we ask our God to forgive us our debts. For it follows:

# CHAPTER THIRTY-THREE

Saying that a servant is not greater than his lord, after the testimony of Scripture he indicates that he will be betrayed by Judas through the offering of the dipped bread, and he exhorts the disciples in many ways.

**VERSES 16–17.**—“Amen, amen, I say to you: A servant is not greater than his lord, nor an apostle greater than the one who sent him. If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” [Col. 0927A]

[Col. 0927D] From St Augustine, Tractate 59, sections 1–3. “He said this because he had washed the disciples’ feet, being a teacher of humility both in word and in example,” so that he might instruct them by word and example in the duty of charity.

**VERSE 18.**—“I do not speak of all of you,” that is, I do not call all of you blessed. “I know whom I have chosen,” for this blessedness, so that they might be followers of my commandments. “But so that Scripture may be fulfilled: ‘He who eats bread with me will lift up his heel against me.’” That is, he will trample me [Augustine: “trample upon me”].

He eats bread not for his salvation but for punishment, because he ate so that he might remain concealed as a betrayer, not advance as a lover. What does he mean when he says elsewhere: “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6:71) And here he says: “I know whom I have chosen.” That Judas was chosen not for blessedness but for the treacherous betrayal that would serve the world’s salvation, not his own, because it was said of him: “It would have been better for that man if he had not been born” (Matthew 26:24).

But those of whom it is now said [Ms.: “he said”], “I know whom I have chosen,” were chosen for the blessedness of eternal glory.

**VERSE 19.**—“From now on I tell you before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe that I am.” That is, I am the one of whom that Scripture spoke beforehand, where it says: “He who eats bread with me will lift up his heel against me” (Psalm 40:10).

**VERSE 20.**—“Whoever receives anyone whom I send receives me; and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me.” When he said this, he did not divide the unity of nature, but showed the authority of the one who sends. Thus each person should receive the one who has been sent in such a way that in him he recognizes the one who sent him. If, then, you look upon Christ in Peter, you will find the teacher of the disciple. But if you look upon the Father in the Son, you will find the Father of the Only-Begotten; and so, in the one who has been sent, you receive the one who sends without any error.”

**VERSE 21.**—“When Jesus had said these things, he was troubled in spirit, and testified and said: Amen, amen, I say to you, one of you will betray me.” [Col. 0927C]

[Col. 0927D] From the same, Tractate 60, section 1. “The approaching passion, the imminent danger, and the impending hand of the betrayer troubled him, whose intention he had foreknown.” {594}

He was therefore troubled in spirit by the betrayer’s great crime. Our weakness was troubled in him, not his power. Just as he suffered for us, so he was troubled for us. Thus he who died through power was troubled through power, so that our distress might not fall into despair but be turned [to] compassion for our neighbors or [to true] repentance for our sins; for his distress is our consolation.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: one of you will betray me today.”

[Col. 0928D] From St Augustine, Tractate 61, sections 2–6. “One in number, not in merit; in appearance, not in virtue; by bodily association, not by a spiritual bond; joined in flesh, not united as a companion in heart. What does ‘one of you’ mean except that one who will betray me will go out from you?

**VERSE 22.**—“The disciples therefore looked at one another, uncertain of whom he was speaking.” Such pious love did they have for their teacher that, although each one’s conscience was known to himself, human weakness nevertheless made each suspect the other [Ms. and Augustine: “made each one stir suspicion concerning the other”].”

**VERSE 23.**—One of his disciples was reclining in Jesus’ bosom, the one whom Jesus loved. What he had called “in his bosom,” he shortly afterward calls “upon Jesus’ breast.” This is John, whose Gospel this is, as is made clear later.

For this was the custom of those who ministered the sacred writings to us: whenever the divine narrative was being told by one of them and he came to himself, he would speak as though of another person, and thus insert himself into the structure [Augustine: “order”] of his narrative as a writer of events, not as his own eulogist. Blessed Moses did this too, narrating everything about himself as though about another person [addition from Augustine: “and he said: ‘The Lord said to Moses’”] (Exodus 6:1).

“He loved him”—not one above all others, but one more familiarly in all things. He loved in him something that he did not love in the others: namely, that he should pass through this life in peace [“from this life, not end this life through suffering”]. “In the bosom of Jesus,” that is, in the secret place from which he poured forth that wondrous mystery unheard by all ages: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

**VERSE 24.**—“Simon Peter therefore signaled to him and said to him.” He speaks by signaling, not by speaking; by indicating, not by making a sound. What does he say by signaling? What follows: “Who is it of whom he speaks?” Peter indicated these words—not with the sound of his voice, but through bodily movement.

**VERSE 25.**—“When he had reclined upon Jesus’ breast”—this is indeed the bosom of the breast, the secret place of wisdom—“he said to him: Lord, who is it [who will betray you]?”

**VERSE 26.**—“Jesus answered him: It is the one to whom I shall give the dipped bread.” And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas, son of Simon Iscariot. “After the bread, Satan then entered into him.” The betrayer was exposed; the hiding places of darkness were laid bare. What he received was good, but he received it to his own harm, because the evil man received the good evilly.”

[Col. 0928D] From the same, Tractate 62, sections 1, 2, 4, 5. From this we are taught how carefully we must guard against receiving a good thing evilly. For it matters greatly not what is received, but who receives it; nor what sort of thing is given, but what sort of person is the one to whom it is given.

Thus, after this bread, Satan entered the Lord’s betrayer, so that he might possess more completely one who had already been handed over to him, into whom he had earlier entered in order to deceive him.”

For the presumptuous reception of the sacrament increased the sin of the betrayal: bread entered the ungrateful man’s stomach, and the enemy entered his mind. Perhaps by the dipping of the bread he indicated the deceit of the one who came to the supper as a feigned friend and went to his teacher as a false disciple.

“‘What you are doing, do quickly.’ He did not command the crime, but foretold Judas’s evil and our good. For what was worse for Judas, and what was better for us, than that Christ should be betrayed by him? ‘Quickly’: this means that he was more ready for the passion than they were eager for vengeance. He did not say, ‘What you are doing, do quickly,’ so much in raging toward the destruction of the traitor as in hastening toward the salvation of the faithful. He did not say this because the one whom you betray is in your power, but because the one who has power over all wills it.

**VERSES 28–29.**—“But none of those reclining knew why he had said this to him.” For some thought that, because Judas had the money box, Jesus had said to him: “Buy what we need for the feast,” or that he should give something to the poor.

The Lord therefore also had a money box, preserving what the faithful offered and distributing it for the needs of his own and for those of others in need. Thus the first form of ecclesiastical funds was established. Here we understand that the command that one should not be anxious about tomorrow (Matthew 6:34) was not given so that the saints should keep no money, but so that they should not serve money in this way or abandon righteousness out of fear of poverty.

{595}

**VERSE 30.**—“When he had received the morsel, he went out immediately; and it was night.” He himself was also the night who went out, the son of darkness, doing the works of darkness. He therefore went out to the service of his own destruction and to the dispensation of our salvation—not out of concern for our salvation, but with the intention of his own denial [Ms.: “business”].

Here is fulfilled what the Psalmist says: “Day pours forth the word to day”—that is, Christ brought forth the word of salvation to the disciples—“and night shows knowledge to night” (Psalm 18:3)—that is, Judas showed the Jews the malice of the betrayer [Ms.: “the betrayal”].

Now the Lord’s words must be considered with greater attention, the words that he spoke privately to the disciples on that very night before the betrayal. They are exceedingly deep in their mysteries; therefore, where the interpreter will labor greatly, the hearer must not be negligent. The sayings of the Most High must be considered more deeply: he conceals them so that we may seek, and reveals them so that we may find. He is the one who closes and opens—he closes so that we may seek, and opens so that we may find—so that the seeker may receive the fruit of his labor and the giver may receive praise and thanks for his goodness.

**VERSE 31.**—“Jesus said: Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him.” In this glorification he signifies something great.

[Col. 0929D] From the same, Tractate 63, sections 2–3. “Judas went out, and Jesus was glorified; the son of destruction went out, and the Son of Man was glorified. When the unclean man went out, all the clean remained, and they remained with their purifier. Something similar will occur when this world, conquered by Christ, passes away and no unclean person remains among Christ’s people: when the weeds have been separated from the wheat, the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13:43).

About this future glorification of the saints he used the past tense, because what is future in the saints is said to have been accomplished in God’s predestination.

“Now the Son of Man has been glorified,” as though he were saying: Behold what will occur in that glorification of mine where no evil person will remain. Here it is not said, “Now the glorification of the Son of Man has been signified,” but, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified,” just as it is not said, “The rock signified Christ,” but, “The rock was Christ.”

When he had said, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified,” he added: “And God has been glorified in him.” For this is the glorification of the Son of Man: that God should be glorified in him. For he is not glorified in himself [Augustine: “For if he is not glorified in himself”], but God is glorified in him; then God glorifies him in himself.

Finally, as though explaining this, he adds and says: “If God has been glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself.” That is: if God has been glorified in him who did not come to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him:

**VERSE 32.**—“God will also glorify him in himself,” so that the human nature in which the Son of Man exists, which was assumed by the eternal Word, may also be endowed with immortal eternity. “And immediately,” he says, “he will glorify him”: clearly foretelling his resurrection, which was to occur immediately—not like ours at the end of the world, but immediately.”

**VERSE 33.**—“Little children, I am with you only a little while.” When he had foretold the glorification of his future kingdom and the glorification of his resurrection, which was soon to occur— [Col. 0930B]

[Col. 0929D] From the same, Tractate 64, sections 1–4. So that they would not think that God would glorify him in such a way that he would no longer be joined to them in the fellowship by which he had been with them on earth, he says: “I am with you only a little while.” It is as though he said: Certainly I shall be glorified immediately by the resurrection, but I shall not immediately ascend into heaven; rather, I shall be with you a little longer”—signifying the forty days during which he was with the disciples, appearing to them at appropriate times.

Nevertheless, it may also be understood as the short period of that night alone, until the hour of the passion, during which he would be with the disciples.

[Col. 0929D] The passage is mutilated both in the printed edition and in the manuscripts; it might perhaps be restored as follows: “Nevertheless, it may be understood as the short period of that night alone, until the hour of the passion, during which he would be with the disciples.” [Col. 0930D]

“There is also another divine presence, unknown to mortal senses, concerning which he likewise says: ‘Behold, I am with you until the end of the age’” (Matthew 28:20). “This certainly is not ‘I am with you only a little while,’” but “with you a little while,” either before the hour of the passion or after the resurrection until the glory of the ascension.

“What does he mean when he says elsewhere to his disciples after the resurrection: ‘These are the words that I spoke to you when I was still with you’ (Luke 24:44), except ‘when I was still in mortal flesh, in which you also are’? For at that time, when he said these things, he had already been raised in the same flesh, but he was no longer with them in the same mortality.

“You will seek me, and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come,’ so I say to you now.” That is, you cannot come now. But when he said this to the Jews, he did not add “now.” These disciples therefore could not then come where he was going, but they could afterward.

Thus, teaching them how they could become fit to go where he was going before them:

**VERSE 34.**—“I give you a new commandment,” he says, “that you love one another. These are the steps by which Christ must be followed”—this commandment of charity.

[Col. 0930D] From St Augustine, Tractate 65, sections 1–2. It is not every love that renews the hearer, or rather the obedient person, but this love, which the Lord added in order to distinguish it from carnal love: “As I have loved you.” This love renews us, so that we may be new people, but heirs of the New Testament. This love gathers a new people to Christ.

It also renewed the ancient Fathers, so that they might be believers in Christ, who was to come to redeem them.

“Let all who wish to be brothers of the only Son of God, who gave himself for us in this love, hear and keep this: ‘I give you a new commandment, that you love one another.’” For in this commandment is also contained that commandment which is stated first: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart [and with all your soul] and with all your mind” (Matthew 22:39 and following).

“But to those who understand rightly, both commandments are found in each one. For the person who loves God cannot restrain himself from obeying him when he commands that he love his neighbor [Augustine: ‘cannot despise the one who commands him to love his neighbor’]; and the person who loves his neighbor holily and spiritually—what does he love in him except the Lord [Augustine: ‘God’]? This is the love distinguished from all worldly love, which the Lord distinguished by adding: ‘As I have loved you.’”

[Col. 0931D] From St Augustine, Tractate 66, section 1. When the Lord Jesus commended to the disciples the holy love by which they were to love one another, Simon Peter said to him: “Lord, where are you going?” Thus the disciple said this to the teacher, the servant to the Lord, as though ready to follow him.

Therefore the Lord, who saw his intention and why he had asked this, answered him:

**VERSE 36.**—“Where I am going, you cannot follow me now.” It was as though he said: You cannot now go where you are asking about. He did not say, “You cannot,” but “You cannot now.” He introduced a delay but did not take away hope. Indeed, he confirmed the same hope—which he had not taken away but rather granted—with the following words, adding and saying: “But you shall follow afterward.”

**VERSE 37.**—Peter answered: “Why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.” He saw what desire was in Peter’s mind, but Peter did not see what strength he possessed. The weak man boasted of his will, but the physician was examining [Ms.: “was directing”; Augustine: “was observing”] his condition. One was making a promise; the other foresaw it. The one who did not know dared, and the one who foresaw taught.”

**VERSE 38.**—Jesus answered: “Will you lay down your life for me? What you promise, you cannot do now. Your life must first be laid down for you, so that afterward you may be able to lay down your life for me.”

“Why are you so presumptuous? What do you think of yourself? What do you believe yourself to be? Hear what you are: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: the rooster will not crow until you have denied me three times.’ Behold how quickly you will appear to yourself—you who speak great things and do not know yourself to be small. You who promise me your death will three times deny your life. For by fearing the death of your flesh, you will give death to your soul. As great as life is in confessing Christ, so great is death in denying Christ.”

Here one must be admonished not to trust in one’s own strength, when so great a pillar tottered at the voice of a single servant girl; nor should anyone despair because of his sins. Peter died by denying and came to life again by weeping. He died because he presumptuously trusted in himself, but he came to life by humbly weeping, because the Savior’s mercy looked upon him kindly. For it follows:

{597}

# CHAPTER THIRTY-FOUR

“Let not your heart be troubled,” he says to the disciples. “I am the way, the truth, and the life. Whoever sees me also sees the Father. I am in the Father, and the Father is in me. Whatever you ask in my name, I will do.” [Col. 0932A]

## CHAPTER 14, VERSE 1

“Let not your heart be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in me.” [Col. 0932D]

From the same, Tractate 67, sections 1–2. So that they would not fear death as human beings [Bede: “so that they would not fear death for him as a human being”] and therefore be troubled, he consoles them, also testifying that he is God. For it follows that, if you believe in God, you ought also to believe in me. This would not follow if Christ were not God.”

**VERSE 2.**—“In my Father’s house are many dwelling places.” Because their merits [Ms.: “of the saints”] are different, there are many dwelling places in the Father’s house.

“No one among them will be excluded from that house, where each will receive a dwelling according to his merit.”

Therefore, let not your heart be troubled. For one denarius is given to all who labor in the vineyard—that is, eternal life is given to all who labor in the Church through faith.

“But the many dwelling places signify the different dignities of merits within one eternal life, and [God] will be all in all, because God is love. For each person possesses this also, when he loves in another what he himself does not possess, because the unity of love reigns in all.”

It follows: “If it were not so, I would have told you, because I am going to prepare a place for you.” If there were not many dwelling places somewhere in the Father’s house, I would certainly have told you. But now I am going to prepare a place for you. [How could the members have reached those dwelling places if the head had not gone before? He prepared a place for us], when he died and rose for us, and indeed also ascended into heaven. He did all these things for us in order to prepare a place for us in the kingdom of his Father.

**VERSE 3.**—“And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself.” If I go away through the absence of the flesh, I will come through the presence of divinity, in which I shall be with you until the end [Ms.: “until the consummation of the age”]. Or also: If I go away by ascending into heaven, I will come again to judge the living and the dead, as the angels testified, saying: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

It follows: “And I will take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be.” This is what he said later: “Father, I desire that where I am, these also may be with me.”

**VERSE 4.**—“And you know where I am going, and you know the way.” You know where I am going—that is, to the Father—and you know the way by which one comes to the Father.

**VERSE 5.**—Thomas said to him: “Lord, we do not know where you are going; how can we know the way?” It seemed to him that he did not know what Christ had convicted him of knowing when he said:

**VERSE 6.**—“I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” It was as though he had said: If you know me, you know the way; and I am the one to whom one goes—that is, the truth; and I am the life in which you stand [Al.: “in which one stands”].

If you know me, you know the way; you know where I am going and where you will remain [Al.: “where you will have remained”]. Those who go to the Father go through me; and those who come to the Father come to me, because “I and the Father are one.” And they remain in me, because this is eternal life: “that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3).

Hence he continued, saying: “No one comes to the Father except through me.” Explaining what he had said, “I am the way,” he immediately adds:
