**VERSE 7.**—“If you had known me, you would certainly have known my Father also, because I am the truth, in the true Father. And from now on you will know him, and you have seen him.” If you know and see me spiritually, [you know and see him], because I and the Father are one—one in nature, not one person.

**VERSE 8.**—Philip said to him, not understanding this: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.” As though the Father were something better than the Son, in whose vision alone blessedness would be sufficient. The teacher rebuked the disciple’s statement, saying:

**VERSE 9.**—“Have I been with you for so long, and you have not known me?” [“You have not known me”] to be in the Father and the Father to be in me. “Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father also. Whoever understands me certainly understands my Father also.”

[Col. 0933D] From St Augustine, Tractate 70, section 3. But the teacher rebuked the disciple because he saw the heart of the one who was asking. Philip desired to know the Father as though the Father were better than the Son; and therefore he did not know the Son either, since he believed that something better than the Son existed.

To correct this understanding it was said: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also.” Why do you say, “Show us the Father”? I see how you spoke: you are not seeking to see another who is like him, but you think that he is better.”

**VERSE 10.**—“Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? Why do you wish to know separately those who are inseparable?”

Then he speaks not to Philip alone but to them all: “The words that I speak to you I do not speak from myself. But the Father who remains in me himself does the works.” [Col. 0933B]

[Col. 0933D] From the same, Tractate 71, sections 1–3. What is “I do not speak from myself” except “I am not from myself, who speak”? For he attributes what he does to the one from whom he himself is. The Father God is not from anyone; the Son, however, is indeed God equal to the Father, but from God the Father. Therefore the Father is God, but not “from God,” and light, but not “from light”; whereas the Son is God from God, light from light.

Finally, he adds and says:

**VERSES 11–12.**—“Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? Otherwise, believe because of the works themselves.”

“Previously he had rebuked Philip alone, but now it is shown that he was not the only one present who needed rebuke. ‘Believe because of the works themselves,’ he says, ‘that I am in the Father and the Father is in me.’ For if we were separate, we could in no way work inseparably.”

But what is it that follows?

Amen, amen I say to you: whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father.” “Let not the servant exalt himself above the master, nor the disciple above the teacher: [Col. 0934A] he said that they would do greater things than he himself did”; but without him, as he said below, what could they have done? “But what, after all, are these greater works? Perhaps that, while they were passing by, even their shadow healed the sick? For it is greater that a shadow should heal than a fringe: the former did so through itself, the latter through them—but in both cases it was he himself.” Or are the apostles’ works greater because they brought salvation to all the nations, whereas Christ’s work brought salvation only to the Jews, and to only a very few of them? Yet he did both: he accomplished the salvation of some in Judea [personally], and the salvation of the nations through the apostles, as well as through other preachers. Hence he continued and said: “Whoever believes in me will do the works that I do, [and will do greater works than these].”

@ [Col. 0933D] From the same author, Treatise LXXII, nos. 1–2. “Not because the disciple is greater than the teacher, or the servant than the Lord, or the adopted son than the only-begotten Son, or [Col. 0934B] man than God: but because through them [he himself] deigned to do the same greater works.”

He immediately showed how they could do greater works, saying: “Whoever believes in me will do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these,” and then immediately added: “because I am going to the Father.” (VERSE 13.) “And whatever you ask in my name, this I will do.” Having said, “he will do,” he later says, “I will do,” as though he were saying: “Do not think this impossible for you; for the one who believes in me will not be able to be greater than I. Therefore he will not do greater works by himself, but through me, because he believes in me. This is not a diminution of power, but a compassion arising from goodness.” Thus the rich man who departed from him sadly, refusing to accept the words of salvation,

@ [Col. 0934D] The passage is corrupt. Read Saint Augustine, at the place cited. “When the apostles preached, many rich people followed poverty willingly [Ms., voluntarily]. [Col. 0934C] Thus what one man heard from him and did not do, many did when the good teacher spoke through his disciples. Behold: when preached by believers, he did greater works than when he spoke to hearers”—but this was through preachers. “Are all who believe in him therefore preachers? Yet he says that those who believe in him will do greater works.” “In this work of faith we do Christ’s works, because believing in Christ itself is also Christ’s work; Christ works this in us, though certainly not without us. First I act, anticipating grace [Ms., more correctly, grace anticipates]; then he too will act [Ms., acts], with subsequent grace, because I act so that it may be done [Ms., so that he may act]. What works are these, unless that the ungodly should become righteous?” Perhaps it is a greater work for us to accomplish our salvation through him than to preach the words of salvation, which he accomplished without us. Having said this, he continued: “Because I am going to the Father, and whatever you ask in my name, this I will do.” In these words he promised great hope to those who pray.

@ [Col. 0934D] From the same author, Treatise LXXIII, nos. 1–4. “Thus he went to the Father without abandoning those in need, but hearing those who ask”; nevertheless, not everything that is asked for, but what pertains to the salvation of those who ask. Therefore he said: (VERSE 14.) “If you ask the Father for anything in my name, I will do it.” What does “in my name” mean except “in the name of the Savior”? If you ask for what pertains to [Col. 0935A] {599} your salvation, you have asked in my name.” “For when evils delight us and good things do not, we ought rather to ask God that good things may delight us than that evils should be granted so as to delight us. Therefore, whoever believes in him, whatever he asks in [his] name that benefits those who believe in him, he does; for he does this as Savior. But if someone who believes in him asks through ignorance for something contrary to his salvation, he is not asking in the Savior’s name: for the Savior will not be his Savior if he does what hinders his salvation. The Savior knows better than we ourselves what benefits us. Therefore we must ask that his will be done in us.” He immediately added:

“So that the Father may be glorified in the Son.” “Therefore the Son does nothing without the Father, nor the Father without the Son. The Father acts in the Son, so that the Son may be glorified in the Father; and the Son acts in the Father, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son, because the Father and the Son are one.” It continues:

## CHAPTER XXXV

He promises that the Paraclete will be sent by the Father to the disciples who love him and keep his commandments, and that he will remain with them forever; he also promises to give them peace and to leave them his peace.

VERSE 15–16.—“If you love me, keep my commandments, and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete.” What does he mean by saying that the Spirit-Paraclete would be given to those who love God and keep his commandments, when God cannot be loved and his commandments cannot be kept except through the Holy Spirit? What else can this mean but that the person who loves God through the Holy Spirit merits, by loving, to possess him more fully, and, by possessing him more fully, to love him more?

@ [Col. 0935D] From Bede’s homily for Pentecost. “Paraclete is interpreted as ‘consoler,’ and the Holy Spirit is rightly called the Paraclete because he lifts up and refreshes the hearts of the faithful with the desires of heavenly life, so that they may not fail amid the adversities of this age.” The disciples therefore had the Holy Spirit, but through a certain hidden inspiration; through him they loved the Lord, but they did not yet possess him in the manner the Lord promised. They possessed secretly the one whom they would later possess through a certain manifestation—that is, when he came in tongues of fire, sat upon them, and they spoke in tongues, magnifying God. “I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete,” thereby showing that he himself is the Paraclete. “But previously they also had a Paraclete, namely the Lord himself, dwelling with them in the flesh. Through the sweetness of his miracles and the help of his preaching [Bede, whose], they were accustomed to be raised up and strengthened so that they would not be scandalized by the persecution of unbelievers.” He said, “I will ask,” on account of his humanity, although he gives together with the Father through his divinity. “That he may remain with you forever.” “For he remains forever with the saints: in this life he always illumined them inwardly and invisibly, and in the future he brings them continually to contemplate the vision of his majesty.

VERSE 17.—“The Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it does not see him or know him.” “He calls human beings ‘the world’—those devoted to the love of this world.” The world, therefore, cannot receive him—that is, worldly people cannot—because they do not possess the invisible eyes of charity, by which alone the Holy Spirit can be seen and known, and through knowing him understood. “But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.” He will be present so that he may remain forever. “Before his passion, unbelievers also saw the Lord and Savior in the flesh; but that he was the Son of God, and that the Paraclete had been sent by God into the world, only believers were able to know. Unbelievers could neither see the Holy Spirit with their eyes nor know him in their minds, because he did not appear to the disciples clothed in humanity. Rather, he chose to come to them and remain with them in such a way that he consecrated for himself a most welcome dwelling in their very hearts. This is what he says: ‘But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.’ Though he remains invisibly with the elect in this life, he visibly indeed [Bede, invisibly indeed] displays to them the grace of his knowledge.” {600}

(VERSE 18.) “I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you.” It seemed to unbelievers that, when the Lord died on the cross, he would leave the disciples orphaned. But he did not leave those orphaned to whom he showed himself alive after his passion through many proofs, for forty days; and ten days after his ascension, he bestowed on them from heaven the gifts of the Holy Spirit. No believer doubts that Christ himself came to them there, if he has understood that the nature of the Holy Trinity is inseparable in power and operation.

VERSE 19.—“A little while, and the world will no longer see me; but you will see me.” “The little while lasted until the time when the passion was completed, after which the reprobate were no longer able to see him. For only the righteous, who had been saddened by his death, were found worthy to see the joy of his resurrection.” “Because I live, you also will live.”

@ [Col. 0935D] From Saint Augustine, Treatise LXXV, no. 3. “What does ‘because I live, you also will live’ mean? Why did he say that he lives in the present, but that they would live in the future, except because he also promised them the life of the flesh—namely, of the resurrected flesh—such as had already preceded in him and was to follow for them? And because his resurrection was soon to occur, he used a verb in the present tense to signify its nearness; but because theirs is deferred until the end of the age, he did not say ‘you live,’ but ‘you will live.’ Thus, in two words—one in the present tense and one in the future—he elegantly and briefly promised two resurrections: his own, soon to come, and ours, to follow at the end of the age.”

(VERSE 20.) “On that day,” he says, “you will know that I am in my Father, and you are in me, and I am in you.” On what day, except the one of which he said, “You also will live”?

@ [Col. 0936D] From the homily of Bede cited above. “At that time the apostles knew that Christ was in the Father through the unity of undivided divinity; they knew that they were in Christ through the reception of his faith and sacraments; they knew truly that Christ was in the Father, [Col. 0937A] and that Christ was in them through love and observance of his commandments. The holy Church of God also knows this, but far better and more fully on that day of which he said, ‘You also will live’—on the day of resurrection, when they truly begin to live, and when they know all that must be known more perfectly because they behold the very source of knowledge more nearly and without end.” To promise this blessedness to everyone, however, and not only to the apostles, he immediately added:

(VERSE 21.) “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me. Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.” “Here we must consider with complete attention that to love Christ truly is to keep his commandments: not merely to profess that love with the lips, [Col. 0937B] but to keep Christ’s commandments, which we possess by learning them, through putting them into practice.” “Whoever has,” he says, “my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me.”

@ [Col. 0937D] From Saint Augustine, at the place cited, no. 5. “The one who has them in memory and keeps them in life; who has them in speech and keeps them in conduct; who has them by hearing and keeps them by doing; or who has them by doing and keeps them by persevering—that one, he says, is the one who loves me.”

@ [Col. 0937D] From Bede, at the place cited. “It should be noted that, when he said in the present tense, ‘Whoever loves me,’ he added the future: ‘He will be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and I will manifest myself to him.’ The Son, together with the Father, loves even now those who love him; but now he loves them so that they may live rightly by faith, which works through love. Then he will love them so that they may attain the vision of truth, which they had tasted through faith. He did not add without reason, ‘And I will manifest myself to him.’” He will manifest himself according to his humanity to all at the judgment; but to the righteous and holy alone he will manifest the glory of his divinity, in which he is equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit, so that they may receive eternal blessedness.

VERSE 22.—Judas—not Iscariot—said to him: “Lord, what has happened, that you are going to manifest yourself to us and not to the world?” He asked in order to learn the reason for the truth. This is the Judas whose Epistle is read in the churches of Christ, not the betrayer. Therefore this man asked in one way, while the traitor asked in another when he said, “Is it I?” The pretender approached the teacher’s table; this seeker of truth questioned the Lord. Jesus answered him:

(VERSE 23.) “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word.”

@ [Col. 0937D] From Saint Gregory, Homily 30, no. 1. “The proof of love, therefore, is the exhibition of a work. Hence the same John says in his Epistle: ‘Whoever says, “I love God,” and does not keep his commandments, is a liar’ (1 John 4:20). We truly love God if we observe his commandments and constrain ourselves away from our own desires [Ms., pleasures] toward his commandments.” “And my Father will love him.” For the works that the Father does, the Son likewise does; whoever loves the Son also loves the Father; and whoever is loved by the Son is loved by the Father. “And we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.” For to the person who truly loves God, and who does not withdraw from the love of God even in a time of temptation, the Father and the Son come through a spiritual approach and have their dwelling with him. That person truly loves whose mind is not overcome, through its own consent, by an evil delight. For each person is separated from heavenly love in proportion as he delights in what is beneath.

@ [Col. 0938D] From Saint Augustine, Treatise LXXVI, nos. 2, 4–5. “Love distinguishes the saints from the world; it makes them dwell together in unity in one house. In that house the Father and the Son make their dwelling: they give both love itself and, at the end, their manifestation to those to whom they give it.” Concerning this manifestation the disciple asked, and he heard that one comes to this manifestation through love.

(VERSE 24.) “Whoever does not love me does not keep my words.” “These are the ones who never see the Father and the Holy Spirit. They see the Son for a brief time, not in order to be blessed but in order to be judged; nor do they see him in the form of God, where he is equally invisible with the Father and the Holy Spirit, but in the form of man, ubi (‘where’) [Ms., in qua, ‘in which’], in which he chose to be contemptible to the world by suffering and dreadful in judgment.” “And the word that you hear is not mine, but the Father’s, who sent me.” Why did he first say “words” in the plural, but now “word” in the singular? Perhaps so that there he might indicate sermones praedicationis (‘words of preaching’) [Ms., praedicationes, ‘preachings’], but here himself, who is the Word of the Father. And therefore he said that it was not his, because he is not from himself but from the Father—just as the image is not his but the Father’s, and the Son is not his but the Father’s. “The equal Son therefore rightly attributes to the author whatever he does, from whom he has precisely this: that he is equally without difference from him.”

VERSE 25.—“I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you.” The dwelling of which he spoke above is spiritual, and is given to the saints alone; the dwelling of which he now speaks is bodily. He spoke only of his bodily presence, which both the righteous and the wicked were able to see.”

@ [Col. 0938D] From the same author, Treatise LXXVII, no. 1. “The former makes the liberated blessed forever; the latter visits those who are to be liberated in time. ‘I have spoken these things to you,’ he says, ‘while remaining with you’—that is, in the bodily presence by which he spoke visibly with them.”

(VERSE 26.) “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and will remind you of everything I have said to you.” He said many things to unbelieving hearers, but they found no place in their hearts because the Holy Spirit did not teach them inwardly. He says many things every day through holy preachers, but those who hear do not receive them inwardly because the Holy Spirit does not inwardly remind them of what they have heard outwardly. Concerning him it is rightly promised: “He himself will teach you all things.”

@ [Col. 0938D] From Saint Gregory, the homily cited, no. 3. “For unless the same Spirit is present in the heart of the hearer, the teacher’s speech is fruitless. No one should attribute to the human teacher what he understands from the teacher’s mouth, because unless the one who teaches is within, the teacher’s tongue labors outwardly in vain.” The Jews therefore heard Christ preaching in one way, and the apostles in another: the former for judgment, the latter for salvation, because the Spirit taught inwardly in the minds of the latter what they had heard outwardly with their ears.

VERSE 27.—“I leave you peace; I give you my peace.” I leave you in peace; I will come to you in peace. Here he says “I leave,” there “I give.” I leave it to those who follow; I give it to those who arrive.”

@ [Col. 0939D] From Saint Augustine, at the place cited, no. 3. “He leaves us peace in this age; he will give us his peace in the age to come. He leaves us peace so that we may love one another; he will give us his peace where we can never disagree with one another.” Why does he say, “I give you my peace,” and not, “I leave you my peace”? Perhaps because peace will be different now and then. Here we wage war against vices; therefore he did not add “my.” There, in eternal peace, there will be eternal tranquility and harmony, and such peace as he had with himself, who had no sin within himself. “Not as the world gives do I give to you.” That is, not as worldly [Ms., unclean] people often agree with one another in their wickedness, but as those who agree with one another in holiness and join themselves to one another in the love of Christ.

{602}

VERSE 28.—“Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it be afraid. You have heard that I said to you: I am going away, and I am coming to you.”

@ [Col. 0939D] From Saint Augustine, Treatise LXXVII, nos. 1–3. “Their hearts could therefore be troubled and afraid because he was going away from them, although he would come to them—lest perhaps the wolf should attack the flock while the shepherd was absent. But from those whom the man was leaving, God was not departing: the same Christ was both man and God. Thus he went away according to what he was as man and remained according to what he was as God; he went away according to what was confined to one place and remained according to what, as God, was everywhere. Therefore God, whom no place contains, departs from the hearts of those who abandon him in their conduct, not with their feet; and he comes to those who turn toward him not with their faces but with faith, and who approach him not in the flesh but in charity.”

“If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I.” As though he were saying: “You ought to rejoice because I am carrying with me your frailty, which is to be consecrated.” “According to that by which the Son is not equal to the Father, he was going to the Father, from whom he will come to judge the living and the dead. But according to that by which he is equal to the Father, he never departed from the Father, but is with him everywhere in his entirety, with the equal divinity that no place contains.”

“Let us acknowledge the twofold substance of Christ: the divine, by which he is equal to the Father; and the human, by which the Father is greater than he. Yet these together are not two Christs but one Christ, so that there is not a quaternity but the Triune God. For just as one man consists of a rational soul and flesh, so one Christ is God and man. Accordingly, Christ is God, a rational soul, and flesh; we confess Christ in all these and in each individually. Who, then, is he through whom the world was made? Christ Jesus, but in the form of God. Who was crucified under Pontius Pilate? Christ Jesus, but in the form of a servant. Likewise, considering the individual elements of which man consists: Who was not abandoned in hell? Christ Jesus, but in the soul alone. Who lay in the tomb for three days, awaiting resurrection? Christ Jesus, but in the flesh alone. Christ is therefore spoken of in each of these individually; yet all these together constitute not two or three but one Christ.

“For this reason he said: ‘If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because I am going to the Father,’ since human nature ought to rejoice because it was so assumed by the only-begotten Word that it was established immortal in heaven, and thus earth was exalted so that incorruptible dust might sit at the right hand of the Father. In this manner he said that he would go to the Father: certainly not to the one with whom he already was, but going to him meant departing from us, changing and making immortal what he had assumed from us as mortal, setting it at the Father’s right hand, [Col. 0940B] and raising it into heaven—the one through whom he had been on earth for us.” Then the Lord Jesus himself continued:

VERSE 29.—“And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it happens you may believe.”

@ [Col. 0940D] From the same author, Treatise LXXIX, nos. 1–2. “He is speaking of the event in which they would see him alive after his death and ascending to the Father. When they saw this, they would believe that he was the Christ, the Son of God, who was able to do this because he had foretold it and proclaimed it beforehand [Augustine, praedicere, ‘to foretell’] before he did it.” They could indeed doubt whether he was the Son of God when they saw him about to die; but when they saw him risen, they believed what they had previously doubted, and the faith in their hearts was confirmed—the faith of the one who had promised with his mouth what he would do and fulfilled through his work what he had foretold.

Then what does he say? (VERSE 30.) “I will no longer speak much with you, for the prince of this world is coming.” “Who except the devil? And he has nothing in me”—that is, absolutely no sin. “Here he shows that the devil is the prince of sinful human beings, not of God’s creatures. And whenever the appearance of the world is mentioned in an evil sense, it indicates only those who love this world, and not God. Far be it from us to believe that he is the prince of heaven and earth and of all the creatures generally called ‘the world.’ The whole world therefore serves its creator, not its deceiver; its redeemer, not its destroyer. It is governed by divine providence, not overthrown by the enemy’s cunning, except for those human beings who belong to that party and subject themselves to the devil by their own will, not by necessity.”

Hence the Apostle also says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood”—that is, against human beings—“but against the powers and rulers of this darkness” (Ephesians 6:12), that is, of sins, who remain in the darkness of iniquity. By calling them “rulers,” he indicates that they are angels who have deserted their station. Yet there are people who, through God’s grace and not through their own merits, are rescued from that power. Of them the Apostle says: “Once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light” (Ephesians 5:8). But thanks be to God, who, as the same Apostle says, rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the glory [Col. 0941A] of his Son [Ms., “of the glory of his own Son”] (Colossians 1:13).

“In him the prince of this world—that is, of this darkness—had nothing, because God had not come with sin, nor had the virgin given birth to his flesh from the propagation of sin. And as though someone were to say to him, ‘Why then will you die, if you have no sin to which the penalty of death was owed?’ he immediately added:

(VERSE 31.) ‘But so that the world may know that I love the Father, and just as the Father commanded me, so I do. Rise; let us go from here.’ He was reclining and speaking to those reclining. ‘Let us go,’ he said—where, except to the place where he was to be handed over? He was therefore handed over to death, though he had no merit deserving death; [but] he had the Father’s command that he should die.” It continues:

## CHAPTER XXXVI

He calls himself the vine and the Father the farmer, and the disciples branches; he testifies that they can do nothing without him. In many forms of expression he impresses upon them another love, by the merit of which they can obtain whatever they ask.

“I am the true vine, and you are the branches.”

The son serves the father out of love, but the servant out of fear. Concerning this service the Lord now said: “I no longer call you servants, but friends,” because they are sons, not servants, and therefore also friends. “Because a servant does not know what his master is doing”: for he does not know the will of his master who serves him through the bitterness of fear and not through the sweetness of love, as though he were serving a father.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

Commending the same love more insistently, he declares that the hatred of the world must be despised. He also foretells what they will suffer for his name and explains that the world will be convicted by the Paraclete concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment.

**VERSE 17.** “I command these things to you, so that you may love one another.”

But the Lord consoles us greatly concerning himself: after saying, ‘I command these things to you, so that you may love one another,’ he added and said:

**(VERSE 18.)** ‘If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you.’ A disciple is not above his teacher. Let the members cling to the head, so that they do not refuse to suffer what the head suffered first.

**(VERSE 19.)** ‘If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own.’ For “world” is understood in one way among the saints and in another among sinners; in one way of those who love God and in another of those who love this age.

“For by the name ‘world’ the Church is often signified, as in the passage: ‘God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself’ (2 Cor. 5:19). Likewise: ‘For the Son of Man did not come to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him’ (John 3:17). The whole world is the Church, and the whole world hates the Church. Thus the world hates the world: the hostile hates the reconciled, the condemned hates the saved, the defiled hates the cleansed. But this world, which God reconciles to himself in Christ, which is saved through Christ, and to which every sin is forgiven through Christ’s body [Augustine: ‘by which every sin is forgiven’], was chosen from the world. Accordingly, after saying, ‘If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own,’ he immediately added: ‘But because you are not of the world, and I chose you from the world, therefore the world hates you.’”

They were therefore of the world, but by grace they were chosen from the world, so that they might not belong to the world in which they were born from the root of sin, but to the world in which they were reborn through grace, so that they might not be in the world but chosen from the world. “I chose you from the world,” he said, so that no one might glory in his own merits; “but whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17).

**VERSE 20.** “Remember my word that I said to you: ‘A servant is not greater than his master.’ If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they kept my word, they will also keep yours.” The perfect teacher recalls the disciples to the example that he had shown in himself, as we read above. Now he exhorts them to keep the teacher’s saying in memory: “A servant is not greater than his master.” Here he signifies the servant who possesses holy fear and remains forever and ever, and in whom there is “the beginning of wisdom” and “good understanding for all who do them” (Ps. 110:10). There, above, he demonstrates the servant of whom he also said earlier: “A servant does not remain in the house forever.” That is the servant who belongs to fear, which love casts out, and who does not remain in the house forever.

**(VERSE 21.)** “But they will do all these things to you because of my name, because they do not know him who sent me.”

One hates ‘without cause’ when he seeks no advantage from his hatred or pursues no benefit [Augustine: ‘when he seeks no advantage from his hatred or flees no disadvantage’].” Those of whom he said this repaid benefits with evils; and because of the excessive wickedness of their hearts they hated the one who loved them and did good to them.

Therefore he promised that they would be strengthened by the coming of the Holy Spirit, both for confidence in preaching and for steadfastness in suffering. We recognize that this happened in the chief of the apostles himself: previously, at the voice of a single maidservant, he was afraid to confess Christ; afterward, strengthened by the Holy Spirit, he preached him openly and more steadfastly than all the others to many thousands of Jews. Thus we read that at his preaching three thousand men believed and were baptized, and not long afterward five thousand also believed (Acts 2 and 4).

Therefore Christ himself, as we have heard, promised this to them, saying: “When the Paraclete Spirit comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth.” He said both “the Paraclete Spirit,” that is, the Spirit of consolation, and “the Spirit of truth,” so that they might have both confidence in preaching through the Spirit of truth and the consolation of grace in the same Spirit.

When he says, “Who proceeds from the Father,” he immediately adds, “whom I will send.” He signifies that the same Holy Spirit proceeds equally from the Father and the Son and is sent equally by the Father and the Son. But because of the distinction of the persons, he is said here to proceed from the Father and to be sent by the Son; and within this same distinction of persons he declares that his operation and will are one with the Father’s will. He also comes of his own accord, because he is coequal with the Father and the Son, so that it may be recognized that the will and operation of the Holy Trinity are one.

## CHAPTER XVI, VERSES 1–2

“These things I have spoken to you so that you may not be scandalized. They will expel you from the synagogues.”

@ [Col. 0950D] From St. Augustine, Tractate XCII, nos. 1–2. “The merciful teacher took care to foretell to the disciples the future battles with the wicked, so that the things coming upon them might disturb them less. For adversities that are foreseen are usually endured more easily than those that suddenly arrive unexpectedly, just as it is read in secular literature that sudden changes of fortune often weary even the strongest soldiers in battle.

“But the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God.” The Jews thought that they were offering service to God when they pursued the ministers of the New Testament with hatred and death. But, as the Apostle testifies concerning them: “They have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10:2). They therefore think, in their zeal for the law [Manuscript: “as zealots of the law”], that they are offering service to God while inflicting death upon the heralds of grace. But they defend in vain the law given through a servant, refusing to accept the grace offered by the Son himself; they judge themselves pleasing to God the Father in vain while striving to despise, indeed even to persecute and blaspheme, the Son of God.”

He said that two things would come upon them from the Jews: that they would expel them from the synagogue and that they would kill them. These things also contributed to the height of that people’s condemnation and would serve the salvation of the nations, as Paul said to those Jews in the Acts of the Apostles: “Since you judge yourselves unworthy of the word of God, behold, we turn to the Gentiles. For thus the Lord has commanded us: ‘I have appointed you as a light to the Gentiles, so that you may be for salvation to the end of the earth’” (Acts 13:46).

It follows:

**(VERSE 3.)** “And they will do these things because they have not known the Father nor me.”

@ [Col. 0950D] From Bede, the passage cited above. “Since the Son is in the Father and the Father is in the Son, and whoever sees the Son also sees the Father, it is plainly evident that all who obstinately reject belief in the Son are proved not to know the Father either.”

**(VERSE 4.)** “But I have spoken these things to you so that, when their hour comes, you may remember that I told you.” It is a great consolation for the disciples to remember that the teacher had foretold what they would suffer, and to know that the same one whose name they had been told they would suffer for is their helper and rewarder.

**VERSE 5.** “I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you.” What are the things that he did not tell them from the beginning? He also spoke of the Holy Spirit, whom he was going to send to them from the Father, and of the consolation and strengthening [Manuscript: confirmation] of that same Spirit, by which they would be consoled and strengthened, so that they would not need to fear in spirit any of the world’s adversities or the scandals and persecutions of the Jews.

“I did not tell you these things from the beginning because I was with you”: because my presence consoled you. But now, as I go to the Father, you need the Holy Spirit to console and strengthen you in every tribulation and suffering that you will undergo.

“And now I go to him who sent me, and no one among you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’”

@ [Col. 0951D] From St. Augustine, Tractate XCIV, no. 3. “He signifies that he is going to him who sent him in such a way that no one would ask what they could plainly see happening before their bodily eyes. For earlier they had asked him where he was going, when he was hastening toward his passion, and he answered that he was going where they could not then come. Now, however, he promised that he would go in such a way that no one would ask, ‘Where are you going?’ For a cloud received him when he ascended from them; and when he went into heaven, they did not ask him in words but saw him with their eyes” [Augustine: “they escorted him with their eyes”].

**(VERSE 6.)** “But because I have spoken these things to you,” he says, “sorrow has filled your heart.” He certainly saw what those words were doing in their hearts. Since they did not yet possess inward spiritual consolation, which they were to have through the Holy Spirit, they feared losing what they saw outwardly in Christ.

**(VERSE 7.)** “But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go.”

@ [Col. 0951D] From Bede’s homily *Cantate*. “It is expedient that the form of a servant be withdrawn from your eyes, so that the love of divinity may be more suitably fixed in your minds. It is expedient that I carry the form known to you into heaven, so that through this you may sigh for it there with greater desire.

“But if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you.” He does not say this because, while present on earth, he could not himself give the Spirit to the disciples, since it is plainly read that after his resurrection he appeared to them, breathed on them, and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). Rather, while he was on earth and living bodily with them, they were unable to raise their minds to him so as to thirst for the gifts of heavenly grace. But when he ascended into heaven, they likewise transferred all their desire there. Thus they were already made capable of the Holy Spirit: they were no longer saddened by his death but rejoiced in the gift of his promise [Manuscript: “of the Holy Spirit”].

It is evident, and requires no laborious exposition, why he called the same Spirit the Paraclete, that is, the consoler: surely because the coming of this Spirit consoles and refreshes the hearts of the disciples, which his departure had made sorrowful.

This does not mean that the Holy Spirit had not previously been in the hearts of the disciples or even in those of the ancient saints. But he had not previously been given with such manifest fullness as when, after the ascension, he is read to have been sent on the tenth day upon the one hundred and twenty persons. Yet in no work of any person of the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit was the operation of the whole Holy Trinity absent. It was necessary, however, for the Trinity to be disclosed in such a way that, although there was no difference of substance, the distinction of the persons would nevertheless be commended individually.

**VERSE 8.** “And when he comes, he will convict the world.” What does he mean by saying, “When he comes, he will convict the world?”

@ [Col. 0951D] From St. Augustine, Tractate XCV, no. 1. “Did Christ, while he was in the world, not convict the world concerning all the things that follow? But Christ convicted the Jewish nation alone, whereas the Holy Spirit, in his disciples spread throughout the whole world, is understood to have convicted not one nation but the world. In what respect does he convict it? In this respect: love has been poured out in their hearts through the Holy Spirit (Rom. 5:5), and love casts out fear, so that they would not fear to convict the world—that is, those who love the world.

“Concerning sin, and concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment.” Christ himself explained this saying:

**(VERSE 9.)** “Concerning sin, indeed, because they do not believe in me.”

@ [Col. 0952D] From the cited homily of Bede. “He designated the sin of unbelief as something particular, because just as faith is the origin of virtues, so persistence in unbelief is the foundation of vices. The Lord bears terrifying witness to this when he says: ‘Whoever does not believe has already been judged’ (John 3:18), because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.” He said “judged,” that is, condemned.

**(VERSE 10.)** “Concerning righteousness, indeed, because I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me.”

“The righteousness of Christ’s disciples was that they believed the Lord, whom they saw as truly human, also to be the true Son of God, and that they continued to worship him with steadfast love after they knew that he had been taken away from them bodily. The righteousness of the other believers, that is, of those who did not see the Lord in the flesh, is this: they believe and love in their hearts as the true God and man the one whom they never saw with bodily sight.

“By this righteousness of faith unbelievers are certainly convicted: why, when they likewise heard the word of life, did they refuse to believe in him for righteousness? For the wickedness of evil people is declared deserving of condemnation not only from its own perversity [Bede: crookedness], but also by comparison with the upright.

“Thus the Holy Spirit convicts the world—that is, unbelievers—concerning sin, because they did not believe in Christ. He convicts it concerning the righteousness of believers, because they refused to follow the example of those who knew that he had ascended to the Father and would no longer live bodily on earth, yet could not in any way be separated from his love. This is what he says: ‘Because I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me.’

“You will not see me, after I have ascended, in the form in which you now usually see me, surrounded by mortal and tangible flesh [Bede: corruptible flesh]; but you will see me coming in majesty for judgment and, after the judgment has been completed, appearing with the saints in greater glory.”

It follows:

**(VERSE 11.)** “Concerning judgment, indeed, because the prince of this world has been judged.” He calls the devil the prince of the world because he held primacy in the hearts of unbelievers, whom he wished to be understood here by the name “world.” In perverse order they love the world rather than the creator of the world. He has been judged by the Lord, who said: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18). He was judged by him when he himself cast out demons and gave the disciples authority to trample upon all the power of the enemy. The world is therefore convicted concerning the judgment by which the devil was judged, when those who might presume to resist God’s will are terrified by the example of the archangel condemned because of pride.”

@ [Col. 0952D] From St. Augustine, Tractate XCV, no. 4. “Let people therefore believe in Christ, so that they may not be convicted concerning the sin of their unbelief, by which all sins are held [Manuscript: ‘by which all sins are detained’]. Let them pass into the number of the faithful, so that they may not be convicted concerning the righteousness of those whom they do not imitate after they have been justified. Let them beware of the coming judgment, so that they may not be judged with the prince of the world, whom they imitate even though he has been judged. For, lest the harsh pride of mortals think that it will be spared, it must be terrified by the punishment of the proud angels.” It follows:

**VERSES 12–13.** “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when the Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all the truth.”

@ [Col. 0953D] From the cited homily of Bede. “It is certain that, when the Spirit came from above, the apostles obtained a much greater knowledge of the truth than they had previously been able to possess in the flesh, and they were inflamed with a greater desire to contend for the truth. Nevertheless, no one should think that in this life anyone can comprehend all truth. Hence the blessed Apostle Paul himself, who was caught up to the third heaven and there heard secret words that it is not permitted for a human being to speak (2 Cor. 12:4), says: ‘We know in part and we prophesy in part; but when the perfect comes, the partial will be brought to an end’ (1 Cor. 13:9).

“Therefore what he says of the Spirit—‘He will teach you all the truth’—should be understood as though he were saying: He will pour love into your hearts, and love will make you love all truth. Instructed inwardly by its teaching, may you advance from virtue to virtue and become worthy of reaching the life in which the eternal brightness of supreme truth and true sublimity—that is, the contemplation of your creator—will appear to you.”

It follows: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak.” The Spirit does not speak from himself, perhaps because he is not from himself but from the Father. For the Son is born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. He does not speak from himself, that is, without communion [Variant: movement] with the Father and the Son. The Holy Spirit is not divided from the Father and the Son; rather, the work of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one.

“But whatever he hears, he will speak”: he hears through unity of substance and distinctiveness of knowledge. He does not speak from himself because he is not from himself. The Father alone is not from another; the Son is begotten from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. The Spirit hears from the one from whom he proceeds, because he is not from himself but from the one from whom he proceeds. From the one from whom he has being [Bede: essence], he also has knowledge. From the one, therefore, comes his hearing, which is nothing other than knowledge.

When he added, “And he will announce to you the things that are to come,” it is clear that some of the saints foretold future events in the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, these words of the Lord should be considered more profoundly, since they can be common to all the saints.

“Therefore the Spirit, when he comes, announces the things that are to come when he recalls to our memory the joys of the heavenly homeland, when through the gift of his inspiration he makes known to us the celebrations of that heavenly city. He announces what is to come when, drawing us away from love [Manuscript and Bede: delight] of present things, he inflames our hearts with desires for the kingdom promised in heaven [Bede: with desire for the promised kingdom in heaven].”

**VERSE 14.** “He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine and announce it to you.” The Spirit glorified Christ because through him such love was kindled in the hearts of the disciples that, after casting off bodily fear, they steadfastly preached the reality of Christ’s resurrection, although shortly before, at the time of his passion, they had fled in fear. Hence it is written: “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with confidence” (Acts 4:31).

The Spirit glorified Christ when the holy teachers, filled with spiritual grace, performed so many and such great miracles in Christ’s name that they converted the whole world to faith in Christ and endured so many and such great struggles of suffering for Christ’s name.

@ [Col. 0953D] The material that is supplied from Bede is lacking. “He glorifies him by pouring love into our hearts and inspiring love of the eternal homeland. ‘Because he will take from what is mine and announce it to you,’ that is, from what belongs to my Father. The Holy Spirit received from the Father because he proceeds from the Father, from whom the Son also was born. But the one who is born from no one proceeds from no one: he alone is the Father.

**(VERSE 15.)** “Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take from what is mine and announce it to you.” He spoke of the things that pertain to the very divinity of the Father, in which he is equal to the Father. In these the Holy Spirit is also equal to the Father and the Son, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one substance, one nature, one majesty, one glory, and one eternity. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one almighty God, invisible and incomprehensible to every creature.” It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

He says that for a little while they will see him, and again for a little while they will not see him. When the disciples ask about this, he introduces the analogy of a woman who, after giving birth, no longer remembers her sorrow because of her joy. He strengthens those whom he signifies to be loved by the Father, as he is about to depart, saying: “In the world you will have tribulation, but take courage: I have overcome the world.”

**VERSES 16–19.** “A little while, and you will not see me; again a little while, and you will see me, because I go to the Father.”

@ [Col. 0954D] From Bede’s Homily, “Rejoice.” It should be noted, however, that the entire sequence of this Gospel reading applies to those who heard it present with the Lord; but it also applies most aptly, first to them [Ms. and Bede: “But that part of it”] and then to us, who came to faith after the Lord’s passion and resurrection. But when he says, “A little while, and you will not see me; again a little while, and you will see me, because I am going to the Father,” this pertains especially to those who merited to cling to his discipleship while he preached in the flesh and, after the sorrow of his passion, to be gladdened by seeing his resurrection and ascension.” There was also a little while from that hour of the night in which he was betrayed until the hour of his passion, during which the disciples saw him bodily; and again there was a little while during which, shut within the tomb and lying there to rise on the third day, he could not be seen by their eyes. This is what he says: “A little while, and you will not see me”; but what he says, “Again a little while, and you will see me,” signifies the period after the resurrection during which he lived with the disciples and appeared to them in many manifestations, until he ascended into heaven while they watched, as is read in Luke’s Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles. This is what he says: “Because I am going to the Father.” “As though he were saying plainly: ‘Because after a little while I shall be hidden from your sight within the enclosure of the tomb, and again after a little while, when the dominion of death has been destroyed, I shall appear for you to behold. For the time has come when, having completed the dispensation of the mortality he assumed, I shall return to the Father with the triumph of the resurrection.’” These words of the Lord, as I said, apply particularly to those who were able to see his resurrection; at that time the apostles were unable to understand them. And the merciful teacher, recognizing their ignorance, answered afterward in accordance with their inward doubt, as though he were about to explain what he had said: “A little while, and you will not see me; and again a little while, and you will see me.”

**VERSE 20.**—“Amen, amen, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you, however, will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy.” “This applies both to their condition and to that of the whole Church. For the lovers of Christ were lamenting and weeping when they saw him seized, bound by his enemies, led before the council, condemned, crucified, killed, and buried. Many lovers of the world [Ms. and Bede: “The lovers of the world”] were rejoicing—those whom the Lord calls ‘the world’ because of their base thoughts—when they condemned to the most shameful death the one who was burdensome even for them to behold. The disciples were sorrowful when the Lord had been placed in death; but when his resurrection was recognized, their sorrow was turned into joy. When they had seen the power of his ascension, they were lifted up by still greater joy, and they praised and blessed the Lord, as the evangelist Luke testifies (Acts 2). But this saying of the Lord also applies to all the faithful, who strive to reach eternal joys through present tears and afflictions: ‘Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy; going forth, they went and wept’ (Psalm 125:5–6), so that they may receive in eternal blessedness the reward of their labor. But the world—that is, the lovers of the world—was rejoicing, those who disdain to prepare themselves for eternal joys through tears and afflictions; you, however, will be sorrowful through labors and pressures, but your sorrow will be turned into the joy of eternal blessedness.” It continues:

**VERSE 21.**—“When a woman is giving birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come.” “He calls the holy Church a woman because of the fruitfulness of good works and because she never ceases to beget spiritual children for God. This woman, when she is giving birth, has sorrow because her hour has come. But when she has given birth to a boy, she no longer remembers her distress because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world. For indeed, as long as the holy Church devotes itself in the world to progress in spiritual virtues, she never ceases to be exercised by the world’s temptations; but when, having overcome the contest of labors, she reaches the palm of victory, she no longer remembers her preceding distress because of the joy of the reward received. ‘The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the glory that is to come, which will be revealed in us’ (Romans 8:18). ‘She does not remember,’ he says, ‘her distress because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world.’ For just as a woman rejoices when a human being has been born into this world, so the Church is filled with worthy exultation when a people of the faithful has been born into the future life. For this birth she now labors and groans greatly, suffering as though in labor. Nor should it seem strange to anyone if one who has departed from this life is said to have been born: for just as one is customarily said to be born when, proceeding from the mother’s womb, one enters this light, so also one who has been released from the bonds of the flesh and raised to eternal light can most rightly be called born. Hence ecclesiastical custom has prevailed that we call the days of the blessed martyrs or confessors of Christ, on which they passed from this age, their ‘birthdays,’ and that their solemn observances be called not funerals but birthdays [Bede: “nativity celebrations”].”

The Lord himself then proceeds to explain the example he proposed concerning the woman: **(VERSE 22)** “So you also now have sorrow; but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.” “This is easily understood of the disciples themselves, because they had sorrow when the Lord suffered and was buried; but when the glory of the resurrection had been accomplished, they rejoiced at seeing the Lord, and no one took their joy from them.” Although they suffered pressures and persecutions in this world, they always rejoiced in hope of the future reward, because they were worthy to suffer insults for the name of Jesus (Acts 5:41). “I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice; and no one will take your joy from you.” “Thus the Lord sees the elect after their sorrow when, after their adversary has been condemned, he rewards their patience.”

@ [Col. 0955D] Thus far from the cited homily of Bede. “I will see you,” that is, when I have taken you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be; and in that perpetual vision of glory your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you, because there will be no adversary there, no persecutor, no one to bring sorrow into your souls, while the God of gods is seen [Ms.: “will be seen”] in Zion (Psalm 83:8); and when Christ appears, then you also will appear with him in glory, as the Apostle says (Colossians 3:4). It continues: **(VERSE 23)** “And on that day you will ask me nothing.” “

@ [Col. 0955D] From St. Augustine, Tractate 101, no. 4. For this word, *rogare*, means not only “to ask” but also “to question,” as the Greek likewise has it, from which this Gospel was translated.” What the Lord says therefore signifies that time when no one will take our joy from us, when we will no longer ask anything or question anything, because nothing will remain to be desired and nothing that must be sought will be hidden.

**VERSE 24.**—“Until now you have asked nothing in my name.” “

@ [Col. 0956D] From the same work, Tractate 102, nos. 2 and 4. This can be understood in two ways: either because you have not asked in my name, a name which, as it ought to be known, you have not known; or because you have asked nothing, since, in comparison with the thing you ought to have asked for, what you have asked for must be counted as nothing.” For whoever asks for what does not pertain to eternal salvation and eternal joy seems to ask for nothing in comparison with that petition which he ought to have made. “Until now you have asked nothing in my name.” Or it should be understood in this way: They had not hitherto asked in the name of the Savior because, while they contemplated the visible presence of the Savior himself, they had raised the gaze of their minds less toward the invisible gifts of salvation. Whoever asks contrary to the reason of his salvation does not ask in the name of Jesus.

Hence the Lord also says next: “Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be full,” signifying what we ought to ask for—that our joy may be full. Therefore he says, “and you will receive.” If we ask for those things that pertain to the fullness of labors and joys, we shall receive them. Thus he calls the fullness of joy the blessedness of perpetual peace. He therefore says: “Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be full,” as though he were saying plainly: “Ask not for the fleeting joys of the age, which are always mingled with sorrow and must end in pain, but ask the singular joy from the Father whose fullness may never be diminished by any disturbance whatsoever, whose eternity may never be dissolved by any end. If, then, you persist in asking for such things—for without doubt you will receive what you ask for if your conduct accords with the mind of the one asking—for it brings little benefit to seek heavenly things through worthy prayer if one does not cease to become entangled in lowly things by living perversely.”

**(VERSE 25.)** “I have spoken these things to you in figures. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will tell you openly about the Father.” For they were still little ones and had not yet been able to understand how the Father was in the Son and the Son in the Father, nor could they yet know the other matters pertaining to the profound mysteries of divinity. Therefore the Lord seemed to speak to them in figures, as in a riddle; but he promises them an hour in which he would speak openly to them about the Father. He was signifying that hour when, after completing his passion and resurrection, he was to give them the grace of the Holy Spirit. For then, instructed inwardly in a spiritual manner and kindled with spiritual delight, they began more perfectly to grasp everything that mortals had to receive concerning knowledge of divinity; and so much more ardently they sought and desired only those things that would help them to merit its vision.

**VERSE 26.**—“On that day you will ask in my name,” that is, you will begin to ask only for what pertains to the salvation of your souls and what appears to belong to eternal joys. And especially so that you may understand what it is that I said: “I and the Father are one,” or how the Father is in me and I am in the Father.” “They ask in his name who ask because, in the mere name of his name [Augustine: ‘in the sound of his name’], they understand not something other than the reality itself which is called by that name. They can in some measure think that our Lord Jesus Christ, insofar as he is human, intercedes for us with the Father; insofar as he is God, he hears us together with the Father”—which I believe he signified when he said: “And I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf.”

For what he says, “And I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf,” can suitably be understood in this way: he does not say, “I ask,” concerning the present, but placed “I will ask” concerning the future [time], because, once the saints have been received into inner peace (ad internam pacem; Ms.: in interna pace), they will no longer need to ask anything concerning them; for they will be endowed with such great blessedness that nothing greater could exist.

**(VERSE 27.)** “For the Father himself loves you, because you love me and have believed that I came forth from God.” What he said—“because you love me”—should not be understood as though they had first loved Christ; rather, it should be understood that the Father, by gratuitous love, went before them and drew them out of the world to love and believe in the Son. Because they preserved the love and faith they had recognized in the Son with a devout and watchful heart, they were rewarded with greater gifts of the Father’s love: he loves them, together with the Son and the Holy Spirit, whom he judges worthy of love. What he added, “because you love me,” must be understood in the same way. Therefore whoever rightly loves [Ms.: “rightly has”] the Son should love him together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, because those whose divine nature is inseparable possess one and the same gifts of virtue. This is what is meant by: “You love and believe [Al.: ‘have believed’] that I came forth from God.”

{615} **VERSE 28.**—“I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I am leaving the world and going to the Father.” He came forth from the Father and came into the world because he appeared visibly to the world in humanity, although he was invisible with the Father in divinity. He came forth from the Father because he appeared not in that form in which he is equal to the Father, but in the created nature he assumed, in a lesser form. And he came into the world because, in the form of a servant that he received, he also offered himself to the lovers of this world to be seen. Again he left the world and returned to the Father because he withdrew from the sight of the lovers of the world what they had seen, and taught his lovers to believe that he was equal to the Father. He left the world and returned to the Father because, through his ascension, he led the humanity he had assumed to the invisible things of the Father’s majesty.

These words of the Lord are mystical and, as he himself testifies, were spoken in figures. But the disciples to whom they were spoken were still so carnal that they could scarcely grasp their depth; and they did not understand not only the hidden meaning of the sayings but even their own ignorance, supposing that what had been uttered simply and clearly—though to those who did not understand them they were figures—was plain speech. And they immediately answered: **(VERSE 29)** “See, now you are speaking openly, and saying no figure.” They therefore supposed that he was speaking openly, although they were not yet able to comprehend the mysteries of his sayings.

But when they add: **(VERSE 30)** “Now we know that you know all things, and you have no need that anyone should question you. By this we believe that you came forth from God,” they openly show that, while speaking to them, the Lord was discussing chiefly those matters which they were pleased to hear and which they wanted to ask him. Anticipating them, he brought these matters forth of his own accord; hence they rightly believe and confess that he knows all things as God and that, as the Son of God, he came from God. For knowing the secrets of thoughts is an evident sign of divinity.

**VERSE 32.**—“Behold, the hour is coming—and has now come—when you will be scattered, each to his own.” The hour of my passion has therefore come, when I alone must tread the winepress, and not even one of you will remain with me; rather, you will be scattered to your own things, that is, through fear of your own faithlessness. It is as though he were saying: “You will be so disturbed that you will altogether abandon even the way in which you now think you believe.” For they came to such despair and forgetfulness of their faith that they did not even remember what they had believed before. See how they had left him, abandoning even the faith by which they had believed in him.

But in the affliction which they endured after his glorification, once they had received the Holy Spirit, they did not leave him; and although they fled from city to city, they fled to him for refuge [Ms.: “they did not flee from him”]. For when the Holy Spirit had been given to them, what is now said to them came about in them: “Take courage; I have overcome the world.” “

@ [Col. 0959B] From St. Augustine, Tractate 103, no. 3. “They took courage and overcame. In whom, if not in him? For the world would not have overcome him if the world had overcome his members. Hence the Apostle says: ‘Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory’; and immediately he added: ‘Through our Lord Jesus Christ’ (1 Corinthians 15:57), who had said to his own: ‘Take courage, because I have overcome the world.’”

He concludes the sermon in this way: **(VERSE 33)** “I have spoken these things to you so that in me you may have peace.” He is not referring only to these words that he spoke to them here at the sacred meal, but to everything that, from the beginning of their discipleship, he either said or did in their presence. All these things pertain to this: that we may have peace in him, although we suffer pressures and persecutions in the world. “And he concludes these words with great hope of consolation: ‘But take courage; I have overcome the world.’ For he overcame the world not only in himself, the head, but also in his members. Therefore the persecutions of this world are not to be feared. And all these things must be done so that we may have peace in him.” “

This peace will have no end in time, and it itself will be the end of all our devout intention and action. {616} **BOOK SEVEN**

**CHAPTER XXXIX**

Speaking to the Father about his glorification, he commends the disciples in a lengthy and manifold discourse, with his passion immediately impending. [Col. 0959C]

**CHAPTER 17, VERSE 1**

—“Jesus, lifting his eyes to heaven, said: ‘Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son.’” The Son could have spoken these same words of prayer silently to the Father; but the Son’s prayer is instruction for the disciples and also for those who might wish to follow their example or read their writings. He said: “The hour has come.” The hour of his passion is therefore approaching. “Glorify your Son,” that is, let the humility of the passion precede the glory of the resurrection, and let the glorification of the resurrection quickly follow.

It continues: “So that your Son may glorify you.” The Father’s glorification is eternal and can neither be increased nor diminished. But this glorification pertains to the knowledge of God the Father, so that, once the glory of the resurrection had been accomplished in the Son, God the Father might become known throughout the whole world, whereas previously he had been known only among the Jews.” “

Full knowledge of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is full and perfect eternal life; perfect eternal life is supreme blessedness; and supreme blessedness exists only in eternal life. Therefore he said: “This is eternal life: that they may know you and Jesus Christ, the only and true God.”

**VERSE 4.**—“I glorified you upon the earth; I completed the work that you gave me to do.” What does it mean that he used the past tense—“I glorified” and “I completed”—and immediately added the future-tense verb “to do,” except that all things are present to God and that, in divine predestination, future things are to be regarded as though they had already happened? For what was destined to happen was, as it were, already completed. “I glorified you,” as though he had said: “I will glorify you by the glory of preaching, which he effects throughout the whole world through his disciples, when I complete the work of my passion and resurrection that you gave me to do.”

He added: “With the glory that I had with you before the world existed.” The order of the words is: “the glory that I had with you before the world existed.” What he says, “And now glorify me,” has this force: as then, so now; as then by predestination, so now by completion. Establish [Ms.: “appoint”] in the world what had existed with you before the world; establish [Ms.: “appoint”] in its proper time what you ordained before all times.

In this passage we should understand the predestination of the glorification of the human nature that is in him, which was to become immortal with the Father from mortal, and that this had already been accomplished by predestination before the world existed, so that it would take place in the world at its proper time. For if the Apostle, seeing the predestination of the Son, said concerning us: “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4),

Although all these things could have been said of all future believers, with the matter still incomplete [Ms.: “with hope perfected”; Augustine: “with hope already perfected”], while they were still future, they can nevertheless be said particularly of the disciples to whom he was then speaking in person. For what follows—“While I was with them, I was keeping them in your name; those whom you gave me I guarded, and none of them perished except the son of perdition”—signifying Judas, who betrayed him and was one of the Twelve—fits this interpretation better, namely, that he was speaking these things particularly about the apostles.

Then he adds: “But now I am coming to you,” by which it is clear that he was speaking of his bodily presence: “While I was with them, I was keeping them,” as though by that presence he would no longer be with them. For by spiritual presence he was always with them and with his whole Church in this world until the consummation of the age.”

But to return to what was said above: “I manifested your name to the human beings whom you gave me.” This does not mean the name by which you are God, but the name by which you are my Father—a name that cannot be manifested without the manifestation of that Son. For the name by which he is God is not, he thought, wholly unknown to any rational nature. This is indeed the true force of divinity: it cannot be entirely hidden from a rational creature as though wholly unknown, except in the few in whom rational nature has been excessively corrupted. Nearly all nations confess that God exists, although diverse errors prevent them from recognizing the true God.

But when it is read in the Psalms, “God is known in Judea only” (Psalm 75:2), this means that they alone knew and worshiped the true God with legitimate worship. But insofar as he is the Father of Christ, through whom he takes away sins, he was unknown before Christ came into the world, except to those to whom God revealed through the spirit of prophecy this great and hidden mystery, which after his coming into the world was preached to the nations, believed in this world, and received into glory.

What he added—“whom you gave me”—is the same as what he said shortly before: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.” “Whom you gave me from the world” means those to whom he granted this through regeneration, not those to whom nature gave it through birth.

What does the following mean: “They were yours, and you gave them to me”? In his humanity he says that he received from the Father the authority to have those whom the Father chose and predestined before the foundation of the world—not the Father alone, but also the Son and the Holy Spirit, so that there might be one work of the holy Trinity, inseparable and altogether equal. Let carnal thinking perish here.

The Son says that human beings were given to him by the Father from the world, while elsewhere he says: “I chose you from the world” (John 15:19). The Son of God chose them from the world together with the Father; the same Son, as human, received them from the world from the Father. “

It continues: “And they have kept your word. Now they have understood that everything you have given me is from you.” That is, they understood what is from you [Augustine: “they understood that I am from you”]. “For the Father gave everything together when he begot [him], who would possess everything,” just as the Lord himself says earlier in this Gospel: “For just as the Father has life in himself, so he also gave the Son to have life in himself,” that is, he begot the Son possessing life in himself.

“Because the words that you gave me I have given them, and they received them,” that is, they understood and held them. For the word is received when it is grasped and held by the mind, lest it perish through forgetfulness. “And they understood,” he says, “truly that I came forth from you, and they believed that you sent me.” Here too “truly” must be supplied. For when he said, “they truly understood,” he wished to explain this by adding, “and they believed.” Thus they truly believed what they truly understood: namely, that “I came forth from you” means “you sent me.”

Yet the disciples were still not such as he says they would become, although he used verbs in the past tense, speaking as though they already were what they would be in the future, once they had received the Holy Spirit, who, as promised, would teach them all things and lead them into all truth. He gave them the words, as he said, which the Father gave him; but when they received those words spiritually, not outwardly in their ears but inwardly in their hearts, then they truly received them, because then they truly understood; and they truly understood because they truly believed.”

But if the words that the Son says he received are understood as pertaining to the unity of divinity, the Father gave words to the Son in the same way in which he begot the Word coeternal with himself. If, however, it refers to humanity, who can understand how he gave or received them—the God who became human from a virgin—when no one can even narrate the generation itself that took place from a virgin? But when he says, “These are in the world,” he signifies that those to whom he was speaking would pass from this world later, since, when he departed from this world, it was necessary that they should remain, through whom his holy name would be preached in the world.

When the Lord had completed the great and lengthy discourse that, after the supper, as he drew near to his passion, he delivered to the disciples who were then with him concerning the pouring out of his blood, together with the prayer that he directed to the Father for his own, the evangelist John began his account of his passion as follows:

## CHAPTER XL

The events of his betrayal and passion are narrated in sequence.

## CHAPTER XVIII, VERSE 1

When Jesus had said these things, he went out with his disciples across the torrent of Cedron [Cedron]. The genitive is plural in Greek, which may be rendered in Latin as “of the cedars.” The time had then approached of which we read in the Psalm: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way.” On the way of this life he drank from the torrent of suffering; therefore he exalted his head (Psalm 109:7), which the Apostle explained in this way: “Christ, obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him” (Philippians 2:8–9).

There was a garden there, into which he himself and his disciples entered. Fittingly he was seized in the garden of our misery, so that he might lead us into the garden of his blessedness. Thus, in the garden of delights—that is, in paradise—the first father of the human race sinned and was expelled from it into this valley of tears. Therefore Christ, the second Adam, wished to be seized in a garden, so that the sin which the first human being committed in the garden of paradise—for “paradise” is interpreted as “garden of delights”—might be erased.

(Verse 2.) Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, because Jesus had often gone there with his disciples.

@ [Col. 0968D] From St. Augustine, Treatise 112, §§1–6. What he narrates here—the Lord’s entering the garden with his disciples—did not happen immediately after his prayer had ended, the words of which are introduced by “When Jesus had said these things.” Some other events intervened, which this evangelist omitted but which are read in the other evangelists, just as many things are found in this evangelist that they likewise omitted in their accounts. The statement “When Jesus had said these things” serves to prevent us from supposing that he came into the garden before he had finished those words and that prayer which, as was recorded earlier, he said or offered after the holy supper.

“Judas also,” he says, “who betrayed him, knew the place.” The order of the words is: “He who betrayed him knew the place.” “Because,” he says, “Jesus had often gone there with his disciples.” There, then, the wolf, covered with a sheep’s skin and tolerated among the sheep by the profound counsel of the head of the household, learned where, for a short time, he might scatter the flock by attacking the shepherd through ambush.

Verse 3.—“Judas therefore,” he says, “having received a cohort and servants from the chief priests and Pharisees, came there with lanterns, torches, and weapons.” The cohort was not composed of Jews but of soldiers. It is therefore to be understood that he received it from the governor, as for apprehending a criminal, with the lawful order of authority preserved, so that no one would dare resist those who were arresting him.
