For this reason such a great band of enemies was gathered, so that no one would dare either to oppose those who apprehended Jesus or to defend him. “Thus his power was concealed and his weakness displayed, so that these measures seemed necessary to his enemies against one whom they could not have overcome unless he himself had willed it [Manuscript: “they would have accomplished nothing unless he himself had willed it”]—he who made good use of the wicked and brought good out of evil.”

But Jesus, as the evangelist goes on to say:

(Verse 4.) “Knowing everything that was to come upon him,” knew and willed that he should be apprehended, because he came into the world for this purpose: that what he willed might happen and be fulfilled when he willed it. He went forward and said to them, “Whom are you seeking?” He went forward prepared for his passion and asked whom they were seeking—not as though he were unaware of their intention, but so that they might know that he himself was the one they were seeking.

(Verse 5.) They answered, “Jesus the Nazarene.” He was called Jesus the Nazarene because he was brought up in Nazareth, so that the prophecy might be fulfilled: “For he will be called a Nazarene.” He said to them, “I am he.” He did not hide himself but showed himself, because he who came into the world by his own will laid down his life for the world by his own will.

(Verse 6.) Judas, who betrayed him, was also standing with them. When therefore he said to them, “I am he,” they drew back and fell to the ground.

“Where now is the cohort of soldiers, and the servants of the chief priests and Pharisees? Where are the terror and protection of weapons? Behold, a single voice saying, ‘I am he,’ struck, repelled, and threw down, without any weapon, such a great crowd, savage with hatred and terrible with arms. For God was hidden in the flesh, and the everlasting day was so concealed in human limbs that he was sought with lanterns and torches to be killed by the darkness. ‘I am he,’ he says, and he cast down the impious. What will he do when he comes to judge, who did this when he was to be judged? What will he be able to do when he reigns, who was able to do this when he was about to die? And now throughout the Gospel Christ says, ‘I am he’; and the Antichrist is awaited by the Jews, so that they may draw back and fall to the ground.”

Why, then, did those who came to apprehend him not seize him—one whom, if he had not willed it, they would not have been able to seize?

@ [Col. 0969D] Manuscript: “Why did those who came to apprehend him not seize him, when they heard from him, ‘I am he’?” [Col. 0970D] “Because they could not do so beforehand, before he willed it who said, ‘I am he.’” They sought to apprehend him [and kill him]; he sought them [to redeem them] and give them life, for this is why he came to us. He showed those seeking him that he had power, because he had power to lay down his life, which he laid down at the hour of his passion; he showed that the mystery of our redemption was to be fulfilled.”

(Verse 7.) Therefore he again asked them, “Whom are you seeking?” If you are seeking him, why do you not seize him, unless it is because it is not in your power to apprehend him [Manuscript: “the hour of apprehending is not in your power”], but in the power of the one who came to be apprehended?

Verses 8–9.—They said, “Jesus the Nazarene.” Jesus answered, “I told you that I am he. Therefore, if you are seeking me, let these men go,” so that the word might be fulfilled which he had spoken: “Of those whom you have given me, I have not lost any.”

“‘If you are seeking me,’ he says, ‘let these men go.’ He sees [Manuscript: “commands”] enemies, and they do what he commands: they let go those whom he does not wish to perish. But were they not afterward going to die? Why, then, if they had died at that time, would he have lost them, except because they did not yet believe in him in the way that all who do not perish believe?”

(Verse 10.) Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the ruler’s servant [thus also in the manuscript; others: “the servant of the chief priests”] and cut off his right ear. The servant’s name was Malchus. This evangelist alone also gives the servant’s name, just as Luke alone records that the Lord touched and healed his ear. Malchus is interpreted as “he who will reign.” What, then, does the ear cut off for the Lord and healed by the Lord signify except hearing renewed by the removal of antiquity, so that it may exist in newness of spirit and not in the oldness of the letter? Whoever receives this from Christ—who could doubt that he will reign with Christ?

He was called a servant because of legal servitude, but he is called sound [Manuscript: “healed”] because of evangelical freedom.

“The Lord nevertheless disapproved of Peter’s act and forbade him to proceed further, saying:

(Verse 11.) ‘Put the sword into its sheath. Shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?’”

“Shall I not drink it?” is to be read interrogatively or reproachfully, as though he had said: “Shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me to drink? Why do you wish to resist the will of the almighty Father—or rather, the cup of your salvation?” In his action that disciple wished to defend his teacher, still ignorant of the dispensation of the Father’s will [Manuscript: “piety”] and of what he had willed would come about through it.

“But when he says that the cup of his passion was given to him by the Father, it is certainly what the Apostle says: ‘If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all’ (Romans 8:31–32). Yet the author of this cup is also the one who drinks it. Hence the same Apostle says again: ‘Christ loved us and handed himself over for us, an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma’ (Ephesians 5:2).”

(Verse 12.) Then the cohort, the tribune, and the servants of the Jews seized Jesus and bound him. They seized the one whom they did not approach—for that day they remained in darkness—and they did not hear: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Psalm 33:6). But when they seized him in that way, they withdrew farther from him; and they bound the one whom they ought rather to have wished to set free.

@ [Col. 0971D] From St. Augustine, Treatise 113, §§1–6. After the persecutors, with Judas betraying him, had seized and bound the Lord, who loved us and handed himself over for us all, and whom the Father did not spare but handed over for us all (Romans 8:32):

(Verse 13.) “They led him first to Annas.” John does not omit the reason why this happened, saying: “For he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.”

Verse 14.—Caiaphas was the one who had given the Jews this counsel: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people.” He was led first to Annas and afterward to Caiaphas, so that their blood relationship and their crime might make them accomplices. Moses, by God’s command, had ordered that high priests should succeed their fathers, so that the succession of priestly generations might be preserved. Josephus reports that this Caiaphas purchased the priesthood from Herod for only one year. It is therefore not surprising if an unjust high priest judged unjustly. Often one who approaches the priesthood through greed conducts himself in it through injustice, and a criminal beginning is brought to completion by a disastrous end.

Verse 15.—“Simon Peter,” he says, “was following Jesus, and another disciple.” Who this disciple was should not be asserted rashly, because he is not named. John customarily identifies himself in this way and adds, “whom Jesus loved.” Perhaps, then, this was the same disciple who stood beside Jesus’ cross, to whom Jesus entrusted the care of his mother. Matthew also says of Peter: “Peter was following him from a distance” (Matthew 26:58). He followed the Lord from a distance because he was about to deny him, either wishing, out of love for his teacher, to see the outcome, or, from human curiosity, desiring to know what judgment the high priest would give concerning Jesus—whether he would hand him over to death or release him after scourging.

(Verse 16.) “That disciple,” he says, “was known to the high priest, and he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest. But Peter was standing outside at the door.” He was standing outside because he was about to deny the Lord; and he was not in Christ, who did not dare confess Christ.

(Verse 17.) Therefore the other disciple who was known to the high priest went out, spoke to the doorkeeper, and brought Peter in. The maidservant who kept the door therefore said to Peter, “Are you also one of this man’s disciples?” He said, “I am not.”

Here it is recognized how true is what Truth itself had said shortly before: “Without me you can do nothing.”

“Behold, the firmest pillar trembled completely at the push of a single breath. Where is the boldness of one who made promises and presumed greatly upon himself? Where are those words when he said: ‘Why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you’ (John 13:37)? This is not following the teacher, but denying that he is a disciple. Is life laid down for the Lord in such a way that the voice of a maidservant is feared lest it happen?”

Certainly, in this passage we must consider how dangerous it is for a Christian to deny that he is a Christian. Peter did not say here that he denied Christ, but that he denied being Christ’s disciple; nevertheless, Christ himself had foretold earlier: “You will deny me three times.” Whoever denied that he was Christ’s disciple denied that he was a Christian; likewise, whoever denies that he is a Christian because of some fear also denies Christ.

(Verse 18.) The servants and attendants were standing beside a charcoal fire because it was cold, and they were warming themselves. There was the cold of unbelief in their hearts, so much so that even the chief of the apostles grew numb in that cold, because he had not yet been inflamed by the warmth of the Holy Spirit. After receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit, he himself no longer feared to confess Christ before the emperor and the Roman people; and even beardless boys and girls, inflamed by the warmth of the Holy Spirit, publicly confessed Christ unto death and did not fear dying for him—the one whom the key-bearer of heaven had feared to confess at the voice of a single maidservant.

Verse 19.—The high priest therefore questioned Jesus about his disciples and about his teaching. He did not question him out of love for learning the truth, but to find a charge by which he could accuse him as well and hand him over to the Roman governor for condemnation.

(Verse 20.) Jesus answered: “I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews assemble, and I have said nothing in secret.” What does it mean that he says he speaks openly and says nothing in secret, when elsewhere he says to the apostles, while speaking to the crowds in parables: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the others in parables”?

“It is to be understood that he said, ‘I have spoken openly to the world,’ as though he had said: ‘Many heard me speaking.’ The statement ‘openly’ was in one way open and in another way not open. It was open because many heard him; and again it was not open because they did not understand. What he spoke separately to the disciples was certainly not spoken in secret. For who speaks in secret when he speaks before so many people, since it is written: ‘Every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses’ (Deuteronomy 19:15)—especially if he speaks to a few what he wishes through them to become known to many? Therefore, even what seemed to be spoken secretly by him—how was it not spoken in secret? [Augustine: “in a certain manner”]—was not said in such a way that those to whom it had been spoken would keep silent about it, but rather in such a way that it would be proclaimed everywhere.”

(Verse 21.) “Why do you question me? Question those who have heard what I said to them. Behold, they know what I said.” As though he had said: “Why do you question me, from whom you do not desire to hear the truth, but whom you wish to condemn? Rather question those against whose testimony you have no ground for resentment.” The Lord tempered his answer in such a way that he neither concealed the truth nor seemed to defend himself.

(Verse 22.) When he had said these things, one of the attendants standing nearby struck Jesus on the face, saying, “Is that how you answer the high priest?” Here what had been prophesied concerning him was fulfilled: “I gave my cheek to those who struck me.” He struck him as though he were guilty because of his answer, but he, unjustly struck, replied meekly:

(Verse 23.) “If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness concerning the wrong. But if I have spoken rightly—that is, truthfully—why do you strike me?” Everyone who speaks against the truth speaks wrongly. But if I did not speak the truth, give testimony against me—show where I spoke falsely. But if I spoke well, that is, truthfully, why do you beat me? What response is truer, gentler, or more just than this?

“If we consider who received the slap, would we not wish the one who struck him either to be consumed by heavenly fire, swallowed up by the opening earth, or seized by a demon and dragged about? For what of these things could he not have commanded by his power, through whom the world was made, if he had not preferred to teach us patience, by him through whom the world is conquered [Augustine: qua, ‘by which [patience] the world is conquered’]?”

Perhaps someone here asks why he did not offer the other cheek to the one who struck him, according to his command (Matthew 5:39). Therefore he not only offered the other cheek to the one who struck him, but also handed over his whole body to be crucified; and the Lord prefers to preserve his commandments in the tranquility of the heart rather than display them through an exhibition of the body.

Verse 24.—Then Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest. These two, Annas and Caiaphas, were chief priests and served the priesthood in alternating years; and it was Caiaphas’s year when Christ suffered. We should believe that, according to Caiaphas’s will, he was first taken to Annas, so that it might seem a lesser fault if the judgment of another fellow priest also condemned him.

“But when the evangelist had said that Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas, he returned to the point in the narrative where he had left Peter, in order to explain what had happened in the house of Annas concerning his threefold denial.

(Verse 25.) ‘Simon Peter,’ he says, ‘was standing and warming himself.’ This repeats what he had said earlier. Then he joins what followed: ‘They therefore said to him, “Are you also one of his disciples?” He denied it and said, “I am not.”’ He had already denied him once at the maidservant’s voice; behold, terrified again by the same fear, he denied him a second time.

Then, so that the third denial might also be completed and the word of the Lord who foretold it fulfilled:

(Verses 26–27.) One of the high priest’s servants, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, said, “Did I not see you in the garden with him?” Peter denied it again as before, and immediately the cock crowed.

Behold, the physician’s prediction has been fulfilled, and the sick man’s presumption has been convicted. What Peter had said did not happen: “I will lay down my life for you” (John 13:38); but what he had foretold happened: “You will deny me three times.”

But this threefold denial caused by fear is washed away by a threefold confession of love. Love was not yet in him—love that would cast out fear. Servile fear still prevailed in his heart, and he had not yet looked upon the one who had foretold these things to him. We must also believe that this happened through the great dispensation of God, so that the one to whom Christ, returning to the Father, was going to entrust his sheep might learn through his own weakness to have mercy on others and forgive the faults of his brothers. Remembering his own sin, he would thus be able to sympathize with the weakness of others, since he was not unaware of his own fall.

When this threefold denial of Peter had been completed, the evangelist returned to the order of his narrative, at the point where he had left it.

Verse 28.—“Then,” he says, “they led Jesus to Caiaphas into the praetorium.”

@ [Col. 0973D] From St. Augustine, Treatise 114, §§1–5. He had said that Jesus was sent to Caiaphas by Annas, his colleague and father-in-law. But if he was sent to Caiaphas, why was he taken into the praetorium? This can mean nothing other than the place where the governor Pilate lived; or Caiaphas went into the praetorium to Pilate for Christ’s condemnation; or Pilate had his praetorium in the house of Caiaphas, and it was large enough to contain both the Lord dwelling apart and the judge sitting apart.

Behold how great is the priests’ zeal for evil [Manuscript: “in evil”!]. “They stayed awake all night in order to commit murder. It was morning, and they themselves—that is, those who were leading Jesus—did not enter the praetorium.” This means the part of the house occupied by Pilate, if it was Caiaphas’s house.

But why did they not enter the praetorium? He explains the reason: “so that they would not be defiled,” he says, “but might eat the Passover.” The days of Unleavened Bread had begun; during those days they considered it a defilement to enter another person’s dwelling. O impious and foolish blindness! They feared being defiled by another’s dwelling, but were not defiled by their own crime.

@ [Col. 0973D] Manuscript: “They thought that they were polluted by another’s dwelling, [Col. 0974D] and did not see that they were stained by their own crime.” They feared being defiled by the house of a foreign judge, but did not fear the blood of an innocent brother.

It should be understood what distinction there is between Passover and the days of Unleavened Bread. “Passover” properly designated the day on which the lamb was killed in the evening, at the fourteenth moon; the following seven days were called the days of Unleavened Bread. They were the days during which nothing fermented was to be found in their houses. Nevertheless, the Passover day is also found to be called one of the days of Unleavened Bread, as it is written in another Gospel: “On the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying, ‘Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?’” (Matthew 26:17).

Verses 29–30.—Therefore Pilate went outside to them and said, “What accusation do you bring against this man?” They answered and said to him, “If he were not a criminal, we would not have handed him over to you.” The Jews had this custom: whoever they judged worthy of death, they bound and handed over to the governor.

Let those freed from unclean spirits, the sick who were healed, the lepers who were cleansed, the deaf who heard, the mute who spoke, the blind who saw, and the dead who rose again be questioned and answer whether Jesus is a criminal. But they said these things of the one who had foretold through the Prophet: “They repaid me evil for good” (Psalm 34:12).

(Verse 31.) Pilate therefore said to them, “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law.” The Gentile judge was more just than they, as though he were saying: “You have a law; judge him according to your law. You know better what your law judges concerning such matters; judge him according to what you know to be just.”

The Jews therefore said to him, “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone.” What is this insane cruelty saying? Did they not kill the one whom they brought forward to be killed? Or did they perhaps not kill him while shouting, “Crucify, crucify”? What did they mean by saying, “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone,” when the law commands that murderers, adulterers, and those guilty of similar crimes be killed or stoned? Perhaps they said this because of the sanctity and veneration of the feast day: according to the law, they were not permitted to kill a person on the feast day, just as, out of reverence for that feast day, they had refused to enter the judge’s praetorium.

How is it, O Jews, O false Israelites, that you did not kill the one whom you seized, whom you led away, whom you handed over to the governor, and whose crucifixion you demanded?

“Hear what the Prophet also cries out against you: ‘The teeth of the sons of men are weapons and arrows, and their tongue is a sharp sword’ (Psalm 56:5). Behold the weapons, the arrows, and the sword with which you killed the righteous.”

Then he continues:

(Verse 32.) “They said this so that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spoke, signifying by what kind of death he was going to die.”

Therefore the Lord is to be understood here as signifying not the death of the cross, but the death by which the Jews handed him over to the Gentiles for execution—that is, to the Romans. For Pilate was a Roman citizen, although his family name was Pontius, and the Romans had sent him as governor to Judaea. Thus, so that this saying of Jesus might be fulfilled—that is, so that the Gentiles might kill him after he had been handed over to them, as Jesus had foretold would happen—this was fulfilled when the Jews handed him over to the Gentiles to be killed. Their crime was nevertheless lesser than that of the Jews, who wished in this way to make themselves appear alien to his killing—not so that their innocence might be shown, but their madness.

Verse 33.—Pilate entered the praetorium again, called Jesus, and said to him, “Are you the king of the Jews?” In these words Pilate showed that the Jews had brought against him the charge that he claimed to be the king of the Jews.

(Verse 34.) Jesus answered, “Do you say this of your own accord, or did others tell you about me?”

@ [Col. 0975D] From St. Augustine, Treatise 115, §§1, 4, 5. The Lord certainly knew both what he was asking and what Pilate was going to answer [Manuscript adds: “and what Pilate was going to answer him”; but this is redundant]. Nevertheless, he wished it to be said—not for his own sake, since he knew everything, but for our sake, so that what he wished us to know would be written.

Pilate answered, “Am I a Jew? Your nation and the chief priests handed you over to me. What have you done?” He removed from himself the suspicion that he might be thought to have said on his own that Jesus was the king of the Jews, showing that he had received this from the Jews.

By saying, “What have you done?” he sufficiently showed that the charge brought against Jesus was presented to him as a crime—as though he were saying: “If you deny that you are a king, what have you done to be handed over to me?” It would not be surprising if a person who claimed to be a king were handed over to a judge for punishment; but if he did not say this, Pilate would have to ask what else he might have done that made him worthy of being handed over to the judge.

### Verse 36

Jesus answered: “My kingdom is not from this world. If my kingdom were from this world, my servants would certainly fight, so that I would not be handed over to the Jews. But now my kingdom is not from here.”

This is what the good Teacher wanted us to know; but first the vain human opinion concerning his kingdom had to be exposed, whether that of the Gentiles or of the Jews, from whom Pilate had heard it—as though he were to be put to death for this reason, that he had unlawfully sought kingship, or because rulers commonly envy those who are about to become rulers. The Lord could have answered the governor’s first question—when he said, “Are you the king of the Jews?”—with the words, “My kingdom is not from this world.” But instead he asks him in turn whether he was saying this on his own, or had heard it from others. When Pilate answered, he wished to show that this had been presented to him by the Jews as a kind of charge against Jesus, thereby revealing to us the thoughts of men, which he himself knew to be vain.”

But when he says, “My kingdom is not from this world,” that is, it is not *in* this world, let all the kings of the earth hear: Christ did not come to take away kingdoms, but to give them; not to diminish them, but to increase them. He did not deny that he was a king, but he said that he did not reign carnally in this world. What is his kingdom except those who believe in him, whom at the end of the age he will hand over to God the Father (1 Cor. 15:24)—that is, whom he will bring to God the Father, so that they may reign with him without end?

But in order to prove that his kingdom was not from this world, he added: “If my kingdom were from this world, my servants would fight, so that I would not be handed over to the Jews.” He did not say, “But now my kingdom is not *here*,” but “is not *from here*.” His kingdom is indeed here, until the end of the age, but in his saints, concerning whom he said in another Gospel: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21). For his kingdom is the holy Church.

Hence also the angel said to the virgin Mary: “And he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32–33), wishing to show that this was a spiritual kingdom, in which he reigns among the saints, not the carnal kingdom that the wicked often possess in this world. For concerning his kingdom he says shortly beforehand: “You are not from the world, but I chose you from the world.”

### Verse 37

Pilate therefore said to him: “So you are a king?”

Jesus answered: “You say that I am a king.”

He did not say this because he was afraid to confess that he was a king, but he said, “You say.” He answered in such a way that he spoke the truth, while his words could not be exposed to accusation. The words “You say” mean: “You, being carnal, speak carnally.”

Then he adds: “For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, to bear witness to the truth.”

“The syllable of this pronoun should not be prolonged when he says, ‘For this I was born,’ as though he had said, ‘I was born in this matter’; rather, it should be shortened, as though he had said, ‘I was born for this purpose,’ or ‘I was born for this,’ just as he says, ‘For this I came into the world.’ In the Greek Gospel there is nothing ambiguous in this expression.

“It is therefore clear that here he recalled his temporal birth, by which he came into the world incarnate—not that birth without beginning by which he was God, through whom the Father created the world. Thus he said that he was born for this, that is, born on account of this, and that he had come into the world for this purpose, namely, by being born of a virgin, to bear witness to the truth.

“But since faith does not belong to everyone, he added: ‘Everyone who is from the truth hears my voice.’ He hears with inward ears—that is, he obeys my voice. This amounts to saying, ‘He believes in me.’

“Therefore, when Christ bears witness to the truth, he certainly bears witness to himself, for his voice is: ‘I am the truth’ (John 14:6). Here he commends grace, through which we have been called. Thus he says: ‘Everyone who is from the truth hears my voice’ (John 8:18). He is not from the truth because he hears his voice; rather, he hears because he is from the truth—that is, because this gift has been bestowed upon him from the truth. And what else is this than believing in Christ through Christ’s gift?”

### Verse 38

Pilate said to him: “What is truth?” Nor did he wait to hear what Jesus would answer him, because perhaps he was not worthy to hear it.

### Verse 39

But after he had said this, he went out again to the Jews and said to them: “I find no case against him. But you have a custom that I should release one prisoner for you at Passover. Do you therefore want me to release the king of the Jews?”

“I believe that, when Pilate had said, ‘What is truth?’ the custom of the Jews immediately came to his mind, by which one prisoner was accustomed to be released for them at Passover. For this reason he did not wait for Jesus to answer him what truth was, lest there be delay, since he had recalled the custom by which someone could be released to them at Passover.”

This custom of releasing a prisoner perhaps remained among the Jews on account of Passover, in memory of their liberation from Egypt, by which they were freed from slavery at Passover.

But when they heard this:

### Verse 40

They all cried out again, saying: “Not this man, but Barabbas.” Now Barabbas was a robber.

This Barabbas is interpreted as “the son of their master,” that is, of the devil, who was master either to this robber in his crime or to the Jews in the impiety of their faithlessness.

“We do not reproach you, O Jews, for releasing a guilty man at Passover, but for killing an innocent man. Yet unless this had happened, the true Passover would not have occurred. But the shadow of the truth was held by the erring Jews, so that, through the marvelous dispensation of divine wisdom and by means of deceitful men, the reality of that same shadow might be fulfilled. For, in order that the true Passover might take place, Christ was sacrificed like a sheep.”

## Chapter 19

### Verse 1

Then Pilate took Jesus and scourged him.”

### From Saint Augustine, *Tractate* 116, sections 1–9

It must be believed that Pilate did this for no other reason than that, once the Jews had been satisfied by his humiliations, they might think that enough had been done and cease their fury before putting him to death. This is connected with the fact that the same governor allowed his cohort to do what follows.

### Verses 2–3

And the soldiers, weaving a crown of thorns, placed it on his head, and clothed him in a purple garment. They came up to him and said: “Hail, king of the Jews!” And they struck him with blows [manuscript: “slaps”].

Thus were fulfilled the things that Christ had foretold concerning himself. Thus the martyrs were instructed to endure everything that persecutors might wish to inflict. Thus, while his terrifying power was temporarily concealed, the patience that was first to be imitated was commended. Thus the kingdom that was not from this world conquered the proud world, not by the violence of fighting but by the humility of suffering. Thus that grain, destined to be multiplied, was sown amid horrifying disgrace, so that it might spring forth in marvelous glory [Augustine: “Thus”].

### Verses 4–5

[Pilate went out again and said to them: “Behold, I am bringing him out to you, so that you may know that I find no case against him.”]

Jesus therefore went out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment, and he said to them: “Behold the man.”

From this it is clear that Pilate was not unaware of what the soldiers had done, whether he had ordered it or permitted it. The reason was the one we mentioned above: that his enemies, seeing these mockeries, might be thoroughly satisfied and thirst no longer for his blood.

Jesus came out to them wearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment, not glorious in authority but filled with disgrace. And he is said to them: “Behold the man.” If you envy a king, now spare him, because you see him cast down: he has been scourged, crowned with thorns, clothed in a garment of mockery, ridiculed with bitter insults, and struck with blows. Disgrace is burning fiercely; let envy grow cold.

But it did not grow cold; rather, it burned more fiercely and increased.

### Verses 6–7

When the chief priests and attendants saw him, they cried out, saying: “Crucify him, crucify him!”

Pilate said to them: “Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no case against him.”

The Jews answered him: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.”

Behold another, greater envy. The former charge seemed small, as though it concerned an attempt to seize royal power unlawfully; and yet Jesus falsely claimed neither title. Both are true: he is the only-begotten Son of God, and he is the king appointed by God over his holy mountain, Zion. He would now demonstrate both, if he did not prefer to be more patient in proportion as he was more powerful.

### Verse 8

When Pilate heard this statement, he became even more afraid. He entered the praetorium again and said to Jesus: “Where are you from?”

But Jesus gave him no answer.

This silence of our Lord Jesus Christ is found, when the accounts of all the evangelists are compared, to have occurred more than once, both before the chief priests and before Herod.

[The missing text should be supplied from Saint Augustine, at the cited passage.]

“Nevertheless, because of those matters to which he did not wish to respond, the comparison with a lamb was given, so that by his silence he might be regarded not as guilty but as innocent.”

### Verse 11

Jesus answered: “You would have no authority against me at all unless it had been given you from above. Therefore the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin.”

“Behold, he answered, and yet he did not answer everywhere” [Augustine: “Behold, he answered, and yet wherever he did not answer, he did not answer as a guilty man,” and so forth]; not as a guilty or deceitful man, but as a lamb—that is, as one simple and innocent—“he did not open his mouth.”

Therefore, when he did not answer, he was silent like a sheep; when he answered, he taught like a shepherd.

Let us learn, then, what he said, which he also taught through the Apostle: “There is no authority except from God” (Rom. 13:1). And because the person who, out of spite, hands an innocent man over to authority to be killed sins more than the authority itself, if that authority kills him out of fear of another, greater authority.

For God had given Pilate such authority that he was himself also under Caesar’s authority. Therefore he says: “You would have no authority against me at all”—that is, whatever slight authority you have—“unless this very thing, whatever it is, had been given you from above.”

But since I know how great it is—for it is not so great that you are altogether free to exercise it as you please—“therefore the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin.” He handed me over to your authority out of envy; you are about to exercise that same authority against me out of fear.

Even out of fear, a man ought not to kill an innocent person; nevertheless, doing so out of jealousy is much worse than doing so out of fear. Therefore the truthful Teacher did not say, “The one who handed me over to you has the sin,” as though Pilate had none; rather, he said, “has the greater sin,” so that Pilate might understand that he too had sin. For the lesser sin does not cease to exist merely because another is greater.

### Verse 12

From that point onward Pilate sought to release him.

What does the expression “from that point onward” mean, as though he had not sought this earlier? Read what precedes, and you will find that for a long time he had already been seeking to release Jesus.

“From that point onward” must therefore be understood to mean “on account of this,” that is, “because of this reason”: so that he would not incur the sin of killing an innocent man handed over to him, although he would sin less than the Jews who had handed him over to him to be killed. Thus “from that point onward” means “for this reason”—not that he began only then, but that from the beginning he had been seeking to release him, lest this sin should be committed [manuscript: “lest this should happen”].

But the Jews cried out, saying: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar.”

They thought they were imposing a greater fear on Pilate by frightening him with Caesar than they had earlier when they said: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.” Pilate did not fear their law when he was about to kill him; rather, he feared the Son of God, lest he kill him.

But now he could not disregard Caesar, the source of his authority, in the way that he could disregard the law of a foreign people.

### Verses 13–14

Pilate, therefore, when he heard these words, brought Jesus out and sat down on the tribunal, at the place called the Stone Pavement, but in Hebrew *Gabbatha* [manuscript: “Golgotha”]. It was the preparation-day of Passover, about the sixth hour.

At what hour the Lord was crucified is a matter that we may discuss, if the Lord wills, because of the testimony of the other evangelist, who said: “It was the third hour, and they crucified him.” A major dispute commonly arises when we reach the very passage where his crucifixion is narrated.

When Pilate had therefore sat down on the tribunal, he said to the Jews: “Behold your king.”

### Verse 15

But they cried out: “Take him away, take him away! Crucify him!”

Pilate said to them: “Shall I crucify your king?”

He was still trying to overcome the fear of Caesar that they had instilled, wishing to break them through their disgrace by saying: “Shall I crucify your king?” He could not calm them by appealing to the disgrace of Christ; instead, he was immediately overcome by fear.

### Verse 16

The chief priests answered: “We have no king except Caesar.”

Then he handed him over to them to be crucified.

For he would seem most openly to be acting against Caesar if, when they professed that they had no king except Caesar, he wished to recognize another king by releasing with impunity the one whom they had handed over to him to be killed on account of these claims.

He therefore handed him over to them to be crucified. But had he not also wanted this earlier, when he said: “Take him yourselves and crucify him,” or even above: “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law”?

Why, then, did they so vehemently refuse, saying: “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone,” and insist in every way that he be killed not by them but by the governor—and therefore refuse to take him for execution—if they now accept him for execution?

Or if this is not what is meant, why is it said: “Then he handed him over to them to be crucified”?

There is indeed a distinction. For it is not said: “Then he handed him over to them so that they might crucify him,” but “so that he might be crucified”—that is, so that he might be crucified by the judgment and authority of the governor.

But the Evangelist said that he handed him over to them in order to show that they were implicated in the crime from which they had tried to distance themselves. Pilate would not have done this unless he intended to fulfill what he saw them eagerly desiring.

The statement that follows—“They took Jesus and led him away”—may therefore refer to the soldiers, the governor’s attendants. For afterward it is said more explicitly: “Then the soldiers, when they had crucified him.”

Even if the Evangelist attributes the whole action to the Jews, he does so rightly: they took up what they had demanded with the greatest eagerness, and they did whatever they had forced to be done.”

### Verse 17

“[The following is] from Saint Augustine, *Tractate* 117, sections 1–5.”

Pilate having judged and condemned the Lord Jesus Christ on the tribunal, about the sixth hour they took him and led him away. And carrying his own cross, he went out to the place called the place of the Skull, in Hebrew *Golgotha*, where they crucified him.

What, then, does the Evangelist Mark mean when he says, “It was the third hour, and they crucified him” (Mark 15:25), except that the Lord was crucified at the third hour by the tongues of the Jews, and at the sixth hour by the hands of the soldiers?

We should understand that the fifth hour had already passed and that something of the sixth hour had begun when Pilate sat on the tribunal, which John calls “about the sixth hour.” When Jesus was led away to be fastened to the wood with two robbers, and when the events narrated took place beside his cross, the sixth hour was completed. From that hour until the ninth, darkness occurred when the sun was obscured, as the authority of the three evangelists—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—testifies.

But because the Jews tried to transfer the crime of killing Christ from themselves to the Romans, that is, to Pilate and his soldiers, Mark suppressed the hour at which Christ was crucified by the soldiers, when the sixth hour had already begun, and instead recalled and expressly stated the third hour. At that hour they could be understood to have cried out before Pilate: “Crucify him, crucify him.”

Thus not only are those found to have crucified Jesus who hung him on the wood at the sixth hour, namely, the soldiers, but also the Jews, who cried out at the third hour that he should be crucified.

Carrying his own cross, therefore, he went out to the place called the place of the Skull, but in Hebrew *Golgotha*, where they crucified him. And with him they crucified two others, one on each side, with Jesus in the middle.

These two were robbers, as we learn from the account of the other evangelists, with whom Christ was crucified. Christ was fastened between them, concerning whom the preceding prophecy had said: “And he was counted among the transgressors” (Isa. 53:12).

### Verses 19–20

Pilate also wrote an inscription and placed it on the cross. It was written: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.”

Many of the Jews read this inscription, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city. It was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin.

These three languages stood out there above the others: Hebrew, because of the Jews who gloried in the Law; Greek, because of the wise among the nations; and Latin, because of the Romans, who at that time ruled over many—almost all—nations.

### Verses 21–22

The chief priests of the Jews therefore said to Pilate: “Do not write, ‘The king of the Jews,’ but rather, ‘He said, I am the king of the Jews.’”

Pilate answered: “What I have written, I have written.”

O ineffable power of divine action, even in the hearts of those who are ignorant! Was not a certain hidden voice sounding inwardly in Pilate, if one may put it so, with a clamorous silence [Augustine: “with clamorous silence”], proclaiming what had been prophesied long before in the words of the Psalms: “Do not corrupt the inscription of the title” (title of Ps. 56)?

For surely it is not therefore untrue that Jesus said, “I am the king of the Jews”?, If what Pilate wrote cannot be corrupted, can what the Truth said be corrupted?

But is Christ king only of the Jews, or also of the Gentiles? Indeed, also of the Gentiles.

For when he had said in prophecy: “Yet I have been appointed king by him over his holy mountain, Zion, declaring the decree of the Lord” (Ps. 2:6), lest anyone say that he had been appointed king because of Mount Zion only for the Jews, he immediately added: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations,” and so forth.

Why, then, do we wish to understand a great mystery in this inscription, in which it was written, “King of the Jews,” if Christ is also king of the Gentiles?

Because, of course, the wild olive has become a partaker of the richness of the olive [Augustine: “olive tree”], not because the olive became a partaker of the bitterness of the wild olive. Since the title was truthfully written concerning Christ, “King of the Jews,” who are to be understood as the Jews except the seed of Abraham, the children of the promise, who are also children of God?

For, as the Apostle says: “Not the children of the flesh are children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as the seed” (Rom. 9:7–8).

And there were Gentiles to whom he said: “If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. 3:29).

Christ, then, is king of the Jews—but of Jews by the circumcision of the heart, in spirit and not in letter. Their praise is not from human beings but from God. They belong to Jerusalem, our free mother (Gal. 4:26), eternal in the heavens, the spiritual Sarah who casts out the slave woman and her children from the house of freedom.

For this reason Pilate wrote what he wrote, because the Lord Jesus said what he said.

### Verse 23

When the soldiers had crucified him, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier, and also his tunic.”

### From Saint Augustine, *Tractate* 118, section 2

From this it is evident that there were four soldiers who obeyed the governor in crucifying him.

For he clearly says: “When the soldiers had crucified him, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier, and also his tunic.” The verb “took” must be understood again, so that the sense is: “They took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier; they also took his tunic.”

He spoke in this way so that we understand that no lot was cast over the other garments, but over the tunic, which they took together with the others but did not divide in the same way [manuscript: “similarly”]. For concerning it he continues by explaining: “The tunic was seamless, woven from the top throughout.”

Why they cast lots for it is then narrated:

### Verse 24

“They said to one another: ‘Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for it, to determine whose it shall be.’”

It is therefore evident that in the other garments they had equal portions, so that there was no need to cast lots; but in the case of that one garment they could not each have an individual portion.

“Someone may perhaps ask what is signified by the division of the garments into four parts and by the casting of lots for the tunic.

“The fourfold division of the garment of our Lord Jesus Christ represented his fourfold Church, spread throughout the whole world, which consists of four regions, and distributed equally—that is, harmoniously—among all those regions.

“For this reason it is said elsewhere that he will send his angels to gather his elect from the four winds (Mark 13:27). What does this mean except from the four regions of the world: east, west, north, and south?

“But the tunic for which the lot was cast signifies the unity of all the parts, which is held together by the bond of charity.

“Speaking of charity, the Apostle says: ‘I show you a still more excellent way’ (1 Cor. 12:31). And elsewhere he says: ‘To know also the charity of Christ, which surpasses knowledge’ (Eph. 3:19). Again, elsewhere: ‘Above all these things, charity, which is the bond of perfection’ (Col. 3:14).

“If, therefore, charity has a more excellent way, surpasses knowledge, and is commanded above all things, it is rightly said that the garment by which it is signified was woven from above.

“It is seamless, so that it may never be torn apart; and it reaches to one point, because it gathers everyone into one. Thus among the apostles, although their number was also twelve—that is, four groups of three—and although all were questioned, Peter alone answered: ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.’ And to him it was said: ‘I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven’ (Matt. 16:16, 19), as though he alone had received the power of binding and loosing.

“Yet he had both spoken that answer on behalf of all and, together with all, had received the power as one representing the unity itself. He spoke for all because unity exists in all.

“Therefore, after saying ‘woven from above,’ he added ‘throughout.’ If we refer this to what it signifies, no one is excluded from it who is found to belong to the whole. From this whole Church, as the Greek language indicates, it is called Catholic.

“And what is commended by the lot except the grace of God? Thus, when the lot pleased everyone, what belonged to one reached all, because the grace of God reaches all in unity. And when the lot is cast, the decision is yielded not to any person’s character or merits but to the hidden judgment of God.

“Nor should anyone say that this did not signify something good because it was done by evil men—not by those who followed Christ, but by those who persecuted him.

“For what shall we say of the cross itself, which was likewise made and inflicted upon Christ by enemies and wicked men? Yet it is rightly understood to signify what the Apostle says: ‘What is the breadth and length and height and depth?’ (Eph. 3:18).

“It is broad in the transverse beam, where the hands of the one hanging are stretched out, and it signifies good works in the breadth of charity.

“It is long from the transverse beam to the ground, where the back and feet are fastened, and it signifies perseverance through the length of time, to the end.

“It is high at the top, where the part above the transverse beam extends upward again [Augustine: ‘where the transverse beam is exceeded upward’], and it signifies the heavenly end to which all works are directed, since all things done well and perseveringly in breadth and length must be done for the sake of the height of divine rewards.

“It is deep in the part fixed in the earth. There it is hidden and cannot be seen, but all its visible and elevated features arise from it, just as our good works all proceed from the depth of God’s grace, which cannot be comprehended or judged.

“But even if the cross of Christ signifies only what the Apostle says—‘Those who belong to Jesus Christ have crucified their flesh with its passions and desires’ (Gal. 5:24)—what a great good this is! Yet this occurs only when the good spirit desires against the flesh, while the enemy, that is, the evil spirit, has made Christ’s cross.

“Finally, what is the sign of Christ’s cross, known by everyone [Augustine: ‘the sign of Christ’], except the cross of Christ? Unless that sign is applied to the foreheads of believers, to the water itself from which they are reborn, to the oil with which they are anointed in chrism [another reading: ‘chrism’], or to the sacrifice by which they are nourished, none of these is properly accomplished.

“How, then, can nothing good be signified through what the wicked do, when through the cross of Christ—which the wicked made—all good is signified for us in the celebration of his sacraments?”

### From Saint Augustine, *Tractate* 119, sections 1–6

After the Lord Jesus had completed everything that he knew had to be accomplished before his death, and had handed over his spirit when he wished, let us see what followed, as the Evangelist narrates.

### Verses 25–27

“The soldiers did these things. Standing beside the cross of Jesus were his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.

“When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple standing nearby whom he loved, he said to his mother: ‘Woman, behold your son.’ Then he said to the disciple: ‘Behold your mother.’ And from that hour the disciple took her into his own home.”

“This is surely the hour of which Jesus had spoken to his mother when he was about to turn water into wine: ‘Woman, what is there between me and you? My hour has not yet come’ (John 2:4).

“He had foretold this hour, which had not yet come then, in which his mother would recognize him as he was dying, though it was from her that he had been born mortally.

“Then, when he was about to perform divine works, he rejected [Augustine: ‘repelled’] the mother not of his divinity but of his weakness, as though she were unknown. But now, while suffering human things, he commended her with human affection, since it was from her that he had become human.

“For then the one who had created Mary was revealing himself in power; now the one whom Mary had borne was hanging on the cross.”

“A mortal speaker is therefore indicated [manuscript and Augustine: ‘A moral passage is indicated’]. He does what ought to be done, and by his example the good Teacher instructed his followers to provide dutiful care for their parents, as though the wood to which the limbs of the dying man were fastened had also become the teacher’s chair from which he taught.”

[Supply from Augustine at the cited passage:]

“For why he did this is indicated by what follows, for the Evangelist says: ‘And from that hour,’ and so forth.”

“From that hour the disciple took her into his own home,” speaking of himself. For he regularly recalled that Jesus loved him. Jesus certainly loved them all, but he loved him above the others and more familiarly, so that at the meal he made him recline upon his breast. I believe that by this means he wished to commend more profoundly the divine excellence of the Gospel that he was to preach through him.

### Verses 28–30

Afterward, knowing that all things had been completed, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, Jesus said: “I thirst.”

A vessel full of vinegar was standing there. They placed a sponge full of vinegar on hyssop and brought it to his mouth.

When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said: “It is completed.” And bowing his head, he handed over his spirit.

Who could arrange what this man who suffered arranged in such a manner? Yet he was the man who is the mediator between God and human beings—the man of whom it had been foretold: “He is both man, and who recognizes him?” For all those through whom these events took place saw the man but did not recognize God.

[Augustine: “For the human beings through whom these things were done did not recognize the man who was God.”]

He appeared as a man, while God was hidden. The one who appeared suffered all these things, and the very one who was hidden arranged all these things.

He therefore saw that everything that had to take place before he received the vinegar and handed over his spirit had been completed. And in order that this too might be fulfilled, as Scripture says, “In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68:22), he said: “I thirst,” as though he were saying: “You have left this undone; give me what you are.”

The Jews themselves were the vinegar, degenerating from the wine of the patriarchs and prophets. And, as though from a full vessel, they had been filled with the iniquity of this world, possessing a heart like a sponge, fraudulent through its cavernous and twisted hiding places.

The hyssop around which they placed the sponge full of vinegar is appropriately understood as the humility of Christ, since it is a lowly herb and cleanses the breast. They surrounded him with it, and thought that they had ensnared him.

Hence the words in the Psalm: “You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Ps. 50:9). We are cleansed by Christ’s humility, because unless he had humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father even unto death on a cross, his blood would not have been poured out for the remission of sins—that is, for our cleansing.

Nor should anyone be troubled about how they could bring a sponge to his mouth when he had been raised above the earth on the cross. As the other evangelists report, in what John omitted, this was done on a reed, so that the sponge containing the drink might be lifted to the height of the cross.

The reed signified Scripture, which was being fulfilled by this act. Just as one speaks of a Greek, Latin, or any other language when referring to a sound expressed by the tongue, so a letter written by a reed can be called a reed. But we ordinarily speak more significantly of sounds expressing human speech as a “language.” That Scripture should be called a “reed” is less customary, and for that very reason it is more richly symbolic.

When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said: “It is completed.” What else was this than what the prophet had foretold so long beforehand [another reading: “shortly beforehand”]?

Then, because nothing remained that had still to be done before he died, like one who had the power to lay down his life and to take it up again, after completing everything that he had awaited in order that it might be completed, he bowed his head and handed over his spirit.

Who sleeps in such a way when he wishes, as Jesus died when he wished? Who lays aside a garment when he wishes, as he put off his flesh when he wished? Who departs when he wishes, as he died when he wished?

How great a power must be hoped for or feared in the Judge, if such power appeared in the one who was dying?”

### From Saint Augustine, *Tractate* 120, sections 1–7

After the Lord Jesus had completed everything that he knew had to be accomplished before his death, and had handed over his spirit when he wished, let us see what followed, as the Evangelist narrates.

### Verse 31

“Since it was the preparation-day, the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away, so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath—for that Sabbath was a great day.”

It was not the legs that were to be taken away, but the men whose legs were broken for this reason: so that they would die and be removed from the wood. They did not want the men hanging on crosses to defile the great feast day with the horror of their prolonged agony.

### Verses 32–34

The soldiers therefore came and first broke the legs of one man, and then of the other who had been crucified with him.

But when they came to Jesus, they saw that he was already dead, and they did not break his legs. Instead, one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out.

The Evangelist used an elegant and vigilant expression: he did not say, “He struck his side,” or “He wounded it,” or anything similar, but “he opened it,” so that there might in some way be opened there the door of life, from which the sacraments of the Church flowed, without which one does not enter into life, which is true life.

That blood was poured out for the remission of sins; that water prepared the saving cup. It both provides a washing and a drink.

This was prefigured when Noah was commanded to make a door in the side of the ark, through which the animals that were not destined to perish in the flood could enter—animals that prefigured the Church (Gen. 6:16).

For this reason the first woman was made from the side of the sleeping man and was called “Life” and “the mother of the living” (Gen. 2:22 and following). It signified a great good before the great evil of transgression, in the form of the man lying and sleeping.

And here the second Adam slept on the cross with his head bowed, so that from his side there might be formed for him a bride who flowed from the side of the sleeping man.

O death, from which the dead come back to life!

### Verses 36–37

“These things happened,” he says, “so that the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘You shall not break a bone of him.’ And again another Scripture says: ‘They will look upon him whom they pierced.’”

He provided two testimonies from Scripture corresponding to the individual events that he narrated as having occurred.

Since he had said, “When they came to Jesus, they did not break his legs,” the testimony “You shall not break a bone of him” applies to this. This was commanded to those who were ordered to celebrate Passover by the sacrifice of a lamb under the old Law, which had gone before as the shadow of the Lord’s Passion.

Hence “Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7). Of this [Augustine: “of him”] the prophet Isaiah had also foretold: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Isa. 53:7).

Likewise, since he had added: “But one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance,” the second testimony applies: “They will look upon him whom they pierced.” In this passage Christ is promised as coming in the very flesh in which he was crucified.

[Col. 0986D] **VERSES 38–39.**—After these things Joseph of Arimathea, because he was a disciple of Jesus—though secretly, on account of fear of the Jews—asked Pilate to take away the body of Jesus; and Pilate permitted it. So he came and took the body of Jesus. Nicodemus also came, who had first come to Jesus by night, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds.

This should not be punctuated as though we were to say, “first bringing a mixture of myrrh”; rather, the word “first” belongs to the preceding sense: for Nicodemus had first come to Jesus by night. John related this same event earlier in his Gospel (John 3:2). Thus it should be understood that Nicodemus came to Jesus not only then, but then for the first time; afterward he kept coming, so that by listening he might become a disciple. This is certainly now made known to almost all nations in the revelation of the body of the blessed Stephen. [MS: *venit*, “came,” for *ventitasse*, “kept coming.”] {634}

**VERSE 41.**—Now there was a garden in the place where he was crucified, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been placed. Just as no one before him and no one after him was conceived in the womb of the Virgin Mary, so no one before him and no one after him was buried in this tomb.

**VERSE 42.**—There, therefore, because of the Jews’ preparation day, since the tomb was nearby, they placed Jesus. He wants the burial to be understood as hurried, lest evening come on: for, because of the preparation day—which the Jews call in Latin *coena pura* (“pure meal”), but which among us is more commonly called *praeparatio* (“preparation”)—it was not permitted to do such a thing.”

## CHAPTER XLI

The manifestation of the Resurrection is likewise explained: Mary Magdalene announces to Peter and John that the body has been taken from the tomb. When they have gone to meet her and returned, she herself, after seeing the angel, supposes that the Lord whom she sees is the gardener; then he immediately calls her back by her own name. Once she recognizes him, she is at once commanded to announce him to the disciples.

## CHAPTER 20, VERSE 1

**“Now on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene came early, while it was still dark, to the tomb; and she saw the stone taken away from the tomb.”**

“The first day of the week, which Christian custom now calls the Lord’s Day because of the Lord’s Resurrection: Matthew alone among the Evangelists called it the first day of the week.”

**VERSE 2.**—So she ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and she said to them: “They have taken the Lord from the tomb, and I do not know where they have laid him.”

Disturbed by excessive love, while she did not find the one whom she sought, she ran to announce it to the disciples, so that either they might seek him with her or grieve with her that the Lord had been taken away. She did not fear to call him “the Lord,” although she was seeking only his body in the tomb.

**VERSES 3–4.**—So Peter and the other disciple went out and came to the tomb. The two were running together, but the other disciple ran ahead, faster than Peter, and came first to the tomb.

“Here the recapitulation should be noticed and commended: how the narrative returns to what had been passed over, and how what follows is added as though it came next [Augustine: “and yet as though this followed”]. For after he had already said, ‘They came to the tomb,’ he went back to relate how they came, and said: ‘The two were running together,’ and so forth. There he shows that the other disciple, whom he signifies as himself, ran ahead and came first to the tomb; but, as is the custom of Sacred Scripture, he narrates everything as though about another person.

@ [Col. 0987D] Thus far from Saint Augustine.”

**VERSE 5.**—“And when he had bent down,” he says, “he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not enter.”

@ [Col. 0988D] From Saint Gregory, Homily 22, numbers 2–5.

“That Mary Magdalene came to the tomb while it was still dark indicates the hour according to the historical sense; according to the mystical sense, it signifies the understanding of one who is seeking. Mary was seeking in the tomb the author of all things, whom she had seen dead in the flesh; and because she did not find him there [alternative: *hunc*, “him”], she believed that he had been stolen. It was still dark, therefore, when she came to the tomb. She ran more quickly and announced it to the disciples; but those ran ahead of the others who loved more than the others, namely Peter and John. The two were running together, but John ran ahead faster than Peter, came first to the tomb, and [Gregory: “but”] did not presume to enter; Peter [supplied in the text], however, came afterward and entered.”

This running of the two disciples contains a great mystery. For what is signified by John, who came first to the tomb but did not enter, except the Synagogue? And what is demonstrated by Peter, except the Church gathered from the Gentiles, which was called later but entered first? The Gentiles and the Synagogue ran together through the successive ages of this world, but they did not come with equal understanding. {635}

“The Synagogue came first to the tomb but did not enter, because although it received the commandments of the Law and heard the prophecies concerning the Lord’s incarnation and passion, it was unwilling to believe in the one who had died. John saw the linen cloths lying there but did not enter, because the Synagogue recognized the mysteries of the Sacred Scriptures and yet deferred entering through faith in the Lord’s Passion. It saw him present whom it had long and widely prophesied, yet rejected him; it despised him as a human being and refused to believe that God had become mortal in the flesh. What, then, does this mean except that it ran more quickly and yet stood empty before the tomb?

**VERSE 6.**—Then Simon Peter came, following him, and entered the tomb.

Because the Church of the Gentiles, following afterward, both recognized the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, and acknowledged that he had died in the flesh, and believed him to be God who lives.

**VERSE 7.**—He saw the linen cloths lying there, and the cloth that had been over his head, not lying with the linen cloths but wrapped separately in one place [alternative Latin: *in unum locum*, “into one place”].

What does it mean that the cloth of the Lord’s head is not found in the tomb with the linen cloths, except that, as Paul testifies, “the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3), and that the incomprehensible mysteries of divinity are separated from the knowledge of our weakness, while his power transcends the nature of creation? It should also be noted that it is said to have been found not only separately but also wrapped [Gregory adds: “in one place”].

[Col. 0988D] For neither the beginning nor the end of a cloth that is wrapped can be seen. Properly, therefore, the cloth of the head was found wrapped, because the height of divinity neither began to exist nor ceases to exist. “In one place” is rightly added, because God is not found in the division of minds. God is in unity, and those deserve to possess his grace who do not divide themselves from one another through the scandals of sects.”

The cloth may indeed [MS: *quoque*, “also”] signify the Passion of our Lord Christ, whose mysteries of suffering are wrapped up for unbelievers: “For although they saw him mortal in the flesh, they did not believe him to be immortal God. The cloth, therefore, which had been over his head is found separately, because the Passion of our Redeemer is far removed from our passion: he endured without guilt what we endure with guilt. He willingly submitted to death, whereas we come to it unwillingly.”

It follows:

**VERSE 8.**—“Then the other disciple also entered, the one who had come first to the tomb.”

After Peter entered, John also went in. The one who had come first entered afterward.

It is known that at the end of the world Judea also will be gathered to the faith of the Redeemer, as Paul testifies when he says: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and so all Israel should be saved” (Rom. 11:25–26).

“And he saw and believed.”

What, then, did he see, and what did he believe? He saw the linen cloths lying there and believed what the woman had said: that the Lord had been taken from the tomb.”

[Col. 0989B]

@ [Col. 0989D] Thus far from Saint Gregory.

For it was still dark in the tomb—that is, in their minds. Therefore it continues and says:

**VERSES 9–10.**—“For they did not yet know the Scripture, that he had to rise from the dead.” So the disciples went away again to themselves—that is, to the place where they lived, and from which they had run to the tomb.

**VERSE 11.**—“But Mary stood outside at the tomb, weeping.”

This Mary—

@ [Col. 0989D] From Saint Gregory, Homily 25, numbers 1–7.

“After she came to the tomb and did not find the Lord’s body there, she believed that it had been taken away and announced it to the disciples. They came, saw, and believed that it was as the woman had said. It is immediately written of them: ‘So the disciples went away to themselves.’ Then it is added: ‘But Mary stood outside at the tomb, weeping.’

Here we must consider how great a force of love had inflamed this woman’s mind: even when the Lord’s disciples were leaving, she did not leave the Lord’s tomb. She sought the one whom she had not found; she wept while seeking him, and, set aflame by the fire of her love, she burned with desire for the one whom she believed had been taken away.”

Her eyes, which had sought the Lord and had not found him, now overflowed with tears. She grieved more that he had been taken from the tomb than that he had been killed on the cross, because no memory even remained of so great a teacher whose life had been taken from her.

“Thus it happened that she alone then saw him who remained behind to seek him. For the power of a good work is perseverance, as the Voice of Truth says: ‘The one who perseveres to the end will be saved’ (Matt. 10:22). Let us therefore see with what result the force of love in this woman multiplies the work of seeking, since she loved in this way and again bent over the tomb she had examined. It follows:

{636}

**VERSE 12.**—“She saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been placed.”

What does it mean that in the place of the Lord’s body two angels are seen sitting, one at the head and the other at the feet, except that in Latin an angel is called a *nuntius*, a messenger, and that the one who was to be announced through his Passion is both God before the ages and human at the end of the ages? The angel sits at the head, as the Apostle John proclaims:

[Col. 0990D] Gregory: “When it is proclaimed through the Apostle John, ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God’” [Col. 0990A] (John 1:1).

And the angel sits, as it were, at the feet when it is said: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

We may, however [MS: *etiam*, “also”], understand by the two angels the two Testaments, one earlier and the other later. These angels are joined to each other by the place of the Lord’s body, because both Testaments, while announcing with one and the same meaning that the Lord was incarnate, died, and rose again, are seated, as it were, with the earlier Testament at the head and the later Testament at the feet.

The angels ask Mary, saying:

**VERSE 13.**—“Woman, why are you weeping?”

She says to them: “Because they have taken away my Lord from the tomb, and I do not know where they have laid him.”

For the sacred words themselves, which stir tears of love within us on account of the goodness of our Savior and the memory of his death, which he endured for our love, also console those same tears when they promise us the sight of our Redeemer.”

The angels asked, “Why are you weeping?” As though they had said: “There is no need to weep for one who is dead; you ought to believe that he is alive.”

But she said: “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.”

Calling her Lord’s lifeless body “my Lord,” she signifies the whole by a part, just as we all confess Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, to be our one Lord—which includes at once the Word, the soul, and the flesh—although, when he was crucified and buried, only his flesh was buried.

“And I do not know,” she says, “where they have laid him.” This was the chief cause of her grief: she did not know where she might go to console her sorrow. But the hour was near when her sadness would be turned into joy.

Therefore it follows:

**VERSE 14.**—“When she had said this, she turned back and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus.”

“It should be noted that Mary, who was still doubtful concerning the Lord’s Resurrection, turned back [alternative: “was turned”] to see Jesus because, through that very doubt, she had, as it were, turned her back [Gregory: “back,” singular] toward the Lord’s face, since she did not at all believe that he had risen. But because she loved and doubted, she saw him and did not recognize him: love had shown him to her, while doubt concealed him.

Her continued ignorance is expressed when it is added:

**VERSE 15.**—“She did not know that it was Jesus.”

He says to her: “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?”

The cause of her grief is questioned so that her desire may increase, in order that, when she named the one whom she was seeking, she might burn more ardently with love for him.

She, supposing that he was the gardener, says to him: “Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him.”

Perhaps this woman was not mistaken even in her mistake when she believed Jesus to be the gardener. Was he not spiritually a gardener to her, who planted and cultivated in her heart the growing seeds of virtues through his love?

But what does it mean that, having seen him whom she supposed to be the gardener, before she had yet told him whom she was seeking, she said to him: “Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me,” and so forth?

Let no one accuse the woman because she called the Lord a gardener and Jesus a teacher. There she was asking him and did not know him; here she recognized him. There she honored a human being from whom she was requesting a favor; here she remembered the teacher from whom she had learned to distinguish human and divine things. She called him “Lord,” although she was not his servant, so that she might come to the Lord whose servant she was.

Thus she spoke of “Lord” in two different ways: “They have taken away my Lord,” and “Lord, if you have taken him away.” In the first case she spoke from the truth; in the second, from honor.

She was seeking him and did not name the one whom she sought, yet she said: “Lord, if you have taken him away.”

“This is what the force of love does; this is what it usually brings about in the mind: that the person whom it is always thinking about, it believes no one else can fail to know. Rightly, then, this woman does not say whom she is seeking, and yet says, ‘If you have taken him away,’ because she does not suppose that the one whom she continually laments with such longing is unknown to another.

**VERSE 16.**—Jesus says to her: “Mary.”

After he had addressed her by the common designation appropriate to her sex, and he was not recognized, he calls her by name. It is as though he openly said to her: “Recognize the one by whom you are recognized.”

To the perfect man also it is said: “I know you by name” (Exod. 33:12). For “human being” is a common designation belonging to all of us, whereas “Moses” is a proper name. It is rightly said that he is known by name, as though the Lord openly said: “I know you not generally, like the others, but particularly.”

Mary, therefore, when called by name, recognizes her Creator and immediately calls him “Rabboni,” that is, “Teacher,” because he was both the one whom she was seeking outwardly and the one who inwardly taught her to seek him.

Now the Evangelist does not add what the woman did, but indicates it by what she heard, for he says to her: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.”

These words show that Mary wanted to embrace the feet of the one whom she had recognized. But the Teacher says to her: “Do not touch me”—not because, after the Resurrection, the Lord refused to be touched by women, since it is written of the two who came to his tomb: “They came and held his feet” (Matt. 28:9).

But the reason why he should not be touched is also added when it follows: “For I have not yet ascended to my Father.”

For Jesus ascends to the Father in our heart when he is believed to be equal to the Father. Whoever does not believe him equal to the Father still does not have the Lord ascended to the Father in his heart. Therefore the one truly touches Jesus who believes the Son to be coeternal with the Father.

“Go instead to my brothers and say to them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.”

Since he says “my” and “your,” why does he not say “our” in common? By speaking distinctly he indicates that he has the same Father and God in a different way from us [Manuscript better: “he has the same Father and God differently from us”].

“I am ascending to my Father,” namely, by nature, “and your Father,” by grace; “to my God,” because I descended; “and your God,” because you will ascend [Manuscript: “because you have ascended”].

Since I too am human, God is my God; since you have been liberated from error [MS: *liberat*, “sets free,” for *liberati estis*, “you have been liberated”], God is your God. {637} Thus the Father and God are distinct in relation to me, because the one whom God begot as God before the ages created me [Manuscript: “created me with himself”] as human at the end of the ages.

**VERSE 18.**—Mary Magdalene came announcing to the disciples: “I have seen the Lord.” And she told them these things.

Behold, the guilt of the human race is cut off at the point from which it proceeded. Because in paradise woman offered death to man, from the tomb woman announced life to men; and she who had recounted the words of the death-dealing serpent now recounts the words of her life-giver.

It is as though the Lord said to the human race, not by words but by deeds: “From the hand from which the drink of death was brought to you, receive the cup of life.”

We have briefly passed through these matters from the exposition of the Gospel reading. Now, with the help of that same Lord of whom we are speaking, let us consider both the glory of his Resurrection and the depths of his mercy. For he wished to rise quickly from death, lest our soul remain for long in the death of unbelief.”

## CHAPTER XLII

When the doors were closed, he comes to the disciples and brings peace, showing them his hands and side. He also signifies the Holy Spirit to them by breathing upon them. Likewise, after eight days, Thomas is confirmed in faith by seeing or touching the Lord’s side and hands, hearing: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.”

[Col. 0992B]

**VERSE 19.**—“When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were closed where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in their midst.”

@ [Col. 0991D] From Saint Gregory, Homily 26, numbers 1–3.

“What is surprising if, after his Resurrection, he entered through closed doors, since he was now going to live forever, when, coming to die, he came forth without the Virgin’s womb being opened?
