But because the faith of those who looked upon that body which could be seen was doubtful, he immediately showed them his hands and side. He offered flesh to be touched, the same flesh that he had brought in through closed doors.”

The nail had fastened his hand, and the lance had opened his side; the traces of the wounds were preserved there for the healing of doubting hearts.

“In this matter he displayed two marvels that, according to human reasoning, are very much opposed to each other: after the Resurrection he showed his body to be both incorruptible and yet tangible. For what is touched must necessarily be subject to corruption, while what is not corruptible cannot be touched. But in a marvelous and immeasurable way our Redeemer presented an incorruptible and tangible body after the Resurrection, so that by showing it incorruptible he might invite us to the reward, and by offering it tangible he might form [Gregory: ‘strengthen’] us in faith. He therefore showed himself to be both incorruptible and tangible, so that he might plainly demonstrate after the Resurrection that his body was of the same nature but possessed a different glory.”

He says to them: “Peace be with you.”

He offered peace who came on account of peace. To those to whom he had earlier said, “My peace I leave you; my peace I give you,” he now says, “Peace be with you.” This is the peace that the angels proclaimed in the world when Christ was born.

And again, a second time he says, “Peace be with you,” to show that the things in heaven and the things on earth had been reconciled through his blood.

**VERSE 21.**—He says to them: “Peace be with you.”

The repetition is a confirmation.

“As the Father sent me, so I send you.”

“The Father sent the Son, appointing him to become incarnate for the redemption of the human race; he willed him to come into the world for suffering. Yet he loved the Son whom he sent to suffer.

The Lord, however, sends the chosen apostles into the world not to the joys of the world but, just as he himself was sent, to sufferings. Therefore, since the Son is loved by the Father and yet is sent to suffering, the disciples too are loved by the Lord and yet are sent into the world to suffer.

Thus it is said: ‘As the Father sent me, so I send you.’ That is: ‘I love you with the same love with which the Father loves me when I send you amid the attacks of persecutors—the same love with which the Father loved me [Manuscript: “loved me”], whom he caused to come to endure sufferings.’”

**VERSE 22.**—“When he had said this, he breathed upon them and said to them: Receive the Holy Spirit.”

We must ask what it means that our Lord gave the Holy Spirit once while remaining on earth and once while presiding in heaven. For the Holy Spirit is not clearly shown to have been given elsewhere except now, when he is received through breathing, and afterward, when he comes from heaven and is manifested in different tongues.

Why, then, is he first given to the disciples on earth and afterward sent from heaven, except that there are two commandments of love: love of God and love of neighbor? The Spirit is given on earth so that the neighbor may be loved; the Spirit is given from heaven so that God may be loved.

Just as there is one love and two commandments, so there is one Spirit and two gifts: first from the Lord while he was standing on earth, afterward from heaven; because in love of neighbor it is shown how one must arrive at love of God.”

When he had said this, he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit.” By breathing upon them he signified that the Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of the Father alone but also his own.

**VERSE 23.**—“Whose sins you forgive,” he says, “they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained.”

@ [Col. 0993D] From Saint Augustine, Tractate 121, number 4.

“Behold the love that is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit: it forgives the sins of those who share in it, but it retains the sins of those who do not share in it. Therefore, immediately after he said, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit,’ he added this concerning the remission and retention of sins.”

It should be understood, however, that those who first possessed the Holy Spirit, so that they might live innocently and benefit some through preaching, received him openly after the Lord’s Resurrection so that they might benefit not a few but many.

**VERSE 24.**—“But Thomas, one of the twelve, who is called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came.”

@ [Col. 0993D] From the cited homily of Saint Gregory, numbers 7–9.

“This one disciple was absent. When he returned, he heard what had happened, but refused to believe what he heard. The Lord came again and offered his side to the unbelieving disciple to touch; he showed his hands and, displaying the scar of his wounds, healed the wound of his unbelief.

What, beloved brothers, what do you observe in this? Do you think it happened by chance that this chosen disciple was absent then; that afterward he came to hear what had happened, hearing he doubted, doubting he touched, and touching he believed? This did not happen by chance but by divine providence.

For heavenly mercy acted wonderfully: when the doubting disciple touched the wounds of the flesh in his Master, it healed in us the wounds of unbelief. Thomas’s unbelief benefited us more toward faith than the faith of the believing disciples, because when he was brought back to faith by touching, our mind, laying aside every doubt, was established in faith.

Thus he allowed the disciple to doubt after his Resurrection, yet did not abandon him in his doubt, just as before his birth he willed Mary to have a betrothed husband, although that man did not come to her marriage. For the disciple who doubted and touched became a witness to the true Resurrection, just as the bridegroom of Christ’s mother had been the guardian of her perfectly preserved virginity.

He touched and exclaimed:

**VERSES 28–29.**—“My Lord and my God.”

Jesus says to him: “Because you have seen me, you have believed.”

When the Apostle Paul says, “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1), it is plainly clear that faith is the proof of things that cannot be seen. For things that are seen no longer require faith but recognition.

Since Thomas saw and touched, why is it said to him, “Because you have seen me, you have believed”? He saw one thing and believed another. Divinity could not be seen by mortal human beings. He therefore saw a human being and confessed God, saying: “My God and my Lord.” By seeing, then, he believed: considering the human being, he proclaimed him to be the true God whom he could not see [Gregory: “who, considering this true human being, proclaimed him God”].

What follows brings great joy:

“Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.”

In this saying we are especially designated: we retain in our mind the one whom we have not seen in the flesh. We are designated, but only if we follow our faith with works. For the one truly believes who practices in action what he believes.”

[“Because he said, ‘Blessed are those who have not seen me and have believed—’”]

@ [Col. 0994D] From Saint Augustine, cited work, number 5.

“He used the verb in the past tense, as though the one thing that was still future was already accomplished in his predestination.” But by these words, as we have said, the faith of the Gentiles is specifically signified.

**VERSE 30.**—“Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples.”

The Evangelist indicates that Jesus performed very many [MS: *plura*, “more”] signs and miracles of salvation and preaching, which were not written down because of the multitude of things that he accomplished.

It follows:

**VERSE 31.**—“But these things are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and so that, believing, you may have life in his name.”

What do those say who assert that Jesus Christ is not the Son of God, when this Evangelist, beloved by God and chosen by God [Alternative: “taught by God”], says that this was his reason for writing the Gospel: so that it might be believed that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God?

The one whose name was announced by the angel and whose name was given as Jesus, when he came to the Virgin, said: “You will bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus” (Luke 1:31). This Jesus, who was born from the Virgin Mary, is the Son of God, as this Evangelist testifies, so that all may be able to have eternal life in his name through this faith.

What should be thought of those who do not believe him to be truly the Son of God but an adopted son, except that perhaps they will never have eternal life? They say that assumption and adoption are the same thing, and that Jesus Christ, insofar as he is human, is necessarily an adopted son because of the assumption of humanity. They do not understand how great is the absurdity that follows from them [MS: *eis*, “them,” for *eos*, “them”].

For if he is adopted because of the assumption, then the person of the Son is adopted, because the Son assumed a human being; and he is then a grandson of God the Father. I think no faithful person is unaware how impious this is.

Let us simply believe that Jesus is the true [Christ], the Son of God in both natures. And just as the Son of God is truly the Son of Man, so the Son of Man is truly the Son of God.

But more on this elsewhere; for now let us consider what follows.

[Col. 0995B]

@ [Col. 0995D] From the same author, Tractate 122, number 1.

“But this chapter seems to indicate the end of this book. Nevertheless, it is next related how the Lord manifested himself at the Sea of Tiberias and, in the catch of fish, commended the mystery of the Church and what the final resurrection of the dead will be [Augustine: “in the final resurrection”].”

Therefore he begins, as it were, from another beginning, because the life of the faithful will then begin from another beginning, when none of the disturbance that we suffer in this life will exist.

Thus he begins by describing how this manifestation took place. For he says:

{640}

## CHAPTER XLIII

He manifests himself again at the Sea of Tiberias to seven disciples in a catch of one hundred fifty-three fish after he had risen from the dead.

[Col. 0995C]

## CHAPTER 21, VERSES 1–3

“He manifested himself again at the Sea of Tiberias; and he manifested himself in this way. Simon Peter, Thomas who is called Didymus, Nathanael who was from Cana of Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two other of his disciples were together. Simon Peter says to them: ‘I am going fishing.’ They say to him: ‘We are coming with you.’ They went out and entered the boat, and that night they caught nothing.”

@ [Col. 0996D] From Saint Gregory, Homily 24, numbers 1–6.

“It may be asked why Peter, who had been a fisherman before his conversion, returned to fishing after his conversion. And since the Truth says, ‘No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God’ (Luke 9:62), why did he resume what he had abandoned?

But if the virtue of discernment is considered [Manuscript and Gregory: “examined”], it is quickly seen that the occupation which had existed without sin before his conversion was not sinful for him to resume after his conversion.

For we know that Peter was a fisherman and Matthew a tax collector. After his conversion Peter returned to fishing, but Matthew did not return to the business of the tax office [Gregory: “did not remain”], because seeking one’s livelihood through fishing is one thing, while increasing one’s activities through the profits of tax collecting [Gregory: “through money”] is another.

There are many occupations that can scarcely, or not at all, be carried on without sins. Therefore, whatever entangles a person in sin must not be returned to after conversion.

It may be asked why, after his Resurrection, the Lord stood on the shore while the disciples were laboring at sea, whereas before his Resurrection he walked upon the waves of the sea before his disciples.

The reason is quickly understood if we consider the cause that was then present. For what does the sea signify except the present age, which strikes itself against the tumult of its circumstances and the waves of corruptible life? And what is signified by the firmness of the shore except that permanence of eternal rest?

Because the disciples were still amid the waves of mortal life, they labored at sea. But because our Redeemer had already passed beyond the corruption of the flesh, after his Resurrection he stood on the shore.

It was as though he were speaking to the disciples through the realities themselves concerning the mystery of his Resurrection, saying: ‘I no longer appear to you in the sea, because I am no longer with you amid the waves of disturbances.’

A great difficulty in fishing was brought upon the disciples so that, when the Master came, a great sublimity of wonder might arise. He immediately said:”

## Verse 6

“Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” Twice in the holy Gospel we read that the Lord commanded nets to be cast for fishing: once before his Passion and once after his Resurrection. But before our Redeemer suffered and rose again, he commands a net to be cast for fishing without specifying whether it should be cast on the right or on the left. After his Resurrection, however, appearing to the disciples, he commands that the net be cast on the right side of the boat.

In that earlier fishing so many were caught that the nets were torn; in this one, many were caught, yet the nets were not torn. Who does not know that the good are represented by the right and the wicked by the left? That earlier fishing, in which no particular side is specified for casting the net, signified the present Church, which gathers good and wicked together. It does not choose those whom it draws in, because it does not know whom it will be able to choose. This fishing, however, which took place after the Lord’s Resurrection, was directed solely to the right, because only the Church of the elect will attain the vision of his glory, and it will possess nothing belonging to left-hand works.

In that earlier fishing the net is torn because of the multitude of fish, since now, together with the elect, so many reprobates enter into the confession of the faith that they even rend the Church itself through heresies. In this fishing, however, many fish, and large ones, are caught, and the net is not torn, because the holy Church of the elect, resting in the continual peace of its author, is no longer lacerated by dissensions.

After such large fish had been caught, “Simon Peter went up and drew the net ashore.” I believe that your Charity already perceives what it means that Peter draws the net ashore. The holy Church was entrusted to him, and to him specifically it was said: “Simon, son of John, do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John 21:15–16). What is later revealed in words is now signified in an action. Since the preacher of the Church separates us from the waves of this worldly life, it is surely necessary that Peter draw the net full of fish to land.

He draws the fish to the firmness of the shore because, through the voice of holy preaching, he displays to the faithful the stability of the eternal homeland. He accomplished this through words, through letters, and he accomplishes it daily through signs of miracles. Whenever we are converted through him to love the repose of eternity, whenever we are separated from the turmoil of earthly things, what else are we than fish cast into the net of faith and drawn to the shore?

But when the net is said to be full of large fish, their number is also added: namely, one hundred and fifty-three. This number is not without a great mystery, and the depth of so great a mystery awaits your attention. For the Evangelist would not have carefully stated the total number unless he had judged it to be full of sacramental meaning.

You know that in the Old Testament every work is prescribed through the commandments of the Decalogue. In the New Testament, however, the power for the same works is given to the faithful through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, multiplied within them. The Prophet announces this when he says:

“The spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord will fill him” (Isaiah 11:2).

But a person receives the power to act through this Spirit only when he acknowledges faith in the Trinity, believing the Father, the Son, and that same Holy Spirit to possess one power and confessing them to be of one substance. Since the seven things mentioned above have been given more fully through the New Testament, while ten are commanded through the Old, all our power and activity can be fully comprehended in the number seventeen.

Let us therefore multiply seventeen by three, and the result is fifty-one. This number, too, is not without a great mystery, since in the Old Testament we read that the fiftieth year was commanded to be called the jubilee year, in which the whole people were to rest from every work (Leviticus 25:11). But true rest lies in unity. One cannot be divided; for where there is the fissure of division, there is no true rest.

Let us therefore multiply fifty-one by three, and the result is one hundred and fifty-three. Since all our activity and power, exercised in the faith of the Trinity, tends toward rest, we multiply seven and ten three times, so that we may arrive at fifty-one. Our true rest exists when we already recognize the very glory of the Trinity, which we firmly hold to be present in the unity of the Godhead. We multiply fifty-one three times and thereby hold the total number of the elect in the heavenly homeland, as though represented by the one hundred and fifty-three fish.

After the Lord’s Resurrection, it was fitting that the net cast should catch as many fish as would signify only the elect citizens of the heavenly homeland.”

There is also another calculation of this number, seven and ten. If you count all the numbers from one through seventeen in this way—one and two make three; add three and the result is six; add four and the result is ten; add five and you have fifteen; and so, with the numbers increasing and being added successively through seventeen—the sum of all these numbers, successively added from one through seventeen, is one hundred and fifty-three.

This calculation corresponds very appropriately to the preceding interpretation, namely, to the law in the number ten and to grace in the number seven. But many other things worthy of wonder can be considered from this, which the shortness of the present time prevents us from saying in full.

But what does it mean that our Redeemer ate a roasted fish after his Resurrection? In another Gospel it is said that he ate a honeycomb together with a roasted fish, while in this one he ate bread with a fish?

“What does the roasted fish signify, then, except Christ who suffered? What does the honeycomb signify, except the sweetness of his divinity? He is a fish because he graciously consented to lie hidden in the waters of the human race and wished to be caught in the snare of our death; and he was, as it were, roasted by tribulation at the time of his Passion.

“But he who consented to become a roasted fish in his Passion became a honeycomb for us in his Resurrection. Or did he who wished the tribulation of his Passion to be signified in the roasted fish wish both natures of his person to be expressed in the honeycomb? A honeycomb contains honey in wax: honey in wax is divinity in humanity.

“This also agrees with the present reading, for he ate fish and bread. He who could be roasted like a fish in respect of his humanity refreshes us with bread in respect of his divinity, for he says: ‘I am the living bread that came down from heaven’ (John 6:41, 52). Thus he ate a roasted fish and bread, showing us through that very food that he endured suffering in our humanity and provided our refreshment from his divinity.

“It should also be noted that the Lord is described as having held his final meal with seven disciples. Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples are mentioned as having been there. Why does he celebrate his final meal with seven disciples, except to declare that only those who are full of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit will be with him in eternal refreshment?

“The whole of this present age also unfolds through seven days, and perfection is often signified by the number seven. Those, therefore, feast at the final meal on the presence of Truth who now transcend earthly things through their pursuit of perfection. The love of this world does not bind them; and although it may in some way disturb them through temptations, it does not blunt their desires once begun.

“Concerning this final meal, John says elsewhere: ‘Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb’ (Revelation 19:9). He says that they are invited not to breakfast but to supper because, naturally, a meal at the end of the day is supper. Those, therefore, who come to the refreshment of heavenly contemplation after the time of this present life has ended are invited not to the Lamb’s breakfast but to his supper.

“This supper is expressed by this final meal, at which seven disciples are said to have been present, because, as we have said, inner refreshment then restores those who now, filled with the sevenfold grace, long for the love of the Spirit.”

---

## From Saint Augustine, Tractate 123, sections 1–3

From Saint Augustine, *Tractate* 123, §§1–3. The Gospel of blessed John the Evangelist concludes with the account of the third occasion on which the Lord manifested himself to his disciples after his Resurrection.

### Verse 12

“Jesus said to them: ‘Come and eat.’ And none of those reclining dared ask him, ‘Who are you?’ knowing that it was the Lord.”

The meaning is this: so evident was the truth, because [Augustine: “by which”] Jesus was appearing to those disciples, that no one dared either to deny it or even to doubt it. For if anyone had doubted, he would certainly have asked. Thus the statement “No one dared ask, ‘Who are you?’” means: no one dared doubt that it was he.

### Verse 13

“Jesus came, took the bread, and gave it to them, and likewise the fish.”

Here, too, what they ate is stated, the significance of which we discussed above. It was also related earlier that, when the disciples came ashore, they saw a charcoal fire laid, with a fish placed upon it, and bread. This should not be understood to mean that the bread, too, had been placed upon the coals; the verb “saw” is merely to be understood as repeated.

If we repeat the verb where it is to be supplied, the whole sentence may be expressed as follows: “They saw a charcoal fire laid, and they saw a fish placed upon it; they also saw bread.” Or better: “They saw a charcoal fire laid, and a fish placed upon it; they also saw bread.”

At the Lord’s command they also brought some of the fish that they themselves had caught. Although the narrator does not explicitly state that they did this, it is not left unmentioned that the Lord commanded it. For he says: “Bring some of the fish that you have just caught.” And who could believe that, when he commanded them, they did not do so?

The Lord therefore prepared a meal for those seven disciples from the fish they had seen placed upon the coals, adding to it some of the fish they had caught, and from the bread which, as has likewise been related, they saw. The roasted fish, as we said, is Christ who suffered; he is also the bread that came down from heaven.

This strengthened the Church so that it might share in everlasting blessedness; [Augustine: “To this is incorporated the Church”], which was also signified in those seven disciples and which, after the labors of this world, will reign with Christ in eternal blessedness.

Here [Augustine: “Here”], then, the Church as it will exist among the good alone is signified by the catch of one hundred and fifty-three fish. In those who believe, hope, and love these things, participation in such great blessedness is demonstrated through this meal.

### Verse 14

“This is now the third time,” he says, “that Jesus was manifested to his disciples after he had risen from the dead.”

We should understand this not as referring to the actual number of manifestations but [editorial supplement: “to”] the days: that is, first, on the day when he rose; then after eight days, when the disciple Thomas saw and believed; and now, when he performed this act concerning the fish. The number of days after which he did this is not stated here.

For on the first day he was seen more than once, as the combined testimony of all the Evangelists demonstrates. But, as has been said, his manifestations are to be counted according to the days, so that this may be the third: the first is to be regarded as one manifestation [Augustine: “is to be regarded, and the same one”] because it occurred on a single day, however often and to whomever he showed himself on the day on which he rose; the second occurred after eight days; and this is the third. Afterward he appeared as often as he wished until the fortieth day, when he ascended into heaven, although not everything he did was written down.”

John himself testifies to this, since he says that Jesus did many things which are not written.

[“We find” is editorially supplied.] By comparing the testimonies of the Gospels, we find that the Lord was seen by human beings ten times, from the first day of his Resurrection until the fortieth day of his Ascension.

First, he appeared to Mary Magdalene, who was weeping at the tomb. Then he appeared to the same Mary and to another woman of the same name as they were returning from the tomb to announce to the disciples what they had seen. Third, he appeared to Simon Peter. Although the place where this occurred is not recorded, we find that it happened from the Gospel of Luke, where the disciples are said to have declared: “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon” (Luke 24:34).

Fourth, he appeared to Cleopas and his companion as he walked with them to Emmaus, where he was recognized in the breaking of bread. They immediately returned to Jerusalem and found the disciples saying: “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon.” For it is not stated elsewhere in full when he appeared to Simon.

Fifth, he appeared to them in the same place, with the doors closed, when Thomas was not present. Sixth, after eight days, when Thomas was with them, the Lord showed him his hands and his side to touch.

Seventh, he appeared to those who were fishing on the Sea of Tiberias and ate with them; there he also asked Peter three times whether he loved him. Eighth, he appeared to the eleven on a mountain in Galilee, as he had appointed for them before his Passion; and he had instructed the women to tell them to go to Galilee, where they would see him.

Ninth, as the eleven were returning, he appeared to them [editorial supplement: “on the mountain”] from which he ascended into heaven, as Mark relates. Tenth, they saw him on that same day, no longer situated on earth but lifted into the air and passing through the heavens, while angels said to them: “He will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

What was done or said at that final meal of our Lord Jesus Christ with his disciples, the Evangelist subsequently explained, saying:

## Chapters 44 and 45

He asks Peter three times, “Do you love me?” because Peter had denied him three times; and, by entrusting the sheep to him three times in succession, he signifies through the extension of his hands that Peter would be crowned with martyrdom by the death of the cross.

“Jesus said to Simon Peter: ‘Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?’” and so forth, up to the words, “he would glorify God.”

### Verse 15

“Jesus said to Simon Peter: ‘Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?’ He said to him: ‘Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.’”

### From a homily of the venerable Bede for the vigil of Saints Peter and Paul

The present question of our Lord shows us the power of perfect love. [Manuscript: “God,” rather than “the Lord.”] Perfect love is that by which we are commanded to love the Lord with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength, and our neighbor as ourselves. Neither of these forms of love can be perfect without the other, because neither can God truly be loved without the neighbor, nor the neighbor truly be loved without God.

Therefore, when the Lord repeatedly asked Peter whether he loved him, and Peter answered that he loved him—God himself bearing witness to it—the Lord added each time, concluding in the same way: “Feed my sheep,” or, “Feed my lambs.” It was as though he were saying openly: This alone is the true proof of an undivided love for the Lord: that you diligently undertake the care and labor required for the brethren.

For whoever neglects to offer his brother the work of mercy that he is able to provide shows that he loves his Creator less than he ought, since he despises his commandments by failing to support his neighbor in need.

Since this charity cannot exist at all without the inspiration of divine grace [Bede: “without the inspiration of the grace of God”], the Lord quietly suggests this when, questioning Peter about it, he calls him “Simon, son of John,” a name by which he never calls him elsewhere [manuscript and Bede: “which nowhere else”]. He says: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?”

Although this may simply be understood as a reference to his earthly father, it is not inappropriate if someone wishes to take the name “John” as mystically indicating the gift of heavenly generation. The apostle John testifies to this when he exhorts us:

“Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God; and everyone who loves is born of God and knows God” (1 John 4:7).

Simon is called “obedient,” while John means “the grace of God.” Therefore it is rightly said to the first of the apostles, when he is questioned about his love, “Simon, son of John,” that is, “obedient through the grace of God,” so that it may be plainly shown to all that the fact that he obeys the Lord’s commands with greater obedience than the others and embraces him with more ardent love is not a matter of human merit but of divine gift.

Thus the apostle Paul, strengthened by the same grace, said: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

The one who is shown to love the Lord more ardently than the others is called the son of John, because the power of that love is received only through the grace of the Spirit.

Yet it should be noted how cautiously and carefully Peter gives testimony concerning his love. When the Lord asked whether he loved him more than the others, he did not dare answer, “You know that I love you more than these.” Instead, in a measured and simple voice he said: “Yes, Lord, you know that I love you.”

This is openly to say: “I certainly know that I love you with an undivided heart, as you yourself know better than I do. But how truly the others love you is unknown to me, while everything is known to you.”

The caution of this answer provides instruction for both our speech and our knowledge [Bede: “thought”]—or our thoughts—so that, following his example, we may learn to presume less upon the purity of our own conscience and to judge less rashly the hidden contents of our brother’s conscience. Especially in doubtful matters, we cannot see the intention or necessity with which we observe others acting.

Peter himself restrained his answer so cautiously in this questioning by the Lord because he remembered that earlier, when the Lord’s Passion was imminent, he had attributed more steadfastness to himself than he possessed. He had promised that he was ready to go with Christ both to prison and to death, although, when danger was at hand, he was not yet capable even of confessing that he knew him or that he had ever been with him.

Instructed, therefore, by his former danger, he spoke more cautiously with the Lord, whom he had learned that the condition of the human conscience [edition: “the constancy of conscience immediately”] was better known to the Lord than the conscience itself could in any way know it. Concerning the hidden things of his brother’s heart he dared to define absolutely nothing. But concerning the integrity of his own love, he offered testimony not from himself alone but also from the Lord who was questioning him: “Yes, Lord,” he said, “you know that I love you.”

O how happy and pure is the conscience that does not fear to say to its Creator, whose eyes see and whose knowledge lays bare all things: “Lord, you know that I love you”! How chaste and holy is the soul that does not doubt that its knowledge lies open before the Lord and knows that it thinks nothing other than what the Lord approves!

In provident compassion, the Lord asks Peter three times whether he loves him, so that by this threefold confession he may release the bonds by which Peter had been bound through his threefold denial. As often as he had denied knowing Christ, terrified by his Passion, so often, restored by his Resurrection, he would testify that he loved him with his whole heart.

In a provident dispensation, after Peter had confessed his love three times, the Lord likewise entrusted his sheep to him three times. It was fitting that as often as Peter had faltered in the shepherd’s faith, so often, with his faith renewed, he should be commanded to care for the members of that shepherd.

For what he says here to him, “Feed my sheep,” is precisely what he had said more openly before his Passion: “But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:33).

To feed Christ’s sheep, therefore, is to strengthen those who believe in Christ so that they do not fall away from the faith, and diligently to work so that they may advance more and more in faith; to assist them as far as one can with secular resources; to correct them, while thinking superfluously about perishable things [manuscript: “to assist them, to correct those who err”]; to console those who mourn; and, with great compassion, to lead everyone to the pastures of eternal life.”

But this must be firmly held in the shepherd’s heart: he must remember that those over whom he presides are not his own but the flock of his Lord, in accordance with what was said to Peter: “If you love me, feed my sheep.” “My,” he says, “not yours. Know that my sheep have been entrusted to you, and remember that, if you love me perfectly, you must govern them as mine. Seek in them my glory, my lordship, and my gains, not your own.”

A clear and distinctive sign of a true shepherd, one whose care for the sheep is sincere, is that he is prepared not only to lack every advantage of temporal life but even to lay down his own life for Christ’s flock.

Therefore, after entrusting his sheep to Peter—that is, the peoples who were to be taught and governed—the Lord immediately adds:

### Verse 18

“Amen, amen, I say to you: when you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish.”

By the stretching out of his hands he indicates the position of his limbs, by which he was to be fastened to the cross. By another’s girding him he expresses the imposition of the bonds by which he was to be restrained by a persecutor. By being led where he did not wish, he indicates the bitterness of death and suffering, which his bodily weakness dreaded, although the spiritual firmness of his soul rejoiced to endure every adversity for the Lord.

For he was not seeking his own will but the will of him who sent him, Christ.

Having first spoken of the feeding of his sheep, the Lord immediately adds, indicating to this first shepherd the triumph of his own Passion as well: “You will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish.”

It was as though he were saying openly: You will clearly prove how great your love for me is when, contending for the life of my little ones, you advance even to death. So that they may be saved both in body and in mind, you will endure [Bede: “you will have endured”] with strong firmness of spirit all the bodily torments that the adversary is pleased to inflict.

The Evangelist also indicates this subsequently when he says: “He said this to signify by what death he would glorify God.” Peter glorified God by his death when, through this testimony, he showed everyone how greatly God ought to be revered and loved, since, when given the choice, he preferred to undergo the torment of the cross rather than cease preaching the heavenly word.

## Chapter 46

The Lord says to Peter, “Follow me,” up to the words, “and we know that his testimony is true.”

### Verse 20

“Jesus said to Peter: ‘Follow me.’ Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who had reclined at the supper upon his breast.”

### From a homily of the venerable Bede for the day of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist

The most blessed Evangelist and Apostle John commends to us the privilege of that exceptional love by which he deserved to be honored by the Lord above the others. He commends the testimony of his Gospel, founded upon divine truth, which no believer is permitted to doubt. He commends the peaceful release from his flesh, which he received when the Lord visited him in a special manner.

After the Lord Jesus signified to Peter by what death he would glorify God, he immediately added: “Follow me.” It was as though he were saying openly: Since I myself was not afraid first to undergo the punishment of the cross for your redemption, why are you afraid to suffer the cross for confessing my name? You will be glorified by an even more glorious crown of martyrdom the more closely you follow your teacher on the path by which that crown is won.

The Evangelist does not add what the Lord and the disciples did after these words had been spoken. Yet he indicates it by what follows: “Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them.”

It is evident that, after [editorial supplement: “when”] saying to Peter, “Follow me”—that is, “Imitate me by suffering the cross”—the Lord rose from the place of the meal and began to depart. Peter followed him also in the movement of his feet, wishing to fulfill what he had heard: “Follow me.” The disciple whom Jesus loved followed as well. He did not think that he should be excluded from following Christ, since he knew that Christ had embraced him with no less grace of love.

It is not incredible that both disciples followed the Lord’s footsteps bodily because they did not yet understand what was signified by his command that Peter follow him.

It is well known to your Fraternity who that disciple whom Jesus loved was: John himself, who wrote this Gospel. For this reason he preferred to indicate his person by the circumstances of events rather than identify him by his proper name.

Jesus loved him—not as though he alone, to the exclusion of the others, were loved, but as one among those whom he loved, whom the special privilege of chastity had made worthy of a more abundant love. He proves that he loved them all when, before his Passion, he says to them: “As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you; remain in my love” (John 15:9).

But he loves this one above all because, chosen by him as a virgin, he remained a virgin forever. History relates that the Lord called him when he wished to marry and that, because he had drawn him away from carnal pleasure, he endowed him with the superior sweetness of his own love.

Finally, while dying on the cross, he entrusted his mother to this disciple, so that a virgin might care for a virgin. And when the Lord himself had ascended into heaven after his death and Resurrection, his mother would not lack a son whose chaste life would protect her through chaste service.

Blessed John also adds another indication of his identity, saying: “The one who had reclined at the supper upon his breast, and who had said, ‘Lord, who is it that will betray you?’”

The preceding passages of this Gospel show more fully how this happened. At the supper which the Savior held with his disciples as his final meal before the Passion, at which he washed their feet and entrusted to them the mysteries of his body and blood for celebration, the disciple whom he loved reclined upon his breast.

When he had said to them, “Amen, amen, I say to you, one of you will betray me,” that disciple, at Peter’s prompting, asked him: “Lord, who is it?” The Lord answered: “It is the one to whom I shall give the dipped bread.”

The fact that this disciple reclined upon the breast of the Master was a sign not only of present love but also of a future mystery. Even then the Gospel was being signified—namely, that the same disciple would write it and that it would contain, more abundantly and profoundly than the other pages of Holy Scripture, the mysteries of the divine majesty.

Since all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in the breast of Jesus (Colossians 2:3), it is fitting that the one whom he endows above the others with the greater gift of singular wisdom and knowledge should recline upon his breast.

We know that the other Evangelists spoke more about the miracles of our Savior and less about his divinity. John, however, writing very little about his human actions, devoted himself rather to explaining the mysteries of the divine nature. He clearly suggests how many streams of heavenly doctrine flowed from the breast of Jesus, streams from which he drew what he would pour forth for us.

The text continues:

### Verse 21

“When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus: ‘Lord, what about this man?’”

Since blessed Peter had heard that he would glorify God through the suffering of the cross, he also wished to know concerning his brother and fellow disciple by what death he himself would pass into everlasting life.

### Verse 22

“Jesus said to him: ‘If I will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me.’”

“I do not wish him to be brought to perfection through the suffering of martyrdom,” the Lord says, “but to await the final day without the violence of a persecutor, when I myself will come and receive him into an eternal dwelling of blessedness. And what is that to you? You must simply remember that you are to follow my footsteps by undertaking the cross.”

At that time the brethren interpreted the Lord’s answer as though John would never die. John himself took care to show that this was not what it meant. After saying that the report had gone out among the brethren that the disciple would not die, he carefully added:

### Verse 23

“Jesus did not say to him that he would not die, but: ‘If I will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?’”

We should not therefore suppose that the disciple did not die in the flesh, since the Lord did not foretell that this would happen to him. The Psalmist says: “Who is the man who lives and will not see death?” (Psalm 88:49).

Rather, the meaning should be understood as follows: after the other disciples of Christ had been brought to perfection through suffering, John awaited in the peace of the Church the coming of the heavenly calling. This is what Jesus meant by saying: “I will that he remain until I come.”

This does not mean that John had not previously endured many labors and afflictions for the Lord, but that he would complete his final old age in peace, with the churches of Christ throughout Asia, which he governed, already firmly and widely established.

In the Acts of the Apostles, he is also found [manuscript: “when”] to have been scourged with the other apostles, who went away rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus (Acts 5:41). Ecclesiastical history also relates that he was sent by the emperor Domitian into a vessel of boiling oil. Yet, protected by divine grace, he emerged as unharmed as he had been free from the corruption of carnal desire.

Not long afterward, because of his unconquerable steadfastness in preaching the Gospel, he was banished by the same emperor into exile on the island of Patmos. Although deprived there of human consolation, he deserved to be strengthened by frequent consolation through divine vision and speech.

Finally, in that place he wrote with his own hand the Apocalypse that the Lord revealed to him concerning the present and future condition of the Church.

It is therefore clear that the promise that he would remain until the Lord came does not mean that he would live in the world without the labor of struggle. Rather, it means that he would pass from the world without the pain of martyrdom.

For, as we find in the writings of the Fathers, when he was worn out by advanced age and knew that the day of his departure was near, he called his disciples together and, through exhortatory admonitions [Bede: “after admonitions”] and the celebration of Masses, bade them his final farewell. Then, descending into the place dug for his burial and offering a prayer, he was gathered to his fathers, as free from the pain of death as he was found to be untouched by the corruption of the flesh.

Thus that truthful saying of the Savior was fulfilled: he willed that John remain until he himself came.

We may also understand mystically that, in what the Lord foretold to Peter and John and in what occurred to them, two lives of the Church are represented: the active and the contemplative. The active life is the common way of life for the people of God; only a very few—and in this [Bede: “and this”] the more exalted after the perfection of pious action—ascend to the contemplative life.

When the Lord says to Peter, “You will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish,” he expresses the perfection of the active way of life, which is accustomed to be tested by the fire of temptations. Therefore elsewhere he speaks of it more openly: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matthew 5:10).

To this he rightly adds: “Follow me.” For, according to Peter’s own words: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we might follow in his footsteps” (1 Peter 2:21).

But when he says of John, “I will that he remain until I come,” he indicates the state of contemplative virtue. Unlike the active life, which ends in death, the contemplative life is to be completed more perfectly after death, when the Lord comes.

Active labor comes to an end with death, to receive an eternal reward afterward. But contemplative happiness, which begins here, is perfected there without end, when the presence of the heavenly citizens and of the Lord himself will be seen not, as now, through a mirror and in an enigma, but face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12).

The text continues:

### Verse 24

“This is the disciple who testifies to these things and who wrote these things; and we know that his testimony is true.”

Here blessed John clearly identifies his person by his office, though he avoids identifying it by name. We must not pass over without attention the words: “Who testifies to these things and wrote these things.”

He testified by preaching the words of God [manuscript and Bede: *verbo Dei*, “by the word of God”]; he testified by writing; he testified again by teaching the same things that he had written; and he continues to testify even now by opening the Gospel he composed for reading in the churches.

[Note: What follows in brackets is also inserted above, col. 740, in the dedicatory Epistle to Gisla and Richtruda.]

[For from the time of the Lord’s Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension into heaven until the final years of the emperor Domitian—about sixty-five years—he preached the word of God without any aid of writing. But when he was sent into exile by Domitian, who was the second persecutor of Christians after Nero, heretics broke into the Church like wolves into sheepfolds abandoned by their shepherd: Marcion, Cerinthus, Ebion, and the other Antichrists, who denied that Christ had existed before Mary. They stained the simplicity of the evangelical faith with perverse doctrine.

But after Domitian’s death, when the pious emperor Nerva permitted him to return to Ephesus, almost all the bishops of Asia at that time, together with embassies from many churches, compelled him to speak more profoundly about Christ’s co-eternal divinity with the Father. For they thought that in the writings of the three evangelists—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—they already possessed sufficient testimony concerning his humanity and concerning what he had accomplished as a human being.

He replied that he would do this only if, after a fast had been proclaimed, they all prayed together to the Lord that he might be able to write something worthy of him. When this had been done, and he had been instructed by revelation and filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, he suddenly dispelled all the darkness of the heretics by the unveiled light of truth: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”]

And, making the whole course of his discourse correspond to these opening words, he taught with the clearest assertion that our Lord Jesus Christ was truly human, truly made temporally from a human being, and likewise truly God, truly born eternally from God the Father, and always existing with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Indeed, he disclosed all the secrets of divine truth and true divinity as fully as no other mortal was permitted to do.

This privilege was rightly reserved for a virgin, so that he might approach the investigation of the mysteries of the incorruptible Word not only with an incorrupt heart but also with an incorrupt body. He himself also took care to show how no one ought to doubt the truth of his words. After saying, “This is that disciple who bears witness concerning these things and wrote them,” he immediately added: “And we know that his testimony is true.”

Since, then, we too, together with the other faithful, know that his testimony is true, let us take care in all things that, by understanding what he taught with right faith and practicing it through right action, we may attain the everlasting gifts he promised.

---

## SUPPLEMENT FROM THE MANUSCRIPT OF ST. EMMERAM

### Verse 25

“But there are also many other things that Jesus did; if they were written down one by one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that would have to be written.”

[Col. 1007C] From St. Augustine, Tractate 124, §8. The statement that the world could not contain the books should not be understood in terms of spatial extent: how could they be written in it if it did not bear the writings? Rather, perhaps they could not be comprehended by the capacity of readers, although, without compromising the truth of the events, words often seem to exceed belief.

This does not happen when something obscure or doubtful is explained by supplying its cause and reason, but when something evident is either magnified or diminished. Nevertheless, one does not depart from the path of signifying the truth, because words exceed the thing indicated in such a way that it is clear the speaker does not deceive. The speaker knows how far one should believe, and in speaking either diminishes or magnifies something beyond what ought to be believed.

The teachers of both Greek and Latin literature call this manner of speech by the Greek name *hyperbole*. This mode of expression occurs here and in several other passages of divine Scripture, as in: “They have set their mouth against heaven” (Ps. 7:9); and: “The crown of the hair of those who walk in their sins” (Ps. 67:22). The holy Scriptures contain many such expressions, just as they contain other tropes—that is, other modes of speech.

I would discuss these at greater length, were I not compelled, since the Evangelist brings his Gospel to an end, to bring my own discourse to an end as well.

**Here ends Book VII.**

# SEVENTH OPUSCULUM

## TREATISE OF MASTER ALBINUS ON THE THREE EPISTLES OF ST. PAUL THE APOSTLE: TO TITUS, TO PHILEMON, AND TO THE HEBREWS

## PRELIMINARY NOTICE

A highly trustworthy writer, contemporary with the life of the blessed Flavius Alcuin, testifies in these words that Alcuin wrote commentaries on four Epistles of the holy Apostle Paul: “He also wrote on four Epistles of Paul, namely, to the Ephesians, to Titus, to Philemon, and to the Hebrews.”

Certain later writers—Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca Sancta*, book III; Trithemius, *De Script. Eccles.* and book II of *De Script. Ord. S. Ben.*, chapter 36; John Bale, *Cent. II Script. Brit.*; and Antonio Possevino, *Apparatus Sacer*, volume I—report that Alcuin wrote fourteen books in all, on all the Epistles of St. Paul. But they give no indication of where they learned this, or what the character of those books or commentaries was. This itself sufficiently reveals that none of them had either seen those commentaries or carefully determined to which author the works they had seen should be attributed. Otherwise, as they do with other works of Alcuin that they know well, they would at least have supplied their beginnings.

We must therefore follow the testimony of the writer of Alcuin’s Life, who was almost his contemporary, and conclude that Alcuin commented on some, but not all, of the Epistles of St. Paul.

This work remained unknown until the present day, and has not yet appeared in complete form. In the distinguished library of the celebrated abbey of Einsiedeln there is preserved a ninth-century parchment manuscript, marked B, 9, containing: “Treatises of Master Albinus on three Epistles of the holy Apostle Paul, namely, to Titus, to Philemon, and to the Hebrews.” That is the title written there by the same hand that wrote the entire book.

The treatise on the Epistle to the Ephesians is therefore missing, although it is the first among the four listed by the author of the Life. The reason for this deficiency in the Einsiedeln manuscript cannot be determined. Perhaps this treatise on the Epistle to the Ephesians was published separately by Alcuin from the other three. Certainly it is listed separately in an old catalogue of the celebrated library of Fulda, cited by Schannat, part I of *Historia Fuldensis*, p. 64.

We therefore received these three treatises from the aforementioned Einsiedeln library through the kindness of the most distinguished Dom P. Meinrad Prenzer, a member of that principal monastery, and transcribed them from the manuscript codex generously communicated to us. Here we now make them available to scholars as the genuine and hitherto unpublished work of our Alcuin, following the testimony of a nearly contemporary codex, confirmed by a writer of the same period.

Moreover, just as Alcuin in his other commentaries on the books of sacred Scripture drew little from his own invention but extracted most of his material from the writings of other holy Fathers long approved by the Church, as we have already noted several times, so too he compiled the treatises before us from the same sources: the first two from the commentaries of St. Jerome, and the last from the homilies of St. John Chrysostom on the Epistle to the Hebrews. In that work he followed the version of Mutianus the scholastic, as it appears at the beginning of volume XII of the works of St. John Chrysostom, edited by Dom Bernard de Montfaucon.

We have therefore compared the text with the published works of those holy Fathers, distinguishing variant readings and Alcuin’s additions and interpolations with brackets for the convenience of readers.

Furthermore, it will not be inappropriate to add to these treatises certain fragments transcribed from a very ancient manuscript in the library of the illustrious metropolitan chapter of Salzburg, marked no. 71. There brief Expositions of several individual passages from the Epistles of the holy Apostle Paul—to the Corinthians, to the Ephesians, to Titus, and to the Hebrews—are attributed to Albinus.

I have no doubt that this Albinus is our Alcuin. The age of the manuscript agrees with his period, and its style resembles Alcuin’s style as closely as one egg resembles another. Someone may object, however, that this exposition does not agree with the exposition of the same passages found in the earlier treatises on the Epistles to Titus and to the Hebrews.

I reply that the difference consists only in saying almost the same thing in another manner, as will be evident to anyone who compares them. It therefore appears that these fragments were not excerpted from the earlier commentaries, but perhaps are individual responses to questions posed to him about those passages, questions of the kind that were frequently put to him.

# EXPOSITION OF PAUL’S EPISTLE TO TITUS

## PREFACE

The Apostle writes this Epistle from the city of Nicopolis, situated on the Actian coast, to Titus, his disciple and son in Christ, whom he had left on the island of Crete to instruct the churches. For he did not want the Cretans to remain in their ancient error during his absence, since the seeds of idolatry had first sprouted among them.

When he asked Titus to come to him because of the needs of preaching, he ordered Artemas or Tychicus to come there, so that through their teaching and consolation the Cretans might be strengthened.

# CHAPTER ONE

## Verse 1

“Paul, a servant of God, but an apostle of Jesus Christ.”

[From St. Jerome’s Commentary on the Epistle to Titus.] In the Epistle to the Romans he began as follows: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle.” Here, however, he calls himself a servant of God, but an apostle of Jesus Christ.

For if the Father and the Son are one, and whoever believes in the Son believes in the Father, then the servitude of the Apostle Paul [and of all the saints] must likewise be referred indifferently either to the Father or to the Son, [because the Father and the Son are one God and are to be worshiped with one service. This service is the service of charity, not of the letter of the law, which kills, but of the Spirit, who gives life.]

That person is a servant of God who is not a servant of sin, because everyone who commits sin is a servant of sin (John 8:34).

“But an apostle of Jesus Christ.” Paul claims great authority for himself among Christians. He prefaced his name with the title “apostle of Christ,” so that by the authority of the name itself he might awe those who would read him [and arouse them to fear his preaching], indicating that all who believed in Christ ought to be subject to him.

“According to the faith of God’s elect and the knowledge of the truth.” This must be referred back to what he said above: “Paul, a servant of God, but an apostle of Jesus Christ.” “According to the faith of God’s elect”—that is, of those who are not merely called but chosen.

There is also great diversity among the elect themselves, according to the variety of their works, thoughts, and words. [Therefore he added: “According to the knowledge of the truth”—that is, those who possess knowledge of the truth in accordance with faith. So that both might agree—true faith and knowledge of the truth—he added: “Which is according to godliness.” For some truth is not according to godliness, such as grammar, dialectic, geometry, and arithmetic.] These disciplines do indeed possess true knowledge for speaking correctly, but that knowledge is not knowledge of godliness.

Knowledge of godliness consists in knowing the law of God, understanding the prophets, believing the Gospel, not being ignorant of the sayings of the apostles, [and knowing how good it is to love God with all one’s heart, with all one’s soul, and with all one’s strength.]

This truth, whose knowledge is according to godliness, is established in the hope of eternal life (verse 2), because it immediately grants the reward of immortality to the person who has come to know it. Without godliness, however, knowledge of the truth gives pleasure for the present but has no eternal reward.

This life was promised by God, who does not lie, before the eternal ages, and he manifested it in its proper times in Christ Jesus (verse 3). To whom did he promise it beforehand, and whom did he later make manifest, except his Wisdom, who was always with the Father, when she rejoiced over the completed world and delighted in the sons of men, promising that all who would believe in her would possess eternal life?

Before the world laid its foundations, before he spread out the seas, established the mountains, suspended the heavens, and made the earth solid by casting down its mass, God made this promise—God in whom there is no falsehood. This is not because he could lie, if he did not wish [Jerome: and does not wish] to break forth into words of falsehood, but because, since he is the Father of truth [and himself truthful], he can contain no falsehood in himself.

It does not seem irrelevant to touch briefly on why the Apostle’s words call God alone truthful and every human being a liar. Unless I am mistaken, the answer is analogous to the question of how God alone is said to possess immortality, even though he created angels and many rational creatures to whom he gave immortality.

In the same way, he is said to be alone truthful—not because others are not immortal or lovers of truth, but because he alone is immortal and true by nature. The others obtain immortality and truth through his generosity. It is one thing to be true [by nature and] through oneself; it is another that what one has should be in the power of the giver.

Nor should we pass over in silence how God, who does not lie, promised eternal life before the eternal ages. From the time when, according to the historical account of Genesis, the world was made, and times were established through the alternation of nights and days, months and years, times have passed in this course and wheel of the world; they come, and either are future or have been past.

Thus certain philosophers do not think that the present exists as time, but only the past or the future, because everything we say, do, or think either passes away as it occurs or, if it has not yet happened, is awaited [Jerome: we await it].

Before these times of the world, therefore, we must believe that there was a certain eternity of ages in which the Father always existed with the Son and the Holy Spirit. To put it so, God’s one time is the whole of eternity. Indeed, there are innumerable times, since he himself is infinite and, existing before times, surpasses every time.

Six thousand years have not yet been completed since the beginning of our world. How many eternities and how many ages, then, must we suppose existed before the origins of the ages, in which angels, thrones, dominions, [and] the other powers served the Creator [Jerome: served God] and, without the alternation or measurement of times, endured at God’s command?

[It is permissible to doubt whether St. Jerome is reporting the opinion concerning the creation of angels before the formation of this visible world from his own view or from the thought of other ancient writers. See his Epistle 18 to Damasus, §7. The opposing doctrine, supported by the authority of many more Fathers of the Church, prevailed: namely, that the angels were created together with the earth and the first light on the first day of the world. Veronese edition.]

Before all these times, then—times that neither speech can express, nor the mind comprehend, nor silent thought dare approach—God the Father promised that his Word, his Wisdom, and the life of those who would believe would come into the world.

Pay careful attention to the text and the order of the reading: eternal life, which God who does not lie promised before the eternal ages, is none other than the Word of God.

“For he manifested,” he says, “his Word in its proper times”—that is, the eternal life he promised is his Word, which in the beginning was with the Father; “and the Word was God”; “and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

That the Word of God, namely Christ himself, is life is also testified elsewhere when he says: “I am the life” (John 14:6). This life is not brief or confined within certain periods, but perpetual and eternal. It was manifested in the last ages through the preaching entrusted to Paul, the teacher and instructor of the Gentiles, so that it might be announced in the world and made known to human beings, according to the command of God our Savior, who willed us to be saved by fulfilling what he had promised.

[“In the preaching entrusted to me according to the command of our Savior God.” We read in the Acts of the Apostles how Paul was suddenly called while traveling on the road to Damascus, and how it was said concerning Ananias: “He is a chosen vessel for me” (Acts 9:15). Again: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas” (ibid. 13:2). This is the Savior’s command: that they preach Christ to the Gentiles.]

The Word—

[The beginning of the Epistle seems to be omitted in the manuscript. It should be supplied from Jerome’s text: “The Apostle writes to Titus, his dearest son.” For the wisdom and teaching with which Titus instructed the churches of Christ made him the Apostle’s own son and separated him from the company of all others. Let us see what follows: “According to the common faith.” Did he call the faith common to all who believed in Christ, or only his own faith and Titus’s? It seems better to me that the faith of the Apostle Paul and Titus was called common than that of all believers, among whom faith could not be common because of the variety of their minds.]

Finally, the preface of the Epistle and the Apostle’s greeting to Titus are completed with this conclusion:

“Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior” (verse 4)—whether this means that both grace and peace come from God the Father as well as from Christ Jesus, so that both may be understood as given by both; or whether grace is referred to the Father and peace to the Son.

“For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what was lacking” (verse 5). [It was the dignity of the Apostle to lay the foundation, like a wise architect; it was the task of Titus and his other disciples to build upon it.]

After Paul had softened the hard hearts of the Cretans toward faith in Christ and subdued them both by his speech and by signs—

[Jerome adds: “and taught them to believe not in their native Jupiter, but in God the Father and in Christ.”]

—so that they would believe in God the Father and in Christ, he left Titus, his disciple, in Crete to strengthen the beginnings of the nascent Church and to correct whatever appeared to be lacking. He himself proceeded to other nations, in order to lay the foundation of Christ anew among them.

Although the Cretans had been corrected by the Apostle, they still needed correction. Everything that is corrected is imperfect.

“And appoint presbyters in each city, as I also appointed you.” [Some bishops do not examine the merits of individuals, but are enticed either by their office or bound to them by blood.]

It is therefore evident that those who, disregarding the Apostle’s law, wish to confer ecclesiastical rank on someone not because of merit but out of favor act against Christ. Through his Apostle, Christ later explained what sort of person should be appointed presbyter in the Church.

[Above all these things, the greatest evil is committed by those who obtain clerical office through gifts. Blessed Peter, the prince of the apostles, terribly strikes all such people in the person of Simon Magus at the beginning of the Church.]

“For a bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward.” A presbyter, then, is the same as a bishop.

[Concerning this opinion of St. Jerome regarding the dignity of bishops over presbyters, see his Epistle 146 to Evangelus and the annotation of the Veronese editor.]

Before divisions arose in ecclesiastical religion at the devil’s instigation, and people began saying, “I am of Paul,” “I am of Apollo,” and “I am of Cephas” (1 Cor. 1:12), the churches were governed by the common counsel of the presbyters.

After each person began to regard those whom he had baptized as his own rather than Christ’s, it was decreed throughout the world that one of the presbyters should be chosen and placed over the others, so that the entire care of the Church might belong to him and the seeds of schism might be removed.

[This can be proved from other Epistles of the same Apostle, or even from the Acts of the Apostles, where it is said that Paul summoned the presbyters from Ephesus.]

To them, among other things, he later said: “Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops, to shepherd the Church of the Lord, which he acquired through his own blood” (Acts 20:28).

[Those whom he previously calls presbyters he now calls bishops.]

And Peter, who received his name from the firmness of his faith, says in his Epistle: “Therefore I appeal to the presbyters among you, as a fellow presbyter and a witness of Christ’s sufferings: shepherd the flock of the Lord that is among you” (1 Pet. 5:1).

[Formerly every presbyter was rightly called a bishop; now, however, every bishop may be called a presbyter, but not every presbyter a bishop. For, in order to exclude the beginnings of dissension, all the care of the churches was delegated to one person, as to a father, so that he might love and govern those subject to him as sons—not with the power of a tribune, but with paternal affection. Likewise, as sons, the individual ranks in the churches should honor their bishops.]

Let us therefore see what kind of presbyter or bishop should be ordained.

## Verses 6–7

“If anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, not accused of debauchery or not subject to sin. For a bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward.”

First, such a steward of Christ’s Church must be blameless, the quality that he calls “irreproachable” in the case of Timothy. For how can someone preside over the Church and remove evil from its midst if he himself has fallen into a similar offense? Or with what freedom can he correct a sinner when he knows that he has committed the very things he censures in another [Jerome: while silently answering himself that he has committed the same things he rebukes]?

When he says “the husband of one wife,” we must understand this [as meaning that the person chosen for the episcopate must have an honorable marriage and must not dare to serve at God’s altar while stained by promiscuous lust]. Yet we should not think in every respect that every monogamous man is better than a bigamist. Rather, a person may exhort others to monogamy and continence if he presents his own example in his teaching [Jerome: if he presents it].

[Some understand the Apostle’s command, “the husband of one wife,” in this way: he is to be a teacher of the Catholic Church, so that he is not carried outside it through heretical perversions into the brothels of various sects. Some also think that, according to this apostolic judgment, bishops are not permitted to move from one church or city to another for the sake of profit, since it is rare for anyone to wish to move from a larger and wealthier church to a smaller and poorer one.]

“Having faithful children, not accused of debauchery or not subject to sin.” The righteous person is not therefore defiled by the vices of his children; rather, the Apostle preserves for the head of the Church the freedom [to correct others].

[How can someone remove the splinter from another’s house [supplement: remove it] who has a beam in his own house, in the sins of his children? The bishop must be such that, because of the vices of his children, he is not afraid to rebuke outsiders, lest some silent brother answer him: “Why do you not take care to correct your own children?” If the sins of children prevent a righteous man from becoming a bishop, how much more must his own sins remove him from Christ’s altar?]

Finally, it must be said that in Scripture sons are to be understood as λογισμοί (*logismoi*), that is, thoughts, and daughters as πράξεις (*praxeis*), that is, deeds. The bishop now being commanded is therefore one who has both thoughts and deeds under his control, who truly believes in Christ, and who is stained by no blemish of creeping vices.

“A bishop must therefore be blameless, as God’s steward.” Among stewards, then, one must be found faithful—not eating and drinking with the drunkards and striking the master’s [the Lord’s] male and female servants, but cautiously awaiting the coming of the Lord [Jerome: God] and giving food to his fellow servants at the proper time [the food of Catholic doctrine].

The bishop and presbyter should know that the people are fellow servants with him, not slaves.

[Therefore he should not oppress them as worthless slaves, but educate them with complete charity as sons.]

“Not arrogant”—that is, not swollen with pride or pleased with himself because he is a bishop, but embracing [good work and] seeking what benefits the greatest number.

“Not irascible” [that is, not moved by a light wind like a leaf hanging on a branch].

Indeed, nothing is uglier than a furious teacher. [A person who becomes angry occasionally is not thereby irascible; rather, one is called irascible who is frequently overcome by this passion.]

“Not addicted to wine.” For the moment it is enough to say that, according to the Apostle, there is debauchery in wine; wherever there are satiety and drunkenness, lust holds sway.

We are surprised, however, that the Apostle condemned drunkenness in bishops or presbyters, since the ancient law also commanded priests, whenever they entered the temple to minister to God, not to drink wine at all (Lev. 10).

[It also commanded Nazirites to abstain from all wine and strong drink as long as they were growing their sacred hair (Num. 6).]

“Not violent.” Taken simply, this instruction edifies the hearer by teaching him not readily to stretch out his hand to strike [or break out into violence with weapons]. Considered more deeply, it edifies still better: the bishop must do nothing that would offend the minds of those who understand and observe him, but must be gentle in speech and honorable in conduct, lest he destroy someone whom he could have instructed through moderation of life and words.

“Not greedy for sordid gain,” and so forth.

[We supply these words, which are absent from the manuscript, by conjecture for the completeness of the sense.]

The desire for sordid gain consists in thinking more about present things than future ones. A bishop who wishes to imitate the Apostle, having food and clothing, ought to be content with these alone (1 Tim. 6). “Those who serve at the altar should live from the altar” (1 Cor. 9). He says, “Let them live,” not “let them become rich.”

Thus far the Apostle has taught what a bishop or presbyter ought not to possess. Now, by contrast, what he ought to possess is explained.

## Verse 8

“But hospitable, kind.”

Above all, hospitality is prescribed [Jerome: announced] to the future bishop. If everyone desires to hear the Gospel’s words, “I was a stranger and you welcomed me” (Matt. 25:35), how much more should this be true of a bishop, whose house ought to be the common lodging of all [and in which strangers and visitors should be received with such kindness that, in humble service, even their feet are washed]?

“Chaste, just, holy.” If laypeople are commanded to abstain from intercourse with their wives [Jerome: from intercourse with wives] for the sake of prayer, what should we think of a bishop, who is to offer to God every day, for his own sins and those of the people, the spotless [Jerome: undefiled] sacrifices [of holy prayers]?

For the priest Abimelech refused to give David and his young men the bread of the Presence unless he learned that the young men were clean from women—not from other men’s women, but from their own wives.

The difference between the bread of the Presence and the body of Christ is as great as that between a shadow and bodies, between an image and reality, between representations of future things and the things themselves that were prefigured through those representations.

Just as hospitality and kindness must therefore be especially present in a bishop, so also must chastity be present in him in a distinctive way. To put it so, priestly purity requires that the mind preparing Christ’s body be free not only from unclean action but also from unlawful touch and errant thought [Jerome: from the casting of the eye and the error of thought].

The bishop must also be just and holy, exercising justice among the people over whom he presides and showing no partiality in judgment, [but discerning—perhaps: deciding—what is just for every person].

“Holy” refers to his own life: he must teach the people entrusted to him not only by words but also by example.

(Verse 9.) “Holding fast to the trustworthy word that accords with the teaching.”

The bishop must be temperate not only in carnal desire but also in moderation of speech, and above all in thought, so that he has control over what he thinks, what he says, and what he does.

Finally, he must hold fast to the trustworthy word that accords with the teaching, so that, just as the word of God is trustworthy and worthy of complete acceptance, he may show himself to be such that everything he says is considered worthy of belief and his words are a standard of truth.

“So that he may be able to exhort with sound doctrine and refute those who contradict.”

That is, he must be able to console those who are shaken by the storms of this age and, through sound doctrine [that is, Catholic doctrine], destroy heretical perversions.

Doctrine is called sound in distinction from weak and unhealthy doctrine. He must also be such that he can [with a free voice] refute those who contradict—heretics, Jews, or the wise men of this age.

The preceding qualities that he assigned to the virtues of a bishop concern [honorable] life. But what he says here—“so that he may be able to console with sound doctrine and refute those who contradict”—refers to [perfect] knowledge.

For if the bishop’s life alone is holy, he can benefit himself by living in that way. But if he is also educated in doctrine and speech, he can instruct others as well—not merely his own people, by instructing and teaching them, but also his opponents, by striking back against them.

## Verses 10–11

“For there are also many disobedient people, empty talkers, and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision. They must be refuted, for they overturn entire households, teaching things that ought not to be taught for the sake of sordid gain.”
