The person who is to become the head of the Church must join eloquence with integrity of life, so that his works do not remain silent without speech, and his words do not blush because of works that fail to support them [Jerome: because of deficient works].

[There are very many, and not merely a few, who corrupt the good seed of the Word of God through empty persuasion. They also try to confirm perverse teachings by sentences from the sacred Scriptures. Therefore the teacher of the Church ought to study the holy Scriptures diligently, so that, if he is struck on the right cheek, he may immediately offer the other cheek to the one striking him.]

These are the Jews of the circumcision, who at that time tried [Jerome: were trying] to subvert the nascent Church of Christ and introduce the legal commands—[circumcision, Sabbaths, and the other precepts of the law].

The teacher of the Church, to whom the souls of the people have been entrusted, ought to overcome such people by the reasoning of the Scriptures and impose silence upon them by the weight of his testimony. They overturn not one or a few households, but entire households together with their masters and families, teaching distinctions among foods [although all things are clean for the clean].

But because their god is their belly, they wish to make their own disciples for the sake of sordid gain, so that, as teachers, they may be fed [Jerome: sustained] [and honored] by their followers.

Every heretic, therefore, who deceives people through certain tricks and is himself deceived, speaks what ought not to be spoken for the sake of sordid gain. [He is a perverse profiteer, aiming at the death of souls rather than at their life.] By contrast, whoever rebukes and corrects his erring brother according to the Gospel [and corrects him] has gained him. What greater gain could there be, or what could be more precious, than to gain a human soul for God?

(Verse 12.) “One of them, their own prophet, said: ‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies.’”

Observe that this can be read in two ways. The statement “one of them, their own prophet,” may be joined with what precedes: “For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what was lacking,” [and the following words may be understood in that connection:] “One of them, their own prophet,” that is, one of the Cretans.

Or it may be joined with what is nearer to it, so that we read as follows: “There are also many who are disobedient, empty talkers, and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision. They must be restrained—those many disobedient, empty talkers, and deceivers, together with those of the circumcision—because they overturn entire households, teaching things that ought not to be taught for the sake of sordid gain.” [Of such people—namely, those who teach for the sake of sordid gain—] “one of them, their own prophet, said”:

Thus, the expression “their own prophet” does not refer specifically to the Jews, and especially to those of the circumcision, but to the many who are disobedient, empty talkers, and deceivers. Since they were in Crete, they must of course be considered Cretans [Jerome: who were certainly].

That verse is said to be found in the *Oracles* of Epimenides, the Cretan poet. Paul playfully called him a prophet for the present purpose, because such Christians deserved to have such prophets, just as there were prophets of Baal and of the idols, as is read in the Books of Kings.

Finally, the book itself bears the title *Oracles*. Since it seemed to promise something divine, I think the Apostle consulted it to see what pagan divination promised, and then used the verse at the appropriate time when writing to Titus, who was in Crete, in order to crush the false teachers of the Cretans by the authority of the island’s own native author [Jerome: to convict them by the teacher of the island].

[The same Apostle is found to have done this elsewhere: in the Acts of the Apostles, for example, he encountered an inscription concerning an unknown god and drew from it the occasion for his preaching.]

[Col. 1017C] VERSE 13.—“The testimony,” he says, “is true”: not the whole poem from which the testimony was taken, nor the entire work, but only this testimony. For this reason, rebuke them sharply, so that they may be sound in the faith.

(VERSE 14.) “Not paying attention to Jewish myths and commandments of people who turn away from the truth.” For he says: “Rebuke them severely”; for they are liars, evil beasts, and lazy bellies, who persuade others to falsehood, who, like wild beasts, thirst for the blood of the deceived; and they do not quietly work for and eat their own bread, whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame. Rebuke such people, so that they may be sound in the faith. Concerning this soundness of faith he speaks in what follows: that older men should be sober, honorable, chaste, sound in faith, love, and [Col. 1017D] patience. [Concerning this soundness of faith he also writes to Timothy:] “If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words [read: sound teaching] of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Tim. 6:3). [He calls them sound words because, when observed, they produce soundness in those who observe them.]

“Not paying attention to Jewish myths and commandments of people who turn away from the truth,” [concerning whom he argues at length in Galatians and Romans. They thought that there was a distinction among foods, since some appeared clean and others unclean. Therefore he now adds:]

(VERSE 15.) “All things are clean to the clean”—that is, to those who believe in Christ and know that every creature is good, and that nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. “But to the defiled and unclean nothing is clean”; rather, [Col. 1018A] their mind and conscience are defiled. Therefore even things that are clean by nature become unclean to them [through guilt]; not because something is either clean or unclean in itself, but according to the character of those who eat it. [Legitimate food, customary in the catholic Church, is clean to the clean; it is unclean to the defiled, whose mind and conscience are unclean.] Therefore even the bread of blessing and the Lord’s cup do not benefit unbelievers and the polluted [but rather make them more polluted], because whoever eats that bread and drinks from the cup unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself (1 Cor. II). Thus it lies within us whether we eat what is clean or what is unclean. For if we are clean, creation is clean for us; but if we are unclean and unbelieving, everything becomes common for us [Hieronymus: “becomes so”], either because of the heresy dwelling in our hearts or because of the consciousness of our sins.

(VERSE 16.) “They profess,” he says, “to know God, but by their deeds they deny him,” since they are detestable and unbelieving, and disqualified for every good work. This accords with what he says in Isaiah: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13). Just as someone honors with his lips while withdrawing far away in his heart, so someone who confesses God in speech denies him by his deeds. But by denying God through his deeds while making a pretended confession, he is rightly called accursed and profane; and, persuaded by no consideration of truth, he is rightly called disobedient and unbelieving. [Nor will a person whose mind is corrupt deny Christ only in martyrdom;] but whenever we are overcome by vices and sins [and act contrary to God’s commandments], so often we deny God; and conversely, whenever [Col. 1018C] we do something good, we confess [and praise] the Lord.

{656}

## CHAPTER II

VERSE 1.—“But you, speak what accords with sound doctrine.” It is one thing to speak sound doctrine and another to teach what accords with sound doctrine, because in the one case there is only simple instruction, while in the other there is, together with what one teaches, also correction of life. For “whoever loosens one of the least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:19). [There will be a teacher who teaches by word but destroys by his conduct what he teaches, yet he will be least; but whoever does and teaches in this way will be called great in the kingdom of heaven, because by his conduct he fulfills what he teaches with his mouth.]

[Col. 1018D] The Apostle now teaches Titus, his son in Christ and his disciple, to speak what accords with sound doctrine, because doctrine is sound when the teacher’s teaching and life agree with one another.

(VERSE 2.) “That older men should be sober, honorable, chaste, sound in faith, love, and patience.” Now, in an orderly way, he establishes appropriate commands for each age and person, so that his speech may be a rule for the conduct of life. Older men, therefore, are to be sober [in good conduct] and honorable, so that the dignity of their age may be adorned by the seriousness [Hieronymus: dignity] of their morals. They are to be chaste, so that they may not indulge themselves at an age not their own, nor, with their blood already chilled toward lust, become an example leading the young to ruin. They are to be sound in faith—not in faith alone, but also in love and patience [and every kind of virtue]—so that, when they possess the original soundness of faith, they may hear from the Savior: “Your faith has saved you” (Mark 10:52). [The blessed Apostle discusses the integrity of this faith more fully, with examples, in the Epistle to the Hebrews.]

Just as there is soundness of faith, so there is the same soundness in love. Who possesses the soundness of love except one who first loves God with all his soul, with all his heart, and with all his strength, and then, hearing Christ’s commandment, fulfills love toward his neighbor [Hieronymus: divides love]? For “on these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets,” [and “the fullness of the law is love,”] because whoever is sound in faith and love must also be sound in patience, which is especially tested in temptations.

(VERSE 3.) “Older women likewise are to be in holy behavior, not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, teaching what is good, so that they may teach prudence.” Although the Apostle Peter commanded that husbands should honor their wives as the weaker vessel, it must not nevertheless be supposed that a wife, who has a weaker bodily vessel, is immediately weaker in soul as well. Hence they are now commanded that in them too the Apostle’s saying may be fulfilled: “Power is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9). [When he says, “Older women likewise,” he wants them to observe the same commands that he previously established for older men,] namely, that they should be sober, honorable, sound in faith, love, and patience; and, according to their sex, they should have this particular quality: that they be in holy behavior.

They are not to be slanderers—not such as seek to please others by speaking ill of others. [If they see some young woman behaving improperly,] they should not so much accuse her before others as correct her privately, in the love of Christ; and they should teach her not to do it rather than accuse her publicly of having done it.

They are not to be enslaved to much wine. Older women are prohibited from excessive drinking of wine because what lust accomplishes in the young, drunkenness accomplishes in old age [Hieronymus: “what lust is among the young, drunkenness is among the old”]. Therefore he expressly says, “not enslaved to much wine.” To occupy a person’s senses with wine is a kind of slavery and an extreme condition [Hieronymus: “to be occupied”]: the person no longer belongs to himself but to wine. Accordingly, he places reins upon them through such teachings [Hieronymus: “he permits the teachings to serve as reins for them”], so that, when they have become such people, they may have the freedom to teach—that is, to teach what is good.

Although he said elsewhere, “I do not permit a woman to teach” (1 Tim. 2:12), this must be understood as meaning that teaching men has been taken away from them. Otherwise, they should teach the young women as their own daughters, first chastity, because the enemy fights against this virtue more fiercely in the flowering of youth, and his strength against women is in the navel of the womb.

VERSES 4–5.—“To teach the young women to love their husbands and love their children; to be prudent, sober, chaste, keepers of the household, kind, subject to their own husbands, so that the word of God may not be blasphemed.”

[The older women are admonished to teach the young women to love their husbands, not with the passion of carnal desire, but in the love of Christ.] He wants them to love their husbands chastely, so that love between husband and wife may be chaste, and so that they may believe that they perform the work of having children before the eyes of God and the holy angels.

They should love their children in such a way that they educate them in the discipline of God. Otherwise, not wanting to distress them by teaching what is good and granting them freedom to sin is not loving children but hating them. [They should also be educated so that they may care kindly for the household—that is, for male and female servants.] He added “kind,” [so that the household might not be ruled with severity.] He also added “subject to their own husbands,” lest, puffed up by wealth and nobility, they forget God’s sentence by which they are subject to their husbands. For God said to the woman: “Your turning shall be toward your husband” [read: “your turning back”], “and he shall rule over you” (Gen. 3:16). It is also said: “The man was not created for the woman, but the woman for the man.” And since the man is the head of the woman, while Christ is the head of the man, any wife who is not subject to her husband [Hieronymus: “to her own husband”] [who is religious and fears God], that is, to her head, is guilty of the same offense as a husband who is not subject to Christ, his head.

“So that my word may not be blasphemed”—either because God’s first sentence is despised and regarded as nothing, or because the gospel of Christ is brought into disrepute when a Christian woman, who according to the law of God and the law of nature is subject to her husband, desires to rule over him, although even pagan women serve their husbands according to the common law of nature.

(VERSE 6.) “Likewise exhort young men to be chaste.” He made this especially the concern of young women: that they should be chaste [Hieronymus: “young men … that they should be chaste”] in all things, both in mind and body, both in conduct and thought, so that there may be no suspicion of disgrace in a young person.

It must also be understood that self-restraint is necessary not only in bodily acts and the desire of the mind, but in all things: that we should not seek undue honors, that we should not be inflamed by greed, and that we should not be overcome by any passion. “In all things” refers to what precedes: exhort them to be chaste in all things.

(VERSE 7.) “Present yourself as an example of good works.” It is of no benefit for someone to have been trained in learning and to have worn out his tongue in speaking, unless he teaches more by his example than by his word. [“In doctrine, in integrity.” In doctrine, he says, so that you may fulfill by your conduct what you teach with your mouth. Integrity properly refers to virginity; hence another translation says, “in incorruption,” for virgins are called incorrupt.]

(VERSE 8.) “In seriousness, in sound and irreproachable speech.” [An ecclesiastical teacher ought to possess seriousness—that is, honorable conduct. Concerning sound speech, the matter was discussed above.] “And irreproachable.” By “irreproachable” we do not mean that someone possesses such eloquence and wisdom that no one reproaches him, but that he says or does nothing deserving reproach, even though adversaries are ready to find fault.

“So that the one who is opposed may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us.” [“The one who is opposed,” that is, the adversary, should have nothing true or plausible to say, even though he is ready to criticize and to find an occasion for contradiction.] This one who is opposed may also be understood as the devil, who is the accuser of our brothers, as the evangelist John declares. When he has no evil that he can bring against us, he is put to shame, [Col. 1021A] and the accuser cannot accuse. In Latin, *diabolus* means “accuser.”

VERSES 9–10.—“That slaves should be subject to their masters in everything, pleasing them, not contradicting them, not defrauding, but showing complete good faith in everything.” For our Lord and Savior, who says in the Gospel, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matt. 11:28), considers no condition, age, or sex excluded from blessedness. Therefore the Apostle now establishes commands even for slaves; [namely, that, having become members of the Church, which is Christ’s body, they may also attain eternal salvation.]

And just as he previously taught what Titus should teach older men, older women, young women, and young men, so now he establishes suitable commands for slaves. [Col. 1021B] First, that they should be subject to their masters in everything—but in all things that are not contrary to God. If a master orders them to do what is not opposed to the holy Scriptures, they should submit to the master’s service [Hieronymus: “the slave should submit to the master”]; but if the commands are contrary, they should obey the spirit rather than the body [Hieronymus: “the spirit should obey rather than the master of the body”].

“Pleasing them” may be understood in two ways: either as pleasing themselves in their service, or also as pleasing their masters by faithfully and humbly carrying out everything they are commanded.

“Not contradicting them.” He says this because it is a serious fault for slaves to contradict their masters and, when they have been ordered to do something, to grumble. For if a slave must fulfill what the master commands, why should he not do the very thing willingly?

“Not stealing.” This corrects another fault of slaves through the teaching of Christ. A thief is judged not only in great matters but also in small ones. For it is not merely what has been stolen that is considered, but the mind of the thief.

Let slaves, therefore, be subject to their masters in everything; let them be content with their condition, so that they do not bear slavery bitterly; let them not contradict their masters or steal; and after this let them show complete good faith in everything, so that they may adorn the doctrine of our Savior God in all things. For if they are faithful in the least matters toward their earthly masters, they will begin to be entrusted with greater things before the Lord [Hieronymus: “before God”]. He adorns the master’s doctrine [the Codex omits “doctrine”] who does what is appropriate to his condition [Hieronymus: “what is suited to his condition”]. For how can someone be faithful in God’s substance [and in ecclesiastical office] who was unable to show faithfulness to an earthly master?

VERSES 11–14.—“For the grace of God our Savior has appeared to all people, teaching us that, denying impiety and worldly desires, we should live soberly, justly, and piously in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself an acceptable people, zealous for good works.”

After the catalogue of doctrine given to Titus—what he should teach older men, older women, young women and young men, and finally slaves—he now rightly adds: “For the grace of God our Savior has appeared to all people.” [Col. 1022A] There is no distinction between free and slave, Greek and barbarian, circumcised and uncircumcised, woman and man; but in Christ we are all one, and we are all called to the kingdom of God.

After offending our Father, we are reconciled not through our merits but through the grace of the Savior; or because Christ himself is the living and subsisting grace of God the Father [Hieronymus: “the grace of God the Father”]; or because this grace belongs to Christ, the Savior God; and because we have been saved not by our merit, according to what is said elsewhere: “You will save them for nothing” (Ps. 55:8).

This grace therefore shone upon all people in order to teach us to deny impiety and worldly desires, and to live chastely, justly, and piously in this age. What it means to deny impiety and worldly desires, I am confident can be understood from what we explained above: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him.”

Worldly desires, therefore, are those suggested by the prince of this world; and because such people are lovers of this age, they pass away with the cloud of this age. But when we have lived in Christ chastely and justly, sinning neither in body nor in mind, we should also live piously in this age. This piety awaits “the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.” For just as impiety dreads the coming of the great God, so piety, secure in its works and faith, awaits him.

Where is the serpent Arius? Where is Eunomius, the twisted serpent? Christ the Savior is called the great God—not the firstborn of all creation, not the Word and Wisdom of God, but Jesus [Col. 1022C] Christ; these names belong to the assumed humanity. Nor do we speak of one Jesus Christ and another Word, as the Nestorian heresy slanders us [Hieronymus: “as the new heresy”]. Rather, we call the same one who existed before the ages, in the ages, and before the world, and through Mary [Hieronymus: “after Mary”]—indeed, from Mary—the great God, our Savior Jesus Christ. He gave himself for us, so that by his precious blood he might redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself an acceptable people, zealous for good works—that is, an emulous people.

(VERSE 15.) “Speak these things and exhort.” What he says by “speak” appears to refer to teaching; what he adds by “exhort” pertains to consolation. When he adds a third instruction, “Rebuke with all authority,” he means that whoever does not listen to teaching and consolation is worthy of rebuke and deserves to hear: “You have forgotten the consolation that speaks to you as to sons.”

“Let no one despise you.” This has the following meaning: Let no one among those who are in the Church live in such a way, while you act negligently, that he thinks himself better. For what kind of edification would it be for a disciple to understand that he is greater than his teacher? Therefore bishops, presbyters, and deacons must take great care to precede the entire people over whom they preside in both conduct and speech.

{659}

## CHAPTER III

VERSE 1.—“Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to obey, and to be ready for every good work.” Something similar is also written to the Romans: “Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God” (Rom. 13:1). [The Lord himself also answered the Jews who were testing him:] “Give to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God” (Matt. 22:21).

In agreement with this answer, the Apostle Paul teaches that those who believe in Christ ought to be subject to rulers and authorities. This command could provide an occasion for those who fear torture to deny Christ [because of this command]; but he cautiously added, “to obey for every good work.” If what the emperor or governor commands is good, obey the will of the one giving the command. But if it is evil and opposed to God, answer him with the words from the Acts of the Apostles: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

Let us understand the same thing concerning slaves with their masters, wives with their husbands, and children with their parents [and disciples with their teachers]: these persons ought to be subject to their superiors only in matters that do not contradict God’s commandments; [and they should be ready only for those things that are not commanded contrary to the Lord’s commandments.]

(VERSE 2.) “To slander no one.” Thus the archangel Michael, when he disputed with the devil about the body of Moses, did not dare to pronounce a judgment of blasphemy, but said: “May God command you” (Jude 9). Therefore, if Michael did not dare to pronounce a judgment of blasphemy against the devil, who was certainly most deserving of a curse, how much more must we be pure from every curse? The devil deserved a curse, but it should not have come forth from the mouth of an archangel.

For now it is enough to have said this: that Christ’s disciples ought not to blaspheme, nor, as is added, to be quarrelsome. For if we are children of peace, and want peace to rest upon us, and have approached the heavenly Jerusalem, which receives its name from peace, then with those who hate peace we should maintain peace; and, insofar as it depends on us, we should be at peace with all people, not only with the gentle but also with the quarrelsome, because there is no virtue in bearing with the gentle. Therefore, “let us give place to anger,” showing complete gentleness toward all people.

VERSE 3.—“For we too were once foolish and unbelieving, wandering, enslaved to various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another.”

Someone may ask how Paul could have been foolish, unbelieving, wandering, and enslaved to various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, when he was educated at Gamaliel’s feet and instructed in the sacred writings from childhood [add: “as we read”] (Acts 22). But from the time when he did not believe in Christ, these things could rightly be said of him: that he was foolish and envious of the salvation of Christians.

Or should we say that Paul was not foolish [Hieronymus: “does Paul not appear foolish to us”] when he had zeal for God but not according to knowledge, and persecuted the Church and guarded the garments of those stoning Stephen? He was so inflamed by hatred against the Savior that he received letters from the priests and went to Damascus [in order to condemn those [Col. 1024A] who believed in Christ (Codex: “to be condemned”; Hieronymus: “to bind them”)].

VERSES 4–7.—“But when the kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared, not from works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Lord, so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.”

Let us attend more carefully, and we shall find in the present chapter a most manifest Trinity. The kindness and clemency of God our Savior—none other than God the Father—justified us for eternal life through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior [Col. 1024B]. The salvation of believers is the mystery of the Trinity [as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” No one will be legitimately baptized unless the name of the holy Trinity is invoked over the one who is to be baptized. Therefore we must hasten to baptism, lest perhaps an infant be snatched from this life without this sacrament of salvation.]

(VERSE 8.) “The saying is trustworthy, and concerning these things I want you to affirm strongly, so that those who believe in God may take care to devote themselves to good works” [read: “those who believe God”]. “These things are good and useful to people.”

What he says, “The saying is trustworthy,” must be joined to the preceding words, in which he promised that, having been justified by his grace, we would become heirs according to the hope of eternal life. The saying concerning God’s inheritance and the hope of eternal life is worthy of faith. Therefore one must believe these things without doubt or fear, and strongly affirm them so that others may believe them as well.

But not only this must be affirmed; it must also be affirmed together with all the others who wish to believe. Therefore he says, “And concerning these things I want you to affirm strongly.” Those who believe these things to be true must necessarily take care to carry out good works [and complete them], through which God’s inheritance and the hope of eternal life are prepared.

Appropriately, to inspire greater faith, he did not say “those who believe people,” but “those who believe God.” It is necessary for them to take care for good works, which, when completed and carried out with every effort, are good and useful for believers.

(VERSE 9.) “Avoid foolish questions, genealogies, contentions, and fights about the law, for they are useless and vain.” [Thus the Apostle recalls us from vain questions that have no rational basis and do not support the catholic faith.] But concerning wise questions, those supported by the authority of Scripture, he rather exhorts and encourages us—provided that our body is not subject to sins—and wisdom will enter into us. Let the mind be exercised daily; let it be nourished by divine reading, and our questions will not be foolish questions.

When he says, “Avoid genealogies and contentions and quarrels that arise from the law,” he especially attacks the Jews, who boast in this respect and think they possess knowledge of the law if they retain the names of each individual [which questions are not suitable for a Christian]. Legal quarrels must be rejected [Hieronymus: “utterly”], and the foolishness of the Jews abandoned; for they are useless and vain, possessing only the appearance of knowledge [Hieronymus: “they possess”]. Otherwise they benefit neither those who utter them nor those who hear them.

VERSES 10–11.—“Avoid a heretical person after one and a second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment.”

The Apostle also counted heresy among the works of the flesh in Galatians (Gal. 5:19ff.). In Greek, *hairesis* derives from “choice,” because each person chooses for himself what seems best to him.

“Avoid a heretical person after one and another admonition.” He says this because it is not enough merely to rebuke or warn once someone who has been corrupted by some error; a second instruction must also be given, so that “every word may be established on the testimony of two or three witnesses.”

But why must he be avoided after the first and second admonition? He gives the reasons, saying: “Such a person is perverted and sins, being condemned by himself.” For someone who, after being admonished once and twice, does not wish to be corrected after hearing his error [has been condemned by his own judgment and separated from the unity of the Church].

A fornicator, adulterer, murderer, and those guilty of other vices are expelled from the Church by the priests. Heretics, however, pronounce the sentence upon themselves, withdrawing from the Church by their own decision; this withdrawal appears to be a condemnation by their own conscience.

They consider the difference between heresy and schism to be that heresy possesses a perverse doctrine, while schism separates from the Church because of disagreement with the bishop.

VERSE 12.—“When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, make haste to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to winter there.” [Here Paul’s paternal affection for the Cretans is demonstrated.] He needed Titus for the ministry of the Gospel; nevertheless, he does not want him to come to him before Artemas or Tychicus has arrived to take his place.

Nicopolis is the city that received its name from the victory of Augustus [Manuscript: Agustus], because he defeated Antony and Cleopatra there.

(VERSE 13.) “Diligently send on Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they may lack nothing.” This is the Apollos about whom he also writes to the Corinthians: “Each one of you says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ or ‘I belong to Apollos,’ or ‘I belong to Cephas’” (1 Cor. 1:12).

He was an Alexandrian man of Jewish origin, very eloquent and accomplished in the law, and bishop of the Corinthians. Because of the dissensions that existed in Corinth, he should be thought to have crossed over with Zenas the teacher of the law to the island of Crete; and, after Paul’s letter had moderated the dissensions that had arisen at Corinth [Col. 1026A], to have returned again to Corinth.

As for Zenas the teacher of the law, we cannot say from another passage of Scripture who he was, except that he had the same apostolic work as Apollos: building the Churches of Christ.

Therefore he commanded Titus that, since they were going to sail from Crete to Greece, he should not allow them to lack provisions, but should ensure that they had what was necessary for their journey.

VERSE 14.—“Let our people also learn to devote themselves to good works for necessary uses, so that they may not be unfruitful.” He says, “Let our people also learn.” He calls his own people “our people”—those who have believed in Christ. Because they belonged to Christ, they rightly deserved to be called Paul’s and Titus’s people.

“You have authority over the disciples,” he says. “Teach them not to be unfruitful, but to minister to evangelists [Hieronymus: evangelists] and apostolic men who serve good works; and let them minister not for just any purposes, but for necessary needs.” For “having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Tim. 6:8).

He calls all those unfruitful who do not minister to evangelists [and do not supply the preachers of the word of God, according to their means, with what is necessary].

VERSE 15.—“All who are with me greet you.” Either he followed his customary practice, saying that Titus was greeted by all who were with him, or, certainly, he addressed Titus particularly because he was such a person that he deserved the love of everyone who was with Paul. It is a great commendation of Titus that all greet him through Paul.

“Greet those who love us in the faith.” [Some people love their own, but not in the faith, as a mother loves her son and a husband his wife. Therefore he added, “who love us in the faith.”] The love of the saints alone loves in faith, to such an extent that even if the one who is loved is an unbeliever, nevertheless the spirit [Hieronymus: “the Holy Spirit”] loves him in faith, according to the saying: “Let everything you do be done in faith” (1 Cor. 16:14). Therefore he says “in faith,” [because he believes that he will receive a reward from God for fulfilling the commandment that says, “Love your enemies” (Luke 6:35).]

“The grace of God be with you all. Amen.” Thus he invokes grace collectively upon the saints and believers, Titus and the others who were with him. And just as the patriarch Isaac blessed his son Jacob, and Jacob blessed the twelve patriarchs (Gen. 27; 29), so now, at the end of his letter, the Apostle invokes grace upon believers [Col. 1026D]. His blessing, accompanied by a prayer, had its effect and lay within the power of believers, if they showed themselves such as the one blessing wished the person blessed to be [Hieronymus reads “blessed” (*benedictus*) for “to be blessed” (*benedici*)].

The exposition of the Epistle of Paul to Titus ends.

# THE EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO PHILEMON BEGINS

[Col. 1025D]

@ [Col. 1025D] From Jerome on this Epistle. He writes a personal letter to Philemon on behalf of his slave Onesimus. He writes to him from prison at Rome.

VERSES 1–3.—“Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy, the brother, to Philemon, our beloved and fellow worker, and to Appia, our most dear sister, and to Archippus, our fellow soldier, and to the Church that is in your house. Grace to you and peace from God our Father [Col. 1027A] and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

[This is as far as the introductory greeting extends. In no other letter does he call himself a prisoner. For he says, “Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ.”] It appears more high-flown to call himself a prisoner of Jesus Christ than an apostle. For the apostles gloried that they had been found worthy to suffer insults for the name of Jesus Christ (Acts 5:41).

But the authority of his chains was necessary. Since he was about to make a request on behalf of Onesimus, a person who could obtain what he asked for had to make the request. Truly blessed is the person who glories not in wisdom, wealth, eloquence, or worldly power, but in the sufferings of Christ.

If Philemon, to whom this letter is written, is the master of Onesimus—indeed, if he began to be his brother from being his master [Hieronymus: “in the Lord”]—and if it is reported to the Colossians that Onesimus was one of them (Col. 4:9), reason and the sequence of events themselves lead us to conclude that Philemon too was a Colossian, and that Onesimus carried this letter to the common Church [Hieronymus: “to the whole Church”] at the same time that he took private letters commending himself to his master.

There is also another indication: in this same letter Archippus is named, and Paul writes to him here together with Philemon: “Say to Archippus: See to the ministry that you have received in the Lord, so that you may fulfill it” (Col. 4:17). What ministry did Archippus receive from the Lord? [In the Epistle] to Philemon we read: “And to Archippus, our fellow soldier, and to the Church that is in your house.”

From this it may be inferred [Hieronymus: “from this I think”] either that he was the bishop of the Church of Colossae, whom he is urged to oversee diligently and carefully, or certainly a preacher of the Gospel.

[Col. 1027C] {662} And Timothy, a brother. He added this so that the letter might have greater authority if it were not written by one man. Thus Paul and Timothy write to Philemon, their most beloved and fellow worker, who is called “most beloved” because he is engaged in the same work of Christ. Also to Apphia, a sister, who has nothing in her [Hier., “who has nothing false and feigned in her”] of fictitious kinship. And to Archippus, a fellow soldier, whom we must suppose to have fought alongside Paul and Timothy against the adversaries on behalf of Christ’s name and to have emerged victorious; hence he is now called a fellow soldier, because he overcame in the same contest and warfare. [And to the church that is in your house. That is, to the congregation of the faithful which was in Philemon’s house.]

Grace to you and peace from God [Col. 1027D] our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. In nearly all the letters there is a similar opening, in which he invokes grace and peace upon them from God the Father and from Christ the Lord. From this it is shown that the Son and the Father have one nature, since the Son can grant what the Father grants, and the Father is said to grant what the Son grants. Grace is that by which we are saved without any merit or work of our own; peace is that by which we have been reconciled to God through Christ.

(VERSE 4.) I give thanks to my God, always making mention of you. You will be able to find this manner of writing in some of his letters: although several persons are introduced, and addressed to several people, in the preface, afterward throughout the whole body of the letter a single speaker is introduced.

(VERSES 5, 6.) Hearing of your love and the faith which you have in the Lord Jesus and toward all his saints, so that the sharing of your faith [Col. 1028A] may become evident in the acknowledgment of every good thing in Christ Jesus. It is believable that Paul always prayed for Philemon, namely that the faith and love which he had in Christ and toward all his saints might be preserved through the sharing of faith and the active acknowledgment of every good thing belonging to Christ, by Christ’s mercy. As for the love which he had in Christ Jesus and toward all his saints, the interpretation is not difficult, since after God we are commanded to love our neighbors.

[But it may be asked how it was said: “In the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints.” Faith must be given to the sayings and writings of the saints, so that they may have spoken truthfully about God, concerning whom they wrote. Therefore we ought to believe concerning the Lord and his saints with the same faith, just as they taught us what we should believe concerning the Lord.]

Nor should we think that faith and love alone toward God and his saints can suffice for us, unless we fulfill in action what we believe [Col. 1028B; Hier., “unless it is completed in action”]. Whatever good is praised in Philemon and taken from the example of the apostles is good because it is drawn from the fountain of Christ.

(VERSE 7.) For I have had great joy and consolation in your love, because the hearts of the saints have found refreshment through you, brother. He more fully emphasizes and teaches why he said: “I give thanks to my God, always making mention of you in my prayers.” It was indeed worthy to give thanks to God for Philemon’s love, since he was showing the inward affection of his heart toward the saints by refreshing their labors [Hier., “since he had refreshed the inward affection of the heart and the deep recesses of the saints’ spirit by receiving them”]. This too is an apostolic idiom: he always calls them “hearts,” wishing to display a love that is complete in the mind. [Col. 1028C]

(VERSES 8, 9.) Therefore, although I have great boldness in Christ Jesus to command you what concerns the matter, I prefer, because of love, to make an appeal, being such a one as Paul, an old man, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ. After first setting forth many praises of Philemon, since the matter for which he is about to plead [Hier., “for which he was asked”] is useful both to the one who is to grant the request and to the one who makes it, Paul could have commanded rather than asked. This confidence arose from the fact that one who had accomplished so many works for Christ could not be unequal to himself in other matters. But he prefers to ask rather than command. Having set before him the great authority of the petitioner, he declares himself to be an old man and a prisoner of the Lord [Hier., “having set this before him, by which the Apostle, as both an old man and a prisoner of Jesus Christ, makes his appeal”].

Everything for which he pleads concerns Onesimus, Philemon’s slave, who had compounded his flight by stealing and had pilfered some of his master’s property [Hier., “household property”]. Going to Italy so that he might not be more easily apprehended nearby, he had squandered his master’s money in extravagance [Hier., “through extravagance”]. Let no one think that this has been rashly and arbitrarily invented by us; let him learn it from what follows. Paul would never have said: “If he has wronged you in anything or owes you anything, charge it to me. I, Paul, have written this with my own hand; I will repay it.” Nor would he have become surety for what had been taken unless what had been taken had been dissipated.

Thus, while Paul was in prison at Rome because of his confession of Christ, Onesimus believed in the Lord Jesus and, baptized by him, wiped away the stains of his former life through worthy repentance [Col. 1029A], to such an extent that the Apostle became a witness to his conversion. [“The master of the fugitive is weighed down by the force of apostolic testimony,” {663}] so that the Apostle might say of the one who, from being a slave, fugitive, and thief, had become the Apostle’s minister:

(VERSES 10–15.) I appeal to you for my son Onesimus, whom I begot in my imprisonment; he was once useless to you, but now he is useful both to you and to me. I have sent him back to you. You, therefore, receive him—that is, my own heart—whom I wished to keep with me, so that he might minister to me on your behalf in the imprisonment of the Gospel.

Wishing to obtain what he requests, he now declares that he is pleading not for Philemon’s slave but for his own son—and for the son whom he begot in the imprisonment of the Gospel, that is, amid the sufferings which he endured for Christ’s Gospel. Formerly Onesimus had been useless only to his master—for a slave [Col. 1029B] who is a thief and fugitive harms no one but his master—but now, in return for the usefulness by which he is useful both to his master [Hier., “to his master himself”] and to Paul, and through Paul to others, he deserves more love than he had previously deserved hatred. Hence he says: “who was once useless to you.” “To you,” he says, “alone, not to others; but now useful to you and to me.”

He is useful to his master because he can serve Paul on his master’s behalf; he is useful to Paul because, while Paul is detained in prison and chains, Onesimus can minister to him in the Gospel. [He did not hesitate to call him his own son as well.]

When he says: “You, however, receive him—that is, my heart,” this means what I said shortly before: “heart” signifies the inward affection and the complete willingness of the soul.

(VERSE 14.) But I wanted to do nothing without your consent, so that your good deed might not be as though compelled, but voluntary. [This statement can resolve the question by which some assert that God ought to have made man unable to sin. God himself is voluntary, not under compulsion [read: “he is voluntarily good, not good by necessity”]; but if man were good from necessity and not by his will, he could not be the image of God.]

The Apostle Paul, therefore, could have kept Onesimus for his ministry without Philemon’s consent; but if he had done this without Philemon’s will, the act would indeed have been good, but not voluntary. What was not voluntary could, in another respect, be argued not to be good. For nothing can be absolutely good unless it is freely chosen. From this we should consider the Apostle’s prudence: he sends the fugitive [Col. 1029D] back to his master so that he may benefit his master, [“who could not have been pleasing if he were kept without his master’s consent”; Hier., “who could not be of benefit if he were kept while his master was absent”].

(VERSES 15, 16.) Perhaps for this reason he departed for a time, so that you might receive him back forever—no longer as a slave, but, instead of a slave, as a most beloved brother, especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord. [Just as, in Joseph’s sale, God made a good outcome—that is, the salvation of many—from the evil will of his brothers,] so also in Onesimus we may understand that evil beginnings became opportunities for a good result. [For he fled from his master and became Christ’s slave and a minister in the Gospel.]

By adding “perhaps,” he fittingly moderated the statement [Col. 1030A]. God’s judgments are hidden, and it is rash to pronounce as certain what is uncertain. Therefore he cautiously said: “Perhaps he departed for a time.” We should understand “a time” as a period; for in comparison with eternity every period is short.

“So that you might receive him forever.” Onesimus, who through faith in Christ has become and is eternal, is eternal for Philemon, since Philemon himself had believed in Christ. Having received the spirit of freedom, he has begun, from being a slave, to be a brother—not merely a brother, but a most beloved and eternal brother.

(VERSE 17.) If, therefore, you consider me a partner, receive him as you would me. What he says amounts to this: If you wish to have me as a partner, have Onesimus also, whom I regard as my partner, my son, and my heart. If you do not receive him [Col. 1030B] or wish to have him, understand that you cannot have me either.

(VERSE 18.) But if he has wronged you in anything or owes you anything, charge it to me. [For if Christ suffered for us and bore our infirmities, Paul, rightly imitating his Teacher, offered himself in place of his son Onesimus. He said all this in order to pacify Philemon’s mind toward Onesimus.]

(VERSE 19.) I, Paul, have written this with my own hand; I will repay it—not to mention that you owe me even your own self. What he says amounts to this: Onesimus took something by theft; I promise that I will repay it. This letter and my own hand are witnesses to the promise, since I did not dictate it in my usual manner but wrote it myself. I say this as though speaking to a stranger. But if I return to my own rights, because I preached to you the word of Christ and you became a Christian, you owe your very self to me. If you are mine, and everything that is yours is mine, [Col. 1030C] then Onesimus also, who is yours, is mine. I could therefore treat him as my own; but I leave him to your will, so that by forgiving him you may receive a reward.

(VERSE 20.) Yes, brother. May I have benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ. When he says: “May I have benefit from you in the Lord,” this is understood in a much fuller sense than is generally supposed. The Apostle does not enjoy anyone except one who contains many and harmonious virtues within himself [Hier., “many virtues joined together”]. Everything that is called Christ according to the variety of circumstances—namely wisdom, righteousness, continence, gentleness, moderation, and chastity—is meant here. He invokes these qualities upon Philemon, so that, when Philemon abounds in them, the Apostle himself may be filled by enjoying him.

And lest you think that “enjoyment” means the pleasure which we often take in one another’s presence [and from which we derive enjoyment], he added: “in the Lord.” “Refresh my heart in Christ.” Just as he wishes to enjoy Philemon in the Lord, so he wishes his own heart—Onesimus, whom above he had likewise called by this name—to be refreshed through Philemon. Onesimus is rightly called the heart of holy Paul [Hier., “Onesimus is rightly called Paul’s heart in Christ”], since he begot him in imprisonment.

(VERSE 21.) Trusting in your obedience, I have written to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say. [For he says, “trusting in your obedience,” so that Philemon would not be ashamed to do what he had been asked. Therefore [Col. 1031A] he added, “knowing,” and so forth. One who knows the goodness of a friend somehow forestalls him, so that he will not dare to refuse what is requested.]

(VERSE 22.) At the same time, prepare a lodging for me. He says this so that, while Philemon expects him to come to him, Philemon may more willingly do what he has been asked. For I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you. [The prayers of the whole Church benefited Paul, while he benefited the whole Church of God. God often granted him to the prayers of the saints, for the benefit of those who would hear him.]

Paul himself says elsewhere that he was frequently in prison and was freed from his chains: “In prisons frequently” (2 Cor. 11:23). From these he was sometimes delivered by the Lord’s help. [For “from which,” read “from these.”]

(VERSES 23, 24.) Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you [Col. 1031B]; so do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas [Ms., “Damascus”], and Luke, my fellow workers.

Who Epaphras, Paul’s fellow prisoner, was, we have received the following account. They say that the parents of the Apostle Paul were from the region of Giscala in Judea; and that, when the whole province was devastated by the Roman hand and the Jews were scattered throughout the world [Hier., “when they were scattered by the Roman hand”], they were transferred to Tarsus, a city of Cilicia. The young Paul followed the condition of his parents, and thus what he testifies about himself can stand: “They are Hebrews, and so am I; they are Israelites, and so am I; they are the seed of Abraham, and so am I” (2 Cor. 11:22). Again, elsewhere: “A Hebrew of Hebrews” (Phil. 3:5), along with the other statements which indicate him to have been more a Jew than a native of Tarsus.

If this is so, we may suspect that Epaphras was taken captive at the time when Paul was captured [Col. 1031C], and that, having been settled by his parents in the city of Colossae in Asia, he later received the word of Christ. Hence in the Letter to the Colossians: “Epaphras greets you, who is one of you” (Col. 4:12).

If this is correct, Aristarchus too, who is called Paul’s fellow prisoner in the same letter, is led to the same conclusion. But if this explanation is not accepted, then, from the fact that “in Christ Jesus” has been added here, we may suspect that he endured at Rome for Christ the same chains as Paul and that, just as Paul was called Christ’s prisoner, Aristarchus too could be called his captive.

So much for Epaphras. Of the remaining fellow workers in the Gospel and in his chains, when he wrote the Letter to Philemon he mentions Mark, who may be thought to have composed the Gospel [Hier., “whom I think to be the author of the Gospel”]; Aristarchus, whom we mentioned above [Col. 1032A]; Demas, concerning whom it is asked elsewhere: “Demas has deserted me, loving this present age, and has departed for Thessalonica”; and Luke the physician, who left the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles to the churches of God. Concerning him he says elsewhere: “I sent with him the brother whose praise in the Gospel is throughout all the churches of our Lord Jesus Christ” (2 Cor. 8:18).

(VERSE 25.) The grace of God be with your spirit. Amen. [Synecdoche is used in the expression “with your spirit,” signifying the whole person by reference to the better part. When grace is in the spirit, it makes the whole person spiritual, so that the flesh serves the spirit, the soul is not overcome by the flesh, and both, transformed together into a spiritual substance, cling to God; for “whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit with him” (1 Cor. 6:17).] [Col. 1032B]

For according to the Hebrews, Paul means “admirable”; Timothy, “beneficent”; Philemon, “wonderfully gifted,” or “mouth of bread”—from “mouth,” not from “bone.” Apphia [Hier., “Apphia”], “self-controlled” or “freedom.” Archippus, “length of work.” Onesimus, “answering.” {665} Epaphras, “fruitful and seeing,” or “growing up.” Mark, “exalted by command.” Aristarchus, “a mountain of greater work.” Demas, “silent.” Luke, “rising up by himself.”

If they wish to understand these names according to their interpretation, it is not difficult to see that he writes especially to one who is admirable and beneficent, to whom every vice [perhaps, “every benefit”] has been granted, so that his mouth may be opened toward the heavenly bread. Then he writes to one who is self-controlled and free, and to one devoted to the length of the work from which we never cease laboring in this age [Hier., “from holy labor”]. Truly he writes on behalf of one who answers to his own testimony, and he has the one to whom the letter is specially dedicated greeted by one who is growing in abundance. [Col. 1032C]

He is also greeted by the one who has been exalted through commands, and by him who has climbed up into the mountain through greater works [Hier., “who has grown up as far as the mountain”]; likewise by the one who has set a guard over his mouth and a fortified door upon his lips—who perhaps was silent for this reason, because he had abandoned the Apostle for a short time. Finally, he is greeted by the one who rises up by himself and daily increases while his Gospel is fulfilled throughout the whole world, growing as often as it is heard [Hier., “as often as, heard and read, it builds up”].

The Explanation of the Letter of Paul to Philemon ends here.

THE EXPOSITION OF THE LETTER OF THE APOSTLE PAUL TO THE HEBREWS BEGINS

CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1031D]

VERSE 1

@ [Col. 1031D] The passages enclosed throughout this work in these typographical signs, « », have been taken from the homilies [Col. 1032D] of Saint John Chrysostom on the Letter to the Hebrews, volume XII of his works. In many parts and in many ways, God formerly spoke to the fathers in the prophets.

The whole intention of the blessed Apostle in this letter was to summon the Hebrews—that is, his own people—to faith in Christ, and to distinguish the superiority of the grace given through the Son from the shadows of the Law, which had been served by angelic ministrations. Therefore he first stated that the prophets had spoken to the fathers in various ways, saying: “In many parts and in many ways God formerly spoke to our fathers in the prophets.” He was indicating what is said elsewhere: “For I multiplied visions, and I was represented in the hands of the prophets” (Hos. 12:10).

«Accordingly, the superiority of the New Testament is not declared merely by this fact: that certain prophets were sent to the fathers, but the Son to us. It is also declared by the fact that none of the prophets or patriarchs [Col. 1033A] saw God except in likenesses, whereas it is established that the only-begotten Son became incarnate and was seen in that flesh,» in which the same man, assumed by the Word of God, is the only-begotten Son of God.

Therefore he immediately added:

(VERSE 2.) In these last days he has spoken to us in the Son. «By saying “in the Son,” he means exactly the same as if he had said “through the Son,” because the preposition in is taken in the sense of through,» just as in many places in his Letters he uses these prepositions interchangeably.

He has not yet mentioned Christ’s name, because he knew that many of them had denied that he was the Son of God. «For he did not say, “Christ spoke,” although it is clear that he did speak. Thus he still did not address the Jews by name openly. For it was evident that nearly all to whom the prophets spoke were wicked and impious [Col. 1033B]; and he did not yet wish to raise the question concerning them, but meanwhile discusses in general terms the gifts which were bestowed upon them by divine generosity.

“Whom he appointed heir of all things.” What does “whom he appointed heir of all things” mean?» Here he is speaking of the Son who became incarnate, of whom he spoke above, just as it is also read of him in the second Psalm: «Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance» (Ps. 2:8). No longer is Jacob alone the Lord’s portion and Israel his lot [Chrys., “Israel alone”], but all nations at once: this Son he appointed Lord of all things.

He uses the name “heir” in order to establish and demonstrate two things through it: that he is the proper Son, and that no loss of dominion can befall him. When he says “heir of all things,” he means the whole world [Col. 1033C]. Then he turns his discourse to higher matters, saying: “Through whom he also made the ages,”» in order to show that the one who came into the world in these last days is the one through whom he made the world as well, displaying the greatness of him who was the bearer and author of the New Testament.

«After this, using certain elegant steps, he arrives at what is much greater than all the things he has said above, and he declares:

{666} VERSE 3. He who is the radiance of glory and the image of his substance. Everywhere we need a devout understanding, but especially when we speak or hear about God, since neither is the tongue sufficient to speak worthily of God nor is the intellect strong enough to comprehend him.» Moreover, where speech fails or thought cannot explain God, [Col. 1033D] «then we should all the more glorify [Chrys., “glorify”] God, because we have such a God—one who transcends both the intellect and the vision of thought.

He rightly called him the radiance of glory, since he knew him to be the one who said: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). He showed that he is light from light, just as he is God from God, illuminating our souls and making the Father known to us. Through the radiance he declared the unity of essence with God the Father, «and in a wonderful manner he showed one substance while revealing two persons [Chrys., “subsistences”] in glory and radiance.

Therefore he also adds: “Who is the image of his substance.” The image [Chrys., “character”] is indeed other than the one whose form it expresses. Yet “other” does not mean other in every respect, but a second person [Col. 1034A; Chrys., “according to substance”]; for here too the image gives an unmistakable indication of equality with that whose image is shown, and certainly admits no suspicion of perverse dissimilarity [Chrys., “does not admit it”].»

Here he calls him “image,” which elsewhere he calls “form,” where he says: “Who, although he was in the form of God,” and so forth. “Form” or “image” declares the equality of one essence.

It follows: Sustaining all things by the word of his power. “Sustaining,” that is, governing all things by that word of power through which he made all things. «For governing the world is no less than creating it. In creating, the substances of things were produced from nothing; in governing, what has been made is preserved so that it does not return to nothing. Therefore, while all these things are governed and things opposed to one another are fitted together, a great and truly marvelous sign of God’s immense power is revealed.» [Col. 1034B]

After this clarity of the divine majesty in the Son, he descends to the lowliness of the incarnation, saying: Having made purification for sins. He signifies two things: namely, that he cares for us, in what he says, “sustaining all things by the word of his power”; and, in adding “having made purification for sins,” that he cleanses our sins.

In these two matters above all we see the Apostle glorying: he demonstrates that these things have been taken away for us through the Son. And when he had reminded us of the cross and passion of this same Son, through which purification from sins was provided for us, he immediately instructed us to lift our minds toward heavenly things and to contemplate [Col. 1034C] his ineffable glory in his resurrection and ascension. For he says: He sits at the right hand of his majesty in the highest places.

By “the right hand” he did not give God a bodily shape, but demonstrated the greatness of his honor. By saying “in the highest places,” he showed that the Son is higher than all and supreme, «for he has reached even the throne of the Father’s glory. Therefore, just as the Father is in the highest places, so also is the Son. Sitting together demonstrates nothing other than equality of honor. For if he wished to show inferiority, he would never have said that he sat at the right hand, but rather at the left.»

He continues to show the excellence of this same Son, when he says:

VERSE 4. Having become so much superior to the angels as he has inherited a name more excellent than theirs. Angels are servants and attendants; he is Son and heir. “So much [Col. 1034D] superior,” he says, “to the angels”—that is, more honorable and more excellent—as he has inherited a more excellent name.

It follows:

(VERSE 5.) For to which of the angels did he ever say: You are my Son; today I have begotten you? And again: I will be his Father, and he will be my Son. This is said without any doubt concerning the incarnation of the Son; therefore he used the future tense: “I will be his Father, and he will be my Son.”

When he said: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you,” he clearly shows that the one of whom he says, “I will be his Father,” and so forth, was begotten from the very essence of the Father. Therefore he used the present time “today,” because for God nothing is past or future, but all things are always present.

«This statement can also be understood according to the flesh [Col. 1035A], because the flesh shares in what is higher, just as the divinity graciously consented to share in what is lowly.» In this passage, therefore, he clearly shows two natures in Christ.

Let us apply these examples to our salvation: «if he himself, although he was God and Lord and the Son of God, did not refuse to assume the form of a servant, how much more ought we to fulfill everything commanded us and to endure all that is humble.» {667} Let us remember Christ saying: “When you have done everything, say: We are unworthy servants” (Luke 17:10).

(VERSE 6.) And again, when he brings the firstborn into the inhabited world, he says: And let all the angels of God worship him. Paul calls Christ’s entrance the assumption of flesh, concerning which the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John [Col. 1035B] 16:28).

Here Christ calls his incarnation an “exit,” whereas Paul calls it an “entrance.” We must ask why Christ and Paul wished to name the same thing by different names.

«The meanings of the statements are clear, and it is evident in what sense each speaks. Christ rightly calls it an exit: we were outside God, like those who are outside royal courts, bound in chains, and who have incurred the king’s displeasure because of their offenses. Such people are excluded outside the royal court. Whoever wishes to obtain pardon for them does not first bring them into the court of the king; rather, he himself goes out, mixes with them there, and enters into conversation with them until he has made them repentant and rendered them worthy to be brought before the king’s face.

Christ does the same. Going out to us—that is, taking flesh—and speaking with us, [Col. 1035C] he made the king’s commands known. Thus, cleansing us from sins, turning us toward God, and bringing us into the royal court like an excellent mediator [Chrys., “brought us in”], he accomplishes this. For this reason he calls the coming of his incarnation an “exit.”

Paul, however, calls it an “entrance,” using a metaphor drawn from heirs who take possession of an inheritance and assume the right of ruling some possession. For when he says: “Again he brings the firstborn into the inhabited world,” he signifies that the inhabited world is entrusted to him. He then possessed the whole world when he was acknowledged by all.»

And let all the angels of God worship him. He raises our minds to higher things, so that we may know that the one who was clothed in flesh and suffered for us was worshiped by the angels. [Col. 1035D]

But in order to distinguish the majesty of the Son from the angels’ ministry, he immediately adds:

(VERSE 7.) He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire. «By this statement he does not signify angels alone, but all the powers that perform heavenly ministries.»

It must be understood that “angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature. They are always spirits, but they cannot always be called angels. Do you ask the name of their nature? It is spirit. Do you ask the name of their office? It is angel. In respect of what he is, he is a spirit; in respect of what he does [perhaps, “acts”], he is an angel, because “angel” is Greek and means “messenger” in Latin—just as “human being” is the name of a nature, while “soldier” is the name of an office.

Thus God the Creator makes those who were already created as spirits [Col. 1036A] into angels by sending them to announce what he has commanded.

And his ministers a flame of fire. We read that fire appeared in the bush; we also read that fire was sent down from above and fulfilled what had been commanded. It can be said that when they are sent to announce gentle things, they are angels; when they are sent for vengeance, they are ministers—that is, burning fire.

These offices also exist in the present Church. Holy preachers, when they proclaim spiritual things and announce the joys of God’s kingdom, are called angels; but when they proclaim the terror of the fire of Gehenna, they are ministers, terrifying sinners with the threat of that fire which will never be extinguished.

(VERSE 8.) But to the Son: Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of equity is the scepter of your kingdom. Here he speaks of the one who exists according to the flesh, concerning whom the Lord himself also says [Col. 1036B] in the Gospel: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son” (John 5:22). And shortly afterward: “He gave him authority to exercise judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5:27).

This throne of God pertains to the future judgment, in which the form of a servant will be seen as judge of the living and the dead. By this judgment Christ truly governs, examines, and distinguishes all things. “Forever and ever,” he says, because the final judgment will stand with eternal separation between the good and the evil, as the one who will judge testifies in the Gospel: “Then these will go away into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:46).

The scepter of equity is the scepter of your kingdom. The scepter signifies the rule of divine equity, which is truly called straight because it is not bent by any crookedness [Col. 1036C]. This scepter governs the righteous and strikes the impious. It is unconquerable strength, the straightest equity, and inflexible discipline. This scepter was anciently called the emblem of royal honor, the scepter itself, signifying in it the king of virtues, the Lord and Savior.

(VERSE 9.) You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity. This is the straight scepter: to love equity and hate wickedness. No one perfectly loves righteousness unless he also abhors evil actions, because truth is love, and falsehood is hatred.

But he explains below what rewards were given to this lover of goodness and hater of iniquity, saying:

Therefore God, your God, has anointed you. Christ’s anointing signifies both king and priest, since these dignities were assumed through the most sacred anointings. Indeed, the very name [Col. 1036D] “Christ” is derived from the sacred chrism.

He is said to be anointed in that nature according to which, through the divine economy, he is truly said to have been born, died, and risen again as Christ; but his divinity had no need to be assisted by any gift or honor. The repetition in the words “God, your God” displays the proclamation of great love.

With the oil of gladness above your companions. He signifies in two ways how that holy anointing came about. The oil of gladness is the absence of the stain of sin; thus the conscience is always joyful when it is not tormented by the harshness of any recollection.

“Above your companions”—among the sons of human beings, whom he himself also calls brothers in the Gospel. It is said “above your companions” because he is known to have received this blessing above the whole human [Col. 1037A] race—whether kings or priests in the Old Testament, or apostles and martyrs in the New—so that, being uniquely anointed, he might anoint the others.

In him is the fountain of blessing, and from it, according to his own will, blessing suitably flows throughout all the elect. But all these things apply to the flesh, to which the perfect and most glorious Word was united for the salvation of the saints.

This ointment is said in another psalm to have descended upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, down to the edge of his garment (Ps. 132:2). And shortly afterward: “For there the Lord commanded blessing and life forever and ever.”

After the excellence of his humanity, the Apostle again turns to the eternity of the divine [nature] in the same Son of God, saying on the testimony of another psalm:

[Col. 1037B] (VERSE 10.) And you, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. When he says: “In the beginning you founded the earth, Lord,” he shows what cannot be denied by sound minds: that the Creator is known to have existed before his creatures, without any beginning.

And the heavens are the works of your hands. Here we must understand “hand” as the power of God’s command. For elsewhere it is said: “He himself spoke, and they came to be; he himself commanded, and they were created.”

### Verse 11

“They will perish, but you remain.” They perish insofar as they cease to be what they are, when creatures are changed for the better. But you remain, so that, just as he showed the Lord’s eternity before he created all things, he might also say that, after the heavens have been changed, he remains in the glory of his majesty.

“And they will all grow old like a garment” (Col. 1037C). What grows old is consumed by death in the manner of clothing, as is human flesh—which nevertheless will be changed for the better through the resurrection.

He added:

### Verse 12

“And like a cloak you will change them, and they will be changed.” By these words the Prophet perhaps intended the transformation of the heavens to be understood: they too are changed, like the other elements, as another prophet reads: “And there will be a new heaven and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17). To show that the works of the Lord, once made, would remain under eternity, he says: “You will change them, and they will be changed,” because they will never again return to this corruptible state.

“But you are the same, and your years will not fail.” In the transformation he indicates what belongs to the same nature; but he himself is what he is, just as he said to Moses, his servant: “I am who I am.” Thus, in these three verses, the transformation of creatures and the Lord’s eternity are described with marvelous brevity (Col. 1037D).

After declaring the majesty of divine eternity in the Son, blessed Paul again turned his discourse to the glorification of that same humanity, saying:

### Verse 13

“To which of the angels has he ever said: ‘Sit at my right hand’?” To the victorious Son, through his holy incarnation the triumphator over the whole world, after the glory of the resurrection, an honored place in the Father’s majesty is offered, so that through this position the glory of the humanity he assumed might be declared—a glory that he ought to have bestowed upon none of the angels.

“Until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.” By the Lord’s feet eternal stability is signified: there he stands, as upon the footprints of his omnipotence. Those who, abandoning the opposition of their vices day by day, return to the Lord must be subjected to these feet; and, like a footstool beneath his feet, they bow before his teachings (Col. 1038A). There is no doubt that this is said of those enemies who, having been converted, are placed at his right hand.

Here the adverb “until” does not designate the end of some period of time, but demonstrates the power of eternity.

### Verse 14

“Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?”

“Why are you surprised if the angels offer service to his Son, when it is also clear that they have been made ministers of our salvation?”

Wishing to lift up the minds of those to whom he speaks, he says that the functions of the angels have been directed by the Lord for the sake of human salvation. The Son, however, saves as Lord; they serve the salvation of those predestined, as servants.

“The books of both the Old and the New Testaments are everywhere full of examples of this. Angels proclaimed the gospel to the shepherds; we read that an angel was sent to the Virgin Mary; at the Lord’s resurrection angels appeared to the women; and many other things are read in the divine Scriptures. Understand, then, how great an honor exists for us, since God appoints his angels to be ministers for us, just as he appoints them for his friends.”

Having introduced these matters concerning the ministry of the angels, through whom the Law itself was also ministered, he immediately added a discussion of the excellence of the grace brought to us through the Son of God, saying:

## Chapter II

### Verse 1

“Therefore we ought to observe more carefully the things we have heard, lest perhaps we drift away.”

“Why did he say ‘more carefully’? That is, more carefully than we were accustomed to do under the Law (Col. 1038C).”

He therefore urges them to attend more diligently to what they have heard through the Son of God than to what was spoken through angels. As is his custom, he joins his own person to theirs in saying “we have heard,” and by “lest we drift away” he does not wish the minds of those hearing to flow away from what they have heard through empty distractions. He explained this more fully in the following words:

### Verse 2

“For if the word spoken through angels was made firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense of reward…”

“What does ‘was made firm’ mean? Clearly, ‘true,’ as though he were saying: ‘faithful at the appointed time.’”

He wished it to be understood that the Law given through angels [the manuscript reads: “that it was given through angels”] was to be firmly observed in its own time. That the Law was given through angels is shown in many passages. Nevertheless, he testifies that the one who did not observe it received a just recompense of reward.

“Why did he say ‘recompense of reward’? Reward is ordinarily used of something good. But this is the Apostle’s practice: he does not pay great attention to the propriety of words, but indifferently uses expressions said of good things or of evil things for one another. Thus elsewhere he said: ‘bringing every thought into captivity to obey Christ’ (2 Corinthians 10:5). Here also he used ‘recompense of reward’ for punishment.”

### Verse 3

“And how will we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?”

“By these words he signifies that there was not so great a salvation in the Old Testament as there is in the grace of God, which the Son of God brought to us.”

For God has not now promised us, as he did them, earthly riches, but the grace of heaven; not vengeance upon earthly enemies, but victory over spiritual enemies; not a happy temporal life, but an eternally blessed and everlasting one (Col. 1039A).

“He briefly indicated all these things by saying: ‘If we neglect so great a salvation.’”

Then he added the surpassing excellence of what had been spoken through the Son of God:

“Which, having first begun to be proclaimed through the Lord…”

“For these things we are discussing were not brought to us by human beings or even by angels, but the only-begotten Son himself bestowed them upon us. ‘By those who heard,’ he says, ‘it was confirmed to us.’ What does ‘was confirmed’ mean? It was believed and brought to completion, because the salvation given to us through that same Son remains perpetual forever.”

God also bore witness to this:

### Verse 4

“…by signs and wonders and various powers, and distributions of the Holy Spirit” (Col. 1039B).

“He is indicating an abundance of graces that was not present among the ancients,” but which was given after Jesus was glorified. The evangelist testifies to this when he says: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39).

As for what he added, “according to his own will,” he attributes everything to the divine will and counsel, so that no one may consider it to depend upon his own merits. It is as though he were saying: “He himself knows what benefits each person, or what is suitable for each.” Therefore he bestowed grace upon each person according to the foreknowledge of his will.

It follows:

### Verse 5

“For he did not subject to angels the world to come, of which we speak.”
