He did not subject to angels our salvation, which was accomplished in the world at the final age and which had formerly been foretold by the prophets as something that would come, but [also…

[Col. 1039D] **Note:** This word is superfluous in the manuscript.

…to his Son, to whom the paternal voice sounded, as was shown above: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.”

He confirms this with prophetic examples, saying:

### Verse 6

“But someone testified somewhere, saying…”

“Why did he not give the prophet’s name, but concealed it? He does this also in other testimonies, as was said above. I think he did not conceal it out of a desire to hide it, but mentioned it with the intention of showing that they possessed extensive knowledge of the Scriptures, so that there was no need for him to give the name of the speaker. He introduced the testimony as though it concerned something evident and readily at hand.”

“What is man, that you remember him, or the son of man, that you visit him?”

The word “man” is to be pronounced with contempt: that is, one who is fragile and perishable, a follower of Adam, bound by the general corruption of original sin. The Lord remembers him when he forgives his sins and bestows the gifts of his mercy.

“Or the son of man, that you visit him?”

Here the voice must now be raised, since this signifies the Lord the Savior. He was not born, like other mortals, from two human beings, but from the Holy Spirit and the womb of blessed Mary, ever-virgin, proceeding like a bridegroom from a glorious bridal chamber.

And observe that above he said “you remember,” but then added “you visit.” He remembered when, from heaven, he showed mercy to the patriarchs; he visited when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (Col. 1040A). For someone is said to visit when a physician enters the sickroom; and this is truly established as fulfilled in the Lord’s advent.

### Verse 7

“You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor.”

Here the humility and glory of the Lord the Savior are recounted. He was made lower, not by the necessity of ministerial service, but by the voluntary choice of his compassion, as the Apostle says: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7).

It follows: “a little lower than the angels”—he who accepted the cross for the salvation of all and who, in that respect, though the creator of the angels, was made lower than the angels. He rightly said “a little lower,” because although he assumed a mortal body, he had no sin.

He was crowned with glory and honor when, after the exceedingly wondrous resurrection, God exalted him and accepted the world’s faith in him as the one who had become human. He was crowned with glory in the resurrection and ascension, and with honor in the confession of the Father’s majesty (Col. 1040B).

### Verse 8

“And you placed him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet.”

His glory and honor were narrated above; now power is also set forth, so that the perfect fullness of Christ the Lord’s majesty may be recognized.

By saying “over the works of your hands,” every creature is shown to be subject to him. For just as nothing is excluded from the work of the Lord, so nothing is proved to be divided from Christ’s power. In subjecting all things to him, he left nothing that was not subject to him.

By saying “all things,” he appears to have excluded neither earthly nor heavenly things (Col. 1040C). The one whom he had previously said was made a little lower than the angels because of the humility of the flesh, he now says, after the ascension, had all things subjected beneath his feet. This distinction removes uncertainty from those who waver and displays the glory of his incarnation.

He says “beneath his feet,” so that every creature may rightly appear to worship and adore him.

“Now we do not yet see all things subjected to him.”

He says this of those who do not believe in him, because the gospel’s preaching has not yet obtained all things. Above he said that nothing was left unsubdued to him; here he asserts that not all things are yet seen to be subject to him. There he signifies universal subjection, whether voluntary or necessary; here, only the voluntary subjection of those who faithfully believe in him (Col. 1040D).

### Verse 9

“But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.”

“Here he shows that the cross of Christ is glory and honor. Because of it he was made a little lower than the angels, just as the Lord himself always calls it, saying: ‘that the Son of man might be glorified.’ If he calls glorious the things he suffered for his servants, how much more should you, a human being, not doubt that the things you suffer for the Lord belong to everlasting glory.”

He added:

“…so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.”

“It was not owed to us that the Son should taste death for us; grace accomplished this. He indeed died for everyone—but what if not everyone believes? Nevertheless, he fulfilled what belonged to him. He said properly ‘tasted death’ because he remained in it for a short time, so that, having conquered it, he might immediately rise again” (Col. 1041A).

### Verse 10

“For it was fitting that he, for whom all things exist and through whom all things exist, in bringing many sons to glory, should perfect the author of their salvation through suffering.”

“It was fitting to perfect salvation through suffering—that is, to bring the salvation of all to completion.”

“Through whom all things exist” means through his death, by which the things in heaven and the things on earth were restored, and through whom all things were also created.

“Do you see how much there is in the midst of us? He is the Son, and we are sons”—he the natural Son, we adopted sons.

“But he saves, and we are saved. Do you see how he both joins us to himself and distinguishes us? ‘Bringing many sons,’ he says, ‘to glory’: here he joined us to himself. ‘The author of their salvation’: here he distinguished us.”

### Verse 11

“For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one.”

“See again how he joins them, honoring and comforting them, and calling them Christ’s brothers, [Chrysostom: ‘making them his brothers’], according to his statement that they are all from one.

“Then, fortifying his argument and showing how he spoke of him according to the flesh, he added: ‘He who sanctifies’—that is, Christ—‘and those who are sanctified’—that is, us. Do you see the difference? He sanctifies; we are sanctified.”

He added, “all from one.” For there is one God, from whom all things come; but he is so in one way, and we in another. He is the natural Son, whereas we are adopted. Nevertheless, we have one Father, God. He, as the natural Son, sanctifies; we, as adopted sons, are sanctified.

### Verse 12

“For this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: ‘I will proclaim your name to my brothers.’”

“In saying, ‘He is not ashamed to call them brothers,’ he demonstrates that our brotherhood is not a matter of nature, but of his mercy and great humility, by which he chose us as his brothers.”

He confirms this also by prophetic testimony, so that it might not be thought to be something new and not foretold long before. For he says:

“I will proclaim your name to my brothers.”

After the sacred passion and resurrection, he says, the glory of the Divinity would be proclaimed throughout the whole world.

“I will proclaim,” he says—that is, “I will cause it to be announced”—just as he said to the women in the Gospel: “Go, tell my brothers” (Matthew 28:10). Those who love and those who are loved are called brothers.

He added:

“In the midst of the church I will praise you.”

In the midst of the saints the Lord’s praise resounds through him who says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to infants” (Luke 10:21).

The true praise of the Lord is proclaimed not only by the mouth, but also by the heart of one who loves and fulfills the Lord’s commandments (Col. 1041D).

### Verse 13

“And again: ‘I will put my trust in him.’”

This was said of the man he assumed, whose entire confidence is unquestionably in God the Father. Thus he himself says in the Gospel, praying for those concerning whom he was supplicating: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24).

To give them confidence, he also exhorted them, saying: “Take courage; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

And again:

“Behold, I and the children whom God has given me” (Isaiah 8:18).

The Apostle brought this testimony from Isaiah, referring it to Christ and the apostles, whom he called children because of their innocence. Concerning them the Lord himself says: “Let the little children come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Mark 10:14).

### Verse 14

“Therefore, since the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same.”

Here he asserts the true brotherhood and humanity of Christ, not a fictitious one. As children consist of flesh and blood, he likewise partook of flesh and blood, so that he would have that by which he might taste death for the salvation of the children.

He immediately adds the reason for this dispensation:

“…so that through death he might destroy the one who held the power of death, that is, the devil.”

“Here he demonstrates something marvelous: the devil was conquered by the very means through which he had possessed power. The weapons that had been strong against the world—namely, death—were the weapons with which Christ struck him. Here he indicates the greatness of the victor’s power by showing how great a good death would accomplish” (Col. 1042B).

### Verse 15

“So that he might free those who, through fear of death, were subject to slavery throughout their entire life.”

“Why do you tremble? Why do you fear what has already been condemned? It is no longer terrifying,” but desirable, as the end of labors and the beginning of rest.

Why does he say, “through fear of death they were subject to slavery throughout their entire life”? All had been slaves of death because they feared death; they had not yet been released from the fear of death, by whose laws they were held.

Now, therefore, the saints mock death: when the contest has been completed and death has been conquered, they are about to pass into the kingdom. Hence Paul himself says: “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23) (Col. 1042C).

### Verse 16

“For he did not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham.”

“Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect.”

Here he honors the patriarch and those who are descended from him, to whom this epistle was written. He recalls God’s benefits, the carnal kinship with Christ, and the promise made to Abraham: “To you and to your seed I will give this land” (Genesis 17:8). For all are from one—that is, from Abraham: Christ according to the flesh, and those to whom he was speaking (Col. 1042D).

What he said above—“since the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same”—he now develops further, explaining from whom he would take flesh and blood. Therefore he says: “He did not take hold of any of the angels,” that is, he did not assume the nature of any angel, but “he took hold of the seed of Abraham.”

No single dignity was granted to the angels such that the Son of God should be united with their nature in one person. Rather, God the Son bestowed this honor and dignity upon human nature, so that God and man might be one person.

Why did he say “took hold”? Because, as though we were withdrawing from him and fleeing far away, he pursued and seized us, and joined the nature of our weakness to himself in one person. Marvelous is the union, in which the eternal and immortal was joined to the mortal and temporal! (Col. 1043A)

How this would happen he immediately explained, saying:

### Verse 17

“Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect.”

“What does ‘in every respect’ mean? He was born, brought up, grew, suffered, and even died, so that he might be like his brothers in every respect—those who are subject to such a condition.”

Above he says that he is the radiance of glory and the likeness of the Father’s substance, through whom he made the ages.

“This one, so great, so marvelous, and so glorious, took such care for our salvation that he became our brother in every respect. For this reason he in a certain sense left the angels and the other heavenly powers in order to seize us—the lost sheep, found through his passion, placed upon his shoulders, and carried back to the heavenly homeland” (Col. 1043B).

This great and exalted priest of ours also wished to offer himself for us before the Father. Therefore he continued and added:

“…so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people.”

There was no other reason for him to be made like his brothers in every respect except that he might be a faithful high priest for us and make propitiation for our sins.

“There is no other cause for this entire wondrous dispensation than this alone. He saw the human race lying upon the ground [the manuscript reads: ‘lying’], bound by the chains of sins, subject to death, and suffering tyranny; and he had mercy on it as a faithful high priest. ‘Faithful’ means true and powerful.”

It is the priest’s ministry to be faithful, so that he may free from sins those whose priest he is. Therefore, to demonstrate his power, he continued:

### Verse 18

“For in that which he himself suffered, having been tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted.”

“In that”—that is, in the humanity in which he suffered—he is powerful enough to free those who have been overcome and to assist those who are being tempted, so that they may not be overcome. For he came to know our temptations not only as Lord, but also as a human being, through his own experience.

Although God in his own nature is impassible, in the nature he assumed the same Son of God was passible, like our nature.

“In the flesh that he assumed he suffered many savage things. He knows what this tribulation is; he knows what the temptation of those who suffer is.”

He himself was tempted, but he was not overcome.

## Chapter III

### Verses 1–2

“Therefore, holy brothers, participants in a heavenly calling, consider the apostle and high priest of our confession, Jesus, who is faithful to him who made him, as Moses also was in all his house.”

He is still speaking of the ministry of Christ’s incarnation. For in the Gospel he himself testifies that he was sent only to the lost sheep—that is, the house of Israel.

*Angelus* is Greek; in Latin it means “one sent.” Recognize what Jesus the priest is and what kind he is; you have no need of any other consolation or comfort.

“For he called him the high priest of our confession—that is, of our faith—to whom this new people has been entrusted, just as the former people were entrusted to Moses for governance. But greater and far better things have been entrusted to this one.”

Blessed Paul wishes to raise the spirits of the Israelites to the excellence of God’s promises, so that they may prepare themselves attentively to receive what God has graciously promised to bring to them. He calls them dearly beloved brothers, called to heavenly things and made participants with Christ in God’s inheritance.

“Who is faithful to him”—that is, to God the Father—“who made him.” He speaks of Christ’s humanity, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, not of his divinity, which was not made but begotten from the Father, of one substance with him.

“As Moses,” he says, “was faithful in all his house.” Since he intended to place Christ above Moses by comparison in the matter of priesthood under the Law, he introduced this statement, asserting that Christ was faithful in his house.

“Faithful” means devoted, defending what belongs to him and not permitting it to be corrupted. That house is us, as he says in what follows: “Moses was faithful in all his house”—that is, in the former people (Col. 1044B).

He immediately went on to show how we ought to be his house, saying:

“Whose house we are, if we hold firmly to the end the confidence and glory of hope,” because “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24:13).

He calls “house” those who are assembled in the Church. He added: “We are the house of God,” God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus.

Until this point he has compared Christ’s incarnation with Moses; from here he turns to describe Christ’s higher dignity, saying:

### Verse 3

“For he has been deemed worthy of greater glory than Moses, just as the builder of a house has greater honor than the house.”

“He did not say that the craftsman has greater honor than the works, but that the builder has greater honor than the house. Do you see how he is speaking not of a temple, but of the whole people”—first, the people whom Moses led out of Egypt, and then the people whom Christ freed from the devil’s slavery and acquired as his house? (Col. 1044C)

### Verse 4

“For every house is built by someone, but the one who created all things is God.”

Here he distinguishes the builder from the building, wishing it to be understood that God is the author of both houses, but in different ways: of the house over which Moses presided in one way, and of the house over which Christ is recognized as leader and Lord in another.

Therefore he continued:

### Verses 5–6

“Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony to the things that were to be spoken; but Christ as a Son over his own house—whose house we are, if we hold firmly to the end the confidence and glory of hope.”

“This one—that is, Jesus—enters into the Father’s possessions as a son [Chrysostom: ‘as lord’]; the other—that is, Moses—as God’s servant. Here again he urges them to stand firmly and not be overthrown [same author: ‘not to overthrow’]. For we will be God’s house if we hold firmly to the end the confidence of hope and glory.”

He rightly said “the confidence of our hope,” because all good things are possessed by the saints in this life only in hope, until they reach the reality of perfect blessedness: “For in hope we were saved.” We cannot possess the good things promised to us in this life of punishment except in hope, awaiting them patiently and holding firm to the end.

### Verses 7–11

“Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says:

‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts,’”

continuing:

“‘until: They shall enter into my rest.’”

Blessed Paul spoke above of hope, because we must hope for what is to come. “Hope that is seen is not hope.”

The history that the Prophet recalls here is very well known:

“When they had gone out from the land of Egypt, traveled a long way, and received many demonstrations of God’s power in Egypt, at the Red Sea, and in the wilderness, they decided to send scouts to inspect the character of the land that had been promised to them. Those men went forth and returned. They greatly admired the land and said that it produced an abundance of fruits, but they also said that the province contained unconquerable and powerful men.

“But the Israelites were ungrateful and foolish. They ought to have remembered God’s many benefits: how he rescued them from danger when they were enclosed in the midst of the great Egyptian army; how he gave them inexhaustible springs of water; how he bestowed manna; and the other miracles he performed for them. Yet they neither trusted God nor remembered any of these things. Terrified by fear, they said: ‘Let us return to Egypt.’

“Therefore God became angry with them, because they had so quickly forgotten God’s benefits and wonders. He swore that that generation would not enter the rest formerly promised to the patriarchs. Thus they all perished in the wilderness, except only two.

“The Apostle mentions three rests in this epistle. The first is the Sabbath, on which the Lord rested from his works; the second is in Palestine, into which the Israelites entered and were to rest from their many miseries and labors; the third is the true rest, namely, the kingdom of heaven. Those who attain it truly rest from their labors and difficulties.”

It is of this rest that the Prophet speaks here against the Israelites, saying:

“Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, lest you suffer what your ancestors suffered and be deprived of the promised rest” [perhaps: “lest you suffer things of the kind”].

Your fathers once heard his voice through Moses, and they became hardened. Thus he spoke through a herald when you hardened your hearts.

Now he speaks through himself. Let your hearts become soft. He who used to send heralds before him deigned to come himself. He speaks with his own mouth—the one who spoke through the mouths of the prophets.

At the voice of the one who sent the herald and who now cried out through himself, do not close your hearts. Remember how your fathers became hardened and how they did not enter the promised rest, but perished in bitterness, murmuring against God.

They were your fathers who perished; do not imitate them. They were your fathers, but if you do not imitate them, they will not be your fathers, although you were born from them. Know that God is able to raise up children for Abraham from stones.

“For forty years I was offended by that generation.”

It was chastised in many ways, yet they always went astray in their hearts. The Lord fasted for forty days in the wilderness when he triumphed over the one through whom they had murmured against God for forty years in the desert.

After he had completed the whole glory of victory through his passion and resurrection, he remained with his disciples for forty days before ascending into heaven (Col. 1046A). In the first forty days he displayed the temptation of this pilgrimage; in the later forty days, the consolation that the saints will possess in their homeland.

The body—that is, the Church—must suffer temptations in this world. Yet consolation is not absent from it, for he said: “Behold, I am with you always, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

“To whom I swore because of their unbelief that they would not enter my rest.”

For God to speak is a great thing; how much greater, then, for him to swear! He intended the oath to serve as confirmation. By whom does God swear, if not by himself? He has no greater by whom he might swear. By himself he confirms his threats (Col. 1046B).

As surely as what he promises is true, so surely is what he threatens certain. He swore that they would not enter his rest; nevertheless, some must enter that rest.

After those others were rejected, we shall enter, because if some branches were broken off on account of dissimilarity and unbelief, we may be grafted in on account of faith and humility.

The apostolic exhortation to the people concerning entering the rest follows:

### Verse 12

“Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, causing you to depart from the living God.”

“Through hardness unbelief is born. Just as hardened and rigid bodies do not yield to the hands of physicians, so hardened souls do not yield to the word of God.

“If your fathers,” he says, “because they did not hope as they ought to have hoped, suffered the things recorded in the history we mentioned earlier and perished in the wilderness because of hardness of heart, you have much greater reason to fear that such things may happen to you, as they happened to them.”

This word was addressed to those who were present or who would come later; therefore he says “today.” For it is always “today,” as long as the world endures.

He goes further in speaking of “today” and adds:

### Verse 13

“But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called ‘today,’ so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.”

“That is: build one another up, correct one another, lest similar things happen to you; lest any of you be hardened when the sin of unbelief deceives him.

“Do you observe that unbelief produces sin? Just as unbelief brings forth an evil life, so the soul, when it has entered the depth of evils, becomes contemptuous. But contempt, or the one who despises, does not allow it to believe, so that it may free itself from the fear of eternal death.”

Then the Apostle continues:

### Verse 14

“For we have become participants in Christ.”

“What does ‘we have become participants in Christ’ mean? ‘We participate in him,’ he says—that is, we have become one with him. For he is the head and we are the members, co-heirs and sharing one body with him according to the spiritual person who was created in him” (Col. 1047A).

“Provided that we hold firmly to the end the beginning of his substance.”

“What is ‘the beginning of his substance’? It signifies faith, through which we subsist and are born of God as sons, and become, so to speak, of his very substance. This must be observed with the greatest care, lest we be corrupted by the stain of any doctrine.”

The Apostle then continues to speak about “today”:

### Verses 15–19

“While it is said,” he says, “‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in that provocation,’” continuing: “‘from those who heard.’”

Here the Apostle begins to explain the prophetic testimony that he quoted above. He said: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the bitterness of the hardened.” He refers to certain unbelievers—surely those whose corpses were laid low in the wilderness.

“What does he mean? They also heard,” he says, “just as we hear; but what benefit did the word they heard bring them? Therefore do not suppose that merely hearing the preaching provides entry into the rest of God. They also heard through Moses, but derived no benefit from hearing, because they did not believe,” nor was the word they heard joined to faith.

He distinguished those who believed the word of the preaching from those who did not believe, for he says:

“But not all.”

“Caleb and Joshua, because they did not agree with the unbelievers, escaped the punishment inflicted upon them. Nor was it the only gift granted to them that they escaped the death by which the others perished; they were also granted entry into the promised land and the honorable possession of their allotted portion.”

## Chapter IV
### Verse 1

Let us fear their destruction and dread God’s just judgment, who will repay each according to his works: everlasting rest to those who have faith—yet faith that works through love—and perpetual punishment to those who do not believe. Let us beware lest, having abandoned the promise that we made to God in baptism, we return again to the works of unbelief that we renounced before many witnesses. Let each person labor on his own behalf, lest he be found unworthy to enter God’s rest.

### Verse 2

For it was announced to us how we ought to enter God’s rest, just as it was announced to them; yet to us through the Son, and to them through a servant. Immediately the Apostle adds words of exhortation, saying:

### Verse 3

“We enter [the critical reading is: ‘we shall enter’] the rest, we who believe, just as he said: ‘To whom I swore in my anger: They shall not enter my rest.’”

He urges us to enter the rest, lest it should be said of us as it was of them: “They shall enter”—that is, “They shall not enter”—my rest. For he hastens to show that there is another rest to which we have been called, namely, the rest of heaven. He does not say that we shall enter the rest that is in Palestine; rather, because of their hardness of heart, he says that they would enter neither Palestine nor the heavenly rest.

He therefore adds that he is speaking about the first rest:

### Verse 4

“And indeed, the works having been completed from the foundation of the world. For somewhere he has spoken of the seventh day in this way: ‘And God rested on the seventh day from all his works.’”

Immediately afterward he speaks of the second rest promised to the people of God:

### Verse 5

“And in this place again,” he says, “‘They shall not enter my rest.’”

The conjunction *if* can be understood as affirmation, negation, or doubt. Above, however, it was used in the sense of negation, where he said that God swore, because of their unbelief, that they would not enter the promised rest. He therefore added: “They shall enter”—that is, “They shall not enter.” Here, however, it can be understood as affirmative, as though he said: “If they enter, they will prosper.” For this reason he added: “Since it remains for some to enter it.”

He means that into that rest—namely, the one in Palestine—few entered: only two, Caleb and Joshua, out of all those who had departed from Egypt. Accordingly he says:

### Verse 6

“And those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief.”

He is indicating those who departed from Egypt, whose corpses were struck down in the wilderness.

Then he begins to discuss, although obscurely, the third rest, which was promised through Christ to those who believe:

### Verse 7

“Again,” he says, “he appoints a certain day, ‘Today,’ saying in David, after so long a time, as has been said above: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.’”

### Verse 8

“For if Jesus had given them rest, he would never have spoken afterward of another.”

Here he shows that there is a certain third rest, of which David said, “Today.” He does not mean the rest into which Jesus led the people, but another rest, much more excellent than that one, into which the true Jesus—not a figure—has led those who belong to him.

“Let us hear, so that this may be certain [Chrysostom: ‘whence this may be certain’]. After so many years,” he says, “David again says: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.’ For if Jesus had given the people whom he led a true rest, David would not afterward have spoken of another rest. It is certain that some will receive the rest signified by that rest which is in Palestine, into which the true Jesus will lead his people.”

### Verses 9–10

Therefore a sabbath-rest remains for the people of God. For whoever has entered his rest has himself also rested from his works, just as God rested from his.

God’s rest is to be understood as the perfection of his works: on the sixth day the original creation of things was completed, and on the seventh he ceased from creating new natures. Through that eternal rest of God he earnestly summons us to eternal rest, which he called a *sabbath-rest*, since he was speaking to Jews.

“He did not say ‘rest’ here, but ‘sabbath-rest,’ its proper name, toward which they rejoiced and hastened, calling the kingdom of God a sabbath-rest. For just as on the Sabbath he commanded them to abstain from every evil [add from Chrysostom: ‘and to do only those things’] that pertained to the service of God, which the priests performed and which benefited the soul, and nothing else [add from the same source: ‘so also then’].”

He does not want such a Sabbath in the kingdom of God that someone might again return from it to laborious works, as they did after the carnal Sabbath. Whoever enters this Sabbath of God rests forever from his works, just as God rested from his.

Therefore, wishing to instruct them about the resurrection and eternal rest, he repeatedly inserted the word “today,” so that they would never despair of entering, as though he were saying:

“If anyone has sinned, let him have hope of returning as long as it is ‘today.’ Therefore let no one despair as long as he lives.”

### Verse 11

Let us therefore hasten to enter that rest, so that no one may fall into the same example of unbelief.

“Faith is indeed a great and saving thing, and without it no one can be saved, as it is said: ‘Without faith it is impossible to please God.’ But faith alone is not sufficient: it is necessary that faith work through love and that one live worthily before God. Therefore Paul also admonishes those who have been found worthy to receive the dignity of the mysteries, saying: ‘Let us hasten to enter that rest.’ He says, ‘Let us hasten,’ because faith is not sufficient; a life worthy of faith must also be added, and great diligence must be applied lest faith be idle. For if those who murmured against God were not found worthy to enter the land, how shall we be found worthy to enter heaven if we live carelessly like the nations?”

Anyone who wishes to possess heaven must adorn faith with good works. The one who lives badly suffers not only this loss—that he does not enter the kingdom of God—but also, what is more terrifying, that he is handed over to perpetual punishment. Therefore he added: “So that no one may fall into the same example of unbelief.”

He terrified his hearers by the destruction of those who perished in the wilderness, lest they fall under the same judgment, as though he had said:

“We are sufficiently instructed by the example of our ancestors not to fall into similar things, not to suffer what they suffered—that is, not to fall into the same example of unbelief.”

Then, to instill greater fear in sinners, he adds:

### Verse 12

“For the word of God,” he says, “is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword.”

Here he shows that we have the same judge who condemned them because of their unbelief. For he said: “The word of God is living.” The Word of God is the Son of God, who said of himself: “If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death” (John 8:51).

Just as they would have lived and entered the promised land if they had kept the word of God, so we too, if we keep his word, shall live and enter the heavenly rest. For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword. A two-edged sword can divide the limbs from the body and penetrate the hidden parts and nature of the flesh. But the word of God is much more penetrating, reaching, as Paul says, “to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow”; and it is a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

We live through the soul, and we understand through the spirit. Carnal life is shared by us with the beasts; spiritual reason with the angels. God’s judgment is so effective that it distinguishes between carnal and spiritual sins—what each person thinks in his mind and with what desire he serves God in his heart.

His gaze is so penetrating that he knows all that we do or think more certainly than we know it ourselves. We always have as the witness of our actions and thoughts the one whom we shall have as judge. Let us fear his presence, whose knowledge we shall in no way be able to escape.

He said that the word of God is a discerner of thoughts and intentions of the heart—that is, the providence of God—showing that everything within us and outside us will be judged by him, because he knows all that is ours and penetrates the entire person throughout.

Nor is it surprising that, being wholly everywhere, he recognizes his entire creation, whether spiritual or bodily, since nothing that has been made was made without him. Therefore he added:

### Verse 13

“And no creature is invisible in his sight. Everything, however, is naked and open to his eyes.”

“He especially terrified them here, lest perhaps, while they still stood in the faith, they should not complete the works of faith with complete satisfaction—works which he himself discerns, since they are in the heart. There he examines, where he considers, repaying each according to his works. And what shall we say about human beings? Whether you speak of angels, archangels, cherubim, seraphim, or any other creature, everything is revealed to his eye; everything is uncovered and manifest. What could remain hidden from him? ‘Everything is naked and open to his eyes,’ to whom we must give an account.”

What does “to whom we must give an account” mean? It means that we shall render to him an account of our deeds.

### Verse 14

Therefore, since we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God.

A little earlier, while discussing his divinity, he said: “Everything is naked and open to his eyes.” Now, however, because he is speaking about the flesh, he discusses the priesthood of the one who offered himself for the sake of our salvation and how he entered the rest before all others.

“For we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens.” Thus Moses, the leader of the people to whom a temporary rest was promised, did not enter the rest that he repeatedly promised to the people. But this priest, guarantor of a better promise, making a way for those who believe in him, first entered the rest promised to the people entrusted to him.

He shows him to be a great priest because he has an everlasting priesthood and is always living to intercede for us. He also shows that this same one is the Son of God when he says: “Jesus the Son of God”—something he nowhere wished to say of Moses. Rather, in the preceding passages he presented him as a servant, while testifying that under the name “Jesus”—the name which the angel, sent by God, announced to the virgin—he is the true Son of God, and therefore the great priest.

### Verse 15

Let us hold fast to our confession. For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses.

What confession does he mean? That he is the Son of God; that Christ is God; that he suffered, was buried, rose on the third day, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father, and will come from there to judge the living and the dead; through him we have every good thing—redemption, resurrection, and an everlasting inheritance with him. Let us confess these things.

That these things are manifestly true [critical reading: “it is manifest”] is shown by the fact that, as high priest, he enters within the veil, sprinkled with his own blood, not another’s, unlike the earlier high priests, who were sprinkled with the blood of a red heifer.

“For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses.”

He does not, he says, ignore what belongs to us. He came by way of the human condition, in every respect without sin, bringing nothing with him by which he would be subject to death, as he himself testifies in the Gospel, saying: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30).

“Many high priests do not know those who are placed in tribulations, nor do they know what the tribulation of each person is. For it is impossible for one who has not experienced affliction and has [the received text: ‘has endured’; Chrysostom: ‘has not endured’] all things perceptibly to know the afflictions of the sinful [Chrysostom: ‘of the afflicted’]. Our high priest endured fittingly everything that was inflicted upon human misery after the sin of the first man, and then he ascended within the veil to the throne of the Father’s majesty.”

He was tempted in every respect according to the likeness of the flesh, without sin. He was indeed tempted in various ways, but not overcome; tested in tribulations, everywhere a glorious victor.

He was tempted according to the likeness of the flesh, without sin. Thus he had the likeness of sinful flesh, yet his flesh was entirely without sin.

This is the temptation by which he was tempted:

“He suffered the persecution of many, received spittle, was accused, endured insult, suffered calumnies, was rejected by his own people, and was finally crucified. ‘According to the likeness,’ he says, ‘without sin.’ When he says ‘in the likeness of flesh,’ he does not mean that the likeness of flesh was in him, but that he assumed true flesh. Why, then, did he say ‘in the likeness of flesh’? The true nature that he assumed is like our flesh, but he had none of the sins that our flesh contracted from our ancestors.”

For the original sin in the flesh of the first man was of such a kind that from it both punishment and remedy could arise. Punishment and sin exist in the whole human race, except in Christ, in whom alone there was salvation and remedy. Sinful flesh was not so predetermined that a remedy could not arise from it. The power of God knew beforehand how, from the same mass, righteousness, equity, and the compassion of mercy could proceed.

### Verse 16

Let us therefore approach with confidence the throne of grace, so that we may receive mercy and find grace for timely help.

“Let us therefore approach with confidence”—that is, let us approach through faith to his throne of grace. Let us have [lacuna], although we are sinners,

> [Some material is missing in the manuscript.]  
> [Col. 1051D]  
> … that we can recover it through his grace, provided that we produce fruits worthy of repentance and retain firm faith to the end.

Now our true high priest, Jesus the Son of God, sits on the throne of grace, ready to forgive our sins through this timely help. Now is the timely season of his help and mercy, as that excellent Teacher said elsewhere: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2).

Long before this, the prophet indicated this timely season of help, saying: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (Isaiah 49:8).

Even now, after baptism, for sinners to find mercy if they repent is the grace of the one who sits on the throne of grace. That he has become timely for us is a great indication of the humility that he assumed from our nature—not of his substance, which he possesses triumphantly with the Father. Let us bring to him, with confidence in his goodness, our faith at this timely hour, when he sits on the throne of grace and grants everything that will certainly contribute to our salvation.

“Now is the time of gifts; let no one despair of himself.”

Let us fear his throne of equity, when he comes to judge everything according to righteousness. Then will be the time of despair for those who now refuse to turn to the seat of grace, when the bridal chamber will be closed and only those who remain with the bridegroom will carry lamps shining with good works.

## Chapter V

### Verse 1

For every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters pertaining to God.

“The blessed Paul now wishes to show how much better this testament is than the old, because there is nothing imaginary in it”—for example, no bodily temple, no fleshly victims, no legal observances—but everything is higher and more perfect, since the whole character of this testament consists in spiritual realities.

But because spiritual things do not introduce the weak in the same way as bodily things, he begins his discussion with bodily things, saying: “For every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings.”

He first defines what a high priest is and indicates what pertains to the high priest, what his ministry is, and what the signs of the priesthood are: namely, that he should offer gifts and sacrifices for sins and be able to sympathize with those who are ignorant and err, since he himself is surrounded by weakness.

“For it was necessary to establish faith in the superior earthly things,” so that they might reach the superior spiritual realities, and so that custom—from the accustomed priesthood according to the manner that existed in the Law—might lead them to something higher, namely, the priesthood of Christ, since they were still weak. For this reason he introduces the example of the carnal high priest.

The duty of the high priest is to stand between God and the people and to entreat God on behalf of the people’s sins. Christ did this by offering himself for our sins, always living to intercede for us: once taken from among human beings, but always interceding [perhaps: “to be interceded for”] on behalf of human beings.

Here the Apostle sets down some things that priests have in common with Christ, and other things that are higher. Thus what he says, “Every high priest taken from among human beings,” is common to them. “He is appointed on behalf of human beings,” is also common. “To offer gifts and sacrifices for sins,” is also common, but not entirely. The remaining points are not common:

### Verse 2

“He is able to sympathize with those who sin in ignorance.” This is already something superior, which he discussed more fully above in the preceding sentence.

But when he adds:

### Verse 3

“And because of this he ought to offer for sins, just as for the people, so also for himself,” this pertains more to the Levitical priests than to Christ.

Unless someone should say that the body of Christ is one body, the Church, and that when he offers for the Church, he also offers for his own members. But this may appear to be a forced interpretation.

Then he undertakes to discuss how one ought to approach the priesthood.

### Verse 4

“No one,” he says, “takes the honor upon himself, but the one who is called by God, just as Aaron was.”

Here he also strikes at priests desirous of honor and eager for the priesthood—not for the salvation of the people, but out of worldly ambition. Aaron was therefore called by God. By the sign of the flowering rod he was shown to be a priest chosen by God, as was also demonstrated by the burning of those who wished to envy his high priesthood.

### Verse 5

So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but the one who said to him: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.”

This is what he himself says in the Gospel: “I did not come of myself, but he sent me” (John 8:42). And again: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing; it is my Father who glorifies me.”

It should be noted that “glorify,” “honor,” and “make glorious” are three words but one reality. In Greek this is *doxazein* [δοξάζειν], but in Latin translation it is rendered in different ways and placed differently. What is said in the Gospel as “I glorify,” the Apostle here calls “glorification.”

The Son was therefore glorified by the Father when, after he had been baptized, the Father’s voice was heard from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

This glorification, or making glorious, was foretold long beforehand through the prophet, inspired by the Holy Spirit: “The Lord said to me: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (Psalm 2:7). “The Lord” signifies the Father.

Let us observe what he said: “He said to me: ‘You are my Son’”—something he would also say to him after baptism: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 17:5). To make you understand that Christ is one person and the only-begotten Son of God, he added: “Today I have begotten you.”

This has nothing in common with the others who are called sons because they are called priests, concerning whom it is said: “I said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Psalm 81:6). Rather, it belongs wholly and uniquely to the only-begotten Son.

### Verse 6

As he also says in another place: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

Melchizedek was not a priest according to the legal commandments, but according to the dignity of a singular priesthood. He offered bread and wine to God, not the blood of brute animals. In the order of this priesthood Christ became a priest—not a temporal priest, but an eternal one. To him this was said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

All the priests were under the Law; he alone was according to the order of Melchizedek, because he was born from a virginal womb before the morning star—not according to the fact that, as God, he was born from the Father, coeternal with the Father who begot him and consubstantial with him, but a priest because of the flesh that he assumed, or because of the victim that he offered for us, taken from us—that is, his flesh and blood.

Concerning this victim he himself says in the Gospel: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54).

But concerning this flesh and blood, let no human mind conceive anything bloody or corruptible, lest, as the Apostle says, “the one who eats the body of the Lord unworthily eats judgment for himself” (1 Corinthians 11:29). Rather, let it conceive a life-giving and saving substance in the bread and wine, through which, when it is received worthily, the remission of sins and possession of the kingdom of God have been granted to us.

The most righteous king Melchizedek established the order of this sacrifice through a mystical likeness when he offered the fruits of bread and wine to the Lord. It is clear that the victims of sheep and cattle, which belonged to the order of Aaron and not to that of Melchizedek, have passed away; but this institution remains, the one celebrated throughout the world in the distribution of the sacraments.

Christ is especially called a priest because he offered himself once for us as a sacrifice, just as Scripture speaks once of Melchizedek and of his priesthood. When he says “forever,” he signifies the Lord Christ himself, who remains in everlasting glory.

### Verse 7

Who, in the days of his flesh, offered prayers and supplications to the one who could save him from death, with a loud cry and tears, and was heard because of his reverence.

Here the Apostle more clearly expresses what our high priest did in his priesthood, saying: “Who, in the days of his flesh.” The days of our Lord’s flesh are the days in which he assumed flesh, in which he was tempted and suffered, in which he offered prayers and supplications to the one who could save him from death.

Everything that Christ did in the flesh consists of prayers and supplications for the sins of the human race. The holy outpouring of his blood is the loud cry by which he was heard by God the Father because of the reverence due to that passion, which he endured without sin for the sake of our salvation.

Although he had no sin, he was made sin for us—that is, an offering for our sins. He accomplished all this with great reverence and perfect love, the one who first loved us and gave himself for us as an acceptable offering to God. He was therefore heard by God because he offered an acceptable offering to God, namely, himself.

What is said here is therefore similar to what is read in the Gospel as having been said by him: “Father, if it is possible, take this cup from me; nevertheless, not my will but yours be done” (Luke 22:42). For he did not come to do his own will, but the will of the one who sent him.

He placed the will of the Father’s dispensation above the will of his flesh, in order to show in himself the true nature of our humanity. Here the blessed Paul says that he poured out prayers and supplications not because of fear of death, but for the sake of our salvation.

For this reason he also says elsewhere that the blood of Christ cried out better on our behalf than the blood of Abel, which cried from the earth to accuse his brother’s crime; but Christ’s blood cries from the earth to the Father to intercede for us.

### Verses 8–10

And although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from what he suffered. And, having been made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him, having been called by God a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek.

I think enough has been said above about the likeness of Melchizedek’s priesthood. Now let us see what the Apostle wishes to be understood when he says: “Although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from what he suffered.”

The obedience that he says the Son of God learned—that is, voluntarily assumed—he also shows elsewhere, where he says: “He became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross; therefore God also exalted him” (Philippians 2:8–9).

But when he says: “Having been made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him,” “made perfect” means “perfected.” He shows how great is the benefit of his passion, which is sufficient for everlasting salvation to all who believe.

Therefore, if the obedience of the Son is the cause of human salvation, how great is our necessity to obey God, so that we may be found worthy of the salvation that he granted us through his own Son?

### Verse 11

Concerning him we have much to say, and it is difficult to explain, since you have become weak in hearing.

He gives the reason why the discourse that he undertook concerning the incarnate Son was difficult to interpret: namely, because they were weak and possessed a fragile understanding for grasping the deep mysteries of God.

Although, considering the time, they ought to have been teachers, they have become weak and need milk rather than solid food. The difficulty of interpretation lay in their slowness, not in apostolic wisdom, to which the mysteries hidden for ages had been revealed, as he demonstrates fully in the Epistle to the Ephesians (Ephesians 3:8).

Then he adds:

### Verse 12

For although, considering the time, you ought to be teachers, you again need someone to teach you the elementary principles of the beginning of the words of God; and you have become such as need milk, not solid food.

He is speaking to those who ought, through the Law and the prophets, to have acquired an exercised understanding concerning the coming of Christ and the grace brought through him to those who believe. If they had believed, they could also have become teachers of others through the mysteries of God that had been given to them.

But now they have become like infants to whom the first elements of letters are taught for reading. Although they ought to have been strong in faith and eager for knowledge, so as to receive the solid food of wisdom that belongs to the mature, they have now become those who need milk.

For he calls milk elementary discourse. He testifies that they needed it because they could not rise to the higher secrets of the mysteries of God. For example, one who cannot understand what the evangelist says—“The Word became flesh”—how can he reach the height of that discourse where he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”?

### Verses 13–14

For everyone who partakes of milk is unacquainted with the word of righteousness, since he is an infant. Solid food, however, belongs to the mature—to those who have their senses trained for distinguishing good and evil.

The palate distinguishes the flavors of foods; the soul tests the words of various teachings, concerning which he says later in this epistle: “Do not be led away by various teachings.”

Just as an infant does not know how to distinguish one food from another and is often endangered by consuming harmful things unless prevented by an older person, so every unlearned person does not know how to discern teachings, is easily deceived, and is endangered on the path of error.

What distinguishes the unlearned from the wise is analogous to the distinction between milk and solid food. Just as milk suits infants and solid food those mature in age, so elementary discourse suits the unlearned, while it is fitting for the wise—who appear to have trained senses—to know the mystery of God.

“How, then, can our senses become trained? Certainly through practice and frequent reading of the holy Scriptures.”

For this reason the Psalmist calls blessed the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night.

## Chapter VI

### Verse 1

Therefore, leaving behind the beginning of the word of Christ, let us press on to perfection.

“Therefore”—that is, because it is fitting for you to have senses trained in the law of the Lord—let us leave behind the beginning of Christ’s teaching,

> [Some material is missing in the manuscript.]  
> [Col. 1055D]  
> … unless the beginning of faith.

“For just as one who is being introduced to the teaching of letters must first hear the elementary principles, so also a Christian must first of all be instructed in the catholic faith, which is the foundation of our salvation.

“But if he needs to be taught about faith, he does not yet possess the foundation. For this foundation must be firm and fixed in the heart of a Christian, so that from it he may become worthy to be transferred to the perfection of the other virtues.

“If someone has heard the word of truth and has been baptized, and after several years needs to hear again about the faith—because he must believe concerning the resurrection and the future age—he does not yet possess the foundation. He is seeking again the beginning of Christianity, because faith is the foundation, while the other things are superstructures.”

The blessed Paul shows this in the words that follow, saying: “Not again laying the foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God.”

“We call that person perfect who possesses a righteous life together with faith. If either one of these is lacking, he will not be perfect; if both are lacking, he may rightly be called an infant. And just as an infant must be taught letters, so this person must again be instructed in the faith.”

He secretly wishes to weaken the Law and call his hearers back to the grace of Christ. Whoever is going to proceed toward virtue must first condemn and cast away wickedness, cleanse the works of death through repentance, and thus approach God.

### Verse 2

The teaching of baptisms [the manuscript reads “of baptisms”; the critical reading is “the teaching of baptism”], the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment.

Repentance alone is not sufficient to cleanse sinners unless they are immediately baptized, as the blessed Peter is read to have answered in the Acts of the Apostles: “Repent, brothers, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus” (Acts 2:38).

For what a person cannot accomplish by himself, he can receive through God’s grace in baptism.

“What is meant by ‘the teaching of baptisms’? It should not be understood as referring to many baptisms, but to one. For just as there is one faith, so there is also one baptism; but he used the plural because of the variety of those who receive baptism.”

The laying on of hands is also mentioned, through which the Holy Spirit can be received. It is believed that after baptism this is customarily performed by bishops for the confirmation of unity in the Church of Christ.

Once these things have been fully received in the Church, one must possess faith in the resurrection and in the future judgment. To live like the angels and to need none of the things that belong to this life—this is the promise of life made to us through the Holy Spirit. The fruit of this promise is the presence of that same life. These two things—faith and judgment—remain for one who has been baptized once; there is no second baptism.

**VERSE 3.**—And this we shall do, if indeed God permits it. For in this faith concerning baptism, the resurrection, and the judgment to come, with God’s permission we are instructing you fully. But lest anyone should in any way think that a second or third baptism could be performed after sins, he immediately adds, saying:

**VERSES 4–6.**—“For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have also tasted the heavenly gift, have become partakers of the Holy Spirit, have likewise tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and then have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt.”

He says “impossible,” not “difficult.” He says “impossible.” He drove them to despair of being baptized a second time, because what is impossible is what cannot be done; whereas what is difficult, although it can be done with effort, is nevertheless possible. If, he says, you have once been enlightened through the grace of the Holy Spirit and have tasted the heavenly gift—that is, have received the forgiveness of sins—and have become partakers of the Holy Spirit in the distribution of God’s gifts, which blessed Paul enumerates in the Epistle to the Corinthians (I Cor. XII, 7 ff.); and have tasted the good word of God—here he means the teaching of the Gospel—and have come to know the powers of the age to come: what is the revelation of the age to come except the resurrection and the blessed life promised to the saints? All these things you received and came to know in the teaching of faith, enlightened by God’s grace through baptism.

Know with absolute certainty that, if you fall again into sins, it is impossible for you to be renewed again to repentance.

“What then? Is repentance excluded after baptism? By no means. But renewal through the washing of sacred baptism cannot take place a second time. He said ‘to be renewed,’ that is, ‘to become new.’ For to make a person new is the work of sacred baptism, concerning which the Prophet says: ‘Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s’ (Ps. CII, 5).”

The power of this sacred baptism rests upon the cross and burial of Christ. Therefore he adds: “Crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt.” That is, our old man was crucified together with Christ, as he says elsewhere: “For we have been conformed to his death”; and again: “You have been buried with him through baptism into death.” For just as it is impossible for Christ to be crucified a second time—that is, to hold him up to contempt—so the person who thinks that he can be baptized a second time seeks to crucify Christ a second time. Yet Christ, having been crucified and having died, rose victorious over death and ascended into heaven with the triumph of glory.

“For just as Christ died once in the flesh upon the cross, so we die once in baptism—not in the flesh, but to sin”; and just as he cannot die again, so we cannot be baptized again, except perhaps through the tears of repentance, not through the washing of regeneration.

“What then,” you ask, “is there no repentance?” There certainly is repentance, but there is no other baptism. Repentance, however, possesses great power even over one who is deeply submerged in sins. If he wills, it can free him from the burden of sins, set him safely on solid ground even when he has reached the very bottom of wickedness; and this is clear from many testimonies. Therefore he adds: “For shall one who falls not rise again, or shall one who turns away not return?” (Jer. VIII, 4).

What, then, is this medicine of repentance, and how is it prepared? First, by exposing one’s own sins: “I have not concealed my iniquity,” he says, “and I will declare my iniquity against myself to the Lord, and you have taken away the wickedness of my heart” (Ps. XXXI, 6; XXXVII, 19). Second, by mourning one’s sins with great humility and thereafter producing worthy fruits of repentance, so that one may never again fall into the same sins. Then he should begin to ransom himself through abundant almsgiving, if he possesses the resources of this world, as it is written: “A man’s riches are the ransom of his soul” (Prov. XIII, 8). Finally, he must not be angry with anyone, return evil for evil, but forgive all who sin against him, as Truth himself says: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven.”

**VERSES 7–8.**—“For the earth, often drinking in the rain that comes upon it and producing suitable vegetation for those by whom it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God. But producing thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near to a curse, whose end is burning.”

“Let us hear the words of God with fear. These are not Paul’s threats; they are not the words of a human being. They belong to the Holy Spirit; they belong to Christ speaking through Paul.”

Here he makes a comparison between the soul progressing in the teaching of God and one neglecting its salvation. He likens the soul that is progressing in the flowers of holy growth to fruitful earth irrigated by heavenly rains, saying: “For the earth, often drinking in the rain that comes upon it.” This shows that those to whom the word was addressed received and drank in the word of heavenly teaching, and received it repeatedly through the Law and through the Prophets, yet even so were not made ready to produce shoots of faith.

He adds further concerning the good earth into which the seed of God’s word fell: “Producing suitable vegetation.” Nothing is so suitable as faith in the Son of God and an excellent life. Such earth receives a blessing from God, so that it may bear thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and even a hundredfold fruit. It should also be noted that all abundance in the crops of the earth and in the fruits of trees can come to the cultivators according to their desire in no other way than through God’s blessing. For it was not the farmers who roused the earth to produce fruit, but God’s command, as the same blessed Paul says elsewhere: “I planted, Apollo watered, but God gives the growth” (I Cor. III, 6).

Thus he aptly produced this example of a soul flourishing in virtues and in God’s blessing, and immediately added another comparison concerning one who neglects his salvation, saying: “But producing thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near to a curse, whose end is burning.”

“For who is clean from these thorns? Even if we were clean, we ought not therefore to be presumptuous, but to fear and tremble lest thorns of sins should sprout in us.” How could a soul or flesh full of thorns take pride? Would it not need to eradicate them with even greater care?

“What, then, are the thorns? Let us hear Christ speaking of thorns, saying that the cares of this world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful.”

“He said ‘producing thorns,’ not ‘generating them’: it is near to a curse. O how much consolation this statement contains! He says ‘near to a curse,’ not ‘a curse’ [Chrysostom: ‘not cursed’]. Whoever has not yet fallen into the curse, but is only near to it, can also be brought far away from it. And he did not console them only in this respect, but also in what follows. He did not say, ‘Rejected and near to a curse, which will be burned.’ But what did he say? ‘Whose end is burning.’”

This burning will occur only if someone remains in his sins to the end. For “on whatever day the sinner turns, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezek. XXXIII, 12).

“If we cut away the thorns through repentance, we shall be able to enjoy a thousand blessings, become approved, and share in God’s blessing.”

After he had sufficiently rebuked them, terrified them, and struck them, he again treats them, lest he make them despair. He neither flatters them in everything nor strikes them in everything. We do not say these things as though we think that you are full of thorns, but because we fear that you may become such. It is better to terrify you with words, lest you should suffer through the facts themselves.

**VERSE 9.**—“But, beloved, we are confident of better things concerning you, and of things nearer to salvation, although we speak in this way.”

Because blessed Paul had no present grounds on which to praise those to whom he was writing, he begins to proclaim to them the hope of future things, saying: “We are confident, brothers, of better things concerning you and of things nearer to salvation, although we speak in this way.”

It is as though he had said: “We have confidence concerning you in certain excellent things that advance your salvation. We are certainly not saying of you what I said above concerning the rejected earth and its nearness to burning, because we believe better things concerning you.”

He also brought their past to mind, so that from their past he might draw them toward every good thing. Therefore he adds:

**VERSE 10.**—“For God is not unjust, so as to forget your work and the love which you have shown in his name, when you have ministered to the saints and continue to minister.”

“See how he revived their souls and strengthened them by recalling ancient things to their minds. Then he caused them not to think that God had forgotten them and his former benefits toward them. For the person who lacks hope for the future must necessarily sin. Then he urges them in every way to hope for future things. For if someone despairs of God’s present benefits, because he does not possess what comes from God, who will be able to strengthen him concerning future things?

“He reproaches the Galatians in a similar way, saying: ‘You were running well; who hindered you?’ (Gal. V, 7). And again: ‘Have you suffered so many things in vain?’ (ibid. III, 4).” But, in order to soften the same statement concerning the present, he immediately added: “If indeed in vain.”

So also in this passage he tempered his statement, saying: “For God is not unjust, so as to forget your work, while you have shown such love toward the saints. We want you to imitate those who through faith and patience have inherited the promises.”

His desire for their salvation he shows in the following citation, saying:

**VERSE 11.**—“For we desire each of you to display the same diligence unto the fulfillment of hope to the end.”

**VERSE 12.**—“So that you may not become sluggish.”

“We desire,” he says, “that you should conduct yourselves not only in words but also in virtues. We are not blaming your former conduct, but admonishing you to be concerned about the future. That is, just as you were formerly, so we desire you to be now and in the future. He did not say ‘I wish,’ which expresses the authority of teaching, but, as befitted paternal affection, ‘we desire each of you to have the same diligence that you once possessed unto the fulfillment of hope in the eternal resurrection.’”

But become imitators of those who through faith and patience will inherit the promises. He urges his hearers to await God’s promises and the inheritances he promised to his saints with genuine faith and perfect patience. And he strives to strengthen this still more firmly by examples, when he says:

**VERSES 13–15.**—“For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom he could swear, he swore by himself, saying: ‘Surely blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you.’ And so, having patiently endured, he obtained the promise.”

The wisdom of blessed Paul is wonderful. Alternately he raises those to whom he writes by praises; alternately he terrifies them with the threats of the preceding history, lest they should be unbelieving and insufficiently trust God’s promise; and alternately he urges them to patience and faith by their examples. And so that they might believe without doubt, he presents not only God’s word but also his oath by himself.

Although he had many examples of saints who through patience inherited God’s promises, he especially selects faithful Abraham “because of the dignity of his person and because this occurred in him above all others” [Supplement: “he mentions”]. Having patiently endured, he obtained the promises in his sons—not only those of past time, which were fulfilled in the people of God, but also those which he proclaimed as future for the sons of Abraham’s faith. His sons are those whom God’s goodness raised up from the stones of the nations and made sons of Abraham in faith.

The long-suffering of the one who heard and awaited the promised inheritance cooperated with God’s promise. The fainthearted and unbelieving [MS: *incredibiles*] did not attain it through the words of God, but a very great multitude of them perished in the wilderness. How impious it is not to believe God when he swears! For he swore by himself because he had no one greater by whom he could swear.

Here, in this oath, the person of God the Father may be understood, who promised the same patriarch concerning his Son, saying: “And in your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXVI, 4). He does not say “in your seeds,” as blessed Paul demonstrates in another epistle (Gal. III, 16), but “in your seed,” that is, in Christ.

Christ himself also swears in the Gospel, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you” (John I, 51), and he swears by himself, because he too had no one greater by whom he could swear.

“Surely blessing I will bless you.” This means: in the stars of heaven, by which the saints who were to come from his seed are signified [lacuna]. “And multiplying I will multiply you”: this means also in the sand of the sea, by which the sinful people of that nation may be signified. For both are recorded as spoken by the Lord, where he says: “Your seed shall be like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the shore of the sea” (Gen. XXII, 17).

**VERSE 16.**—“For human beings swear by one greater than themselves, and the end of every dispute among them, for confirmation, is an oath.”

If, then, the promises of human beings are to be believed for the future, although it is said by the Prophet, “Every human being is a liar,” how much more ought God’s oath to be believed, since he is truth and can neither be deceived nor lie?

“For human beings swear by one greater than themselves, and the end of every dispute among them, for confirmation, is an oath.” It is as though he were saying: “By this the discussion of the entire dispute is resolved—not of one particular dispute, but of the whole matter.” Certainly one ought to believe God without an oath; yet, he says, God swears.

**VERSE 17.**—“In this matter God, desiring to show more abundantly to the heirs of the promise the unchangeableness of his purpose…”

“Therefore he also mentions this promise, which was made commonly to us” [Chrysostom: “communally”]. “He inserted an oath. Since among human beings something appears trustworthy when an oath intervenes in their disputes” [Chrysostom: “when an oath has intervened”]. “It is not the same for a human being to swear by himself as for God. A human being does not possess power over himself”; but God has power over all things that exist.

“But because the human race is unbelieving, he accommodates himself to us. For just as he swears on our account, although it is unworthy of him not to be believed, as was said above, so also ‘he learned from what he suffered,’ because human beings think that something is especially worthy of belief when [through] experience someone passes to faith.”

**VERSES 18–19.**—“So that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have the strongest consolation, we who have fled for refuge to hold fast the hope set before us. We have this hope as a secure and firm anchor of the soul.”

He mentions two things: the promises of God the Father concerning his Son and the coming of the Son into this world for our salvation. The hope set before us is the truth of the events that were promised to the patriarchs and fulfilled for them, so that from things already accomplished we may believe the things that are future.

“We have this hope,” he says, “as a secure and firm anchor of the soul.” Just as an anchor, cast from a ship, does not allow it to be driven about, even when winds shake it, but makes the ship firm when it has been cast down, so faith, strengthened by hope, introduces us into the reality of those things which we now possess through faith and hope.

Therefore he adds, saying: “And entering into the interior of the veil.” A storm and heavy rain shake a small vessel, but an anchor does not allow it to sink. Thus our hope, which we have fixed in the interior of the veil, cannot be submerged by any unbelief if we say truthfully with the Prophet: “Cast your care upon the Lord, and he will nourish you” (Ps. LIV, 23).

If we did not possess this hope, we would be utterly submerged, not only in spiritual matters but also in bodily ones; for, as the Apostle says, “the one who plows plows in hope,” and all our labor is consoled by hope of whatever reward.

Hope penetrates into the interior of the veil when it believes, hopes for, and loves heavenly things without any doubt, and demonstrates by its works what it believes and what it hopes for.

To add a firmer hope to us, he adds:

**VERSE 20.**—“Where Jesus, our forerunner, has entered for us, having become a high priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,” and so forth.

“It is necessary, therefore, that those of whom he is high priest should also be better; and whatever difference there is between Aaron and Christ, there is, in a certain sense, the same difference between the Jews and Christians. Let us offer superior sacrifices of such a kind as can be offered in that heavenly sanctuary—not now sheep and an ox, not blood and fat. All these things have been dissolved, and in their place rational service has been introduced.

“What, then, is rational service? That which is offered to God through the soul and through the spirit. ‘God is spirit,’ he says, ‘and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth’” (John IV, 24).

What is it to worship God in spirit except to worship him in charity and perfect faith, in undoubting hope, and in the holy virtues of the soul, which the Apostle abundantly enumerates elsewhere?

## CHAPTER VII

**VERSES 1–2.**—“For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the enemies and blessed him, to whom Abraham divided a tenth of everything…”

The Hebrews transmit that this man was Shem, the first son of Noah, and that at the time when Abraham was born he was two hundred and ninety years old. It would not be surprising if Melchizedek went out to meet Abraham after his victory, brought bread and wine for the refreshment both of Abraham himself and of his warriors, and blessed him—a blessing which he gave to his descendant by right of fatherhood; and if he received from him a tenth of the spoil and victory, as the priest of the Most High God who was also king of Salem.

Salem, however, is not, as Josephus and many of our people think, Jerusalem—a name composed of Greek and Hebrew, which the mixture of foreign languages shows to be absurd. Rather, it was a town near Scythopolis [the manuscript reads “Schitopholim”], which is still called Salem to this day. There the palace of Melchizedek is pointed out, its great ruins displaying the magnificence of an ancient structure.

Jacob is also read to have descended to this city, which was in the land of Canaan, in the region of Shechem. It should also be considered that when Abraham was returning from the slaughter of the enemies whom he pursued as far as Dan, Salem lay not on the road to Jerusalem but on the route to the metropolitan town of Shechem. Concerning this we read in the Gospel: “John was baptizing in Aenon near Salim, because there were many waters there.”

**VERSE 3.**—“First, because he is interpreted ‘king of righteousness’; then also ‘king of Salem,’ and so forth. Without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God, he remains a priest forever.”

Blessed Paul frequently introduces this same Melchizedek as a type of God the Savior.
