Although nearly all the saints, patriarchs, and prophets of earlier times expressed figures of the Savior in some respect, this Melchizedek more particularly, since he was not of the Jewish race, went before as a type of the priesthood of the Son of God, concerning whom it is said in Psalm CIX: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

They interpret his order in many ways: he alone was both king and priest; he exercised the priesthood before circumcision, so that the nations did not receive the priesthood from the Jews, but the Jews from the nations; he was not anointed with priestly oil, as Moses’ commands prescribe, but with the oil of gladness and the purity of faith; he did not sacrifice victims of flesh and blood or receive the blood of brute animals in his right hand, but consecrated the priesthood through the simple and pure sacrifice of Christ, bread and wine.

Yet it must not be believed that this Melchizedek was without father or mother, since Christ too, according to both natures, has a father and a mother. Rather, Melchizedek is suddenly introduced in Genesis as having met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the enemies, and neither before nor afterward is his name or genealogy found written.

The Apostle affirms by this example that Aaron’s priesthood—that is, the priesthood of the Jewish people—had both a beginning and an end, whereas the priesthood of Melchizedek—that is, the priesthood of the Church of Christ—is eternal, both in the past and in the future.

This Melchizedek is interpreted as “king of righteousness.”

“Who is the true king of righteousness except our Lord Jesus Christ? Then he is ‘king of Salem,’ that is, ‘king of peace,’ which pertains to Christ. For he made us righteous, making peace between all things in heaven and all things on earth”—he alone is the king of righteousness and peace, our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his divinity is without beginning and without end, an everlasting king, eternally from the eternal Father [read: *Patre*, “Father”], although according to his temporal mother he was temporal.

“For just as we do not read the beginning or end of this Melchizedek in Scripture because it has not been written, so we do not know the beginning or end of the Son of God because he has none. The likeness consists in this: neither the beginning nor the end of the one or the other is read. In the case of Melchizedek, because it was not written; in the case of the Son, because it does not exist at all.”

**VERSE 4.**—“See how great this man is, to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils.”

He now turns his discourse toward those who boast that they are sons of Abraham and that their nobility descended from his origin, whom they strive to exalt with divine praises and are read in the Gospel to have placed above the Lord, saying: “Are you greater than our father Abraham?”

It is as though he were saying: “The one whom you consider superior to all others was offering a tenth to Melchizedek, and that from the chief portion of the victory—he who was made like the Son of God and became a priest forever.”

**VERSE 5.**—“Those indeed of the sons of Levi who receive the priesthood have a commandment, according to the Law, to take tithes from the people, that is, from their brothers, although they themselves have come from the loins of Abraham.”

“So great is the excellence of the priesthood that even those who were similar by descent and had the same ancestor were nevertheless [judged] much better than their brothers”—those who are made worthy of the priesthood. Aaron, for example, is read to have stood between the living and the dead to appease God’s anger that had broken out; he could do this on behalf of the people, although all had one and the same ancestor.

“Therefore Abraham himself would in no way have given a tenth to a foreigner unless his honor had been very great and superior,” since he gave him a tenth of the spoils after discovering that he was pleasing to God.

“He also showed that an uncircumcised priest was much higher than a circumcised priest. How, then, did he show this? Because Levi himself” [Chrysostom: “because Levi gave him tithes”], from whom the priestly race arose, was tithed in the loins of his ancestor.

**VERSES 6–10.**—“But the one whose genealogy is not counted among them received tithes from Abraham and blessed the one who had the promises. Without any contradiction, the lesser is blessed by the greater” [the manuscript reads “by the better”].

That one whose genealogy is without record was tithed in Abraham—not only Levi, but also Aaron himself, who used to receive tithes from the people, and through him the whole Levitical priesthood.

Nor is he content merely to stop here, but he further exalts him, who belonged to another race, with greater honor, saying: “And he blessed the one who had the promises.”

“He showed that Melchizedek was more honorable according to the common judgment of all; and, ‘without any contradiction,’ he says—that is, it is clearer than daylight to everyone that the lesser is blessed by the greater. Therefore the type of Christ is better even than the one who had the promises.”

Who is the one who lives? He also is the one who was made priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

“According to the order of Melchizedek,” who bears the type of our high priest, who offered himself as an offering pleasing to God—not from any necessity, but through the will of his own power [supplement: “excellence”]. He is designated as one who owed nothing to death; therefore, through the priestly sacrifice of his body, he washed away the sins of all.

**VERSES 11–12.**—“If, therefore, perfection had been through the Levitical priesthood—for under it the people received the Law—what further need was there for another priest to arise according to the order of Melchizedek, and not to be called according to the order of Aaron? For when the priesthood of the body [MS: *corporis*] is transferred, there must also be a transfer of the Law.”

“Here he begins to show the differences between the Old and New Testaments,” saying: “If perfection—that is, completion—was through the Levitical priesthood, what need was there for another priest to arise?”

No one doubts that Aaron was the first priest from the tribe of Levi after the Law had been given. Therefore he called the priesthood in which Aaron served “the Levitical priesthood.” In the priestly order, Melchizedek was much better than this Levitical priesthood, since he bore the type of our priest, that is, the Lord and Savior of the world.

He would certainly not have said “according to the order of Melchizedek” if Aaron’s priesthood had been better, under which the Jewish people had received the Law. If, therefore, there is a transfer of the priesthood, there must also be a transfer of the Law. For a priest cannot exist without a testament, without a law, and without commandments.

**VERSES 13–14.**—“For the one concerning whom these things are said belongs to another tribe, from which no one attended the altar. For it is evident that our Lord arose from Judah, a tribe concerning which Moses said nothing about priests.”

“For the one concerning whom,” he says—that is, the one concerning whom these things were spoken—meaning the Lord, namely the Savior.

“When the priesthood was transferred, the testament was transferred at the same time—not only in order and commandments, but also in tribe. For it was necessary that the tribe should also be changed. And how was the priesthood transferred from tribe to tribe, from the priestly tribe to the royal one? So that the same tribe might be both royal and priestly.

“Observe the mystery: first there was the royal priesthood of Melchizedek, according to the sequence of this discourse; second, there was the priesthood in Aaron; third, in Christ it was again royal. He was always king, but became priest when he assumed flesh and when he offered the sacrifice.

“Do you see the change of things? For the things that came about through transfer appear, as it were, from the continuity [Chrysostom: ‘consequence’] of events to return as something new.”

**VERSES 15–17.**—“And it is still more evident if another priest arises according to the likeness [the manuscript reads ‘order’] of Melchizedek, who was made not according to the law of a carnal commandment but according to the power of an indestructible life. For he testifies: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.’”

Here he establishes a new [Codex: “our”] distinction between Aaron’s priesthood and Christ’s priesthood: the former was carnal, the latter spiritual; the former temporal, the latter eternal.

For he says of Aaron’s priesthood: “According to the law of a carnal commandment.” That Law was carnal in many respects: in the circumcision of the flesh, the cleansing of the flesh, carnal sacrifices and offerings, distinctions of foods, days, and seasons, and also in the rewards by which peace, security, prosperity, abundance of crops, and royal power were promised to those who did good and kept the Law—all of which had to come to an end in death.

But Christ’s priesthood is not like this; it is according to the power of an indestructible life.

“Who is this priest of such a kind? Not Aaron; not Melchizedek himself, but the one whom that Melchizedek represented as a type. Concerning him God the Father himself testifies by an oath: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.’ That is, he is not temporal and does not have an end, but exists according to the power of an indestructible life.”

He possesses indestructible life in himself, although for a time he was dead in the flesh. Nevertheless, he lives forever in divinity and humanity, the mediator between God and human beings, always living to intercede for us.

**VERSES 18–19.**—“For there is indeed an annulment of the preceding commandment because of its weakness and uselessness—for the Law brought nothing to perfection.”

“What, then? Did the Law accomplish nothing? It certainly accomplished something, but it accomplished nothing in the sense that it could make those who served under it perfect. Therefore it was annulled, so that room might be given to grace, when grace should come, in which perfection would take place.

“The Law was useful, but for those who had faith in Christ, not for those who had fixed their entire hope upon it: ‘the introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God.’”

**VERSE 20.**—“And inasmuch as this was not without an oath.”

Some indeed became priests without an oath.

“‘The introduction of a better hope.’ The Law too had hope, but not such hope. For those who pleased God and kept his Law hoped to possess the land, suffer nothing distressing, and live prosperously, as it is said: ‘The one who does it shall live by it.’

“But here we hope that, pleasing God and keeping the commandments of the Gospel, we shall not possess the earth but heaven. More than that—and this is much better than heaven—we hope to stand near God, reach the Father’s own throne, and minister to him with the angels.”

This priesthood, through which we shall possess this glory, will not be without an oath, so that we may believe God’s promise to be firm. For he promised all these things to us in his own Son, whom he delivered up for us all, so that through him we may have all these things [supplement, perhaps: *habeamus*, “may have”]. Concerning him it is said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

**VERSES 22–24.**—“To such an extent has Jesus become the guarantor of a better covenant. And the others indeed became priests in greater number because they were prevented by death from continuing; but he, because he remains forever, possesses a permanent priesthood.”

“He sets forth two distinctions, because our priest has no end, unlike the legal priesthood. He says this from the person of Christ, who entered, as he says, according to the power of an indestructible life.” And he testifies to this by an oath, as was said above.

“Just as he remains, so also the Law that he brought will remain. In it there is true forgiveness of sins and the perpetual reception of grace. For if the former Law was excluded because of its weakness, since it could lead nothing to perfection, this Law, which the great high priest brought, has power, is strong, and remains.

“He demonstrates this from the high priest. How? Because he is one. He would not be one unless he were immortal. For just as there were many priests under the Law because they were mortal, so there is one because he is immortal even to this day. He has become the guarantor of a better covenant to such an extent that, according to what was sworn concerning him, he will always remain.”

**VERSE 25.**—“Therefore he is also able to save forever those who approach God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them.”

You see that he is speaking of the one who exists according to the flesh. “For when he is high priest, then he also intercedes”; because, in the nature according to which he is high priest, he intercedes for his own.

Who is it that intercedes except the union of human nature with his divinity, which he brought to the Father’s throne, always living and able to save?

The other high priests, because they did not exist forever, did not intercede forever. He not only saves in this life through the intercession of his humanity, but also glorifies in the future, when he will hand over the kingdom to God the Father and lead the saints to the vision of the Father’s majesty.

**VERSE 26.**—“For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens.”

It was fitting that he should also be such a high priest for those concerning whom he himself says: “I will no longer call you servants but friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV, 15).

The legal servants had mortal and sinful high priests, offering sacrifices for themselves. But the sons and friends of God have an immortal high priest, separated from sinners—that is, from the former priests—who is innocent and holy.

“Innocent,” because he is without malice, as the Prophet says: “No deceit was found in his mouth” (Isa. LIII, 9).

“Holy,” because he is preeminent in every goodness.

“Undefiled,” because he possessed no sin.

“Made higher than the heavens,” because all the angels of God adore him.

**VERSE 27.**—“Who has no daily necessity, like the priests, first to offer sacrifices for his own sins and then for those of the people; for this he did once for all when he offered himself.”

Here he shows the greatness of the sacrifice. Although it was one, it was offered sufficiently for eternity; it prevailed to an extent that all other sacrifices did not; and what he offered, he did not offer for himself but for the people.

Nor was this to be offered daily for the people. Rather, this sacrifice possessed such holiness and honor before God that, once offered, it benefited the people of God forever.

Source/review notes: The omitted Chapter IX–X continuation has been restored in full. Printed corruptions, conjectures, alternate readings, citations, and the terminal fragment remain explicit.

**VERSE 28.**—For the law appoints as priests men who have weakness; therefore they always offered sacrifices for themselves as well as for the people. But this man is so powerful that, once he had been offered in the sacrifice of his flesh, no believer needed to offer anything further on his behalf. The word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints the Son perfect forever.

Here, too, the name “Son” is used to distinguish him from the servants who were under the law, because those servants were weak—either because they were sinners or because they were mortal. He demonstrates that this Son is perfect because he lives forever and is forever without sin. The Apostle says both things, wonderfully comforting his hearers and fearfully alarming the negligent. He comforts them in saying: “They have drawn near to a priest of great power [the manuscript’s reading is corrupt] through sacrifice.” He terrifies them lest they sin, because that sacrifice will never again be offered for sins.

“There is no other sacrifice; one sacrifice cleansed us, but after this there will be judgment. Let all of us who have been redeemed remain in this sacrifice, preserving our dignity and our honor.”

## CHAPTER VIII

**VERSES 1, 2.**—“Now the chief point in what has been said is this: We have such a high priest, who sits at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heavens, a minister of the holy things and of the true tabernacle, which God established, not man.”

When he says, “The chief point in what has been said,” he signifies something supreme and important, as though recapitulating the preceding argument and bringing the hearer to the matter itself. “We have such a high priest,” he says, “who sits at the right hand of Majesty”: he mingles lowly things with exalted, human things with divine, showing that the one who is God is also high priest. Nor is there another who sits at God’s right hand except the one who is the minister of the holy things and of the tabernacle which God established, not man.

This tabernacle is the souls of the saints, for whom the great high priest ministers eternal joys, and it is also the veil of heaven. He sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high, the Father. When you hear that the same person sits at God’s right hand and ministers to the saints, “sitting signifies divine dignity, while ministering signifies the abundant mercy and great love that he has bestowed upon us.”

It is a wondrous mystery that the same person should sit in the glory of divinity whom his persecutors saw hanging upon the cross; and in that cross of his passion there is the ministry of our salvation. We believe that this took place, and we know that it profits us for salvation.

But what should the human mind, still carnal, understand by the statement that he sits at God’s right hand? Holy Scripture accommodates itself to our weakness and customary ways of thinking, so that feeble humanity might be instructed, since human beings could not reach that secret glory of divinity. Therefore, after the glory of the resurrection, an honorable seat is offered to the victorious Son, the triumphator of the whole world through his holy incarnation, so that the glory of the humanity he assumed might be declared through this position. For by the word “sit” it is indicated that Christ our head is recognized as placed at the Father’s right hand—that is, in the sublimity of divine Majesty. Those are to be placed in that region who, through the gift of the same Savior, are separated from the faithless.

**(VERSE 3.)**—For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; hence it is necessary that this one also have something to offer.

The high priests of the Old Testament were appointed to offer legal gifts and sacrifices for their own sins, as he said above, and also for the sins of the people. Hence it was necessary that our Savior, in the days of his flesh, should have something to offer for us. Since in the eternal nature of his divinity he had nothing that he could offer, he took from us what he could offer for us, namely, human flesh.

What is so suitable for sacrifice as mortal flesh for mortals? And what is so pure, for cleansing mortal faults, as flesh born in a womb, from a virginal womb, without any contamination of carnal desire? And what could be offered and received with such favor as the flesh of our sacrifice, made the body of our priest?

And how is this to be understood? Four things are considered in every sacrifice: to whom it is offered, by whom it is offered, what is offered, and for whom it is offered. Therefore sacrifice is owed to no one except the true God alone. Accordingly, our high priest offered himself for us, being both priest and sacrifice.

**VERSES 4, 5.**—“If he were on earth, he would not be a priest, since there are those who offer gifts according to the law, who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things.”

If, therefore, he were an earthly high priest like Aaron, he would not be a priest according to the eternal order of Melchizedek. Aaron died and is no longer a priest; but because Christ lives forever, he is an everlasting priest—not like those who served a copy and shadow of the heavenly things.

All the priests appointed under the law exercised a priesthood that was a copy and shadow of the heavenly things, that is, of spiritual realities, signifying the true and everlasting priesthood of Christ. Is not our faith a heavenly altar on which we offer prayers every day?

“It contains nothing of a carnal sacrifice that dissolves into ashes, spreads out in smoke, or disperses into vapor. These sacrifices, however, are made bright and more festive. How could those who are told, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose sins you retain, they are retained’ (printed as John XXVIII, 23; the verse is John XX, 23), fail to celebrate heavenly sacrifices?”

All the sacrifices of the Levitical priesthood were signs of these sacrifices: “For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John I, 17).

“As Moses was instructed when he completed the tabernacle: ‘See that you make everything according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain’ (Exodus XXV, 40). Since hearing seems less suited than sight for receiving instruction—for we do not commit everything we hear to memory as we do what we perceive with our own eyes—he therefore says, ‘See that you make everything as it was shown to you on the mountain.’”

But one may ask what he meant by “everything”: whether the construction of the tabernacle, or the sacrifices and offerings that they were to offer in it. It is better understood as referring to both.

**(VERSE 6.)**—“But now he has obtained a more excellent ministry, just as he is the mediator of a better covenant, which has been established [the manuscript reads *sanctificatum*; another reading is *sancitum*, ‘enacted’] upon better promises.”

“You see,” he says, “how much better this is than that celebration. For the former was a copy and form, whereas this is the truth,” as it is said in the Gospel: “The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.”

Of this grace the Apostle speaks here subsequently, saying: “Which has been established upon better promises.” As heavenly things are better than earthly things, and eternal things than temporal, so Christ God is the better mediator and priest of the covenant.

“Passing from place, priest, and sacrifice, he finally establishes the difference between the covenants. Here he raises us to heaven and shows that we have heaven as our tabernacle,” in the promises of God.

**VERSES 7, 8.**—“For if that first covenant had been without fault, no place would have been sought for a second.”

In condemning them he says this: if those who observed the first covenant had been blameless, a place for a second would never have been sought. But because the first was not perfect, a suitable place was found for the second covenant, just as the Lord says through the Prophet: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a new covenant over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah” (Jeremiah XXXI, 33).

**(VERSE 9.)**—“Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, because they did not remain in my covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord.”

Here he carefully specifies whom he means by saying that they did not remain in his covenant. When he says, “On the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt,” he refers to the law given on Mount Sinai, which is known to have been given on the fiftieth day. Their fathers did not remain in it, but made a calf at Horeb and worshiped it.

He is not speaking of the covenant that he proposed to their fathers—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. All the children of faith can be called children of Abraham, as it is written of the Lord himself in the Gospel: “I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matthew III, 9).

This is the covenant that God will complete—that is, perfect—among all nations, so that whoever believes in Christ may truly be a child of Abraham according to spiritual generation.

**(VERSES 10–12.)**—“For this is the covenant that I will establish with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and I will write them upon their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And no one will teach his neighbor, and no one his brother, saying, ‘Know God’ [another reading: ‘the Lord’], for all will know me, from the least to the greatest. For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.”

There is a great difference here between law and law, between Scripture and Scripture, between the letter and grace. The letter of the law was written on stone tablets, which Moses himself broke when he saw the people playing before the calf. Grace, however, was given to the hearts of believers through the Holy Spirit, through whom love has been poured into the hearts of believers.

What had been hidden in the letter and was read by the people through the traditions of their teachers, the Holy Spirit, when he came, taught to the apostles. This is what the Prophet says: “No one will teach his neighbor and no one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for all will know me, from the least to the greatest of them.”

The Gospel likewise says of the Lord: “Then he opened their minds so that they understood the Scriptures” (Luke XXIV, 45).

**(VERSE 13.)**—By saying “new,” he made the first old. And what becomes obsolete and grows old is near destruction.

“Taking confidence from the Prophet, Paul attacks that covenant still more vigorously, aptly showing that our things are now flourishing, while those things are old and near destruction.” But our youth will be renewed like the eagle’s if we run to the fountain of life and stretch our wings and eyes toward the sun of righteousness.

## Chapter IX

**Verses 1–2.**—“The former covenant indeed had ordinances of worship and an earthly sanctuary.” [Col. 1071A] For the first tabernacle was made, in which were the lampstands, the table, and the setting forth of the loaves; this is called the Holy Place.

We read in Josephus that the tabernacle was made in the likeness of this world, while its outer parts bore the figure of the present age. Therefore the holy priests minister daily, approaching—or, by conjecture, *kindling*—the light of doctrine and feeding God’s people. The loaves must remain ready upon the table from Sabbath to Sabbath: from the Sabbath of our hope, in which we are secure as though in Christ and safe from the storms of this world, until that Sabbath in which—or, by conjecture, *so that*—we may possess what we now hold in hope.

The lampstands are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which shine in the Church for those who understand through him upon whom shall rest the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord.

The inner tabernacle, called “the Holy of Holies,” signifies heaven itself. **Verses 3–5.**—“The veil is heaven,” within which Christ our priest entered, not without blood. He has a golden censer in which the prayers of the saints are offered. There the cherubim in glory overshadowed—or, as the proposed correction reads, *overshadowing*—the mercy seat; this is the fullness of knowledge. The mercy seat is fittingly said to be placed above the ark because it was specially granted by God the Father to the Mediator between God and humanity that he should be the propitiation for our sins (1 John 2:2). Hence Paul also says: “Jesus Christ, who died—indeed, who also rose—who is at the right hand of God, [Col. 1071C] who also intercedes for us” (Romans 8:34).

“And the ark of the covenant.” This is the flesh of our Savior, in which were the manna of divinity, the tablets of the two Testaments, and Aaron’s rod, which flowered in Christ’s priesthood. Of these there is no time now to speak individually.

**Verse 6.**—“When these things had thus been arranged, the priests always entered the first tabernacle, completing the services of the sacrifices.” He now shows more clearly what he called above an earthly sanctuary: it was the tabernacle in which the sacrifices were earthly and brought those serving in them to no perfection.

**Verse 7.**—“But into the second, the high priest alone entered once a year, not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the people’s ignorance.” This high priest signifies Christ in part, because Christ entered heaven once, within the veil into the Holy of Holies, to appear before God’s face for us. As for the statement that he offered for his own and the people’s ignorance, this is what he himself said on the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), followed by “the words of my offenses.” What are the words of the offenses except those of his body?

**Verses 8–9.**—“The Holy Spirit signifying by this that the way of the saints”—the text reads *life*, with *way* proposed—“had not yet been disclosed while the first tabernacle was still standing. This is a parable for the present time, according to which gifts and sacrifices are offered.”

> These things, he says, were constructed in this manner so that we might learn that the Holy of Holies—that is, heaven—was still ordinarily inaccessible to mortals.

We must not suppose that we cannot enter the place where our high priest went before us, not without blood, as the prophet foretold: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bosra?” (Isaiah 63:1). [Col. 1072A] Rather, we patiently await the time of our resurrection, in which, when he appears, we know what we shall be: like him, that is, immortal. Just as death will no longer have dominion over him, neither will it have dominion over our flesh.

“These sacrifices cannot perfect the worshiper according to conscience, being only matters of foods and drinks”—**Verse 10**—“and various washings and ordinances of the flesh imposed until the time of correction.” These fleshly ordinances concerning foods, drinks, and various washings were imposed until the time of correction. Consider what this means: the law brought nothing to perfection. According to the supplied, grammatically compressed reading, however, the cleansing of the flesh could remove filth and ignorance; concerning adultery and capital crimes it could purify nothing, but stood ready to condemn without mercy.

For this reason the Pharisees brought the adulterous woman before Jesus (John 8:3), so that they might accuse him if he ordered her acquittal contrary to the law, or so that he might lose his praiseworthy gentleness if he commanded that the law’s order be observed. But God’s Wisdom avoided both, as though he had said: The law is indeed just, if only it had just ministers. If one wishes to remove a speck from another’s eye, it is right that he first remove the beam from his own.

The washings of the Jews are treated more fully in the Gospel according to Mark, where the Pharisees reproached the Lord and his disciples for eating with unwashed hands (Mark 7). In vain the Pharisees, and in vain all the Jews, wash their hands and bathe when they return from the market as long as they disdain to be washed in the Savior’s fountain. The Pharisees understood carnally the spiritual words of the prophets, which commanded chastening of heart and deed: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isaiah 1:16), and “Be clean, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isaiah 52:11). They hoped only in bodily washing. Yet it is certain that Moses and the prophets, when for any reason they ordered the vessels of God’s people to be washed with water, purified by fire, or sanctified with oil, commended to us not the cleansing of material things but rather the chastening and holiness of minds and works and the salvation of souls.

[Col. 1072D] **Verse 11.**—“Christ, appearing as high priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made by hand, that is, not of this creation.” The tabernacle not made by hand signifies heaven, from which we hope that future, eternal, and imperishable goods will be given to us. “Not of this creation” means that it is not of the same kind as the tabernacle a human being erected in the wilderness; it was created by God himself in a far different manner, spiritually rather than carnally. In that tabernacle now dwell the souls of the righteous and the spirits of their angels, waiting until the number of their fellow servants is complete.

**Verse 12.**—“Neither through the blood of goats and calves, but through his own blood, he entered the sanctuary once, having obtained eternal redemption.” [Col. 1073A] Everything has been changed. There the blood of goats washed away sins of the flesh; here Christ’s blood washes away sins of the spirit. Having obtained eternal redemption, he entered the sanctuary—that is, heaven—once, to appear before God’s face for us. The phrase “having obtained eternal redemption” shows that no eternal redemption existed in the former sacrifices and legal ceremonies.

**Verse 13.**—“For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled upon the defiled, sanctifies for the cleansing [of the flesh], how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself immaculate to God?”

> If the blood of bulls, he says, could cleanse the flesh, much more will Christ’s blood wash away the soul’s stain. Lest anyone, on hearing “sanctifies,” suppose the washing to be perfect, he immediately adds the cause of the difference: “who through the eternal Holy Spirit offered himself immaculate to God.” That is, he offered an immaculate sacrifice. This sacrifice was clean from sins: it was offered through the eternal Holy Spirit, not through fire or anything else.

“And he will cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God.” He rightly said “from dead works.” Anyone who touched a dead body was defiled; likewise, one who touches a dead work is contaminated in conscience. Dead works are sins. “Whoever touches pitch will be stained by it”; so one who has been washed from dead works through repentance and then does them again is more grievously contaminated. As the apostle Peter says, “The dog returned to its vomit” (2 Peter 2:22); so too does one who repeats his folly.

[Col. 1073C] “To serve,” he says, “the living God.” Here he shows that those who possess dead works cannot serve the true and living God, because those works are dead and false. Rightly, no one possessing dead works enters here. If a person who touched a dead body was not permitted to enter the temple, how much less can one who has dead works enter heaven? All works that possess no life are dead.

**Verses 15–17.**—“Therefore he is the mediator of the New Testament, so that, death having intervened for redemption from the transgressions committed under the former testament, those who are called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance. For where there is a testament, the death of the testator must intervene. A testament is confirmed upon the dead; otherwise it has no force while the testator lives.”

> Perhaps many who were more weakly disposed would, especially because Christ died, disbelieve his promises. Paul therefore adds this out of abundance and, taking examples from common custom, speaks as though answering a doubtful heart: it was therefore necessary to confess [lacuna]. For testaments become firm and receive force not while testators live but when they have died. A testament is made near the last day of death; at the same time it ought to have witnesses. Notice him saying: “I am the one who bears testimony concerning myself, and the one who sent me bears testimony concerning me” (printed John 20:18; the wording corresponds to John 8:18).

The printed commentary marks an alternative in Chrysostom: “it was necessary to have confidence. Why? Because,” in place of the corrupt words surrounding “it was necessary to confess.”

[Col. 1074A] “And in your law it is written that the testimony of two persons is true.” If the testimony of two is not to be rejected, how much more the testimony of the Father and the Son, and also of the Holy Spirit, of whom it is said: “He will bear testimony concerning me.” Of the apostles it is said: “And you also bear testimony concerning me, because you have been with me from the beginning” (printed John 5:36; compare John 15:27).

> We were under liability, and it was necessary for us to die. He sent his Son, made from a woman, who could die for those who owed death and who died for us the death that was owed—or, by the proposed reading, *owed to us*. He made us worthy of the testament and the promised inheritance. In this manner the testament was made firm. Our sin was so great that we could never have been saved unless the only-begotten Son of God had died for us.

The statement that a testament is weak while the testator lives signifies that as long as the testator lives, he can alter his decision and introduce different heirs into his inheritance.

**Verse 18.**—“Hence not even the first was dedicated without blood.”

> Hence, he says, not even the first testament was dedicated without blood—that is, made firm and ratified. The word “hence” is as if he said that it was therefore necessary for the solemnity of the testament to be completed also through Christ’s death.

**Verses 19–22.**—“For when every commandment of the law had been read by Moses to all the people, taking”—the codex has the plural *taking*, with the singular proposed—“the blood of calves and goats with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, he sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying: ‘This is the blood of the testament that God commanded for you.’ [Col. 1074C] He likewise sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels of ministry with blood, and according to the law he cleansed almost everything in blood; without the shedding of blood there was”—with *there is* proposed—“no remission.”

What does it mean that the book, the people, and the tabernacle were sprinkled with blood, except that the precious blood of Christ our Savior was foretold from the beginning in that figure? Why hyssop? Hyssop is a lowly herb that grows upon rocks; through it are signified Christ’s humility and the strength by which our inner parts are cleansed, for disorders of the lungs are customarily purged by this herb. Why water? It shows the future cleansing through the water of baptism. Why scarlet wool? So that it might retain the blood. Here it shows that the water and the blood are the same. Our baptism too—Chrysostom reads, *for his baptism*—is his passion; therefore Paul says elsewhere: “For you were buried with him in baptism” (Romans 6:4).

Why does he say that without the shedding of blood there was no remission? Because among them remission was not full but only half-full, in the smallest part. Now, however, he says: “This is the blood of the New Testament, which was poured out for us for the remission of sins.” What is the book sprinkled with mystical blood, what are the vessels of anointing, and what is the tabernacle, except the people? They themselves are the book, the vessels, and the tabernacle. Therefore the Lord says: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Corinthians 6:16; the source prints verse 15).

[Col. 1075A] The whole cleansing of the Old Testament was bodily; now the cleansing by Christ’s blood is spiritual and occurs in the soul. Therefore he says: “This is the blood of the New Testament for the remission of sins” (Mark 14:24).

> Among them it was sprinkled on the surface and the sprinkled person was washed again; the people did not always walk around bloodstained. It is not so in the soul: the blood is mingled with its very substance, making it strong and clean and leading it to that ineffable beauty.

For this reason the lamb was slain and its blood smeared upon the lintels of those who were to be delivered. For this reason also all the sacrifices of the Old Testament are recorded: so that they might signify—or, as proposed, *so that there might be signified*—this one sacrifice through which there is true remission of sins and cleansing of the soul forever.

[Col. 1075B] **Verses 23–24.**—“It is therefore necessary that the copies of heavenly things be cleansed by these, but the heavenly things themselves by better sacrifices than these. For Jesus did not enter handmade sanctuaries”—another reading has the singular, *a handmade sanctuary*—“copies of the true ones, but heaven itself, so that he may now appear before God’s face for us.”

How are these copies of the things in heaven? He calls our way of life “heavenly”; the exemplar and signification of this way of life was everything performed in the Old Testament. Hence the Apostle says: “Our way of life is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

> Therefore those things that are ours are in heaven, and these things of ours are heavenly, even though they are celebrated on earth.

What is this way of life of ours? It is the true philosophy that Christ taught and the apostles followed, which leads to heavenly things. Hence the Apostle also says: “The first man was earthly, from the earth; the second is heavenly, from heaven. As was the earthly man, so are the earthly; and as is the heavenly man, so are the heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15:47–48).

[Col. 1075D] > “By better sacrifices,” he says, “than these.” What is better is better than something good. The copies of the things in heaven were therefore good—Chrysostom reads, *their copies*—but the heavenly things themselves far surpass the copies by which they are signified. If, therefore, we are heavenly and have obtained so great a sacrifice, let us fear to remain on earth. We seem somehow both to be and not to be on earth when in will we are in heaven, although in body we are on earth. If in mind we draw near to God, we are in heaven. What concern is heaven to me when I see the Lord of heaven, when I myself become heaven? “I and the Father,” he says, “will come and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). Heaven of itself is serene and clean; it does not change in winter or at night. Thus let us not fear to suffer this either amid the tribulations of the world or the adversities of the devil, but let us remain immaculate and clean.

Heaven has its sun; let us too have Christ, the sun of righteousness, always shining in our hearts.

**Verse 25.**—“Nor was it so that he might offer himself often, as the high priest enters the sanctuary every year with another’s blood.” Above he said “copies of the true things,” calling all of them copies; yet he also calls true the sanctuary that the high priest enters. This one temple was more venerable than any other in the whole world, and people came to it from every direction, [Col. 1076A] as is read in Acts (Acts 2:5) concerning the holy day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit was given to the apostles speaking in all languages, so that those gathered from different regions of the world might hear and see the heavenly miracle.

> But Paul set the whole heaven over against this temple. He showed not only this difference but also the greatness of the high priest, “that he may appear before God’s face.”

The next sentence of the source is corrupt. Its apparent sense is that the matter is made more venerable not merely by heaven but also by the entrance: not simply through certain signs, as here, but because Christ stands before God himself, always living to intercede for us.

> Observe how great the differences are: often and once; in another’s blood and in his own blood. The difference is therefore great. He himself is sacrifice, priest, and victim.

[Col. 1076B] **Verses 26–28.**—“Otherwise he would have had to suffer frequently from the foundation of the world. But now he has appeared once at the consummation of the ages to destroy sin through his sacrifice. And as it is appointed for a human being to die once, and after this comes judgment, so Christ also was offered once to exhaust the sins of many; he will appear a second time, without sin, to those awaiting him for salvation.”

Christ suffered after sins had become many. He fittingly appeared then, as Paul also says elsewhere: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20). If his single offering had not sufficed to exhaust the sins of all who believe in him, he would have had to suffer repeatedly from the foundation of the world. To prevent that, he suffered once at the consummation of the world to exhaust the sins of many.

[Col. 1076C] > Why “of many” and not “of all”? Because not all believe. He died for all—that is, as far as lay in him. That one death is of as great a weight as the perdition of all. He did not take away the sins of all because they refused to believe.

Chrysostom’s variant reads, “that death is of such weight,” in place of “the death of one is of such weight.” It is appointed for everyone to die once, and after death each person will be judged according to his merits. So too Christ died once for the sins of others; because he died voluntarily and not from necessity, at his second coming he will appear without sin. Every victim offered for sin is called “sin”; at that time he will no longer be a victim for sin, because there will be no sin, but justice, whether in the reward of the righteous or in the requital of sinners.

## Chapter X

[Col. 1076D] **Verse 1.**—“For the law, possessing a shadow of the good things to come and not the very image of the realities—”

> That is, not the reality itself. So long as someone looking at a painting sees only the outlines of shadows, indicating what the painter intends to paint, it is a kind of shadow and not an image. But if the painter applies the actual bloom of the colors to the outlines, then the image comes into being. The law too was something like this: a shadow of the truth.

“Year after year, by the very same victims that they offer without ceasing, it can never make those who approach perfect. **Verses 2–4.**—Otherwise they would have ceased to offer”—another reading has the passive, *to be offered*—“because the worshipers, once cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sin. [Col. 1077A] But in those sacrifices a remembrance of sins is made every year, for it is impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of bulls and goats.”

> This victim, he says, is one, whereas those victims are many. They lacked strength precisely because they were many. Tell me, what need would there be for many if one sufficed? The fact that many were offered continually shows that they never cleansed those who offered them. When a medicine is strong, effective for health, and able to repel the whole illness, one application accomplishes everything. If, therefore, one application has accomplished everything, it displays its power by not being applied again. [The source repeats: “and this is its work, that it should no longer be applied.”] But if it is continually applied, that is a clear indication that the medicine had too little power. Its strength, indeed, is shown by being applied once and not frequently. So too here: for what reason were they always treated with the same sacrifices? If they had been freed from every sin, no one would offer sacrifices every day. Thus there was a remembrance of sin, not absolution,

because the priests themselves and the people alike were cleansed daily by the same victims.

[Col. 1077B] > With Christ, by contrast, the victim was offered once, powerful for everlasting salvation. What then of us? Do we not offer every day? We do offer, but in order to make a memorial of his death. This victim is one, not many. How is it one and not many? Because it was offered once. That victim was offered in the Holy of Holies; this sacrifice is its representation. [Col. 1077C] We always offer the selfsame thing—the manuscript reads *to that very thing*. We do not offer one lamb today and another tomorrow, but always the selfsame. Therefore this sacrifice is one. Otherwise, because it is offered in many places, would there on that account be many Christs? By no means. Christ is one everywhere, existing fully here and fully there: one body. For just as he who offers everywhere—or, in Chrysostom, *is offered*—is one body and not many bodies, so too the sacrifice is one. Our high priest is he who offered the victim that cleanses us. We offer that same victim even now, which, though offered then, cannot be consumed. What we do is done in commemoration of what was done. “Do this,” he says, “in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). We do not offer another sacrifice, as the high priest did, but always the same; rather, we perform the memorial of the sacrifice.

[Col. 1077D] [The supplied chunk ends here.]

### VERSES 5–9

Therefore, when entering the world, he says:

> Sacrifice and offering you did not desire,  
> but you prepared a body for me;  
> burnt offerings and sin offerings did not please you.  
> Then I said, “Behold, I come;  
> in the heading of the book it is written of me:  
> I desired to do your will, O God.”

Above, he says: “Because you did not desire sacrifice and offerings and burnt offerings for sin, nor were the things offered according to the law pleasing to you.” Then I said: “Behold, I come to do your will, O God.”

The signs that promised have been taken away, because the promised reality has been presented. Therefore he says: “You did not desire burnt offerings and sacrifices, but you prepared a body for me.” This means that the sacrifices prescribed by the law could not atone for the sin of the human race. “But you prepared a body for me.” He said this in the person of the one who assumed the body of our mortality, so that he might have something to offer on our behalf.

“Then I said: Behold, I come.” When the time came for the signs to be taken away and the promised reality to arrive, then I said: “Behold, I come.” Those things were taken away; these have been fulfilled. Where are the sacrifices of the Jews? They have passed away and are not in the Church of Christ, because the one whom those sacrifices prefigured has come, of whom it is written at the beginning, or in the heading, of the book.

Which book? Certainly the Psalter, where it says:

> Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly,  
> nor stood in the way of sinners,  
> nor sat in the seat of pestilence,  
> but his delight is in the law of the Lord (Psalm 1:1).

Some call this psalm the heading of the entire book [thus the manuscript]. Therefore the Apostle also says here: “In the heading of the book it is written of me, that I should do your will, O God.” This is what is said in the Gospel: “I have not come,” he says, “to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38).

“He takes away the first, in order to establish the second.” That is, he takes away the first testament, which was given to Moses on Mount Sinai, in order to establish the second—that is, the Gospel brought through Christ—as firm.

### VERSE 10

In this will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ, once for all.

This offering was made once, but it always has power to cleanse all who believe and all who desire to be purified by it. Therefore he added—and blessed Paul, explaining more fully the power of this sacrifice, said the same thing:

### VERSES 11–13

> Every priest indeed stands daily, ministering and repeatedly offering the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins; but this man, after offering one sacrifice for sins forever, sits at the right hand of God, from that time waiting until his enemies are placed as a footstool for his feet.

“For he first shows that the former sacrifices were useless for complete cleansing, but that they were rather a form and possessed much less efficacy. Yet, since the following objection occurred to him—namely, if they were forms, why, when the reality came, did they not cease and disappear, but are still celebrated?—he therefore continues to speak about them, showing that they are no longer celebrated, not even as forms; for God does not regard them as acceptable” [Chrysostom: “Therefore he says this to them”].

This is possessed only by those who have always resisted the Holy Spirit. Consequently, he rebukes them by prophetic testimony, saying:

> You did not desire burnt offerings or offerings for sin.

“This is said of no one other than Christ. And what wonder is it if now the will of God is not in the blood of goats and bulls, when it is said through the prophet Isaiah: ‘Who has asked these things from your hands?’ (Isaiah 1:12) Since you did not desire these things, then I said: ‘Behold, I come’; in this will we have been saved. How have we been saved? That is, through the offering of the body of Jesus, once for all.

“Every priest indeed stands daily, ministering. To minister is the task of servants, but to sit is the task of lords; therefore he also says: ‘He sits at the right hand of God.’ Consequently, after offering one sacrifice, which can save forever, he sits at the right hand of the Father, from that time waiting until his enemies are placed as a footstool for his feet.

“Who are his enemies? The Jews, certainly, and all unbelievers,” who will be condemned by him on the day of judgment.

“And here he signifies the enormity of his power. He did not say, ‘Let them be subjected,’ but ‘that they may be placed beneath his feet.’ Let us therefore not become part of the number of his enemies. For not only are unbelievers his enemies; so also are those who are filled with an impure life. The mind of the flesh is hostile to God, for it is not subject to the law, nor indeed can it be” (Romans 8:6).

### VERSES 14–18

> For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are being sanctified.  
> The Holy Spirit also bears witness to us.  
> For after saying, “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws into their hearts, and I will write them upon their minds,” he also says:  
> “And their sins and their iniquities I will remember no more.”  
> [Manuscript: “True”; read: “Where”] Now, where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer an offering for sin.

For by one offering of the body of Christ he has perfected forever those who have been sanctified; it effects the complete forgiveness of sins.

He also proved this from prophetic testimony, saying: “The Holy Spirit also bears witness to us: ‘This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws into their hearts.’”

Not as the law was written on tablets of stone, but he was perpetually writing it on tablets of fleshly hearts.

What is this law that has been written in the hearts of individuals? Certainly charity: that we should not do to another what we do not want done to ourselves. This is the law that covers a multitude of sins (James 5:20), as it is said in the Gospel: “Whatever you want people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matthew 7:12).

Therefore it is not necessary to cleanse oneself daily through daily sacrifices, as under the old law.

### VERSES 19–21

> Therefore, brothers, having confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Christ, a new and living way that he inaugurated for us through the veil, that is, through his flesh, and having a great priest over the house of God—

Here he shows the difference between the high priest and the priest, between the sacrifices, the tabernacle, the testament, and the promise, and a very great difference indeed: those things were temporary, whereas these are eternal; those appeared for a time, whereas these endure; those were weak, whereas these are perfect; those were forms, whereas these are the truth.

This is the new testament, possessing forgiveness of sins; the former possessed nothing of the kind. The former was made by hand; this was not made by hand. The former had the blood of goats; this has the Lord’s [Chrysostom: “this has God”]. The former had a priest standing; this has one sitting.

Since, therefore, those things are lesser and these greater, he says: “Therefore, brothers, having confidence.” From where does this confidence arise? For just as sins produce shame, so the forgiveness of sins produces confidence; and so do the fact that we have become heirs and that we enjoy such great love.

“In the entering of the holy places,” he says. Here he means heaven and access to spiritual realities. “Which he dedicated,” that is, which he constructed and inaugurated. Dedication is called the beginning of use.

“Which he prepared,” he says, “and through which he himself proceeded—a new and living way.” “Through the veil of his flesh,” he says. For this flesh first penetrated that way and dedicated it, inasmuch as he himself proceeded through it. We rightly call it a veil: when he was raised into heaven, then the heavenly things appeared.

### VERSE 22

“Let us draw near,” he says, “with a true heart and in the fullness of faith, our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.”

By what should we draw near? Certainly by faith, by spiritual worship, with a truthful heart, without hypocrisy, in the full assurance of faith, because none of these things is visible. There are no longer priests, no sacrifice, no altar. Therefore he says, “in the fullness of faith.”

We must believe as firmly as we are certain of visible things. Indeed, even more firmly: here the senses of the flesh sometimes err concerning things that are seen, but there they cannot err, because by the spirit we perceive spiritual realities, and we are not permitted to doubt them.

Therefore he says: “Our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience.” He shows that not faith alone is sought, but also a life of virtue, because faith without works is idle. They cleansed their bodies, but not their consciences.

“And washed,” he says, “with pure water.” Here he means the washing of baptism. Baptism is not merely the cleansing of the body but of the soul, if faith is present in the one baptized—whether the faith of the parents or the person’s own faith, if he has reached the age of reason.

### VERSE 23

> Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.

“Do not investigate anything further, and expect no rational demonstration; all these things require faith,” because without faith it is impossible to please God.

Just as God is faithful in his promises, so he wants us to be faithful in our promises, those that we have vowed. We must resist the devil and serve Christ.

### VERSES 24–25

> Let us consider one another, provoking one another to charity and good works, not abandoning our assembly, as is the custom of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the day approaching.

What does “let us consider one another” mean? If someone is believed to possess virtue [another reading: “if someone is endowed with virtue”], let us imitate him and direct our attention toward him, so that we may love and be loved; for good works arise from love.

Assembly is a great good, since it produces more abundant charity, and from it all good works are generated. Nothing is good that is not done through charity. Let us therefore strengthen one another in this, because “charity is the fullness of the law” (Romans 13:10).

We do not need labors or sweat: if we love one another, a path leading to virtue and heavenly things is laid before us spontaneously.

“As is the custom of some.” In this passage he not only admonished but also blamed and terrified those who were splitting the unity of charity.

“But encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the day approaching.” What day does he indicate except the day of judgment, on which the merits of each person are examined? Or perhaps the final day of our life. For elsewhere he says: “The Lord is near; do not be anxious about anything” (Philippians 4:5–6)—that is, about earthly matters. And again: “Now our salvation is nearer than when we believed” (Romans 13:11), for the time has been shortened.

### VERSE 26

> For if we sin deliberately after receiving knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins.

If we sin willingly after receiving recognition of the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains for us, as under the old law it was permitted to offer sacrifices repeatedly for sin.

For Christ himself is not to be sacrificed again for our sins. This was done once, and there is no need for a second time. Rather, after receiving grace, we must remain in faith and in the truth of good works.

“You have been cleansed; you are free from crimes; you have become a son of God. If you return to your first vomit, another judgment awaits you,” unless you are renewed through repentance.

Therefore he continues:

### VERSE 27

> But a fearful expectation of judgment and the fury of a fire that will consume the adversaries.

“By this he did not exclude repentance, nor the propitiation that takes place through repentance. He does not repel or cast the sinner down into despair, for he is not so hostile to our salvation.

“But what does he exclude? He excludes a second baptism. He did not say, ‘There is no further repentance,’ nor did he say, ‘There is no further forgiveness.’ Rather, he says, ‘There is no further sacrifice’; that is, there is no second cross.

“For by one offering he perfected forever those who are sanctified, unlike the Jewish sacrifices. He wishes to make us cautious, so that we do not thereafter expect either the cross of Christ or Jewish sacrifices for sins.”

Whoever neglects the remedy of repentance will be devoured by the fury of the fire. Therefore each person should flee to the remedy of repentance while he has time, lest he be handed over to eternal fire.

### VERSE 28

> Anyone who violates the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses.

He instills terror in Christians by speaking of the punishments of those who sinned under the law.

“Without mercy,” he says, so that there may be no pardon and no compassion, although that law belonged to Moses. If two or three witnesses, as he ordered, testify against a person, the judges of the people immediately sentence him to death if he has acted contrary to the law or disobeyed it.

“And if this is so under the old law, where the law of Moses is violated—

### VERSE 29

“how much worse punishment,” says the Apostle, “do you think will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, regarded as polluted the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?”

The greater Christ is than Moses, and grace than the law, the greater the punishment that such a person will deserve.

And how does someone trample underfoot the Son of God? When we partake of him unworthily through the sacraments, does that person not commit a grave sin? Does he not trample upon him? Does he not despise him?

For just as we regard the things we trample upon as worthless, so those who sin freely, without fear and without repentance, consider Christ worthless,” and do not fear that he will be their judge.

Through grace he has become the body of Christ, but he makes himself the body of the devil. He makes the undefiled blood of Christ defiled [reading: “defiled”], by which he was cleansed, returns to his former vomit, and neglects to cleanse himself again through repentance [perhaps: “neglects”].

### VERSE 29, CONTINUED

“And insulting the Spirit of grace.”

“Whoever does not receive the benefit of the giver with a grateful mind commits an injury [perhaps: commits it] against the benefactor. He makes you a son, but you wish to become a slave of sin. For he comes to dwell with you;” but you do not prepare for him a house worthy of his dwelling, procuring another inhabitant for yourself—that is, the devil.

### VERSE 30

> For we know him who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.”  
> And again, “The Lord will judge his people.”

He said this about enemies and about those who neglect to cleanse themselves through repentance, yet act wickedly in security.

“To judge his people” is understood as separating the good from the wicked, the faithful from the unfaithful, within his people.

### VERSE 31

> It is fearful to fall into the hands of the living God.

A person falls into the hands of God on the day of judgment—that is, into the power of the judge who will repay each person according to his merits—if he does not now forestall God’s face by confession and repentance while there is time.

If he does not repent of his sins, he falls into the fearful judgment of almighty God.

### VERSE 32

> But remember the former days, in which, after being enlightened, you endured a great struggle of sufferings.

“After Paul had shaken their minds by saying, ‘It is fearful to fall into the hands of the living God,’ proving that the one who insults the grace of God and commits an affront against the Holy Spirit must perish in every respect, he also teaches this from the law of Moses.

“Therefore, lest he cause one who was despairing through excessive fear to be swallowed up by grief and despair, he consoles them with praises and exhortations, bringing before them their own former zeal.

“‘After being enlightened’ means strengthened by divine grace. You endured a great struggle of sufferings. He does not simply say ‘struggle,’ but adds ‘great.’ Nor does he say ‘temptations,’ but ‘combat,’ which is a matter of great praise and a proclamation of our praises,” namely, suffering for the name of Christ.

### VERSES 33–34

> At one time being made a spectacle through reproaches and tribulations, and at another time becoming companions of those who were treated in this way. For you also shared the sufferings of prisoners.

Little by little, in separate parts, he sets forth their praises, saying that they not only endured sufferings manfully for Christ, but also announcing that they had compassion on those in prison.

“And being made a spectacle through tribulations and reproaches.”

“Reproach is a grievous thing, capable of overturning the strength of the soul and powerful enough to blind the mind, since the human race is exceedingly desirous of glory. Therefore it is easily ensnared even by reproaches.

“He did not simply say ‘through reproaches,’ but increased the expression by saying ‘you were made a spectacle’ [the manuscript consistently has *expectaculum*]. When someone is reproached in secret, he is certainly saddened; but much more so when it happens before everyone.”

> And you accepted with joy the plundering of your possessions.

He praises them wonderfully for their faith. If they had not possessed faith, they would not have accepted with joy the seizure of their property, believing that they had received better things in exchange for the substance taken from them.

Therefore he adds the confidence of faith:

> Knowing that you have for yourselves a better and enduring possession.

As though he were saying: “Seeing your future riches as though they were already present, you endured with joy.” What was not yet visible, you perceived as though it were present.

“This is entirely apostolic work and worthy of those strong souls: to rejoice in scourging, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: ‘They departed from the council rejoicing that they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus’ (Acts 5:41).

“‘Knowing,’ he says, ‘that you have a better and enduring possession,’ as though he were saying: a firm and stable possession that cannot perish, unlike these earthly things, which perish.”

Then, praising them, he says:

### VERSE 35

> Therefore do not abandon your confidence, which has a great reward with God.

It is evident that they possessed great confidence toward God. He urges them most earnestly not to lose it, for it is easier to preserve something intact than to recover it once lost.

You need nothing except to stand firm and persevere in your strength, which has a great reward with God.

### VERSE 36

> For you need endurance, so that, after doing the will of God, you may receive the promise.

Oh, how great is the exhortation and consolation contained here! You have only one task: to persevere in the contest until you receive the crown corresponding to your labor.

For it is not the one who begins who will be crowned, but the one who perseveres in the contest to the end; this one will be saved (Matthew 10:22). “In your endurance,” the Lord says, “you will possess your souls.”

“Receive,” he says—that is, receive God’s promises.

### VERSE 37

> For yet a very little while,  
> and the one who is to come will come  
> and will not delay.

It is no small consolation amid labor to hope that the judge, the one who rewards, and the one who consoles will come soon and reward steadfastness in the contest.

### VERSES 38–39

> But my righteous one lives by faith;  
> and if he withdraws, my soul has no pleasure in him.  
> But we are not children of withdrawal unto destruction,  
> but of faith unto the gaining of the soul.

The Apostle introduced this prophetic testimony as an exhortation to faith. Just as the one who doubts will be displeasing, so the one who believes will live in his upright faith.

Therefore let us believe that Christ the judge will come swiftly [perhaps: “will come”], and let us prepare to meet him with good works, lest we be children of withdrawal from eternal light, but children of acquisition unto glory, hearing with the saints on the great day the desirable voice:

> Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world (Matthew 25:34).

*Here the manuscript ends. The remaining three chapters of this Epistle to the Hebrews have been omitted, either by Alcuin himself or by the copyist.*

# A BRIEF COMMENTARY ON SOME SAYINGS OF THE HOLY APOSTLE PAUL

Albinus, on what the Apostle says to the Corinthians:

> Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body (1 Corinthians 6:18).

This can be explained as follows. It is one thing to sin through the body and another to sin in the body. Theft, robbery, murder, and similar acts are committed through the body; fornication and the uncleanness of lust are committed in the body. The body performs the former; it suffers the latter.

Alternatively: “He sins against the body” who takes the members of Christ and makes them members of a prostitute, and makes the temple of God a shrine of the devil (1 Corinthians 6:15).

Alternatively: “He sins against the body” who, on account of fornication, loses virginity, which he can never recover, as the Prophet testifies:

> The virgin of Israel has fallen; she will not rise again (Amos 5:1–2).

Fornication may be washed away through repentance, but the crown of lost virginity cannot be regained. There are also those who want this to be understood of a wife.

There is another question in the place where the Apostle speaks to the Ephesians:

> Rise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will illuminate you (Ephesians 5:14).

This is also said to those who lie in the darkness of sins, indeed even to those who are dead. If they rise through repentance, they immediately perceive the light of divine grace present with them.

But who, you ask, would have said this? Certainly the Holy Spirit through the Apostle, in order to exhort us to repentance. Therefore what the Spirit was speaking within him he suddenly brought forward, so that by the authority of the speaker within him he might establish what he wished to persuade his hearers to accept.

Some think that he brought this testimony from the hidden books of the ancients, as we read that he did in other places. But the question is why he first says, as though to someone living, “Rise, you who sleep,” and afterward, as though to someone dead, “Rise from the dead.”

We read of the death of the soul, as in: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:20); but we do not read of the death of the spirit. Therefore “Rise, you who sleep” can be referred to the spirit, while “Rise from the dead” can be fitted to the soul.

> See Saint Jerome on this passage.

## On the Epistle to Titus

Why did the Apostle approve the testimony of a certain gentile poet:

> Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, and lazy bellies (Titus 1:12)?

Clearly, he approves it because he understood that they were indeed such as their own prophet had foretold—whom he playfully called a prophet—namely, that such Christians deserved to have such prophets.

He took this verse from the book of Epimenides of Crete, the poet, whose title is *On Oracles*. I believe that the Apostle had read this book in order to know what the oracles of the gentiles promised—not because he approved the whole book, but because, finding gold in dung—that is, truth among falsehoods—he brought that saying into the treasury of God, and in order to confound the Cretans’ inborn vice of falsehood by means of their own author above all.

“For Cretans are liars,” he said, “and evil beasts and lazy bellies”: people who persuade others of falsehoods and thirst for the blood of the deceived like wild beasts, and who do not quietly work and eat their bread, whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shame (Philippians 3:19).

The fourth question concerned the Epistle to the Hebrews, where the Apostle says:

> For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have become participants in the Holy Spirit, who have nevertheless tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and who have fallen away, to be renewed again unto repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt [reading: “as an object of contempt”] (Hebrews 6:4–5).

This entire passage, both what precedes and what follows it, is wrapped in great obscurity. Nevertheless, let us say something about the exposition of this sentence alone, and briefly open its depth.

It is thought that the Apostle said this concerning the sacrifices of the Jews, or concerning the baptism of Christians: that it is impossible—for what is impossible cannot happen—for those who have once been enlightened through faith, who have tasted the heavenly gift, that is, forgiveness of sins through baptism, and who have become participants in the Holy Spirit, having indeed received the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands; who have nevertheless tasted the good teaching, the saving word, and the powers of the age to come, namely, the hope of the future glory promised to the saints; and who have fallen into some sin of unbelief—it is impossible for such people to be cleansed through Jewish sacrifices or to be renewed again to repentance through baptism.

For just as Christ died once for the salvation of all, so each person ought to be baptized once for salvation. Therefore he said “renewed,” because a person becomes new in baptism.

If we knew that we could always be cleansed through baptism, when would we stop sinning? For it is likewise impossible for Christ to be crucified a second time; this is what it means to hold him up to contempt.

What is our baptism except the crucifixion of Christ? For just as Christ died on the cross, so we die to sins in baptism. And just as he remained three days in the tomb, so we are immersed three times, as the Apostle says: “We were buried with Christ through baptism” (Romans 6:4).

And just as, after his resurrection, death will no longer rule over him, so sins ought not to rule over us after the resurrection of baptism, as the same Apostle commands:

> Brothers, if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, not the things that are on earth; for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. But when Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory (Colossians 3:1–4).

# FIVE BOOKS OF THE COMMENTARY OF BLESSED ALCUIN ON THE APOCALYPSE

These commentaries are not found in Frobenius’s edition; we have excerpted them from Mai’s Vatican Collection.

## MAI’S NOTICE

A Vatican codex of excellent quality and extraordinary antiquity—of the ninth century, or certainly the tenth—presented me with five little books of commentary on the first twelve chapters of the Apocalypse. Alcuin’s name is inscribed upon these booklets.

Although this work is entirely absent from the fullest edition of Alcuin prepared by Frobenius, nevertheless Johannes Trithemius in *Ecclesiastical Writers*, Sixtus of Siena in the *Sacred Library*, and Balaeus in *British Writers*, century II, expressly mention Alcuin’s Commentary on the Apocalypse. It therefore remains for us to suppose that this work has until now lain among the lost.

It makes no difference that the writers mentioned above speak of a single book of the work, since our five booklets are so brief that, to those who saw their size, they could have appeared to be equivalent to one book.

So that my readers may not easily wonder that this little work remained hidden for so long in our codices, let them remember, I ask, that my predecessor in the prefecture of the Vatican, Petrus Fogginius, brought to light another unknown work of Alcuin’s from the Vatican Palatine codex: namely, a little book against the heresy of Felix of Urgel. He had supplied it with a preface and prepared it for the press, and afterward sent it to Frobenius so that it might be inserted into the new edition he was preparing with such splendor (volume I, p. 659 and following).

That example of Fogginius, together with the style of the work—which differs in no way from Alcuin’s—the great antiquity of the codex, and the name of Alcuin inscribed upon it, as I have said, encouraged me to publish the work confidently.

Its learned preface enumerates those who had expounded the Apocalypse before him, down to his contemporaries, Bede the Venerable and Ambrose Autpertus. The method of the work is pious, moral, and mystical, referring everything, as is fitting, to Christ and to the Church.

Nor will philologists despise the fact that in columns 1098 and 1106 Alcuin also displays another translation of the Apocalypse.

If anyone is reasonably offended by the minute etymology of proper names and explanation that it sometimes pursues, let him know that it conforms to another little work of Alcuin’s (*Works*, volume I, p. 449), in which he gives a literal, allegorical, and moral interpretation of Hebrew names.

Every age, of course, suffers its own ghosts; yet this does not prevent Alcuin from having been the torch of his age, as Baronius says under the year 802: second to no one in knowledge of divine and human letters, certainly the most learned of the English after blessed Aldhelm and Bede, founder of the Parisian academy, and the dear teacher of Charlemagne, as the ancients call him.
