God opposed him in the West as a champion against the Adoptian heretics, just as in the East he opposed Cyril to the Nestorians.

# BOOK ONE

## ALCUIN’S PREFACE TO THE EXPOSITION OF THE APOCALYPSE BEGINS

Blessed Bede says that the Apocalypse consists of seven sections.

In the first, after the greeting, he recalls the Lord’s sufferings and glories to strengthen the weak. Then, after recalling what has been done and what will be done in the seven churches, he describes the struggles and victories of the universal Church.

In the second, he sees four living creatures, twenty-four elders, the Lamb standing, and a book sealed with seven seals. He also narrates the struggles and triumphs of the Church.

In the third, under the image of seven angels sounding trumpets, he describes various events of the Church.

In the fourth, under the figure of a woman and a dragon, he narrates the struggles and victories of the Church, where through seven angels he recalls sayings and deeds, although not as previously.

In the fifth, through seven angels and seven plagues, he strikes the earth.

In the sixth, he narrates the condemnation of the prostitute.

In the seventh, he says that the wife of the Lamb, adorned, descends from heaven.

There are also Tichonius’s seven rules: the first concerns the Lord and his body; the second, the true and simulated body of the Lord; the third, promises and the law; the fourth, species and genus; the fifth, times; the sixth, recapitulation; and the seventh, the devil and his body.

These seven rules are found not only in the Apocalypse but also in other books, especially the prophetic books.

Victorinus the martyr was the first to comment on the Apocalypse. Blessed Jerome followed him, removing some things that Victorinus had understood literally and adding some things of his own, and composed a single book on it. He promised that he would labor on it especially if he had sufficient time in life, but it is uncertain whether that work was completed.

The Donatist Tichonius also published an extensive exposition of it, but mixed it with the poison of his false belief.

After him, Primasius, bishop of the African Church, a wholly Catholic man learned in the divine Scriptures, explained it in five books. As he himself says, he wove together not so much his own material as that of others, drawing out what Tichonius had understood well; nevertheless, he also appended certain chapters expounded by blessed Augustine. Although he explained it more fully than the others, he composed it in an exceedingly lofty style.

Finally, although few in number, certain chapters were explained with great brilliance by Saint Gregory in his various works.

At last, the blessed presbyter Ambrose Autpertus treated the subject most beautifully, inserting some material from these authors but much from himself.

*The preface ends.*

# EXPOSITION OF THE PROPHECY OF THE NEW TESTAMENT

Frobenius indicates that the following verses should be placed before the subsequent Commentary—although he could not find it, despite the fact that it was not wholly unknown—among the additions and supplements at the end of the works of blessed Alcuin. He took them from a very ancient codex, concerning which this distinguished scholar writes:

“Shortly before this work had been completely finished in print, by a fortunate accident a very ancient manuscript codex, previously mentioned by no one, came into my hands. It was preserved in the famous college, or episcopal school, of Saint Paul in our city of Regensburg.

“As the verses written on the first page testify, it was written at the command of Liutpram, archbishop of Salzburg. The verses read as follows:

> The archpriest Liutpram, the rector,  
> had this book written;  
> may life and salvation be his.

“Liutpram held that metropolitan see from the year 836 until the year 859; the writing of the codex agrees perfectly with that period.

“Moreover, in this codex I discovered many poems of our Alcuin, some already included among the published works, some mutilated there, and others entirely unpublished,” and so forth.

[Col. 1088C] Among the remaining books of the New Testament, the Apocalypse alone is called a prophecy, in accordance with the statement: “Blessed is the one who reads and those who hear the words of the prophecy of this book,” and so forth. Since, therefore, it is a new prophecy, it surpasses the ancient prophecy just as the Gospel surpasses observance of the Law: for what the ancient prophecy foretold as destined to be revealed concerning Christ and the Church, this prophecy now declares to have been revealed. Hence it is entitled Apocalypse, that is, “Revelation.” This book has great authority because it is sent from the Trinity through an angel to John: from the Father, as in the words, “which God gave him to make manifest”; from the Son, as in, “I, Jesus, sent my angel to testify these things to you”; and also from the Holy Spirit, as in, “The Lord God almighty, the Spirit of the prophets, sent his angel,” and so forth. Therefore, since it conveys nothing historical, its very words are understood to teach. For there are not craftsmen in heaven who forge breastplates, nor could a woman give birth in heaven.

It remains now that we examine the character of its vision. Our fathers taught that three kinds of vision are to be understood: bodily, as when we see the sun, the moon, and other things with our eyes; spiritual, which occurs through an ecstasy of the mind, whether men are awake or asleep, when through the spirit they perceive not bodily things but likenesses of bodily things—for example, when Pharaoh saw seven cows, Nebuchadnezzar a stone cut from the mountain without hands, and Peter a sheet; and the third, which is called intellectual, through which neither bodily things nor their likenesses, but the very truth of things, is manifested to those who behold it. Blessed Jerome attributes the Apocalypse alone to this kind of vision. Saint Augustine, however, teaches in every possible way that a spiritual vision is to be understood here, displayed through likenesses of bodily things. But let them determine among themselves which of them spoke more truly.

The order of the narrative is as follows. At times it begins with the Lord’s advent and carries the account through to the end of the age. At times it begins with the Lord’s advent and, before reaching its conclusion, returns to the beginning; repeating in different figures what it had left aside or already said, it proceeds to the Lord’s second advent. At times it begins with the final persecution; but before it reaches the end, it joins both matters together by recapitulation. At times, in explaining what it has undertaken, it interrupts itself briefly and inserts something unrelated to that subject; [Col. 1089C] afterward, in a shortened sequence, it fully explains what it had begun. At times, within the very kind of expression, the figure is so changed that it mingles something apparently different, although it signifies nothing other than what it had begun to narrate.

Note also that very rarely in this revelation do either the angel or John retain their own individual persons. The discourse returns from species to genus, as when, after specifically rebuking Jezebel, it adds: “And I will give to each of you according to your works.” This appears to apply generally both to the good and to the wicked. Again, it passes from genus to species when, speaking of the Church that dwells among the wicked under the figure of the shepherd of Pergamum, it says: “I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is,” and so forth. Immediately afterward it addresses the negligent shepherd: “I have a few things against you,” and so forth. From this species it passes to another when it immediately adds: [Col. 1089D] “So you also have those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.” For since he does not say, “You also have there,” but “you also have,” he plainly indicates that the discourse has turned from one species to another.

Genus is also found within species. For by saying, “I, John, your brother,” and so forth, he indicates in his own person the persecutions of the whole Church, which it suffers daily for the word of God. Genus is joined to genus when the throne is said to have been set in heaven. For each of these, taken separately—that is, both heaven and the throne—frequently signifies the Church in this revelation; when they are joined together, they represent one and the same Church.

## CHAPTER ONE

### Verse 1

**“The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ.”**

First, it must be noted that the meaning would be fuller if it said, “This is the Apocalypse”; but it is the custom of Scripture, for the sake of brevity, to leave such previously mentioned particles implicit. Hence Solomon does not say, “These are the parables of Solomon,” or, “These are the words of Ecclesiastes.”

As stated, *Apocalypse* is interpreted from Greek into Latin as “revelation.” *Jesus* is Hebrew; in Greek, *sotir* [σωτήρ], and in Latin it is called “saving” or “salutary.” *Christ* is Greek, “anointed” in Latin. For *chrisma* means “anointing.” Moses is said to have first prepared *chrisma* at the Lord’s command in the book of Exodus; kings and priests were anointed with it, prefiguring Christ, invisibly anointed by the Father.

**“Which God gave him to make manifest to his servants, the things that must soon take place.”**

Here too it must be noted that it would more ordinarily be said, “Which God gave him”; but [Col. 1090B] it is the custom of Sacred Scripture frequently to use the accusative without a preposition in place of the ablative. Thus in the Psalm: “Hear, O Lord, my voice, with which I cried to you.” And Paul says: “I have fought the good fight.” These words show that this revelation belongs to Jesus Christ and that he received it from God so that by his revelation he might make manifest to his servants the things that must soon take place.

For this reason the punctuation should be: “The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ”; and then one should continue: “which God gave him to make manifest to his servants,” and so forth. The first clause pertains to his divinity, according to which he himself, together with the Father, reveals all mysteries; the second pertains to his humanity, according to which he received from the Father and the Holy Spirit, and also from himself, the task of declaring by his own revelation to his servants the things that must soon take place. [Col. 1090C] Hence it does not say, “which God the Father gave him,” but indefinitely, “which God gave him,” that is, the Trinity.

Note also that by saying “to his servants,” he shows that the Son, even in the form of a servant, is not himself a servant, since his humanity is proclaimed Lord over servants. He says “his own,” that is, those subject to divine grace, in accordance with the words: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to infants” (Matt. 11:25).

In the statement that follows, “the things that must soon take place,” although innumerable matters may be understood, he nevertheless weaves together his discourse with singular attention to the temporal pressures and everlasting joys that will come upon the Church, and to the present prosperity and future eternal torments of the wicked. All these things take place soon, because the present age is compelled to fly to its end without any interval, however brief, being interposed. Hence the same John says elsewhere: “Little children, it is the last hour” (2 John 2:18).

**“And he signified it, sending it through his angel to his servant John.”**

“He signified,” that is, “he sealed.” For a sign is called a seal. Hence Daniel is told: “The words are closed and sealed” (Dan. 12:9); and Isaiah says: “I sealed the vision among my disciples” (Isa. 8:16).

But what does it mean that this vision is said to have been sealed, when later it says, “Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book,” unless it is because it is opened to the devout but closed by a seal to the impious? For riches are sealed not on account of faithful servants, but on account of thieves. Hence Daniel is told: “The impious will act impiously, but the instructed will understand” [Col. 1091A] (Dan. 12:10).

By saying “he signified,” he shows that it should not be understood according to the letter, but that through the word “signification” he has directed us to search more deeply into the mysteries.

This vision, therefore, was sent through an angel. But the uncircumscribed Spirit who sent it was in the one through whom he sent it and in the one to whom he sent it. The same angel who appeared bore the figure of the incarnate Word alone and of his body, which is the Church. John himself, to whom he appeared, also presented a type of the Church. It must not, however, be thought that the angel and John prefigured two Churches. Rather, when the angel holds the type of the head, John represents the preachers; when the angel represents the preachers, John represents the hearers; and when the preceding members are signified through the angel and the following members through John, the Church is understood in the angel as glorified after the resurrection, and in John as presently being instructed by Christ.

Moreover, it must be understood that after the ascension the Lord appears in the same way in which he appeared to the fathers before the incarnation, namely, through an angelic creature. By this action he plainly shows that he should not now be expected to teach bodily, since he is present everywhere in majesty. For it must not be supposed that the humanity taken from the Virgin was present in the angel; rather, the angel expressed its figure.

Nor is it surprising that he is called “like a son of man,” since the prophet Daniel is reported to have called the angel Gabriel a man. Thus through this angel he is said to declare: “I am the first and the last,” and so forth, just as before the incarnation God, in the assumed person of an angel, says: “I am the God of Abraham,” and so forth. For just as Moses calls the one who appeared to him in the bush sometimes an angel and sometimes the Lord, so John testifies that this revelation was sent to him through an angel and confirms that the one in the mystery and figure was the Lord Jesus Christ.

Thus the Lord also appeared to Paul on the road through an angel; for if he had needed to appear in the substance of his own flesh, he would have appeared to John, whom he specially loved. It should also be noted that, following the custom of others, John speaks of himself as though of another. Moses says: “Now Moses was a very meek man” (Num. 12:3). And Job says: “There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job” (Job 1:1), and so forth. For it was not they themselves who spoke from themselves, but the Holy Spirit spoke through them.

### Verse 2

**“Who bore witness to the Word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, to all the things that he saw.”**

John bore witness then; now the Church bears witness, whose figure he represented when he saw this Apocalypse. He distinguishes “the Word” and “Jesus Christ” because of Christ’s two substances, concerning both of which he bore witness when he said: “In the beginning was the Word.” And again: “The Word became flesh.” “He saw” refers to both: with spiritual eyes he saw the Word, but with bodily eyes he saw all the things narrated concerning his humanity.

### Verse 3

**“Blessed is the one who reads and those who hear the words of the prophecy of this book, and keep the things written in it. For the time is near.”**

Here the great authority of this book is evident: among all the prophecies, it promises blessedness in a uniquely explicit manner. By saying “the one who reads” and “those who hear,” he indicates the persons of teachers and hearers. What follows, “and keep the things written in it,” applies to both, because “it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified.” And to stir the minds of both toward observing these things, he adds: “For the time is near”—namely, the time when either the righteous will be rewarded after observing the commandments or the unjust will be punished after neglecting them.

### Verse 4

**“John to the seven churches that are in Asia.”**

The universal Church is expressed through the number seven, because of the seven gifts of the one who filled the whole world. Hence Elisha caused the child over whom he had lain to yawn seven times, because the people, dead through unbelief, are brought to life through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. The number seven, therefore, is perfect, being formed from three and four.

Three is regarded as perfect in the divine Scriptures because of the mystery of the Trinity; or because of the three virtues—faith, hope, and charity; or because of the three orders of the faithful: preachers, abstainers, and married people.

Four is perfect because of the regions of the world; or because of the four principal virtues, namely prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice; or because of the books of the four Gospels.

Since, therefore, the knowledge of the Trinity embraces the four quarters of heaven; or since hope, faith, and charity perfect the sum of the four principal virtues; or since the three orders of believers submit themselves to the precepts of the four Gospels, the universal Church is rightly figured through this number seven.

Nevertheless, it must be understood that he specifically entrusted these mysteries, written from exile, to the seven churches of Ephesus. The species is not therefore excluded; rather, the genus is shown within the species—that is, the universal Church, which is rightly said to be in Asia. For Asia is interpreted as “exaltation.”

Exaltation is not always used as a fault, but sometimes for the summit of virtue, as in: “I will make you the pride of the ages” (Isa. 60:15)—that is, “I will make you despise all pleasures and the lowest honors.” And elsewhere: “He lifted you above the heights of the earth.”

The Church, therefore, stands in this lofty exaltation. Alternatively, if “exaltation” is used as a fault, it must not be understood that the holy Church remains exalted, but that, once formerly raised up in the pride of exaltation, it has been predestined through heavenly grace to become humble. In accordance with the words: “Have you entered the storehouses of snow, or have you seen the storehouses of hail, which I have prepared for the time of the enemy, for the day of battle and war?” (Job 38:22–23).

### Verse 5

**“Grace to you and peace from him who is, and who was, and who is to come, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne, and from Jesus Christ.”**

Grace is forgiveness freely bestowed. By its radiance we have been adopted from servants of sin as sons of righteousness. Peter and Paul placed this grace before the faithful as the title of their greetings when they wrote to them, showing that, when they wished to exhort peoples to grace, the whole substance of greeting consisted in it. Grace is appropriately placed before peace, because no one could come reconciled to the peace of God unless the grace of mercy had gone before him.

What he says, “from him who is, and who was, and who is to come,” must be assigned specifically to the only-begotten Son of God. He exists essentially with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and mutability never affects him, in accordance with Paul’s words: “There was not in him ‘is’ and ‘no’; but in him ‘is’ was ‘was’” (2 Cor. 1:18). For before he was born in time from the Virgin, he made all times together with the Father. Hence the same John says: “In the beginning was the Word.”

He is also the one who is to come in the humanity he assumed, to judge the living and the dead, as it is written: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

Since it is certain that the Church received this grace from the Son and the Holy Spirit, and likewise from the Father through the Son and the Holy Spirit, why is the person of the Father omitted in this passage? It is because it is the custom of Sacred Scripture that whenever one or two persons of the Trinity are mentioned, the whole Trinity is understood together.

He says “from the seven spirits” because of the sevenfold operation of the one Spirit. The Spirit is said to be alone before the throne—that is, the Church, or the memory of the saints—because the forgiveness of sins is assigned especially to him, in accordance with the words: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven” (John 20:22–23). Or, certainly, the whole Trinity is understood in the Spirit.

By saying “from Jesus Christ,” he repeats the person of the Son because the one who is said to have existed before the ages became man at the end of the ages.

**“Who is the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth.”**

In an evident manner of expression he calls Christ specifically the faithful witness, although there are three who bear witness—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—and the three are one God. The Son may also specifically be called the faithful witness in the man he assumed, because for the testimony of truth he endured the death of the flesh.

For although the whole Church bears witness to Christ through its holy preachers, those who endured bodily death for Christ are called martyrs, that is, witnesses, in the primary sense. He is called the firstborn because no one before him who would not die again rose from the dead. Alternatively, all the saints have died to the world, as in: “For you have died”; but he died uniquely, since there was no sin in him.

By “kings” he either means all the saints who know how to rule themselves well, or certainly the preachers, who associate themselves with the good but raise themselves above the wicked, as Peter did over Ananias, and as Paul brandishes the scepter when he says: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod?” (1 Cor. 4:21).

**“Because he loved us.”**

How he loved us is shown by the evils he endured. He did not love us as we were—that is, as impious people—but as the people whom he made us through that very love. Hence it immediately adds:

**“And washed us from our sins in his blood.”**

The order in which he washed us in his blood the Apostle indicates when he says: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death” (Rom. 6:3).

### Verse 6

**“And made us a kingdom, priests to God and his Father.”**

Because our head is both king and priest, all his members are therefore kings and priests, as the Apostle Peter says: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2:9).

They are kings by ruling themselves; they are priests by offering themselves to God, in accordance with the words: “I appeal to you by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice.”

By saying “to God and his Father,” he indicates one person, although the Holy Spirit is understood there according to the rule stated above, just as the Apostle also says: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 1:3), wishing “God and Father” to be understood as one person.

Therefore it must be said: “To him be glory forever and ever.” “To him,” that is, to the one who made us kings and priests—to the Father and the Son. Here we understand the love of both, which is the Holy Spirit: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit.”

It is fitting that the Church attributes glory for these things not to itself but to the one from whom it received them, in accordance with the words: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. 113:1).

### Verse 7

**“Behold, he comes with the clouds.”**

If we understand this according to the letter, when the Lord comes to judgment there will be a bright cloud that, overshadowing the saints, will protect them from the fire that consumes the world. It will be terrifying, and the wicked will be frightened by its thunderous crashes. Nevertheless, in this Apocalypse nothing should easily be understood according to the letter.

Thus, in sacred speech, when clouds are mentioned in the plural, they signify holy preachers, who are light through purity of mind and do not cease to water the hearts of their hearers with the drops of their preaching. With these clouds, therefore, the Lord will come to judgment, in accordance with the prophet’s words: “Behold, the Lord comes to judgment with the elders of the people” (Isa. 3:13).

**“And every eye will see him, and those who pierced him.”**

Every eye will see him—that is, every human being, the whole understood from a part, who will then rise, either to life or to death. This does not mean the animals, to whom it has not been granted to rise after death.

Every human being will see him in the form of a servant, in which he was judged by the impious, not in the form of divinity, which cannot be seen by the impious. Note that another translator says, “Every land will see him,” as though he were saying: “They will see him as the impious did not believe he would be when he was placed here.”

**“And all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him.”**

Here it must be noted that he says “the tribes of the earth” with an added qualification, as though he were saying: those desiring earthly things and devoted to avarice, to whom it is said: “Woe to you who are rich” (Luke 6:24), and again: “Woe to you who laugh” (ibid., v. 25).

The cause of their sorrow is disclosed when it says, “over him.” Although there will be mourning there because of many miseries, nevertheless no weeping will compare with the weeping caused by seeing Christ’s glory. For then the wretched will grieve more because they have lost such a Lord than because they have fallen into the most dreadful torment.

But behold, he confirms what has been said by inserting an oath when he adds: “Yes, amen.” What is “yes” among the Latins is *amen* among the Hebrews. Both are adverbs of affirmation. Thus he says, “Yes, amen,” as though repeating it: “It is true, it is true.”

### Verse 8

**“I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end,”** says the Lord God, “who is, and who was, and who is to come.”

By saying “I am,” he plainly indicates that God himself was speaking. Hence the Apostle says: “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3). And David says: “Attend, my people, to my law” (Ps. 77:1), although David was neither the people nor the law.

“Alpha and Omega” signifies “the beginning and the end.” For among the Greeks, Alpha is the beginning of the letters, while Omega is their end. Christ is called the beginning because every creature receives its beginning from him; he is called the end because, as its boundary, he brings all things to completion.

Alternatively, he is called the beginning and the end because he is God before the ages and man at the end of the ages. Hence John says: “In the beginning was the Word.” And again: “The Word became flesh.”

### Verse 9

**“I, John, a brother and fellow participant in the tribulation, kingdom, and patience of Jesus, was on the island called Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.”**

Here John designates both his own particular person and, generally, the person of the Church. It should be noted that the kingdom pertains to the head, tribulation to the members, and patience to both; all of this is found in the one Jesus.

The head suffered tribulation together with the members when he said: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

The kingdom is in the head, as in the words: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34). This is plainly to say: “Come, members; reign with the head, because I am the kingdom.” He will give himself to his own, as it is written: “The oath that he swore to Abraham our father, that he would give himself to us” (Luke 1:73).

Patience awaits us, in accordance with the words: “Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance?” (Rom. 2:4); and, “In your patience you will possess your souls.”

Through the island of Patmos, which is interpreted as “strait” (*fretus*: so the manuscript reads), where John had been confined, persecutions and afflictions are signified—afflictions that John and the Church suffer, that is, the species and the genus—but for the sake of the word of God, not because of their own wrongdoing, in accordance with the Apostle Peter’s words: “Let none of you suffer as a thief, but as a disciple of Christ” (1 Pet. 4:15).

### Verse 10

**“I was in the spirit on the Lord’s day.”**

From this point onward, we must speak separately of the species and separately of the genus. John’s spirit did not entirely abandon the flesh when he saw this, for the body would not live without the spirit. Rather, he was placed in ecstasy and could neither perceive nor understand anything through the body.

Note that he says he was in the spirit not on the Sabbath but on the Lord’s day, because that ancient law, which brought about death, had already passed away, and the new law, which gives life, had shone forth in Christ’s resurrection.

Allegorically, the Church, because in its elect it mortifies the deeds of the flesh by the spirit, so that it may rise in the spirit into a manner of life, is shown to be the Lord’s day. Hence the Apostle says: “You are not in the flesh but in the spirit” (Rom. 8:9).

### Verse 11

**“And I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet saying: ‘What you see, write.’”**

It must be understood that, just as John heard in the spirit, so the voice addressed to him was spiritual. But one may ask what kind of back the spirit could have, so that he heard a voice behind him.

It appears, therefore, that the face of that spirit was the very vision of divine contemplation, while the back was forgetfulness of present things. For this reason he heard a voice concerning the things he had forgotten: so that he might turn the face of his mind toward them and write in a book whatever he saw.

It was as though the voice itself said to him: “The things that you are beginning to see in the Spirit of God, here, where you hear me sounding without sound—that is, on earth—are either things that have happened or things that are going to happen.”

Thus it says, “What you see, write,” as though it said, “What you are going to see,” for he had not yet seen anything.

Allegorically, the Church hears behind it a voice concerning the union of Christ and itself, from the Law and the prophets, as in: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24). This voice is rightly called loud, whether in the Church or in John, because it speaks of the highest mysteries. It is therefore compared with a trumpet and spread through the mouths of preachers. Hence one of them is told: “Cry aloud like a trumpet” (Isa. 58:1). In John this voice admonishes the Church to write down what it sees, that is, to store it in its memory.

**“And send it to the seven churches: to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea.”**

It must be explained how the interpretation of these names suits the universal Church.

*Ephesus* is interpreted as “will” or “my counsel”—

> [Note: What learned person would approve these and the following interpretations of city names? And whose [will or counsel] is it, except his who rejects the counsels of princes, while his own counsel remains forever (Ps. 32:10)?]

The Church is the will of God, to which it is said through the prophet: “You shall be called My Will” (Isa. 62:4).

Note that “will” pertains to charity, while “counsel” pertains to correction. For the one who is the will of God is the person who submits himself to the Creator voluntarily, not through fear of punishment. But the one who wishes to commit himself neither through fear nor through love, by divine mercy at work, is addressed with a word of correction, so that, abandoning error, he may receive the counsel of salvation.

*Smyrna* is translated into Latin as “their song,” that is, the song of the elect. That song is the new commandment. The Church sings this song daily when, by loving God and neighbor, it fulfills the new commandment.

*Pergamum* is interpreted as “dividing their horns.” And whose horns could these be except Christ’s and the devil’s? In the horns of Christ, therefore, his kingdom—that is, the Church—is shown; in the horns of the devil, his kingdom also, that is, the impious.

Hear, then, the division of the horns: “I will break all the horns of sinners, and the horns of the righteous will be exalted” (Ps. 74:11).

*Thyatira* means “illuminated.” And what other illuminated thing is understood except the one to whom it is said through Isaiah: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem” (Isa. 60:1)? The Church is appropriately called illuminated so that it may remember that it was once darkness. Hence the Apostle says to its members: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8).

*Sardis* sounds in Latin as “prepared for the prince of beauty,” with “prepared” or “made ready” understood. The prince of beauty is the one of whom the Psalmist says: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44:3). And who has been prepared for him except the one concerning whom the prophet says to that same prince: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a garment of gold, surrounded by varieties” (ibid., v. 10)?

*Philadelphia* is interpreted as “saving the inheritance for the Lord.” Hence it aptly signifies the Church of the elect, which strives, with divine assistance, to save itself. Concerning this inheritance it is said: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. 2:8).

*Laodicea* is interpreted as “a tribe beloved by the Lord,” or “they were in vomit.” This interpretation shows the good mingled with the wicked in the Church.

### Verse 12

**“And I turned to see the voice that was speaking with me.”**

By saying “to see,” he shows that the voice was not bodily, since a bodily voice cannot be seen, but spiritual; and to see it is nothing other than to hear it.

Allegorically, the Church turned in order to see the voice because, through the desire of its mind, it turned toward the words of the Law and the prophets, so that it might now behold their mysteries fulfilled.

**“And when I had turned, I saw seven golden lampstands.”**

### Verse 13

**“And in the midst of the seven golden lampstands, one like a son of man.”**

The sevenfold Church is signified by the seven lampstands, and Christ is in its midst. He is called “like a son of man” because he was already immortal, or because he appeared not with sin but in the likeness of sinful flesh.

He is read to have appeared in the midst in accordance with the words: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. 18:20).

The Church is appropriately figured by the seven golden lampstands. For the sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit is represented by the number, and the splendor of eternal wisdom by gold. Thus, just as gold tested by fire and shaped by blows becomes a lampstand, so the Church, refined to purity by the fire of tribulation and stretched through the blows of trials into endurance, is brought to perfection.

Hence Isaiah says: “The Lord spoke, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31:9).

Moreover, it must be understood that both through the seven lampstands and through the son of man one Church is signified, since Christ and the Church are one person. Hence the same Lord who appeared clothed in the *podere* in the midst of the lampstands was clothed in the lampstands themselves. Therefore the garment of Christ is the seven lampstands, that is, the Church.

Genus is joined to genus when the Church is understood both through the seven lampstands and through the son of man. Note also that the likeness of the son of man pertains to us, because just as our head has risen in reality, so we have risen in hope.

**“Clothed in a *podere*.”**

*Podes* is Greek; in Latin it means “feet.” What, then, do we understand by the *podere*, that is, the ankle-length tunic which Zechariah says is priestly, except specifically Christ’s flesh and generally the whole Church?

He exercised the priesthood by offering himself to God the Father on the cross. But this priestly garment reaches to the ankles because his body, which is the Church, fulfills, down to its final members, the things lacking in Christ’s sufferings. Or certainly, his garment reached to the ankles because the work of charity continued to the passion of death.

**“And girded at the breasts with a golden belt.”**

It must be understood that Daniel saw a man girded at the loins, while John sees one girded at the breasts, because the Old Testament restrains the lust of the flesh, whereas the New also restrains the lust of the mind.

That double girding does not pertain to the head but to the members, since it is clear that our Redeemer was touched by the lust neither of the body nor of the heart. This belt is therefore rightly said to have been golden, because whoever is a citizen of the heavenly homeland abandons uncleanness not through fear of punishment but through love of heavenly splendor.

When the apostles are commanded in the New Testament, “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35), this is commanded in their person to those who, not yet restraining the fornication of the flesh, still belong to the old human being. They had previously abandoned the uncleanness of the flesh.

Alternatively, the angel is girded with a golden belt at the breasts because the Church, coming from two peoples, is united in Christ by the bond of charity.

### Verse 14

**“His head and his hairs were white, like white wool and like snow.”**

The head of Christ is God the Father; hence the Apostle says: “The head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3). His eternity is represented, according to the custom of human speech, by the whiteness of the head.

Allegorically, the head of the Church is its Redeemer, in accordance with the words: “The head of the man is Christ” (ibid.). The hairs are the distinguished members of the Church, who, because of their innocence, are compared with lambs—that is, with wool—and, because of the resurrection, with snow.

Because Christ manifested both things in himself—that is, innocence and resurrection—and we are commanded to imitate the one and await the other, not only the hairs but also the entire head is compared with white wool and snow.

[Col. 1098C] **“And his eyes were like a flame of fire.”**

These are the eyes of which it is said below: “I saw a Lamb as though slain, having seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God” (Rev. 5:6). Since the Holy Spirit both enlightens the Church for faith and burns it with love of God, he is rightly compared with the lights of the eyes and with a flame of fire.

Through these eyes, spiritual angels in the Church may also be signified: they illuminate that same Church with the light of knowledge and provide the fire of love.

### Verse 15

**“And his feet were like burnished bronze, as though burning in a furnace.”**

The nature of burnished bronze is said to be such that bronze placed in a furnace, subjected to an intense fire and also treated with a certain medicinal substance, acquires greater strength and is transformed into the radiance of gold.

Hence the feet like burnished bronze are appropriately referred to the final members of the Church, which must be refined under the intense fire of persecution in the time of Antichrist. But when the medicine of endurance has been applied, they will be found stronger and brighter.

And because the affliction will be more intense in Judea, where the Lord was crucified by the impious Jews, another translation has “burnished bronze of Lebanon,” which is said to be a mountain in Judea.

**“And his voice was like the voice of many waters.”**

Above, he compared the voice of the one who appeared with a trumpet; now he compares it with the voice of many waters, because what a few preachers first proclaimed, the whole world afterward cried out.

Alternatively, the voice of the trumpet may be understood as the voice of the Old and New Testaments, and the voice of many waters as charity, whose law is manifold, in accordance with the words: “And you will know that his law is manifold” (Job 11:6).

**Verse 16.**—“And he held seven stars in his right hand.” By the seven stars, as the same angel explains below, angels are understood. Not, however, the spirits of the heavenly homeland, in whom nothing blameworthy is found, but the preachers of the Church, of whom it is said: “The angels of peace shall weep bitterly” (Isa. XXXIII, 7). They are rightly represented by stars and angels, because they shine amid the night of this age through the purity of their life, and, announcing heavenly things to their hearers, become angels of truth. Since the number seven is not used numerically but as a sign of universality, this figure embraces all the preachers of the churches. Thus, in its symbolic meaning, it is no longer seven but one angel—that is, the perfect order of preachers. Likewise, the seven lampstands signify not only the churches of Asia but the universal Church. And if we attend carefully, we find lampstands also in these seven stars—that is, the universal Church in the holy preachers. Hence, when the Lord speaks to one angel, he adds: “Let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Apoc. II, 29).

The right hand in this passage should be understood as the highest blessedness, which is now possessed in hope but will then be possessed in reality. Hence Isaiah says: “The right hand of my righteous one shall uphold you” (Isa. XLI, 10). Therefore, when we hear that the Church is held in the right hand, we should understand the part from the whole: namely, the Church, which will in the future be placed at the right hand.

“And from his mouth came forth a sword sharp on both sides.” What is signified by the sword except the preaching of the Old and New Testaments? As Paul says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. [Col. 1099C] VI, 17). It is rightly called sharp on both sides, because on one side it cuts away sins of action, and on the other it cuts away unlawful thoughts. Or because it instructs the imperfect externally according to the literal sense, while inwardly it teaches the perfect according to the mystical understanding.

“And his face shone like the sun in its strength.” By the face shining like the sun, the elect may be understood, as in the statement: “The righteous shall shine like the sun” (Wis. III, 7). If in this statement we wish to understand the visible sun, we should know that then it will possess greater brilliance than now, and the glory of the saints will likewise be greater, as Isaiah testifies: “The light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, like the light of seven days, on the day when the Lord binds up the wound of his people” (Isa. XXX, 26). Hence it is added here: “in its strength.” [Col. 1099D]

Alternatively, what is signified by the angel’s face except the manifest incarnation of the Redeemer? It had, as it were, a rising in his birth, a setting in his death, and again a rising in his resurrection. And because his resurrection had already shone throughout the whole world, he had, as it were, ascended to the noonday hours of the sun when John saw these things. Therefore the phrase is added: “like the sun in its strength.”

**Verse 17.**—“And when I had seen him, I fell at his feet as though dead.” Here John signifies the members of Christ, while the angel specifically signifies Christ. John, therefore, falls at the angel’s feet as though dead, because the Church follows Christ’s footsteps so that she may die to the world. He is appropriately said to be “as though dead,” because although the Church dies to the world and to vices, she nevertheless lives to God.

“And he laid his right hand upon me, saying: Do not be afraid.” By the angel’s right hand, preachers are signified in this passage. Hence it is said through Moses: “In his right hand was a fiery law” (Deut. XXXIII, 2)—that is, the doctrine of the Holy Spirit in the holy preachers. The text does not explicitly say what the angel did by placing his right hand upon him; but we gather with certainty that he raised either John or the Church, represented in him, from the ground. But was the Church removed from imitating Christ’s sufferings? Certainly not. [Col. 1100B] Therefore, for the angel to place his right hand upon John, lying at his feet as though dead, and to raise him from the ground, means that the Lord Redeemer, through holy preachers, lifts the Church—which imitates his sufferings—from sorrow of heart to hope of future glory by exhorting her, as in the statement: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

He appropriately says, “Do not be afraid,” as though the Lord were saying to the Church: “Having received confidence from above, drive human fear far away.”

**Verse 18.**—“I am the first and the last, and I was alive and was dead, and behold, I am living forever and ever.” Here it is made clear that this angel specifically represented the person of the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom all these things apply.

“And I have the keys of death and of the underworld.” By the keys, the power of divine judgment is signified, from which no one can escape, but which encloses everyone as with keys, according to the statement: “He shuts and no one opens” (Apoc. III, 7). By “death,” however, he is meant of whom it is written: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wis. II, 24). By “the underworld,” those who belong to him are indicated. By these keys, therefore, the devil is released to test the Church, and by these same keys he is bound. Hence it is written: “God is faithful, and he will not permit you to be tested beyond what you are able to endure” (I Cor. X, 13).

**Verse 19.**—“Write therefore what you have seen, and what is, and what must take place after these things.” He passes from the general to the specific. For here John specifically designates the preachers. And observe that he repeats what he had already said, so that the fault of sluggishness might be removed. “Write therefore,” he says, [Col. 1100D] as though he were saying: “Write what you saw in the Law and the Prophets concerning what was to come about me; and what is,” namely, what has been fulfilled through me; “and what must take place after these things,” that is, what must be fulfilled in my members.

But this book must now be closed at its proper ending, lest we become weary on the level plain of the fields before we come to climb the mountains of this Apocalypse.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1099D] As we have already said in the preceding book, some assert that this vision was spiritual, others intellectual. If it was intellectual, he speaks [the manuscript reads *discit*, “learns”] not in his own person but in that of others. If it was spiritual, in some places he says how he received the understanding of the vision, while in others he remains silent. This is done with moderation: if the vision were open throughout, it would become cheap; if it were entirely closed, it would be despised. [Col. 1101A]

**Verse 20.**—“The mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands: the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches.” Enough has already been said about these matters.

## CHAPTER II

**Verse 1.**—“And to the angel of the church of Ephesus write: Thus says he who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands.”

**Verse 2.**—“I know your works, your labor, and your patience.” Here blessed John, either in his own person or in that of the preceding preachers, writes at the Lord’s command his words to the universal Church, which is represented by the angel. In this angel, at one time the entire body of the elect, consisting of holy preachers and good hearers, is raised up by praise; at another time, a particular part among the wicked is also identified.

What, then, does it mean for the Lord Redeemer to hold the stars in his right hand, except that he has predestined his elect to the blessedness of prosperity? What does it mean for him to walk in the midst of the lampstands, except that, bestowing upon each of the saints the grace of his gifts through inward discernment, he is present everywhere? But if by the stars and lampstands we understand the whole body of the Church, which consists of the elect and the reprobate, then by Christ’s right hand we should understand the power of his divinity, which no one can escape, because “all the ends of the earth are in his hand.” He walks among the lampstands by visiting the righteous and abandoning the unjust.

The Lord declares that he knows the works, labor, and patience of the saints—that is, he approves them through the grace of election. But now the discourse returns to a particular weakened part of the body, when it adds:

“And because you cannot bear the wicked.” It is not an indication of praise but of great weakness that the angel cannot bear the wicked. It should be noted that below he says to this same angel: “You have endured for my name’s sake.” This is not contrary to the present passage, because in one place the weakness of the members is shown, and in the other their strength.

“And you tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and you found them liars.” We should believe that false apostles had then sprung up in the church of Ephesus. John calls them antichrists in his epistle, and in their person the treachery of all heretics is indicated. Testing sometimes has reference to proving, as in the statement: “The Lord your God tests you” (Deut. XV, 3). The Church therefore tests false teachers when, through its preachers, it questions heretics about the faith, asking whether they are disciples of truth or of falsehood.

**Verse 3.**—“And you have patience, and you have endured for my name’s sake, and you have not grown weary.” Since these things are clear, let us pass on.

**Verse 4.**—“But I have this against you: that you have abandoned your first charity.”

**Verse 5.**—“Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent, and do the first works.” Far be it from us to believe that the one whom he praised so highly in the preceding verse had abandoned his first charity. Rather, he turns the discourse from this aspect to another, which he judges worthy of condemnation. By “first charity,” using ordinary human speech, he means the charity of an earlier time.

“Otherwise, I am coming to you, and I will move your lampstand from its place, unless you repent.” What does it mean to say to the unrepentant, “I am coming to you,” except: “I will make you feel the presence of my anger”? And because the angel and the lampstand are one in their symbolic meaning, what does it mean to say, “I will move your lampstand from its place,” except: “I will move you”? Here the whole angel should not be understood, but rather the unrepentant part of him, whose place is the Church. Since he touches not the general category but the particular form represented by the angel, he consequently points out the place of that particular form within the general category.

It should also be noted that he does not say, “I will cast it out,” but “I will move it,” showing that the unrepentant person, so long as he remains in this life, is not altogether torn away from the Church. Yet, because of his unrepentant heart, he is not worthy of the gift of holiness by which he formerly shone before human eyes. The Lord is said to move the lampstand—that is, not to establish it—just as he is said to harden Pharaoh’s heart.

Whenever someone commits a crime, his lampstand is moved in the sight of human beings. If he quickly rises again through repentance, then, because he is mercifully placed in the same position, many stand before God who appear to lie fallen before human beings. Therefore he says: “I will quickly move your lampstand from its place unless you repent”—that is, you will not receive the gift of holiness after your fall unless you take care to soften your heart through repentance.

**Verse 6.**—“But you have this: that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.” It is as though the universal angel were being told: “Not in the aspect that I have just reproved, but in another aspect you have this: that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.”

Blessed Augustine explains the particular deeds of the Nicolaitans in his book *On Heresies*, saying:

> “Nicolaus, as the story goes, was one of the seven deacons who were appointed by the apostles. When he was reproached on account of the jealousy of his exceptionally beautiful wife, he is said, in order to clear himself, to have permitted anyone who wished to use her. His deed was turned into a most shameful sect, which approves the indiscriminate use of women. His followers also do not separate their food from what has been sacrificed to idols.”

In general, however, all heretics are Nicolaitans. For Nicolaus is interpreted as “foolish people.” Therefore, whoever does not hold a true understanding of the wisdom of the Father, who is the Son, demonstrates himself to be foolish according to God, even if he is wise according to the world.

We also find Nicolaitans in the Church—namely, those whom we see foolishly storing up treasures in earthly love. Finally, it should be noted that he does not say, “You hate the Nicolaitans,” but “the deeds of the Nicolaitans,” because the Lord, and those who are on his side, are shown to hate in them not the nature that was created good in them, but their utterly evil deeds.

**Verse 7.**—“He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.” By saying this, he clearly shows that in the one church of the Ephesians he embraces the whole community of believers. He seeks ears not of the body but of the heart, according to the statement: “I say to you who hear.”

But since the angel specifically represented the person of the Son, what does it mean that the text does not say, “What the Son of God says,” but “what the Spirit says to the churches”? It means that, for the instruction of human conduct, the words of the Son are the words of the Spirit. Or the person of the Holy Spirit should not be understood specifically; rather, the whole Trinity is to be understood in the Spirit.

“To the one who conquers I will grant to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God.” The tree of life is the wisdom of God the Father, according to Solomon’s statement: “Blessed is the man who finds wisdom, the tree of life” (Ecclus. XXV, 13), and what follows. It is appropriately called the tree of life because in the present it protects his elect from the heat of vices, while in future blessedness it provides food of eternal contemplation to those who desire it. Hence the statement: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is manifested to me” (Ps. XVI, 15).

Whoever conquers—that is, whoever overcomes the temptations of the ancient enemy in Christ and through Christ—Christ will grant, according to his humanity, to eat from the tree of life, because when he comes for judgment he will lead him to contemplate the majesty of his divinity. The paradise in which the tree of life is found is eternal life, which is in the tree of life. And note that he says that he has God, speaking according to the humanity that he assumed for us.

Moreover, because he praises this angel in part and censures him in part, this is done according to his name, since Ephesus is interpreted both as “great fall” and as “my will.”

## Verse 8

“And to the angel of the church of Smyrna write: Thus says the first and the last, who was dead and lives.”

**Verse 9.**—“I know your tribulation and your poverty, but you are rich.” This is said not so much to one person as to the unity of the saints, whose tribulation is manifold. Hence another translation has “tribulations” in the plural.

We should understand poverty in two ways. One is poverty through renunciation of earthly possessions; the other is poverty through contrition of spirit, by which pride is diminished and humility increased. Concerning this the Lord says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V, 3). The one who is poor in spirit is the person who, while doing good, always regards himself as useless.

Thus let it be said: “I know your poverty, but you are rich,” as though he were saying: “By the very thing through which you consider yourself poor in humility of spirit, you are shown to be rich in every respect.” The statement “I know” is equivalent to “I make you know.”

Any elect person may also be called poor and rich because he does not yet possess in reality the riches of the heavenly homeland, though he possesses them in hope.

“And you are blasphemed by those who call themselves Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan.” This is said to the universal Church, which is blasphemed by enemies in individual members throughout particular places and in her whole body throughout the world. We should not believe that blaspheming Jews existed or exist only in Smyrna.

But it must be asked when the Jews lost their proper name, since even after the Redeemer’s death Holy Scripture continues to call them by that name, as in the Acts of the Apostles. We should understand that although they outwardly display the name according to the letter, they lost it inwardly in spirit when they refused to confess Christ. For “Jew” is interpreted as “confessor.” Figuratively, however, this applies to heretics, who falsely assume for themselves the name of Jews—that is, of confessors.

**Verse 10.**—“Fear none of these things that you are about to suffer.” This accords with the Gospel saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. X, 28).

“Behold, the devil is about to cast some of you into prison, so that you may be tested, and you will have tribulation for ten days.” Here it is plainly shown that different persons are being addressed in one angel. For after using the singular number—“fear”—he introduces the plural—“some of you”; likewise, he does not say “that he may be tested” or “that he may have,” but “that you may be tested” and “you will have,” thereby indicating that many are contained in one.

He designated all the distresses of affliction by the name of prison. And because he does not say “you,” but “some of you,” he wishes those to be understood who emerge victorious from the tribulations inflicted upon them.

But what does it mean that he confines the Church’s tribulation to the number ten days, except that she struggles against the various sufferings of persecutions and the diverse allurements of desires, subject to the commandments of the Decalogue?

“Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.” This is said generally to the whole Church and specifically to each faithful person. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22).

**Verse 11.**—“He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches: the one who conquers shall not be harmed by the second death.”

Since Holy Scripture is accustomed to posit three deaths—one of sin, another of the flesh, and another of condemnation—why in this passage is the final condemnation called not the third but the second death? It is because those deaths appear here which are shown to cause harm: the death of sin and the death of eternal punishment. In comparison with these, the death that belongs to the flesh ought not to be called death. By the word “harm,” the corruption of misery should be understood.

## Verse 12

“And to the angel of the church of Pergamum write: Thus says he who has the sword sharp on both sides.” This was said above.

**Verse 13.**—“I know where you dwell, where the seat of Satan is.” This is said generally to the Church, which dwells throughout the whole world, where the devil reigns.

“And you hold my name, and you have not denied my faith, and in those days Antipas, my faithful witness, was killed among you, where Satan dwells.” This sentence has either been corrupted through the fault of scribes or must be explained through ellipsis, so that the order of the words is as follows: “In those days Antipas, my faithful witness, who was killed among you, did not deny my faith”; or certainly: “In those days Antipas appeared as my witness, who was killed among you.”

In this martyr all witnesses are raised up by praise. By “among you” he does not mean that Antipas was killed by them, but that he was killed among them by those in whom Satan dwells. And observe that “you hold” is introduced in the singular, while “among you” follows in the plural, because he addresses many in one person.

**Verse 14.**—“But I have a few things against you: you have there those who hold the doctrine of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat and to commit fornication.” These words do not apply to the one whom he had previously praised by saying, “You hold my name,” and so forth. Rather, the discourse turns to another category.

He calls the doctrine of Balaam the counsel that Balaam gave to Balak: that he should place exceedingly beautiful women before the children of Israel, so that, delighted by their appearance, they might rush into illicit embraces and, softened by their blandishments, eat from the sacrifices of Beelphegor; thus, abandoned by God, they would fall before their enemies.

But if we turn from the literal sense to the figurative, we find how these things apply after events that have taken place or are yet to take place. Balaam is interpreted as “varied people”; hence he aptly represents heretics, who waste away in diverse errors. Balak, interpreted as “one who destroys,” represents the powers of this age, which, often at the persuasion of heretics, temporarily bend the dignity of the Church. Israel, interpreted as “a man seeing God,” represents the elect.

Thus, while Balaam teaches, Balak places before the children of Israel a stumbling block consisting of women—that is, deception, by which they eat from idol sacrifices and commit fornication. For, at the persuasion of heretics, the princes of this age display their sects outwardly, as though they were beautiful, in forms of speech that are known inwardly to be full of every impurity.

Alternatively, Balaam—that is, the devil—teaches Balak—that is, the flesh—to send women—that is, the pleasures of the world—by which souls perish.

**Verse 15.**—“So you also have those who hold the doctrine of the Nicolaitans.” Enough has already been said about the deeds of the Nicolaitans. By saying not “you have there,” but “you also have,” he shows that the discourse is turning from one category to another.

And because it makes no difference whether someone is reproved for keeping silent concerning the doctrine of Balaam or that of the Nicolaitans, he rightly adds: “In the same way, repent.” By this statement those also are secretly urged to repentance whom the same sluggish preachers are noted not to have corrected while they remained negligent. Hence he adds:

**Verse 16.**—“Otherwise, I am coming to you, and I will fight against them with the sword of my mouth.” Why does he not say, “I will fight against you,” but “I will fight against them”? Because, as has been said, he also urges those to come to lamentation whom he knew to have perished through the sluggishness of the preachers. It is as though he were saying: “I am coming to you, and I will fight against you,” as another translation makes clear. Or: “I am coming to you all, and I will fight with you all.”

What does it mean to say, “I am coming to you,” except: “I will make you feel the visitation of my anger”? Or what does “I will fight against them with the sword of my mouth” mean except: “I will condemn them with the sharp judgments of my words”?

**Verse 17.**—“He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches: to the one who conquers I will give the hidden manna.” He calls the hidden manna the invisible bread that descended from heaven, which became man so that man might eat the bread of angels. This manna is now received in the sacrament through faith, but at some time it will be received in reality through vision, according to the Psalmist’s statement: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is manifested to me” (Ps. XVI, 15).

“Manna,” when interpreted, sounds like “What is this?” We say this only of something we have not previously seen. The fullness of heavenly glory is therefore aptly called manna, because, according to Paul’s words, “eye has not seen, nor has it entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. III, 9).

“And I will give him a white stone, and on the stone a new name, which no one knows except the one who receives it.” A *calculus* is a precious stone, also called a carbuncle. For just as a burning coal, when placed in darkness, shines whatever its size, so this stone too is said to shine.

What, then, is signified by the white stone except Jesus Christ? He appeared among human beings pure, without any obscuring stain of sin, and by the light of his divinity illumined the darkness of our mortality. The meaning is this: “I will make the one who triumphs over the author of death my coheir in the kingdom of the Father.”

Another translation has “pearl” instead of “stone.” By the “new name” he means “Christian,” formerly unheard of, concerning which the Lord says to the Church through Isaiah: “You shall be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord will utter” (Isa. LXII, 2).

But since many who have been conquered by the devil are counted by this name, how does he promise to give it only to those who conquer? It is because the giving must be understood as that by which we know that those predestined to life in the heavenly city have been chosen. Hence he appropriately adds that “no one knows it except the one who receives it,” as though he were saying: No one defends the dignity of the Christian name by his life and conduct except the one whom divine predestination has destined to eternal life.

To know the name of Christ pertains to keeping his commandments; to receive it refers to the grace of divine predestination.

## Verse 18

“And to the angel of the church of Thyatira write: Thus says the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire, and whose feet are like orichalcum.”

**Verse 19.**—“I know your works, your charity, your faith, your ministry, your patience, and that your last works are more numerous than the first.” These things are said to the universal Church, whose works, charity, and faith the Lord knows because he approves them through the grace of election.

But these are listed in an inverted order. The first thing is to believe; then to love what one believes; finally, to do what love and faith compel one to do. By “ministry” he means the generous exercise of mercy with one’s utmost resources.

But it must be asked why the Church’s last works are praised as more numerous than the first. We should know that at the beginning the apostles commanded only four matters to be observed by the Gentiles converted to Christ: namely, that they abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from fornication, from what has been strangled, and from blood.

But when, as time passed, small intervals had elapsed, they grew toward the summit of perfection, so that many believers set aside all the things of the world. Alternatively, because a greater power of action will shine forth in the Church during the persecution of Antichrist. What now struggles only among the Gentiles will then labor twice as much, leading the Jews also to the faith.

**Verse 20.**—“But I have this against you: that you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce my servants to commit fornication and to eat things sacrificed to idols.” These things do not apply to the one whom he praised above with such honor, but specifically to wicked preachers who through their negligence allow fornication and idolatry in the Church.

We should not believe that Jezebel, the wife of Ahab, remained bodily alive until that time—she whom we know to have been trampled under the hooves of horses. Rather, because at that time there were people who imitated her intercourse, she herself, the mother of fornications, was identified in them. For the reprobate, joined by similarity of vices, form one body of the ancient enemy, just as the elect, joined by the bond of virtues, constitute one body of Christ.

Jezebel’s fornication is fourfold. There is fornication of desire, as in the statement: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 28). There is also fornication of action, concerning which the Apostle says: “Flee fornication, brothers” (I Cor. VI, 18). There is fornication of idolatry, according to the statement: “She committed adultery with stone and wood” (Jer. III, 9). There is also fornication of avarice, according to the statement: “Avarice, which is the service of idols” (Col. III, 5).

It should also be noted that Jezebel calls herself a prophetess, and for this reason seduces God’s servants. When someone says to a chaste person, “Come, let us enjoy the things you desire, for if God did not want this to happen, he would not have created male and female,” he attempts, as though prophesying, to seduce God’s soldier.

Jezebel is therefore interpreted as “a flow of blood,” or “flowing,” or “a dung heap.” Sins are represented by the name of blood, according to the statement: “Deliver me from bloodguilt” (Ps. L, 16). It is said to be the custom of women to discharge a flow of blood when the accumulated blood of many days is expelled in excess at the arrival of the menstrual period.

This is shown to happen universally to Jezebel: for a shameful desire, long accumulated, leaps forth into the deformity of open action when the time arrives. Then the mind becomes more intensely anxious, and, like wax before the face of fire, the person melts completely. Hence she is rightly called “flowing.” Finally, through the repeated commission of the lust already perpetrated, the stench of an evil reputation is emitted far and wide. Hence Jezebel is consequently interpreted as “a dung heap.”

**Verse 21.**—“And I gave her time to repent, and she does not wish to repent of her fornication.” Hence blessed Job says concerning any reprobate: “The Lord gave him a place for repentance, and he abuses it for pride” (Job XXIV, 23).

But since in the preceding verse he reproved the sluggish preacher for Jezebel’s fornication, why does he not say, “I gave you,” and “to her,” but only “to her”? This is especially puzzling since the Apostle testifies that not only those who do evil but also those who consent to those who do evil are punished by eternal death (Rom. I, 32).

We should therefore understand that the word of God passes from the particular to the general, and within it reproves, as though secretly, the reprobate part of that particular category as unrepentant—a part he had openly rebuked above. Thus one and the same category appears now guilty and now worthy, since both the openly negligent and the secretly unrepentant are rebuked. This is done so that the part of the category consisting of holy preachers might not appear joined to that which consists of the reprobate.

**Verse 22.**—“Behold, I am casting her onto a bed, and those who commit adultery with her will be in the greatest tribulation unless they repent of her works.”

**Verse 23.**—“And I will strike her children with death.” Jezebel, those who commit adultery with her, and her children are one body of Satan. This body is placed upon a bed not so that it may rest, but so that it may fall into frenzy; for by the name of the bed the boldness and security of sinning are understood.

She is said to be placed there by God, not because he himself drives her into it, but because by chastising he does not rescue her from this deception of security. And because the growth of vices is itself a kind of punishment, the bed is rightly called great tribulation.

The bed may also signify eternal punishment. Hence it seems to me that another interpreter rendered “bed” as “mourning.”

“And all the churches shall know that I am the one who searches the kidneys and hearts.” By the kidneys he wishes the wickedness of bodily lust already committed to be understood, because the seed of human conception comes forth from men’s loins; by the heart, the incentives of spiritual adultery. Hence the Psalmist says: “Burn my kidneys and my heart” (Ps. XXV, 2).

But does the Church not know beforehand that the Lord is the knower of hidden things, before he publicly exposes and destroys idolaters and fornicators? Or how can the Church be said to know this if she knows it by the outcome of events rather than by faith?

Therefore it must be held with certain faith that, insofar as concerns the condition of the present time, they are punished by a hidden death. The meaning is this: when I condemn the reprobate in hidden and secret places, the faithful nevertheless do not doubt that I know the deeds of all.

“And I will give to each one of you according to his works.” He returns from the particular to the general. There is no need here to explain further what ought rather to be feared.

**Verse 24.**—“But I say to you who remain in Thyatira, who do not hold this doctrine, who have not known the depths of Satan.” Here the word returns to the elect.

The “depths of Satan” should be understood as his ruinous pride, by which he first rose up against God and swelled with arrogance. The elect are said not to know it—that is, they do not receive it for imitation by any consent. In the same way, Holy Scripture says that unmarried women did not know men, meaning that they had in no way experienced the works of men in intercourse; and in the same way we say that a truthful person does not know how to lie.

“As they say, I will not place any other burden upon you.” Who are those who say this except the Jewish people, who say that the ceremonies of the Old Law ought to be imposed upon the shoulders of believers? Hence the evangelist Luke says: “Certain men came down from Judea and taught the brothers that unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved” (Acts XV, 1).

**Verse 25.**—“Nevertheless, hold fast to what you have until I come.” That is: Do not reject the light burden to which you have been called, namely, the grace of the Redeemer. By saying “until I come,” he shows that the Church will remain under grace until the times of restoration.

**Verse 26.**—“And to the one who conquers and keeps my works until the end, I will give authority over the nations.”

**Verse 27.**—“And he will rule them with an iron rod, and they will be broken like a potter’s vessel.”

**Verse 28.**—“As I also received from my Father.” The Son received this authority from the Father not in his divinity but in his humanity, in which he is less than the Father. Hence the statement: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII, 18).

And because the elect are his members, they too receive this authority in their head, according to the statement: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 18), and what follows.

By the iron rod, the rule of the preachers is expressed. An iron rod possesses uprightness without softness. Likewise, the holy preachers know neither how to spare themselves nor how to spare others in opposition to vices; rather, they strive to direct both themselves and others along the path of justice alone. Hence it is said to Christ: “Your rod is a rod of uprightness, the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. XLIV, 7).

Believers are appropriately compared with earthen vessels. They are vessels because they carry the treasure hidden for ages; they are earthen because they are weighed down by the corruption of the flesh. Hence the Apostle says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Cor. IV, 7).

The statement that these vessels are broken by the touch of the rod should be understood of the part of the vessels that is still being shattered so that it may be reformed into something better. Hence it is said to the potter of the human race: “Overturn the wicked, and they will be no more” (Prov. XII, 7); “the wicked” is understood, but the righteous are implied.

But what does it mean that the text first says, “the one who conquers and keeps my works until the end”? Does no one rule believers before triumphing over the devil by reaching the end? Or will he rule only afterward?

We should therefore understand that the Lord, using the future for the past, signifies through the grace of predestination that those to whom he declares he will give authority over the nations have already conquered and have already kept his works until the end. It is as though he were saying: “I will grant the capacity to rule well to the one whom I have seen as victorious and as destined to persevere in my works until the end.” This is because future things are present to him.

“And I will give him the morning star.” In Holy Scripture, the morning star in the singular signifies Christ. Hence below: “I am the morning star.” In the plural, however, it signifies the angels.

The Lord will therefore give the morning star to those who conquer when he reforms the body of our lowliness—that is, when all who are in the tombs hear the voice of the Son of God and come forth. He will lead them to the perfect day when he reveals to them the brilliance of his divinity.

## CHAPTER III
Source/review notes: Explicit source lacunae and codex variants are retained; useful column anchors are placed at their corresponding translated clauses.

**Verse 1.**—And to the angel of the Church in Sardis write: “Thus says he who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars: I know your works, that you have a name that you are alive, but you are dead.” (**Verse 2.**) “Be watchful, and strengthen the rest that were about to die.”

The Lord has the seven spirits in one sense, and the stars in another. For he has the sevenfold Spirit, equal to himself in the nature of divinity; he has the sevenfold Church subject to him like a handmaid under the authority of his power. But if he designates this angel—[Col. 1109D] whether among preachers or among certain of his hearers—as having a name that he is alive by the mere confession of faith, yet dead in works, how does he immediately add, in admonishing him: “Be watchful, and strengthen the rest that were about to die”?

We must therefore understand that he shows him dead in part through sins, but alive in part through good works. Yet how does one live in part who has died through even a single crime? Unless it is because, if he rises from sin through repentance, he does not lose, once alive, those good works that he performed while dead, since they too are brought to life with him.
