Therefore he hears: “Be watchful, and strengthen the rest that were about to die”; that is, if you revive in that part by which you are dead, strengthen the rest that still live in you, lest they die.

[Col. 1110A] Alternatively, there are many within the bosom of the Church who, guarding their life from every crime, are judged alive by human beings; but because their right intention does not proceed, they are reckoned dead by God. To them it is said: “Be watchful, and strengthen the rest that were about to die,” as if it were said: “If you wish the structure of the virtues to live, take heed to the intention of your action; pride will live.” For I do not find your works complete before my God. That is: because the head, intention, has grown weak, the limbs of virtue do not flourish as full or vigorous, but waste away, emaciated and almost dead.

**Verse 3.**—“Remember, therefore, how you received and heard; keep it, and repent.”

This statement applies to both senses. For he had heard: “Whoever observes the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all” (James 2:10); likewise: “If your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness” (Matthew 6:23). “But if you are not watchful, I will come to you like a thief, and you will not know when I will come.”

To watch is to rise from the sleep of sin to righteousness through the tears of repentance. The comparison with a thief is suitably introduced here: when he comes unexpectedly, he finds everyone asleep, slaughters them, and plunders their goods. So the heavenly Judge, when he comes unlooked-for, destroys the unrepentant by the sentence of punishment and scatters their deeds like the most powerful robber.

**Verse 4.**—“But you have a few names in Sardis who have not defiled their garments, and they will walk with me in white, because they are worthy.”

They do not stain their garments with filth who, after the sacrament of baptism, do not commit a mortal crime. But because they are few, “a few names” is mentioned first.

Where, then, Lord, will they walk with you? From where and to where, unless from you into you? For they walk with you daily because, following the traces of your Passion, they keep watch. You go before them by giving examples; they follow by imitating those same examples.

When he says “worthy,” he means either clean or worthy of my gracious favor. But should those who defile their life after baptism despair? By no means. Let them therefore hasten to the blood of the Lamb—not so that they may again be dipped in it through baptismal water, but so that they may be washed from the stains of sins in the fountain of tears. Hence it immediately follows:

**Verse 5.**—“The one who conquers will thus be clothed in white.”

That is, the one who, fighting with the enemy to recover his garments, conquers will shine once more clothed in them, just like those who kept them unstained.

This may also be applied to unbelievers, who are urged to conquer—that is, to believe in Christ—for “this is the victory that conquers the world: our faith.” And I will not erase his name from the book of life.

A great question arises for us at this point. The words seem to sound as though the name of the one who does not conquer were erased from the book, although it is clear that no one except the elect is held enrolled in the heavenly book of blessed predestination. It therefore remains for us to understand, according to the customary expression of sacred Scripture, that the names of the reprobate are erased from the book of life; that is, they are not written there on account of the merit of their rejection—just as Pharaoh’s heart is said to have been hardened by the Lord.

[Col. 1111A] This book, moreover, is a certain divine power that, before the ages, predestined the fixed and determined number of the elect who were to be glorified. Let it therefore be said of the victor: “I will not erase his name from the book of life,” as if he were saying: “The one whom I know will become a victor, I already hold as having his name written in heaven.”

“And I will confess his name before my Father and before his angels.” What does it mean for the Son of God to confess the victor’s name before the Father and the angels, except to show that the one who has conquered is united to him through good works? This will chiefly take place when he says to the elect: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matthew 25:34), and the rest.

**Verse 7.**—“And to the angel of the Church in Philadelphia write: Thus says the Holy and True One, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens. (**Verse 8.**) Behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one can shut.”

The Lord is called uniquely holy and true because, in comparison with him, no one is holy or truthful. For it is written: “No one is clean from defilement”; and again: “Every human being is a liar” (Psalm 115:11).

We understand the key of David as the incarnation of our Redeemer, which he assumed from the seed of David. The door that this same key opens or shuts is Christ himself, according to the saying: “I am the door,” and the rest (John 10:9). Thus the key and the door are like the shepherd, the doorkeeper, and the door, of whom the Gospel speaks simultaneously.

The open door, therefore, is Christ, born according to the flesh, who suffered and was raised on the third day; open not to unbelievers but to believers. The Jews tried to shut this door when, after beating the apostles, they commanded that they should not speak in the name of Jesus. But because, when he opens, no one shuts, they immediately replied: “We cannot not speak of what we have heard” (Acts 4:20).

The apostles had attempted to open this door, which was shut to the Asians; but because, when he shuts, no one opens, the Spirit of Jesus prevented them.

The open door may also be understood as Scripture, through which we enter into Christ by the steps of faith. He therefore opens the door with the key of David, and no one shuts it, because no veil of the Jews can obscure within the hearts of the elect the words of sacred Scripture, which he enables them to understand spiritually through the grace of his incarnation. Conversely, he shuts it to the unbelieving Jews, and it cannot be opened by anyone.

This may also be examined morally: “Because you have little strength, and have kept my word, and have not denied my name.” Here a considerable question arises: how can one have little strength who keeps the word of God and does not deny his name? We must understand, therefore, that this is said according to the judgment of human weakness, because the elect, although they can do many things through Christ, presume that they can do little. Thus it says, “You have little strength,” as if it said, “You think that you have little strength.”

**Verse 9.**—“Behold, I will give some from the synagogue of Satan, who call themselves Jews and are not, but they lie. Behold, I will make them come and worship before your feet, and they will know that I have loved you.”

Here the faith of the Jews is foretold, according to the saying: “Until the fullness of the nations enters, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25). [Col. 1112A] At present they call themselves Jews but are not, because the name they bear outwardly according to the letter they have inwardly lost according to the spirit. For the expression of the name “Jews” is a confession of Christ.

When Elijah and Enoch preach, they will come to worship before the feet of the Church, because they will venerate it by imitating the examples of its conduct.

**Verse 10.**—“Because you have kept the word of my patience,” and the rest.

The word of patience is what the Lord demonstrated by his example when, hanging on the cross, he prayed for his persecutors, and taught in words, saying: “In your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

What follows—“And I will keep you from the hour of temptation that is going to come upon the whole world to test those who dwell on the earth”—must be referred to the times of Antichrist, under whom there will be such tribulation as there has not been from the beginning of the world. The wounds of the bodies will indeed be severe, but the darts of the adversaries will be more grievous [the manuscript reads: “miracles”]. But the saints will be preserved from the temptation of deception, because they will not be provoked to deny Christ.

**Verse 11.**—“I am coming soon; hold fast what you have.”

The Lord says that he is coming soon, so that no one may fail in the contest. For everything that passes happens quickly. He urges him to hold fast the manner of heavenly life, and gives the reason, adding: “So that no one else may receive your crown.”

In this statement we see included the fixed and determined number of the elect, contemplating with truly wondrous consideration that no one can be added to it or subtracted from it.

**Verse 12.**—“The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God.”

The temple of God is the Church, according to the saying: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3:17). And because not only preachers but also good hearers triumph over the ancient enemy, and everyone who conquers is said in this verse to become a pillar in the temple of God, we are compelled to confess that the pillar is the same as the temple—that is, the universal Church.

But in what follows—“and he will go out no more”—it is plainly shown that the Church had long ago, in the younger brother, passed from the unity of faith and conduct that it had maintained in the prophets under the Law into the error of faithlessness and wrongful action; but, after receiving the slaughtered fattened calf, it was restored.

Alternatively, in Adam we all went out, both Jews and Gentiles; but, brought in as victors to the second Adam, we become pillars of the temple of God. For, by overcoming the temptations of the ancient enemy through the blood of that same Mediator of ours, we are established in the heavenly glory of the saints by that stability of the commandments which we are shown to have lost in the first Adam.

But we go out no more, because we will not be torn away by any persuasions of the enemy from that common happiness of the heavenly homeland.

And note that he says that he has God, speaking according to his humanity.

“And I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which descends from heaven from my God, and my new name. (**Verse 13.**) Whoever has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.”

For the Father’s name to be written upon the victor is for him to become his son by adoption through the Spirit. With what pen, indeed, is it written, except with the grace of the Spirit belonging to both? [Col. 1113A] Hence the Apostle says: “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God” (Romans 8:16).

“Jerusalem” is interpreted as “vision of peace.” It is said to descend from heaven from God because the Church of the elect, which advances by the steps of love toward the vision of heavenly peace, descended with the Lord, whose body it is, predestined into the womb of the Virgin; or because its number is increased daily by heavenly grace.

It is called “new” because through baptism and love it is stripped of the oldness of the earthly human being and clothed in heavenly newness. [Col. 1114A] Hence the saying: “The old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

The name Jerusalem is therefore written upon the victor when he is joined to the number of the saints. From where all these things come is made clear when it adds, “and my new name”—with “I will write” understood—namely, that which accrued to the same Mediator in time: Christ.

From him come our dignity; from him our exaltation; from him we are called sons of God, the new Jerusalem, and Christians. Therefore, where the whole sum of salvation resounds, let the book at last receive its proper conclusion.

## Book Three

**[Column 1113B] Verse 14.**—And to the angel of the Church in Laodicea write: “Thus says the Amen, the faithful and true witness, who is the beginning of God’s creation.”

“Amen” is interpreted as “true,” which must be referred to that Truth who says of himself: “I am the truth” (John 14:6).

Although the Lord has many faithful and true witnesses, he is appropriately called uniquely faithful and true, because in comparison with him no one is faithful or truthful. He is faithful, truthful, and good by nature; we are so by participation in him.

How the Son alone can be called the witness, when there are three who bear witness, has already been said in the first book.

Finally, the Son is called the beginning of God’s creation because all things receive from him the beginning of their existence. For, as it is written: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3).

**Verse 15.**—“I know your works, that you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were hot or cold! (**Verse 16.**) But because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I am about to vomit you out of my mouth.”

The cold are those whom either Jewish faithlessness or the error of the Gentiles holds bound, since the one who said, “I will sit on the sides of the north” (Isaiah 14:13), constrains them with his ice. Conversely, the hot are those whose hearts the Spirit—*auster*, that is, the Holy Spirit—touches when he comes with the warmth of faith, so that, once the hardness of unbelief has been dissolved and the coldness of error lost, they pour forth the fervor of good works.

The lukewarm person, moreover, may arise either from the cold or from the hot: one person turns from the coldness of iniquity but does not advance to the perfect fervor of righteousness; another descends from the warmth of righteousness into the torpor of sluggishness.

We have all learned by experience that something cold or hot is easily taken into the body, whereas something lukewarm is expelled from the mouth itself with nausea. Thus, thus (so the codex), teachers can more easily draw an unbeliever to faith, or a perverse Christian to the fervor of good works, than a lukewarm person. Therefore they abandon him, like a farmer who leaves barren land and cultivates land from which he has already removed the thorns and which is fruitful, or land that is still full of thorns but is foreseen to become fruitful.

**Verse 17.**—“Because you say, ‘I am rich and have grown wealthy, and I need nothing,’ and you do not know that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind.”

Whoever boasts that he is rich on account of his confession of right faith, unless he ceases to do evil, is not rich but poor. Because any lukewarm person does not understand this, he is rightly rebuked by the Lord as wretched, pitiable, poor, naked, and blind: wretched because he deceives himself; pitiable because he does not understand what mocks him; poor and naked because he is empty of true virtues; but worse still, because he is not even conscious of this—and therefore deservedly blind.

But because divine mercy calls some lukewarm people to the fervor of righteousness, it rightly adds:

**Verse 18.**—“I advise you to buy from me gold refined by fire, so that you may become rich.”

By gold here the incarnate Wisdom of God is understood, of which it is said elsewhere: “Receive wisdom as gold.” This gold is appropriately called refined and tested by fire, because our Redeemer was tested by the fire of suffering.

The meaning is: If you wish to be rich in virtues, take me as the one to imitate, so that you too may become gold refined by fire. And what price will a poor person give for this gold, except a devoted desire in petition? To this he adds:

“And that you may put on white garments, so that the shame of your nakedness may not appear.”

The one who purchases gold refined by fire is clothed in white garments to cover the shame of nakedness; he is transferred into a new life to avoid the disgrace of lukewarmness; he merits to cling, through the virtue of imitation, to the new and heavenly human being.

“And anoint your eyes with salve, so that you may see.”

As if he were saying: Apply the divine commandments to the blind mind, so that, seeing the nakedness of virtues that you suffer, you may hasten to cover it. For unless the divine commandments were salve, the Psalmist would not say: “The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes” (Psalm 18:9).

By the salve made from earth, which drives the dust of the earth from the eyes, the temporal poverty of our Redeemer, assumed for our sake, may also be signified. Therefore, let the one whose eyes have been blinded by dust apply salve, so that he may receive light; that is, let the one who is carried away by earthly delights recall to mind the temporal poverty of his Redeemer, so that with the inner eyes he may contemplate the future rewards of the saints.

**Verse 19.**—“Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline.”

Reproof pertains to words; discipline pertains to scourges. In this statement there is nothing more that ought to be explained, but much that ought to be willingly embraced.

“Be zealous, therefore, and repent.”

As if he were saying: Unless you receive scourges with them here temporarily, you will undergo eternal torments without them.

[Col. 1115A] **Verse 20.**—“Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me.”

This standing is not bodily but must be understood without location, because the one whom the Lord inhabits he does not abandon by passing elsewhere.

The door signifies the entrance of the mind. The Lord knocks either by himself, without an intermediary, through inspiration; and whoever keeps the admonitions of his commandments through the love of charity hears his voice. He opens the door when he enlarges his heart to see the supreme good of eternity.

Once the door has been opened, the Lord enters him because, through inward sweetness, he enlightens the soul burning with desire.

Thus the head dines [lacuna], because by doing the Father’s will daily [lacuna], the members with the head, who, in order to do the Father’s will, die daily with him; as in the saying: “For you are dead,” and the rest.

**Verse 21.**—“The one who conquers, I will make him sit on my throne, just as I conquered and sit with my Father on his throne.”

The conquering Lord sits on the throne of the Father because, after his Passion and resurrection, he showed himself to be equal to the Father. He says that we too will sit because we receive the power of judgment through the Son’s authority, according to the saying: “You who have followed me will sit upon thrones,” and the rest (Matthew 19:28).

Nor is it contrary to the truth that elsewhere he says they will sit upon twelve thrones, while here he says they will sit upon his throne. For by the twelve thrones universal judgment is shown; by the Son’s throne, the singular summit of judicial power. What is designated by the twelve thrones is therefore designated by the one throne of the Son.

But it must be asked how (the codex reads “when”) he can say that all victors will judge, when not all will judge, but some among the victors will judge and others will be judged. We must understand, therefore, that they will have authority over others which they do not possess in themselves, just as the whole human body has the power to speak through the mouth and to see through the eyes.

But if we examine this statement more subtly—“just as I conquered”—we find that it designates those who are more glorious in victory and superior through it.

## Chapter IV

**Verse 1.**—After this I saw, and behold, a door opened in heaven.

The birth of the Redeemer is recapitulated here, the things already said under other and various figures being repeated—as if someone were narrating one matter in different ways: the narratives would have different times, but not the matter itself, which took place at one time.

But it must be asked: since other prophets have ordinarily revealed through kings how great an interval there was between one vision and another, why does John not disclose the time of the prophecy? For this reason, namely, that he teaches that the whole time of the Church must be referred to that continuous day of resurrection of which it is said: “Blessed is the one who has a share in the first resurrection” (Revelation 20:6).

For the first resurrection—that is, the resurrection by which souls rise from the death of sin to the life of righteousness—is taking place throughout the present age.

But with what eyes did John see this door? Certainly, as far as the figurative manifestation is concerned, not with the eyes of the flesh but of the mind. As far as the truth of the matter itself is concerned, however, which had already been manifested when the Lord appeared in the flesh, [Col. 1116A] he saw it not only with the eyes of the flesh but also touched it with his hands.

By the open door, therefore, Christ is signified, already manifested to all the faithful by being born, dying, and rising again. He is appropriately seen in heaven—that is, in the Church—because our Redeemer is preached and believed in it as having been born, suffered, raised, and ascended into the heavens.

“And the first voice that I heard was like a trumpet speaking with me, saying: Come up here.”

Where, except to the door and heaven—that is, to Christ and the Church? And by what steps, except those of faith?

John is rightly invited to this by the first voice because each of the elect is strengthened by the teaching of the Old Testament—which precedes the new—in order to reach, through the Gospel and with an unimpeded step of belief, the mysteries of true faith.

This voice is rightly compared to a trumpet because it summons to spiritual battle. Hence the saying: “Raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isaiah 58:1).

But when it adds, “I will show you what must take place after this,” it does not deny that there are exaltations of the Church; rather, it shows that they will remain until the end of the age.

**Verse 2.**—And immediately I was in the spirit.

If this is referred to John, it says that he was taken up into ecstasy; but if it is referred to the Church, this statement declares its spiritual manner of life.

“And behold, a throne was set in heaven, and one seated upon the throne.”

The Church is signified both by heaven and by the throne. For one kind is joined to another in such a way that one thing, not two, is understood.

The throne is therefore set in heaven when heaven itself—that is, the Church—merits to be presided over by the Lord. The one seated upon the throne is nothing other than the Son of Man appearing in the midst of the golden lampstands, except that there he walks—that is, he bestows gifts—whereas here he sits—that is, judging each person, he exercises judgment on account of the gifts bestowed.

That the Son is designated by the one seated here is made clear when it adds:

**Verse 3.**—“And the one seated was like in appearance a jasper stone and a sardius.”

By jasper, which consists of a green appearance, the green pastures of paradise are signified. And what are these except the divinity of Christ, in which all things live? As the same John says: “Whoever has the Son has life” (John 3:36).

By the sardius, which resembles red earth, the humanity of our Redeemer is expressed, because “truth has sprung from the earth.”

The Church may also be signified through the appearance of these stones.

“And there was a rainbow around the throne, like the appearance of an emerald.”

Through the rainbow—which in both Greek and Latin is called an *arcus*, an arch—the reconciliation of the world accomplished through the dispensation of the incarnate Word is signified.

When the sun illuminates a cloud, a rainbow appears; so when the Father’s Word, which is the sun of righteousness, irradiated human nature by assuming it, that very assumption of his humanity—which is called a cloud by the prophet—became the reconciliation of the world.

The interpretation of the name itself agrees with this. For if one letter is added to *iris*, one obtains *irini* (Greek: εἰρήνη), which is translated from Greek into Latin as “peace.”

When he illuminates the solid hearts of the saints, which are called clouds, they produce the appearance of an arch, because through prayer they bend God toward mercy.

[Col. 1117A] The connection of the figures is also fitting, because below the flashes and thunder are said to proceed from the throne as from a cloud.

Since the rainbow shines principally with two colors—water and fire—it signifies either the baptism of water and the Holy Spirit, or the judgment preceding it through the Flood and the judgment following it through fire.

So that the divinity reconciled to the world might be shown more clearly here through it, the rainbow is compared to an emerald appearance. For this stone is of an extremely green color, which is not unfittingly applied to the nature of divinity.

**Verse 4.**—And around the throne were twenty-four seats, and upon the thrones twenty-four elders seated.

When the Lord mentions twelve thrones in the Gospel, what does John mean by saying twenty-four, except that, because of the twofold Testament, the number of the twelve tribes is also doubled?

Thus, with regard to the distinction between the two Testaments, there are twenty-four thrones and an equal number of elders; but with regard to their unity and harmony, there are twelve.

Nor should we understand things so carnally as to think that one seat signifies one thing and the twenty-four thrones another. Since the Lord will judge the entire Church uniquely and principally, the elders and thrones are therefore said to be one seat. But because the holy preachers of both Testaments will examine the peoples subject to them together with him, it follows that around the seat an equal number of elders sit upon twenty-four thrones.

What follows concerning the elders—“clothed all around in white garments, and on their heads golden crowns”—pertains to the whole Church, which is clothed in white garments, that is, in the inviolable sacraments of baptism. It has golden crowns on its head because it truly triumphs over the author of death.

Alternatively, by this number the holy Church may be represented on account of the perfection of six, which is completed through the four books of the Gospel; or certainly because it uses the twenty-four books of the Old Testament.

**Verse 5.**—And from the throne proceed flashes of lightning, voices, and thunder.

Here it is plainly shown that the Church is signified by the throne, since all these things are appropriate to it. In the flashes of lightning we understand signs of miracles. Hence the Psalmist says: “Your flashes of lightning illumined the world” (Psalm 76:19).

By the voices and thunder, the preaching of truth is expressed, as the same Psalmist says: “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel” (ibid.).

And note that, as though passing obliquely from one figure to another, he says that these things proceed from the seat, although they belong not to a seat but to a cloud. He therefore wants the seat itself to be understood as a cloud.

The Church of the righteous is appropriately represented by a cloud, because its preachers rain through their words, thunder through their threats, and flash through their miracles.

“And seven burning lamps before the throne, which are the seven spirits of God. (**Verse 6.**) And before the seat was something like a glassy sea, resembling crystal.”

The Holy Spirit is appropriately compared to lamps because he kindles the souls of the elect to love of God and neighbor.

What is signified by the glassy sea except baptism? And why glassy, except because the faith of those passing through it is shown by a figurative expression? The effect is named from its cause. [Col. 1118A] For just as in glass nothing appears outwardly except what is contained inwardly, so the faith of the Church is inwardly simple in belief and shown outwardly as truthful in confession.

But lest it be thought fragile like glass, “resembling crystal” was added. For just as ice, compressed by winter cold, becomes hardened over many years into the likeness of stone and becomes crystal, so the faith of the saints is solidified amid pressures through the passage of time.

[Col. 1119A] “And in the midst of the seat and around the seat were four living creatures, full of eyes in front and behind.”

No one doubts that by these four living creatures the four evangelists are represented. But if they are in the midst of the seat, how are they said to be around the seat—especially since it has already been said that the Lord is in the midst of the seat and that the twenty-four elders sit around the seat?

We must therefore understand that the living creatures are in the Lord and the Lord in the living creatures; and again, the living creatures are in the elders and the elders in the living creatures.

The universal Church may also be represented by the appearance of the four living creatures. The living creatures are therefore full of eyes because, as many as are the sayings of sacred Scripture, so many are the spiritual lights of the elect by which they are illuminated for faith.

They have eyes in front and behind because they contain within themselves the mysteries of the Old and New Testaments. Here “in front” is used for the past.

Alternatively, they have eyes in front and behind because they announce some things already fulfilled and others still to be fulfilled; or because they lament past sins and guard against future ones.

**Verse 7.**—And the first living creature was like a lion, the second living creature like a calf, the third living creature had a face like a human being, and the fourth living creature was like a flying eagle.

It must be asked why John said that the first living creature was like a lion, when Ezekiel says that the first creature had the appearance of a human being.

Therefore, either the historical order was changed, which the mystical words of Scripture do not always preserve; or, because people believed in Christ not on account of his birth or Passion but on account of the resurrection, which is represented by the lion, he placed the lion’s form first.

Since Matthew began with human generation, he is rightly represented by the human being; since Mark began with the cry in the wilderness, he is rightly represented by the lion; since Luke began with sacrifice, he is suitably represented by the calf; and since John began with divinity, he is worthily represented by the eagle.

These things may also be referred to Christ and to all his members. But it is sufficient to have said this briefly.

**Verse 8.**—And the four living creatures, each of them, had six wings.

In the wings of the four living creatures we understand the sayings of the two Testaments. Since these wings are two, nevertheless, on account of the doubled number twelve—which is found in the tribes of Israel and in the apostles—they are multiplied twelve times and produce twenty-four.

Likewise, because they spread throughout the whole world knowledge of the Trinity, they are multiplied three times and appear as six in all.

Alternatively, the six wings may signify six laws: the first natural law, the second the law of Moses, the third that of the prophets, the fourth the law of grace, the fifth that of the apostles, and the sixth that of the councils. By these the Church flies to heaven.

“And around and within they are full of eyes.”

The living creatures are full of eyes both around and within because the holy Church displays the light of preaching to believers but closes it to unbelievers; or because the holy preachers show the path of faith and holiness to the minds of the simple outwardly, through history alone, and to the perfect inwardly, through allegory; or because they look unceasingly outwardly to offer good examples to their brothers and inwardly to persist in right intention.

And they have no rest day or night, saying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty, who is, and who was, and who is to come.”

“They have no rest,” that is, they do not cease from crying out. Hence it is clear that the four living creatures signify the whole Church: for not only the evangelists, but all the faithful, day and night—that is, in prosperity and adversity—do not cease to praise God.

In saying “holy” three times, they designate the three Persons. By saying “Lord God almighty,” they show that in these three there is one substance.

But how can the words “who is to come” in this praise correspond to the Trinity, when only the Son will come in his humanity to judge? We must therefore understand that the invisible Trinity will examine the righteous and sinners through the assumed person of the Son.

He will come not by passing from place to place, but by displaying manifest power through the assumed form of a human being, which will descend from heaven to the lower regions.

The present coming of the divinity may also be understood here, by which his saints are illuminated daily.

**Verse 9.**—And when those living creatures gave glory, honor, and blessing to the one seated upon the throne, who lives forever and ever, (**Verse 10.**) the twenty-four elders fell down and worshiped the one who lives forever and ever.

Here the living creatures no longer signify a genus but a species—that is, the evangelists. Through the twenty-four elders, however, the universal Church is expressed in its leaders and subjects.

The living creatures therefore give glory and honor to the one seated upon the throne when the holy evangelists teach that he should be praised for all good things, as in the saying: “Every good gift,” and the rest.

While they say these things, the twenty-four elders—that is, all the saints—fall down by thinking humbly of themselves. Wherever they fall, there they worship, because in not attributing anything to themselves, they honor God.

The falling and worship must be understood spiritually, according to the saying: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24).

“And they cast their crowns before the throne, saying,” and the rest.

This repeats the same point. For the elders’ placing their crowns before the throne means that the elect, through a pious confession of mind, lay aside the swelling of pride over the virtues they have received before their consciences, over which God presides, and attribute everything to the one who presides over them.

Hence they say:

**Verse 11.**—“You are worthy, Lord our God, to receive glory and honor and power.”

As if they were saying: “These things belong principally to you, from whom, through whom, and in whom are the glory, honor, and power of the saints.”

But what does the following mean: “Because you created all things, and because of your will they existed and were created”? For if they were created, how did they exist before they were created?

We must therefore understand that they existed in predestination before they came to be in actual work.

## Chapter V

**[Column 1120A]**
**Verse 1.—** “And I saw in the right hand of the One seated upon the throne a book written within and without.” By the One seated upon the throne the person of the Father is indicated; by the right hand of the One seated, however, the Son of that same Father is signified, through whom all things were made, and concerning whom the Father’s voice says: “I will lift up my hand to heaven and swear by my right hand.”

The book written within and without appears to contain both Testaments, namely, the Old and the New. The Old, according to the letter, lay open on the outside, but according to its mystical meaning concealed the New within. Or else the book is shown written within as allegory, and without as history. The Old and New Testaments are rightly called one book, because neither can the New be distinguished from the Old, nor again the Old from the New. **[Col. 1120B]** The book is also rightly said to be in the right hand, because the principal intention of the divine Scriptures refers to the dispensation of our Redeemer.

“Sealed with seven seals.” The number seven often signifies totality. The book is said to have been sealed with seven seals because, before the Lord Savior’s dispensation had been revealed in the fullness of time, it was hidden in the divine books in the complete abundance of all manner of concealed mysteries.

If this interpretation is not sufficient for someone, let him know that the seven seals comprise seven modes of expression: the indicative, as in what is said to the prophet who was asking: “I am the Lord who speak righteousness” (Isa. 45:19); the declarative, as in: “Hear me, Jacob and Israel, whom I call,” and so forth (Isa. 48:12); the imperative, as in: “Cry aloud; do not cease” (Isa. 58:1); the optative, as in: “Would that you had heeded my commandments!” (Isa. 48:18); the subjunctive, as in: “If you will keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession” (Exod. 19:5); the infinitive, as in: “To restrain oneself from evil is understanding”; and the impersonal, as in: “Who can proclaim the mighty deeds of the Lord?” (Ps. 105:2).

**Verse 2.—** “And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice: Who is worthy to open the book and loose its seals?” By the mighty angel the herald of the law should be understood; for “the lips of the priest guard knowledge,” and “they seek the law from his mouth,” because “he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.” What does it mean to ask who is worthy to loose the book, except anxiously to desire Christ, who could show in himself that the law had been fulfilled and revealed, so that it should now be observed and understood not carnally but spiritually?

The book is rightly opened first, and then its seven seals are loosed, because first the proclamations of the divine law were fulfilled in Christ, and afterward, in the whole body, in a certain manner—as the opening of the individual seals makes clear. And because Christ had not yet come, it is rightly added:

**Verse 3.—** “And no one was able, neither in heaven”—that is, an angel—“nor on earth”—that is, a human being—“nor under the earth”—that is, a soul—“to open the book or to look upon it.” For none of these could accomplish the dispensation of human salvation.

But blessed John, how could no one look upon the book, when you yourself say: “I saw a book in the right hand of God”? Perhaps you were neither in heaven, nor on earth, nor under the earth? So that there may be no contradiction, “to look upon” must be understood as “to comprehend.” For who is sufficient to comprehend how God became incarnate without seed? How the God-man came forth from the closed womb of a virgin? How the Lord of glory was crucified, when only the flesh died?

**Verse 4.—** “And I wept greatly, because no one was found worthy to open the book or to see it.” John is by no means believed to have wept in his own person—he who was writing these things after the opening of this book—but in the person of the Church that existed before Christ’s coming. Burdened by the weight of sins, she anxiously sought the presence of her mediator. In her person David also says: “My tears have been my bread day and night, while they say to me every day, ‘Where is your God?’” (Ps. 42:3).

Consolation is directed to her in what follows:

**Verse 5.—** “And one of the elders says to me, ‘Do not weep. Behold, the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he may open the book and loose its seals.’” By one elder the order of the prophets is understood, through whose oracles the Church was consoled, according to the saying: “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent.”

Note that Christ is called a lion here because he conquered the devil; in the following verse he is called a lamb because, offering himself, he redeemed the world. “The Root of David” means David’s lineage and son.

It should further be noted that by saying “he has conquered,” he uses the past tense for the future, as in: “They pierced my hands,” and so forth (Ps. 22:16).

**[Col. 1121C] Verse 6.—** “And I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth.”

As has already been said, the throne, the living creatures, and the elders signify the Church, in whose midst the Lamb stands, according to the saying: “I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the church I will praise you” (Ps. 22:22). It is not contradictory that elsewhere we read: “The Lord is round about his people” (Ps. 125:2), because, presiding in the midst, he governs and judges, while surrounding them on every side, he protects and defends.

But why is he read as standing here, whereas above he is read as seated? It is because there the examination and kingdom are shown, while here assistance is shown. To sit belongs to one who reigns and judges; to stand belongs to one who helps.

Note also that he is seen not slain, but as though slain, because although he was crucified in weakness, he nevertheless lives by the power of God. In another sense, Christ is not slain but appears to be slain whenever his members either willingly mortify themselves or endure persecutions, so that they may fulfill in themselves what is lacking in Christ’s sufferings.

By the seven horns, as he himself explained, the sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit is signified. This operation is shown to have rested not only upon the Head but also to have enlightened the whole body; hence, in this passage, the seven spirits of God are said to have been sent into all the earth. This sevenfold operation, which is represented because of kingship and strength, is rightly also represented by eyes because of the Church’s illumination.

Alternatively, by the horns, which rise above the flesh, those who are more eminent in the Church may be understood, to whom it is said: “You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit” (Rom. 8:9).

**Verse 7.—** “And he came and took the book from the right hand of the One seated upon the throne.” The right hand of the One seated upon the throne and the Lamb, as though slain, in the midst of the throne are the same, because the Son of God, through whom the world was created, and the Son of man, through whom it was redeemed, are not two Christs but one.

Therefore the Lamb—that is, the Son of man—received the book from himself, that is, from his divinity: the book is the dispensation of human salvation, to which all the pages of Scripture bear witness.

**Verse 8.—** “And when he had opened the book, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell before the Lamb, each holding a harp and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.”

**[Col. 1122B]** The Lamb opened the book when he accomplished the work of voluntary suffering. What does it mean for the living creatures and the elders to have harps, except that the Church of the elect fulfills what is lacking in Christ’s sufferings? Sufferings are appropriately represented by harps. On a harp some strings are stretched more tightly and others more gently; yet, though stretched differently, they produce by no means a different song. Thus, in Christ’s body, different members imitate his sufferings—some more fully, others less—but together they resound one hymn of concord.

The living creatures and the elders therefore fall before the Lamb with harps, because all the saints attribute whatever they suffer for Christ to Christ, not to themselves.

By the golden bowls charity is understood. Charity knows how to intercede not only for friends but also for enemies; hence the bowls are said to be full. And the bowls are appropriately placed after the harps, because first the Lord endured the gallows of the cross, and then, with incomparable charity, prayed for his persecutors, saying: “Father, forgive them,” and so forth (Luke 23:34).

**Verse 9.—** “And they sang a new song, saying: ‘You are worthy, Lord our God, to receive the book,’” and so forth. Christ sang a new song by preaching in words and imitating through deeds.

What does it mean to say, “You are worthy, Lord our God, to receive the book and to open its seals, because you were slain and redeemed us for God by your blood from every tribe and tongue and people and nation,” except that, in comparison with our victories, your victory alone is judged worthy—the victory by which we were redeemed from the prince of death and from the curse of the law?

In the fact that the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders say that they were redeemed from every tribe, tongue, people, and nation, it is openly shown that through them the universal Church is signified.

**Verse 10.—** “And you made us a kingdom and priests for our God, and we shall reign upon the earth.” The elect are kings when, by restraining their bodies, they reign over the earth subjected to them by the law of virtue. Hence they affirm that they have received a kingdom upon the earth. They are priests because, chastising themselves daily, they offer themselves to God, according to the saying: “A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit” (Ps. 51:17).

**Verse 11.—** “And I saw and heard the voice of many angels around the throne and the living creatures and the elders.” By saying that he heard a voice, he shows what kind of vision this was. That vision hears, and that hearing sees.

But if the living creatures and the elders are around the seat, as has already been said, how is an angel around it, unless the same living creatures and elders are angels? Of them it is said: “The angels of peace will bitterly weep” (Isa. 33:7). The heavenly host of angels may also be understood by the name “angels.” Whether these or those are intended, however, an innumerable multitude is shown when it follows:

“And their number was thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice:

**Verse 12.—** ‘Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power, and divinity, and wisdom, and strength, and honor, and glory, and blessing.’”

**Verse 13.—** “And every creature that is in heaven, and upon the earth, and under the earth, and in the sea, and those that are in it.”

The sea and the things in it signify the present age.

“I heard all saying: ‘To the One seated upon the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and power forever and ever.’”

By saying “all,” he repeats those whom he previously said constituted the whole Church: the living creatures, the elders, and the angels. In the One seated and the Lamb—that is, in the Father and the Son—the Holy Spirit also is understood, according to the rule already stated.

“And the four living creatures said, ‘Amen.’ And the twenty-four elders fell down and worshiped the One who lives forever and ever.”

Because the living creatures and the elders are one—that is, one Church—the living creatures fall and worship with the elders, and the elders affirm with the living creatures that these praises are true, responding with a word of confirmation: “Amen.” Their falling and worship, as has already been said, must be understood spiritually.

Therefore, lest we grow excessively weary through prolonged exposition, let us close this book at this point.

## Book Four

### Chapter VI

**[Col. 1123B] Verse 1.—** “And when the Lamb had opened one of the seven seals, I heard one of the four living creatures saying, as with the voice of a great thunder: ‘Come and see.’”

The opening of a seal is the revelation of a mystery. But because the mysteries are not one but many, and it would take a long time to treat each individually, they can all be comprehended in these three modes: speech, knowledge, and action. Speech includes within itself all the commandments. Knowledge, when properly applied, conveys forms of understanding. Action agrees with both.

When one of the seven seals was opened, one of the four living creatures, in the manner of great thunder, invited John to come and see, because, once the truth has been manifested, the Church which goes before in the apostles summons its successor to faith.

**Verse 2.—** “And behold, a white horse, and the one seated upon it had a bow.” By the white horse Christ’s humanity without the obscurity of sin is signified, which the Word of the Father uniquely chose to preside over; or else all the elect are signified.

By the bow the Old and New Testaments are expressed, from which as many arrows proceed as there are utterances of the Testaments. Concerning this bow it is said to the same rider: “Bending and extending your bow over the scepters.”

What follows—“and a crown was given to him”—refers not only to the head but also to the body.

“And he went out conquering, so that he might conquer.” From where did he go out, except from the opened seal? For from the revealed mystery of Scripture, the truth of the mystery itself appeared openly. He went out conquering, first as the Head, so that afterward he might conquer daily in the body the temptations of the devil and the persecutions of evil people.

**Verse 3.—** “And when he had opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature saying: ‘Come and see.’” Why is a similar admonition given in a dissimilar circumstance, except because, just as there is joy there over a victory accomplished, so here there is concern over a future battle?

**Verse 4.—** “And another horse went out, a red one, and to the one seated upon it it was granted to take peace from the earth.” The red horse is the body of the ancient enemy; all the reprobate are blood-red through the slaughter of souls.

The rider of the elect says: “I give you my peace” (John 14:27). The rider of the reprobate, however, takes peace from the earth, because the former is the author of concord, whereas the latter is the author of discord. Note that he takes peace not from heaven but from the earth—that is, from those who seek earthly things.

“And that they should slaughter one another.” In this statement not bodily but spiritual slaughter must be understood. How the reprobate slaughter one another is disclosed when it is added concerning the ruler of the Jews: “And a great sword was given to him,” that is, a spiritual and malignant sword, by which not the bodies but the souls of the reprobate are slaughtered.

The devil wields this sword in two ways: either he deceives inwardly by his own spiritual speech, or, striking outwardly through the tongue of his carnal followers, he reaches the soul for its destruction.

All these things are said to have been given to him—that is, permitted, while the just God disposes all things.

**Verse 5.—** “And when he had opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature saying: ‘Come and see.’ And behold, a black horse, and the one seated upon it had a balance in his hand.”

In the blackness of this horse that hunger of the wicked is signified by which they eagerly desire to devour Christ’s body and transfer it into the belly of their malice. Its rider holds a balance in his hand because he seeks to purchase the life of the good with temporal rewards, so that he may satisfy his own hunger and that of his followers.

He held this balance in his hand when he offered one apple to be eaten and purchased the whole world for destruction. For it must be understood that the devil first takes away the nourishment of hearing the word of God, so that, when those afflicted by hunger for spiritual food are weakened, he may more easily take them as an increase to his own body.

Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “Behold, I will send a famine upon the land—not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God” (Amos 8:11). The Lord brings this about by abandoning; the devil, by invading.

But how can those who are God’s grain, wine, and oil suffer this famine? Rather, let the chaff, the grape-skins, and the olive dregs suffer it; let them come to the balance, unworthy of any price—not those who have been redeemed by Christ’s blood.

Hence it immediately follows:

**Verse 6.—** “And I heard something like a voice in the midst of the four living creatures saying: ‘A two-pound measure of wheat for one denarius, and three two-pound measures of barley for one denarius; and do not harm the wine and the oil.’”

This voice sounded in the midst of the four living creatures—that is, in the midst of the Church—when, with the nations united in faith, divine power restrained the devil from harming the elect. It was as though he were mockingly told: “The rider of the white horse has taken away and purchased the wheat and barley, the wine and the oil, with his denarius; but he has left you the chaff, the grape-skins, and the olive dregs.”

One two-pound measure, which is made from two sextarii, is the Church, consisting of the two Testaments in love of God and neighbor. In this passage, however, we should understand one Church as represented by holy preachers or men of great virtues, not by all believers generally.

For it is not without reason that barley is placed here after wheat. Let one two-pound measure of wheat, from the two peoples, designate the new preachers of the Church and men eminent in virtues, who, crushed in the mill of tribulations and cooked in the fire of persecutions, have deserved to become Christ’s beautiful and white bread.

Let the three two-pound measures of barley designate the life of the subordinate and weak, coming from both peoples. Note that the price of wheat and barley is one and the same: although the labor of the saints differs, they have nevertheless been purchased at one price, and after their labor they will receive one denarius.

It should further be noted that the same statement is repeated when it follows: “Do not harm the wine and the oil.” For how is the Church not wine and oil, when she is trodden like a grape in the winepress of tribulations and, like an olive crushed in the press of distress, is melted and poured out?

**Verse 7.—** “And when he had opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature saying: ‘Come and see.’”

**Verse 8.—** “And behold, a pale horse, and the one seated upon it was named Death; and Hades followed him.” Those who are also represented by the red horse are designated by the pale horse; their spiritual death is now represented in the pallor of that horse.

Death—that is, the devil—is rightly said to sit upon them, preparing to fight against the living, because through the service of those whom he has already killed spiritually, he seeks to extinguish the life of the elect.

They are called Hades in whom death dwells. Hades therefore follows Death, because the wicked imitate the devil. More particularly, heretics may also be understood by the pale horse.

“And authority was given to him over the four parts of the earth, to kill with sword, with famine, with death, and with the beasts of the earth.”

There are two parts in this world: Christ’s and the devil’s. Christ’s part is not divided, according to the saying: “My dove is one” (Song 6:9). The devil’s part, however, is divided into four parts: pagans, Jews, heretics, and evil Catholics. Thus there are as many plagues as there are parts of the devil. How he kills with sword, famine, and death has already been explained.

By the beasts, savage movements of the soul are signified. Our enemy therefore kills the souls of the reprobate with beasts, because, when carnal movements of the soul are not held back by the cages of the divine commandments, they become savage, so to speak, through the impulse of diabolical suggestion, and hurl the life of the wretched headlong over every precipice.

**Verse 9.—** “And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been slain because of the word of God and the testimony that they held.”

In the souls of the slain we understand the souls of all the elect who are harassed either by bodily or by spiritual attacks from the reprobate. There are two kinds of martyrs: one public, the other hidden.

By the altar Christ is understood. Upon it we offer our sacrifices to God the Father when, imitating his only-begotten Son, we appear before him as a living victim. The souls of the slain are therefore beneath the altar because they are subject to our mediator.

If the elect themselves are understood by the altar, they are beneath themselves because they have not yet been clothed with the immortality of the body.

**Verse 10.—** “And they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell upon the earth?’”

What does it mean for the souls of the saints to ask vengeance for their blood from their persecutors, except to await the day of the final judgment? The words of the souls are not formed through an organ of the throat by air drawn into the belly; rather, their great cry is their great desire.

But since the mind that asks is ordinarily moved in one way, and the mind that is asked in another, and since the souls of the saints cling so closely to God that by clinging they rest, how are they said to ask, when it is certain that they neither ignore God’s will nor what is to come?

It must therefore be understood that, since they are placed in God, they are said to ask something from him—not because they desire vengeance that would conflict with the will of the One whom they behold, but because they receive from him the knowledge to ask for what they know he intends to do.

**Verse 11.—** “And a white robe was given to each of them, and they were told to rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers who were to be killed as they had been should be completed.”

What is signified by the white robes except the reward of the martyrs? Before the resurrection, the elect are said to have received individual robes because they already enjoy eternal blessedness in the soul alone.

Note that this is the voice of souls expressing what lovers desire; God’s response is that they must await the gathering of their brothers, graciously instilling in their minds the delay of waiting. They desire the resurrection of their bodies, but they hear that they should willingly await the gathering of their brothers.

**Verse 12.—** “And I saw when he had opened the sixth seal, and there was a great earthquake; and the sun became black like a sackcloth garment, and the moon became like blood.”

By the earthquake the final persecution under Antichrist must be understood. It is called great because, according to the Lord’s word, there will then be tribulation such as has never been and never shall be.

The sun is Christ, according to the saying: “For you who fear God the sun of righteousness shall rise” (Mal. 4:2). He will be darkened at the end of time, when those who seemed to shine as though in Christ’s body fall into the darkness of manifest error.

The radiant life of preachers may also be signified by the sun. At the end of time, therefore, the sun will be like a sackcloth garment, because the radiant life of preachers will appear harsh and contemptible before the eyes of the reprobate. Sackcloth is suited to criminals and sinners.

By the moon turned into blood we recognize the holy Church, stained in the elect by the blood of suffering. It is said to be wholly stained because no one who remains in faith in the mediator will be exempt from that final persecution. Hence Joel says: “The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and manifest day comes” (Joel 2:31).

**Verse 13.—** “And the stars of heaven fell upon the earth, as a fig tree casts its unripe figs when it is shaken by a great wind.”

Heaven is the Church of the saints, which, during the night of the present life, shines as though with stars radiating from above, while it contains the innumerable lives of the saints.

For the stars to fall from heaven to earth means that those who appear to cling to holy faith or works fall from earthly love into the iniquity of manifest error.

This is also what it means for the fig tree to cast its unripe figs. The fig tree is shaken by a great wind when the whole Church is shaken by the final persecution. Another translation has “bitter fruits.”

**Verse 14.—** “And heaven withdrew like a scroll when it is rolled up.”

Just as the reprobate fall away from the Church not bodily but through transgressions, so the same Church, in her elect, withdraws from the midst of the wicked not by bodily departure but by faith and action.

The Church is rightly represented by a book, because she contains within herself the commandments of the entire heavenly life, written not merely with a pen on parchment but also, by the Spirit of God, on tablets of the heart of flesh.

Note that the book is said to be rolled up. Just as it is not apparent what a rolled-up book contains except to those to whom it is opened by the will of the one who opens it, so, in the time of persecution, the Church of the elect closes her inner things to outsiders and opens them discreetly within to her own.

“And every mountain and island was moved from its place.” By mountains we must understand men of lofty dignity, who surpass others in words and virtues. Of them it is said: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains” (Ps. 121:1). By islands we understand people of lesser righteousness, still tossed about amid tribulations.

The statement that the mountains and islands are moved from their places therefore belongs to the preceding meaning, according to which the Church of the saints withdraws from the company of the wicked in faith and action. The mixed association of the wicked was, so to speak, her place.

**Verse 15.—** “And the kings of the earth, and the princes, and the tribunes, and the rich, and the strong, and every slave and free person hid themselves in caves and among the rocks of the mountains.”

Kings are those who rule themselves well. Likewise, princes are those who, though not like kings, resist vices as best they can. Tribunes have less power than princes; nevertheless, they too resist the devil as best they can. He speaks of the rich in virtues, not in possessions; and of the strong not in body but in spirit.

In the final persecution, therefore, these people, presuming on nothing of their own virtues, hide themselves in the caverns and caves of the mountains, because they seek the intercession of the saints. The saints are rightly called mountains because, lofty in virtues, they despise earthly things. They are rightly called rocks because they are strong in firmness, having been strengthened in Christ, who is the Rock.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains” (Matt. 24:16). Solomon says: “The little rabbit, a feeble people, makes its nest in the rock” (Prov. 30:26). And Isaiah says: “They shall enter into the caves of the rocks and into the hollows of the earth, before the face of the Lord’s strength and the glory of his majesty, when he rises to strike the earth” (Isa. 2:19). He also urges that this be done, saying: “Enter into the rock; hide yourself in a pit in the ground” (ibid., v. 10).

These may also be understood as the heavenly powers, according to what is read in the book of Job: “He dwells in the rocks and makes his home in precipitous flint and inaccessible crags” (Job 39:28).

But let us hear what those who flee—whether to angels or to holy human beings—say.

**Verse 16.—** “And they say to the mountains: ‘Fall upon us and hide us from the face of the One seated upon the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb.’”

It is as though they openly say: “Bend your hearts toward mercy, and cover us by your holy intercessions from the wrath of the Judge.” They do not ask to be hidden from the face of one who spares, but from the face of one who is angry.

Why they fear so greatly is added:

**Verse 17.—** “For the great day of his wrath has come, and who will be able to stand?”

It is as though they say: “If the saint fears the wrath of that God, who among us will endure?”

All these things that have been said about the saints may be passed over and understood of the reprobate. The mountains are the proud; the islands are the greedy, according to the saying: “Be silent, you who dwell on the island; the merchants of Sidon” (Isa. 23:2). Kings, princes, and tribunes designate the reprobate according to their respective qualities.

He calls those rich who do not need another’s assistance for evil; the strong are those who are strong for mixing drunkenness; the slave is the slave of sin, and the free person is free for righteousness.

There is no doubt that all these, when the future judgment draws near, run for the demons’ aid, since, in despair, they do not dare approach any of the saints. This is what it means for them to seek hiding places in the caves and rocks of the mountains. But how will those who will first receive the wrath of fury themselves defend others from it?

In any case, all these things, even according to the letter, instill great fear in those who hear them. But figurative expressions should not therefore be forcibly bent toward a literal interpretation.

## Chapter VII

**[Col. 1128D] Verse 1.—** “After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds of the earth, so that the wind should not blow upon the earth, or upon the sea, or upon any tree.”

It should be noted that, from the first seal through the sixth, he appears to have preserved the order. But, passing over the seventh, he returns to the beginning of Christ’s incarnation and briefly recapitulates what he had set forth, changing the figures of the enigmas. He concludes the same two narratives with the seventh seal. This recapitulation does not always occur in this manner but in various ways.

What, then, can be represented by the four angels except the body of the ancient enemy? Because of the four principal kingdoms of the world—namely, those of the Assyrians, Medes, Persians or Macedonians, and Romans—in which the devil reigned through the worship of idols, four angels are assigned to the reprobate side.

Hence Nebuchadnezzar saw a statue whose head was of gold, its chest and arms of silver, its belly and thighs of bronze, and its legs of iron. In the gold the Assyrian kingdom is represented; in the silver, that of the Medes; in the bronze, that of the Persians or Macedonians; and in the iron, that of the Romans.

It is not surprising that evil human beings are represented by angels, since it was said concerning Judas: “One of you is a devil” (John 6:70).

It should also be understood that the four angels are the four winds, according to the prophecy of Daniel, which says: “Behold, four winds were fighting in the great sea, and four beasts were descending from the sea, different from one another” (Dan. 7:2). He indicates that the winds and the beasts are one and the same thing: the four kingdoms mentioned above.

Therefore, when the angels hold the winds, they are holding themselves. And because all such beings are the body of the devil, he himself is also understood in them.

What, then, did it mean for the four angels to hold back the four winds of the earth so that they would not blow? It meant that the hidden adversary, together with his entire body, united and restrained itself, and so throttled the mouth of everyone that no one dared to breathe forth a word of truth against the worship of idols.

By the earth the diversity of provinces is signified; by the sea, the multitude of islands. In the trees also, because the text reads “the kind was silent” [so the manuscript], various human occupations are signified according to their diversity. But because they were being suffocated by the devil, they were rescued by the coming of their Lord.

Hence it immediately follows:

**[Col. 1129C] Verse 2.—** “And I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, having the seal of the living God; and he cried with a loud voice to the four angels to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea,

**Verse 3.—** saying: ‘Do not harm the earth, nor the sea, nor the trees, until we seal the servants of our God upon their foreheads.’”

Christ is the angel because he is known to have announced to the world the joys of the new life. Concerning him it is written: “The angel of great counsel” (Isa. 9:6, according to the Septuagint).

The ascent from the rising of the sun is understood as that by which, from the very resurrection—which shone forth like a new sun—he filled the whole world by growing and enlightened it with evangelical doctrine.

By that voice he also restrained the harmful power of the four angels from causing injury, and at the same time shattered it in both its authors and its ministers. Hence Nebuchadnezzar saw the stone cut from the mountain without hands strike the aforesaid statue on its iron feet and shatter it.

By this stone the Lord Jesus Christ is signified, begotten from the stock of Judah without marital activity. He struck the statue on its feet, and it fell, because by the preaching of the word he touched the extremity of the Roman kingdom and turned the aforementioned kingdoms of the world toward a salutary restoration.

The same mediator is said to have the seal of God, that is, the mystery of the cross. The fact that he does not say “let me seal” but “let us seal” shows that there are many in him through whom that mystery is fulfilled.

By saying “upon their foreheads,” he indicates the interior reality. We smear both doorposts with the blood of the Lamb, but it does no good for anyone to bear it outwardly unless he also receives it inwardly, because faith without works is idle.

**Verse 4.—** “And I heard the number of those who were sealed: one hundred and forty-four thousand sealed, from every tribe of the children of Israel.”

A finite number is used for an infinite one. It does not pertain only to the twelve tribes of Israel; rather, the whole Church is represented through this number in the elect.

For three is a perfect number in sacred Scripture, especially because it reveals the Trinity. Four is likewise significant because of the four parts of the world, the four Gospels, or the four principal virtues. When these are multiplied by one another, we arrive at twelve, which is itself sacred because of the twelve tribes or the twelve apostles. The thousand signifies totality, according to the saying: “For a thousand generations.”

**[Col. 1130B]** Since the Church is gathered from all nations through knowledge of the Trinity and is watered by the books of the four Gospels, she is rightly represented in twelve thousands.

But in order that she may be perfected in what she has believed, it is necessary that the number twelve thousand be joined to a fourfold solidity. Let twelve thousand therefore be multiplied by four, and forty-eight thousand result. And so that she may reach what she has believed—that is, contemplation of the Trinity—let forty-eight thousand be multiplied three times, and it produces one hundred and forty-four thousand.

### Verse 5 (continued)

“From the tribe of Judah, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Reuben, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Gad, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Asher, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Naphtali, twelve thousand sealed; [Col. 1130C] from the tribe of Manasseh, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Simeon, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Levi, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Issachar, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Zebulun, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Joseph, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Benjamin, twelve thousand sealed.”

If we return to the historical account in Genesis, we find that these names were certainly not inserted in this order according to the birth of each one. For Judah is placed there fourth, but here first; Reuben there first, here second; Gad there eighth, here third; Asher there ninth, here fourth; Naphtali there seventh, here fifth; Manasseh there ninth, here sixth; Simeon there second, here seventh; Levi there third, but here he is substituted in the eighth place. Only Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, and Benjamin are placed here as they are there. [Col. 1130D] Dan, however, Jacob’s fifth son, is altogether excluded from this spiritual catalogue.

But we readily understand why this was done if we withdraw the mind’s attention from carnal birth and seek in them a spiritual lineage according to the interpretations of their names. Judah, then, is interpreted as “confession,” or “praise.” What else does the interpretation of this name signify but confession of sins and praise of virtues? Although the term “confession” appears to be used for praise—for this reason the Lord, who had no sin at all, says: “I confess to you, Father,” and so forth (Matt. 11:25).

In Reuben, whose name is said to mean “seeing a Son” or “those who see the Son,” the very works of virtue are signified. For the fruits of good works are often represented by the term “sons,” [Col. 1131A] according to the saying: “May you see the sons of your sons” (Ps. 127:6)—that is, virtues born from virtues. And because the works of virtue ought to serve the advancement of others, he is rightly called “seeing a son”: namely, so that we may make visible to others those things in which we see that we ourselves have progressed, according to another saying of the Lord: “That they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). Judah, therefore, is rightly placed first.

Then Reuben follows, because unless through confession we renounce evil deeds, we are not formed in what is upright and pleasing. Who, then, would not now see that, if he had begun with the firstborn according to the flesh and placed Judah fourth, he would certainly have confused the spiritual lineage of the Church?

But because temptation always tests those who act well, Gad—meaning “temptation”—is rightly substituted after Reuben. And because those who are girded with divine power stand firm against it, what is said of Gad also rightly applies to them: he is likewise called “girded.” Since, however, we ought to direct the end of good struggles toward God and not toward the face of human praise, the aforesaid Gad is called “a robber,” as though he secretly acquired good things of the heart and offered them to God for approval, rather than exposing them to human eyes as things to be displayed.

Therefore, because the tribulation inflicted upon them tests the elect and crowns them after their testing, Asher—who is called “blessed”—is rightly placed after Gad. And because, strengthened by the promise of blessedness, the warriors of the Church expand among the wicked through the breadth of charity, Naphtali—who is called “breadth”—is fittingly placed after Asher.

For, running through this most ample commandment of love, they both forget what lies behind and stretch forward toward the eternal riches that are to come. Accordingly, Manasseh is suitably inserted after Naphtali; his name is understood to mean “forgetful” or “necessity”: “forgetful,” because he has abandoned the one thing that lay behind; “necessity,” because he has not yet reached that toward which he stretches.

Since their desire is often deferred for a long time, Simeon is rightly placed after Manasseh. Simeon is interpreted as “I have heard sorrow.” But those who hear sorrow must also hear the name of a dwelling-place, which Simeon likewise seems to signify, so that those who mourn in the tabernacle of corruption may rejoice in the dwelling-place of eternal rest.

What sort of people all these are, Levi, which follows, indicates; [Col. 1131D] its name means “added.” For such people, surpassing many general commandments, add things that are not commanded—for example, the celibacy of holy virginity and other things of this kind. Since these are not commanded but advised, they are certainly added to the commandments as counsels.

Issachar is therefore rightly joined after Levi; his name is interpreted as “reward.” For those who do such things, a special and distinguished reward is owed. Hence Jeremiah says to one of them: “Let your voice cease from weeping and your eyes from tears, for there is a reward for your work, says the Lord” (Jer. 31:16).

But persecutions inflicted upon those who do such things ordinarily test them before they are rewarded, though they do not overcome them. Hence Zebulun, who is called “the dwelling-place of strength,” follows Issachar not inappropriately. For each of these becomes a dwelling-place when strength is perfected in weakness.

Therefore, because they distribute the talent of the divine word freely not only to friends in a time of peace but also to enemies amid persecution itself, Joseph, whose name is interpreted as “increase,” is aptly joined after Zebulun. For they do not hesitate to distribute what they have received even to their enemies, so that they may return profit from the money entrusted to them.

Thus, so that you may understand that all these are to be placed at the right hand of the eternal King, Benjamin—“son of the right hand”—is beautifully substituted in the final place, as though he were the end of the order in which the happiness of eternal reward is promised.

Holy Church, therefore, is praiseworthy for confession in Judah. In Reuben she shines, fruitful in pious works. In Gad she is tested through the exercises of temptation. In Asher she is blessed after overcoming temptations. In Naphtali she is enlarged through the love of charity. In Manasseh she forgets what lies behind and stretches toward what is to come. In Simeon she is still as though sorrowful in the valley of weeping, but rejoices in hope concerning the dwelling-places of the citizens above. In Levi she is adorned with virginity and exceedingly rich in merciful goodness. In Issachar she is suspended in expectation of the future reward. In Zebulun she is crowned through martyrdom. In Joseph she is enriched with the doubled talent of spiritual substance. In Benjamin she is shown to have obtained the right hand of eternal happiness.

No one should, however, suppose that there are twelve professions in the Church, since there are only three kinds of virtue: that of virgins, that of the continent, and that of those who are good spouses.

Among these matters, we must by no means pass over the question of why Dan, certainly a son of Jacob, whether in Genesis or in Exodus numbered among all his brothers, was cast out of the spiritual catalogue in this Apocalypse, while Manasseh, born among foreigners and therefore not a son—although adopted as a son—appears to have been substituted in the sixth place.

Dan, then, is interpreted as “judgment,” or “judging the Hebrews who pass over.” And what is this judgment of the Hebrews who pass over except the rejection of the former priesthood?
