Dan, therefore, expelled from the spiritual catalogue, teaches by the interpretation of his name itself that, in the sixth age of the world, by a hidden but just judgment, the faithless Jewish people were altogether expelled from their place and lost the dignity of the priesthood; and in its place Manasseh—that is, the people of the Gentiles—by grace deserved to be substituted.

### Verse 9

“After this I saw a great multitude, which no one could count, from every nation and tribe and people and language.” Here it is clearly manifested that the number mentioned above belongs not only to the Jews but to all the elect. For they are designated by the innumerable multitude, just as the one hundred and forty-four thousand are designated by those who were sealed. This multitude is innumerable not to God but to us. For he himself says: “I will number them, and they will be multiplied beyond the sand” (Ps. 138:18).

“Standing before the throne.” Although this innumerable multitude itself is the throne of God, it is nevertheless said to stand before the throne because the vision, shaded by figures, varies, while the reality displayed through the figures does not vary at all.

But does it signify anything that this multitude is said to stand, when earlier it was described as sitting around the throne with the elders? [Col. 1133A] It certainly does. It sits when, through certain members of itself, it examines the deeds of others; but it stands when, in all its elect, it strengthens the mind in firmness of faith and love.

“And in the sight of the Lamb, clothed in white robes.” What is signified by the white robes except the condition of the mind? Yet these were not white before the Lord’s coming, because the hearts of the human race were stained with the blemishes of original sins.

“And palms in their hands.” By palms, victory is expressed; by hands, action. To have palms in one’s hands, therefore, is to triumph over the ancient enemy and the pleasures of the world.

### Verse 10

“And they cried out with a loud voice, saying.” This cry is understood not as bodily but as a cry of the heart. For this great voice is a great feeling of devotion, since each person cries out with the voice all the more loudly the more greatly he loves God.

“Salvation belongs to our God, who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb.” The order is: “Salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb who sits upon the throne.” In these words the person of the Holy Spirit is also understood according to the rule already stated.

And note that, in a remarkable form of expression, they show one substance in the Father and the Son and two persons. Moreover, it must be understood that, when they attribute all their salvation to God, the doctrine of Pelagius and Coelestius [Cod., Celestinus] is nullified. They defend free will to such an extent that they say human beings can be saved without the grace of God.

### Verse 11

“And all the angels stood around the throne, and the elders, and the four living creatures, and they fell upon their faces before the throne.” Through the angels, the throne, the elders, and likewise the living creatures, the Church is signified. One and the same reality is represented in different ways.

For, since Christ alone reigns and judges in the Church, all the saints are rightly represented by one throne. Since the Church itself examines the deeds of others, it is fittingly represented by the elders. And because in some of its members it still clings by faith alone to the verdant pastures of paradise, while in others it already enjoys them by sight, it is suitably represented by the living creatures.

Because it announces what is to come by preaching, it is appropriately represented by the angels; and because it is gathered from different nations, it is rightly represented by the multitude.

These, therefore, fell upon their faces before the throne—that is, in the secret place of their mind, where the inner Judge sits. “And they worshiped” [Col. 1133D]—saying:

“Amen; blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and strength be to our God for ever and ever.” All these things suitably belong to the Trinity.

### Verse 13

“And one of the elders answered, saying to me: These who are clothed in white robes—who are they, and from where have they come?”

Since no question preceded it, what does it mean that one of the elders is said to have answered? It is the custom of Sacred Scripture to use this word in this way; it seems to have no particular significance. Therefore neither ignorance of this usage is harmful nor knowledge of it praiseworthy.

In the one elder, then, the unity of the preachers of both Testaments is understood; or the elder of the elders himself is understood, namely the Lord Jesus Christ. He asks John for this reason: that John may seek, and while seeking may hear and understand, and may kindle himself to imitate him.

In the white robes are signified both purity of mind and the glory that will be bestowed upon them in the future. To this the blessed John, speaking in the person of good hearers, replied: “My lord, you know.” Then he again adds, speaking in the person of the Lord or of his good preachers:

### Verse 14

“These are those who came out of the great tribulation,” and so forth.

In the verb “came” three tenses are contained, standing for “they have come,” “they are coming,” and “they will come.” Since, therefore, the entire number of the elect is brought to an end by this statement, we must greatly fear that, if anyone comes from elsewhere, he may not attain to the fellowship of the elect.

The tribulations of the righteous, as the Psalmist says, are many (Ps. 33:20). Among them is that universal tribulation concerning which none of us knows whether he will attain to the fellowship of the elect, as Solomon bears witness when he says: “A person does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but all things are reserved uncertain for the future” (Eccl. 9:1–2).

“And they washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.” All the elect whiten their robes in the blood of the Lamb; that is, they adorn the condition of their minds through the sufferings of Christ and prepare it to receive future joys.

### Verse 15

“Therefore they are before the throne of God and serve him day and night in his temple, and he who sits upon the throne will dwell over them.”

It is as though he were saying: The throne of God and the temple are the same, because those clothed in such garments and washed in the blood of the Lamb are seen to be both. And note that he does not say, “He dwells in them,” but “over them,” in order to show that they are simultaneously the throne and the temple. By “day and night” he means in prosperity and in adversity.

### Verses 16–17

“They will hunger no more, nor thirst any more, and the sun will not fall upon them, nor any heat; for the Lamb, who is in the midst of the throne, will rule them and lead them to fountains of the waters of life.”

For this reason they suffer no hardship: because the Lamb rules them. But where does he lead them except to the fountain of waters—that is, to the Trinity, which is signified by the fountain? And by what way except by himself? For he says: “I am the way” (John 14:6).

It should also be noted that one and the same fountain removes hunger because it is living bread, and thirst because it is the drink of life. For, as the Apostle says: “God will be all in all” (1 Cor. 12:6). One fountain, therefore, is mentioned because of the unity of the nature of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The fountain of waters, however, is introduced so that the multiplicity of God’s gifts in the saints may be expressed through this statement.

Thus, whoever is led by the Lamb’s rule to the satisfaction of this water suffers neither sun nor any heat, because he is not burned by the heat of vices.

“And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.” O expression of wondrous tenderness! He shows himself to be a father and reveals himself as a mother, wiping away the tears of his weeping children. Hence Isaiah rightly says: “For you are our Father, and Abraham did not know us; you, Lord, are our Father” (Isa. 63:16).

But what are these tears? One person weeps because of the evil he has done; another because he has not done good; and there are many other things of the same kind. These tears of the children, however, will then be wiped away when they have returned from exile to their homeland.

## Chapter VIII

### Verse 1

“And when he had opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.”

Heaven, as we have often said, is called the Church. When, through certain of its members, it withdraws from the multitude of bodily affairs and seeks the innermost retreat of contemplation, it prepares, as it were, silence for God. Because this cannot be perfect in the present life, it is said that silence lasted “about half an hour.”

And note that he ended the recapitulation there where he said: “After this I saw a great multitude”; now, however, he concludes the narrative with the seventh seal.

### Verses 2–3

“And I saw seven angels standing in the sight of God, and seven trumpets were given to them. And another angel came and stood before the altar, holding a golden censer.”

At this point he reverses and interrupts the order of the narrative. For, as what follows will show, the one who came with the censer first stood before the altar, before the seven angels received the trumpets. He interrupts the narrative because, before finishing his account of them, he inserted this figure with the censer in the middle.

What, then, do we understand by the seven angels except the holy Church in its preachers, who are announcers of eternal life? They are also rightly called seven because they are filled with the sevenfold Spirit, or because they are set over the whole body of believers.

They are said to stand in the sight of God because, having trampled earthly desires underfoot, they cling to divine contemplation.

What else is signified by their seven trumpets except the perfect preaching of the Old and New Testaments, according to the saying: “Raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58:1)?

Since it is the duty of a priest to assist at the altar and to burn incense prepared with aromatics, we recognize that this angel is the mediator between God and human beings, the angel of the seven angels, and, so to speak, the high priest of the seven priests. Concerning him the prophet says: “The Angel of great counsel” (Isa. 9:6, according to the Septuagint). Hence we clearly gather that he came before the seven angels received the trumpets.

By the altar, the elect are signified, in whom spiritual sacrifice is celebrated. The angel, therefore, came through the flesh and stood through divinity. What else is signified by the censer except the humanity of Christ? It is appropriately called golden because the flesh assumed by the Word of God is one wisdom with him, concerning which it is said: “Receive wisdom as gold” (Prov. 16:16).

The censer in which the aromatics are burned may also signify the Church, which, kindled by the fire of divine love, says daily: “Let my prayer be directed like incense,” and so forth (Ps. 140:2).

It is rightly added, with singular reference to Christ:

“And much incense was given to him, so that he might offer it from the prayers of the saints upon the golden altar, which is before the throne;” [Verse 4] “and the smoke of the incense rose from the prayers of the saints from the hand of the angel before God.”

Just as smoke rises from burning aromatics, so the power of compunction is generated from devotion to prayer. But, in order that prayers may become acceptable to God, incense is given to the angel—that is, devotion to prayer is entrusted to our Redeemer. The body cannot speak to God at all except through the office of the head.

That incense is offered upon the golden altar shows that the sacrifice of prayer is received from him nowhere except in the body of Christ, which wholly shines with the wisdom of the divine Word.

And note that the throne and the altar before the throne signify not two Churches but one, just as Noah’s ark and the eight souls within it signify one reality.

### Verse 5

“And the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and cast it upon the earth.”

The angel took the censer when the Lord joined human nature to himself within the Virgin’s womb; or we may understand it of the body, when he first chose disciples in Judea.

Since the angel, the censer, and the altar are one body, and since the censer is said to have been filled with fire from the altar, it should be understood as though he were saying: Both the head and the body were kindled by no fire other than their own—that is, by the Holy Spirit.

He cast it upon the earth—that is, he brought it to this Gentile world. Hence it is appropriately added: “And there were peals of thunder and voices,” that is, the terrors of preaching; “and flashes of lightning,” that is, signs of miracles; “and an earthquake,” that is, persecutions.

### Verse 6

“And the seven angels prepared themselves to sound their trumpets.”

What does it mean for the holy teachers to prepare themselves to sound, except to search the divine utterances so that they may know what they ought to say, to whom, and how?

The reader should therefore be advised that in what follows he should understand not seven angels but one angel; yet in each one he should always recognize the seven, since, for reasons arising from the figurative forms of speech—which cannot be narrated under a single figure—he finds them distinguished into seven.

[Col. 1136C]

### Verse 7

“And the first angel sounded his trumpet, and hail and fire mixed with blood came about, and it was cast upon the earth; and a third of the trees was burned up, and all green grass was burned up.”

By hail, the anger of almighty God is expressed, according to the saying: “The anger of the Lord descends like hail.” By fire, zeal or hatred is signified. It is rightly said to be mixed with blood because, according to John’s statement: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15).

The Lord promises through Isaiah that the Church cannot be consumed by this fire, saying: “When you walk through fire, you will not be burned, and the flame will not burn you” (Isa. 43:2).

It must be noted, however, that when he says a third has perished, we must not suppose that two parts remained among the elect, contrary to the saying: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16). This number appears to pertain not to the literal quantity but to the quantity represented by the figure. The variation itself demonstrates this, since in one place he relates that two thirds, in another three, and elsewhere one third came into the lot of the reprobate.

Above, indeed, he divided the whole body of the devil into four parts; now into two thirds, later into three, and then into one. But one third is not smaller than two or three. For when he divides the devil’s body into four parts, he wishes one to be understood as within the Church, among false brothers, and three outside: heretics, Jews, and pagans.

When he describes the whole body in three thirds, one single part is to be understood within, among wicked believers; another outside, consisting of the twofold group of Jews and heretics; and a third outside, among the Gentiles, likewise single.

When he figures one part of the body by the same threefold and third-based number, constituting two parts out of the three thirds, he wishes both hidden and manifest heretics to be understood. One third remains inside and outside, retaining in itself the forms of all.

When he speaks of two thirds, he wishes one simple part to be understood inside, among wicked Christians, and the other threefold part outside, among Jews, heretics, and pagans.

It should be understood that “earth” here means the same as “trees”: the totality of the wicked, contained in two thirds, one simple and the other threefold. They are earth because they seek earthly things, and trees because they waver in instability. Concerning them Jude says: “These are autumn trees, fruitless, uprooted, twice dead” (Jude 12).

When, therefore, hail and fire mixed with blood are cast down, two thirds are burned; one remains unharmed, because, as the anger of the heavenly Judge increases, the society of the ancient enemy, since it is not gathered in by the preaching of the saints, is set ablaze by the flames of its own hatred. The congregation of Christ is exercised by that hatred of the wicked but is not consumed.

What follows—“All green grass was burned up”—appears to be a repetition of the statement. In the two thirds, all green grass was burned up; that is, the part of the wicked already mentioned was consumed by the flames of its own hatred.

The greenness of the grass is used here on account of the allurements of the flesh, according to the saying: “All flesh is grass,” and so forth (Isa. 40:6). Hence the crowds who are fed by the Lord are said to sit upon the grass—that is, to subdue the pleasures of the flesh by pressing them beneath themselves.

[Col. 1137C]

### Verse 8

“And the second angel sounded his trumpet, and something like a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea. And a third of the sea became blood; [Verse 9] and a third of the creatures that have souls died in the sea, and a third of the ships perished.”

The great mountain is called the devil, either because he wished to be like the one concerning whom it is said, “In the last days the mountain will be prepared” (Isa. 2:2), or because at the end he will exalt himself above everything that is called God or worshiped as God.

He is burning because he is tormented by his own malice and envy. When the angel sounds his trumpet—that is, when the Church preaches—he is expelled by the saints and cast into the sea, that is, into unbelievers. This does not mean that he was not previously in them, but that, having been expelled by these people, he begins to dominate them more fully.

In the one third that is changed into blood, the kind of death by which the two thirds perish appears to be represented, so that death is indicated in one and the number of those dying in two.

Water changed into blood is carnal wisdom, which kills souls. Hence the Apostle says: “To set the mind on the flesh is death” (Rom. 8:6). This wisdom signifies both evil belief and perverse action. For a wicked doctrine it is said: “The letter kills” (2 Cor. 3:6); for a wicked deed: “Deliver me from bloodshed” (Ps. 50:16).

### Verse 10

“And the third angel sounded his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, like a burning torch.”

The devil is called a star either because of his former preeminence or because he transforms himself into an angel of light. He is called great because he was placed above the other angels. He is a burning torch because of the heat of his malice.

This fall is not to be understood as the fall by which he was previously expelled from the heavenly dwelling, but as the fall by which, when the angel sounds—that is, when the Church preaches—he is excluded by the elect.

Heaven is the Church, which the Lord inhabits by presiding over it.

“And it fell upon a third of the rivers and upon the springs of waters”—that is, upon human nature, which from its origin flows onward through the waves of carnal pleasures and runs toward death.

### Verse 11

“And the name of the star is called Wormwood.”

Because the devil, recoiling from the sweetness of truth, was changed into the bitterness of falsehood, he rightly received the name “wormwood.”

And because many perish through the examples of the wicked, it is fittingly added: “And many people died from the waters, because they had become bitter.”

For people die, as it were, from bitter waters when carnal persons, enticed by the doctrines of the perverse or by examples of their deeds, perish spiritually.

### Verse 12

“And the fourth angel sounded his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of them was darkened, and a third of the day did not shine, and likewise the night.”

The Church is represented by the sun, the moon, and the stars. Their obscurity is properly referred to the faithlessness of heretics.

Although two parts are formed from three thirds—one, namely, of the day through the sun, and the other of the night through the moon and the stars—the two nevertheless make one, or one is subdivided into two. This is so that the heretics’ manifest error may be signified by day and their hidden error by night: namely, their public conflicts and their concealed machinations.

It is not said, “A third was struck and darkened,” but, “It was struck so that it might be darkened at the appropriate time,” because heretics are truly darkened when they are openly separated from the Church. Previously they are wounded, as it were, secretly.

They are struck by the light of faith and the brightness of the divine word. This destruction is not to be attributed to God but is to be understood in the same way as the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart.

### Verse 13

“And I saw, and I heard the voice of one eagle flying through the midst of heaven and saying with a loud voice: Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell upon the earth.”

With respect to the remaining voices of the three angels who were going to sound their trumpets, John, the eagle, and the angels all bear the figure of the Church. It is rightly called one eagle because it abides in the unity of faith and, having trampled earthly pleasures beneath its feet, is raised up to heavenly things.

Thus, in John it sees itself; in the eagle it flies; and in the three angels it announces the evils that are to come in the final age.

And note that in spiritual vision, to see is the same as to hear. In the fact that the Church is said to mourn not over the preceding voices but over those of the angels who follow, it is shown that it mourns and preaches the future blows of various calamities at various times: it mourns in the eagle and preaches in the angels.

It is therefore said to fly through the midst of heaven because it possesses the whole world on every side. Its preaching is called a loud voice because it has resounded throughout the entire world.

## Chapter IX

[Col. 1139A]

### Verses 1–2

“And the fifth angel sounded his trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth, and the key of the pit of the abyss was given to it. And it opened the pit of the abyss, and smoke rose from the pit like the smoke of a great furnace.”

What is signified by the angel and the star has already been stated. By the abyss are signified the hearts of the wicked, darkened by the obscurity of errors. By the pit of the abyss, the preachers of errors are to be understood.

For if the mouth of the abyss is a pit, they are rightly represented by the pit through whom the iniquity of the wicked pours forth the poisons of its heart.

By the key of the pit, temporal power is expressed, through which the ancient adversary opens the mouths of the reprobate to perverse doctrines. These doctrines are rightly compared with smoke because they turn the light of truth into darkness for themselves and appear to obscure the brightness of faith even in others.

The great furnace, however, is the persecution of Antichrist, from which smoke emerges—that is, perverse teaching, which turns the souls of those who are perishing into darkness.

But how is this smoke said to be like the smoke of a great furnace, when the Lord says concerning that tribulation: “Then there will be great tribulation,” and so forth (Matt. 24:21)? It must therefore be understood that it is not called greater than all others because of the torments or false doctrines in which it resembles them, but because of the signs of miracles by which it will deceive more powerfully.

“And the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke of the pit.” Here the fifth angel says that what the fourth had foretold would happen to the sun, moon, and stars has already happened to the sun and air.

### Verse 3

“And locusts came out of the smoke upon the earth.”

Heretics are fittingly represented by locusts. For just as the locust appears neither to fly perfectly like birds nor to advance step by step, but to gnaw the crops of the earth by making leaps, so these people, possessing neither the flight of full knowledge nor the step of perfect action, but moved only by leaps of pride, kill the souls of the wicked by preaching unheard-of things.

Locusts come out of the smoke when heretics are born from heretics.

“And power was given to them, like the power of the scorpions of the earth.”

The power of scorpions is in the extremity of their body, in the tail. Thus temporality, failing from itself, is left behind; for everything that passes is, as it were, behind, while what endures is before.

The locusts therefore receive power to harm like the scorpions of the earth because heretics, supported by temporal powers, harm others only through those things that lie behind.

### Verse 4

“And it was commanded them not to harm the grass of the earth, nor any green thing, nor any tree, except those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.”

The preceding meaning is repeated. The angel ascending from the rising of the sun commanded the four angels—who are now understood in the locusts—not to harm the earth, the sea, or the trees.

By grass, which is food not for human beings but for animals, little ones in Christ are signified, concerning whom the Apostle says: “The natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:14).

By green things, from which much food for human beings usually comes, those who are progressing in faith are signified, being in some way more suited to desire the green things of paradise.

By trees, the strong are signified, rooted with a certain stability amid the winds of temptations.

What does it mean that the locusts are forbidden to harm every green thing or every tree? A part is to be understood from the whole, and that part is preserved from their harm.

The people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads are those who do not possess the faith that works through love.

### Verse 5

“And it was given to them not to kill them, but to torment them for five months.”

If those who do not have the seal are reprobates, how are the locusts forbidden to kill them? Or do those who do not have the seal of God perhaps live?

Therefore an ellipsis is supplied from the preceding statement. Let it be said: “It was given to them not to kill them, but to torment them for five months”—that is, so that heretics would not be able to deceive those who were sealed, but, by tormenting them in the present life, which is governed by the five bodily senses, would test them; to these the following statement appropriately corresponds:

And their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it strikes a person. This means that the elect, scorning what lies behind and stretching themselves toward what lies ahead, are believed to be afflicted by others because of what they themselves seem to have rejected through contempt for the world—that is, either by secular power or by the error of false belief.

(VERS. 6.) And in those days people will seek death and will not find it; they will desire to die, and death will flee from them. These days run from the Lord’s coming until the end of the age. The elect seek death when they desire to cling to God in a hidden way of life; but death flees from them because either the unbreakable bond of governance or the constraint of a lower rank holds them fast.

(VERS. 7.) And the likenesses of the locusts were like horses prepared for battle, and upon their heads were likenesses resembling crowns of gold. Because of their swift movement, heretics are rightly represented by horses. They are prepared for battle against those of whom Habakkuk says: “You sent your horses into the sea, stirring up many waters” (Hab. III, 15). But since, with the Lord’s favor, they do not prevail, they are said to have not crowns but things resembling crowns. It is as though one said: They were neither crowns nor made of gold, but a certain fabrication of falsehood.

And their faces were like human faces (VERS. 8), and they had hair like women’s hair. The locusts’ faces, resembling a human face, signify a pretence of reason. The hair of women signifies the effeminate conduct of heretics. Alternatively, by “human faces” men may be understood, and by “women’s hair” the sex itself. For women’s approval was also given to the heretics. And their teeth were like lions’ teeth. Lions’ teeth naturally produce fear; in them the stench of the heretics is revealed.

What follows—(VERS. 9) “And they had breastplates like iron breastplates”—shows their hearts hardened and made rigid against the truth, so that they could not be pierced by the arrow of truth. And the sound of their wings was like the sound of chariots, like the sound of many horses running into battle. By the locusts’ wings we understand the exalted knowledge of the heretics, whose sound is rightly said to resemble that of many chariots and horses running together into battle: by their doctrines the heretics divide themselves, and yet, united, they fight against the Church.

(VERS. 10.) And they had tails like scorpions, and there were stings in their tails. Their power was to harm people for five months. The matter of the scorpions’ tails has already been discussed. Note that the Apostle calls sin a sting. The five months were also discussed above. But there he speaks of the good, here of the wicked: those [the locusts] torment but do not kill, whereas these do not torment but kill by inflicting harm, whether through perverse teaching or temporal power.

(VERS. 11.) And they had over them as king the angel of the abyss, whose name in Hebrew is Abbaddon, in Greek Apollyon, and in Latin his name is Exterminator. The ancient enemy is called king of the wicked, not because he created or rules them, but because, by God’s just permission, he exercises the tyranny of domination. Note that, as has already been said, they themselves are the abyss. Therefore, because he deceitfully attempts to usurp Christ’s name through the condemned man, he is expressed by the words of three languages, in which, as the authority of the Gospel testifies, the Redeemer’s name was written by Pilate in the inscription.

But since blessed Jerome, in his interpretation of Hebrew names, gives not Abbaddon but Labbaddon, it is clear that the first letter was lost through the error of the scribes. The devil is appropriately called “Exterminator,” because through him many are expelled from the boundary of the elect and led into exile under everlasting death.

(VERS. 12.) One woe has passed. That is, it has preceded in the narrative, or has been fulfilled in the work of past time. Behold, two woes are coming after these things—that is, they are to be fulfilled in the narrative or in the work of the future.

(VERS. 13.) After these things the sixth angel sounded his trumpet, and I heard a voice from one of the horns of the golden altar that is before God (VERS. 14), saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet: “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.”

The altar is the Church; it is golden because it is illumined by heavenly wisdom. Note that the altar is before God’s eyes, because “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous.” The horns of the altar are the holy preachers. By one horn, however, the chief of the preachers is understood, namely Christ. This one speaks to the sixth angel sounding the trumpet—that is, he commands the Church to release the four angels, because he grants it the power of binding and loosing both in heaven and on earth, according to the saying: “Whatever you bind” (Matt. XVI, 19), and so forth.

In the four angels we recognize the entire body of the reprobate, which consists of evil spirits and wicked people: distinct by nature, but joined by iniquity. The number four is customarily used for universality. Thus, at the end of the age, the elect are said to be gathered by angels from the four winds of heaven.

By the Euphrates, which is usually used in a negative sense, the power of worldly rule opposed to Christ and the Church is signified. The ancient enemy is said to be bound there with his body because he is not permitted to harm as much as he wishes. Thus it may be said: “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates,” as though the Church were told: Release human beings in the angels, and angels in human beings.

And consider how patiently you must endure the constraints of persecution, which the adversaries cannot inflict except by your judgment—that judgment which is established in the Head and which cries out for you and in you: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII, 18).

(VERS. 15.) And the four angels were released, who had been prepared for the hour, and day, and month, and year, so that they might kill a third of humankind. The release of these angels signifies the beginning of the final persecution. He says that they were prepared because the devil always awaits the downfall of the good.

By the hour, day, month, and year we understand, by a transference of expression, the four periods—that is, the three years and six months during which that persecution will rage. The third part of humankind that is said to be killed consists of rulers and subjects, that is, of persuaders and those persuaded, because the dead will kill the dead.

(VERS. 16.) And I heard the number of the cavalry army: twice ten thousand times ten thousand. This number is referred specifically to the preachers of error, yet the deceived multitudes are understood in the deceivers, since the army is shown as coming against the number of the elect, doubled and multiplied two times ten thousand. For of the elect it is said: “The chariots of God are ten thousand” (Ps. LXVII, 18); but of these: “twice ten thousand times ten thousand.” It is therefore double because it consists of evil spirits and reprobate people. It remains, then, that the single good must fight against the twofold evil.

(VERS. 17.) And in this way I saw the horses in the vision, and those sitting upon them had breastplates of fire, and hyacinth, and sulfur. These horses—that is, the preachers of error, in whom the deceived are also understood—have demons as riders, not for guidance but for destruction. By the name of breastplates the harsh torments of the impious are signified, which no prayer can remove. The hyacinth-colored ones should be understood as smoky, for smoke proceeds from fire. The color itself also indicates this, since hyacinth has the appearance of air.

And the heads of the horses were like the heads of lions. The heads of the horses are the authors of error, who are both strong enough to crush the weak and full of foulness. Hence it is rightly added: “And from their mouths proceed fire, smoke, and sulfur.”

(VERS. 18.) By these three plagues a third of humankind was killed: by the fire, smoke, and sulfur that proceeded from their mouths. This is because the preaching of the wicked prepares eternal punishments for their followers, which are figuratively represented through it: what is procured is named from what it procures.

(VERS. 19.) The power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails. In the mouth, the knowledge of the teachers is signified; in the tail, temporal power, which must be placed afterward. Their power is therefore in mouth and tail because they preach by persuading people to perversity, while, supported by temporal powers, they exalt themselves through the things that lie behind.

For their tails are like serpents, having heads, and with these they inflict harm. Here, conversely, the wicked teachers are signified by the tails, and secular power itself by the heads. False preachers are appropriately compared to serpents because they persuade to evil by the voice of the one whose hissing delighted Eve. And because, supported by the favor of the powerful, they violently drag many into unlawful acts, they are rightly said to have heads, which according to another interpretation are called the heads of dragons.

And to show that the gentiles also belong to this body, he added:

(VERS. 20.) And the rest of humankind, who did not die and did not repent of the works of their hands, so as not to worship demons and golden, silver, bronze, stone, and wooden images, which can neither see nor hear nor walk.

(VERS. 21.) And they did not repent of their murders, nor of their fornication, nor of their thefts. It is as though one said: These people too appear to belong to the number mentioned above.

BOOK FIVE

CHAPTER X

[Col. 1143A]

Whereas in the other prophecies we find many things concerning our Mediator that apply to earthly matters, and few that apply to heavenly matters, John has more frequently designated his coming in this prophecy through an angel. Why? Except that he might show this prophecy to be richer than the others. Hence it is now said:

(VERS. 1.) And I heard another mighty angel descending from heaven, clothed with a cloud. He is rightly called an angel because he appeared to human beings as the new messenger of eternal life, of whom we read: “The angel of great counsel.” He is mighty because he is proved to have conquered the powers of the air by dying; hence the saying: “The Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. XXIII, 8).

When he says “another,” this does not indicate a difference in the reality but the customary manner of recapitulation. He saw another angel because he repeated another vision. The angel appeared clothed in a cloud because the Lord was seen among human beings clothed in flesh; his descent from heaven is the very assumption of flesh.

And there was a rainbow upon his head. The head of Christ, as the Apostle says, is divinity itself. A rainbow is called an arc, through which the reconciliation of the world, accomplished through the dispensation of the incarnate Word, is represented; its mystery has been described above.

Note that, after the final struggle has been described and the seventh seal has been passed over—the seal under which both the consummation of the end and the Lord’s second coming are expected—he returns to the beginning of Christ’s incarnation, of which mention has just been made, and describes his preaching. When this narrative has been completed, he returns to the matters that he had briefly omitted.

Let us remember that, when he has carried this narrative through to the end, the conclusion must be joined to the abbreviated sequence. For that passage where it is said below, “The second woe has passed,” has this implicit reference: the conclusion of the preceding book, in which we dealt with the destruction of the most wicked horses and nations. Note that in this narrative he does not proceed in the usual manner, but concludes both narratives not with one ending but with two, distinguishing separately both the omitted sequence and the recapitulation, as will shortly become clear.

And his face was like the sun. The angel’s face is Christ’s incarnation, by which he was known to mortals; concerning it the Psalmist says: “Show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. LXXIX, 4). It is compared to the sun not because of its brightness, by which it is incomparably greater, but because, like the sun, he had a rising in his birth, a setting in his death, and another rising in his resurrection. Hence Solomon says: “The sun rises and the sun sets,” and so forth (Eccl. I, 5).

The saints too may be understood by the face. And his foot was like a pillar of fire. The angel’s feet are the preachers, through whom the wisdom of God incarnate traversed the whole world, so to speak. They are rightly compared with pillars and with fire, since they both support the superimposed building of the Church and, kindled by the Holy Spirit, inflame the hearts of their hearers with the love of God through preaching.

(VERS. 2.) And he had in his hand a little book that was open. The angel’s hand is the working of our salvation, that is, Christ’s incarnation. The open little book is the grace of the New Testament made manifest. Note that, unless the angel’s face had first shone forth, he would not have held an open book in his hand, because in his dispensation the whole sum of the Scriptures has been revealed.

And he placed his right foot upon the sea, but his left upon the land. This statement shows a distinction among preachers and among times. Those who are stronger are, as it were, the right foot: neither prosperity lifts them up nor adversity casts them down, and they say: “As is his darkness, so also is his light” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 12). These are placed upon the sea, that is, for enduring the persecutions of the wicked. The left foot signifies those of lesser virtue, who, when they are sent in a time of peace, are placed, as it were, upon the solidity of the land. For just as a king directs his forces against the stronger, so does Christ.

(VERS. 3.) And he cried out with a loud voice, as when a lion roars. Just as a lion’s roar strikes fear into beasts, so Christ, through holy preachers, strikes fear by threats into bestial human beings, according to the saying: “The lion has roared; who will not fear?” (Amos III, 8).

And when he had cried out, the seven thunders spoke their voices. The seven thunders signify the same thing as the lion’s voice, namely the preaching of the word, as in the saying: “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel” (Ps. LXXVI, 19). Note that the thunders are said to have spoken after the lion’s voice, because what the Lord taught, the sevenfold Spirit also taught the apostles to preach; hence they are called “sons of thunder.”

They spoke their own voices because holy teaching does not admit into its doctrines either the fables of the Jews or the empty songs of the philosophers.

But a very perplexing question arises from what follows:

(VERS. 4.) And when the seven thunders had spoken, I was about to write, and I heard a voice from heaven saying: “Seal what the seven thunders have spoken, and do not write it.”

For if holy preaching had not been written down, how would it have come to us? It seems, therefore, that some manner of description must be understood here. We should know that we close something under a seal so that it will not be open to everyone but may be unsealed at the appropriate time for those whom we trust. What we write openly, however, we make known to everyone.

We are therefore commanded not to disclose indiscriminately to all the mysteries of God’s utterances, but to supply them according to measure and, as it were, from beneath a seal, insofar as we see those receiving them to be capable; to give some the drink of milk and others solid food. Divine mysteries are also closed under the sign of custody so that they may not be disclosed to those who will not believe, since, when they do not accept them, they begin to mock them.

(VERS. 5.) And the angel whom I saw standing upon the sea and upon the land lifted his hand toward heaven (VERS. 6), and swore by him who lives for ever and ever. Since the Lord forbids swearing, what does it mean that he himself swears? Nothing other than this: human beings are often deceived by an oath, but he who is truth is never deceived.

The angel’s lifting of his hand toward heaven therefore signified that our Redeemer, by his power, would raise his humanity to the Father’s throne. To swear by him who lives for ever and ever was to show that he himself, who is the Word of the Father, and the flesh, which signifies the whole human being composed of flesh and soul, are one person, true God and man; or certainly he swears by the Father because he attributes everything to him.

When it follows—“who created heaven and the things in it, and the earth and the things in it, and the sea and the things in it”—he destroys the error of the heretics, who do not hesitate to assert that some things were made by the good principle and some by the prince of darkness.

But let us hear what he swore: “That time shall be no more” (VERS. 7), but “in the days of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound his trumpet, the mystery of God will be completed, as he announced through his servants the prophets.”

The seventh angel and the seventh trumpet are the end of the Church’s preaching, at whose completion the Lord’s second coming is expected. But if time shall be no more when holy preaching has reached its end, how does the Psalmist say: “Their time shall be for ever” (Ps. LXXX, 16)?

We must therefore understand that, for the righteous whom eternity receives into immortality, no time of change follows; whereas for the unrighteous, whom everlasting ruin will take up, times of mutability will, as it were, occur. Since time fails moment by moment, the ruin of the wicked is appropriately called by the name “time.” What the Lord denies concerning the righteous, the Psalmist confirms concerning the unrighteous.

Finally, when he says that the mystery of God will be completed, this is said not of destruction but of perfection. He says that it was foretold through the prophets because nearly their entire concern was with the Lord’s first and second coming and with the consummation of the age.

[Col. 1145D]

(VERS. 8.) And the voice that I had heard from heaven, speaking to me again and saying: “Go, take the little book from the hand of the angel who is standing upon the sea and upon the land.”

That voice, which earlier had commanded the voices of the thunders to be sealed because of those who would not believe or because of the little ones, now invites the holy Church, in its preachers, to the open book. This voice is understood spiritually: through it God instructs the hearts of preachers to understand the truth of the Law and the Prophets as it has been revealed, a truth entirely closed to those destined for destruction, either in the seven thunders or in the seven seals.

The steps by which the holy Church approaches the angel are not bodily but spiritual: namely, the desire of the mind by which it appears to draw near to God. Therefore, because the saints’ eager disposition (*affectus*; Cod.: *effectus*, “effect/result”) follows the voice of the one commanding with complete readiness, it is rightly added:

(VERS. 9.) And I went to the angel, telling him to give me the little book. And because the one who invites to the promises deceives no one, it is aptly added: “And he said to me: ‘Take the little book and devour it.’”

To devour the little book is to store the understanding of the Scriptures in one’s inmost being. We must know that in obscure passages sacred Scripture is food for us; unless it is chewed through interpretation, it cannot be swallowed. In clear passages, however, it is drink, which we easily drink as we find it without interpretation.

Therefore, although the holy preachers, in the person of John, already understood the mysteries of the Scriptures revealed concerning the Lord, nevertheless, because they still needed an explanation of how those mysteries related to him, he does not say of the open little book, “Take the book and drink,” but “Devour it.” It is as though he said: Chew it over as you eat and understand it; then swallow it.

And it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey. The order is reversed, though it is rightly found a little later. For it follows:

(VERS. 10.) And I took the little book from the hand of the angel and devoured it, and it was sweet as honey in my mouth; and when I had devoured it, my stomach became bitter.

By the mouth, from which preaching proceeds, those are represented who meditate on the law of God day and night and who say with the Psalmist: “How sweet are your words to my palate” (Ps. CXVIII, 82). By the stomach, from which excrement comes out, carnal people devoted to earthly pleasures are represented, concerning whom the elect say: “Our stomach has clung to the earth” (Ps. XLIII, 25).

Thus, as food descends through the mouth into the stomach, so knowledge of the Scriptures reaches, through the preachers of the Church, even those who live carnally. Hence the book is sweet in the mouth but grows bitter in the stomach. For what is more bitter to such people than the Lord’s command: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (Deut. V, 21), and everything that belongs to him?

Alternatively, the book is sweet in the mouth when eternal joys are promised to those who read in it, as in the saying: “The righteous will shine like the sun” (Matt. XIII, 43). It is bitter in the stomach—that is, in the secret place of the mind—when austere commandments are set forth in it, as in the saying: “Unless you become like this little child, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XXVIII, 3).

(VERS. 11.) And he said to me: “You must prophesy again concerning peoples, nations, kings, and many languages.” This is said specifically to John and generally to preachers, who are commanded to prophesy again—that is, to preach—in order that what they proclaim with their mouths they may repeat through their deeds.

CHAPTER XI

(VERS. 1.) And a reed like a rod was given to me, saying: “Rise and measure the temple of God, and the altar, and those worshiping in it.”

This is spoken generally in the person of the preachers. By the reed, which is called *arundo* in Latin, divine preaching is figuratively signified, since it is written through it. It is said to be like a rod because holy preaching is not flexible but straight.

The faithful are the temple of God, to whom it is said: “You are the temple of the living God” (II Cor. VI, 16). The altar within the temple is the life of religious people among the faithful, in whom the unfailing fire of holy compunction principally and continually remains. He says “those worshiping in it” in relation to the temple and the altar; by this expression they themselves are represented.

What, then, does it mean to measure the temple and the altar with a reed, except to distribute through holy preaching the grace of gifts? The Church does this in Christ, that is, in its head. Note that the one who must measure the temple of God is admonished to rise—that is, to ascend through the exercise of works to the lofty heights of virtue—so that he may become taller than the building he measures.

(VERS. 2.) But cast out the courtyard that is outside the temple, and do not measure it, because it has been given to the nations. “Cast out what is outside,” he says, using the kind of expression by which we command that someone knocking be cast outside if we do not wish to let him in.

What, then, do we understand by the courtyard except the Jews, heretics, and gentiles? It is said to have been given to the nations because all pass into the number of unbelieving nations. And they will trample upon the holy city for forty-two months.

The holy city—that is, the temple and the altar—is the heavenly Jerusalem, which is built as a city. What, then, does it mean for the Church of the saints to be trampled by those who are outside except to be persecuted by words and torments?

The forty-two months signify “a time, times, and half a time,” that is, the time of Antichrist. Nevertheless, they also signify the whole period of the present life, because of the seven ages and the seven divisions through which the day revolves. Six times seven makes forty-two. This was also signified by the fact that the children of Israel entered the promised land at their forty-second encampment.

[Col. 1147C]

(VERS. 3.) And I will grant to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for twelve hundred and sixty days, clothed in sackcloth.

The martyr Victorinus understands the two witnesses as Elijah and Jeremiah, for he says that Jeremiah’s death is nowhere recorded. Others, however, more appropriately understand them as Elijah and Enoch. We should understand a class through the figure: by the two witnesses, the Church; and by the twelve hundred and forty days, not only the time of Antichrist but also the elapsed times of the past.

The Church is appropriately represented by two witnesses because of the two Testaments, the two peoples, the two commandments of love, and the two kinds of martyrdom. By sackcloth we understand either the confession of humility or the glory of the saints despised by the wicked.

(VERS. 4.) These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth. The Church, whether in those two or generally in all preachers, is represented by the olive tree because of the anointing of the Holy Spirit, and by the lampstands because of the light of faith and works.

Although it is one Church formed from two peoples, it is called two olive trees and two lampstands because of the two Testaments. They stand before the Lord because they cling to their Creator in inward contemplation. Hence Elijah, to whom this is specifically attributed, says: “As the Lord lives, before whom I stand” (IV Kings III, 14).

In another interpretation this may refer specifically to Elijah and Enoch, who, withdrawn from human sight, cling more secretly to God.

(VERS. 5.) And if anyone wishes to harm them, fire will come out of their mouths and devour their enemies; and if anyone wishes to injure them, in this way he must be killed.

What is signified by fire except holy preaching, kindled by the flames of the Holy Spirit? It is not surprising if the wicked die through preaching, since the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ for God among those who are being destroyed,” and so forth (II Cor. II, 15).

Alternatively, fire proceeding from the witnesses’ mouths kills their enemies because the Church strikes those who persist in evil with the flash of anathema. Alternatively, the part may be understood from the whole: it is burned so that it may be converted to something better. Fire of glory therefore goes out from the Church, by which the wicked are converted to something better.

(VERS. 6.) These have power to shut heaven, so that it may not rain during the days of their prophecy. What is meant by heaven except what we understand through the two witnesses, that is, the holy preachers of the Church? When they shut heaven so that it does not rain, they certainly shut themselves.

They shut it not so that it may not rain at all, but so that it may not rain upon the thorny ground, which is near to being cursed. The members possess this power in the Head. And they have power over the waters to turn them into blood.

The sword of the letter, which the Church uses spiritually to pierce the hearts of the elect, so that it may enliven them by the Spirit, causes blood to flow in the hearts of people who understand wrongly. And to strike the earth with every plague whenever they wish.

Whenever they close the divine mysteries to the faithful, they strike them with an incurable plague. Whenever, however, they open God’s mysteries to the faithful, they draw some toward life and others toward death. Note that they are said not merely to be going to have power, but already to have it, so that we may understand this as spoken not only of those two but also of the preachers of the present.

(VERS. 7.) And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the abyss will make war against them, and will conquer and kill them. “When they have finished” means when they have reached the completion of their testimony—that is, the time of Antichrist.

It is therefore clear that these things occur before the final persecution. Because of the shortness of those days, of which the Lord says, “For the sake of the elect those days will be shortened” (Matt. XXIV, 22), when that time has arrived, the Church’s testimony is said to be as though already finished.

The beast—that is, the whole body of the devil—is therefore said to rise from the abyss because it is permitted by divine judgment to speak forth. For “the judgments of the Lord are a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV, 7); it rises from the place from which it is permitted to be lifted.

If, however, by the beast we understand only Antichrist, his ascent from the abyss is a carnal birth from the people of the Jews, sunk in the deepest impiety—that is, from the tribe of Dan. The battle will be both bodily and spiritual.

In the statement “and he will conquer them,” a certain part joined to the body of Christ is included, a part that is said to be capable of being conquered either by terrors or by flatteries. Therefore the preceding sentence was not spoken only of the two witnesses. If it were, God forbid, the beast would conquer them.

They should therefore be understood in that part of the Church concerning which it is said, “and he will kill them”: that is, in the elect part, which can be killed but cannot be conquered.

(VERS. 8.) And their bodies will lie in the street of the great city, which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was also crucified.

By the description of the Church of the saints lying dead in the street of the great city, it is shown to be severely afflicted and spiritually subjected to its enemies by God’s judgment. Note that we must understand not only the bodies of those who are killed by the sword, but also those who still live, concerning whom the Apostle says: “For you have died,” and so forth.

And because the persecution will be more savage in Jerusalem, the martyrs of the saints are said to be there. This shows that the Jews will principally adhere to Antichrist until those who are to be saved are converted through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch.

That city is spiritually called Egypt and Sodom because of its imitation of them. And because that persecution will take place throughout the whole world, the entire world raging against the Church may be understood through this city.

The Lord also suffered not within that city but outside its gates, so that, being crucified throughout the world, he might be believed to have occupied the whole world. By Egypt and Sodom the wickedness of the persecutors is signified.

(VERS. 9.) And people from peoples, tribes, languages, and nations will see their bodies for three and a half days, and will not allow their bodies to be placed in tombs.

As tombs conceal bodies from human eyes, so the tranquility of time conceals the saints from tribulation. Since there will therefore be no peace for the saints, they are said to remain unburied.

Let no one object that the dead may be understood to mean not only those who have been killed but also those who have been afflicted, since, figuratively, he indicates whole people by their bodies. Thus, in the space of three and a half days, the total of three years and six months is described—the whole from a part.

(VERS. 10.) And those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and celebrate, and will send gifts to one another, because these two tormented those who dwell on the earth. How they are tormented by them has been explained a little above: namely, by the devouring of spiritual fire, the withholding of saving rain, and the conversion of waters into blood.

(VERS. 11.) And after three and a half days, the spirit of life from God entered them, and they stood upon their feet. Here the general resurrection of all the saints, which will come after that final persecution, is declared.

The spirit of life will enter them from God, not because they receive another spirit, but because they will receive again the same one they had. To stand upon their feet means no longer to totter through any changeability of spiritual things.

Let us therefore hear what the reprobate suffer when the saints awaken: “And great fear fell upon those who saw them.” It is not surprising if fear seizes the reprobate, since even the elect themselves, although with secure fear, will nevertheless tremble.

(VERS. 12.) And they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them: “Come up here.” This is the voice of which the Apostle says: “The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God” (I Thess. IV, 15).

And they ascended into heaven in a cloud, and their enemies saw them. They ascend in a cloud—that is, in the power of the one judging. Hence, after conquering death, the Lord ascended in a cloud to the Father’s throne.

We have already stated that the bodies of the two witnesses consist of both the living and the dead. To confirm this we introduce Paul as a suitable witness, saying: “We who live, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (ibid. V, 16).

If, then, as the Apostle says, the living who are found will be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, is the Psalmist a liar when he says: “Who is the person who lives and will not see death?” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 49). And is the book of Genesis a liar when it says: “You are earth, and to earth you will go”?

Far from it. For, as Father Augustine says, in that very rapture of the clouds they will taste momentary death. This is what it means for the body to return to the earth: when the soul departs, the body remains, and the body is earth. How swift each transformation will be, the Apostle indicates, when he confirms that all things will happen “in the twinkling of an eye” (I Cor. XV, 52).

(VERS. 13.) And in that hour there was a great earthquake. After the resurrection has been shown, he recapitulates from the final persecution. It is not surprising that he calls this shortened time, on account of the elect, an hour, since elsewhere he speaks of this whole period: “Little children, it is the final hour” (I John II, 18).

Note that he calls the earthquake great because, according to the Lord’s word, “there will be tribulation such as has not been from the beginning” (Matt. XXIV, 21).

And a tenth of the city fell. The tenth part of the city falls in those who do not belong to the number of the elect. For the elect, joined to the nine orders of angels, restore the ruins of the demons by their own number and fill the tenth place of the order.

It is therefore not the whole tenth that is to be understood as falling, but a part of the tenth: namely, that which, not reaching the nine orders of angels, does not occupy the place of the tenth order at all.

And seven thousand names of people were killed in the earthquake. In these we should understand that part which now lies hidden among the sheep but, when the final persecution occurs, is led into open error and transferred into the body of the beast to be devoured.

And the rest were struck with fear and gave glory to the God of heaven. Whom does he call the rest? Those who remained in the faith, or those who denied and afterward returned, or those who were without faith and afterward would believe through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch? We can truly understand all of them.

(VERS. 14.) The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is coming soon. This is the end of the twofold recapitulation, but the second woe is not assigned to this place. It had been said above, after the battle of the locusts had been completed, that one woe had passed and two others were to come.

After the matters belonging to the second woe had been narrated—that is, the release of the four angels and the rest—the second woe was not repeated. This is because the recapitulation followed from Christ’s coming; if “the second woe has passed” had been said there, we might have thought that the third woe belonged to the recapitulation.

The second woe therefore has an implicit reference not here but to the preceding passage. For when the recapitulation that interrupts the sequence has been narrated, the abbreviated sequence is restored to its order.

What the third woe is becomes clear when he adds:

### Verse 15

“And the seventh angel sounded his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven” [Col. 1151A]. When the Lord appears for judgment, this seventh angel sounds the trumpet. In him the Church is understood—not now preaching, but singing aloud to the Lord of mercy and judgment. Hence the angel standing upon the earth and the sea swears that there will be no more time, but that fulfillment will come at the seventh trumpet.

The loud voices in heaven—that is, in the Church—are acts of thanksgiving. They are rightly called loud, because great desire arises from great things. John shows from whom these voices come when he adds: “saying: The kingdom of this world has become [the kingdom] of God and of his Christ,” that is, the world in which the ancient enemy previously reigned. “And they shall reign forever and ever.” In these two, that is, in the Father and the Son, the Trinity is understood.

### Verse 16

“And the twenty-four elders, who sit in the presence of God upon their thrones” [Col. 1151B] “fell upon their faces.” It has already been said that the elders signify preachers, so that the kind is to be understood in the form. The twenty-four rightly stand for the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles. Through the thrones and the elders, one throne of Christ is understood, in rulers and subjects.

The elders are rightly said to sit in the presence of God because, examining the deeds of those subject to them, they seek not human favor through this but the glory of God. They fall upon their faces because they attribute every good not to themselves but to God.

“And they worshiped God, saying:

### Verse 17

‘We give you thanks, Lord God Almighty, who were, and who are.’” In the fact that they do not say “who are to come,” it is clear that all these things are to be said or done at the final judgment.

But what follows—

### Verse 18

“Because you have taken your great power, and the nations were angry”—belongs to his first coming. He took great power in his humanity, which he always possessed through his divinity. But what follows, “because your wrath has come and the time of the dead,” is said of his second coming.

Yet since the Lord says, “Love your enemies” (Matt. 5:44), how are these people said to give thanks for the coming of his wrath upon the reprobate? They therefore rejoice not over the destruction of the wicked, but over their own resurrection and glorification, which they know cannot be fulfilled unless the condemnation of the impious has preceded it.

In accordance with this understanding, the souls of those slain are said to cry beneath the altar of God: “How long, O Lord,” and the rest (Rev. 6:10). For they do not demand vengeance, but [Codex: *in* in place of *sed*] that they themselves may be rewarded after vengeance has been taken upon the wicked. Hence the Psalmist says: “The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance” (Ps. 57:11). The wrath of the Judge therefore signifies not disturbance of mind but uprightness. As a person has borne his conscience, so he will see Him.

“To judge and to repay your servants the prophets, and the saints, and those who fear your name, the small and the great.” Since the Apostle says that we have been saved by grace, how is the Lord here said to repay a reward? We must therefore understand that when God repays his servants, he rewards his own gifts in them. We could not possess the work deserving reward unless we had received from him the ability to perform it.

Note also that the apostles are designated by the name of prophets. Meanwhile, let no one despair of his perfection, provided that he strives to perform perfect works and is unable to do so, because even the small attain that reward. Hence blessed Job says: “The small and the great are there” (Job 3:19).

“And to destroy those who corrupted the earth.” They are therefore said not to be killed but to be destroyed, so that the perpetual exile of condemnation may demonstrate their eternal deprivation. To corrupt the earth is to pervert life through wicked works. From this, then, hangs the third woe of the wicked, which was foretold as coming quickly in the seventh angel.

### Verse 19

“And the temple of God in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen in his temple.” This expression returns to the beginning of faith and introduces the Church’s conflict under other figures. For what does the temple of God signify except Christ, in whom “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2:9)?

It is said to be opened because Christ has now been born, suffered, risen, and exalted. Since all these things are preached as having been done by Christ in the Church, the temple is therefore said to be opened in heaven.

The ark of the covenant is called the Church. In it the power of the two Testaments is written by the finger of God. According to the faith of Exodus, it has four golden rings, by which it is carried on four poles—that is, the four Gospels, through which it is governed by holy preachers. In it is the golden urn containing manna, that is, the wisdom of the divine word together with the food of life; and also Aaron’s rod, that is, the approval of the royal priesthood.

“And there were flashes of lightning, voices, thunderclaps, an earthquake, and great hail.” The flashes of lightning are signs of miracles, by which the minds of unbelievers were struck and subjected themselves to humility. Hence the Psalmist says: “You will multiply the flashes of lightning and trouble them” (Ps. 17:15).

Voices—that is, preachers—are rightly placed after the flashes of lightning, because preachers first displayed new miracles so that, by speaking, they might lead unbelievers to faith. After the words come thunderclaps, so that those who despise the voices may be shaken by fear of judgment. Then comes the earthquake, that is, persecution, which is signified by the hail.

For just as hail crushes the crops of the earth by breaking them, and the earth again bears fruit, so the raging crowd of the nations, while attempting to remove the name of God from the earth, was itself reduced to nothing, either in strength or through transformation for the better. For many of them returned to the faith of Christ.

## Chapter XII

### Verse 1

“And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet.” The woman clothed with the sun is the blessed Virgin Mary, overshadowed by the power of the Most High. In her the kind—that is, the Church—is also understood. She is called a woman not because of softness, but because she gives birth daily to new peoples, from whom the universal body of Christ is formed.

Thus the Church is clothed with the sun, in accordance with the saying: “All of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27). For Christ is “the sun of righteousness” and “the brightness of eternal light” (Wis. 7:26).

Through the moon, which wanes as time progresses, the mutability of time is expressed. The Church despises this and, as it were, treads it beneath her feet. Note that certain things in what follows apply not to the individual form but to the kind.

“And upon her head a crown of twelve stars.” The twelve stars fitted into the crown are the twelve apostles, through whom the head of the Church, that is, Christ, first won victory. They are called stars because the reasoning of truth illuminates the darkness of ignorance.

### Verse 2

“And being with child, she cried out in labor and was in anguish to give birth.” These words cannot be applied specifically to blessed Mary, but to the Church, which, while giving birth again to those whom she had already borne, undergoes here a certain difficulty of birth, until, in the Apostle’s words, “we all attain to the perfect man” (Eph. 4:13).

### Verse 3

“And another sign appeared in heaven; and behold, a great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns, and upon his heads seven diadems.” The Devil is called a dragon because of his malice, great because of the multiplicity of his snares, and red because of murder. He is seen in heaven—that is, in the Church—not because he possesses it, but because he opposes it.

In the heads and horns his entire kingdom is displayed: as though the seven heads were against the seven Churches; the seven evil spirits against the sevenfold Spirit of God; and the ten horns against the ten commandments of the Law. More will be said about these matters below.

### Verse 4

“And his tail dragged a third of the stars of heaven, and cast them down to the earth.” The dragon’s tail consists of perverse preachers, in accordance with the saying: “The prophet who teaches lies—he is the tail” (Isa. 9:15). Those who outwardly appear to cling zealously to the heavenly life are led by false preachers, through love of earthly things, into the wickedness of open error. Concerning them Job says: “Let the stars be darkened by its gloom” (Job 3:9).

Since the tail is the end of the body, Antichrist and his preachers may be understood through it, if we take the past in reference to the future. And truly, at that time the fall of these stars will be more manifest.

“And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she had given birth he might devour her child.” The dragon then stood ready to swallow the head when it was born; he always stands ready to swallow the members of the head. But, as what follows shows, the woman’s son escaped the dragon’s bite because he was snatched up to the Father’s throne.

Here a serious question arises. For Christ did not bodily ascend into heaven immediately after he was born and sought by Herod; nor do his members avoid the dragon’s teeth because, abandoning the body altogether, they reach their head.

We must therefore understand that the right faith, which preserves the commandments of life and is declared through the sacred pages of Scripture, is an ascent of the mind to God, by which the dragon’s malice is avoided. Accordingly, the text does not speak of a bodily ascent. Note also that they are said to stand before, not behind, those by whom his craftiness is recognized.

### Verse 5

“And she gave birth to a male child.” The former gave birth to the head; the latter gives birth to the members of the head. But why did he add “male,” when he had already said “son”? Evidently because the term is used for good in the sense of excellence in strength, or for evil in the sense of the enormity of wickedness. Just as it is used here in a good sense, so it is used of evil when Jeremiah says: “Cursed is the man who announced to my father, saying, ‘A male child has been born to you’” (Jer. 20:15). In any case, the Church does not give birth to anything effeminate or weak.

“Who is to rule the nations with an iron rod.” This refers both to the head and to the body. Through the rod the uprightness of justice is expressed. Hence the Psalmist says: “An upright rod,” and so forth.

But what does the statement that follows mean: “They will be shattered like a potter’s vessel” (Rev. 2:27), except that the censuring of justice shatters the muddy works among those subject to it, so that vessels of contempt may become vessels of honor and sanctification? This may also be referred to the reprobate of Christ.

“And her son was caught up to God and to his throne.” This has been said somewhat above.

### Verse 6

“And the woman will flee into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, so that there they might feed her for one thousand two hundred and sixty days.” For the woman to flee into the wilderness is the same as for her son to be caught up to God: the Church flees not by a bodily ascent but by a spiritual one.

The wilderness is the hidden place of the mind. Holy men make themselves a wilderness in order to escape the serpent’s poison, despising all transitory things and carnal desires.

Note that it belongs to preachers to feed this woman. The place where she is fed is the same place to which it is said: “Be for me a protecting God and a place of refuge” (Ps. 30:3). It is also the food with which she is fed, of which he says: “I am the living bread” (John 5:35).

This number of days signifies the time of Antichrist, yet in such a way that it embraces the whole period of the present life from the preaching and passion of Christ. For the Gospel preaching was given by the Lord for the same number of days in which it will be brought to an end at the close of the age by the final preachers.

### Verse 7

“And there was a great battle in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon, and the dragon fought, and his angels.” Far be it from the hearts of the faithful to believe that this battle occurred at the time when the ancient enemy, through pride, fell from heaven with his followers. It must without doubt be understood as taking place from the beginning of the Christian faith until the end of the present life.

From that beginning, in heaven—that is, in the Church, where the apostolic voice cries, “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12)—that dragon, namely the Devil, is proved always to resist and oppose.

But if we fight, why is Michael said—contrary to this assertion—to fight? It must therefore be understood that both our battle and that of the angels against the Devil are shown in many other passages. Peter says: “Resist him, firm in faith” (2 Pet. 5:9), and James: “Resist the Devil, and he will flee from you” (Jas. 4:7). Yet David declares that this very resistance is carried out through angels, saying: “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him and will deliver them” (Ps. 3:8).

These examples show that neither do we fight without the angels, nor do the angels fight without our conflict.

Michael and his angels are not called so because Michael created them, according to the impiety of certain heretics, but because he received them from God for assistance; or because they are believed to serve under one king and from one city. Similarly, the dragon’s angels are called his because they are proved to belong to him and to accomplish his will. Wicked human beings are included among their number, just as we are included among the good angels.

### Verse 8

“And they did not prevail, and their place was no longer found in heaven.” How are the evil spirits said not to prevail when they deceive many, and those who were the dwelling place of the Redeemer become the place of the deceiver?

A part must therefore be understood from the whole: the multitude of evil spirits cannot prevail over that part unto eternal death. He gives place to the ancient enemy who commits a mortal sin.

Alternatively, this prophecy concerns the time of Antichrist, when the evil spirits, excluded by the elect, will no longer have opportunity to deceive.

### Verse 9

“And that great dragon was cast down, the ancient serpent, who is called the Devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world; he was cast down to the earth, and his angels were cast down with him.” Our enemy is called a dragon because of his malice; great because of the enormity of his crime; a serpent because of his snares; ancient because of the long duration of his seduction; and the Devil because of his fall from heaven and his accusation of the faithful and elect. For *diabolus* signifies both “flowing downward” and “accuser.” Satan, however, means “adversary.”

When he says “who deceives the whole world,” he has put the whole for a part.
