From where, then, and to where was he cast, except from heaven to earth—that is, from the minds of the elect into the hearts of the reprobate? This does not mean that he was not previously in them, but that, after being excluded by them, he rules them more fully.

### Verse 10

“And I heard a loud voice saying in heaven: ‘Now salvation and power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, because the accuser of our brothers has been cast down, who accused them before our God day and night.’”

Since the dragon falls daily from heaven to earth, it is clear that this voice—that is, the mind’s desire expressed in praise—begins from the Lord’s coming and does not cease to cry out until the end of the age in heaven, that is, in the Church. Hence the adverb “now” embraces the whole period.

They say that salvation has come because we have been saved by the gratuitous goodness of God; power, because we have been strengthened; authority, because we have been raised to the glory of exaltation. All these things have been accomplished in human beings, though not through a human being but through Jesus Christ.

The Devil accuses day and night when he sees some people exalted in prosperity and others broken by adversity. The Devil’s accusation of the saints is not by speaking outwardly but by listening inwardly. His own malice is an accusation against the saints.

### Verse 11

“And they conquered him because of the blood of the Lamb and because of the word of their testimony.” They conquer because of the blood of the Lamb because they follow Christ’s sufferings. They conquer because of the word of their testimony because they preserve the uprightness of faith. Concerning them it follows: “And they did not love their lives even unto death”—that is, they exposed themselves to death so that they would not love their lives wickedly.

### Verse 12

“Therefore rejoice, heavens, and you who dwell in them.” He invites the heavens to rejoice in the plural because he indicates the multitude of Churches, all of which produce one Church from themselves. By those who dwell in heaven he means angels or holy human beings, with whom it is fitting to rejoice harmoniously in the Lord when human beings, having conquered the enemy, return to the fellowship of the angels.

There is nothing else here that requires exposition, except that, while this joy remains, the book should reach its proper conclusion.

*[The exposition of the remaining chapters is absent from the manuscript, whether Alcuin wrote it or not, although in fact this chapter, at verse 3, promises that he will write more.]*

Naphtali, that is, “blessedness,” 1131, 29 ff. Who the Nicolaitans, that is, the heretics, were, 1102, 30 ff. — And their deeds, 1105, 24 ff. Nicholas is interpreted as “foolish people,” 1102, 44 ff. The new name is called “Christian,” 1106, 10 ff. — For the name of the Father to be written upon the conqueror means that through adoption he is made his son by the Spirit, 1112, 56 ff. — What is meant by “king of the heretics,” or “of heretics,” 1141, 8 ff. The cloud, when the Lord comes to judgment, will be white, overshadowing the saints; but it will be terrifying, and by its crashing the reprobate will be frightened, 1094, 20 ff. — Mystically it designates preachers, ibid., 27 ff. The number seven indicates the universal Church, 1092, 11 ff. — It is perfect because it is formed from three and four, ibid., 16 ff.; 26 ff. — Three is perfect because of the mystery of the Trinity, the three theological virtues, and the three orders of the faithful, ibid., 17 ff. — Four is perfect because of the regions of the world, the cardinal virtues, and the four books of the Gospels, ibid., 22 ff. — The number of the elect is certain and definite, 1112, 25 ff. — The twelve tribes are doubled because of the twofold Testament; hence the twenty-four elders are mentioned, 1117, 10 ff. — The number of those sealed with the seal of the living God is almost infinite, 1130, 3 ff. — Three is for the Trinity, while four is for the four Gospels, 1130, 7 ff. See above. — The number of the elect is almost infinite, 1132, 44 ff. See above.

The eyes represent the Holy Spirit, who illuminates the Church, 1098, 31 ff.

— The spiritual lights of the living creatures are the elect, 1118, 18 ff. — The four living creatures figure the preaching of the Church, ibid., 56 ff. — The seven signify the sevenfold working of the Spirit, 1121, 51 ff. The two olive trees are the two witnesses, or the Church, on account of anointing, 1147, 43 ff. Omega. See Alpha. All things existed in predestination before they came into being in actuality, 1119, 57. The sevenfold working of the Spirit is signified by the seven horns, the seven eyes, and the seven spirits, 1121, 51 ff. See Sevenfold. Prayer, in order to be effective, must be offered to God through Christ the mediator, 1135, 49 ff. The door which the key opens is Christ, 1111, 21 ff. — It is the entrance of the mind, at which the Lord knocks by inspiring it, 1115, 5 ff. — An open door figures Christ, 1116, 2 ff.

The palms designate the victory of the elect, 1133, 9 ff.

Paradise is eternal life, 1103, 20. Christ’s portion is undivided, but the devil’s portion is divided into four, 1125, 50 ff. Patmos signifies the persecutions and afflictions of the Church, 1095, 35 ff. Patience pertains both to the head and to the members of the Church, 1095, 22 ff. Why the twelve patriarchs are listed in Revelation in a different order from that in Genesis, 1130, 36 ff. A poor man is one who boasts of being rich merely because of his confession of the true faith, unless he ceases from doing evil (*regere* printed; perhaps *gerere*), 1113, 52 ff. Poverty is of two kinds, 1103, 33 ff. The feet resembling bronze refer to the final members of the Church, which must be refined in the great fire of persecution under Antichrist, 1098, 40 ff. The Pelagians assert that a human being can be saved without grace, 1133, 23 ff. Pergamum is interpreted as “Dividing their horns,” 1096, 42 ff. Let each person suffer persecutions on account of the word of God, not on account of his own evils, 1095, 39 ff. — The persecution of Antichrist is foretold, 1112, 14 ff. — It is depicted, 1148, 58 ff. — It is recapitulated, 1150, 18 ff. The person of the Father is signified by the one seated on the throne, and that of the Son by the right hand of the one seated, 1120, 1 ff. The golden bowls indicate charity, 1122, 29 ff. Philadelphia is interpreted as “Saving the inheritance for the Lord,” 1097, 4 ff. Divine piety does not abandon the lukewarm, 1114, 16 ff. What the plague of the sixth seal signifies, 1126, 49 ff. — What it signifies when the first angel sounds the trumpet, 1136, 30 ff. — What it signifies when the second angel sounds the trumpet, 1137, 30 ff. — What it signifies when the third angel sounds the trumpet, ibid., 54 ff. — What it signifies when the fourth angel sounds the trumpet, 1138, 19 ff. — What it signifies when the fifth angel sounds the trumpet, 1139, 1 ff. — The plague of the four angels who were released, 1142, 4 ff. The feet of Christ figure, specifically, his flesh, and, generally, the whole Church, 1097, 49 ff. — The garment is priestly, 1097, 50 ff. The power over the nations, which the Son received from the Father, he received not in divinity but in humanity, 1108, 50 ff. — It figures the Church’s power of binding and loosing, ibid., 52 ff. — The power given to Death and Hell when the fourth seal was opened, 1125, 48 ff. — The power given to the two witnesses, 1148, 12 ff. Only four commandments were imposed upon the Gentiles converted to Christ, 1106, 38 ff. The double girding which either Daniel or John saw, 1098, 1 ff. The herald of the law is to be understood through the strong angel, 1120, 39 ff. Predestination is necessary for eternal life, 1106, 18 ff. Only the predestined are inscribed in the book of life, 1110, 54 ff. The preaching of the Old and New Testaments is figured by the sword, 1099, 28 ff. — It is expressed through voices and thunder, 1117, 42 ff. — It is signified through the eyes of the four living creatures, 1118, 56 ff. — It reached the extremities of the Roman Empire, 1129, 51 ff. Preachers are designated by the seven stars, 1099, 6 ff.; 1106, 47 ff. — The wicked, who through their negligence permit fornication and idolatry in the Church, are rebuked, ibid., 49 ff. The great battle in heaven between Michael and the dragon, 1154, 32 ff.

Four. See Living creatures, Evangelists, etc.

The Root of David is Christ, 1121, 26. Reproof pertains to words, 1114, 47 ff. Kings, whose anointing prefigured the anointing of Christ, 1090, 11 ff.

— They are the elect, 1122, 52 ff. The kingdom pertains to the head of the Church, 1095, 21 ff. The kidneys figure bodily lust, 1108, 7 ff. The first resurrection is that which takes place from present death, 1115, 53 ff. — It is figured in the lion, 1118, 36 ff. — The resurrection of the saints after the persecution of Antichrist is introduced, 1149, 39 ff. The reprobate were given time to do penance, 1107, 34 ff. — They are erased from the book of life, that is, they are by no means written in it, 1110, 56 ff. Reuben is interpreted as “Seeing a son,” 1130, 57 ff. The sword is sharp on both sides, 1104, 36 ff.

Priests, whose anointing prefigures the anointing of Christ, 1090, 11 ff.

— They are the elect, 1122, 55 ff. Salvation can be accomplished through Christ alone, 1120, 55 ff. The saints are called kings because they know how to govern themselves well, 1093, 44 ff. Blood figures sin, 1107, 18 ff. Sardis in Latin means “prepared for the beauty of the prince,” 1096, 54 ff. Sardius signifies the humanity of the Redeemer, 1116, 41 ff. Satan, first raised up against God, swelled with pride, 1108, 29 ff. See Dragon. Scripture is the open door, 1111, 35 ff. The one seated on the red horse is the devil, who takes peace from the earth, 1124, 20 ff. See Person. What the twenty-four elders signify, 1117, 10 ff. — They figure the universal Church, 1119, 32 ff. The living creatures around the throne are angels, 1123, 3 ff. The seven stars are said to be the angels of the churches, or the preachers, 1099, 3 ff. — The stars indicate the perfect number, that is, the entire order of preachers, ibid., 11 ff. — The stars also include the lampstands: that is, the preachers [include] the whole Church, ibid., 17 ff. — The lampstands designate the universal Church, ibid., 15 ff. — The sevenfold spirits are the Holy Spirit, 1109, 40 ff. — The stars are the sevenfold Church, ibid. See Lampstands, Seals, Horns. The sevenfold working of the Holy Spirit is designated by the number seven, 1097, 28. See Seven, Six. See Wings. The seven seals indicate seven modes of expression, 1120, 17 ff. — The first seal is opened, 1123, 17 ff. — The second, ibid., 47 ff. — The third, 1124, 35 ff. — The fourth, 1125, 36 ff. — The fifth, 1126, 5 ff. — The sixth, ibid., 49 ff. — The seventh, 1135, 2 ff. “Sign” is used for “seal”; hence significare (“to signify”) has been used in place of sigillare (“to seal”), 1090, 48 ff. — The sign of the living God is the mystery of the cross, 1129, 54 ff. Simeon. “I heard sorrow” is the interpretation, 1131, 38 ff. The emerald is spoken of in connection with divinity reconciled to the world, 1117, 6 ff. Smyrna is rendered in Latin as “their song,” that is, the song of the elect, 1096, 38 ff. Sodom. See Egypt. The sun is Christ, 1026, 55 ff. The Holy Spirit, whose sevenfold working is called the seven spirits, 1093, 19 ff. — In the memory of the saints he is declared to be alone, because remission of sins belongs specially to him, ibid., 21 ff.; in him the whole Trinity is understood, ibid., 25 ff. — He did not utterly abandon John’s flesh when he had the vision, 1095, 44 ff. — The Holy Spirit in whom John was is believed to be the very power of contemplation, 1096, 4 ff. — The Holy One who illuminates the Church is figured by the eyes, 1098, 51 ff. — How he is to be heard when he speaks to the churches, 1102, 55 ff. — The Holy Spirit is compared with seven lamps, 1117, 50 ff. What is the balance held by the rider on the black horse, 1124, 41. The morning star figures Christ, 1109, 26 ff. — The stars falling from heaven are those who appear to be holy but who at that time, under Antichrist, will rush into iniquity, 1127, 17 ff. See Seven. White robes are the reward of martyrdom, 1126, 35 ff. — White garments signify the state of the mind, 1133, 6 ff.

The temple of God is the Church, 1112, 30. Time. Why it is said to be near, 1092, 7 ff.

— It is also granted to the reprobate so that they may do penance, 1107, 34 ff. Temptation sometimes pertains to testing, 1101, 45 ff. The lukewarm person is one who, having turned away from the coldness of iniquity, does not pass over to the perfect fervor of righteousness, 1113, 37 ff. — He is difficult to convert, ibid., 44 ff. — In what sense he is wretched, pitiable, poor, and blind, 1113, 52 ff. The earthquake of the sixth seal foretells the final persecution of Antichrist, 1126, 52 ff. The Old Testament restrains the lust of the flesh, while the New also restrains that of the mind, 1098, 2 ff. — The Old is indicated by the twenty-four elders and the throne, 1117, 35 ff. — The Old and New are figured by the bow, 1123, 35 ff. See Book. The two witnesses who will prophesy for 1,260 days are Elijah and Jeremiah, or Elijah and Enoch, 1147, 30 ff. Thyatira is called “illuminated,” 1096, 48. Thunder. See Preaching. The twelve thrones express universal judgment, while the throne of the Son signifies the singular summit of judicial power, 1115, 24 ff. — What is meant by twenty-four, 1117, 10 ff. Tribulation pertains to the members of the Church, 1095, 22 ff. — The tribulation of the saints is manifold, 1103, 30 ff. The tribulations of the Church are prefigured by the island of Patmos, 1095, 35 ff. The whole Trinity gave [this] to Christ, so that he might disclose to his servants the things that must soon take place, 1090, 30 ff. — The whole Trinity is understood whenever one or two persons of the Trinity are mentioned, 1093, 16 ff. — It is demonstrated by the threefold cry of the four living creatures, 1118, 14 ff. The seven trumpets indicate the perfect preaching of the Old and New Testaments, 1135, 27 ff. Trumpet. See Plague.

One woe is emitted, 1141, 26 ff. — The second, 1150, 44 ff.

— The third, ibid., 57 ff. Not to stain the garments with filth means not to admit mortal sin, 1110, 29 ff. The four winds held by the angels are the principal kingdoms of the earth, 1129, 12. The words of the Son are words of the Spirit, 1103, 4 ff. Manifested truth summons one to faith, 1123, 27 ff. The victory of Christ is celebrated above all victories, 1122, 40 ff. Watchfulness is rising from the sleep of sin to righteousness through the tears of repentance, 1110, 19 ff. Twenty-four. See Elders. The iron rod signifies the rule of the preachers, 1108, 57 ff. The Virgin Mary and her glory are described, 1152 ff. Why the vision is called sealed, 1090, 52 ff. — John’s vision is asserted to be both spiritual and intellectual, 1099, 53 ff. The will of God is the Church and is designated by Ephesus, 1096, 29 ff. — It pertains to charity, ibid., 32 ff. The voice addressed to John was spiritual, 1096, 2 ff. — Allegorically, it is said of the law and the prophets, whose voice the Church hears, ibid., 13 ff. — It is called great because it speaks of the highest mysteries, ibid., 16 ff. — The voice of many waters figures charity, 1098, 58 ff. — It is compared with a trumpet because it summons to spiritual warfare, 1116, 16 ff.

Zebulun, that is, “dwelling-place of strength,” 1131, 57 ff.

# PART ONE OF THE WORKS OF BLESSED ALCUIN.—LETTERS. 135

**Froben’s Notice.** Same page.

**The Notice of the Editor of the Patrology.** 137

## Letter I. To Aeric, duke.—He praises him for his devotion to sacred reading and his humility; wishes him victory over the unbelievers; and proposes Saint Paulinus of Aquileia as a teacher of Christian piety. 139

## Letter II. To Arno.—He desires to have him present; urges him to exercise diligent care for the souls entrusted to his governance; wishes to be remembered to Laidrad; and indicates that, because of the recent change of regime, he is still being detained in his homeland, England. 140

## Letter III. To Colcu, lector in Scotland.—He recounts various things that he either saw or heard on his journey. 142

## Letter IV. To Felix, bishop.—He commends himself to the prayers of Felix, bishop of Urgell, whom he appears to praise for his piety. 144

## Letter V. To Cudradus, presbyter.—After the devastation of the holy places, he exhorts the presbyter Cudradus to steadfastness. Same page.

## Letter VI. To the brethren of the Church of York.—He gratefully declares that he was educated by the people of York from infancy to manhood. He commends himself to the prayers of all of them and urges them to guard against vices. 145

## Letter VII. To the brethren of York.—He expresses his joy at the letter received from them; urges them to follow in the footsteps of their fathers; and commends himself to their prayers. 147

## Letter VIII. To Beornwinus, presbyter.—He declares that he has never withdrawn from his loyalty to King Offa and the English people; advises him to urge kings, bishops, and princes alike to follow God’s will; and commends peace. 149

## Letter IX. To the people of Lindisfarne.—He laments the devastation of the Church of Lindisfarne and exhorts them to pray; urges them to correct their conduct and observe the rule; and advises them not to be disheartened. 150

## Letter X. To Aedilhard, archbishop of the city of Dorchester.—He urges him to follow the footsteps of his predecessors and to carry out fearlessly the office of shepherding souls, and to preach the word of God without fear together with his fellow bishops. 152

## Letter XI. To Aedilred, king, and to the princes and people of the Northumbrian nation.—He urges them to be grateful to God; to desire heavenly things rather than earthly ones; not to seek riches through injustice; to flee vices and sins; to be fathers to widows and orphans; to preserve concord and peace; and to submit to the preaching of the priests. 157

## Letter XII. To King Aedilred.—He urges him to practice royal virtues. 160

## Letter XIII. Fragment.—To King Aedilred.—He speaks of the affliction of the Church and city of Lindisfarne. 161

## Letter XIV. To the brethren of the Churches of Wearmouth and Jarrow.—He urges them to an orderly charity; to observance of the regular or canonical life and of the Rule of Saint Benedict. He terrifies them by the example of the people of Lindisfarne; dissuades them from extravagance in clothing; and commends confession of sins and penance. 162

## Letter XV. To the brethren of the Church of Jarrow.—He urges them to virtues worthy of monks and to follow in the footsteps of their fathers and teachers. 166

## Letter XVI. To the brethren of the Church of Saint Peter.—He commends himself to the friendship formerly agreed upon with them; praises their regular way of life; and urges them to the virtues proper to monks. 167

## Letter XVII. To Charlemagne.—He praises him for his secular power and his preaching of the divine law, as ruler of the people and teacher. He refutes the error of the Adoptionists. 168

## Letter XVIII. To Pope Adrian I.—He commends himself to the pope’s favor, professes him to be the vicar of Saint Peter and heir of his authority, and at the same time asks him to grant the requests that he is to make through Angilbert. 170

## Letter XIX. To Theophilus.—He praises his writings on the apostolic faith and wishes to be instructed by him. 172

## Letter XX. To Usualdus.—He urges the monks to virtue; says that he has supported their requests before the king; and commends himself to their prayers. 173

## Letter XXI. To certain persons.—Among the people of York, Alcuin excuses his absence and urges them to concord with their father, Eanbald. 174

## Letter XXII. To a certain person.—He stimulates a son and companion of his pilgrimage to virtue. He recalls and commends the pursuit of wisdom and brings to mind teachings formerly given. 175

## Letter XXIII. To the brethren of Saint Martin in the city of Tours.—He wishes to be with them and urges them to virtues suitable for monks. 176

## Letter XXIV. To Pope Leo III.—Through Angilbert, he commends himself to the supreme pontiff’s apostolic solicitude, as vicar of the apostles and prince of the Church. 178

## Letter XXV. To his sweetest son Homer (Angelbert).—He commends his own memory to the patronage of the saints and advises him to bring back to him something of ecclesiastical beauty. 180

## Letter XXVI. To Angelbert, first officer of the palace of King Pippin.—He commends Angilbert, who is making a pilgrimage to the sacred thresholds of the apostles, to his favor, and asks that sacred relics be sent to him. 181

## Letter XXVII. To Homer.—He sends two solutions to grammatical questions proposed to him by the king. Same page.

## Letter XXVIII. To Homer, his son. 183

## Letter XXIX. To Paulinus, patriarch.—He commends himself to Paulinus’s constant remembrance and the bearer of the letter to his patronage. 185

## Letter XXX. To Paulinus.—He expresses his desire to converse with Paulinus. He sends him three small lists and recalls a gift sent by Liutgard. 186

## Letter XXXI. To Aginus, bishop.—He asks that the relics of the saints formerly promised to him be sent through Angilbert. Same page.

## Letter XXXII. To Itherius.—He consoles a sick man and kindly advises him to prepare himself for eternity. 187

## Letter XXXIII. To the lord king.—He rejoices over the submission of the Huns and explains how they should be instructed in the faith and what order should be observed. Same page.

## Letter XXXIV. To Arno.—He eagerly desires his return and wishes to be informed about various events. He indicates that he will go to the palace in July. He urges him to beware of the error of the Spaniards. 190

## Letter XXXV. To … (Arno).—He tells him that he has received his letter. He commends the soul of Archanbald (Eanbald) to his prayers. He sends a letter to the king, written concerning preaching among the pagans. 191

## Letter XXXVI. To Arno.—He instructs him concerning the preaching of the faith among the recently converted Avars. 192

## Letter XXXVII. To the lord king.—He prays for those captured in the Hunnic war and for the enemies. 196

## Letter XXXVIII. To Pippin.—He offers excellent instructions for the conduct of life. 197

## Letter XXXIX. To Paulinus, patriarch.—He wishes to know what Paulinus intends to do for the conversion of the nation after the Huns have been conquered, and repeatedly asks that letters be sent to him. 198

## Letter XL. To a certain person (Paulinus).—After Paulinus’s long silence, he expresses his joy at now having received letters. Thereafter he launches into praise of Paulinus; and, recalling his approaching death and his own sins, humbly commends himself to Paulinus’s prayers. 200

## Letter XLI. To Paulinus, patriarch.—He asks Paulinus to remember him during the holy Mass. He requests that a piece of the holy cross and other relics be sent to him, and urges him to labor in preaching. 202

## Letter XLII. To Megenfrid.—He instructs him about the order and manner of preaching; rebukes greed and the excessive collection of tithes; and grieves that many seek the honors of the priesthood while avoiding its ranks and ministry. He wishes Charles to be asked to send more good laborers into the harvest. 204

## Letter XLIII. To Charlemagne.—He expresses his joy at the king’s prosperity. To advance his studies, he asks that his books be brought from England. He lists the benefits of literary study and advises that the young men of the palace devote themselves to it. 207

## Letter XLIV. To Damoetas, his son.—He prays for prosperity for him as he goes to war and grieves at the absence of his friends. 210

## Letter XLV. To Riculfus, archbishop of the city of Mainz, surnamed Damoetas.—He is saddened by the absence of his friends and urges love of eternal things. 211

## Letter XLVI. To Damoetas.—He gives thanks for a gift; urges him to render justice to everyone; and sighs for the arrival of his friend. 212

## Letter XLVII. To Offa, king of the Mercians.—He announces that Charles is angry with the Northumbrian people because of the killing of King Ethelred. 213

## Letter XLVIII. To the same.—Wishing to return to his homeland, he is held back because of the perjuries and devastation of the people. Same page.

## Letter XLIX. To the same.—He sends a student back to England at the king’s request, so that he may teach in the schools there. He urges him to royal virtues. Same page.

## Letter L. To Ecgfrid, king of the Mercians.—He exhorts him to virtue. 214

## Letter LI. To the monks of Saint Vedast.—He sends several verses and Masses; commends himself to their prayers; and urges them to religious virtues. 215

## Letter LII. To the brethren in the Church of Saint Liudgar, bishop.—He excuses himself for not having come to them and urges them to virtues suitable for monks. 217

## Letter LIII. To the brethren of Corbie.—He praises the good way of life that he formerly experienced among them. He commends himself to their prayers and urges them to pursue virtue. 218

## Letter LIV. To his dearest friends at York.—He urges them to avoid the stain of simony in the election of a bishop. 219

## Letter LV. To a certain person.—He asks him to defend the Church from every act of violence while a new bishop is to be elected and to keep the eternal days in mind. 220

## Letter LVI. To Eanbald, bishop.—He congratulates him on having attained his dignity; urges him to pastoral care and to arranging everything well; and commends himself to his remembrance and prayers. 221

## Letter LVII. To Aethelred, bishop.—He consoles him in persecution and tribulation and urges manly perseverance, so that he may not flee from his sheep. 226

## Letter LVIII.—A consolatory letter to a mother concerning the death of her son. Same page.

## Letter LIX. To Edilburga.—He recalls teachings formerly given to her; grieves over the infidelity of his homeland; and commends to her prayers Liutgard, a noble woman. 227

## Letter LX. To King Eardwulf.—He urges the king, raised to the throne, to secure both his own salvation and that of his people. He terrifies him by the example of his predecessors. 229

## Letter LXI. To Osbald.—He urges Osbald, whom he suspects because of regicide and disturbances among the people, to change his life and provide for the salvation of himself and his nation. 230

## Letter LXII. To a certain archbishop.—He announces that, having laid aside the occupations of the world, he is preparing for the Lord’s coming. 231

## Letter LXIII.—To Coenwulf, king of the Mercians.—Having been raised to the kingship, he is urged to royal virtues. 232

## Letter LXIV. To Simeon.—He recalls the teachings once given to him and adds new ones. 233

## Letter LXV. To Simeon, priest.—In prosperity and adversity he advises moderation of spirit; he sends gifts and advises that the clergy be taught the Roman Order. He reports that he is feeling better after his illness. He commends the study of sacred reading and wisdom. 234

## Letter LXVI. To Arno.—He rejoices at the news of his arrival; wishes to learn many things from him; and informs him about his own residence. 235

## Letter LXVII. To ***.—He indicates where he is staying, wishes to learn what is new, and sends certain small gifts. 236

## Letter LXVIII. To Arno.—He states that he has received his letters and complains about the silence concerning many matters. 237

## Letter LXIX. To Arno, bishop of Salzburg.—He commends a certain son to him; wishes to be informed about the king’s return, the case of Saint Paul, and other matters; sighs for the vision of God; and urges him to desire heavenly things. 238

## Letter LXX. To Bishop Speratus.—He dissuades him from the vanities of this life and impresses upon him the duties proper to bishops. 241

## Letter LXXI. To the same.—He eagerly desires his continuing friendship and urges him to live a life worthy of a bishop. 244

## Letter LXXII. To Simeon, priest.—He urges him to carry out the episcopal office diligently in the dangerous circumstances prevailing in Britain. 245

## Letter LXXIII. To Calvinus, presbyter.—He urges contempt for the riches and honors of the world; wishes Simeon, the high priest, to be admonished frequently; and advises him to guard against flatteries, attend diligently to the care of souls, and practice Christian virtue. Same page.

## Letter LXXIV. To the nation and people of Canterbury.—He exalts their faith and nobility with praise; exhorts the priests and nobles; laments their calamities; and advises them to try to bring Archbishop Aedilhard back from his flight. 249

## Letter LXXV. To Athelard, archbishop of Canterbury.—He urges him to repent of his flight from his see and to restore order to the Church; and to restrain the clergy from vanity in clothing and from excessive feasting. 251

## Letter LXXVI. To the lord king.—On the calculation of the lunar leap. 254

## Letter LXXVII. To Ethelard.—He prays for a prosperous journey for him as he goes to Rome and asks him to remember him before the holy apostles. 257

## Letter LXXVIII. To the same.—He prays for his safe return from the Roman embassy, in view of the restoration of the dignity of the Church of Canterbury. Same page.

## Letter LXXIX. To the lord king.—He commends his friends who have traveled from England to Rome. 258

## Letter LXXX. To the same.—On the calculation of Septuagesima, Sexagesima, and Quinquagesima. 259

## Letter LXXXI. To Abbot Albinus.—Charlemagne replies to the preceding letter concerning the calculation of Septuagesima. 263

## Letter LXXXII. To the lord king.—He replies to the preceding letter and sends calculations of the lunar leap. 266

## Letter LXXXIII. To the same.—On the sun’s course through the signs of the zodiac, and how the leap day arises from it. He praises the study of astrology, arithmetic, and every branch of philosophy. He asks for assistants in refuting Felix and encourages the king to defend the truth. 269

## Letter LXXXIV. To the same.—He replies to Charlemagne’s letter concerning the composition of a poem, the appearance of the star of Mars, the refutation of Felix’s treatise, questions put to him by his daughter, and the correction of calculations according to the Egyptians. 274

## Letter LXXXV. To the same.—He replies from memory to Charles’s various questions concerning the courses of the stars. 278

## Letter LXXXVI. To the same.—The reasons are assigned why the moon appears smaller or larger than the calculation of the astronomers would indicate. 281

## Letter LXXXVII. To Arno.—As he is setting out for Hunia, he urges him to carry out the apostolic work well. 284

## Letter LXXXVIII. To the same.—He urges him to perform the apostolic office zealously and not to allow himself to be hindered either by bodily illness or by care for his own sheep. 285

## Letter LXXXIX. To Liobradus.—He eagerly desires the friendship of that elected bishop of Lyon. 286

## Letter XC. To the brethren of Lyon.—He warns them to beware of the various errors of the Spaniards. He replies to a question concerning observance of the Sabbath before the Sunday of the Resurrection. 287

## Letter XCI. To Arno.—He desires to see him and laments the dangerous times. He indicates that he has been summoned to the palace and that Felix is to be brought by Laidrad to the king, and so forth. 294

## Letter XCII. To the same.—He states that he has received a letter with gifts and that he will be with the king in the middle of May, when Felix too is to be brought there. 296

## Letter XCIII. To the brethren of the Church of Juvavum.—He praises their regular way of life and urges them to carry out the duties of monks well. 297

## Letter XCIV. To Arno.—He sends Easter poems and wishes the parishioners, or officials, of his diocese to be admonished to uprightness of life and to the proper performance of their duties. 300

## Letter XCV. To the lord king.—He gives thanks for the good things received; complains of the disturbance of the Church and kingdom; and urges the king to devote the greatest care to the Church, with somewhat less severity toward the Saxons. Same page.

## Letter XCVI. To the same.—He gives thanks for being remembered in the king’s letters and for the many benefits received. He praises and urges the king to render justice to the apostolic see. He excuses himself from undertaking the journey to Rome. He wishes for peace with the Saxons. 303

## Letter XCVII. To ***.—He eagerly desires his presence; laments a terrible event at Rome; urges him to the work of preaching and the practice of virtue; and congratulates him on receiving the pallium, while urging him to fulfill his ministry well. 306

## Letter XCVIII. To Arno.—He advises him to guard himself against the dangers of the world and expresses his love for him. 308

## Letter XCIX. To ***.—A letter enigmatic at the beginning. He seeks his affection. 309

## Letter C. To the lord king.—He replies to Charles’s repeated letters. He praises his zeal for religion, piety, and royal power, and mentions certain computational tables. 311

## Letter CI. To the same.—He gives thanks for the book against Felix that was read and sent back, and excuses certain of its errors. Concerning Felix’s disputation with a Saracen and that of a certain Jew with Master Peter. He sends certain kinds of words. 313

## Letter CII. To Arno.—He teaches that the world must be despised and that one must strive toward eternal things. He says that he has come to the dwelling of Saint Amand in order to visit Arno, but nevertheless grieves that he did not find him there. 315

## Letter CIII. To the same.—From the letters received from Arno, he learns of his return, but nothing about the Christianity of the new people, nothing about his residence, and nothing about the hope of a mutual conversation, although he greatly desires it. 316

## Letter CIV. To the same.—He grieves over Arno’s presence, awaited in vain; but he mitigates his sorrow with sighs for the heavenly homeland. He gladly receives the gifts sent to him. 318

## Letter CV. To the same.—He rejoices at Arno’s visit but grieves over the brevity of his presence; he raises his longing toward joy that will always remain. He urges him to give pious exhortations to the brethren and to all the sheep. 319

## Letter CVI. To the lord king.—The epitaph of Liutgard, a noble woman. 320

## Letter CVII. To the same.—A consolatory letter concerning the death of Liutgard. 322

## Letter CVIII. To Arno.—He urges him to defend Pope Leo against his adversaries. He complains that the Huns have defected from submission and that pagan ships are ravaging the shores of Aquitaine. He relates that he has established a new congregation of monks. He sends greetings to the bishops Alimo, Remedius, and Paulinus. He reports certain matters concerning Elipandus and Felix. 324

## Letter CIX. To the lord king.—He replies to Charles’s letter announcing victory over the enemies and the miraculous recovery of Pope Leo. He declines to continue the journey to Rome. 329

## Letter CX. To the abbots and monks of Gothia.—He refutes the error of the Adoptionists, which, he says, he has already refuted in a short treatise sent through the blessed Benedict and will now refute in a larger work. 332

## Letter CXI. To the brethren in Gothia.—He urges them to penance, observance of the regular life, and courage in the tribulation that has arisen. 334

## Letter CXII. To the brethren in the province of the Goths.—He refutes those who refuse to confess their sins to priests and establishes the necessity of confession. 337

## Letter CXIII. To Paulinus, patriarch.—He praises his treatise on the exposition of the faith and urges him to combat certain errors arising in the Church. 341

## Letter CXIV. To Aedilhard, archbishop.—He praises him for his meeting with Eanbald concerning the honor of the churches and the reform of the clergy. He advises him to return quickly to his flock after completing his embassy and sends him his saddle and horse. 343

## Letter CXV. To Eanbald, archbishop of the Church of York, surnamed Simon.—He consoles him in his affliction and urges him to patience; he dissuades him from fleeing his Church. 345

## Letter CXVI. To Calvinus and Cuculus.—He suggests what should be suggested to Simeon (Eanbald), the bishop placed in tribulation. He indicates that he has laid down the burden of pastoral care. 347

## Letter CXVII. To Aquila, pontiff.—He replies to the letters received from him and gives thanks for his gifts; recalls a certain impious and cruel murder; and narrates what was done in the case of Felix of Urgell in the presence of the king and the Fathers. 348

## Letter CXVIII. To the same.—He expresses his affection to Arno, whom he calls his son, and wishes him every good thing. 352

## Letter CXIX. To the young King Charles.—He congratulates Charles, son of Charlemagne, on having received from the apostolic authority the royal name together with the crown, and offers excellent advice for ruling well, after the example of his father. 353

## Letter CXX. To the same.—He again urges Charles to royal virtues and to imitate his father’s example. He prays for his prosperity. 354

## Letter CXXI. To the sons staying in the palace with the lord emperor.—He displays his affection for his sons and commends his own memory to the thresholds of the apostles. 355

## Letter CXXII. To Riculfus, archbishop.—He urges him to apostolic labors and virtues. 356

## Letter CXXIII. To Damoetas, archpriest.—Damoetas being in Rome, he urges him to work at repairing the breach in the Church; reproves disagreement among the peacemakers; and wishes not for new arrangements to be established but for the old ones to be restored. 357

## Letter CXXIV. To George, patriarch of the city of Jerusalem.—He congratulates George on his dignity in the holiest place and urges him to patience in persecution by unbelievers. He commends himself and his people to George’s prayers. 359

## Letter CXXV. To Gundrada, a virgin, surnamed Eulalia.—He instructs Gundrada how to live virtuously at court. He wishes to be commended to the king through her and to have his inability to reach him excused. 360

## Letter CXXVI. To his dearest sister.—He praises her piety and exhorts her to labor for eternity; he gives thanks for the cross bestowed. 362

## Letter CXXVII. To his most beloved sister.—He gives thanks for a cloak and other gifts; he mentions Angilbert, his sister Ava, and Columba. Same page.

## Letter CXXVIII. To Gisela, daughter of Charlemagne.—He grieves that, because of illness, he cannot see the king’s face or enjoy Gisela’s conversation; and he urges her to virtue. 363

## Letter CXXIX. To the lord king.—He expresses his joy at Charles’s return from Italy and sends Candidus with gifts to meet him. 364

## Letter CXXX. To Arno.—He replies to his letter and removes an unfavorable suspicion from himself. He says that he advised the king to choose envoys to administer justice. He wishes God to be entreated for him and commends himself to Pope Leo, Paulinus the patriarch, and Peter of Milan. Finally, he urges efforts to restore peace among ecclesiastical persons. 366

## Letter CXXXI. To the lord king.—Through his servant, he sends sacred books that he himself collected and corrected into a single volume. 369

## Letter CXXXII. To the same.—Summoned to court, he excuses himself on account of old age and declares that the most wise king has no need of his counsel. Same page.

## Letter CXXXIII. To the same.—He announces the death of Maganfred. He intercedes for the brethren and the Church of Saint Peter in the city of Benevento and begs that the Beneventans be treated mercifully. 370

## Letter CXXXIV. To the same.—He gives thanks for the benefits conferred and begs that, because of bodily illness, he may be allowed to rest at Saint Martin’s. 372

## Letter CXXXV. To Nathanael.—He arouses him to piety and commends to him the care of instructing the virgins Lucia and Columba. He entrusts to him a letter to be delivered to King Charles together with a gift of sacred Scripture. 374

## Letter CXXXVI. To the same.—He encourages an honorable and religious way of life and advises him to avoid the crowned doves flying through the chambers of the palace. 375

## Letter CXXXVII. To Chrodgarius, count.—He indicates that he is undertaking the education of a little boy and his brother. He urges faithful service and the provision of counsel to the king. As Chrodgarius is about to depart to ravage the city of Benevento, he advises him to beware of the harmful air of Italy. 376

## Letter CXXXVIII. To his sister and daughter.—He indicates how highly he values their friendship. He informs them of the favorable news received from Rome. He sends certain treatises of the venerable Bede to be copied. He informs them about his own health. 377

## Letter CXXXIX. To the same.—He commends charity and the reading of sacred Scripture together with prayer. 378

## Letter CXL. To the same.—He advises them to preserve equanimity in prosperity and adversity, after the example of the saints, whose lives he wishes them to read from the *Dialogues* of Pope Saint Gregory. 379

## Letter CXLI. To Aquila or Arno.—He recalls with joy the king’s prosperity and exaltation. He wishes to be informed about the case of the lord Apostolicus, the Beneventan controversy, and what was done at the assembly of the bishops. He reports the state of his health. 381

## Letter CXLII. To the brethren of Fulda.—He urges them to religious virtues. He sends a storax-colored pallium for the body of Saint Boniface and a small liturgical booklet. Same page.

## Letter CXLIII. To Arno.—He invites him to come to Saint Martin’s; he aspires to heavenly things and asks that he be prayed for. 383

## Letter CXLIV. To the same.—He desires to see Arno at Saint Martin’s and to confer with him about the conduct of his life before he is compelled to depart from this life. 384

## Letter CXLV. To the same.—He replies to a letter sent to him. Again he desires to enjoy Arno’s presence, although he himself is prevented from coming to the palace. 387

## Letter CXLVI. To the same.—He expresses his affection for Arno. He partly refuses and partly promises to answer his questions. He praises the king’s love of justice and censures the greed of his ministers. He sends him a little work on Solomon’s Ecclesiastes to be copied. 389

## Letter CXLVII. To Theodulf, archbishop.—He praises his virtues; congratulates him on receiving the pallium from the apostolic see; and urges him to persistent preaching. He prays for good fortune on his journey. 391

## Letter CXLVIII. To the same.—A wholly allegorical letter in which Theodulf is compared to the father of the vineyards. 394

## Letter CXLIX. To Charles, emperor.—He intercedes for the brethren of Saint Martin and defends both them and himself against accusations concerning asylum granted to a cleric of Orléans; he reveals the true cause of the disturbance that arose. 395

## Letter CL. To Maurus.—He asks him for the little book promised to him. 398

## Letter CLI. To Arno.—He complains that no reply has been sent to several letters. He grieves that his friend is entangled in secular affairs and that shepherds of souls are disturbed by worldly concerns. Sick in body and spirit, he commends himself to Arno’s prayers and sighs for heaven. 399

## Letter CLII. To the same.—He commends to Arno the care of the canons, the monks, and the members of the third order, who stand between them. He complains of simoniacal depravity, which has even crept into the apostolic see. He mentions a letter concerning confession and a little book on the Catholic faith. 401

## Letter CLIII. To the same.—He indicates that he has received a letter of affection through Bishop Adalwin, who is coming to Saint Martin’s. He wishes Odulf to be admonished to administer justice, the chaplains to an exemplary way of life, and the brethren of the monastery of Saint Rhodbert to sincere charity, and so forth. 402

## Letter CLIV. To the same.—He consoles him, afflicted by secular occupations. He sends letters through Bishop Adalwin. He promises grateful remembrance for the chasuble. 404

## Letter CLV. To the same.—He commends himself, as a sick old man, to his sacred remembrance. He sends two table vessels and again gives thanks for the Mass chasuble. 406

## Letter CLVI. To the same.—Through Fredegisus he sends various little works and commends this son of his to him. 407

## Letter CLVII. To Candidus and Nathanael.—He advises them to conduct themselves wisely at court. He instructs them concerning their dispute with Theodulf, bishop of Orléans. 408

## Letter CLVIII. To Albinus, master, and to the congregation of the monastery of Saint Martin.—He rebukes the congregation for defending a certain matter involving a cleric who had fled to them, against the judgment of his bishop and against the king’s command, and so forth. 415

## Letter CLIX. To Arno.—He commends to him a student of grammar whom he calls “the calf.” 416

## Letter CLX. To ***.—He commends himself to the affection of a friend. 417

## Letter CLXI. To Arno.—He explains how the terms *substance*, *essence*, *subsistence*, and *nature* are predicated of God. Same page.

## Letter CLXII. To the lord king.—He explains the difference between *eternal* and *everlasting*, *perpetual* and *immortal*, *saeculum* (age), *aevum* (duration/age), and *time*. 419

## Letter CLXIII. To Charles.—He explains the text of Saint Luke 22:36 and related passages concerning the two swords. He complains about certain bishops who wish to prevent priests and deacons from exercising the ministry of preaching, and about the profanation of altars. 422

## Letter CLXIV.—To the same.—He replies to questions concerning the hymn sung after supper in Matthew and Mark. 428

## Letter CLXV. To the same.—He replies to a question concerning the price of human salvation and to whom it would be paid. 431

## Letter CLXVI. Or, a capitulary of admonition to the same.—The points that should be remembered at such a time. 437

## Letter CLXVII. To Peter, archbishop.—He commends himself to his paternal affection and sacred prayers. 438

## Letter CLXVIII. To the same.—He expresses his gratitude for his paternal benevolence and commends Liutgard, from whom gifts are being sent to him. 440

## Letter CLXIX. To Bishop Rigbod of the city of Trier, surnamed Macharius.—He complains of his friend’s absence and of the interruption of their exchange of letters. He reproves in him an excessive love of Maro [Virgil]. 441

## Letter CLXX. To the same.—He grieves at his friend’s absence. 442

## Letter CLXXI. To the same.—He complains about the interruption of their correspondence. For the moment he asks for certain writings of Saint Leo and the venerable Bede. He invites him to Saint Martin’s. Same page.

## Letter CLXXII. To the same.—He grieves at his absence and expresses joy at the news that Macharius has recovered his health. 443

## Letter CLXXIII. To Joseppus.—He sympathizes with him in bodily illness and encourages him to patience. He commends himself to his prayers and urges the restoration of the house of God, and so forth. 444

## Letter CLXXIV. To Remigius, bishop.—He commends to him a merchant traveling to Italy and the soul of Joseppus to his prayers. 445

## Letter CLXXV. To Remedius, bishop.—He gives thanks for the gifts of his affection and stimulates him to good works. Same page.

## Letter CLXXVI. To the same.—He commends himself to his prayers on account of their longstanding friendship. 446

## Letter CLXXVII. To the same.—He expresses his confidence in his prayers and urges him to carry out the episcopal office well, in hope of an eternal reward. Same page.

## Letter CLXXVIII. To Aedilbert, bishop.—He commends himself to the prayers of all and of each person; urges him to follow in the footsteps of his fathers, to read sacred Scripture, and to instruct the younger men. 448

## Letter CLXXIX. To a certain bishop.—He sighs for eternal things. He urges him to carry out the pastoral office diligently. He wishes omens, the singing of birds, and sneezing to be abolished. 449

## Letter CLXXX. To a certain bishop.—He grieves over his friend’s illness and urges him to patience, virtue, and care for the students. 451

## Letter CLXXXI. To a certain person.—He urges him to piety and the remaining virtues and commends to him care for divine praise in the churches entrusted to him. 452

## Letter CLXXXII. To Hechstanus, presbyter.—He urges him to virtue and wishes himself to be commended to the prayers of his friends. Same page.

## Letter CLXXXIII. To Monna, presbyter, and his brother.—He urges contempt for the world and humility. 454

## Letter CLXXXIV. To Eada, presbyter.—He gives thanks for gifts; grieves that he has been snatched from a condition of poverty into the abyss of riches; and commends himself to his prayers. 455

## Letter CLXXXV. To a certain student.—He rejoices at the student’s prosperity and devotion to letters; urges him to penance and to battle against the enemies of the soul; and reproves bodily adornment. 456

## Letter CLXXXVI. To a faithful friend.—He expresses the ardor of his affection and urges him to be an example of life to everyone. He commends reading the holy Gospel and Saint Gregory’s *Pastoral Rule*. 457

## Letter CLXXXVII. To a certain son.—He praises the student’s devotion and pursuit of wisdom. He urges him to follow not his own conduct but his exhortations and the examples of the saints; commends reading sacred Scripture, the practice of virtue, and care for young men, and so forth. 458

## Letter CLXXXVIII. To an ailing son.—He consoles him and urges him to confess his sins. 460

## Letter CLXXXIX. To Antonius.—He complains of being forgotten, condemns spectacles, and says that he has written to Homer about these matters, and so forth. 461

## Letter CXC. To the same.—He announces that the brethren of the island of Lérins have arrived and that the brother of Adalhard has been summoned to the palace, and so forth. 462

## Letter CXCI. To the same.—He expresses his joy at Antonius’s intention to visit him. He censures Homer’s vanity concerning actors; complains about the interruption of their correspondence, which he says is not contrary to the regular life; and desires that he be remembered after his death. 463

## Letter CXCII. To the same.—He greatly desires Antonius’s prayers, so that he may always be able to love and praise God. 466

## Letter CXCIII.—Enigmatic. Same page.

## Letter CXCIV. To the congregation of Saint Mary and Father…

To Moroaldus.—He desires to enjoy their companionship and friendship. 467

**LETTER CXCV. To his mother and daughter.**—He exhorts them to good works and commends himself to their prayers. Same place.

**LETTER CXCVI. To his daughter Eugenia.**—He exhorts her to courage amid the tribulations that, though innocent, she suffers with God’s servants at the hands of wicked kings. 468

**LETTER CXCVII. To the same.**—He commends chastity together with generosity in almsgiving. 469

**LETTER CXCVIII. To the woman Hundrud.**—He exhorts her to devotion and an exemplary life in the king’s palace. He prays for the welfare of the queen and of Egfrid. 470

**LETTER CXCIX. To Aedilthyd, a servant of God and formerly a queen.**—He instructs her with the best precepts for living. 471

**LETTER CC. To Edilthruda.**—He consoles the mother over the death of her son. 473

**LETTER CCI. To Count Magenharius of the city of Sens.**—He exhorts him to virtue and to care for his official responsibilities. 475

**LETTER CCII. To Amicus.**—He expresses his affection to his friend. 476

**LETTER CCIII. To Gallicellula.**—On the comparison of the numbers of the Old and New Testaments. Same place.

**LETTER CCIV. To Fridugisus.**—On the three kinds of visions. 478

**LETTER CCV. To a certain disciple.**—He removes the cause of their disagreement and asks that they return to friendship. 479

**LETTER CCVI. To a disciple.**—He reproves him for the perversity of his life and exhorts him to reform. 481

**LETTER CCVII. To a prodigal son.**—He reproves the disciple’s perverse conduct and urges him to amend his life, using as an example a certain man who is now a bishop but was formerly his fellow student. 482

**LETTER CCVIII. To the same.**—He laments the disciple’s perverse conduct and tries to recall him to better things through fear of Gehenna. 484

**LETTER CCIX. To a friend.**—He exhorts a man converted to better things to remain steadfast. 485

**LETTER CCX.**—A letter of recommendation from a certain priest, Fordradus, to his friends. 486

**LETTER CCXI.**—A letter of recommendation from Noroberet to all his friends. Same place.

**LETTER CCXII.**—A recommendation to friends on behalf of pilgrims traveling to the thresholds of the apostles. Same place.

**LETTER CCXIII. To Bishop Ragaubertus.**—He complains about the new exactions by which the bishop’s officials were harassing the priests serving in the churches of Saint Martin. 487

**LETTER CCXIV. To Bishop Nifridius.**—He begs him to remember him in his prayers and commends Benedict, who is departing from him. 488

**LETTER CCXV. To his most beloved Fathers.**—He exhorts them to charity and to the labors of the monastic life. 489

**LETTER CCXVI. To Bishop Cunibertus.**—He commends the memory of the friendship once contracted between them. He exhorts him to the work of preaching, which must not be hindered by any worldly power or vanity. 490

**LETTER CCXVII. To Bishops Alchardus and Tifredus.**—He exhorts them to fulfill the duty of preaching. 491

**LETTER CCXVIII. To Ardbertus.**—He exhorts him to works of justice and mercy; praises his goodness; and commends to him the case of Abbot Lullus. 492

**LETTER CCXIX. To Bishop Leutfredus.**—He consoles him in tribulation. 493

**LETTER CCXX. To Benedict.**—He commends a certain brother, whom he calls his son, to his charity, while commending himself, tossed about amid the storms of the world, to that brother’s prayers. He returns thanks for medicinal herbs, etc. 494

**LETTER CCXXI. To the same.**—He sends letters to the king and others, to be delivered by Benedict; he wishes to receive letters from Benedict more frequently. 495

**LETTER CCXXII. To the brothers of Hilliria.**—He recalls the reputation for their good way of life that has reached him; commends himself to their prayers; and exhorts them to mutual charity and peace. 495

**LETTER CCXXIII. To Abbot Teotgarius and the brothers whom he appears to govern.**—He sends back the brothers traveling to Saint Martin with a letter and begs forgiveness for their disobedience and negligence. He wishes those who have gone astray to be recalled, not cast away. 497

**LETTER CCXXIV. To Friduinus.**—He congratulates him on having undertaken responsibility for the monasteries of Saints Benedict and Ceolfrid, and exhorts him to govern his flock by a good example. He commends himself to his prayers. 498

**LETTER CCXXV. To the brothers who appear to be serving God in various places on the island of Ireland.**—He rejoices at the report of their excellent way of life that has reached him; he praises the good deeds their Fathers once performed in Britain, Gaul, and Italy. He exhorts them to a life according to the rule; he teaches what the life of rulers, monks, nuns, and all Christians ought to be. 500

**LETTER CCXXVI. To the brothers serving God in the church of blessed John the Baptist.**—He welcomes the abbot and brothers of the monastery of Mount Olivet into his friendship, and exhorts them to fight for the Catholic faith and persevere in observance of the rule. 503

**LETTER CCXXVII. To certain monks.**—He seeks their friendship and prayers. He exhorts them to charity, humility, obedience, care for regular discipline, and the praise of God. 504

**LETTER CCXXVIII. To Abbot Arnoldus.**—He praises their way of life and exhorts them to religious virtues, especially poverty at banquets, in money, in clothing, etc. 506

**LETTER CCXXIX. To the priest Eanulfus.**—He commends himself to his prayers and exhorts him to fraternal fellowship and a life according to the rule, to care for souls, etc. 507

**LETTER CCXXX. To the priest Onias.**—He says that charity is sweet when present but bitter when absent. He exhorts him to virtue. 508

**LETTER CCXXXI. To the same.**—He commends charity toward God and toward the poor, the wretched, and pilgrims. Same place.

**LETTER CCXXXII. To Gisla.**—He expresses his affection for her, exhorts her to every kind of virtue, and commends the reading of Holy Scripture. 509

**Fragment I.**—To the brothers of Saint Ninian, at Candida Casa. 511

**Fragment II.**—To the people of York. 512

**Fragment III.**—To Osbert, patrician of the Mercians. Same place.

**Fragment IV.**—To the same Osbert, patrician. Same place.

**Alphabetical order of the persons to whom Blessed Flaccus Alcuin addressed his letters.** 511
## Part Two of the Works of Blessed Alcuin 515

### Exegetical Works, or Commentaries on Sacred Scripture

Here begin the Questions and Answers. 517  
On the Blessings of the Patriarchs. 558  
Sayings of Blessed Albinus the Levite on the passage in Genesis: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” 565  
On the Ten Words of the Law. 567

An old hymn on the fifteen Gradual Psalms. 637

The Compendium begins. 642

Solomon’s Prayer at the Dedication of the Temple. 721

## Book One

### Chapter One

“In the beginning was the Word,” with God, through whom all things were made. John was sent before him; he makes those who receive him children of God through grace. On the same page.

**Chapter II.** John denies that he is the Christ, but says that he was sent before him, and declares, according to Isaiah, that he is “the voice of one crying in the wilderness.” 753

**Chapter III.** Of the two disciples of John who had followed the Lord, one, Andrew, brought his brother to Jesus; Jesus named him Peter. Philip, too, when called, tells Nathanael. He immediately confesses, among other things, that Jesus is the Son of God. Then Jesus changes water into wine, and his disciples believe in him. 760

## Book Two

771

**Chapter IV.** As the Passover of the Jews approaches, he drives the sellers and buyers from the Temple. On the same page.

**Chapter V.** Among many other things, he tells Nicodemus that no one can enter the kingdom of God unless he is born again, and that he came into the world not to judge it but to save it. He also declares that the works done in God are to be made manifest. 778

**Chapter VI.** While John is baptizing at Aenon, his disciples tell him that the one to whom he bore witness is baptizing and that everyone is coming to him. John declares that he is the Bridegroom, that he must increase while John himself must decrease, and that he is from above and is above all. He confirms that the believer in him has eternal life, whereas the wrath of God remains upon the unbeliever. 784

**Chapter VII.** At Jacob’s well, Christ reveals himself to the Samaritan woman and speaks many things mystically. Many Samaritans believe in him, saying: “Truly this is the Savior of the world.” 791

**Chapter VIII.** The sick son of a certain royal official is healed by the absent Lord’s word. 801

## Book Three

803

**Chapter IX.** Jesus heals a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years by saying, “Take up your pallet and walk,” and does so on the Sabbath, making himself equal with God. On the same page.

**Chapter X.** Just as the Father raises the dead, so also does the Son; and the Son must be honored equally with the Father. Those who believe in him pass from death to life. He also announces that an hour will come when the good and the wicked will rise from their tombs. 810

**Chapter XI.** He calls John a lamp. He also says that the Father and the Scriptures bear witness about him. He testifies that the Jews, who do not receive the one coming in the Father’s name, will receive another coming in his own name. He further testifies that Moses wrote about him. 816

**Chapter XII.** As the Passover of the Jews approaches, he feeds five thousand men with five loaves and two fish. Because of this sign they want to make him king, but he flees to the mountain. Thereafter, walking upon the sea while the disciples are afraid, he says to them: “It is I; do not be afraid.” 819

**Chapter XIII.** Sought and found by the crowds, he says: “Work for the food that does not perish, but that endures to eternal life.” He declares himself to be the true bread from heaven and the life of the world. 826

**Chapter XIV.** He declares that he is the bread of life, and that those who believe in him will rise on the last day. 830

**Chapter XV.** The Pharisees, murmuring, call him the son of Joseph. He himself, among many other things, says that he will give his flesh as bread for the life of the world. He bears witness to many other things of this kind concerning his bread and flesh. 832

**Chapter XVI.** He declares that his words are spirit and life, and calls one of the Twelve a devil. 838

## Book Four

839

**Chapter XVII.** Since the Jews are seeking to kill him, he goes secretly to the feast of Tabernacles, where various things are said about him and by him. When they seek to seize him, they cannot, because his hour had not yet come. On the same page.

**Chapter XVIII.** With many among the crowd believing, he speaks at length, including these words: “Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink.” The Pharisees also oppose Nicodemus on the question of giving him a hearing. 849

**Chapter XIX.** A woman caught in adultery is brought before him. Since her accusers do not condemn her, he himself releases her on the condition that she sin no more. 853

**Chapter XX.** He declares that he is the light of the world. Refuting the Pharisees’ objection that he bears witness concerning himself, he rebukes them. He himself confirms that his judgment is true. 855

**Chapter XXI.** He tells the Jews that they will die in their sin. When they ask him who he is, he replies that he is the beginning, adding: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he.” 861

**Chapter XXII.** To the Jews who believe, he says: “If you remain in my word, the truth will set you free.” When they reply that they are free, he says: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.” 867

**Chapter XXIII.** He says that whoever keeps his word will never see death. Among many other things, affirming that he existed before Abraham, he leaves the Temple. 875

## Book Five

877

**Chapter XXIV.** After giving sight to a man blind from birth and greatly troubling the Pharisees, he declares that he is the light of the world. Later, recognized by the man who had been blind and received his sight, he is worshiped by him. On the same page.

**Chapter XXV.** He says that whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the door is a thief, and that he himself is the door and the shepherd of the sheep. He declares that he will lay down his life for them and bring in other sheep, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd. 882

**Chapter XXVI.** He says that he has authority to lay down his life and to take it up again. When the feast of the Dedication takes place in Jerusalem, and when the Pharisees question him about many things, he says: “I and the Father are one.” Many believe in him. On the same page.

**Chapter XXVII.** He says that Lazarus, his friend, who has been dead for four days, is sleeping. Calling out in a loud voice, he raises him and commands him at once to be released and to depart. Many of the Jews believe. 896

**Chapter XXVIII.** The chief priests assemble a council against him, in which Caiaphas prophesies that one man ought to die for the people so that the whole nation might not perish. Six days before Passover, Judas is rebuked for murmuring about the price of the ointment poured over the Lord’s feet. 903

**Chapter XXIX.** The crowd, coming to meet him with palm branches, cries, “Hosanna.” He himself sat upon a young donkey, while the Pharisees say: “The whole world has gone after him.” 909

**Chapter XXX.** When it is announced that the Gentiles wish to see him, he says that it is the hour of his glorification, and declares that a grain of wheat, when it dies, will bear much fruit. He also promises that whoever serves him will be honored. 911

**Chapter XXXI.** Saying that his soul is troubled and asking the Father to glorify him, he hears a voice from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.” After this he continues at length, including his testimony that he came into the world not to judge it but to save it. 913

## Book Six

923

**Chapter XXXII.** Rising from supper, he washes the disciples’ feet, saying that he has given them an example, so that they too should do for their fellow servants what he, acknowledged as Lord of all, has done. 923

**Chapter XXXIII.** Saying that a servant is not greater than his master, after the testimony of Scripture he indicates, by offering the dipped morsel of bread, that he is to be betrayed by Judas, and he exhorts the disciples in many ways. 926

**Chapter XXXIV.** “Let not your heart be troubled,” he says to the disciples. “I am the way, the truth, and the life. Whoever sees me sees the Father also. I am in the Father, and the Father is in me. Whatever you ask in my name, I will do.” 932

**Chapter XXXV.** To the disciples who love him and keep his commandments, he promises that the Paraclete will be sent by the Father and will remain with them forever. He also promises that he will give them peace and leave them peace. 935

**Chapter XXXVI.** Calling himself the vine, the Father the gardener, and the disciples the branches, he testifies that they can do nothing without him. In many forms of speech he impresses upon them mutual love, by virtue of which they can obtain whatever they ask. 941

**Chapter XXXVII.** Commending the same love even more urgently, he says that the world’s hatred must be despised. He also foretells what they will suffer for his name, and declares that the Paraclete will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment. 946

**Chapter XXXVIII.** He says that in a little while they will see him, and again in a little while they will not see him. When the disciples ask about this, he introduces the comparison of a woman who, after giving birth, no longer remembers her sorrow because of her joy. He signifies that they are loved by the Father and strengthens them as he prepares to leave, saying: “In the world you will have tribulation, but take courage; I have overcome the world.” 954

## Book Seven

959

**Chapter XXXIX.** Speaking to the Father of his glorification, he commends the disciples in an extensive and many-sided discourse, while his Passion is immediately impending. On the same page.

**Chapter XL.** The events of his betrayal and Passion are narrated in sequence. 968

**Chapter XLI.** The manifestation of his Resurrection is likewise explained. Mary Magdalene announces to Peter and John that the body has been taken from the tomb. When they come and then return, she herself, after an angelic vision, supposes that the Lord whom she sees is the gardener; he immediately calls her back by her own name. Once she recognizes him, he commands her to announce him without delay to the disciples. 987

**Chapter XLII.** Although the doors are closed, he comes to the disciples and brings them peace, showing them his hands and side. By breathing upon them, he also signifies the Holy Spirit. Likewise, eight days later, Thomas is confirmed in faith by seeing or touching his side and hands, hearing: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.” 992

**Chapter XLIII.** After rising from the dead, he manifests himself again to seven disciples at the Sea of Tiberias, when they catch one hundred and fifty-three fish. 995

**Chapters XLIV–XLV.** Three times he says to Peter, “Do you love me?” because Peter had denied him three times. Likewise, by entrusting the sheep to him a third time, he indicates through the extension of his hands that he would be crowned with martyrdom by the death of the cross.

Jesus says to Simon Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” and so on, up to the statement that he would glorify God. 1000

**Chapter XLVI.** The Lord says to Peter, “Follow me,” up to the words: “And we know that his testimony is true.” 1003
